{\small\noindent\textit{Translator's note.} This is the whole of Høffding's
history of modern philosophy in English, in the order of the work. The first
volume (1903) runs from the philosophy of the Renaissance and the new natural
science through the great systems of the seventeenth century and English empiricism
to the French Enlightenment and Rousseau; the second (1904) from the German
Enlightenment and Kant through the philosophy of Romanticism and positivism to the
philosophy of Germany from 1850 to 1880. Each volume opens with its title pages and
its table of contents, the printed page numbers kept, and ends with Høffding's
notes, as in the original; those to the Tenth Book are given as footnotes. The
second volume closes with the index of both volumes, its headwords translated, its
order (the Danish alphabet's) and its page references as printed.
The numbers in the margin are the pages of the second Danish edition (1903--04);
each volume is paged separately.

\noindent The translation is made from the diplomatic transcription of that edition
published in this collection, which keeps the printer's errors as printed; the
English gives the intended sense. The Introduction and the Tenth Book were
translated first, from the e-book text of the same edition, and then checked
against the transcription. The Third and Ninth Books, with their notes, were
translated from the transcription with Claude (an AI model) in fifteen parts,
working from one brief and one glossary of terms; each part was checked by
script against the Danish, printed page by printed page (page numbers, notes,
paragraphs, emphasis, Greek), and where the Danish was corrected afterwards the
English was mended to follow it. The rest of the work --- the First,
Second and Fourth to Eighth Books, the remaining notes, the title pages, the tables
of contents and the index --- was then translated in the same way, in thirty
further parts, from the transcription of the whole work, with the glossary extended
to the terms of these Books. The Introduction and the Tenth Book, too, were
translated with Claude. Until now the work was available in English only in
B.~E. Meyer's translation of 1900, made from the German edition of the first
Danish edition.\par}

\hhchapter{Introduction}
\label{ch:indledning}

\opage{XI}It will be natural that, when a new presentation of an important period in the
history of philosophy appears, the question should be asked what conception of
philosophy the author takes as his ground, and what significance and value he
ascribes to the history of philosophy. My answer is that the studies whose
provisional conclusion is marked by the publication of this book had precisely
the aim of orienting me with respect to what philosophy really is. As we come to
know a person through his biography, so we must be able to come to know a
science through its history. And it will be all the more natural to try this
road, since experience constantly shows that in the domain of philosophy
conflicting ways of seeing assert themselves, so that there is no presentation
of philosophy to which one could point as giving an exhaustive concept of it. It
will then be natural here --- as in the domain of religion --- to apply the
comparative method. The history of philosophy treats the attempts which
individual thinkers have made to discuss the ultimate problems of knowledge and
of life. The most important result will be to get clear about which problems
philosophy occupies itself with, how those problems are posed at different
times, and by what the different ways of posing them, and of attempting to solve
them, are determined in detail. If such a result can be approximately reached,
the study of the history of philosophy will be of no slight importance for
continued philosophizing.

For my own part I have been strengthened, by the study of the history of modern
philosophy, in the assumption I had arrived at by another \opage{XII}road: that
philosophical inquiry turns upon four principal problems. These four problems
are now to be briefly characterized. A more searching discussion and comparison
of them I have given in the treatise \textit{Filosofiske Problemer} (University
Programme 1902).

\medskip

1. \emph{The problem of knowledge} (the \emph{logical} problem). However
different the several sciences may be in respect of subject and of method, they
all nevertheless work with human thinking. Every time they form a concept, utter
a judgment or draw an inference, they presuppose the general forms and
principles of thinking. Here, then, there shows itself the possibility of a
peculiar discipline, one which investigates the forms in which thinking moves
and the principles it must by its nature take as its ground, whatever the
objects it may concern. This discipline, \emph{formal logic}, treats however
only one part of the problem of knowledge. Those forms and principles do not
lead beyond thinking itself, but only make it possible for thinking to be in
agreement with itself, to be consistent. Every time they are applied to given
phenomena, which our thinking has not itself constructed but must take as they
come, the question arises with what right that application takes place ---
with what right we assume that not only our thinking, but existence itself,
which expresses itself in the given phenomena, is consistent, agrees with
itself. Herewith shows itself the possibility of a discipline which investigates
the conditions of a knowledge of existence, and the limits of such knowledge.
This discipline is \emph{epistemology}.

2. \emph{The problem of existence} (the \emph{cosmological} problem) arises
when it is asked how the existence of which we are members must be supposed to
be constituted, when we draw the ultimate consequences of all that we know, or
can conjecture with the help of the most probable hypotheses. We call this
problem the cosmological (from \textit{kosmos}, world, and \textit{logos},
doctrine), because it leads to a discussion of the possibilities that present
themselves to thought when it seeks to work up what is given in experience into
a general world-view, or when by speculation's bold road it attempts to
construct one. The \opage{XIII}different philosophical systems are attempts in this
direction --- attempts whose value depends on how significant and how
comprehensive are the experiences they take as their ground, and how much
consistency and power of combination is displayed in their constructions.

3. \emph{The problem of valuation} (the \emph{ethical-religious} problem)
arises through this, that we do not merely stand to existence in an intuiting
and understanding relation, but also have our feeling set in motion by it, so
that we utter judgments which ascribe value to it or deny it value. Of
particular importance are the judgments we utter upon human actions, our own and
others'. All such appraisal rests --- like all knowledge and understanding ---
upon certain presuppositions, which it is a matter of exhibiting and
determining. This task belongs under the ethical problem. When the valuation
concerns not merely human actions and institutions but existence, life as a
whole, the religious problem arises, which leads especially to a discussion of
the relation between the ethical ideals and actual existence, so that it becomes
a combination of the cosmological and the ethical problem.

4. \emph{The problem of consciousness} (the \emph{psychological} problem).
For all three of the problems indicated it shows itself that their treatment
presupposes an empirical acquaintance with human conscious life. Psychology
presents the \emph{actual} development of human knowledge, which must be known
before one can discuss the conditions of knowledge's \emph{validity}. And since
the relation between the spiritual and the material is a principal point within
the problem of existence, psychology is presupposed in cosmology as well. As
regards the problem of valuation, finally, psychology discusses partly the
constitution of the very feelings that lead us to make valuations, partly the
possibilities which actual conscious life presents for a further development in
the direction valuation demands. In consequence of this close relation to the
philosophical problems, psychology is itself to be reckoned a part of
philosophy; and one will therefore also, conversely, quite naturally come in
psychology to touch upon philosophical problems. And even if one were to declare
all three of the preceding problems insoluble, or arisen through
misunderstanding, the psychological problem --- the question \opage{XIV}of the nature and
the laws of conscious life --- would still remain as philosophy's last
stronghold.

\medskip

--- If it is asked what factors will, in the nature of the case, come to
influence the treatment and the answering of these problems, the first to be
named must be the personality of the one who philosophizes. The problems named
have this in common, that they lie at the boundary of our knowledge, where the
exact methods fail; it cannot then be otherwise than that the inquirer's
personality must come to determine his train of thought, without his needing to
be conscious of it. The ``personal equation'' must be of greater importance in
philosophy than in other scientific domains. The historical, comparative method
therefore becomes of particular importance here; by its help the personal
element can most easily be exhibited. That personal element is not always
something to be pushed aside; its presence is often a condition of a problem's
being able to come to be at all. There are thoughts which can come to be only
upon a determinate psychological soil. --- It will, in the second place, depend
upon which observations are taken as the ground. Here the development of natural
science acquires especially great importance for modern philosophy. As will
appear, the decisive problems of modern philosophy are determined by the very
fact that modern natural science came into being. But to this there come as well
--- especially as regards the problem of valuation --- historical conditions,
intellectual movements in other domains. --- Finally, the posing of problems and
their solution are determined by the consistency with which the starting points
once seized are held fast and carried through.

Both the characterization and the criticism of every philosophical attempt will
always lead back to these three points. Among them I lay most weight, in the
presentation that follows, upon the first two. An inconsistency in a great
thinker is often precisely a natural consequence of \emph{several} trains of
thought having opened themselves to his genius, without his having been able to
pursue them far enough to discover their mutual conflict. And it may be of the
greatest importance that these different trains of thought be brought out. Best
of all, of course, is when profundity and consistency are united.

An attempt at posing or at solving a problem may \opage{XV}have a twofold interest. In the
first place it may be regarded as a symptom, as the historical expression of
intellectual currents. From this side the history of philosophy is a part of
general cultural history. In the second place it may be examined with respect to
the real, definitive clarity that has been reached by it. This consideration is
more specifically philosophical and technical. The two sides from which the
philosophical phenomena can be regarded will of course, in the case of different
phenomena, stand in very different relations to one another. Sometimes the
cultural-historical interest may even stand in inverse relation to the purely
philosophical.

If I am briefly to indicate wherein my presentation of the history of modern
philosophy differs from its predecessor in our literature --- Brøchner's work of
1873--74 --- I would name first the particular weight I lay upon the personal
factor, upon the relation to empirical science, and upon the cultural-historical
significance of the philosophical phenomena. Next I would point to my endeavor
to give the posing of problems precedence over their solution. Solutions may
die, and the problems live on; otherwise philosophy would not have had so long a
life as it has had. Finally it goes without saying that a renewed study of the
sources, as well as the use of the abundant literature of recent years, has set
many phenomena in a new light. But in spite of all this it has been a dear
thought to me, in this work, to be able to continue Brøchner's labor in the
field of the history of philosophy; and I can only hope that my book may not be
unworthy to be consecrated to the memory of that noble inquirer, whose
admiration for the heroes of thought was at once so deep and so understanding.

\begin{center}---\end{center}

% --- p. 1 ---
\hhchapter{First Book}\opage{1}

\begin{center}\textsc{The Philosophy of the Renaissance.}\end{center}

\bigskip

\subsection*{1.\quad The Renaissance and the Middle Ages}

The period in the European life of the spirit that is called the Age of Rebirth is marked
partly by a break with the unfree, incoherent and limited view of life of the Middle Ages,
partly by a widening of the gaze to new domains and an unfolding of new spiritual powers.
In every birth both go together: the tearing loose from the old and the unfolding of the
new life. But it is surely unique in the life of the human spirit that both sides stand out
so fully at the transition to a new age as here. In other periods of transition, as a rule,
either criticism and negation or the new and positive fullness takes on an overwhelming
character. It is characteristic of the Renaissance in this respect that it is chiefly the
new life that brings with it the criticism of the old. On this rest its health and
strength. It laid the foundation of a new, free, human conception of nature and of human
life, which it was itself able to express only in broad outline, and which, when worked
through in detail, proved to contain problems enough for centuries of thought and research,
but which in its great main features has undergone no essential change. Every attempt to
orient oneself, with the help of history, with regard to the great theoretical and practical
problems must therefore look back to this time, which has the freshness and power of the
breakthrough and, in a richness full of presentiment, embraces what more divided research is
often able to grasp only one-sidedly.
% --- p. 2 ---
\opage{2}

Before we proceed to set forth the philosophizing of the Renaissance as it appears in its
most important thinkers, we must cast a glance back at the Middle Ages, from which it was a
matter of breaking loose.

It would be wrong to take the Middle Ages for an age of sheer darkness. Not only did there
unfold, beneath or outside the official dominion of the Church, a bright folk life, fresh
with nature, which has left its monuments in the new, budding national literatures. But
even within the learned world it will be very difficult to fix a definite boundary between
the Middle Ages and the age of rebirth. Especially in the Romance countries, and most of all
in Italy, the connection with antiquity was really never wholly broken. The justification
for speaking of the Renaissance as a special period must then be sought in the fact that
there came a time when the knowledge of nature and of human life became so full that it
could not be contained within the bounds of the ecclesiastical notions. And even this point
in the development will not be easy to fix definitely. But this difficulty does not concern
us more closely here, since we shall confine ourselves to setting forth the philosophy that
took shape at the close of the Renaissance, that is, in the course of the sixteenth century,
and can therefore disregard germs and beginnings, which moreover have a literary-historical
rather than a philosophical interest.

Even if one disregards the germs of further development that are found within the spiritual
life of the Middle Ages, and keeps to medieval thought in its classical form, one will find
that the Middle Ages made their significant contributions to spiritual development and were
by no means the desert or the world of darkness for which they are still often given out.
They deepened the life of the spirit and sharpened and exercised its powers in a significant
way, and in any case they stand behind no other period in the energy with which they used
the means of culture at their disposal, although these, owing to the historical conditions,
such as they happened to be, were very limited. In later, happier periods, which commanded a
rich material, the working-up and inward appropriation of this wealth has hardly taken place
with so great a power as that which the
% --- p. 3 ---
\opage{3}Middle Ages applied to their meager material. Some individual points on which
medieval thinking especially offers advantages and has had a preparatory effect shall be
indicated here.

Medieval thinking was theological. The theology of a monotheistic religion proceeds from the
fundamental thought that there is one first cause of all things. Apart from the great
difficulties this thought presents, it has the great and beneficial effect that it accustoms
one to look beyond the differences and particulars and prepares for the assumption of a
lawful connection in all things. To the unity of the cause the unity of the law must
correspond. The Middle Ages educated men to this thought, to which natural man, who,
overwhelmed by the multiplicity of phenomena, inclines to polytheism, is not disposed. They
thereby mark a preparation for a conception of the world determined by science. For all
science endeavors to lead the phenomena back to as few principles as possible, even if it
must indeed acknowledge that the thought of one single, highest law is an unattainable ideal.

For carrying out its ideas in detail, medieval thinking, as already remarked, had only a very
poor material at its command. But all the greater was the labor it spent on it. The poverty
of realities had to be outweighed by the wealth of formalities. Thinking displayed a formal
acuteness, a skill in making distinctions and in setting up arguments, that is altogether
unique. One wishes this skill a better application, but a skill it was, and it has been of
great importance for the development of the spirit. It trained organs that could come into
function in more fruitful domains. It was bound in the long run to lead to a testing
criticism of the very presuppositions which for a long time had stood as the fixed framework
that men did not dare to examine.

The greatest merit of the Middle Ages lies in their absorption in the inner world of mental
life. Classical antiquity stopped at a harmonious relation between the inner and the outer,
and took an interest in the inner life only in its relation to the outer life in nature and
the state. For medieval faith the eternal destiny of the personality was determined by the
events of the inner life. It was a question of life and death whether the mental growth
% --- p. 4 ---
\opage{4}unfolded as it should. No wonder that a fine and deep sense developed for what went on
within. The self-absorption of the mystics has the same significance for the development of
the psychological sense as the distinguishing and arguing of the scholastics for the
development of the logical sense. It became clear that the spiritual world is, after all,
just as much a reality as the material world, and that it is in it, after all, that man has
his true home. The way was paved for a more thorough discussion of the great problem of mind
and matter than antiquity had been able to undertake. But first and foremost there was won
for human life a domain of experience that was its own in the very narrowest sense, where no
outer powers could penetrate. Thereby the possibility of a more deeply reaching spiritual
liberation was given.

Yet it was precisely the great misfortune of the Middle Ages that none of these motives,
fruitful in themselves, could stir freely and fruitfully. There is in medieval thinking, as
in medieval architecture, a craving toward the great and the infinite, and there is at the
same time a striving to fit all the elements of the knowledge of the world that men
possessed, as bearing stones and pillars, into the great edifice of thought. At the bottom:
the world of nature, as Aristotle had set it forth; above it: the world of grace, broken
forth in Christ; and highest: the prospect of the eternal world of glory. The ideal was a
harmonious gradation of \textit{natura, gratia} and \textit{gloria,} such that the higher
domain did not break off but completed the lower. This endeavor is most perfectly expressed
in \textsc{Thomas Aquinas} (1227 --- 1274), the perfecter of scholasticism, one of the
greatest systematizers who have ever lived. He inspired Dante, was canonized in 1323, was
called \textit{doctor angelicus} in the theological schools of the Middle Ages, and still
stands as the classical thinker of the Roman Church, Pope Leo XIII having decreed in the year
1879 that his philosophy is to be made the foundation in the Catholic institutions of
learning. But despite the grandeur of a doctrinal edifice which for so many still contains
the elements of existence and throws light on their connection, it has nevertheless had,
from its very beginning, highly questionable defects. Only in an artificial way were the
elements, drawn from such
% --- p. 5 ---
\opage{5}different sides, joined together. In order to unite the natural knowledge which,
it was believed, Aristotle had summed up with the supernatural presuppositions of the
Church, this knowledge had partly to be reinterpreted, partly to be prevented from working
out all its consequences. Aristotle's philosophy was really designed to present existence as
a harmonious gradation. The fundamental concepts with which Aristotle operated were taken
from the phenomena of organic life. He saw nature as a great process of development, within
which the higher stages were related to the lower as form to matter, or as reality to
possibility. What on the lower stage was only possible (potential) became real (actual) on
the higher stage. Aristotle himself was not able to carry through this significant view. In
what direction its consequence lies is clear enough. As an ecclesiastical thinker, Thomas
Aquinas had nevertheless to break completely with this consequence, to push back the
doctrine of unity (monism) to which it led, and to put a doctrine of duality (dualism) in
its place. This shows itself in a characteristic way in his psychology and in his ethics.
According to the Aristotelian psychology the soul is the ``form'' of the body: what is given
in the body as mere possibility comes forth in mental life in full activity and reality. But
so intimate a relation between soul and body conflicted with the ecclesiastical
presuppositions, and although Thomas in words adheres to Aristotle and calls the soul the
form of the body, he nevertheless in reality treats the soul as a being wholly different
from the body, just as he does not hesitate to assume ``forms'' without matter --- in order
to make room for the angels! In ethics a similar dualism shows itself. From the Greeks he
takes over a series of natural cardinal virtues: wisdom, justice, courage and self-control;
but whereas for the Greeks these made up all virtue, he places above them, as a higher layer,
the three ``theological'' virtues: faith, hope and love, which arise only in a supernatural
way. The development is thus broken, and Thomas does not even inquire whether the forms of
will denoted by the theological virtues might not very well find their place within the
natural virtues, as special forms of these. --- As regards the conception of the world as a
whole, the idea of
% --- p. 6 ---
\opage{6}natural development stood in sharp opposition to the dogma of creation and the
assumption of miraculous intervention. On closer inspection dualism shows itself on one point
after another. But such closer inspection medieval thinking had to keep away. It
\textit{had to} agree with the teaching of the Church. There was to be no thinking, no
understanding of the world, that was independent of theology. And since men had once
acquired the conviction that the Aristotelian philosophy was particularly well suited to
represent natural knowledge in the erection of the scholastic edifice of doctrine, it came
to be regarded as heretical to depart from Aristotle, and, be it noted, from Aristotle as he
was known and understood in the Middle Ages. In other words, inquiry and thought were
arbitrarily brought to a halt, so that the building that had been erected should not be
shaken. The Aristotelian philosophy, which for its time marked so extraordinarily great an
advance, was fixed as eternally valid. For the doctrine of organic life and of mental life
the damage done by this was not the greatest; for in these domains lay Aristotle's real
merit, already in his own time. But the development of an exact natural science was
hindered, of a science that could explain through what elementary processes and according to
what general laws the development of forms that Aristotle assumed took place. The trouble
with the Aristotelian philosophy was that it fixed organic growth as the type of everything
that happens in nature. It could therefore at most give a description of forms and
properties, not a real explanation of their coming into being. The mechanical view of nature
was thus excluded in advance. Men cut themselves off from the way of progress --- without,
however, being able to overcome the difficulties by the means at their command. The
principle of authority hindered a freer and wider discussion of the problems and fixed
dualism as a permanent result. The principle of authority is, of course, itself a form of
dualism, since it presupposes an irreconcilable opposition between human knowledge and the
goal that is to be reached. Men were then reduced to living on the meager content they had,
and to interpreting this content, by artificial distinctions and argumentations, as the
Church wished it. No wonder that a strong
% --- p. 7 ---
\opage{7}hunger for fullness of content was bound to arise, and a great enthusiasm for the
new wealth that streamed in from all sides in the centuries of the Renaissance!

Even in the domain into which the Middle Ages particularly delved, these defects show
themselves. Self-absorption was anxiously religious. It was not allowed to develop into free
knowledge of the spiritual world. The dogmatist always stood on guard against the mystic,
the surge of whose inner life so often led him beyond what the Church sanctioned as true and
right feeling. Just as little as the Church could give the new experience free play, just as
little did it dare to let inner experience go its own ways. It saw a danger in the
possibility that man, by withdrawing into himself, might be able to place himself in an
immediate relation to what is of highest value and thereby become independent of the Church.
It sensed that self-knowledge, just as well as knowledge of nature, offered possibilities of
spiritual liberation and opened the way to a quite different conception of the world from
the theological one. --- Yet it was not only the anxious restriction to religious moods that
hampered the development of inner experience. Here too dualism was at work and prevented the
recognition of a real lawfulness in the inner domain, as well as of a natural connection
between the mental and the bodily. Mental life could not be rightly understood until a freer
and more comprehensive view of nature developed. ---

The significance of the Renaissance, then, is that it marks the period in which the limits
and one-sidednesses of the medieval view of life could be combated with the help of new
experiences and points of view. However diverse the phenomena that meet us within the
philosophy of the Renaissance, they nevertheless have in common a great enthusiasm for, and
confidence in, nature, a striving to carry through a unified conception of existence and to
assert the lawfulness and legitimacy of natural human life. The Renaissance begins with this
last point, with ``the discovery of man'' (to use Jacob Burckhardt's expression), and leads
later to the development of a new world-picture and a new investigation of nature.
% --- p. 8 ---
\opage{8}

\section*{A.\quad The Discovery of Man}

\subsection*{2.\quad Humanism}

It was no accident that Italy became the home of the Renaissance and thereby the cradle of
modern thought. In Italy the connection with antiquity had been best preserved, and when the
literature of antiquity was brought forth again, the Italians could appropriate it in a quite
especially independent way, because it was the work of their own antiquity, flesh of their
flesh and blood of their blood. Toward Greek literature too, which in the fifteenth century
once more became the object of enthusiastic study, the Italians stood in several respects
with more understanding than the northern peoples. This whole return to the literature of
antiquity, to the study of ancient history, poetry and philosophy, had the great significance
for the history of culture that men now became aware that outside the Church and
Christianity too there existed a human life of the spirit which followed its own laws and had
its own history. The spiritual world was widened, and a comparative consideration of human
affairs became possible. In several of the thinkers of the Renaissance we already find the
comparative method applied to the understanding of what is human. Moreover, the works of
antiquity could serve as models that guided thought until it could work in a more independent
way. Many germs of thought, which in antiquity itself had only just begun their growth, only
to be checked by the age of the Middle Ages, so harsh for free spiritual development, could
now unfold. After a long slumber thought sought to take up its work where it had laid it down
at the close of antiquity.

But that a living understanding and an independent appropriation of the literature of
antiquity became possible was due in turn to the historical conditions in Italy. The division
into the many small states, constantly tossed about by internal political struggles in which,
as a rule, no means were shunned to obtain and secure power, brought with it a dissolution of
the medieval order of society. In the Middle Ages man was valued according to his connection
with the Church and the corporation. Natural man, with his purely
% --- p. 9 ---
\opage{9}individual life of feeling, was not heeded and not regarded as legitimate. The
political struggles round about in the cities had now, on the contrary, developed a reckless
striving to assert one's personality, a striving that naturally led to fuller results only
in the fortunate holders of power. On the other hand, the dominion of power that prevailed in
the Italian states was bound to draw many individuals away from public life and, since the
need to assert individuality had after all been awakened, to direct them to develop their
personality as widely and freely as possible in the relations of private life and in
artistic and literary interests. It is \textsc{Burckhardt}'s merit (in his work on the
culture of the Renaissance) to have shown how the bent toward individualism and the need for
purely personal development were bound to arise in Italy in the fourteenth and fifteenth
centuries under the influence of the historical conditions. It was not, then, merely the
outer discovery of the literature and art of antiquity that conditioned the Italian
Renaissance. In that case it would have been a merely learned movement, a predominantly
receptive process. It was first and foremost the practical discovery of human nature as a
domain --- for each individual the domain lying nearest, --- in which there was ample room
and occasion both for gaining experiences and for undertaking a work of development. What the
Middle Ages had made possible only in the form of religious mysticism was now carried further
and freed from limits and bonds. Individual mental life is felt as a reality and awakens
interest in and for itself, apart from what it is attached to. It was a discovery of no less
significance than the discovery of the new continent on the earth and of the new worlds in
the heavens. In the poets (Dante, Petrarca) the interest in, and occupation with, one's own
self and its events naturally appears first and in the grandest style.

Humanism therefore denotes not merely a literary tendency, a school of philologists, but
also a tendency of life, which was characterized by interest in the human, both as an object
of consideration and as a basis for action. It is, both in literature and in life, a
tendency that presents extraordinarily many differences. The Church for a time showed itself
% --- p. 10 ---
\opage{10}favorably disposed toward it, and humanistic interest even prevailed for a while on
the papal throne. When Pius II had a crusade preached, it was presumably essentially in order
to save civilization; in his conviction Rome was now, after the fall of Constantinople, the
last refuge of literature, and he had perhaps mourned the fall of the Greek imperial city
fully as much from humanistic as from religious motives. Humanism has something indeterminate
in its character. It denotes the discovery of the human; but how this human element is
conceived, and how its development is sought, still remains uncertain. For a time it looked
as if the humane and the traditional might be able to go together in a peaceful way. But the
new content soon burst the old leather bottles.

Here we now have the task of showing how, on the basis of the practical interest in the
human, there appears in the thinkers of the time a series of attempts to conceive and
understand it theoretically as well. It is attempts to emancipate psychology and ethics from
theology that we have here to bring forward.

\subsection*{3.\quad Pietro Pomponazzi and Niccolò Machiavelli}

The whole of medieval thinking had, as we know, rested on an ancient foundation, since it
built on Aristotle, whose ideas it had bent toward what the dogmas demanded. But opposed to
this ``Latin'' interpretation of Aristotle stood partly the old Greek interpreters, who
conceived his doctrine more naturalistically, partly the Arabian interpreters, first and
foremost Averroës, who conceived his doctrine in a pantheistic spirit. On the question whether
Aristotle taught the immortality of the soul the three groups of interpreters clashed.
According to the Greek interpreters, whom men in the Middle Ages took no account of, Aristotle
taught a natural development of mental life from lower to higher stages, but in such a way
that even the highest stage was not independent of the natural conditions. According to the
Averroist interpretation the highest form of thinking becomes possible only by man's being
made to partake in an eternal reason; but this partaking lasts only for a time, and it is not
the individual souls but
% --- p. 11 ---
\opage{11}the universal reason, in which they momentarily partake in their highest acts of
thought, that is immortal. The theological Aristotelians, on the other hand, with Thomas
Aquinas at their head, maintained the immortality of the soul as a doctrine grounded on the
soul's capacity to know and to will the universal and eternal.

\textsc{Pietro Pomponazzi} discussed this much-disputed question in a remarkable little work
\textit{(de immortalitate animi} 1516). Rightly has this work been seen as the introduction to
the philosophy of the Renaissance. It deserves this place by the manner in which the problem
is treated. It does discuss what Aristotle's real meaning is, but declares at the same time
that it will examine the question according to natural reason, independently of all
authority. And its endeavor aims at asserting the natural connection within mental life and,
at the same time, the possibility of an ethical conduct of life on the ground of nature.
Pomponazzi was a celebrated teacher of philosophy, first in Padua, later in Bologna. He was
born in Mantua in 1462 and died in Bologna in 1525. Of his personal circumstances little is
known. He was an excellent disputant and speaker; his writings, however, do not distinguish
themselves in a literary respect.

Against Thomas as well as against Averroës, Pomponazzi lays weight on the lawful and
continuous development of nature which Aristotle taught in his Physics, and which permits no
leaps, nor the introduction of wholly new principles not prepared by the preceding
development. He carries this thought through even further than the master Aristotle himself,
who taught that the highest activity of reason (``the active reason'') could not be explained
from the successive development. How it was then to be conceived and explained, Aristotle had
not pronounced, and precisely thereby he had given occasion to the conflicting
interpretations. That even the highest thinking cannot be independent of natural conditions,
Pomponazzi proves especially by the proposition, expressly set up by Aristotle, that all
thinking presupposes representations which must at the outset be given through sense
perception. And he maintains that the Aristotelian definition of the soul as the form of the
body, or its perfect reality,
% --- p. 12 ---
\opage{12}likewise does not make it possible to assume an independent subsistence of the
soul.

Will there not, then, arise from this result questionable consequences in an ethical respect,
since for natural man the prospects of reward or punishment after death cannot then become
motives? Pomponazzi maintains, on the contrary, that these prospects are questionable in an
ethical respect, since they hinder man from doing the good for its own sake. The full
development of man's nature in the various domains has its satisfaction in itself. And while
scientific and artistic development does not fall in equal measure to everyone's lot, there
is one development from which no one is excluded: ethical development. And this has its goal
and its value in itself. The reward of virtue is virtue itself, and the punishment of the
vicious is vice itself. Whether, therefore, man is mortal or not, death is still to be
despised, and however things may stand with the state after death, one must still not turn
aside from the way of the good. --- These utterances, which are found in the fourteenth
chapter of the book, recall on the one hand the Apology of Socrates and point on the other
forward to Spinoza's and Kant's conception of the ethical. Several humanists had, it is true,
come forward with the idea of an independent ethics; but in Pomponazzi this idea acquires a
special significance through the connection with a specifically religious problem in which
it appears.

The question of immortality is, according to Pomponazzi, an insoluble problem (problema
neutrum); one may add in his spirit: a neutral problem also in the sense that no real ethical
values depend on its answer. But with such questions the point is to get it settled how far
our knowledge can really reach. Evidently, for Pomponazzi the chief interest of his
investigation is bound up with the light it throws on the nature of our knowledge. The
problem is only the occasion. He distinguishes sharply between the standpoint of the
philosopher and that of the legislator. For the legislator the point is to find motives that
can make men upright, and he may perhaps find it right to make use of the faith in
immortality as an educative motive; but the philosopher has only to ask after the truth
without letting himself be
% --- p. 13 ---
\opage{13}moved by fear or hope. A similar opposition can, as Pomponazzi teaches, be found
within the individual man. With his reason he seeks only to draw correct conclusions from
given presuppositions; what results reason is to arrive at therefore does not depend on man's
will. With his will man can hold fast to a faith that his reason cannot ground. Pomponazzi
thus distinguishes between faith and knowledge, and he can therefore, with regard to the
final decision of the problem he treats, submit to the doctrine of the Church. Whereas the
scholastic Duns Scotus had declared two centuries before that something can be true for the
philosopher which is not true for the theologian, Pomponazzi's meaning would rather be
expressed in the proposition that something can be true for the theologian which is not true
for the philosopher. It must be remembered, after all, that as a philosopher he ended with a
problema neutrum. There is therefore no reason, either, to doubt that this doctrine of faith
and knowledge was meant in full earnest, or to take it for irony or for a mere
evasion\textsuperscript{1}). He gives the impression of a seeking nature, for whom inquiry is a
matter of full earnest. He compares the philosopher to Prometheus, because he is constantly
gnawed by restless thoughts in his craving to search out the divine secrets. It may very well
be that reason was more developed in him than the will that was to bind him to faith, but it
may nonetheless have been his earnest when he held fast to the claims of both. Only, a closer
development of the connection between will and faith is lacking in him. He confines himself
to pointing to the will as the foundation of faith without giving further explanation,
although such an explanation would be of great interest. ---

Besides the work discussed here, Pomponazzi also wrote on sorcery and sought to give a natural
explanation of events that were interpreted as effects of supernatural agency. This work is of
interest through its endeavor to assert the principle of natural causes, although the causes
he makes use of themselves, in our view, belong under the concept of superstition. For it is
especially the influence of the stars that he relies on, an influence which the age, of
course, did not regard as supernatural. --- In a third work he discusses the question of
% --- p. 14 ---
\opage{14}divine predestination and man's will. He acutely demonstrates the conflict between
them. As a philosopher he keeps to what stands firm in experience: the reality of the human
will; its relation to divine agency he leaves standing as an insoluble problem, here too
making use of the distinction between faith and knowledge.

This distinction did not help him, however. In Venice the Inquisition had his work de
immortalitate burned, and if he had not had a powerful protector in Pope Leo X's friend
Cardinal Bembo, he might perhaps not have escaped sharing the fate of his book. ---

At first glance it might seem strange to place Machiavelli beside Pomponazzi. The Florentine
statesman seems to have nothing to do with the Bolognese scholastic. And yet the common
enemies of these two contemporary thinkers were hardly wrong when they held them to be of the
same leaven. It was the ancient faith in human nature that they both, each in his own way,
wished to see reborn. And both were strongly influenced by the authors of antiquity. As
Pomponazzi sought to continue Aristotle's naturalistic psychology and ethics, so Machiavelli
shows himself on important points influenced by the Greek historian Polybius, who in turn
points back to older Greek thinkers' conception of the course of development of states. But
it was Machiavelli's own observations of the events of his time, in which he himself was
involved, that begot in him the need to go back to antiquity. \textsc{Nicolo
Machiavelli} was born in Florence in the year 1469 of an old and respected family that had
come down in the world. He early entered the diplomatic service of the republican government
of his native city and visited as its envoy Pope Julius II, Cesare Borgia, the Emperor
Maximilian and King Louis XII. He thereby had ample opportunity to gather observations of men
and events. Of fateful significance for the development of his views was the fact that
precisely this period in the history of Italy was one in which cunning and intrigue,
treachery and cruelty were the means by which political decisions were carried out. He
himself, in his Florentine History (in the introduction to the fifth book), made the
% --- p. 15 ---
\opage{15}remark about the history of Italy in the fifteenth century that one cannot admire
the conduct of the Italian princes of that time for its greatness and nobility of heart,
though it does not on that account afford less material for consideration, when one sees how
such noble peoples were kept in check by weak and badly led arms. It was bound to stand for
Machiavelli as the result of what he had experienced that cunning and strength were the one
thing needful for the statesman. He himself does not show himself to be any superior
politician; his greatness is in the world of thought, not in that of action. And yet he
grieved deeply when he was forced to exchange the latter world for the former. When the
Medici overthrew the free constitution of Florence (1512), Machiavelli was dismissed, and
during the enforced private life that he then led for a number of years he composed his
celebrated works. Had he borne his political misfortune with greater dignity, his literary
works too would perhaps have been kept in a higher style. As it was, he worked out
especially that one of his works which has become most famous, the book on the prince
\textit{(Il principe)}, with the purpose in view of gaining the favor of the Medici. He partly
attained this purpose, but it cannot be denied that a stain was thereby put on his
character, and that by having the political power of a single family in view he came to
stress individual arbitrariness and recklessness in politics more strongly than he would
perhaps otherwise have done. Often it looks in his exposition as if it were in the last
instance indifferent what purpose the ruler wished to carry through, and as if he in any case
regarded it as his task to give directions for the various purposes one might happen to set
oneself. Not only in ``The Prince'', but also in his real chief work, the \textit{Discorsi,}
the discourses on the first ten books of Livy, this shows itself. Whoever would found a
republic must go about it thus; whoever would found a monarchy, thus; whoever would found a
tyranny, thus. And yet it is certain that there was one purpose for which Machiavelli's heart
beat, and which in his innermost being he embraced with his thought in the midst of the
diplomatic intrigue as well as in the working-out of his works, namely the unity and
greatness of Italy. It is certain, too, that he always felt himself a
% --- p. 16 ---
\opage{16}republican; this is seen from the advice he gave the Medici concerning the
constitution of Florence. And there also stood before his mind an ideal of man, of health,
strength and wisdom, which was to tower high above the wretchedness by which he felt himself
surrounded, and above the cowedness that the medieval Church had brought over human nature.
It was on this point that he himself looked to antiquity and demanded that it be imitated.
Although he was himself a poet and lived with the poets, and although he himself had a good
deal of the unrestrained man of pleasure in him, the aesthetic Renaissance was not enough for
him, any more than the gospel of pleasure was for him the highest. It was the Renaissance of
strength and greatness that he demanded. ``When I,'' he says (in the introduction to the
first book of the Discorsi), ``consider the reverence that antiquity inspires in all, how,
e.g., men give a great sum of gold for a fragment of an ancient statue in order to have it
constantly before their eyes, for the adornment of their houses and as a model for artists,
while on the other hand I see that the marvelous deeds which history relates to have been
performed in the ancient states by their princes, generals, citizens and legislators, and by
all those who have labored for the greatness of their fatherland, are coldly admired rather
than imitated, nay, that everyone on the contrary seems to avoid everything that can recall
them, so that we now have not the least trace of ancient virtue left, then I must both wonder
and lament at it.'' In his highest ideas he is akin to the great spirit that appears in
Michel Angelo's finest works. But his tragic fate was that the great purposes so often
receded behind the multiplicity of the means. He was so taken up with the thought that it is
of no use to have a purpose, be it ever so noble, when one has not powerful means to carry it
out, that in the end he forgot the purpose over the means, or omitted to examine whether the
means he admired would also in reality and in a lasting way work in the direction of the
great purposes that were undoubtedly the highest for him. He became so taken up with the
strength of the means that he came to attribute value to it in and for itself, detached from
the purpose that was to sanctify it. As a true man of the Renaissance he admires the display
of strength in and for itself, indifferent as to the
% --- p. 17 ---
\opage{17}direction in which the strength works. Although he declares himself against the
purely aesthetic Renaissance, he has nevertheless himself introduced it into a domain where
the point is precisely always to have strength determined by the purpose. The contradiction
that expresses itself on this point in his writings, and especially in ``The Prince'', has
often led to his being judged most unjustly. And the same contradiction was the fate of his
life, if one will not call it his guilt. When the Medici were again driven out, after the
taking of Rome by the imperial troops in 1527, and the free constitution was restored, his
countrymen would not accept his service, because they regarded him as a turncoat. His last
days were thereby embittered. A contemporary who is otherwise not favorable to him said of
him after his death: ``I believe that his own circumstances pained him; for he truly loved
freedom, and that in more than the usual way. But it tormented him that he had involved
himself with Pope Clement.'' He died in 1527.

There runs, like an undercurrent, through Machiavelli's works a constant comparison between
ancient and Christian morality. He has (in the ``Discorsi'') set himself the task ``of
comparing ancient and modern events''; but even where he does not expressly undertake such a
comparison, it can be traced in his conception and manner of exposition. He will not content
himself with relating and describing; he will also find the causes of the difference between
the old and the new, and this he cannot do except by going back to the great opposition
between the ancient and the medieval view of life. Machiavelli thereby becomes the most
consciously pronounced representative of the opposition to the Middle Ages.

In the Middle Ages it stood as the task of the state to help men toward their highest goal,
blessedness in the world beyond. The prince was not, indeed, to work for this directly, but
still indirectly, especially by providing for the preservation of peace. In this direction
goes the conception of the state in Thomas Aquinas. For Machiavelli, on the contrary, the
national state has its purpose in itself. Its strength and health within, its power and
expansion without, on these everything depends. And it is not an ideal state that he is
thinking of, but definite, actually given states. ``Since I,''
% --- p. 18 ---
\opage{18}he says (The Prince. ch. 15), ``intend to write things that may be useful to those
who read me, it seems to me better to keep to the reality of things than to give myself up
to empty speculations. There are many who have imagined for themselves republics and
principalities such as have never been seen or known. But what purpose do these fantasies
serve? There is so great a distance between the way in which men live and the way in which
they ought to live that by studying only the latter one learns rather to ruin oneself than to
keep oneself up. He who in all things and everywhere would show himself an honorable man
cannot avoid perishing among so many who are bad. A prince who wishes to maintain himself in
power must therefore learn not always to be good, but to make use of good and evil according
to necessity.'' And in accordance with this it is said in the discourses on Livy: ``Wherever a
decision has to be taken on which the welfare of the state depends, one must not let oneself
be stopped by considerations of justice or injustice, humanity or cruelty, honor or dishonor,
but, disregarding everything else, keep to what can save the state and assert its freedom.''
(Discorsi. III, 41). Whoever cannot in this way free himself from the usual moral notions
must live as a private man and not venture forth among those who govern (I, 26).

What is not clear in Machiavelli is whether he regards the justice and sense of honor that
in certain cases hinder the necessary political action as real virtues or only as imagined
virtues. In some places (as The Prince ch. 8) he speaks of qualities that seem to be virtues
and that can bring about the prince's ruin. He does not go further into the great problems
that arise here, namely those of the relation between the ethics of the private man and that
of the statesman. Is there here an opposition in principle, two kinds of virtue? Or should it
not be a misunderstanding when one calls a quality a virtue that hinders the attainment of
something which is a good for the whole circle that the valuation concerns? Machiavelli is
not free from a certain ambiguity here, which several modern declaimers against ``morality''
share with him. It looks as if he wishes to get
% --- p. 19 ---
\opage{19}beyond the opposition between good and evil, and yet it is only a new valuation,
thus a new application of the concepts good and evil, that he aims at. This new valuation
itself becomes, as has already been shown, uncertain in him because of the unclear relation
between power and the purpose that power is to serve. The aesthetic admiration for the
reckless display of strength pushes aside the thought of the sanctifying purpose. What he
blames men for is that they show energy neither for evil nor for good: of small crimes men
are not afraid, but from crimes in the grand style, ``whose greatness would blot out their
infamy'', they shrink back. In the year 1505 Pope Julius II ventured with his cardinals,
without an army, into Perugia to depose Baglioni, who held power in this city. Now when
Baglioni did not use the opportunity to seize the foolhardy pope and thereby at one stroke
free himself from his mortal enemy, seize great riches and give the princes of the Church a
salutary lesson for the future, it was certainly not for moral reasons; for Baglioni was a
man who did not shrink from incest and from the murder of near relatives. ``The conclusion was
drawn from this that men do not know how to preserve any dignity in crime, any more than they
are able to be perfectly good, but that they shrink back from a crime when it bears the stamp
of greatness and loftiness.'' (Discorsi. I, 27).

What Machiavelli turns against, then, is the petty, the dull and the timid. That was his
real complaint against his contemporaries, as is also seen from his Florentine History. When,
then, he asked the reason why men had moved so far from the greatness of antiquity, he found
this reason in education, which has caused weakening and cowedness, and education in turn is
bound up with religion. The ancients loved honor, greatness of mind, bodily strength and
health, and the ancient religions bestowed divine esteem on those mortals who had won merit as
great generals, heroes or legislators. Their religious ceremonies were magnificent and often
connected with bloody sacrifices, which were bound to dispose minds to fierceness. Our
religion, on the contrary, places the highest goal in another world and teaches us to despise
the honor of this world. It
% --- p. 20 ---
\opage{20}glorifies humility and self-denial and places the quiet, contemplative life above
the practical, outward-turned one. If it demands strength of us, it is rather strength to
suffer than to act. This morality has made men weak and handed the world over to foolhardy
men of violence, who have discovered that most men, in the hope of paradise, are rather
disposed to put up with insults than to avenge them. (Discorsi. II, 2). Machiavelli does add
that this is a false interpretation of Christianity, due to human cowardice; but it is hardly
his meaning thereby to take back his whole comparison between ancient and Christian morality,
and it is clear enough to which side his own sympathy goes. Religion is for him essentially a
means in the hand of the legislator. The legislator needs it as a support for the laws. The
wise man foresees much that the multitude does not suspect and will not believe, and then
the gods must step in and sanction the necessary laws. The history of Lycurgus and Solon
bears witness to this, and Savonarola worked so powerfully on his countrymen because it was
believed (whether rightly or wrongly) that he stood in immediate intercourse with God.
Religion is especially a firm foundation for the maintenance of unity and good manners among
the people. Numa's religious institutions were an essential cause of the strength and
greatness of the Roman Empire, and every prudent prince must uphold the national religion,
even if he personally regards it as an error. (Discorsi. I, 11---12).

Machiavelli has no feeling that in religion he stands face to face with a spiritual power
which unfolds according to its own involuntary laws, and which politics therefore cannot
always, without further ado, take into its service or have at its disposal. He relies on the
whole too much on shrewd calculations, on arbitrary intervention and on the uniformity of
circumstances, and overlooks that the greatest things in history often come like a stream
that suddenly rushes forth from springs hitherto invisible. He himself, it is true,
emphasizes the multiplicity of great and unforeseeable events to which the age had been
witness, and which might lead to the belief that ``God and fortune'' ruled everything. But he
does not think that the human will is therefore powerless. Against a raging flood there is
perhaps
% --- p. 21 ---
\opage{21}nothing to be done at the moment; but when the storm is over, we can dig canals and
throw up dikes, so that the damage becomes less the next time. Fortune comes to rule
especially where no resistance has been prepared. (The Prince. ch. 25). It is, however, a
rather external relation that he here sets up between the involuntary and the arbitrary. The
statesman who stands wholly outside the great spiritual currents will hardly have such an
understanding of them that he can draw canals and build dikes in the right way. ---
Machiavelli lays great weight on the necessity that institutions and constitutions ---
religious as well as political --- be reborn from time to time by being ``led back to their
principle.'' In the course of time there come additions and changes that can corrupt the
source of their essential strength. The point then is to remember the beginning, to reflect
upon one's origin. The occasion for this can be given by external misfortunes, as when Rome
was reborn after the Gallic war, or by definite institutions, such as the tribunes and
censors of Rome, or by eminent men whose personalities become models, as when St. Francis
and St. Dominic again set the original Christian model before men's eyes and thereby saved
the Church from the ruin that would otherwise have been near. (Discorsi. III, 1). This is one
of the most brilliant considerations to be found in Machiavelli. But it shows at the same
time the limits of the shrewdness that he believed he could reduce to a system. The greatest
event that occurred in his lifetime was precisely such a renewal according to the original
principle in the religious domain, but at the same time a renewal that was not a mere
repetition. Through the Reformation spiritual development was led into new paths, and no
politician who would regard it merely as a means, without having a deeper understanding of
its value, has been able to exert any lasting influence on the course of things. That
through the ``renewal'' wholly new forces can come forth, he will not understand. ---
Machiavelli on the whole had no eye for the causes working in secret. There were many sides
of life besides inward religiosity that escaped his attention. The development of the
practical interests, of trade and industry, of mechanics and economics, and the way in which
these interests and the new
% --- p. 22 ---
\opage{22}social strata that represented them had grown strong enough to determine to an
essential extent the politics of the new age --- this was something to which his
predominantly formal conception of politics as a game of intrigue and a struggle for power
blinded him. His politics hovered in the air, because they were not tied to the great ideas
in which the constantly working forces find expression. Like so many realists he missed
reality, because he wished to seize it on the surface of events.

It was natural that Machiavelli, in his striving for an understanding of history, had to keep
to the causes he could catch sight of, or thought he caught sight of. So, after all,
Pomponazzi in his criticism of superstition had to content himself with astrological
explanations. The merit of both is this: to have asserted the principle of natural causes.
They were on the way, and they made it possible for their successors to get further along
this way. As regards Machiavelli in particular, he stands not only as the founder of
scientific politics in modern times, but also as the founder of comparative ethics. What he
had indicated in broad outline, it became the task of later times to carry out in detail,
avoiding the rocks on which he had run aground.

Shortly after the death of Pomponazzi and Machiavelli there was an end of the free Italian
life of the spirit. When Florence lost its freedom for the second time (1530), the turning
point had come. Reaction now broke forth mightily, and the Inquisition was organized anew to
meet the Protestant movement. Exile or martyrdom now became the lot of those Italians whose
religious or scientific views led them into new paths. And yet it was, as we shall see later,
precisely in this period that the new world-view and the new method of natural science were
developed by Italian thinkers, Italy's great contribution to the spiritual development of
modern times. First we follow the conception of man, and have to bring forward some
significant phenomena that show us how the fundamental thoughts of the Renaissance worked
outside Italy.
% --- p. 23 ---
\opage{23}

\subsection*{4.\quad Michel de Montaigne and Pierre Charron}

The various sides of the Renaissance show themselves in hardly any of the thinkers of the time
so clearly and fully as in Montaigne. He has, in the first place, the pronounced
individualism which in France in the sixteenth century, no less than in Italy in the
preceding centuries, was developed through the political struggles, and in Montaigne's case
also through the religious conflicts he witnessed. France, moreover, had its humanism in the
sixteenth century. Montaigne was born (1533) of a noble family in southern France, received a
careful and learned education, made journeys in Italy and afterwards lived for the most part
on his estate, enjoying his freedom and pursuing his studies, carefully guarding himself
against being drawn into the political and religious movements of the time, which he looked
upon as upon a play. That he held back was certainly not grounded merely in his being led to
skepticism by seeing the many parties and the changing views, but chiefly in his wish to
preserve his own personality, such as it happened to be. It was this that was the most
important object of his study. His \textit{Essais} (whose first two books appeared in 1580,
the third book in 1588) are a book personal in a high degree, both in content and in form.
``I study myself more than any other object,'' he says (III, 13); ``that is my metaphysics,
that is my physics.'' And the book does indeed give us full information about his interests,
studies, habits and manner of life. It is written in a free form, without systematic
connection. Thinking is for him a kind of play or pastime; he lets his thoughts go as they
will, and gives them in turn to his readers just as unbound and unordered as he himself
received them. And he declares at once in the preface that he really writes only about
himself (je suis moy mesme la matiere de mon livre), and that, had manners and custom
permitted, he would gladly have gone still further in giving particulars about himself. In
the third book of the ``Essais'' he goes further in this respect than in the first two,
appealing to the greater freedom that age gives. This self-preoccupation, this giving oneself
up to one's own thoughts and rocking oneself in one's own moods, is a
% --- p. 24 ---
\opage{24}modern trait; it bears witness that the individual is freed from traditional
presuppositions and, without troubling himself about any authority, confidently dares to
abandon himself to the currents in his own nature and let himself be carried by them.

Another characteristic trait is his great reading, especially in the literature of
antiquity. His writings swarm with quotations, and he has a great store of characteristic
traits with which to illustrate human opinions, feelings and drives. The comparative method
he has applied to the spiritual domain to an even greater extent than Machiavelli. And that
not merely, as has often been thought, in order to draw skeptical consequences from the
multiplicity of characters, views and tendencies that he brings forward. He is interested in
the individual nuances, and he has at the same time the humanist's joy in the rich material.
It is the gaze out into the immeasurable world of spiritual phenomena that captivates him,
not merely the mutual difference or conflict that there may be between them.

To be sure, both his individualism and his humanism were bound to make him an opponent of
every attempt to force upon men and carry through, dogmatically, one single general doctrine.
He attacks both theological and philosophical dogmatism (especially II, 12). If --- he says
to the orthodox --- we were really in earnest about faith in the supernatural, --- ``if we
were really touched by the ray from the Deity,'' --- then our life would have to look quite
different from what it does. All relations would be transformed in accordance with the holy
demands, and the wars of religion with their ignoble passions could not have split us. It is,
then, hardly divine powers, but rather custom and tradition, that lead us, in so far as it is
not the passions that determine our faith. In the wars of religion God's cause alone could
hardly have raised a single company. And apart from the influences that make themselves felt,
it is clear that our representation cannot grasp anything that lies wholly beyond the limits
of our being. Our own qualities we can think of as heightened or diminished, but beyond them
we cannot get. Moreover, every being is most interested in itself, in its
% --- p. 25 ---
\opage{25}peculiar nature. From this it follows that we represent the Deity to ourselves in human
shape and think that everything in the world is governed for the good of men. But would not
the animals reason in a corresponding way from their nature? He who thinks he knows something
about God inevitably drags God down into what is low. Of all human opinions about religion
that one seems to be the most probable which acknowledges God as an incomprehensible power,
the author of all and the sustainer of all, pure goodness and perfection, graciously
receiving the worship that men render it, under whatever form they may conceive it and in
whatever way they may show it their reverence.

But because the orthodox assertions must be rejected, there is still no reason to presume upon
human reason. Man is at once the most wretched and the proudest of all creatures. Pride is
his innate disease. He feels himself highly exalted above the rest of creation, and yet there
is (as Montaigne seeks to show through a detailed enumeration of traits that bear witness to
the understanding and feeling of animals) not so great a distance between him and the
animals as he thinks. He has no reason to set himself apart from the host of beings. With
his knowledge things stand badly. The senses are uncertain and erring. We cannot convince
ourselves that they teach us the truth. They present the world to us as their nature and
condition bring with them. It is not the external object but the senses' own condition that
appears to us in sense perception: les sens ne comprennent pas le subject estangier, ains
seulement leurs propres passions. If we were to be able to rely absolutely on sense
perception, we should have to have an instrument that could check it --- and then in turn a
means of checking this instrument, and so on to infinity. Nor does reason lead to any final
decision: every reason that is adduced for an assumption itself needs a reason in turn, and
so we could go on going back to infinity. --- To this is added that both we ourselves and the
objects change and alter incessantly; there is nothing fixed and constant. And the wealth of
differences is so great that it is hopeless to attempt to set up general laws or types. No
law can exhaust the
% --- p. 26 ---
\opage{26}multiplicity of cases. The more exact the investigation, the more differences are
discovered. And in the attempt to bring the differences found under common points of view,
one will find that they conflict with one another, so that the comparison cannot lead to any
result. --- The constant changes and the great differences show themselves also as regards
the moral and civil laws. No natural law can be pointed out that is followed by all. Manners
change with time and place. What kind of goodness is it that yesterday was in force, but
tomorrow no longer, and that becomes a crime when one crosses to the other bank of the river?
Can truth be bounded by mountains, so that it becomes a lie on the other side? --- Doubt then
becomes the last resort. But neither may doubt be fixed as something that definitely holds.
We dare not say that we know nothing. Our result is: \textit{what do I know? ---}

This whole line of thought in Montaigne has often been taken as skepticism, men seeing in it
Montaigne's last word. Pascal already took him so. But this does not reach the ultimate
foundation of Montaigne's view of life, the point about which everything finally turns in
him, and by which he comes to suggest an entire world-view. Montaigne is, to be sure, too
much a causeur to develop his world-view in purely philosophical form. But his last word is
not the bewildering diversity of phenomena, not skepticism, nor individualism either. Behind
everything in him there rises an infinite background: the idea of nature in its majesty and
infinity as that from which the fullness of phenomena derives, and as that whose power
branches out in a peculiar way into each individual being\textsuperscript{2}).

Montaigne will not merely refute puffed-up knowledge. He even downright praises ignorance,
because it gives nature free play and does not, with reflection and art, hinder ``our great
and mighty mother Nature'' from leading us. By ignorance he does not then mean raw and
thoughtless emptiness, but the ignorance that is the fruit of an understanding of the limits
of our being. Only by knocking against a door can we convince ourselves that it is shut, not
by standing passively before it. Only for ``a good head''
% --- p. 27 ---
\opage{27}(une teste bien faiste) is ignorance a good and wholesome pillow. Both in great
things and in small the concept of nature plays a role in Montaigne. If the talk is, e.g., of
illness, he will have nothing to do with the physicians, who only corrupt nature and hinder
it in its own right development. Like every other being, every illness has its definite time
to develop and to end, and it is in vain to intervene. Let nature rule; it understands the
matter better than we. In the order of nature one must acquiesce. Like the harmony of the
world, our life is composed of opposites, of different tones, all of which belong to the
great connection, illness and death as well as health and life. --- If the talk is of
education, then likewise the point is to let nature have its free course. The communication
of knowledge is to be only a means for the development of feeling and character, and the
experience of life is the best school for self-control. --- His very skepticism he really
takes back outright when he comes to the concept of nature. The only way, he says, in which
one can secure oneself against measuring things with a false yardstick is to set before one's
eyes ``our mother Nature in her whole majesty'': she shows us a pervasive and constant
multiplicity, within which we discover ourselves, and everything we call great, as a
vanishing point\textsuperscript{3}). We thereby avoid drawing arbitrary and narrow limits.
Thereby tolerance arises. As we have already seen, Montaigne's final result in a religious
respect is that the unknown Deity is worshipped by the various nations under just as many
different forms. --- And by this consideration Montaigne grounds his conservatism. I am weary
of the new, he says, under whatever shape it presents itself. Not because the existing laws
are always reasonable. The validity of laws does not rest on their being just, but on the
very fact that they are laws: c'est le fondement mystique de leur auctorité! Custom is the
mistress of the world. Conscience feels itself bound to what it is accustomed to respect, and
cannot tear itself loose from it without pain. The wise man must indeed inwardly free his
soul in order to judge things without prejudice; but outwardly he ought to follow the
existing laws and customs. It is foolish pride to presume oneself able to put
% --- p. 28 ---
\opage{28}something better in its place. Although Montaigne does not say it outright, it
seems nonetheless to lie in his line of thought that nature makes itself known in what
becomes manners and custom, and his conservatism thereby falls under his faith in nature,
although, of course, the new --- on Montaigne's own view --- would have to be just as
``natural'' as the old.

By the concept of nature, finally, the first trait we emphasized in Montaigne is grounded, his
individualism. Everyone, he thinks, by listening attentively to what goes on within him
(s'il s'escoute), will discover in himself a manner of being peculiar to him, a ruling
character (forme sienne, forme maistresse, forme universelle), which resists outer influence
and keeps away emotions that are incompatible with it. This character is in its innermost
ground unchangeable. I can wish myself another ``form'', loathe and condemn the one I have.
But what has its deepest root in my nature cannot really be repented of, since repentance can
concern only what it is in our power to change. It is through this ruling form that nature
stirs in us, and in each of us in a peculiar way, for which reason everyone ought to be
judged by his own measure. Montaigne thus asserts nature in the single individual, just as he
asserts it in the great whole. In opposition to the Church's demand for an absolute rebirth
he claims that a complete transformation is impossible. He denies the reality of repentance
if it is to be such a transformation. Repentance is possible only if there is an inner
foundation that can be wounded by the full and clear picture of the evil action that has been
committed. While reason remedies the other sorrows and pains, it produces the pain of
repentance, which is the heaviest, because it arises within, just as the heat or cold of
fever is more penetrating than that which comes from without. In a corresponding way there is
felt an inner satisfaction, a noble pride, in doing good and having a good conscience. To
build the reward for good actions on the approval of others would be to build on an all too
uncertain foundation, especially --- Montaigne thinks --- in times like the one he lives in,
where to be an object of people's esteem
% --- p. 29 ---
% scan: „proud'hommie“ (p. 29)
\opage{29}is a bad sign. Everyone must have an inner pattern (un patron au dedans) by which he
can judge his actions. Only you yourself can judge your conduct. Others see not so much your
nature as your art. Even those nearest to us look differently on our actions from strangers.
Through the greater insight into our nature that they have occasion to gain, they perhaps
discover that the brilliant outward deeds are only fine jets of water that shoot up from a
swampy ground. From the outer no conclusion can be drawn to the inner. (Essais. III, 2).

Montaigne does not explain more closely how that ``patron au dedans'' develops, and how it is
related to the ``forme maistresse''. Here he leaves a great problem to subsequent thought.
But it is clear that, just as he praised ignorance and confident surrender to nature only for
him who has a good head, so too in the practical domain it cannot be his meaning that one
should without further ado let nature provide. The individual nature develops into its
peculiar form only when reflection and will work with it, and the ``ruling form'' can be
preserved from distortion only by watchfulness and labor. Montaigne is aware that he is no
hero of the will. If he has any virtue, it is, he thinks, rather the favor of fortune than
the work of the will. He is grateful for belonging to a good family (une race fameuse en
preud'hommie) and for having received a good education. He has a natural abhorrence of most
vices (particularly cruelty), but he does not vouch for how it would have gone with him if
his nature had not been so happy; inner strife and debate he cannot endure. His reason does
strive to take the seat of honor in his soul; but it often has enough to do not to let itself
be corrupted by the drives, and cannot always reform them. And yet it was his conviction that
the highest pleasure was bound up with virtue; the struggle could only be a transition. The
lower enjoyments are only momentary and fleeting and easily bring repentance with them. A
perfect satisfaction, equally far removed from sensual enjoyment and from a toilsome struggle
to hold fast to the commands of reason, is found only where it is the very innermost nature
of the soul that expresses itself in
% --- p. 30 ---
\opage{30}good actions. To have developed such a nature in oneself that every occasion for
inner struggle falls away --- that is for Montaigne the highest. He knows that he himself
stands only in the third rank, belonging neither to those who fight bravely nor to those who
do not need to fight. But he admires the ``loftiness of heroic souls''. His own weakness does
not make him blind to the strength of others. Although he himself creeps on the earth, he
can still see their high flight. And neither does he regard it as a small matter that he has
kept his moral judgment sound in an age in which virtue seems to be nothing but a ``jargon du
collège''. (I, 19; 36. --- II, 11. --- III, 13).

There is an ancient character in the way in which Montaigne asserts the concept of nature.
But this concept is carried by him beyond the limited form it has in the Greek thinkers. It
