is made infinite by being brought into so close a connection with the concept of
individuality. When Montaigne sets nature in opposition to men's artifices, it is partly
because these fix certain single forms as alone legitimate and thereby overlook the fullness
of nature, partly because they violate the single peculiar individuality, whose right to
develop ``sur son propre modele'' is the same as that of every other. The two thoughts, that
of infinity and that of individuality, had the future before them. And through his
skepticism, his great power of observation and his humanist learning Montaigne gained the
freedom of mind and the material for impressing the significance of these concepts. His
skepticism --- which is really an assertion of the right of thought --- led him to seek
beyond the artificial barriers, and his rich experience and learning taught him what was to
be found on the other side of the barrier: new individual forms, in which the one and the
same infinite nature expresses itself. ---

Montaigne died in 1592. A thinker of his kind could really have no disciple. His thinking is
too personal for that. There were combined in him elements that could not recur in the same
combination in others. He who stands nearest as his disciple, and as the one who systematized
his ideas, accordingly represents only a single side of his world of thought, even if it is a
very significant side. It was
% --- p. 31 ---
\opage{31}acquaintance with Montaigne that led \textsc{Pierre Charron} to philosophical
ideas. He was born in Paris in 1541, was first an advocate, but later went over into the
clerical estate and became a celebrated preacher. He published apologetic writings for the
Catholic faith against Protestants and freethinkers. But for all that, the most remarkable
thing in the book of lasting interest that he left behind, and which appeared at Bordeaux in
the year 1600 (three years before his death) under the title \textit{De la sagesse,} is
precisely a thoroughgoing defense of the main thought that we have found in Pomponazzi,
Machiavelli and Montaigne alike: the thought of human nature as the foundation of ethics and
politics. He lays great weight on the ignorance that follows from true self-knowledge. Human
nature, on closer investigation, appears to us both in its wretchedness and in its greatness.
Natural reason cannot be the measure of all things; one ought therefore, in Charron's
opinion, to keep to the old doctrine of the Church without entangling oneself in new
doctrines. Like Montaigne, and in an even higher degree than he, Charron thus draws
conservative consequences from doubt. But what is remarkable is this: he goes more closely
into the relation between religion and morals, which Montaigne had not directly touched upon.
Religion and morals belong together, but must not be confused, since each has its own
mainspring (ressort). Above all, goodness must not be made dependent on religion, since it
thereby becomes something accidental and does not have its source in ``the good mainspring of
nature''. I want, says Charron, a man to be a good man even if there is no paradise and hell.
It is to me a terrible saying when someone says that if he were not a Christian, if he did
not fear being damned, he would do this or that. I want you to be a good man because nature
and reason will it so, --- because it is demanded by the general order of things, of which
you are only a part, --- and because you cannot act against yourself, your being and your
purpose; --- let come of it what will. If this stands firm, then religion can come
afterward. But the reverse relation is pernicious.

So resolute a recognition of the independence of ethics is
% --- p. 32 ---
\opage{32}remarkable in the mouth of a Catholic cleric. It is a psychological riddle how
Charron, who not long before had come forward as a zealous Catholic preacher, came to it.
But in any case it bears witness that a strong tendency in this direction was stirring in the
age.

\subsection*{5.\quad Ludovicus Vives}

The great interest that the age of the Renaissance took in the human was bound, naturally, to bring about an eager
psychological study of mental phenomena. In all the thinkers named so far, psychological observation and psychological
interest play an essential role, without the psychological inquiry, however, appearing as a distinct endeavor,
separated from the farther-reaching philosophical consequences that were drawn from it. But a purely theoretical
psychological study was also pursued at this time. And if any single person is to be named as the representative of
pure psychology at this time, it must be the Spaniard LUDOVICUS VIVES. He was a quiet scholar, an eager
humanist, the friend and collaborator of Erasmus of Rotterdam, but his chief significance lies in the domain of
psychology and pedagogy. He was born in Valencia in 1492, studied in Paris, and later lived in Bruges right up to his
death (1540). For a time he was tutor to the daughter of the English king Henry VIII, but broke with the English court
over the divorce case. Vives was a serious Catholic, but his peace-loving, sound and mild way of looking at things led
him, in a candid letter to Pope Hadrian VI (1522), to speak for a general council that should heal the breach in the
Church by distinguishing between what is necessary for piety and morals and what can be left to free discussion. Later,
too, he worked for tolerance and for a mild and free conception of Christianity. As a pedagogue he has an
extraordinarily great significance for his time. Many of the good pedagogical ideas that the Jesuits afterwards carried
out are said to derive from Vives, with whom Loyola is said to have been personally acquainted. His occupation with
philological criticism and with pedagogical problems led him on to the question of the method of
% --- p. 33 ---
\opage{33}science in general, and he demands that experience be the foundation of all knowledge. As regards psychology, he
himself sought to carry out this demand, standing as he does as the founder of modern empirical psychology. Like his
whole age, he builds on a great body of material taken from antiquity; but he seeks to confirm it by his own
experience, and his work \textit{De anima et vita} (Bruges 1538) is rich in original observations. His description of
particular mental phenomena, especially of the emotions, is still instructive, and his book had an extraordinarily great
influence on the psychological theories of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries\textsuperscript{4}).

Vives's clear empirical standpoint shows itself especially in the section of the first book of De anima that bears the
heading ``What the Soul Is''. After pointing out the difficulties bound up with answering this question, since it is
easier for us to say what the soul is not than what it is, he remarks that it is not really of interest to us either to
know \textit{what} the soul is, but \textit{how it acts,} and that the commandment to know ourselves concerns not the
essence of the soul but its functions. It is established here with great assurance that it is the mental phenomena we
have to do with directly, and that empirical psychology can disregard entirely every purely speculative theory of the
essence of the soul. To this standpoint Vives on the whole remains faithful in his purely descriptive procedure. It
could not, of course, be otherwise than that much had to stand for him as certain experience that was later to fall
before criticism; but Vives nevertheless did much toward letting the psychological standpoint be separated off from the
speculative and the theological on the one side and the physical on the other, a separation that Descartes carried out
in a clear and decisive way. Descartes owes Vives more than one would think from the particular passages where he
mentions him.

As is evident already from the title of Vives's book, he places the concepts of soul and life in close connection with
each other. He conceives the soul as the principle of life, the principle of all organic life, not merely as the
principle of the life of consciousness. He endeavors to conceive the lower forms of life as the foundation of
% --- p. 34 ---
\opage{34}the higher. His psychology is a physiological psychology, which lays great weight on describing the phenomena, as
far as possible, from the physiological side as well. Here, naturally, he uses the physiology of his time. He shows
himself an inquirer emancipated from the Aristotelian school by referring cognition to the brain. There were still
Aristotelians who denied that the nerves (as the later Greek anatomists had already shown) issued from the brain and not
from the heart. According to Vives, on the other hand, the vital force has its seat in the heart, where the first and
the last sign of life is given, and whose hampered or free function finds expression in the emotions. The brain he
takes, in agreement with a doctrine handed down from the Stoics and Galen, to be filled with fine air or breath
(spiritus tenuissimi ac pellucidi). Its vibrations were supposed to stand in connection with what went on in
consciousness; but Vives does not express himself more precisely on this. What the relation is between the soul that
acts in the brain and the one that acts in the heart, he likewise leaves undecided. In his view it was only the
properly human soul that was created immediately by God; the plant soul and the animal soul (that is, the principle of
organic life and of sensation) are produced by the force of matter. The human soul, in thought and aspiration, is not
content with the finite and the sensible, but seeks an infinite object; from this its divine origin is derived, for the
cause must correspond to the effect. Vives shows himself here a decided spiritualist, as one would also have to expect
from his religious presuppositions. On this point too he leaves great problems for the thinking that followed.

His psychology confines itself to setting out the various mental phenomena. Only later inquiry sought the principles of
the mechanics that could lead over from one phenomenon to another.

\subsection*{6.\quad The Development of Natural Law}

Italian humanism had an intellectually aristocratic stamp. Its great significance was the founding of a free life of
the spirit. But it did not much concern itself with how things went with
% --- p. 35 ---
\opage{35}human life in the wider circles. Church, state and social life it left to look after themselves; it was essentially
intellectual and aesthetic tasks that it busied itself with. Even Machiavelli forms no real exception to this, in spite
of his great interest in nationality and politics; for it is, after all, the ruler's display of force that most draws
his gaze, and the deeper-lying forces and conditions of social life he does not heed. Humanism fell when political
freedom fell in Italy; but that political freedom fell, and that no national political life developed, was owing to
this narrow conception of the human in humanism, its fear of going into depth and into breadth. This was also the
reason why it left the religious question alone and was content to push it aside. The northern nations, among whom the
Renaissance appeared with less brilliance, carried the liberation deeper in and farther out.

It was the great merit of the \textit{Reformation} that it was not content to go around the religious question, but
went directly into it and in the religious domain proclaimed the same principle of personality that humanism had
pronounced in other domains. The Reformation is the application of the thought of the Renaissance to the religious
domain. Not to be understood as if Luther and Zwingli had first appropriated that thought and then applied it. What is
great about these personalities is precisely that in their own experience of life they discover that thought anew and
cast it in an altogether peculiar form. They assert the immediate personal experience of life itself as the real
foundation of religion, and, supported by it, they wage their struggle against the medieval Church and theology. The
inner, human forces were freed from the artificial forms. Christianity was here really --- to use Machiavelli's
expression --- led back to the principle from which it had originally issued. Even if \textit{Luther} did not enter on
a critical investigation of primitive Christianity, he nevertheless seized on an important point in the notions of the
earliest congregation, building as he did on the Pauline doctrine of justification by faith. It was the inward, personal
adherence to Christ by which man was raised above all external relations. This thought he developed especially
% --- p. 36 ---
\opage{36}in his writing ``\textit{Von der Freiheit eines Christen-Menschen''} (1520). When personality was thus freed from
all external authority in its innermost relation, the one on which its eternal destiny was supposed to depend, it could
not but seem natural to carry out a similar liberation in other domains as well. Nor can it be denied that the Lutheran
Reformation had an awakening effect in many respects. In his struggle against the Church Luther was also bound to come
to speak for the right of what is naturally human. He asserts the independence of the family and the state over against
the Church, and above all he asserts --- in natural connection with his doctrine of justification by faith alone --- the
significance of the conduct and activity of ordinary human life over against Catholicism's undervaluation of it in
relation to asceticism. But a positive relation to the natural human interests Luther could not, after all, ground.
Toward science he stood --- especially in his earlier period --- suspicious, by reason of his principle of faith, and in
political life he held to the principle of passive obedience. For when he wrote on ``the freedom of a Christian'', he
divided his consideration into two parts: first he shows the inner freedom that the Christian has, then he refers the
full unfolding of this freedom to the world beyond and maintains that the Christian, according to his outer man, is
precisely ``ein dienstbarer Knecht und Jedermann unterthan''. In this dualism between the inner and the outer lay the
reason why Lutheranism did not come to play the role in the spiritual and political development for which there might
in itself have been the possibility, given the great and powerful personality of its founder. The religious and the
human were merely placed side by side like Sunday and weekday, without inner, essential connection. And so it went in
particular with the relation of faith to science. At Worms Luther appealed to the Bible and to clear, evident reasons.
But as to the mutual relation between these two principles, no clarity was reached\textsuperscript{5}), except in so far
as it can be called clarity that a scholasticism was soon developed in Lutheran theology which was less grand and more
narrow-hearted than the medieval one.

Yet at Luther's side there stood a man who with quiet enthusiasm sought to unite the thoughts of the Reformation and of
the general
% --- p. 37 ---
\opage{37}Renaissance. \textsc{Philip Melanchton}, ``the Teacher of Germany'', represents, in contrast to Luther, a more
rational side of Protestantism. He was not only a theologian, but a philologist and philosopher, and when the harsh
condemnation of unregenerate man by Luther and the Lutherans grated on his ears, it was presumably not only because it
conflicted with his mild conception of the human in general, but especially because it fell upon his beloved classics.
At the University of Wittenberg Melanchton lectured not only on theology, but also on natural philosophy and on
philosophical sciences such as psychology, logic (``dialectic'') and ethics. An elegant presentation and a great
knowledge of ancient literature distinguish these lectures. Of greatest interest is his ethics. In natural philosophy he
polemicizes (as will be mentioned later) against the new Copernican doctrine, and as a psychologist he cannot measure
himself against Vives, whose work is roughly contemporary with his. Of great significance for his ethics was his
doctrine of \textit{the natural light,} in which he is especially influenced by Cicero's rendering of the Stoic
philosophy, though in such a way that he also relied on the Apostle Paul's words about the law as written in men's
hearts. At the basis of all inferring, counting and calculating, of all acceptance of the first principles of the
sciences and of all moral judgment, there lie certain representations implanted by the Deity and innate in everyone
(noticiæ nobiscum nascentes, divinitus sparsæ in mentibus nostris), which make it no accident that scientific knowledge
and moral valuation never die out in the human race. (This doctrine Melanchton develops partly in his \textit{Liber de
anima,} partly in his \textit{Erotemata dialectices).} This natural light was, however, darkened by the Fall, and
therefore its essential moral content had to be proclaimed in the ten commandments on Mount Sinai. This assumption, that
it is the same content that is proclaimed in the ten commandments and in the natural moral law, was common to the
Reformers. It is found in both Luther and Calvin, and it goes far back in the Middle Ages. Through this doctrine, renewed
by Melanchton, it came to stand firm that one could arrive by the way of clear reasons at the same result as the Old
Testament revelation. But although Melanchton thus gives the natural law, which for him meant both
% --- p. 38 ---
\opage{38}the moral law and the highest principle for all relations of right, an independent, natural and rational
grounding, it nevertheless followed from his theological presuppositions that the ethical conduct of life possible on
this foundation could concern only the outer, civil life, not the innermost stirrings of the soul. He defines moral
philosophy as ``the knowledge of the commandments concerning all moral actions (honestis actionibus) of which reason
sees that they agree with human nature and are necessary in civil life, so that one seeks, as far as possible, to find
the origin of these commandments by scientific means''. The most inward and deepest element in mental life was thus, in
the Reformer's view, not to ``agree with human nature,'' but could only be set in motion by supernatural influence. He
does indeed hold (in his \textit{Philsophiæ moralis epitome}) that philosophy can teach that there is one God, that he
ought to be worshipped, and that it is God's will that upholds the great difference between good and evil. The first
three commandments fall within moral philosophy just as well as the last seven. But the real, inward relation to God,
that ``in which we have to do immediately with God,'' falls outside philosophy. Here the error shows itself of setting
the content of the ten commandments equal to the natural law. For it was surely hardly Melanchton's meaning to deny to
Old Testament piety an immediate and inward relation to God. And on the other hand, that equation bore witness to the
theological prejudice that what is most inwardly human could be thought only in religious form. For Melanchton the
humane was only the outer, civil sphere. We meet here again, even in this humanist, the opposition between the inner and
the outer. But the concession that had been made, namely that human life in its outer relations could be ordered by laws
that could be rationally grounded, was nevertheless of great significance. Civil life, the whole life of the state,
could then unfold independently according to its own purely human principles.

And in Melanchton's school this independence was developed still more sharply than had happened with the master
himself. The Danish theologian \textsc{Niels Hemmingsen}, who has been called the Teacher of Denmark, just as his
teacher Melanchton was called that of Germany,
% --- p. 39 ---
\opage{39}set out in his writing \textit{De lege naturæ apodictica methodus} (1562) the demand for a strictly scientific
development of natural law. As he himself states at the close of the writing, he has deliberately kept all theological
considerations away, so that it may become clear ``how far reason can reach without the prophetic and apostolic word''.
He wants by way of inquiry to gain a clear and distinct knowledge of the essence of right. Only that is a true law which
does not merely rest on the authority of the prince and the magistrate, but has its ``firm and necessary ground'',
which cannot be sought anywhere else than in the very nature and purpose of the law. In human nature there are given
germs of the moral and the just, and besides these a judgment for distinguishing the just from the unjust. These means
one must use if one wants a law in the true sense of the word. Hemmingsen then shows that there is in man's being a
sensuous and a rational element, and that the animal drive awakened by sense-sensation is to obey reason, which contains
the true human law of nature (lex naturæ seu recta ratio). The purpose of human life is the knowledge of the true and
the practice of the good. Above family life and political life there rises the spiritual life (vita spiritualis as
opposed to vita oeconomica and politica) in the worship of God, in which the highest purpose is to be sought. At this
point the natural forces no longer suffice, for no one can know the right way of worshipping God except by divine
revelation. But as far as the knowledge of natural law itself is concerned, revelation is not needed. Hemmingsen, like
Melanchton, does regard the ten commandments as a brief epitome of natural law,
(epitome legis naturæ), but only after having developed the natural law does he examine its agreement with the ten
commandments. Here, then, the advance has been made that ethics and the doctrine of right (``natural law'' comprises
both) are independent of theology and do not rest on supernatural authority.

But with this the movement also comes to a halt within Lutheranism. Individual jurists such as Oldendorp and Winkler did
indeed hold fast to the thoughts that had been developed. But it was only in the Reformed countries that the inner and
outer conditions were present for a
% --- p. 40 ---
\opage{40}more thoroughgoing liberation of ethics and the doctrine of right. In Zwingli and Calvin there was not that
anxious separation between the freedom of personality in the inner life and bondage in everything outer. Here the
break with the principle of authority is far greater than in Lutheranism. The man made free by virtue of election by
grace feels his right to self-determination in all spiritual and worldly things. Zwingli, that clear, powerful nature,
in whom the reformer's religious inwardness was joined with the thinker's consistency, with the humanist's love of
antiquity and with the republican's political impulse toward freedom, spoke for self-government in both the civil and
the ecclesiastical domain. And Calvin continued his work, with less talent and greater narrowness. It was their
thoughts that lay at the basis of the great struggles in France, the Netherlands and England in the sixteenth and
seventeenth centuries, the struggles in which the civil, religious and scientific freedom of modern times came into
being. The modern state and modern science owe their existence to these struggles. What Italian humanism, from softness
and intellectual aristocracy, and what Lutheranism, from an anxious impulse toward inwardness and obedience, could not
lead to, the disciples of the Swiss reformers accomplished with the weapons of the spirit and of the hand. Here too,
indeed, a hard struggle had to be fought out to burst the confessional barriers within which the Reformed Church, just
as well as other churches, sought to hold the spiritual movement. But it was of great significance that this Church had
a bolder conception of the relation between the inner and the outer and did not set the innermost personal life in
sharp opposition to all human interests. Thereby the Reformed countries became the second home of modern philosophy,
after its first home, Italy, had been subjugated by the powers of reaction. And thereby modern natural law in particular
had its origin in these countries: the conception of right that lies at the basis of all political and social
endeavors at reform, right into the nineteenth century.

The wars of religion in the Netherlands and in France, and the publicistic literature to which they gave occasion,
became of great significance for the development of the idea of popular freedom and of the independence of the state
over against the Church. The struggle to assert
% --- p. 41 ---
\opage{41}religious freedom was closely bound up with the struggle to preserve civil freedom. The right of subjects,
through their lawful representatives, to resist and in the extreme case to depose a prince who violated the right of the
people was asserted with great force. And as its ground the claim was put forward that all governing authority springs
from a transfer that is conditional on the fulfillment of definite duties on the part of those who govern. Thus the
principle of popular sovereignty was proclaimed, and the idea of an original contract between people and government was
laid at the basis of all discussion of constitutional law. The contract theory had already been used in the medieval
strife between Church and state as a weapon against the Church's claims to supremacy. The memory of the origin of the
Roman imperial power in the Roman democracy here worked together with consequences that were drawn from the notion of a
paradisal state of nature without relations of right or of the state. Now this theory was used on the side of the people
against the princes, whereas in the Middle Ages it had been employed in the service of the princes against the Church. A
series of Protestant publicists, in the first rank \textsc{Hubert Languet} and \textsc{François} \textsc{Hotman}, built
their writings of agitation on it. But it was also taken up on the Catholic side. Over against the power of princes ---
especially where it was lukewarm or heretical --- one found one's account in appealing to the right of the people,
which was derived from an original contract. In this spirit a series of Jesuit writers, in part men of great acuteness
and energy, expressed themselves. The Church was then to stand as the only society that had arisen from above, whereas
the state had come into being from below.

The wars of religion, both the physical and the literary, were naturally bound to lead patriotic men who were concerned
for the subsistence of the state, threatened as it was by the struggle of the confessions, to fix their gaze on the
conditions of political life that were independent of the disputed religious assumptions. There then formed in France,
in opposition to Huguenots and Leaguers, a party of ``politicians'', whose view was expressed in literature by
\textsc{Jean Bodin} in his book on ``the State'' \textit{(La republique),} which appeared in 1577. This remarkable man,
who by his superstition recalls the darkest side of the Middle Ages, while his political and historical conception
% --- p. 42 ---
% print: „Suverænitetetens“ (p. 42) (misprint)
\opage{42}points far beyond his time, was a French jurist who for a time stood in the favor of Henry III, but later
forfeited it by speaking for the rights of the estates and of the people over against the king. For a time he stood
close to the chief of the ``politicians'', the Duke of Alençon, and was later among the first to join Henry IV, when
the latter ended the civil wars by gathering the contending parties under the protection of tolerance. He died, however,
two years before the Edict of Nantes appeared. In the history of the doctrine of right his significance rests on the
clear and consistent way in which he developed \textit{the concept of sovereignty.} He distinguishes definitely between
sovereignty and government. The highest power is not one with sovereignty. For power can be transferred for a time. And
power can be divided, whereas sovereignty is indivisible. Just as little as there can be several gods, if God is to be
an absolute being, just so little can there be several sovereigns in a state. Bodin distinguishes between the form of
the state and the form of government. The difference between the forms of state rests on who has sovereignty. And the
marks of sovereignty are legislative power, the right to declare war and peace, the right of pardon and the right to
appoint the highest officials. Sovereign authority can lie with the whole people, with the aristocracy or with the
prince. But the form of government can quite well be monarchical although the form of state is democratic; such is the
relation where the whole people elects the king.

Bodin felt a need, over against the Protestant and Catholic stirrers-up of unrest, to insist on the concept of absolute
sovereignty. Yet he is not for that reason a denier of the right of the people. Sovereign authority is subordinate to
morality and natural law; it cannot abolish the personal right of property, and therefore it cannot impose taxes either.
Bodin did not see that legislative authority could not in the long run be maintained without the authority to grant
taxes, and that when he placed the latter with the people he in reality also transferred sovereignty to them, so that
the difference between the various ``forms of state'' fell away and only the difference between the ``forms of
government'' remained. This consequence was first drawn from the concept of sovereignty by his successors.
% --- p. 43 ---
\opage{43}

Bodin's political theory is distinguished by the weight he lays on the family and the smaller societies or
corporations. He demands that their independence and peculiar character be preserved and developed, in so far as they
are compatible with the common tasks of the state. He has on the whole a sound eye for real human life in its various
directions, and he reproaches Machiavelli, of whom he says that he ``has never sounded the waters of political
science'', for his belief in tyrannical subtleties as the most important thing in politics. In a special little writing
(on the method of history) he shows the significance of the comparative and historical method for the doctrine of right.
``In history,'' he says, ``the best part of universal law is contained, and what is very useful for a correct judgment
of the laws is that from them we can come to know the manners of the nations, the foundations of the state, its course
of development, forms, revolutions and downfall.'' He holds that by this way one must get away from the assumption of a
golden age: ``in comparison with our time the so-called golden age would stand as an iron age!'' His belief in progress
he builds especially on the development of industry. He strongly emphasizes the inventions and discoveries of modern
times, as well as the livelier intercourse between the various nations. Yet he distinguishes between progress in culture
and progress in morality; in the latter respect his belief is not so confident. --- Of his writing on the philosophy of
religion and its significance there will be talk later.

The one who first really founded the theory of natural law in modern times was \textsc{Johannes Althusius.} This man,
whom it is GIERKE'S merit to have drawn forth from a most undeserved oblivion, was born in Diedenshausen in 1557,
studied in Basel and probably in Geneva, was for a time professor of law at Herborn and later, through a long series of
years, burgomaster of the East Frisian town of Emden, whose rights he zealously defended against the encroachments of
the East Frisian counts and knights. He was an ardent Calvinist and followed with enthusiasm the struggle for religious
and political freedom waged by the Netherlanders, kin to the East Frisians. In his writings he alludes several times to
this struggle. In Friesland the old freedom of the peasants had survived,
% --- p. 44 ---
\opage{44}while in the rest of Germany it had perished, and Althusius accordingly asserts the rights of the peasant
estate alongside those of the nobility and of the burghers. Thus both his religious faith and his studies, both the
events of the day in the neighboring country and the social conditions in his own narrower fatherland, combined to
nourish in him the view in the philosophy of law and of the state that he developed in his writing on politics
\textit{(Politica methodice digesta atque exemplis sacris et profanis illustrata.} 1603). Of his other writings,
besides several purely juridical ones, mention should be made of his writing on the virtues that find application in
intercourse with other men \textit{(Civilis conversationis libri duo).} He died after a long and active life in the
year 1638.

Althusius agrees with Bodin that sovereignty is one and indivisible. There can be only one sovereign in a state, just
as there can be only one soul in a body. But he polemicizes against Bodin's assumption of several forms of state.
Sovereignty can lie in only one place, and it cannot be transferred or alienated. Princes and aristocrats can exercise
government, but never possess sovereignty; it must have its seat in the whole people, which never dies, and to which
every ruler is answerable for his administration. It is the welfare and need of the people that the state is to further
and help; here lie the cause and the purpose of the state. The individual ruler dies, but the people does not. And the
ruler is only the single man, but the people is the many. From the people, therefore, all authority must go out, and to
it it constantly returns.

Only the form of government, not the form of state, can differ. It is the people bound together by common conditions of
life (corpus symbioticum) that is the source of all authority, and that cannot permanently hand over its power to any
magistracy whatever. All who exercise governing authority stand as representatives of the people, and as soon as they
overstep the limits that are set to their activity by the natural law contained in the ten commandments and by the
welfare of society, they cease to be servants of society and become private men, to whom one owes no obedience in that
in which they overstep the limits of their authority. Yet it is not every individual's business to assert the limit of
% --- p. 45 ---
% scan: „hele.“ (p. 45)
\opage{45}the power of the magistracy. In every well-ordered state there is, besides the magistrates, yet another kind
of ``administrators'', namely overseers (ephori), whose office it is to elect the supreme magistrate, to assert the
inalienable rights of the people, to remove the magistrate who violates them, but also to defend and support every
magistrate within the limit of his authority. Such ephors were known both in the states of antiquity, as senators and
tribunes of the people, and in modern states as the estates, electors and councillors. Under one form or another a
supervisory authority must always be organized\textsuperscript{6}).

A historical proof of his idea of the sovereignty of the people Althusius finds not only in the fact that there is thus
in most states an authority which, on behalf of the whole people, is to criticize the conduct of the supreme magistracy,
but also in the fact that the people has thrown off the rule of a tyrannical prince. He refers to the Netherlanders'
struggle for freedom, and in the preface to the third edition he states that he has dedicated his work to the estates of
Friesland because they, like the other Netherlanders, had seen that sovereignty could not be inseparably bound to the
person of the prince, but that he could have only the use of it, while the real right of majesty belonged to the people,
--- and because they had fought for this principle with such great bravery, good sense and endurance.

A philosophical proof he finds by looking to the purpose and the cause of political life. The purpose is, after all,
the welfare not of the magistracy but of the whole people. And the cause of men's joining together and forming states is
the helpless and needy condition of the individual. The feeling and need of the \textit{individual} persons are the
ultimate cause of political life. First, narrower societies are formed, such as the family and the neighborhood. These
narrower societies are the nursery of the larger societies, which are formed by the union of several small ones. Then a
political, not merely a private, society is obtained. The state is the universal society, which includes all the
smaller ones within itself. Althusius here recalls Bodin, who, as we saw, laid such great weight on the significance of
the smaller societies within the large. It is the people, represented in the various circles of society and by
% --- p. 46 ---
\opage{46}the ephors, that is the holder of sovereignty. On this point these older writers have a great advantage over
the teachers of natural law of the eighteenth century, who really knew only the single individual and the state as a
whole. It must be added, however, partly that the corporations had by then shown themselves bound up with many abuses,
partly that absolute monarchy in France and its imitations elsewhere had done everything to press the intermediate
links lying between the individual and the state down to as great an insignificance as possible.

Society in its simplest form, which lies at the basis of all others, has arisen by agreement, which in turn has its
motive in human wants. To understand rightly the contract theory thus put forward, one must consider somewhat more
closely how Althusius conceives the agreement that is to lie at the basis of all social life. It is need that leads to
it. But Althusius seems not to conceive this need as purely egoistic. Especially where he speaks of the origin of the
family and of the community of neighbors, he uses as explanation not only ``necessity'' but also ``natural feeling''
(naturalis affectio). He agrees with Aristotle's statement that man is a ``social animal'' in a far higher degree than
bees or other animals living in societies. It remains unclear how that ``natural feeling'' and this social inclination
are related to individual self-preservation. Althusius felt no need of a closer psychological analysis. Yet it would
have lain all the nearer to hand for him in that he confines the purely individual compact to the simplest society and
lets the other societies grow out of it. The assumption of a natural growth of society obviously stands in a certain
opposition to the immediate arbitrariness of the single individual. Even if, according to Althusius, it is the will of
the individuals who found society that lets society come into being, it is nevertheless, by his own doctrine, only the
first push that they can give; later on they appear not as individuals but as members of corporations, not as
independent atoms but as elements in a compound molecule whose motions do not depend on the single atom alone. There
are no \textit{pure} individuals; all individuals are involuntarily
% --- p. 47 ---
\opage{47}socially determined. From the beginning, the contract theory, by its assumption of pure individuals, stands in
opposition to the historical conception of the development of social life, which regards individuals as the
\textit{products} of society, not merely as its \textit{active forces.} Althusius wanted to unite both points of view.
Here too the decisive problem came forward later.

Connected with this is another question: was the original contract that founded society entered into consciously or
not? It is clear that only if it was entered into consciously can it be meant as a real historical event, taking place
at a definite time and place. Althusius seems not to conceive the matter so. Society, he says, is formed by an
\textit{express or tacit} compact (pacto expresso vel tacito). But what lies in a ``tacit'' compact? The assumption of a
contract is, according to Althusius, necessary not only for understanding the origin of society, but also for
understanding the transfer of governing authority to the magistrates. There is thus first a social contract, then a
contract of rulership, the former between the individuals among themselves, the latter between the whole people and
those who are to govern. With regard to this latter contract Althusius now says (and it must hold for the first contract
too) that the rights the people has not expressly transferred to the prince it keeps for itself, and that even where the
people submits to a magistracy without express conditions, the general demands of equity and justice and the content of
the ten commandments must nevertheless be understood as implied: ``for it is not probable that the people, to its own
ruin, has given the prince unbridled freedom, and the people has not wished to deprive itself of the capacity for
self-preservation or to give one individual a power greater than that of all the others together.'' In other words:
Althusius infers from what must \textit{reasonably} be the people's meaning to the content of the \textit{original}
contract, and he
therefore presupposes that the people behaved reasonably when the contract came into being. But unfortunately the people
behaves reasonably always just as little as the princes do, and the justification for assuming a ``tacit'' reason on that
occasion is therefore unprovable. It is evident, then, that that contract (especially in its ``tacit'' part) rather
% --- p. 48 ---
\opage{48}expresses Althusius's ideal of a society than a historical event. Natural law, and especially its contract
theory, is a mythological expression of the ideal demand that must be made on the order and development of society. It
places its ideal of the future back in the past. It is perhaps a question whether most of the teachers of natural law
really conceived the original contract as a historical fact. Bodin already saw that the idea of the golden age rested on
an illusion, and so it goes with every notion of an absolute state of nature. The great significance of natural law
rests on its having had, in the idea of the original contract, a form in which the right of the individual over against
society and its authorities could be asserted with clarity and emphasis. But it was only Kant who taught that there is a
difference between a guiding, regulative idea and something factually given. With the help of this distinction one can
see at once the defects of natural law and its great significance. ---

Bodin and Althusius continue Machiavelli's work of making political theory a purely human science. Althusius does rely,
as the very title of his work shows, on biblical history just as well as on profane history. But it is only purely
historical examples that he takes from it. He does not operate with theological arguments. He assumes with Paul that
all authority is of God; but God's working is here not immediate but mediate: the forces and drives that lead to the
formation of society and the installation of authority stem from God through nature. The authority of the prince and of
the ephors stems \textit{immediately} from the people, \textit{mediately} from God. Not to the prince alone, but to the
ephors or estates as well, has God committed the care of the state. The theological hypothesis has thus been pushed
further into the background. As an ardent Calvinist, however, Althusius sets the furtherance of religion as a chief
purpose of the state. He declares himself decidedly against religious freedom, with reference to Deuteronomy 13, 12,
which demands the death penalty for him who speaks for another faith than that of the fathers. Religious freedom, he
holds, would make faith uncertain and abolish the unity that ought to reign in the state; he that is not with me is
against me. Althusius's theological standpoint also comes
% --- p. 49 ---
\opage{49}to light in his denying the independence of individual ethics over against theology. What the individual is
obliged to do he learns from the ten commandments, in so far as it does not belong to what political theory and the
doctrine of right enjoin. What then remains for ethics is only the rules for worthy conduct in word and deed, which
Althusius treated in his writing on ``cultivated social intercourse'' (civilis conversatio). He thus consistently holds
fast to the opposition, fixed by Melanchton, between the inner and the outer man, although he cherishes a disquieting
interest in outer human life and considers its ordering by purely natural laws possible. He recognizes the natural
forces in social life with an energy that would have aroused offense in Melanchton. What the Emden councillor formulated
in his ``Politics'' were ideas that had been fostered during the Dutch war of liberation and that later, after passing
through Rousseau's passionate mind and being sharpened there to their extreme formal consequence, came to make up the
circle of dogmas that ruled the French National Convention. It was the gospel of political freedom. Melanchton and his
school would never have admitted that there was such a gospel. In glaring contrast to this gospel stands Althusius's own
rejection of religious freedom, a testimony to the inner discord in the line of thought that had been inherited from the
Middle Ages and that even the boldest tendency within ecclesiastical Protestantism could not get beyond.

That it was not Althusius but \textsc{Hugo Grotius} who for the age that followed came to stand as the real founder of
natural law in modern times had its reason partly in the radical, democratic standpoint that the author of the
``Politica'' represented, and which was most different from the one taken by the leading statesmen and teachers of
constitutional law of the seventeenth century, partly in the larger and fuller historical grounding that Grotius gave the
principles of natural law, and partly, not least, in the fact that Grotius, in his famous work ``On Law in War and in
Peace'' \textit{(De jure belli ac pacis} 1625), took as his point of departure the question of the justification of war
and of the law that holds in war. Thereby he tied natural law to the law of nations and started from a
% --- p. 50 ---
\opage{50}phenomenon that occupied the thoughts of statesmen and touched the interests of all. It was not the inner
relation between magistracy and people, but the outer relation between sovereign states, that was the point of
departure for his consideration. What put the pen in his hand was the sight of the many wars that were often begun
without reasonable ground and that let loose all wild passions, as if men, once war had begun, were transformed into
raging beasts. He was then led to inquire how far all right must really vanish here, and this question led him back to
the ultimate foundation of right.

Hugo de Groot was born in Delft in 1583. In his student days at Leyden he already won great renown for learning. At
sixteen he accompanied Oldenbarneveldt to Paris, where Henry IV is said to have presented him to his court as the prodigy
from Holland. He early attained high posts in his fatherland as jurist and statesman. When Maurice of Orange, with the
help of the orthodox clergy, overthrew Oldenbarneveldt and had him executed, Grotius was sentenced to imprisonment for
life, from which he escaped through his wife's stratagem. He now took up residence in Paris, where for a time he
received support from the French government. Here he worked out the work to which his name is attached. Later he became
Swedish ambassador in France. He died in Rostock in 1645, on the way home from a visit to Sweden.

Grotius remarks that it is easier to say what wrong is than what right is. Wrong is everything that conflicts with the
nature of the social life that is led by rational beings. --- It is seen here that Grotius stands nearer to experience
and history than his predecessors. For that human social life rests on definite conditions is seen best when these are
lacking; there is then a kind of experiment before us. If those conditions were always present, one would not notice
them. --- It is an involuntary need that leads man to live together with others. Even if we did not directly need
others, we would still seek intercourse and fellowship with them. It is true that we cannot do without the help of
others; but the real ground of social life does not lie in that. Already in children one can trace an
% --- p. 51 ---
\opage{51}inclination to do good to others and to have pity on them in misfortune. This natural impulse (appetitus
societatis) is developed and clarified when fellowship with others becomes, by the help of language, a spiritual
intercourse, and when man acquires the capacity to lay general principles at the basis of his knowledge and his action,
so that he treats similar cases in a similar way. In the care to preserve a social life of this kind natural law has its
origin. Human actions are now judged by their agreement with, or their conflict with, what such a social life requires.
Natural law thus springs from principles that lie in man himself (ex principiis homini internis), and would hold even if
there were no God. Yet God can be called the author of natural law, since he is the author of nature and has thus willed
that this law should hold.

The first and most important provision of natural law is that agreements and promises are to be kept. This is contained
in the very original will that brings society about. Every obligation has its ground in a preceding agreement or in a
given promise. Positive law (jus civile) here springs from natural law. For social life could not subsist if men could
not bind themselves to one another. The whole of civil life here rests, then, on an eternal and unchangeable justice,
which holds for God as well as for all rational beings. Human nature, which is the mother of natural law, is thus the
grandmother of positive law, since the source of positive law is the necessity, grounded in natural law, of standing by
one's word.

But what, then, is it that gives the principle of the keeping of promises and compacts its original force? Here it
appears how the contract theory lies at the basis in Grotius as well as in Althusius. The very principle that compacts
are to hold is in fact laid down by an original compact! Only this original compact need not have been entered into
with full consciousness. It can be tacit, understood, lie in the nature of the circumstances, that is to say: it is only
another expression for the will to keep society up, which in turn is the condition of all
% --- p. 52 ---
\opage{52}social life. Society is regarded as the product of a free association, in which each sets in his will as part
of the common will. All particular relations ought to be judged by this original will (ex primæva voluntate). The state
is a body that has a voluntary origin (corpus voluntate contractum). From this is derived, among other things, the
important provision that the right of the individual can never wholly vanish over against society: it surely cannot
have been his will to annihilate himself! He cannot give up the right of self-preservation that he had before he
entered society.

As in Althusius, the mythological notion of the state of nature and of its replacement by political life through an act
of will appears here. Yet where Grotius, with the help of this notion, derives special relations of right (such as the
injustice of lying\textsuperscript{7}), private property, prescription, customary law), he readily uses the idea of a
\textit{tacit} agreement, an expression of what the beneficial ordering of the relation requires (aut expresse, aut ex
negotii natura tacite promittere, silentio convenire), so that it may be doubtful in his case too how far he conceived
the social contract as a historical event. But it is remarkable that, although Grotius starts from wrong and the absence
of peace as the leading facts, he nevertheless has a very idyllic conception of human life as it would look if it were
not ordered by society. He conceives the social need as direct, disinterested, and its relation to self-preservation
remains, as in Althusius, unclear. Only Hobbes here brought the stir from which greater clarity about the psychological
presuppositions of right could arise.

Grotius parts from Althusius in maintaining that the people, after it has been constituted by the social contract, can
transfer sovereignty permanently to a prince or an estate, just as well as the individual can give himself into
slavery. He polemicizes directly against Althusius's doctrine of popular sovereignty, although, for what reason is
unknown, he does not name him. He insists that the question here is not which form of state is the best --- something
on which there can always be different opinions, --- but the will that is the
% --- p. 53 ---
\opage{53}source of right (ex voluntate jus metiendum est). And what should stand in the way of the people's being able
to deliver itself wholly into the power of one or of several? Even in a democratic state the minority must, after all,
subordinate itself to the majority, and women, children and the poor have no share in the decisions, and so none in
sovereignty either. The original will can produce a necessity that binds for all time. It is of no use to say that the
state exists for the sake of the whole people, not for the sake of those who govern; for a guardianship exists for the
sake of the wards, not for the sake of the guardian, and yet he has authority over them. --- By thus giving the contract
by which power is transferred to those who govern a different character from the one by which the people is constituted
as a people, Grotius becomes the forerunner of Hobbes; it thereby becomes possible for absolute monarchy, too, to rely on
the contract theory. His arguments do not, however, shake Althusius's claim that it is hardly probable that the people
should have wished to sign away its freedom for all eternity. Althusius's conception obviously agrees best with the
contract theory, both in its mythological and in its rational meaning.

It is, as already remarked, war that gives Grotius the occasion for his inquiry into the concept and origin of right.
War can, in the first place, take place between individuals among themselves. But on the presupposition of a social
condition and a political life, just war between individuals is confined to self-defense, and the power of punishment is
in the hands of the government. In the second place, war can be raised by the individual against the state. This is
rebellion, and its inadmissibility stands firm for Grotius, who here too polemicizes against Althusius. He holds that
those who have granted the representatives of the people a right of rebellion have accommodated themselves too much to
the circumstances of a particular time and place. Grotius himself, on the other hand, seems to have taken too little
account of his countrymen's struggle against their ruler, a struggle grounded on the ``right of nature''. In the third
place, war can be waged on the part of the state against the individual. Such a war is just when it is directed against
one who has himself done wrong. The inquiry into this point thus leads to an inquiry into the nature and justification
of punishment.
% --- p. 54 ---
\opage{54}Grotius treats this point in a very interesting way. He is a decided opponent of the theory of retribution.
Punishment does not have its purpose in itself; only a savage and inhuman mind can find satisfaction in any pain whatever
being inflicted, when no further good is thereby attained for the person himself or for others or for the whole of
society. In the fourth place, there can be war between states among themselves. This subject is treated at the greatest
length. The conditions for the justice of a war and the considerations of humanity that ought to be observed during war
are derived from the principles of natural law. The chief principle is that men do not cease to be men because they
become enemies, and that war, which exists only for the sake of peace, must be waged in so honest and humane a way that
it does not make a peace impossible. Grotius is fully aware that the law of nations lacks the sanction that the power of
the state affords within the single people. Great states seem able to permit themselves anything. But even they need
ordered intercourse with other peoples, and the public opinion of humanity cannot be indifferent to them, just as war,
too, can be waged with vigor only when the people itself believes in the justice of the cause. By this insistence on the
demands of humanity and by pointing out the analogy between the conditions of intercourse among peoples and the
conditions of intercourse within the single people, Grotius made an extraordinary impression on the statesmen of the
seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Gustavus Adolphus is said always to have had his book with him in his tent. It is
said to have been Grotius's authority that kept Louis XIV from making good his threat of giving no quarter in his war
with the Dutch, just as the indignation that the devastation of the Palatinate aroused would hardly have risen with such
force in advance of the temper that Grotius's work had awakened. And to this very day the instructions of most states for
their officers in wartime are in essential part built on the rules set up by Grotius\textsuperscript{8}), which it is
not, however, our task here to follow out in detail. The point was only to show that the famous philosopher of law and
teacher of the law of nations has his place among those who discovered the human.
% --- p. 55 ---
\opage{55}

An important question in constitutional law and the law of nations at that time was how far men ought to be punished for
their religious opinions, and how far one state might make war on another for the sake of religion. As to the first
point Althusius stood at a narrowly confessional standpoint, and the wars of religion bore witness to what the general
view of the second point was. Grotius begins by asking what is to be understood by the true religion. It must be the one
that is common to all times, and its content he finds to be: the unity and invisibility of God, God as the author of all
things and as the one who cares for everything. These assumptions, he holds, can be proved in a natural way, and their
general diffusion testifies moreover to ancient traditions. At least the existence of God (whether one then assumes one
god or several) and the government of providence are self-evident, generally diffused and morally necessary truths. Those
who deny them violate human society and ought to be punished. Another people should be warred against for religious
reasons only when its worship of God has an immoral and inhuman character. When it is asked whether one should make war on
a people because it will not accept Christianity, Grotius answers that, apart from the quality of the Christianity that
is offered it, the rejection of a faith that rests on historical testimony and arises only through supernatural influence
cannot fall under human judgment. There is a wider horizon here than in Althusius, and a natural theology is set up. On
this point Grotius shows himself akin to the endeavors that we now pass on to discuss.

\subsection*{7.\quad Natural Religion}

It could not be otherwise than that the powerful spiritual movement of the
Renaissance, and the widening of the spiritual horizon that took place, must
reach into religious life. The Reformation itself is already evidence of this.
But the Reformation is at the same time precisely an attempt to set definite
limits to the religious movement. Among the most remarkable phenomena of the
Renaissance, especially toward its close, belongs
% --- p. 56 ---
\opage{56}on the other hand the endeavor to find a religion laid down in human
nature itself and independent of external forms and traditions. And just as
with natural law, two ideas here go hand in hand: for what really has its
ground in human nature must also be found again in the various historical forms
under which the human life of the spirit appears. The comparison between the
various contending confessions, whose number was, after all, being increased
precisely at that time, worked together with the newly awakened belief in the
self-sufficient power of human nature. Already within Italian humanism there
appear endeavors to develop a circle of religious ideas that was to be
independent of the doctrine of the Church. It was above all Plato's doctrine
that was taken as the foundation, as it was conceived by the Neoplatonists. The
Platonic Academy in Florence became of great influence here, beyond the borders
of Italy as well. In the heartfelt faith in a personal God and in the
immortality of the soul the individual found a satisfaction of his religious
need which at once set him free with respect to so many of the dogmas and
ceremonies of the Church and yet made it possible for him to find a deeper
symbolic meaning in them. In Germany and the Netherlands this humanist current
was joined by the mystical tendency, which already in the Middle Ages had worked
in quiet for a more inward and freer religiosity. The Swabian
\textsc{Sebastian Franck} and the Dutchman \textsc{Coornhert} came forward in
this spirit against the new Protestant dogmatism. They pointed to an inner
religious experience that can be lived through under very different
confessional forms. For Franck the invisible Christ was one with the natural
light, whose spark is found in every human mind and which could therefore be
kindled among the heathen too. One can, said Coornhert, follow the law of
Christ without knowing his name. These two men
% scan: „Mæud“ (p. 56; the e-book's reading, set by sense: scan-artefact rule)
are forerunners of the philosophy of religion of a later time, which sought the
understanding of positive religion and of its significance not by external
criticism of the finished dogmas, but by immersion in the spiritual ground of
nature and in the inner experiences that are the ultimate source and constant
abode of all dogmas. They themselves were made to feel confessional fanaticism.
The name by which it was customary
% --- p. 57 ---
\opage{57}to designate those who took an independent stand toward the
confessions was attached particularly to Coornhert, whom the Dutch preachers
called ``the prince of the Libertines''\textsuperscript{9}).

Natural religion was developed into still more definite forms in France and
England. The long and violent wars of religion in France could not but awaken
the need to get beyond the strife of the confessions and open the eye to the
human side of each of them. In the year 1577 Henry of Navarre (the later Henry
IV) wrote: ``Those who straightforwardly follow their conscience belong to my
religion, and I belong to the religion that all brave and good people have''.
Montaigne had at the same time, by his own path, arrived at the notion of a
universal religion that could be found in all, no matter how they conceived the
Deity. The most remarkable contribution in this direction, however, was made by
\textsc{Jean Bodin}, whose ideas in the domain of political theory have already
been brought forward. He left behind a dialogue between seven men
\textit{(Colloqvium heptaplomeres),} each of whom stands at his own religious
standpoint, which they develop each for himself without reserve, but in the
greatest friendliness and with the finest understanding of the personal relation
to religious notions. A rich Catholic in Venice gathers a circle of friends
around his table for conversations on various subjects, among which the question
of religion then comes for a time to take first place. Among the participants,
besides the host, who is a Catholic, are a Lutheran, a Calvinist, a Jew, a
Mohammedan and two men who, each in his own way, profess a universal theism.
Remarkable is the objective, dramatic manner in which the various standpoints
are brought forward. Only the Lutheran perhaps stands somewhat in the shade; at
any rate he does not shine by acuteness. When one day the host had mixed
artificial apples among the natural ones that had been set on the table, the
Lutheran guest was the only one who confidently bit into one of them without
suspecting anything amiss. The host, who himself always holds to the doctrine of
the infallible Church but is no fanatic, draws from this the moral that if
sight, the keenest of our senses, can thus be mistaken, how then should our
mind, bound to the senses, be able to arrive at certain knowledge of the highest
things! ---
% --- p. 58 ---
\opage{58}After all the standpoints have come forward, on several points with
the display of great learning, the dialogue ends without a definite conclusion.
A choir sings the hymn: ``Behold, how good and how pleasant it is when brethren
dwell together in unity!'' Then the participants embrace one another and part.
``Thereafter they practiced piety and integrity in admirable concord, in their
life together and in common studies, but never again held any debate on
religion, although each maintained \textit{his} religion in holy conduct.''

Bodin wrote this work in his 63rd year, that is, in 1593. It was not published,
but was spread in copies and was well known among the learned of the
seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. It is mentioned not infrequently, and as
a rule with the greatest abhorrence. Only a few, such as Leibniz in his later
years, declared themselves in favor of its being published. But only in the
year 1841 was it published (in a somewhat abridged translation) by Guhrauer, in
1857 complete in Latin by Noack, and it can now serve as a measure of what,
a couple of centuries ago, people were fairly well agreed in calling
ungodliness.

Since Bodin himself has not directly given us to understand which of the
persons expresses his own views, there have been differing opinions on the
matter. For a time people were inclined to think that Bodin sympathized with
Judaism, whose representative is drawn with particular force and expertise. But
if one attends to what is otherwise known of Bodin's religious tendency, and
compares it with what is put forward in the course of the conversations, one
arrives at another result. There is extant from Bodin a letter of an earlier
time to a friend, in which he expresses himself in the spirit of universal
theism as we already know it. ``Do not let yourself,'' he says, ``be confused by
the different opinions about the religions. Only hold fast in your mind that the
true religion is nothing other than the turning of a purified soul to the true
God.'' ``This is my religion, or rather Christ's.'' There follows an account of
how men would lie in eternal darkness if exalted men did not from time to time
come forward as exemplars. To their number belonged, besides the Jewish
patriarchs and prophets, the Greek and Roman
% --- p. 59 ---
\opage{59}sages as well. Plato is especially praised as the one who proclaimed
the idea of God and of the immortal soul. What he intimated Christ fulfilled,
and after him chosen men have worked in his spirit. This same idea of a
continued revelation through a series of sages, both before and alongside the
Mosaic, Christian and Mohammedan religion, now appears also as characteristic of
Toralba, one of the two persons in ``Heptaplomeres'' who maintain universal
theism. He argues that the best religion must be the oldest. The first man
received his knowledge and his piety from God himself. Faith in one God goes
back, according to the testimony of the Bible, to before the Jewish religion; it
was the religion of Abel, Enoch and Noah; it was the religion of Job. When men
abandoned this natural religion, which together with reason is implanted in men
(cum recta ratione mentibus humanis insita), they went astray in intricate
labyrinths. The natural law and the natural religion are sufficient; the other
religions --- of Christians, Jews, Mohammedans and heathens --- are superfluous.
For natural religion one needs no special learning or upbringing; one is created
for it, one has it given in one's own nature. The reason that is implanted in
us discerns and judges what is good and what is bad. But in some chosen ones
this religious and moral capacity appears with greater power than in others.
Toralba praises (just as Bodin does in that letter) Plato because he --- ``not
without divine help and enlightenment'' --- attained so high a wisdom concerning
divine things. The essence of the Deity is infinite, cannot be comprehended by
thought, let alone expressed in words. One comes nearest to it by calling God
the eternal being, exalted above everything bodily, infinite wisdom, goodness
and might. And in this Greek philosophers meet with Hebrews and Ishmaelites, so
that this idea must be assumed to be implanted by nature.

To this is added yet another trait in Toralba that recalls Bodin himself.
However far advanced Bodin was in several respects in relation to his time, in
one respect he was nevertheless deeply sunk in it. He believed with a convinced
heart in witchcraft and demonic possession, and he even wrote a
% --- p. 60 ---
\opage{60}book against the ungodly men who recommended caution and leniency in
the punishment of witches. It was the devil himself, he thought, who brought
forth such mildness toward the possessed. In the second book of the dialogue
this point is touched upon in a discussion between Toralba and Senamus, who is
otherwise the one among the interlocutors who stands nearest to Toralba. Toralba
declares that it is a mistake of the more recent physicists that they want to
explain everything by natural laws and recognize no intervention of God or of
the demons. Senamus replies to this that all natural science is thereby
overturned, since it presupposes definite laws of nature. Toralba adduces
several demon stories as proof of his view, and here can rejoice in the full
assent of the Lutheran. Senamus replies that even if there were demons who
could intervene in the corporeal world, it was still not thereby said that
wonderful phenomena were to be explained by them; and on the other hand: if one
assumes the intervention of demons, why then does one not explain everything in
nature by demons? Moreover he urges the necessity of criticism toward the
witch stories.

Toralba's standpoint is Bodin's own, as it is known from his personal
utterances. And yet he puts into the mouth of Senamus a criticism that Toralba
is unable to refute. Senamus is on the whole the critical spirit in the
dialogue. To the question who is to be judge in religious disputes, the Lutheran
answers: Christ, who is God! Senamus points out to him that the dispute
concerns, among other things, precisely the divinity of Christ. The Calvinist
refers to the witnesses and the documents. Senamus asks where the genuine
witnesses and testimonies are to be found. The Catholic refers to the Church,
--- but Senamus asks which of the many churches is the true one. The Lutheran
appeals to the Bible, the Mohammedan to the Koran; Toralba rejects this appeal
to authorities and holds that the wise must decide the matter; but Senamus then
asks who is wise. And when at last the Catholic wants a distinction drawn
between what is essential and what is inessential in religion, Senamus shows
that the great dispute arises precisely when this boundary is to be drawn.

Senamus takes the same stand toward Toralba's natural religion as toward the
heathen, the Mohammedan,
% --- p. 61 ---
\opage{61}the Jewish and the Christian religion. He thinks that they are all
well-pleasing to God when they are practiced with a sincere mind. He himself
gladly visits all kinds of temples, wherever they are found. He will offend no
one: him who believes most, the Catholic, who is ``religiosissimus'', just as
little as those whose religion is merely faith in one God. He thus does not set
up natural religion as a particular religion in opposition to the positive
religions. In Senamus Bodin has let thoughts come forward that contain a
corrective to the dogmatism into which, as history shows, natural religion can
lapse just as well as the positive religions. Even if his own standpoint
coincides with Toralba's, he has nevertheless intimated a more far-reaching
consideration than the latter's. It is not impossible that Bodin in his last
years had begun to entertain doubts about his own earlier assumptions in the
domain of theology and demonology, and that he let these doubts find a voice
through Senamus, without having been able to form a new conception on the basis
of what he has Senamus say.

The idea of natural religion was brought forward in fully finished form before
wider circles by Lord \textsc{Herbert of Cherbury}, in his book \textit{De
veritate} (1624). Like Althusius, Grotius, Coornhert and Bodin he was a
statesman who took part in the public affairs of his time and had occasion to
gather extensive experience and to make comparisons. He belonged to a noble
family in Wales; his forefathers were doughty knights, and he himself did not
deny their warlike spirit. War and duels are a main subject of his
autobiography. He was quick to get his sword out of its sheath, although he
asserts that it was always for the sake of others that he drew it. He was born
in 1582 or 1583 and received a careful education, which he afterwards
constantly continued on his own. It was his wish to form himself into a citizen
of the world. After having been married to a rich heiress already in his 16th
year, he studied at Oxford and then came to court. Later he was in the camp of
Maurice of Orange, traveled in Germany and Italy, and was then for a number of
years English ambassador in France. But neither at court, in the camp nor in his
diplomatic post did he forget his ``beloved studies''. His
% --- p. 62 ---
\opage{62}famous book he finished in Paris, where he let Grotius read it.
Although Grotius's judgment was highly favorable, he still had misgivings about
publishing it, since he knew it would meet much opposition. Once, when he sat
irresolute in his room, which was open to the south, he resolved to obtain a
supernatural decision of his misgivings. With the book in his hand he threw
himself on his knees and implored God, who is not only the author of the
outward light but from whom all inward enlightenment comes, for a sign that
might urge him to publish; if the sign failed to come, he would suppress the
book. At once he heard a faint sound, which came from the clear sky and
resembled nothing on earth; and now he confidently let the book go
forth\textsuperscript{10}). This event does not stand, as has been thought, in
any contradiction with the conception Herbert develops in his book. For he
assumes that God not only works in human reason but also answers men's prayers
through particular manifestations. Like Bodin's Toralba, he assumes miracles.
Shortly after the book's publication he was recalled from his post as
ambassador, because his brisk conduct did not suit the hesitant policy of
James I. The rest of his life he spent partly in London, partly at his castle in
Wales, occupied with historical and philosophical studies. During the Civil War
his conduct was wavering; but in the end he joined Parliament. He would have
liked best, as before, to combine public activity with his studies, and he
could not get over his political disappointments. He died in the year 1648.

Herbert makes his way to his doctrine of natural religion by an epistemology
that is not without historical interest. --- If the truth is to be grasped by
us, there must be faculties in us for it. Besides discursive reason and the
inner and outer sense there is a natural instinct that leads to the development
of certain truths common to all men (notitiæ communes). This Stoic doctrine we
have already found in Melanchton and his school. In Herbert it serves as the
foundation for the universal truths that the comparison of the various
religions led men to assume. But peculiar to him is the way in which he connects
the
% --- p. 63 ---
\opage{63}origin of these common notions with the instincts that lead to the
self-preservation of the individual and of the species. For the natural
instinct from which they spring is the fundamental force in every man and in
the whole world: the instinct of self-preservation in the widest sense, through
which divine providence manifests itself. Without conscious reason everything in
the world strives after what is best for it. And since the ``common notions''
serve preservation and the maintenance of peace, the instinct of preservation
leads to their being developed and recognized. It is thus the truths most
important for the individual and for society that become the object of
instinctive recognition. When they are separated from impure admixtures and
methodically ordered, they constitute a sum of divine wisdom. Such truths are
the following: mutually contradictory assertions cannot all be true; there is a
first cause of everything; nature does nothing in vain; do not do to others
what you would not have them do to you. Thus the most important logical,
ethical and religious ideas are to be grounded, in the manner indicated, on
natural instincts. Herbert gives no more than intimations. The relation between
the fundamental truths and the natural instinct remains unclear. There are
evidently a good many psychological intermediate links to be understood between
the instinct and the fundamental truths. The task is --- to use modern
expressions --- to understand how the struggle for existence can lead to fixing
certain representations as self-evidently valid. But these intermediate links
Herbert does not seek out, whereas he sometimes makes the natural instincts and
the fundamental truths wholly one.

Herbert makes a front on three sides. First, against those who set faith above
knowledge, and by faith understand what their sect assumes, while they seek to
gain entry for this faith by threats of punishments in another life. With this
the assumption of the corruption of nature is usually connected. An ungodly
faith, for it conflicts with the providence that manifests itself in the natural
instincts! Second, against those who want to prove everything by way of
reasoning (by discursus luxuriosus). This scholastic pedantry does not see that
natural instinct, just as well as the inner and the outer sense, stands above
reason. It manifests itself before the capacity to reason stirs, and works
% --- p. 64 ---
\opage{64}independently of it; it is found in all, works without hesitation and
uncertainty, and is a necessary condition of self-preservation. Third, he turns
against those who derive all knowledge from the senses and take our mind to be
originally an unwritten tablet (tabula rasa). Those fundamental notions are
precisely the conditions of our being able to have experiences! And it surely
cannot be the objects themselves that make us act back upon them! The agreement
between men's representations proves the existence of a natural instinct, which
besides could also be inferred from the goodness of God, who could not leave
man to stand helpless.

Natural religion is now grounded precisely on such an instinctive foundation.
In his autobiography Herbert occasionally develops this more closely. There
arise in us faculties and drives which cannot find full employment or reach full
satisfaction in anything that experience can offer; only the perfect, the
