eternal and the infinite could bring rest. The Deity itself is their real
object. In every sound and normal man there is therefore the same capacity for
religion, even though it is developed in the most different ways and perhaps
finds no expression in any outward cult. At the foundation of all religion lie
five propositions which have validity everywhere: there is a highest, divine
being; it ought to be worshipped; the most important part of its worship
consists in virtue joined with piety; faults and crimes are to be atoned for by
repentance; there is reward and punishment after this life. Whatever in the
individual religions does not conflict with these propositions but serves to
confirm them may be accepted. That there are those who deny them is to be
explained by the fact that so many false and unworthy notions have arisen in
the religions that some are thereby led to reject all religion, without
excepting the natural one. The five propositions are in themselves sufficient;
one should keep to them and let the disputed questions lie. Through the
instincts on which natural religion is grounded, a constant inner revelation
takes place to individuals, so that they become independent of what the priest
says.

It is natural to apply to Herbert Senamus's
% --- p. 65 ---
\opage{65}remark that it is by no means easy to draw the boundary between the
essential and the inessential in religion. It would also be impossible to give
a proof that those five points really recur in all religions. Even if they could
be shown to be universal, it would by no means follow, moreover, that they are
grounded on natural instincts. And even if they had such an instinctive origin,
it would --- as already touched upon --- still remain to be shown \textit{how}
they develop. Herbert proceeds too briskly and dogmatically. On his way he
passes by a whole series of epistemological, psychological and religious
problems. But the point of view he sketched in broad outline was shaped with a
vigorous hand and became of great historical significance. It was established
that there is a religious consciousness which is independent of all existing
church communities and takes a critically testing stand toward them.

\subsection*{8.\quad Religious Speculation (Jakob Böhme)}

Lord Herbert busied himself by turns with sword and with book, and from
diplomatic negotiations at the court of Paris he went back to his closet to work
on his work ``on truth''. But the need of the age for new thoughts, and for
bursting the rigid ecclesiastical forms in which the movement of the Reformation
had so early settled down to rest, manifested itself under less brilliant
circumstances too. \textsc{Jakob Böhme} let awl and last lie in order to write
his ``\textit{Morgenröte im Aufgang}''. He too had looked about him in the world
before he took up the pen. As a journeyman shoemaker he had traveled at his
trade; later he settled in Görlitz, and in the quiet workshop thought worked in
a race with the hand. He was not a wholly unlearned man; he calls himself a
naturalist and philosopher, and had made the acquaintance of astronomical
writings; remarkably enough he is a Copernican, inasmuch as he lets the earth
and most of the planets move round the sun; he had made the acquaintance of the
physician Paracelsus's writings on the philosophy of nature, and probably also
of the works of the mystic Valentin Weigel, spread in copies, in which
Paracelsian ideas were worked together with the doctrines of earlier
% --- p. 66 ---
\opage{66}mystics. He was at the same time a pious man who knew his Bible and the
Lutheran doctrine. But his problems he set himself, and he treated them with a
spiritual freedom and strength that still make his writings valuable and that
led him beyond the dogmatic barriers. While Bodin and Herbert come to the
religious problem more from without, for Böhme it presents itself within the
confessional notions themselves; he goes on working with these until the stream
of thought breaks through all dams. In his naive but vigorous self-confidence
the shoemaker of Görlitz too bears the stamp of the Renaissance, just as the
elements of learning that he uses for his edifice of thought point back to the
philosophical and scientific movements of the time, which had found their way to
him too through many intermediate links and transformations. He uses what is at
his disposal to solve the problems that for a time were bringing him to despair.
A remarkable example of how the philosophical intellectual tendency can break
forth even where inner and outer circumstances seem bound to exclude it! So long
and so hard had he struggled with the tormenting thoughts that it stood before
him as a revelation, a higher enlightenment, when he caught sight of the
possibility of a solution. In the 19th chapter of ``Morgenröte'' he has
described his doubts, and how the light then dawned on him, and it was to him
``as though life had been born in the midst of death''. He was then 25 years
old, and according to the legend it was in an ecstatic state, into which the
sight of a shining metal dish put him, that he first saw his fundamental
thoughts clearly before him. And they still had to ripen for twelve years before
his first work (Morgenröte) was written (1612). That the shoemaker dared to
philosophize so boldly aroused great offense in the parish priest, who had got
hold of a copy of the book. He denounced Böhme as a heretic from the pulpit and
got the authorities to forbid him to write. Only for some years did Böhme
observe the prohibition. In the last period of his life he unfolded a fruitful
activity as an author. He died in Görlitz in 1624.

The religious problem presents itself to Böhme under two main forms. --- He fell
into ``hard melancholy and sadness'' on
% --- p. 67 ---
\opage{67}seeing how small a place man occupies in the outer world. It is high up
to heaven, where the learned say that God dwells. And globes and elements, which
fill space, seem to go their way without any heed being paid to how things stand
with man! God's remoteness and man's vanishing place in nature was thus the one
stumbling block. But to this was added: the struggle between good and evil, both
in the human world and in nature, together with the sight of how the ungodly
fare just as well in the world as the pious, and how the barbarous peoples hold
the best parts of the earth and have better fortune with them than the
believers. That was the other stumbling block: How is the existence of evil
compatible with the existence of God? ---

The first problem, the one posed by the fact that the world of matter is so
great and the world of spirit so remote or so small, he solves by means of the
thought that it is God's force and essence that stirs in everything, in us as
well as in the outer masses. God is not separated from nature, but is related to
it as the soul to the body. Heaven is not up there above the blue; it is in your
own innermost being, where the divine life stirs in you. God is not remote; you
live in God, and God in you, and if you are pure and holy, you are God. The same
forces stir in you as in God and as in the whole of nature. Fire, air, water,
earth --- everything is God. Or else you are not God's image. You cannot be any
other matter than God himself. When you see the stars, the globes and the deeps,
you see God, and in the same God you too live and are. The globes and the
elements, to be sure, are not the clear Deity itself; but the force from which
they draw their life rules in you too. The inner motions in man's being are of
the same nature as those that take place in God. In all processes of nature God
is hidden; only in the spirit of man is he known. One understands nothing of
God as long as the soul is separated from him, as if it were a separate being.

If one wants to call this line of thought heathen, Böhme answers: ``Hear and
see, and mark the difference. \textit{I write not heathenishly, but
philosophically.} Nor am I a heathen, but I have the deep and clear knowledge
of the one great God, who is all.''
% --- p. 68 ---
\opage{68}And he knows how much it has cost him to reach this thought, which has
made the world alive for him and taught him that spirit is not remote and alien
in it, but one with what stirs innermost in everything. He has tried to push
such thoughts aside, but great anguish and temptation have then led him anew to
seek them out. (Morgenröte im Aufgang. Ch. 19 and 25). The religious need of
inward unity with the Deity, of abolishing God's remoteness, here meets with the
philosophical need to find connection in everything, and both are supported by
the doctrine, set up by the natural philosopher Paracelsus, that man consists of
the same elements as the universe.

But Böhme does not stop at nature as it now is. The question arises for him how
this outward, sensible world came into being? why is everything not in such
inward and harmonious connection that temptations such as those he had
experienced could not arise? Already Paracelsus, the revolutionary chemist and
physician, by whom Böhme is evidently strongly influenced, could put him on the
way here, since he had taught that the diversity of the elements had arisen by a
process of separation and splitting. Böhme follows this track with his usual
boldness, and it leads him at the same time to a solution of the second and most
serious problem. But the problem of the origin of evil had been sharpened for
him by the fact that he will not have God separated from the world and from the
souls, but would conceive their life as a part of God's own life. Evil consists
for Böhme precisely in wanting to separate oneself from the whole connection, in
wanting to be a whole, although one is only a part. Thereby arise the hard
division, the externality, the strife and the torment in the world.

Böhme gives his elucidation of this question in mythological form, using
biblical and alchemical representations, often in a baroque, but also often in a
magnificent poetic combination. Of this mythological or symbolic form of
exposition he is clearly aware. That he is able at all to solve the lofty
questions that press upon him he explains by the fact that the same spirit and
the same elements that stir in the world, and have stirred there from all
eternity, also stir in him.
% --- p. 69 ---
\opage{69}In other words, it is his own inner experiences and struggles that he
uses to interpret nature and its history and to understand what is innermost
moving in everything. And when he depicts a series of processes and
catastrophes, a whole world-drama in vivid images, he does not thereby mean that
such things took place literally thus, at a definite time and place, --- nor
that it was something that unfolded historically and successively. He wants to
depict what takes place everywhere and at all times, an eternal fundamental
relation between the forces of the world, a strife that has not been fought once
for all, but is constantly being fought, and in which he feels that he himself
stands. His utterances on this are surprisingly clear. ``The meaning is not that
there is in heaven a particular place or a particular corpus where the fire of
the divine life rises . . . but \textit{I speak in a corporeal manner for the
sake of the reader's want of understanding} . . . For you cannot name any place,
either in heaven or in this world, where the divine birth does not go on.''
``And although I have here written how everything comes into being, and how
everything is formed and fashioned, and how the Deity rises, you must not think
that there was first to be quiet and extinction and then the rising to take
place. O no, but \textit{I must describe piecemeal for the sake of the reader's
want of understanding.}'' ``The birth of nature goes on to this very day in the
same way as in its first beginning.'' ``In the divine forces (Qualitäten) there
is neither beginning, middle nor end.'' ``You must know that what I write here
is not a story that has been told me by others, but I must myself stand in this
battle, and often I get, like other men, a broken leg.'' --- In presenting
Böhme's thoughts it is therefore justified to let the mythological form play a
subordinate part.

Böhme declares himself decidedly against creation out of nothing. ``Many writers
have indeed written that heaven and earth were created out of nothing; but I
wonder that among so many excellent men there was found none who could describe
the right ground, since after all the same God who now is has been from
eternity. Where nothing is, nothing comes to be either; everything must have a
root, otherwise nothing grows forth, and had not the spirits of nature
% --- p. 70 ---
\opage{70}existed from eternity, then no angel, no heaven and no earth would have
come into being.'' It is Böhme's conviction that nothing can be explained from
an absolute unity. There must lie in the essence of the Deity a plurality of
moments; a difference must assert itself in it which cannot from the first have
been arbitrarily produced, but is precisely as a dark source of universal life.
In purely logical or psychological form Böhme expresses this (in his
``Theosophiske Fragen'') by saying that God is not merely a Yes, but that a No
must step into opposition to this positive moment, since otherwise there would
be no joy and sensation, on the whole nothing that could stand out definitely
(no \textit{Erheblichkeit}). Without such an inner original opposition between a
positive and a negative moment there would be no will either; pure unity has
nothing in itself that it can will. This original element of opposition Böhme
calls, in his mythological language, God's wrath and the foundation of hell.
There is originally in God wrath just as well as love, a foundation for hell
just as well as for blessedness. Where indeed should wrath, all that is sharp,
bitter, hard and poisonous in the world, come from, if it did not have its root
in God? But originally wrath is only a moment that serves to let love step
consciously forth. Life demands such opposition; only because there are
different ``qualities'' in nature is there mobility, growth and drive in
everything. The word quality Böhme interprets by a naive etymology, which
expresses a brilliant thought, as coming from quallen, Quelle: ``Qualität ist
die Bewegligkeit, quallen oder treiben eines Dinges.'' ``Qualificirung'' is one
with ``Bewegung''. He will not stop at ascribing dead and resting properties to
things, but dissolves everything into active forces and tendencies. That heat,
e.g., is a ``quality'' thus means that it shines, warms, dissolves, melts. The
plurality of the qualities --- i.e. of the fundamental forces --- thus stands
firm for Böhme, since no motion, no life and no consciousness would be possible
without such a difference. But from the first the fundamental forces are in
harmonious interplay. The bitterness in the root of nature serves only to let
the sweetness come forth all the more strongly. The bitter quality is in God
too, but as ``a triumphant source of joy''.
% --- p. 71 ---
\opage{71}

But even if this original unity of opposition is recognized, the riddle remains
standing. How can there be reconciled with it the experience of a hardness and a
bitterness in the world which are by no means merely moments in an inner
harmony, and above all of the sharp strife between good and evil in the inner
and in the outer world? Here is the crux of all religious speculation. Just as
little as it is possible to derive plurality from absolute unity, just as little
is it possible to derive disharmony from absolute harmony. No wonder that
Böhme's mythologizing fantasy, at this point, where his feeling is moreover in
such strong motion, gets the better of his thinking completely. It will not be
possible to give a vivid account of the drama in which the persons of the
Trinity, the original ``Qualitäten'' and ``Quellengeister'' and the host of
archangels appear. The main thing is that one of the elements in the original
nature of the Deity, the element of wrath, the No, pushes forward with a
tendency to spread over the whole. It was not content to be a moment, but wants
to be totality. That was Lucifer, who was blinded by his splendor and his power
and his seat in the highest center, and now would triumph over the whole Deity,
have a prouder and more splendid ``qualification'' than God himself. Then strife
and torment were born in the world; a fire was kindled that has never since been
quenched. The opposites were loosened from the original harmonious connection,
hard matter was hurled out into space, and only then did the world come into
being as we now know it. Evil thus existed before man; man received the germs of
it in his nature. Only now has Böhme come to the point where the story of
creation in Genesis begins, a story for which he otherwise has not much respect,
since there is a good deal in it that conflicts ``with philosophy and sound
reason'', for which reason he also cannot believe that ``the dear man Moses''
wrote it. On the whole he follows his own thoughts, trusting in the inner
testimony of the spirit. Nor does he let himself be impressed by the learned:
``I do not need the formula and art of philosophers, astronomers and
theologians, since I have not learned from them, but have another teacher,
which is the whole of nature.''

Above all Böhme is indignant at those who teach that God has
% --- p. 72 ---
\opage{72}purposely chosen some for blessedness and destined others for
damnation. Even if Paul or Peter had written it, he will not believe it. God
does not will evil. Nor did he know beforehand that it would go as it went. And
yet evil must have its root in God, who is the author of everything! This root
is the negative moment, ``the foundation of hell'', --- that in God which is not
God, if by God one understands only love (not wrath). And yet it is after all a
divine element that breaks loose from the original harmony --- it was ``God
against God'', as Böhme (Morgenröte. Ch. 14 § 72) expressly says. Thereby the
strife in the world becomes so serious and so violent; there are divine forces
on both sides. Hence the anguish and agony that the struggle brings, and from
which Böhme saved himself only by fleeing to the thought of the heart of the
Deity, which constantly works to force hardness and bitterness back within their
bounds.

In his theological speculation Böhme applies the psychological truth that the
involuntary precedes and forms the foundation of the voluntary. He finds the
origin of evil not in God's voluntary willing, but in the involuntary ground of
nature, which contained different elements. But the great leap from difference
to strife, from opposition to division, he overlooked. How pride comes to be in
Lucifer he cannot explain. Here he narrates instead of giving grounds. And yet
his thought has ventured as far as the thoughts of so inwardly religious a man
seldom venture. From the theological side one must consistently regard him as
he regards Lucifer. He has set a dangerous ``quality'', thought, in motion, and
once this source has begun to flow it cannot be stopped again. Yet it is not
pride but an inward need of understanding that leads him on from step to step.
The naive self-confidence of newborn thinking keeps him from wavering and
stopping. He expressly regards his task, as we have already heard in a
characteristic utterance, as a purely philosophical one. ``What is still
hidden?'' he asks in another place, ``Christ's pure doctrine? No, but
philosophy.'' This, then, he wants to bring, and he attaches such great
significance to the understanding he has won that he calls his
% --- p. 73 ---
\opage{73}first book ``Dawn Breaking Forth''; the time of fulfillment must now be
near! There is in reality dawn in his thinking. He felt the new forces, even if
he did not see whither they led.

Two great laws Böhme laid at the foundation of his speculations: the law of
opposition as the condition of all motion and of all consciousness, and the law
of development as the progressive unfolding of differences. In the law of
opposition it is clearly enough psychological experiences that he starts from,
as can be seen especially from the characteristic proposition: ``Kein Ding ohne
Widerwertigkeit mag ihm selbst offenbar werden.'' In the thought of development
as the arising of diversities he is influenced by Paracelsus. The word
development he introduced into the German language\textsuperscript{11}). --- By
the consistent use of these laws he carried religious thought to its limit, a
limit that no later attempt of a similar kind has been able to move.

There might seem to be a great difference between Böhme's religious speculation
and the natural religion maintained by Bodin, Cherbury and Grotius. Böhme was,
or thought he was, a positively believing Lutheran. But he saw consistently
that if divine light and life work in the whole of nature as a counterweight to
hardness and bitterness, access to the light cannot be limited. Everyone can work
his way or grow forth through ``wrath'' to ``love''. Jews, Turks and heathens,
who know nothing of Christ, nevertheless stand on an equal footing with
Christians. ``Whoever has love in his heart and leads a merciful and meek life
and fights against wickedness and presses through God's wrath into the light, he
lives with God and is one spirit with God. For God needs no other service.''
These words Bodin might very well have put into the mouth of his Toralba.
\textsc{Martensen} finds them ``strange and without foundation''. But they have
a secure foundation in Böhme's own fundamental thoughts. Later ``speculative''
theologians might wish for his steady gait as a thinker. What interests us here
is that in the midst of the territory of Lutheran orthodoxy, in an unlearned
artisan, we find the same universal tendency in religious respects that is
peculiar to the philosophy of the Renaissance, and that is so
% --- p. 74 ---
\opage{74}closely connected with the fact that men again believe in the natural
forces and dare to use their own thoughts.

\section*{B.\quad The New World-View}

\subsection*{9.\quad The Aristotelian-Medieval World-Picture}

Just as little as man and the world can be separated from each other, just as
little can the conception of man be separated from the world-view. There is
therefore something artificial in following the change that the conception of
man undergoes without regard to the changes in world-view. There is a constant
interaction between them. Böhme's religious speculation is thus evidently in
part conditioned by the new world-view (especially by Paracelsian and Copernican
ideas) and can properly be understood only when one takes it into account too,
although what predominates in him is his conception in terms of the psychology
of religion. Conversely, in several of the thinkers whom we shall here consider
as founders of the new world-view there will be found valuable ideas and points
of view in psychological and ethical respects, which in and of themselves could
entitle them to a place among those who have discovered man. But it must be
permitted to give them their place under the point of view that indicates their
decisive significance in the history of thought.

To understand the magnificent change in world-view that is the greatest deed of
the Renaissance beside its art and its discovery of man, we must first bring
forward the main features of the world-picture that still in the fifteenth
century stood unshaken for learned and lay alike. It derived from Aristotelian
physics and Ptolemaic astronomy and had been interwoven with biblical
representations, a combination that was very easily possible, since the whole
world-picture kept to what the senses immediately taught and merely gave it a
more exact determination and a systematic execution.

Even for the ordinary conception there is a great
% --- p. 75 ---
\opage{75}difference between the motions in the heavens and what happens here on
earth. Here there seems to reign a constant change. Phenomena wane and wax,
arise and pass away. Motions arise, but they cease again after a shorter or
longer time. Otherwise up yonder: the stars go their regular course without any
change being noticed, and their path leads them always back along the same ways
in an eternal circular motion without rest. \textsc{Aristotle} laid this
opposition between the heavenly and the earthly or sublunary region at the
foundation of his world-view. He relied on what observation seemed to teach,
while he also referred to the old belief, among Hellenes and barbarians alike,
that makes heaven the seat of the eternal gods. The heavenly region is
incorruptible; motion in it is eternal and absolutely regular. The sublunary
region, on the other hand, is the home of corruptibility, where motion and rest,
coming into being and passing away, succeed one another.

The two regions must then also consist of different matter. The heavenly bodies
must consist of a matter that does not belong in any definite place and can
therefore continue its motion eternally. This matter, ``the first body'',
Aristotle calls the ether. It is what fills the space of heaven, and in which
the eternal circular motion takes place. Only circular motion can be eternal,
since it always returns into itself and from every point in the circle passes
to every other point. In the sublunary region every motion stops at a certain
point, namely when the body has reached its ``natural place''. Here rectilinear
motion reigns, which goes either from the center of the world outward and
upward, or toward the center of the world inward and downward. That whose
natural place is at the center of the world or near it is called heavy; that
whose natural place lies upward toward the upper boundary of the sublunary world
is called light. The constant changes in the earthly regions now come from the
elements' not always being in their natural place. The heavy element is earth,
the light one fire; between both lie water and air. Fire, after all, constantly
rises aloft, and the stone thrown aloft always falls down again. Each element
has a craving for its definite place in the space of the world. The four
elements can
% --- p. 76 ---
\opage{76}pass into one another, but cannot themselves be dissolved into simpler
constituents, whereas all bodies are composed of them.

There can be only one world. If one imagined for a moment that there were
several, the heavy elements would at last have to gather around one center, and
there would then be only one world. The earth is, as observation shows, at the
center of the world, and from it we come, going outward and upward, first
through the three other sublunary layers and then to the region of the ether,
whose matter is the purer the farther it is removed from the earth. The heavenly
bodies, first the moon, the sun and the other planets, then the fixed stars, sit
fastened in solid but transparent spheres that turn about their axes. This
assumption Aristotle took over from the astronomer Eudoxus. That the globes
could float freely in the space of heaven the ancients could not conceive. All
the spheres move about the earth as their center; the moon, the sun and the
other planets each have their own sphere; all these spheres, and thus the whole
system of the world, are enclosed by ``the first heaven'', the sphere of the
fixed stars, which is moved directly by the Deity itself, while lower principles
or spirits guide the motions of the lower spheres. The highest is what encloses
and limits. The uppermost or outermost part of the world is the most
perfect\textsuperscript{12}).

The Aristotelian world-scheme offered a framework that not only corresponded to
what sensory observation seems to teach, but could also take into itself the new
observations made by the astronomers of later antiquity. It turned out, to be
sure, that one had to conceive the motions of the planetary spheres as very
complicated when one took into account the forward and backward motions of the
planets; but this was remedied by conceiving each single planet as attached at
once to several spheres, each corresponding to one of its motions. The motions
were conceived as taking place not in simple circles, but in smaller circles,
epicycles, whose centers moved on larger circles. And this system of epicycles
then became, as research advanced, ever more complicated. Ptolemy of Alexandria
(in the 2nd century after Christ) gave an account of the system of the world
that became the authority in the astronomical domain throughout the Middle Ages,
% --- p. 77 ---
\opage{77}just as Aristotle became so in the philosophical domain.

Since the Aristotelian-Ptolemaic system, like the Bible's conception of the
world, took its stand on the standpoint of sensory observation, for which the
earth stands still while the sun and the stars move, it was well suited to be
combined with the religious notions prevailing in the Middle Ages. As Aristotle
had remarked, it also agreed, after all, with the old belief in heaven as the
seat of the Deity. An essential difference made itself felt, however, between
the ancient and the medieval conception of the world. Aristotle by no means
placed the earth at the center of the world because he thought that everything
else in the world existed for its sake or for that of its inhabitants. On the
contrary, for him the highest was what encloses and limits, and the earth was
the place of the lowest matter. But for the medieval conception of the world it
was precisely the earth and the events on it around which everything turned.
Nevertheless it could well use the Aristotelian scheme and the idea of the
imperfection of the sublunary world, since it let the heavenly forces descend to
intervene in earthly affairs and lead them to the right goal.

The whole mode of representation was --- apart from the difficulties that the
compound spheres and the epicycles caused --- clear and vivid. It amounted to
this: that sensible space was absolute space, and that in this space there were
absolute places. The globe on which the philosopher or the astronomer found
himself he took, just as the practical man constantly does, for the absolute
center of the world. And the world that took form around this center in the
various spheres had its limit in the outermost sphere, beyond which there was
nothing. It belonged to the ancient view of nature to think everything formed
and limited. The unlimited was one with the dark and the unformed, if not with
evil. Here too the scheme could rely on sensory intuition and fantasy, which
always stops at a certain point without any need to ask what lies beyond it.

A world-picture such as this could be attacked from two sides.
% --- p. 78 ---
% print: „Selvbestemmelse“, for Stedbestemmelse (the author's slip) (p. 78) (misprint)
\opage{78}First and foremost by bringing forward observations and calculations
that conflict with it or at least make another conception possible or probable.
But also --- and this interests us here not least --- by contesting the naive
trust itself in the absolute validity of sensible space. If it turns out that
every determination of place depends on the observer's position, the absolute
difference between the heavenly and the earthly region, and between the natural
places within the earthly region, falls away. Along both paths the
Aristotelian-medieval world-picture was attacked in the research of the
Renaissance. And as will appear, the latter path was entered upon first.

\subsection*{10.\quad Nicolaus Cusanus}

Already at the close of antiquity there showed itself within philosophy a need
to burst the clearly articulated and limited Aristotelian world-picture.
Plotinus, the founder of the Neoplatonic school, expressed a thought which, when
carried further, was bound to lead beyond every dogmatic limitation and
partitioning of nature. For him, as for Plato and Aristotle, harmonious
limitation was not the highest. The highest was something that lay beyond, or
led beyond, every barrier. The infinite was thus no longer something
negative, but became the expression of a positive, unsurveyable fullness, before
which thought and language are at last powerless. The finite forms, beings and
regions are then each of them only limited revelations of the infinite. Although
Plotinus still stands on the ground of Greek thinking, thought in him
nevertheless often threatens to lose itself in mysticism. He became the
forefather of the mysticism of the Middle Ages, a tendency which again and again
came forward with its protest against the conceptual dogmatism of Scholasticism.
In the view of nature this tendency led to an emphasis on the connection of the
inner forces in spite of the differences of the outer phenomena, and to a
feeling of dissatisfaction with fixed forms and limits in every domain.
Mysticism has thereby prepared the way for the doctrine of evolution. It was
therefore of great significance that
% --- p. 79 ---
\opage{79}the Neoplatonic philosophy in particular was cultivated with zeal in
the period of the Renaissance. The Academy in Florence has especial merit here.

\textsc{Nicolaus Chryffts}, called \textsc{Cusanus} after his native town, did not
first come under the influence of Neoplatonic ideas through these new studies. He
was brought up at Deventer by the ``Brethren of the Common Life'', who were
strongly influenced by German medieval mysticism. He was born in 1401 at Cues, a
small town near Trier, but fled from there as a boy because of his father's
ill-treatment. A nobleman with whom he took refuge then had him study at
Deventer. Later he studied law, mathematics and philosophy at Padua. But the
mystical keynote, and the problems which it set in motion in him, never left him.
For a time it seemed as if he would pass wholly over into practical life. He was
first an advocate, then became a cleric, and took part with zeal in the
negotiations on the reform of the Church, at first attaching himself to the
Council of Basel, but later seeing the only possibility of a reform of the Church
in the strengthening of the papacy. Later still, as Bishop of Brixen, he had a
hard struggle to sustain with the sovereign of the land, Archduke Sigismund of
Austria. For a time he was even imprisoned. Pius II made him a cardinal and sent
him to Germany to visit churches and monasteries. Here too he had hard struggles
to sustain through his zeal to reform the manners of the clergy and of the
monasteries. In particular he combated superstition in a way that betrays a great
spiritual superiority over his age. He censured the use of superstition for
ecclesiastical purposes, and the procuring of ecclesiastical revenues by means
of relics and bleeding hosts. Witchcraft and sorcery he regarded as remnants of
paganism, which were kept alive by the very persecutions with which they were
visited. He found that there were most witches where people most believed in
witches. Two old women who had the reputation of being witches he examined
himself; they were half mad, and ``what they believed had really happened to
them, the Devil had put into them in dreams''. --- But amid all this
participation in the struggles of his time he was occupied with his problems. The
fundamental thought of his most interesting and best-known work \textit{(De docta
% --- p. 80 ---
\opage{80}ignorantia)} came to him, by his own account, as he was sailing back to
Italy from Constantinople, where he had been on a papal errand. It was followed
by a whole series of other writings, in which he partly developed his ideas
further, partly modified them. He died at Livorno in the year 1464, during the
preparations for the crusade, planned by his friend Pius II, against the enemies
of faith, of science and of literature.

Cusanus stands on the border between the Middle Ages and the Renaissance, and
between theology and philosophy. His innermost interest is, to be sure,
theological. It is the problem of the Trinity that he wants to solve. But he
treats it in such a way that he comes to develop epistemological and
scientific thoughts of great interest. It is bound up precisely with his mystical
tendency that the sharp distinction between the domains of concepts does not
exist for him. The obscure and abstruse element which is found in his writings
beside the many excellent ideas arises from this confusion. --- It is of no
interest for us to go through the whole of Cusanus's philosophy. The point is
only to show how he arrived at thoughts that shook the world-picture supported by
the testimony of the senses, the inquiry of antiquity and the authority of the
Church.

Cusanus conceives cognition as a connecting and assimilating activity. Sense
perception apprehends the scattered impressions, but already in this apprehension
thought expresses itself, partly in that the separate impressions are put
together into a whole, and partly in that there arises a wonder which spurs one
to go further. The various sense images are connected by the faculty of
representation (phantasia), the various complexes of representations by reason
(ratio); but at all these stages thought (intelligentia) is at work, which at
last seeks to lead all differences back to absolute unity. But at this point the
difficulty arises, for without plurality and difference (alteritas) our thought
cannot know. At its summit, then, thought finds precisely its limit. It can only
approach absolute unity in that a mystical vision, for which all the radii of
existence run together in one center, takes the place of the cognitive process
and gives thought rest. The perfection of thought is thus its cessation.
% --- p. 81 ---
\opage{81}

This conception of cognition (which is developed in the work \textit{De
conjecturis} ch. 16) makes clear what Cusanus means by ``conscious ignorance''
(docta ignorantia), an expression which already occurs in Bonaventura. It is
thought's consciousness of its own limit, joined with the mystical presupposition
that the best and highest lies beyond this limit, though in continuation of the
process that led to the limit. In the very work that bears the name De
docta ignorantia the matter is developed thus: Our cognition seeks to reach
beyond the oppositions and contradictions which experience presents. It discovers
on closer investigation that even the greatest oppositions, even mutually
contradictory states, coincide in one, if only the point of unity can be shown.
Thus maximum and minimum coincide by means of the concept of magnitude: both are
absolute quantities, each in its own direction; both are superlatives, and that
on one and the same scale. The concept of magnitude itself embraces them both.
But all the intermediate terms on the scale our cognition cannot find. It
remains forever stuck in oppositions. It works its way forward from term to term,
but cannot reach the perfect unity of the oppositions, any more than one can
produce a perfect circle by giving a polygon ever so many sides. Our thought is
related to truth, which is the perfect unity of oppositions, just as the polygon
is related to the circle.

The infinite is the measure and ideal of the finite. In it the oppositions meet.
An infinite curve is the same as an infinite straight line. But every line that
we apprehend is either straight or curved. We cannot reach beyond the finite
determinations. And yet that is necessary if there is to be a knowledge of God.
God can be thought only by the canceling of all particular determinations: but
for us nothing remains when all particular determinations are removed. God as
unity in all, as comprehending all, even what is mutually contradictory (omnium
rerum complicatio, etiam contradictoriarum), is therefore incomprehensible. No
name can be ascribed to him. For every name derives from a distinguishing and
separating, by which the one is set against the other. But God has no
opposite, any more than the concept of magnitude
% --- p. 82 ---
\opage{82}has any opposite on the whole scale from maximum to minimum. In the
religious cult conscious ignorance is replaced by holy ignorance (docta
ignorantia by sacra ignorantia), negative theology by positive. Definite
predicates and names are then ascribed to God; but none of these can then be
taken in the proper sense. When God, e.g., is called light, what is meant is not
a light that forms an opposite to darkness; in the infinite light even darkness
is light, just as the minimum lies on the same scale as the maximum.

The Aristotelian school has failed to recognize this truth, without which no
access stands open to a mystical theology. That is why it has not been able to
comprehend the doctrine of the Trinity rightly; for it has not seen the necessity
of a principle that can connect the oppositions expressed by the Father and the
Son: Spiritus sanctus est nexus infinitus! And that is why it has not led to any
true knowledge of nature. It stops at the difference between possibility and
actuality, between matter and form, between what produces and what is produced,
and does not seek a bond that can embrace all these oppositions and express their
unity. This bond is motion. Motion is neither merely produced nor merely
producing, but both at once, and so it is too with the other oppositions. And
this juxtaposition of the connecting principle in the Trinity and in nature is
not accidental for Cusanus: the Holy Spirit is the bond of nature, is one with
nature as the sum of all that happens through motion. --- Cusanus does not
distinguish between the coincidence (coincidentia), the comprehension
(complicatio) and the connection (connexio) of the oppositions, although these are
indeed quite different relations that are denoted by the three expressions. His
examples point mostly to a connection of extremes through transitions and
intermediate terms, and to a comprehension of them through the continuity thus
brought about. But that is something other than a complete canceling of the
oppositions. There is a want here of full clarity about the nature of the very
concept that denotes his highest point of view. And this is bound up with the
lack, mentioned before, of a distinction between the different domains of
knowledge.
% --- p. 83 ---
% print: „Udfoldelse“, no point before „Men“ (p. 83) (misprint)
\opage{83}

It is especially characteristic of Cusanus that he slides easily from mystical
inquiry into the divine processes over to the processes of nature, and can use
the same points of view in both places. That the two processes, the life of the
Deity and the life of nature, nevertheless do not coincide is, to be sure, clear
to him. The relation between them is that between the closed unity (coincidentia,
complicatio, connexus) of the oppositions and their separated appearance in time
and space. Nature is an unfolding (explicatio, evolutio) of what was joined in
complete unity in the Deity, just as the line is the unfolding of the point (by
repeated positing), and just as actuality is the unfolding of possibility. But how
this conversion from the complicative to the explicative form takes place, ---
how the absolute coincidence of the oppositions is replaced by their appearance as
contending powers, --- how the confusion of multiplicity replaces the harmony of
unity, --- that is a riddle which our thought cannot solve. Every finite existence
is a limitation, and the great riddle is precisely how the infinite can limit
itself. In one place Cusanus says that there is no positive cause of
multiplicity, since only the unity in things can derive from God. If you appeal
to omnipotence to explain how multiplicity comes into being, that is the same as
saying that you do not understand it!\textsuperscript{13})

But even if Cusanus ends at this point in dualism, since a gulf remains between
his knowledge of God and his knowledge of nature, he has nevertheless, in the idea
of motion as the connecting principle in nature and as that which makes the world
a whole, and no less in the idea of the development of the world as a progressive
process of complication and explication\textsuperscript{14}), expressed fruitful
points of view which anticipate the thoughts of later philosophers. They made it
possible for him to maintain at once the peculiar character of individual beings
(as distinct complications or contractions) and also the continuous connection
and transition between them. Whereas for antiquity and the Middle Ages alike the
completed actuality was the highest, the significance of possibilities and of
development now began to come into its own. And that again was closely bound up
with the change which the
% --- p. 84 ---
\opage{84}concept of infinity had undergone. In place of the finite, firmly
limited forms, the emphasis was now laid on infinite variation, on the constant
transitions which let the oppositions stand as the extreme cases or stages on a
continuous scale.

In religious respects a difficulty arose for Cusanus from his denial, on
principle, of the right to apply any concept whatever to the Deity. To be
consistent he would then have had to declare all religious representations
symbolic or mythological; but this step he could not take as a believing
Catholic. In Docta Ignorantia he helps himself by making a certain distinction
among the predicates. Though all predicates must be denied of the Deity, the
negation of the greatest imperfections is nevertheless to be ``truer'' than the
negation of the highest predicates. It is thus to be truer to say that God is not
a stone than that he is not life or spirit; --- and from this it follows in turn
that one may with greater right call God life or spirit than stone. It is clear
that, when \textit{all} oppositions are to coincide or vanish in the Deity as in
the infinite principle, even the greatest difference between predicates that we
can make from our standpoint becomes of altogether vanishing significance. In his
later writings Cusanus therefore also sought more positive determinations and
laid more weight on positive theology in relation to negative, without, however,
succeeding in removing the difficulties which he himself had pointed out.

Within the knowledge of nature the fundamental thoughts of Cusanus find several
very important applications. In canceling the absolute oppositions through the
constant transitions, he is led to discover the relativity in our
representations. The epistemological law of relation has in him one of its first
representatives. Thus he maintains the relativity of the concept of the atom.
\textit{In our thought,} he says, we can always carry the division of things
further; but the \textit{real} division always stops at a part which is in fact
indivisible for us. Such a magnitude, in fact indivisible because of its
smallness, is an atom. This actual stopping is therefore no proof that an
absolute minimum has been reached, any more than the actual stopping in the
summation of magnitudes is proof of
% --- p. 85 ---
\opage{85}an absolute maximum. --- Just as an infinite division is impossible in
reality, because we always stop at a certain point in the process of division, so
an infinite motion is also impossible, because every body, owing to its own
nature and that of its surroundings, will always meet with resistance. A perfectly
round sphere on a perfectly smooth base would continue forever in the motion into
which it had once been brought, if nothing in its state were altered. It would
have to be regarded as an atom, and the force imparted to it could not cease to
act. A sphere that was not perfectly round could not take up the imparted motion
in such a way that it became a natural motion which as such could not cease. This
is one of the most remarkable intimations of the law of inertia that occur before
Galilei. And it springs from Cusanus's great capacity to think every thing in the
definite relations through which it first acquires its full peculiar character.
--- Of still greater interest is his doctrine, arising from the same way of
looking at things, of the relativity of the determination of place and of motion.
The world can have neither center nor circumference, for then it would have to
stand in relation to something outside it by which it was limited, and it would
not be the whole world. Wherever a man may be: on the earth, on the sun or on
another star, he will think himself to be at the center. Now put together these
various possible points of view, and you will see that it is impossible to ascribe
any figure to the world, any more than to ascribe motion to it. Every point in the
world can with equal right be called the center and be said to lie on the
periphery. And since the earth does not stand at the absolute center of the
world, it cannot be at rest. But we do not notice its motion, since we have no
absolutely fixed point to compare it with. It is with us as with one who is on
board a ship that drifts with the current, when he does not know that the water is
flowing and cannot see the shores: how should he discover that the ship is being
moved? --- Cusanus thus moves the earth out of the midpoint of the world, because
on the whole no absolute midpoint can be given, and with the central position
absolute rest must also fall away. On the other hand, he does not teach that the
earth moves round the sun; he cancels the geocentric theory,
% --- p. 86 ---
\opage{86}but does not establish the heliocentric. Those who might think that the
earth thereby loses in dignity he consoles with the thought that perfection does
not depend on size. The inhabitants of the earth are the more perfect the more
they approach the ideal that accords with their nature; but it is not said that
this ideal is the same as that which holds for the inhabitants of other globes.
Man does not strive after another nature, but only to become more perfect in his
own nature. Nor can the perishability on the earth prove its imperfection, for
nothing is absolutely perishable. It is only the peculiar form of existence that
ceases, in being dissolved into its elements. And such processes of dissolution
can take place just as well on other stars as on the earth, since they, no less
than the earth, must be assumed to be subject to external
influences\textsuperscript{15}). By this doctrine a decisive blow was dealt to the
Aristotelian-medieval world-picture. The security which the closedness of this
picture presupposed was broken. Reflection had lifted the world-sphere from its
foundation and set it in a motion that could now no longer stop. At the same time
the sharp opposition between heaven and earth was canceled within the picture;
the possibility that the same laws and relations hold in both regions had been
expressed. An important contribution had thereby been made to the new world-view,
and a contribution that sprang from the innermost core of the profound thinker's
system. If the ancients did not arrive at the doctrine of the relativity of motion,
that was, says Cusanus, because they lacked Docta Ignorantia. They did not see
that all our concepts hold only in certain relations and fall away with these.
Thus the same thought which according to Cusanus makes a knowledge of God
impossible makes it possible to know that the world-picture cannot be so limited
and so at rest as had hitherto been supposed.

\subsection*{11.\quad Bernardino Telesio}

The philosophy of the profound cardinal is the greatest work of thought that the
fifteenth century produced. It prepared the way for a new world-view by
dissolving the rigidity into which
% --- p. 87 ---
\opage{87}concepts had fallen under the dominion of Scholasticism. But not only
from the inner workshop of thought itself, from the world of outer experience too,
important preparatory steps were taken. In the sixteenth century experience began
to become the watchword. People no longer wanted to read in old books, but in the
ever-young book of nature itself. This need expressed itself, as was natural, at
first in an unclear but all the more passionate way. People wanted to stamp out
of the earth the fullness of content which they missed in books. And they had not
critical sense enough to sort out the genuine experiences, nor to keep their own
mystical inspirations or favorite ideas away. As representatives of this titanic
impulse toward experience and knowledge of nature may be named the German
physician and chemist \textsc{Paracelsus} and the Italian physician and
mathematician \textsc{Cardanus}, both restless, storm-tossed men, who besides
ideas of genius in the domain of their special sciences also expressed
philosophical views. They contested the Aristotelian view of nature on several
points, especially the doctrine of the four elements, and they maintained the
unity of the different parts of the universe as regards matters and forces, in
opposition to the Aristotelian-medieval duality of a celestial and a sublunary
world. But although they regard themselves as pioneers, especially as regards
method, their inquiry is nevertheless far from scientific and methodical. They
do not yet know the stricter requirements for the method of the knowledge of
nature which were impressed by Leonardo da Vinci, Galilei and
Baco\textsuperscript{16}). Nor do their thoughts arrange themselves into an
easily surveyable whole, as --- in spite of all methodical defects --- was the
case with \textsc{Bernardino Telesio}, whom we shall therefore consider as the
representative of the philosophy which, supported by experience, precedes the
founding of modern natural science and has yet freed itself from the
Aristotelian-medieval conception.

With Telesio we set foot on the soil of southern Italy, which in antiquity
nurtured so many thinkers, and which was to win this fame again in the period of
the Renaissance. It was the homeland of Telesio, Giordano Bruno and Campanella.
These three thinkers stand in the same line; the tendency of their ideas is the
same, however characteristic the differences they otherwise present. Telesio
influenced the two
% --- p. 88 ---
\opage{88}others. He was born at Cosenza near Naples of a noble family, and used
his fortunate outward circumstances to undertake comprehensive studies. After
studying in Milan he came to Rome, where he suffered ill-treatment when the city
was taken by the Imperial troops under the Constable of Bourbon. Later he went to
Padua, and here the break with Aristotle is said to have taken place in him. The
foundation was thereby laid for a sharp opposition between the northern Italian
and the southern Italian schools. While in Padua and Bologna people went on
cultivating Aristotle and more or less blindly swearing by his word, in southern
Italy they struck out in new directions and opened new paths, seeking at the same
time to build as far as possible on the awakening natural science. After a stay
in Rome with Pope Paul IV, who valued him highly and even wanted to make him an
archbishop, Telesio returned to southern Italy. He lectured in Naples and founded
an academy in Cosenza. In the year 1565 the first part of his chief work ``On the
Nature of Things'' (de rerum natura) appeared; later (1587) appeared the part that
treats of man in his psychological and his ethical aspect. Telesio died in the
year 1588. In his last years he was the object of sharp attacks from the monks,
who thought that everything fell with the Aristotelian concepts, and a few years
after his death his works were put on the list of forbidden books.

Telesio sets his endeavor in opposition to that of all his predecessors: they, in
their great self-confidence, wanted to fathom nature with their reason, just as
if they were God's equals in wisdom; he himself has greater humility and wants to
reach only a human wisdom, limited to what the senses teach and what can be
inferred from the likeness with things sensed. He wants, then, to rely on sensuous
experience, and on that alone. Thereby he thinks he can reach a surer knowledge
than his predecessors. Non ratione, sed sensu! is his motto. But he is convinced
that sense perception will never lead him into contradiction with itself, nor
(as he adds, however, only in a later edition --- perhaps taught by experience)
into conflict with the Church. Aristotle, on the other hand, contradicts
experience, himself and the Church alike!
% --- p. 89 ---
\opage{89}

The most significant feature of Telesio's philosophy of nature is his endeavor to
put the relation between matter and force in place of the relation between matter
and form that runs through Aristotle. It was characteristic of the aesthetic view
of nature of antiquity that it found the explanation of natural phenomena in the
forms in which they appeared; the natural processes were understood through the
fully developed results to which they led. The new view of nature goes further
back and asks about the acting forces. According to Telesio there are two such
forces (principia agentia), an expanding one, which he calls heat, and a
contracting one, which he calls cold. Heat and cold are thus for him not matters
or mere properties, but forces which express themselves in two different kinds of
motion. It would thus not have lain far from Telesio to conceive everything that
goes on in nature as motion. These two forces act on matter, which is never
either increased or diminished, but under their influence takes on the most
various forms, according to the different relation between contraction and
expansion. Besides, it is uniform everywhere, without there being any ground to
make a difference between celestial and terrestrial matter.

Next, he also comes into definite opposition to Aristotle by teaching that space
is something different from matter, whereby the Aristotelian doctrine of the
natural places of the different elements received its death-blow. The different
places in space have no different properties. There can even be an absolutely
empty space; it is pure imagination when Aristotle believes that nature shudders
at the void. Aristotle's doctrine of the elements fell away not only through the
falling away of their ``natural places'', but also through there remaining only
the one and imperishable mass (moles), which takes on different shapes because of
the different relations between expansion and contraction. If different elements
are to be assumed, there ought to be only two: one in which the expanding force
acts, another in which the contracting force acts. The first has its center in
the sun, the second in the earth. Telesio adheres on this point to the
Aristotelian world-picture, except that he conceives the mass as uniform in both
and only the forces as different, and
% --- p. 90 ---
% scan: „enkelte.“ (p. 90)
\opage{90}assumes a livelier interaction between the celestial and the
terrestrial than Aristotle. He also expressly opposes the way in which Aristotle
lets the celestial spheres be guided by special spirits. Not compelled by an alien
principle, and not by craving for something that lies beyond it, but because it
is its own nature, the heaven moves round. And likewise the earth keeps still
because it is its nature, cold and dark as it is. God does not intervene in nature
at particular points; but he has endowed every being with its nature and its way
of acting. And there is harmony between the impulses of self-preservation of the
particular beings, just as in an organism there is harmony between the particular
organs, in that they serve the whole by each acting according to the peculiar
character of its nature. There are therefore no special final causes, but it is a
satisfaction for every cause to follow its own nature, and thereby harmony arises
between the particular beings. In place of an outward adjustment and intervention
on God's part, Telesio assumes that the divine wisdom shows itself precisely in
this, that what happens according to the necessary laws is in itself serviceable
to a purpose. The heaven does not move round for the sake of the earth, but in
accordance with its own nature; and yet its motion benefits the earth.

There is in Telesio an evident endeavor toward a more correct and more fruitful
setting up of concepts than the Aristotelian philosophy of nature offered. But he
gives no methodical, inductive demonstration of the validity and necessity of his
fundamental concepts, and so far denies his own program, according to which he
wanted to build merely on sense perception. Against the fundamental concepts
themselves objections could be made, and were made. A contemporary philosopher,
the Platonist \textsc{Patrizzi}, who on essential points was dependent on Telesio,
directed against him, in an interesting discussion partly with Telesio himself,
partly with one of his disciples\textsuperscript{17}), various telling objections,
and remarked among other things that what Telesio called matter could not be
apprehended by sense perception, which shows us only the particular, changing
qualities, not absolute, passive matter. He asked, moreover, how it was possible
to derive the whole multiplicity of phenomena from the two forces. These
objections both
% --- p. 91 ---
\opage{91}struck home, and the latter was especially confirmed by the highly
arbitrary and naive explanations that Telesio gives of particular natural
phenomena. There was as yet no material for scientific explanations in detail,
and on this point Telesio did not show the same critical spirit as in setting up
the fundamental concepts valid for the whole knowledge of nature. It was arbitrary
too when Telesio called the fundamental forces heat and cold. Among other things
it had the consequence that the origin of heat through motion always had to be
regarded as secondary or as the awakening of a pre-existing heat, while the origin
of motion through heat was to be the original fact, which --- as Patrizzi likewise
showed --- is an arbitrary assertion. When, finally, heat was centralized in the
sun and cold in the earth, this was not, according to Telesio, to exclude that the
earth produced heat under the influence of the sun; but then --- declares
Patrizzi --- the earth must surely also be able to move, since heat produces
motion. Telesio himself did not answer this remark; one of his disciples, on the
other hand, stated that there were indeed now those who thought that the earth
moves, but they had proved nothing but their own acumen. The time when the
Copernican theory could gain decisive influence on the world-view had not yet
come. Telesio's philosophy of nature would have had to be radically altered in
its details to agree with the new astronomy, which let the earth, the ``cold''
body, move, and the sun, the ``warm'' body, stand still! But that does not exclude
that Telesio on important points played into the hands of the new world-view. This
is best seen from the indignation he aroused among the Aristotelians. Throughout
Italy great disputations were held, in which ``the forces'' contended with ``the
forms'', and in which the struggle at times --- as at a disputation in Venice in
the year 1573 between Telesians and Paduan students --- was on the point of being
fought out with bodily weapons. The philosophy of southern Italy and that of
northern Italy here stood face to face. ---

The mental nature stands, according to Telesio, in an intimate relation to the
material, is indeed not really different from it at all. The material forces,
``heat'' and ``cold'', must have the capacity for sensation, for otherwise they
could not
% --- p. 92 ---
\opage{92}subsist, since, in order to be able to gather themselves to resist each
other, each of them must notice the opposite force approaching and feel
satisfaction in its own subsistence and activity. Every material thing has,
besides, a need of contact with other things, for which reason it follows them
when they are removed; this too presupposes sense perception and feeling. Special
sense organs therefore need not be ascribed to things; a sense organ is, after
all, only a path along which an impression is conducted, and which can be
dispensed with in immediate contact. Telesio thus finds, in mythological,
animistic fashion, the necessary presupposition of the interaction of bodies in
their ensoulment. Of more lasting significance is another argument on which he
bases his theory of ensoulment, namely that, if the fundamental forces and the
fundamental matter did not possess sensation, its origin in the beings that
consist of them would be altogether inexplicable, for what one does not have, one
cannot give either. He maintains, then, the impossibility of explaining the origin
of consciousness from matter, if one does not assume consciousness as an original
capacity of matter. But he thereby at the same time bears witness that the
fundamental matter and the two fundamental forces with which he began are by no
means sufficient for the explanation of everything in the world. Here, surely, a
new force is added! And yet --- Telesio would not admit the justice of this
criticism. For just as he ascribes consciousness to matter, so he conceives the
soul as a material being. If the soul were not material, how then could it be
affected by material forces? How should it be able to notice expansion and
contraction if it were not itself expanded or contracted? In pleasure the soul is
expanded, in pain it is contracted. And since this can happen quickly and easily,
it must consist of a very fine matter. This soul-matter (spiritus) has its place
in the cavities of the brain, which is proved partly by the nerves springing from
the brain, not, as Aristotle believed, from the heart, and by the matter of the
nerves resembling that of the brain, not that of the heart, partly by death
setting in when the cavities of the brain are filled with too thick a matter, or
when the brain is injured in some other way, just as unconsciousness in apoplexy,
fainting and sleep can also set in without alterations in the other parts of the
body.
% --- p. 93 ---
% print: „»Aanden»“ (p. 93) (misprint)
\opage{93}Already in Vives and Melanchton we have met with this animal spirit,
which is now the seat of the soul, now, as here in Telesio, the soul itself, a
representation that had been handed down from Greek physicians and philosophers.
--- It is evident, of course, that when Telesio thinks of all matter as endowed
with consciousness, he cannot have so much against thinking of consciousness
itself as something material. Yet it turns out that he makes a distinction
between consciousness itself and what goes on in that ``spirit'' which moves in
nerves and brain. For in pointing out that a uniform motion in the ``spirit'' is
never connected with sense perception, but that an alteration in the motion of the
``spirit'', determined by the action of things, must set in if sense perception is
to become possible, he remarks: Sense perception (sensus) is therefore an
apprehension (perceptio) of the outer impressions and the inner alterations, first
and foremost of the inner alterations, since it is only through them that we know
the outer influences\textsuperscript{18}). When sense perception is thus not
simply one with the alterations of motion in the inner soul-matter, but is the
``apprehension'' of them, the new question arises, of course: how then does this
apprehension become possible? By the inserted ``perceptio'' Telesio has expressed
an involuntary admission that the matter is not so simple after all. He thinks he
has solved the problem by making the soul material; but the goblin moves house
with him and asks how, then, what goes on in the material soul is
\textit{apprehended! ---}

In an interesting way Telesio seeks to show that all knowledge is sense
perception. He denies the difference between sense perception and thinking in
such a way that he makes all thinking into sense perception. Once a motion has
been aroused in the ``spirit'', it can later be called forth again, a habit forming
itself of coming into this motion, or perhaps the motion itself in part
persisting. The knowledge connected with such accustomed or repeated motion is
memory. Now when a thing that has earlier been sensed as a whole later presents
only some of its properties to our immediate apprehension, we can nevertheless, by
virtue of the likeness with what was earlier apprehended, supply what is missing
and intuit the thing as a whole, although it is given only as a
% --- p. 94 ---
\opage{94}fragment. We can represent to ourselves fire with all its properties,
although we perhaps only see it shine and do not notice the heat or the consuming
power. In such an apprehension as a whole of what is given in fragments consists,
according to Telesio, the understanding (intelligere), which he would therefore
rather call a memory or an estimation. Even the highest and most perfect knowledge
contains no more than the capacity to discover the unknown properties and
conditions of things by means of the likeness with a case that is known to us as a
whole. The absolutely unknown cannot be known. There must always be a point of
contact with something given, and thus a point of attachment for sense and for
memory, the latter of which is nothing but prolonged sense perception. To infer is
only to know the missing properties in the manner described. Even pure logic and
mathematics have their origin in sense perception, since this shows us something
similar to what the logical and mathematical fundamental propositions contain.
Sense observation gives me immediate examples of the whole being greater than the
part, and of my not being able at once to affirm and deny the same thing, just as
well as it immediately shows me that snow is both white and cold, and that man is
two-legged. Through all degrees of approximation the simplest sense observations
hang together with the ideal scientific principles. There is therefore no ground
for splitting our cognitive faculty in two. It is in its essence one and rests
throughout on the relation of likeness --- or perhaps on several very compound
relations of likeness --- between the objects apprehended by immediate sense
perception, and therefore it is sense perception throughout.

The presupposition of this whole doctrine is that likeness and difference are
``sensed'' just as well as other properties. ``The spirit'', says Telesio, ``notices
the likeness and difference of the things sensed; what has the same effect it
notices as one, what has different effects it notices as different things.'' The
question is whether these are quite simple acts of sense. There is in any case
this discrepancy between likeness and difference and other properties, that the
former --- more than the latter --- presuppose a process of comparison, so that one
must distinguish within
% --- p. 95 ---
\opage{95}sense perception between a passive and an active side. In the
apprehension of likeness and difference the active side outweighs the passive. It
is then only a terminological question whether one will use the word sense
perception of both sides, or will say (with Cusanus) that in all sense perception
there is a thinking. Yet Telesio himself sometimes came to set the apprehension of
likeness in opposition to sense perception. When Patrizzi reproached him with
despising reason (ratio), he answered: ``I by no means despise reason, that is to
say: the knowledge of things which \textit{not sense perception, but the likeness
between the things apprehended by sense perception} affords us, and I would never
think either that it ought to be despised. But I shall always maintain that one
must believe sense perception more than reason.'' To this Patrizzi in turn answers
very rightly: ``But of this likeness, then, you do not seem to assert that it can
be apprehended by sense perception; by what, then, is it apprehended, if not
precisely by reason?'' --- In the apprehension of likeness, then, something is
added that does not lie in the simplest acts of sense. Telesio's attempt to make
knowledge absolutely alike at all stages has thus not succeeded, but it was in
itself a justified attempt, a counterpart to the attempt made by Cusanus. Both
sketches contain fruitful thoughts in psychological and epistemological respects.
---

Just as all matter does, the soul too seeks to preserve itself. It strives after
many different goods and has many different drives; but when it makes a choice and
subordinates all goods to one single good, it always appears clearly that the
standard in this choice is self-preservation and its conditions. All goods get
their value from their relation to self-preservation, and to the natural activity
by which a being is preserved and maintained an immediate feeling of pleasure is
attached. No being, and therefore not the ``spirit'' either, can strive after any
other end than self-preservation. It appears especially that all knowledge is a
means to it. Wisdom becomes the sum of all virtue, since right knowledge is of so
great importance for being able to find the means of self-assertion. The various
particular virtues are the various capacities that self-assertion has need of.
The individual cannot live securely and comfortably except in
% --- p. 96 ---
\opage{96}interaction with others, and in order that this interaction may become
intimate and fruitful, individuals must be joined as closely as if they made up a
single compound being, so that they work together like the organs in an organism.
In this way the social virtues are motivated, whose sum is humaneness (humanitas),
and whose possibility rests on the need of social life, intimacy and goodwill. But
the highest of all virtues\textsuperscript{19}) is nevertheless magnanimity
(sublimitas), which regulates the impulse toward honor. Man will not be despised;
he cannot bear to be regarded as unfit to do his part, or as impure or as harmful.
He then seeks a support in the judgment of others, since his own power does not
always bear sufficient witness. Magnanimity now holds fast that only that honor
is to be sought which is grounded on the individual's own inner goods, and that
these goods themselves are to be preferred to the honor that may be connected with
them. Honor is for magnanimity not a necessary, an inner good; what matters is to
be worthy of honor; there is a sufficient source of satisfaction in purity and
ability themselves. ---

But all this, both knowledge and self-preservation, concerns, according to
Telesio, only the material soul, the one that develops from the seed (spiritus e
semine eductus). But now there shows itself in man, besides this sensuous
knowledge and natural self-preservation, also a higher need and sense, which
points beyond the present life and its preservation, and which must therefore be
explained by God's having implanted another soul, which as an incorporeal form
joins itself to the naturally developed one when the body is fully formed. Only
thus is it understood that man in his contemplation can forget his sensuous
necessities, and, on the whole, that he is not satisfied with the present life.
How this ``form added from above'' (forma superaddita) is related to the natural
soul, Telesio does not explain more closely. By this doctrine, which is perhaps
due merely to an accommodation to theology, he breaks the integral character of
his philosophy. And he overlooks that already within natural ethics he has
described a state of character that is raised above merely physical
self-preservation. Several psychological intermediate terms are missing for an
understanding of how
% --- p. 97 ---
\opage{97}magnanimity can develop out of the original impulse of
self-preservation. The endeavor ought rather to have been directed to filling up
these gaps than to taking up supplements that do not fit the whole foundation.
---

With all its imperfections Telesio's system nevertheless stands as one of the most
remarkable that the period of the Renaissance produced. Earthbound and sensuous in
its foundation, it nevertheless rises boldly toward the heights. It drew
consequences and indicated ways of looking at things which could be developed with
ample grounding only much later. And yet it also set its own time in strong
motion, and gained considerable influence on thinkers like Bruno, Campanella and
Bacon.

\subsection*{12.\quad The Copernican World-Picture}

The traditional conception of the world had been shaken by Cusanus's criticism of
the doctrine of absolute motion and by the polemic of Paracelsus and Telesio
against the Aristotelian elements and forms. But the ground was first drawn out
from under it by Copernicus's new world-picture. He showed that there was every
reason to regard things in the opposite way from that to which people were
accustomed. That was what Luther, who had himself turned so many things upside
down, complained of: that the Copernicans wanted to stand the world on its head.
No wonder that the new world-picture aroused the greatest enthusiasm in some, by
reason of the infinite horizon it seemed to open, and the greatest indignation in
others, because they seemed to lose the clear and surveyable frame within which
everything that one believed one knew about the world and the forces of the world
had hitherto fitted. A hard struggle began, which cost noble blood and what is
dearer than blood. It was not only a struggle against religious misgivings, but
also a struggle against trust in immediate sense perception. Human knowledge was
to learn that existence in itself can be constituted quite otherwise than it
immediately presents itself to us. It was a lesson in distinguishing between the
subjective apprehension and existence itself which became of great philosophical
significance.
% --- p. 98 ---
% print: „Fordannelse“ (p. 98) (misprint)
\opage{98}Freedom of mind was then especially needed in this matter, the capacity
to disregard what the senses immediately seem to teach and what religious ideas
seem to demand. Among the champions of the new hypothesis the necessity of a
``free mind'' is accordingly constantly emphasized. Copernicus's first disciple,
Joachim Rheticus, says with regard to his master's relation to the old
astronomers: ``Whoever would inquire must have a free mind''; Kepler too regarded
Copernicus's free mind (animus liber) as an essential condition of his work; and
Galilei again used the same expression (ingegno libero) of
Kepler\textsuperscript{20}). It was a process of liberation that was at stake.

The founder of the new conception of the world stood on the ground of humanism.
\textsc{Nicolaus Copernicus} (whose real name is said to have been Coppernick) was
born of a well-to-do family at Thorn on 19 February 1473. Poles and Germans have
contended over his nationality; probably he descends from a German family that had
long lived in Polish lands. He is not known to have spoken or written Polish. At
Cracow, where there was a flourishing university, he studied the humanities,
mathematics and astronomy. Through the influence of his uncle, the Bishop of
Ermland, he was received as a canon or member of the cathedral chapter at
Frauenburg. This brought with it, to be sure, a lower degree of clerical dignity,
but no theological training was required, and only very few of the canons were
able to perform clerical functions. They lived more as noblemen and humanists than
as clerics. It is a wrong picture that has been formed of Copernicus when he has
been imagined as a monk in his cell. For the time being the young canon spent ten
years in Italy, where at Bologna, Rome and Padua he pursued astronomical, medical
and humanistic studies. Of his teacher at Bologna it is related that he is already
supposed to have had his doubts about the correctness of the
Aristotelian-Ptolemaic system. After his return home from Italy he stayed for some
