years with the Bishop of Ermland, partly as physician, partly as courtier. In this
period, between his thirty-third and thirty-sixth years, the main features of his
system took shape in his mind. He says himself that from 1506 he began to write
down the scientific exposition and grounding of his
% --- p. 99 ---
\opage{99}doctrine. After his uncle's death he lived the greater part of his life
in the castle of Frauenburg; an exception is formed by some years in which he
managed some of the chapter's estates. It was thus not only astronomical studies
that occupied him. He was an administrator and a physician, and took part besides
in negotiations on reforms of the coinage, and he had not laid his humanistic
studies wholly aside. In 1509 he published a Latin translation of Theophylact's
Epistles. He was thus active in many directions. He followed, moreover, what went
on in the world. As a physician he belonged, to be sure, to the old school and
took Avicenna as his basis. But he and several of his colleagues stood freely and
sympathetically toward the religious movement. A reform was wished for, and in any
case people wanted the struggle to be fought with spiritual weapons. It seems to
have been the intellectual tendency of Erasmus that prevailed among the canons of
Ermland.

In many years Copernicus let his work rest. He was constantly polishing it, and he
felt great misgivings about publishing it. His ideas nevertheless became known far
and wide, perhaps especially through a little abstract (commentariolus) which he
composed, and which has been found in manuscript in recent years. The decisive push
toward publication came from a young, enthusiastic adherent, \textsc{Joachim
Rheticus,} who was a teacher at the university of Wittenberg. He traveled (1539)
to Frauenburg and stayed for two years with Copernicus in order to study his work.
From his hand the learned world received the first detailed report of the new
system (Narratio prima de libris revolutionum. Printed in Danzig 1539---40). He
also got the master to overcome his misgivings and to permit the printing.

Copernicus's last years were not good. The Catholic reaction began, and the freer,
humanistic spirit that had hitherto prevailed among the canons was now hampered and
persecuted by a new bishop, Johannes Dantiscus, formerly a man of the world and an
erotic poet, now a fanatical churchman. In spite of his earlier friendship with
Copernicus he now seemed to make a special point of vexing him. Copernicus was
compelled to break off his connection with various persons close to him, whom the
bishop regarded as heretical. He lived his last years in
% --- p. 100 ---
\opage{100}spiritual solitude. In the spring of 1543 he was struck by hemorrhage
and paralysis and died on 24 May 1543. On the day of his death he received a copy
of his work, but by then consciousness had already gone.

It does not belong here to bring forward all the astronomical questions that
Copernicus comes to touch upon. What interests the general history of thought are
the presuppositions from which the reformer of astronomy starts, and the great
features in which his new world-picture appears. By its presuppositions his system
bears the spiritual stamp of the time, and by the character of the world-picture it
intervened in the progressive development of the time.

Among the presuppositions there are two which are of special interest.

It was the artificial and intricate character of the old world-picture which led
Copernicus to think about the possibility of conceiving the celestial phenomena in
another way. This whole system of manifoldly connected spheres and epicycles seemed
to him to conflict with the simplicity and purposiveness that nature otherwise
displays. The sagacity of nature (naturæ sagacitas) otherwise reaches its end by
the simplest ways, without circumlocution and with harmonious connection between
the acting elements. It prefers to attach many effects to one cause rather than to
multiply the number of causes. This principle of the simplicity of nature was for
Copernicus and his successors not merely a methodological but a metaphysical
principle. They would have been at a loss had they been asked how, then, they knew
that nature always acts in the simplest way. It was for them an immediate
certainty, a religious faith. They still felt themselves near to the heart of
nature. It became an essential task for the philosophy of the following age to
discuss the justification of such presuppositions. For the time being people boldly
took hold, and it turned out that the presupposition had in this case been happily
chosen. It set the task of finding a point of view from which the order of the world
could be surveyed and the present confusion removed. In particular, by virtue of the
principle of simplicity, it could not but appear absurd that the whole universe
should move
% --- p. 101 ---
\opage{101}round the earth, the great mass round the small. Would it not be simpler
if the great mass rested and only the small ones moved?

With the principle of simplicity was combined the principle which had already led
Cusanus beyond the old system of the world (without, however, leading him to a new
one), the principle of relativity. When a motion takes place in space, then ---
says Copernicus --- sense perception cannot immediately tell us what it is that
moves. It may be the thing sensed that moves. But it may also be that the one who
senses is himself moving. And it may finally be both the thing and the one who
senses that move, with different speeds or in different directions. When we sail,
the shores, after all, seem to move away from us, although in reality it is we, not
they, that move. Let us then suppose that the earth, the place from which we sense
what goes on in the universe, moves, and let us then see whether we do not get a
simpler and more natural conception of the world out of it than when we assume that
it is the objects of sense perception that move!\textsuperscript{21}) ---
Copernicus's whole work is a mathematical demonstration that under this
presupposition the phenomena would look precisely as sense perception shows them
to us.

The new world-picture, then, has the sun as the midpoint of the world and the source
of light. Round it move, fastened to concentric spheres, the planets, in whose
series the earth now takes its place between Venus and Mars. The earth moreover
moves round its own axis. Outermost, the whole universe is enclosed by the fixed
sphere of the fixed stars, which is immovable. Whether the world is finite or
infinite, Copernicus will decide nothing. But so much stands firm for him, that the
diameter of the earth's orbit must be vanishing in relation to the earth's distance
from the sphere of the fixed stars, since no such apparent advance and retreat is
observed in the fixed stars as in the planets, which are nearer to the earth. This
enormous enlargement of the universe, which for Copernicus himself was nevertheless
not a bursting of the old frame, was one of the great stumbling blocks of the new
theory\textsuperscript{22}), and Copernicus felt it himself. He consoles himself
that one must after all rather grant it than assume such a swarm of circles as
% --- p. 102 ---
\opage{102}would be necessary if the earth were assumed to be at the center. And is
it not, after all, more reasonable that what is enclosed should move than that the
all-enclosing frame itself should be in motion? The sphere of the fixed stars is for
Copernicus the absolute place, that in relation to which every place and every motion
is determined (communis universorum locus). The heaven is, besides, the most
venerable thing in the universe; immobility must therefore belong to it. And should
it move, this would have to happen with so violent a speed that there would be far
greater reason to fear that it would break to pieces than to entertain, with
Ptolemy, such a fear for the earth's part, if it were to move. That water and air
are not left behind in the earth's revolution comes from their making up one whole
with the earth itself and therefore sharing in its motion. It is just the same with
the objects on the earth. --- Thus Copernicus seeks briefly to answer the physical
objections that might be made against his theory. Of the cause that makes the
planets move round the sun he says nothing. With the ancients he takes circular
motion to be the natural motion of bodies. A rectilinear motion occurs only when a
part is loosened from its connection with the whole to which it
belongs\textsuperscript{23}). It is then always a sign that something is not as it
ought to be. --- Copernicus's theory has a descriptive character. It is an attempt
to show how the things in the world must look from a definite position. But the
compelling necessity of taking up this position he could not establish. And many
difficulties in detail still remained unexplained.

And yet one of the greatest among his successors praised him precisely for the
courage with which he developed his view without letting himself be stopped by any
difficulty, trusting more to reason than to sense perception. Galilei even finds it
understandable that he did not go more at length into the counter-arguments; he paid
no more heed to them than the lion pays to the barking of dogs. Without such courage
the new view would not have come forward and would not have been tested.
Copernicanism stands in the history of thought as a great example of how
% --- p. 103 ---
\opage{103}necessary it is that ideas and hypotheses be set up which can show
investigation the way. The venture has its right in science too.

Yet Copernicus did not conceive his doctrine as a mere hypothesis. --- He did not
himself see to the publication of his work. It was entrusted to the preacher
Osiander in Nuremberg, who, so that the book should not arouse indignation, put a
preface in front of it, in which the new doctrine was presented as a mere
hypothesis, which one could, purely mathematically, have the pleasure of trying to
take as a basis. The new assumptions, he says, may be just as good as the old, and
no one must expect that astronomy can teach anything that is certain. This preface,
which the reader could not but believe derived from the author himself, no doubt did
much to keep the theory from arousing great attention for the time being. If the
author was not in earnest with it, it was, after all, of no great interest. Luther
mocked at it in his Table Talk, and Melanchton declared in his lectures on physics
(Initia physices) that it was only from a need of something new and of showing one's
acumen that people invented these strange things, but that it was nevertheless not
seemly (honestum) and could set a harmful example when, merely to exercise one's
mind, one engaged in absurd assumptions of this kind, instead of receiving with
reverence the truth that God reveals and resting content with it, especially since
the new doctrine obviously
% scan: „aabenhart“ (p. 103)
conflicts with the statements of the Bible. Melanchton therefore also regarded his
young colleague Rheticus as a restless head. Only comparatively few still joined
the new doctrine in the course of the sixteenth century. Among the most enthusiastic
of these were Giordano Bruno and Kepler, while Galilei still held back for fear of
ridicule, and Tycho Brahe let only the planets, but not the earth itself, move round
the sun. Bruno already protested in strong words against the idea that the timid
preface could derive from Copernicus himself. He intimates that there were those who
contented themselves with reading the preface and then dismissed the matter when
they saw that it was only a question of mathematical speculations. Bruno asserts
that that preface must have been added by ``some ignorant and presumptuous ass'',
who wanted to make the book palatable
% --- p. 104 ---
\opage{104}to the other asses, and he appeals to Copernicus's own foreword, from
which it is seen that the theory was his serious opinion, just as he also, after
all, speaks in the book itself not only as a mathematician but also as a physicist.
And later Kepler, relying on letters from Osiander himself, gave an express proof
that the preface was not genuine\textsuperscript{24}).

Even in Italy, where the ecclesiastical reaction was now in full swing, it was some
while yet before the new world-picture became so well known that it could arouse a
persecution. That it came so far was due perhaps not least to the enthusiastic
thinker who not only took up the new world-picture and wove it into his train of
thought, but at the same time enlarged it and drew the most important consequences
from it with regard to the general world-view, while in return his struggle for the
new ideas led to his ruin.

\subsection*{13.\quad Giordano Bruno}

\subsubsection*{a.\quad Biography and Characterization}

In Bruno we find the ideas of Cusanus, Telesio and Copernicus bound together into a
distinctive whole, the greatest philosophical edifice of thought that the Renaissance erected,
and in several respects of a prophetic character. The scientific world-view of the modern
age was founded in some of its most essential features. On the other
hand, Bruno sacrifices at the altar of his time and shares its superstition and its extravagant fancy,
to which his passionate and impatient mind disposed him. Clear methodical
thinking was not his affair; only the great lines took clear shape and were followed
with an enthusiasm that stood its test. But in particulars he was not clear
about himself or his thought; he did not know how far it had
moved away from the old, to which he still felt himself bound, however much he
could mock and scorn it. He is a figure in whom neither the
intellectual nor the moral physiognomy is drawn purely and clearly. He
himself felt the contradictions and the inner struggles within him. They
% --- p. 105 ---
\opage{105}sprang from his nature, but they were nourished by the circumstances under which he and his
thinking developed.

His fate was decided early. He himself said that when one has buttoned
the first button of one's coat wrongly, none of the others can be buttoned
rightly. This fits the step that Filippo Bruno, who was born at Nola in
southern Italy in the year 1548\textsuperscript{25}), took when, at fifteen years of age, he entered
a monastery in Naples. His family seems to have been noble, and he had received
a good preparatory education; otherwise nothing is known of the years of his childhood,
and in particular not what determined him to become a monk. It was perhaps
in an exalted mood that he took this resolution. Strong oscillations between
boundless enthusiasm and deep dejection, and between mystical rapture and critical
inquiry, belonged to the peculiarities of his character. He took a step
that cannot be undone, and yet his whole following life was an attempt to take
this step back. In the monastery, where he took the name Giordano, it soon
showed how little he could bend his spirit under discipline. He was
repeatedly accused of heresies. First he made himself suspect by
removing all images of saints from his cell and keeping only a crucifix; later, when
he had already been ordained a priest, by defending the Arian doctrine. He declared
later, during the examination before the Inquisition in Venice, that from his eighteenth year on
he had harbored doubts about the dogma of the Trinity. When he noticed that an
accusation was being prepared against him, he fled, to escape imprisonment, to Rome, and when
the accusation followed hard on his heels there, he fled, after laying aside his
monk's habit, from Rome as well. That was at the end of the year 1576. And now began
his restless wandering from place to place, amid passionate intellectual labor and
no less passionate struggle for the new ideas he had arrived at. There is, however,
much that suggests that it was not only the intellectual side of his
nature that rebelled against monastic discipline. He was a strongly sensual nature and
himself declared that not even the snows of the Caucasus could cool his fire. He
had a hard struggle to go through in order to ennoble his drives, so that a ``heroic affect''
could develop out of the ``animal affect,'' and
% --- p. 106 ---
\opage{106}it was not through asceticism that he could strive toward this goal. A
series of poems which he later interprets allegorically (in De gl' heroici furori), but
which were surely love poems originally, bears witness to this. In a comedy whose material
must have been gathered during his stay in his native region, circumstances are depicted and
expressions used whose coarseness is striking, even when one knows that the inhabitants of Nola
were known for their free speech. Though he entered a monastery early, he did
not thereby make himself a stranger to life, which indeed stirred so strongly in
him that it soon drove him out again. Essentially, however, it was
intellectual doubts that led him to a break. --- After his flight from Rome he
wandered about northern Italy for some years. At Noli near Genoa he ran
a school for small boys for a time and at the same time taught some young noblemen astronomy.
Probably he was already at this time an adherent of Copernicus;
he himself dates his acquaintance with him back to his very young years. At first
he could regard the new doctrine as nothing but madness, but soon its truth
and significance dawned on him, especially when he had learned enough mathematics to
follow the grounding in detail. He then felt the need to go further than
his teacher, who, with ancient and medieval astronomy, still held to
the limitation of the world and the immobility of the eighth sphere. For Bruno the universe is
unlimited, since every attempt to posit an absolute limit is unjustified,
and it includes within itself an infinity of worlds like ours, each with
its own center. The Deity works at every point of this infinite universe as
the inner soul that embraces and animates all things. Such were the thoughts that now
developed in Bruno. Besides by Copernicus he is, as already remarked,
strongly influenced by Cusanus and Telesio. How the influence of these thinkers
appears in him will become clear in the exposition of his doctrine in its
particular motivation. Here it need only be stressed that this altered
conception of the world brought him into sharp opposition to the reigning Aristotelian
philosophy, on which the theology of the time also relied, and which stood and fell
with the old world-picture. Since he found no
% --- p. 107 ---
\opage{107}lasting place in northern Italy, though he roamed through it as far as Venice, he crossed
the Alps and came to Geneva (1579). Here he seems to have been counted as a member of the
Reformed Church, although he himself, during the examination before the Inquisition in Venice, denied
having gone over. For his name has been found entered in the register of the university,
even in his own hand, and a condition of this was assent to the
Calvinist confession of faith. Moreover, records have been found which show that he
carried on a violent quarrel with a professor at the academy and with the town's ministers; it
is laid especially to his charge that he called these last ``pedagogues''; he has also
taught heretical doctrine. He is therefore excommunicated and must --- in order that
the excommunication may be lifted --- express repentance for what he has done.
This episode evidently presupposes that Bruno at any rate outwardly
joined the Reformed Church. He then at once got to feel Calvinism's
theocratic rule, and this has surely, together with other
experiences from his stay in Protestant lands, laid the ground for the sharp
judgment he later passes on Protestantism, especially in its Calvinist form.
What was historically to develop out of Calvinism, Bruno did not suspect; he got
to feel only its dark sides, and they caused him to leave Geneva after a few months' stay
and go to southern France. At Toulouse he began to lecture at the
university to great applause and was appointed professor, a
position he held for two years. Here too he lectured on astronomy and on
Aristotelian philosophy. It was his calmest time, although here too he came into
conflict with the learned, probably on account of the new things he had in mind.
It is worth noting, in order to understand Bruno's relation to Catholicism rightly,
that already here in Toulouse he took steps to be readmitted to the
Catholic Church, steps which he later took again in Paris. He thought he could
live in harmony with the Church without returning to the monastery. He hardly
regarded his relation to the Church as broken.
What was essential in Christianity he thought he could unite with his new ideas, and the interpretation of the dogmatic
representations that was the presupposition of this reconciliation he believed the Church
could
% --- p. 108 ---
\opage{108}permit. The repellent impression he had received of Protestantism
nourished the need for union with the Church he had left, even though he thought
that it needed a thorough reform. But he was told --- both in Toulouse
and in Paris --- that the first condition was that he should go back to his
monastery, and to that he could not agree. His wish was to live in
quiet for his studies, without again coming under the monastic rule. --- This
conception of Bruno's relation to Catholicism is supported by his statements during
the examinations before the Inquisition, just as, on the whole, his return to Italy only
becomes intelligible on this presupposition.

When the civil war put a stop to Bruno's university activity in Toulouse, he went to
Paris (1581), and appeared here as an academic teacher with great applause. He
expounded here, besides scholastic subjects, partly the so-called Lullian art,
a kind of schematism of thought with which he was much occupied and which he treated in a whole
series of writings, partly the art of memory, to which he also ascribed great importance.
King Henry III had him summoned in order to obtain information from him about his ideas. By the
king's favor and recommendation he came, when in the year 1583 he had gone over to
England, into the house of the French ambassador. In the writings he published in London
he praises in lofty tones the hospitality and high culture of the ambassador (the Marquis de Castelnau) and his family.
He was less satisfied with the English, who
struck him as barbarians. Even the learned on the whole formed for him
no exception to this. Especially in the first of a series of Italian writings he
published in London, \textit{Cena de le ceneri} (The Ash Wednesday Supper), his
ill will toward the learned and unlearned rabble found vent. The fact was that here in England he
appeared for the first time as a reformer of the world-view and now, in his
own expression, learned what it is to cast pearls before swine. Bruno was now
not only enthusiastic about the new ideas that took shape more and more for him, and
the time for whose proclamation had now come, but he also had a sense of his own
importance, to which he gave vent in a rather bombastic way. It was not only conservative
pedants who could feel irritated by the letter to the vice-chancellor of the
university
% --- p. 109 ---
\opage{109}at Oxford with which he announced his appearance there. He presents himself here as
a teacher of pure and blameless wisdom, as a philosopher famous at the other European academies,
who is a stranger only among barbarians and brutes, an awakener of sleeping
souls, a vanquisher of ignorance, whose gaze is directed only at spiritual culture,
hated by the stupid and the hypocrites, greeted with jubilation by the honest and the earnest, etc.,
etc. Much in this bombast must of course be put down to the taste of the
time. The University of Oxford opened its doors to him, and for some
time he gave lectures there on his psychological and astronomical theories. His
ideas of the unity of mental life under the many different forms under which it
appears in the world simultaneously and successively, and of the infinity of the universe, since
the earth, far from being the absolute center, was only one of the infinitely
many globes in constant motion, none of which whatever has any right to
stand as absolute center --- these ideas might well make the scholastics at Oxford
dizzy and give them offense. The lectures had to be broken off. At a
public disputation in Oxford too, where by his own account he reduced
his opponent, ``the coryphaeus of the university,'' to silence fifteen times, he thought he had received
proofs of the ignorance of the specialists. And the same thing happened at the
disputation he has described in detail in ``Cena de le ceneri.'' Yet he did not give up
the hope of progress for his ideas, but used his stay in the French
ambassador's house to work out a series of writings in Italian and in dialogue
form, in which he has given the fullest and grandest picture of his
views. However restless and however quickly broken off his life was, he
nevertheless attained the greatest happiness a thinker can attain: to have his ideas developed as
fully and clearly as was possible at the stage at which he stood. In spite of all
opposition, his stay in London was therefore a happy time for Bruno. Some
distinguished men such as Phillip Sidney and Fulco Greville showed him friendship; he
came into contact with aristocratic circles and was even received by Queen
Elizabeth, whom he praises in his writings as Amphitrite, the queen of the sea. His
severe judgment of the English he does indeed limit more closely in a later
% --- p. 110 ---
\opage{110}writing. Yet it would surely be too bold to
suppose that even within narrower, more select circles any
real understanding of his views was formed. Of this not the slightest trace can be
shown; of Bruno's stay in England we know anything at all only through
his own accounts. Philosophical interest in England went in a different
direction from Bruno's, both now and in the following time; the time for the understanding of
Bruno came only later. The ideas related to Bruno's which are found in
Shakespeare, especially in Hamlet, are rather to be derived from Montaigne and other
contemporary authors, in so far as they are not due to the great poet's own
thinking\textsuperscript{26}).

It was an astonishing productivity that Bruno developed during his stay in London.
Besides a mnemotechnic writing (with the introductory letter to the
Oxford chancellor mentioned above) he published here five important Italian dialogues which
contain an exposition of his philosophical ideas. In the first, ``The Ash Wednesday Supper,''
the Copernican theory is treated, with the grounding and
the extension Bruno gave it. Then followed ``On the Cause, the Principle and
the One'' \textit{(De la causa, principio et uno),} Bruno's chief work, in which
his speculative ideas and his ideas in the philosophy of religion are developed. It is continued in
the dialogue \textit{On the Infinite Universe and the Worlds,} which sets out more closely
his doctrine of the infinite, divine principle that reveals
itself in an infinity of worlds and beings. After he had in these writings
developed his views from the theoretical side, he gives in
``The Expulsion of the Triumphant Beast'' \textit{(Spaccio de la bestia
trionfante),} to which is joined \textit{the secret doctrine of the Pegasean ass}
and ``On the Heroic Affects'' \textit{(De gl' heroici furori),} his
moral philosophy and his practical view of life. These writings are distinguished in
many passages by profundity and by an exposition full of mood and poetry.
But with these alternate passages where the old scholasticism still sticks its head
out, or where imagination passes over into extravagant fancy, or where there is a struggle with
language to utter the unutterable. Perhaps this last is what is most
characteristic of Bruno. His world-view is essentially motivated by
the new way of seeing which Copernicus
% --- p. 111 ---
\opage{111}put forward. But Bruno sees that the consequence leads much further, and that
in the same moment one removes the earth from its resting place at the center of the universe,
one properly loses the right to posit rest and limit anywhere
in the world. Together with the endeavor to ground the world-view on given
experience there then goes a movement that leads beyond the limits of experience. And as
convinced as Bruno was that the highest reveals itself in nature, so
convinced was he also that any revelation whatever, or series of
revelations, is insufficient to express its fullness and its unity, so
that no oppositions hold for it and no word fits it. No thought,
no number and no measure suffice here, although nature is determined throughout by
thought, number and measure. He is equally convinced of the necessity of the scientific
conception and of its insufficiency. In one of his philosophical poems he says:
``My thought and my sense teach me that no act of thought, no measurement and no
calculation can comprehend a force, a mass and a number that extends beyond
every lower limit, every middle, every upper limit.''

Con senso, con raggion, con mente scerno,

Ch'atto, misura, et conto non comprende

Quel vigor, mole, et numero, che tende

Oltr' ogn' inferior, mezzo et superno.

The ``learned ignorance'' (docta ignorantia) that we know from Nicolaus a Cusa is
Bruno's last word too. But he stands nearer to the world of experience and has a greater
interest in it than the theologian, for whom the inquiry into the nature and
limit of thinking was essentially a ladder to mystical absorption in the thought of the Deity.
Bruno uses the ideas he owes to Cusanus above all for the grounding and development
of the new world-picture. Yet he does not lose himself in the intuition of the external
world. He holds the conviction that the Deity works in the innermost part of the world, and
that this innermost part is found at every point. The external, childish distinctions between
heaven and earth have fallen away, but only (just as later in Böhme) to make
room for the feeling that the highest is everywhere where the sense is open to
it. But
% --- p. 112 ---
\opage{112}then the work begins anew in the domain of the inner life. Here too the
strong oppositions stir, a surge of waves without limits, a craving toward an infinite goal.
Especially in the writing on ``the heroic affects'' this is expressed in a wealth of
poems, allegories, psychological reflections and ethical ideas. Pleasure and pain
are bound together, so that the one cannot be chosen without the other; only through
danger and ruin does the way go to victory; and the danger is not only outer but inner too;
the will must fall in order to be able to rise high enough; in repentance the soul soars
upward like the swan from the marsh. There is for Bruno a tragic relation between
knowledge and truth, and between the will and its goal. But the highest is
for him to feel this disproportion in the constant striving. ``Even if the
goal desired is not reached, and even if the soul is consumed by the strong craving,
it is enough for it that so noble a fire is kindled in it'':

Eh bench' il fin bramato non consegua,

E'n tanto studio l'alma si dilegua.

Basta che sia si nobilmente accesa!

In his own nature and in his own fate Bruno had oppositions in full measure.
Ideal craving and a passionate need of knowledge on the one side, fantastic
self-esteem and sensual ardor on the other: here tasks enough were set,
and here there were reefs enough on which the development of character could founder, even apart
from the external circumstances. And how complicated and changing were these! A
runaway monk who could not find his place in the Protestant lands
where he went about, but passed a far severer judgment on Protestantism than
on the Church under whose ban he lay! A thinker who wanted to overthrow all
inherited systems for the sake of a new one, which his thought constantly strove to
shape, and which could find no understanding among his contemporaries! A southerner who felt
himself in northern Europe as in exile among barbarians! ---

After two years' stay in England Bruno went back with the French ambassador to
Paris, where he made his second vain attempt at a rapprochement with the
Catholic Church. At the university he held a public disputation, at
which he
% --- p. 113 ---
\opage{113}attacked the Aristotelian philosophy and defended the new conception of the world.
The freedom of thought was asserted here in strong and clear words. The invitation piece for
this disputation \textit{(Acrotismus,} probably printed first in Paris 1586,
later in Wittenberg 1588) is one of Bruno's clearest writings. It gives in concise
form the most important ideas that had been developed in the Italian dialogues. He
left Paris soon after the disputation, probably on account of the political
disturbances. Thereafter he wandered about among various German universities. At
Marburg he was refused the right to teach, which led to a violent scene
between him and the rector of the university, who thereupon struck him off the list
of students, on which he had already been entered. Probably it was
as a Catholic that he was excluded; his writings were hardly known. At Wittenberg,
on the other hand, he was allowed to lecture, and here he lived two quiet years. But a new
duke came, and he then had to move on. In his farewell oration he praises German
science, represented by Cusanus, Paracelsus and Copernicus, and glorifies
Luther for his struggle against the power of the Church: like a new Hercules he had fought
Cerberus with the triple crown! ---

Once more the wandering life began. After short stays in Prague and Helmstädt he went
to Frankfurt, where he settled for about a year in order to print a series of
writings which, partly in the form of didactic poems, were to give a systematic
exposition of his doctrine. Unlike the London writings, these
writings are composed in Latin, probably because they were meant for the
German learned. This series of works is remarkable, moreover, in that Bruno approaches
an atomistic view of nature (in the writing \textit{De triplici Minimo),} and
that in his exposition of the new world-picture (in the writing \textit{De
Immenso)} he uses Tycho Brahe's investigations of the orbits of comets, which excellently
supported the ideas he had developed earlier. But side by side with this there are found in these
writings several abstruse and symbolizing developments, which are of interest only
in showing what one could resort to at that time for want of
scientific data. On this point as on other points Bruno has a certain
likeness to Kepler, in whom too great scientific
% --- p. 114 ---
\opage{114}ideas and symbolizing speculations were joined in a remarkable way.

Before the printing of these books was finished he had to leave Frankfurt. In
the preface to De triplici Minimo, whose publication he did not manage to see through, the
publishers say that the author was taken from them by a sudden accident (casu
repentino avulsus). Probably he was expelled; documents have been found
which establish that the magistracy of Frankfurt had been unfavorably disposed toward him
from the very time of his arrival. The expression the publishers use does not suggest a
voluntary departure. Yet he had received an invitation to come to
Italy, which he would surely have followed in any case. In a sonnet he has
compared himself to the moth that flutters toward the light. By this he was thinking of
the irresistible but painful need of truth. But a similar
need seems to have stirred in him at the thought of his fatherland. A new
fatherland he had not been able to find during his long wanderings north of
the Alps. But how much danger must not threaten the runaway monk when he
returned? Perhaps the circumstance that the invitation came from Venice
made him feel safe. A young Venetian nobleman, Giovanni Mocenigo, who had
studied one of Bruno's mnemotechnic writings, learned from his bookseller that
the author was staying in Frankfurt. He then invited him to Venice in order to be able to
receive instruction from him. It seems as if he believed that Bruno also
understood secret arts, and that it was really these he wanted to be initiated
into. Bruno accepted the invitation. After his sudden departure from Frankfurt
he stayed for a time in Zürich, where he gave lectures to some young men,
and then he set out on the fateful journey across the Alps (autumn 1591). In
Venice he taught Mocenigo and at last had his lodging in his house. But
his pupil complained, when some time had passed, that he was not learning all that
he wished. And he also came to have scruples of conscience about harboring a heretic.
At the bidding of his confessor he then denounced Bruno to the Inquisition and
shut him up in his house until he was fetched to the prison of the Inquisition
(May 23, 1592).
% --- p. 115 ---
\opage{115}

In the examination Bruno broke down. He protested against several detached and
wanton statements which, on Mocenigo's information, were ascribed to him; he declared
that he had always held fast to the faith of the Church in his innermost being, even if as a
runaway monk he had been prevented from taking part in the Church's divine service, and even
if in his philosophy he taught things that indirectly led to conflict with the dogmas
--- and at last on his knees he begged pardon for all his errors and expressed the wish for
a penance that might open the bosom of the Church to him again. --- In order to understand this
denial of what he himself had so enthusiastically proclaimed, one must
hold fast to the fact that Bruno himself never thought that the bridge between him and the Catholic
Church had been broken. His repeated attempts at reconciliation bear witness to this. And the
repellent impression he had received of Protestantism must also have disposed
him to reconciliation. While still in Venice he had declared to various persons, who
confirmed it to the Inquisition, that he had a writing in hand which he
meant to lay before the Pope, and which he hoped would make it possible for him to live
in Rome, occupied with literary pursuits. He meant also to lay before the Pope the
writings he now acknowledged, and hoped to be able to obtain absolution for what
he had transgressed. He perhaps thought that the symbolic truth he could
ascribe to the ecclesiastical representations in his philosophy might cause it to be
tolerated, especially since, by virtue of ``learned ignorance,'' he granted faith an
independent place outside the domain of science. He therefore begins boldly
to tell the inquisitors his life and to set out his philosophy for them; he
tells them, e.g., that what the Church calls the Holy Spirit is for him
the world-soul that holds the universe together, and that while souls ``catholicamente
parlando'' went after death to paradise or purgatory or hell, he taught,
``seguendo le raggion filosofiche,'' that mental life was imperishable and constantly
took on new forms, which he found expressed in the old doctrine of the transmigration of souls.
He does not properly appeal, like Pomponazzi, to the claim that something can be true in
theology which is not true in philosophy. He assumed not a double truth
but a double form of truth. The relation between his philosophy and the doctrine of the Church
% --- p. 116 ---
\opage{116}stood for him roughly as the relation between the Copernican theory and
sensuous intuition. Yet it must be granted that he did not come to full clarity
with himself. All the easier is it to understand that he --- the man of moods who
swung between exaltation and dejection --- could break down, and that,
in order to save the prospect of a quiet literary life such as he had imagined for himself after the restless
years as a wandering scholastic, he --- just like Galilei later
--- made the confession that was wanted, instead of setting his understanding
of Christianity against the ecclesiastical-dogmatic one.

Perhaps he would have escaped with this, and then he would not have come to stand in
history as the heroic figure we now know. But the Roman Inquisition
had received word of his case and demanded his extradition, partly because he
was guilty of such grave heresies, partly because by flight he had evaded
earlier accusations in Rome and Naples. After some hesitation the
Venetian government handed him over, and a new trial now began in Rome. Of the records of
this trial only a few fragments are known, and the rest is said, without its being known
how, to have disappeared from the papal archive\textsuperscript{27}). One does
not know, therefore, how it came about that Bruno sat over six years in prison in Rome.
It is only seen that the Roman inquisitors, among whom the later Cardinal
Bellarmine especially distinguished himself, showed more zeal than the Venetian ones. Bruno's books
were gone through and a list drawn up of eight grave heresies, whose
retraction was demanded. Probably, among other things, the assumption that there are infinitely
many worlds was laid to his charge\textsuperscript{28}). It was heretical
because it seemed to conflict with revelation, which cannot have taken place
more than once. For the same reason the assumption of
antipodes had been found heretical in the Middle Ages. Yet it is seen from the remains of the examinations that are known that the Pope
wished to restrict the retraction to be demanded of Bruno to
such propositions as the Church had condemned from of old; the propositions
directly connected with Copernicanism were then to be left
aside. But Bruno stood firm against this precise demand. He denied that
he had made
% --- p. 117 ---
\opage{117}himself guilty of any heresy; it was the inquisitors who had interpreted his
opinions in a heretical sense; he had nothing to retract. This attitude of his
confirms the conception set out above of his relation to
Catholicism. With death before his eyes he held fast to his conception of
Christianity as against the Church's, and he was no more willing to
abjure his religious than his philosophical views. He composed a
defense which he wished laid before the Pope; it was opened, but not read.
On February 9, 1600, the sentence was pronounced to Bruno. He was degraded,
excommunicated and handed over to the secular power, the governor of Rome, with the
usual hypocritical request that he might be punished mildly and without
the shedding of blood. To this Bruno answered with a threatening look: ``You who pass sentence
on me perhaps feel greater fear than I on whom it is passed!'' He meant,
no doubt, that they felt fear of the truth, while he himself had now overcome
the fear of what there may be to suffer in the service of truth. Now he saw
clearly what he had not seen in Venice: that it was the free search for truth itself
that had to be asserted. Now he did not waver. On February 17, 1600, he was burned
on the Campo di fiore and suffered death with steadfastness. He turned away a priest who
wanted to hold out a crucifix to him, and died without any outcry. His ashes were scattered to
the wind. --- But on the spot where he was burned his statue was erected in the year 1889
by contributions from the whole civilized world, and the
Italian state is now defraying the cost of a splendid edition of his works. ---

Having come to know the life and personality of this greatest philosopher of the Renaissance,
we now pass on to set out his philosophy in detail.

\subsubsection*{b.\quad The Grounding and Extension of the New World-Picture}

Giordano Bruno is one of the first thinkers to have a clear consciousness that
great thoughts are owed to a long, successive series of experiences. He thinks he has
uttered great thoughts, but he is also conscious of what he owes to his
predecessors, especially the great astronomers on whose observations he builds.
% --- p. 118 ---
\opage{118}While in the Renaissance men were still inclined to look back to antiquity
as the source of truths, just as the Church looked back to the time when
the revelations took place, Bruno maintains that it is those now living who are older than
``the ancients,'' since they have more experiences to build on than these. Eudoxus did not know
as much as Hipparchus, and he not as much as Copernicus. And
Copernicus he praises not only as the one who continued the work of his predecessors,
but above all as the one who had loftiness (magnanimita) and strength enough of mind to
raise himself above the prejudices of the multitude and the illusions of the senses and set forth a new
world-picture. In the Latin didactic poem ``on the immeasurable and the innumerable
worlds'' he breaks out in a hymn in honor of Copernicus. But he reproaches
Copernicus with having stopped too early and not drawn all the consequences of his
thought. There was needed, then, an interpreter who could find out all that lay in
Copernicus's discovery, and this dignity he ascribes to himself. He has
opened our eyes to the infinity of the universe, shown that there could be no
absolute limits to it, any more than there could be fixed ``spheres'' that
marked off the different regions of the world from one another --- shown that one law and
one force rule in the whole universe, so that wherever we go we do not get away from
the Deity who rules in it, any more than we need at all to seek it
outside ourselves. --- The task will now be to find the grounds on which Bruno
supports his setting up and carrying further of the Copernican world-picture. They
can be traced back to two main considerations, the one of an
epistemological, the other of a religious-philosophical kind.

The old world-picture, with the earth in the center and with the sphere of the fixed stars as
outermost limit, cannot rightly appeal to the testimony of the senses. If we take
up the different sense-images we receive when we move, we see
that the horizon is constantly shifted when we change our standpoint. So far is it, then,
from sense perception establishing an absolute center of the world and an absolute limit of the world, that
it, rightly interpreted, rather establishes the opposite: namely the possibility of
constantly changing and extending the limit of our world. And with this testimony of sense perception
agrees the capacity of our imagination and our thought
% --- p. 119 ---
\opage{119}constantly to add number to number, magnitude to magnitude, form to form, just as
there also stirs in us a drive and craving that never rests content with
what has been attained. It would be --- Bruno thinks --- unthinkable that our
imagination and our thought should surpass nature, and that to this constant
possibility of new intuition there should not correspond realities in the world. From the subjective
impossibility of setting a limit and positing an absolute center he
then concludes that there is no limit and no center. In this proof he relies,
as he himself says, on the fundamental condition of our knowledge (la conditione del modo
nostro de intendere). It is in good consistency with this consideration --- a
consequence, however, that he only occasionally hints at --- that Bruno remarks in one place
that one cannot properly conceive the universe as a totality when it has
no limit.

Since the horizon always forms itself anew around the place of the beholder as center,
every determination of place must be relative. The universe looks different according
as one thinks of it as beheld from the earth, from the moon, from Venus, from
the sun, etc. One and the same point will, according to the different points from which
it can be seen (respectu diversorum), be center, pole, zenith, nadir.
Determinations such as up and down therefore do not mean, as the old world-picture
presupposes, anything absolute. Only by fixing definite points of view can one
give such expressions a definite meaning. --- And with the relativity of place
follows the relativity of motion. Motion is apprehended only in relation to a fixed
point, and it then depends on where one thinks of this fixed point. One and
the same motion will look different seen from the earth and from the sun, and wherever
I then imagine myself to be, my standpoint will always appear to me as motionless.
The distinction between what is at rest and what is in
motion can therefore not attain absolute certainty. The old world-picture presupposes as given what
was precisely to be proved: that the earth is the fixed point by which every
motion is to be measured. --- With the relativity of motion follows the relativity of
time. For an absolutely regular motion cannot be demonstrated, and we have
no sign that can establish that all the stars
% --- p. 120 ---
\opage{120}have taken exactly the same position in relation to the earth that they had
before, and that their motions are absolutely regular. An absolute measure of time
we therefore cannot obtain. Since motion looks different from the
different stars, there will, when it is to serve as the measure of time, be just
as many times in the universe as there are stars.

No more than the determinations of place can the concepts of heaviness and lightness have
absolute meaning. Heaviness was indeed for Aristotle a tendency to seek toward
the center of the world, and since earth is the heaviest element, the earth had to be at
the center of the world! But the properties heavy and light belong to the parts of each single globe
in relation to the whole globe. When what is heavy falls, it is because it
seeks back to the place where it belongs, and where it can best
abide. The particles of the sun are heavy in relation to it, just as the earth's
particles are in relation to it. In relation to the universe as a whole the
concepts of heaviness and lightness hold just as little as determinations of time and place and
motions. They acquire meaning only in relation to a particular globe or a
particular system. --- It is the same theory of gravity we have already met
in Copernicus, only that Bruno lays the main weight on the parts' seeking back to
their whole from the impulse of self-preservation. Copernicus also relied on
the relativity in our determinations; but he stopped halfway. Bruno's
merit is to have carried this principle through and shown what consequences
it leads to. In Bruno we also find for the first time a decisive answer to
one of the most important objections to Copernicus, namely that things which fall
down to the earth would not be able to strike it perpendicularly below the place from
which they fall, but must strike it some distance to the west. For Bruno shows that
a stone thrown down from the top of the mast will fall at the foot of the mast,
because from the outset, by impressed force (virtu impressa), it shares in the ship's
motion. If, on the other hand, the stone were thrown down from a point that did not itself belong
to the ship, it would fall some distance further back. Bruno here strikes
the significant line of thought that later led Galilei to the discovery of
the law of inertia.
% --- p. 121 ---
\opage{121}

In close connection with the principle of relativity stands, in Bruno, the principle that
nature is everywhere essentially like itself (indifferenza della natura). From
conditions as they are here with us he concludes to the conditions elsewhere in
the universe. An experience from his childhood years led him onto this path. From
the mountain Cicada near Nola, which lay before him covered with forests and vines, he looked
across toward distant Vesuvius, which seemed to him both small, bare and barren.
But when he had once wandered there, he saw that the two mountains had exchanged
character; now Vesuvius was the large and wooded one, and Cicada the small and naked one.
The
same principle that leads him to ground Copernicanism and to extend
it by asserting the infinity of the universe leads him quite naturally also
to assume essentially the same conditions everywhere, where particular experiences do not
speak against it. He then thinks of the other globes as like the earth, and of the
other systems as like the solar system, so that the fixed stars become suns
surrounded by planets. There is no ground for assuming anything other than that the same
forces work everywhere. It is therefore unjustified when Copernicus, with the
usual conception, lets all the fixed stars be at an equal distance from us,
seated in one and the same sphere. It is perhaps only in appearance that they always
keep the same distance from us and from one another. Distant ships seem to us
motionless, and yet often move with no small speed. Whether this is the
case with the fixed stars, only very long-continued
observations, which have not yet been begun, will certainly be able to show. But that such
observations have not been begun comes precisely from men's having been so
convinced that the fixed stars did not change place in relation to us and to
one another. --- Thus the principle of ``the indifference of nature'' too (or,
as it is called nowadays, the principle of actuality) shows itself, no less than
the principle of relativity, from which it can be derived, fruitful in leading to
new investigations. --- Bruno has a far clearer eye for the fact that theoretical and
subjective considerations need confirmation by way of experience than the
usual expositions credit him with. ``What could we think if the
many observations were not before us?''
% --- p. 122 ---
\opage{122}he asks. He is by no means merely an enthusiastic visionary of the infinite.
By critical intellectual labor he has sought to show on what dogmatic
presuppositions the old world-picture rested, and to establish
the justification and naturalness of adopting other presuppositions. And
the burden of proof here rests, he thinks, rather on the one who asserts the limitation of
the universe, since experience shows that the limit always shifts for us wherever we
go. Why, too, should the universe stop precisely at the eighth sphere, as
even Copernicus thought? Why not assume a ninth and a tenth, and so
forth? Because our sense perception has a limit, one is not entitled to conclude that
the universe too is limited. --- Bruno's great merit is the energy with
which he has thought his way into the new world-view and demanded that it be tested
in detail. Thereby his doctrine became more than an anticipation of genius. The
epistemological foundation on which he builds has its lasting significance.
It is not to be denied for all that, that the passionate consistency with which
he proceeds often makes him speak with greater certainty than he
strictly has a right to. It is no wonder that the momentum with which he comes, and
which is necessary to be able to overcome the resistance, carries him beyond the mark.

By the relativity of the determinations of place Bruno had, as we have seen, overthrown the
old doctrine of the elements, which characterized them by heaviness and lightness as
absolute properties and assigned each of them to its ``natural'' place in the universe.
The distinction between the heavenly and the sublunary world was thereby also
abolished, and with it the prejudice that no changes could take place
in the heavens. But what lay especially close to Bruno's heart was to overthrow the assumption of the
fixed spheres. He shows how this assumption is connected with the assumption
of the earth as absolute center. As soon as one thinks one's way into the idea that each globe
is in a certain sense a center and can move freely in space, just like
the earth, the necessity of assuming the spheres falls away. And why should
the globes need external forces in order to be moved? Each of them has, like every
being in the world, an inner impulse of
% --- p. 123 ---
\opage{123}motion that carries them along; every globe and every little world has a source
of life and motion in itself, and space is the great ethereal medium in which
the all-embracing world-soul works, without any need of particular sphere-spirits
to set the individual regions in motion. A confirmation of his conception
Bruno found in TYCHO BRAHE'S investigation of the comets. The Latin didactic poem ``on
the immeasurable and the innumerable worlds'' he perhaps even worked out in order to
be able to show how these investigations confirm the assumptions he had developed on other
grounds in the Italian dialogue ``on the infinite universe and the
worlds.'' He praises here the Danish inquirer as the first among the
astronomers of the time (Ticho Danus, nobilissimus atque princeps astronomorum nostri
temporis) and as the one who has put an end to the fixed spheres which were to enclose
our world in layers\textsuperscript{29}). The comets indeed went right through the
``spheres'' whose crystal masses were to separate the regions of the world from one another! ---

So much for the considerations in Bruno that can be summed up under the point of view
of an epistemological grounding of the new world-picture. We now pass
on to what might be called the religious-philosophical grounding. This
is drawn from the idea of the infinity of the Deity, which stands firm for
Bruno from the outset, and which he could presumably also presuppose that his readers and opponents
shared with him, even if they did not make clear to themselves what lay in this idea. For
Bruno it stood as a contradiction that to the infinite cause there should not
correspond an infinite effect. If the Deity, which in its original unity
embraces all that unfolds itself in the universe, is infinite, the universe,
which is the unfolded form of God's being, must be so too. No force limits
itself, and the infinite force has nothing that can limit it. If
the Deity is conceived as the principle of the good, must it not then be assumed that it will
impart all that it is able to? Should it be envious or niggardly? The
infinite perfection must manifest itself in infinitely many beings and
worlds. It is not justified to ascribe to the Deity a force or a
possibility that does not become actuality. This
% --- p. 124 ---
\opage{124}opposition between possibility and actuality holds only for finite beings and
may not be transferred to the Deity. We should then get two gods, one possible and one
actual or acting, in opposition to each other, and that would conflict with
God's unity and be blasphemous. --- Of this blasphemy Jacob Böhme, as we have
already seen, was not afraid. His religious-philosophical speculations
recall Bruno's in several respects, just as the new world-view also
plays a part in him. But it was the problem of evil, not the problem of
the connection of the world, that chiefly occupied Böhme. --- Of the religious-philosophical
proof on which Bruno relies he is, moreover, not the first originator.
It had, as he himself mentions, already been put forward by \textsc{Pietro Manzoli} of
Ferrara, who under the name of Palingenius published a Latin didactic poem
\textit{(Zodiacus vitæ,} printed in Lyons 1552), in which the infinity of the universe
is taught (see the poem's 12th book), with a religious motivation similar to Bruno's,
although the world-picture is otherwise conceived in the traditional way with fixed
spheres; outside the eighth sphere Palingenius imagines an incorporeal and
infinite world of light. It does not lessen Bruno's originality that he thus
makes use of earlier thinkers, here Palingenius, as on other points Cusanus,
Copernicus and the old atomists (see LUCRETIUS: \textit{De rerum natura} I, v.
944---1013). Everywhere he brings their thoughts into a larger connection and
carries them through with greater consistency and on a fuller basis of experience than
they had been able to.

For Bruno it was as if he first breathed freely when the limits of the universe had
widened out for him into the infinite, and when the fixed spheres had fallen away.
There was no longer any barrier to the flight of the spirit, no ``thus far and no
further''; and the narrow prison in which the old faith had held the spirits
must now open its doors, and the pure air of a new life could be breathed in by him.
These thoughts he has expressed in some sonnets prefixed to the dialogue on ``the infinite
universe.'' The picture of reality which his thought had labored so
enthusiastically and assiduously to shape acquired for himself a symbolic meaning. The
outer infinity became for him a
% --- p. 125 ---
\opage{125}symbol of the inner. Not all symbolism is built up on such firm ground.

\subsubsection*{c.\quad Fundamental Philosophical Thoughts}

Bruno's great achievement as a thinker is the grounding which, starting from the nature of our sense perception and
thinking, he gives of the new world-picture, and the extension of it which he at the same time shows to be
necessary. But in close connection with this world-view of his stand his general fundamental thoughts, his doctrine
of the ultimate principles of existence. On the basis of a thorough study of Bruno's Latin writings and a comparison
between them and the Italian writings,
\textsc{Felice} \textsc{Tocco} has sought to show that, with regard to Bruno's fundamental philosophical conception,
three stages are to be distinguished. At the first stage he stands close to the Neoplatonists, in that he sees in the
world as well as in human knowledge an emanation of the Deity. This stage is represented above all by the work De
umbris idearum (The Shadows of Ideas). At the second stage he conceives the Deity as the infinite substance which
subsists beneath all the change of phenomena, as the unity of all the oppositions of existence. This stage is
represented by his chief works, the Italian dialogues published in London. At the third stage he conceives that
which lies at the ground of phenomena as an infinity of atoms or monads, without, however, giving up on that account
the thought of the substance that stirs in all things. This stage appears in the Latin didactic poems published in
Frankfurt, especially De minimo. With this conception of Bruno's philosophical development in the last ten years
(1582---1592), during which he was at liberty, I can on the whole agree, especially when sufficient weight is laid on
what Tocco states, that the transitions and differences between these stages were not conscious to Bruno himself. In
particulars I believe that several points must be conceived somewhat differently than the indefatigable Italian Bruno
scholar conceives them.

Bruno began as a Platonist. In an eternal idea, which is one with the essence of the Deity, all things have their
ultimate ground. It is
% --- p. 126 ---
\opage{126}the task of our knowledge to raise itself from the confused multiplicity of the sensible to the unity
which stirs in all things, even though the highest knowledge we can attain is only a shadow of the divine ideas. But
on one, and probably very essential, point Bruno differs from Plato. While Plato by ideas means the general concepts,
what is common to the individual phenomena, the universal, Bruno declares expressly that the concepts by which we
raise ourselves above the confused multiplicity of the senses are not a graded series of general concepts
(universalia logica), but concepts which express the real connection between phenomena, so that instead of an
unformed multiplicity of parts one obtains a firmly connected and formed whole, whereby the individual parts become
more intelligible than as long as they are held each apart, just as we understand the hand only in its connection
with the arm, the foot in its connection with the leg, the eye in its connection with the head. The highest unity,
which is set up as the ideal goal of knowledge, is thus not an abstract idea, but the principle of the real, lawful
connection which alone gives the individual phenomena subsistence and makes them intelligible to us. Bruno here puts
forward a thought which in various forms extends through the whole history of modern philosophy. While ancient
philosophy turns its attention above all to the \textit{idea} or the \textit{form,} modern philosophy turns its
attention above all to the \textit{law.} The lawful connection of existence is the fundamental fact which it seeks
to think through and interpret. Bruno only touches on this thought in the work on ``the Shadows of Ideas.'' He does
not go further into it, because his chief interest is mnemotechnical: he recommends linking the representations
together in memory in the same way as the corresponding phenomena belong together in reality, since this connection
makes both recollection and practical application easier. --- It thus becomes not difficult to understand Bruno's
transition to the conception which he develops in the Italian dialogues in close connection with the consequences of
the new world-picture. What he really seeks, already at his first stage, is the inner principle which lies at the
ground of the real connection between the individual things as well as
% --- p. 127 ---
\opage{127}of these themselves. Inward, not outward or upward, is his watchword from the first.

In the dialogues ``on the Cause, the Principle and Unity'' we find the full development of Bruno's fundamental
thoughts. The constant endeavor is to grasp the universe as a whole moved by inner forces, within which all things
stand in close connection, and which is itself the unfolding of what the infinite principle, which is the highest
thought to which we can attain, contains within itself. When Bruno distinguishes between the cause and the principle,
he means by this that the infinite unity can be seen partly in its opposition to what springs from it, --- and then
Bruno calls it cause, --- partly as that which stirs in the multiplicity of phenomena, --- and then he calls it the
principle or the world-soul. In the former form it is not accessible to our thought, but only an object of faith.
The true philosopher and the believing theologian differ from each other in that the latter seeks the Deity outside
and above nature, the former in nature. As already appears in the discussion of the world-picture, Bruno lays great
weight on the infinite cause having to have an infinite effect. But precisely because the effect is infinite, it
cannot be surveyed, and the knowledge which can be had of the Deity, even when it is regarded as principle (immanent
cause) or world-soul, must therefore always remain imperfect. That knowledge is possible at all rests on this
principle stirring in us just as well as in everything else in the world. The new world-picture proves the
illusoriness of seeking the seat of the Deity outside us, and teaches us that it is to be sought innermost within us,
``in a more inward relation to us than we stand in to ourselves'' (di dentro piu che noi medesmi siamo dentro à noi).
The Deity is the soul of our soul, as it is the soul of the whole of nature.

The world-soul is in Bruno the principle which connects and orders all things in nature; through space, which is not
empty but an infinite ethereal medium, it produces interaction between the individual things. Just as space does not
exclude bodies, but precisely makes the intuitable connection between them possible, so the world-soul, as the bearer
of the world-ideas (
% --- p. 128 ---
% print: „fr.“ (p. 128) (misprint)
\opage{128}mundus intelligibilis. De immenso VIII, 10 cf. De la causa ed. Lag. p. 267)
acts not from outside or as something foreign to things, but precisely as the law of their own being. It is an artist
who from within develops and produces the forms which natural phenomena assume: not a spirit that sets the world in
motion from outside, but the inner principle of motion. It acts in its wholeness at every single place, in every
single part. The universe is not as a whole in its individual parts; but in each of these parts the world-soul stirs
as a whole: Anima tota in toto et qvalibet totius parte!\textsuperscript{30}) There stirs an inner impulse of
motion, a vital force in every thing, a will, which leads things along the ways that make self-preservation possible
for them. It is this inner need that leads the iron to the magnet, --- that lets the drop of water as well as the
whole earth assume the spherical form, which best holds the parts together. This inner principle of motion, in which
the world-soul makes itself known in every single being in the world, stands in Bruno in opposition to the external
moving spirits of the old philosophy of nature, and marks an advance, insofar as it rejects external causes where the
inner ones are sufficient. It prepares for the discovery of the law of inertia, which Bruno hints at in his
astronomical dialogues. But it is at the same time for him, as is already clear from what has been adduced,
% scan: „Anforte“ (p. 128)
a purposive, teleologically acting principle. It leads with inner necessity to preservation and development.
Teleology and mechanics are united in it. The various beings and worlds are moved by the inner principle in such a
way that their subsistence is secured and the systems of the world are not dissolved before their time. Providence
and the acting force in nature (la provida natura) are thus not different, but one and the same. In the Latin
didactic poem De immenso (V, 3) Bruno shows more closely how this unity of teleology and mechanics appears in nature.
Those combinations of the elements which are not purposive quickly perish: male adorta cito pereunt. Through
constant tossing (exagitatio) of the elements there must then at last arise combinations which have subsistence and
viability for a longer time. In this way it can be explained that systems of the world can be formed which subsist
for centuries. While Bruno
% --- p. 129 ---
\opage{129}in this mechanical explanation joins the atomists of antiquity, who --- as is seen from Lucretius's
didactic poem --- had similar ideas, it is nevertheless his firm conviction that a providence is not excluded
thereby: in the tendency which drives toward constantly new, at last victorious attempts, he sees the expression of a
governing will, he traces a mens paterna cuncta moderans. This is characteristic of Bruno's attempt to unite Platonic
idealism with a realist view of nature. At the first stage (in ``the Shadows of Ideas'') it was the connection of
nature in which he found the idea; here he goes a step further and finds the idea in the very struggle to subsist.
--- Yet Bruno's view of nature, through its emphasis on the inner force, retains a poetic character. On some points
he approaches a purely natural-scientific mode of consideration, but his need to find again everywhere the same
motives which he knew from himself prevented him from taking the step fully. He has expressed points of view which
can be of interest also \textit{after} a mechanical natural science has been founded, but which could not themselves
lead to its foundation. Among the points where he approaches the mechanical view of nature belongs especially his
statement that motion in space is the principle of all change. It is the thought on which modern natural science
rests.

Bruno's philosophy acquires a realist stamp through his sharp polemic against Plato and Aristotle, who set the idea
or the form in opposition to matter. Thereby these became fantastic, and matter is degraded to a purely passive and
unfruitful principle. In agreement with the older Greek philosophers of nature (perhaps also influenced by
Paracelsus) Bruno states the doctrine of the conservation of matter. From the seed comes the stalk, from the stalk
the ear, from the ear bread, from bread chyle, from chyle blood, from the blood semen, from the semen an embryo, from
the embryo a man, from the man a corpse, from the corpse earth! There thus takes place a constant metamorphosis of
matter. It subsists beneath the change of the ``forms.'' And the forms which it assumes in the individual cases it
receives not from outside, but from its own womb. Art produces the forms by joining together or dissolving the
matter; nature, on the other hand, produces its forms
% --- p. 130 ---
\opage{130}by unfolding what is present in it as disposition, by explicating what is complicated in the original
principle of nature. Far from being something low and mean, matter is therefore a divine being (cosa divina), the
origin and mother of natural things, indeed is one with nature itself. Bruno says that this consideration of the
significance and originality of matter for a time even led him toward the view that the forms were something merely
external and vanishing in nature. Presumably it was Telesio's philosophy of nature that influenced him then. But he
nevertheless saw that there must be an original principle by which the forms find their explanation. Form and
matter, actual acting and passive receiving, must originally be united in the being that lies at the ground of all
things. The divine activity does not have its matter outside itself, nor does it need to be set going from outside.
Possibility and actuality here coincide, just as matter and form, passivity and activity. Bruno distinguishes between
two kinds of substance, which he calls now form and matter, now spiritual and material substance, and both have
eternal subsistence. The world-soul is both the eternal form, which comprises within itself the individual forms that
arise and vanish, and the infinite spirit, which subsists beneath the change of the finite spirits. All that exists
is ensouled and formed, in different degrees and kinds, at least in disposition (secondo la sustanza), if not in
actual development (secondo l'atto). But both substances are for him in the end nevertheless only one and the same
substance; they spring from one root, are to be traced back to one being. No plurality of substances can be assumed
in the world, but only \textit{una originale et universale sustanza,} which lies at the ground of all the differences
that existence presents. Indeed, he even declares that what produces the differences in things does not belong to
the essence of things, but only to their sensible appearance. In the highest unity, which is the goal of knowledge,
the difference between spirit and matter is thus to be overcome, as well as the difference between form and matter,
acting and suffering, actuality and possibility\textsuperscript{31}). In short, all oppositions and differences in
existence are in the eternal being joined into unity and agreement (unità et convenienza), without any change in the
one
% --- p. 131 ---
% print: „Modsætningrenes“ (p. 131) (misprint)
\opage{131}or the other direction being possible, and without anything being able to set itself in opposition to it,
any more than anything can stand in a relation of likeness to it, since there is nothing other than it. In its
eternal subsistence the difference between hour, day, year and century falls away, and likewise the differences of
the finite beings among themselves, --- between ant and man, between man and star, --- become vanishing in relation
to the infinite being which embraces all things. But for that very reason our thought cannot grasp this infinite
unity and fullness either. Only a \textit{negative} concept of it can we form, in that we strive to keep differences
and oppositions out. All that we comprehend we shape as unity, but the absolute unity surpasses our capacity. --- In
this negative theology Bruno shows himself a disciple of Cusanus, just as in his doctrine of the relativity of
knowledge. He halts (De la causa. ed. Lagarde. p. 268) at the difficulty of how the Deity can be \textit{both}
possibility \textit{and} actuality, when it is to be an absolute unity. Like Cusanus, he endeavors to bring life into
the concept of the Deity by ascribing to it possibility and not merely the actuality concluded once and for all, but
he takes this determination back by the mystical declaration that possibility and actuality are to be one. Thereby,
at the same time, dualism breaks forth in his system; for in the finite world possibility and actuality are
separated, and there then arises a strong opposition between this finite world and the eternal substance, where the
opposition between possibility and actuality does not exist. If the eternal substance, which in its unity
(complicamente et totalmente) comprises the whole content of existence, is perfect, what significance then has the
process of unfolding which advances through the surging of the oppositions and the constant transition from
possibility to actuality? Only when one admits an original imperfection or incompleteness (that which consists in
having the content \textit{only} complicatively, not also explicatively) or --- with Jakob Böhme --- a fall in the
Deity, can the finite development become compatible with the idea of God. It is Böhme's merit to have seen this
clearly. Bruno oscillates, without quite noticing it himself, between mystical contemplation of the unity
% --- p. 132 ---
\opage{132}and enthusiastic devotion to multiplicity. Yet his thought is most occupied with tracing the eternal unity
beneath the constant development and through all oppositions. He refers to a series of confirmations by experience
(verificationi) of his doctrine. The constant conversion of matter into new forms is the expression of the infinite
unity, which cannot be realized exhaustively in any single form. Only by means of a common, underlying principle could
oppositions such as minimum and maximum, dizzying fortune and sudden ruin, birth and death, love and hate, pass over
into each other. Through continuous transitions the highest degree of heat and the highest degree of cold stand in
connection with each other, which indicates that one single principle lies at the ground (a consideration which
Bruno directs against Telesio). On the whole, he who would understand the greatest secrets of nature must attend to
how the oppositions in their minima and maxima pass over into each other. Everywhere in nature the oppositions work
together, and on closer consideration there always appears a common ground to which they each lead back. --- When one
notices the manner in which Bruno thus ``verifies'' his doctrine of the unity of oppositions, this doctrine loses a
good deal of its mystical character. It is the continuity between the oppositions, not their absolute identity, that
he proves. Thereby his doctrine acquires a realist character; it calls for seeking all intermediate links and
intermediate causes and for finding the highest in that which makes their connection and cooperation possible. This
is also the significance of his doctrine of the world-soul, just as it was the same thought that came forward already
in the work De umbris idearum. This whole line of thought puts him in an optimistic mood. All perishing,
dissolution, malformation and suffering do not touch that which has true subsistence. They belong to the sensible
world, where possibility and actuality do not always go together, and where the oppositions come forward in sharp
conflict. They vanish when the gaze is turned to what eternally subsists. But they vanish also when one conceives each
thing in its individual nature, according to the definite manner in which it fills a place in the great connection,
where even the smallest link has its
% --- p. 133 ---
\opage{133}significance: ``All is perfect, because in its own peculiarity (De imm. II, 12: in sua individuitate) it
is a being which is not limited by anything else; this is the inner measure of perfection''. And even what in certain
respects and for some beings is evil is for other beings and in other respects good. For him who turns his gaze to
the whole connection, discord therefore dissolves into harmony. Nature is like a choirmaster who has many voices in
