his choir, but also knows how to make them sound together harmoniously. --- Yet it is only when Bruno's thoughts
dwell in these high regions that he is able to hold fast this harmony. Where he immerses himself in the actual
oppositions of life, he feels them to be so much in conflict that the fundamental mood becomes more complex and
acquires a tragic character, or in any case bears the stamp of resignation. From this side he conceives existence in
his work ``on the heroic affects.''

Those statements of Bruno's in which individual peculiarity is set up as the measure of perfection and the
significance of the small elements for the great results is emphasized are found in the Frankfurt writings, thus in
the last group of works, which, according to \textsc{Felice Tocco}'s demonstration, express Bruno's third standpoint.
Here he moves even further than in the London writings from the Neoplatonic absorption into a supernatural
principle. And whereas in the London writings he emphasized above all the connection and the interaction, here he
emphasizes above all the individual elements between which the interaction takes place. The individual is emphasized
in its peculiarity: there are, he asserts e.g., no two things, two cases, two times which are entirely alike. And
these elements, of which all things in the end consist, are what is properly substantial. What presents itself to
our senses as something continuous consists of small bodies, just as number consists of units. The atom (or minimum
or monas) is that which has no part, and which is itself the first part of a phenomenon. Within every domain we must
go back to these constituent elements, which are what is not dissolved when the whole phenomenon is dissolved. A
composite being cannot be substance. Bruno states definitely that division cannot
% --- p. 134 ---
\opage{134}go on to infinity, and he reproaches not only the physicists but also the mathematicians for assuming such
an infinite division. However, it is not really his meaning to establish absolute atoms. He conceives atoms of
different kinds, and atoms of the one kind can enclose atoms of another kind. It is then clear that the concept of the
atom is with him a relative concept. Of the two members of which his definition of the minimum consists:

Est minimum, cujus pars nulla est, prima qvod est pars, he can really hold fast only the second. The atom is the
first constituent element we need for the explanation of a sensible phenomenon; but there is no reason to lay it down
that it itself has no parts; that we do not take account of them is another matter. Bruno himself accordingly uses
the concept of minimum of great wholes too: thus the sun with its whole planetary system is a minimum in relation to
the universe. Indeed, even the universe is called a monad. And further: the minimum is not merely a part of matter,
but acting force, soul and will. The purpose lies implanted in it --- whereby it becomes possible to hold fast the
unity of teleology and mechanism. Seen from this side too, Bruno distinguishes between atoms (or minima or monads) of
different degrees: the world-soul too, God himself, is called a monad. This determination is necessary: for what is
not one, is not. God is the monad of monads, that is, he is the being in all individual beings. This says the same as
when God in the Italian writings was called the soul in souls. Bruno has thus not given up his fundamental thought
from the earlier stages of one single substance that stirs in all things. Even though he has seen the necessity of
the concept of the atom for an exact view of nature, he nevertheless applies it only to material phenomena, and it
remains an unsolved problem how the individual mental beings are related to the spiritual substance whose individual
forms they are\textsuperscript{32}). From his interest in the old doctrine of the transmigration of souls one might
conclude that he assumed that the individual souls after death passed over into new bodies. But this fantastic notion
he has not seriously embraced. He stopped at the thought that the spiritual substance, just as well as the material,
% --- p. 135 ---
\opage{135}subsists beneath constantly changing forms, but the new forms need not be identical with the earlier ones.
He lays great weight on the need for continuation of life and for constant development; and this need is not
disappointed, he thinks, even if it is an illusion when we believe we know about the form of existence into which we
pass\textsuperscript{33}). ---

Beside many ideas in which the poet gets the upper hand over the thinker, and beside many allegorizing and arbitrary
speculations (especially in the work De monade), which we have not brought forward here because they no longer have
any interest, Bruno's philosophy presents an attempt, remarkable for his time, to unite an ideal fundamental
conception with the scientific world-view. Bruno did not, to be sure, know the exact grounding of this world-view
which Galilei and Kepler first brought; but in several of his thoughts he has approached them.

\subsubsection*{d.\quad Theory of Knowledge}

The endeavor that rules in Bruno is to come to know nature. And for him that is to come to know the Deity. An advance
in the knowledge of nature is for him like a revelation. Hence his enthusiasm over Copernicus and Tycho Brahe and his
zeal to think through the consequences of their discoveries. Thinking, reason, is for him only the means of finding
the essence of nature; it must not put itself and its forms in the place of nature. It is his complaint against Plato
and Aristotle that they have set up logical differences, oppositions of thought and distinctions as if they were real
oppositions in the very essence of nature. It is, as he states several times, the foundation of all ``natural and
divine knowledge'' to distinguish between logical opposition and real unity, so that one does not --- as Aristotle
does, e.g., with his distinction between form and matter --- divide with reason what is undivided according to nature
and truth. Reason is to conform to nature, not nature to reason. In Bruno's view it is in particular quite arbitrary
to think that in nature the oppositions are as sharply separated as in
% --- p. 136 ---
\opage{136}our thinking. In nature itself the oppositions do precisely pass over into each other and thereby show
themselves closely related, whereas in a logical system they are placed as far from each other as possible.

As regards sensuous knowledge too, Bruno inculcates the critical distinction between what belongs only to our
cognitive activity and what belongs to nature. This distinction comes forward especially at his last stage, where the
atomistic turn in his way of looking at things gave particular occasion for it. In the work De minimo, where the
doctrine of atoms is set up, it is taught that the minima (atoms or monads), which are what is properly real, are not
themselves perceived as such. It is thus only through their united action that sense perception arises. To the
differences which our sensations present there need not, therefore, correspond equally great differences between the
physical elements. Yet Bruno will not go so far as to assume only one homogeneous matter (communis materia), because
it would then be difficult to understand how the differences for sense perception could arise. That light, the fluid
and the dry (the atoms) should consist of one and the same matter, he cannot conceive. This is connected with the
fact that his atomism holds only for the ``dry'' or solid matter (materia arida), not for light and for the ethereal
fluid which brings about connection between the small bodies. He does not see that the difficulty of understanding
the origin of the differences of sensation must in any case present itself as regards the ``dry'' matter, to which,
after all, different qualities of sensation correspond. He approaches the principle of the subjectivity of the sense
qualities, but he does not adopt it fully. Only as regards the elements of feeling attached to the sensations does he
teach that they have merely subjective and relative significance. Their validity depends on the perceiving subject,
whose valuation they express. They hold \textit{ex latere potentiarum,} not \textit{ex
latere objectorum.} (De minimo. ed. 1591. p. 59). The same consideration can in part be applied to the moral and
aesthetic concepts; yet Bruno holds fast that there is something good in and for itself (simpliciter), which it is
the business of thinking to find, in that it leaves the limited human standpoint. The good can,
% --- p. 137 ---
\opage{137}he thinks, be determined in such a way that it does not merely express a relation to human nature (ad
speciem humanam contractum). The consequence of Bruno's view of nature would seem, however, to have to be this: that
just as little as any absolute determination of place --- that is, any determination of place without relation --- is
possible in the universe, just as little is moral or aesthetic valuation possible except in relation to a definite
subjective basis. On this point Bruno is not yet a Copernican.

And this is connected with his being unable to give up the presupposition that our knowledge itself does after all
express in itself the innermost nature of existence and is a testimony to it. It is, he says, one and the same ladder
by which nature in its producing descends to the individual things, and by which we in our knowledge ascend to the
universal laws. Nature's producing is an unfolding, an explication; our knowledge is a gathering together, a
complication. The two processes correspond entirely to each other. To understand something is to give it an
abbreviated, simplified expression. All knowledge is a simplifying, because it seeks unity --- and from this, says
Bruno, it is clearly seen that the essence of things consists in unity! --- It is clear that he here himself
transfers his form of thought to existence itself, only that it is not the form of distinction but the form of
unity. This he takes to be more essential than the other. Neither of them, however, can be dispensed with. Here lies a
great problem which was taken up only much later.

The highest object of knowledge marks for Bruno at the same time its limit. The absolute unity is inaccessible to our
discursive and distinguishing thinking. We cannot form any concept that can express it. It is the object of faith.
Only as revealed in nature, as world-soul, is it an object for philosophy. And yet --- the world-soul too, God as the
soul in nature, the being in all beings, is surely to be raised above all oppositions (between form and matter,
actuality and possibility, spirit and matter etc.)! It too must then withdraw from knowledge. --- While Nicolaus a
Cusa, by whom Bruno is here strongly influenced, swings over on this point into positive theology, and ever more the
older he grows,
% --- p. 138 ---
\opage{138}Bruno halts only for a moment to state that ``the deepest and most divine theologians'' have taught that
God is honored and loved more by silence than by speech, and to praise the superiority of negative theology over the
scholastic, --- and thereupon he turns back again to nature. The ladder of knowledge which he builds does not reach
quite to the top, and Bruno himself is also most at home in the middle of the ladder, where the place of those who
strive is.

Positive theology has, according to Bruno, only practical, not theoretical significance. The new astronomical system
for which he fought, and which met with such great opposition from the believers in the Bible, he defended (like
Galilei and Kepler later) by saying ``that the holy books do not treat of proofs and speculations concerning natural
things, as if it were science that was at issue, but on the contrary, for the good of our mind and our heart, would
guide moral action by their commandments''. Therefore, he adds, they had to speak a language which all understand.
With this he meant to stop the mouth of some ``impatient and strict rabbi''. He himself is convinced that the new
philosophy which he teaches will support true religion far more than any other philosophy, by teaching that existence
is infinite like its cause, and that in spite of all change no absolute perishing takes place. This statement (Cena.
p. 169---173) contains the clearest account of Bruno's relation to positive religion that is to be found. In other
places (De l'infin p. 318. De gl' her. fur. p. 619) he expresses himself in a more intellectually aristocratic way,
as when he says that faith is for the crude people who are to be governed, but thinking for the contemplative natures
who know how to rule both themselves and others. It is no wonder that the relation had to present different sides to
him, especially during the violent struggle he had to wage against prejudices that supported themselves on religious
notions. --- Where he occasionally attacks or alludes to Christianity, it is Protestantism rather than Catholicism
that must bear the brunt. And this is surely precisely because he fears that the beneficial practical consequences of
positive religion will be lost through Protestantism (especially through Calvinism), which produces a rebellious
disposition, strife between those closely related, civil war and endless dogmatic polemic.
% --- p. 139 ---
\opage{139}Every pedant, after all, has his catechism, which he is planning to publish, if he has not already
published it, and to which he demands that all others conform. What offends Bruno not least is the Protestants'
praise of faith in opposition to works. It opens the way to barbarism, he thinks. It leads people to appropriate and
consume what their forefathers founded, without increasing it. Hospitals and poorhouses, schools and universities are
owed not to the new but to the old Church, and it is unjustified when these decriers of works appropriate them.
Instead of reforming, they take away precisely the good from religion. These statements (in Spaccio p. 446
f. 466 f.) have evidently arisen from Bruno's experiences in Geneva, France and England. The new shoots of life in
the Protestant spirit he did not catch sight of, and it was probably also difficult, in the midst of the ferment and
under the mutual denunciations of heresy, to catch sight of them. His sympathy is evidently on the side of the old
Church, and one understands that he felt homeless. As freely as his thought moved in infinite cosmic space, so hard did
it find it to settle into the motley human world. He did not see that Protestantism was a Copernicanism in the
spiritual domain: that it would make each individual a center of the world. The fanaticism and pedantry of the
Protestant theologians made him blind to the process of liberation which had here been begun. Admittedly, also only
begun.

In his symbolizing writings (Spaccio and Cabala) Bruno satirizes several dogmatic notions, thus the incarnation and
transubstantiation. It was, after all, precisely this that brought him down, however much he asserted that in his
philosophy he brought out the viewpoints of true religion. It is interesting to see what a definite difference he
makes between the dogmatic notion of Christ and the historical Christ. In ``Spaccio,'' where the constellations are
to be reformed, the centaur Chiron also comes under treatment. Momus, the god of mockery, makes a number of
witticisms on the subject of his double nature, which is nevertheless to constitute one person, but he is ordered to
take his understanding captive like a good boy. Zeus recalls that this Chiron,
% --- p. 140 ---
% scan: „mode“ (p. 140)
\opage{140}while he lived on earth, was the most righteous of men, that he taught men the art of healing and the art
of music and showed them the way upward to the stars. Therefore he is not driven out of heaven, but gets his place at
the altar as its only priest. This trait is illuminating with regard to Bruno's relation to Christianity. That it
meant nothing in the eyes of Cardinal Bellarmine goes without saying.

\subsubsection*{e.\quad Ethical Ideas}

Bruno has not given a coherent ethics, although he says (in the preface to Spaccio) that it is his intention to give a
moral philosophy ``grounded on the inner light''. We meet here again ``the natural light,'' which in the sixteenth
century was brought forward in its independence. This plan Bruno did not come to carry out. On the other hand, he has
given what he calls ``preludes'' in two symbolizing writings: Spaccio (The Expulsion of the Triumphant Beast) and De
gl' heroici furori (On the Heroic Affects).

These two writings, although they came out shortly after each other, stand in a certain mutual opposition. Spaccio is
more optimistic, more directed to human life as a whole, particularly to its social life. The work on the heroic
affects, on the other hand, leads us into the inner struggle and opposition in the single striving individual; the
pain of the constant striving is emphasized, although it is seen precisely as a testimony that one is setting up ideal
demands; it is the striving of the individual, not of society and the species, that is depicted. The latter work is
an ethics for the chosen few, whose inner life goes into the depths and the heights; the former is for all.

In Spaccio the frame is this: Zeus, by whom is meant not the highest Deity but each one of us, insofar as there are
divine forces in him, makes the resolution to reform heaven. He says to the gods: Our scandalous stories are there to
be read in the constellations. Let us now return to justice, that is, to ourselves. Let us reform the inner world,
and then the outer will be reformed too. ---
% --- p. 141 ---
\opage{141}And this reformation is now depicted in the form that the constellations receive new names, the various
virtues taking the place of the more or less ambiguous figures of gods and animals. In discussing which virtues
should be represented in heaven, Bruno has occasion to undertake a ``revaluation of values'' (to use a modern
expression). The account of this is very prolix, but has a number of interesting episodes. There is occasion here
only to dwell on a couple of characteristic traits.

In the first and highest place in the new order truth is set, for it rules over all things, and it determines the
place of each thing; on it all things depend. If one would conceive something that could surpass truth and determine
its validity, then this something would be precisely the real truth! Thus nothing can precede truth. It is desired by
many, but beheld only by few. It is often combated, but nevertheless needs no defense; it grows precisely the more it
is disputed. --- This valuation is evidently connected with Bruno's struggle for the new world-view and with his
conviction that the new ideas would widen the outlook and ennoble the mind.

In Bruno's world-view the necessary connection of the oppositions and their passing over into each other play a great
role. The same law he finds in the domain of mental life, especially in that of feeling. If there were no change, no
pleasure could be felt. Every feeling of pleasure consists in a transition, a motion. And pleasure presupposes pain as
its background. Hence no pleasure without an admixture of sorrow. This kinship of the oppositions is what makes
repentance possible. It gives birth to the need for a higher stage of life than the one on which one has hitherto
stood. It is by virtue of this that Zeus resolves to reform himself and the whole world of the gods. Beneath all
changes only truth subsists, and it is in its light that the reform is to take place. These are, after all, the two
thoughts which Bruno (like Heraclitus in antiquity) constantly holds fast: the oscillation of all things through
oppositions, and the eternity of the world-law beneath all change. From this it is understood how both truth and
repentance receive a
% --- p. 142 ---
\opage{142}place in his ethics. Repentance is to take the place of the swan in the new order. Like the swan it emerges
from rivers and marshes and strives through purification to attain shining purity. It consists in a displeasure at
the present state, sorrow at having found satisfaction in it, and a need to raise oneself from the lower regions up
toward the sun. Although error is its father and injustice its mother, it nevertheless has a divine nature in it; it
is like the rose that is plucked among thorns, or like the bright spark that flies out of the dark flint. ---

Among those who seek a place in heaven under the new order is also freedom from labor (ocio). It praises the happy
childhood of the human race, when it did not need to labor and was free from all cares and from the unrest of
endeavor, and when there was neither misfortune nor vice and sin. But to this praise of the golden age Zeus replies
that man has hand and thought in order to use them, and that it is his task not merely to follow the promptings of
nature, but to produce another nature, a higher order, by the power and freedom of his spirit, without which he cannot
maintain his dignity as the god of the earth. In the golden age, with its freedom from labor, men were no more
virtuous than the animals now are; indeed, they were perhaps even duller than these. Want and need have produced
industry, sharpened thought and led to the discovery of art, and thus, from day to day, under the pressure of
necessities, ever new and wonderful inventions are developed out of the depths of the human spirit. Thereby it moves
away from the animal and approaches the divine. Injustice and wickedness grow at the same time, it is true. But in
the animal state the virtues are lacking as well as the vices; for one must not confuse virtue with the absence of
vice. Self-control is present only where there is resistance to overcome; otherwise animal dullness becomes a virtue.
Chastity is no virtue in a cold and dull nature. In northern Europe it is therefore hardly a virtue; but in France,
still more in Italy, most of all in Libya. --- The result is that freedom from labor can be acknowledged only as the
necessary opposite of labor (ocio --- negocio). Labor and
% --- p. 143 ---
\opage{143}rest ought to form a natural rhythm. For a high-born spirit, freedom from labor will be the greatest burden
when it does not come as relief from strenuous activity. ---

In the work on the heroic affects too, weight is laid on the point that, since existence is composed of great
oppositions, the life of feeling in those who are not animally narrow must be of a complex character, and this is made
a measure of the development of feeling. The stupid man keeps to the present state without thinking of what goes
before and what follows after, of the opposite, which nevertheless lies so near, of the absent, which nevertheless is
always a possibility. His joy can therefore be without care, without fear and without repentance. Ignorance is the
mother of sensuous bliss and of the animal paradise. He that increases his knowledge increases his pain. With growing
knowledge one sees more possibilities, sets oneself a higher goal, --- and it then becomes so much the more difficult
to reach it. The heroic affect arises when one does not let oneself be held back from craving toward a high goal
because pain and danger are bound up with this striving. The butterfly which is attracted by the light does not know
that it is death; the heroic man knows it, and seeks the light nevertheless, because he knows that pain and danger are
evils only for the limited and sensuous consideration, not seen from the standpoint of eternity (ne l'occhio de
l'eternitade). It is even a necessity that with all higher striving a pain must come along, since the goal constantly
rises the further one advances. One steps carefree into the boat to begin the voyage --- and soon one is out on the
infinite sea, which overwhelms sense and thought. The further one reaches, the more one sees that absolute
satisfaction is impossible. One discovers that its object is infinite, and thereby strife and unrest come into the
finite nature. But one then feels satisfaction in the noble fire being kindled, even if pain is bound up with it. It
is a higher form of self-preservation that leads one to continue the ideal striving in spite of the harmony that has
been abolished. What binds the will (vinculum voluntatis) is at every stage a love, but this love can concern
something that lies high beyond the finite existence of the individual.

---
% --- p. 144 ---
\opage{144}This whole line of thought has interest not only through containing an answer to objections that have
often been directed, right up to the most recent time, against the ethics which uses happiness or welfare as its
measure, but also through the opposition in which Bruno here stands both to the ancient and to the medieval
conception. To be placed in the strife of oppositions and to be out on the ocean of infinite striving is for Bruno
the highest. It brings with it a richness and fullness in the inner life which he cannot imagine that any resting
state that could be attained would bring with it. However much the work on the heroic affects reminds one of Plato
and Plotinus, to whom he himself refers, it nevertheless characterizes Bruno precisely as a modern thinker. He is
here a forerunner of Lessing's and Kant's idea of eternal striving as the highest, just as his position toward the
notion of the golden age also recalls the culture-historical conception of a later time. As in his conception of the
world, so also in his ethical ideas he works with a wide horizon --- and with the notion that it can always become
wider.

\subsection*{14.\quad Tommaso Campanella}

Like Bruno, Campanella too was a monk who came into contact with the new thoughts of the time and had a receptive mind
for them. But he already belongs to the reaction. With the Renaissance philosophers he demands that a new science and
a new philosophy must come, because the book of nature is now opened as never before. But he has at the same time
another reason for his demand, namely that the old philosophy is heathen. It was impossible, he thought, to unite the
Aristotelian philosophy with the faith of the Church, although in the Middle Ages, to be sure, this had been held
possible. A new doctrine of nature and a new political theory, a whole new philosophy must be founded, in order that
the Church may subsist, and in order that it shall not, in face of the new peoples in the other parts of the world,
be ashamed to come with a culture which has not been produced within the Church itself. The bold hopes of the
Renaissance thinker are united in Campanella with the believing Catholic's humility toward the Church. He denies that
Bruno was burned on account of his
% --- p. 145 ---
\opage{145}scientific assumptions; in his apology for Galilei he urges the Church to let research grounded on
experience go its free course, since the book of nature, when it is thoroughly studied, will surely agree with Holy
Scripture. But when the Church condemns the new astronomy in Galilei's doctrine, he bows. It is probably also a
satisfaction to him that he now need not give up the view of nature which he had learned from Telesio and stated in
his earlier writings. By his attempt to set up a philosophy other than the scholastic, he nevertheless incurs a
bitter enmity, which was probably a contributing cause of his long imprisonment. There is something tragic in his
figure, in that his struggle against scholasticism is regarded with displeasure by those in power in Church and state,
because they had now learned to fear any change in what had been handed down. All his enthusiasm for the cause of the
Church did not help him. Nor was he able in his inner self to triumph over the forces of the past. There are
significant thoughts working their way forward in him; but they are clothed in scholastic and mystical forms; and when
he had succeeded in bringing them out, they had already been stated by another road, in clearer form and in better
connection with the science of the time, by Descartes.

Campanella was born in Stilo in Calabria in the year 1568. His first name was Giovan, which he exchanged for Tommaso
when, at fourteen years of age, he entered the Dominican order. It was, by his own account, not only religious need,
but perhaps just as much the hope of being better able to pursue his studies in the monastery, that led him to take
this step. By his zeal and his acuteness he soon aroused attention and fear among the monks. He attacked the
Aristotelian philosophy with such good arguments that it was thought he had not come by them in a natural way, and his
inclination to the ``secret sciences'' could strengthen this opinion. Telesio's philosophy of nature aroused his
enthusiasm, and it was a grief to him that he was not allowed to visit the old thinker; only when Telesio lay on his
bier did he get to see him. In essential points he follows the Telesian philosophy, as whose eager defender he came
forward. To escape the enmities he had aroused, he traveled to
% --- p. 146 ---
% print: „udlevet“ (p. 146) (misprint)
\opage{146}Rome and from there to Florence and Padua. He did not succeed in obtaining a chair from which he could
proclaim his ideas. People were wary of the new doctrine. His manuscripts were even stolen from him, --- and he saw
them again only when, on the way home from northern Italy, he had to appear before the Inquisition in Rome. He seems,
however, to have come off fairly lightly from the trial to which he was here subjected. A harder one awaited him in his
homeland. Amid the prevailing ferment of minds and the discontent with the Spanish regime, disturbances broke out in
Calabria. Campanella, who had already drawn attention to himself by his philosophical opposition, could not but become
an object of suspicion through the socialist ideas which he took up early, and no less through the manner in which,
from the signs of nature and of the times, he believed he could predict great upheavals in the year 1600. He was
accused of plans hostile to the state and of heresy, was repeatedly subjected to the most terrible torture and held in
prison for 27 years. The best time of his life passed in this way. The vigorous man's enthusiasm, however, was not
crushed. In prison he wrote poetry and thought, and when he got his underground hole exchanged for a better abode, he
gave himself up to eager studies. His manuscripts were seen into print by friends who visited him. At last, however,
he became free by being handed over to Rome. The Pope protected him and let him flee to France, where he lived his
last years in peace, with a pension from the French government. He died in 1639, two years after Descartes's first
epoch-making work had appeared.

Campanella wants a philosophy which proceeds from experience. That is why he was enthused by Telesio's program and
overlooked the imperfect manner in which this program had been fulfilled. That is also why he took a lively interest
in Tycho Brahe's and Galilei's observations and was, as already touched on, for a time wavering in his view of the
universe. If Galilei is right in his conclusions, he said, we must philosophize in a new way. And since Galilei
constantly relies on observations, one can refute him only with other observations. It lies very close to
Campanella's heart as a Catholic that the Church should not expose itself to ridicule by
% --- p. 147 ---
% scan: „Fgenskaber“ (p. 147)
\opage{147}condemning the new doctrine. Therefore he wrote in prison his \textit{Apologia pro
Galileo,} which one of his friends saw into print in Frankfurt in 1622. But the Church would not (as we shall later
have occasion to discuss more fully) go the way which Campanella so urgently called on it to take: to let the book of
nature and the book of revelation be interpreted each according to its own rules, in the conviction that they would
surely agree in the end, especially when one holds fast that the Bible quite naturally keeps to the sensuous and
popular conception of the world. When the judgment on Galilei then came, Campanella was so eager a Catholic and at the
same time so eager a Telesian that he bowed to
it\textsuperscript{34}). Only, on the strength of Tycho's and Galilei's investigations, he rejected the fixed spheres.
Like Telesio he assumed two world-forces struggling against each other, the expanding (heat) and the contracting
(cold), and the first had its source in the sun (as centrum amoris), the second in the earth (as centrum odii). The
sun, with the other stars as its helpers, moves around the earth.

Campanella's view of nature has, like Telesio's, an animistic character, in that he thinks that the interaction of
things, and especially the mutual attraction of the opposite forces, would be unthinkable if they were not ensouled.
In order to be able to act on each other, they must perceive each other. He repeats Telesio's arguments with closer
elaboration. Of greatest interest is the consideration that sensation cannot arise from the cooperation of the
elements, since the origin of such an entirely new capacity or property would be a creation out of nothing. In
antiquity the answer had been given to this (by Lucretius) that nature after all presents so many examples of the
product having other properties than the producing elements. But Campanella replies that in all such cases it is for
us, too, a production out of nothing, since we do not understand what it is in the elements that contains the
possibility of the new property. That sensation arises from material elements is thus just as much a creation out of
nothing as that the bodily arises from the incorporeal. That in the elements which contains the possibility of the new
property must be essentially akin (ejusdem rationis) to it, without
% --- p. 148 ---
\opage{148}the latter therefore needing to pre-exist in the same way as it appears in the result (eodem modo qvo
nunc). --- Conceived in this way, the idea of the ensoulment of all things has a significance which is entirely
independent of animism, and which comes into its own precisely only when animism gives way to the mechanical
explanation of nature. --- It is, however, only the sensuous or bodily soul that Campanella will in this way bring into
connection with the rest of nature. The higher, spiritual part of the soul he assumes to be created out of nothing,
as Telesio assumed.

Campanella's philosophy of nature develops, like Bruno's, into an entire metaphysics, which in turn is brought into
connection with religious ideas. All that is appears as power (potestas), knowledge (sapientia) and drive (amor). ---
To be is first and foremost to be able, to have the capacity to assert oneself. In its highest, infinite degree and
form power is found in the Deity; it is limited in every finite being, in which the fullness of being is always
restricted in greater or lesser degree by non-being: there is nothing that God is not; with his essence, not by
external influence (essentiando, non exterius agendo), he stirs in all things; --- but there is much that a finite
being is not. The multiplicity of the finite beings shows this relative non-being; they limit each other and to that
extent negate each other. --- What holds of power holds also of knowledge and of drive. Without knowledge power cannot
act. But this knowledge is inherent in power, is one with power. The capacity to perceive what is to be acted against
cannot be separated from the very capacity to act. The instinct of self-preservation in animals shows us this
clearly; but it holds for everything in nature. Therefore knowledge must be original, not first the product of
external influence. The presupposition of all other knowledge is knowledge of oneself. Such an original
self-knowledge is found in every thing, but ``hidden'' (as intellectio abdita), since no opposition and change asserts
itself. Campanella attempts to show how self-knowledge is possible, as against Telesio's proposition that all
knowledge presupposes a change. This proposition, Campanella thinks, holds only for the knowledge acquired through
external experience. In order to know other things, one must be influenced by them and thereby
% --- p. 149 ---
\opage{149}changed. But in order to know oneself one need not be influenced or changed: for what one is here to know,
one \textit{is}, after all, and need not become it. Of itself the individual being has an ``original, hidden thought''
(notio abdita innata), which is one with its nature. When it is objected: why then do we not at once have clarity
about ourselves, but must learn to know our nature from our actions? Campanella answers that this self-knowledge lying
in our nature is constantly hindered or checked by influences from outside. It is necessary for self-preservation to
learn to know other things and thus to be constantly changed. Thereby the original knowledge is obscured: the soul
lapses into self-forgetfulness and ignorance of itself. The lower animals in particular are strangers to themselves
and live as in constant madness owing to the constant influence from outside. But that ``hidden'' self-knowledge is
nevertheless the necessary presupposition for anything being able to be known about other things. That I perceive
heat means that I perceive myself as heated. Every knowledge of other things is a particular determination, a
modification of my consciousness, and presupposes it. Only in the infinite being can the original self-knowledge
unfold freely and clearly, because external influence here falls away. But in the finite beings the doctrine of the
original self-knowledge has the significance that all knowledge is built on our immediate sensation. The skeptics may
be right with regard to all derived knowledge; but this always presupposes a consciousness of our own immediate states
and their modifications, and this consciousness is a reality which cannot be doubted. It goes with our knowing as with
our being able: when I can lift a burden, it is because I can lift my arm; and thus I can know something about other
things only because I can know my own state as determined by these other things. I can be mistaken in the
interpretation of my state, but not in my apprehending it in a definite way. Campanella refers to Augustine, who had
already shown that immediate consciousness does not deceive. ``For me,'' said Augustine, ``it is the most certain of
all things that I am. Even if you deny that I am, and say that I err, you nevertheless thereby precisely admit that I
am; for I
% --- p. 150 ---
\opage{150}cannot be mistaken if I am not.'' --- It is by this doctrine that Campanella reaches the point which in
Descartes became the starting point of the whole of modern philosophy. Campanella's Metaphysics, in which this
doctrine was stated, appeared, it is true, only the year after Descartes's \textit{discours sur la methode,} but it
was certainly for the greater part written already during his time in prison. Moreover, the thought of immediate
consciousness as the foundation of all knowledge is found earlier in several of the thinkers of the Renaissance, in
Cusanus, in Montaigne, in Charron and in Sanchez (the last of whom we have not yet had occasion to discuss). --- But
Campanella goes further back still. His ``hidden'' knowledge is what might now be called potential consciousness; it
is possibility of consciousness rather than actual consciousness, and Campanella also teaches that it is constantly
hindered by external experience. Real self-knowledge is, after all, also won, not by withdrawing from all changes (for
an unchangeable being we could not conceive as conscious), but by noticing how our being unfolds by means of the
changes and through our actions. And this Campanella then also admits when he says that ``the manifold changes veil
our original being and constantly make us into new beings, whereby the comparison with what is past and the unity in
our being, and thus also acquaintance with ourselves, is hindered.'' Here another kind of self-knowledge is hinted at
than that half-mystical one which is to be independent of all change. ---

As power and knowledge stir in all things, so too does drive. This shows itself in every thing seeking to preserve
itself. The stone will continue to be stone, and when it is hurled into the air, it seeks back to the earth, where it
belongs. Plants and animals seek
% scan: „soger“ (p. 150; the e-book's reading, set by sense: scan-artefact rule)
even through propagation a self-preservation that extends beyond the life of the single individual. Indeed, in the
need of light and heat to spread themselves over and into all things, Campanella sees the same eternal drive or
``love'' (amor) at work. And just as power to move oneself is the presupposition of power to move everything else, and
knowledge of oneself the presupposition of knowledge of everything else, so too love
% --- p. 151 ---
% print: „»skjult»“ (p. 151) (misprint)
\opage{151}of oneself is the presupposition of love of everything else. The special forms which love assumes toward
different objects presuppose the ``hidden'' love (amor abditus) with which every being holds fast and asserts its own
being. Happiness for man, as for every being, consists in such self-preservation; if it consisted in something else,
self-annihilation would be the consequence. Virtue is the rule which must be followed in order that the highest
purpose, full self-preservation, can be attained; what the law is for society, virtue is for the individual man. By
three ways the goal can be reached here in the world; by preserving one's own personality, by continuing one's life in
one's children and by leaving behind honor and fame. A fourth way leads to eternal life in God, where man gets a share
in the infinite being from which his own existence has been separated by the admixture of non-being. All morality and
religion Campanella thus sets in close connection with self-preservation. The relation is most intimate in the case of
religion: for the unconscious or ``hidden'' love of oneself, which lies at the ground of all else that we love, is in
turn, in its innermost ground, love of the infinite being which stirs in the limited being of all things, and only by
participation in it can the highest blessedness be reached. Therefore there is an original ``hidden'' religion
(religio abdita) in all, just as well as a ``hidden'' knowledge and drive, and really as one with these. The
individual, positive religions may err, but not that inner, original religion which is their common presupposition. A
revelation is a necessity only because the positive religions (religiones superadditæ) present differences and
errors.

In his individual ethics Campanella quite recalls Telesio. Like the latter, he sets magnanimity (sublimitas) as the
summit of all virtue, in that it expresses the true nobility, the inner self-preservation, which looks down on
external honor and, in its striving to win freedom for itself and others, does not deny itself under the harshest
tortures or the longest imprisonment. In his social ethics he goes through the various societies, from the narrowest,
family and household, through commune and state to the world-empire, a universal human society, whose highest leader
% --- p. 152 ---
\opage{152}is the Pope, and whose senate is formed by the secular princes. Campanella occupied himself eagerly with
politics. Perhaps in his youth he even nourished bold plans for the future of his fatherland and regarded himself as
called to be a religious-political reformer. Great obscurity still rests over the conspiracy in which he was accused
of having taken part. Utterances that occur in his portrayal of the magnanimous man might indicate that he had had
great plans which he \textit{would} not confess. But however that may be, later he looked toward a theocratic
world-dominion with the Pope at its head, spread over the whole earth, so that Spain (as is developed particularly in
the work \textit{On the Spanish Monarchy)} has the task of bringing the peoples of the other parts of the world under
the Church, while the ``most Christian'' King of France (according to the preface to \textit{Universalis philosophia)}
has the charge of subduing the heretics in Europe. Campanella's reactionary position comes forward here in his
politics, as above in his view of nature. He stands above all in sharp opposition to Machiavelli, whom (especially in
\textit{Atheismus triumphatus} 1636) he regards as the representative of the evil principle.

But the remarkable thing is that Campanella here, as in the domain of the view of nature, is extraordinarily strongly
influenced by the thoughts which he wants to, or must, combat. As an appendix to his ethics and politics his ideal
portrayal of the future, ``The City of the Sun'' (\textit{Civitas solis)}, has been published. It came into being in
prison, while the pressure of the present lay heavily upon him. A century earlier the English chancellor Thomas More,
and at about the same time as Campanella, Bacon of Verulam had given such social ideals; the common model for them all
Plato gave in his ``Republic.'' Campanella describes an ordering of society in which science, that is, natural science
and philosophy, rules, and in which material labor has come into its own. There is no priesthood and no nobility.
Those who govern are those who have received the best theoretical and practical education. The inhabitants of the
City of the Sun find ridiculous the thought that the craftsmen should not be just as noble a class as other members of
society. No private property, no separate dwellings
% --- p. 153 ---
% print: „Arbejsudbyttet“ (p. 153) (misprint)
\opage{153}and no private family life are permitted, since thereby egoism would be favored and the burning love of
fatherland which animates the inhabitants of the City of the Sun would be diminished. The authorities regulate sexual
unions according to physiological considerations, so that the state may obtain healthy and well-endowed citizens. It
is, after all, they think, the species and not the individual that is to be preserved through propagation! Pride is
regarded as the worst vice. Each is set to the activity which best suits his abilities, and from the yield of labor
each receives what he needs and deserves. Chance is not to be allowed to rule over breeding, over vocational activity
or over distribution. That would only result in injustice and the distress of many. ``There now live 70,000 people in
the city of Naples; of them hardly ten or fifteen thousand work, and these are worn out and ruined by excessive,
constant and daily labor, while the rest give themselves over to idleness and fall into sloth, avarice, sickliness,
lust and love of pleasure. But in the City of the Sun, where services, arts, labors and occupations are distributed to
all, each individual need work barely four hours a day; the rest of the time he can use to acquire knowledge in a
pleasant way, to discuss, read, tell stories, write, walk or exercise mind and body in an enjoyable fashion.''

This picture of the future, which hovered before Campanella while he sat in his prison ``in chains and yet free,
solitary and yet not alone, silent and yet raising his cry'' --- as it says in one of his sonnets, stands in a certain
opposition both to the philosophical and to the political-religious view which he develops in his other writings. With
the strong emphasis on self-assertion it does not agree that the individual in the ``City of the Sun'' must so entirely
renounce finding his own way to his goal. Among other things Campanella forgets that he has expressly regarded
propagation as a form of the preservation of the \textit{individual}; here it is to be \textit{only} the preservation
of the species that is at stake. Still more remarkable is the opposition between the ``City of the Sun'' and the
theocracy which Campanella in his philosophical and political writings sees as the goal. All hierarchy and all
absolutism has here vanished. There is really no room for positive religion either. The ``
% --- p. 154 ---
\opage{154}hidden'' religion seems here to be enough, and it is even stated that Christianity really only sanctions
what natural thinking leads one to assume, --- a sanction which, in so perfect a social order as that of the City of
the Sun, no longer seems to be necessary. One can, to be sure, as \textsc{Sigwart} remarks in his excellent treatise on
Campanella and his political ideas, find an agreement between the plan of the theocracy and the plan of the
scientifically guided state of the future; but it is nevertheless characteristic that Campanella has worked out his
ideas in this double form, and in such a way that not the theocracy but the socialist state, where the right of labor
and of science stands in the first line, is the final ideal. The powers of his time, the very representatives of the
reaction in state and Church, he thus regarded as means and as educative forces which were to lead forward toward the
ideal goal, which was diametrically opposed to the existing order. Although Campanella is in so much a man of the
reaction, he nevertheless still has the blood of the Renaissance in him, and he looks out beyond the limits of the
given social world with the same enthusiasm as Giordano Bruno beyond the limits of the outer, sensible heaven.

\begin{center}---\end{center}


% --- p. 155 ---
\hhchapter{Second Book}\opage{155}

\begin{center}\textsc{The New Science.}\end{center}

\bigskip

\section*{1.\quad The Task}

Practice precedes theory, and art precedes science --- even if a new practice may
later develop out of the theory, a new art out of the science. Humanism developed, as
we have seen, out of the political and social conditions in the Italian states, and
out of humanism as a tendency in the practical conduct of life there developed in turn
a new doctrine of man. In a corresponding way mechanical natural science developed out
of the industry that flourished in the Italian cities. In order to procure means of
power and splendor, the rulers had to favor handicraft and industry, and the personal
strength and strong self-esteem of the citizens of the cities found expression in eager
and ingenious activity in the domain of industrial labor and industrial inventions.
There was a contest between the cities in this respect. They sought to outdo one
another in professional skill and brooded jealously over new inventions and machines.
The practical application of the forces of nature increased acquaintance with their
mode of operation and was bound to awaken interest in finding their laws. Neither
Leonardo's nor Galilei's appearance is intelligible except in connection with Italian
industry, any more than Pomponazzi and Machiavelli are intelligible except in
connection with the development of the Italian spirit and Italian politics.

To take a single example. Galilei began his famous
\textit{Investigations concerning Two New Sciences} by having the
% --- p. 156 ---
\opage{156}principal character in the dialogue, Salviati, say: ``The inexhaustible activity
in your famous arsenal, gentlemen of Venice, seems to me to offer thinkers a large
field for speculation, especially in the domain of mechanics, since machines and
apparatus are constantly being made there by numerous craftsmen.'' To this Sagredo
replies: ``You are quite right, sir, and since I am by nature eager for knowledge, I
often come here, and the experience at the command of those whom, on account of their
outstanding mastery, we call `the first,' has often opened to me the causal
connection of wonderful phenomena that were formerly held to be inexplicable and
incredible.''

The development of the new world-picture also had a preparatory effect in this
direction. It led to seeking a connection in nature other than the one that sense
perception immediately offered, and was bound to lead to the question by what forces
and laws the system of the world that thought constructed on the basis of observation
was held together and kept in activity. This question the new world-view did not
itself answer, or when it attempted to, it was in a fantastic, poetic, animistic
manner. It was indeed a significant advance that Telesio put the concept of force in
the place of the Aristotelian form. By this it was established
% scan: „siaaet“ (p. 156)
that the explanation could not be sought in the quality of the phenomenon itself, its
completed shape, as with an artist's work, which is understood when one discovers what
model hovered before him. But the concept of force is still too vague and unfruitful
so long as it is not constructed on the basis of insight into the regular connection
between phenomena. If one knows according to what law phenomenon B follows
phenomenon A, then one also knows what force and how much force must be ascribed to
A; for force then means only the conditions that A contains for the occurrence of B.
But to discover this, observation and description are not enough. One must go back to
the simplest relations and investigate by way of experiment the conditions on which
the occurrence of phenomena depends. It is no longer merely a matter of a picture.
The picture must be analyzed into its individual features, and their connection
investigated. Only thereby can full certainty of the
% --- p. 157 ---
\opage{157}picture's validity be won. Several of the investigators who stand as founders
of the new mechanical natural science therefore also worked further on the
development of the new world-picture, just as they in part got the problems for their
mechanical investigation from its relations.

Here too it was a thought of antiquity that was taken up. Archimedes, the founder of
statics and hydrostatics, had already in the third century before Christ expressed
thoughts that contained the germ of a mechanical view of nature. Through the disfavor
of the times this germ did not develop until after the lapse of millennia. Archimedes,
now that his intellectual tendency had found favorable conditions of life, was among
the authors who were eagerly studied, edited and translated in the 16th century. It
was, however, in reality a new science that was to be founded. The philosophical
interest of this event lies in its significance for the life of the spirit, and this
significance is of a many-sided kind. --- In the first place, a new method developed
here, and with it a new use of the human cognitive faculty, which reached deep into
the character and direction of the development of the spirit. New spiritual needs and
habits arose. Experiment and analysis pressed forward ahead of contemplation and
construction, if they did not actually displace them. --- In the second place, it was
especially the material side of existence to which the new method could be applied.
The question then had to arise what scope the results found here had --- whether they
contained a knowledge of the whole of existence, or what their relation was to the
mental side of existence. The revolution that took place through the new world-view
had already led profound thinkers to see that the riddles of the world do not merely,
as the naive conception supposed, lie essentially outside us and beyond us, in the
great cosmic relations, but hide in our own inner self and in the very smallest
natural phenomena accessible to us. Through the new method and its results this
became still more evident. --- Finally, it could not be otherwise than that the more
exact knowledge of nature, and the ability, following upon insight into the laws of
nature, to foresee and in part to control the course of phenomena, must strengthen
human
% --- p. 158 ---
\opage{158}self-esteem and carry further what humanism had begun in a more aesthetic and
theoretical form.

\section*{2.\quad Leonardo da Vinci}

With this great artist we come back again into the Renaissance. He ought to be named
in the history of philosophy because in the scattered thoughts that have been
extracted from his posthumous manuscripts there is found the first clear statement of
the principle and method of exact natural science. Not only in the visual arts but
also in anatomy, engineering and mechanics was this most versatile mind of the
Renaissance at home, and he had the need to give himself an account, in philosophical
ideas, of the path he took in his research, as well as of the impressions he received
of the human life around him. He was born near Florence in the year 1452 and received
instruction in the art of painting from Verocchio, who himself, besides the visual
arts, practiced weaving, metal casting and the goldsmith's art. He was called by
Ludovico Moro to Milan, where he founded an academy of sciences. It has been supposed
that a part of his notes were intended to be communicated here. In Milan Leonardo
worked not only as painter and sculptor but also as engineer, musician and arranger of
court festivities. After Ludovico Moro's fall he worked chiefly in Florence and Rome.
His last years he spent in France, where he died in 1519. His wandering life and
many-sided activity brought it about that he did not come to work out the works on
scientific and philosophical subjects that he had sketched. They would have reached
deep into the development of scientific thinking and hastened it considerably.
Thoughts that one has been accustomed to attribute to Galilei or Bacon are already
found expressed by Leonardo, but lay buried in his manuscripts, which have only in the
most recent times become more closely known. The main thoughts that interest us in
this connection aim partly at emphasizing the significance of experience, partly at
enjoining that without the application of mathematics no full certainty is reached for
the results of our knowledge. Wisdom is the daughter of experience, and therefore it
is also a product of time.
% --- p. 159 ---
\opage{159}He rejects speculations that do not find their confirmation in experience,
which is the common mother of all sciences. But he will not stop at mere observation.
It is his conviction that to every active element (potentia) in nature are attached
effects of a definite kind, which unfold in a definite order. Necessity is the eternal
bond, the eternal rule in nature (freno e regola eterna). It is into this that we must
penetrate, and --- so Leonardo's meaning must presumably be understood --- it is by
virtue of necessity that mathematical knowledge can be applied to experience: it makes
it possible to infer from the given phenomena to others that stand in a relation of
condition to them. In mechanics this shows itself most clearly and simply: mechanics
is ``the paradise of the mathematical sciences.'' --- In the thoughts that thus appear
to us through a combination of Leonardo's aphorisms, the fundamental problems of
modern epistemology are already contained. Through his practical application of them
he became one of the founders of modern mechanics and engineering.

What else is available of Leonardo's ideas bears the stamp of a robust naturalism. He
regards the soul partly as the principle of sensation, memory and thinking, partly
also as the formative principle of the organism. Insofar as we wish to know anything
about the soul beyond this, he refers us to the monks, ``those fathers of the people,
who by inspiration know all secrets.'' He expresses (as Montaigne and Bruno later did)
the idea of the circulation of matter through the organic and inorganic world, and
draws from it a peculiar conclusion, which only after a long lapse of time crops up
again in Diderot: ``In the matter that dies, life continues to exist without its being
noticed; and when that matter is then taken up again into the nutritive organs of
living beings, it awakens once more to sensuous and mental life''. In agreement with
this he finds in man's constant craving and expectation a testimony to what stirs in
nature itself, of which man is the model. His hope of attaining a clear knowledge of
nature is supported by the thought that nature follows the simplest paths, a thought
that on the whole played a great part in the first times of modern research.
% --- p. 160 ---
\opage{160}

Interesting as these hints are, it is nevertheless not they but the idea of the
combination of experience and exact thinking that gives Leonardo a prominent place in
the history of thought. A century was to pass before this idea, through great
investigators who had to discover it by their own path, could be carried further.

\section*{3.\quad Johannes Kepler}

Attention has already been drawn to how the new world-view, in the form of mystical
speculation, stirred at the beginning of the 17th century even in Böhme's quiet
workshop. His contemporary and, on certain points, kindred spirit
\textsc{Johannes Kepler} succeeded in finding a more exact foundation for the new view
than it had hitherto been able to rest on. Through a rare union of apparently
conflicting faculties and interests he was led, by enthusiastic and faithful work,
from lofty, soaring speculations to the founding of an exact science of experience. In
common with Bruno, Kepler has the great need of a wide horizon and of expressing the
thoughts that move his mind. ``I know,'' he says, ``no greater torment than not to be
able to bring out what I feel within me --- let alone to state the opposite of what I
think''. He did indeed come to feel opposition on the part of orthodoxy; this, in
connection with the slight spiritual sense and great superstition of the time, cast
dark shadows into his life. But his love of truth and untiring zeal for work held him
up despite all adversities.

Kepler was born in the year 1571 in Weil in Würtemberg. He is a Swabian, like so many
of Germany's most profound minds. He received his education at the theological
seminary of Tübingen, where humanities, philosophy, mathematics and astronomy were
studied to no small extent. Here he was introduced to the Aristotelian philosophy of
nature, to which he long held fast. In astronomy he had Maestlin as teacher, who
privately doubted the correctness of the Ptolemaic system, although officially he
continued to lecture on it. Theology was laid aside when he
% --- p. 161 ---
\opage{161}reluctantly took up a post as teacher of mathematics at the gymnasium in Graz.
This call became decisive for his --- and for science's --- future. He now formed the
plan of giving a new philosophy of nature that combined Copernicus's system with the
old doctrine of psychical beings as movers of the heavenly bodies. He separates himself
\textit{(Epitome Astronomiæ Copernicanæ.} Op. ed. Frisch. VI,
p. 136 f.) expressly from Bruno by assuming the sphere of the fixed stars as the
boundary of the universe, since he holds that on Bruno's theory the fixed stars must
be so far removed from one another that we could see only far fewer of them than we
actually see. The sphere of the fixed stars encloses a hollow, in whose middle the sun
is found, about which the planets, among them the earth, move. Bruno has here seen
more rightly than Kepler. But in return the latter was able to subject his ideas ---
despite their originally mystical form --- to a more exact verification than Bruno had
been able to. Kepler's first writing \textit{(Mysterium cosmographicum.} 1597)
proceeds from theological and Pythagorean presuppositions. He wants to conceive the
universe as an image of the Trinity: to the Father corresponds the center, to the Son
the surrounding sphere, and to the Spirit the relation between the two, expressed in
the geometrical relations between the different spheres in which the planets move.
The divine spirit reveals itself, namely, in the harmonic proportions of magnitude in
the universe. Kepler seeks to show that in the different spherical surfaces in which
the planets move one can inscribe the five regular solids set up by Pythagoras, that
is, the solids that have nothing but equal faces with equal sides and equal angles.
The fundamental forms of geometry and the distribution of the globes in space are also
supposed to correspond exactly to each other. This is the cosmographic mystery over
which Kepler was enthusiastic, and which he carried with him as a guiding idea that
partly furthered, partly hampered his subsequent investigations. It expressed his
never-failing conviction that definite mathematical relations must be demonstrable in
the universe, and guided
him therefore always to renewed research; but it caused him lasting trouble through
the presupposition, from which he set out with all antiquity
% --- p. 162 ---
\opage{162}and the Middle Ages, that the heavenly bodies moved in circles, since the circle was
the most perfect figure.

Among the men to whom Kepler sent his writing was also Tycho Brahe, whom he greeted as
``the prince among the mathematicians of the century.'' Tycho answered kindly, but
declared that, relying on 35 years of observations, he could not go along with
Kepler's speculations, however much ingenuity he found in them. In particular he
advanced his objections to the Copernican theory. The connection thus begun between
the two men led to Kepler --- when Tycho shortly afterwards moved to Prague --- also
taking up his residence in Prague and later, after Tycho's death, being entrusted with
his great body of material, about which he had earlier written to his teacher
Maestlin: ``My opinion of Tycho is that he possesses riches which he --- like so many
rich men --- does not use in the right way''. Now he had himself inherited these riches
and with them the possibility of a further development and confirmation of his ideas.
It was on the basis of Tycho's observations that he found the laws named after him
and --- what interests us most in this connection --- was at the same time led to set
up the mechanical view of nature in place of the animistic one he had hitherto
embraced.

Kepler lived his later years in Linz, in hard struggle against Protestant and Catholic
fanaticism and in painful efforts to procure means for the publication of his works.
To his native region in Würtemberg he had to return home for about a year to save his
mother, who was accused of witchcraft and threatened with the stake. He died in 1630
in Regensburg, where he had traveled to claim a sum owed to him by the Imperial Diet.
---

Through his idea of the significance of quantitative relations in nature Kepler became
one of the founders of exact natural science. He arrived at this idea partly by a
theological, partly by a psychological, partly by a natural-philosophical path. --- The
theological path we know already. In order that the universe might become the
beautiful image of the essence of the Deity, it was ordered in definite quantitative
relations. Kepler, like Copernicus and Leonardo, had the conviction that nature works
according to simple
% --- p. 163 ---
\opage{163}and clear rules. Simplicity and ordered regularity (simplicitas atque ordinata
regularitas) in a view of nature therefore speak in its favor in his eyes from the
outset. The task is to lead everything back to as few and simple principles as
possible. --- The psychological grounding lies in the fact that the human mind sees
through quantitative relations most clearly; it seems to be quite properly created to
apprehend these. In qualitative respects the activities in nature appear very
different to different subjects (pro habitudine subjecti); full certainty is attained
only by keeping to the quantitative side; this side therefore brings the real truth.
--- Finally, the natural-philosophical grounding lies in matter itself, as we know it
from experience: ``where there is matter, there is geometry'' (ubi materia, ibi
geometria). The world shows itself in fact to partake of quantity (mundus participat
quantitate).

The question \textit{which} quantitative relations, then, lie at the ground of the
universe, Kepler at first (in Mysterium cosmographicum) believed he could answer
purely a priori. From this error he was led away by immersing himself in Tycho Brahe's
material of experience and in his own observations. It is well known how
indefatigably he worked until he had found the relation that agreed entirely with the
observations, and that he was thereby led to put the ellipse in place of the circle,
idolized since antiquity.

In his doctrine of hypothesis Kepler has given a clear account of his conception of
the nature of scientific research. He had occasion in several ways to set up such a
doctrine. Tycho had sharply rejected Copernicus's hypothesis as pure fancy (imaginatio)
and protested against every method that proceeded a priori (or, as it was also said at
that time, ab anteriore). But besides this, both Tycho's and Copernicus's theories were
regarded by opponents (e.g. Ursus of Dithmarschen) as purely arbitrary assumptions that
aimed only at making fools of people. And Osiander, as we know, had in his day, to
avert offense, declared Copernicus's conception of the world to be a hypothesis that
was merely to make the mathematical relations intuitive, but not to be held
% --- p. 164 ---
\opage{164}seriously. In his unfinished \textit{Apologia Tychonis contra Ursum} (cap. 1)
Kepler now discusses the whole question of the significance of hypotheses, and he
comes back to it many years later, in the first book of \textit{Epitome
astronomiæ Copernicanæ.} All science --- he says --- rests on certain presuppositions,
and one does not wait to do research until one has found absolutely first
presuppositions, any more than one waits to build one's house until one has
investigated whether the interior of the earth is solid. Hypothesis means, in the
widest sense of the word, what one assumes as certain in a proof. In this sense
geometry too rests on hypothesis, and the observation on which one builds in natural
science is also a hypothesis. In a narrower sense an astronomical hypothesis is the
sum of representations by whose help an investigator demonstrates the ordering of the
motions of the heavenly bodies. Such representations can by no means be formed
arbitrarily. They are to stand their test by the conclusions drawn from them agreeing
with the actual phenomena and not leading to absurdities in physical respects. And
they can be dispensed with as little as a physician can avoid forming a representation
of the disease instead of stopping at the bare symptoms. Science begins with
observations, builds its hypotheses on them, and next seeks the causes that bring
about the assumed connection. There is in Kepler still some uncertainty concerning the
relation between the first and second members of this threefold division. For when he
regards Tycho as the one who has supplied the observations on which astronomy builds,
and Copernicus as the one who has supplied the best hypothesis, then the hypothesis
has, after all, come before the observations. This can very well be the case, when it
is the hypothesis grounded on a preliminary investigation that guides toward the
understanding of the facts found and toward the search for new facts. So it went with
Kepler himself: it was his Copernican presuppositions and his ideas of the
significance of quantity in the world that gave him an eye for what lay in the riches
that Tycho himself did not rightly value.

As regards the third member, the demonstration of the causes,
% --- p. 165 ---
\opage{165}Kepler gradually made stricter demands than he had made in his first, animistic
period. He began (in Mysterium cosmographicum) by having the planets guided by souls,
or else the whole system by the world-soul in the sun. But later he broke with
animism. In his epoch-making treatise on Mars (\textit{Astronomia}
\textit{nova s. physica coelestis,} tradita commentariis de motibus stellæ Martis. 1609)
he declares that it is physical causes that must be demonstrated. ``True'' causes
\textit{(veræ causæ)} or probable causes now become a frequent demand with him. He
approaches the conviction that the causes assumed for natural phenomena must
themselves be demonstrable as operating in nature. In the second edition of his
animistic youthful writing he adds to the expression ``moving souls'' (animæ
motrices) the following note: ``In my treatise on Mars I have shown that there are no
such things,'' and remarks that in place of the word soul one ought to put the word
force. ``Formerly,'' he continues, ``I believed that the force that moves the planets
was really a soul . . . . But when I considered that this moving force decreases with
distance, . . . . I concluded that it must be something corporeal.'' (Opera I.
p. 176). --- In place of the Mysterium cosmographicum there now came for Kepler the idea
of a Physica coelestis, which he still lacked the means, however, to carry through. It
was carried a mighty step further by Kepler's great contemporary

\section*{4.\quad Galileo Galilei}

When Galilei, in a letter some years after Kepler's death, says that ``he has always
esteemed Kepler as a free (perhaps all too free) and acute mind, but that his own way
of doing research is different from Kepler's,'' he is no doubt thinking in this
characterization essentially of Kepler's earlier, animistic theories. He has hardly
had clearly before him the turning point that came for Kepler through the
investigation that led to the famous laws. The two great investigators work in reality
in the same spirit: they seek to combine deduction and induction, mathematics and
experience, and they thereby stand as founders of the exact
% --- p. 166 ---
\opage{166}science of experience. Only that Kepler begins more from the a priori, deductive
side, Galilei more from the experimental, inductive side. In Galilei the really
decisive step is taken by which natural science was constituted as an independent
science and a great ideal for all research was set up.

Galilei, like Bruno, became a martyr for the new world-view. There is in him an
interesting interaction between his astronomical and his physical investigations. His
experiments and his study of Archimedes led him to find difficulties in the
Aristotelian-Ptolemaic system, and conversely he was led by his zeal to ground the new
world-picture to find new physical laws. Only slowly and hesitantly did he come forward
as a declared Copernican. He was born in Pisa in 1564 and studied philosophy, physics
and mathematics there, just as he was also an enthusiastic cultivator of poetic
literature. He preferred Plato and Archimedes to Aristotle, and thereby the foundation
of his later views was already laid in his student years. As professor, first in Pisa,
later in Padua, he lectured on the old system after he had long been convinced in his
heart of the truth of the new. He writes in a letter to Kepler (in August 1597): ``It
is a misfortune that those who seek after truth, and who do not follow a wrong method,
are so rare. Many years ago I came to Copernicus's opinion, and from this standpoint I
have found the causes of many natural phenomena that are certainly inexplicable by the
usual hypothesis. I have written down many reasons and refutations, which, however, I
have not dared to bring to light, since I am deterred by the very fate of our teacher
Copernicus, who, though he has won immortal fame with a few, has with countless others
(so many fools are there in the world) become an object of laughter and scorn.'' Only
when he had constructed a telescope for himself and discovered the moons of Jupiter
did he declare himself publicly (in the year 1610) for the Copernican system. With that
the signal for persecution was given. Although Galilei made one brilliant discovery
after another that could support his hypothesis --- thus he discovered the sunspots and
the phases of Venus --- monks and theologians nevertheless spoke out
% --- p. 167 ---
% scan: „Heftigked“ (p. 167)
\opage{167}against him with increasing vehemence. Aristotelian philosophers would not even
look through Galilei's telescope themselves, so as not to see the offensive sight of
changes in the heavens and thereby lose their faith in the old world-picture. Galilei
was right when he said that even if the stars themselves came down to earth and bore
witness, his opponents would not let themselves be convinced. He sought in vain to
show that his views did not conflict with the Bible. Had he remained in Padua, which
stood under the dominion of Venice, he would no doubt have been safe in his person. But
in order to have more leisure and a more favorable financial position, he accepted a
position in Florence as the Grand Duke's ``mathematician,'' and here he could easily be
reached from Rome. The College of the Inquisition now (in the year 1616) took the
momentous step of putting Copernicus's work on the list of forbidden books (``until it
had been corrected'') and of declaring his doctrine heretical. Galilei was summoned
before Cardinal Bellarmine and is said --- according to what is claimed on the Catholic
side --- to have received an express injunction not to embrace and spread the condemned
doctrine; proof that such an injunction was really given cannot, however, be
furnished. Galilei did not, however, give up his research on that account. Through his
investigations of the comets he came into conflict with the Jesuits, and the mighty
order stood as one man against him. He was moreover working constantly on a complete
account of the struggle between the two systems of the world, which he had often
announced in earlier writings. If he merely expressed himself hypothetically, there
was, he thought, no danger. He thus used the same method that Osiander had used when he
published Copernicus's work. In the year 1632 his famous work appeared, which is
described on the title page as \textit{``Dialogue, in which in conversations on four
successive days the two most important systems of the world are discussed,} the
Ptolemaic and the Copernican, in such a way that, without any decision being made
(indeterminatamente), the philosophical and natural grounds for the one and for the
other of the two parties are set forth''. The persons conversing are Salviati and
Sagredo, two of Galilei's friends, and Simplicio, who is the representative of the
Aristotelian philosophy. Salviati is the deliberate, critical investigator; he sets
forth the grounds, but prefers to draw
% --- p. 168 ---
\opage{168}no definite conclusion and seeks to hold back the fiery Sagredo, through whom
Galilei gives vent to the freest of his ideas, so as then, if need be, to have
Salviati call them back. Yet it is clear enough to every reader in which direction the
author's sympathy goes, and in Rome they did not let themselves be fooled. The book was
forbidden, and Galilei was summoned to Rome. He seems not to have been actually
tortured, but only threatened with the rack, and then on the 22nd of June 1633 had,
kneeling, to abjure ``the false doctrine that the sun is the center of the world and
immovable, the earth not the center, but movable,'' and to swear ``that he would not in
future either orally or in writing state anything from which this doctrine could be
derived, but on the contrary would denounce to the Inquisition any heretic or anyone
suspected of heresy whom he came to know!'' --- That he swore a false oath there is no
doubt. His conviction he did not give up. Instead of burning him bodily, they punished
him with the burning pain caused by having to keep silent about one's conviction. Even
if Galilei, by his nature, did not feel this pain as strongly as a Kepler would have
felt it, it was nevertheless strong enough to embitter his life. To this were added
