grief and blindness. He lived under constant supervision in the neighborhood of
Florence, always occupied with scientific ideas. The life he saved by his false oath
was still to be of extraordinary value through the publication of his second main
work: \textit{Investigations (Discorsi) concerning Two New Sciences,} which --- to
escape the censorship --- was printed in Holland (1638). This work, which contains the
founding of modern physics, had, as has been aptly said, to sneak its way into
literature. Galilei died in 1642; he was mentally active right up to his last moment.
--- We shall now bring forward the most important points of view from which Galilei
has significance for the general history of thought\textsuperscript{35}).

\subsection*{a.\quad The Method and the Principles}

Galilei objects to the old logic that it is excellent for regulating and correcting the
train of thought, but is not a means for the discovery of new truths. Such discovery
% --- p. 169 ---
\opage{169}comes about when one derives an assumption from certain experiences and then
seeks by deductive means to show that the assumption set up agrees with other
experiences. The analytic method (metodo risolutivo) and the synthetic method (metodo
compositivo) thus mutually supplement each other. If by induction one meant an
investigation of all possible cases, inductive inference would be either impossible or
useless: impossible when one could not get hold of all the cases, useless when one
could manage all the cases. It is therefore only a matter of investigating the most
characteristic cases; from them one then infers to the others. But one must set up a
proposition as a conjecture before one can find the real proof of it. Confidence that
the proposition is correct contributes much to one's finding the proof of it. On the
other hand, what one infers from general principles must be proved in the particular
case by experiment. Thus Galilei proved by experiments on the inclined plane his
assumption, derived a priori, that the paths traversed with uniformly increasing
velocity are to each other as the squares of the times.

But when deduction and induction are thus to work together, a difficulty arises from
the fact that in our deductive reasonings we assume the relations to be simpler than
they are in reality. The mathematical propositions hold only for ideal figures. It is
no defect in real things that their figure never coincides entirely with any of the
figures that geometry constructs. The irregular figure that the stone has, it has to
perfection. But in the application of abstract reasoning to concrete relations, the
manifold and intricate conditions must be taken into account. It is our art of
calculation, not the figure of things, that is imperfect. In empty space --- we
assume --- all bodies would fall with the same velocity. Since we cannot produce an
absolutely empty space, we investigate how the relations are in denser and in thinner
media, and when we see that the velocities approach one another the thinner the media
are, we consider the proposition proved. That a body thrown along a horizontal surface
will continue to move when all obstacles are kept
% --- p. 170 ---
\opage{170}out is proved by the fact that the more one manages to exclude the obstacles,
the longer the motion is continued.

In order to be able to find points of attachment for deduction in experience, and in
order to be able to establish to what degree experiences approach the ideal
presuppositions on which deduction rests, Galilei --- like Kepler --- lays great weight
on quantitative relations. Only by the measurement of phenomena does it become possible
to decide how far they agree with what deduction requires. Therefore it is Galilei's
principle to measure everything that is measurable, and to make measurable what is not.

Galilei's chief method is the one that Stuart Mill much later called the method of
proportional changes, and that one could also call the method of limits. It makes it
possible to combine abstract thinking with concrete observation. Through approximations
the concrete cases come to share in the ideality of the abstract rules. As with Plato
the ``idea'' was the model for real things, so with Galilei
the law is the ideal expression of the connection between things.

When the law is thus found by analysis of what is given in experience, it follows of
itself that the causes by which phenomena are explained must themselves be given in
experience. Galilei embraces the same principle that Kepler expressed in the demand
for ``true causes'' (veræ causæ). In a very apt way Galilei shows that the appeal to
the divine will explains absolutely nothing, precisely because it explains everything
equally easily. It is as easy for God to let the universe move about the earth as to
let the earth move about the sun. Here the one becomes just as simple as the other. But
if we keep to what is moved, there is evidently a great difference in simplicity
between the two assumptions; the one requires a far greater expenditure of force than
the other. Before the infinite the finite differences vanish, but they remain when one
compares two finite things with each other. To such a comparison science must keep.
If one appeals to a miracle, the one can be assumed just as well as the other; every
criterion is lacking. Besides, one overlooks that all the works of nature
% --- p. 171 ---
\opage{171}and of God are miracles, even if they can be explained in a natural way.

Not only the theological but also the animistic explanation of nature is excluded by
the method employed. To explain the mutual influence of things, e.g. the attraction of
the magnet, by ``sympathy'' is merely to dispose of a whole host of questions with a
fine-sounding word. Thus gravity too is only a name. We do not know what it is that
draws the stone down toward the earth, any more than what it is that holds the moon in
its orbit around the earth, or what keeps the stone in motion after it has left the
throwing hand. Galilei therefore rejects the assumption put forward by Kepler that the
moon has an influence on ebb and flood. Here his fear of ``occult qualities'' leads
him astray.

\subsection*{b.\quad The New System of the World}

However often Galilei says in his dialogues that he will not settle on any view, his
own standpoint is nevertheless clear enough, even if we did not know it from his
letters. He admires Copernicus because, despite the testimony of the senses, he managed
to gain and hold fast his conviction of the motion of the earth. And he himself, through
his astronomical discoveries, brings forward a series of proofs that the universe
cannot, as the Aristotelians held, be divided into an unchangeable, heavenly world and a
changeable, earthly one: the sunspots and the new fixed stars show that changes also
take place in the heavens. And --- Galilei remarks --- with what right does one really
ascribe a higher value to the unchangeable than to the changeable? ``I for my part,''
he has Sagredo say, ``consider the earth to be most noble and admirable precisely on
account of the many diverse changes and productions that take place on it without
ceasing''. Simplicio objects to this that while the changes that take place on the
earth may be for the good of men, the heavenly changes would be altogether purposeless.
A similar reasoning he applies to the enormous extension that the universe (as Tycho
Brahe
% --- p. 172 ---
\opage{172}had already pointed out) must have on Copernicus's system: of what use is the
enormous space between the outermost planet and the sphere of the fixed stars? In his
answer Salviati applies to final causes the same consideration that Simplicio applies
elsewhere to natural causes: how dare we presume to know the purposes of the Almighty!
There is, after all, so much in our own body whose significance we do not know; how
then should we be able to know the significance of what is more remote? And how
difficult is it not to discover how a thing enters into the whole connection to which
it belongs, when one has no possibility of seeing what effect its removal will have?
It is to set limits to the divine power to believe that the enormous dimensions of the
universe should make its working at all points impossible. The sun shines on the grape
and ripens it as if that were the only thing it had to do, and so God and nature too
may well provide for every single thing, even if the content of the universe extends to
infinity. Galilei's standpoint here recalls Bruno's and Böhme's line of thought in face
of the same problem. --- Galilei is rather inclined (like Bruno) to assume the infinity
of the universe; he doubts the right to speak of a center of the world; and if he does
not express himself definitely on this, it is perhaps because Bruno's fate made him
wary.

It has rightly been a matter of wonder that Galilei, in his discussion of the systems of
the world, has not mentioned Kepler's laws, whose derivation from the law of gravitation
in Newton's hands was to become so mighty a support for the new system. Galilei
presumably attributed to them only a purely mathematical interest and did not suppose
that they could bear witness to the physical connection of the universe.

\subsection*{c.\quad The First Propositions of the Doctrine of Motion}

In support of the new world-picture Galilei appeals, like his predecessors, to the
principle of simplicity. Nature does nothing in vain, and therefore it always goes the
simplest ways and seeks by few and simple causes to attain a multiplicity of effects.
This principle of simplicity, which in
% --- p. 173 ---
\opage{173}astronomy he set against the complicated systems of Ptolemy and Tycho, led him in
physics to set up the first laws for the changes of material phenomena. It seemed to
him to be the simplest thing that a thing should remain in the state in which it was,
when no change occurred. Kepler had already set up the proposition that a body could
not of itself pass from rest to motion. Galilei now discovered that a body also cannot
of itself change its motion or pass from motion to rest. This is the law that was later
(with an expression used by Kepler) called the law of inertia. Galilei does not,
however, set it up as a general proposition. That both the direction and the velocity
are preserved he has nowhere stated. In the ``Dialogues'' it is the preservation of
velocity that he chiefly dwells on; he is thinking here chiefly of horizontal motion,
and he assumes that circular motion will continue just as well as rectilinear motion.
In the ``Discorsi'' the proposition appears more clearly. A motion, it is said here,
can only increase when new force (impeto, momento), is supplied, and only decrease when
an obstacle (impedimento) is applied, in both cases, then, only under the influence of
external causes. If external causes are kept away (dum externæ causæ tollantur), the
motion will be continued with the velocity once attained\textsuperscript{36}). That this
is a thought experiment Galilei expressly states; but he proves the correctness of the
proposition by experiments showing that the more external causes are kept away, the
longer the motion continues unchanged. Here the interaction between deduction and
induction by means of the limiting cases shows itself, and Galilei here at the same
time himself gives an example of his claim that the way of proof is other than the way
of discovery. For to appeal to the simplicity of nature is no proof, even if this
thought can lead to significant discoveries.

In his investigations of falling motion too Galilei uses the principle of simplicity as
his starting point. ``To the investigation of naturally accelerated motion I have been
led by attentive consideration of nature's usual procedure and ordering in all its
operations, since it is wont to employ the simplest and easiest means . . .
% --- p. 174 ---
\opage{174}When therefore I observe that a stone falling from the position of rest from a
considerable height gradually acquires new increments in velocity, why should I not
believe that such increments come about in the very simplest way? And we shall not be
able to find any increment simpler than the one that always comes in the same way''.
--- But here too it is only in the finding and setting up, not in the proof proper,
that the general principles are used. ---

As Galilei begins his investigations of motion, he says: ``On a very old subject I bring
an entirely new science''. He emphasizes in particular that no one has yet investigated
the quantitative variations of motion in free fall or of projectile motion. In finding
laws for these variations Galilei is conscious of having founded a new science, ``into
whose deeper secrets it is reserved for more superior minds to penetrate.'' But already
Galilei himself saw clearly that if motion is to
be thought of in continuous connection, account must be taken not only of the actual,
sensible motion, but also of the force or incitement (energia, momento, impeto) to
motion that is present at every moment --- whether a body is at rest or in motion
(Discorsi III).

The step that was taken by this founding was of extraordinary significance. The later
history of natural science has shown that the laws of motion contain the key to all
scientific knowledge of material nature. Galilei himself had a presentiment of this. In
the ``Dialogues'' he states that he has never been able to comprehend how a
transformation of substances into one another was possible. When a body presents
properties it did not have before, he does not consider it impossible that this
happens through a mere change in the arrangement of the parts, without anything being
annihilated or anything coming into being. With this it was clearly stated that the
understanding of the qualitative changes in nature becomes possible only when these can
be conceived as quantitative changes, that is to say here, as motions in space. The
great question for the philosophy of the modern age now became how it would take its
stand toward the great principle that was hereby set up,
% --- p. 175 ---
\opage{175}and that triumphantly established its applicability in one domain of nature after
another.

\subsection*{d.\quad The Subjectivity of the Sense Qualities}

Already in Copernicus and Bruno it appeared that the new conception of the world led to
posing the problem of knowledge in a new way, in that, in place of the picture of the
world that immediate observation gave, an entirely different one had to be put when
thought drew its consequences. In Galilei this appears still more clearly.

When he lays the principle of simplicity at the ground of so many important questions,
he distinguishes expressly between the ease and simplicity with which nature works and
the often intricate and laborious procedure we must employ to convince ourselves of
nature's simplicity. What is difficult for us to understand is very easy for nature to
do. There appears here, then, a definite opposition between existence and knowledge. It
was Galilei's view that in the clearest knowledge we have, the mathematical, this
opposition in a certain way falls away. Here human knowledge shares in the necessity
with which the Deity thinks the truths that lie at the ground of the connection of
existence --- only that what we think successively, laboriously working our way forward
from inference to inference, the Deity knows by a simple beholding (di un semplice
intuito, as opposed to: con discorsi). To that extent the same opposition between
simplicity and multiplicity remains on this point too. And it is only in intensity, in
rigor and necessity, that human knowledge at its summit thus becomes one with the
divine. In extent it falls infinitely far behind, and the most insignificant thing that
goes on in nature is impossible to see through even for the deepest inquiry. Socrates
saw clearly this imperfection of our knowledge, and yet he was praised as the wisest of
all. --- Thus both by its simplicity and by its infinity existence stands in
% --- p. 176 ---
% print: „Egenskaaer“ (p. 176) (misprint)
\opage{176}opposition to our knowledge. Galilei teaches a docta ignorantia just as Cusanus and Bruno do.

The opposition between knowledge and existence comes out no less in the distinction
that Galilei, like all Copernicans, enjoins between absolute and relative motion. Only
in relation to something unmoved do we apprehend motion. The motion common to several
things is --- as far as their relations to one another are concerned --- as if it were
not present. While the ancient conception of the world confidently presupposed visible
space as one with absolute space, the thought now had to make its way that absolute
space, as the immovable container of all material things, was not an object of sense
perception at all, since the apparently resting frame might itself be in motion in
relation to a point lying outside it, and so on. Copernicanism, especially under
Galilei's acute treatment, trained people generally in the application of the
epistemological law of relation. While the Peripatetic philosophy would otherwise keep
change out of the heavens, it nevertheless regarded the rising and setting of the sun
and the stars, the alternation of day and night, as real changes. Galilei's
representative in the Dialogues replies to this: ``All this is only change from the
earth's point of view. Think the earth away: then there is no sunrise or sunset, no
horizon, no meridian, no day and no night!''

When a whole series of changes in the heavens thus lost their absolute character and
were explained merely by the standpoint of the beholder, Galilei also found occasion,
for earthly phenomena, for a similar transfer of the differences from the objective to
the subjective domain. We have already seen that he denied the transformation of
substances and would assume only a rearrangement of parts; with that the principle of
the subjectivity of the sense qualities was really already given. But Galilei has stated
this principle in a still more definite form. In a remarkable section of an astronomical
polemic \textit{(Il
Saggiatore.} 1623) he has stated that the only properties we must of necessity ascribe to
bodies are figure, magnitude, motion or rest. These properties, which he therefore calls
the first and the real properties (primi e reali accidenti), we cannot even
% --- p. 177 ---
\opage{177}by the strongest exertion of the imagination separate from things. On the other
hand, it is due only to a prejudice nourished by the senses when we regard taste,
smell, color, heat etc. as absolute properties of things. They are only names we give
to things when these call forth certain sensations in us. They have in reality their
seat not in things but in the sensing body (nel corpo sensitivo). Take the sensing being
away --- and all those qualities fall away at the same time\textsuperscript{37}). ---
The parallelism between this consideration and the line of thought employed in the
defense of the new world-picture is easily seen. It became of great significance for
modern epistemology, as soon as the latter could work its way entirely out of the
swaddling clothes of dogmatism.

\section*{5.\quad Francis Bacon of Verulam}

\subsection*{a.\quad Predecessors}

The new science, which was founded under the influence of the experiences and inventions of practical life,
was bound to lead to an extension of the inherited logic. But even among those who did not stand especially
under the influence that called the new science to life, even in the circle of the humanists, the need of a
new logic expressed itself, and ever more vividly, through the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. From this
sprang a series of attempts at reform, programs and announcements, with manifold presentiments of what should
be put in place of the scholastic logic, which was really suited only to drawing formal conclusions from
presuppositions already given by authority. In the Middle Ages it was, after all, chiefly theology and the
doctrine of right that made use of logic, and both started from presuppositions fixed by authority. This whole
series of attempts at reform culminates in Francis Bacon of Verulam. This man, who has often been represented as
the founder of empirical science, hardly deserves even the name of a Moses who looks into the promised land.
There is certainly something prophetic about him, and he has often expressed, in a brilliant way, thoughts that
% --- p. 178 ---
\opage{178}illuminate the course and conditions of human inquiry, just as he is also clearly conscious of his
opposition to scholasticism; but the promised land had --- without his having noticed it --- been conquered by
Vinci, Kepler and Galilei. He declares modestly that he is not himself a warrior, but the herald (buccinator) who
rouses men to the battle. But the inquirers who founded modern empirical science did not need the notes of his
horn to be fired for the struggle. Bacon does not for that reason lose his significance in the history of
philosophy. To a rare degree he took into himself the thoughts and hopes that were bound to stir in the age in
which the new science came into being. If he did not help to found it, he was touched by the medium in which it
developed, and he prophesied of the way in which such a new science was bound to intervene in human life. He has
the consciousness of a fundamental change in lines of thought and interests, far more clearly than any other of
the thinkers of the period of transition. He will therefore keep a great name, even if a good deal must be
subtracted from the idolization his countrymen have practiced with him, and which neither his works nor his
personality deserve. --- Before we go on to consider the man and his work more closely, we must dwell a moment on
his predecessors in the 16th century.

From the circle of the humanists came PIERRE DE LA RAMÉE (Petrus Ramus). In the middle of the 16th century he
waged a violent battle against the Aristotelian logic. To be sure, he only continued\textsuperscript{38}) thereby
the endeavors which, already from the preceding century on, had sought to bring logic nearer to practical
applicability, especially for rhetoric. And he himself declared that he had had the German humanists and
pedagogues Agricola and Sturm as his teachers. But the whole tendency nevertheless finds in him its most gifted
and most accomplished representative, and he waged the battle with an energy that contributed mightily to shaking
the absolute rule of scholasticism at the universities of Western Europe.

Ramus was born in 1515, the son of a charcoal-burner in north-eastern France. That he was a charcoal-burner's son
he often had to hear --- after that age's manner of polemic --- from his
% --- p. 179 ---
\opage{179}opponents. But he was not ashamed of it. Not because his family was noble (though it had come down in
the world); but because by his passionate eagerness to learn he had worked his way up to a high scholarly
position. He began as servant to a rich student in Paris, and when he had done his day's work, he studied at
night. It was the scholastic logic into which he was first introduced; but he felt dissatisfied with it and came
with enthusiasm to know Plato's dialogues, which seemed to him to describe the living, actual activity of thought
to a far higher degree. In his master's disputation of 1536 he defended the radical proposition that everything
Aristotle has said is false. The bitterness of the Aristotelians was great, and it grew with his detailed
criticism of the old logic. The university demanded that Ramus's books be suppressed, since he was an enemy of
religion and of public peace in imparting to the young a dangerous love of the new. Francis I then prohibited
Ramus's books by an edict, and at the same time prohibited Ramus from attacking Aristotle and other ancient
authors! Under Henry II, however, Ramus received freedom to teach again and now worked at the Collége de France,
where his lectures gathered nearly 2000 listeners. It was a movement such as had not been known since Abailard's
days. In 1554 Ramus published his logic \textit{(Institutiones dialecticæ)} in Latin, and the year after in
French. The fundamental thought of his doctrine is that one must first investigate how thinking is used by
nature, before one sets up rules for it. He therefore refers to the first philosophers, who as yet had no
artificial logic. And not only these philosophers, but also the great statesmen, orators and poets, as well as
the mathematicians of antiquity, show us in their works the involuntary use of the faculty of thought. Here we
find the rules unconsciously applied. Ramus's humanist interest finds satisfaction in the fact that the study of
the ancient authors can thus be taken into the service of logic. Like his humanist predecessors, he sets up two
principal logical functions: the finding (inventio) of arguments, and the use of these arguments by the judgment
(judicium) for the closer grounding and illumination of the subject. The judgment is therefore often called, in
the school language of the following period, secunda pars Petri.
% --- p. 180 ---
% print: „Krag 1558—1600)“, no opening parenthesis (p. 180) (misprint)
\opage{180}Ramus occupied himself mostly with this latter part and especially worked out the doctrine of the
syllogism, and the striking thing appears here, that at bottom he does not depart much from the Aristotelian
logic. The purely formal character of Ramus's reform shows itself in the great weight he lays on divisions into
two (dichotomies). Without regard to the nature of the subject, the exposition is divided at every point into two
members, since (according to what logic teaches) a certain predicate in question either holds or does not.
Hereby a new scholasticism was really introduced. --- There did, however, stir in him a lively need to return to
nature, and he did good by simplifying exposition and by insisting that art always builds on nature. But nature
he found in the books of antiquity instead of in ever-living thought. He did not immerse himself in the study of
the psychology of thinking, and he could not yet use the procedure of the new science as a model in his
description of the method of thinking.

Ramus, who had gone over to Protestantism, was murdered on St.~Bartholomew's Night 1572. It is not impossible
that the hatred of a fanatical scholastic showed the murderers the way. His corpse was maltreated by the Catholic
students.

But his reform of the teaching of the liberal arts made its way abroad. Ramism flourished in Germany, Switzerland
and Scotland. In Denmark it was represented by \textsc{Anders Krag} (1558---1600), who after studying in France
became professor in Copenhagen. At the University of Cambridge in England, Ramism was combated by the zealous
scholastic and mystic \textsc{everard digby}, who was probably Bacon's teacher. But here too it found a zealous
defender in \textsc{William} \textsc{Temple} (the Elder), who led it to victory and by his polemical writings
against scholasticism laid the foundation for a freer tendency in philosophy, which since that time has always
characterized Cambridge in contrast to conservative Oxford. The heated dispute about method between Digby and
Temple was bound to arouse great attention and was surely of no small significance for Bacon's
development\textsuperscript{39}).

While Ramism went on its triumphal march in northern and western Europe, there stirred at the same time in many a
deep
% --- p. 181 ---
\opage{181}need of real knowledge, a thirst for well-grounded acquaintance with actual nature. The writings of
Telesio and Campanella, and in part those of Bruno too, bear witness to this. A remarkable example of a
deep-going criticism of inherited knowledge, of a clear notion of how much is required in order rightly to know
anything, but at the same time of an inability to find a positive realization of this ideal, is offered by
\textsc{Franz Sanchez}, the author of the ``Treatise on the noble and lofty science that nothing is known''
\textit{(Qvod nihil scitur),} which appeared in 1581. Sanchez was the son of a Spanish physician who had moved
to Bordeaux, and he himself worked as a professor of medicine, first in Montpellier, later in Toulouse. Although
the title of his chief work might seem to stamp Sanchez as a skeptic, it would surely be unjustified to regard
him merely from this side. He has a lively feeling of the imperfection of human nature and especially of human
knowledge. But doubt is for him not an end but a means. His skeptical work is only the introduction to a series
of works of a special and empirical kind. It was also his intention to work out a separate treatise on method.
He praises observation and experiment, in union with judgment, as the right paths to knowledge. His motto is: Go
to the things themselves! But he does not have the great hope, which animates his contemporary Bacon, of how far
it will be possible to advance along this path. He sees how many riddles even the smallest thing contains, ---
and also that all things in the world hang closely together, and that the world extends into the infinite:
therefore a perfect knowledge of things stands before him as an unattainable ideal. The attempts he himself made
in the direction of the philosophy of nature, which recall those of Telesio and of Bacon, do not give him the
satisfaction that these two thinkers felt in their similar attempts.

On one single point Sanchez goes deeper than both Bacon and Ramus. He goes back, namely, to the source of all
certainty in the human mind itself. No external knowledge, he says, can be as certain as that which I have of my
own states and my own actions; this is immediate as that can never become. I am more certain that a thought, a
drive or a
% --- p. 182 ---
\opage{182}volition stirs in me than I can be that I see a certain object or a person outside me. On the other
hand, inner experience falls short of outer experience in distinctness and exactness. --- By this line of
thought Sanchez stands as a predecessor of Campanella and Descartes. But he was as little able as Campanella to
make it fruitful. This was reserved for Descartes.

In Bacon both the demonstration of the defects of knowledge and that of the right method appear far more fully
than in any of the humanists and empiricists who before him had sought to reform logic. And the explanation of
this has rightly been sought not only in Bacon's peculiar personality, but also in his position in the midst of
the luxuriantly pulsing life of England. He has --- as has rightly been said --- as his predecessors not only
philosophers and men of science, but practical investigators of nature, engineers, seamen and adventurers.

\subsection*{b.\quad Bacon's Life and Personality}

There has been a long dispute about Bacon's character. His honor as a man, not merely as a thinker, has been
alternately destroyed and rescued. This dispute falls away for anyone who attentively reads his \textit{Essays}
and his diaries, published some years ago. He has been so sincere in them that we cannot be mistaken about him,
especially when we connect with these direct or indirect self-confessions the traits of character that come to
light in his philosophical writings.

Francis Bacon was born in 1561. He was a son of Queen Elizabeth's Lord Keeper of the Great Seal, Nicolas Bacon,
and a nephew of the first minister, Lord Burleigh. After having studied at Cambridge, where he probably studied
scholasticism under Digby, he accompanied an embassy to Paris. The brilliant prospects that opened before him
fell away with his father's early death. He was the youngest son and now had to make his own way; his powerful
uncle would do nothing for him. A strong desire for power, wealth and honor animated him, but it was nevertheless
not the only motive that drove him forward. In one of
% --- p. 183 ---
\opage{183}his earliest treatises he says: ``Is not the pleasure of the feelings greater than the pleasure of
the senses, and is not the pleasure of thought greater than that of the feelings? Is not the pleasure of thought
the only one of which one is never surfeited, and is it not knowledge that frees the mind from all unrest?'' The
need of knowledge and the desire for power, wealth and honor did not merely go side by side in him, but he found a
justification for the latter motive by subordinating it to the former: he sought power and wealth in order to
have means for carrying out the great scientific plans --- nothing less than a complete renewal of science
(instauratio magna) --- over which he brooded. And here a third element in his character must now be noted ---
one to which his writings above all bear witness --- namely his great sanguineness and his no less great
self-esteem. He saw a great work before him, and it needed great means. By this he excused to himself the
crooked moral paths he took, and even baseness faded for him in the brilliant light in which he saw his striving.
In order to carry out his plan he needed leisure and means to collect observations and make experiments.
Therefore he threw himself into a political career. But in him, as in Machiavelli, the means gained the upper
hand over the end that was to have sanctified it. Had he, instead of laying out his plan on so great a scale, as
regards both end and means, attentively followed the works of his great contemporaries Tycho Brahe, Gilbert,
Kepler and Galilei, he would have found there enough to think about and a sufficient foundation for working out a
program for the future. His sense of the grandiose led him astray and, with the help of his lust for power,
entangled him in relations that corrupted his character and plunged him into misfortune. He lacked a living moral
sense to form a regulating counterweight to the other motives. In his ``Essays'' he says: ``The best character
consists in having a reputation for openness, but practice in proceeding secretly and, should occasion arise,
in being able to dissemble.'' And in another place: ``There are no two more fortunate qualities than to have a
little of the fool and not too much of the honest man.'' Bacon's ambition led him into worldly
% --- p. 184 ---
% print: „sørger“ (p. 184) (misprint)
\opage{184}and political life, and he thereby obtained material for observation and for knowledge of men, which
he has used in his writings (especially in the ``Essays'' and in the seventh and eighth books of \textit{De
dignitate et augmentis scientiarum).} He praises Machiavelli because he sets forth so openly and honestly what men
are accustomed to do, not what they ought to do. Knowledge of this is necessary, in order that the simplicity of
the dove should not come to lack the wisdom of the serpent. But here again the means became an end for him. For
to get on in the world one must direct one's conduct by men's actual conduct, and he therefore warns against
remaining the same when circumstances change; the thing is to let the mind adapt itself to occasion and
convenience (ut animus reddatur occasionibus et opportunatibus obseqvens, neqve ullo modo erga res durus aut
obnixus). And he urges always having several ends before one, so that one may attain the subsidiary end even if
the principal end is not attained. A piece of advice especially dangerous for his own character! ---

Bacon first tried to make his way as a petitioner for office. It did not succeed. In Parliament he spoke against
a government bill and thereby fell into decided disfavor with the queen. His friendship with Essex (if it can be
called friendship) helped him for a time out of difficult pecuniary circumstances. But when Essex was about to
fall, Bacon drew back from him. Indeed, during his trial Bacon even offered the queen his services, which were
accepted. And when Essex had made his desperate attempt at rebellion, Bacon appeared as a witness against him and
after his execution wrote a piece in justification of the government's conduct. A zeal that cannot be explained by
concern that justice should take its course, but which is understood when one reads the following utterance in an
essay (of followers and friends), printed in 1597, thus a few years before Essex's catastrophe: ``There is but
little friendship in the world, and least of all between equals. The friendship that exists is between superior
and inferior, where the fortune of the one comprehends that of the other.'' Of this kind was Bacon's
``friendship'' for Essex, and he took care in good time that his ``friend's'' fortune should not come, in an
unpleasant way, to comprehend his own. Whether men really are accustomed to
% --- p. 185 ---
\opage{185}behave in this way is a question by itself. The William Temple mentioned earlier, who had been Essex's
secretary, at any rate did not behave so, and therefore also had to go into exile.

In spite of all Bacon's attempts to adapt himself to circumstances, he nevertheless had no success under Queen
Elizabeth. Things went better under James I, especially since he knew how to ingratiate himself with the king's
various favorites. The dark sides of Bacon's character here had unhappy and far-reaching historical consequences.
He was himself of the conviction that the king ought to comply with the justified wishes of the House of Commons,
but then use his sovereign power to carry through the codification of the laws and the colonization of Ireland,
and, in external affairs, to act energetically by making himself the head of a Protestant league. The attention of
the people would thereby be diverted from constitutional questions. But with the unstable and weak king, who was
puffed up with a sense of his power, it was impossible to carry through such a course. Herbert of Cherbury, who
held a similar conception of foreign policy, had, as is known, to lose his post as ambassador in France a little
later for this reason. Bacon adapted himself to the king's whims --- whether quite unconsciously, as his
biographer \textsc{Edwin Abbot} thinks, is surely a great question. And yet vigorous action on his part could have
been of great significance. For himself the adaptation had, for the time being, favorable consequences. He
advanced at last to Lord Chancellor, Lord of Verulam and Viscount of St. Albans. But to reach this high goal he
had not only to adapt his political views, but also to work in favor of the king's favorites. This caused his
abrupt fall (1621). Bacon had declared certain monopolies, which were favorable to Buckingham's relatives, lawful
and beneficial. When Parliament grew bitter at this, the king put the blame on his advisers. People then turned
against Bacon and struck at him with a charge of bribery. Bacon at once declared himself guilty and was deprived
of his dignities by the House of Lords and sentenced to a large fine and to sit in prison as long as the king
pleased. Since --- apart from his own guilt --- he fell as a victim of the conduct of the king and his
favorites, he got off lightly. He was
% --- p. 186 ---
% print: „encypklopædisk“ (p. 186) (misprint)
\opage{186}imprisoned only a couple of days and never paid the fine. His last years he lived in quiet, occupied
with scientific works. This quiet he could have procured for himself earlier and at a cheaper price. He obtained
what he had declared in his Essays to be the most desirable thing: to die in the midst of serious work, since
the wound is not felt when one falls in a fierce battle. He died in 1626. --- By his friends and his servants he
was loved and admired. That belongs, together with his great interest in study and the great faith he had that
human culture would be able to develop so richly and gloriously as had never yet been dreamed, to the traits
that cast a reconciling light over his character after all the dismal things that are otherwise to be told of
him.

During his activity as judge, statesman and courtier he had not forgotten his studies. The plans for his chief
works arose in him early. A writing of 1607 \textit{(Cogitata et Visa)} is the first detailed draft of Bacon's
most famous work, \textit{Novum Organum} (``The New Logic''), which appeared in 1620, after Bacon had reworked it
twelve times. It investigates the grounds of the imperfection of the sciences, sets forth the obstacles to true
knowledge that lie in the very nature of the human mind and in the conditions under which it develops, and then
goes on to describe the inductive method. The work is unfinished, and it is laid out on a scale that it was
impossible to carry through in Bacon's time. Only two hundred years later did Stuart Mill, in his Logic, do the
work that Bacon, with his imperfect material, had dared to undertake. --- A writing of 1605 \textit{(Advancement
of learning)} is the first draft of \textit{De dignitate et augmentis scientiarum} (On the Worth and Advancement
of the Sciences), which appeared in 1623. This work is an encyclopedic survey of the sciences, which contains many
apt remarks, especially concerning the gaps that still remained to be filled. --- The rest of Bacon's works are
for the most part collections of material which now have as good as no interest.

As an author Bacon is vigorous and apt in expression, and often extraordinarily happy in the choice of images. But
% --- p. 187 ---
\opage{187}it is incomprehensible how anyone could have compared him with Shakespeare\textsuperscript{40}). His
imagination is abstractly intuitive and symbolizing, and lacks Shakespeare's glowing energy, individual nuancing
and atmospheric inwardness.

\subsection*{c.\quad The Obstacles, Conditions and Method of Knowledge}

Science, says Bacon, has been cultivated for only a very short time, and this holds especially of natural
science, which is the mother of all science. The Greeks occupied themselves mostly with moral philosophy, the
Romans with the doctrine of right, and after the rise of Christianity the most gifted threw themselves upon
theology. Only in idle hours and as a handmaid was natural science cultivated, not as a principal task, not with
the end in view by which alone it can become truly fruitful: to make human life richer and better. And besides,
wrong methods were employed. It was held that the human mind was too exalted to occupy itself with experiments,
especially since it was supposed able to spin the truth out of its own interior. People were content with what had
been handed down. They had too great a reverence for the past and its great thinkers, whom they called the
ancients, though it is in fact precisely we who are the ancients, since we can look back on a far greater
experience than they. To this was added a false religious zeal, which did not see that natural science teaches us
to know God's power, just as religion teaches us to know God's will. As faith is to restore to us the innocence we
lost by the Fall, so science is to restore to us the power over nature that we then lost. But most of all, men's
faint-heartedness and distrust of their own strength have done harm. They have lacked the courage and the hope to
set themselves great tasks.

There is reason now to have good hope, precisely because our own faults are to blame for the imperfection under
which we suffer. The right method must be capable of being found. It is the one that will not, like the spider,
spin everything out of itself, nor, like the ant, merely collect material, but which, like the bee, takes the
material into itself and works it up. If the material is collected, and if one is able to keep prejudices and
preconceived opinions away, then
% --- p. 188 ---
% scan: „frem.“ (p. 188)
\opage{188}the right interpretation of nature will soon be found. The most important step of all that must be
taken is then to procure as rich and many-sided a collection of facts as possible. Then the human mind will, by its
own involuntary drive, work them up and interpret them. --- In this assertion of the involuntary activity of mind,
which comes into operation as soon as the material is merely at hand, Bacon is perhaps influenced by Ramus, whom he
mentions with recognition, though he objects against him that his method is too simple. The difference between
them rests on Bacon's having seen the necessity of a large mass of material of experience, in order that the
faculty of invention and the judgment may work in a fruitful way. --- The most important error that can be
committed is, according to Bacon, that of going forward too quickly, of hastening to the general fundamental
propositions instead of ascending slowly to them through many intermediate steps. The human mind needs lead, not
wings.

The end is to enrich human life through the inventions that can be made when one knows nature. Knowledge is
power; for we have the possibility of producing things when we know their causes. By the help of inventions and
mechanical skills men have gradually worked their way out of barbarism and have attained a civilized life. Only
along this path can the misery and misfortune that men still suffer under be remedied. The thing is to gain
greater dominion over nature; but that is gained only by obeying it. --- Yet one would do Bacon an injustice by
attributing to him the opinion that science is to be cultivated only for the sake of practical utility. Above the
external yield that knowledge can procure he places the very contemplation of things (comtemplatio rerum above
fructus inventio). We rejoice in the light because we can work, read and see one another by its help; but the
very sight of the light is nevertheless more glorious than its manifold uses.

But there is hope of reaching the great goal only if one comes without prejudices. As with the kingdom of heaven,
one can enter the kingdom of man, which is to be founded on science, only by becoming as children. Prejudices and
preconceived opinions must be laid aside. The thing is, after all, to interpret nature, not to anticipate nature:
interpretatio, not
% --- p. 189 ---
\opage{189}antecipatio. Bacon therefore seeks to give a comprehensive doctrine of the unjustified anticipations.
This is his famous doctrine of the illusions of the mind (idola mentis), which must be purged away in order that
the mind may become a clean and smooth tablet (tabula abrasa), on which things can write their true nature. Bacon
distinguishes four classes of such illusions.

Some illusions are grounded in human nature itself and are therefore common to the whole species (idola tribus).
To these illusions of the species belong those which arise because we conceive things according to their relation
to us and in likeness to ourselves (ex analogia hominis), and not in relation to and in likeness to existence (ex
analogia universi). Our mode of conception, our way of sensing and thinking, surely cannot be the measure of
things! In particular we have an inclination to presuppose greater order and regularity in things than is actually
found there. The evenness (æqvalitas) of our own mind we presuppose in things too. And what conflicts with
assumptions we have once formed, we are inclined to overlook. The negative cases are easily passed over when one
draws conclusions from experience. To what acts suddenly and immediately upon us we ascribe the greatest
significance, and we are inclined to take what is more remote to be of the same nature. On the other hand, we also
carry the unrest and constant craving of our own mind over into nature, so that we will posit no limits to its
extension or to the series of causes. Or one settles down content by finding the explanation in a purpose and
positing final causes (causæ finales), an explanation that is evidently taken from our own nature, not from that
of the universe. Finally, our results are very easily determined by our feelings and drives, by our hope or our
fear, and this influence of feeling on knowledge often takes place in an altogether imperceptible way.

Another class of illusions springs from the individual nature of the single person. Bacon calls them (alluding to
a passage in Plato) ``cave-illusions'' (idola specus), since each one's individuality is, as it were, the cave
from which he looks at existence, and in which the light of nature is refracted in a peculiar way. These illusions
of individuality are determined by original
% --- p. 190 ---
\opage{190}nature, upbringing, company and reading. There are some who are most inclined to dwell on the
differences of things, others who are most inclined to dwell on their likenesses, --- some who most love the old,
others who turn with predilection toward the new, --- some who seek the elements of things, others who stop at the
compound phenomena as they are immediately given.

As the worst of all illusions Bacon regards those that are due to the influence of words on thinking. He calls
them ``idols of the market-place'' (idola fori). Words are formed according to the needs of practical life and
according to the popular understanding (ex captu vulgi), and the boundary lines they fix between things often
cannot be used by sharper thinking. Words are formed for something that does not exist at all, and on the other
hand words are lacking for things that experience actually offers. Hence much verbal dispute.

While the first three classes of idols have their ground in the nature of man, the last class, ``idols of the
theater'' (idola theatri), is due to the influence of inherited theories. These theories may be very ingenious and
sharply thought out and yet miss the goal. He who follows the right path reaches the goal with slight gifts more
quickly and surely than the best runner once he is off the right path; indeed, precisely by his skill as a runner
the latter will move further and further from the goal. The method of experience that Bacon recommends, in
contrast to the brilliant speculations of earlier times, leaves --- in his view --- no great room for acuteness
and strength of mind to exercise themselves. The right method levels the difference between minds. When a circle
is to be drawn freehand, differing gifts may become of significance; but when compasses are used, such difference
falls away. --- This fourth class of idols is hard to keep apart from the second, since Bacon makes reading,
tradition and authority contribute to the coming into being of individual peculiarity.

Bacon's doctrine of the idols is a small piece of critical philosophy, an attempt to distinguish between what
belongs merely to the subjective nature of
% --- p. 191 ---
\opage{191}knowledge and what belongs to existence. In Montaigne, Cusanus, Bruno and Galilei we have met beginnings
in the same direction. Unfortunately Bacon lacks the grand point of view that comes forward, especially in
Galilei, through the Copernican theory, which inculcates the relativity of the standpoint. And Bacon is inclined to
regard the ways of viewing that we involuntarily adopt as purely deceptive. Thus it is for him a deception of the
senses (fallacia sensuum) when the senses show us things otherwise than science explains them. He has, moreover,
not investigated more closely how it is possible to purge the mind so that it becomes a blank tablet. The
conditions and forms that lie in our original individuality and in common human nature we surely cannot abolish,
even if we can discover them. At this point a contradiction comes out in Bacon. For, as we have seen, it is his
conviction that when the material is laid ready, the mind works it up involuntarily according to its own inner
capacity (vi propria atqve genuina). But is not something then added here to the material --- and by what right is
it added? What guarantee is there that the mind's own inner power can lead us to see things no longer according to
their relation to ourselves, but according to their relation to the universe? How do we convince ourselves that we
have really reached analogia universi? --- Here later epistemology took hold. Bacon is its forerunner by his
doctrine of the idols. And especially interesting is the thought that the presupposition from which Leonardo,
Copernicus, Bruno and Galilei so confidently started, namely that nature always follows the simplest paths, could
have a purely human and subjective origin, so that its justification must be discussed. ---

The method that must be followed in working up the material is induction. This method had, to be sure, long been
used, but Bacon found in its usual application an essential error, which he brought under the illusions of the
species, namely that one keeps to the cases in which a phenomenon has shown itself and regards them as sufficient
to ground an insight into its nature. This kind of induction Bacon calls induction by simple enumeration (inductio
per enumerationem
% --- p. 192 ---
\opage{192}simplicem). He demands that it be supplemented by an investigation of the ``negative instances'', that
is, the cases in which the phenomenon does not occur, although the circumstances are akin to those under which it
occurs. And besides he demands a table of degrees, which shows under what circumstances the phenomenon decreases or
increases. By this procedure we can get so far that we can form a provisional conception of the nature of the
phenomenon, or, as Bacon calls it, its ``form''. By the form Bacon understands the property that is always present
when the phenomenon is present, always absent when it is absent, and which decreases or increases in the same
proportion as it does. After having eliminated the properties that do not satisfy these requirements, we retain the
form. In investigating the nature of death we must thus disregard whether it takes place by drowning, by burning,
by piercing, by apoplexy, by
lack of nourishment, etc. With heat we must disregard the special ways in which heat is produced, the composition
of the hot substances, etc.

When Bacon is often accused of conceiving induction as a mere collecting of material, it must be noted that he lays
great weight on the formation of provisional hypotheses for survey and orientation. The first interpretation is only
an attempt. It is the ``first vintage'', which serves merely as a trial (Nov. Org. II. 20). It is undertaken because
truth is more easily won through an error, if only it is clearly thought through, than through a chaotic heaping up
of material. It is one of Bacon's most famous aphorisms: citius emergit veritas ex errore qvam ex confusione. As
such a provisional hypothesis Bacon sets up, as regards the ``form'' of heat, the proposition: heat is motion. ---
And his method of induction is now continued after the setting up of this provisional hypothesis and with it as
guide. The thing now is to find, or to produce experimentally, such cases as are especially suited to illuminate
and more closely ground the assumption that has been set up. Of such ``prerogative instances'' Bacon enumerates a
whole multitude. Among other things he mentions (as instantiæ solitariæ) cases that present the property under
discussion under circumstances that otherwise have absolutely nothing in common with
% --- p. 193 ---
\opage{193}all the other cases in which it occurs, or which do not present it, although they otherwise have all
other circumstances in common with the cases in which it occurs. These are the methods that Mill later called the
method of agreement and the method of difference. As instantiæ viæ he designates cases and experiments that show us
the phenomenon ``on the way'', in its coming into being, during which its nature (``form'') will most readily
reveal itself. As instantiæ irregulares et deviantes he designates cases in which the phenomenon has, as it were,
``gone astray'', varies, assumes irregular forms. Through such variation the thing more readily discloses its
proper nature. Akin to these are the transitional forms (instantiæ limitaneæ), which present some properties that
can be brought under one form, and others that can be brought under another form.

Bacon intimates that a whole series of further operations still belongs to the complete carrying through of the
method of induction. But Novum organum ends with the enumeration of the various kinds of prerogative instances. ---

The detailed description of the method of induction that Bacon gives was a real advance for its time. It betrays a
clear understanding of essential points. What he overlooked, and what puts him in the shade beside the founders of
the new science, is the subordinate position he assigns to quantitative determination and to deduction. Exact
empirical science becomes possible only when, by exact measurement of the phenomena, one obtains a foundation for
mathematical deduction. He does, to be sure, give quantitative determination a place in the inductive process; a
special kind of prerogative instances is the instantiæ qvanti, also called doses naturæ. But he did not see their
decisive significance. And with this his underestimation of deduction is connected; the most brilliant deductions
are the mathematical ones. Even if Bacon did not, as he has been accused of doing, altogether misjudge the
significance of deduction (the ``first vintage'' speaks against that), he nevertheless gives the deductive process
an altogether subordinate place in his method of experience. He had no inkling that a deduction gives the real
proof of the correctness of the inductive conclusion.
% --- p. 194 ---
\opage{194}

What Bacon wants to reach by way of induction is a determination of the nature or ``form'' of things, of their
peculiar essence, each by itself. But properly speaking such a determination is not an induction in the modern
sense of the word. It states not the dependence of one phenomenon on another, not a law, but a concept. It is (as
FRIES has already remarked in his history of philosophy) rather to be called abstraction than induction. And Bacon
himself here refers to Plato as his model. There is, he says, a difference between the idols of the human mind and
the ideas of the divine mind. It is these latter that he wants to seek: they are the eternal forms of things. The
form is the definition of the thing, the thing itself (ipsissima res). He praises Plato because he saw that the
``form'' is the true object of science. Plato's error was, partly, that he separated the forms or ideas from the
things themselves, whereas they are precisely to be sought in the individual phenomena themselves, and partly that
he did not resolve the compound forms or natures into the simplest, purely elementary ones. What must be
established is, according to Bacon, precisely the simplest, indissoluble properties (naturæ simplices) of
things\textsuperscript{41}). Such simple properties are color, heaviness, solubility, expansibility, etc.

Seen from this side, the concept of ``form'' in Bacon points back to ancient and scholastic philosophy. But he
wavers not a little in his conception of this concept. In some places the ``form'' means not a definition or a
determination of the nature of the thing, but the law according to which the activity proceeds in which the
phenomenon consists. ``The forms'', he says in one place, ``are fictions (commenta) of the human mind, unless one
is willing to call the laws of activity or of motion forms''. The form of heat is thus the same as the law of the
phenomena of heat. By this he wanted to distinguish his ``forms'' from those that had hitherto been assumed. This
law one must know if one is to be able to produce the phenomenon. Both in theory and in practice it is then the law
that must be found. This practical side Bacon no doubt also gets expressed when he speaks of the form as the
expression of the essence of things, in that he calls the form the active nature of the thing (natura naturans),
the source from
% --- p. 195 ---
\opage{195}which its individual properties spring (fons emanationis). Plato too, after all, regarded the ideas as
the true causes. But the nuance that --- without Bacon himself noticing it --- comes out in the concept of form,
in that it designates now the essence of the thing, now the law of its production, is nevertheless characteristic
of his doctrine of method. He shows himself here to stand at the transition between the old and the new
philosophy. He starts --- like Plato and the scholastics --- from the assumption that there is a certain number of
``simple natures'', whose combination makes up the various phenomena. But the presupposition that things are
subject to definite laws he does not set up or investigate.

A connection between the two meanings of the concept of form arose for Bacon from his asserting so definitely that
one could learn to know the essence of things only by investigating the process by which they come into being, as
well as the inner connection between the parts of which they consist. But both of these lead us beyond the
sensible. For the changes in nature take place by degrees, through small transitions (per minima), so small that
we notice them as little as we can sense the minute parts of which things must be assumed to be composed, and
whose kind of composition (schematismus) produces the properties (forms!) that they present to us. The task of
inquiry is then to find the hidden process (latens processus) that continuously connects the various stages of
development which our leaping and periodic observation apprehends, and the hidden arrangement (latens
schematismus) that underlies the sensible properties. Nature is too subtle for our senses. The motion in which the
essence of heat consists we do not sense as such. The hidden process escapes us here. It goes similarly with the
development of the organism, with the process of nutrition (when one is to have all the stages, right from the
taking up of the nutritive matter to its complete working up into flesh and blood), with voluntary motion (when one
is to have all the members, right from the first motion in the representation through the inner processes to the
bending and motion of the limbs). And the task becomes especially difficult to solve when one must find at every
point what is lost, what remains, and
% --- p. 196 ---
\opage{196}what is added; for Bacon regards it as certain that the total sum of matter is neither increased nor
diminished. --- This doctrine (Nov. org. I, 10, 50; II, 5---7. 40---41) of the continuous process, and of its
individual members as the conversion into a new form of what is given in another form, without anything being lost
or gained as regards quantity, belongs to the most brilliant anticipations in Bacon --- although he himself, by
his method, wanted to exclude anticipation and put interpretation in its place. He set up the principle of
continuity, which has later proved so fruitful. Bacon here comes involuntarily to admit that every interpretation
must start from certain principles. His whole doctrine of the hidden continuous process and the hidden arrangement
he sets forth purely dogmatically, merely illustrating it with a few single examples.

By drawing the consequence of the doctrine of the hidden process one discovers that the two meanings of the
concept of form in Bacon are in conflict with each other. According to the first meaning (form = simple nature =
property that makes up the essence of the thing) we start from the assumption that the properties which
observation establishes also belong to the things themselves. By the second meaning (form = law of the process by
which things come into being) it turns out that things in reality consist of minute parts and arise through
minute changes, none of which can be observed by itself. With the latter meaning the subjectivity of the sense
qualities agrees (since heat in itself or in ordine ad universum is motion), while it conflicts with the first
meaning (heat as natura simplex, like color, etc.). Just as Bacon by the first meaning recalls Plato and
scholasticism, so by the second meaning he recalls Democritus, without, however, having really been an atomist.
It is characteristic that the utterance cited above, that the ``forms'' are fictions and illusions of the species
unless by form one understands law, occurs precisely in a context where he has just before praised Democritus
because of his demand that nature be resolved into its elements rather than that abstractions be made. --- It is
again here the relation between quality and quantity at which Bacon stops short. Entangled in Platonic and
scholastic
% --- p. 197 ---
% scan: „Ufrugtbarked“ (p. 197)
\opage{197}presuppositions, he did not consistently carry through what lies in his brilliant idea of the continuous
process by which qualitative differences are resolved into quantitative ones; and therefore he does not recognize
the subjectivity of the sense qualities in the resolute way that Galilei does.

\subsection*{d.\quad Theory of Science, Theology and Ethics}

The inductive method is to hold for all sciences, for the human sciences (ethics, politics, logic) as well as for
the natural sciences. Bacon on the whole strongly emphasizes the unity of science in spite of its division into
special subjects. The complete isolation of the single subject will condemn it to unfruitfulness. If one asks where
the common foundation of the various sciences is to be found, he answers somewhat differently in his two chief
works. In Novum organum natural science is called the great mother of all sciences. But in the work on the
advancement of the sciences (De augmentis scientiarum) the honorary name of mother of the sciences is given to the
science that contains the fundamental propositions common to the various sciences. This science of the common
fundamental propositions Bacon calls prima philosophia. But such a science has not yet been developed, though it
would be of great significance, since a system of such common fundamental propositions would contain a testimony to
the unity of nature. As such common fundamental propositions Bacon names (Nov. org. I, 80. 127. De augm. III, I):
Equals added to unequals produce unequals; things that agree with one and the same third agree with each other;
nature reveals herself especially in minima; everything changes, but nothing perishes. These are in part
propositions with which Bacon confidently operates in his doctrine of method. Of their origin and grounding he does
not speak more closely, but it is of course his opinion that they are themselves a fruit of induction. There
undeniably arises thereby a circle in his line of thought, since on the one hand he uses these fundamental
propositions as presuppositions of the inductive method, and on the other hand regards them as results of
induction, a circle that is unavoidable for all forms of pure empiricism. And
% --- p. 198 ---
\opage{198}Bacon wanted, after all, as we have seen, to have the mind made a blank tablet before the work of
knowledge begins.

Of the grounding of the first fundamental propositions by induction he speaks not in his doctrine of prima
philosophia, but in quite another context, namely where he wants to draw the boundary between philosophy and
theology. Bacon warns strongly against mixing philosophy and theology together; one thereby gets a fantastic
philosophy and a heretical theology. Their sources are altogether different. Philosophy starts from sense
observation; theology builds on divine inspiration. In science the human mind is affected by sense perception; in
faith it is affected by another spirit; therefore faith is nobler than science. And the more absurd and incredible
a divine mystery is, the greater the honor one shows God by believing it nevertheless, the more glorious is the
victory of faith. Once one has accepted the principles of religion, one can draw logical consequences from them,
just as from the first philosophical principles. But the significant difference is that in philosophy the
principles themselves are subjected to a closer testing by induction, like all other propositions; but in religion
the first principles stand fast by divine authority, as in the game of chess, where the first rules of the game
cannot be discussed. Yet Bacon thinks that there is still wanting a closer investigation of how far reason can be
applied in the religious domain, as well as of the question how far agreement in religious assumptions is
necessary.

Besides the ecclesiastical theology, which Bacon mainly has in view in these determinations, he nevertheless also
takes a natural theology to be possible, even if it is not of great extent. It can only refute atheism and show the
necessity of assuming a first cause. When one begins to find natural causes (causæ secundæ), one often becomes so
captivated by them that one thinks one needs no first cause. But later it is precisely the fixed mutual connection
of the causes that shows the existence of a Deity. Here belongs also the point that, even if natural science has no
use for final causes, which on the contrary corrupt science by applying a merely human motive to nature, the
justification for assuming
% --- p. 199 ---
\opage{199}final causes does not fall away, and these can very well be united with the continuous process which it
is the task of natural science to find. The final cause is like a nun; it is barren in science, but has religious
significance.

In his Essays Bacon discusses the relation between atheism and superstition. Here too he says that beginning
inquiry leads to atheism, but deeper inquiry to the assumption of a God. The chief causes of atheism, however, he
finds in religious controversies, in scandals among the clergy, in a bent for mockery, and in enlightened, peaceful
and happy times (for misfortune and adversity bend the mind to religion). Atheism degrades man, since man needs a
support for his spiritual being, so that the bodily may not drag him down too far toward the animal, and since man
is ennobled by his relation to a higher nature, as the dog is ennobled by its relation to man. But superstition is
nevertheless worse than atheism. Better no opinion of God than an opinion unworthy of God; the former is only
unbelief, the latter is insult. Superstition produces immoral qualities far more readily than unbelief does. It is
dangerous to the state, since it founds a power in the people that can exceed the power of the government. Then the
wise are forced to follow the fools. It is especially in barbarous times that superstition arises.

The duality that appears in Bacon's doctrine of faith and knowledge, and which clearly bears the stamp of being a
compromise, consistently casts its reflection into his psychology and his ethics. --- The sensible soul of man is,
like that of the animal, material. It consists of a fine fiery air (aura ex natura flammea et aërea conflata), which
streams out from the brain through the nerves and is nourished by the blood. Bacon here follows Telesio. He misses,
however, a closer demonstration of how this fine air can move the dense and hard body. With Telesio he also agrees
in ascribing to all things a receptivity to impressions, which he would rather call perception (perceptio) than
sensation (sensus). He misses a closer investigation of how the former can pass over into the latter, that is, how
the general receptivity to impressions can become sensation, or how unconscious mental life can pass
% --- p. 200 ---
\opage{200}over into conscious mental life. --- Besides the sensible and material soul Bacon assumes, like Telesio,
a spiritual soul implanted by God; but about this only religion, not philosophy, can teach us anything. --- The
special psychological observation of the phenomena of mental life, which goes its way independently of materialism
and spiritualism, Bacon does not know. Here he falls short of Sanchez and Campanella, to say nothing of Descartes.
Only in passing does he intimate it, in the proposition that we know nature through direct light, God through a
light refracted in the world as a medium, and man, who is his own object, by reflected light (radio reflexo).

As regards ethics, Bacon distinguishes between the doctrine of the exemplars and the doctrine of the means and
ways of approaching these exemplars. This latter doctrine (de cultura animi) has, he thinks, been greatly
neglected, and for the same reason that explains the imperfection of the sciences generally: people have preferred
to revel in notions of the ideal rather than laboriously to inquire how it can be realized. As regards the
exemplar, in its highest form it belongs to religion, not to philosophy, since it is supernaturally revealed. The
philosophical doctrine of the exemplar has on the whole been well set forth already by the ancient philosophers.
Bacon misses, however, investigations of the first sources of the ethical (fontes ipsi rerum moralium). He thus
demands a doctrine of the psychological development of the ethical. And he himself gives the main outlines of such
a doctrine. In every thing there is found a twofold need: by the one it seeks to assert itself as a whole; by the
other it seeks to act as part of a greater whole. The first has the individual good, the second the common good, as
its object. The ancient philosophers wrongly laid the greatest weight on the individual good, in that they set
knowledge, contemplation, as the highest, whereas the active life is surely to be set highest. Our task here in
life is not to be mere spectators. --- Political theory Bacon will not go into more closely. For the work (De
augmentis sc.) of which it was to form a part is dedicated to King James I --- and before such a master of the art
of government silence was for him the most seemly course! ---
% --- p. 201 ---
\opage{201}

Here at last we meet Bacon again as courtier. It was the misfortune of his life that he entered upon that career,
just as it was the misfortune in Bruno's life that he became a monk. But in spite of this he was able to develop
thoughts that were good expressions of the new paths on which inquiry was about to enter, and which especially
heralded the philosophical inquiry that was to contribute mightily to giving his fatherland an eminent place in the
history of the modern development of the spirit.

\begin{center}---\end{center}


% --- p. 202 ---
\hhchapter{Third Book}\opage{202}

\begin{center}\textsc{The Great Systems.}\end{center}

\bigskip

\noindent After the time of the new ideas and discoveries there comes a time of attempts to
order and systematize, to lead the many thoughts and facts back to
simple and fixed fundamental thoughts. These attempts were made with great confidence that the
right foundation had been found. In place of analysis, construction was put. This
had the great importance for thinking that it could now become fully
clear what lay in the points of view which the Renaissance and the new
natural science had brought forward. They were established with a dogmatic
assurance of which the minds of the preceding time had not thought, because
they did not give themselves so clear an account of the individual principles and their
range. What had earlier hovered more or less obscurely before the mind
% scan: „bavde“ (p. 202)
was now formulated with express consciousness. And out of the presuppositions so formulated
systems were built up, each of which laid claim to
take the place of the old scholastic system, which was only now wholly overthrown.
From scholasticism, however, was inherited the endeavor to give knowledge an absolute
conclusion, to bring thought to rest in a principle which itself should
contain no problem. Men wished to build as high as the building that had been
torn down had reached. The natural need, which always stirs more or
less strongly in the human mind, to bring coherence into all
representations that are taken to be valid, expressed itself here so vividly and energetically,
and at the same time in so brilliant a manner, as in no other period of
% --- p. 203 ---
\opage{203}the history of modern philosophy. This was connected with the fact that tasks had been set which
had been set neither before nor later with the same novelty and sharpness. It
was the new picture of the world and the new science that had to be worked together with the
rest of the spiritual content that stood firm for consciousness. It therefore had to be
the problem of existence that came to stand in the first rank. Bruno had treated
it on the basis of the new picture of the world. But now the new mechanical
explanation of nature had been added, and the great question of the relation between the
material and the mental was thereby set before thinking. The most important of the
hypotheses that are possible concerning this relation were put forward by the systems of the seventeenth
century with a clarity and energy that give these attempts of thought a
lasting value. But other problems weave themselves together with this one. The question of the
relation between God and the world even presses forward for a while in front of it. With
it, in turn, the question of the unity or multiplicity of existence is connected.
And finally it becomes an important problem whether the mechanical
explanation of nature makes it possible to ascribe any real significance to the concept of purpose.

The problem of knowledge and the problem of valuation recede before
the problem of existence, although they constantly exert their influence as more or
less consciously motivating and impelling forces. In Descartes, the first
in the series of the great systematizers, there is still, in the presentation as well, a
clear endeavor to find the way to constructive thinking through analysis.
In Hobbes and Spinoza construction overshadows analysis. In Leibniz the
analytic tendency begins again to work its way forward, as a transition to the
predominant importance the problem of knowledge and the problem of valuation were to acquire
in the eighteenth century.

The conditions of cultural history in the seventeenth century present an analogy to the
concluding, systematic tendency that at this time formed the main current in
philosophy. There is one fundamental mood that pervades the different domains,
politics, church and thinking. It is the time of the absolute sovereignty of the state. The state
has freed itself from ecclesiastical tutelage
% --- p. 204 ---
\opage{204}and now demands absolute submission of individuals and of the smaller circles.
The principle of sovereignty is even carried through, in its very sharpest forms, by the two
thinkers who mark the high point of construction. The individual now seeks shelter and rest
after the storms of the Renaissance and the age of the Reformation. Intellectual contemplation and
mysticism draw many to them. A tendency to quietism makes itself felt. But in the
philosophical systems these tendencies are satisfied through a thinking elaboration
of the new ideas and discoveries. They thereby acquired the significance of experiments for
testing the carrying power of important trains of thought.

\section*{1.\quad René Descartes}

\subsection*{a.\quad Biography and Characterization}

This man, the founder of modern philosophy, was born in Touraine on 31 March
1596, of a noble family. The sickly boy early showed unusual gifts,
and his father used to call him ``my philosopher'' on account of the many
questions he had to ask. So that he might receive a careful upbringing, he
was sent to the Jesuit college La Flèche, recently founded by Henry IV. He
always remembered his Jesuit teachers later with gratitude, and it was a
great sorrow to him that the Jesuits came forward as opponents of his philosophy. At La
Flèche he learned natural philosophy and philosophy according to the scholastic system, but was
