most occupied with mathematics, and very early he seems to have busied himself with
ideas that led him to his great mathematical discovery, the founding of
analytic geometry, the application of algebra to geometry. He has himself described
his development in the years of his youth in his epoch-making work \textit{Discours de
la méthode,} since it is at the same time the history of the genesis of his philosophy. On
leaving school he felt dissatisfied, despite the much he had learned.
Many facts he knew, and many fine thoughts had been imparted to him; above all he
admired the stringent method of mathematics. But those facts and thoughts stood
before him as disconnected fragments, and mathematics was to him only useless
cobweb-spinning.
% --- p. 205 ---
\opage{205}He then laid his studies on the shelf and threw himself into the worldly life of
Paris. His theoretical interest, however, he could not wholly deny: among
his papers was found a treatise on the art of fencing that dates from this time.
Soon he grew weary of the thoughtless life and suddenly vanished from his
friends, withdrawing to a solitary part of Paris in order to study in
peace. It now became more and more his ideal to lead a retired life devoted to
reflection and study. His motto became: ``Happy he who lived in
concealment!'' (Bene vixit, qvi bene latuit!). His friends found him after the lapse of two
years, and he was torn out of his solitude. Then he resolved to come to know
``the great book of the world.'' Perhaps practical life, which puts all
thoughts to the test, had taught men truths that learned speculation could not
discover! And besides, he wished to try himself under the vicissitudes of life.
He then went as a volunteer, at his own expense, into military service under Maurice of
Orange, though he used every quieter time for studies, especially
mathematical ones. From Holland he went to Germany, where the Thirty Years' War was about
to break out. He joined the army the Elector of Bavaria was gathering against the
rebellious Bohemians. While he lay in winter quarters (1619---20) at Neuburg on the
Danube, a scientific breakthrough took place in him, as he found the
general method that later guided him both in his philosophical and in his
mathematical studies. In a memorandum from that time, which was found among his
papers, he has even given a definite date for the emergence of the decisive thought:
--- ``the 10th of November 1619, when I was filled with enthusiasm and found
the foundation of a wonderful science!''\textsuperscript{42}) He lived
shut up in his room and gave himself up to thoughts that led him to his
general doctrine of method. It occurred to him that, as in general a work done by
many in common will be more imperfect than one carried out by a single person,
so our imperfect knowledge derives from the many different teachers who
each instill their opinions in us, from the influence of the different drives, from the
different conflicting judgments we hear from scholars and from practical people. Let us
then, in order to remedy this
% --- p. 206 ---
\opage{206}imperfection, begin afresh, disregard what has been handed down, and slowly erect
our building on one single foundation! The right method consists in accepting only
what is thought clearly and distinctly, in resolving every difficulty into its individual
parts, and in starting from what is simplest and most easily understood, so as then
step by step to come to the more composite questions. It was the
analytic method that stood before his inner sight in its whole generality. In
the mathematical domain this method led him to the idea of a science that
was more general than the individual mathematical sciences, since it investigates
relations, proportions in general, no matter whether they obtain between
figures or numbers or other things. It was a general theory of magnitude or
of functions, of which analytic geometry was a special application.
--- His thoughts worked so eagerly with these ideas that he fell into an exalted
state. He had remarkable dreams, and the next day he promised the Holy
Virgin to make a pilgrimage to Loreto, so that she might give his thoughts
success. (He did not fulfill this vow, however, until a convenient opportunity
offered itself). This vow of pilgrimage is a peculiar introduction to modern
philosophy --- a counterpart to the supernatural voice in which Herbert of
Cherbury a few years later heard a sanction of his ``natural religion''! ---
Yet he still thought it was too early to proceed to the working out of his
philosophy. After having taken part in the capture of Prague and in a campaign in
Hungary, he returned home to France and took over some estates that had fallen
to him by inheritance. His family would gladly have seen him married and placed in an
official position; but his mind was not set on that. He formed the resolution to devote
his life to science, and in order to be able to pursue it in peace, he moved to
Holland (1629). Before that he had repeatedly had occasion to
develop his philosophical ideas, especially about method, in literary circles in Paris. Two
remarkable unfinished treatises, which were first published long after his death,
``Rules for the Direction of Thinking'' and ``The Search for Truth by the Help of the
Natural Light,'' probably date from this time. They give a significant
% --- p. 207 ---
\opage{207}presentation of the analytic method. In the first period in Holland he (as
is seen from Discours de la méthode, parts 3 and 4) occupied himself with the
speculative ideas he later presented at length in his ``Meditations.'' He
laid the foundation of his theology and his psychology and found a way that, through doubt
itself, leads him to the starting point of all coherent philosophical knowledge.

When Descartes settled in Holland, it was surely not only because he
sought peace and because --- as he said --- he could philosophize better in a
cooler climate. A contributing reason was that he expected to find
greater freedom there for his inquiry. The reactionary movement that brought Bruno to
the stake and Galileo under mental torture had spread to France. When
some young investigators in Paris in the year 1624 wished to defend atomism
against Aristotelian physics in a public disputation, the theological
faculty declared the doctrine that everything consisted of atoms heretical, since it conflicted with the
Catholic doctrine of the Eucharist. The disputation was forbidden at the last moment, after nearly
a thousand people had assembled to attend it. The authors
were arrested and sent away from the city. And on 6 September 1624 the
Parlement forbade --- on pain of death! --- the putting forward of fundamental propositions that conflicted with
the old and tried authors, and the holding of disputations not approved
by the theological faculty! --- This certainly could not but make the atmosphere in
Paris less agreeable for a philosopher. In Holland he could expect to find
freer air. Besides the purely philosophical speculations mentioned, he occupied
himself in his new place of residence with studies in natural science and worked out a
treatise that was to be called ``The Universe'' (le Monde) and to give a presentation of
the development and structure of the world according to purely mechanical laws. He supposed that God
had created matter as a chaos and thereafter ordered it according to the same laws
that he now constantly follows in the preservation of the world. In this way he reconciled
his faith in the dogma of creation with the idea of a development according to natural, still
demonstrable laws, in the application of which to the genesis of our world-system he
stands as the predecessor of Kant and Laplace. But then came the
% --- p. 208 ---
% scan: „for“ (p. 208)
\opage{208}news of Galileo's condemnation and of the Inquisition's condemnation of the
Copernican doctrine, which Descartes had presupposed in his hypothesis --- and he
then laid the work aside. He would not, he wrote to his friend Father Mersenne, teach
anything that conflicted with the faith of the Church, and besides it was, after all, his motto that one
lived best in concealment (bene vixit, qvi bene latuit); he wanted above all to
have peace and be free from fear and vexation; and therefore under
the present circumstances he would confine himself to studying for himself alone. ---
Descartes's fine motto thereby received an ugly application, and this whole affair has
rightly been called a stain on his character. From his letters it is seen that he is
in full agreement with Galileo in his results. And even if one now has every reason to
suppose that Descartes was a sincere Catholic, there is nevertheless hardly any question
that fear, and perhaps most of all the need of peace, was the predominant
motive for his reticence. Later (in ``Principia philosophiæ'')
he presented his hypothesis of cosmic development --- but in disguised form.
He threw, as his first biographer says, sand in the eyes of the Inquisition.

Descartes had not yet had anything printed. And yet his philosophical and
scientific ideas were known in wider circles, partly in Paris, partly also in
Holland. The Cartesian philosophy, as has rightly been said, was
taught before it could be studied in print. Several of his disciples brought it
forward at the Dutch universities, where it occasioned hard struggles, which also
caused its founder much disquiet. Only in the year 1637, at the urgent
requests of his friends, did he have four treatises published
(\textit{Essays philosophiques.} Leyden 1637), which were to give
characteristic examples of his inquiry and its results. In the
first treatise (Discours de la méthode), the only one that has direct
philosophical significance, he gave here the history of his ideas and the main features of a new
epistemology and metaphysics. In the second and third treatises (Dioptrique,
Météores) he gave examples of a strictly mechanical explanation of nature, and in the
fourth (Géometrie) he founded analytic geometry. --- The
% --- p. 209 ---
\opage{209}complete presentation of his philosophy he gave some years later in his
\textit{Meditationes} (1641) and in \textit{Principia Philosophiæ} (1644).
He had had the Meditations sent in manuscript to several of the thinkers of the time,
e.g. the famous Jansenist Antoine Arnauld, Gassendi, Hobbes, and their
objections, with Descartes's replies, were printed together with the work itself,
which thereby acquires an interesting dialogical character. The discussion with Gassendi
continued for a long time and took on a rather bitter character. While the opposition
on the side of Gassendi and Hobbes was purely philosophical and therefore always very
instructive, the new philosophy met resistance for quite other reasons on the side of the Jesuits
and of orthodox Protestantism. At Utrecht, Gröningen and Leyden hard struggles
were fought, since the theologians held to the scholastic philosophy as a bulwark
for the faith. At last prohibitions against new opinions were issued. The Dutch, says
Descartes in a letter, honor the beard, voice and bearing of the theologians more than their
integrity. He considered the Protestant theologians worse than the Catholic ones.
He had come under a double fire. The Protestant theologians accused him of
skepticism, atheism, the dissolution of universities and of church and state, but
besides warned against his philosophy as papism; and the Catholic theologians
accused him not only of heretical opinions, e.g. the assumption of the motion of the
earth (which he had nevertheless sought to conceal), but also of inclining to
Protestantism and attending Protestant services.

The last work of Descartes that appeared in his lifetime was the interesting
treatise on the emotions \textit{(Les passions de l'âme),} which appeared in
1649. Its origin is owed to Princess Elisabeth of the Palatinate (a daughter of the
unfortunate Bohemian king Frederick of the Palatinate), with whom he was in lively
correspondence. In his letters to her he developed his ethical ideas. With
another gifted princess too he came into correspondence, namely Queen Christina
of Sweden. At her invitation he traveled to Stockholm in order personally to
introduce her to his philosophy. This stay ``in the land of bears, ice and rocks''
(as he calls it in a letter), as well as the life of the court, cannot have been favorable to his
health. The year after his
% --- p. 210 ---
\opage{210}arrival he contracted an illness that caused his death (1650).

The main features of Descartes's character appear clearly in his life. A love
of study and thinking, which was faithfully preserved through his whole life, and which in
particular moments, when new ideas dawned on him, could pass over into affect and
enthusiasm, was the most important and finest trait of his nature. His favorable and
independent circumstances made it possible for him to carry through the plan of life he had
laid down, which aimed above all at preserving peace and equanimity for the sake of his
studies. He did not lack courage, as he showed on his travels; but he
was too anxious and deferential toward authorities. The least attractive
trait in him is his lack of ability to acknowledge the merits of others. He
had a great feeling for what was new in his standpoint and firmly denied having
learned from his predecessors, maintaining that even the assumptions he had
in common with them received in his hands a quite different justification. He names Plato,
Aristotle, Epicurus, and among the moderns, among others, Telesio, Campanella, Bruno as
authors he has known, but --- despite all agreement --- has not learned
from, since his principles were quite different. Only Kepler does he acknowledge having learned
from; in particular, the German investigator's mechanical view of nature, his emphasis on
the importance of the concept of quantity and his partial discovery of the law of inertia were of
great influence on Descartes's philosophy of nature. But this trait too is connected
with his complete absorption in his own thoughts. As a thinker, sharp
distinction, the clear leading back to simple points of view, was his
chief quality. He has thereby done a deed of lasting significance:
definitively put an end to arbitrariness and fantasticality as far as method is concerned.
If errors are committed in his thinking, it is in any case easy to see where the error
lies. Descartes found an essential difference between geometry and metaphysics in
this, that in the former there is no difficulty about the first principles, whereas what matters
is to draw consequences from them, while in metaphysics, on the contrary, the great dispute
stands precisely about the principles themselves, or about the right determination of the
fundamental concepts, since it
% --- p. 211 ---
\opage{211}requires great effort of thought to work oneself free of the prejudices we are
inclined to cherish. This he himself gives (Resp. ad sec. obj.) as the reason
why in his Meditations he has followed the analytic method. But his
ultimate purpose was nevertheless a construction, a synthesis, that could present the whole system of our
knowledge in its logical grounding. And he often makes the transition from analysis to construction
all too quickly, takes the fundamental concepts as
finished before they are. Moreover, it was his conviction that concerning the
special relations of nature we can only arrive at hypotheses if we do not wish to
remain standing at
% scan: „vod“ (p. 211)
the individual data of experience. In putting forward such hypotheses he was very
bold, and his historical significance rests in part precisely on the
enthusiasm and the resistance he thereby aroused.

\subsection*{b.\quad The Method and Presuppositions of Knowledge}

Since in all knowledge, whatever object it concerns, we use our understanding,
it is, Descartes thinks, of importance to investigate this itself closely. The understanding
works alike everywhere; therefore the science of it becomes the universal science,
and the true method can therefore be only one. It consists essentially in
starting from what is simple and clear, and from that seeking to understand what is
composite and obscure. First of all one must by experience (\textit{induction}
or enumeration) bring together everything that is needed to throw light on the
question to be treated. This material is then ordered in such a way that the
% scan: „do“ (p. 211)
simplest, immediately evident relations are laid at the foundation. To find something
immediately evident is the first condition for being able to think. Every
transition of thought takes place by immediate intuition, \textit{intuition.} It is by
intuition that I learn that a triangle is bounded by three lines, that a sphere has
only one surface, that when I think, I must exist. By such immediate
intuiting the first principles are apprehended. There are propositions that are so simple
that we cannot think them without holding them to be true. To these belong:
that the same thing cannot both be and not be, that nothing cannot be the
% --- p. 212 ---
\opage{212}cause of something, and that there cannot be more in the effect than there is in the
cause. It is not, however, Descartes's meaning that such propositions immediately
are \textit{given.} He expressly maintains that intuition relies on
individual cases; but in the individual example a general truth can be found contained,
and we then know it immediately as self-evident (simplici mentis
intuitu), even if it is not yet formulated as a general proposition. The great
question of how general principles can be derived from individual cases,
so that intuition can pass over into a fundamental proposition, Descartes does not go into more
closely. He only admonishes us to be very cautious in putting forward
principles\textsuperscript{43}).

From the propositions that are clear in themselves we derive further consequences by \textit{deduction}.
It consists in a series of intuitions, in that by a
continuous movement of thought one goes from link to link and so connects
what was not immediately evident in its connection. If one here comes upon
something that cannot be comprehended, one must stop, since it would be fruitless to
go further. Either one lacks sufficient experiences, or one stands before
questions which, by the nature of the human mind, cannot be answered. If one succeeds
in carrying the deduction through, we have led the unknown back to the
known, and the first, simple truths have been extended to hold for
a larger domain. The items of knowledge accessible to us are mutually
connected by a wonderful bond and can be derived from one another by way of inference,
so that one will be able to find them if one only advances gradually
from the very simplest items of knowledge. --- Descartes, as is seen from the
way in which deduction is conditioned by intuitions of simple relations of experience,
is no opponent of the method of experience, just as he was always eager to
gather experiences and make experiments. But he maintains that scientific
knowledge is reached only by strict thinking, and that experience has its proper
significance in giving occasion for it. He does not, on the other hand, discuss searchingly
whether it is possible to reach a complete collection of everything that can
throw light on the subject (complete induction or enumeration), and he
% --- p. 213 ---
\opage{213}underestimates besides the necessity that the results of deduction be
verified. Science arose for him through inferences from data of experience and
consisted in logically deduced hypotheses. ---

But how far must I now go back to find the very simplest? Where
do I find an unshakable foundation for my knowledge? These questions Descartes answers
in Discours de la méthode (Chap. 4) and --- more fully --- in the
Meditations. About every content of knowledge, every object of knowledge, we can
doubt. All assumptions and sense perceptions may rest on illusion. Let us suppose
that an evil being had created us and incessantly instilled errors into us! Even
then there would still be one thing we could not doubt: our own thinking, our own
consciousness. All doubt, all error is after all a thinking, an activity of consciousness.
However many incorrect, non-existent things I represent to myself, the
very faculty of representation (vis imaginandi) still constantly proves its reality.
In so far as I think (or: have consciousness), I exist: Je pense, donc je
suis (Cogito, ergo sum). It is, as already remarked, an immediate
intuition that cannot be further grounded, any more than it can be further
defined what thinking or existence is. It has an immediate clarity and
distinctness that is the model and measure for every other insight. ---
Descartes declares it a misunderstanding to take that proposition as an
inference, but he has undeniably himself given occasion for this misunderstanding
by saying \textit{donc} (ergo)\textsuperscript{43\,b}).

That simple intuition, which cannot be shaken by any doubt, is not yet any
knowledge. How do we get further? How can we ground the objective validity of our
knowledge, the reality of what we represent and think? ---
To answer these questions Descartes uses the causal principle, or
rather the proposition that effect and cause must correspond to each other. This
proposition belongs, as we have seen, according to Descartes to those that can be discovered by
intuition. The natural light teaches us that there cannot be more in the effect
than there is in the cause. From this it follows that nothing can arise from nothing, and that the
perfect cannot arise from the imperfect. If we
% --- p. 214 ---
% print: „siges“ (p. 214) (misprint)
\opage{214}apply this to our representations, then it is clear that some of these
can be explained as having arisen from external causes, others as produced by ourselves.
But in neither of these ways can the representation of God as the infinite
being, the sum of all perfection and reality, be explained. Since I myself am
a finite being (of which my doubt and my desire convince me), I cannot
have produced such a representation. It cannot have arisen through the
combination of individual observed perfections; for then it would not
contain the unity and indissolubility that is the distinctive mark of the representation of God.
Every external cause is also finite. There remains, then, only that God himself is
its author. It is innate in us in the sense that our faculty of thinking, as soon as it
awakens to clarity, can by its own power grasp this representation as true. ---
By an innate representation (idea innata), then, Descartes understands not a
representation that is \textit{given} from the first, but one that we have the
capacity to develop. The idea of God, says Descartes, is innate in the same sense
as the representation of myself is. ``The innate representations proceed from
the faculty of thinking itself''\textsuperscript{44}). --- But the word ``innate'' was
fateful; it gave occasion to many misunderstandings.

When the reality of the representation of God has thus (be it noted: by virtue of the
causal axiom) been secured, a firm foundation, according to Descartes, has been won for the
reality of our knowledge. Everything I know belongs to the infinite
reality that this representation expresses, is one of the perfections the
concept of God contains, and thereby stands firm for me. Only a finite being
can err; the possibility of erring falls away in the infinite being, in whose
perfection I share through my clear and distinct representations.
Popularly, Descartes expresses this by saying that God, who is the ultimate cause of all
our sensations and representations, cannot deceive, since he is a perfect
being. But, when one looks more closely, he indicates a less external
connection between the representation of God and the reality of our knowledge. Since I can
perceive my imperfection only with the help of a more or less distinct
representation of perfection, and since the representation of God is the
% --- p. 215 ---
\opage{215}representation of the highest perfection, which comprehends everything, this
representation serves me as an ideal by which I can measure and correct my
imperfect knowledge\textsuperscript{45}). When Descartes draws the concept of God
into epistemology, it is not really God in the religious sense
he means; the idea of God is for him one with the idea of the continuous and
all-embracing connection in existence, in which everything that is to have
reality must be able to find its place. Thus it is said in the sixth Meditation:
``By nature as a whole (natura generaliter spectata) I mean nothing other than
either God himself or else the connection (coordinatio) of created
things established by God.'' What I am to acknowledge as true must be able to find its place in
this connection, which, then, could just as well be called nature as God. It is
by its connection with everything else that the individual thing acquires reality for me. The criterion
for distinguishing between dream and the waking state is that the experiences of waking life
I can connect with all my experiences and memories without a break in the
connection (perceptionem earum absqve ulla interruptione cum tota reliqva
vita connecto). --- This is the deeper meaning of Descartes's theological
grounding of the validity of knowledge. But interesting as this line of thought is,
the theological turn could nevertheless have been avoided altogether, since already
the causal principle, which is after all in its turn a presupposition of the reality of the representation of God,
is sufficient to bridge the gap between the knowing subject and
existence. The causal principle and the other first fundamental propositions Descartes
(in Responsiones secundæ) expressly exempts from the knowledge that is first
to be grounded by the representation of God. On a closer development of what
lies in the causal principle, it would appear that it leads precisely to the
assumption of a connection within which the individual phenomena have their
definite place. But the time for a closer discussion of the causal relation and the causal principle
came only a century after Descartes's time.
% --- p. 216 ---
% print: „Posiviteten,“ (p. 216) (misprint)
\opage{216}

\subsection*{c.\quad Theological Speculation}

Descartes begins analytically and critically, but very quickly leaps over into
theological and spiritualistic speculation. In his ``Je pense, donc je suis'' he finds
the starting point for both; for the present we keep to his theological ideas,
which are of interest to us in that they provide a stricter development and grounding
of the content of ``natural religion.''

Descartes denies that the existence of God can be proved from the world given in
experience. The series of causes could after all go on to infinity, and we must not confuse
the impotence of our understanding to follow such an infinite series with the necessity
of assuming a first cause. Moreover, the concept of God is presupposed as known
beforehand when I am to prove the right to call such a first cause
God. His proof is more direct. It consists, as we have already seen, in the
impossibility that the representation of an infinite being could be formed by a
finite being. This representation is indeed even a presupposition of the representation
of myself as a finite, limited being; for the finite presupposes a
limitation of an infinite; the infinite is the positive, by whose limitation
the finite comes into being. The concept of God is then formed by removing the
limitation (thus by the negation of a negation found to hand). With this
last determination Descartes comes considerably closer to the view that
the concept of God is formed as we form all our ideals: by extension and by
the removal of barriers (besides by the combination of features from different
contexts). Gassendi pointed out against Descartes that we in fact form ideal
representations by extension and combination; but Descartes answered that
this very capacity to extend the representation of the relatively perfect given in experience
presupposes that we have our origin from God. Instead of
following Gassendi to the study of the psychology of the formation of ideals (a subject that even
to this day has been very little treated), Descartes keeps to the
\textit{finished} representation of God: since it concerns something infinite, it supposedly cannot
have been produced by a finite being. This inference itself would after all only be
% --- p. 217 ---
% scan: „af“ (p. 217)
\opage{217}correct if it were the representation itself, and not merely its object, that
had to be infinite. ---

Yet Descartes has still another proof, the ontological. While there he went from
the representation of God back to the cause of this representation, here he seeks to
show that when we clearly and distinctly think the concept of an infinite and
all-perfect being, we must also assume the existence of such a being: for by
denying it existence we would deny it a perfection and so
contradict ourselves. Against this reasoning (which is found in the fifth Meditation)
Gassendi already objected that existence is certainly the condition for
something's being able to have perfections or imperfections, but is not in itself
any perfection. Descartes held to the point that we do after all ascribe
existence to things in the same way as we ascribe properties to them. ---

Descartes is clear that the concept of God whose validity he thinks he has
proved by the two proofs cited is not the popular one. Most people
do not regard God as an exalted and infinite being, the sole author of everything, but
think by the word God of a finite being that can be worshipped by men. It is
no wonder that there are those who deny the existence of such a God. His own
higher concept of God Descartes develops further by determining God as the
absolute substance. That God is a substance means that he is a being which is
able to exist by itself (per se), needing no other thing
in order to exist. Descartes does indeed also use the concept of substance of finite
beings (thus of soul and matter, which we shall go into more closely in what
follows); but he declares that it cannot be used in one and the same sense (univoce)
of the infinite being and of the finite beings. Since the finite beings
all depend on the infinite, they can only improperly be called substances. Especially
in his letters Descartes carries the strict concept of substance through. ``One cannot,''
he writes, ``prove the existence of God without regarding him as the most
perfect being of all; but he would not be so if anything happened in the world
that did not proceed from him. Natural philosophy already teaches that
% --- p. 218 ---
\opage{218}not the least thought can come up in the human mind without God's willing it
and having willed from eternity that it should come up.'' This is also one of
the reasons why Descartes rejects atomism: an atom would be something that
subsisted by itself; but only one being, the highest of all, can be independent
of every other being! --- In his writings Descartes expresses himself more vaguely,
since a wider and more popular definition of the concept of substance slips in
beside the strict one. According to the laxer usage, substance means the same
as thing or being. Substance is that which has certain properties. From
the properties we infer a substance. In this sense (as bearer of
properties) a finite being can very well be a substance. It is clear that
it must lead to unclarity when the two meanings of the word are not kept sharply
apart. But Descartes conceives soul and matter as substances also in the
sense of absolutely independent beings. And just as he thus applies the
strict concept of substance to finite beings, so too he conversely applies
the loose concept of substance to the infinite being, since the content of this concept
is after all all possible reality and perfection --- thus all possible
properties! It was therefore a criticism that cut deep into Descartes's system when
Hobbes and Gassendi objected against him that we have no positive
concept at all of substance as bearer of properties, since we know only properties
(accidents, attributes --- or, as we would now say, phenomena). Descartes
conceded that we do not apprehend substance immediately, but infer it
from the properties; but he maintains that we can think it, even if we cannot
form any image of it\textsuperscript{46}). Here too lay a problem
that came to play a great role in the subsequent philosophy. ---

It was with the help of the causal principle that Descartes arrived at the assumption of God's
existence. But this same proposition might seem to lead beyond the concept of God: for
must not God then also have a cause? From this difficulty Descartes seeks to
free himself by distinguishing between that which has its cause outside itself and that which
has its cause in itself. God
% --- p. 219 ---
\opage{219}must be, in relation to himself, what the cause is in relation to the effect,
thus be the cause of himself (causa sui). As the infinite being, God has an
inexhaustible power in himself, so that he needs nothing other than himself in order
to exist. In this way the concepts of substance and cause of itself are
closely connected. Antoine Arnauld, the great Jansenist theologian, who later became
an ardent Cartesian, objected (with a line of thought that already occurs in
Thomas Aqvinas) that the concept of cause of itself contained a self-contradiction and
in any case could not be applied to God. For, he said, no one can give
what he does not have, and for anyone to be able to produce himself, he would have to
exist already beforehand. And if God is cause, he is also effect;
the cause precedes the effect in time; but in God there can be no distinguishing
between past and future or between possibility and actuality. Descartes
answers that when we prove the existence of God by means of the causal principle, we must
also apply this principle to God himself, which is possible only by conceiving
him as the cause of himself. But he adds that the expression cause is used of God only
by analogy, on account of the imperfection of human knowledge,
and that one may well call God the cause of himself, but not the effect of himself,
since thereby something in him would come to stand lower than something else! The relation of time
has, moreover, no validity at all for God, since it is due only to human
apprehension, is a modus cogitandi. --- There seems then undeniably not to remain
much of the concept of cause in its theological application. The Cartesian
philosophy of religion could not but give rise to a need to discuss the justification and
significance of the application of our fundamental concepts in theology.

The proposition that the relation of time has no validity in God must particularly
be remembered when Descartes teaches that the eternal truths (such as, e.g., that a thing
cannot both be and not be, --- that the sum of the angles in a triangle is equal to two
right angles) depend on the absolute will of God. God's reason and his willing are not
distinguished. God has not first perceived the eternal truths and then laid
them down. His willing is eternal and
% --- p. 220 ---
% scan: „tit“ (p. 220)
% print: „hviken“ (p. 220) (misprint)
\opage{220}unchangeable like his essence. Here too the great difference shows itself between
Descartes's concept of God and the current one. There is really not a single
psychological expression that can be transferred to God. But this consequence
Descartes did not yet draw.

One difficulty remains, even if one grants Descartes to be right in all his
assumptions. Through our doubt we perceived our imperfection, and its concept
presupposed the concept of the perfect. Thus we rose up to the concept of God. But
after we have risen to this height, imperfection nevertheless continues to
subsist --- and how is it at all possible that imperfection could have
come into being, when it is an ideal and perfect being that lies at the foundation of
everything? Descartes answers that imperfection necessarily clings to everything
finite, and everything created is finite. It is, besides, only a negation that
brings about imperfection; and this negation makes the world more perfect than it
would otherwise be, since the multiplicity in the world thereby becomes greater. Even if
the eye is the most beautiful thing in the body, the other parts of the body still have no reason
to complain, since the body could not consist of nothing but eyes. Descartes
indicates in these remarks
% scan: „Bemærkuinger“ (p. 220)
a theodicy similar to the one Leibniz later presented at length.

\subsection*{d.\quad Philosophy of Nature}

By virtue of the criterion of truth Descartes had found, he concludes that our
sense-sensations must derive from something that is different from our
consciousness. But this something need not --- according to Descartes --- by any means be
so constituted as the senses present it to us. The significance of sense perception
is first and foremost practical; it is to inform us of what is beneficial
or harmful to us. And even if we regard it as the task of sense perception to
help us to a knowledge of things, it is not necessary that our
sensations \textit{resemble} things, provided only that they correspond to them as the word
corresponds to the thought. If we look to the way in which sense perception takes place, we find
that all impressions on the senses are contacts; it is thus only the
surface of things that we come into relation with. If we wish to think how
% --- p. 221 ---
\opage{221}things are constituted apart from the way in which they affect us, then
there remain only extension, divisibility and mobility as properties
we cannot --- even in our imagination --- think away. They are the simplest and
clearest representations we can have of matter, and it turns out that by
keeping to them --- thus to the purely geometrical properties --- we can reach
a simple and clear understanding of everything that goes on in the material
world. It is the phenomenon of motion that contains the explanation of all other
phenomena. On the other hand, nothing is explained by assuming ``forms'' or qualities
in matter. The qualities belong to our consciousness; but what really goes
on in the material world is only motions outside our organism or
within it. In science we must think of the material world as it
would be if no human being perceived it. --- It is the principle of simplicity that
played so great a role in the struggle for the new picture of the world, and that is now
used to ground the leading back of all the properties of matter to
extension and motion. A consequence of this leading back is that the
qualities are relegated to the subjective domain. Since Descartes can hardly have known
Galileo's ``Saggiatore,'' he has probably come to the principle of the
subjectivity of the sense qualities by his own path, through the attempt to
think through the conditions for a purely objective and strictly necessary
explanation of material processes. From notes in Descartes's hand from
the years 1619---20 it is seen that he did not yet at that time adhere to the mechanical
explanation of nature. The transition to it must have taken place in him in the years
1620---29, in connection with his studies in natural science, especially in the domain of optics
and physiology. Besides Kepler's influence, there has probably also been at work here
the influence of a circle of younger French investigators who adhered to
atomistic views and were especially influenced by \textsc{Sebastian Basso}, the
real renewer of the atomistic doctrine in modern times; Descartes himself names
Basso among his predecessors. It was two young men of this circle who wished to
hold the disputation in Paris mentioned earlier and thereby gave occasion to the
% --- p. 222 ---
\opage{222}terrorist decree against new opinions. Since Sebastian Basso in turn seems to have
been influenced by Giordano Bruno's writings, a historical
connection appears here between Descartes and the philosophy of the Renaissance. ---
\textsc{Harvey's} discovery of the circulation of the blood too has (as we shall see later)
intervened strongly in Descartes's line of thought.

In the attempt to explain all material phenomena by means of
extension, divisibility and mobility as the fundamental properties of matter,
Descartes proceeds deductively. He goes from cause to effect. He is fully
conscious that by this path only a hypothesis can be reached, since there is always the
possibility that the given phenomena could have been produced by other causes than
those we start from. Here, then, experience and experiment must come in as
confirming, and Descartes declares that for this so great a quantity of
experiments is needed, and such costly ones, that they far exceed his means and can be brought
about only by the cooperation of many. Descartes, then, has in no less a degree
than Bacon an eye for the significance of experience, but he lays greater weight than the latter
on the guiding principles and hypotheses. From Galileo he likewise differs
in his interest in principles and deductions. He took the deductive
procedure to be the properly scientific one and lacked Galileo's ability
to throw light on great and comprehensive relations through investigations of particulars ---
and this although he himself, in his doctrine of method, sets the intuition bound up with
individual observation as the starting point of thinking. But his task was a different one
from Galileo's. His mission was to bring to full clarity and consciousness that the
time was past when an explanation of nature could be reached by assuming mystical
forces or supernatural intervention. He set up the ideal for all
natural science: the derivation of phenomena from their causes with the same
transparent necessity with which a mathematical conclusion follows from the presuppositions laid down.
The principle of simplicity, to which he appeals, is really
at the same time the principle of transparency. In the ideal thus set up he was
not mistaken. But he ascribed to the deductive application of general principles,
and to the hypotheses grounded on it, greater significance
% --- p. 223 ---
\opage{223}than they have in reality, and his philosophy of nature thereby acquired
a dogmatic character, which, especially in the hands of the Cartesians, stood out markedly
and provocatively. In many a mechanical scholasticism took the place of the scholasticism of
substantial forms and qualities. ---

From the fundamental properties of matter it follows that there can be no absolute atoms, since
no limit can be set to divisibility --- that there can be no empty space,
for space means extension, and extension presupposes an extended being,
thus matter --- that the material world is infinite, for it is impossible for us
to set limits to extension, and where there is extension, there is also
matter. Further, it follows that when material changes occur,
these must all be explained according to the laws of motion, which thus become the highest
laws of nature. These laws too Descartes seeks to derive by deduction, and
the foundation for this deduction he finds in the concept of God, which in his
philosophy of nature comes to play a role analogous to the one it plays in his
epistemology. From the unchangeableness of God, which is part of his perfection,
Descartes derives that the sum of motion produced at the creation
is preserved during the preservation of the world (which according to Descartes is a constantly continued
creation). Motion can be distributed differently among the different parts of the
world, but no motion is lost and none begins anew. --- There lies
in the theological grounding Descartes gives of the old proposition of the
constancy of motion an involuntary admission that the fundamental properties of
matter from which he starts in his philosophy of nature are too simple and abstract. For
it turns out that it is really the divine force constantly at work in the world
that is constant; the constancy of motion is derived from the constancy of this
force. Had Descartes seen this clearly, he would also have found
a more correct proposition than the one he sets up. For it is not motion but
force, energy, that is constant. With his proposition Descartes gets into
difficulty at every transition from motion to rest or the reverse. But even
in its imperfect form his proposition is an interesting predecessor of the modern
principle of the
% --- p. 224 ---
\opage{224}conservation of energy. --- Special laws of motion too Descartes derives from God's
unchangeableness. So first and foremost the law of inertia, which in him for the first
time is consciously and systematically set up. It would, Descartes thinks,
conflict with the divine unchangeableness if any thing that can be regarded
as simple and undivided could lose the state it is in without an external cause.
Thereby the possibility is rejected that such a thing could of itself (sua sponte) and without
external influence pass over from motion to rest or the reverse.
Descartes probably arrived at the principle of inertia under the influence of
Kepler, who set up one half of it, but independently of Galileo. Already in
the treatise ``Le Monde,'' which was worked out before Galileo's Dialogues appeared, he had
in fact set it up. --- In setting up the principle of inertia Descartes makes a
reservation, leaving open the possibility that souls and angels could
act upon matter. This reservation is made in the interest of his
spiritualistic psychology, which we shall consider later.

Descartes's concept of matter bears the stamp of simplicity and clarity and is indeed also
grounded by the principle of simplicity. It is a natural outcome of the tendency
that also found expression in Kepler and Galileo and sought to lead all
qualities back to quantitative relations, whereby exact natural science became
possible. But just as he is inclined to overlook the hypothetical character of his deductive
results, so he is also inclined to regard his definitions, set up by
abstraction and by virtue of the principle of simplicity, as
exhaustive. He thinks he knows the essence of matter completely by the determinations
extension, divisibility and mobility, without, however, being able to give any guarantee
for it. When he speaks of matter as \textit{the extended substance,} he does not notice
that it is an abstraction he has made into a being subsisting by itself.
He has not proved the justification for regarding the geometrical properties of things
as absolute. For it does not necessarily follow from the fact that these
properties are the most important for the knowledge of nature. Properties such as extension,
divisibility and mobility may very well be due to the action of things upon us
(like colors, taste, smell, etc.), without their therefore
% --- p. 225 ---
\opage{225}\textit{resembling} the things themselves. And besides there is --- as already shown --- a
determination that is still more fundamental than the three properties Descartes
keeps to, namely force, energy. --- It became the business of subsequent inquiry
to discuss the questions indicated here. Descartes's philosophy of nature signified
for the time being, in all its one-sidedness, an immense advance in clarity. We shall now
briefly consider some of the most important applications he makes of the
general principles he has set up. It is always the fundamental thoughts we keep to; in
detail his explanations are often very unfortunate and arbitrary.
Spinning hypotheses was his fault; his greatness was the happy grasp of
general points of view.

When everything in material nature is to be explained from extension, divisibility
and mobility as the only properties of matter, it follows of itself that
final causes cannot be applied. But Descartes gives a theological rather than an
epistemological grounding for the exclusion of the
teleological explanation of nature. Since God is an infinite being, there must be much
in his working that we cannot grasp; it would be presumptuous to wish to search out his
purposes. There is, after all, in the unbounded world infinitely much that does not
affect us at all; what meaning can one then attach to its having been
created for our sake? The only purpose that can be thought for everything that happens
must be God himself. It is thus because we dare not set limits to the essence of the world
and of God that the teleological view is rejected.

If we are now to understand nature in detail, then according to Descartes we must start
from the simplest, most easily seen-through phenomena, from the processes we
constantly see going on before our eyes, and by means of them explain what
goes on in the small and in the hidden, and what has gone on in the past.
The principle of simplicity thus passes over, for Descartes, into the principle of actuality, which
requires the distant and unknown to be explained by the near and known. Best of all,
we must take as our foundation insight into the construction and working of our machines, since we
have the most distinct representations of these. Therefore, says Descartes,
% --- p. 226 ---
\opage{226}I describe the world as if it were a machine (terram totumqve hunc mundum
\textit{instar machinæ} descripsi). The present state of the universe we explain
to ourselves by supposing that the parts of matter from the very first (for matter and
motion were created at the same time) were in whirling motion about certain centers. In
these centers the smaller parts had to gather, which arose during the whirling
motion through the friction of the larger parts against one another. Thus arose the
various larger and smaller globes. Some of these globes gradually lost
their independence and were swept along by the vortices that go on about larger
globes. So it has gone with the earth. Descartes thinks that according to his theory he can
call the earth immovable, since it does not change place within the medium that
whirls it along with itself around the sun, and since, besides, outside the part of the universe
we can observe, there may be stars in relation to which the earth is
immovable! By such a subtle application of the relativity of motion
Descartes seeks --- as it turned out, in vain --- to escape standing as a
Copernican heretic. Gravity is explained as a consequence of the pressure of the vortex currents on
the parts in space, whereby they are pressed toward the globes or in any case held
in their vicinity.

Descartes is the first in modern times who has attempted to give a mechanical
theory of the evolution of the world-system. He does indeed make a polite reservation toward
theology, conceding that the world was created perfect and finished; he only wishes
to show the \textit{possibility} that the present state of the world can have developed according to
natural laws from a more imperfect initial state.
If one asks how this initial state is then to be thought, he answers that
it will not matter much whether we think of it in the one way or the
other: for by virtue of the natural laws matter will run through all the
states it is capable of assuming, so that after the exhaustion of more
or fewer imperfect states the present state will in any case be
reached. This declaration (Princ. phil. III, 47), which contains the program for all
mechanical theory of evolution, is of greater interest than Descartes's attempt to
depict the cosmogonic process in detail. --- A chief
% --- p. 227 ---
\opage{227}defect of his hypothesis was that it made no attempt to explain
the connection that Kepler's laws had established. These laws continued to stand as
an indifferent fact until Newton's brilliant thought discovered the physical
connection from which they could be derived, and which could be derived from them. ---

Just as Descartes seeks to explain the connection and development of the world according to
the general laws of nature, so he also seeks to explain the organism and
organic life according to purely mechanical laws. Not only astronomy, but also
physiology was in his view to be a purely mechanical science.
Just as in his cosmogonic hypothesis he abstracts from theology, so he abstracts
in his organic mechanics from psychology and thinks of the human
body as formed of material parts and working according to the laws of heat and motion,
without any soul (whether ``vegetative'' or ``sensitive'' or ``rational'')
intervening. This view, which is a consequence of Descartes's general
principles of the philosophy of nature (since the organism, as a material being, must fall
under the general laws of matter), received for him a confirmation from experience in
\textsc{William Harvey's} discovery of the circulation of the blood (1628). Harvey stands in the first
rank among the founders of modern natural science; he is for physiology
what Galileo was for physics. He gave the mystical forces their deathblow in the
domain of physiology by showing that the motion of the blood is not due to its own
force or that of the soul, but is determined by the contraction of the heart, which presses it
out into the body. The general laws of motion thus hold in the organism as
outside it. Descartes was one of the first eminent men to adhere
to Harvey's doctrine, and his adherence, which was declared in Discours de la méthode
(chap. 5), was a powerful support for the new doctrine, which had so much resistance
to overcome, since it stood in sharp conflict with the old view of
organic life\textsuperscript{47}). Descartes depicts in various writings
(especially in Traité de l'homme) how the human body can be conceived as
a mere machine. Here too his general way of looking at things has brought clarity
about, even if his special explanations were
% --- p. 228 ---
\opage{228}unfortunate. One of the greatest anatomists of the time immediately following, \textsc{Niels
Steensen}, acknowledged that the method Descartes introduced serves to
show the insufficiency of what had earlier been taught about the significance of the various
organs, and to put the questions about it in a clearer way.
Descartes extended the mechanical view that Harvey had carried through for
the circulation of the blood to the domain of the physiology of the nerves. In the nerves he assumes,
in agreement with ancient physiology, currents of ``animal spirits'' (esprits
animaux), which are formed by the fine parts of the blood, after being heated in
the heart, being carried up to the brain and filling its cavities, while the rest of the
bloodstream continues its way through the vessels. From the brain they stream out through
the nerves to the muscles. These currents can now, according to Descartes, be set in
motion by impressions that do not become conscious to us; this happens in involuntary
movements, as when in falling we put out our hands, or when we continue our
walk without thinking of it. Such involuntary movements can take place purely
mechanically, even against our will (mente invita et \textit{tanqvam in machina).}
Descartes expresses what goes on here by saying that the ``animal spirits'' are reflected
(esprits réfléchis), and he gives a clear description and explanation of what
is now called reflex movement. In animals there is, he thinks, no reason to
assume anything other than that all functions and actions go on in the involuntary
and machine-like way. There is no reason to ascribe a soul to them. When
the lamb flees at the sight of the wolf, it is because the rays of light that from the wolf's
body strike the lamb's eye, through the ``reflected'' currents of ``animal spirits,''
set its muscles in motion. And when the swallows come in spring, it is to be
explained in analogy with a clock's striking its strokes at a definite time. One sees, after all,
that animals cannot adapt themselves to new and more complicated conditions,
any more than a machine can. In any case: when we can explain the
behavior of animals purely mechanically, there is no reason for assuming an animal soul.
And when man can make wonderful automata, should not
nature be able to produce still more wonderful ones? --- The assumption that animals are
% --- p. 229 ---
\opage{229}mere machines recommends itself to Descartes also for the reason that, in
his view, one would otherwise have to ascribe immortality to them
% scan: „llghed“ (p. 229)
--- and should an oyster or a sponge be immortal? It is otherwise with
man, in whom, on account of the consciousness that makes itself known in each of us,
we must assume a soul, a thinking substance in interaction with the material
substance, with the capacity to intervene in directing the motions of the ``animal spirits.''
Immediately, according to Descartes, the soul stands in connection only with a single part of
the brain, the pineal gland (glandula pinealis), which drew Descartes's
attention because it is not, like so many other parts of the brain, a
double organ, and because it seemed to him to be placed about in the middle of the brain
and above the passage through which the ``animal spirits'' from the anterior cavities of the brain
are in connection with the posterior ones. The ``animal spirits'' strike against the pineal gland and
thereby affect the soul, awaken sensation, feeling and drive in it, and the soul
answers in turn --- likewise by striking (!) against the pineal gland and thereby directing
the animal spirits in a certain direction. Often (as in self-control) thrust and
counter-thrust go in opposite directions, and it then depends on who can strike
hardest!\textsuperscript{48})

Descartes has the merit of having described and analyzed reflex movement
and thereby thrown clear light on the involuntary activity in us. He has
also the merit of having maintained that mental activity is bound to
the brain, and immediately only to it. And finally he has --- despite the
imperfect anatomical presuppositions at his disposal --- the
merit of having presented the spiritualistic psychology with great
vividness and in its full consequence. His psychological theory we shall now
consider somewhat more closely.

\subsection*{e.\quad Psychology}

Only in man does Descartes assume a soul, and he conceives it as a being
distinct from the body, a substance of its own, the bearer of the mental
properties, just as the body is the bearer of the material properties. Since,
as we have seen, he carries his mechanical view of nature through into the
% --- p. 230 ---
\opage{230}domain of organic life as well, he must assume that in the organism, as little
as in the rest of material nature, can any motion arise that is not a
continuation of earlier motion, or any motion vanish that is not continued in a
following motion: for the principle of the constancy of motion is indeed a
chief proposition of his philosophy of nature. But when he now lets the soul
``push'' the pineal gland in order to set the ``animal spirits'' in motion, and
in turn itself receive ``pushes'' through the action of the ``animal spirits''
on the pineal gland, then motion must indeed arise or vanish at this point
without compensation! Even if one could attach any meaning to the soul's
pushing or being pushed, Descartes's spiritualistic psychology nevertheless
comes here into open contradiction with his philosophy of nature. In reality he
thinks of the soul as a material being when he lets it push and be pushed; this
is what always happens to spiritualism when it is thought through with full
clarity. Descartes's gifted correspondent, Princess Elisabeth of the Palatinate,
remarked quite rightly that it was easier to conceive the soul as material than
to understand how, if it is not material, it can move matter and be moved by
it. In one single place Descartes seems to want to restrict the soul's action
to bringing about a change of direction in the ``animal spirits'', which in
themselves could just as well move in the one direction as in the other; but
even this mere directing would then conflict with the principle of inertia and
could only be set up as an arbitrary exception to it.

When Descartes in general sets up the soul as a peculiar being, distinct from
the body, it is because consciousness and extension are such wholly different
properties that he can conceive them only as borne by different beings. Je
pense, donc je suis! was his starting point, and by thinking he meant, as he
expressly explains, consciousness in general (omnia, qvæ nobis consciis in nobis
fiunt). He could therefore, he remarks, just as well say: I feel, therefore I
am, or: I will, therefore I am. It is the fundamental fact of consciousness
that he wants to bring out. And he has deserved well of psychology by having
set up consciousness (mens) as the starting point, whereas
% --- p. 231 ---
\opage{231}the concept of soul (anima) is --- and especially was --- an ambiguous and
mystical concept. He thereby paved the way for modern empirical psychology. It
is not impossible that in this he was influenced by Vives, who distinguished so
clearly between mental phenomena as what is really given and the essence of the
soul in and for itself; Vives's psychological work is cited in several places
by Descartes. But Descartes thinks that in thinking or consciousness he has a
perfectly clear and exhaustive concept of the essence of the soul, just as in
extension he thinks he has a perfectly clear and exhaustive concept of the
essence of matter. Now if, says Descartes, I can think the concept of the soul
clearly and completely without needing to presuppose the concept of matter, and
can think the concept of matter clearly and completely without needing to think
of the concept of the soul, is this not proof that we have before us here two
wholly different beings or substances, independent of one another? (It is ---
as Descartes himself expressly remarks in one place --- not the individual body
that is substance in the strict sense, but matter considered as a whole: corpus
generaliter sumptum). --- We have earlier mentioned the double meaning in which
the concept of substance appears in Descartes. It does not merely denote a
bearer of properties, a something that ``has'' the peculiarities that
experience presents. Even in this vaguer meaning of the word Descartes infers
too much when he makes the ``something'' of thinking different from the
``something'' of extension; it could indeed be the same ``something'' that had
both properties! But in the stricter meaning substance is a wholly
self-subsistent and independent being. It lies, says Descartes, in the nature of
substances that they \textit{mutually exclude one another.} And this he assumes
of soul and matter, because he can think of each of them by itself alone
without needing to think the other party along with it. Man, then, is to
consist of two beings that mutually exclude one another! Thereby the
interaction between them becomes incomprehensible. When the one substance
affects the other, they cannot be wholly independent of one another; something
then takes place in the one that cannot be understood without my thinking of
the other. The relation becomes
% --- p. 232 ---
\opage{232}incomprehensible, and Descartes himself admits it. Those who never
philosophize, he says in a letter, have no doubt that soul and body interact
and make up one being. But philosophically it is impossible to think at once the
difference and the connection between soul and body. No inference and no
comparison, he says in another place, can teach us how consciousness, which is
incorporeal, can set the body in motion; but a sure and evident experience
teaches it to us daily; it is one of those things that must be understood
through themselves, and that are obscured when we compare them with other
things. --- Descartes speaks here as though he had seen the soul push the pineal
gland and receive a push in return! The knot of the problem is precisely that
immediate experience cannot decide the matter, but that inference and
comparison are our only way to an intelligible hypothesis free of
contradiction.

It is a common assumption that medieval dualism recurs in Descartes's theory of
soul and body. But what really led Descartes to his theory is his endeavor to
form clear and distinct concepts. From the independence of the concepts of one
another he then infers the independence of the corresponding beings of one
another. It is the clear and sharp characterization of the difference between
mental and material phenomena that is Descartes's great merit; but it is also
this that leads him astray. As a dogmatist he trusts in the completeness of his
concepts and in the agreement of existence with his concepts. The psychological
dualism that we have met in Telesio, Bacon and Campanella Descartes carries
through in extreme form --- and he has thereby contributed much toward leading
beyond it. He has formulated the popular metaphysics of soul and body so sharply
that its difficulties and contradictions stand out clearly. --- \textsc{Gassendi}
and \textsc{Arnauld} rightly objected against him that, because consciousness and
extension are the chief properties of the soul and of the body, it does not
follow that their essence is thereby exhausted. They have thereby struck
precisely the decisive point in Descartes's theory. ---

The consequence of Descartes's sharp distinguishing between soul and body is
felt in his special psychology. He investigates
% --- p. 233 ---
\opage{233}carefully which mental activities and phenomena derive from the soul itself,
and which are due to the body's influence on the soul.

Sense perception is due to the body; it arises through the ``animal spirits''
acting on the soul by way of the pineal gland. Yet Descartes emphasizes that
popularly more is counted as belonging to sense perception than should be. For
a distinction must be made between the motion in the brain produced by the
impression (which can also be found in animals), --- the action of this
brain-motion on the soul, whereby the sensation (e.g.\ of color) arises, --- and
thirdly the judgments that are involuntarily passed on external things on the
occasion of the motions of the bodily organs. Such an involuntary judgment
underlies the conception of things as external and as situated at determinate
places in space. It is the motions of the eye and of the head that, through the
corresponding motions in the ``animal spirits'', occasion the soul to pass such
a judgment. This third moment in sense perception is due to the soul itself.

Likewise there are two kinds of memory: one of material things, which rests on
after-effects or traces of the impressions in the brain, and one of mental
things, which rests on lasting traces in consciousness itself. --- Thinking
proper (intellectio) and representation (imaginatio) are distinguished from one
another in that in thinking proper the soul acts alone, but in representation
it makes use of bodily images. Representation, like sense perception and
material memory, belongs to the soul only insofar as the soul is united with
the body; the soul in its purity (anima pura) can be thought without
representation and sense perception. --- The difference between drive and will
likewise rests on the drive's being called forth by the body, while the will
belongs to the soul itself. Descartes ascribes to us an immediate consciousness
of the causal freedom of the will, although he admits that the indifference of
the will is rather an imperfection in our knowledge than a perfection in our
will. The will has a greater scope than the intellect; we can choose and hold
fast to something that we do not understand. The will is unlimited, the
intellect limited: by this Descartes explains the possibility of error. ---
The emotions (passions) are due to the body's influence
% --- p. 234 ---
% print: „(êmotions“ (p. 234) (misprint)
\opage{234}on the soul, but the inner feelings (émotions intérieures) arise in the soul in
consequence of its own thoughts and judgments. The inner, purely mental feeling
is indeed, so long as the soul is united with the body, accompanied by an
emotion, a sensuous feeling: but this is then due to the soul's action on the
brain, inasmuch as, e.g.\ in intellectual love, the mood of the soul affects the
pineal gland. In emotion joy precedes love, in inner feeling the reverse.
Although by this dualistic conception Descartes really blocks his own way to a
coherent history of the development of the feelings, he has nevertheless
deserved well of the psychology of the feelings by his attempt to trace the
various feelings back to certain elementary forms from which they arise by
combination. As elementary feelings he assumes wonder, love, hatred, desire, joy
and sadness. Of these and their combinations he gives a purely descriptive and
analytical account, constantly making use of his physiological theory. In
explaining the physiological conditions of the emotions he lays the chief
weight on the interaction between brain
% scan: „Hjørne“ (p. 234)
and heart. Only in the case of admiration, which he conceives as a purely
intellectual feeling, does he not think that any influence of the brain on the
heart takes place. He emphasizes the connection of the emotions with the
instincts: they dispose the soul to will what is useful and to shun what is
harmful; even without the soul's intervention, the motion in the ``animal
spirits'' that calls forth the emotion leads to the performance of purposive
actions. But the purposiveness that shows itself here is not absolute;
therefore experience and reason must intervene to correct it. Of importance for
the development of the feelings is the connection between a representation in
the soul and a certain state of the ``animal spirits''; only through such a
representation, not quite directly, can the will intervene determiningly in the
bodily motion. The struggle between reason and sensuousness is carried on,
according to Descartes, not within the soul itself, but is a struggle between
the soul or the will on the one side and the body or the ``animal spirits'' on
the other, and the struggle is over which can push the pineal gland the harder!
(Passions de
% --- p. 235 ---
\opage{235}l'âme. I, 47). --- Here too we find the spiritualistic theory carried
through by Descartes with all desirable consistency.

\subsection*{f.\quad Ethics}

When Descartes set up universal doubt as the starting point of his philosophy,
he provisionally excepted the moral domain, although he saw that his
philosophizing must have consequences for it too. So that his conduct of life
should not be left without guidance while he analyzed everything theoretically,
he set up (in the Discours de la méthode, chap. 3) the following provisional
rules for his conduct: 1. To keep to the religion and manners of his
fatherland. 2. To carry out consistently what he has once
% scan: „Gaug“ (p. 235)
resolved. 3. To strive to conquer himself rather than fortune, to subordinate
his wishes to the order of the world, and to remember that our own thoughts are
the only thing that is wholly in our power.

Later, when he had developed and published his philosophical views, he was
wary of venturing into the moral domain. The theologians, he says, who were so
angry with him on account of his physics, would certainly not leave him in
peace if he wrote on ethics. Apart from some statements in the work Passions de
l'âme, it is in his letters to Princess Elisabeth, to Queen Christina and to
Chanut (French envoy in Sweden) that we find his ethical ideas developed. They
are only a further unfolding of the provisional rules of the Discours de la
méthode; they betray the influence of Stoic philosophy, particularly of Seneca.

What means, asks Descartes, can philosophy teach us for attaining the highest
happiness, which vulgar souls vainly expect from the course of things, but which
we can only get from ourselves? Three means present themselves: clear knowledge
of what is right, firm willing of it, and the suppression of every wish and
every want that is directed at what is not in our power. Only through the
intervention of the will does knowledge come to rule in us, so that the motion
of the ``animal spirits'' follows it. Whereas the sensuous feeling or emotion
confuses our thought and
% --- p. 236 ---
\opage{236}makes it overvalue external goods, it now becomes possible to hold fast to
the inner enjoyments of the soul, which are eternal like the soul itself,
because they are built on the firm ground of the knowledge of truth. The most
important knowledge is the knowledge of God as the author of all things, as the
all-perfect being of whom our mind is an emanation, and the knowledge of the
soul as a being distinct from the body. Next comes the knowledge of the
infinity of the world, which roots out the belief that everything should exist
for the sake of the earth and the earth for our sake. Knowledge teaches us to
regard ourselves as parts of a whole (family, society, state) and to prefer the
interest of the whole to our own interests. But above all it is a matter of
distinguishing between what is in our power and what is not. Only the use of
our will is wholly in our power. In the feeling of this consists
\textit{magnanimity} (générosité), which is the key to all virtues. The
magnanimous man feels at once his own power to accomplish great things and his
own limitation. Instead of the notion of a capricious fortune, which is a mere
phantasm, it is a matter of holding fast to the conviction that everything
rests on the eternal and unchangeable will of Providence. Thereby the passions
are purified, and room is made for the spiritual love (amor intellectualis) of
God, the sweetest and most beneficial of all the feelings we can have in this
life (although it must be left to the theologians to decide whether it, such as
the natural man can have it, is sufficient to bestow eternal blessedness on
man). By sufficient exertion of heart and thought this feeling can also become
the strongest of all. --- As in Descartes's epistemology and in his philosophy
of nature, so in his ethics too thinking culminates in the idea of the infinite
being as the ultimate foundation. A mixture of rationalism and mysticism is
characteristic of Descartes, as of the seventeenth century as a whole. This side
of Descartes's philosophy was particularly developed by his immediate
successors.
% --- p. 237 ---
% print: „Udbredelee“ (p. 237) (misprint)
\opage{237}

\section*{2.\quad Cartesianism}

The Cartesian philosophy could not but exercise great influence on the age. By
its demand for methodical doubt and analysis, for disregarding all inherited
presuppositions, it could not but awaken free inquiry and lead to independent
thinking. On this point its most important significance doubtless lies. It has
thereby exercised influence on many more than those who became Cartesians in
the narrower sense of the word. By its demand for a purely mechanical
explanation of nature it intervened as a reforming force in natural science,
especially in physics and medicine, even though several of its special
hypotheses soon proved unfortunate. It stated the principle of mechanism with
an energy that has been of lasting significance. By its spiritualistic
psychology and its theological speculations it appealed to the current
conception, for which the resolute and absolute distinction between soul and
body was very clear and appealing, and which also found in the Cartesian proofs
a new foundation for agreement between theology and science, in place of the one
that was falling with the scholastic philosophy. In the last part of the century
we accordingly see the greatest minds of the French Church, \textsc{Bossuet} and
\textsc{Fénélon}, as zealous Cartesians. In eminent Jansenists, such as
\textsc{Arnauld} and \textsc{Nicole}, it likewise found adherents, although the
greatest figure of Jansenism, \textsc{Pascal}, here took up a special position,
which will be characterized later. Under Arnauld's direction an excellent
account of logic was worked out in this circle \textit{(La logique ou l'art de
penser.} 1662), which is still of interest and value. In the learned Order of
the Oratory too Cartesianism found great support. In wider circles it was
spread by popular lectures in Paris and the provinces. From Madame de Sevigné's
letters one sees what interest it aroused in the high aristocracy, among women
too. It gained no small spread in Holland through the appearance of several
younger university teachers. But both in France and in Holland it also met with
violent opposition. The Jesuits and the orthodox Protestant clergy sought in
every way to crush it. The new philosophy ascribed too much to free human reason
and gave
% --- p. 238 ---
\opage{238}doubt a dangerous significance. It taught the subjectivity of the sense
qualities, which was not compatible with the dogma of the Eucharist (especially
in its Catholic form), and besides it assumed the motion of the earth and the
infinity of the universe. The cause of theology seemed to be bound up with the
old scholastic doctrine. At several Dutch universities Cartesianism was
forbidden; in any case the Cartesians were kept away from theological chairs
and from offices in the ministry. In Rome Descartes's works were put in 1663 on
the list of forbidden books, and in France repeated royal decrees forbade the
teaching of Cartesianism at the universities. All this did not prevent it from
becoming the ruling philosophy, whose dominion was first broken by the tendency
proceeding from Locke and Newton, a tendency which it had, moreover, itself
prepared.

Among the more independent Cartesians the difficulties and contradictions in
Descartes's doctrine could not, in the nature of the case, but lead to attempts
to develop the master's thoughts further. In the dogmatic part of the Cartesian
system there were especially two points that contained stings. The one was the
relation between the absolute substance, which played so great a role in
Descartes's theory of knowledge, doctrine of nature and ethics, and the finite
substances, the finite world as a whole. How can an absolute being have a finite
world outside itself, and what reality can such a finite world have? This
problem could not but press forward particularly in an age that had a bent for
mysticism and for the recognition of absolute powers; it is indeed the age of
absolutism in politics, and it became so by a natural analogy in philosophy
too. Soon the Cartesian philosophy glides over into mysticism. The other point
was the relation between soul and body as substances that mutually excluded one
another and yet were to stand in interaction with one another. The master
himself had indeed even declared that this could only be understood so long as
one did not philosophize. There were some of the disciples who went on
philosophizing on this point, and who found here an incomprehensibility that
for them recurred everywhere in experience where different things were to act
on one another. By this road Cartesianism was led on to restricting knowledge to
establishing the succession and external connection of phenomena,
% --- p. 239 ---
\opage{239}while the inner connection between them was declared incomprehensible. Thereby
the treatment of the problem of causality by the later epistemology was
prepared. --- Both points work together in the so-called
\textit{occasionalism,} yet in such a way that the mystical element, the
tendency to gather all reality and all causality in the absolute substance, is
the predominant one. We consider in all brevity the most important
representatives of this tendency.
