Louis \textsc{De La Forge}, a French physician, stated clearly (in his
\textit{Tractatus de mente} \textit{humana,} 1669, in French as early as 1661)
that just as difficult as it is to see how the mind moves the body, just so
difficult is it to comprehend how one body can move another body. Perhaps,
however (cf.\ \textit{L. Stein} in Archiv für Gesch. d. Philos. I. p. 56),
another Cartesian before him, \textsc{Géraud De Cordemoy}, a Parisian advocate
who later became tutor to the Dauphin, had stated this thought; in that case he
must be regarded as the real founder of occasionalism. And while de la Forge
declares that the relation between the soul and the body is intelligible only
on the assumption that God has originally put them in connection with one
another, Cordemoy goes further and teaches that it is just as impossible for the
soul to get new representations as for the body to get new motions, if God does
not intervene. The finite beings, souls as well as bodies, are only occasions
for God to intervene. Thus, e.g., our will is the occasion for God to move our
arm. How the tendency to concentrate all activity in an absolute being
cooperates in the development of occasionalism is seen from the following
statement of the Cartesian \textsc{Sylvain Régis} (in his \textit{Cours de
philosophie)}:``In order to produce actions properly so called one must act of
oneself and by oneself, i.e.\ by one's own power, and it is certain that only
God can act thus. From this it follows that only God is a truly efficient
cause.''

These thoughts came to consistent development in the Netherlandish Cartesian
\textsc{Arnold Geulincx} (the name is pronounced Gölinks). He was born in
Antwerp in 1623 of Catholic parents, studied at Louvain and became professor
there. As a Cartesian he was in ill favor, and they contrived to drive him from
his
% --- p. 240 ---
\opage{240}post. He then went to Leyden, where he went over to Protestantism. In Leyden
too Cartesianism was struggling with the old scholasticism, and Geulincx met
with much opposition. After a series of straitened years, in which he worked as
a teacher of philosophy, he died of the plague in 1669, shortly after having
obtained a professorship at the university. The most important of Geulincx's
works that appeared in his lifetime is the \textit{Ethica} (1665) (which,
however, appeared complete only later, in 1675). The occasionalist doctrine
appears partly as the background of his ethics, partly --- more fully --- in
the Metaphysics published after his death (1695). --- His collected works have
recently (1891---93) been published by \textit{Land,} who has also written an
interesting monograph on him. \textit{(Arnold Geulincx und seine Philosophie.}
Haag 1895). In the following characterization we shall keep especially to the
thoughts that are of significance for Geulincx's ethical standpoint.

It is a peculiar mixture of rationalism and mysticism that characterizes
Geulincx's philosophy. And at the same time it shows itself clearly in him how
the problem of causality grows out of the Cartesian doctrine of substance.

Geulincx sets his ethics in sharp opposition to the prevailing, Aristotelian
ethics, which built on man's striving after happiness and laid great weight on
practice and unconscious habit. The ethical consists, according to Geulincx, in
obedience to the law of reason that God has implanted in us. Not in obedience
to God's will; for this is fulfilled whatever we may do, and besides:
everything, be it ever so exalted and holy, is subject to the discussion of
reason. Ethics presupposes the knowledge of nature. For man must come to know
his position in the world in order to be able to act rightly. Self-examination
(inspectio sui) is the foundation of ethics. It teaches me that only my thought
and my will belong to me, whereas my body is a part of the material world. And
in the material world I have produced nothing and can produce nothing. For by
what right dare I assert that I produce something, when I do not know at all
how it comes to be? And besides: my acting cannot reach beyond the limit of my
being, cannot flow out to other things. My will has significance only for my
own soul. Just as little
% --- p. 241 ---
\opage{241}can things act on one another or on me. How can the acting of a thing, which
is its own inner state, acquire significance for other things? It does not
itself know, after all, how the change outside it is produced; its inner state
does not, after all, extend wholly over into the other things! --- If you think
that you yourself move your limbs, although you do not know how it happens, you
might just as well think that it is you who composed the Iliad, or who makes the
sun go across the sky, and the child in the cradle could with the same right
believe that its will directly sets the cradle going when the mother fulfills
its wish to be rocked. If my willing and acting are to have significance beyond
my own being, the Deity, the only true and real cause, must intervene. The same
one who put motion into matter and gave it laws also formed my will and united
it with the material body in such a way that will and motion come to correspond
to one another, just as two clocks that go alike and strike at the same time,
not because the one acts on the other, but because they are produced by the
same one. Better than this image, which had already been used by Cordemoy and
has become classic in the discussion of the relation between soul and body, is
an image that Geulincx uses in his \textit{Annotata majora in principia
Cartesii.} When I can procure food and clothes for money, it is not the metal's
own natural power that brings this about, but its value rests on human
institution (ex hominum instituto, qvo valor iste ei consignatus est); in a
similar way it is not the material motion itself that is able to produce
sensations and representations in me, but this happens by virtue of divine
institution (nulla vi sua, sed instituto qvodam decretoqve divino). --- So
strongly does Geulincx emphasize the Deity as the \textit{only acting} being
that \textit{Land} is probably right that the expression occasionalism does not
quite fit his conception, since what \textit{occasions} does after all to some
degree \textit{cooperate.} He stands in any case nearer to the standpoint of
Spinoza and Leibniz than the other ``occasionalists''.

By the sharp emphasis on the difference and self-containedness of the
individual beings the problem of causality, which concerns the
% --- p. 242 ---
\opage{242}possibility of a transition and connection between them, clearly emerges. And
since the divine will is conceived as the unifying power that embraces all the
individual beings and acts in them, it is also intimated that the problem
becomes wholly insoluble if a unity in existence is not assumed behind all
differences, a continuity that extends through them all and beyond them all.
Since, finally, it is said that not motion itself, but an element that is put
into it or attached to it, is able to produce the mental states, a deeper
solution of the problem of soul and body than the Cartesian one is intimated.
Admittedly all this appears in Geulincx in a theological or mythological form
that prevents full clarity and consistency. But his philosophy offers great
interest through its energetic emphasis on the point that the acting of a thing
and its being cannot be separated.

Geulincx himself draws from his doctrine the ethical consequence that we stand
as spectators before the world, or rather before God (for the world cannot
itself produce a picture of the world in me; only God can do that, and as a
spectator of what takes place in the world I am therefore a constant miracle:
ego ipse spectator mundi maximum sum et juge miraculum!). We are absolutely
dependent on the will of the Deity. The supreme principle in ethics then becomes
that where I can accomplish nothing, I shall also will nothing: ubi nihil vales,
ibi nihil velis! The chief virtue in Geulincx's ethics therefore becomes
humility. A characteristic contrast to the magnanimity of Descartes and of
Telesio and Campanella! The vigorous self-assertion of the Renaissance had given
place to its opposite. I have, says Geulincx, no right to anything, not even to
myself. It cannot then be my task to further my happiness, but only to do my
duty. Yet happiness is perhaps furthered in just this way in the best manner;
for, thinks Geulincx, our misfortunes really come from our all too eager
striving after happiness. --- Into the details of this ethics of thoroughgoing
resignation we cannot go either. In many of Geulincx's ethical remarks a fine
and heartfelt mood comes to light. ---

Occasionalism gets its extreme form in \textsc{Nicolas
% --- p. 243 ---
\opage{243}Malebranche}. The mystical side of Cartesianism decidedly presses forward
into the foreground here. Malebranche, the son of a high official in Paris,
entered the Oratory in the year 1660, at the age of 22. His weak health had
already, while he was a child, nourished in him the desire for a quiet,
contemplative life, and the last part of his life he spent for the most part in
his cell. By chance he came one day upon one of Descartes's writings (Traité de
l'homme), and the clear development of thought interested and inspired him to
such a degree that for emotion he could scarcely finish reading it. From that
moment his life was dedicated to philosophy. His chief work is the
\textit{Recherche de} \textit{la vérité,} of which the first volume appeared in
1674. Of his other works, particular mention must be made of the
\textit{Entretiens sur la Métaphysique} (1687), which many regarded as his
finest work. As an author Malebranche is clear, elegant and witty, but also
somewhat verbose. The religious and the philosophical interest go together in
Malebranche, and he thought he had found the way to a complete reconciliation
between them. He did not see that his thinking led him to results similar to
those that Spinoza, whom he abhorred (le misérable Spinoza, as he calls him), had
already reached earlier. Just as little as Spinoza does Malebranche seem to have
known the earlier occasionalists (Cordemoy and Geulincx), a proof that a natural
tendency of development was stirring here. Malebranche kept his freshness of
mind into his high old age and died in 1715.

Malebranche begins in his Recherche de la vérité by investigating the causes of
errors and the means of freeing oneself from them. A chief source of error is
the belief that the senses, which are given us for practical purposes, should be
able to teach us to know the essence of things, and that we rightly transfer the
sensuous qualities that we sense to the things themselves. Material things are
in themselves only extended, not colored, hard, soft etc. The imagination leads
us astray, since it stands under the influence of sense perception and is also
dependent on our feelings. Malebranche undertakes an interesting investigation
of the psychological and physiological nature of the feelings and here states
% --- p. 244 ---
\opage{244}views (particularly on the role that the influence of the nervous system on
the blood vessels plays in emotion) that to this very day have attracted
attention. --- The errors both of sense perception and of the imagination
derive from the action of the body. But the understanding too, which after all
belongs to the soul in itself, must be subjected to a critique. The chief
question is, whence our representations (ideas) come. Only our own mental
states and activities do we apprehend immediately; other things we know only
through the representations or ideas we have of them. Now these ideas can be
produced neither by the things nor by ourselves: for no finite being can be an
absolute cause. To be a cause is something divine, and it is therefore
paganism to ascribe causality to finite things. There can be only one cause, the
Deity; the natural causes are only occasional causes (causes occasionelles ---
hence the name of this whole tendency of philosophy). When a ball is set in
motion because another pushes it, this other ball is not the cause. There is no
necessary connection between the motions of the two balls\textsuperscript{49}).
The collision of the balls is only the \textit{occasion} for the author of all
material motion to carry out the decree of his will by imparting to the pushed
ball a part of the motion of the pushing one. The moving force of bodies is only
his will, which upholds the bodies. And it is likewise with the human mind:
without God's action it can neither sense nor will. One cannot help oneself by
assuming that God has given bodies and souls the capacity to act, imparted to
them a part of his power. For God cannot do that: God cannot create gods! Just
as the true religion teaches that there is only one God, so the true philosophy
teaches that there is only one cause.

Our knowledge, then, can only be explained by our being dependent on God with
regard to all our thoughts. God stands in an immediate relation to every mind;
he is ``le lieu des esprits''. Through this connection with God, the author of
all things, our mind beholds the created things: the representations of them
must indeed be in God, since he could not otherwise have created them. Strictly
speaking, all the particular representations we have are only
% --- p. 245 ---
\opage{245}limitations of the representation of God, the infinite being. Every act of
thought is a closer determination of an indeterminate representation of what
is, which never lets go of us. In a similar way all our striving is at bottom a
striving toward God; only in union with him is true happiness, and it is he who
awakens the need of happiness in us; but we often stop at a finite, limited
good and regard it as the highest good --- just as we regard the finite beings
as true causes. Malebranche's ethics thus forms a complete analogy to his theory
of knowledge.

A difficulty in Malebranche's doctrine that we behold everything in God is
this: why it is then really necessary to assume an actual material world. Our
knowledge of nature, according to Malebranche, finds its full explanation in
God's action on us, and the actual material world is not needed at all: God's
representation of it (the intelligible extension, as Malebranche calls it) is
enough. According to one report \textsc{Berkeley}, on a visit to Malebranche
shortly before the latter's death, is said to have made this objection to him.
The same objection also came out in a correspondence that Malebranche's former
pupil, the mathematician \textsc{Mairan}, carried on with him. Mairan puts to
Malebranche the alternative: either material extension does not exist (since,
according to Malebranche, it is not needed to explain our knowledge of it), or
else material extension, as Spinoza taught, belongs to the very essence of God
(it then being not merely the intelligible extension, not merely the
representation of extension, but actual extension itself that we behold in
God). The old mystical philosopher was ill at ease at these objections, and the
correspondence with Mairan closes with his appealing to religious faith as the
ultimate foundation of all certainty. ---

While Cartesianism in the series of thinkers we have discussed here led over
into a theological idealism, in another circle of thinkers it helped to produce
new forms of skepticism. It contained several elements that could lead in this
direction. In the first place the principle of methodical doubt, the whole
critical tendency with which Descartes's philosophy
% --- p. 246 ---
\opage{246}began. Not everyone could pass over from doubt and analysis to dogmatic
settlement with the same speed as the founder of Cartesianism. In the second
place the very dogmatism of Descartes could not but challenge criticism,
especially as the dogmatic results themselves raised new problems, or old
problems in a new form. In the third place Descartes himself maintained an
opposition between positive religion and scientific knowledge, an opposition
that, when more sharply stressed, could lead to denying any decisive value to
the philosophical results Descartes might have reached, since they did not, after
all, lead to the highest truth. These motives worked in varying degree and form
on a series of men at the end of the seventeenth century who, for all their
differences, have this in common, that at least for a time they stood under the
influence of the Cartesian philosophy and later went over to a more or less
pronounced skepticism in philosophical respects. Only a quite brief
characterization of them can be given here.

\textsc{Joseph Glanvil} (1636--- 1680) worked his way in his youth out of
Puritanism and the scholastic philosophy that reigned in Oxford during his time
as a student. He became a great admirer of Bacon and Descartes, especially of the
latter, and cherished great hopes for the future of the science of experience. In
his chief work \textit{(Scepsis scientifica} 1665), which he dedicated to the
Royal Society, he spoke up for unprejudiced inquiry; he counted himself a
skeptic only in the original meaning of this word, in which it denotes one who
seeks. He joins Descartes entirely in the demand for a mechanical explanation of
nature (the mechanical hypothesis) as opposed to the scholastic doctrine of
qualities and forms. Nature is for him the great machine (the great automaton).
But he stresses more strongly than Descartes that all our knowledge of nature is
hypothetical; he traces out with great zeal all the grounds that indicate that
our knowledge will always be afflicted with imperfection; and he shows how
precisely the advance of experience brings new phenomena that may necessitate a
change in the hypotheses we formed earlier. Like the occasionalists, but
independently
% --- p. 247 ---
\opage{247}of them, he emphasizes very strongly the difficulties of conceiving an
interaction of soul and body, and like Geulincx
% scan: „Geulinex“ (p. 247)
and Malebranche, but before them, he comes to see the difficulties that lie in
any causal relation whatever. ``No cause'', he says (Scepsis scientif. cap. 23),
``do we know by immediate intuition, but only through its effects. When we infer
that one thing is the cause of another, we build only on its constantly going
together with it; for \textit{the causal relation itself cannot be sensed}
(causality it self is unsensible). But an inference from concomitance to causal
relation is not compelling.'' Glanvil here anticipates Hume. He lays particular
weight on such cases in which cause and effect are highly unlike one another,
and where we therefore can have no clear and necessary insight into the relation
between them. When, for all his critical and empirical sense, he defended the
belief in witches, it was because he held it dogmatic to deny witchcraft, since
one could not know a priori what causal relations took place in the world. His
skepticism thus led him not to put full trust in the ``mechanical hypothesis''.
He is here, like the kindred spirits who are to be named in what immediately
follows, evidence that the new thinking had not succeeded in driving out the
medieval notions.

High above all the men in this group, and high up into the sphere of eminent
minds as a whole, towers the figure of \textsc{Blaise Pascal}. Pascal too
(1623---1662) was influenced by Descartes and always kept some Cartesian views
in his circle of ideas. But his violently and deeply stirred inner life led him
to turn his back on philosophy. And yet there is always a certain kinship
between Pascal's religious thinking and Descartes's philosophizing: both
proclaim conviction free of authority. In his \textit{Fragment d'un traité du
vide} Pascal speaks out against the power of authority in the scientific domain,
and in the treatise \textit{De} \textit{l'esprit géometrique} he gives clear
indications of a doctrine of method, with express acknowledgment of Descartes's
Discours de la méthode. Later, after his religious breakthrough, he fights on
the side of the Jansenists against the validity of papal authority in the face
of facts. From Rome
% --- p. 248 ---
\opage{248}he appeals to heaven. And on the occasion of Galileo's condemnation he
utters (in the 18th Provincial Letter) the often repeated saying that if the
earth really goes round, no decree will be able to prevent it; it will go round
with all men, whether they believe it or not. Like Bruno and Descartes he
assumes the infinity of the universe and uses this thought in his religious
agitation to make the soul dizzy with the feeling of being a vanishing element.
He agrees with Descartes in his conception of soul and body. The body is to him
only a machine, an automaton. The sharp opposition between thought and extension
he uses to impress upon us man's spiritual worth: as a material being man is
admittedly to be reckoned as nothing over against the enormous masses; he is
only a reed --- but a \textit{thinking} reed! This is a genuinely Cartesian
thought. But even though this thought could fill Pascal with enthusiasm, it did
not for him contain the highest. Above the world of matter and of mind there
stood for him the supernatural world of love, which comes into being for man
through God's immediate revelation. Religion is the heart's immediate experience
of God (dieu sensible au coeur). What philosophical proof can lead to is at best
an abstract God, perhaps the God of truth, but not the God of love, the one true
God. Deism and atheism come for Pascal to much the same thing. What he yearns
for is to have his heart filled, and no inquiry could help him to that. But
besides this direct need to attach his feeling to an infinite object, another
psychological motive is also at work in Pascal, which conditions the decisive
difference between him and a figure such as Malebranche. It is the anguish with
which he feels himself existing in a world without limits, without stability, a
world concerning which knowledge can arrive at no firm results. Skeptics and
dogmatists contend; neither of the two parties can be proved right --- and yet
one of them must be right; the very contention between them shows that the
skeptics are at bottom right. It is no use wanting to ground the first
principles of knowledge on human nature: for where is human nature to be found?
It changes constantly, or else it is ruled by habit. In practical
% --- p. 249 ---
% print: „\textit{(Pens}\textit{è}\textit{es)}“ (p. 249) (misprint)
\opage{249}respects man is driven on by restlessness and vanity, or he follows custom and
usage. Man is full of oppositions and contradictions. Doubt and uncertainty
reign within him. ``He is to be judge of all things and is yet a wretched worm;
he is to be the bearer of truth and is yet a sewer of uncertainty and error; he
is at once the glory of the universe and its disgrace!'' --- In the face of all
these contradictions Pascal knows only one rescue: to take refuge in the
historically revealed Christianity. There his own loving and trembling soul
found rest. In order to lead others there he had devised an account that rested
on the biblical history and was to show how all oppositions and contradictions
in the nature and condition of man fell away through the revelation given in the
biblical writings. It is certainly a piece of good fortune for Pascal's memory
that the positive part of his apology for Christianity was not carried out, so
that his thoughts \textit{(Pensées)} on human nature and its
condition, which were only to make up the preparatory part of the apology, can
now act by their own power. It is the strong feeling of the weight and value of
life that animates Pascal. In opposition to the rationalistic tendency, which in
Descartes's philosophy received such good support, Pascal appeals to the living
personality, to the heart, to conscience as the ultimate decisive motive in the
view of life. A century before Rousseau he raises the question of the value of
scientific knowledge for personal life. In the face of his need of love and his
anguish of soul the answer becomes that ``the whole of philosophy is not worth an
hour's trouble!'' And he had the plan of writing against those who go too
deeply into the sciences (qui approfondissent trop les Sciences). That he
himself found the solution in the Christian, particularly the Catholic, more
particularly the Gallican, and most particularly of all the Jansenist doctrine,
he would not regard as the result of habit or tradition; he would not see that
here he still left a place open for the skeptical arguments that he himself had
brought into the field. And when he was asked what one was then to do --- what
one was to resort to in order to bring the doubting thoughts to rest, he
answered as a good Cartesian: We are automaton as well as we are mind.
% --- p. 250 ---
\opage{250}Both must be brought to believe, the latter by conviction, the former by habit.
And when conviction will not come, then begin with habit: act as if you
believed; take holy water and have masses said; it will make a beast of you and
make you believe (cela vous fera croire et vous abêtira)! That is cutting the
knot --- with the help of the philosophy that he at once uses and combats. ---

\textsc{Pierre Daniel Huet,} Bishop of Avranches (b. 1630, d. 1721), likewise
wished to abolish free inquiry in favor of religious faith, which in him appears
more pronouncedly than in Pascal as the faith of the Church. (Cf.\
\textit{Barach: Huet als Philosoph.} Wien 1862). He also still holds to
essential parts of the scholastic philosophy. For a time he had been a
Cartesian, and he felt great enthusiasm for the clear and simple method of the
new philosophy. But he later came to doubt whether there could be any rational
criterion of truth at all: we must then again have a criterion that this is the
right criterion of truth --- and so on to infinity! Descartes urges us to begin
with the simple and from it to pass over to the composite; but there is nothing
so easy and simple that it could stand as indubitable! Descartes thinks that we
cannot doubt thought itself; why not? We know thought, after all, only in the
same way as everything else: by directing our attention to it --- that is, by a
new thought. An absolute beginning is therefore not reached. Descartes's
``Cogito, ergo sum'' is an inference whose legitimacy can be called in doubt, and
his proof of the existence of God falls away when one sees that existence is not
a property. Only the authority of tradition and of the Church could furnish a
foundation for knowledge, and Huet, who was a learned humanist, offended at the
Cartesians' disdain for the ancients, therefore seeks to show that the religions
and philosophical systems of antiquity are due to a tradition stemming from the
Jewish people.

\textsc{Pierre Bayle} (1647---1706) had come to know Cartesianism during his
student years in Geneva, and in him it now displaced the scholastic philosophy
into which he had been introduced at a Jesuit college. He admired especially the
Cartesian demand for clear and
% --- p. 251 ---
\opage{251}distinct concepts and for leading complicated questions back to simple and
immediately evident principles. To several of the doctrines of Cartesianism he
later (during his university work at Sedan and in Rotterdam) took up a critical
attitude. He was quite as much a scholar and man of letters as a philosopher; he
took an interest in literary phenomena and speculative opinions in their motley
multiplicity, and the need of clear and distinct concepts led him to sharp
pointing up of the difference between standpoints, to decided emphasis on the
sting of problems, and to the unmasking of illusory solutions. In his masterly
characterization of Bayle \textsc{Ludwig Feuerbach} shows that Bayle was by no
means a systematic doubter, but that it was the difficulty and multiplicity of
the individual subjects that gave birth to doubt in him. Philosophy was for him
essentially criticism, its significance more negative than positive. Its results
decidedly conflict with those of theology, which Bayle shows in the case of a
single dogma (that of the Fall) by setting up a series of theological and
philosophical fundamental propositions that prove to be wholly incompatible with
one another. By this setting up (in his \textit{Réponse aux questions d'un
provincial)} Bayle opened the most important debate on the problem of evil since
Jakob Böhme's ``Aurora''. Already in his \textit{Dictionnaire historique et
critique} he had maintained (especially in the article on the Manichaeans) that
the assumption of two principles in the world, a good and an evil one, would be
very difficult to refute if it were defended by unprejudiced and acute thinkers.
If Augustine had not left Manichaeism, he would, thought Bayle, have been able to
make something of it that could have confounded the orthodox. By the way of
reason this doctrine could not, in his view, be refuted. According to Bayle a
choice must be made between reason and faith, and faith shows itself all the
more glorious the more contrary to reason the dogma is that is to be believed.
Bayle himself had certainly made his choice and was sincere in his sharp
distinction. But this choice has not prevented him from acknowledging a humanity
independent of all dogmatism. He lays (especially in \textit{Pensées diverses à
l'occasion de la comète)} great weight on the natural instincts that keep the
individual and the species
% --- p. 252 ---
\opage{252}alive without conscious reasoning. And as regards in general the conduct of
men in public and private life, he maintains that it is determined far more by
their natural temperament and their character than by their belief or unbelief.
He can therefore (which aroused great offense) very well conceive of a state of
atheists. \textsc{Ludvig Holberg} later remarked, precisely on the occasion of
this line of thought of Bayle's, that it made ``the whole disputation'' on
whether freethinkers could live morally ``in vain'' (Ep. 210). This line of
thought stands in natural connection with Bayle's zealous struggle for
toleration, and no less with his maintaining the independence of ethics over
against theology. The Cartesian method is applied by him here in an interesting
way: just as the proposition that the whole is greater than the part is so clear
and distinct that no revelation can be accepted if it conflicts with it, --- so
too the simplest ethical judgments, by which we distinguish between good and
evil, are so clear that no revelation can abolish them, but the validity and
value of every revelation must conversely be tested with them as the standard.
If one rejects the natural light here, one has no standard at all. On this point
a possibility comes out in Bayle that would make the conflict between faith and
knowledge lose its significance: namely this, that the natural instincts and the
immediate sense for the true and the good were sufficient to carry life! It
became the task of the eighteenth century to develop this possibility, which the
Renaissance had already seized in its discovery of man, but which the victorious
reaction had not allowed to get beyond the narrow circle of the thinkers. The
thought also still needed a fuller development. ---

\section*{3.\quad Pierre Gassendi}

formed a counterweight to Descartes, especially in the French world; yet more by
his method than by his results. He wished to be a philosopher of experience and
to plead the cause of sense perception against Descartes's intuitive and
deductive method. While Descartes, with
% --- p. 253 ---
% print: „Bevægelsesarsager.“ (p. 253) (misprint)
\opage{253}greater speed than his own method allowed, rose to the highest ideas and tended
to ascribe to them an immediate grounding in the human mind, Gassendi maintained
the empirical origin of our concepts. The very polemic \textit{(Disqvisitio
metaphysica.} Amsterodami 1644) that he published against Descartes is among the
most interesting documents in the debate between the empirical and the deductive
school. When Gassendi nevertheless ends in spiritualistic results, this is due to
his clerical position, which made it necessary for him to combine theology and
empirical philosophy. He was born near Digne in the south of France in 1592,
became a priest in 1617 and later professor of philosophy at Aix, a position he
later exchanged for a professorship of mathematics in Paris, in which he worked
until his death in 1655. In his youth Gassendi published a sharp critique of the
scholastic philosophy; after that the severe decree of 1624 against the new
doctrines and the condemnation of Galileo caused him to hold back. He occupied
himself with physical and astronomical studies, but did not venture to declare
himself for the Copernican doctrine. In his later writings he developed the
atomistic doctrine partly in the form of a renewal of the Epicurean doctrine. He
defends the personality and philosophy of Epicurus against the current attacks.
These works became of great significance, since the atomistic theory, which
Bruno and Basso had prepared, was excellently suited for use by modern natural
science. Gassendi was an admirer of Galileo, and the fundamental propositions
that he sets up for the knowledge of nature betray Galileo's influence
\textit{(Opera omnia.} Lugd. 1658). Starting from the premise that nothing can
become nothing or arise from nothing, and that something must therefore subsist
through all changes, he shows that if change is to be explicable at all, the
something that subsists through all changes, i.e.\ matter, must be a
multiplicity of solid and indivisible elements, i.e.\ atoms. Mathematically,
division can be continued to infinity, but physically divisibility has a
determinate limit. All changes in nature are to be explained by the motions of
the atoms: all causes are causes of motion. Between the atoms there is an empty
space; otherwise their motion would not
% --- p. 254 ---
\opage{254}be possible. Space, like time, is a thing of its own kind, to be called neither
a being nor a property. Only by contact can motion arise and cease; therefore all
causes must be material. The soul moves the body only insofar as it (as
vegetative and sentient soul) is itself material. Gassendi differs from
Descartes by maintaining that solidity, not merely extension and mobility, must
be ascribed to matter, and by setting a limit to physical divisibility. He
teaches moreover (under the evident influence of Galileo) that it is not motion
itself, but the impulse of motion (impetus), that is constant; the impulse of
motion does not fall away because motion passes over into rest. These
improvements of the new mechanical view of nature mark a significant advance. On
the other hand Gassendi recalls the predecessors of Descartes and Galileo,
especially Telesio, by assuming sensation in all atoms and using this
assumption, as well as the notion of a world-soul, in his philosophy of nature.
A similar half-heartedness appears in his attempt to combine spiritualistic
notions with his atomistic and mechanical doctrines: the atoms are created by
God; and to the proposition that all causes are material God and the
supernaturally implanted soul or part of the soul (anima rationalis or
intellectus) form an exception. This compromise was even more inconsistent than
the Cartesian one, since the soul itself was split into two parts, a material and
an immaterial. But it brought the advantage that the learned, and especially the
theological, world grew used to not regarding atomism as an absolutely godless
doctrine. Natural science could then make use of the atomistic hypothesis
undisturbed, as its needs required.

\section*{4.\quad Thomas Hobbes}

\subsection*{a.\quad Biography and Characterization}

When in the year 1588 the Spanish Armada was about to put to sea in order to attack
England, the terrifying
% --- p. 255 ---
\opage{255}rumors of war caused the wife of the clergyman in Malmesbury to give birth prematurely to a little
son. She bore, says the latter later in a versified autobiography, twins,
namely me and fear. He derived from this his timorous, peace-loving
temperament, which nevertheless --- as his life shows --- did not exclude energetic
thinking and a delight in literary feuds. The boy, Thomas Hobbes, received his first
instruction in his native town and at the age of 15 came to Oxford, where he learned the
scholastic logic and physics, which interested him very little. He left
the university early and became tutor to a young nobleman of the family of
Cavendish. To this family he remained attached all his life.
His position gave occasion to repeated journeys round Europe. He gathered
experience of the world and cultivated literature with zeal, especially the classical
historians and poets. He followed the events in his native country with
an attentive eye, and a translation of Thucydides which he published in 1629 was not
prepared without regard to the political storm clouds that already in the first
years of the reign of Charles I threatened on the horizon. For a time, however, his
interests were drawn in an entirely different direction. By chance he came upon
Euclid's geometry and thereby discovered that there existed a rigorous deductive
science. He had not suspected this until then, for mathematics did not yet belong to the
regular subjects of instruction in England, and was indeed even regarded as
devilry. He now obtained a model for his thinking. A mathematician by profession
he did not, to be sure, become; his later attempts in that direction turned out most unfortunately and
involved him in long literary feuds in which he decidedly drew the
shortest straw. But the foundation of his philosophical tendency had now been laid.
The great weight he lays on deductive thinking places him close to Descartes,
while it places him in decided opposition to Bacon, with whom he had
stood in a personal relation, having in Bacon's last years been
of assistance to him as secretary and in the translation of his books into Latin. From Bacon
he received no decisive philosophical impulses, even if one can perhaps show on
individual points that, after his own peculiar philosophizing had been set going by
impulses from other quarters, he
% --- p. 256 ---
\opage{256}took up Baconian ideas and wove them into his system. The problem that set
his thinking going he is said, according to what his first biographer relates, to have
received in a conversation that probably took place in a scientific
circle in Paris, and in which the question was raised in passing
what sensation is. As this question was not answered, Hobbes set himself to
think about it. It then dawned on him that if material things and all
their parts were always at rest or in uniform motion, all difference
(discrimen) between things, and consequently all sensation, would fall away. From this he then
concluded that difference of motion (diversitas motuum) is the cause of everything. Now he thought,
by his own account, of nothing but motion day and night, waking and
sleeping. It had dawned on him that the deductive method, which he had not long
before come to know in its most perfect form, was excellently suited to
application on the basis of the fundamental proposition that everything is motion. Probably he
also at the same time (c. 1630) arrived by his own path at the conviction of
the subjectivity of the sense qualities\textsuperscript{50}). That Galilei had already in 1623
stated this principle, Hobbes did not know. Only after it had dawned
on him does he seem to have become aware of Galilei's writings, and later
on a journey to Italy he came to know the man of whom he himself later
(in the dedication of De Corpore) said that ``he first opened to us the first
gate to the whole of physics, namely the nature of motion.'' Thereby his already
begun line of thought received a more definite form and a firmer basis. Galilei is said
also to have drawn his attention to the possibility of treating ethics
deductively in analogy with physics. If this account is correct, then
Hobbes's whole system had thereby found its provisional conclusion for him. For a long time yet, however,
only in his mind and thought and in the confidential exchange of ideas that took
place within a circle of men whom the monk Mersenne, Descartes's and Gassendi's
friend, gathered about him in Paris, and to which Hobbes also belonged. ``From the
moment,'' says Hobbes in his autobiography, ``that I had communicated my ideas to Mersenne,
and he in turn had made others acquainted with them, I too was counted among
% --- p. 257 ---
\opage{257}the philosophers. His cell was better than all schools.'' It was also Mersenne who
later sent Descartes's Meditationes round to various thinkers, among
others Gassendi and Hobbes, and thereby called forth one of the most remarkable philosophical
discussions of the 17th century. Hobbes's critique of Cartesianism is an
interesting document for the illumination of his own philosophy. Hobbes, to whom the
late Lord Cavendish had secured economic independence, now intended, when in
the year 1637 he came back to England after several years' absence, to
work up his ideas into a threefold system: Corpus --- Homo --- Civis, a
doctrine of the laws of matter, of man and of society, as far as possible by the deductive
method on the foundation of the general laws of motion. But the execution of this great plan
was prevented for a long time by the outbreak of the English Civil War. His
temperament made him look with anxiety on the political strife growing in
passion. It seemed to him to shake the foundation of all ordered
social life. He feared that the elementary drives would stir with
unbound and unconditioned violence. His experience of the world had taught him how much
the impulse of self-preservation and egoism can work not only for good but also
for evil, and that a strong authority is needed to keep the stream of these forces
within its proper bed. He was ultra-conservative precisely because in his
theory he was ultra-radical and went back to the purely elementary presuppositions.
But surely his moving in the circles of the high nobility also contributed much to
determining his political sympathies. He therefore misjudged the significance of the
English Revolution, although the grounds he gave for his condemnation were purely
naturalistic and thereby diametrically opposed to the grounds that held the
adherents of the Stuarts together. For Hobbes the principle of authority was a derived principle; for
them it was an absolute, divine, supernatural principle: this was the great
opposition that came out as soon as Hobbes worked out his political theory. And
it is the grounds given, not the results, in Hobbes's political theory that have given
it its lasting and in a certain sense unique significance in modern ethics and
political theory. In the year 1640 he composed a work that contained his
% --- p. 258 ---
% print: „ecclesiatical“ (p. 258) (misprint)
\opage{258}psychological and ethical-political theory in its main features. This work, which
circulated in copies and was later published in two parts, Human Nature and De
Corpore politico, has recently (1888) been published by TØNNIES from the oldest
manuscripts and with the original title \textit{Elements of Law.} It is one
of his freshest and most instructive works and ought to form the foundation of every
study of Hobbes. It was composed with the troubled circumstances of the time in view and as a
word of warning. Hobbes believed that he would have been exposed to personal danger
from the side of the opposition if the King had not dissolved Parliament. When
the unrest increased, and when the new Parliament began to proceed severely against
the King's men, he fled (at the end of 1640) over to France in order there
to be able to continue his studies in peace. But the grave circumstances of the time gave him no
peace to turn his thoughts away from political problems, and he then worked up
the last part of ``Elements of Law'' into an independent work \textit{(De
cive),} which appeared in 1642 in a small, in 1647 in a larger edition. It was intended
to be the third part of the whole system. From the earlier treatise it differs
by stressing far more strongly the opposition between the state of nature and life
in the state, and by insisting on the necessity of the sole authority of the power of the state in
religious matters. Hobbes was an opponent on principle of all hierarchy, the
Protestant as well as the Catholic. This made his stay in a Catholic
country and in a circle of exiled clerical royalists insecure. There came a
formal breach when he had once more laid his studies in natural philosophy aside
in order to write a political work. This was the famous work \textit{``Leviathan}
or the Matter, Form and Power of a Commonwealth ecclesiastical and civil'', which
appeared in London in 1651. It was named after the mighty sea monster mentioned in
the Book of Job, of which it is said: ``Upon earth there is none like him; he is
made without fear.'' With this mighty one Hobbes compares the absolute
power of the state. He here carries through the doctrine of sovereignty founded by Bodin and Althusius
to its extreme consequences --- but on a naturalistic basis and in an
antihierarchical spirit. That it was not especially the absoluteness of the royal power but of the power of the state
that he asserted
% --- p. 259 ---
% scan: „1651.“ (p. 259)
\opage{259}was interpreted as if with this work he were angling for Cromwell's favor. And the
episcopal royalists were indignant at the statement (in a concluding section which
was left out in the later Latin edition of 1670) that just as Elizabeth had
overthrown the Catholic hierarchy, the Presbyterians had overthrown the Episcopalians, only
to be overthrown themselves by the Independents --- ``and so we are brought back
to the independence (independency) of the first Christians.'' The consequence was that Hobbes
lost his position as teacher of mathematics to the young King Charles II and was
denied access to the court. In England conditions were now calmer; there was again
a firm and ordered power of the state, an exerciser of sovereignty, and Hobbes thought that
it was now safest for him to return home. After a toilsome journey in
wintertime he came home to England at the end of 1651, and he could now enjoy
the benefit of complete freedom of the press to work in peace on the publication of his works,
which he had never lost sight of. In 1655 appeared \textit{De corpore,}
which comprises logic, the doctrine of fundamental concepts (philosophia prima), the doctrine of
motions and magnitudes, and the doctrine of physical phenomena. In 1658 appeared
\textit{De homine,} which for the most part is an optics (to illuminate the
nature of the sense of sight) and otherwise gives only brief outlines of the psychology of
language and of the feelings. This second part of the system can measure itself neither in content nor in form
with the first part of Elements of Law or with the opening chapters of
Leviathan. The third part of the system was the earlier published work De cive, and
the whole system was thus now complete. Then came the Restoration, which Hobbes greeted
with joy. He came into favor with his former pupil Charles II, who often conversed
with him. He lived with the Cavendish family as an old student, much
occupied with mathematical and theological polemics. His antihierarchism was made into
atheism, and a Hobbist counted as the same as what was later called a
freethinker. Although he ascribed to the power of the state the sole right to determine what
should be taught, he himself interpreted the Bible in a critical and rationalistic spirit. For
him the original faith of Christianity was only this, that Jesus was the Messiah, not
any speculative doctrine whatsoever. The eternity of the punishments of hell he rejected. He
assumed no incorporeal spirits.
% --- p. 260 ---
\opage{260}But for the most part he referred to the incomprehensibility of the doctrines of faith and advised
accepting them without thinking about them, just as one does best to swallow
bitter pills whole without chewing them. Hobbes preserved his physical and mental
energy into his high old age; at 87 years of age he translated the whole of Homer into iambic
meter. He died at 91 years of age (1679).

Hobbes is an acute and energetic thinker. Thinking, he says in the preface
to De corpore, will be esteemed the highest enjoyment if one but once experiences the
joy that is caused by the meeting between our mind and the glorious universe (pulcherrimi
mundi cum anima congressus). He made the most thoroughly considered attempt in
modern times to make the knowledge of natural science the foundation of all
our knowledge of existence. It is the most profound materialistic system
that has been set up in modern times. But Hobbes's writings, which
are distinguished by their vigorous and clear exposition, contain besides many interesting
remarks in logical and psychological respects. He may be called the founder of
English psychology, and thereby of the properly English school in philosophy.
Above all, however, it was his ethical and political points of view that became of
far-reaching significance. By his bold, though one-sided naturalism he set
people's thoughts in motion, partly by provoking them. He broke with scholasticism in
the domain of the human sciences, just as Copernicus had broken with it in the domain of
astronomy, Galilei in that of physics and Harvey in that of physiology. By the
side of these men Hobbes, with justified self-esteem, places himself as
founder of the science of society: this (he says in the preface to De
corpore) is no older than his book De cive. By his naturalistic grounding of
ethics and politics he roused a movement which has aptly been compared with
the one Darwin roused in the 19th century.

\subsection*{b.\quad First Presuppositions}

Science stands for Hobbes in opposition partly to sensation and memory, partly
to theology. It does not, like
% --- p. 261 ---
\opage{261}sensation and memory, stop at the individual phenomena, but seeks to know them
from their causes; now it goes from cause to effect, now from
effect to cause. From this it follows that science can only concern what has an
origin; thereby theology is excluded, the doctrine of the eternal God, who has not
come into being. --- So at least I define science, says Hobbes.
Perhaps someone wishes another definition; that is his affair. Definition is a free
and arbitrary matter, a mere explanation of what we mean by a name, and the use of
names is arbitrary. Science begins with the definition of the underlying
concepts. One arrives at these concepts by analysis (resolutio) of what is
given to sensation (a sensibus ad inventionem principiorum). The validity of the
principles, the fundamental concepts, itself cannot be the object of
proof, only of definition. They are known in themselves --- otherwise they are
not principles. Since they are fixed by arbitrary naming, they are
produced by ourselves. It is art or construction, not science, that
fixes the principles: here we ourselves produce the truth: ratiocinationis prima
principia, nempe definitiones, \textit{vera esse facimus nosmet ipsi} per
consensionem circa rerum appellationes (De corpore. cap. 25, 1., cf. cap. 3, 8---9).

This sharp emphasis on the purely arbitrary in the setting up of the first presuppositions
Hobbes makes properly only in the work De corpore; in Elements of Law
it does not appear so clearly. It is due to the ever more predominant
deductive method: when all true science is deduction, the presuppositions of deduction,
which cannot themselves be deduced, must come to stand as purely
arbitrary. But then it cannot be understood what Hobbes means by saying that
the principles must be ``known by themselves'' (per se nota), if this is to
mean more than that one is conscious of what is meant by the words employed. And
this immediate consciousness itself is then a presupposition which properly ought to be
set up by itself. It is a kind of intuition or, as Hobbes himself in one
place\textsuperscript{51}) calls it, a reflection. Besides, Hobbes declares, as we know,
that we arrive at the principles by resolution or analysis (resolutio, analysis) of
% --- p. 262 ---
\opage{262}the given; it is then not altogether arbitrary what principles we set up, and
there is more in the setting up than mere naming. Indeed, Hobbes says
expressly that analysis is an inference from the given to the principles or
definitions (analysis est ratiocinatio a supposito ad principia, id est, ad
definitiones. De corp. cap. 20, 6): thus the first principles of inference are
themselves set up by inference, in so far as they are set up by analysis. It turns out,
then, that the situation in setting up the principles is more complicated than the
pure theory of arbitrariness assumes.

Hobbes has also in another way limited the arbitrariness in setting up the principles,
or in naming. One cannot, for instance, give one and the same thing
two mutually opposed names. Of this principle Hobbes declares (De corp. cap. 2,
8) that it is the principle of all inference, and so of all science. But it is
surely not itself set up arbitrarily; it precisely restricts arbitrariness: if
I have given a thing a name, I cannot add to it \textit{any whatever}
other name. The same holds everywhere we construct: only the first step
can be purely arbitrary; the following ones are determined by the first. --- Apart from
the wavering and one-sidedness that shows itself here in Hobbes, it is his great
merit to have brought out so sharply the active and constructive element in
knowledge. Neither in Descartes nor in Bacon did this come sufficiently
forward, and the decisive point where one turns from induction and analysis to
deductive thinking therefore did not receive sufficient illumination with them. ---

When we have now arrived by the way of analysis at the first principles, the task is to
derive the phenomena from them. As a general principle Hobbes sets up that there is
a single cause of all the properties that the phenomena present, namely
\textit{motion.} This assertion, he thinks, needs no proof; it will be
granted by anyone who thinks it through without prejudice (De corp. cap. 6, 5). To
this proposition, that all change is motion, a series of other
propositions attaches itself, which Hobbes sets up on occasion without examining their closer
relation to one another or to the one first set up. Thus the general
causal principle (which is set up in the work on freedom
% --- p. 263 ---
\opage{263}and necessity), the principle of inertia, the proposition that the cause of motion must always
lie in the motion of a contiguous body, and the proposition of the conservation of matter.
In a single place, however, Hobbes proves the proposition that all change is motion
by means of the causal principle and the principle of inertia, and for these two
propositions too he sets up proofs on occasion, which, however, on closer examination
turn out to presuppose precisely what was to be proved\textsuperscript{52}).

From the proposition that all change is motion, and the propositions more
or less closely connected with it, Hobbes now wishes to build up his system by the deductive way.
After logic has first examined the method, and philosophia prima the
most important fundamental concepts, geometry discusses the mathematical laws of motion,
mechanics the effects of the motion of one body on another body, physics
the effects of the motions that take place in the small parts of bodies, the doctrine of
man and the state (what would now be called the human sciences) the motions
that take place in men's minds and determine their conduct toward one another. If
the system could be developed purely deductively, we should in these various disciplines merely
have progressive special applications of the general laws of motion, starting from
the first self-created presuppositions, through the series of steps Corpus --- Homo ---
Civis. And this is evidently the ideal that stands before Hobbes. But just as we
have seen that the doctrine of the self-creating activity in the fixing of the presuppositions
is, by his own account, subject to considerable
restrictions, so it turns out also that at three places in the system
there is a break in the strict deductive connection, since the relations are too
complicated for a single, progressive method to manage them. These three
points lie at the transition from geometry to mechanics, from mechanics to physics, and
from physics to psychology.

In the first place, the system would form a strict unity if mechanics could
without more ado be derived from pure geometry, without wholly new presuppositions being
taken up. But in mechanics the cause, or the concept of force, comes forward,
% scan: „from“ (p. 263)
while geometry presupposes only extension and the general
% --- p. 264 ---
\opage{264}logical principles. That Hobbes lays no weight on the difference between geometry and
mechanics is connected with his not distinguishing between ground and cause. Yet
he admits the difference in so far as he concludes the geometrical section of
De corpore with the remark: ``In this section we have considered motion and
magnitude in themselves, and in an abstract manner. The next section deals with
the phenomena of nature, i.e. with the motion and magnitude of real bodies.''
(De corp. XXIV, 9).

Although Hobbes lets science go partly from effects to their causes,
partly from causes to their effects, he is nevertheless clear that only when one
goes from cause to effect does knowledge have strict necessity. When we
begin with a given phenomenon and regard it as effect, the knowledge of
the cause can always be only hypothetical: what one can find out can only be
the manner in which the phenomenon \textit{could} have been produced; but whether it
really \textit{has been} produced in this manner cannot be decided purely
deductively. When we start from the given and seek its real causes,
we do not ourselves produce the principles, but must try to find the principles which
have been employed by the Author of nature in producing it. Herein physics differs
from geometry and mechanics (De corp. cap. 25, 1. De homine, cap. 10, 5). ---
We must therefore, at the transition from mechanics to physics, halt our deduction in order to
examine what phenomena are given, and form our hypotheses by analysis
of them. The question is whether something analogous does not already hold for the presuppositions of logic,
of ``the first philosophy,'' of geometry and of mechanics, so that these too
are not apodictic but of a hypothetical character. This seems to follow
from the fact that analysis is necessary in order to find them\textsuperscript{53}).

The third point where the successive advance in the system gives place to
more complicated relations is at the beginning of the human sciences. For, says Hobbes,
the causes of the mental motions can be found not only deductively, that is,
from the propositions of mechanics and physics; here everyone has, by
self-observation (per uniuscujusqve proprium animum examinantis experientiam),
access to knowledge of the principles on
% --- p. 265 ---
\opage{265}which political theory builds: the human feelings and drives and their
tendencies. One can therefore come to political theory not only by the long
series of deductions from geometry through mechanics and physics, but also directly, inductively,
from the facts of self-observation, which are set up as new starting points
for deduction. (De corp. cap. 6, 7). It is the independence of empirical psychology
over against the science of material nature that Hobbes here
acknowledges. He had all the more occasion to call attention to
this point since he had himself, as we know, published psychological and political-philosophical
writings (Elements of Law, De cive and Leviathan) before the work which in
the system comes before the human sciences (De corpore). He ought here to have
gone a step further. For what could be grasped deductively from
physics can in any case only be the physiological processes that
are connected with the mental phenomena. As phenomena of consciousness the
mental phenomena can be known only by the inductive way of self-observation, and the break
in the deductive process is therefore greater than Hobbes sees.

The last two points are, moreover, on closer examination connected. For the reason
why at the transition from mechanics to physics we must break off deduction is
properly this, that physical phenomena appear to us as qualities, but
these as such are due to the sentient subject. What is given in physical phenomena
is thus subjective phenomena, whose objective cause is to be sought, which
cause must necessarily --- on Hobbes's presuppositions --- be motion.
(De corp. cap. 25, 3). It is thus the mental phenomena that at both
points break the unity of the method and of the system.

\subsection*{c.\quad The Object of Science}

In agreement with his first fundamental proposition, that all change was motion,
Hobbes declares that the object of science is the corporeal. By body (corpus)
is understood everything that is independent of our thinking and fills a part of
space. As independent of us it is called substance.
% --- p. 266 ---
% print: „Fremgangsmaede,“ (p. 266) (misprint)
\opage{266}Body and substance are one and the same. An incorporeal substance is for Hobbes a
contradiction. But substances and bodies we do not perceive immediately, only by
inference. It is only the properties (the accidents) that we observe; of substance
as such we have properly no representation, although we infer that there
is something that underlies the properties. The essential properties of body
are extension and motion. All other properties are only subjective
phenomena in the sentient consciousness. Space and time too are, according to Hobbes,
subjective, since he understands by space and time such representations as
the extension and motion of bodies call forth in us, and which we could retain
even if all bodies disappeared.

One might interpret this to mean that Hobbes renounces knowledge of
the essence of things and keeps only to their properties, in so far as these can
be apprehended with the help of sensation. And Hobbes has even a very lively
understanding of the fact that the very circumstance that something can appear to us and be apprehended by us
is for the philosopher the most remarkable of all facts. ``Of all phenomena,
the very fact that something appears to us as phenomenon (id ipsum \textit{τὸ
φαίνεσθαι)} is the most wonderful of all, so that, since the phenomena are principles for
the knowledge of everything else, sensation is the principle for the knowledge of the
principles themselves, and all science is derived from it, while its own causes can only
be found by beginning with it.'' (De corp. cap. 25, 1). Here the
sentient consciousness is set as the first starting point for all knowledge. It is a
statement that recalls Descartes's ``Cogito, ergo sum,'' and which might seem to
conflict with the assumption that Hobbes's system is materialistic. It is also
only in so far as Hobbes proceeds strictly deductively from his original
postulates or definitions that he can be called a materialist. His materialism
falls away every time the strict deductive procedure, which would derive everything
from the one proposition that change is motion, is broken. That Hobbes wants such a
derivation is certain, though it is also certain that he cannot achieve it, and
that he sees that he cannot achieve it. Whether one will call him a materialist
% --- p. 267 ---
\opage{267}or not therefore easily becomes a dispute about words. \textsc{Edv. Larsen} understands (in
his monograph on Hobbes, Copenhagen 1891. p. 186) the matter thus: Hobbes
is a materialist only in his doctrine of method, because our knowledge in his opinion could
only give an account of motion, but he does not wish to give a materialistic
metaphysics. Hereby, I believe, a distinction between method and system is
put into Hobbes which he does not know. He is too much of a dogmatist to distinguish
in this way. He trusts that things are such as they must be according to our
definitions. He is a materialist in the same sense as Descartes is a
spiritualist. Both become entangled in contradictions through their assumptions; but of these
contradictions they were not conscious.

We therefore also see Hobbes, just after he has brought out with great emphasis
what problem lies in the very fact that something becomes a
fact for us, pass with great composure to asking whence, then,
sensation, the principle of all knowledge, comes, and answer this question in
consistency with his first fundamental proposition: since all change
% scan: „Forandriug“ (p. 267)
is motion, sensation too, which is due to a change, must be motion.
Sensation, he says, is \textit{nothing but} a motion in the small parts of the sentient
body. (De corp. cap. 25, 2, cf. Leviathan, cap. 6). And what he
here says of sensation he says, in the objections to Descartes, of
consciousness as a whole (mens \textit{nihil aliud erit} præterqvam motus in
partibus qvibusdam corporis organici). Thus for Hobbes psychology
properly belongs entirely under the doctrine of motion. And even if he distinguishes between
motion itself and its appearance (apparition) to us, as when he
insists on the subjectivity of the sense qualities, he nevertheless maintains that \textit{what
really exists,} when we have sensations or feelings, is only
motion. The feeling of pleasure is, e.g., nothing but a certain motion in the heart
(pleasure is nothing \textit{really} but motion about the heart, Elements of
Law, VII. 1). Appearance, apprehension, feeling, consciousness become for
Hobbes, where he speaks strictly deductively, only a seeming (nothing really, El. of
Law, I. 2, 5). --- But a seeming, we must add, that presents a great
% --- p. 268 ---
\opage{268}problem: for motion, according to Hobbes, can produce only motion, and it then stands
as an inexplicable marvel that at certain points, besides motion, there
comes into being the seeming, the ``apparition'', which we call consciousness. It is Hobbes's
great significance that he has so clearly established the limitation of the materialistic hypothesis.
His energetic deductive thinking has here led him to the
decisive point. No later materialistic attempt has been carried through with the
clarity and freedom from prejudice of his. He has thereby given a contribution of lasting
value to the elucidation of the place of mental phenomena in existence. What is
cast in one piece always carries its reward with it. ---

As regards Hobbes's special doctrine of nature, it need only be remarked that he no more
than Descartes assumes an empty space, but conceives the smallest solid particles as
moving in an ethereal fluid. Motion vanishes for him no more than
for Gassendi in the transition to rest. He conceives space and time as composed
of small parts, each smaller than any part experience can show us (minus
qvam datur); even in such vanishingly small parts of space and time there is
motion, but only as tendency to motion (conatus, endeavour). And this
tendency to motion does not vanish because an equally great opposite tendency to motion
holds it in check; it then becomes tension (nixus). By the help of these concepts, set up (De
corpore, 15, 2; 22, 1), it becomes possible for Hobbes, who here (like
Gassendi with his corresponding ideas) stands under the influence of Galilei,
to maintain the continuity of motion in a more perfect manner than Descartes. And he
has (as is seen from a treatise first printed in the appendix to
Tönnies's edition of Elements of Law) applied these thoughts in a polemic against
Descartes (El. of Law p. 215).

\subsection*{d.\quad The Limits of Knowledge. Faith and Knowledge}

Every representation we can form is, according to Hobbes, finite and limited.
A knowledge of the infinite is therefore excluded. When one hears the words ``eternal and
infinite,'' one must be prepared to hear absurdities. ``Infinite'' can only
% --- p. 269 ---
% scan: „16:“ (p. 269)
\opage{269}be used in a negative sense, of that for which we can set no limits.
This word signifies nothing in the thing itself, but a lack of power (impotentia)
in our mind. We express by it our own limitation, not a positive property
of any being. --- For Descartes, conversely, the infinite was the positive
concept: the finite arose by limitation of the infinite. These are two
different views of life that express themselves in this opposition.

Just as little as there can be a knowledge of the infinite, just as little can there
be a knowledge of the world as a whole. Only a few questions can be raised about
the whole of the world --- and none of them can be answered. Science cannot
say anything about the world's magnitude, duration or origin, not even whether
it has an origin at all. The knowledge of the first things,
the first fruits of wisdom (primitiæ sapientiæ), is reserved for the theologians, just as in
Israel the first fruits of the harvest were offered to the priests. So Hobbes expresses himself
in De corpore (cap. 26, 1). He further argues here that we cannot
close the causal series in such a way that we could know for certain that it could not
be continued further back. Even if we assumed a first cause, this cannot
be something unmoved, for nothing can be set in motion by something that is not itself
in motion; what we stop at must then be something eternally moved. But there is in
itself no contradiction whatever in assuming that the world has no beginning.
Therefore, says Hobbes, I cannot praise those who boast that they
have proved by natural reasons that the world has an origin. --- In a
remarkable opposition to this stands the manner in which Hobbes expresses himself in his
political-philosophical writings, (El. of Law I, 11, 2; De cive, cap. 14---16;
Leviathan, cap. 11---12). He here acknowledges, to be sure, the incomprehensibility of God, but he
finds no difficulty in inferring back from the world to God: by continually
going back, we must necessarily come to an eternal cause which in turn has
no cause! Yet it is not only theoretical but especially practical reasons that
lead to natural religion, since man, on account of his weakness and
dependence, renders God obedience. --- This opposition is
% --- p. 270 ---
\opage{270}all the more striking as it cannot be explained by the
political-philosophical writings being older than De corpore. For in the objections to
Descartes, which were written at about the same time as De cive, it is
expressly maintained that the creation of the world cannot be proved. The matter can hardly be explained
in any other way than that Hobbes in his political-philosophical writings, from
practical motives, attributed greater probative force to the grounds of reason than he
strictly could. --- But he always maintains that we can form no representation
of God. It goes with us here as with the blind man who warms himself at the fire: of
the cause of the warmth he can form no representation. We dare not transfer our
properties and states to God --- neither pain nor need nor understanding
nor will; for they all presuppose a limited being in order to have any
meaning. Only negative, superlative and indefinite expressions are permissible, and they
are then used to express our obedience and admiration, not what God in himself
is. The word incorporeal too, applied to God, is only an honorific predicate. For since everything
that is, is body, God must also be so, which also agrees with the opinions of the
old Fathers of the Church. --- Natural religion is not sufficient,
for reason is imperfect and the affects are strong. A revelation is then
necessary. But the discussion of it belongs in political theory. For since it goes beyond
human comprehension, it can be grounded only on authority, and authority
a private man can obtain only by working miracles; since now the time of miracles is past,
the state ought to decide all religious questions. Religion is not philosophy but a law;
it demands not discussion but obedience.

\subsection*{e.\quad Psychology}

Hobbes opens the series of eminent investigators in the domain of psychology who
are the pride of English philosophy. With his usual vigorous grasp and his
eye for the great, elementary lines he has given valuable contributions to
the understanding of mental life. It was properly the endeavor to obtain an
empirical foundation for ethics and political theory that led him into
% --- p. 271 ---
% scan: „Descartes.“ (p. 271)
\opage{271}psychology; but this gains independent interest in his exposition. --- We
first bring forward Hobbes's physiological theory, in so far as it concerns the conception
of the life of consciousness. --- What goes on in the external world is, as we
have seen, only motion. When this motion propagates itself inward through
sense organs and nerves to the brain and from this to the heart, it meets here with
a certain resistance and reaction, since the inner organs are themselves constantly in a
certain motion. It is on account of this reaction, which is like a striving
outward, that we place the object of sense-sensation outside us. How
the relation more precisely stands between these inner processes (action and reaction) and
sense-sensation, Hobbes, as we have already seen, does not go into. --- As
is seen, Hobbes stands somewhat closer to ancient and scholastic physiology than
Descartes, since he (though only in De corpore, cap. 25, 4, not in Elements of
Law, I, 2, 8) regards the heart as the place where sense-sensation arises. This
assumption was probably called forth by the effects on feeling attached to
sense-sensation, in which the heart plays an essential role. In the heart is
the source of life, and according to the manner in which the impression from without alters
the vital motion, which is one with the motion of the blood, namely either facilitates or
impedes it, there arises pleasure or pain respectively. Thereby is called forth in turn
an involuntary striving to hold fast the motion that brings pleasure
with it, or to check the motion that brings pain with it. Already in
the movements of the fetus this original need (conatus primus) makes itself known.

What really takes place in the world is, as we have seen, according to Hobbes only
motion --- motion outside us and in us. The subjectivity of the sense qualities is
therefore in Hobbes a consequence of his metaphysics of motion. But not only by the
deductive but also by the inductive way he seeks to establish the subjectivity of the
qualities. He points to the fact that we see images of things in places where
they in fact are not, as in reflection, in dreams and in sense illusions, --- that
different persons can apprehend the properties of things differently, --- that we
sometimes see things double, --- that by a blow on the eye or
% --- p. 272 ---
\opage{272}pressure on the optic nerve light arises, which nevertheless in fact is not an external light. From this
he concludes that the content of our sense-sensations is always only ``appearance''
of motions in brain and nerves, nothing real.

Sensation arises when there is a reaction from the interior of the organism against the impression (a
reactione cordis versus exteriora). But, says Hobbes, one cannot turn the
proposition round and teach that everything that reacts has sensation. Then all bodies would
be able to have sensation! Even if a glimmer of sensation always arose in such a reaction
(phantasma), it would at once vanish if there were no capacity \textit{to
hold it fast and recall it,} and it would not be sensation proper
(sensio). To sensation proper belongs a judgment about the objects, built on
comparison of the sense impressions. (Nam per sensionem vulgo intelligimus aliqvam
de objectis per phantasmata judicationem, phantasmata scilicet comparando et
distingvendo, De corp. XXV, 5). Sensation therefore presupposes memory and
comparison. The individual sensations must be capable of being distinguished from one another. It is
therefore a necessary condition of sensation that the sense impressions
\textit{vary.} Under entirely uniform influence all sensation falls away.
Just as little as I have any sensation of the bones in my arms, although they
are surrounded by very sensitive membranes, just as little would a man be able to have
sensation if he stared motionless at one and the same unchanging thing.
To sense the same thing constantly and not to sense at all come to the
same. --- This was, as we have seen, the point with which Hobbes's whole philosophizing
began: that without change there would be no sensation. Through the proposition
that all change is motion he then passed over into his philosophy of motion, from
which (as he certainly does not himself notice) he has difficulty in
coming back to sensation. No wonder that he so strongly stresses that the very
fact that something is apprehended by us (or can be phenomenon for us) is the
most remarkable of all phenomena; about it his whole philosophy turns, since it
constructs partly the causes of sensation, partly the effects of sensation. ---

Just as several different sense impressions obscure one another,
% --- p. 273 ---
\opage{273}so the memory images, which are nothing but sense-sensations
weakened by the removal of the object, will be further weakened by the new
sense impressions that come. In dreams, where such new impressions do not come, the
memory images come forward as the expression of something present, often together with
features and properties that are taken from other representations. ---
The memory images arise according to certain laws. They follow the same order as the
original sense perceptions. The motions in the brain are connected in such a way that
when the first is repeated, the others follow after on account of cohesion, just as
water on a smooth table is drawn after the finger that leads a part of it in a certain
direction. Thus the representation of the apostle Andrew can bring us to
think of the apostle Peter, his name can bring us to think of a stone,
etc. This is the law that is now called the law of contiguity. But Hobbes also lays
great weight on what might be called the law of interest. The course of representations
is regulated not only by the connection between the original sense-sensations,
but also by the influence of feeling and drive. A certain order and
connection comes into our representations from the fact that we always have a purpose we seek
to reach, and which makes us seek for means to reach it. It is the
constant regard to our purposes (freqvens ad finem respectio) that brings
system into our thoughts. In dreams (besides the external impressions) this
consciousness of the purpose is lacking, and thereby the capriciousness of dream representations
is better understood. --- For the origin of language, the involuntary
association between an object that sets feeling in motion and a vocal
outburst or an action in which the feeling finds vent is for Hobbes not a sufficient
explanation. Language arises, as already mentioned, according to Hobbes by arbitrary
naming. Man sets a mark in order to be able to recognize a thing again, as
when seafarers set a mark on a rock they pass by, in order to be able to recognize
the place again. Language is a mark (nota) for the individual before it is
a sign of communication (signum) for him over against others. And only when signs of communication
