have thus been introduced --- does a society become possible. --- There lay in Hobbes's
own doctrine of association conditions for a
% --- p. 274 ---
\opage{274}more natural and more correct psychology of language than this theory, which ascribes too much to conscious
reasoning and arbitrariness. --- Arbitrary naming
plays, as we have seen, a great role in his epistemology. It makes possible the
construction of the first fundamental propositions or definitions. And when
such construction has once taken place, all thinking, according to Hobbes, proceeds as an
addition or subtraction of names. He seeks to make all thinking a kind of
algebra of names. In a judgment, e.g., it is expressed that one name denotes the same thing
as another name. Since Hobbes has not seen the significance of the relation of similarity in
the involuntary association of representations, he consistently stops at this
wholly external conception of thinking, which at the same time suits so well his
deductive tendency. ---

Pleasure and pain are, as we have seen, closely bound up with the facilitation
or checking of the vital process. The impulse of self-preservation is the fundamental need in man.
Pleasure and pain arise from its momentary satisfaction. When
experiences have been made and there is a capacity to form representations of the future,
the more composite feelings arise. These can, according to Hobbes, be traced back to
the feeling of power or of impotence. When I feel pleasure in something that in the future may
cause pleasure, this presupposes that I have power to procure it for myself. This power
may be my own mental or bodily strength, or that of my friends, on whose
assistance I rely, or an authority by whom I feel myself protected; perhaps
even God the Almighty alone disposes of the power that makes it possible for me to feel pleasure
in the representation of the future. The feeling of pain arises, on the other hand, from
the representation of impotence to procure future goods or avert
future evils. All men have a constant and restless craving for power,
which only death brings to an end. It is not always that one expects greater joy
than that which one possesses; but one wishes
% scan: „vii“ (p. 274)
constantly to secure better what one has. The special feelings arise during
the struggle or race between men. There arises triumph in those who come
before others, humility in those who fall behind, hope when one is in breath,
despair when one is tired, anger at a sudden obstacle,
the feeling of pride when
% --- p. 275 ---
\opage{275}a strong obstacle is broken through, weeping when one suddenly falls, laughter when
one suddenly sees others fall, pity when we see one whom we wish well fall
behind, indignation when we see one whom we wish ill get ahead, love when we
help another during the race, the feeling of happiness when we constantly get ahead of those
before us, the feeling of unhappiness when we constantly fall behind, --- and only with death
does the race end! As long as we live, we set ourselves purposes and feel craving. All
feeling of pleasure is bound up with a craving toward a goal. If we conceive a highest goal,
and that it has been reached, then not only all craving but also all feeling would fall away.
Unhindered
% scan: „Ubindret“ (p. 275)
progress to ever more distant goals would be the greatest of all goods. The
enjoyment itself of what has been reached is a craving: the soul of the one who enjoys moves
through the parts of what is enjoyed. For life is motion, and if this cannot
proceed straight forward, it becomes circular motion.

In his closer explanation of pity and love Hobbes traces these
feelings back to the impulse of self-preservation and the feeling of power. Pity arises
from our coming, at the sight of others' misfortune, to think of a possible misfortune for
ourselves; love consists in the feeling of one's own power that one has in being able to
help others. The joy of knowledge, too, is a kind of feeling of power, as well
as the joy of wealth and rank; only science gives very little power, since so few
understand it. Yet Hobbes also assumes an immediate joy of knowledge, which
is an inconsistency. --- Cruelty, he explains, is contempt for another's pain
and sorrow; it springs from the assurance of being oneself in safety; on the other hand,
Hobbes takes it to be impossible that anyone, without something being gained for him thereby,
directly rejoices in the suffering of others. Hobbes's explanation of all feelings
from the impulse of self-preservation becomes artificial and one-sided in detail. But he
nevertheless always has firm and natural ground under his feet in regarding the feelings in
their appearance and motivation during the struggle to subsist and to get ahead. There is
not the refinement in him that there is in his contemporary \textsc{La Rochefoucauld},
who in his ``Maxims,'' in which he set down his ``experiences'' of the Fronde and
of salon life, constantly operates with the trick of putting a conscious
% --- p. 276 ---
\opage{276}ulterior motive into every feeling. Hobbes has far more sense for the involuntary.
He would hardly have been able to write down an assertion such as the one La Rochefoucauld has
put forward, that one weeps only either to get a name for tenderness of heart, or to
be pitied, or to avoid the shame of not weeping! ---

As regards the psychology of the will, there are found in Hobbes good remarks on
the relation between drive, deliberation and willing, directed against the scholastic
psychology, which makes ``the will'' a peculiar, abstract faculty, without connection with
the more elementary expressions of activity. Besides, Hobbes has given a brilliant
plea in defense of determinism in the little work ``Of Freedom and
Necessity,'' which was called forth by a discussion with an English bishop.
The bishop held that if the will were not free of causes, the laws would be
unjust when they forbid actions; deliberation would be useless,
admonition, praise, blame and punishment in vain, and books, weapons, instruments and
medicines of no use! Hobbes answered: the law acts as a deterrent, and so as a
motive; punishment is not meant to torment the criminal for what cannot be
otherwise, but to make him better and to deter others; without deliberation
the action often turns out badly, does not become what it otherwise can become, and for the same reason
instruments and medicines etc. often cannot be dispensed with; praise and blame
are conditioned by the goodness or corruptness of the action and have nothing to do with
necessity or non-necessity.

\subsection*{f.\quad Ethics and Political Theory}

With the same energy with which Hobbes founds his whole conception of existence
on the laws of mechanical motion, he founds his whole conception of ethical and
social life on the impulse of self-preservation. If one asks about the relation
between Hobbes's ethics and political theory on the one side and the rest of his
system on the other, Hobbes has already conceded that one can arrive at ethics
and political theory by two roads, partly through deductions from the doctrine of
% --- p. 277 ---
\opage{277}bodies, partly through immediate psychological experience. But the
deductive road he has not attempted at all, which is connected with the fact that
his ethico-political writings were composed before his writings on natural
philosophy. He makes no attempt to derive the impulse of self-preservation from
mechanics; he does not see self-assertion as a general tendency in all that
exists, as Telesio and Bruno did before him, and Spinoza later. He contents
himself with establishing it as a fact. There is, however, yet a third road by
which, according to Hobbes, ethics and political theory could be introduced: by
arbitrary definition, arbitrary fixing of the first principles.
% scan: „Priuciper“ (p. 277)
For in ethics and political theory we are dealing with our own life; its
valuation and ordering rest on our will. Therefore, according to Hobbes, ethics
and political theory can be constructive sciences like geometry and mechanics.
For all moral and political laws presuppose a contract among men to lead a
social life on certain conditions. From this contract the particular moral and
political rules can be deduced. As with the general scientific presuppositions,
however, regard for experience plays an essential role here too in the setting
up of the principles; this setting up is not unmotivated. On the contrary, it is
not the least interesting part of Hobbes's ethico-political theory that sets out
to show how men come to construct a social life for themselves.

It is experience of bitter need and danger that leads them to it. It is wrong to
suppose (with Aristotle and Grotius) that man has an original need of and
capacity for social life. On the contrary. Since each individual's need and
feeling of power lead him to take possession of as much as possible of what
nature offers, he comes into collision with the others, who have a like need and
feeling of power. Fear will perhaps even lead them to try to forestall one
another in using violence, so as not to be taken by surprise themselves. That
this is how matters stand is shown by the accounts of our barbarian forefathers
and of savages; and it is seen in the precautions for safety that we all take,
and in the relations of states to one another. The state of nature, i.e. the
condition of man as it is apart from the life of the state, is a \textit{war of
all against all} (bellum omnium contra
% --- p. 278 ---
% scan: „bor“ (p. 278)
\opage{278}omnes). Here no other rule holds than the individual's need and
power. Where power is slight, cunning takes its place. --- This does not mean
that all men are evil by nature. It is not human nature itself that is evil; but
ruinous actions can spring from it. And even if there were fewer evil men than
good, the good would still have to take precautions against the evil.

There would be no way out of this dismal condition if reason did not have its
root in human nature just as much as passion does. Right reason leads men to seek
better means for their preservation than they have so long as they fight each
for himself. They discover that the evil is common, and that there are common
means to employ against it. Thereby \textit{the first and most fundamental moral
law of nature} comes into being: peace is to be sought, and if it cannot be
attained, aid for war is to be sought! But the condition for this is that the
individual give up the unconditional right that he has in the state of nature.
It is the impulse of self-preservation that dictates this surrender. From this
there further follows: keeping one's word, gratitude, obligingness, forbearance
and equity are to be practiced, but arrogance and encroachment avoided; what
cannot be divided is to be used in common; mutual strife is to be settled by
arbitration; each individual is to keep his mental faculties unimpaired (for
otherwise right reason and its commands cannot come to prevail). All these
consequences can be summed up in the old saying: Do not do to others what you
would not have done to yourself. --- Should anyone think that these commands of
reason could have no power against the passions, Hobbes concedes that fear and
hope, anger and ambition, greed and vanity can indeed prevent their being
acknowledged; but --- he adds --- there is no one who does not at times have a
calm mind (sedatus animus), and then he will acknowledge them in their necessary
connection with the impulse of self-preservation. All duties and virtues follow
from the one proposition that peace is to be procured; they are means to peace.
Therefore the natural moral law is also the will of the Deity; reason is
implanted by God, and Christ, the apostles and the
% --- p. 279 ---
\opage{279}prophets proclaim the same commands that can be derived from right
reason.

It is not impossible that Hobbes was influenced in this line of thought by
Herbert of Cherbury, who, as we know, saw the significance of the natural law in
its preventing mutual destruction, and saw in the right setting out of the
``common notions'' a means to peace. It is known from Hobbes's biography (Vitæ
Hobbianæ Auctarium) that Hobbes stood personally close to Lord Herbert. ---

When Hobbes appeals to right reason, he is fully aware that he is not assuming,
with Plato and the Scholastics, a special mystical faculty that could furnish a
common standard in all decisions about what is good and evil. He expressly
denies (Elements of Law, II, 10, 8) that any such ready-made recta ratio is to be
found in the world: Right reason is not existent. What stands firm is only the
end after which all living beings strive, and when reason awakens to clarity, it
will also find the necessary means of reaching this end. Hobbes gives reason its
basis and content in self-preservation and its means, and is fully clear that
reason works only when the mind is calm (De cive III, 26: sedato animo). In
constructing the presuppositions of ethics and political theory he takes such a
calm state of mind as his basis. And it is experience that has taught him that
only through the union of the impulse of self-preservation with the composure
that makes deliberation possible can there be any question of ethical laws for
human actions. An idealization of the given is thus necessary, for passionate
excitement, shortsightedness and inconsistency must all be kept away if reason is
to be ``right.'' The ideal and consistent demands that peace requires must,
moreover, be upheld by a constant will. It is not merely a matter of outwardly
observing the commands, but of inward adherence to them for their own sake. The
natural moral law binds the individual before the tribunal of his own conscience
(in foro conscientiæ). --- Hobbes has undeniably not noticed to how high a degree
he is idealizing here. If the impulse of self-preservation in its elementary
form is always to be the only motive, then such a conscience as Hobbes here
conceives, a
% --- p. 280 ---
\opage{280}feeling or will that holds fast to the necessary conditions of peace
for their \textit{own} sake, becomes impossible. It goes with him here as when he
assumes a desire for knowledge as an immediate feeling of pleasure; this too
cannot be directly derived from the impulse of self-preservation. Hobbes lacks
the idea of a displacement of motives, by which what first stands as a means can
pass over into becoming a purpose. Such a metamorphosis is quite conceivable on
the basis of the impulse of self-preservation: it might well be that one uses the
means best when one does not use them \textit{as} means!

It is of little use, now, that the individual acknowledges the natural law before
the tribunal of his conscience. An authority must be brought into being before
which all bow. The individual must hand over his natural right to such an
authority on the presupposition that all others also hand over theirs to the same
authority, and this authority, the power of the state, then concentrates in
itself all the right that in the state of nature was distributed among the many.
This contract, by which the life of the state replaces the state of nature,
contains at once an agreement of the individuals among themselves and a common
submission to an authority (whether this be a single person or an assembly of
several persons). In this Hobbes's doctrine differs from that of Althusius, who
distinguished between the social contract and the constituting of the authority;
for Hobbes the two coincide. But Hobbes, no more than the earlier teachers of
natural law, assumes that this contract is entered into with full consciousness.
It can be understood or supposed (a supposed covenant, pactum subauditum), and
need not be express (pactum expressum). Examples of understood contracts are found
in the relation between the victor and the vanquished whose life he has spared:
had he not trusted in his obedience, he would not have spared his life. Likewise
a tacit compact is entered into between the infant and the one who brings it up
and protects it, as a rule the mother. That the contract has taken place Hobbes
\textit{infers} from the nature of the relation. When the contract is understood
or tacit, it comes close to being a mere point of view, used for illumination and
valuation. But it is then characteristic of Hobbes that he uses precisely this
% --- p. 281 ---
\opage{281}point of view. The contract presupposes (where it is express) the
individuals standing over against one another as independent beings, each with
his impulse of self-preservation, and society is now to be the product of their
interaction. By this point of view it becomes possible for Hobbes to deduce the
life of the state from individual self-preservation. He imagines men sprung up
out of the earth like mushrooms, each in his own place, and afterwards joining
together. This is a thought experiment that is necessary for the constructive
method. But Hobbes does not inquire expressly how experience is related to this
thought, as indeed in general the relation between experience and the arbitrary
presuppositions of constructive thinking remains unclear with him.

The contract theory is meant to show that it is in every individual's
well-understood interest to obey. The authority that is to be obeyed must be
unconditional. The power of the state must be as strong as possible, so that each
individual over against it is utterly insignificant. It must have the authority
to punish, the right to wage war and make peace, disposal over all property, and
the decision as to which opinions and doctrines may be proclaimed. To absolute
authority on the one side corresponds absolute obedience on the other. Only what
would be worse than death --- e.g. to kill oneself or one's nearest --- the power
of the state cannot command. When this enormous power is abused, there is a
breach of the moral law of nature, by which the holders of the power of the state
are also bound before the tribunal of their conscience, --- but not a breach of
the laws of the state, which cannot bind the very authority whose will upholds
them. If one finds these hard conditions, Hobbes answers that with the power to
protect there follows unavoidably the power to oppress. Human life simply cannot
be free of inconveniences. The freedom of the state of nature is bound up with
insecurity and strife, the constraint of the life of the state with security and
peace. It is impossible to limit the power of the state. For power can be limited
only by power, and to limit power is therefore the same as to divide it. If one
restricts the sovereign's power, then sovereignty in reality lies with the one or
those who can punish or dismiss the so-called sovereign. This
% --- p. 282 ---
\opage{282}holds whether one wishes to distinguish between ecclesiastical and
secular power, or between executive and appropriating power. --- Hobbes regards
monarchy as the best form of government. Democracy is in reality an aristocracy
of orators. Monarchy has the advantage that there is only one who can commit
abuses, but above all that party strife is avoided and secrets are more easily
kept. It is (by virtue of the original contract) in reality the people that
governs; its will is carried out through the monarch, to whom in the original
contract everyone's natural right has been transferred.

In all religious and moral questions it is for the sovereign to decide. The
sovereign is to determine how God is to be worshiped: otherwise what is worship
for one would be blasphemy for another, and a constant source of strife and
dissolution would be present. Just as little can individuals decide what is good
and right in practice; that would be a constant seed of rebellion. It is clear,
too, that only when the definitions are common can there be certainty that the
conclusions will be common. When Hobbes calls ethics and politics constructive
sciences because ``we ourselves'' fix the first principles, then in practice this
``we ourselves'' becomes one with the sovereign. Here the strangeness of Hobbes's
whole standpoint comes clearly to light. His free, naturalistic inquiry has led
him to see the necessity of an absolute authority whose reason must be
acknowledged as recta ratio. But he then nevertheless himself gives a grounding
of this authority, grounds its recta ratio by his own recta ratio, and in this
grounding makes use of the freedom of thought and of expression whose
extirpation he demands. The fruits of knowledge that he himself has plucked he
uses to impress on us the necessity of a prohibition against eating of the tree
of knowledge. He used the freedom of the press under the rule of the
Independents to publish the first edition of Leviathan (1651), and later, under
the Restoration, he took refuge in the Dutch freedom of the press to bring out
the second edition of Leviathan (1670); Charles II had expressly refused him
permission for a new edition of the heretical work. Like so many of the best men
of the seventeenth century, Hobbes
% --- p. 283 ---
\opage{283}unites in himself the Renaissance's vigorous self-confidence and
feeling of freedom with the conviction of the absoluteness of the great
sustaining powers. In his doctrine he marks the strong reaction against the
Renaissance and the Reformation. The rebellious opinion concerning freedom of
conscience and concerning the right of individual knowledge in the moral and
political domain he derived partly from the study of the Roman and Greek authors
(especially Aristotle) at the universities, partly from the free access to the
reading and interpretation of the Bible that came with the Reformation. Against
this he set up the strictest caesaropapism: Christ's kingdom begins only with his
coming again to judgment; until then God speaks only through his vice-gods: the
holders of the power of the state. He declares himself against Catholics,
Anglicans and Puritans alike. If the pope is to be the shepherd of the faithful,
he becomes their real sovereign, and the state is dissolved. If each individual
believer is to be considered a partaker of the divine wisdom, there will be a
strife of all against all. If the bishops are to have any authority beyond what
follows from royal appointment (the Anglicans think that they have ``something
more, they know not what, of divine right''), there will also be strife between
church and state --- and an ecclesiastical tyranny besides. The Protestant clergy
thought that the papacy had been overthrown so that they could step into its
place. But --- asks Hobbes --- what then have we gained by deliverance from the
pope's tyranny, if these insignificant men (these petty men) are to replace him?
Especially since they are people whose mental qualities are not favorable to a
peaceful social life (qvorum ingenium paci et societati aptum non est)! Hobbes
thus begins with polemic against free discussion, but ends with polemic against
the small authorities who had pushed themselves forward in the place of the great
one. It is really they whom he means to strike. And in this relation lies the
explanation of his strange position.

Hobbes shares the tendency to seek a center, the concentration and the
resignation that are characteristic of the seventeenth century, and that in
philosophy find expression not only in his political theory but appear in
analogous features in the mysticism of Fenelon and Malebranche and in Spinoza's
pantheism. And he has the great merit in political theory of having established
that in a state there
% --- p. 284 ---
\opage{284}can be only one center of gravity. But he mistakes the center of
gravity: all forces other than gravity vanish for him, and consistently, then,
all masses gather at the center. Power and obedience become all in all. The
spontaneous content of life, manners and custom, public opinion, the quiet and
hidden ways by which even the holders of power are dependent on what moves among
the many, and on the other hand the whole unfolding of life which it is the task
of power to protect and to subordinate itself to as its serving foundation ---
for all this Hobbes has no eye. His eye is held captive by that one point. And
his thinking is in the lapidary style; the finer nuances escape him. All the
greater is his sense for the great, elementary conditions of life of human
society. He belongs to the same side of the English mind from which Malthus and
Darwin, both of whom can be said to continue Hobbes's thought, have sprung.

Nevertheless there are, as already touched on, hints in him that lead out to a
wider horizon.

The duty of the ruler is summed up in the proposition that the welfare of the
people is the highest law. For the state is not instituted for the sake of the
rulers, but for the sake of the citizens. The despotism for which Hobbes speaks is
of the same kind as that which appears in the enlightened, reforming statesmen of
the eighteenth century (Frederick II, Joseph II). He is not only an ardent
opponent of hierarchy in all its forms, but also of every kind of class rule, such
as may be found even in ``free'' countries. By the absolute center of gravity that
he establishes he means to abolish the small centers of gravity, so that all the
elements can come to move in natural orbits. And the absolute authority itself is
grounded by way of reason. Hobbes makes use of free discussion. He hoped that his
``Leviathan'' would ``fall into the hands of a prince who would consider it
himself, without the help of any interested or envious interpreter, and then use
his sovereign authority to protect the public teaching of the doctrine it
contains, so that the theoretical truth might be converted into practical
utility''\textsuperscript{54}). But he hopes not only for the enlightenment of
princes, but also for that of the
% --- p. 285 ---
\opage{285}people. Against the hierarchy he relies not only on the jealousy of
the power of the state, but also on the advancing intellectual culture and
criticism of the people: Paulatim eruditur vulgus! (De homine, XV, 13).
Self-contradiction between the propositions of the doctrine, or between the
doctrine and the life of its preachers, will sooner or later be discovered. A
wide horizon opens here, wider even than the one that stood before the heroes of
the Enlightenment in the eighteenth century; for Voltaire and Diderot expressly
disclaimed the thought of an enlightenment of the vulgus. And this wide horizon
does not, properly speaking, come about through an inconsistency, when one goes
to the bottom of Hobbes's presuppositions. For by the ``contract'' through which
individuals give up their self-will, this will is not really meant to vanish, but
only to be taken up into a higher connection. What is lacking in Hobbes is the
means of showing how the isolated will can undergo a metamorphosis by being thus
worked into a larger whole. But by his first and his last word he points beyond
the imperfection of his own doctrine, an imperfection that is outweighed by the
natural force and the acuteness in the foundation and construction of the
doctrine.

\subsection*{g.\quad Opposing Tendencies in English Philosophy}

The history of English philosophy in the seventeenth century is not exhausted
with Bacon, Herbert of Cherbury and Thomas Hobbes and with the tendency they
represent. Besides this tendency, which takes its foundation in what is given in
external or internal nature, and works on this foundation by means of the
inductive or the deductive method, there is also another tendency, which
historically points back to Neoplatonism, and which assumes a foundation raised
above all experience for the highest ideas, especially for the ethical ideas. To
this belongs \textsc{Robert Greville, Lord Brooke}, who in his thirty-fifth year
fell at Lichfield (1643), fighting for the cause of Parliament. In his work on
``The Nature of Truth,'' which appeared two years before his death, and for which
he perhaps received the impulse from Lord Herbert's work, he protested against
knowledge's being merely a human faculty, empty in itself, that would first have
to go looking for
% --- p. 286 ---
\opage{286}its content: only light is receptive to light, and knowledge is a ray
of the divine nature itself. True knowledge raises us above sense perception ---
of which the Copernican system is an example. All plurality, all relations of
space and time are mere appearance; thinking finds rest only in the knowledge of
the one cause of all things. The knowledge of the unity of all things in God
frees us from envy, shows me the happiness of others as my own, disperses the
darkness of the soul and heals all pain. Experience, on the other hand, can show
us no real causes; it can only show us that the one phenomenon precedes the
other\textsuperscript{55}).

The Platonic tendency to which Lord Brooke belonged found a home about the middle
of the century at the University of Cambridge, while Oxford continued to hold to
Scholasticism. A year after Leviathan had appeared, there appeared (1652)
\textsc{Nathaniel Culverwel's} ``Discourse of the Light of Nature.'' Culverwel had
died in 1651; he was Master of Arts and Fellow at Cambridge. His writings are
Platonizing like Brooke's, but not so mystical, and he lays greater weight on
psychological experience. But he assumes eternal and universally valid truths in
both the practical and the theoretical domain. These truths are one with God's
essence and are upheld in the world by God's will. Thus for him, as for Brooke,
philosophy and theology merge into one, whereas Bacon and Hobbes drew a sharp
boundary between them\textsuperscript{56}). In a more systematic form the same
tendency, whose distinguishing mark is a close union of Platonic philosophy and
Christian theology, appears in \textsc{Ralph Cudworth} († 1688) and
\textsc{Henry More} († 1687), both attached to the University of Cambridge.
Whereas for Bacon and Hobbes it was a principal matter that truth must work its
way forward in the world, come into being in man's consciousness through strenuous
labor, these men returned to the Platonic doctrine of the eternal truth, which
does not come into being, and to which man's consciousness need only open itself
in order to have a share in it. This tendency turned both against Puritanism,
which was hostile to philosophical thinking, and against Hobbes (and, in More's
case, also against Spinoza), who set philosophy in opposition to theology. It is
characteristic
% --- p. 287 ---
\opage{287}that Henry More was led into philosophical studies through doubt about
the truth of Calvinism; he had been brought up strictly Calvinist, and the fact
that he was able to work his way out of the doctrine that had been impressed on
him by the energy of his own thinking was to him a testimony to the independence
of thought over against everything external, an independence that he then
asserted not only against the narrow Puritan theology but also against the
realist tendency of Bacon and Hobbes. More was in touch with Descartes and took
up several of his ideas, only not the sharp distinction between mind and matter;
for him the mental was extended, though not an object of touch. In his work
\textit{De anima} (Rotterdam 1678. cap. 1) he defines a mind as a substance that
can indeed be penetrated but not divided (substantia penetrabilis et
indiscerpibilis), whereas body is a substance that can be divided but not
penetrated (substantia impenetrabilis et discerpibilis). What is characteristic of
body is not that it is extended, but that it is impenetrable. Everything that
exists has extension in length, breadth and depth, the mind as well as the body.
\textit{(De anima.} cap. 8: Responsiones ad Hobbesiana). In this way he mediates
between Hobbes and Descartes and thinks he has refuted Hobbes's objection to
spiritualism, that we cannot form any concept of an immaterial substance.
Extension is to be common to both kinds of substance, and More goes even a step
further, in that he, like several of the philosophers of the Renaissance, regards
space as a divine attribute: that God has extension follows from his
omnipresence. \textit{(De anima.} cap. 2, §
4---5). The difference between God and the individual soul is only that God is
unlimited, the soul limited. In this bold mysticism More is influenced by the
Kabbalistic doctrine. His mystical conception of space recurs in Newton, who on
the whole was influenced by More. --- From Descartes More differs not only in
assuming that all substance is extended, but also in taking activity (in the case
of mind original activity, in the case of matter communicated activity) into the
concept of substance. \textit{(De anima.} cap. 1
§ 3). Hereby he prepares (like Gassendi and Hobbes)
% --- p. 288 ---
\opage{288}Leibniz's philosophy of nature. --- We cannot go further into this
tendency here; it is more a learned mysticism than new philosophical thinking. It
has had great significance for the spiritual development of England, but has not
brought new thoughts into the history of philosophy.

A greater interest attaches in this respect to an author who met Hobbes on his own
ground, the inquiry into the psychological foundation of ethics and social life.
\textsc{Richard Cumberland} (b. 1632, studied at Cambridge, died as Bishop of
Petersborough 1718) published in the year 1672 a work remarkable in the history
of ethics: ``Philosophical Inquiry into the Natural Laws'' \textit{(De legibus
naturæ disqvisitio philosophica),} which is expressly directed against Hobbes. He
declares that he means to continue the work of Hugo Grotius by another road than
the one the famous Netherlander followed. Instead of inquiring how the moral laws
of nature make themselves known in experience and history, he means to inquire
into their origin and their causes. In this inquiry he means to start from
experience and to reason his way forward from the nearer to the more remote
causes. He is sure that by this road he will at last come back to a divine source
of those laws; but he will not use the easy method of the Platonists, which lets
the innate ideas bear immediate witness to this lofty origin: ``I have,'' he
says, ``not been so fortunate as to arrive at the knowledge of the natural laws
in so convenient a way.'' And in any case he will not build his ethics on such a
hypothesis, although he acknowledges the sound and good influence of ``our
Platonists'' in moral respects. Against Hobbes, on the other hand, he points to
the spontaneous tendencies in human nature, whereas Hobbes had taken the arbitrary
adaptation of wills as his basis. From birth onward there takes place an
unfolding of the human faculties and powers, a spontaneous use of the organs,
which is bound up with an immediate satisfaction. Sense impressions are met by a
spontaneous inclination to receive them, to turn toward them. In this way the
first experiences are had and the first mental operations performed:
remembering, comparing and counting. In this immediate
% --- p. 289 ---
\opage{289}need (impetus), which is not produced by the impressions, but only
released by them, the natural and self-evident truths of reason (naturalia
rationis dictata) have their ground. And such an immediate need also underlies
the first striving to produce goods and shun evils --- and that without the
individual's own goods and evils being at once separated from the common ones: on
the contrary, it is spontaneously acknowledged that the good that is common to
all rational beings stands above that which falls to a single being only, and
that the single being attains its peculiar happiness precisely by striving after
what is good for the whole to which it belongs. Clear consciousness and arbitrary
willing can only develop further what the spontaneous tendencies already lead
to; art can work on the foundation of nature, but cannot take its place. ---
While Cumberland thus stresses the original natural instinct, in opposition to
Hobbes's construction of society out of clearly conscious, independent
individuals, he maintains on the other hand that the natural is not only what can
be traced in the first manifestations of life, but also what appears as ripe
fruit when growth and development are complete. Human nature is therefore to be
sought not only in the elementary drives, but just as much in what the highest
spiritual development displays. Even if man, then, at first confines his interest
to himself, it is not on that account unnatural for him to attach his interest to
what brings happiness to all. The state of nature is not given up because there
develops a magnanimity (generositas) for which the good is what works toward the
preservation and perfecting of the whole human species, nay perhaps even of the
whole universe, so far as we have a concept of it. --- What Cumberland urges,
then, is partly the possibility of a development from the elementary drives to
magnanimity, without the external and mechanical notion of contract needing to
form the middle term, partly the harmony between individual and common goods. In
both respects he put forward thoughts that were more fully grounded and developed
within English philosophy in the eighteenth century, and that already, in
Cumberland's own time, were quietly taking shape in
% --- p. 290 ---
\opage{290}Spinoza's Ethics and Leibniz's philosophy of law. Cumberland's
exposition is still unclear and imperfect, but he has pointed to decisive points.
Even if his work (to judge by its title page and preface) was called forth chiefly
as a plea against Hobbes, it nevertheless has an independent significance in the
history of ethics.

\section*{5.\quad Benedict Spinoza}

\subsection*{a.\quad Biography and Characterization}

Spinoza is the central thinker of the seventeenth century. All the threads of
thought run together in him: mysticism and naturalism, theoretical and practical
interest, which in the century's other thinkers stand in greater or lesser
opposition to one another, and --- where they appear in the same personality ---
awaken inner discord, are here sought to be carried through consistently, and the
reconciliation between them is found precisely in their being carried through
consistently. Whereas so many know no other way of connecting the threads of
thought than to cut each of them off separately and then tie them together in an
external fashion, the greatness of Spinoza's thinking is that he will set no
arbitrary limits, but trusts in the harmony of the trains of thought in their
innermost essence. Through the quiet labor of thought to which he devoted his
life, he sought to shape a work that could take the new world-view and the new
science into itself and let them unfold all their consequences, and yet maintain
the reality and independence of the mental in existence, --- a work in which the
multiplicity and individuality of phenomena could be fully acknowledged, and yet
the unity, the all-embracing order of the world, be seen as the power that in its
innermost bears all and works in all. And this work was for him not a purely
theoretical labor; it was to him the satisfaction of a personal need of clarity
and self-understanding, and it helped him to the cheerful fundamental mood that is
won by working one's way through the unrest and darkness of existence to the
understanding of eternal laws. His chief work (\textit{Ethica}) has thereby become
a work of art, not merely a purely speculative work. It has aptly been compared,
in its five books, with a
% --- p. 291 ---
\opage{291}drama in five acts. And this comparison can be carried through in
detail. In the first book the most general propositions are given, which unroll
before our eyes a great, infinite background for human life. In the second book
there is added to these a series of propositions borrowed from physics, by which
the strictly mechanical view of nature is laid down, and the book then passes on
to an inquiry into human knowledge. A provisional conclusion is offered by the
end of the second book --- and, on a not unfounded conjecture, the first two
books originally formed a whole by themselves. There appears a prospect of
attaining what Spinoza had set as his goal: the knowledge of the connection in
which our mind stands with the whole of nature. In this knowledge he saw (in an
autobiographical fragment) the only good that was closely bound up with his
personality, and of which no external accident could rob him. But so swift a
conclusion of the drama is prevented by a cloud appearing over the horizon: it
is not only thoughtlessness and false combinations of representations that hinder
true knowledge; it is first and foremost the feelings and passions by which we
are tossed about. Here a new and serious resistance is to be overcome --- and in
order to be overcome it must first and foremost be known. In the third book,
then, Spinoza gives a masterly natural history of the feelings. He demonstrates
the connection of the feelings with the impulse of self-preservation, and shows
how they are transformed under the influence of representations. His chief
endeavor is to find a fixed causal connection in the mental as well as in the
material domain. He wants to find the law of the swell of waves by which we are
tossed about. In this very law he finds deliverance. In the fourth book the
light begins to break through again. No passion, it is true, can be directly
extirpated; but it can be checked by another passion that is stronger. Once this
has been seen, the task is to make the knowledge of the good, that is to say, of
the conditions of the preservation of our being, a power in the mind, and this
comes about by this knowledge itself awakening pleasure in us, both through the
end it shows us and through its being itself a mental activity, an expression of
our power. This knowledge will unite us with individuals akin to us in essence,
since it turns out that
% --- p. 292 ---
\opage{292}we are subject to common conditions, and that only common striving
leads each of us to the goal. With this the drama approaches its conclusion a
second time. But there still remains a question: that of the individual's
complete working-through of his personality by uniting the scientific knowledge,
whose possibility the first two books showed, with the practical course of
development, the discipline through the struggle for existence, that the third
and fourth books depicted. In the fifth book it is shown how the clear
understanding of our passions in their natural connection raises us above them,
and unites with all our other knowledge of nature into an immediate beholding of
our being as one single one of the forms in which the eternal Deity, working in
the world of mind as in that of matter, unfolds its being. As we thus see
ourselves --- and all things --- ``under the aspect of eternity,'' all the unrest
and obscurity of time and finitude vanish, and with the mental freedom whose
development the fourth book depicted there is now united the inward feeling of
being one with the eternal and infinite being. --- Thus within one frame Spinoza
finds room for philosophy of religion, physics, theory of knowledge, psychology
and ethics, just as the carrying through of realism by the strict application of
the law of causality does not hinder, but for him precisely makes possible, the
mystical unity with the Deity. If we add that this whole great and manifold
connection of thought is set out in the form of propositions and proofs after the
mathematical pattern (more geometrico), we have the picture of a work unique of
its kind. No wonder that it was not understood in its own time; nay, that the time
of understanding began only a hundred years after its appearance, so far as the
idealist side of its content is concerned, and came only in our own day, so far
as the realist side of its content is concerned. For the history of philosophy
the task with regard to a work such as this is first and foremost to inquire how
it came into being, and on what historical presuppositions it rests. It stands
before us like a cut crystal; if possible, we should discover something of the
process of crystallization. Here Spinoza's personality and personal circumstances
and his philosophical development may perhaps be able to help us. There can
hardly be any doubt that the
% --- p. 293 ---
\opage{293}manifold content that is here gathered into so peculiar a frame is
held together first and foremost by the personality of the author. After that, an
analysis of the system itself will show us how the presuppositions and elements
that the author has taken into himself are used by him, and how far he has
reached his goal. ---

Baruch Spinoza was born on 24 November 1632 in Amsterdam, the city in which his
parents, Spanish Jews who had fled from the Inquisition, had taken refuge. The
gifted boy made his first studies at the Jewish academy in Amsterdam, where he was
introduced to the Talmud and to medieval Jewish philosophy. Thereby the foundation
was laid for an essential side of his thinking, the endeavor to hold fast to and
carry through the thought of the Deity as the one infinite being, as this thought
comes forward in the higher popular religions, especially in Judaism. In the
course of his studies, Maimonides (a Jewish philosopher of the twelfth century)
and Leo Hebraeus (a Jewish mystic of the time of the Renaissance) seem in
particular to have been of significance for him. Their books were in his library.
The oriental or mystical tendency always lay at the basis of his thought and gave
him the quality of being cast in one piece, the determined direction toward one
point, that distinguishes his thinking. Early on he harbored doubts concerning the
Mosaic theology, and he therefore became an object of suspicion on the part of the
Jewish theologians, which in turn led to his withdrawing from the synagogue. He
felt the need of a wider intellectual horizon and began to study the humanities
and natural science. In Latin he was taught by the physician van Ende, who had a
name as a freethinker. The most important source for Spinoza's biography, the
pastor \textsc{Colerus}, who --- in spite of his great abhorrence of Spinoza's
doctrine --- collected information about his life with great love of truth, thinks
that in this ``school of Satan'' Spinoza no doubt learned other things than Latin.
According to Colerus's account, Spinoza is said to have been in love with van
Ende's gifted daughter, who helped her father with the teaching, but to have been
rejected for a fellow pupil who knew better how to make his way as a suitor. There
is, however, some difficulty in reconciling this account
% --- p. 294 ---
\opage{294}with what is known of the ages of the two persons. --- Colerus says
that Spinoza at this time left theology and gave himself wholly to ``physics.'' It
is probable that among the authors he studied in order to become acquainted with
the newer view of nature, Giordano Bruno was one of the most important. Bruno, it
is true, is never named by Spinoza, and his books were not in Spinoza's library,
but the latter's first work (especially a little dialogue that is incorporated in
the work \textit{On God, Man and his} \textit{Happiness}) clearly recalls Bruno.
Here he found a philosophical conception that made it possible for him to unite
what was for him the essential element in the religious ideas with a scientific
understanding of nature. Bruno's doctrine of the infinity and divinity of nature
made it possible for him to unite the concept of God and the concept of nature in
an inward way. This influence of the philosophy of the Renaissance on Spinoza has
become probable only since the discovery (some thirty years ago) of Spinoza's
first work. Previously one held to Colerus's remark that Spinoza, after he had
given up theology for ``physics,'' was long in two minds about which teacher he
should follow, but that then Descartes's works had fallen into his hands and had
appealed to him by their endeavor to build everything on clear and distinct
grounds. It was thought that Spinoza began in philosophy as a Cartesian and only
gradually turned critically against Descartes. Against this stands the fact that
the very first work we know from Spinoza's hand criticizes Cartesianism on some of
the most decisive points. Spinoza was never a Cartesian, but he learned much from
Descartes and used several of his concepts, and in part followed him in his
terminology. But in this period of transition, too, before his own system took
more definite shape for him, he must have studied the more recent Scholastic
authors, who at that time --- before the philosophy of Bacon and Descartes had
made its way --- dominated philosophical teaching in Germany and the Netherlands.
Many expressions and propositions in Spinoza's later as well as in his earlier
works point to such a Scholastic influence, just as Spinoza himself in several
places refers to the Scholastics. It
% --- p. 295 ---
\opage{295}appears --- when one takes all this together --- that they are very
comprehensive and diverse circles of thought, and no small literature, that
Spinoza traversed in the course of his philosophical development. Closed and cast
in one piece as his chief work stands before us, it nevertheless has its roots
branching out to many sides within the philosophical
tradition\textsuperscript{57}). This does not diminish his originality; it is the
mark of genius to be able to take in and work over as no one else can. The
peculiarity and originality of the building do not suffer from the stones' having
been fetched from many places.

Under the influence of all these motives of thought, which streamed in upon him
from many sides, Spinoza in his views moved further and further away from the
synagogue. His open apostasy was foreseen, and in order to avoid it attempts were
made to hold him back by offering him a pension. But neither this nor a fanatic's
attempt to assassinate him kept him from following the way of his thought. He was
then solemnly expelled by the Jewish clergy (1655). They even succeeded --- since
the Protestant congregation too regarded him as a dangerous man --- in having him
banished from Amsterdam for a time. He took up provisional residence with a
friend in the country near Amsterdam. He supported himself by grinding optical
lenses, a skill he owed to his rabbinical upbringing, since every future rabbi
had to learn a trade. His friends in the city fetched his lenses and sold them
for him. It seems that already at this time a circle of younger men had gathered
around him and his thoughts. At this time the work on God and man (the ``short
treatise'') and perhaps the first draft of the later ``theological-political
treatise'' came into being. Spinoza turned with indignation from the fanaticism
of the positive churches, and with ever greater inwardness and self-understanding
found the task of his life in the independent working out of a circle of
thoughts that could spread clarity over the nature of man and his position in
existence. Experience had (as he says at the beginning of the unfinished treatise
``on the Improvement of the Intellect'') taught him that neither riches, sensual
enjoyment nor honor could be a true good for
% --- p. 296 ---
\opage{296}man, but that the only thing that could fill the mind with ever new
satisfaction was the constant striving after knowledge, by which the soul is
bound to what endures while all else changes. Spinoza's thinking had --- however
speculative and abstract the forms it took, and however remote from ordinary
human life it might seem to lie --- a decidedly personal and practical motive.
Full mental clarity was to him a necessity of life.

In the year 1661 he moved to Rhynsburg, a small town near Leyden. Here he began
the working out of his famous chief work. It is mentioned in letters to his
friends (especially in the letters to Oldenburg and to Vries). Copies of the
worked-out part of the work existed early, and Spinoza's young friends in
Amsterdam, mostly medical men, studied the book together and in cases of doubt
turned to the master for explanation. His life was not so solitary as it has
often been depicted. His correspondence, of which we have had fuller knowledge
only since the find of manuscripts that was made some forty years ago, and in
which the ``short treatise'' was also discovered, shows him in touch with a not
inconsiderable circle of men of different station and intellectual tendency. The
study of this correspondence is of considerable interest for the understanding of
Spinoza and his thoughts as well as of the spiritual condition of the time; in my
popular account of Spinoza I have treated this subject in a separate chapter,
``Spinoza og hans Korrespondenter,'' to which I must refer here. In the nearby
university town of Leyden he had several friends. Thus he came here into a
confidential relation with the Danish naturalist \textsc{Niels Stensen}, who was
studying in Leyden at this time. Later, when Stensen had gone over to Catholicism,
he addressed to Spinoza in an open letter (Epistola ad novæ philosophiæ
reformatorem), in which he calls him his former very intimate friend (admodum
familiaris), an appeal to follow him into the bosom of the one saving Church.
Niels Stensen's biographer, the keeper of the national archives
\textsc{a. d. jørgensen}, explains Spinoza's silence in the face of his former
friend's appeal in the following way: ``The restless spirit of love of
Christianity drove Steno
% --- p. 297 ---
\opage{297}to an attempt to make his friend a partaker of its happiness;
philosophy's infinite indifference to the individual personality with its desires
and its cares let Spinoza see that this man was irretrievably lost to the
knowledge of the truth, and that the right answer to his address was therefore
silence.'' I believe that the excellent historian (who was the first to bring to
light the interesting relation between Steno and Spinoza) here does both Spinoza
and philosophy a great injustice. I have great reverence for the figure of Steno,
for his religious as well as for his scientific personality. But I nevertheless
believe that in all propaganda, however noble the name it calls itself by, other
motives are at work besides the spirit of love (if this is always present at
all); and in any case this spirit of love did not prevent Steno and many others
from looking forward to a blessedness from which, they believed they knew, very
many would be excluded. It is in any case unjust to deny Spinoza the spirit of
love because he will not force his views on others. His loving faith was directed
to man, and he found what is human behind very different forms of faith. An
unwilling witness, the pastor Colerus, relates of him how sympathetic he was
toward others, and how he comforted and cheered the members of his household when
they were visited by sorrow or sickness. When his landlady in the Hague asked him
whether she could be saved in the religion she had, he answered her that her
religion was good and that she should not seek any other; she would surely be
saved by it if she led a pious and quiet life. He sympathized most with the freer
tendencies within Protestantism. He had a different view of the significance of
Protestantism from that of his kindred spirit Bruno, and quite naturally so, since
he lived in the freest country in Europe, which admittedly did not mean much at
that time. When later a young man, Albert de Burgh, who had lived in Spinoza's
household and who had gone over to Catholicism, repeated Steno's attempt at
conversion, Spinoza answered him in a letter in which he maintains the validity of
free knowledge and sets justice and love as what is essential in all true
religion. It must not be
% --- p. 298 ---
\opage{298}forgotten that what not least offended Steno in Spinoza was that the
latter had spoken up for freedom of religion. To work for freedom of religion was
for Steno to do harm to one's soul! Should there not lie in Spinoza's conviction
that a true faith cannot be forced on anyone either by spiritual or by bodily
violence, and in his caution about shaking the faith of others when only there
was seriousness in it, a greater and truer interest in the individual personality
than the one that finds outlet in passionate propaganda?\textsuperscript{58}) ---

After a couple of years' stay in Rhynsburg Spinoza moved to Voorburg near the
Hague (1663) and later (1670) to the Hague itself. Here too he had many friends,
in part men in high positions, such as the brothers de Witt. His way of life was
frugal, and he showed great unselfishness toward relatives and friends in money
matters. A bright and cheerful mood marked his way of taking life. ``Why,'' he asks
in a passage of his Ethics, ``should one rather still hunger and thirst than drive
away melancholy? In my conviction no deity, and in general no one who is not
envious, can take pleasure in my impotence and my misfortune, or count tears,
sobbing and fear as merit; but on the contrary, the greater the joy we feel, the
greater the perfection to which we pass, that is to say, the more we partake of
the divine nature. Therefore the wise man will refresh and strengthen himself with
food and drink, as well as with fragrance, flowers, music, tasteful dress, bodily
exercise and plays.'' In spite of his mystical vein Spinoza was no ascetic. In his
life as in his philosophy an energetic seeking to be absorbed in one thought went
hand in hand with a sense for the manifold reality whose inner law, in his
conception, this thought precisely expresses. Both his life and his philosophy are
distorted if one does not hold fast to the different currents that actually moved
in him, even if he had perhaps not (as he believed) found the redeeming word that
could let all these currents come into their full right and into reconciliation
with one another.

The first work Spinoza published was an exposition of the Cartesian philosophy
(1663), originally intended for a young man (the Albert de Burgh already
mentioned) whom he did not yet
% --- p. 299 ---
\opage{299}want to initiate into his own philosophy. It is characteristic that he
thus regards Cartesianism as an introduction to his own doctrine. On the
``Ethics'' he worked and polished constantly. He was very cautious about
communicating it to others; before he allowed his disciples to show the manuscript
to strangers, he gathered careful information about their character and
circumstances. Thus he refused his friend Tschirnhausen permission to show the
Ethics to Leibniz; only after a longer personal conversation with Leibniz did he
himself show him his chief work. According to a hypothesis put forward by
TØNNIES\textsuperscript{59}), the first two books of the Ethics were worked out by
themselves, whereas the realist psychology of the third book, which betrays the
influence of Hobbes, who also strongly influenced Spinoza in political theory,
seems to be due to a later working out. This explains several discrepancies
between the conception in the second and in the third book. In relation to the
``short treatise'' the ``Ethics'' marks the advance that Spinoza no longer
conceives the relation between mind and matter as a causal relation, but as a
relation of identity. Spinoza made several attempts at publishing this chief work
of his, but gave it up again when even the rumor of its publication aroused great
agitation. He was in ill repute after the publication of his theological-political
treatise (1670), although he had not yet developed his real system there. The
book defended freedom of religion as a human right, with particular reference to
the fact that the diversity of personalities must also bring with it diversity in
faith. It further undertook a purely historical inquiry into the biblical
writings (especially those of the Old Testament, whose late origin is maintained)
and a psychological characterization of their authors. A definite distinction was
made between religion, whose purpose is practical, in that it aims at bending the
minds of men to obedience and morality, and science, which has a purely
theoretical purpose; and on the basis of this distinction the complete freedom of
science was maintained. Finally there was polemic against the assumption of
miracles, since the laws of nature are the laws of God's own essence. --- This
work, which contained so many thoughts of the future, was regarded as the epitome
of all ungodliness. The experiences Spinoza had in this way led
% --- p. 300 ---
\opage{300}him not only to hold back his ``Ethics,'' but also to decline an
invitation to take up a professorship at Heidelberg; he feared that he would ---
in spite of all promises --- not have sufficient freedom of teaching. --- A
disease of the chest that was hereditary in his family, and that had been
consuming him for a long course of years, brought on his death (21 February
1677). About his death, as about his life, wild rumors were spread, which the
truth-loving pastor Colerus refuted after careful inquiry --- although he himself
is astonished that a freethinker could live so beautifully and die so calmly, and
although he is offended that Spinoza's barber, in a bill submitted to the estate,
calls his deceased customer ``the late blessed Mr. Spinoza!'' ---

In Spinoza's personal development we thus see the different elements of his
system come forward from different sides. It will now be the task, through an
analysis of the finished system, to see how he has united these elements, and how
far the union has really succeeded.

\subsection*{b.\quad Theory of Knowledge}

If in setting out Spinoza's system one wished to follow his own ``Ethics,'' one
would have to begin with certain definitions and fundamental propositions and
from them in turn derive a series of propositions. The question would then remain
unanswered how Spinoza came to his definitions and fundamental propositions, which
contain the whole system within them, --- and yet it is really this question that
is of the greatest interest historically. If one begins with the definitions and
fundamental propositions on bare ground, as Spinoza himself does in his chief
work, the most natural supposition is that these first principles are either set
up quite arbitrarily (as Hobbes thought) or else are the object of an immediate
intuition. Neither was Spinoza's meaning. By following the fashion of the time,
which demanded a strictly deductive exposition, he has therefore given occasion
to misunderstandings of his system. From the unfortunately unfinished treatise
``on the Improvement of the Intellect'' it is seen that he gave serious thought
to scientific method
% --- p. 301 ---
\opage{301}and had in mind to write a kind of inductive logic. In a certain sense
it can be said that the principles on which Spinoza builds the deductive
exposition in the ``Ethics'' came about for him by reflection on, and construction
of, the presuppositions on which our empirical knowledge of existence rests.

If by experience one understands merely an apprehension of things as they present
themselves to us spontaneously and by chance, it gives us no true knowledge. It
stops at the given as it appears at a definite time and place, and an assumption
then settles fast in consciousness merely because no contrary facts have so far
shown themselves, without there being any guarantee that such are not to be
found. This kind of experience Spinoza calls experientia vaga; it corresponds to
Bacon's inductio per enumerationem simplicem. True knowledge must be a knowledge
of reason, which does not stop at the single given phenomenon, but sees it as the
consequence of a general law, as a single expression of a general order of things
that extends far beyond it. Knowledge of reason considers the phenomena given in
experience in their definite connection with one another, and finds in this
connection the explanation of each single phenomenon. Knowledge of reason (ratio)
starts from the given. Spinoza urges the necessity ``that we always derive our
concepts from real beings, proceeding as far as possible along the series of
causes.'' First, then, an account of the facts must be procured, and after that
the fundamental concepts and fundamental propositions must be derived from them.
In his ``theological-political treatise'' Spinoza draws an analogy between the
interpretation of a book (the Bible) and the explanation of nature. First it must
be established what the given content is. Next one must make sure of certain
general relations and laws that hold good at every point. In the case of physical
nature these are the laws of motion; in the case of mental nature Spinoza would
most likely name the laws of the association of representations. It is, in a
word, the idea of the lawfulness that reigns in all things, which reveals itself
in the single changing phenomena and makes each one of them explicable to us. In
this lawfulness there is revealed for Spinoza
% --- p. 302 ---
\opage{302}the true, eternal essence of things. Not to the advantage of clarity,
he distinguishes between ``the fixed and eternal things, on which the changeable
single things depend in so inward and essential a way that without them they can
neither be nor be conceived,'' and ``the laws that are written in those fixed and
eternal things as in law books.'' What he calls the fixed and eternal things can
be nothing other than the order of nature itself in the material and in the
mental domain, that is, the very fact that definite laws hold for the phenomena.
These laws reveal themselves equally completely in nature as a whole and in its
single parts. It is to them that one must go back if one wishes to reach a
completion of knowledge. The series of phenomena is infinite, inexhaustible;
there we could go on passing from link to link. But true knowledge concerns what
connects the links, and what is therefore present everywhere, --- those fixed and
eternal things, which thought is able to grasp, while the series of phenomena
extends to infinity, without completion. --- Spinoza distinguishes expressly
between the real connection that those fixed and eternal things (entia realia)
express, and the mere general concepts (abstracta et universalia), which have no
objective reality.

The truth and validity of our knowledge rest, according to Spinoza, on no
external criterion, not on agreement with anything outside it. It is the clarity
and distinctness that go with perfect consistency that give the assurance of
truth. Error always rests on something limited and isolated having been made into
a whole. Error vanishes when one simply proceeds with strict consistency from the
erroneous presuppositions in which one is entangled. Intellectio fictionem
terminat. In strict logical consistency, then, our thinking has a norm of truth
that it can apply everywhere, even where it is in error. Truth, says Spinoza,
illuminates both itself and error (veritas norma sui et falsi est), just as light
makes known both itself and darkness. The starting point of all our inquiry
naturally becomes, then, the investigation of the rule of truth that is given in
the very nature of our intellect. This is the foundation on which we build in our
% --- p. 303 ---
\opage{303}inquiry after what is eternal and necessary in things, after what
underlies all things (res omnium prima).

Spinoza here hints that it is only by means of our subjective reason that we can
find ``the eternal things,'' ``the first of all things,'' in nature. Had he
pursued this hint further, the problem of knowledge in all its sharpness would
have presented itself to him: by what right do we assume that existence itself
follows the norm that holds for the relations of our thoughts to one another? But
this problem does not arise for him. It stands fast for him that our rational
presuppositions are also those of things, nay, that what is eternal in things
corresponds to them; an objective order of the world corresponds to the
subjective order of thought. There is the same relation between the objective
objects of our thoughts (which Spinoza denotes by the Scholastic expression
essentiæ formales) as between our thoughts among themselves. To what is for us
the first thought, from which all other thoughts are derived, there corresponds
what is in existence the first thing, the origin and source of all else. When
Spinoza has the laws that explain the single phenomena be ``written in the fixed
and eternal things as in their law books,'' he means thereby (we could say from
our standpoint) to express that the connection that makes things intelligible is
just as much a reality as the single detached ``things'' each by itself, nay, that
it far rather than they deserves the name of reality, since it is eternal and
all-embracing. And here too we must see the origin and meaning of what he in his
deductive exposition calls substance. For by substance he understands that which
exists in itself and is conceived through itself, and through which all else
exists and is conceived. Spinoza's substance, the fundamental concept of his whole
philosophy, is thus really causality represented as a thing or a being. For
causality, the causal relation, is according to Spinoza understood through itself
and is what makes everything else intelligible to us. And since the causal
relation is the presupposition of a knowledge of real existence, which makes
itself known to us through experience, we see that Spinoza's whole philosophy can
be said to be a construction of the presuppositions that hold for all scientific
experience, in such a way that these presuppositions are made one with the
innermost
% --- p. 304 ---
\opage{304}essence of things. But causality, or the causal relation, which
Spinoza thus thinks of as a real power on which the single things depend and in
which they exist, corresponds in turn for him to the necessity with which we
derive conclusions from premises, or in other words: Spinoza does not distinguish
between ground and cause; the causal relation is for him not a relation in time,
where the cause goes before and the effect follows after, but an eternal relation
of ground; the relation between ``the fixed and eternal things'' (or ``the first of
all things'') and the single phenomena is not that the former were first and then
the latter arose as their effects. For true knowledge, according to Spinoza, the
relation in time drops away. Knowledge of reason is, according to Spinoza, an
apprehension of things ``under the aspect of eternity'' (sub specie æterni): it
keeps to that in things in which the eternal necessity makes itself known in
them, and sees them only as examples of it. The causal principle itself Spinoza
regards as a necessary presupposition. In the Ethics he sets up as a fundamental
proposition that a thing must have its cause either in itself or in something
else. Now since substance, that which exists through itself and is conceived
through itself, cannot have its cause in something else, it must have its cause
in itself and thus exist with necessity. If one denies this proposition, one must
also deny the proposition that there must necessarily be a cause of every thing
(either in it or outside it). And that it is a proposition of reason is evident
also from the fact that for two things to be related as effect and cause means
that the concept of the one thing can be derived from that of the other; the
knowledge of the effect is only the knowledge of a particular property of the
cause; there is something common in their concepts. Only when in this way the
relation in time, and in general \textit{the difference between cause and effect,
drops away,} so that the effect is seen as the logical consequence of the cause
(which would admittedly be the ideal completion of knowledge), can substance or
``the eternal things'' be called the cause of phenomena. And only on the
presupposition of this confusion of ground and cause does it become intelligible
how Spinoza could hope to build up a purely rational knowledge of existence, or,
as
% --- p. 305 ---
\opage{305}one can also express it, to know existence as being rational in its
innermost essence. The counterpart to Spinoza is formed here by the conception
that Brooke and Glanvil (as well as the occasionalists) had already hinted at and
that Hume later carried through: that cause and effect are \textit{wholly
different} things, an assumption that must lead to doubt about the
intelligibility of existence. ---

Knowledge of reason (ratio) does indeed lead us to see what is eternal and
necessary in things, but it is nevertheless, according to Spinoza, not the
highest form of knowledge. In it the universal law and the single phenomena still
stand in opposition to one another, and thinking here is still discursive, and
wins its result by comparison and inference. The highest form of knowledge,
according to Spinoza, is the intuitive, where the single phenomenon is seen
immediately as if shone through by the general order of things, as when I see
immediately that two lines are parallel to each other when each of them is
parallel to one and the same third, or as when in the knowledge I have of
something I at the same time see immediately what belongs to knowing something.
The difference between the universal and the individual has here dropped away
entirely; their unity is seen at one glance. It is Spinoza's highest aim to
understand as much as possible in this immediate, intuitive way; he declares,
however, that it is very little that he has so far been able to understand in
this way. In the last book of the ``Ethics'' he seeks to understand the single
soul in its inward unity with the eternal being: an intuition that forms the
conclusion of all his theoretical and practical striving. The chief condition for
rising to this intuition is that one tear oneself loose from external, accidental
experience and find the necessary connection with the help of knowledge of
reason. --- Yet it is not easy to hold fast to a sharp difference between
knowledge of reason and intuition; for both show us things ``under the aspect of
eternity,'' and moreover: in his description of intuitive knowledge Spinoza says
that it \textit{``proceeds} from an adequate concept of the essence of certain
divine attributes to an adequate knowledge of the essence of things'': here, then,
the discursive has not entirely dropped
% --- p. 306 ---
% scan: „have.“ (p. 306)
\opage{306}away. --- What Spinoza aims at is nothing less than the highest goal of
all knowledge: to unite individuality and continuity, the single and the whole
connection, in as inward a way as possible. He succeeds in this only by
postulating an intuition that can recall now the artistic apprehension, now
mystical beholding, according as the weight is laid on the individual or on the
universal moment. ---

It is a great pity that Spinoza did not get his theory of knowledge finished. But
the fragment we have nevertheless shows that the fundamental definitions and axioms
do not come in him as if shot out of a cannon, but are constructed on the basis of
a reflection on the presuppositions of all understanding of existence. What is
dogmatic in Spinoza appears in the confidence with which he sets up these
presuppositions and treats them as realities, not in his having altogether
overlooked the existence of such presuppositions.

\subsection*{c.\quad The Fundamental Concepts of the System}

\textit{α.} When Spinoza begins his deductive exposition by defining
what he understands by cause of itself and by substance, and by laying down
as a fundamental proposition that what does not have its cause in something
else must have it in itself, he has really thereby only postulated the
possibility of a conclusive knowledge of existence. Existence could not be
known if the causal principle did not hold, and causal knowledge could not be
completed if there were not something which had its cause in itself and did
not again point the inquiring thought beyond itself, as every single
phenomenon does. When Spinoza defines substance as ``that which subsists in
itself and is understood through itself, that is to say, whose concept does
not need the concept of any other thing from which it should be formed'' (per
substantiam intelligo id, qvod in se est et per se concipitur, hoc est id,
cujus conceptus non indiget conceptu alterius rei, a qvo formari debeat), he
has nevertheless, in his view, not thereby given a purely subjective
determination of a concept, but formulated an objective
% --- p. 307 ---
\opage{307}fact, a reality. For him there is no doubt that substance exists. Its
existence is given; but when we reflect on what substance is, we see that its
existence is also necessary, since there is nothing that can exclude it,
inasmuch as it has its cause in itself. Likewise it follows from the essence
of substance that it cannot be produced or pass away; that it cannot be
divided; that it cannot be limited; that there cannot be more than one
substance. Everything else to which we ascribe existence can then only be
properties (attributa) of the one substance or single phenomena (modi, ways)
in which it reveals itself. That there appear in existence different
properties (such as consciousness and extension) which we cannot reduce to a
common form does not justify (as Descartes thought) the assumption of
different substances: they must be conceived as different properties or
attributes of one and the same substance. Just as little does the fact that
experience shows us a multiplicity of finite things or phenomena, separated
in time and space, justify us in assuming a multiplicity of substances. The
existence of finite things or phenomena is conditioned through and through,
and true subsistence (substantiality) can be ascribed only to the universal
order of things, the comprehensive being which bears them all.

\textit{β}. With the concept of substance, the concept of God and the
concept of nature coincide for Spinoza. Through the concept of substance he
points back to Cartesianism and scholasticism, through the concept of nature
also to Bruno and the Renaissance, and through the concept of God to the
religious ideas which first of all set his thinking in motion. God is called
substance as the infinite being which reveals itself under an infinity of
attributes. Everything that is said of substance must then hold of God too,
so that everything that is, is in God and can neither be nor be conceived
without God. Both matter (extension) and mind (consciousness) are then divine
attributes and do not denote beings outside God, and just as little are the
single things or phenomena (modi) outside God. Just as little as God has
anything outside himself, just so little are there differences or
oppositions in God's essence; here there is no difference between
possibility and
% --- p. 308 ---
\opage{308}actuality, no difference of time. Everything that follows from his
essence follows with eternal necessity; God's freedom consists precisely in
this necessity determined by his essence. When God is called the cause of
things, it must be well noted that cause and effect are here not two
different things, but the effect a revelation of the essence of the cause.
God's work is not different from himself, as the work of a human master is.
God is the cause of things in the same sense in which he is his own cause; he
is an indwelling (immanent), not a transcending (transscendent) cause; his work
remains in him, and he in it; he cannot go beyond the compass of his essence.
A distinction must indeed be drawn between God and the sum of all the single
phenomena (modi): the phenomena make up the produced nature (natura
naturata); God is the producing nature (natura naturans). But an external
