separation does not exist. According to Spinoza it is a purely
\textit{abstract} way of regarding things when we regard the single phenomena
isolated from ``the whole order of nature,'' that is, from substance, the
producing nature. We thereby throw away the condition of understanding them.
To see existence \textit{abstractly and superficially,} as it appears to the
senses and the imagination, through the isolated appearance of the phenomena,
is for Spinoza the opposite of seeing it \textit{as substance} and with the
aid of the intellect. Every single phenomenon is only a limited form of the
one infinite substance, arising through a negation, a canceling of all the
other forms under which it appears. Every particular determination is a
negation\textsuperscript{60}).

\textit{γ.} Substance, God or nature, appears under different properties or
attributes. ``By attribute I understand,'' says Spinoza, ``that which the
intellect perceives of substance as making up (constituting) its essence.''
Of the infinitely many attributes which the infinite being that we call God
or nature has, we know only two, mind and matter. The essence of God or nature
appears to us only under these two forms, as working partly in the world of
material phenomena, partly in that of mental phenomena. Spinoza's relation to
experience appears clearly here. Not only is it a matter of experience that
we
% --- p. 309 ---
\opage{309}know only two attributes, but the very definition of the concept of
attribute rests on experience, namely on the fact (which must have dawned on
Spinoza in the interval between the ``short treatise'' and the definitive
working out of the ``Ethics'') that the mental and the material are each
understood according to its own laws. The difference between them is then
irreducible; we cannot derive the mental from the material or the material
from the mental, but within the mental world by itself and within the material
world by itself we can demonstrate connection and causal relation. The fact
that the mental and the material are irreducible differences in existence is
what Spinoza expresses by calling them attributes and by defining the
attribute as that which expresses the essence of substance: for substance is,
after all, that which subsists in itself and is understood through itself.
One must therefore not leap over from one attribute to another. ``So long,''
says Spinoza, ``as things are regarded as mental phenomena (modi cogitandi),
we must (debemus) explain the order of nature, or the causal connection,
through the attribute of mind alone; and so long as we regard them as material
phenomena (modi extensionis), the whole order of nature must (debet) be
explained through the attribute of extension alone.'' There is thus only one
substance, one causal connection, but it can be regarded in two ways. It has
hardly been Spinoza's meaning, however, that the attributes should be only
points of view which \textit{we} apply to
substance\textsuperscript{61}). He says expressly, after all, that an
attribute is what the intellect perceives as \textit{constituting} the essence
of substance, and a doubt whether what our intellect perceives as constituting
also really constitutes cannot be shown in Spinoza. When he says, then, that
we \textit{must} explain the mental by the mental and the material by the
material, this is a necessity which, like all necessity for him, is an
expression of the eternal essence of existence.

If it is asked what it really comes from that one cannot explain the mental
side of existence by the material, or conversely, the answer lies contained
in the ideal of causal explanation which Spinoza has set up, and according to
which cause and effect must be homogeneous (4th and 5th axioms of the
% --- p. 310 ---
\opage{310}first book of the Ethics). In a letter (Ep. 4) Spinoza says still more
clearly: ``When two things have nothing in common with each other, the one
cannot be the cause of the other; for since there would be nothing in the
effect which was also in the cause, everything that was in the effect would
have arisen out of nothing.'' When this fundamental proposition is
consistently held fast, one has the key to Spinoza's whole system. For from
it follows the doctrine of God or substance as the \textit{indwelling} cause
of all phenomena (modi), and so the abolition of the theological dualism of
God and world. And from it follows further the impossibility that the cause
can be material and the effect mental, or conversely, and so the doctrine of
mind and matter as expressions of one and the same existence, one and the
same causal connection, and with that the abolition of the spiritualist
dualism of soul and body. Just as it was the \textit{general}
epistemological consideration of the conditions for understanding what is
given in experience that led Spinoza to set up the concept of substance (as
the concept of hypostatized causality), so it was the \textit{special}
consideration of the possibility of understanding the mental and the material
that led to the doctrine of attributes. This doctrine is essentially
conditioned by the conviction of the possibility of conceiving the material
side of existence as a continuous whole, and of the impossibility of deriving
the mental side of existence from it. Spinoza makes a stand against Descartes
and against Hobbes alike. His theory of attributes is an attempt to solve the
difficulties from which Cartesianism and Hobbesianism (spiritualism and
materialism) suffer. He has set a new, original hypothesis over against
spiritualism and materialism.

Now Spinoza has not strictly held fast to this meaning of the doctrine of
attributes. With the problem of the relation between mind and matter he has
in several places confused the problem of the relation between knowledge and
its object. It is easy to see that these are two different problems; for both
mind and matter (existence from its mental as well as from its bodily side)
are objects of knowledge, and the problem of knowledge comes up with regard to
all the sides from which existence can be
% --- p. 311 ---
\opage{311}seen.
But since Spinoza, as a dogmatic philosopher, confidently relied on the
agreement between our reason and the essence of things, he had to assume ---
as already set forth --- that to every relation of thought there corresponded
a relation in existence. And this \textit{epistemological} doctrine of
identity he then confused with the \textit{psychophysical} doctrine of
identity which his doctrine of attributes expresses. When he lays down the
proposition: ``The order and connection of representations is the same as the
order and connection of things'' (Eth. II, 7), this proposition is ambiguous,
since it can be understood both epistemologically and psychophysically.
Spinoza himself understood it rather epistemologically. This is seen from his
example: to my concept of the circle corresponds the circle existing in
reality (Eth. II, 7 Schol).
% scan: „Sehol“ (p. 311)
Psychologically it would have had to run: to my representation of the circle
corresponds the state my brain is in when I have this representation. But
when Spinoza, in immediate connection with this, maintains that mental
phenomena are to be explained by mental phenomena, material phenomena by
material ones, it is an entirely different problem that he has to do with. In
the third book of the Ethics, where the point of view is psychological, not
epistemological, he accordingly applies the doctrine of attributes purely
psychophysically. --- This confusion is naturally connected with the fact that
the problem of knowledge in Spinoza does not appear as an entirely independent
problem. Only through a critical revision of our knowledge --- with regard to
its capacity to know the mental as well as the material side of existence ---
does the difference between the two problems come clearly to
light\textsuperscript{62}).

Just as, according to Spinoza, there is an inward relation (an indwelling
relation, a relation of immanence) between substance (God or nature) and the
single phenomena, so for him the great fundamental forms and fundamental
properties that existence presents must also be substance's own attributes.
It was a bold consequence of this when Spinoza declared matter or extension a
divine attribute. Matter, on the usual theological conception, is only
something derived, a product of mind. Just as little as Bruno and Böhme could
Spinoza rest content with this conception, which conflicts above all
% --- p. 312 ---
\opage{312}with his fundamental thought of the indwelling causal relation. With
regard to Spinoza's doctrine of matter as a divine attribute it must be well
noted that by matter he here means what is substantial in material phenomena,
that in them which subsists through all changes and in spite of all divisions,
and which can neither suffer, arise nor pass away. The material side of
existence is, just as much as the mental side, a revelation of the Deity or of
substance; to its ``infinite power of thought'' (potentia infinita cogitandi)
corresponds the infinite material extension, of which the single phenomena
are parts. What lies at the ground of existence, from whichever side it is
regarded, is the causal connection and the unity to which the causal
connection bears witness.

\textit{δ}. The single phenomena (modi) are, as will be remembered from what
has gone before, the particular ways in which substance comes forth within the
different attributes. Since the attributes hold for substance, they hold also
for the single modi: every single phenomenon can therefore be regarded from
infinitely many sides, just as well as the whole of existence, of which it is a
member or part, only that we know, after all, no more than two of these
sides. The definition of modus is: a determination of substance, or: that
which has its subsistence in something else, through which it is also
understood. As affectio substantiæ a modus is understood only through
substance and has its subsistence in it --- just as, one might say, the single
wave subsists only as part of the sea and is understood only by being seen as
part of the sea. In every single phenomenon there stirs an impulse of
self-preservation which is a part of the divine power working in all things.
But in each single modus this power stirs only in a limited way; one cannot,
then, understand the way in which the single modus acts or suffers without
seeing it in its interaction with all other modi. The state of the single
modus is therefore understood only through something other than itself. Here
an external (transscendent) causal relation comes into play. But however
externally the single phenomena stand over against one another, they are
nevertheless, all together and each by itself, only determinations
(affectiones, modificationes, determinationes) of the one infinite substance.
In
% --- p. 313 ---
% scan: „modi.“ (p. 313)
\opage{313}the produced nature (natura naturata) the producing nature (natura
naturans) is at work at every point.

Within natura naturata Spinoza distinguishes between necessary and infinite
modi, which follow immediately from God's eternal nature, and finite modi,
which need other modi for their coming into being. Within the attribute of
extension he names (Ep. 64) as infinite modi motion and rest; here he seems in
particular to be thinking of the conservation of motion, or of the law that
through all the changes of matter the same relation between motion and rest is
preserved, --- the law which makes it clear that every single body is only a
part of the whole universe. Within the attribute of thought he names the
``infinite intellect'' (intellectus infinitus), which is an immediate effect
of the infinite divine power of thought, and which --- since it is placed in
analogy with the constancy of motion --- must be taken to mean the mental
energy that constantly remains the same in the world, however much the single
mental phenomena may change. (Perhaps it is chiefly the conservation of motion
and ``the infinite intellect'' that Spinoza, in the treatise on the
improvement of the intellect, has in mind with the expression ``fixed and
eternal things.'')

ε. For a closer characterization of the system set forth here, a series of
problems and difficulties to which the system leads shall only be indicated
further. --- God or substance is spoken of as acting, although the form of
time is to hold only for the modi, natura naturata, not for substance, natura
naturans. This is connected with the confusion of ground and cause mentioned
above. --- There subsist two causal relations: one among the modi mutually, an
external, transscendent one, and one between substance and the modi, an
immanent one. How are the two to be reconciled? --- The unity of substance
and the multiplicity of the attributes and modi are not brought into harmony;
no answer is given to how the one substance can appear under different points
of view, or how an infinity of effects can follow from the one substance. ---
And when for Spinoza the concepts substance, nature and God cover one another,
he introduces with the designation God a determination of value which is
grounded only by his
% --- p. 314 ---
\opage{314}defining perfection as reality; the question whether this definition
can be held fast is not examined more closely, and at a later point in his
exposition he even sets up --- as we shall see --- a concept of perfection
according to which not all reality is perfect. --- Thus even the boldest
speculative system leaves unanswered questions enough behind it. What is great
in Spinoza is his resolute carrying through of the thought that existence must
be rational; from this he concludes that its essence must be identity,
absolute unity. Consistently, he would have had, instead of several systematic
fundamental concepts, only a single one: substance. To this concept one may
perhaps ascend --- but once one has reached it, one can in any case not get
down again. --- These objections to Spinoza's system do not, however, strike
his fundamental endeavor, the fundamental direction of his thinking, but are
made possible for the most part by the dogmatic procedure he employs.

\subsection*{d.\quad Philosophy of Religion}

It will be of interest to stop for a moment to see in what relation Spinoza's
philosophy stands to the current religious views. When he named his highest
concept (substance) God, he had himself at once given occasion for such a
comparison. Already in his correspondence we see this point discussed. On a
particular occasion he writes (Ep. 73): ``I hold an opinion of God and nature
far different from the one which the modern Christians are accustomed to
defend. For I maintain that God is (as one says) the indwelling, not the
external, cause of all things. That is to say, I assert with Paul that in God
all things are and are moved . . . But when some think that the
`theological-political treatise' aims to show that God and nature, where by
nature one understands a mass or corporeal matter, are one and the same, they
are entirely mistaken.'' --- From the usual theological conception Spinoza's
philosophy separates itself especially on two points: in not conceiving God
and the world as two different beings, and in not ascribing human properties
to God. In the first period one
% --- p. 315 ---
\opage{315}made short work by calling his conception atheism and materialism.
\textsc{Henry More}, e.g., says in a writing in which he sets out to refute
Spinoza's ``gross atheism'' (crassissimus atheismus) that God and matter are
one in his system. Therefore, says More, stones, dirt, lead, dung are God, since
these things are, after all, matter! So Spinoza is then a ``sordid and
befouled atheist'' (sordidus et lutulentus atheus)\textsuperscript{63}). A
small sample of the polemics of the seventeenth century! --- People were at a
loss with the new system on account of its peculiarity; it could not easily be
fitted into the current rubrics of heresy, and in its sharply cut forms it
nevertheless provoked offense on several points. Later the expression
pantheism came up (first, it seems, in Toland). Here one had a word that hit
the mark better. And yet there is no full agreement about its use. According
to some it denotes a view that conceives God's relation to the world as
immanent; according to others what is essential to pantheism is that God is
not thought of as a personal being\textsuperscript{64}). By the first of these
marks there is no doubt that Spinoza's system is pantheistic; by the second it
is less clear how one is to designate it.

In one of his letters (Ep. 54) Spinoza says that, so as not to confuse the
divine nature with the human, he does not ascribe to God human properties such
as will, intellect, attention, hearing, etc. The more precise grounding of this
is found in several places in the ``Ethics.'' --- It is clear that the
applicability of the psychological determinations must fall away with the
falling away of the relation of time, and time holds for Spinoza only for
natura naturata, not for natura naturans. With the relation of time all change
falls away too; God can pass neither to greater nor to lesser perfection and
can therefore feel neither joy nor sorrow, love nor hate. Further, God as
substance has nothing outside himself, no external object toward which feeling
or will could direct itself. Our consciousness, our intellect as well as our
feeling and our will, is determined by such external objects, and when they
fall away, consciousness too falls away for us. --- If one wants to use words
such as intellect and will of God, one must make
% --- p. 316 ---
\opage{316}it clear to oneself that their meaning must undergo such a change
that at bottom it is only the word that is common to the two uses, much as one
uses the word dog both of the constellation the Dog (Sirius) and of the barking
animal on earth. The whole impulse to transfer human properties has therefore
no objective validity. If triangles could think, they would conceive God as
triangular; if circles could think, they would conceive God as round.

On the other hand Spinoza recognizes the mental as an independent side of
existence. God is substantia cogitans as well as substantia extensa; cogitatio
(thinking, mind) is one of God's attributes, and so expresses God's essence!
Intellect and will belong only to the produced nature, not to the producing;
but there must be a ground in the latter for their being able to arise, and if
the ``infinite intellect'' has eternal subsistence through all the change of
mental phenomena, this too must have its ground in the essence of the Deity.
One might perhaps express Spinoza's conception thus: God is mind, but not
personality, because only a limited being can be a personality. (Spinoza
mentions the expression personality in a single place only, but declares it
obscure.) It must be noted, however, that Spinoza, by declaring cogitatio a
divine attribute and by speaking (as will be mentioned later) of God's
infinite love of himself (of which man's love of God is a part), himself
undertakes just such a sublimation of the psychological properties as he
denies on other points. Against cogitatio as a divine attribute objections
could be raised similar to those which Spinoza himself brings against the
current conception. --- Those to whom it is absolutely a matter of bringing a
philosophical system under one ``ism'' or another will to that extent be at a
loss with Spinoza, especially since every thinking theism must undertake
sublimations of the same kind as Spinoza's.
% --- p. 317 ---
\opage{317}

\subsection*{e.\quad Philosophy of Nature and Psychology}

By setting up extension as one of the attributes of existence and by demanding
(by virtue of the very definition of the attribute) that in the explanation of
a phenomenon one is to keep to the attribute under which one regards it,
Spinoza has already established a purely mechanical explanation of nature as
the only scientific one. As falling under the attribute of extension, all
bodily phenomena are to be explained only by bodily causes, by causes that act
from other points of space than the one at which they themselves are. It is
therefore very easy for Spinoza to give a proof of the principle of inertia:
this really lies already in the setting up of extension as an attribute. Just
as dogmatically as Descartes and Hobbes, Spinoza sets up the fundamental
propositions of mechanics as eternal truths --- although he must concede that
he cannot derive motion from extension itself\footnote{\emph{Spinoza} makes
this concession in the last letter we have from his hand (of 15
July 1676), an answer to the philosopher and mathematician
\textsc{Tschirnhausen}, who had asked with great acuteness how one could derive
from the general concept of extension the figure and motion of bodily
things. Tschirnhausen pointed out that this difficulty does not exist in
Descartes, who assumed that God created matter in motion; but Spinoza, for whom
extension is a divine attribute, then lacks the concept of force which in
Descartes was conceived in theological form. Spinoza declares the
definition of matter as extension insufficient and announces a closer
discussion of the question, which he did not manage to give.}. There can be no
differences of essence between bodies; these differ only in respect of motion
and rest, speed or slowness. The laws of motion are eternal laws of nature and
of reason. --- In the doctrine of attributes is contained also the rejection of
every assumption of purposes in nature. Since the one attribute cannot
determine the other, no material phenomenon as such can have its ground in a
thought, which the teleological explanation presupposes. In a longer note to
the
% --- p. 318 ---
\opage{318}first book of the ``Ethics'' Spinoza seeks to show that the
teleological conception springs from man's practical need and wish, from his
impulse of self-preservation in connection with his original ignorance of the
real causes; he assumes that everything is arranged for the good of men and
that the gods work for this; where no reasonable purpose can be found, they
content themselves with finding the explanation in God's will, this refuge of
ignorance (asylum ignorantiæ), which is always at their service. If
mathematics had not pointed out a rational way to knowledge, the teleological
conception would forever have hindered the knowledge of nature. The
teleological conception, however, not only hinders the knowledge of nature but
also presupposes unworthy representations of the Deity: if God acts according
to purposes, he is, after all, not perfect, but becomes so only when he has
reached his purposes! Men make bold to apply moral and aesthetic concepts to
nature, find order and confusion, beauty and ugliness, good and evil in it,
supposing that it is designed to appeal to their feeling. They do not see that
the perfection of nature is one with its might, and that this might is
infinite, so that it is able to produce all possible degrees and forms of
existence, those which to us stand lowest just as well as those which to us
stand highest.

In a series of lemmas in the second book of the Ethics Spinoza indicates how
he conceives a mechanical view of nature carried through. --- According to the
law of inertia every body is determined to motion or rest by another body, this
by a third, and so on. The way in which a body is determined depends partly on
its own nature, partly on the nature of the body that acts on it. --- When
bodies of the same or different size are so held together by other bodies that
they touch one another, or when they communicate their motions to one another
in a certain ratio, they are said to be mutually united and all together form
one body or one individual, which is distinguished from other individuals by
the definite union between the single bodies of which it consists. Such an
individual continues to be the same even if some parts are taken in and others
given off, and even if the size of the parts and the
% --- p. 319 ---
\opage{319}direction of the motions change, provided only that the whole form of
the composition continues to be the same. Several such individuals can be
united into an individual of the second order, and several individuals of the
second order into an individual of the third order, and so on, until at last
the whole of nature stands before us as one single great individual, whose
single parts vary infinitely without the whole individual undergoing any
change.

In all its stages and degrees nature is animated. This too follows from the
doctrine of attributes: since each attribute expresses the whole substance,
to every form under the one attribute there must correspond a certain form
under the other attribute. To the different stages of individuality in
material nature, then, there correspond different stages of mental life in
mental nature. Just as the human body consists of many composite individuals
of different constitution, so the thought which makes up the nature of the
human mind is also composed of many different thoughts. The mind and the body
are, after all, one and the same substance, or rather one and the same part
(modus) of substance, and what under the attribute of extension appears as
more or less composite forms of motion appears under the attribute of thought
as more or less composite forms of thought. When I have a drive or make a
decision, there takes place simultaneously under the attribute of extension a
bodily determination according to the general laws of motion and rest, and
this is to be understood in such a way that at bottom it is one and the same
thing that happens. By this assumption, as Spinoza shows, one is spared from
maintaining an influence of the soul on the body or conversely, something of
which no one can form a clear concept. To say that the soul sets the body in
motion is at bottom to say that one does not know how this motion comes about.
This assumption has the further advantage that one does not set arbitrary
limits to the activity of material nature. No one, after all, has yet found
the limit of what can be effected by the laws of material nature itself, so
that one has no right to invoke the intervention of the soul because the body
seems to act in a marvelous way.
% --- p. 320 ---
\opage{320}Nor does the appeal to the ``freedom'' of the will help. This so-called
``freedom'' (real freedom, according to Spinoza, is that which consists in
following the necessity of one's own nature) is an illusion which arises from
one's not knowing the causes of one's own acting. The chatterer thinks he acts
freely when he lets his tongue run, just as the stone, if it could think, would
think that it fell to the ground of its ``free'' will. Besides, the decision is,
after all, dependent on memory, and of this we are not always masters! ---

Although Spinoza rejects every explanation of mental phenomena by material
causes, he nevertheless uses --- which is also fully justified on his
presuppositions --- the connection between the material and the mental to
throw light on mental phenomena where these cannot be understood immediately.
Every sense-sensation corresponds to a bodily state. Now this state has indeed
its cause in the influence of other bodies, but this influence is modified by
the constitution of our own body: from which it follows that the
sense-sensation corresponds not only to the nature of the external bodies but
first and foremost to the nature of our own body. Nevertheless we
involuntarily regard every sense-sensation as the expression of something
real, until other sensations or representations arise in us which exclude the
assumed reality. According to Spinoza, then, it is through the mutual struggle
of sensations and representations that our conception of reality is cleared
and determined. --- Sensations call up representations of what resembles, or
has occurred together with, the object of the
sensation\textsuperscript{65}). The laws of the connection of representations
are for Spinoza mental laws of nature, the counterpart of the laws of motion
within the attribute of matter. Spinoza distinguishes sharply between the
association of representations and thinking proper. This difference has been
discussed in the section on his theory of knowledge. Sense-sensation and the
association of representations express man's state as a member of the series
of phenomena, of the infinite natura naturata. The higher stages of knowledge,
rational knowledge and intuitive knowledge, are reached by going back to that
which stirs in everything as common law and essence, that is, to the infinite
substance,
% --- p. 321 ---
\opage{321}and seeing everything taken up into it, or seeing it sub specie
æterni. --- Hobbes's psychology has here the advantage over Spinoza's that it
shows the possibility of how thinking proper, by concentration on a purpose or
a task, can develop out of the involuntary association of representations.
Spinoza still, in scholastic fashion, posits thinking proper as an entirely
peculiar activity, different in essence from ordinary representing. All the
more remarkable, then, that he nevertheless confuses the epistemological and
the psychophysical points of view in the doctrine of attributes --- although
on the other hand this confusion would hardly have occurred if he had seen
that the laws of the association of representations are in reality not
suspended in thinking proper. ---

The treatment Spinoza gives of the psychology of the feelings belongs to the
finest he has accomplished, and that has been accomplished in psychology at
all. In the first place he has the merit of maintaining the necessity and the
justification of a purely natural-historical investigation of the human
feelings and passions. He will (as an inquirer) neither mock them, laugh at
them nor weep over them, but seek to understand them, and will therefore
regard them with the same equanimity as if it were material phenomena of
nature or geometrical figures that he had before him. Next, he has brought
forward the most important points of view that come into application in the
explanation of the feelings.

As regards the position and significance of feeling in mental life, Spinoza
held different views at the different stages of his philosophical
development. In his first work, ``the short treatise'' (II, 16, 5), his
conception is entirely intellectualistic. It is knowledge, the
representations, that determine all the phenomena of mental life. The will is
merely a consequence of the representation, an affirming or rejecting. And
here, moreover, the representations themselves are still determined by the
influence of the objects, since in this writing he assumes an influence of the
one attribute on the other. Already in his writing on the Cartesian philosophy
he indicates that the representations are themselves expressions of our
activity, so that one cannot distinguish between the arising of the
representation and its affirmation or rejection. And with the definitive
doctrine of attributes this indication is carried further, but in such a way
that intellect and
% --- p. 322 ---
\opage{322}will are now made completely one. To think is an activity of the mind,
and all activity of the mind is thinking: so, roughly, one might express
Spinoza's conception here; it is formulated in the corollary to the 49th
proposition of the 2nd book of the ``Ethics'': Voluntas et intellectus unum et
idem sunt. But in the 3rd book of the ``Ethics,'' where the natural history of
the feelings is given, an entirely new conception of the will appears, since
the will is here determined as conscious impulse of self-preservation (Eth.
III, 9 Schol). It is now so far from being one with, let alone a consequence
of, knowledge, that knowledge is precisely dependent on the will: ``we do not
seek, will, desire and wish for anything because we think that it is good, but
conversely, we think that something is good because we seek, will, desire and
wish for it.'' Here, then, need and will are one, and the representations
dependent on them. In his treatise on the history of Spinoza's development,
in which \textsc{Tönnies} has thrown light on this point in a brilliant way,
he conjectures with great probability that it is Hobbes's influence that has
produced this last change in Spinoza's conception. Hobbes puts drive and will
in close connection with each other and with the impulse of self-preservation,
and he also stresses the influence which the thought of a purpose has on the
connection of representations. In Spinoza's work as it lies before us there is
an evident contradiction between the definition of will II, 49 Coroll. and the
definition given III, 9 Schol., so that it is highly probable that two drafts
have been worked together without all traces of different conceptions having
been removed.

From the impulse of self-preservation as the expression of the nature of each
single being Spinoza now proceeds in his exposition of the psychology of the
feelings in the 3rd book of the ``Ethics.'' Even if he thereby changed
something in his psychology, he changed nothing in his general philosophy. In
every single being the infinite nature, the Deity itself, is at work. The
striving of each single being to preserve itself is then only a part of the
infinite divine working in the whole of existence. Already in the ``short
treatise'' (I, 5) he saw (like Bruno) in this impulse of self-preservation,
living in all beings, the revelation of divine providence. And this need is one
with the very nature of things, takes on
% --- p. 323 ---
\opage{323}a different character according to the nature of the single beings:
to exist is to strive to preserve oneself. This striving is called drive when
it is bound up with consciousness: by drive, then, is understood the very
essence of man, insofar as it is thought of as determined to activity by
reason of a change in its state. When this drive is regarded in particular
from the mental side, it is called will. Pleasure arises when this striving is
furthered, pain when it is disappointed. Be it noted: it is the very
transition to a more favorable (``more perfect'') state that is bound up with
pleasure, and the very transition to a less favorable (``imperfect'') state
that is bound up with pain. The states themselves, as at rest, are not bound
up with feelings. Nor, however, is any express comparison made between the
states: the feeling corresponds immediately to the very change of the states.

Just as Spinoza here states what we now call the biological significance of
feeling, its connection with the advance or decline of life, and just as he
also has a clear eye for the significance of the relation of contrast for the
arising of the feelings (``the law of relation in the domain of the
feelings''), so he has also put the third main point in the psychology of the
feelings, the significance of the representations and the combinations of
representations for the development of the feelings into special kinds, in an
excellent light. --- From drive, pleasure and pain he derives, with the help of
the laws of the combination of representations, the special kinds of feeling.
We love what causes pleasure, but hate what causes pain. We love further what
furthers what we love, just as we hate what harms what we love. And when we
represent to ourselves a being that resembles ourselves as having a certain
feeling, we involuntarily get the same feeling ourselves. From this compassion
can arise --- but also envy and wounded ambition, namely when we wish to
possess alone what the other enjoys, or when we wish the other to be disposed
entirely as we are disposed. --- According to these general principles
Spinoza now carries out his consideration in detail. He has founded the theory
of evolution in the domain of the feelings, by showing how our feeling, under
the influence of the representations and by
% --- p. 324 ---
% scan: „al“ (p. 324)
\opage{324}mutual composition and mixture, can take on forms that are highly
different from the elementary initial forms. It is the conditions of growth of
feeling that he has formulated. --- How far it is possible to keep exclusively
to the one starting point he has seized on, the individual impulse of
self-preservation, is a question that cannot be discussed here.

\subsection*{f.\quad Ethics and Political Theory}

It is characteristic of Spinoza that there is a practical motive for his
thinking, and that his thinking nevertheless rises high above the world of
finitude and experience in which alone practical motives and practical
striving are possible. Spinoza rejects the validity of every valuation of
existence; existence follows its eternal laws, and our ethical judgments,
which rest on a comparison between the more or the less perfect in relation to
the ideal of human life that we form for ourselves, cannot find application to
the eternal essence of nature itself, for which time, measure and number do
not hold. Spinoza insists on the subjectivity of the ethical qualities as
energetically as the subjectivity of the sense qualities had been insisted on
from Galilei's time onward. Insofar as Spinoza holds fast to his conception of
existence ``under the aspect of eternity,'' he can have no real ethics, and
needs none either. Of ethics there can be question only in a world where the
relation of time holds, where there is becoming and development, change and
opposition, and where models can be formed and purposes set up. As Spinoza has
aptly expressed it: the judgments of good and evil rest on comparison --- but
in the eternal unity with itself of the infinite, divine nature all comparison
falls away, because all difference and opposition has fallen away. The
investigation of Spinoza's theory of knowledge showed us that all
\textit{riddles} fall away under ``the aspect of eternity''; we now see that
all \textit{tasks} fall away too.

But just as Spinoza distinguishes between natura naturans and natura
naturata, he also distinguishes between the purely theoretical standpoint and
the practical standpoint. The practical standpoint holds only within natura
naturata. Spinoza sets up
% --- p. 325 ---
\opage{325}an ethics with the same right as that with which he maintains the
significance of the modi of the world of experience, the finite world. There is
no greater inconsistency in his setting up an ethics than there is in his
setting up, at all, other concepts than the concept of absolute substance.

The possibility of an ethics is closely connected in Spinoza with his
psychological doctrine of the feelings. The foundation of ethics is the
impulse of self-preservation which lies at the ground of the manifold
feelings and passions. For out of the impulse of self-preservation there can
develop a need not to be tossed about by all the feelings and passions which
external causes call up in us. As a part of nature, as a modus among other
modi, man is dependent and is tossed about like the waves of the sea without
knowing goal or direction. We naturally strive, then, to assert our being,
after full, inward activity. The fundamental ethical virtue is
\textit{strength of mind} (fortitudo), an inward might which makes man free
and independent. Virtue is the very essence or nature of man, insofar as he
has the might to produce effects that can be understood through the very laws
of man's nature. For man to be able to attain this character, he must make it
clear to himself that no feeling and no drive can be checked in us except by
a stronger feeling or drive. (This proposition was already maintained by BACO:
De Augm. Scient. VII, 3). Spinoza builds his proof of this proposition on the
law of inertia, which, by virtue of the identity of mind and matter, has its
counterpart within the mental side of existence. Ethical development becomes
possible through the fact that feelings can be called up which gradually
displace the feelings by which they themselves were originally called up.
When, by comparing different forms and stages of human conduct of life, we
form for ourselves an ideal of human nature (idea hominis, tanqvam naturæ
humanæ exemplar), we call everything that brings us nearer to this ideal good,
everything that hinders us from approaching it evil, and there arises a drive
to approach the ideal as much as possible. The knowledge of good and evil is
--- since it concerns what is truly useful and harmful to us --- nothing other
than conscious joy at approaching
% --- p. 326 ---
\opage{326}the ideal or conscious sorrow at moving away from it, and this
knowledge can, precisely because it is one with a feeling, become a might in
the soul. Man now soon sees that he cannot attain full strength of mind and
freedom of mind by his own help. The whole of outward and inward life must be
ordered and made secure. Above all it is a matter of developing a true
knowledge; this too is reached only by united strength, just as, on the other
hand, there is nothing that better unites men than the striving after such
goods as can be common to all. The passions that bring strife among men always
concern something which the individual alone can possess. The more each
individual attains freedom and strength of mind, the less strife will there be
among men, and the more will they act in common, because they all seek what is
truly useful to human nature. Nothing is so useful to men as men. Best of all
would it be if all could become as one soul and one body, seeking the common
utility. Those who strive after their own true utility therefore wish nothing
for themselves which they do not wish for other men, and thereby they become
just, faithful and honorable in their conduct. The strength (fortitudo) in
which virtue consists therefore appears not only as \textit{courage}
(animositas), by which man immediately asserts his personality, but also as
\textit{magnanimity} (generositas), in that man strives to help others and to
bind them to himself in friendship. --- By distinguishing between courage and
magnanimity Spinoza makes an advance in relation to Hobbes and the thinkers of
the Renaissance, in that he gets an eye for the different elements and
possibilities, of which some can lead more in an individual, others more in a
social direction. Courage is a predominantly individual virtue, magnanimity a
social virtue. But Spinoza is hindered, already by his starting point in the
pure impulse of self-preservation, from entering on a closer investigation of
the relation between self-assertion and devotion.

Characteristic of Spinoza is the valuation which, after setting up the model
of human development, he makes of the different feelings. The feeling of
pleasure is in itself good, the feeling of pain in itself evil. Therefore
hatred, fear, contempt,
% --- p. 327 ---
\opage{327}pity, remorse and humility are evil --- insofar as they are not
necessary intermediate links for the arising of feelings of pleasure. This is
grounded by the fact that the feeling of pleasure corresponds to an advance in
perfection, the feeling of pain to a decline. He who is led by true knowledge,
the spiritually free man, has his gaze directed toward the positive
development of life in himself and in others. He thinks of nothing less than
of death; his wisdom is a meditation on life (meditatio vitæ), not on death. He
strives, as far as he can, to outweigh the hatred, anger and contempt of others
by love or magnanimity. He who fights hatred with hatred lives a wretched life;
but when hatred is conquered by love, the conquered yield with joy, not because
their strength diminishes but because it grows. There is no way in which a man
can better display his strength of mind than by developing others to live
according to their own free knowledge\textsuperscript{66}).

While Spinoza's ethics leads in this way from the impulse of self-preservation
as its foundation out to practical action and the founding of society, there
also stirs in him another tendency, which from the same starting point leads in
a mystical and individualistic direction. From his earlier psychological
standpoint there still constantly presses forward the presupposition that
man's real essence consists in pure knowledge: the more this can develop, the
more does man's real nature come forth, the more is he truly self-active, and
the true impulse of self-preservation therefore leads to the development of
knowledge. It was, after all, also the knowledge of the connection in which our
mind stands with the whole of nature that stood for Spinoza as the only good
which could not be taken from us by external causes. Therefore Spinoza can,
almost in the same breath (cf.
% scan: „smign.“ (p. 327)
Eth. IV, 22 Coroll. with 26 Dem.), set up the two propositions that the
striving after self-preservation is the first and only foundation of virtue,
and that the striving after knowledge (conatus intelligendi) is the first and
only foundation of virtue. Alongside the realistic psychology, according to
which Spinoza conceives feelings and passions as positive powers in our being,
there runs another conception, according to which feeling is defined as
imperfect or confused
% --- p. 328 ---
\opage{328}representation (idea inadæqvata sive confusa, see the concluding
explanation in the 3rd book of the ``Ethics''). According to this other
conception feeling falls away with the full and clear development of
knowledge. The more we understand ourselves and our states as determined by
the infinite nature, by the Deity which stirs in us as well as in everything
that acts on us, the more do we see ourselves not as single, isolated,
powerless beings, but as taken up into and as one with the Deity. We feel
pleasure at this thought, since it is the fruit of our mind's highest
activity, and pleasure at the thought of the being that is the cause of the
joy of knowledge we feel. Thereby there arises a spiritual love of God (amor
intellectualis dei), which gives us the highest peace. God does not stand here
as an external object; our own innermost power is a part of the infinite power
that stirs in everything, and our love of God is one with the infinite love
with which God loves himself: God's love of men and men's love of God are one
and the same. We see ourselves and everything under the aspect of eternity.
--- Spinoza the mystic comes into conflict with Spinoza the psychologist; for
the intellectual love (the human and the divine) is to be raised above
becoming and opposition, but Spinoza has himself, after all, explained feeling
as corresponding to a \textit{transition ---} either an advance or a decline!
Only by explaining feeling as unclear thinking and abolishing the law of
relation can Spinoza hold fast to the mystical conclusion of the ethics.

In the fifth book of the ``Ethics,'' where this mysticism prevails, is found
also Spinoza's doctrine of immortality. In that intellectual love of God,
grounded on the understanding of our unity with the absolute being, our true
essence expresses itself: this essence, then, is not dependent on time, but is
a part of the infinite intellect (intellectus infinitus), which continues to
subsist although the single mental phenomena arise and pass away, just as
motion subsists through all material changes. As an immediate form of the
divine working we are immortal. But this immortality --- which is not a
\textit{continued} subsistence but an \textit{eternal} subsistence, since the
relation of time has no significance at all here --- seems able to belong only
to those in whom
% --- p. 329 ---
\opage{329}the highest knowledge, and with it the full and clear
self-activity, is developed\textsuperscript{67}). Whether this subsistence as
an eternal element of thought (modus cogitandi æternus) is personal or not
cannot be seen from Spinoza's exposition; his notion of immortality is in any
case very different from the popular one. And at the close he remarks that the
assumption of the eternity of our mind is not a condition of ethics, pointing
out that he himself has developed his ethics without using this assumption.
Blessedness is not the reward of virtue but is one with virtue itself. For only
when we can feel joy in our mind's highest working can we master our passions.
---

The deep and sound thoughts in Spinoza's ethics would have come to a fuller
unfolding if he had carried out his psychological theory in detail. As it is,
intellectualism gains the upper hand in him, especially when he is to depict
the highest forms of spiritual life. His ethics thereby becomes too much an
ethics for philosophers. The significance of immediate devotion and of
artistic intuition does not come into its own, although in his
``intellectual love,'' grounded on intuition, there are hints in these
directions. But no one will be able, with an unbiased sense, to immerse himself
in Spinoza's wonderful work without confirming Goethe's words about the
boundless unselfishness that shines forth from every proposition, about the
lofty resignation that once and for all bows to the great laws of existence
instead of scraping through life with the help of petty consolations, and about
the air of peace that runs through the whole book. ---

But peace, according to Spinoza, must be won through strife. It is won by the
individual through the struggle with the passions, in which a new, higher
passion is developed, and it is won by men in union through the savagery of
the state of nature, where everyone takes as much right as he has might,
being replaced by the life of the state through the establishment of an
authority that can subdue the conflicting drives and bring harmony between
the impulses of self-preservation of the individuals. In his political theory,
as in his psychology, Spinoza is decidedly influenced by Hobbes. Only he does
not have Hobbes's blind and one-sided fear of the multitude. He is
% --- p. 330 ---
\opage{330}consistent enough to hold fast that human nature is the same in all, and
that safeguards are needed just as much against those who rule as against
those who are to be ruled. One can just as little presuppose the best motives
in the rulers as in the multitude. And if it is thought that the multitude has
no understanding of public affairs, Spinoza answers that this comes from its
being kept in ignorance of them. Spinoza is one of the first democratic
philosophers of law in modern times; but since his ``political treatise'' was
not completed, we do not know his doctrine of democracy in detail. It is
characteristic that while Hobbes maintains that a democracy is in fact always
an aristocracy --- of orators, Spinoza maintains that a monarchy is always an
aristocracy --- of officials. In reality, of course, the political functions
must always be exercised by a few --- but it depends on where one finds the
ultimate source of authority. According to Spinoza it depends on the state's
being built on the united might of the many, in that they are united into one
will, just as the strength of the individual also grows by being united with
that of the others. But this spiritual unity, which is the condition of the
unity of might, can be present only where the state strives after what sound
reason points out as useful to all. One can put up with much for the sake of
peace; but if slavery, barbarism and isolation are to be called peace, then
peace is the most wretched of all things for men. The state is not to make men
into beasts or machines, but precisely to bring it about that their mental
and bodily activity can unfold freely, and that they can use their free
reason.

Only on the free adherence of individuals does the might of the state rest,
and the individual therefore does not give up his natural right on entering
the state, but has it precisely secured and developed. The state would act
against its own purpose by suppressing the individuals' freedom of thought and
of speech; it would first and foremost make the noblest and best men in the
land its opponents.

As Spinoza maintains the freedom of expression, so he also maintains religious
freedom. It is the main subject of his ``theological-political treatise.'' He
wants to show here that religion has nothing to do either with the state or
with science,
% --- p. 331 ---
\opage{331}and that the state, by its nature and its purpose, must let the inner
spiritual life develop with full freedom. The state can have power only over
outward action, not over disposition. It can lay down an outward cult, and its
dominion in this respect is to be preferred to a hierarchy. But even when it
uses its might in this way, it does best to let religious worship consist
merely in the exercise of love and justice. The mental nature of men
(ingenium) is so various that what awakens reverence in the one causes laughter
in the other. It is therefore best to let everyone keep his free conviction
and right to interpret the religious documents according to his own
intellectual tendency (ex suo ingenio). --- From science religion separates
itself by its practical character. It aims at piety, not at truth. The
prophets were not men who were especially highly gifted in intellectual
respects. Imagination was stronger in them than understanding. Their task was
to impart to the people, through images and symbols, representations that
could bring it to live in that obedience to God which shows itself in love of
one's neighbor. The multitude, which cannot follow the inferences of reason,
must have historical models for guidance. Only thereby does it come to obey not
out of mere fear but out of its own will and devotion. What theoretical
opinions men have of God --- whether they think he is fire or spirit or light
or thought --- is a matter of indifference, so long as they have in him a
model that can lead them on the right way. --- While according to Spinoza the
prophets do not see the truth in its pure form, but only in images, the
divine wisdom was revealed immediately in Christ, the only one who has had the
capacity to apprehend something which is not contained in, and cannot be
derived from, the first grounds of our knowledge. In a letter (Ep. 73) Spinoza
declares that he does not understand what the Church means by the doctrine
that God has taken on human nature; it seems to him as absurd as that the
circle should take on the nature of the square. But he assumes that God's
eternal wisdom, which reveals itself in all things and especially in the human
mind, has revealed itself most of all in Christ. --- Spinoza demands that the
biblical writings be subjected
% --- p. 332 ---
\opage{332}to a purely historical investigation. The Bible is to be explained by
itself, just as nature is explained by itself. Only when one has established
what the Bible really teaches can one raise the question whether this teaching
is true or not. Just as Spinoza has maintained the independence of the
investigation of nature and of ethics, so he here maintains the independence
of the historical method. His historical eye shows itself in the demand that
in the interpretation of the writings one is to take account of what one
knows of the individualities of the authors. One is also to investigate the
origin of the writings. The investigation Spinoza undertakes leads him to
assume that the five books of Moses were composed in the time of the Exile.
Even if more recent research does not always go so far, it nevertheless has a
forerunner in Spinoza.

It was through his philosophy of religion that Spinoza first had an
influence. Before Lessing and Goethe, and after them the speculative
philosophers, pleaded his cause at the end of the eighteenth century, his
views had an influence of no small extent in the Netherlands, both in such a
way that individuals quietly found nourishment for their life of thought and
feeling in his ideas, and in such a way that religious sects were even formed,
now of a more mystical, now of a more rationalist character, whose conception
and application of Christianity derived, through more or fewer intermediate
links and modifications, from the writings of the solitary philosopher. Right
up to the end of the eighteenth century Dutch orthodoxy had frequent occasion
to denounce Spinozist thoughts as heresy; his books were repeatedly forbidden
and confiscated. In its more mystical form religious Spinozism united with the
influence of Jakob Böhme's writings, which from the end of the seventeenth
century were eagerly read in the Netherlands. --- Remarkably enough, the three
elements which were bound together into a peculiar unity in Spinoza's thinking
have later each in its own time won enthusiastic adherence: first the
religious, in the Dutch sects, then the idealist, in the German Renaissance at
the end of the eighteenth century, and finally the realist, among philosophers
and natural scientists in our own day. And even thinkers who officially would
not acknowledge him were nevertheless deeply and strongly influenced by him.
This holds in particular of
% --- p. 333 ---
\opage{333}the man who has often been set up, by himself and by others, as
Spinoza's antipode: Leibniz.

\section*{6.\quad Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz}

\subsection*{a.\quad Biography and Characterization}

In Descartes, Hobbes and Spinoza we find three great systems developed which,
for all their differences, have this in common, that they assert a purely mechanical
connection of nature as regards the material side of existence. In these systems the
consequences had been drawn from the principles whose establishment had made the
rise of exact natural science possible. They were attempts to show how
existence looks when these principles hold absolutely for all
material phenomena (whether one then holds that there are other phenomena
than the material ones, or not). To many of the old school these new
principles and systems were the epitome of arbitrariness and ungodliness. A reaction
makes itself felt in various forms at the end of the seventeenth century. In
philosophical respects the reaction of greatest interest is the one which will not give up
what had really been won in scientific respects, and which, not in an external
way, by compromising or by patching incompatible elements together, but in an
internal way, through an investigation of the presuppositions that lay at the basis of
the mechanical view of nature itself, sought to lead beyond it and to reconcile it
with the ancient and medieval conception on which men had turned their backs with such great
energy. In this sense Leibniz signifies a reaction against those three great
thinkers. But perhaps never has a reaction been carried through in so
profound a way, even if Leibniz, consciously and unconsciously, accommodated himself in his
manner of expression to conservative views far more than his standpoint entitled
him to. What from the first offended Leibniz in the modern ideas, for all
his admiration for them and for those who bore them, was that they threatened the aesthetic and the
religious contemplation of nature. The legitimacy of the concept of purpose was rejected
in the world-view,
% --- p. 334 ---
\opage{334}and the world seemed to become a mere machine. The aim of his life was to bring about a
reconciliation between ideas from opposite regions of the world of the spirit, and
in working to reach this aim he developed a wealth of thoughts and
points of view, of discoveries and hints, which is perhaps unique in the
history of thought. In almost every scientific field he intervened creatively
and stimulatingly, and there is an inner agreement between, a common type for,
his thoughts in the widely different fields in which he worked.

Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz was born in Leipzig on 21 June 1646. His father,
who was a jurist and professor of moral philosophy, died early, and the boy, who
was often left to himself, was very fond of spending his time in his father's
library, where he read all the books he could manage, at first
chiefly novels and historical works, later scholastic works. Despite all
the obstacles of foreign languages and of the abstruse character of the content, he nevertheless sought
by his own efforts to understand what he got hold of. Those around him, he relates
in an autobiographical sketch, feared first that he would become a poet, and next
that he would become a scholastic: ``they did not know that my mind could not be filled
exclusively by one kind of thing''. The struggle between the mechanical and the
teleological view of nature began early in his mind. He relates that as a
quite young man he wandered about in a wood near Leipzig and pondered whether he
should hold to the scholastic philosophy or join the new doctrines.
The need of an all-round education and of acquainting himself with the exact
sciences led him away from Leipzig. On the occasion of a slight he gave
up taking the doctor's degree in his native city. He took the degree in law at Altorf
and then went to Mainz, where, despite his youth, he was taken into the
Elector's service. Plans for the improvement of the science of law and of
the law-books occupied him greatly in these years alongside his philosophical and
scientific studies. He wanted to root out the scholastic barbarism in
jurisprudence, just as at the same time he became more and more convinced of the
decisive victory of modern natural science over the scholastic doctrine of nature. There was
% --- p. 335 ---
\opage{335}even, by his own later statement (in the Nouveaux Essais), a time when
he inclined very strongly to ``the side of the Spinozists''. But the ruling thought in
him was nevertheless this: to maintain the assumption that existence is determined by purposes
without giving up mechanical natural science. With zeal he defends the new
scientific conception against the men of the older time, his teacher Jakob
Thomasius and the famous jurist and physician Herman Conring. But it was his
endeavor to show that the mechanical connection of nature, far from excluding,
actually presupposes a divine thought of providence. In a small treatise
\textit{(Confessio naturæ contra Atheistas)} and in his letters to Jakob
Thomasius from the years 1668---69 this double endeavor appears clearly.
Leibniz is here still a dualist; there is still for him a gulf between the two
principles he wants to connect. In studying Kepler, Galilei and Descartes he feels, by his own account,
``as if transported into another world''; but the old
world is to be connected with the new. A journey to Paris on a mission for his government
gave him the opportunity for new studies. Alongside his practical business and
alongside the remarkable proposal he laid before Louis XIV for a French
conquest of Egypt (in order to divert the lust for conquest from Germany), he immersed himself
in mathematical studies in Paris under the guidance of Huyghens and was led to
the invention of the differential calculus, at the same time as he zealously studied
the Cartesian philosophy. His standpoint around the year 1670 bears the stamp of
the influence of Hobbes's writings. In a treatise on natural philosophy
\textit{(Hypothesis physica nova.} 1671) he asserts, in a manner similar to
Hobbes and Gassendi, the continuity of motion by means of the thought of tendencies of motion
(conatus) in the smallest moments and the smallest parts. This thought stands in
connection with the discovery in the following years of the significance of infinitely small
quantities in mathematics. From this time on he combats Descartes's doctrine of
the conservation of motion and begins to put the conservation of force in its place.
He finds the difference between mind and matter in this: in the material
domain a tendency which does not pass over into motion can exist only in the
single moment, but in mental life the tendency can, by
% --- p. 336 ---
\opage{336}means of memory and thinking, reach beyond the moment. He has expressed
this pregnantly in the proposition that a body is a momentary mind or a mind
without memory. In a letter from the year 1671 we read: ``As the activity of bodies
consists in motion, so the activity of souls consists in striving (conatus)
or, so to speak, in a minimal or punctual motion, just as the soul
properly is only in a point in space, while the body occupies a place''. We
have in these hints what one might call Leibniz's second philosophy. He
seeks to go beyond dualism and asserts continuity by putting mental striving
into the differentials of matter, but is still not clear about the relation between
the material and the mental. An obscure point of union is found in the concept of
striving; beyond this indefinite hint Leibniz does not here get. Only this stands
firm for him, that the solution can be found only by going back from what is given in
the phenomena to its elements and presuppositions.

Just as Leibniz worked in the fields of various sciences, it was also
his endeavor to come into personal contact with eminent men of
various intellectual tendencies. In Paris he associated with Huyghens, to whose mathematical and
scientific ideas Leibniz owes much: through him he was surely
led to the principle of the conservation of force, which plays so great a part in
his thinking. Even earlier he had addressed himself to Hobbes in writing,
though no correspondence seems to have come about. During his stay in
Paris his attention was directed to Spinoza, whose ``Theological-Political
Treatise'' had appeared a few years before, while the ``Ethics'' was as yet accessible
only to a narrow circle. The mathematician and philosopher Tschirnhausen, who
belonged to this circle and was one of Spinoza's most acute correspondents, was
together with Leibniz in Paris and gave him a survey of Spinoza's views.
Through a common friend Tschirnhausen informed Spinoza that he had
met in Paris ``a man well versed in the various sciences and free from the usual
theological prejudices, by the name of Leibniz, with whom he had formed a
friendship, since he was a man who,
% --- p. 337 ---
\opage{337}like himself, worked at developing his mind and regarded this as the
most important thing''. Tschirnhausen considers his new friend worthy to know the ``Ethics'' and
asks the master for permission to show it to him, reminding him that
Leibniz had already earlier written Spinoza a letter concerning the
``Theological-Political Treatise''. Spinoza answers: ``I believe I know this
Leibniz through his letters. But I do not know why he, who is a court councillor in
Frankfurt (i.e.\ Mainz), has gone to France. So far as I have been able to see from his
letters, he is a man of a free mind and well versed in every science. Yet
I believe it would be unwise to entrust my writings to him so quickly.
I should first like to know what he is doing in France, and to hear
what my friend Tschirnhausen thinks of him when he has associated with him longer and
come to know his character better''. Spinoza evidently did not have real
confidence in Leibniz, whose many-sidedness and pliancy were certainly not always
favorable to his intellectual character and in any case gave his spiritual
life and his activity a stamp that was entirely opposite to Spinoza's withdrawn and
concentrated existence as a thinker. Spinoza's mistrust was justified. For however
near Leibniz stands to Spinoza in his final results, and when he is consistent,
he nevertheless in his later writings seizes every opportunity to distance himself from
him, and that often in expressions one would not have expected of a man who was
``free from the usual theological prejudices''. At this time, however, he was
very eager to come into contact with Spinoza. After a four years' stay in
Paris (1672---76), where he --- a proof of how different minds he
knew how to value and learn from, --- associated with the great Jansenist theologian and
zealous Cartesian Antoine Arnauld, he went by way of England to Holland, where he
stayed for two months, during which he repeatedly visited Spinoza and
discussed philosophical subjects with him. Only through the most recent literary
finds\textsuperscript{68}) has this personal relation between the two
great thinkers been discovered, a relation which became so intimate that Spinoza at last overcame his
misgivings and showed him the ``Ethics''. Leibniz himself does mention in a single place
(in the ``Theodicy'') his visit to Spinoza, but
% --- p. 338 ---
\opage{338}gives the impression that the conversation turned on the events of the day! It was
not commendable to have been so near to Spinoza. One sees accordingly that several
of the letters in the edition of Spinoza's works which his friends saw to immediately after his death
have been abridged, and the names of the writers of the letters often omitted, and Leibniz,
who had looked forward to the publication with great longing, was very dismayed to
find one of his own letters (an entirely innocent one, to be sure) printed with his name
given. That Leibniz had written Spinoza several letters, no one had previously
suspected. --- Spinoza's line of thought exerted a strong influence on Leibniz,
especially in leading him definitively beyond the dualistic theory. One finds
Spinoza's thought again in him when at this time he objects against the Cartesians that
the difference between mind and matter did not exclude their being properties
of the same being. We have marginal notes and excerpts of Leibniz's dating
from his first reading of Spinoza's ``Ethics''. There are three points on which
he at once raises objections, and all three are characteristic of his line of thought.
The first is the fifth proposition of the first book, which asserts that there can be only one
substance; the second is the exclusion of intellect and will from ``the
producing nature'' (Eth. I, 31); the third is the appendix to the first book with
the famous polemic against final causes. --- As little as Leibniz ever
was a Cartesian or a Hobbist, so little was he ever a
Spinozist. But he received mighty impulses from his predecessors. As regards
Spinoza it must especially be noted that Leibniz embraces the identity hypothesis
put forward by Spinoza and carries it further. Hardly any
greater misunderstanding of Leibniz could be conceived than to conclude, from his assertion of
the plurality of substances, that he disputed the identity hypothesis. His
endeavor aimed precisely at uniting both assumptions; how far he
succeeded is a question in itself. ---

At the end of the year 1676 Leibniz took up a position with the Duke of
Hanover (Braunschweig-Lüneburg) as court councillor and librarian. A mass of
administrative, historical and political work laid claim to him, and his
restless zeal
% --- p. 339 ---
% scan: „kalolske“ (p. 339)
\opage{339}to keep up in every field brought with it an enormous correspondence. In the
library in Hanover are kept the correspondences he carried on with over a thousand
different persons. But just as it was the main thought of his philosophy that existence
consists of a multitude of individual beings, each peculiar in itself, in mutual
harmony and continuity, so too there is a connection between his
endeavors in the various fields. He had an eye for small relations,
for the vanishing differences which nevertheless, by their joining together and totalization,
can prove to be realities. His mathematics, his physics and his philosophy
show us this trait. But no less weight did he lay on continuity, the
inner connection between all things. It was the connection between past and present
that interested him in his historical studies, and it was a similar
interest that led him to procure information about China through
the missionaries of the Jesuit order. He had a sense for the practically useful as well
as for science and Church. He saw to the development of the mines in
the duchy, worked for the founding of academies, proposed that the monasteries
be transformed into scientific institutions, negotiated with Bossuet about a union
between the Catholic and Protestant Churches and later with Protestant
theologians about a union between the Lutheran and the Reformed Churches. To Peter the
Great, whom he highly admired and with whom he had several meetings, he put
proposals for reforms and for measures to promote philology and
natural science. As a philosopher of language he had so sound an eye and asserted
with such energy the significance of experience for the study of language that Max Müller has
been able to say of him that, had he been understood and supported by the
learned men of his time, the science of language would have been founded a century earlier
as an inductive science. In the field of medicine too he put forward
significant ideas. --- No wonder that he can declare in a letter: ``How
extraordinarily distracted I am cannot be told. I make researches in the
archives, bring out old papers and collect unprinted documents. I receive
and answer letters in great number. But I have so much that is new in mathematics, so
many thoughts
% --- p. 340 ---
\opage{340}in philosophy, so many other literary observations which I do not like to let
be lost, that I often do not know what I should do first.'' Nor, accordingly, did
Leibniz succeed in collecting himself for a work typical of his personality and his line of
thought. He was not a ``man of one book'' like Spinoza. His ideas he expressed
in an infinity of letters and small treatises, which are not yet all printed.
The most important philosophical works brought to light so far are found in Gerhardt's edition
(7 vols.); but much still lies in the library in Hanover, and a
new collected edition of his works is being planned, arranged by the international
association of the scientific societies of the various countries. An incredible
capacity for work and mobility of thought this man had. And just as existence in
his system is mirrored in countless ways in the individual souls, so too
he had a need to make his system intuitive from the very different
standpoints with which he came into contact. It was during his correspondence with the Jansenist
Arnauld that he developed his system to full consciousness in himself. But he had
nothing against giving it a scholastic form in order to make it acceptable to his
friends among the Jesuits. He cast it in a more popular form when he
philosophized with the Electress of Hanover or with the Queen of Prussia,
or when he was to give Prince Eugene an exposition of his doctrine (the later
so-called ``Monadologie'').

But we have not yet followed the development of Leibniz's philosophical views to
their conclusion, to the point where he could say that he believed he had
found ``a new expression for the inside of things'' (une nouvelle face de l'intérieur des
choses). We have seen how he held fast to the legitimacy of mechanical natural science,
but wanted to reconcile the teleological way of looking at things with it,
first in a more dualistic manner, later (following Hobbes and Spinoza)
in a more monistic way. It was his conviction that ``the moderns had carried
the reform too far'' by making everything into machines, but it is no less his
conviction that hitherto men had only ``prostituted themselves'' by trying to
refute the strict mechanical
% --- p. 341 ---
% print: „mètaphysique),}“ (p. 341) (misprint)
\opage{341}connection even in the material processes that proved to be most closely
bound up with mental phenomena.

In a letter from the year 1697 Leibniz wrote: ``Most of my opinions have been
matured at last after a deliberation of twenty years; for I began at a
very young age to think . . . Yet I have changed and changed again my
views according to the new knowledge I acquired, and only about twelve
years ago did I feel satisfied.'' This statement points to the year
1685. In that year Leibniz worked out a small treatise \textit{(Petit
discours de métaphysique),} which at the beginning of the following year he sent
to Arnauld. It states that existence consists of individual substances; in
each of these the world is expressed from one of the infinitely many possible sides
from which it can be seen in the divine thought; each one is a divine thought
--- realized by constant ``emanation''. Extension and motion are
only phenomena, just as much as the sense qualities. Only force, not motion,
persists; and force is one with substance. This treatise had been prepared by an
earlier one (of 1680), in which it is first developed that the innermost nature of
motion --- motion, to which the modern systems reduced everything in the
material nature! --- was not yet sufficiently cleared up (intima
motus nondum patent), and then it is asserted that to subsist (to exist, to be
substance) and to act are one and the same, and that all force or striving is an
acting\textsuperscript{69}). The proposition that every substance acts, and that everything
that acts is substance (omnem substantiam agere, at omne agens
substantiam appellari), is perhaps the most important in the whole Leibnizian
philosophy. By it an end was made of the mysticism or mythology that conceives
the essence of things as a resting essence, an unchangeable subsistence in itself.
Leibniz himself found in it the possibility of his union of teleology and
mechanism, in that the forces which make up the innermost nature of individual beings and
phenomena, and are that which persists through all changes, are assumed to
flow out from the divine being and to act in the direction of valuable
purposes. The divine purposes are then fulfilled in nature without a breach of the
% --- p. 342 ---
\opage{342}lawful connection, but precisely through it. The advance in the ``Discours'' of
1685 over the treatise of 1680 consists chiefly in this, that the \textit{individual}
character of the substances is asserted, and that they are conceived in analogy with
the souls of men and animals. Each individual being is a little world, develops
according to its inner laws, by its own force, a peculiar radiation of the
divine force, and this development takes place, on account of the common
origin, in harmony with the development of all other beings. --- With this Leibniz's
system was complete. It first came before the public in a treatise which was
printed in the Journal des Savants in 1695 \textit{(Système nouveau de la nature et de
la communication des substances).} And the name monad he used only later
(1696). He hardly borrowed the name from Bruno; on the whole no direct influence of
Bruno on Leibniz can be shown historically, however much kinship
there is in several of their ideas. Rather (according to what has been conjectured
in the most recent time) he took the name from the mystical chemist van Helmont
the Younger, with whom, just shortly before it is first found in him, he had
come into personal contact. ---

Leibniz fulfilled his own definition of substance as that which constantly acts.
Even after his system was formed, he went on working to shape its
fundamental thoughts to the greatest possible clarity. His extensive
correspondence and his wide personal acquaintance gave him ample opportunity for this.
Thus during a stay in Vienna he worked out (1714) for Prince Eugene an
exposition of the doctrine of monads, which after his death was printed under the title
\textit{Monadologie.} At the same time he followed attentively what was stirring in his
time. With two eminent thinkers he entered into a discussion, which he conducted with great
chivalry. John Locke's attempt to derive all knowledge from experience
he criticized in his \textit{Nouveaux Essais} in a way that is brilliant and still to this
day instructive, asserting in particular the significance of the inner dispositions, of the conditions lying
in the knowing beings' own nature. As Locke died
