before Leibniz had his work finished, he would not publish it, and so it came
not to exert the influence
% --- p. 343 ---
\opage{343}on the philosophical discussion that it would surely otherwise have had. Only in 1765
did it appear. The other contemporary against whose views Leibniz felt
called upon to take up his pen was Pierre Bayle. Bayle had given a critique
of the attempts of various theologians and philosophers to demonstrate a harmony between
the assumption of an almighty divine government and the moral and physical evil
in the world, and had asserted that philosophically the assumption of two opposite
principles, a good and an evil one, could be defended far more easily given the world's
actual constitution. Against this Leibniz sought in his \textit{Théodicée,} which
appeared in 1710, to show the agreement between theology and philosophy and to ground
the claim that the actual world is the best possible world. It is
Leibniz's weakest work, diffuse and loose in form, vague and in a bad sense
popular in its line of thought. Nowhere, moreover, does he accommodate himself more to
notions to which, by strict consistency, he could give no place in his
system. It was unfortunate that it was above all this work through which Leibniz
was known in the eighteenth century. The ``Nouveaux Essais'' lay forgotten in the library in
Hanover, and the brilliant and inspired small treatises in journals in which
he had expressed his real fundamental thoughts were accessible only to few.

There can be no doubt that Leibniz meant his attempt to
unite and reconcile religion and philosophy honestly. It was a thought which from his youth
on runs through his whole life. But a properly religious nature he was
not. This is shown by the ease with which he could disregard confessional
oppositions. It was natural rather than positive religion that lay
close to his heart. And it was his sense for the individual and characteristic
that made it easy and at the same time interesting for him to familiarize himself with the various
ecclesiastical systems, just as it was his faith in the harmony among all
individual peculiarities and endeavors that led him to the wish for a
reconciliation between the contending Churches, a wish which was not shared by men like
Bossuet and Spener, who could see no legitimate peculiarity in confessions
other than their own. Arnauld urged him rather to be converted
to the true faith than to
% --- p. 344 ---
\opage{344}speculate about the connection of things. Characteristic of Leibniz is a story he
liked to tell about two brothers, one of whom had become a Catholic and
then sought to convince the other, while the latter just as eagerly sought to
win him back for Protestantism; the result was that they both
mutually convinced each other, --- and the end of the whole thing was that God, on
account of their great zeal, had mercy on them both! What interested
Leibniz was the inner force and striving in the monads, not merely the particular
way in which force manifests itself in the individual monad, and which is often
regarded by the latter as the only right one. Leibniz's faith concerned the universal harmony, which
for him was not first a result of the future, but was already present in
minds, if only they could become conscious of it. In every book Leibniz
read --- and he read many books --- he found something that was
interesting and instructive to him, and since he knew how differently things can
look from different points of view, he was inclined to defend and
excuse even where he could not approve. With people of all
stations in life he knew how to talk about their interests. His recognition of
the monads extended to the lower forms. He avoided killing animals, and if
he had used an insect for microscopic examination, he put it carefully
back on the leaf from which he had taken it. Mild and cheerful, not
subject to strong emotions, constantly occupied with thinking and study ---
so he went through the world. --- His last years were lonely. Because of
his many labors he had, as he himself said, not had time to marry
--- before it was too late. Whereas in an earlier time he had been in favor at
the Hanoverian court, and had advanced to ``Geheime-Justizienrath'', he seems
in later years --- after the death of his princely patrons --- to have been in a
kind of disgrace. The clergy and the people suspected his orthodoxy because
he did not go to church; his name was interpreted in Low German as Lövenix, i.e.\
Glaube-nichts. When he died (1716), his bier was followed by only a
few. --- His motto was: ``As often as an hour is wasted, a part of
life is lost'';
% --- p. 345 ---
% print: „fænomale“ (p. 345) (misprint)
\opage{345}it was set on his coffin together with a symbol he had been fond of: a spiral
with the superscription: Inclinata resurget (it bends only in order to rise).---

\subsection*{b.\quad The Doctrine of Monads}
% print: „b“ without its point (p. 345) (misprint)

Now that we have gained a survey of the historical development of
Leibniz's philosophy, the task is to give a systematic exposition of it. The
writings which must chiefly be taken as the basis here are \textit{Discours de
métaphysique} (1685), \textit{Système nouveau} (1695), \textit{Lettre à
Basnage} (1698), \textit{De ipsa natura} (1698) and \textit{Monadologie} (1714).
But a mass of letters and smaller treatises must be compared with these.

It is by an analysis of the fundamental propositions of natural science that Leibniz grounds
his philosophy. He acknowledges these fundamental propositions as unconditionally as Hobbes
and Spinoza, but he finds them to be derived from presuppositions lying
deeper. Physics has its ground, for him, in metaphysics. The first and foremost
thing, then, is to see how, according to Leibniz, the transition from physics to metaphysics is to be
made.

When the new science aimed at reducing everything in nature to motion,
Leibniz entirely approves of this endeavor. But as a philosopher he asks: what
reality has motion itself, and what cause has it? --- All motion is
relative. Whether something is assumed to be moved will depend on the standpoint from which
it is seen. The real reality is not motion itself, but the force which is
its cause, and which persists even if the motion ceases. The Cartesians, who
taught that the sum of motion in the world is the same, but also that motion passes
over into rest and conversely, are forced to assume constant breaches of continuity,
since both the transition from motion to rest and the converse became inexplicable. Only
by means of the \textit{concept of force} (or tendency, conatus) can the connection
be maintained. There is then only a relative difference between motion and rest: they are
different phenomenal forms of force. It is force that persists. There is
no absolute rest. Not in the smallest moment one may think of is a moved
% --- p. 346 ---
\opage{346}body in one and the same place in space. If one asks what force then is, Leibniz
answers: \textit{that in the present state which brings with it a change in
the future} (ce qu'il y a dans l'état présent, qui porte avec soi un changement
pour l'avenir) (Lettre à Basnage). This is what is real in existence. Leibniz
also arrives at this concept through a critique of the concept of the atom as the
atomism of the time conceived it. The assumption of absolutely hard atoms would
conflict with the conservation of force and with continuity, since in every
collision force would be lost. The atoms must therefore (as Huyghens already
taught) be elastic --- and must accordingly consist of parts; absolute atoms are
consequently a self-contradiction. There is, when we examine the matter thoroughly,
activity everywhere. ``The atoms are,'' says Leibniz in a letter, ``only the effect of
a weakness in our imagination, which likes to rest and therefore
hurries to come to an end with the divisions and analyses''. (Letter to
Hartsoeker 1710). In his polemic against the Newtonian Clarke, Leibniz distinguishes
between a body's losing motion, considered as a whole, in a collision with another body,
and force's being lost: the motion which the body considered as a whole
(in relation to other bodies) loses passes over to the parts, which
by the impact are set in an inner vibration; the forces are not annihilated, but
distributed among the small parts. The same thing happens here as when one changes large
money into small coin. (Cinquième écrit de Mr. Leibniz § 99). The difference between the
solid and the fluid is relative, just as motion is relative. From this point of view too
only force has a real reality.

That force is the real reality Leibniz expresses, in the language of the time, by saying
that force is substance and that all substance is force. But the concept of force is
in turn closely connected with the \textit{concept of law:} force is, after all, only that in a
state which brings it about that a change occurs in the future. The presupposition of
every application of the concept of force is then a lawful connection between the
changing states. The principle of sufficient reason, which says that there is a
ground for everything, is therefore the real fundamental proposition of Leibniz's philosophy,
although
% --- p. 347 ---
\opage{347}he sets it up as an express fundamental proposition only in his later writings (the Theodicy and the Monadology).
And with the concept of law another main concept
of Leibniz's is in turn connected: \textit{the concept of individuality.} For individuality means
for him the law according to which changes in a being's states succeed
one another. Each individual has, so to speak, its formula. And just as in a
mathematical series one can infer the following terms when one has found the law
for the succession of the first terms, so it is also with the inner changes of an individual
being. In the law for their succession consists
individuality itself: \textit{la loi du changement fait l'individualite de chaque
substance particulière} (Lettre à Basnage). In the ``Discours de métaphysique'', where
the concept of the individual substance is introduced for the first time, the
relation between the substance and its changing states is compared with the relation between
subject and predicate in a logical judgment: just as in a logical judgment it must be
possible to find the predicate contained in the subject as soon as one knows the subject
completely, so he who knows the nature of the individual will be able to
derive from it all its changing states. There is continuity between these,
since the following one always has its ground in the preceding one. Each of these
substances is therefore a little world for itself, develops from its own
inner drive and has its own inner life. Only in a miraculous way can such an
individual substance arise or pass away. And each substance has its own inner
law, different from others.

If it is asked why the real, the persisting (the substance) must be individual,
Leibniz answers: because only \textit{unities,} individual beings, can exist. He
reproached the Cartesians not only for ascribing absolute reality to motion,
but also for ascribing absolute reality to extension and making
it substance. Already in his notes on reading Spinoza's ``Ethics''
he writes that he is not sure that bodies are substances; it is otherwise
with souls. This remark indicates the direction in which his
thinking went. In his later works the following line of thought recurs constantly under manifoldly varied
turns of phrase: extension
% --- p. 348 ---
\opage{348}presupposes something which is extended, that is, repeated several times.
Extension means multiplicity, composition, aggregate. But the nature of the
composite depends on what composes it (the components). Not the
aggregate, but the ones of which it consists, have reality. If there were not
absolutely simple substances, there would therefore be no reality at all.
The assumption of the reality of extended matter brings with it, moreover, the difficulty that
its divisibility, by virtue of the law of continuity, goes on to infinity. The true
unities therefore cannot be material, extended; if, on the other
hand, no such absolute unities existed, matter would be a mere
seeming without any real significance. Only the absolutely simple and indivisible can be
substance, and it cannot be material.

Before we ask what, then, it is, one more important determination must be
brought forward. Leibniz started from the fundamental propositions of natural science. The
most important of these was for him the principle of the conservation of force\footnote{As
already remarked, this law derives from \textsc{Huyghens,} who in his doctrine of
the pendulum further developed hints which Galilei had given, and which we have also
found in his disciples Gassendi and Hobbes. (See E. MACH: Die Geschichte
und die Wurzel des Satzes von der Erhaltung der Arbeit. Prag 1872. p. 10 f.).
Leibniz maintained the principle of the conservation of force against the Newtonians, who
denied it. See his interesting polemic against Clarke (Opera philos. ed.
Erdmann. p. 746 ff.). On the relation between Descartes, Newton and Leibniz with
regard to this principle see \textsc{Rosenberger:} Isaac Newton u. seine
physikalischen Principien. Leipzig 1895. p. 409---412.}. It was for him
\textit{the foundation of the laws of nature} (fundamentum naturæ legum). This very
foundation of the laws of nature can, according to Leibniz (see especially De ipsa natura,
Erdmann's edition p. 155), be understood only by a teleological argument: it is
necessary that the same quantity of force be preserved in the world; but this necessity
depends on the divine wisdom and order reigning in the world; the
first principle or ``sufficient reason'' of mechanism is a final cause, \textit{a
teleological principle.} In a small
% --- p. 349 ---
% print: „Leipniz“ (p. 349) (misprint)
\opage{349}treatise directed against the physicist Papin \textit{(De legibus naturæ,} Dutens' edition, III, p.
255) Leibniz carries this out as follows: cause and effect must always correspond to
each other, be equivalent. If there were more in the effect than in the cause,
we should get a perpetuum mobile; if there were less in the effect than in the
cause, the same cause could never be brought about again, nature
would constantly go backward, perfection would be diminished. Both would conflict
with the divine wisdom and immutability. When the equivalence of cause and
effect obtains in nature, to the exclusion of the two other possibilities, then
this, according to Leibniz, cannot be grounded purely mathematically or mechanically, but must
be explained teleologically.

The law according to which the individual beings, which are the true
realities, unfold their changing states is for Leibniz a law according to
which they advance to more perfect states, not merely to new states.
The relation between cause and effect is thus here identical with the relation between
means and purpose. In its innermost ground existence is so disposed that the
purely mechanical laws act in the direction of what the laws of justice and of love
demand. In the law inherent in its own being (lex insita) both kinds of laws are
united in the case of every individual. --- Leibniz is, as one sees, so
occupied with the law of the conservation of force that he overlooks that, teleologically seen,
what matters is not that the same quantity of force is preserved, but that it is preserved in a
form favorable and useful for the subsistence of life and for continued development. This is,
moreover, a consideration which has come clearly to light only through the investigations of the most
recent time. --- But although Leibniz thus grounds the mechanical
connection of nature teleologically, it is nevertheless not his intention to reintroduce
final causes and to permit an explanation of natural phenomena by appeal
to inner forces or to purposiveness. In particulars one must proceed
strictly mechanically; it is only mechanism as a whole, or rather the
first principles of mechanism themselves, that prove to become intelligible only through
teleological consideration. The mechanical connection of nature
% --- p. 350 ---
% print: „degrès“ (p. 350) (misprint)
\opage{350}is the fact from which Leibniz's whole philosophy proceeds, just as much as
Hobbes's and Spinoza's. ---

The technical name for the absolute individual beings which for Leibniz make up the
true reality is \textit{monads.} It is a Greek word which means unities,
and which thus designates the beings only from the formal side. If we now ask what
these individual unities, with their inner states unfolded according to a definite law,
really are, Leibniz answers that we must conceive them in analogy with
our own souls. In the ``Discours'' this is not stated definitely. But in the following
correspondence with Arnauld we read: ``The substantial unity presupposes a
complete (accompli), indivisible and naturally indestructible being,
since its concept encompasses everything that is to happen to it. Such a thing cannot
be found in figure or motion, . . . but only in a soul or a substantial
form \textit{in the likeness of (à l'exemple de)} what is called an I''. (Letter to
Arnauld, Nov. 1686). The objective analysis is thus here supplemented by a
subjective analysis. In ourselves we find, by way of self-observation, inner
states (sensations, feelings, thoughts) which change, and a need or
drive which leads us to pass over from one state to another. By
means of this subjective observation we must --- by way of analogy --- make
the nature of the monads intelligible to ourselves. Our soul is only a single monad, but we have
no reason to believe that we stand alone in nature. On the contrary. By virtue of
the law of continuity, which excludes leaps in nature, we must assume that there
are infinitely many degrees of the kind of existence we know from ourselves:
c'est partout et toujours la même chose, aux degrés de perfection près.
The law of analogy bids us everywhere to embrace the principle: ``Just as with us''
\textit{(tout comme ici)\textsuperscript{70}). The law of
analogy,} according to which we conceive all other existence as differing only in degree
from our own, is for Leibniz only a special form of the law of continuity and
springs, like it, from the principle of sufficient reason. If one does not
assume such a general ensoulment of lower and higher degrees, it becomes
entirely unintelligible how sensation and consciousness can arise. Just as
the origin of motion became inexplicable for the
% --- p. 351 ---
\opage{351}Cartesians because they did not go back to force, so the origin of consciousness
was also a riddle for them, because they took no account of the obscurer
degrees and forms of mental life, the unconscious mental life, the need and craving which
first awaken to the clarity of consciousness at higher stages of life. In ourselves
we constantly observe, after all, an alternation of clearly conscious, obscure and unconscious
states. In analogy with this we must conceive monads of all degrees with respect to
clarity and obscurity. There are slumbering, dreaming and more or less waking
monads. The uniformity of nature leads to this assumption. The part of matter
which makes up the human body cannot, after all, alone be endowed with the capacity
to sense and to will. Something analogous (whether one wants to call it soul
or not) must be found at lower stages. In a letter (of May 1704) Leibniz calls
this application of analogy ``mon grand principe des choses naturelles''.

The way by which all mythologies and earlier speculative systems --- without
being conscious of it --- had come to the assumption of the mental as
ruling in existence, this way Leibniz goes in full consciousness. He points
clearly to the point where all metaphysical idealism springs up. And it is again
the presupposition of the complete intelligibility of existence that guides him here.
From this presupposition follow the continuity of all existences and the analogy of all beings
with our own being.

But as Leibniz has come to this point in the development of his thought, he stands at
a turning point. He builds his philosophy on an analysis of material phenomena,
guided by the endeavor to find what is real and persisting in them. Now that he
has arrived at the assumption that, properly speaking, only representing beings exist,
with differing obscurity and clarity in their representations, matter becomes for
him a \textit{mere} phenomenon. It is a seeming for the senses when bodies seem
to exist. The senses do not deceive us, however, any more than they deceive
us when we believe that the sun goes round the earth. The phenomena are real
insofar as there is a regular connection between them, a law according to which
they succeed one another.
% --- p. 352 ---
\opage{352}It is this law that is the mark of what is reality for us. But
it does not force us to assume that anything exists other than monads and their
representations. --- At this point there would be the possibility of an entirely new
line of thought: a testing of whether, from the purely subjective standpoint, from
the assumption that the world exists only in the form of representation, one would arrive at the
same result as by the objective way Leibniz has gone so far. This new way
Leibniz did not take, and when in his last years he heard of Berkeley's
attempt in this direction, it struck him as a mere paradox (see his letter to
des Bosses of 15 March 1715). Leibniz himself evidently did not become clear about
the great difference between being a phenomenon \textit{of} something and being a phenomenon
\textit{for} someone. Both relations can lie in the concept of phenomenon; Leibniz
begins with the first relation and ends in the second. And it is only after
he has set up the concept of substance as force and as individual unity
that he --- in accordance with the law of analogy --- finds its essence to consist in
representing activity. Precisely because this last assumption is the end point of
his train of thought, it is understandable that he does not draw all the consequences of
it\textsuperscript{71}). Leibniz continues to treat material phenomena
as the expression of an objective order of things. By virtue of the law of continuity everything
in the material world stands in reciprocal action; a change in one part of the world
extends to all parts. And from this it is concluded that it is the \textit{whole}
universe which is represented by each monad in a more obscure or clearer way. Every
monad represents the whole universe, just as every single point in the physical
universe feels everything that happens in the whole universe. The very assumption that there
is a multiplicity of monads shows that Leibniz did not go the purely
subjective way, for then he would have had to do with only one monad and its
picture of the world. The assumption of other consciousnesses than my own
already presupposes, after all, the application of the inference from analogy on which Leibniz
builds his metaphysical idealism. ---

An empirical confirmation of his hypothesis that there is force, life and soul behind
all apparently dead mass he found
% --- p. 353 ---
% print: „Mangfoldigded“ (p. 353) (misprint)
\opage{353}in the discovery of the small organisms which Swammerdam, Leeuwenhook and other
naturalists found with the help of the microscope. There opened up here for him a
world of infinitely small beings in the domain of organic life, just as he
himself had helped to open up the world of infinitely small quantities, and
just as in his philosophy he had asserted that behind the apparently homogeneous
mass the true reality was found, consisting of individual beings with a
nature akin to our own. Arising and passing away, birth and death were
for him only phenomena, expressions of processes of contraction or unfolding,
of obscuration or clarification in monads. The absolute leaps and
differences fell away (no less than the homogeneous mass) the more clearly he
became aware of the infinite individual nuances of life. With visible satisfaction
Leibniz in all his later expositions refers to the works of the great contemporary
naturalists just named.

With his concept of the monad Leibniz apparently enters into a sharp opposition to
Spinoza. For the latter there was only one substance, and all individual beings stood
to it as the waves to the sea. For Leibniz the true reality is a
multiplicity of individual forces, each acting according to its inherent law,
so that all its effects unfold from its own original
character. Leibniz himself often sharply emphasized this opposition, most clearly in a
letter to Bourguet (Dec. 1714): ``I do not know how one can
extract Spinozism from my doctrine. It is precisely by the monads that Spinozism is dissolved. For there are as
many true substances, . . . as there are monads, whereas according to Spinoza there is only
one single substance. He would be right if there were no monads; then
everything outside God would be vanishing and be dissolved into simple modifications''. But
it is the same fundamental concept of substance from which both Leibniz and Spinoza
proceed. All the determinations and states of the substance are to follow from its own
inner nature, not to be due to influence from outside. Leibniz asserts this just as
definitely in the case of each of his monads as Spinoza asserts it in the case of his
one and only substance. The difficulty of this absolute
concept of substance became for Spinoza
% --- p. 354 ---
\opage{354}this: how the multiplicity of the attributes and of individual beings could be explained
from the assumption of a single substance. The difficulty of the same concept
became for Leibniz this: how there can be agreement between the states of the
different monads when each of them is determined only from within, and
none of them has holes, windows or doors (to use Leibniz's own
images) by which something from outside can come into them. And the difficulty became
for Leibniz, besides, that of reconciling the doctrine of monads with his theological presuppositions.

Leibniz regards both these difficulties as solved by one thought. That there is
agreement between the states of the different monads he takes as a
fact: there is a universal harmony or concord (accord) between all
beings in the world. Clearly enough, as already touched on, he starts here from
the observation of the general physical reciprocal action in the world and from the
empirical (and yet grounded on an inference from analogy) assumption that the observations and
representations of the individuals agree in such a way that a common
picture of the world can be constructed in its broad outlines. But since the real
reality is a multiplicity of entirely self-subsistent and independent beings which
(as Leibniz says in a letter) are to be regarded as little gods, since they have
life in themselves, there must --- he concludes --- be a common origin of that
harmony. ``God alone'', we read in the ``Discours'' (§ 32), ``brings about the connection
or coherence between the substances, and it is through him that the phenomena of the one
meet with and agree with those of the other, so that there is
reality in our representations''. God has from the first created the individual monads
in such a way that in the one regard is taken of the other; the agreement
between them is due to the common origin. They arise from God by an outflowing
or radiation (émanation, fulguration), as individualizations of the one
divine force, just as each of our thoughts is a radiation of the force of our
mind. God sees the universe from infinitely many different points of view, and
each of these different points of view he realizes by creation as an
individual substance. The
% --- p. 355 ---
% scan: „sig.“ (p. 355)
\opage{355}states of the individual monads thus correspond to one another as the different views
one gets of a town from different vantage points agree with one another
(Discours § 14). The spontaneity in the monads and the conformity between the monads
thus both find their explanation in the fact that it is the divine force and
thought that make up their innermost essence. The harmony between them is present
from the first, is ``pre-established''. Each of them is a peculiar concentration of
the universe which stood before God's creating thought, is a universe en miniature, and
the universe consists only of such concentrations. Leibniz is a metaphysical
Copernicus: he shows how the world can be seen from far more points of view
than one is accustomed to think, and that the one point of view in itself has the same
legitimacy and validity as the other. The world is for him not something that
lies outside or between the individuals, but consists precisely of and in the
individual beings.

Leibniz thus puts the whole problem back into the thought of the creating God. He
passes over from philosophy to theology. But that does not free him from
the difficulties: for how does there arise in the divine thought or imagination
a world that can be seen from infinitely many points of view? And these possible
points of view do not stand in the divine imagination as resting images; but
just as Leibniz constantly asserts that all possibility is a little actuality, an
incipient reality, so he assumes here too an original need or
craving for existence (inclinatio ad existendum, exigentia existendi):
the possibilities seek to press forward to full reality, which is granted only to those
that fit together best into a harmonious world-whole. It is a mythological
prelude which decides the struggle for existence before actual existence
begins, so that the latter can then be a harmonious unfolding of inner germs in
each being. In the exposition of the Theodicy we shall return to this
point. It has been to the decided detriment of the clarity and significance of Leibniz's
philosophizing that theological points of view play so great a part in him from first to last.
And it does not help at all toward the solution of the problems to clothe
them in a theological form. A certain feeling of devotion makes one rather
% --- p. 356 ---
% scan: „on“ (p. 356)
\opage{356}stop asking questions and raising objections; but such a stopping is no solution.
It is easily seen that the problem, in the form in which it comes to present itself to Leibniz,
is insoluble. If the monads are absolute substances, they cannot be
produced. Only the appeal to a supernatural creation covers over the evident
self-contradiction. Just as Leibniz, by virtue of his concept of substance, excludes
real reciprocal action between the monads, so he would consistently have had to exclude
their coming into being out of a substance different from them. Here Malebranche
said the redeeming word: God cannot create gods! --- Leibniz's difference from
Spinoza --- if one disregards that evident self-contradiction --- in
reality falls away, since the creation of the monads is not concluded at
any point of time once for all, but constantly takes place: the radiation
or outflowing of the monads goes on uninterruptedly (Discours § 14. 32. ---
Monadologie § 47: Dieu seul est l'unité primitive ou la substance simple
originaire, dont toutes les Monades créées ou dérivatives sont des productions,
et naissent, pour ainsi dire, par des fulgurations continuelles de la divinité
de moment à moment). Leibniz lays weight on its being the source, the force to
act, that thus uninterruptedly wells out from the Deity into the monads; but
Spinoza too, after all, explains the striving which leads each individual being to assert itself
as a single manifestation of the power that acts in all individual beings.
Consistently carried through, Leibniz's philosophy here differs from Spinoza's only in that the
individual beings are drawn more into the foreground and their common origin
stands as an obscure background (which is lit up more strongly only when Leibniz seeks
connection with the theologians), whereas in Spinoza the individual beings are seen more
as offshoots or ramifications of the infinite being which is his first
and his last thought. The difference between the two systems can be reduced to the
same difference as there is, according to Leibniz, between two views of the universe, produced
by a turning of it. For both, existence is a pyramid, which Spinoza sees
from the apex, Leibniz from the base\textsuperscript{72}). --- There falls,
as already emphasized, a shadow both on Leibniz's intelligence and on his
% --- p. 357 ---
\opage{357}character when, despite this state of the case, he so often distances himself from Spinoza in more or less
heresy-hunting expressions. ---

Leibniz's theory of the relation between soul and body is a simple consequence of
his doctrine of monads. What we call our body is a group of monads, each of which develops
for itself according to inner laws and by inner force, just as our soul does.
From the state of one monad one can, by virtue of the universal harmony,
infer the states of other monads; it is this that is popularly expressed by saying
that one being acts on another. The monad from whose state one can, by such an
inference, derive those of the others is said to act. When the inner development
of the individual monad is hindered, this is due to the obscurity, the chaotic state of
the elements in its own interior. But since the nature of every monad, that is, the degree of
obscurity or clarity and the force to pass over to new states with
which it is endowed, depends from the first on a regard to the other monads
together with which it is set into existence, there correspond to the inner
hindrances definite states in other monads, which are therefore popularly called
their causes. When Leibniz wants to express himself quite popularly, he uses
the image of two clocks adjusted to each other once for all to designate
the relation between soul and body. Popularly and accommodatingly he also calls
the body a composite substance. But this manner of expression is too crude for his
real conception. Matter is for him, after all, only a phenomenon, a world of external
multiplicity whose states express for the senses the inner changes in
the monads, which are the real reality. One thing ``expresses'' or
``represents'' another, in Leibniz's usage, when there is a constant and
regular relation between what can be asserted of the two things (Letter to
Arnauld, Oct. 1687). What is concentrated, united into unity, in the interior of the monads
appears to sense perception as an extended multiplicity. In a letter
of 4 Nov. 1696 (to the Electress of Hanover) Leibniz writes: ``Souls are
unities, bodies multiplicities . . . But although the unities are indivisible,
they nevertheless represent the multiplicities,
% --- p. 358 ---
\opage{358}much as all lines from the periphery meet in the center. \textit{In this
union (réunion) consists the wonderful nature of consciousness (sentiment);} and
it is also this that makes every soul like a world for itself''. --- The
stringency with which Leibniz, in agreement with Hobbes and Spinoza,
asserts the mechanical connection of nature makes it impossible for him to keep to the
usual dualistic conception. The identity hypothesis stands, on his
presuppositions and according to his whole system, as the only possibility. The
difficulties to which this hypothesis is subject Leibniz has made still greater by
the very absolute substantiality he ascribes to the monads. From the stamp of unity
which consciousness has, he concludes with dogmatic haste that the conscious
being must be an absolute, indestructible unity which can receive nothing from outside.
Had he, instead of merely conceiving the bodily in analogy with the
mental, \textit{also} conceived the mental in analogy with the bodily,
he would have seen the necessity of assuming that the individual consciousnesses,
despite their wonderful stamp of unity, stand in reciprocal action with the rest of
existence by virtue of the law of continuity on which he himself lays so great weight,
but is able to apply only within each individual monad, not to the relation
between them. Development comes for Leibniz to mean only unfolding. The
individual organism, for him, really does not come into being at all; it exists from the
first; its birth and growth consist only in its being freed from its envelope and in
its dimensions being enlarged. It was the so-called encasement hypothesis (the one
germ being thought to lie inside the other up through the series of generations) which
Leibniz embraced like many naturalists of his time. And so in the
mental domain too development became not a taking up of new content, but
only a clarification of the content which was given from the first in a chaotic and obscure
form. --- Concentration cannot come into being according to Leibniz; new centers, new
monads cannot form. Here he cuts the knot. The problem of individuality perhaps contains
an insoluble knot for human thinking; but
to cut it is not to solve it.

Yet this very cutting is --- just as much as the
% --- p. 359 ---
\opage{359}distance he felt between himself and Spinoza --- only an outcome of the energy with
which Leibniz thought through the concept of individuality. It appears in him
with a brilliance and clarity as in no other thinker. And the peculiar
turn he gave the concept of substance by applying it to the individual elements of
existence (the monads) is characteristic of the transition from the
seventeenth to the eighteenth century. In place of mystical resignation and
submission to the absolute powers there now enters the free,
peculiar striving of the individual for clarity, for the unfolding of its own being. It is
a revolution in the world of thought --- a prelude to the revolution in the external
world. But one presupposition Leibniz's system shares with the other great systems:
the presupposition of the complete rationality of existence. It is the
principle of sufficient reason that guides him in his theological speculation and in
his doctrine of monads as in his mathematical and scientific works. This
presupposition too passed as an inheritance to the new century, whose typical initiator he was.

\subsection*{c.\quad Psychology and Theory of Knowledge}

From the significance that the analogy with the life of consciousness has for Leibniz as the foundation
of his metaphysical idealism, it follows that his real point of departure must be
the same as Descartes's: immediate self-observation, inner experience.
It gives us the first term of the analogy. Leibniz is also clear that here
lies a point of departure for his thinking, and he has devoted great attention
to it. It is the ``Nouveaux Essais'' that is the chief work here. The polemical side
of this work could only be properly assessed once Locke's theory of knowledge, against
which it is directed, had first been set out. But in this context the weight lies
on Leibniz's own psychological and epistemological views. The
work mentioned gains significance as a verification of Leibniz's general
philosophical ideas, since in the introduction he declares that here he will disregard
his doctrine of monads and take his stand on purely empirical ground.
% --- p. 360 ---
% print: „Spontanietet,“ (p. 360) (misprint)
\opage{360}

The chief question that presents itself is whether the soul is empty from the outset,
like an unwritten tablet (tabula rasa). Long before, in the ``Discours'' (§
27), Leibniz had expressed himself on this question. Even then he found
that this notion of an unwritten tablet was false. It is due to inexact
observation. One overlooks the small, obscure stirrings in the soul and keeps only
to what is clearly conscious, which arises only later, when outer experiences have long
been at work. The Cartesians made themselves guilty of this error just as much as the empiricists.
The less difference and opposition there is between our sensations,
the less any single thing in us stands out in relation to the rest of the content, the
more obscure, in a word, the life of consciousness is, the more easily one overlooks it.
More exact observation will be wary of setting limits. There are all
possible transitions between obscurity and clearness. The obscure changes in us that
do not come to real consciousness Leibniz calls perceptions. Already in them
a multiplicity is united in a single state. At this stage stand the
lowest beings (in Leibniz's system: the monads at the lowest stage). The expression
consciousness (sentiment)\footnote{Sentiment in Leibniz should be translated by
consciousness. By conscience Leibniz understands something more than necessarily
lies in the word consciousness, namely connaissance \textit{reflexive,} thus
rather ``self-consciousness''.} Leibniz first uses where the sensation
(the perception) is more distinct and is accompanied by memory. The highest stage of
mental life presents express attention (apperception) or reflection, which
is directed toward the obscure sensations. (These three degrees are best described in the
little treatise \textit{Principes de la nature et de la grâce} § 4, cf.
\textit{Monadologie} § 14 ff.). But at every stage it is an activity, a
spontaneity, that unfolds itself. We are active, even in the most obscure states.
Just as there is no tablet that does not by its constitution have an
influence on what is written on it, so our nature is preformed from the outset.
In an involuntary, instinctive way we apply principles of which we
can only later become conscious. What is contradictory
% --- p. 361 ---
% scan: „smaa.“ (p. 361)
\opage{361}we reject, even if we have never heard tell of the principle of contradiction. There
are both practical and theoretical instincts. The impulse of self-preservation and the
need to help others work involuntarily. There is on the whole far
more in us than we think of. Here, as in material nature, it is the
small magnitudes that underlie what comes forth distinctly and to the senses.
No more than motion can consciousness arise from nothing or all at
once. Corresponding to the conservation of force (or properly --- by virtue of
the identity hypothesis --- as one with it) Leibniz assumes the uninterrupted
subsistence of mental life through states of consciousness and of unconsciousness, through clearness and
obscurity. The apparent disappearance of mental life is only a conversion into a
more obscure, more elementary form. The question whether there are innate ideas
Leibniz thus answers to the effect that there are innate capacities, dispositions, which
unfold as soon as experience gives occasion for it, and which underlie
all theoretical and practical activity. As an example of the obscure elements
we easily overlook, he points to what may be called sensations of life, the as a
rule faint sensations that correspond to the organic functions, and that have an
influence on the state we are in at every moment. Our outer senses are
indeed more distinct; but since the qualities of sense are utterly different from the
motions that correspond to them within matter, Leibniz assumes that our
sense-sensations are only apparently simple, but are in reality
just as compound as the corresponding motions. What comes forth clearly
for consciousness is for him always something compound that presupposes more obscure
elements, just as, when we hear the roar of the sea, we really gather
the impressions from thousands of waves into one sensation. If we pay attention to it,
we shall find that we are never without sensation. Our soul is constantly active.
Constantly we receive small sensations, and constantly they release our activity. We are
never altogether indifferent; the assumption of indifference is only an expression of our
inattentiveness to the small differences. Involuntarily we turn to the right
or to the left, even where there are no outer grounds for the choice. Our
nature is always working in us to produce greater
% --- p. 362 ---
\opage{362}satisfaction (à se mettre mieux à son aise). A certain unrest always makes itself
felt, a lack of full satisfaction, which drives us forward, a spur
which as a rule we notice only when from unrest it turns into pain. There are always small
hindrances to overcome, and demands are always made for exertion of strength.
No feeling of pleasure is possible without such unrest, without minimal hindrances; indeed, the
hidden spur maintains itself in joy itself and heightens it, so that a constant
progress becomes possible. Only through these small sensations (petites perceptions)
does the connection between the different periods of life of one and the same individual become clear;
for the clearly conscious states often stand as contradictory. And as they at once
explain the difference and the connection between the states of one and the same individual,
so they also explain both the difference and the connection between different
individuals. Even if one will call the soul an unwritten tablet from the outset, one must
nevertheless grant that no two tablets are alike in constitution. If one looks at the small
nuances and differences, one will find in the whole of nature no two altogether alike
beings. There are not two leaves that are alike, let alone two human beings. Here too
the assumption of indistinguishability is due only to our ignorance. But in the obscure
sensations of which the individual does not become conscious, the rest of
existence makes itself known in him and determines him, without his knowing it. Through them
he is connected with the rest of existence. Even in sleep this connection is not
suspended. There is only a difference of degree between sleep and waking: the turning away of attention
is a partial sleep.

It is a great merit that Leibniz has earned in psychology by drawing
attention to the significance of the vanishingly small elements. He has opened a new
world for self-observation, admittedly a world where it feels the want of an
instrument that could correspond to the microscope in the domain of outer observation. And
he has indicated points of view by which it becomes possible to maintain
the continuity of the mental side of existence to a far higher degree than the
usual conception assumes, and indeed at bottom also than Leibniz himself assumed when
he let the monads be without windows and thereby
% --- p. 363 ---
\opage{363}shut them off from unconscious influences from the rest of existence.
The elements of existence (monads) differ from one another only by the degrees of
clearness or obscurity of their inner states, and likewise the states of the same
individual differ only by such differences of degree. It is a herald of the fact
that we are entering the century of the Enlightenment. All the conditions are assumed to be
present --- only the light must be brought: on this optimistic faith
Leibniz and his posterity built. Yet it must be noted in a purely psychological respect
that Leibniz points toward a deeper view of mental life than the one
rationalism and the age of the Enlightenment took as their foundation. In the first place it is for
Leibniz an \textit{infinite} content that is given in obscure form, and full
clarification of it is thus impossible for a finite being. Secondly, he assumes,
as an independent element beside the sensations or representations,
the need and the tendency (appétit, tendance) to pass over to new sensations.
Striving or willing is to that extent for him what is innermost in man, and it is a
striving that cannot cease. Toward the passions (passions) he takes a somewhat wavering
stand. At times he regards them as obscure thoughts (pensées confuses); and
on this view they must then fall away with sufficient clarification; --- at times he declares
that they are different both from representations and from feelings of pleasure and
pain, but are tendencies that are aroused by representations and accompanied by
feelings of pain; on this view they are thus closely connected with the never resting
striving or willing\textsuperscript{73}). By carrying the latter point of view
through, Leibniz would have arrived at a more realistic conception of
mental development than the one that sees it exhausted by the concept of enlightenment. ---

Self-observation gives us, as we saw, the first facts from which we
proceed in our thinking, \textit{the first truths of fact. The first necessary
or a priori truths} we have in identical judgments, that is to say,
those in which subject and predicate can be shown to be one and the same concept.
Common to the first truths of fact and to the first a priori truths
is the immediate relation: in the one case between the understanding and its object, in the other between
the subject and the
% --- p. 364 ---
\opage{364}predicate of the judgment. This immediate relation is in both places proof that nothing more certain
can be reached. Leibniz came early to this distinction between a priori truths and truths of fact.
As early as 1678 (in a letter to Conring of 3 Jan.) he makes this
distinction and demands that all a priori fundamental propositions be traced back to
identical judgments. He therefore divides the axioms into identical and a priori.
The significance of identical judgments rests on this, that when other judgments can be traced back
to such, their validity is thereby given. Leibniz thus demands that proof
be given for all fundamental propositions one lays down, in so far as they are not
identical. He sympathizes with Locke's criticism of ``the innate ideas,''
in so far as Locke thereby wished to combat indolence and prejudice. But Locke
ought to have distinguished between necessary truths and truths of fact. Even if a truth
is innate in the sense in which Leibniz uses this word, a proof of it must nevertheless, on
his view, be given; ``innate'' truths must be \textit{learned}
like other truths. The clarification may be a hard labor, and full
clearness is found only in identical judgments. Leibniz has great merit in logic
for having laid down the principle of identity, whereas the Aristotelian and
scholastic logic kept to the principle of contradiction. He sketched
a logic in which every judgment is formulated as a relation of identity, and has
thereby anticipated a method that English logicians (Boole and Jevons) have taken up in our
day. But these sketches were not published before 1840, so they have
not exercised any influence. --- Just as the principle of identity is our
criterion of truth for pure thinking, so the lawful connection
that the principle of sufficient reason demands is the criterion of truth in
the domain of experience. And just as Leibniz is the first to lay down
the principle of identity as the fundamental logical principle, so he is also
the first to lay down the principle of causality as a special principle for actually
given relations. He thereby brings forward the principle that bears all real knowledge,
and since he at the same time distinguishes it sharply from the purely logical principles,
he makes it natural to discuss its nature more closely. It is not to be a formal
logical principle; nor is it to
% --- p. 365 ---
% scan: „Sprog.“ (p. 365)
\opage{365}be drawn from experience; but it is nevertheless to be a principle of reason and to hold for
all actual relations (and that both in the supernatural and in the natural
world!): how is this possible? That was the problem Leibniz left
to his successors. He himself was content to analyze it out of the
confusion, partly with general logical, partly with special physical
principles, in which it had occurred among his predecessors. Indeed, he does not even distinguish
clearly between ground and cause, which is connected with the fact that the principle is at
once to be a principle of reason and to hold for actual relations, --- and in
the last instance with the fact that the laws of facts are seen as testimony to the
divine reason that is the origin of the world\textsuperscript{74}).

His whole life long Leibniz occupied himself with plans for a kind of alphabet of thought
(Alphabetum cogitationum humanarum), which was to be formed by a thoroughgoing analysis
of our knowledge, so that one arrived at the fundamental concepts that condition
it. By combination of these fundamental concepts he then thought one would be able to
find new truths. And by a suitable system of signs one would at the same time be able to
obtain a universal language, something corresponding, for all concepts, to
what the mathematical language of signs is for magnitudes. It was thus
to be at once a logic, an encyclopedia and a grammar, at once
a means of gathering what had been learned and of making new discoveries. As
the sharp distinction between a priori truths and truths of fact dawns on
him, he nevertheless restricts his ``Ars combinatoria'' or ``Characteristica
universalis'' to the a priori domain. The plan was, despite many attempts,
never carried out, essentially, no doubt, because he gradually saw that such a
general language of signs really presupposed that our knowledge was already
complete. But the plan is characteristic of dogmatic philosophy.

\subsection*{d.\quad Theodicy}

It was Leibniz's task as a thinker to lead beyond the mechanical view of nature
without breaking it. The way he
% --- p. 366 ---
\opage{366}took was to try to show that the forces at work in the mechanism are
determined by purpose, so that the whole graded series of mechanical causes and
effects, seen from within, is a graded series of means and ends. What is innermost in the
world is at every point striving, development, progress. In this thought, which
besides bringing harmony between mechanism and teleology also brought harmony
between the states of the different monads and between soul and body, he thought
he also had a means of reconciling religion (both the positive and the
``natural'') with reason\footnote{In a recently published statement by
Leibniz he places his conception of the relation between \textit{God and the world}
in a characteristic way together with his conception of the relation between
\textit{soul and body} and between \textit{teleology and mechanism:} ``The
general mechanical laws are expressions of the will of the Deity (decreta voluntatis
divinæ), and the special mechanical laws in each body are expressions of will
or forms of the soul in its striving after perfection . . . Everything in
nature can be proved by final causes (causæ finales) just as well as
by efficient causes (causæ efficientes).''
% scan: „officientes“ (p. 366)
\textsc{(Bodemann:} Die Leibniz-Handschriften der kgl. öffentl. Bibliothek zu
Hannover. 1895. p. 89).}. It was his conviction that his philosophy
satisfied the demands the strictest orthodoxy could make. But the
religious problem was just then sharpened by a contemporary writer for whom
Leibniz cherished the greatest esteem. Pierre Bayle maintained, as we have mentioned in its
place, a disharmony between religion and reason and found especially the
doctrines of positive religion contrary to reason. He relied here especially
on the problem of evil and found the Manichaean doctrine of two principles in the world, one
evil and one good, more in agreement with experience than the orthodox doctrine, to
which he nevertheless bowed in the obedience of faith. Leibniz's gifted disciple,
the Queen of Prussia, was strongly influenced by Bayle's misgivings and asked
Leibniz to refute them. Leibniz thought himself well prepared for it. From his first
sketches on he had had an eye for the problem of a theodicy, i.e. the problem
of how the assumption of the world's origin in an almighty, all-good and all-wise
being can be reconciled with experience
% --- p. 367 ---
% scan: „det.“ (p. 367)
\opage{367}of the physical and the moral evil in the world. Early on he had
planned a work on this; Bayle's ``Reponse à un Provincial'' and the Queen's
request led him to work out and publish his \textit{Essais de
Théodicée sur la bonté de Dieu, la liberté de l'homme et l'origine du mal,} which
appeared in Amsterdam in 1710.

Against Bayle's assertion that the doctrines of religion are contrary to reason and yet must be
believed, Leibniz sets the distinction between something's \textit{being above}
reason and its \textit{being contrary} \textit{to} reason. This distinction
is connected with his division of truths into eternal truths (which
are grounded in the principle of identity) and truths of fact (which belong under
the principle of sufficient reason). Against the first kind of truths of reason
nothing that is to be believed can be contrary. The existence of God, e.g., is possible only if
the content of the concept of God, the properties ascribed to God, are not
self-contradictory. But an assumption can be raised above what
experience teaches, since the rational necessity we find, with the help of the principle of sufficient
reason, in the connection of phenomena is always conditioned: the very
fundamental propositions of natural science, according to Leibniz, find their
explanation only in a thought of providence, a teleological principle. It is the very principle
of the truths of fact, the principle of sufficient reason, that leads us beyond
experience, since the harmony between the monads and the lawful connection in
all that happens finds its explanation only in an absolute being that has
produced the world by a rational choice. Each single thing, each single event
by itself is contingent: we then obtain no completion of the series of grounds or causes,
no full satisfaction of the principle of sufficient reason, unless
we go outside the series (extra seriem, see Opera ed. Erdm. p. 83) to a
cause that is the cause of itself. That the divine choice by which the
given world came into being was a rational choice is inferred from the fact that several worlds were
possible besides this actual world: this one can then only have come into being because
it was the best. But the best world does not mean a world that has no
dark sides and defects; it means merely a world in which the defects
% --- p. 368 ---
% print: „medes“ (p. 368) (misprint)
\opage{368}are vanishing in relation to the perfections. Every possible world that
was to consist of finite beings would have to present imperfections, since
finite nature brings limitation with it and therefore cannot fully take the
divine nature into itself. From limitation (metaphysical evil) spring
suffering (physical evil) and sin (moral evil). Evil thus has
in a certain way its origin in God: but not in God's will, which always wills the
good; rather in God's intellect, in which the possible pictures of the world dwell from
eternity. God has created actuality, not the possibilities. The source of evil is the
imperfection that clings to every possible world of limited beings; but
by the divine choice of creation this imperfection is reduced to the
least possible and made to serve as means and as foil for so much the
greater perfection. --- In a somewhat more mythological form and carried out in livelier
colors, Leibniz's conception becomes really the same as Jakob Böhme's. And
both approach Bayle, since they (as Leibniz himself remarks), like him,
assume two principles, only that they think they can bring them to agree within
one and the same nature of God, whereas Bayle found it necessary to assume two gods.
Leibniz and Böhme let the possibilities press forward and struggle within the
divine nature, a prelude to the struggle in actual existence.

Bayle had maintained that the Manichaean doctrine had its strength in the testimony of experience
to misfortune and sin in the world, while an a priori consideration
would rather maintain the unity of the ground of the world. Leibniz must then follow him over into
the domain of experience. Frequently, to be sure, he confines himself to saying: this world
must be the best possible; otherwise God would not have chosen it! He overlooks the
objection that could be made (and that Schopenhauer, Leibniz's antipode, put forward much
later), that even if the chosen world was the best possible, it was
not thereby said that it was good enough to be actualized! The need to
exist, the craving for actualization, which Leibniz ascribes to the eternal
possibilities (he can, after all, everywhere think of possibilities only as minimal
actualities), might well
% --- p. 369 ---
\opage{369}be of evil! Leibniz must then try to show that the actual world
deserves to exist, since for a thorough and comprehensive consideration there
remains a surplus of light and perfection. --- He demands that one must not look
merely at a single part of the world, but think of the whole. A sound that by itself
would sound ill can make an excellent effect in a musical ensemble.
Cover a painting except for a small spot: it will then seem a
meaningless and unclear juxtaposition of colors; but in the whole painting it
helps to determine the impression. A bitter ingredient in a dish serves to
heighten the flavor, while by itself alone it would be unpalatable. --- But how
far, then, is the consideration to be extended? Existence, Leibniz answers, is
infinite. The thought of providence, the purpose that underlies existence
and conditions its stepping forth into actuality, we therefore cannot reach. Only a
small, vanishing part of the world do we know --- and it is perhaps the one where the
most evils are found! Human purposes and ideals must not be made the
only thing or what is decisive in the last instance. God pursues purposes that comprise
the whole of existence, in which there are surely many other beings than
human beings\textsuperscript{75}). --- And should this great, infinite work then be
altered or taken back for the sake of our misfortunes and sins? All the more since everything
hangs together in such a way that if, e.g., Tarquinius's deed of rape or Judas's
betrayal were taken away, the whole historical development would become a different one. God
has placed the single beings in the world; but of their actions they are themselves
the cause; the source, not the stream, he has created. And although he knew what
would stream from this source, he nevertheless created it, because the world in which
it occurred was after all better than any other. Without Judas's betrayal
the Savior's atoning death falls away: all the more reason, then, to say with the old church hymn:
O felix culpa! --- When the evil in the world is emphasized so
strongly by many, it is because it draws attention to itself, and because
habituation weakens the sense for the good we possess. Hindrances and resistance
there must be, so that our activity may constantly be aroused anew and we may not
become dulled. Even the blessed and
% --- p. 370 ---
\opage{370}the angels must meet resistance if they are not to become ``stupid.'' Although
existence in itself is continuous and harmonious, it is nevertheless
purposive that apparent leaps should appear, breaks in
the connection, disharmony: it exercises thought and increases the beauty of the whole. ---
Leibniz even undertakes to justify the dogma of eternal damnation: in
existence as a whole he assumes such a fullness of light and perfection that
even if the majority of human beings were eternally tormented, their pain would nevertheless be
vanishing in relation to that infinite sum of happiness!! --- Whether existence regarded as
a whole advances in perfection, or whether the perfection it
possesses merely varies in form through changing states, is a question
Leibniz will not decide. But he is in no doubt that the fundamental mood of
one who looks at existence with a widened and understanding gaze will be joy
in the beauty and perfection of things and in the constant development, a joy
that is widely different from Stoic patience in the face of necessity. ---

Leibniz comes, without noticing it, to grant Bayle far more right than he
wishes. Apart from the fact that in a certain sense he too assumes two principles, he must
in fact concede to Bayle that when the consideration is confined to
\textit{experience,} it is very difficult to maintain teleological
optimism. Leibniz's appeal to the infinity of existence and the limitation of our knowledge
is really an abandonment of the proof: for whence does he know anything
of how things stand in other regions of the universe? It is a faith he
appeals to; but thereby he declares the question insoluble by way of reason.
In a letter contemporary with the Theodicy (to Bourguet, printed in
Gerhardt III, p. 550 f), he accordingly also says: ``We can survey only a small part
of the chain of things, and it is this part that presents the most evils and is therefore well
suited to exercise our faith and our love of God.'' --- Nor does the appeal
from the single to the whole untie the knot: for precisely in Leibniz's own system,
where there is life and soul at every single point in existence, it becomes
impossible to ground the sacrifice of the single for the whole. The suffering in the single
monad does not fall away because it increases the
% --- p. 371 ---
\opage{371}beauty of the picture of the world that the monads together form. The single monad will
rightly be able to complain of the role assigned to it, and say that it
would rather not be than be in hell, even if this hell could not
be dispensed with as a kind of bass in the great orchestra of existence. Leibniz's own sense
for the infinitely small, for individual differences, ought consistently here
to have led him away from teleological optimism.

\subsection*{e.\quad Philosophy of Law}

Leibniz's ethical ideas and his ideas in the philosophy of law are closely connected with his general
philosophy. His doctrine of monads culminates in the idea of existence as a ``City of God,''
ordered according to the fundamental law of justice, according to which the forces that underlie all
mechanism act. The teleological point of view is common to his
conception of the world and his ethics.

The foundation of all ethics and philosophy of law (both are comprised for him in the concept of
natural law) he finds in the immediate, instinctive need of happiness. Each
single feeling of pleasure corresponds to a progress, a ``perfection,'' which either
consists in the force being increased, or in a greater inner harmony being attained in the
content the force comprises. ``Perfection,'' he says (in a little treatise
\textit{Von der Glückseligkeit,} one of the few German works we have from
his hand), ``shows itself in the force to act, as indeed every being consists in
a certain force, and the greater the force, the higher and freer is the being.
Further: in all force there shows itself --- and the more so, the greater it is --- a
multiplicity springing from a unity and contained in a unity (Viel aus Einem
und in Einem), since there is one thing that determines a multiplicity outside itself and
forms it beforehand in itself. Now unity in multiplicity is nothing other than
agreement.'' Leibniz means by this to express that the feeling of pleasure is conditioned by
the fullness of and the harmony between the forces that sustain life, whether one is
conscious of these conditions or not. Happiness consists in a constant feeling of pleasure.
The condition for the production of happiness is wisdom: the clarification of the
% --- p. 372 ---
\opage{372}understanding and the exercise of the will. But involuntary striving already leads in this
direction. Leibniz assumes, like Grotius, the ``incomparable Grotius,'' as he
calls him, an involuntary need to act not merely for one's own but also
for the happiness of others. Love is joy in the happiness of others, in that one has made it
one's own; even disinterested love is possible only through the happiness of others
as it were shining back upon ourselves. As the chief ethical virtue Leibniz,
following Aristotle, lays down justice, which he defines
as the love of the wise man (caritas sapientis): love sets the end, and
wisdom knows how to find the right means and the right distribution. Justice
consists in giving each his own, in distributing goods in the right way, both in
the ordering of public relations and in the imparting of what the individual has
at his disposal. Justice in this sense (as legislative and distributive
justice) aims at benefiting all and is different from strict right
(jus strictum), whose purpose is the preservation of peace in society. (See the treatise
\textit{De rationibus juris et justitiæ.} 1693).

There is something prophetic in Leibniz's philosophy of law in spite of his partial use of
ancient and scholastic elements. By setting universal utility or happiness
as the end of law and morality he is a forerunner of so-called
utilitarianism. His ideas recall Cumberland's, and he was himself gladly
surprised to find a kindred line of thought in his younger contemporary Shaftesbury.

Although ethics and the philosophy of law are built in Leibniz on a purely psychological
foundation, they nevertheless cannot, in his view, do without a theological
sanction. He agrees with Grotius that morality and law are not to be grounded
on the arbitrary commands of the Deity. But like all the highest principles and laws,
the laws of morality and of law too spring in the end from the divine thought and
are upheld by the divine will. In disinterested love, to be sure,
the striving after one's own happiness becomes one with the striving after the happiness of others. But it
is found only in chosen natures (les âmes bien nées). One cannot, without
presupposing divine reward and punishment in an
% --- p. 373 ---
\opage{373}other life, prove that the moral good \textit{and} what is most useful to the individual himself
\textit{always} coincide. Therefore natural religion is necessary
as a guarantee of morality. And it gives at the same time the highest point of view for
human morality and doctrine of right, since the consideration is widened to the divine law
that reigns in the whole of existence.

In Leibniz's philosophy of law, as in his whole system, the fundamental thought of
harmony between individual beings comes forth. It was this thought that bore his inquiry
in all domains, and that he bequeathed to the new century, for
which his system is in so many respects typical.

\section*{7.\quad Christian Wolff}

What Leibniz had expressed in letters and treatises that were accessible and
intelligible only to a few, Christian Wolff developed broadly, flatly and systematically in
voluminous works. He has an extraordinarily great significance for having introduced
rational thinking into wider circles and made ``the principle of sufficient reason''
valid in all domains. Whereas Leibniz wrote predominantly in French or
Latin (although for a time he thought of writing his ``Theodicy'' in German, precisely on
account of that language's philosophical ``virginity''), Wolff used the German
language and in part created the German philosophical terminology. A popular
Wolffianism became an essential component of the German Enlightenment in the eighteenth
century. Through Wolff a whole series of thoughts from the great systems of the seventeenth century
found their way out into the educated public. Another circle of thoughts came from
England through the movement awakened by John Locke, which the following main division
will set out.

Christian Wolff, who was born in Breslau in 1679, studied mathematics and philosophy
besides theology and became professor of mathematics at Halle in 1706, but lectured chiefly on
philosophy. He was strongly influenced by the writings of Descartes and Leibniz, but
through Tschirnhausen also by Spinoza, whose theory of knowledge Tschirnhausen (without
naming Spinoza's name) had carried out in broader
% --- p. 374 ---
\opage{374}form in his \textit{Medicina mentis.} Although Wolff himself did not like to be
regarded as Leibniz's disciple, and although he modified Leibniz's thoughts in various ways,
it was nevertheless with full right that the philosophy he introduced into the
German universities, and which reigned there right up to Kant's time, was called the
Leibniz-Wolffian philosophy. To be sure, the innermost kernel of Leibniz's
line of thought, his metaphysical idealism and the doctrine of monads, did not lend itself to such a
popular systematization as Wolff gave. But the tendency to unite
natural science and theology by conceiving the world as a great mechanism that is
designed to serve divine purposes and brought by ``pre-established harmony'' into
agreement with mental life is pervasive in
Wolff\textsuperscript{76}) as in Leibniz. The world is conceived as a law-determined
whole of individual beings with God as the ultimate ground. And the logical bearer of the
whole system is the principle of sufficient reason.

It is interesting to see how Wolff is not merely the popularizer of dogmatic philosophy
but also becomes its completer. It was a
significant step in Leibniz that the principle of identity and the principle of sufficient
reason were laid down as two different principles, the one holding for all
truths of reason, the other for all truths of fact. Wolff now tries to
derive the latter principle from the former. He wants, then, to make it
self-evident that there is a ground or a cause for everything that happens, and
he found it a defect in Leibniz that he had given no proof of
``the principle of sufficient reason,'' which nevertheless plays so great a role in his
as well as in the other great systems. Wolff's proof (which is found in
\textit{Vernünftige Gedanken von Gott, der Welt und der Seele des Menschen,
auch allen Dingen überhaupt,} den Liebhabern der Wahrheit mitgetheilet von
Christian Wolffen. 1719. § 30) is as follows: ``Where there is no ground
present, there is also nothing from which one can comprehend why something exists, and
so it must arise from nothing. Now since it is impossible that something can arise from
nothing, everything that exists must have its sufficient ground why it
exists.'' --- It is easy to see that this proof moves in a circle; for that
something cannot arise
% --- p. 375 ---
\opage{375}from nothing means, after all, the same as that everything has its ground or its cause, and
that was precisely what was to be proved. But by this line of thought Wolff got
dogmatism set completely into a system. All certainty was traced back to
the principle of contradiction, and philosophy became a system of propositions that could all
be grounded purely logically. The principle of contradiction contains, as must indeed
be noted so as not to do Wolff an injustice, the guarantee for all empirical assumptions
as well as for all inferences. When I observe something, I cannot at the same
moment not observe it; this demand every observation must
satisfy. Wolff by no means wants to make all science formal logic. But
he wants to show that rational principles reign everywhere. It was
rationalism that made its entry.

Wolff applies it not merely to the conception of the world but also to theology.
Just as from the principle of sufficient reason he derives propositions of natural science
such as the principle of inertia and the law of continuity (nature makes no leap,
because the transition from one state to another would then be incomprehensible),
so he also wants to derive from this principle not merely the existence of God
(the world must have its ground, which has its ground in itself), but also the
conditions to which every positive revelation must be subject. There must --- Wolff
thinks --- be definite marks by which revelation can be distinguished from empty
imagination and false pretense. Revelation cannot be contrary to God's
perfection and cannot contain contradictions. Although it is a miracle and
to that extent is contrary to ``contingent'' (factual) truths, it must not be contrary
to the necessary truths: God can make the sun stand still, but cannot change
the relation between the diameter and the circumference of the circle. And Wolff maintains that a world in
which miracles are rare is more perfect than a world in which they are
frequent; miracles require only might, but the natural order requires in addition
a wisdom that thinks of the whole, not merely of the single.

Wolff himself became a victim of ``the principle of sufficient reason.'' The
pietist theologians in Halle saw a danger in the
% --- p. 376 ---
\opage{376}rationalism he proclaimed, and when in a university oration he had praised the
Chinese philosopher Confucius for his pure morality and declared it to agree
with his own, the storm broke loose. With King Friedrich Wilhelm I people are said to have
made use of Wolff's application of the principle of sufficient reason to
human actions, representing to the soldier-loving king that
when one of his grenadiers deserted, one could not, according to Wolff's doctrine, hold
him responsible. According to what Wolff relates in his autobiography, the king is said to have been
shown a passage in the writings of one of his theological opponents where this
consequence of his determinism was drawn. There then came (1723) a royal
cabinet order according to which Wolff, on account of his ungodly doctrines, was to be
dismissed and within 48 hours be out of the King's realms and lands; if not,
he would be hanged. Wolff went to Marburg, where he continued his
activity until the new King of Prussia, Friedrich II, who was himself among
his admirers, called him back to Halle, where he worked until his death (1754).

\begin{center}---\end{center}


% --- p. 377 ---
\hhchapter{Fourth Book}\opage{377}

\begin{center}\textsc{The English Philosophy of Experience.}\end{center}

\bigskip

\noindent The great systems sprang from the confidence that there was sufficient material
and sufficient clarity of thought to erect edifices that could take the place
of the medieval world-view, which had been overthrown by the inquiry of the
Renaissance and by the coming into being of the new science. In a certain sense
this confidence was not unfounded either; through the new discoveries, methods
and fundamental propositions a decisive light had been cast on the direction in which human
thinking had to move with regard to some of the most important
problems, and it is the special significance of the seventeenth century that it worked out with energy
and consistency the most important hypotheses concerning the relation between
the mental and the material in existence. But the very fact that
several hypotheses were possible was bound to arouse the attention of the critical thinker. And
to this was added that those who with such great confidence and genius erected those
edifices of thought had indeed discussed the nature and working of thinking, but only
as an introduction to their real work. With dogmatic haste they hurried from
the examination of thinking to finding the solution of the riddles of existence. The
significance of the classical English school in the history of philosophy is marked by the fact that
it makes the investigation of the development of human knowledge and of the forms
and presuppositions at its disposal into an independent problem. John Locke and
his successors secured the independence of the problem
% --- p. 378 ---
\opage{378}of knowledge over against the problem of existence, which in the great systems
had entirely overshadowed it. They pushed epistemology forward ahead of
metaphysics. If (following Kant's usage) one understands by dogmatism a
tendency which, without sufficient examination of the conditions and limits of knowledge,
uses our concepts to fathom the essence of things, while the critical
philosophy examines the cognitive faculty itself before it begins to speculate about
existence, then the critical philosophy decidedly begins with John Locke.

But behind this purely philosophical opposition between dogmatic and critical philosophy
