lies a more comprehensive historical opposition. It is not only the philosophical
systems that are criticized: the critical examination turns against every
authority, every established power. The concept of substance in philosophy had, as we
have seen, its analogue in absolute authority in the life of the state. Now comes
the age of emancipation, together with that of criticism. The process of which Leibniz's monads are
symbols, the individual's becoming independent, appears with sober clarity in
Locke's great settling of the accounts of thought with authorities and traditions in the
domains of science, education, the state and the church. Leibniz and Wolff
asserted the principle of sufficient reason and practiced applying it. John Locke
and his successors subjected all principles --- in the end even the principle of sufficient reason
itself --- to a thorough investigation.

Together with the energetic treatment of the problem of knowledge goes a no less
energetic discussion of the problem of valuation. In the English school ethics comes
to a more independent position than it could obtain within the great systems,
whose real interest led the gaze far out beyond human life. And through the
method of experience employed in this school, the foundation of philosophical ethics
now receives a more thorough illumination.
% --- p. 379 ---
\opage{379}

\section*{1.\quad John Locke}

\subsection*{a.\quad Biography and Characterization}

The first critical philosopher was born in the same year as the greatest of the dogmatists.
John Locke was born on 29 August 1632 in the neighborhood of Bristol. His father was
an attorney, but took part as a cavalry captain in the Civil War on the side of Parliament.
His independent and liberal cast of mind passed by inheritance to the son. The
upbringing the future philosopher received from his father was of such a kind
that he could draw on memories of it in working out his epoch-making
treatise on education. In particular the feature \textit{(Thoughts on Education} §
40) that the relation of obedience necessary in childhood is gradually to be
replaced by a free relation of friendship is taken from the upbringing the author himself
had received. It was more by the effect of contrast that the experiences he had at school
and at the university gained significance for his philosophy. For six years he went to school in
Westminster, where he learned the ancient languages by a strictly grammatical method and
was plagued with learning by rote and with composing Latin dissertations on subjects
he did not understand. Natural science was not taught --- only in summer a little geography
after supper. His warnings against learning by rote and against beginning
the teaching of languages with grammar are grounded in what he had thus himself
experienced at school. When he came to Oxford (1652), Puritanism and
scholasticism reigned there. Locke felt dissatisfied with both. His philosophical awakening
he received (by his own later statement) through the study of Descartes's writings.
Acquaintance with these was a great encouragement to him, since he had put down his
small progress in scholastic philosophy to his lack of talent in the
philosophical direction. Gassendi and Hobbes too he studied, and they had great
influence on his intellectual tendency.

Great tolerance was shown in Oxford at that time. Not only the university's
chancellor John Owen, but the mighty Protector Oliver Cromwell asserted
freedom of thought for all Protestants. This time set its lasting marks on
Locke's thinking
% --- p. 380 ---
\opage{380}throughout his whole life. With the Restoration the episcopal church came to
power again. Locke had at first thought of becoming a clergyman, but his free,
``broad-church'' (latitudinarian) conception of Christianity now made it
impossible. In a treatise of 1667 (which was later expanded into his famous
\textit{Letter on Toleration)} he denies to anyone whatsoever the right to force
speculative opinions and particular forms of worship on others. And in a treatise headed
\textit{Error} (which, like the preceding one, is printed in
\textit{Fox Bourne's} excellent ``Life of Locke''. London 1876) he says:
``He who inquires, and who after honest inquiry accepts an error instead of
a truth, has done his duty better than he who accepts the
profession of the truth (the truth itself he does not accept) without having
inquired whether it is right or not''. He lays the chief weight on the moral
side of religion and demands as few dogmas and ceremonies as possible. The
episcopal church with its thirty-nine articles and numerous ceremonies was then closed
to him.

He decided to become a physician and studied chemistry and medicine. Thereby was laid
the foundation of a friendship with the famous chemist Robert Boyle, as well as with the
no less famous physician Sydenham. Locke's endeavors as a philosopher form an
analogy to those of his two friends. --- \textsc{Boyle} (who was six years older than Locke)
asserted the experimental method in chemistry over against alchemists and medical
chemists, who set themselves other purposes than the purely scientific one. He was
the first to make clear what chemical analysis aims at: namely, to
find the elements of compound substances, that is to say, the demonstrable constituents that cannot
be further dissolved. He predicted that far more
elements would be discovered than were then imagined, and disputed the uncompounded character of
many substances that had hitherto been regarded as elements. Boyle also
emphasized the peculiarity of chemical compounds that the product has
other properties than the elements. --- \textsc{Sydenham} asserted
the method of experience in medicine and paid homage to the same principles that Locke
expressed in a small treatise \textit{On Medicine,} where the necessity
is impressed
% --- p. 381 ---
% scan: „forst“ (p. 381)
\opage{381}of building on observations, not on axioms. Locke often accompanied Sydenham on
his visits to the sick.

Yet medicine did not become Locke's life's work either. He made the acquaintance
of the Earl of Shaftesbury, the well-known politician under Charles II, and was soon
attached to his family as friend, secretary, physician and tutor of two generations.
Locke's political views were (as can be seen from short treatises of his
younger days) liberal, like his religious views. He stood with zeal and
conviction on the side of the Whig party and became entangled in its fate.
Shaftesbury's fall in 1672 drew Locke's with it. He had to give up the posts
Shaftesbury's confidence had procured him. He now spent some years traveling in
France. His travel notes have historical interest and testify to his good
power of observation and his attention to all sides of life. When later his
noble friend had become entangled in a conspiracy and had to flee to
Holland, Locke did not consider himself safe in England either and likewise went
(1683) to Holland, where by degrees a good many exiled Whigs gathered.
For a time he had to live in hiding, since the English government demanded his
extradition. In these years he worked on his writings, especially on
\textit{Epistola de tolerantia} (1685), which appeared in English some years later,
and on his chief work ``on the human understanding''. At the same time he was, so far as
one can see, occupied with the preparations for the Revolution. He stood in close
connection with the Prince of Orange and his consort, and returned to
England at the beginning of 1689 together with the Princess.

Locke forgot neither philosophy for politics nor the reverse. At the beginning of
1690 his chief work \textit{Essay} \textit{on Human Understanding} appeared, one of
the most remarkable and most influential works in the history of philosophy. The first
germ of it lies far back in Locke's development. He relates in the preface
that the occasion of the work's coming into being was a discussion he had with some
of his friends. When they could not solve the problems they had set themselves, it
occurred to Locke that it would perhaps first have been necessary ``to examine our own
% --- p. 382 ---
\opage{382}powers and see what objects our understanding was fitted to deal with, and
what not''. In a copy of Locke's Essay which is in the British Museum,
Locke's friend James Tyrrell has written: ``I remember that I myself was one of those who
were present when the principles of morality and revealed religion were discussed''.
It was thus a discussion of ethical and religious subjects that led to the
closer investigation of knowledge. This first beginning was made in the
winter of 1670---71. Later Locke worked on his work during his stay in
France and during his exile in Holland. In 1687 the work was finished. An abstract
of it was printed the following year in the Dutch journal ``Bibliothèque
universelle'', and in 1690 it appeared complete in English. It consists of four
books: the first criticizes the doctrine of innate ideas and principles; the second
shows that all ideas derive from experience, and resolves the
complex ideas into their simple constituents, so that agreement may thereby
more readily become possible; the third investigates the influence of language on
thinking, combats the scholastic philosophy of words and impresses that our
concepts of species may not without further ado
% scan: „tor“ (p. 382; the e-book's reading, set by sense: scan-artefact rule)
be regarded as valid for nature; the fourth distinguishes between the different kinds of
knowledge and determines the limits of knowledge. The epistemology proper
is thus contained in the fourth book. It and the second book (on the origin of ideas
from experience) seem to have been written first; the first
(the critique of innate ideas) and the third (on language) were added later.

Under King William Locke had no small influence. He stood close to the king and to several
of the leading men. He worked for freedom of the press, tolerance, sensible
coinage and trade legislation and for a better poor-relief, and held various
offices. His \textit{Two Treatises on Government,} which appeared in 1690, avow,
besides having a theoretical aim, that they are also a defense of the
Revolution that had led to the new order of things. Of his other writings
there must be named (besides \textit{Thoughts on Education} 1692) the book on
``the reasonable nature of Christianity, presented according to Scripture'' \textit{(The
Reasonableness of Christianity as delivered in Scripture).} In his
% --- p. 383 ---
\opage{383}conception of Christianity Locke lays the weight on the fact that the faith of the oldest church
was comprised in the proposition that Jesus is the Messiah. Christianity is for him
the gospel of love; it would not torment men with incomprehensible
dogmas (of the Trinity, the Atonement, eternal damnation), but extend the law of nature and
of reason by showing how men can attain eternal
blessedness. He himself believed he was a believing Christian, and his letters as well as
his life testify to religious inwardness. He was a zealous reader of the Bible and
in his last years worked out a commentary on the Epistles to the Corinthians. But he felt
most attracted by the Christian tendencies that had least dogmatics and
hierarchy. During his stay in Holland he lived for a time with a Quaker, with whom
he formed a faithful friendship. Later, in London, he accompanied King William when
the latter visited the Quakers' meetings in disguise in order to get to know this sect.
To an English Quaker woman Locke wrote that, just as it was women who first
saw the risen Savior, so perhaps it was also women who were now to
proclaim the resurrection of the spirit of love. He became the object of violent
attacks on the part of the theologians, and since the source of his theology was found in his
philosophy, this too was sharply attacked, especially by Stillingfleet, Bishop of
Worcester, whom Locke answered repeatedly in very lengthy
polemical writings. It was the last single combat between the scholastic and the
modern philosophy. What sharpened the ill will toward Locke's theological standpoint
was that it lay so near to that of the deists that a writing such as John Toland's
``Christianity not mysterious'', which appeared in 1696 and was publicly burned the year
after in Dublin, seemed only to draw an obvious consequence from it. Since Locke's
writings were also read by the student youth, the heads of the colleges in
Oxford resolved that Locke's Essay might not be used at the university. Locke
remarked, when he heard of this, that because there are those who put on blinkers
or turn their heads away, not everyone will put up with doing without his eyes; and
in this history proved him right.

In his last years Locke, who was never married, lived in the house of Mr. Masham
at Oates near London. Lady Masham was
% --- p. 384 ---
\opage{384}a daughter of the Cambridge philosopher Cudworth and a highly gifted lady. After several
years of suffering from asthma he died there in the year 1704. A gentle disposition, great love for
his friends, sincere search for truth and firm faith in the significance of personal and
political freedom, these are the traits of character that stand out especially in
Locke, as we know him from his works and letters. Characteristic of him
is what he wrote, the year before his death, to a young friend, the later deistic
writer Anthony Collins: ``To love truth for truth's own sake is the
most important part of human perfection in this world and the seed-plot of
all other virtues.''

\subsection*{b.\quad The Origin of Ideas}

Since Locke means to call human knowledge to account, his first
task is to investigate where the ideas (ideas) with which it operates
derive from. By idea (idea) he means everything we can think of.
This task would fall away if there were innate ideas in the
literal sense, and it is against this assumption, then, that he first turns his criticism.
It has been held that the idea of God was such an innate idea;
likewise the most fundamental logical and moral principles were supposed to be so.
Such propositions as that every thing is what it is, and that we are to do
to others what we would that they should do to us, are assumed to be originally
implanted in human consciousness. But in that case --- Locke holds ---
they would have to be the very first ideas to appear to consciousness.
That this is not so one can easily convince oneself by investigating children,
idiots, savages and unenlightened people. The consciousness of such beings contains
only single, definite, concrete ideas and observations, no
general principles. And experience shows us individuals and peoples without
an idea of God and without the moral ideas proper. --- If one would
infer innateness from the fact that such ideas and principles are understood and
assented to as soon as they are made distinct to consciousness, that is an
unwarranted inference, for what has to be made distinct and
% --- p. 385 ---
\opage{385}proved is not innate, but must be learned. There must of course be an original
capacity (capacity) to learn, and one may rightly speak of natural laws or
fundamental propositions, inasmuch as there are assumptions at which man arrives by the natural use of
experience and of his power of thought. Among these Locke counts, besides the
logical and mathematical truths, also the most important religious and moral
assumptions. But a \textit{natural} law --- he insists --- is by no means
the same as an \textit{innate} law. The doctrine of innate ideas springs in
great part from indolence; one would be spared the investigation of the
development of ideas.

This polemic seems to be directed especially against the scholastic philosophers,
the Cambridge Platonists and Herbert of Cherbury; this last is the only
representative of ``innate ideas'' who is named by name. Descartes is
hardly aimed at in the first instance, just as the closer explanation
Descartes gives of the unfortunate expression ``innate'' means that he is not hit by
Locke's criticism. --- Locke himself used an expression that has been misunderstood,
namely the old image of consciousness as an unwritten tablet (tabula rasa).
It was not his meaning thereby (as has often been believed) to deny original
powers in the soul prior to experience. --- It is an unfortunate side of philosophical
catchwords that they easily convey too crude notions. Even with the said
correction of Locke's doctrine, Leibniz's criticism is nevertheless to the point, since Locke partly
overlooks the significance of the obscure, more or less unconscious elements, partly the
involuntary, spontaneous way in which original tendencies assert
themselves. The very moment of activity that Locke still recognized in the
formation of ideas was reduced by some of his successors and
in the end abolished. ---

Locke's own answer to the task is that all ideas, by which is
meant all content of consciousness, stem from experience, partly outer experience
(sensation), partly inner experience (reflection). Outer experience arises when an
impression or a motion produced in some part or other of the body
awakens a sensation (perception) in the soul. Inner experience arises when
the soul also receives impressions of the activity
% --- p. 386 ---
\opage{386}that is unfolded (e.g. in memory and comparison) in working up the ideas derived from
outer experience. By ``reflection'' we thus apprehend
our own states and activities, by ``sensation'' the influences of other things.
In every such immediate apprehension or reception of ideas
consciousness behaves as good as (for the most part) passively. It is however
only the simplest ideas that come into being through such immediate and
passive reception.

The simple ideas that arise through outer experience need no more resemble the
properties of the things that call them forth than the word resembles the idea. Only
the so-called primary qualities, solidity, extension, figure, mobility,
cannot be separated from the outer things themselves; the secondary qualities, such as color,
taste, smell etc., correspond only to the power that things, by means of the primary
properties, have to produce certain ideas in us. --- The expressions
primary and secondary qualities Locke seems to have taken over from Robert Boyle;
the doctrine itself, which has often been ascribed to Locke as its first originator, stems,
as we have seen, from Galilei, Hobbes and Descartes. Locke does not go further
into the problem that lies in there being here so great a difference between the outer
cause and the inner effect. ---

The simple ideas are the material of consciousness, which it works up in
different ways. The activity of consciousness shows itself partly in the formation of
\textit{complex} ideas by combination of simple ideas,
partly in the formation of \textit{ideas of relation} by bringing simple
ideas into a certain mutual connection, partly in the formation of
\textit{abstract ideas} by separating simple ideas from
others with which in reality they occur together. All ideas that
are not due to immediate impressions have, however exalted and significant they
may be, come into being through the compounding, uniting and
abstracting activity of consciousness and on the foundation of immediate observations. --- Of
these three kinds of derived ideas it is the first two that have most
interest. They are formed, moreover, with the co-operation of abstraction.
% --- p. 387 ---
\opage{387}

1) To \textit{complex ideas} belong \textit{properties} (modes) such as
space and time. In forming the idea of space we rely on the senses of sight and
touch. At the same time we here employ abstraction, distinguishing between
space and solidity, a distinction that is as clear as that between the bushel
and the grain. The idea of time we form by means of the inner sense, which shows
us a succession of ideas. And when it appears that our power of
representing space and time to ourselves as enlarged remains the same however many
additions we have made, the idea of infinity arises. ---
To the concepts of properties belong also the ideas of power and motion as well
as all ideas of compound colors, forms etc., and in the domain of the
inner sense the ideas of sense perception, memory, thinking,
attention etc.

While the concepts of properties present no difficulty, it is
otherwise with the \textit{idea} \textit{of thing, being or substance.}
It too is formed by compounding. Our idea of a thing or a
substance is the idea of the properties or powers we ascribe to it. But
the remarkable thing is that we nevertheless represent the thing or the substance itself to ourselves as
something different from the properties and powers, namely as their bearer or
foundation (support). From experience stems everything we ascribe to substance.
This holds even of the idea of God, which is an idea of substance that
is formed by enlarging and heightening our ideas of mental
properties, which are taken from the inner sense.

2) As an example of \textit{ideas of relation} (ideas of relation) may be
named the idea of cause and effect. This idea we form on the
foundation of the observation that properties and things arise, and that their arising
is due to the influence of other properties and things. Other examples are
the ideas of relations of time and space and of identity and difference. The
moral ideas too belong to the ideas of relation, since they are formed from the
simple ideas of our actions compared with the idea of a
law. --- While by compounding we combine several ideas into one
idea, ideas of relation are formed by two
% --- p. 388 ---
\opage{388}ideas (simple or complex) being placed together so that they can be
apprehended at once without becoming one. Locke does not investigate whether the
idea formed by compounding does not have another nature than the
simpler ideas of which it is formed, in analogy with what Boyle had
emphasized in chemical compounding. Nor does he investigate whether
ideas ever occur except in some relation or other, and whether
the idea of relation is produced by mere juxtaposition; the relation, after all, does
not lie in any of the elements each taken by itself.

3) By \textit{abstraction} we separate an idea from other
ideas with which in reality it occurs together. Thus
we form the idea of white by disregarding the other properties
it occurs together with in chalk, snow or milk, and the idea of space in
and for itself by distinguishing between space and content, just as we distinguish between
the bushel and the grain.

\subsection*{c.\quad The Validity of Knowledge}

After the coming into being of ideas has been shown, the question of
their validity arises. Now there is for Locke no doubt that the simple
ideas have real validity. They stem from reality and must therefore
agree with reality. The secondary qualities, to be sure, do not resemble the things that
call forth the ideas of them, but they correspond to the things because they are
the latter's constant effects. --- As regards the derived ideas,
their validity cannot be established in this way, since they are after all formed by
compounding, juxtaposition and extraction, thus by our activity. That they
contain no self-contradiction is not enough to establish their real
significance. They are not copies of things, but their significance consists in being
models or patterns (archetypes, patterns), which consciousness uses when
it orders and names things (thus in mathematics and moral philosophy). In
mathematics and moral philosophy we take account only of the content of things, of the ideas
formed by us by free choice, not
% --- p. 389 ---
\opage{389}of the connection things have in nature (Essay IV, 4, 5). Yet this holds
only of the ideas of properties and relations (modes and relations).
The concept of substance, the idea of an unknown bearer of the properties, can only
have validity when there is in reality such a combination of
properties as it indicates. The idea of a centaur is a false,
the idea of God a true idea of substance. The concept of substance is not
itself a model, but its model must be outside us if it itself is to
have validity. But what it is that underlies the properties of things
we do not know. We know the material substance as little as the mental,
and the Cartesians therefore have no right to assert that matter cannot think.

Knowledge is the perception of the mutual agreement or
disagreement of ideas. In its simplest form it is intuition, immediate
intuiting. On this point Locke decidedly approaches Descartes, as when he
says that we have an intuitive knowledge of our own existence; doubt itself
says so: for if I know that I doubt, I have as certain a perception
of the existence of the doubting thing as of the thought I call doubt. Besides
our own existence we apprehend by such immediate intuiting the simplest
fundamental relations between our ideas. A proof (demonstration)
arises when a series of intuitive cognitions is joined together. Each step in
the demonstration is an immediate intuiting. These two kinds of knowledge are the
only strictly reliable ones. All other knowledge is only assumption, more or
less probable conviction; to this belongs the sensuous knowledge of
the things outside us.

Demonstrative knowledge concerns not only mathematical propositions, but also
the existence of God --- and this is the only case in which we can, by way of
proof, know real existence besides our own. Locke's proof
of the existence of God is the usual one: from the world (or from our own
existence) one infers God as its cause. But it acquires a special interest from the fact
that it builds on the causal principle, which is declared to be an intuitive truth:
we have an immediate certainty
% --- p. 390 ---
% print: the mark „76)“ for note 77 (p. 390) (misprint)
\opage{390}that what does not exist cannot produce reality (nonentity cannot
produce any real being)! (Essay IV, 10, 3). There must then be an eternal being. And
it cannot be matter, Locke continues, for matter cannot produce
understanding. --- Only apparently is there a contradiction between this last
proposition and the one cited earlier about the possibility that matter can think. For in
the earlier proposition he asserts that we do not know the innermost essence of matter;
here he proceeds from matter as we know it\textsuperscript{76}).

Just as there is in Locke's doctrine of the origin of ideas a sharp
opposition between the passivity in the reception of simple ideas and
the activity in the formation of derived ideas, so there appears in
his doctrine of the validity of knowledge a no less sharp opposition between
sensuous knowledge, which only attains to probability, and intuitive
and demonstrative knowledge, which brings full certainty and necessity with it.
Remarkably enough, this opposition appears in setting up the proposition on
whose validity Locke's proof of the connection of knowledge with reality rests,
the causal principle. The very concept of a causal relation we form by sensuous
experience: ``That which produces a simple or complex idea we denote
by the general name cause, and that which is produced, by the name
effect.'' (Essay II, 26, 4). The validity of the causal principle is established by
intuition (Essay IV, 10, 3), and the causal principle itself is used confidently both in
inferring from the simple ideas to the things that have produced them, and
in the proof of the existence of God. The idea of God is --- like
the idea of cause --- taken from experience, though with the co-operation of the
combining and enlarging (idealizing) activity of the mind; the existence of God
is proved by inference with the help of the causal principle. Locke's standpoint as
empiricist as regards the origin of ideas, and as rationalist as regards
their application, appears clearly here. By the boldness with
which Locke sets up and uses the causal principle he still belongs to
dogmatism. But by the demand for psychological explanation and epistemological
% --- p. 391 ---
\opage{391}grounding he has led onto the path of the critical philosophy. Locke's
transitional position is, however, seen most clearly in the concept of substance. It was the
self-evident fundamental concept in the great systems, the last, absolute
resting point of thought. Only Hobbes shook it, and here, as on several
points, he is Locke's predecessor. Locke treats it with a certain irony, calls
substance an ``I know not what'' and compares the belief in it with the Indians'
belief in the elephant as necessary to bear the earth; --- and yet he does not reject
it. He explains it as a self-made concept, just as the mathematical and
moral-philosophical concepts are; and yet he ascribes to it an outer model
and foundation.

\subsection*{d.\quad Philosophy of Religion}

Locke's religion did not stand in opposition to his philosophy. He did not need as
many surreptitious moves as Leibniz in order to unite them. Since he believed he had given
a philosophical proof of the existence of God, he believed he had at the same time asserted the
truth of natural religion by way of reason, just as he thereby also obtained the
theological presuppositions without which, in his conception, no ethics was
possible. His ethics is a theological doctrine of happiness: from the natural need of
happiness springs the law that states the conditions under which our own happiness
can be attained in connection with that of others; but this law, found by the natural way of reason,
which is summed up in the old saying that we are to do to others what we
would that they should do to us, must, in order to obtain authority, be regarded as
sprung from and upheld by the will of God.

Although Locke held that tolerance in the state ought to be extended to all who
professed natural religion, his own personal standpoint was nevertheless
that of faith in revelation. In the spring of 1695 he writes to Limborch: ``This winter
I have carefully considered wherein the Christian faith consists. I have drawn from
Holy Scripture itself, but kept the opinions of sects and systems away.''
The results of his investigations he set down in his writing on ``the reasonable
nature of Christianity''.
% --- p. 392 ---
\opage{392}Revelation is for him an extension of natural religion, which can be grounded by reason,
and on the other hand reason is the constant control of faith in revelation.
In his chief work (Essay IV, 18, 2) he defines faith as assent
to a proposition that is not set up by inference of reason, but is built on trust
in him who puts it forward as coming from God and communicated in an extraordinary
way. Whether something really is revelation, reason must decide, and faith can
never convince us of anything that conflicts with reason: for the knowledge we
have that revelation stems from God can never be as certain as the
knowledge we ground on the very agreement or
disagreement of our ideas. Revelation is nevertheless necessary. For although nature
testifies sufficiently to God, men have not rightly used their reason. From
indolence, sensuality and fear they came under the dominion of superstitious priests,
since the few who followed reason could gain no influence on the
great multitude. The greater part of men lack time and ability to follow
the proofs of reason. Christ was then sent to enlighten, strengthen and help.
Faith in him as Lord and Master has the promise of an eternal life. Even the
most unlearned, even those whose life passes in heavy toil, can understand Christ's
example and teaching as it appears in the Gospels. To the doctrinal developments of the Epistles
Locke attaches less weight. The dogma of the Trinity he can find neither in
the Gospels nor in the Apostles' Creed.

Beside Christian Wolff (who on other points too, e.g. in the
unfortunate grounding of the causal principle, recalls Locke) Locke stands as the
founder of religious rationalism. His writings and especially his religious
standpoint influenced the greatest minds of the eighteenth century; Voltaire and
Frederick II stand here in the first rank. Most remarkable, however, is to see how
religious rationalism breaks forth as a democratic movement, --- as indeed,
for that matter, every new religious current does. In combating the theology of the church,
Locke pays special regard to the needs of the unlearned and of those who labor hard: he
demands a Christianity that can be
% --- p. 393 ---
\opage{393}accessible and comprehensible to them. But Locke's standpoint was nevertheless still
dogmatizing: he ascribes to ``natural'' religion so great a certainty as regards
proof, and so great a necessity as the foundation of ethics, that he
even excludes those who reject it from the benefits of religious freedom! Not only
Catholicism and Protestantism, but rationalism too has its intolerance.

\subsection*{e.\quad Philosophy of Law and of the State}

Locke's writing on ``civil government'' is an occasional piece. He says in
the preface that his intention is ``to establish the throne of our great restorer King William,
to make good his title by the consent of the people, which is the only title
for a lawful government, and which he possesses in far higher degree than any other
prince in Christendom, and finally to justify before the world the English
people, whose love of their lawful and natural rights and firm
resolution to uphold them saved the nation when it stood on the brink of
slavery and ruin.'' In the first part of the writing Locke refutes the doctrine set up by
the royalist Filmer of kingship as a divinely
instituted, patriarchal institution. Political power, Locke asserts, is
different from the father's power over his children, the master's power over his journeymen and
the lord's power over his slaves. It is the power to give laws, to execute these
laws and to defend society against outer violence, and all this only for the sake of the
common good. Such a power can only be established by free agreement. Such an agreement
is entered into tacitly even now, when the state of nature has ceased, as every
time the son takes over the father's place in society. This agreement amounts
essentially to this, that the will of the majority is to be law, because it is the only
way in which society can come to act as a whole.
The state of nature is not, indeed, as Hobbes held, a state of war; but it
nevertheless brings with it inconveniences that can only be remedied by fixed laws, impartial judges
and executive power of the state. The state of nature is already a state of freedom, but
freedom is better upheld in society. It is then very far from the case that the natural
rights are given up on entering
% --- p. 394 ---
% print: „77)“, the mark for note 78 (p. 394) (misprint)
% scan: „Ulemperne;“ (p. 394)
\opage{394}into society. The right of property, e.g., is a natural right, grounded in
man's working of the soil or of other material. God has given
the world to the industrious, not to the lazy, and all economic value springs from
labor. The state can therefore as little abolish the right of property as ground
it, but has only to secure and uphold it. As it is with
the right of property, so it is also with personal freedom; slavery
conflicts with nature and ought therefore not to be maintained by the state.

In Locke's political theory his strong emphasis on the legislative power is especially of
significance. By the introduction of a legislative authority no
arbitrary power is established; for one leaves the state of nature precisely in order to avoid
arbitrariness. What is aimed at is the greatest possible regard for the
general good in all decisions. Only with the approval of the majority ought
taxes to be levied: otherwise the right of property is abolished, for I do not own what
another can take against my will! --- Locke demands that the legislative power be separated from
the executive and the judicial\textsuperscript{77}); but the legislative power is
nevertheless the highest: with its establishment the constitution of the state is given, and moreover
he who gives the laws stands above him who executes them (Of Govern. II, 141. 143).

The highest power nevertheless remains with the people, and it comes into
use when the executive power comes into conflict with the legislative. No
power on earth except the people can decide such a conflict. By virtue of the last,
inalienable right, the right of self-preservation, the people appeals to heaven and
carries out its will. This is not rebellion: the rebellion is committed by those who break
the laws. Nor does it lead to the dissolution of the state, for in the first place
the presupposition is that the majority of the people feels the inconveniences that are to be
remedied, and in the second place the people does not so easily get out of its old forms
as is believed. ---

Locke's free spirit of inquiry, united with his warm and practical participation in the
great events of his people's history in his time, led him to
formulate the great fundamental propositions of popular freedom in a way that became of
decisive significance
% --- p. 395 ---
\opage{395}not only for later doctrine of law and the state, but also for the history of the peoples in the
following centuries. Montesquieu and Alexander Hamilton are his disciples,
Rousseau's doctrine of popular sovereignty can rest on him, and the
North American and the French Revolutions were illustrations of what Locke
calls the appeal to heaven. The constitutional life of the modern states is
essentially built on Locke's fundamental propositions. The limitation of this whole
political philosophy coincides with the limitation of the constitutional question.
Behind it rises the social question. By deriving the right of property from
labor Locke had, without knowing it, posed this problem, which only in a
much later time was to come to the fore.

\section*{2.\quad Discussions in Moral Philosophy and the Philosophy of Religion}

\subsection*{a.\quad The Doctrine of the Moral Sense}

Through the Renaissance and the seventeenth century self-preservation can be traced, under different forms,
as the foundation on which the conduct of life is thought to be
built. With quite few exceptions all attempts to ground an
ethics proceed from the individual, its craving and need, its subsistence and its welfare. It makes
here in principle no difference whether one thinks only of the individual's subsistence in
this world, or whether one (as e.g. Locke) also takes its subsistence in another
world into consideration. Over against this way of considering things, which in Hobbes
found its sharpest and most consistent defender, there was set up within
philosophical ethics especially the appeal to reason as that which is to regulate
men's conduct. Spinoza's profound attempt to show what
metamorphoses or displacements the impulse of self-preservation can undergo was
little heeded. It is \textsc{Shaftesbury's} merit to have brought out the significance of
immediate feeling, determined by instinct, for ethical valuations.
It is a salutary and fruitful opposition to the rising rationalism that
Shaftesbury initiates; and as so often,
% --- p. 396 ---
% scan: „Det“ (p. 396)
\opage{396}where a refreshing current of thought breaks forth in modern times, it is ancient
influences that determine his ideas. The ancient harmony and self-limitation
and the ancient trust in nature are found again in Shaftesbury, to be sure
combined with a certain amount of modern sentimentality. Anthony Ashley Cooper
Shaftesbury, born in London in 1671, was a grandson of Locke's friend. Locke
assisted as physician at his birth and was later his teacher. The greatest
influence came from the careful instruction in the classical languages. He had a
woman teacher who spoke Latin and Greek with fluency, so that he learned to speak
these languages as his mother tongue. Sound Greek thoughts were stamped early on the
boy's mind. His further development he received on travels in Italy and France,
which brought him knowledge of men and gave him occasion to cultivate his
artistic interests. For some years he was a member of the House of Commons. King William
valued him highly and wished to give him a high office, but he declined;
his health was weak, and his mind was set on a quiet, literary life. He died
comparatively young in Naples in 1713.

Shaftesbury's works, of which he himself collected most in three volumes under
the title \textit{Characteristicks of Men, Manners, Opinions, Times} (London
1711), are not written in the form of calm, systematic development of concepts; they give
outbursts and reflections, often in the form of letters or dialogues, often with great
poetic swing and mood, but also often with sentimental rhetoric instead of
reasons. He is, both in a good and in a less happy sense, the first
philosopher of feeling. The significance of immediate feeling is asserted in opposition to
reasoning reason, calculating egoism and outer sense perception. He asserts
the connection between the beautiful and the good, taking up again the ancient
conception of virtue as a harmony between the drives in the single human being and
among men in their mutual relations. Finally he asserts the independence of ethics from
religion, while at the same time it is his conviction that ethical feeling,
through faith in the harmonizing Deity working in all things, is perfected as
religious feeling.

While Shaftesbury regarded his teacher Locke with great
% --- p. 397 ---
% scan: „tit“ (p. 397)
\opage{397}respect and directs his sharpest polemic against Hobbes, he nevertheless declares (in his
\textit{Letters to a young Man at the University),} that Locke by his criticism of
innate ideas has overthrown the foundation of morality. He grants that there
is a meaning of the word ``innate'' in which ``innate ideas'' are absurd.
He himself uses it in the same meaning as natural, in agreement with nature,
instinctive, in opposition to what is due to art, culture and discipline.
(Cf. also \textit{The Moralists,} III, 2). The question is surely not,
he says, of the moment at which one body comes out of another, or of
the point of time at which our ideas are formed, but of whether the human
constitution is such that certain ideas arise naturally in the course of
development. And one cannot assert that we get the ideas of love and
justice only from experience and the catechism. Then there would also have to be a
catechism that teaches the bird to fly and to build its nest and teaches man and woman
to find each other! --- It is, says Shaftesbury, who here agrees with
Grotius, Cumberland and Leibniz, an instinct that binds the individual to the species,
an instinct that is just as natural as the instincts of propagation and of
care for offspring. Man cannot and never could subsist outside
society. Wrongly is the state of nature set in opposition to
the state of society. On closer investigation of the development of the human
species one finds a whole series of different states of nature, without in any of
them social life and the drives that bear it falling away entirely. --- By this
consideration (which is found in The Moralists II, 4) Shaftesbury places himself in
opposition to the contract theory of natural law, which let society arise through the
association of independent individuals. He goes back to the obscure
standpoint of instinct, where individual and society do not yet stand in opposition to
each other, and he sees at the same time that the state of nature and the state of culture are relative
concepts. It is one of the most important germs of thought to be found in him. But the
spiritual atmosphere of the eighteenth century was not favorable to its further development.

Although Shaftesbury lays great weight on instinct, he
% --- p. 398 ---
\opage{398}does not overlook the significance of thinking. It makes a reflection on our inner
states possible, and thereby these become objects of feeling and judgment. It
is Locke's inner experience to which he here appeals. Through reflection on what
stirs involuntarily in us, peculiar feelings arise: of esteem or
contempt, of admiration for the noble and right, of aversion to the ignoble and perverse
in ways of thinking and acting, feelings that are akin to aesthetic pleasure and
displeasure, but are distinguished from these by their active character, prompting to action.
Such a feeling Shaftesbury calls a ``reflected feeling'' (reflex
affection) or ``moral sense'' (moral sense). As springing from natural
instincts it is itself natural, original \textit{(Inquiry concerning Virtue
and Merit).}

There is, to be sure, a ``cool philosophy'' which teaches that there is no natural faith
or justice, no real virtue, because self-love and
striving for power are the only forces at work. Shaftesbury thinks that this doctrine
perhaps springs from an aversion to letting oneself be led by nature to serve
purposes that lie beyond oneself. He himself teaches that all beings strive after
happiness. But, he says, it makes a great difference whether one finds happiness in
striving after common purposes, or whether one narrows one's interest to one's own
advantage, perhaps even to one's own self-preservation. There is no absolute
opposition between the selfish and the sympathetic feelings: for on the one hand
love and friendship bring self-satisfaction, since by a kind of
reflection one comes to share in the happiness one prepares for others, and on the other hand our
conditions of life are so closely bound up with those of others that we cease to provide for ourselves
when we cease to provide for the common goods. The point is to bring harmony
among the different promptings that stir in the mind. That man is the
architect of his own happiness who acquires for himself an inner foundation of order, peace and
concord. Happiness rests on what is inward, not on what is outward. The
harmony and beauty of the feelings condition the forms and manners of true social life: what
satisfies the demands of social life is also what brings harmony into the
individual's inner being. And therefore --- writes Shaftesbury in his ``Letters to a young man
at the University'' ---
% --- p. 399 ---
\opage{399}seek the beautiful in everything, even in the smallest things! --- He intimates the ideas of a modern
evolutionist aesthetics when he says (in his \textit{Miscellaneaus
Reflections)}: ``The forms that are ugly produce at the same time discomfort
and disease, and the forms and proportions that are beautiful yield advantage by making
fit to act and to be of use.''

The sense of order and harmony in which, according to Shaftesbury, moral feeling
consists is directed not only to human society, but turns to
the whole universe and thereby becomes religious reverence. The order of nature stands
as admirable. Misfortunes and evils exist only for the limited consideration:
our finite thought must often take for imperfect what would prove to
be a perfection if we could see it from the standpoint of the whole. The universe
meets no outer resistance. It follows its own inner harmonious order, which has
its ground in the thought of God. Ethics thus leads over into religion, and Shaftesbury
speaks up for ``a noble theism, which conceives God as the all-loving and
protecting one and therefore as ideal model.'' On the other hand, it would be to begin
at the wrong end if one would (with Locke) build ethics on religion.
Disinterestedness would thereby fall away. Virtue is its own reward. What reward
could better suit it? ---

With \textsc{Francis Hutcheson} (1694---1747), a Scot who was born in the
north of Ireland and, after having directed a private academy in Dublin, worked as
professor of moral philosophy in Glasgow, Shaftesbury's ideas received a more systematic
form and were at the same time spread in wider circles. His \textit{Inquiry into the Ideas
af Beauty and Virtue} (1725) gives an investigation of aesthetic and ethical
feeling which contains many interesting observations and gives a closer
determination of several points that in Shaftesbury had been left more indeterminate. After
his death his \textit{System of Moral Philosophy} was published (1755). It is
his endeavor to ground ethics on observation of real
human nature. He finds there, besides the selfish instincts, also an
immediate need to help and gladden others. And he finds on the other hand
an equally immediate feeling
% --- p. 400 ---
\opage{400}of joy and approval in the face of actions that spring from such a need to
help and gladden. Reason is only the power of finding means to given purposes;
it enters the service of sympathy and cannot be dispensed with, since that immediate
feeling otherwise works blindly and shortsightedly; but it is not reason alone that
leads to the valuation of human actions. Just as little as the moral
sense can do without reason, just as little can it do without experience, which alone
can teach us the effects or tendencies of actions. The moral
sense works only when it is confronted with observations of human
actions and their effects. When Hutcheson observes how the
moral sense works on the foundation of such observations, he finds that, with
equal degrees of happiness that can be expected to result, the action is valued
highest whose effects in happiness extend to the greatest number of persons, ---
yet so that the dignity or moral significance of the persons can make up for
the number, --- and that when the number of persons who benefit by the actions'
effects is the same, the action is valued highest that causes the highest
degree of happiness. He sums up these observations in the principle that has so often
been repeated since: that action is best which causes the highest happiness
for the greatest number (the greatest happiness for the greatest number)
(Inquiry, 2. ed.p. 177.). --- Among the many interesting investigations to be
found in Hutcheson's writings, there is especially to be singled out his discussion of how
the moral judgment on an action is determined by the relation between the
feeling of humanity (benevolence) that is its motive, and the power and
skill (ability) found in the agent. He assumes that the action's
moral goodness stands in direct proportion to the feeling of humanity to which
the action testifies, and in inverse proportion to the power the agent is presupposed
to possess. (Inquiry. 2. ed. p. 194 f).

The moral sense cannot be explained by experience, for it manifests itself quite
immediately and instinctively, --- nor by education, custom and
association of ideas, for in that way --- Hutcheson holds (System, I,
p. 32. 57) --- no entirely new senses or ideas can arise. He grants that
% --- p. 401 ---
\opage{401}there is to that extent something mysterious in the moral sense. He assumes it to be
originally implanted by God and sees a proof of the Creator's wisdom in the fact that the
moral sense approves only actions that serve the welfare of others, or that
serve one's own welfare in a way that agrees with the welfare of others. But it works
even in those who do not believe in any God. The ethical is for Hutcheson as
independent of theological ideas as of egoistic ulterior motives, although he
grants that where the moral sense is weakened, the command of authority may be the
only means that can take up the fight with the affects. --- Not always,
moreover, in Hutcheson's conception, does the moral sense work as an immediate
instinct. There can develop out of it a feeling of obligation, inasmuch as ---
even where the immediate prompting does not lead to doing or forbearing
--- a consciousness can assert itself that by not making a
particular decision one would come into conflict with what love of humanity demands,
and thereby suffer harm to one's inner peace (serenity), perhaps also bring upon oneself
other inner or outer inconveniences. The feeling of duty is thus, according to Hutcheson, a
derived and a vicarious feeling. ---

In particular ethical questions Hutcheson applies the principle of welfare as
a standard. There are found in his System of Moral Philosophy a multitude of acute,
humane and liberal remarks on particular moral, social and political
matters. --- An excellent biography and characterization of Hutcheson and his
significance has been given by \textsc{W. R. Scott} in his book \textit{Francis Hutcheson} (1900).

\textsc{Joseph Butler,} who after having studied at a Dissenting academy
later went over to the established church and died as a bishop in 1752, an energetic thinker and
able observer, gave Shaftesbury's doctrine of the moral sense a still more
theological form than Hutcheson had done. Connected with this was the fact that Butler
had an especially sharp eye for the dark sides of life and felt himself very far from
Shaftesbury's enthusiastic optimism.

His conception of ethics he developed in his religious discourses
\textit{(Sermons} 1726). He does indeed, like Shaftesbury and
% --- p. 402 ---
\opage{402}Hutsheson, set the ethical in close connection with the single human being's immediate
relation to the species, but he stresses still more strongly than they the quite
immediate inner compulsion that makes itself known in the moral sense, which he would rather
call conscience. We are too shortsighted to find out what in the
particular case will bring happiness. Over happiness the Lord of the world disposes. But we are
so constituted that, quite apart from the outcome, we condemn falsehood, violence
and injustice and approve love and benevolence. For the principle of welfare set up by Hutcheson
there is no use here; Butler keeps merely to the inner, subjective side of the
ethical. In Shaftesbury he blames especially that the authority of
conscience, the inner moral feeling, over against all other
elements and promptings in the soul is not brought out in his doctrine. Conscience
is of a higher nature than all other powers. It is destined to rule over
the world. By a fine psychological analysis Butler shows how such an
immediate satisfaction as moral feeling gives is different from
the feeling of pleasure attained by egoistic calculation: in the immediate instincts
we do not consciously make ourselves our purpose; on the other hand, egoism proper presupposes
experience of the feelings of pleasure won by immediate devotion and the conscious
setting up of them as purposes; but this reflection and calculation can then precisely
hinder the attainment of full satisfaction.

Although according to Butler there is an immediate satisfaction in following
the commands of conscience, he nevertheless has so sharp an eye for the oppositions in human
nature that he cannot rest content with Shaftesbury's joy in
the harmony of our own nature. If it is not specially guaranteed to us that in the end we
shall quite personally have our need of happiness satisfied by the good and the right,
this will not hold us fast: ``Though virtue or moral perfection consists in
feeling for and striving after what is in and for itself good and right, yet we
shall nevertheless, \textit{when the enthusiasm is gone} (when we sit down in a cool hour),
be unable to justify either this or any other pursuit to ourselves
before we are convinced that it will serve our happiness or at
least not conflict with it''
% --- p. 403 ---
% print: „umennneskelige“ (p. 403) (misprint)
\opage{403}(Sermon XI). The ``cool'' hours Shaftesbury esteemed as little as the ``cool''
philosophy. For Butler it is in the last resort only the prospect religion gives
of another life that can help us over such hours. Yet he knows also
another way by which ethics leads over into religion. The need to feel
love and admiration that lies in our nature finds in God the highest possible
object. Religion widens our feeling and alters its direction, but creates
no entirely new kind of feeling; our nature cannot be transformed. So for
Butler the opposition between self-interest and admiring devotion withdraws from the
ethical relation into the religious one, without receiving any definitive solution.

Butler's opposition to Shaftesbury is the opposition of the pessimist to the optimist.
The eighteenth century began decidedly optimistically. Nature and human life were seen
in a bright light, and great hopes of happiness and progress were cherished. Leibniz, Locke
and Shaftesbury expressed this optimism under different forms. By Shaftesbury
and the freethinkers natural religion, which built on the consideration of
the connection and harmony of nature, was praised in opposition to the obscure mysteries and inhuman dogmas
of revealed religion. Both personal mood
and theological conviction led Butler to oppose this opposition. In
his remarkable writing \textit{Analogy of Religion, Natural and Revealed, to the
Constitution and Course of Nature} (1736) he sought to show that the most important
objections urged against revealed religion also strike the
faith of natural religion in a providential government in nature. Observation of
nature cannot establish that it has a wise, just and good cause. When one
is offended at the doctrine of election and damnation, one must not forget that
countless germs in nature perish without unfolding, and that it is only
few men who come to full moral development in this life! When one
is offended at the dogma of the Atonement, one must not forget that in nature the innocent in fact suffer
for the guilty! If one takes offense at Christianity, one must also take offense
at nature. The mystery is at bottom equally great in both. --- What helps
Butler himself
% --- p. 404 ---
\opage{404}over this difficulty --- as regards both nature and revelation --- is
the thought that both in the natural and in the supernatural world we are only
parts of an immeasurable whole which we cannot survey from our place.

By this consideration Butler strikes the smooth, veiling optimism that
overlooks the real conditions. There is just as much a thoughtless cult of nature as
a thoughtless faith in revelation, and the dogmatism of natural religion can become
no less questionable than that of positive religion. But Butler's proposition can be turned round and
then comes to declare that the same contradictions are found in Christianity as
in nature: the question then becomes what solution of the riddle of existence has been
reached in revelation, when it becomes only a kind of doubling or reflection
of nature and its riddles? The spear with which Butler wounded his
opponents wounds himself.

On the other hand, the author of the ``Fable of the Bees'', \textsc{Bernard De Mandeville} (born in
Holland of a French family, lived as a physician in London and died in 1733), seems to have
avoided wounding himself. The Fable of the Bees is a poem that appeared in 1708 and was sold as
a broadsheet in the streets of London. It depicts a society of bees in a most
flourishing and mighty condition. All worked zealously to satisfy the
common necessities. Restlessness, discontent, voluptuousness, vanity,
fraud prevailed --- but all of them helped toward the common good. Precisely
the viciousness in the single parts of the state made it as a whole a paradise,
just as the single discords in a piece of music contribute to the harmony of the whole. Even
the poor lived better than the rich had formerly lived. But then there were some
who began to cry: Away with corruption! Good God, if only we were honest!
And the cry won assent. The most zealous cheats were also the most zealous to
join in the cry for honesty. The gods heard the cry. Hypocrisy vanished.
Luxury ceased. Wars of conquest fell away. Priestly rule and officialdom were
curtailed. The poor were provided for by the public. People contented themselves
with the products of their homeland and needed no import of costly goods.
Seafaring therefore ceased. The population declined --- and in the end the whole swarm
withdrew into a hollow tree.
% --- p. 405 ---
\opage{405}Contentment and honesty had been attained --- but the splendor and the power were
gone. --- The moral is clear enough: the contentment and morality of the individual cannot
coexist with the culture of society.

In a later edition \textit{(The Fable of the Bees, or Private Vices Publick
Benefits.} 6th. ed. London 1732) Mandeville added notes, partly in
dialogue form, in which he sharply develops the difference between his own views and
Shaftesbury's. --- Two systems, he says, could not be more
contradictory than Lord Shaftesbury's and mine. It is man's egoistic
interests, his need of food and drink, his ambition, envy,
love of enjoyment, laziness or impatience, that lead to labor, culture and
social life. Contentment and virtue, on the other hand, lead one to be satisfied with
what one has. An original social impulse there is none. Without hypocrisy
society cannot subsist: only think what the consequence would be if we
were to give honest expression to all our ideas and moods! The
task of the true statesman is this: to make society mighty by getting
men's egoistic interests to work together for the general good;
but it would be foolish to root out the necessary evils. The current virtues
were invented by ambitious politicians, who could more easily secure their dominion
and power when they could get men to become self-sacrificing and obedient; only
thereby did it become possible to rule over great masses. But with increasing
civilization the connection between the individual's vice and constant
discontent and the good of the whole shows itself. Philanthropy, which would abolish poverty,
has a harmful effect. In a special treatise \textit{(On Charity and Charity
Schools)} Mandeville insists how dangerous it is to give the poor
more enlightenment than befits their station: how then will one get the
simplest and least attractive kinds of work done? --- One must make one's choice
between nature and culture, between morality and social progress. The dirt in the streets of London
cannot vanish without the magnificent traffic vanishing too.
Evils and goods are inseparably bound up with each other in the course of development.
% --- p. 406 ---
\opage{406}

Mandeville thus dissolves the harmony of Shaftesbury and Leibniz. He makes the
most forceful plea that comes from the pessimistic side in the eighteenth century and
has real merit in the treatment of the problem of culture. In order to come to terms with
the theologians, he declares that since the author of nature is incomprehensible to us, we have no
right to call it cruel. Indeed, he even believes he is working in the interest of faith in revelation
and of Christian morality by establishing the vanity of the world and
the insufficiency of human reason as well as of pagan virtue --- in
opposition to Shaftesbury, who favored deism and set pagan virtue
above Christian (Fable of the Bee's. 6th. ed. II, p. 431 f.). This
theological finale seems rather stuck on --- but it had its effect.
The clergy came out far more sharply against Shaftesbury than against Mandeville.

An interesting monograph on Mandeville is available by P. \textsc{Sakmann}
\textit{(Bernard de Mandeville und die Bienenfabel-Controverse.} Freiburg in B.
1897).

\subsection*{b.\quad Freethinkers}

Under a great many different forms and in a great many different directions, thought had, ever since the dawn of the
Renaissance, tried its powers on the great problems of life. It was no wonder, then, that in wider circles too the
conviction could arise that a view of life and a conduct of life needed no authority as a support, but that the insight
into the laws of nature and of human life that man can procure for himself by the powers of his own mind can suffice as
a guiding star. Early on, therefore, there appeared, in Italy from the fifteenth century onward, in the more northern
countries in the following centuries, men for whom natural religion was enough, or who perhaps did not even need it in
its usual form. From the sixteenth century onward the name \textit{Deism} became common for those who did not accept a
revelation in the Church's sense of the word; later it was stressed as the special mark of this tendency that it denied
the miraculous intervention of the Deity in the course of things. Often no great distinction was made between deists
and atheists.
% --- p. 407 ---
\opage{407}Every new conception in the philosophy of religion people were for the time being inclined to call atheism.
From the beginning of the eighteenth century the word \textit{Freethinker} appears in English literature. It denotes
thinking freed from authority. The word can --- like the word deist or atheist --- denote the most diverse views; none
of these expressions therefore has any philosophical value. But it is a sign of the times that the so-called
freethinkers become more numerous and more self-conscious from the beginning of the new century. (Cf. FR. EILSCHOW:
\textit{Philosophiske Breve.} Copenhagen 1748. p. 119 ff.). The deistic or freethinking literature is for the most part
of very slight value in a philosophical respect, which does not diminish its great significance in a
cultural-historical respect, as a symptom of the spread of scientific and philosophical ideas and in general of what is
stirring in wider circles. But to follow such symptoms in detail is the business of the history of literature more than
of the history of philosophy. As regards the English deists, \textsc{Leslie} \textsc{Stephen} \textit{(History of the
English Thought in the 18th Century,} Chap. 3) remarks, no doubt rightly, that on the whole they were inferior to their
opponents, while the reverse was the case in France. The explanation is presumably to be sought partly in the fact that
the greater resistance the Catholic Church could offer provoked the attackers and set greater forces in motion, partly
in the fact that in France it was not a purely abstract dogmatic discussion that was carried on, but the social and
political opposition was closely bound up with the religious and theoretical. For both reasons there arose an
enthusiasm that English deism lacked.

Only a single man among those usually called the English deists has made contributions of value to the history of
thought. That man is \textsc{John Toland}. He was born in 1670 in the north of Ireland and was brought up in the Catholic
religion; that is all that is known of his childhood. In the preface to \textit{Christianity not Mysterious} (1696) he
says: ``After I had been brought up from the very cradle in the grossest superstition and idolatry, it has pleased God
to make my own reason, and men who used their reason, the instruments of my conversion.'' He found no difference
between the authority of the Pope
% --- p. 408 ---
% print: „Mond“ (p. 408) (misprint)
\opage{408}and the authority that the Protestant clergy laid claim to. For him it was now a matter, just as at the
beginning of Christianity, of choosing between the clear teaching of Christ and the intricate doctrines of the scribes.
What Toland took to be the clear teaching of Christ he has set out in the work named. Locke's friend, the physicist
Molyneux in Dublin, at first speaks of Toland with respect in his letters to Locke; he calls him (letter of 6 April
1697) ``an honest freethinker and a learned man'' (a candid free-thinker and a good scholar). (This is, as far as I
know, the first time the word freethinker occurs). But later he was repelled by Toland's vanity and his inclination to
make propaganda in coffee-houses and other public places. No less offended were the clergy and the magistrates. Such
zealous preaching was directed against him that a pious man (according to what Molyneux relates) would no longer go to
church, because more was said there about a certain Toland than about the Lord Jesus. The book was burned, and an Irish
member of parliament wanted to have the author burned as well.

In the period that followed, Toland occupied himself with works of literary history and of politics. He came forward as
a defender of the Protestant succession and thereby came into favor at the court in Hanover, where he met Leibniz.
With Leibniz's pupil, too, the gifted Queen Sophia Charlotte of Prussia (a Hanoverian princess), Toland came into high
favor. It interested the Queen to hear discussions between the Berlin theologians, Leibniz and Toland. In the preface
to his \textit{Letters to Serena} (1704) Toland praised woman's capacity for intellectual work on the strength of the
experiences he had had here. Serena is Sophia Charlotte. --- Through his activity as a publicist Toland came into such
good circumstances that he could buy himself a house in the country. He could now satisfy his feeling for nature and
live ``free from care as well as from ambition, always with a book in his hand or in his head''. Later things went
downhill for him again, and his last years were weighed down by poverty and illness. He died in a village near London
(1722).

We come to know Toland's relation to Christianity from
% --- p. 409 ---
\opage{409}the work mentioned above, in which he seeks to prove ``that there is nothing in the Gospel either
\textit{contrary to} or \textit{above} reason, and that the Christian doctrine cannot rightly be called a mystery.'' By
reason he understands the mental faculty that leads us to certainty by comparing the doubtful and obscure with what we
clearly know. This faculty we must make use of in religion too; for only by it, not by the authority of the Church, can
we convince ourselves of the divinity of Scripture. The dogma of creation or the stories of miracles do not conflict
with reason. What we do not see through completely is not on that account at once a mystery. In the New Testament the
word mystery --- Toland maintains --- is never used of what is in and of itself incomprehensible to us, but of what had
hitherto been hidden, but had been revealed and can therefore now be grasped. Why, moreover, should God require that we
believe what we cannot grasp? Our diligence is not increased by it, and there is reason enough anyway to apply
ourselves to humility! It was only priests and philosophers who had made Christianity a mystery. ---

The later deists, Collins, Tindal, Morgan etc., went further than Toland, in that they explained away or denied the
miracles. The dispute was conducted, on their side and on their opponents' alike, with great vehemence, but in an
unscientific manner. Both parties lacked historical sense. What the orthodox explained as arbitrary miracles the deists
explained as equally arbitrary inventions of cunning priests. ---

Toland's most important work is his ``Letters to Serena''. It is directed against the Cartesian school's concept of
matter, which was still held fast --- though with misgivings --- by Spinoza. Toland maintains that motion must be
regarded as just as essential and original a property of matter as extension and solidity. If one conceives matter as
passive and at rest, one must assume a supernatural cause that sets it going. But on closer investigation we find motion
everywhere in nature; it is only to the senses that there seem at particular points to be rest and standstill; to the
conception of thought there is an inner activity (internal Energy, Autokinesis) in everything. Every motion must be
explained from
% --- p. 410 ---
\opage{410}another motion, and this holds also of the motions that, like those of animals, seem to arise of themselves
without a cause. Consciousness does not mark any break in the succession of motions. God must be assumed to have
created matter as active. The order and harmony in the universe testify that he guides the motions of matter; without
such an assumption the origin of organic life in particular will be inexplicable.

This line of thought of Toland's came to have an influence on French materialism around the middle of the century. It
was not entirely new; Huyghens and Leibniz had already corrected the Cartesian philosophy of nature in a similar
direction and in a far more profound way. But Toland carried the doctrine of the eternity of motion out into far wider
circles.

Toland developed his concluding ideas in \textit{Pantheisticum} (1720). He depicts here, in a fictitious account, how
there are, here and there throughout Europe, circles of unprejudiced men who gather for frugal social meetings, at which
they discuss various important questions with calm and good sense. They are called pantheists (a word that seems to
derive from Toland himself), because they hold that God is one with the force that works, creates and orders in the
whole universe, and can therefore be distinguished from the world only conceptually (ratione). They are entirely at odds
with Epicurus and are not materialists.
All individual beings, each after its kind, they take to have sprung from motion and thought, thought, which is the force
and harmony of the universe. They have a liturgy of their own, and they practice an unconditional tolerance. Their
endeavors concern the welfare of the state and of humanity without regard to parties. Their doctrine they keep hidden,
as an esoteric doctrine (accessible only to the initiated); for there are erring and obstinate people, whom one must
handle as nurses handle their stammering little ones. --- Toland wrote this work in a mood similar to the one from
which the Freemasons' movement, which \textsc{Hettner} has called the inner mission of English deism, sprang at about
the same time. The new ways of looking at things need cultivation in narrower circles, and in part new symbols as well.
Only, the age of criticism and enlightenment was not fitted for the founding of such societies or for the creation
% --- p. 411 ---
\opage{411}of viable symbols. Free individualism and critical examination had (and have) a long work still to do, and
neither societies nor symbols are created by conscious arbitrariness.

\section*{3.\quad Newton and His Significance for Philosophy}

Just as at the transition from the Renaissance to the seventeenth century we had to insert an examination of the
founding of modern natural science, without which the subsequent philosophical development could not be understood, so
here too, at the beginning of the eighteenth century, we must bring forward a great figure from the history of natural
science, perhaps the greatest it presents. In Newton not only is the ideal of inquiry that the new science had set up
brought to completion, so that his work stands as a model of scientific method as a whole; but his discoveries and
results in natural science themselves gain great influence on the subsequent philosophical development, not only in his
own country but also in France and Germany. And finally Newton himself has his own peculiar philosophy, which is of
interest for the history of philosophy both as the expression of a great natural scientist's world-view and by the
influence it exerted.

\textsc{Isaac Newton} was born at Woolsthorpe near Nottingham on 25 December 1642. Already as a child he had an interest
in mechanics and constructed machines, mills and clocks. He was at first destined to be a farmer, but when, as a
shepherd boy, he let cows and sheep look after themselves while he became absorbed in his reflections, he got his wish
to be allowed to study. At the University of Cambridge he soon went so far by studying on his own that he surpassed his
teachers. Very early he got the ideas for his great scientific discoveries in the domains of mathematics, optics and
astronomy alike. Like several others of the greatest minds in the history of science, he kept ideas conceived early
through long periods of silence and quiet work, until he could give them full execution and demonstrability. The idea
of the differential calculus
% --- p. 412 ---
\opage{412}he had, it seems, before Leibniz, although the latter published his method first; together with the proof of
the composition of light and of gravity as a universal law, it makes up his great discoveries, on which it is not our
task here to dwell more closely. His chief works are \textit{Principia philosophiæ naturalis mathematica (1687)} and
\textit{Opticks} (1704). After he had been professor at Cambridge for a number of years, he lived in his later years in
London, where he held a high position at the Mint. He died at a great age in 1727.

The great philosophical significance of Newton's discovery of the law of gravitation was first and foremost that it was
now established that the physical laws that hold at the surface of the earth hold also in the universe, as far as we
are able to survey it. Newton's fundamental thought, which according to the legend dawned on him in a happy moment, was
to extend what we see taking place on the earth beyond its domain and to test whether the inferences we can draw in
this way agree with the observations. Gravity is greater in the valleys than on the mountain heights; but there is no
reason why it should cease because we thought of ourselves on the moon or on one of the planets. Might not the motion
of the moon be conceived as a motion of falling, so that in the direction of its motion it constantly deviates from the
line it would follow by virtue of the law of inertia just as much as the law of falling bodies requires according to
the distance at which the moon is from the earth? What guided his thought in this conjecture he has formulated in his
chief work as a special rule of inquiry (regula philosophandi): ``such properties as cannot be intensified or
diminished, and which belong to all bodies of which one can have experience, ought to be taken as properties of all
bodies whatever \ldots\ For one ought surely not lightly to invent dreams that conflict with the connection of
experiments (tenor experimentorum), and one ought not to abandon the analogy of nature, since nature is wont to be
simple and always to agree with itself \ldots\ It is by virtue of this rule that we learn that all bodies gravitate
mutually toward one another.'' --- What Newton has set up in this rule of inquiry is the principle on which the whole
of modern science and philosophy
% --- p. 413 ---
\opage{413}rest. We have met it in Copernicus, Bruno, Galilei and Leibniz under various forms and in various
applications. In Newton it finds its most scientific application.

It was a magnificent widening of view. It now became clear that the fixed, law-governed order of nature reigns not only
here on earth but in the whole universe. The mechanical view of nature founded by Kepler, Galilei and Descartes thereby
became both more certain and more comprehensive. The world now came to stand as a great machine. People had, no doubt,
surmised that it was one; but only now had they found what held it together. And only now was a scientific proof given
of the Copernican hypothesis. If the heavenly bodies follow the law of gravity, the larger globe must necessarily stand
at a center in relation to the smaller ones, and a small globe like the earth could not be the absolute center. --- A
great confidence in the method of natural science, a self-esteem on behalf of the human mind for having solved such a
task, was bound naturally to develop even in those who could not see at first hand how the task had been solved.

The very method Newton employed was quite as important as his results. The ingenious idea that, by virtue of the
principle of actuality,
% scan: „Aktualitetsprineipet“ (p. 413; the e-book's reading, set by sense: scan-artefact rule)
extends what has been established for narrower circles of experience to wider circles, is only the first step. The
next step is the strict deduction of the consequences that the idea set up contains. And the third step is the proof
that what thus follows consistently from the idea agrees with experience. An unsurpassed cooperation of deduction and
