induction makes Newton's chief work a model for all scientific inquiry. First he derived the consequences of the
assumption that all the planets move according to the same laws as falling bodies at the surface of the earth, and next
he showed that these consequences were also actually confirmed by experience. From this he then concluded at last that
it is the same force that acts in both places. He goes from the phenomena to the law, and from the law to the force
(like Leibniz, see above).

This force he calls attraction, adding expressly that by this designation he does not wish to establish anything
% --- p. 414 ---
\opage{414}about the nature of the force, but merely to express that it acts so as to bring one body nearer to a larger
body. At bottom he does not assume any force acting at a distance. For both in the ``Principia'' (2, 11) and in the
``Opticks'' (Query 18---24) he declares that the centripetal force should rather be called impulse (impulsus) instead
of attraction (attractio), since the most reasonable hypothesis would be the assumption of an ethereal matter that
pervades everything and is thinner in the neighborhood of the globes than farther away; by this assumption perhaps not
only gravity but also light and heat could be explained. But his chief standpoint is nevertheless the one stated in the
Scholium generale (at the end of the third Book of the Principia): ``The ground of the properties of gravity I have not
yet been able to derive from the phenomena, and I do not occupy myself with inventing hypotheses''. \textsc{Pemberton}
\textit{(A View of Sir Newton's Philosophy,} London 1728. p. 407) relates that Newton complained to him of having been
misunderstood, as if by the word attraction he had meant to give an explanation, although it was only his intention to
draw attention to a force in nature whose cause and mode of action it must be the business of further inquiry to seek.
Yet he (and still more his disciples) was inclined to regard it as an immediate effect of God. --- Newton's doctrine
does not stand in the irreconcilable opposition to Cartesian physics that the Cartesians, Leibniz and also many of
Newton's friends supposed. At bottom he agrees with Descartes in his general points of view, although he corrects his
special assumptions by his more perfect method. Quite unjustly was he accused of wanting to reintroduce the
``occult qualities'' of scholasticism. He has satisfied his own demand: to set up only demonstrable causes (veræ
causæ).

But Newton does not enter the history of philosophy only through his results and his method. There appears in him as
well, partly as the background of his doctrine in natural science, partly as its consequence, a peculiar world-view,
which it will be of interest to bring forward.

There is a remarkable connection between Newton's religious conception and his mathematical doctrine of nature, a
connection that
% --- p. 415 ---
\opage{415}is brought about by his doctrine of space. (The chief passages are the Scholium after the Definitions in the
``Principia'' and Query 31 in the ``Opticks''). Wrongly, says Newton, does the popular conception (vulgus) assume that
the sensible times, spaces, places and motions are the true ones. It determines them by their relation to sensible
things. But it is by no means certain that there is any body whatever that is at absolute rest, so that we could use it
as a starting point for the determination of place and for distinguishing between real and apparent motion. For there
to be real motion (such as, e.g., the principle of inertia presupposes), there must be an absolute space and an
absolute time, which are not determined by relation to anything external whatever (sine relatione ad externum
qvodvis). There must be absolute, immovable places in order that absolute determination of place can take place; but
such places sensation cannot show us. The absolute places (loca primaria) are places both for themselves and for all
other things. True space and true time are mathematical space and time, which are not objects of sensation. ---
Strangely enough, we find in the great natural scientist the dogmatic tendency to leap from the phenomenal and relative
to the absolute. He postulates a space in itself (a kind of locus sui), just as Descartes, Spinoza and Leibniz postulate
a cause of itself (causa sui). He does not let the mathematical way of considering things be merely a point of view
that can guide us in calculating the relations of phenomena, but sets it up as the \textit{true} one in opposition to
the sensible or vulgar one, which does not get beyond the relative. A mathematical abstraction is made into the true
reality. In practice (in rebus humanis) we may keep to sensible space and forget that sensation can show us no
absolute places; but as thinkers (in rebus philosophicis) we must disregard the senses!

Some wavering can, to be sure, be shown in Newton's statements on this point\textsuperscript{79}), but the assumption of
absolute, ideal space as a reality is bound up with what is innermost in Newton's world-view. Space is for him not an
empty form, but God's organ, through which he acts in the world
% --- p. 416 ---
\opage{416}as omnipresent and at the same time immediately perceives the states of things. It is a ``boundless and
uniform sensorium''. --- Extension, then, is for Newton (as for Henry More) not the decisive distinguishing mark of
material things. Only that is material which besides extension also has solidity. In his conception of space Newton
stands, on the side of philosophy of nature, closest to Gassendi by his own account, while as regards its application
in the philosophy of religion he is influenced by Henry More. --- From Gassendi he also took over the atomic theory,
which thereby came to play an important role in the natural science of the following period, especially in chemistry
(since the founder of chemical atomism, John Dalton, had his concept of the atom from Newton). ---

As for the existence of God itself, Newton proved it from the purposive and harmonious arrangement of the world, and he
thereby struck up a theme that was varied endlessly throughout the whole eighteenth century. --- Whence comes it that
nature does nothing to no purpose, but always follows the simplest ways? Whence comes all the order and beauty we see in
the world? The motion of the planets about the sun in orbits that are concentric with the sun and lie practically in
the same plane, --- in short, the whole wonderful framework of our solar system (elegantissima compages) cannot be
explained according to mechanical laws, and cannot have developed in a natural way. Only in a supernatural way can the
masses, distances, velocities and densities of the various globes have been fitted to one another, and only by a
supernatural force can it be explained that the planets move in circles instead of following gravity and plunging into
the sun. And to this is added the remarkable structure, organs and instincts of animals! --- (Besides in the Scholium
generale in the ``Principia'' and Queries 28 and 31 in the ``Opticks'', Newton discusses this subject in his letters to
Bentley. Cf. BREWSTER: \textit{Life of Newton,} II. p. 125 ff., and \textsc{Rosenberger}: \textit{Isaac Newton,} p.
267---273).

Yet the world-machine was not quite perfect in Newton's opinion. The attempts to prove God's existence from the
purposiveness of nature easily come to work against themselves: for if nature is created perfect, it can surely go
% --- p. 417 ---
\opage{417}its way by the forces that are laid down in it, and God's continued activity is unnecessary. This
awkwardness does not appear in Newton's theology, since he assumes that through the mutual influence of comets and
planets irregularities have arisen in the system that would make a divine regulation necessary. --- This point was
sharply attacked by \textsc{Leibniz}, who mockingly compared Newton's system of the world to a clock that from time to
time has to go to the clockmaker. Newton's disciple CLARKE defended his doctrine by maintaining that it surely would not
do to make God superfluous. So: one first wants to prove God's existence by the ingenuity of the mechanism of nature
--- but then becomes afraid that, if the ingenuity is too great, God's existence will be refuted by it, --- and this
although the ingenuity would surely, properly speaking, have to be infinitely great in order to furnish a proof of the
existence of a God! --- This part of Newton's thinking is untenable. Fortunately, the great natural scientist's own
spirit and method led his successors beyond his unfortunate philosophy. \textsc{Kant} and \textsc{Laplace} showed the
possibility that the solar system may have developed in a natural way into its present form, and the great French
mathematicians, especially Lagrange and Laplace, established that the irregularities were periodic and compensated
themselves. There lay in Newton's doctrine and method a deeper philosophy than he himself got out of it. Kant and
Laplace were better Newtonians than Clarke. --- How dangerous an appeal to the supernatural can become in a scientific
respect can be seen from a cavalier remark of Newton's disciple \textsc{Maclaurin}, who has given an excellent
exposition of his doctrine. Apropos of the upheavals that seem to have taken place on the earth in earlier times, he
says: ``Since God has formed the universe in dependence on himself, so that it must be renewed from time to time by
him, it does not seem to be a very important question whether those great changes have been produced by the action of
external circumstances or by the same forces that formed things at the first''. All doctrine of evolution is thereby
declared superfluous, a whole series of scientific tasks is struck out. Nothing lay further from the spirit in which
Newton's real doctrine was thought out.
% --- p. 418 ---
\opage{418}

\section*{4.\quad George Berkeley}

\subsection*{a.\quad Biography and Characterization}

We put off for a while following the ideas of Locke, Newton and the deists on their wanderings through Europe, and,
having shown the source of these ideas, we turn to a thinker who, partly continuing, partly opposing, takes them up for
a new philosophical working-through, which leads him far away from the line of thought in which popular consciousness
moves and alone can move. What is peculiar to George Berkeley, one of the finest and clearest minds the history of
philosophy knows, is, however, that he pleads the cause of immediate, practical consciousness against scientific
abstractions and speculations, while at the same time by his own results he comes to stand in the sharpest opposition
to this consciousness and to offend it in the sharpest way by his paradoxes. In other respects too Berkeley unites in
his way of thinking opposites that might seem irreconcilable. Sharp criticism and childlike religious faith, the love
of inquiry and glowing missionary zeal have perhaps never been joined in so intimate and peculiar a way as in Berkeley.

\textsc{George Berkeley} was born at Dysert in County Kilkenny in Ireland on 12 March 1685. He belonged to an English
family that seems to have come to Ireland immediately after the Restoration and was a collateral branch of the noble
family of Berkeley. George Berkeley's friend Swift is said to have presented him to the Earl of Berkeley with the words:
``My lord, here is a young man of your family. I can assure your lordship that it is a far greater honor for you to be
related to him than for him to be related to you''. This much is certain, that the young man early showed brilliant
abilities. He studied in Dublin, where the writings of Boyle, Newton and Locke were at that time taken as the basis at
the University. Very early the fundamental thought of his later philosophy dawned on him. In his notebook
\textit{(Common-place Book)} from his young years, which \textsc{Fraser} has published in his excellent biography of
Berkeley \textit{(Life and Letters of George Berkeley,} Oxford 1871) and later in the first volume of
% --- p. 419 ---
\opage{419}\textit{The Works of George Berkeley} (Oxford 1901), we see his ideas in their successive unfolding. It was early his
conviction that when science and philosophy are freed from meaningless abstractions and foggy words, the conflict
between knowledge and faith will also be done away with. He works to lead men back to immediate experience and
intuition. He wants to put an end to the scholasticism that still remains, and to the one that has stepped into the old
one's place. His central thought is the proof that in the literal sense of the word there are no abstract ideas. With
this thought his ingenious discoveries as well as his personal outlook on life are very closely bound up.

Berkeley's first significant work was \textit{New Theory of Vision} (1709); he showed here how the sense of sight and
the sense of touch work together in our perception of space, and that space ``in itself'' was an abstraction to which
no immediate sensation corresponds. The following year his chief philosophical work appeared, \textit{Principles of
Knowledge,} in which he first criticizes the old theory of abstraction and then seeks to establish that the concept of
matter is an invalid abstraction, and that we have no other immediate objects of knowledge than our own
sense-sensations. How from here he makes the transition directly to his theological notions will be shown later. A few
years after these works appeared he went to London, moved in literary circles and began to combat the freethinkers in
articles in Steele's periodical ``The Guardian''. His polemic has a childlike and naive character. So, for example, when
(in \textit{Remarks on ``Collins' Discourse of Free-thinking'')} he wonders that the freethinkers do not seek in
sensual enjoyments a substitute for supernatural blessedness, but for the most part live a retired life in their
studies! The freethinkers --- he thinks --- proclaim publicly that they have less reason for virtue than others. One
knows the strength of passion but poorly if one thinks that the beauty of virtue is a sufficient counterweight in the
hour of temptation! --- After publishing a brilliant popular exposition of his philosophical ideas in the form of
dialogue \textit{(Dialogues between Hylas and Philonous,} 1713), he spent several
% --- p. 420 ---
\opage{420}years traveling in France and Italy. His travel diary shows us his open eye and his great feeling for nature,
history and social conditions. When he came home, he took up a clerical office in Ireland, but did not have peace for
long. He despaired of being able to carry out his plans of leading the men of old Europe back to nature and simplicity
in thought and life. Europe seemed to him decrepit. From the new virgin land on the other side of the Atlantic he
expected a new golden age, for faith, science, art and life alike. With this was joined zeal for spreading
Christianity among the heathen and a romantic feeling for free nature. In a poem (``On the Plan of Transplanting Arts
and Sciences to America'') he has expressed these thoughts. He formed the plan of founding a college in the Bermudas for
the training of missionaries for America. When after long exertions he had obtained a promise of state support for this
undertaking, he settled on Rhode-Island to direct the preparations for the establishment of the college. But it turned
into a great disappointment. The promise was not kept, and after three years' stay in America he had to return (1731).
He never got over the shattering of this great hope. His view of life was darker from this time on. --- Memories of the
beautiful natural surroundings in which he lived on Rhode-Island are found again in the rich scenery of the dialogue
\textit{Alciphron} (1732), in which he resumed his polemic against the freethinkers, besides seeking anew to give a
clear and popular exposition of his philosophical ideas. In this work he expresses an idea, similar to the one his
friend Butler developed at length a few years later in his ``Analogy'', of the difficulties common to natural and
revealed religion. He directs the polemic against two types of freethinkers, those of Mandeville's kind as well as
those of Shaftesbury's kind, and he triumphs when he can show how they fall out with each other, Mandeville's
representative declaring that natural religion is a half-measure when it is not supported by the supernatural. ---
Berkeley's dialogues still have no slight interest, both through the philosophical and theological problems that
% --- p. 421 ---
\opage{421}are discussed in them and through the beautiful language and the on the whole successful form of dialogue.

As Bishop of Cloyne in the south of Ireland (from 1734), Berkeley showed himself equally zealous as a pastor,
philanthropist and patriot. He was loved and respected not only by the Protestants but also by the Catholics (who made
up almost five-sixths of the population of his diocese). He spoke up for the admission of Catholics to the
universities. In his \textit{Querist} (1735---37) he set a multitude of social and Irish-patriotic questions in motion.
Even medicine did not lie outside his interest. In ``tar-water'' he believed he had found a universal remedy against
various diseases, which he sought to explain more fully in one of his last works \textit{(Siris} 1744), which is
remarkable as well for the mystical-Platonizing direction his thinking takes here. The last works from his hand were
treatises on fossils and on earthquakes. For this subjectivist and idealist nothing in the world of reality was
indifferent and alien. He spent his last years in Oxford, where he died in 1753.

By the chief purpose Berkeley set himself in his philosophy, his position in the history of thought forms an analogy to
Leibniz's. Both want to carry thought beyond the purely mechanical view of nature without, however, denying it. They
undertake an examination of the concepts with which Descartes, Spinoza, Newton and, still to a great extent, Locke
confidently operate as realities. They take the world-picture constructed by natural science and philosophy not as an
absolute reality but as a phenomenon. But whereas Leibniz dissolves the mechanical world-picture chiefly by the
objective road, by leading motion back to force and making force one with the monad's subjective impulse toward new
states, Berkeley goes chiefly by the subjective road, seeking to show psychologically how our ideas of space and matter
--- on which, after all, the whole mathematical-physical knowledge of the world rests --- come into being. Berkeley
continues Locke's investigation of the origin of ideas and discusses the question what we can really claim to know
beyond the reality that is given in our own sensations and ideas. He pursues his consistency with a
% --- p. 422 ---
\opage{422}ruthlessness he would perhaps hardly have possessed, for all his love of truth, if his living religious faith
had not stood ready to fill in at once what his philosophical criticism cut away. In the rejection of absolute space and
absolute matter to which his philosophy led him, he felt himself nearer to his God, indeed felt himself in immediate
contact with him. His intimate and primitive religious feeling could not be content with the clockmaker theology, the
external relation between God and the world, that Locke, Newton and most of the theologians and freethinkers of the time
professed. Yet it is not as a religious thinker but as a psychologist and critical philosopher that he has his
significance. In our exposition we follow him only to the door that leads him into theology. For him his philosophy was
itself a crusade aimed at winning back the Holy Land. But it went with him as it went with the crusaders: he came to
work for other tasks and purposes than those he had set himself.

\subsection*{b.\quad On Space and Abstract Ideas}

In his ``Theory of Vision'', one of the most ingenious psychological works ever written, Berkeley investigates the
psychological nature of the perception of space. He shows that distance and size are not perceived immediately from the
first. The perception of distance and size arises in that visual sensations are combined with sensations of the
movement or straining of the eyes (sensations Berkeley calls sensations of touch, whereas nowadays they are called
sensations of movement) as well as with memories and associations (or, as Berkeley calls them, suggestions) of
sensations of touch that we have previously had in immediate relation to the object. The idea of touch that the visual
sensation calls up fuses with it to such a degree that afterwards we immediately ``see'' the object before us at a
certain distance and with a certain size. The practical significance of the visual sensation lies in its giving warning
of the sensations of touch we would get at closer quarters. But the connection between the two kinds of sensation
% --- p. 423 ---
\opage{423}is due to experience and practice. We ``see'' distance and size in the same way as we ``see'' shame or
remorse in a man's look. Sight and the sense of touch have nothing in common; only custom joins them in a common result.
But to this result --- space --- no real single sensation corresponds. Space corresponds only to the practiced subjective
association between the two kinds of ideas of sense. In and of itself it is an empty word.

One sees how Berkeley takes Locke's demand in earnest: to test the validity of ideas by investigating their origin.
Space no longer hovers as an incomprehensible general something above all the senses; its source is led back to a
process of association. This is what we know about it. Berkeley himself, however, conceives it also as a divine
language of signs, in which we are trained by way of association.

In his investigation of abstract ideas (in the Introduction to \textit{Principles of Knowledge)} his polemic is
directed against Locke as the last important representative of the old theory of abstraction, which ascribed to us a
faculty of abstraction in the sense of a faculty of forming ideas that contain only marks common to several objects.
From three ideas of a green, a red and a yellow thing we should, e.g., be able to ``abstract'' the idea of a color in
general (neither green, red nor yellow). That ideas of this kind exist in consciousness Berkeley denies. We can of course
divide an idea, e.g. represent to ourselves a part of an object without the others. But we cannot form new ideas whose
content would be what is ``common'' to several qualities. We have words that denote this common element, but not ideas
of the common element. This does not exclude our being able to form general ideas that hold for a whole group of
phenomena; but this comes about in that an idea that is in itself concrete, individual (particular), is used to
represent (represent or stand for) all other concrete ideas of the same kind. We think in examples!

In this investigation too Berkeley has made a significant contribution to psychology. Leaving it to
% --- p. 424 ---
% scan: „som.“ (p. 424)
\opage{424}psychology to show what is still lacking in Berkeley for a complete theory of general ideas, we pass on to
see what philosophical consequences Berkeley draws from his psychological investigations.

\subsection*{c.\quad Epistemological Consequences}

Whereas --- says Berkeley (in the \textit{Principles)} --- as regards the objects of the inner sense, no one thinks of
ascribing existence to them when they are not perceived, it is held that the objects of the outer sense exist whether
they are perceived or not. But this is an unprovable and unreasonable assumption. Objects of knowledge, by the nature of
the case, exist only in so far as they are known; their being consists in being perceived (their esse is percipi). If
one looks more closely at what underlies that assumption, one finds the old theory of abstraction again. For surely it
is the most violent abstraction of all to represent to oneself the object without everything that makes it an object
for us. We should then have to disregard all our sensations! It is held, to be sure, that it is only the secondary
qualities (color, taste, smell etc.) that are to be disregarded, not the primary ones (extension, solidity). By matter is
meant something that has only the primary qualities, something that has extension and figure and can move. But it is
overlooked that the primary qualities are not perceived without the secondary ones, and that they themselves, just as
much as these, exist for us only by means of sensations. If extension, e.g., is to be assumed to exist outside
consciousness, one must ask: is it extension as sight shows it to us, or as touch shows it to us? Perhaps as both
together show it to us --- but then we have already seen that the idea of it is due only to an association. There
cannot exist an extended and moving something that is neither large nor small, far nor near, and moves neither fast nor
slowly! Even if there were solid, figured and moving substances outside consciousness, whence would we know it? How can
one appeal to the testimony of the senses for something that is not sensed at all?
% --- p. 425 ---
\opage{425}

But is not the difference between reality and imagination thereby done away with? This Berkeley most emphatically
denies. Real nature, he says, I do not deny; I deny only abstract matter. Everything that is seen, felt, heard or in
general perceived by the senses I take to be real, but not matter, this unknown something (somewhat --- if indeed it
may be termed somewhat) without sensible properties and inaccessible to all sensation and comprehension. The difference
between reality and imagination rests on the difference between sense-sensation and memory or fantasy. Sense-sensations
make a stronger impression on us, are more distinct, and appear in a definite order that we cannot break. We have as
well the consciousness that we have not produced them ourselves. On this rests my concept of reality, says Berkeley;
let others then see whether they can find more in the concept of reality they have! --- Nor is the validity of natural
science shaken by that overthrow of the concept of matter. Natural science, after all, seeks to explain phenomena by
other phenomena, by causes that can themselves be sensed, not by assuming mystical substances. To explain the phenomena
is merely to show that under such and such circumstances we get such and such sensations. What natural science
establishes is a definite and law-governed relation in the occurrence of our sensations, so that the one sensation can
stand as a sign of the other. We thereby become able to infer forward and backward. By careful observation of the
phenomena accessible to us we discover the general laws of nature, or we set up certain formulas for the phenomena of
motion. Natural science has to do neither with force nor with matter, only with phenomena. --- Every proof of a law
among the phenomena and every inference from such a law rests in the end on the fundamental presupposition that the
author of the phenomena always acts uniformly and in observance of general rules --- a presupposition that, according to
Berkeley (Principles § 107 in fine), cannot, to be sure, be proved.

What, then, is the author of the phenomena or sensations, in so far as I do not produce them myself? While Berkeley
holds the causal principle to be unprovable in so far as it concerns
% --- p. 426 ---
% scan: „Vil lie“ (p. 426): one word; a gap in the word is no division (as II.388 Uendel ighed)
\opage{426}the relation of the phenomena among themselves, he has no doubt of its validity when the question becomes
one of the origin of our passively received sensations. There must be an activity that comes into force where we
ourselves are passive. Now our own power of calling up and altering ideas is the only example of activity we have. In
this power Berkeley finds our real essence expressed: the soul is the will (the soul is the will), he says
(Commonplace-book ed. 1871 p. 428). ``As far as I can see, the words will, soul and spirit do not denote different
ideas'' (Principles § 27). All inner activity Berkeley calls willing, thinking too: ``What I think of, whatever it may
be, I call idea (idea). Thought itself, or thinking, is no idea, but an act, that is to say willing, or --- in
contrast to the effects --- will'' (Commonplace-book p. 460). Its being is not to be perceived but to perceive (its
esse is percipere). Will is the only form of activity we know. About the knowledge we have of our willing, and so of the
real essence of our spirit, Berkeley is not at one with himself. Only this stands firm for him, that our knowledge of
our own active nature cannot be an idea (idea), since every idea is passive and therefore presents nothing active to us.
``The will is purus actus, or rather pure spirit, which cannot be imagined, sensed or grasped'' (Commonplace-book p.
462). Not an idea but a concept (notion) is what we have of ourselves. But in one place (Principles § 27) he teaches
that we know spirit, or that which acts, through its effects (that is, the changes of ideas); in another place
(Dialogues between Hylas and Philonous, 3rd Dialogue) he ascribes to us an immediate knowledge of our spirit and its
ideas, in that we perceive them by self-observation (by reflection). But however we may perceive it: for forming the
thought of the source of the phenomena we have only the \textit{analogy} with our own spirit to hold to. We think of God
in analogy with our spirit, only with its powers raised infinitely. The real ideas now become those he implants in us,
and we now understand as well how objects can exist even if we do not perceive them: they exist potentially, as
possibilities, in God as
% --- p. 427 ---
\opage{427}their constant cause. (Cf. Commonplace-book p. 489). The divine will makes itself known to us in the order
and connection of our sensations, and divine providence in the purposiveness this order presents. If nature is to be a
being distinct from God, it is a heathen chimera. The usual conception has God first create matter and then matter act
upon us. Why this detour? Why not have God produce our sensations immediately? The more clearly we think, the more we
shall find ourselves in immediate relation to God. There are no secondary causes. In God we are, live and move, says
Berkeley, and he thinks he has more right to say it than Spinoza. ``Every sensation that I receive from without
according to the general laws of nature, i.e. independently of my will, proves the existence of a God, i.e. of an
unextended, incorporeal spirit''. (Commonplace-book p. 463). --- To this mystical-pantheistic conception Berkeley, as
is seen from \textit{Siris,} gave himself up more in his later years; but we cannot go further here into the more
detailed form he gives his thoughts in this direction. We merely draw attention to a point of likeness between Berkeley
and Leibniz at the transition from their philosophy of experience to their speculative philosophy: they both make use of
the principle of analogy, which is the principle of all metaphysical idealism. In the dialogue Alciphron (IV § 21)
Berkeley maintains --- against those who deny that we have any concept of God, --- that we know God by way of analogy,
relying on such human properties as are real perfections.

Berkeley's merit is above all this, that with an energy not weakened by the paradoxical results to which his thinking
led him, he held fast to the question: whence do we know that things are more than our sensations and ideas? By what
right do we leap from consciousness, which alone is immediately given, over to things, which are never immediately
given? --- As regards Berkeley's own answer to this question, it is seen from the foregoing exposition that he by no
means makes existence a mere series of sensations. In the first place he distinguishes between the sensations and
% --- p. 428 ---
\opage{428}spirit; only the being of the former consists in being perceived (esse = percipi); the being of the latter is
to perceive (esse = percipere), that is, to act. What is innermost in existence is for him willing and acting. In the
second place he acknowledges the principle of causality and uses it to solve the question raised. But whereas the
usual conception (popular metaphysics) starts from the assumption that the cause of our sensations must resemble them,
Berkeley starts from the assumption that the cause of our passive states must be thought in analogy with what acts in
ourselves. --- He is an idealist, but not a subjectivist. But his idealism at once takes on a theological form. His
theological notions lie ready, poised to spring, while he philosophizes, and as soon as he has drawn the knot tight and
shown an open question, they press forward to fill in what is lacking. Thinking thereby halts too early. The theological
notions themselves are not tested. The whole conception of the world becomes anthropomorphic. The connection of nature
becomes only a connection in the divine will, which holds the phenomena together, and the phenomena become only a
collection of arbitrary signs. The principle of causality itself is not examined more closely, and yet it carries the
whole solution of the problem. On this last point Berkeley's nearest successor took hold, continuing and opposing, just
as Berkeley himself had done toward Locke.

\section*{5.\quad David Hume}

\subsection*{a.\quad Biography and Characterization}

English philosophy has this great significance in the history of the development of the life of the human spirit, that
by its method of experience it demands that account be rendered not only for the edifices of thought that speculative
philosophers erect, but also for the unconscious and unproven presuppositions on which the popular conception of the
world and the special sciences build. Thus Locke had demanded an account of where our ideas in general come from, and
Berkeley had shown what problem, when one takes this account in earnest, lies in
% --- p. 429 ---
\opage{429}the idea of space and in the idea of the material world. This critical investigation of knowledge reaches its
high point within the English school of the eighteenth century in the philosophy of David Hume. He undertakes an
investigation of the two concepts on which the whole earlier philosophy rested, and which Locke and Berkeley had not yet
attacked in earnest: the concept of substance and the concept of cause, the two concepts that were the binding cement in
all speculative, scientific and popular edifices of thought. On the causal principle, or the principle of sufficient
reason, rested Leibniz's great system of harmony, Newton's mechanics of the world and the popular conception of a world
of things subject to certain laws. All started from the reasonableness of existence, its rationality, presupposed with
greater or less consciousness that existence contained in itself something corresponding to our reason. This
presupposition Hume tests. And he is the first who has in earnest undertaken such a test and has descended into the
depths in which the forces that hold the inner and the outer world together for us spring up, depths that lead away from
the regions in which speculative philosophers, special inquirers and common sense move. Hume himself felt, and expressed
in a characteristic way, the strange state of solitude and dissolution in which the thinker finds himself who
perseveringly pursues the problem of knowledge down into these depths, and the opposition there is between the strictly
theoretical and the instinctive, practical and popular conception of the world. Only the intellectual passion that
awoke ever anew, together with the hope of winning fame by going the way consistently to its end, made it possible for
him, by his own statement (in the concluding section of the first Book of his chief work), to complete his work.

In Hume's character intellectual zeal and ambition were united with good nature, benevolence and a mild view of
weaknesses and prejudices, but at the same time also with a certain love of ease, which did not want to be disturbed by
polemic in the cultivation of literary interests. He was born on 26 April 1711 on the estate of Ninewells in the south
of Scotland, the second son of a
% --- p. 430 ---
\opage{430}landowner. In his autobiography he says: ``Very early I was seized by a passion for literature, which has been
the ruling passion of my life and a great source of enjoyment to me.'' His family wanted him to be a lawyer, but he
``felt an insurmountable aversion to everything but philosophy and learning''. His ideal was a carefree existence in
which he could satisfy his inclinations for inquiry and cultivate the company of a few chosen friends; but he wanted as
well his literary activity to make his name honored. While still quite young he believed himself on the track of new
thoughts: a new ``scene of thought'' opened up for him. But an attack of hypochondria (which he describes in a letter to
a physician, printed in \textsc{Burton}: \textit{Life and Correspondance of David Hume.} Edinburgh 1846 I p. 30 ff.)
halted his meditations for a time. Presumably he here noticed at once the strange opposition between the world of
reflection and the world of practical daily life which he later described in his chief work. He resolved to lay his
studies aside and become a merchant. But practical life could not hold him. He sought out solitary places to stay in
France and wrote there his chief work: ``Treatise on Human Nature, an Attempt to Apply the Method of Experience to the
Mental Domain'' \textit{(Treatise on Human Nature etc.).} It came out in London 1739---1740 and consisted of three parts,
of which the first deals with knowledge, the second with the feelings, the third with the foundation of morality. It
carries the treatment of these various questions considerable steps further, and still stands in the front rank among
the classic works of philosophy. But for the time being it had no success. ``It fell'', he says himself, ``dead-born
from the press, and did not even attain the honor of exciting a murmur among the zealots''. Hume's literary ambition,
which seduced him into declaring his excellent brainchild dead-born, had a fateful effect. The fame he did not win by it
he sought to win by a series of smaller treatises (Essays), partly of philosophical, partly of economic and political
content; for a time he went away from philosophy altogether to cultivate history; indeed, in the end he even
% --- p. 431 ---
\opage{431}disowned his significant work of youth entirely, declaring --- so as not to be molested by his theological
critics (who, then, had after all begun to ``murmur'') --- that he acknowledged only the exposition of his philosophical
doctrine he had given in the ``Essays''. But brilliant as many of these smaller works are, they could not gain so great a
significance in philosophical discussion as the chief work could have gained if Hume had used the literary fame he later
won to bring life into the ``dead-born'' child, and had not disavowed it so that it should not cause him disturbance. As
regards the problem of knowledge in particular, it was above all through the abridged and muted exposition in
\textit{Enquiry concerning Human Understanding} (1749) that Hume's philosophizing gained influence on the further
development of thought, while the radical exposition in the ``Treatise'', which cuts the very bond between our thoughts,
and in general between the elements of our being, lay forgotten for a long time. --- That the motive of Hume's
disavowal of his work of youth is the one given here is seen from \textit{Letters of David Hume to William Strahan}
(Oxford 1888. p. 289 f.). There is no question, as has sometimes been thought, of Hume's really having changed his views
on main points. Yet it is psychologically understandable that the highly strung intellectual state in which Hume wrote
his work of youth could not last. After having thought with the learned, and better than the learned had thought
hitherto, he felt a need to talk with the unlearned. After giving a popular exposition of his philosophical and
economic ideas in his ``Essays'', he threw himself into history. ``As you know'', he wrote to a friend, ``there is no
post of honor on the English Parnassus that can more truly be said to stand vacant than that of history''. The place
he had obtained --- after strong opposition on the part of the orthodox --- as librarian of the Advocates' Library in
Edinburgh gave him good opportunity for learned studies. His History of England made him still more popular than his
Essays had done. As a historian he has the merit of being the first who sought to make history more than a history of
wars, in that he
% --- p. 432 ---
\opage{432}took account of social conditions, manners, literature and art. His historical work began to appear two years
before Voltaire's famous ``Essai sur les moeurs''. While he was liberal in his philosophical views, in his judgment of
historical personalities he started from royalist and Tory points of view. --- Yet he did not put philosophy on the shelf
altogether. Studies in the philosophy of religion especially occupied him in his later years. To this his
\textit{Natural History of Religion} (1757) and his \textit{Dialogues on Natural Religion} bear witness, the latter work
of which he held back for reasons of caution, so that it appeared only a couple of years after his death.

Hume was not only a philosopher and historian. He had a need to take part in practical life. As secretary of an embassy
he made (1748) a great journey through Holland, Germany, Austria and northern Italy. And later he exchanged his post as
librarian in Edinburgh for a post as secretary to Lord Hertford, when the latter, after the Peace of Paris in 1763, went
to France as English ambassador. Hume was by then already famous and was received in the most brilliant way at court and
in literary circles. He was, like Franklin later, in fashion, perhaps precisely because of his plain, little elegant
manner. When after three years' stay he traveled back to England, he took Jean Jacques Rousseau with him, to procure a
refuge for the man, now driven out of both Switzerland and France. Hume's fine conduct toward Rousseau was repaid by the
latter with insane suspicion, and after a spectacular break Rousseau fled back to France again, where the storm had now
abated. --- After Hume had held the post of Under-Secretary of State for Scotland for a year, he took up residence in
Edinburgh and now led a quiet learned life with chosen friends, until, after a lengthy illness that did not rob him of
his equanimity and cheerfulness, he died on 25 August 1776.

\subsection*{b.\quad Epistemological Radicalism}

All the sciences, and not least the human sciences, stand in a definite relation to
human nature. With this
% --- p. 433 ---
\opage{433}proposition Hume begins his investigation of knowledge, and from it he draws the
conclusion that by the study of human nature one will discover the foundation of
all human science. But this study ought to be undertaken by means of the method of
experience, which has already been applied with success in natural science, and
whose application to the study of human nature Bacon, Locke and Shaftesbury have
already begun. As his \textit{fundamental proposition} Hume now sets up, appealing
to experience, the proposition that all our ideas (ideas) spring from sensations
(impressions); ideas can never be original. In testing the validity of an idea we
have then first and foremost to ask of which sensation it is an after-effect.
Dispute and doubt arise when the ideas are unclear and indefinite. Since it now
turns out that the sensations from which the ideas derive are on the whole clearer
and more distinct than the ideas themselves, disagreement and uncertainty will be
brought to an end when one seeks out the corresponding sensations; --- if such
cannot be shown, the idea must be invalid (Enquiry Sect. 2). In the origin of the
sensations Hume sees a problem insoluble for our knowledge, but a problem whose
solution is also not necessary for the treatment of his task (cf. Treatise I. 3,
5, where he leaves it open whether it is the external things that call forth the
sensations, or God who creates them, or the soul itself that unconsciously forms
them; --- in other places, as II, 1, 1, he follows the usual mode of expression).
--- By means of that fundamental proposition (which Berkeley had applied only to
the ideas of space and matter) Hume then tests a series of important ideas. ---
The idea of substance or essence must be declared invalid, since we have no
corresponding sensation. We immediately sense only single qualities, more or less
firmly connected with one another, but no ``essence.'' --- The mathematical ideas
of time and space are formed by idealization. Experience shows us only imperfect
equality in the magnitude of times and spaces; every standard of measurement that
we have is imperfect; --- but after experience has given us occasion to compare
% --- p. 434 ---
% scan: „2. 4“ (p. 434)
% print: „Evidens“, the quotation does not close (p. 434) (misprint)
\opage{434}different degrees of equality and different standards, we form the idea of perfect
equality and of a perfect standard (a perfect line, e.g.), since the imagination,
once it has been set in motion, continues its course even if experience cannot
keep up. Since geometry concerns such ideal objects, it cannot, in its application
to real objects, lead to complete exactness. --- Just as little as the concept of
substance and the mathematical concepts does the idea of existence correspond to
any sensation. To think of a thing and to think of it as existing are not two
different things. Our idea of the object remains a mere idea even if we think the
object as existing, and we do not add a new quality to a thing by conceiving it
as existing.

In testing the validity of our knowledge as a whole, Hume distinguishes between
the knowledge that consists only in clarifying the relation of our ideas to one
another (the formal sciences: logic and mathematics),\footnote{With regard to
mathematical knowledge there is a wavering in Hume. In the Treatise he lays strong
emphasis on the fact that we can conceive no absolutely regular line or figure,
and he therefore declares that geometry cannot be a strict science, whereas
algebra and arithmetic can attain complete exactness, since we can always convince
ourselves that two numbers contain an equal number of units (Treatise I, 3, 1).
But he nevertheless acknowledges that there is both a geometrical and an
arithmetical necessity, which springs from an act of the understanding by which we
compare two ideas (I, 3, 14), --- and that in geometrical relations too we have a
standard, although it is owed to a ``fiction'' (I, 2, 4). And in the later
epistemological work he puts geometry and algebra on an equal footing: ``Even if
there never existed any circle or triangle in nature, the truths that Euclid has
demonstrated would still always retain their certainty and evidence (Enquiry III,
1).} and the knowledge that leads us beyond the given sensations and convinces us
of the existence of something that is not given. This latter kind of knowledge
rests on the assumption of the validity of the causal relation, --- and here Hume
then performs his great philosophical deed by posing in a decisive way the
\textit{problem of causality,} the
% --- p. 435 ---
\opage{435}problem on whose solution all appraisal of the significance of the real sciences
depends. At the root of all inquiry lies a need to find ``what holds the world
together in its inmost core''; in every single problem of the real sciences lies
the same fundamental problem, and Hume was the first to see it in its whole scope.
It must be firmly kept in mind that Hume never at any time doubts that we must of
course apply the causal principle without interruption in theory and practice; he
asks only whether this application can be \textit{grounded,} --- and it is here
that he finds only a negative answer. He discovers that what makes us assume
causal relations is the same as what makes us assume something as existing even
if it is not given to sensation. One and the same investigation casts --- in
accordance with Hume's psychological method --- light on the two concepts of cause
and belief (belief).

One cannot, in grounding the validity of the causal relation, appeal to immediate
certainty or intuition; for such we have only concerning simple relations of
resemblance and quantity. Nor to logical demonstration; for all our ideas can be
separated by us from one another. The motion of the one billiard ball is an event
wholly different from the motion of the other billiard ball. There is no object
that it is not easy for us to think as existing at one moment and as not existing
at the next. There is then no self-contradiction whatever in something's beginning
without a cause. The proofs that earlier philosophers (Hobbes, Locke, Clarke ---
to whom Wolff could be added) have attempted are only sham proofs. It is also
clear, of course, that if the causal principle were grounded on reason (either on
intuition or on demonstration), we should come into conflict with the
``fundamental proposition'': for then reason would possess the capacity to produce
wholly new ideas that did not derive from experience! --- But is the validity of
the causal relation not grounded by experience? --- To this the answer is that
experience only shows us the one event following upon the other, but not the inner
necessity in their mutual relation, which is what is meant by the word causal
relation. This holds whether by experience we mean inner or outer experience. Hume
refutes in particular the assumption (which
% --- p. 436 ---
\opage{436}Berkeley had embraced) that in the immediate consciousness of our willing we
should have an apprehension of power or activity. A single experience cannot give
us the idea of cause, and several experiences give us only a relation of
succession. When we have very often seen one phenomenon followed by another, we
involuntarily expect this other when the first occurs again; but that is a
custom, and therein lies no proof of our right to infer from the past to the
future.

In his explanation of the tendency we have to go beyond a given sensation and to
assume or expect something that is not given, Hume first takes as his basis the
experience that every strongly moved state or mood (disposition, feeling) into
which consciousness comes has a tendency to maintain itself and to spread out over
the new ideas that emerge. When consciousness is heightened and enlivened by an
object, every act of consciousness will be livelier than otherwise as long as the
enlivenment lasts.
It was indeed this same law that explained the idealization of the mathematical
ideas. --- In the second place he lays weight on the fact that experience shows us
a propensity in our ideas to call one another forth. Every idea has an associating
tendency; a gentle power (a gentle force) leads from the one over to others. As
various grounds of such association Hume names resemblance, contiguity in time and
space, causal relation. There manifests itself here an attraction in the inner
world which is as significant for that world as physical attraction is for the
outer world. But it is at the same time no less mysterious in its nature: its
causes must lie in qualities of human nature that we do not know. The uniting bond
between our ideas is just as incomprehensible as the uniting bond between external
objects; and it is known only through experience. Indeed, Hume finds (in the
Appendix to the first book of the Treatise) the associative connection not merely
incomprehensible but even self-contradictory: how can there be a connecting
principle \textit{(uniting principle,} Tr. I, 3, 4; \textit{principle of
connection,} Tr. I App.), when all our sensations and ideas are distinct,
independent existences? Of this difficulty Hume
% --- p. 437 ---
\opage{437}declares that it is too hard for his understanding. --- But the two facts (which we
may call expansion and association) stand firm. And by their help it is explained
how a lively sensation, which itself --- precisely because of its liveliness ---
stands before us as the expression of something real, can communicate its
liveliness, and with it also its stamp of reality, to the ideas that it calls
forth by association. What we call belief (belief) is nothing other than the
lively stamp that ideas can acquire in this way. Belief is not owed to any new,
peculiar impression, but signifies only the peculiar manner in which an idea comes
to stand for feeling (feeling or sentiment). We cannot refrain from passing over to
the idea associated with the lively sensation, and cannot refrain from holding it
fast and seeing it in a stronger light than otherwise. --- And since now (in the
third place) consciousness (as the ideas of the sense qualities, of time and
space, and of substance show) has a propensity to regard its own inner states as
external, objective phenomena, we understand how we come to assume causal
relations between the things in the world, although the necessity in question
here is found, of course, only in ourselves, and is a compulsion which for
psychological reasons manifests itself in us to pass over from one sensation or
idea to another. The necessity is subjective, just as the sense qualities, space
and time are. What we call reason (reason, Treatise I, 3, 16 in fine, cf. Enquiry
IX: experimental reasoning) is only an obscure instinct in us, which arises through
the repetition of experiences in a definite order. The very arising of this
instinct, the very influence of custom, is just as incomprehensible as all
connection between the elements of our consciousness in general is. But since the
mental activity by which we infer from the same cause to the same effect is of
extraordinary practical importance, nature has not been willing to entrust it to
uncertain thinking (reason = subtile reasoning Treatise I, 4, 1 and 2), but has
let it be owed to the sure, though obscure, instinct, which will not be shaken by
any critical examination whatever: nature is stronger than reflection (nature is
too strong for principle! Enquiry XII, 3).
% --- p. 438 ---
\opage{438}Whereas dogmatic philosophy in its various forms believed that by the help of pure
reason it could build trains of thought that led far beyond sense perception, as a
consequence of Hume's investigations the imagination (imagination) comes to stand
as the only faculty that can lead to the assumption of something that is not an
object of present sense perception (Treatise I, 4, 7). On the imagination, then,
rests the assumption of an external world independent of consciousness. We do not
experience the uninterrupted existence of objects, only a certain constancy and
coherence --- but this is enough for our imagination, which of course continues to
move in the direction in which it has once been led, to conceive as great a
uniformity and coherence as it is at all able to. The intervals between our
sensations we fill up by feigning constant beings. --- By quite the same principle
the idea of the ego or the self is explained. The invalidity of the concept of
substance has already been shown. Our sensations and ideas can very well subsist
without leaning on or inhering in such a substance. If one wishes to ground one's
assumption of a soul-substance, one must show a sensation on which it is grounded,
and that one cannot do, since all our sensations change. If one takes the word
substance in a vaguer sense, of that which has separate subsistence, why then
should our sensations and ideas, each of which can subsist separately, not be
substances? --- Hume warns theologizing metaphysicians in particular against the
assumption of a soul-substance in which the single sensations and ideas subsist as
particular modifications, since one would thereby give Spinozism a dangerous
support: it was in just this way, after all, that Spinoza conceived the relation
between God and the things in the world! --- But even if we disregard the idea of
a soul-substance and merely ask how matters stand with the idea of the self as the
expression of our personal identity, we are entangled in great difficulties. No
sensation or idea is unchangeable and constant. We always find a special inner
state given, never ``ourselves'' as a whole. The identity that we ascribe to
ourselves is of the same nature as that which we ascribe to external objects: it
is owed only to the ease with which we
% --- p. 439 ---
\opage{439}pass over from one sensation or idea to another, an ease that makes us overlook
the enigma in the fact that one element can lead over at all to another, different
from it! ---

Hume is a poser of problems of the first rank. He is able, as few have been able,
to think a concept or a relation through in such a way that the hidden
difficulties come to light. By his energetic labor of thought he succeeds in
drawing forth the fundamental concept that bears all the practical thinking of
men, all their exact science, all their speculation and all their religion. He has
shown that there are problems enough for philosophy even after the time of the
great systems is past. But to see his significance rightly, one must study him in
his chief work (Treatise). In his Essays\textsuperscript{80}) the investigation is
essentially limited to the concept of cause, and the radical manner in which Hume
pursues ``the uniting principle'' under all its forms (in mathematical knowledge,
in the concept of the self), as well as the method he follows, in particular the
thoroughgoing application of the law of expansion, one would not suspect from the
abridged and subdued exposition. --- The uniting principle, whose
incomprehensibility he shows, he nevertheless acknowledges as operative: partly in
assuming that we have ideas not only of single things but also of their relations
(time and space, resemblance and difference, e.g.), partly by assuming the
association of ideas as a fact, partly, finally, by the weight he lays on the
imagination's tendency to spread and extend itself, a tendency which is, of
course, a tendency in consciousness to preserve its identity with itself in spite
of all differences. All this certainly stands in a wonderful contrast to the
absolute, ``substantial'' difference between the single sensations and ideas which
is the presupposition from which Hume starts, --- a presupposition that marks the
limit of his thinking. One could with greater right find the difference between
the elements of our consciousness incomprehensible: for to comprehend is to
connect, to find connection!
% --- p. 440 ---
\opage{440}

\subsection*{c.\quad Ethics}

The second part of Hume's chief work treats of the feelings. It is of great
significance for the history of psychology; but we can treat it here as an
introduction to the ethics, which forms the third part of the work, and which Hume
later rendered in shorter form in his \textit{Enquiry concerning the Principles of
Morals} (1751). --- In his conception of the psychological nature of the feelings
he has Spinoza as his predecessor and was probably influenced by him. His
exposition is richer and fuller than Spinoza's. The conception of both rests on
the significance that the ideas and their mutual connection have for the
development of feeling. Hume shows how one feeling connects itself with another
feeling by means of the connection between the ideas of their objects. His
statements waver on the question whether a direct association between feelings
takes place: for the most part he does ascribe to the feelings --- as to the
ideas --- a tendency to reproduce other feelings (II, 1, 4, cf.
\textit{Dissertation of the Passions} in Essays), but in other places (II, 2, 8)
he teaches that the connection of feelings does not take place when there is no
connection of ideas. At the root of this wavering there probably lies the
recognition that feeling does not play a wholly passive role in these processes,
something for which Hume, by his doctrine of expansion, which is of such
far-reaching significance in his theory of knowledge, has shown that he has a
clear eye. --- As a psychologist he is significant also for strongly emphasizing
that only feeling, not mere reason, can give rise to acts of will. He points out
that sensations and ideas are easier to establish than drives and tendencies when
these are not violent. Therefore the first germs of the will are easily
overlooked. And just as the will arises only from feeling, not from reason alone,
so too it is only feeling that can check feeling and prevent action (II, 3, 3).
Here too he agrees with Spinoza in a psychological proposition that is often
overlooked but is of great scope. Feeling is an original and immediate state, but
reason manifests itself in reflection and comparison and therefore gains influence
on
% --- p. 441 ---
% scan: „Bevægelse;“ (p. 441)
\opage{441}feeling only in so far as it can test the ideas connected with the feeling.
--- An imperfection in Hume's psychology is that he does not bring out the
connection of feeling with original instincts\textsuperscript{81}). Shaftesbury
saw more clearly here than he. Hume is inclined to regard the instincts as merely
derived (as when in his theory of knowledge he explains the causal instinct by
custom). Here his conception is limited by his empiricism. A related trait shows
itself in his writing of history, for it has been objected against it that he
takes no account of the racial peculiarities of the peoples whose history he
depicts. ---

The psychological investigation of the relation of feeling to reason gains
immediate significance for Hume's ethics by containing the answer to the question
whether morality is grounded on reason or on feeling. Reason merely establishes
relations or facts. But a moral judgment arises only when a feeling is set in
motion by the idea of an action, after all the relations and facts that concern
this action have been brought forward. Only because our feeling is set in motion
do we call something good or evil. The moral qualities (good and evil) therefore
have validity only from the standpoint of feeling beings --- just as the sense
qualities have validity only from the standpoint of sentient
beings\textsuperscript{82}). But this does not rob these qualities of their
significance: in practice we apply moral valuations just as confidently as the
sensible qualities, although none of them expresses objective and eternal
relations. (See, besides Treatise III, 1, 1, especially the essay \textit{The
Sceptic} in ``Essays''). Hume (who on this point again agrees with Spinoza) stands
here in sharp opposition to the moral philosophers who would derive morality from
reason alone and regarded the moral principles as eternal truths, a standpoint that
even after Locke's time was maintained by Clarke and Price (just as Cudworth had
maintained it against Hobbes). In this connection Hume makes the following remark
(Treatise III, 1, 1 in fine): ``In every ethical system that I have hitherto met
with, I have always remarked that the author for a time reasons in the usual way,
asserting the existence of a God or bringing forward
% --- p. 442 ---
\opage{442}observations on human affairs; --- but suddenly I am surprised to find that
instead of the usual words \textit{is} and\textit{ is not} I meet with
propositions in which \textit{ought} or \textit{ought not} forms the connection.
It is an imperceptible transition; but it is of the very greatest significance.
For this \textit{ought} or \textit{ought not} expresses a new relation, which ought
to have been explained, and it ought to have been shown how this new relation can
be derived from other relations that are altogether different from it. But authors
are not usually so careful.'' Hume finds in this transition, and in the
impossibility of explaining it by the establishing and comparing reason alone, a
sign that it is feeling that is at work here (Treatise III, 1, 2).

The next question is what feeling it is, then, from which morality springs. In all
actions and qualities that are the object of moral approval one common trait is
found again: that they are, mediately or immediately, to the good and utility of
the agent himself or of others. This trait wrings from us --- independently of all
upbringing and authority --- approval, esteem, perhaps admiration. And since we
approve actions that do not benefit ourselves, the feeling that lies at the root of
the approval cannot be of a selfish nature. He who pronounces moral judgments
leaves his private standpoint and takes up a standpoint that is common to him and
others. If we were to value merely according to selfish interests, we could arrive
at no common valuation. Even if the recognition of justice as a virtue were
originally owed to each single individual's need of peace and security, the
interest in the general order of law can nevertheless be explained only by
sympathy with that which preserves human life as a whole; the motive that
originally makes something a virtue need not be the one that can later lie at the
root of the valuation. It is, then, sympathy or fellow-feeling (fellow feling) that
is the real foundation of morality. Even the valuation of the virtues that bring
advantage only to the agent himself (such as prudence in one's own affairs) is best
understood from sympathy. --- Sympathy itself Hume explains in accordance with the
``fundamental proposition'' of his theory of knowledge: it arises in that the sight
or
% --- p. 443 ---
\opage{443}the lively idea of the expressions or the causes of others' joy or pain calls forth
in us a lively feeling of joy or pain, that is, in that a mere idea (idea) passes
over into \textit{sensation} (impression) by virtue of its connection with a
lively sensation.

Hume's ethics bears the stamp of a clear head and a warm heart. One must not seek
in it light on deeply penetrating ethical crises and oppositions. He does not even
take up Hutcheson's interesting attempt to derive the feeling of duty from
sympathy. The inner and outer resistance that the working out of an ethical
character may meet he does not stop to consider. But he has a full and clear
conviction of the foundation of morality in human nature, and he indicates the
fruitful distinction between
% scan: „meilem“ (p. 443)
the first motive for the development of a quality of character or an institution
and the motive from which the later valuation springs. If he has often been called
a skeptic, this designation at any rate does not fit him as
an ethicist. In a special investigation \textit{(A Dialogue,} in Essays) he
discusses the objections that could be raised from the mutually conflicting moral
ideas, manners and customs of different peoples and times. One could, he says,
just as well find a difficulty in the fact that the Rhine flows to the north and
the Rhone to the south! Both rivers flow in opposite directions because of one and
the same law, the law of gravity, owing to the different slope of the ground.
Because men come to different results under different circumstances, they may very
well start from the same principle. Everything that men have called good or evil
has been something that was regarded as directly or indirectly useful or harmful.
The differences, then, do not shake the principle. ---

As an economist Hume is Adam Smith's most important predecessor. In his economic
essays he asserts the importance of awakening the acquisitive drive. By compulsion
no one is brought to work ably. New wants must arise in order that the desire for
advancement may come into being. If no other wants show themselves than those that
can be satisfied by the meagerest yield of the soil, the soil
% --- p. 444 ---
\opage{444}will not be cultivated as well as possible. Agriculture flourishes only in
interaction with commerce and industry. And thereby is also formed the middle
class, which is the surest and best support of public freedom. --- Into the
problem of the relation of the acquisitive drive to sympathy Hume enters as little
as his friend and successor Adam Smith. They seem to have assumed a harmony between
the effects of the two motives.

\subsection*{d.\quad Philosophy of Religion}

Hume's most important merit with regard to the religious problem rests on his
clear distinction between the question of the possibility of grounding religion by
the way of reason and the question of the actual origin of religion in human
nature, a distinction that has analogies both in his theory of knowledge and in his
ethics. The first question is discussed in his ``Dialogues on Natural Religion,''
the second in ``Natural History of Religion.''

As regards the latter, the historical question, Hume seeks to show that it is not
a need of understanding that leads to faith in divine beings. On the contrary,
what for the thinker is a great stumbling block, the misfortunes and disorders in
nature, is for the common man precisely a motive to believe. Faith is called forth
by feelings that arise in the course of life: fear and hope, suspense and
uncertainty, anxiety before the enigmatic. With this cooperates the general
tendency to conceive all other beings in likeness to oneself. History seems to show
that polytheism is the original religion. And this agrees with the natural course
of development: consciousness rises gradually from lower to higher stages, and as,
in the strong agitation into which it is put, partly by fear, partly by
enthusiasm, it exalts its object for the imagination and thinks it ever more
perfect and nobler, it at last arrives at the idea of a single, infinite and
incomprehensible God. There takes place here, in the domain of religious feeling, a
process of idealization similar to the one that according to Hume lies at the root
of the formation of the mathematical principles and of the principle of causality.
The transition from polytheism to monotheism cannot be explained by merely
% --- p. 445 ---
\opage{445}intellectual motives; but by the way of feeling men have reached the same result
to which rational consideration leads: that there can be only one God. Now when
this exalted stage has been reached, a reaction easily takes place, as history
shows. A need is felt of intermediate beings between the one, infinite, purely
spiritual God and the world. Between these two opposite poles --- the exalted,
non-intuitable and the limited, intuitable conception of God --- a constant
oscillation takes place. --- On closer investigation Hume finds conflicting
tendencies and qualities in the nature of religion. Sublimity and coarseness, faith
and doubt, purity and immorality, grandeur and horror are mixed together in a
remarkable manner. There is so much that is enigmatic in religion, and so much
conflict between the different religions, that Hume prefers to withdraw into the
calm, though obscure, regions of philosophy. --- In his essay ``on miracles'' Hume
discusses in particular the question of the supernatural. His main thought here is
that no testimony is sufficient to ground a miracle unless the falsehood of the
testimony itself would be a greater miracle than that which it concerns. But he
maintains that there is no miracle that has been able to be supported by such
testimony. ---

As regards the question of the truth of religion, there is difficulty in finding
out Hume's real standpoint, since he has discussed this question in dialogue form.
He puts forward three different standpoints. Demea represents a mystical orthodoxy,
which builds partly on a priori grounds of reason, partly on postulates of feeling.
Cleanthes represents a rationalist deism, which relies especially on the
purposiveness in nature. Philo appears partly as a skeptic, partly as a
naturalist. That Demea does not represent Hume's own standpoint there can be no
doubt. Cleanthes he has, by his own account, made the hero of the dialogues; but it
is evident, and he also says so in letters (Burton I p. 332. Letters to Strahan p.
330), that Philo's considerations interest him himself the most, although he lets
him give up his standpoint at the end. Philo's standpoint undoubtedly comes closest
to Hume's own. The main thoughts that Philo urges are the following. ---
% --- p. 446 ---
% scan: „den.“ (p. 446)
\opage{446}Who could blame us if, faced with such great and difficult questions, we declared
that we knew nothing? We go here, after all, far beyond the domain of experience,
and system stands against system! Against Cleanthes's inference from the order and
purposiveness in nature to the existence of God, Philo makes a series of
objections. 1) Why seek the cause of the order and purposiveness outside the
world? There could, after all, be forces at work in the world itself that bring
order and harmony with them --- perhaps through many upheavals and provisional
adaptations. Nothing, after all, can subsist entirely without order and connection.
And just as skill develops through attempts and trials, different systems of the
world could have succeeded one another until the present system could arise as the
one that offered the most favorable conditions for continued subsistence. 2)
Experience shows us mind and thought as finite, limited phenomena. With what right
does one explain the whole of the world from a part of it? Thought itself --- and
so also the plan of the world that is ascribed to God --- needs explanation just as
much as everything else in the world, and when we stop at it as the last cause, is
that not because of the satisfaction of finding our own nature again behind things,
just as we are inclined to see our own shapes in the clouds? 3) Is there any
special problem to pose concerning the world as a whole? When we have explained the
coming into being of the single parts or phenomena, it is no special problem how
all these parts together have come into being. It is only an arbitrary act of
consciousness that makes us conceive them as one collected whole. 4) From the world
as experience shows it, with all its imperfection, pain and want, one can at any
rate not infer a \textit{perfect} cause. In one of his Essays \textit{(Of a
Particular Providence and of a Future State)} Hume poses the following dilemma: if
there is justice in the world, there is no reason to seek another world, and if
there is no justice in the world, this world cannot be assumed to have been created
by God. --- Philo, however, will not deny the existence of God. He only warns
against conceiving God in too close an analogy with man. He declares that the
difference between the theist and
% --- p. 447 ---
\opage{447}the atheist, the dogmatist and the skeptic is in the end only a verbal difference:
the theist after all admits that the divine mind is extremely different from the
human, the atheist that the principle which rules in the world nevertheless has a
certain analogy with the human mind; the dogmatist admits that there are great
difficulties connected with his assumption, and the skeptic that in spite of the
difficulties we cannot remain in mere doubt. What matters is that no prejudices
weaken the natural love of mankind and the feeling of justice. ---

Hume's treatment of the religious problem marks a great advance. His dialogues
stand as a lasting monument beside Kant's critique of theology in ``Kritik der
reinen Vernunft.'' An answer to these two works has not really been given. As
regards the psychological side of religion, there is surely need of a greater
depth and fullness than Hume's sober mind could give; with respect to the
historical understanding of religion, too, his material was insufficient. But in
both respects he has indicated thoughts that later inquiry has carried further. His
sound method of experience gives his investigations lasting value. He is the most
important predecessor of modern positivism.

\section*{6.\quad Hume's Successors and Critics in England}

Hume marks the high point of the development of philosophical thinking in England
in the eighteenth century. From the points of view that Bacon and Hobbes already,
but above all Locke, had urged, the last consequences that could be drawn had been
reached; the line of thought once struck up had been carried to its end through a
labor in which one eminent thinker took hold where the other let go. Only from
wholly new points of view, which did not lie within the horizon of the English
school but had to come --- and did come --- from another side, could the
development be carried further. This does not exclude that even after Hume's time,
before philosophical work in England comes to a long pause that lasts into our
century, there appears a series of
% --- p. 448 ---
% scan: „Smith.“ (p. 448)
\opage{448}significant works, partly supplementing and continuing Hume's work, partly opposing
and reacting against it.

a. Hume's work in the domain of ethics and economics was continued in an
independent manner by his friend \textsc{Adam Smith}, who was born at Kirkaldy in
Scotland in 1723 and studied at Glasgow, where he heard Hutcheson with admiration,
and later at Oxford. To judge from the manner in which he later speaks of the
English universities in his famous economic work, the conditions at Oxford did not
appeal to him. According to what Lord \textsc{Brougham} relates (\textit{Lives of
Philosophers of the Time of George III} p. 179), he is said to have experienced the
narrow-mindedness of the university authorities himself: his copy of Hume's
``Treatise,'' which he was studying, was confiscated, and he received a reprimand
for reading such a work! A trait characteristic of the manner in which Hume and his
works were regarded in the chief seat of English learning, where, moreover, Hobbes
and Locke had earlier been treated in a similar manner. For a number of years (from
1751) Adam Smith worked as professor at Glasgow. His course on moral philosophy
consisted of four parts: natural theology, ethics, natural law (after Montesquieu's
historical method) and economics. Only the second and the fourth part of this course
did he succeed in working out into independent works. As regards the natural
theology, we know only what can be inferred from his writings. In religious
respects he was more conservative than Hume; perhaps he stood to Hume as Cleanthes
to Philo (in Hume's Dialogues). Of the third part of Smith's course we can form a
notion from a set of lecture notes which was found a few years ago, and which,
besides the doctrine of right, contains an exposition of economics (the first draft
of the Wealth of Nations). (See \textit{Lectures on Justice, Police, Revenue and
Arms.} Delivered in the University of Glasgow by \textit{Adam Smith.} Reported by a
student 1763. Edited by Edwin Cannon. Oxford 1896). He lays weight here on showing
the development of public and private law under the influence of economic and
industrial progress. His ethical and economic works too bear witness to his zeal to
use the study of real,
% --- p. 449 ---
\opage{449}historical conditions to illuminate questions of principle, and it is one-sided
when \textsc{Buckle}, in his otherwise instructive characterization of Adam Smith
in his English history of civilization, describes his method as purely deductive.
Interesting essays from his hand on the origin of language and on the history of
astronomy also bear witness to his historical sense. --- A short time after the
