publication of \textit{Theory of Moral Sentiments} (1759) he withdrew from his
university work and thereafter stayed some years in France, where in particular his
acquaintance with Quesnay, Turgot and Necker became of significance for his
economic studies. After his return home he lived for ten years in his native town
Kirkaldy and here worked out the work that above all has made him famous, since the
beginning of scientific economics is usually dated from it: \textit{Inquiry into the
Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations} (1776). (Danish translation by DRÆBY
under the title: Undersøgelse om Nationalvelstands Natur og Aarsag. Copenhagen
1779---80). In his last years Smith held a post in the customs service at
Edinburgh, where he died in 1790.

The two works on which Adam Smith's significance as a thinker rests stand in a
peculiar contrast to each other, since in his economic work he takes the
acquisitive drive, in his ethical work sympathy, as his basis. \textsc{Buckle} has
held that it was Smith's intention to set up two tendencies of human nature, each
in its abstract form, in order thereby to make a clear, deductive line of thought
possible. Against this stands the fact that the contrast between the two works is
indeed characteristic but not absolute, and that Smith's method is not purely
deductive. It remains an unsolved question how Smith himself conceived the
relation between his two works; a psychological and historical investigation of
the relation between the two tendencies in human nature he has not given. But he
has often been done an injustice by forgetting that he is the author not only of
the work on national wealth but also of the work on the moral feelings.

As an ethicist Smith lays great weight on the fact that the moral feeling arises
only when man lives in society with
% --- p. 450 ---
\opage{450}others. There then manifests itself in him a natural instinct to imitate the looks
and conduct of others, to put himself in their place, to feel and suffer with
them. It is an involuntary propensity which the most selfish man cannot entirely
subdue. This instinctive sympathy acquires its more definite character through the
arising of ideas of the causes and the effects of the mood and action of others. We
approve the feelings of others when we are conscious that under the same
circumstances we would have feelings of the same kind and strength. The feeling
must stand in a certain proportion to the cause that has called it forth if we are
to be able to sympathize with it. But when the other's feeling becomes the motive
for actions that bring about effects for a third person, we put ourselves in his
place too, and we can then sympathize with the action only when its effect stands
in a suitable proportion to the original cause of the motive. In the case of
benevolence and love of mankind we sympathize with both giver and receiver. In the
case of gratitude and revenge, sympathy with the agent ceases when the effect stands
out of proportion to the original cause. In opposition to Hume, Smith maintains
that regard to the utility of the qualities of character that are approved is not
the original ground of approval. It is a factor that comes in later and lends
support; but it is an ``after thought,'' a thought that comes after the
involuntary judgment which springs from one's putting oneself in the place of the
agent and of the one affected.

Our first ethical judgments concern others, whose conduct we follow as impartial
spectators. But we soon learn that others also observe and judge our conduct, and
we
then learn to judge it ourselves --- provisionally from the standpoint of the
others. Only by living together with others do we thus learn to hold up a constant
mirror to our own actions. We divide ourselves into two persons, an agent and a
spectator. And this inner spectator does not now go on being a mere representative
of the outer censors: we quite naturally ascribe to him a greater knowledge of us
than other men can have, and involuntarily equip him as an inner judge, to whose
superior wisdom and justice we appeal from the short-sighted and unjust judgments
of those around us,
% --- p. 451 ---
\opage{451}just as, on the other hand, remorse can arise when our will is in conflict with
what the inner, impartial spectator can approve, even if no man knows of what stirs
within us. --- The internalization and idealization of the moral feeling that
Smith here depicts he could have explained better if he had made use of Hume's
doctrine of the imagination's tendency to hold fast and to heighten its objects.
But Smith's exposition, although some intermediate links are missing, is of
extraordinary interest and marks a significant step toward the understanding of
the development of the moral feeling. He rejects the assumption of a peculiar,
original moral sense that would be complete once and for all, just as he rejects
the explanation of all morality from egoism or from pure reason. The great
significance of reason for moral development he does not deny; but the single
moral experiences from which the general moral propositions of reason can be
derived we come, in his view, to make by means of that involuntary and instinctive
sympathizing with the state and conduct of others. Only in generalization, not in
the original observations of good and evil, does reason cooperate. On this point
he agrees with Hutcheson, whom he praises as the one who first saw clearly here.
--- In the last part of the ``Theory of Moral Sentiments'' Smith gives an excellent
criticism of earlier theories, which is still of great interest.

What has given occasion to assume not merely a certain contrast but even a
contradiction between Smith's two chief works is the great weight that he lays, in
the work on national wealth, on the individual's acquisitive drive being allowed to
move freely. The source of all wealth is thrift and industriousness, and these
develop only where the acquisitive drive is not cowed. ``The drive that moves us to
thrift,'' says Smith (Om Nationalvelstand. Danish trans. I, p. 469), ``is a desire
to better our condition, a desire which is indeed in general calm and without
passion, but which nevertheless follows us from the cradle to the grave.'' How the
individual can satisfy this drive in the best way, he himself finds out best of
all. The state is not to intervene here
% --- p. 452 ---
\opage{452}with commands or prohibitions. Let everyone buy where it is cheapest, whether at
home or abroad. Supply and demand will regulate everything in the best way. Under
the influence of the relation between supply and demand, the division of labor,
which is the condition of all development of culture, has come into being, since
both the individual himself and the others found their account in his limiting his
labor to what, according to his abilities, he could do best. This shows itself both
in small things and in great. What is prudence in every private household can
surely not be folly in a great kingdom! (Om Nationalvelstand, II, p. 42---44). The
task of the government is only to protect against external violence, to maintain
internal peace, and to establish and maintain such public works and institutions as
private persons cannot find it to their advantage to provide. By this last
determination (Om Nationalvelstand, II, p. 333) Smith thus does acknowledge that
there are tasks that cannot be accomplished through the interaction between the
single individuals, each led by the acquisitive drive. In general it should be well
noted that Smith himself, in composing his economic work, stands at the standpoint
of the ``impartial spectator.'' The ethical standpoint is so far from being pushed
aside that it is precisely what lies at the basis. When he praises the system of
liberty, it is because it is ``generous and liberal'' (Om Nationalvelstand, II, p.
320). When he demands free movement for the individual according to his own
calculation of what brings advantage, it is because he believes that the
individual can ``be led by an invisible hand to promote an end that he has not set
himself.'' ``By seeking his own advantage he often promotes that of society in a
more effective way than if he really sets out to promote it'' (II, 42). --- Let the
word ``often'' be noted. People have (as KNIES: Die politische Oeconomie vom
geschichtlichen Standpuncte. Neue Aufl. Braunschweig 1883 p. 226 has shown) quoted
this statement of Smith's with the omission of ``often,'' and thereby his doctrine
has come to stand as a doctrine of the absolute harmony of egoistic interests,
which makes all sympathy and ethical action superfluous, indeed harmful. Thereby
% --- p. 453 ---
\opage{453}there would certainly arise an insuperable contradiction between Smith's two
works.

In order to understand Smith's significance as an economist rightly, one must
remember what a burden lay upon the whole of civic life, even in the most advanced
countries. He pleads the cause of the industrious and thrifty citizens against
ignorant, extravagant and arrogant governments, relying on the experience that
England, in spite of war and extravagance, has advanced in prosperity owing to the
good husbandry of private persons and their uninterrupted efforts to better their
own condition (Om Nationalvelstand I, p. 476). He demands recognition for the labor
that is done in obscurity and in small things, and which is nevertheless what
produces the main sum of the nation's strength. And he rejoices at the rise of
wages in the immediately preceding period, because the laborers make up the
greatest part of society. --- Smith's point of view, then, is of an ethical-social
nature in his economic work too, even if he lays greater weight on production than
on distribution, and even if he assumes too trustfully that the points of view of
private economy can without further ado be transferred to those of national
economy. In his lectures he treated, under the common name of doctrine of right
(jurisprudence), justice, economy (police), public revenue and preparations for
war (Lectures p. 3). The third and the fourth part of his course belonged closely
together. ---

b. When \textsc{David Hartley} is named among Hume's successors, it is not because
he was particularly influenced by Hume, but because he has illuminated from a new
side questions with which Hume occupied himself. He himself declares that he
received the decisive influences from Newton and Locke. He was born near York in
1705. His study was at first theology, but he gave it up, since he could not
subscribe to the 39 Articles, and went over to medicine. Early on he conceived the
plan of writing a work in which he would work his religious, philosophical and
physiological ideas together. The main thought of this work he got from an attempt
by a less well-known author, \textsc{Gay}, to explain all higher feelings as having
arisen by association of the lower ones. Gay asserted that Hutcheson, with the
concept of ``sympathy,''
% --- p. 454 ---
\opage{454}had introduced an occult cause (vis occulta), and then attempted to explain
compassion as having arisen by the association of ideas. Hartley's work
\textit{(Observations on Man, his Frame, his Duty and his Expectations)} appeared in
1749. Hartley worked as a physician and is described as a noble and humane man (†
1757). --- His significance in the history of psychology rests on his attempt to
explain all higher mental phenomena by the association of quite simple sensations
and ideas. All thinking and feeling, even the most ideal and exalted, is supposed
to have developed in this way, and the power that our will can have over ideas,
feelings and actions is likewise owed to association. The laws of association are,
according to Hartley, the highest mental laws of nature. Hartley does indeed define
association as a connection between ideas that are given simultaneously or in
immediate succession
(Observations. London 1792. I, p. 66); but he nevertheless also describes the
phenomenon that is now called association by resemblance (I, p. 291 f.), just as
he also speaks of an immediate relation of coincidence (coincidence) between ideas,
such as appears in the intuitive certainty that is the foundation of all other
certainty. --- On the physiological side there corresponds to association a
connection between different vibrations in the minute parts of the brain, such
vibrations uniting by repetition into one vibration. On the mutual relation between
ideas and vibrations Hartley will set up no theory; in their ultimate source they
are closely connected, but he will join neither spiritualism nor materialism. ---
By virtue of the law of association mental life develops step by step from lower
to higher forms. Thus complex ideas are formed that can make up so complete a unity
that the single ideas from which they have arisen are no longer noticed, just as a
compound matter can have other qualities than its elements. Further, activities
that were at first carried out with full consciousness will by repetition become
unconscious, or become what Hartley calls secondarily automatic activities.
Finally, the life and strength with which certain ideas appear can later pass over
to other ideas that are connected with them by
% --- p. 455 ---
\opage{455}association. It is on these three derived laws that all mental development rests,
in particular the process by which the primitive, sensuous feelings and expressions
of will give place to more ideal expressions. In this way egoism can be worn down
and abolished, and a disinterested and universal compassion can develop. On the
other hand, envy and cruelty can also develop according to these same laws.

In manner of exposition and in conception Hartley recalls Spinoza. He has carried
association psychology a significant step further by setting up the theory of
psychical combinations with other qualities than those of the elements, and by
bringing out the phenomenon of the displacement of motives. And like Spinoza,
Hartley is convinced that by virtue of such psychological laws a transition between
the greatest mental opposites is possible: self-preservation can pass over into
mystical self-forgetfulness through association and displacement of motives. The
love of God arises, it is true, says Hartley, partly from egoistic grounds; but
since God is the cause of all things, infinitely many associations will gather in
the idea of him, and this idea can thereby become so predominant that the ideas of
everything else, ourselves included, vanish in relation to it. --- A peculiar
union of mysticism and realism is found in Hartley as well as in Spinoza; but he
lacks the latter's superior clarity.

Hartley's theory was not much heeded until the natural scientist and theologian
\textsc{Joseph Priestley} (1733---1804), famous for his discovery of oxygen, for his
struggle against the doctrine of the Trinity and for his enthusiasm for the French
Revolution, came forward toward the end of the century as its adherent and
popularized it. Priestley himself describes his general standpoint as materialism,
but he assumes --- following a theory set up by the Jesuit \textsc{Boscovich} ---
that the essence of matter consists in force, attractive or repulsive force, and
that the atoms are to be conceived as points of force, since this is in reality all
that we know of them. Solidity is only a sensible quality, which does not express
the essence of matter but only an effect of it on the senses. If this is how
matters stand,
% --- p. 456 ---
\opage{456}there is (as Priestley develops in his \textit{Disquisitions on Matter and
Spirit.} London 1777) no reason to assume two different substances; it may very
well be the same substance to which both the physical and the psychical forces
belong. Priestley is convinced that this conception agrees far better with the
original Christian conception than the spiritualistic one, which was taken over
from heathen philosophy.

Another eminent natural scientist also took up Hartley's theory, the physician
\textsc{Erasmus Darwin} (1731---1802), grandfather of Charles Darwin, a man who had
talents as a natural scientist, as a poet and as a philosopher. In his chief work
\textit{Zoonomia or the Laws of Organic Life} (London 1794 ff., German trans. by J.
D. Brandis. Hannover 1795 ff.) he explains the origin of the instincts by
experience and association under the influence of the impulse of self-preservation
and of adaptation to circumstances. He goes further than Hartley by laying weight
(see especially the remarkable 39th chapter of the 1st part) on the fact that the
qualities acquired in this way can be inherited; thereby the psychological doctrine
of association is developed into a biological doctrine of evolution, which has a
good deal in common with the hypothesis that Lamarck set up some years later
concerning the evolution of species, and which, like that hypothesis, is a
forerunner of the great hypothesis to which the name Darwin was to be attached.

c. Of quite another kind is the position that \textsc{Thomas Reid} and his
successors took up toward the philosophy of Locke and Hume. In opposition to the
persevering analysis that was the strength and greatness of the classical English
school, but that threatened to undermine the foundation of the secure, popular
conception of the world no less than that of the speculative and the religious
one, appeal is made here to the judgments of naive consciousness and of sound
human understanding, and philosophy is given the task of giving an account of what
lies in these judgments and of systematizing their content. Tired of analysis and
wary of it, one turns toward the immediate and demands its right. It is a reaction
which, in various forms, makes itself felt in the course of the century, as herald
of the thoroughgoing reaction against the whole tendency of the eighteenth century
that came at the beginning of the new
% --- p. 457 ---
\opage{457}century, --- a reaction that in many respects was fruitful and justified in
asserting the right of historical facts, but that at the same time was often highly
uncritical when it came to determining what in the single case was given as a real
fact. The Scottish school (so the tendency founded by Reid was called, which can
already be traced in Hutcheson and Smith, but which with Reid became dominant at the
Scottish universities) has deserved well of the human sciences by its sound,
descriptive psychology; but it suffers from the fault of confusing description with
explanation and of putting theoretical points of view into the description.
---Thomas Reid (1710---1796), the most important man of this tendency, was first a
clergyman, later professor at Aberdeen and at Glasgow. In his most considerable
work \textit{(Inquiry into the Human Mind on the Principles of Common Sense.} 1764)
he relates that he had been an adherent of Locke's and Berkeley's philosophy, but
that Hume's ``Treatise'' had shown him that it leads to dangerous consequences: to
the overthrow of all science, all religion, all virtue, all sound human
understanding (common sense)! He therefore subjected the whole tendency to a
criticism and discovered that it conflicted with experience; it is also on the
ground of experience that he wants to combat it. He wants to follow the method of
Bacon and Newton. --- What Reid presented in shorter form in his ``Inquiry'' he
later carried out, with application to the special psychological domains, in his
larger works: \textit{Essays on the Intellectual Powers of Mind} (1785) and
\textit{Essays on the Active Powers of Mind} (1788).

At the root of all our knowledge there lie, according to Reid, certain instinctive
presuppositions that no doubt can shake. They are the same that irresistibly guide
the assumptions and conduct of all men in the ordinary circumstances of life. They
are the principles of sound human understanding (principles of common sense), which
are older than all philosophy and therefore have greater authority than it. They
are components of our original constitution, which stems from the hand of God.

To these original principles belong first and foremost the belief in a material
external world and in the existence of the soul.
% --- p. 458 ---
\opage{458}Every sensation that I receive awakens by a natural prompting (natural suggestion)
the assumption of an external object of the sensation, as well as of a self that
has the sensation. Between sense perception and memory on the one hand and
imagination on the other there is not merely a difference of degree but a
qualitative difference, which cannot be explained further. The belief in what is
perceived or remembered is a simple act of consciousness that cannot be described
further, any more than it can be explained by association. It is certainly a
remarkable trait of our nature that we face here: by a kind of natural magic (by a
natural kind of magic) the sensation calls forth for our consciousness something
that we have never experienced, and which we nevertheless at once apprehend and
believe in! --- Related to perception by the senses (perception, which besides
sensation also includes that natural suggestion) is the causal instinct, a natural
but inexplicable propensity to believe that the connections between phenomena that
we have observed in the past will also continue in the future. On this principle
all science is built, as well as all superstition; it may be called the inductive
principle. All sound human understanding acknowledges it, and we would put in the
madhouse anyone who did not acknowledge it. --- In the practical domain we have the
moral sense as an example of an original principle. ``Just as we,'' says Reid
(Active Powers, p. 238), ``by the external senses obtain not only the original
ideas of the various qualities of bodies, but also the original judgments that this
body has this quality, that one another quality, so by our moral faculty we obtain
both the original ideas of good and evil in action, of worth and unworthiness, and
the original judgments that this conduct is good, that one evil, this character
worthy, that one unworthy.'' The testimony of nature makes itself known through the
moral sense in a manner similar to that in which it does through the external
senses. The first principles, in the theoretical as in the practical domain, have
an intuitive certainty (intuitive evidence) that cannot be resisted when the mind
is mature, calm and unprejudiced. ---

Reid and the Scottish school mark a reaction against Hume similar to the one that
the Cambridge school in its time marked against
% --- p. 459 ---
\opage{459}Hobbes. It is characteristic that this reaction now itself appeals, not to eternal
truths, but to the testimony of experience. It believes, to be sure, and this is
its great misunderstanding, that it can read eternal truths straight off from the
simplest observations, and it assumes as many original instincts as there are
enigmatic phenomena. A very easy manner of explanation! Moreover, it extends
intuition far beyond what Descartes, Locke and Leibniz had called by that name: the
simple apprehension of likeness or difference. The most complicated acts of
consciousness are declared intuitive and are thereby regarded as justified. This
tendency was bound to lead to a halt in all inquiry and analysis. And it does not
really touch Hume at all, since he had himself declared that in practice he
embraced ``the principles of sound human understanding,'' but only found
extraordinarily great difficulties in grounding them. Reid's justification against
Hume lay in the fact that Hume overlooked the original and constant connection
between the sensations, which is just as much a fact as the single sensations each
by itself. But he cut himself off from a scientific refutation of Hume by his
appeal to Common Sense, which was an abandonment of all philosophy.

After Hume there came in general a long ebb in the history of English philosophy,
which is quite understandable. As already remarked, the line of thought that had
been entered upon in the English school was now carried through; the line had run
out. And on the other hand, partly the political, partly the religious interest now
pressed forward into the front rank: politics again laid claim to eminent powers,
after people had long lived on the after-effects of the Revolution of 1688, and the
religious feeling, which latitudinarianism and deism had damped down, now flared up
in Methodism, a strong and deep popular reaction against the preceding rationalist
period. But these conditions cannot be illuminated more closely here. An excellent
characterization of them is given by \textsc{Leslie Stephen} in his work:
\textit{History of English Thought in the 18th Century.}

\begin{center}---\end{center}


% --- p. 460 ---
\hhchapter{Fifth Book}\opage{460}

\begin{center}\textsc{The Philosophy of the French Enlightenment and Rousseau.}\end{center}

\bigskip

\section*{General Characterization}

Through David Hume philosophical thinking had been brought to a point where
further progress was possible only by the adoption of entirely new points of view. The answer
to the question Hume posed in the ``Treatise'' of 1739 came only with Kant's
``Kritik der reinen Vernunft'' of 1781. The interval lying between these two
great works is significant in the history of thought above all because
philosophical thinking was made into a weapon of battle. The peaceful labor of thought
was interrupted when the call to arms was sounded, the call to a spiritual battle against
the traditions and institutions of the past, which the impatient human spirit now
called to account. In the domain of material nature the new science had
led to a magnificent result, magnificent not only in its wide horizon but
also in its exact grounding. In the domain of mind one had, in the principle set up by
the English school, that the validity of every idea must be
proved by its origin in experience, a means of testing all ideas
for which respect was demanded. And in the social and political domain
one had, in the fundamental propositions of natural law that had been formulated on the basis of the struggles of the sixteenth
and seventeenth centuries, a standard which one boldly set up against the
principle of authority that had hitherto upheld the social order. Had one then finished
the
% --- p. 461 ---
\opage{461}investigation, so that one now had the right to proceed to practical application? One
certainly had no other right than that which life's own mighty need gives. The
solitary thinkers would hardly have concluded; but their time was over for the present.
Some years before Hume went over to France in order to work out his chief work there in
greater solitude, two young Frenchmen had visited England, not, however, in
order to ripen their thoughts in solitude, but on the contrary to open mind and senses to the
English life of the spirit and to take into themselves the living movement that the healthy English
soil had fostered. Voltaire and Montesquieu brought home from England, as from
an entirely foreign world, entirely new notions of philosophy, religion, church and
state. It was a traveler's acquaintance that they made with English thoughts and conditions, and
their purpose was not to keep what they had learned to themselves in order to develop it further,
but to let it go out into the world in as free, light and simple a form as possible
so as to awaken, provoke and transform. And for this
purpose one used not only the method and results of English inquiry: the whole
development of thought from the Renaissance through the great systems to the
philosophy of experience supplied means for waging the battle. Behind the violent and
radical criticism that was now applied to everything handed down lay a dogmatism that
believed itself essentially complete as regards conception of the world and view of life. One
had to stand firm oneself in order to be able to overthrow what existed. When one wants to settle accounts all at
once, as in an instant, with everything that history has produced in the
spiritual and the social domain, one must have great confidence in one's own
standpoint. But so it goes everywhere in history: when the day of judgment is to be held,
there is no time to wait until all the premises are in order.
Christianity and the Church did not wait to destroy ancient culture until
they could give a full grounding of their superiority. Ancient culture was
shattered. Spiritual currents are ruthless. When a spiritual need has long been
dammed up, there comes a point where it breaks through, however much of
value it may destroy on its way. That the Church had not really
overcome ancient culture became clear in the Renaissance. And that the
% --- p. 462 ---
\opage{462}philosophical and political revolution at the end of the eighteenth century did not
really overcome the old order of things became clear in the Romantic
reaction at the beginning of the nineteenth century. In reality one had not
finished philosophizing in the chambers when one began to philosophize, first in
the salons and then in the streets and lanes. But the philosophical incompleteness of the
weapons of thought with which one took the field takes nothing away from the significance
of the historical mission of the men who opened the battle. Where
life is at stake, one must use the weapons one has. And although one does not always get
the impression of intellectual superiority from the French philosophers of the middle of
the eighteenth century, indeed, although by their eager striving to
simplify and popularize they often came to make the great small and to
profane what was truly exalted, there nevertheless lay, even behind their dogmatism,
their shortsightedness and their pettiness, a flaming faith in light, in
progress, in humanity, for whose sake many sins may be forgiven
them. What Voltaire exclaims in his memorial words on a young, early departed,
noble thinker (Vauvenargues): ``Whence did you get that mighty flight in this
century of pettiness?'' --- this can serve as the motto of the whole
movement. Particularly when one treats the French philosophy of the eighteenth century
not in a history of literature and culture but in a history of philosophy, the
strong subjective undercurrent must not be forgotten; what the surface current presents may
often seem petty and insignificant. Yet --- there was one in whose deeply stirred
mind the subjective undercurrent became all but sole master, so that he gained the power
to plead, in a way it had never been done before, the cause of immediate
feeling, of individual mood, the cause of nature against culture and
reflection, the cause of the great, simple, human values of life against every kind of
aristocracy and refinement. In Jean Jacques Rousseau a new element of life, a
new side of the life of the spirit, came forward and set itself in opposition both to the new
critical wisdom and to the old order of things. Deeper down than any
relation of authority and any critical reflection reaches, he pointed out living
human feeling as that
% --- p. 463 ---
\opage{463}whose assent no tradition and no thinking can do without, and as that
which is the foundation of all value of life. The significance of feeling had never before been asserted
in this simplicity and purity, however often mystical tendencies
had pleaded its cause. Not so much by his ideas and theories as by his very
personality (despite all its frailties) does Rousseau mark a great
turning point in philosophical respect: with him the problem of valuation becomes decisive,
whereas the problem of existence and the problem of knowledge had hitherto all but
dominated everything. And in turning both against the old order of things
and against the new criticism, he proves that there is something that neither of them allows
to come into its own. Of the philosophers of the eighteenth century he is the one who most
decidedly points toward the future and has its seeds within him. He is, after all, also the thinker of
his time who takes the greatest interest in the child.

That the radical consequences --- both in their negative and in their positive form
--- were drawn precisely in France and not in England itself, where the decisive
principles had come forward, had its good historical reason. \textsc{Taine} has
shown in a brilliant way (in ``L'ancien régime'') how the French language
and the French spirit had been polished at court, in the salons and in
classical art into organs for simple and clear ideas, for a thinking
that wants to discuss the greatest problems with the least possible preparation, and that does not
strive to extend its domain but only wants to work through what has been
won. Yet the classical spirit and the polished language would not be a
sufficient explanation. They explain only the form, not the content and the
direction. The real cause of the practical consequences of
English philosophy being drawn in France and not in England is to be sought in this, that the
old order of things on French soil stood far more rigid and stubborn
against the new than in England, and that at the same time it was far more hollow and
rotten than on English soil. The English social order had absorbed the
new forces and was able to use them as awakeners to continued development.
In France the old social order was
% --- p. 464 ---
\opage{464}so consistently carried through that it either had to crush all criticism or be crushed by it.

\section*{1.\quad Voltaire and Montesquieu}

In his \textit{Lettres sur les} \textit{Anglais,} which were written 1728---1730
and appeared in Amsterdam in 1735 (after they had already appeared in 1732 in an English
translation in London), \textsc{Voltaire} (b. 1694, d. 1778) set before
his countrymen a new natural science, a new philosophy and a new social order. He
set Locke and Newton against Descartes, Socinians, Quakers and other
Dissenters against Catholics, parliamentary constitution against absolute monarchy. Even where he did not
directly allude to a comparison but meant to remain purely
descriptive, the meaning was clear enough, and no one mistook it; the book was
burned. Many Frenchmen, moreover, regarded Voltaire (as later
Montesquieu) as a bad patriot because he admired the English character.
But those letters mark a turning point in the history of culture: the grafting of English
thoughts onto the Continent. Later Voltaire published a good popular exposition of
Newton's physical theories (\textit{Eléments de la philosophie de Newton,} mis à
la portée de tout le monde. 1738), which contributed much to winning the new
natural philosophy diffusion and victory. Voltaire has significance not as an independent
thinker but as the great abridger and popularizer. The title of one of his
most important philosophical writings: \textit{Dictionnaire philosophique portatif}
(1764) is characteristic in this respect. The views are ready-made; it is
only a matter of shaping them so that they can easily be carried about. He praises
Locke because he has given us the history of the soul, whereas so many ``raisonneurs''
had previously given us its romance, and because he derives everything that is in
the understanding from sensation. But he is not disinclined to go further and
regard all memory and thinking as merely continued and altered sensation; when
Condillac (who will be discussed later) had set up this doctrine,
Voltaire subscribed to what ``the great philosopher'' had said (Art. Sensation in Dict.
phil.).
% --- p. 465 ---
\opage{465}But if everything comes from the senses, what can we then know of the eternal and
infinite and of the nature of the soul? As good as nothing. Peculiar to Voltaire
--- in contrast both to Condillac and to Locke --- is the skeptical
result he extracts from the proposition that everything in our consciousness comes from
sensation. Officially, to be sure, he assures us, with an irony there is no
mistaking, that revelation has taught us about the soul as a spiritual substance. But
his conviction of ``the limits of the human mind'' (see Art. ``Bornes de l'esprit
humain'' in Dict. phil.) finds expression in the words with which he ends the article on
the soul in his philosophical Dictionnaire: ``O man, God has given you
understanding to guide you to what is right, not to penetrate into the essence of created
things!''

That everything comes from sensation, Voltaire nevertheless has no doubt. But
sensation itself? Locke had said, to Voltaire's great delight, that there was surely nothing to
prevent God from having given matter the capacity to sense. That the communication
of this capacity could, according to Locke, take place only by a \textit{miraculous} act,
Voltaire did not notice; he seizes on the remark and uses it as a weapon against the
spiritualists. Here, however, there is also expressed an endeavor in his system
to trace everything back to two principles: God and matter. He then had no
use for minds as intermediate links. But what, then, is matter? Well, that we
really know just as little as we know what soul is. Yet Voltaire does not doubt
its existence, and he even ascribes to it an eternal existence: ``No
fundamental proposition,'' he says (Art. ``Matière'' in Dict. phil.), ``is more generally
recognized than this, that \textit{nothing comes from nothing.} The opposite is surely
inconceivable.'' ``Perhaps my reason is led astray by this old and generally
accepted idea [that nothing comes from nothing]; but it tells me that matter must
be eternal, since it exists; if it existed yesterday, it has existed
before. I see no probability that it should have begun to come into being,
nor any cause why it should have come into being at one moment
rather than at another.'' (Le philosophe ignorant. 1766. p. 32). --- And he
seeks to show that religion does not suffer from this assumption of an eternal matter
that is ordered
% --- p. 466 ---
% print: „»le bien commun)“, no closing « (p. 466) (misprint)
\opage{466}in a purposive manner by the Deity. ``To be sure, we now happily know
by means of faith that God drew matter forth out of nothing, but'' etc. The assumption of an eternal matter
also presents various difficulties, it is true, and
one must not flatter oneself that one can overcome them; philosophy cannot give
an explanation of everything. But the belief in an eternal matter ordered by God
presents no moral misgivings: we have the same obligations whether we have an
ordered or a created chaos under our feet! --- Voltaire maintains the slight significance
of speculative and dogmatic decisions in practical and moral respect. It
is perhaps on this point that he has his greatest significance in philosophical
respect, and here too his skepticism proves to be different from mere
blasé indifference. Of the practical earnestness Voltaire could show when it mattered,
his appearance as defender of the oppressed and the
innocently condemned bears sufficient witness. He showed in deed that even if it was irony or
malice when he so often referred to what revelation taught, his
whole will was in it when he set practice in opposition to speculation.
Toward the belief in immortality his attitude seems to have been that it was
necessary for upholding morality in humanity. (Le bien commun de
tous les hommes demande qu'on croye l'âme immortelle. Lettres sur les Anglais.
XIII). For the belief in God he nevertheless sought (although here too he relied on ``le bien
commun'')\textsuperscript{83}) to give a grounding, relying (like
Newton) on the purposive order in nature. He defends the
assumption of final causes (causes finales); only one must keep to the
effects that are invariably the same at all times and everywhere, not to
the special and derived effects. Voltaire emphasizes sharply and with teasing
relish the dark sides of the world, and he combats the optimism which, with its gaze
turned on the great laws that govern the whole, overlooks or disdains the
sufferings and misfortunes that this general order of things may bring to the
individual beings. The destruction of Lisbon by earthquake gave him, as is well known, special
occasion for mockery of the best of all possible worlds. He strikes Leibniz's
optimistic system right in the
% --- p. 467 ---
\opage{467}heart when he has his Candide (as he was being flogged at an auto-da-fé that
was held as a festival of atonement after the destruction of Lisbon!) say to himself: ``If
this is the best world, what then are the others like?'' Voltaire
was indignant that Leibniz, Shaftesbury and, after them, Pope in verse declared that
all was good, and that one could not demand that God should change his eternal
laws for the sake of so wretched a being as man. ``One must surely admit,'' he says
(Art. ``Tout est bien'' in Dict. phil.), ``that this miserable being has the right
to cry out in all humility and --- all the while it cries out --- to seek to
understand why those eternal laws have not come into being for the sake of each single
individual!'' For Voltaire himself the answer to this last question was given
in his doctrine of God and matter, which was perhaps motivated precisely by reflection
on the evils that the lawful order of nature brings to individual beings. He believes
in a good God, but the suffering in the world is to him a testimony that this God
is not almighty but constantly has a resistance to overcome, and this resistance
he finds in eternal matter. The moral side of religion was to him the
essential thing. ``After our holy religion,'' he says, beginning with his
usual official bow (Art. ``Religion'' in Dict. phil.), ``which is quite certainly
the only good religion, which, pray, is then the least bad? Should
it not be the simplest? Should it not be the one that teaches much morality and
very few dogmas? the one that strives to make men just without
making them absurd?'' Everything in religion that goes beyond the worship of a highest
being he declares to be superstition. The thought of simplicity, which the
thinkers of the Renaissance applied to the understanding of the natural world, is now applied by
the thinkers of the Enlightenment to the supernatural. Over against positive religion
Voltaire's criticism keeps to the fully finished dogmas; about their origin,
about their springing from the human need of feeling, about the symbolic value they
might have as expressions of dearly bought mental experiences, he does not ask.
He amuses himself over the capriciously arranged islands in the ocean of religion and does not
consider that what thus appears scattered, contradictory
% --- p. 468 ---
% print: „honnètes“ (p. 468) (misprint)
\opage{468}and irregular on the surface may have its subterranean connection and perhaps
be the effect of volcanic forces in the depths. The unconscious or half-conscious,
the involuntary and spontaneous, the obscure movement of feeling he did not understand.
He saw everything as in clear daylight. Dawn and twilight were for him signs of
ambiguity, insanity, stupidity, absurdity or knavery. Against
such things he operates with the alternative that one must be either mad or a
knave (fou --- fripon) to believe them. What produces superstition is
the madness and stupidity of fanaticism, which can rise to insolence (insolente
imbécillité); but then the knaves come and make use of the follies for their own
ends\textsuperscript{84}). An elementary psychology of religion that undeniably
satisfies the principle of simplicity and is in a high degree ``portable''!

Voltaire was convinced that the moment had come when accounts could be settled
with all prejudices. It was not his meaning that all prejudices were bad: there
are those that are approved by reason (Art. ``Préjugés'' in Dict. phil.). But of
the sufficiency of reason, of what was then called reason, he had
no doubt. He rejoiced (in his letters to d'Alembert) that ``the age of
reason'' had come. On every point he saw the power of the Church give way, in the
consciousness of the educated as in the state. To be sure --- there was a limit to
the spread of enlightenment: ``the rabble,'' ``the cobblers and the servant girls'' could
not have a share in it. But Voltaire consoles himself: ``It is not a question of
preventing our lackeys from going to Mass or to sermon; it is a question of
tearing the fathers of families from the tyranny of the impostors and of spreading the spirit
of tolerance''\textsuperscript{85}). He had no inkling that the lackeys too would soon begin
to philosophize; he had, after all, himself made philosophy ``portable.'' Beyond the dualism
between ``decent people'' (honnêtes gens) and ``the rabble'' (canaille) he did not see. Here
again he kept to the salient oppositions without being able to find
the connection, often hidden, to be sure. Yet it must not be forgotten that the gulf
between the different parts of the people was, just in his time, as great and
yawning as we no longer know it,
% --- p. 469 ---
\opage{469}and that Voltaire saw the solution in the care of an enlightened absolutism for the great multitude. ---

\textsc{Montesquieu} (1689---1755) had essential qualities that Voltaire
lacked, especially that of thinking in such a way that things were seen in their definite
connection and not torn loose for the sake of the point. He rises high above the usual line of thought of the eighteenth
century by the idea that underlies his
chief work \textit{(Esprit des lois} 1748): that institutions and laws
are not arbitrary productions but presuppose definite natural conditions
in order to subsist and to act. He emphasizes the connection of the laws with climate,
manners and way of life, with religion and with the whole national character. ``The laws must,''
he says (Esprit des lois, I, 3), ``be so peculiar to the people for
which they are written that it is a pure accident when the laws of one people can
suit another.'' The more recent historical school has in Montesquieu one of its
most important predecessors. --- But it is nevertheless his endeavor to reach
general ideas through the study of historical conditions. On several points
he is able, precisely by carrying through his historical method, to prove the
sophistry in the defense that had been made of traditional abuses, as in the
investigation of personal and political freedom. And his admiration for
antiquity and for England leads him to give ideal descriptions that became
so many condemnations of the existing conditions in France. As after
his return home he transformed his garden into an English park, so his
political ideas too acquired an English coloring. And here it should be well noted that in his
famous description of the English constitution (Esprit des lois, XI, 6) he
builds rather on his study of Locke's book ``Of Civil Government'' than on more deeply
searching investigations of English constitutional life itself in its connection
with the history and manners of the nation. Locke's treatise was, after all, a theoretical defense
of the Revolution; it was not to describe what historically existed, but
to ground the right to develop what historically existed further in a definite
direction. Montesquieu now goes even further than Locke, in that he develops, far more sharply
than the latter, the theory of the threefold division of power into legislative, judicial and
executive.
% --- p. 470 ---
% scan: „on“ (p. 470)
\opage{470}He did not see that this threefold division in fact fitted only tolerably a definite
stage of English history, precisely the time just after the Revolution.
Earlier the king had had a greater share in the legislative power, and later
Parliament has acquired an ever greater share of the executive
power\textsuperscript{86}). And yet Montesquieu regarded this system as
primordially Germanic: ``this beautiful system was invented in the woods.'' He knew it only
as fully finished and as an external form of the people's political life; the whole
foundation of self-government in the smaller circles that supports the English
parliamentary constitution he did not see. Just as Voltaire took the results of Locke and Newton
without taking along the spirit, the investigator's mind, out of which they had grown,
so Montesquieu took the form of the English constitution and systematized
it without taking along the firm subsoil that in reality supported it. Seen from
this side he is akin to the French philosophy of the Enlightenment and belongs
in its ranks. One notices in him too ``the classical spirit.''
\textsc{Albert Sorel} says aptly of him: ``He does not follow governments in
their historical development . . . He presents them as fixed,
complete, definitive . . . No chronology and no perspective; everything lies
in the same plane. It is the unity of time, place and action, transferred from the theater
to legislation.'' --- It was not, however, Montesquieu's meaning that
English forms could be transferred to France without further ado. His thoughts went
rather in the direction of a revival of the old French monarchy with an enlightened
official class and especially with an independent judiciary. But the spirit of his time put
tendencies into his work that conflicted with his own historical method; and especially
in his readers this spirit was so powerful that his work acquired a revolutionary
significance he had not intended.

\section*{2.\quad Condillac and Helvétius}

The epistemological and psychological foundation of the French
philosophy of the Enlightenment was worked out by \textsc{Condillac} (1715 ---
% --- p. 471 ---
% print: „Traitè“ (p. 471) (misprint)
\opage{471}1780), a peaceful thinker who, after early becoming a clergyman and after
having directed the education of an Italian prince, spent his last years in an
abbey whose revenues he enjoyed. In his chief work \textit{(Traité des
sensations,} 1754) he carries
% scan: „gennemforer“ (p. 471; the e-book's reading, set by sense: scan-artefact rule)
through, with clarity and breadth and more by a deductive than by an inductive path, the proposition
that everything in our consciousness, not merely --- as Locke had taught --- all content,
but also all activities and forms, was merely the transformation of simple passive
sensations (sensations transformées). The single sense-sensation appears
as a purely passive change in the soul. When this change is so strong that
other sensations are excluded, attention arises. When we have two
sensations simultaneously, we are said to compare and judge. Memory is only the after-effect
of a sensation. Abstracting is the separating out of a sensation from other
sensations. The condition of all comparison, judging, remembering and abstraction
is attention, which is thus the fundamental phenomenon in knowledge. With its help
we are able to conceive distinctly and separately what at first appears in a
chaotic conception of the whole. On such separate and thereby distinct conception of
what first appears in chaotic mixture --- thus on analysis --- rests
all knowledge. When with the help of language we form signs for each of the elements
that analysis presents, we can, by combining these signs and by
substituting for one another signs that mean the same, develop a logical
calculus, a scientific language of complete clarity and exactness. Only
with the help of a language of signs can analysis be completed; but analysis in turn reacts
on the language of signs, and all science is really a system of signs whose
meanings and mutual relations are completely clear. (Cf. Condillac's
work: \textit{La langue des calculs.} Introduction). Languages are analytical
methods, since man involuntarily analyzes, led by his need to
make gestures or break out in cries in the face of what arouses his attention.
Later, then, conversely, science, exact analysis, becomes the same as a
perfect language.

Condillac's theory of knowledge is an attempt to derive everything
% --- p. 472 ---
% scan: „forst“ (p. 472)
\opage{472}from experience in such a way that experience itself is conceived as completely passive,
but also in such a way that the possibility of a science on the
ground of experience is nevertheless shown. By its clarity and simplicity his doctrine won great
adherence, and it displaced Cartesianism in the official institutions of learning.
It became the philosophy that was taught at the end of the century, during the Revolution
and the Empire, until new tendencies asserted themselves. In
``Traité des sensations'' Condillac employs the mode of exposition of imagining a statue
whose senses awaken to activity one at a time; there arises one sensation at a
time, and it is investigated how the life of consciousness successively develops
and, under the influence of the impressions, acquires its various faculties (attention,
comparison, memory etc.), which thus are not original dispositions in
nature. Characteristic especially is his attempt to describe attention as
a purely passive state and his description of comparison as simultaneous
attention to two impressions. --- The successive arising of the various
faculties takes place under the influence of man's drives and wants. Drive
and want arise through comparison of feelings of pleasure and pain, which are a
special kind of sensation. Instead of equipping us with a multitude of original
faculties, the Author of nature has given us the feeling of pleasure and pain to arouse
attention and thereby set analysis going, first in its simpler,
then in its higher forms.

Although Condillac's doctrine, seen from one essential side, stands in sharp opposition to
the Cartesian, it has points of contact with it not only in the weight
laid on the analytical method but also in the spiritualistic point of view
that ultimately underlies it. For Condillac maintains decidedly that sensation is
different from motion, and that the latter can therefore only be the occasional cause of
the arising of sensation in a soul different from the body. To be sure, we know (concedes
Condillac, like Locke) the substance of the soul just as little as that of the body. But the capacity
to compare (according to Condillac: to have two sensations at once)
nevertheless presupposes a \textit{simple} substance as the bearer of the sensations. (See especially
\textit{De l'art de raisonner}
% --- p. 473 ---
\opage{473}I, 3 and\textit{ Discours préliminaire du cours d'étude,} Art. 4). Moreover,
Condillac's doctrine concerns only our sensations; these are only the ``statue's'' own states;
if the first sensation is the smell of a rose, then the soul is only the smell of a rose and nothing
else. Extension, which according to Condillac derives only from the sense of touch,
originally not at all from the sense of sight, is only the most constant element in our
sensations, that around which the others gather; but has one therefore the right to
regard it as the expression of absolute reality? Extension is a sensation
that is aroused in us, as are other sensations, by something whose essence we do not
know. (Traité des sensations, I, 1; II, 11; IV, 5). Condillac betrays
the influence of Berkeley (``Barclai,'' as he calls him), in any case of
his ``Theory of Vision,'' whereas it is doubtful whether he knew his
chief writings; his doctrine of abstraction does not suggest it.

We have already heard Voltaire refer to Condillac as the great philosopher. As
can happen in wartime, the results of the peaceful thinker were used as
weapons of war. His doctrine of the transformation of sensation was taken up and his
spiritualism left aside. In direct cooperation with the free tendency and with growing
sympathy for it, on the other hand, \textsc{Helvétius} (1715 --- 1771) wrote his
works \textit{(De l'esprit,} 1758. --- \textit{De l'homme,} 1773 --- 74).
The book De l'esprit was treated as one of the most impious books that have ever
been written. It was condemned by the Archbishop of Paris, by the Pope and by the
Parlement of Paris, and Helvétius, who had expected literary fame from the
book, had to stay abroad for a time, among other places for a while with
Frederick the Great, who set great store by his unselfish character and after
his death wrote to d'Alembert: ``With infinite pain I have learned of his
passing. His character seemed to me admirable. Perhaps one might have
wished that he had consulted his heart rather than his mind.'' Helvétius was
a liberal-minded, mild-thinking and philanthropic man, who used the wealth he
had won as a farmer-general in the service of literature and of charity.
With great sorrow and indignation he followed (as one sees especially from the
% --- p. 474 ---
\opage{474}posthumous work De l'homme) the degradation and inner dissolution of his fatherland.
His writings are borne by the conviction of the unhappy consequences of
individuals being excluded from active participation in public life. Characters
then do not get sufficiently great motives and objects for action. Both
literature and morality suffer from it. For both talent and virtue, ``mind'' (esprit)
and ``rectitude'' (probité), are conditioned and developed by the form of government and by
the education that is in turn determined by the form of government. This is the great, serious
chief thought that lies behind Helvétius's works. He continues Condillac's
theory of the development of all faculties through experience and external influence. Even
love of ourselves is acquired: for we cannot feel love without
first having felt pleasure and pain. Susceptibility to pleasure and pain is thus the
only gift that nature originally gave us. It arouses and sharpens
attention, and it determines our action. What comes to fix our
attention depends on education --- this word taken in the very widest
sense, so that it designates everything in our surroundings and circumstances that has
an influence on our development, down to the smallest trifles. Since
Helvétius takes the word education in this wide sense, he can maintain that two
human beings never receive quite the same education (De l'esprit, III, 1). Endowment
he assumes to be the same in all --- but the conditions for its development are
different. All differences of character Helvétius derives from education, and
since this in turn is bound up with public conditions and the form of government, one sees
how his theory motivates his sorrow and indignation at the internal
conditions of France.

The corruption of manners consists not so much in the excesses to which individuals
give themselves up as in the general split between individual and
social interest. It is hypocrisy when the moralists attack the private vices of individual
persons instead of directing their attack against public
abuses and against oppression from above. Morality, the art of legislation and pedagogy
are not three different endeavors but rest on the same principle, namely
the principle of public utility, the utility for the greatest possible number of
human beings who
% --- p. 475 ---
\opage{475}are united into a state. (De l'esprit, II, 17). What is recognized as good
and as virtue (probité) depends on interest. Most people recognize as good only
what agrees with their own limited interest. Only comparatively few
possess --- especially under bad social and political conditions --- the enlightened
pride, the spiritual nobility, to be able to pass their moral judgments from
consideration of public utility without being led astray by the narrow interests of themselves or of their
nearest surroundings. Such nobility of soul by no means presupposes
the giving up of love of oneself. Such a giving up is an impossibility. But
it presupposes that one's own interest is inseparably bound up with the
public interest, especially through the need of power and honor. ``No one,'' says Helvétius
(De l'homme, V, 1), ``has ever contributed to the public good to his own detriment.
The citizen who heroically risks his life to cover himself with honor, to deserve
public esteem and to free his fatherland from slavery, follows the feeling that
for him is bound up with the greatest pleasure.... The good man thus obeys only
a noble interest.'' --- It remains unclear in Helvétius whether the need of power
and honor does not become of a somewhat different nature when it is inseparably
tied to consideration for ``bien public'' than when it stands isolated and therefore
seeks satisfaction by any means whatever. The expression nobility of soul
(noblesse d'âme) seems to presuppose that the feeling must after all undergo a certain
metamorphosis when --- through an excellent education --- one has succeeded in
connecting the representation of justice so closely with the representation of power and
happiness that they fuse completely into one single representation (Note 33 to De
l'homme, Sect. 4). What is lacking in Helvétius (as in Condillac) is a
closer investigation of the way in which the feelings are altered under the
influence of representations and combinations of representations, investigations
that Spinoza, Hume and Hartley had begun.

A chief proposition in Helvétius is that we can recognize only ideas and
traits of character that agree with our own ideas and feelings. Mind (esprit
--- in the sense of capacity for new combinations of thought) we recognize only where the
new
% --- p. 476 ---
\opage{476}combinations of thought we encounter have a certain analogy with our own thoughts and agree with
our own interests. And what holds for the recognition of mind holds
also for the recognition of rectitude (probité). Without our own interest
being set in motion, we recognize nothing. But --- says Helvétius --- there are two
kinds of interest: ``There are men who are animated by a noble and enlightened
pride, and who keep their mind in a suspended state (état de suspension)
that gives new truths free entry. To their number belong some philosophical
minds and some young people who have not yet formed opinions so fixed
that they blush at changing them . . . . There are other men --- and
they are the majority --- who are animated by a less noble vanity. These can
recognize only such ideas as agree with their own, and that justify
the high opinion they all have of the ability of their minds'' (De l'esprit, II, 3.
Cf. De l'homme, IV, 6: ``Genius has as its protector and eulogist youth and
a few enlightened and upright men''). --- Yet besides
ignoble vanity Helvétius also names indolence as a hindrance to the recognition of
new ideas and new virtues. Both hindrances can, in his view, only
be overcome by a sufficiently strong feeling tearing man out of his
torpor and his limitation. --- Both of Helvétius's works (whose tendency has often
been misunderstood) investigate the conditions for the arising of great minds and
significant traits of character and for their recognition once
they have arisen, and the fundamental condition for him is the close connection of the
individual life with the public one. His theories of the original
uniformity of individuals, of self-interest as the fundamental thing and of the omnipotence of education
all serve to impress one and the same fundamental thought.

Helvétius's religious standpoint is the deistic, with strong emphasis on
the unknowability of the Deity. He polemicizes against theological morality because it
merely attacks private vices and not the source of evil in public conditions,
and against the priesthood because its interest cannot go together with that of the whole
people. There runs, in general, a polemical undercurrent
% --- p. 477 ---
\opage{477}through his books --- even stronger in De l'homme than in De l'esprit, which Diderot
nevertheless was not wrong to call a club-blow against all prejudices.

\section*{3.\quad La Mettrie, Diderot and Holbach}

Already in Voltaire, natural science and its results play an essential role alongside the philosophy of experience.
But the influence of natural science comes forward first and foremost in a group of French philosophers who,
it is true, avail themselves of Locke's doctrine that everything in consciousness comes from sensation,
but whose chief thoughts nevertheless concern material nature. Their philosophy
is to be a simple consequence of natural science. They take up again Hobbes's
materialistic tendency, but in such a way that they attempt to proceed inductively,
whereas Hobbes proceeded predominantly deductively. Their appearance is a testimony
that the method and results of natural science demanded, with increasing energy,
influence on the view of life and the world-view. And the more impossible it was for them to
explain to themselves or to justify the ecclesiastical dogmas and the existing
institutions on the basis of the fundamental propositions of natural science, which stood for them
as eternal truths, the more these dogmas and institutions had to appear to them
as purely arbitrary, as sprung from stupidity, fanaticism or fraud.
Voltaire's dilemma, madness or knavery, was here carried out to its
ultimate consequences and was hurled forth with a defiance and a passionateness that
Voltaire, who does not leave the atmosphere of the court and the salons, had not known.
And yet these writers too are clear that their ideas cannot find
entry with the great multitude.

The revolutionary tendency in these writers, their conviction that one
must reform heaven before one can reform earth, does not prevent their
works from having philosophical value. They combat the spiritualistic doctrine, not, it is true,
with arguments of principle going beyond what Hobbes and Spinoza had
provided, but with a greater wealth of
% --- p. 478 ---
% print: „La Metrie“ (p. 478) (misprint)
\opage{478}particular experiences. They rely not merely, like the thinkers of the seventeenth century, on the general principles of
mechanical natural science, but also on the results that
the science of organic life had produced in the last century.
Particularly to be named here is \textsc{La Mettrie} (1709---1751), the real founder of
French materialism in the eighteenth century. He was an army physician,
but lost his post partly because of his attacks on the prevailing medicine,
partly because of his \textit{Histoire naturelle de l'âme} (1745), where he
first expressed his views. For a time he now stayed in Holland; but
from here he had to flee because of the offense his \textit{L'homme
machine} (1748) aroused. He now found a refuge with Frederick the Great,
whose reader he became and with whom he seemed to have stood on a very
intimate footing. He died suddenly in 1751; evil tongues (especially Voltaire's) said
that his death was due to his gourmandise, but there seems to have been a
case of poisoning. La Mettrie's character appeals by its boldness and a certain
amiable lightheartedness. But he could also be impudent instead of bold, and
frivolous instead of lighthearted, and his philosophical reputation has had to suffer from
these unfortunate sides of his character, which are undeniably noticeable in his
writings too. In recent times especially \textsc{Albert Lange} in his ``Geschichte
des Materialismus'' and \textsc{Dubois Reymond} in his ingenious lecture on La
Mettrie have paved the way for a juster judgment.

La Mettrie wants to build on experience and observation and to apply the comparative
method. As a natural scientist he is a pupil of the famous physician \textsc{Boerhaave},
who applied the fundamental propositions of the Cartesian natural philosophy to the study of
organic life. The title of La Mettrie's well-known work ``L'homme machine'' points
back to Descartes and could very well have come from the older
Cartesian school, if only the soul-substance that now and then touches
the pineal gland is pushed out. By the path of the comparative method La Mettrie seeks to
show that there is only a difference of degree between animal and man, and that there is therefore
no ground for assuming that in man an entirely new kind of
substance is added. In order not to misunderstand La
% --- p. 479 ---
\opage{479}Mettrie one must note that he has not only written an ``L'homme machine''
but also a work with the title: \textit{Les animaux plus que machines.} His
task is, by bringing out the kinship in structure and mode of operation between the
human and the animal organism, to prove that what acts in them
is not different in essence. And he goes still further. He emphasizes not only
the similarities between man and animal but also the similarities between man and
plant (\textit{L'homme plante).} And from the whole graded series that the study of the
structure and functions of living beings shows us, he then draws the conclusion
that if there is mental life above, it cannot be wholly lacking below. The capacity for
sensation he extends to everything living, indeed to everything material: everything in the universe
is full of souls, and he refers here (Les animaux plus que machines. Oeuvres
philos. Berlin 1755. II, p. 82) to Leibniz's slumbering monads. --- This
graded series does not, for La Mettrie, consist of forms finished once and for all.
He assumes --- following partly the naturalist Maillet, whom Voltaire mocked,
partly Epicurus and Lucretius --- a development from lower to higher
forms. As it seems \textit{(Système d' Épicure} § 13. 32---33, 39), he
assumed eternal organic germs from which, in interaction with the external
conditions, the various forms of life have emerged with progressive
perfection. The driving force is need, the wants. A higher
mental life arises only when wants other than the purely
vegetative appear. Plants need no real soul. The transitional forms between
plants and animals have all the more intelligence the more they are obliged to
move in order to find their food. And man stands highest because he has the
most wants (L'homme plante). --- It is an interesting anticipation
of the idea of the struggle for existence that meets us here. And when La Mettrie
sets up the proposition: ``Beings without wants are also without mind,'' it is
not impossible that he thereby gave Helvétius the motive for one of his chief thoughts.

This whole side of La Mettrie's doctrine set forth so far has its interest quite
apart from the materialistic views
% --- p. 480 ---
% scan: „pétitesse“ (p. 480)
\opage{480}that he draws from it. The necessity of the materialistic consequence lies
for him in the fact that we see nothing around us but matter, under constantly changing
forms. He admits, to be sure, that we do not know the real essence of matter. But we
know its properties, namely: extension, motion and sensation. That
sensation is a property of matter he derives from experience, which shows
us that certain organic states are always accompanied by sensation, and he
appeals here particularly to comparative investigation, which shows us
mental life varying with organization. If the soul is not material, i.e.
extended, how then can it be explained that enthusiasm makes us warm, and that
conversely the heat of fever affects the representations? (L'homme machine. Oeuvres, III,
p. 75 f.). All our thoughts must be material modifications. And since
a great multitude of thoughts is in fact contained in our brain, these must be
extraordinarily small in order to be able to ``lodge'' there \textit{(Traité de l'âme,} p.
103: De la petitesse des idées)! --- La Mettrie regards the assumption of a
soul-substance as a useless and self-contradictory hypothesis; he wants to content himself
with what anatomy and physiology teach us --- and he believes that he does so.
He maintains that the question of the truth of materialism must be decided purely
theoretically. The loftiness of our mind does not depend on whether we can use of it the
meaningless word incorporeality, but on its strength, its range, its clarity.
It need not then blush at having been born in the mire. La Mettrie has
rightly seen here that materialism is compatible with practical idealism. His
own moral philosophy, insofar as he has one, is to be sure far from having
this stamp. The standard of justice is the welfare of society, he maintains; but
this standard he really uses only to distinguish between debauchery
(débauche), the feeling of pleasure that brings harm to society, and enjoyment
(volupté), the feeling of pleasure that does not harm others. When he has made this
distinction, he keeps to enjoyment and gives detailed instructions
concerning it \textit{(L'art de jouir),} instructions in which
sentimentality and sensuality work together in a way that arouses disgust.
% --- p. 481 ---
\opage{481}

\textsc{Denis Diderot} (1713---1784) marks at once the high point of
philosophical thinking and of revolutionary spirit in the French literature of the eighteenth century.
He was a warm-hearted man with a great capacity for entering into
subjects and circumstances of the most diverse kind, a French Leibniz, who was able
to find life everywhere and had an eye for peculiarities, but also a need
to find the connection in the whole. The poet in him often strove with
the thinker; many of his thoughts express only the mood of the moment with crude
one-sidedness, without his having sought to find the thread that could connect them with
other thoughts which it was nevertheless also his will to maintain. A cynical delight in
the coarse and the vulgar could alternate in him with the most exalted ideas and
moods. And in his works sentimental effusions stand side by side with
brilliant developments of thought. His literary fate has been strange. By
his contemporaries he was known only as a writer of comedies, as the author of some
writings on the philosophy of nature in a deistic direction and as the editor of the great
Encyclopedia, in which consideration for the censorship forced on him the role of a smuggler
when he wanted to bring out his own ideas. The work on the Encyclopedia took most of his
strength and time. With incredible endurance he carried this giant work
through despite all opposition. His many-sided interest showed itself here in a magnificent
way, since he wrote not only a series of philosophical articles but
also articles on crafts and factories, which rested on thorough
study of his own. This work marks a turning point in the history of culture by bringing
enlightenment and knowledge out into wide circles. But Diderot did not bring out his real views
here. They must be sought in his correspondence (especially in the letters to
Mademoiselle Voland, which depict the radical salons of Paris in a way both
interesting and delightful) and in his dialogues (especially \textit{Conversation with
d'Alembert} and\textit{ d'Alembert's Dream),} which were written in 1769 but only
appeared in 1830 (under the title: Mémoires, correspondances et ouvrages inédits). Only
through these works has one come to know the real Diderot. We keep here
to his purely philosophical ideas, all the more since our literature received a few years
ago a fine and detailed account
% --- p. 482 ---
\opage{482}of Diderot (\textsc{Knud Ipsen}: \textit{Diderot, hans Liv og hans Gerning.}
Copenhagen 1891).

In his first writings Diderot still uses, in the manner of popular theology,
the representation of God to explain what science seemed unable to explain.
But more and more it dawns on him that such an explanation is something quite
other than what science understands by explanation. In his work
\textit{Interprétation de la nature} (1754) he maintains that the true method is
an interplay of observation and thinking, induction and deduction, in which one
goes from experience through reason back to experience. At the same time he here
takes up again, in a more realistic spirit, questions he had already touched on
earlier, namely the great question of how the purposive phenomena of nature are
to be explained. Instead of appealing to a cause outside nature, he states the
possibility that in the chaos of matter there have been from eternity elements
with the capacity for life and consciousness, and that these elements have
gradually been brought together and, through many stages of development, have
become animals and men, the combinations and formations that were not viable
being successively eliminated. Like La Mettrie, Diderot seems to have come to
such ideas partly through reading Lucretius, partly by carrying through
Leibniz's doctrine of continuity in the graded series of the monads and
connecting it with the investigations of contemporary naturalists into the small
organisms. Even if it would be wrong to present Diderot as a mere disciple of
Leibniz\textsuperscript{87}), the influence of the founder of the doctrine of
monads is nevertheless clear in him. He may well have got the idea of motion as
an original property of matter from Toland, and the conception of the state of
rest as a state of force or tension (nisus) (in the little treatise
\textit{Principes philosophiques sur la matière et le mouvement)} may well derive
from others than Leibniz. But when Diderot, in his brilliant dialogue
``Conversation between d'Alembert and Diderot'', not only, like La Mettrie and
several of the naturalists of the time, conceives the capacity for sensation,
sensibility, as a general and essential property of
% --- p. 483 ---
\opage{483}matter, but, in working out this thought more closely, introduces a
distinction between potential and actual sensibility (sensibilité inerte ---
sensibilité active) in analogy with the distinction between ``dead'' and
``living'' force, one will hardly be able to avoid finding an influence of one
of Leibniz's most significant thoughts. For Diderot life and mind are eternal in
nature. They are never mere products or results of purely mechanical processes.
Their germs are present from the first, and the only question is whether the
conditions of development are present. The transition from the potential to the
actual form takes place, after all, every time the organism converts food into
blood and nerves! However much weight is to be laid on the external conditions,
the internal, original conditions are nevertheless for Diderot the essential
thing. To suppose that by adding one, two or three dead particles to a dead
particle one should be able to form a living system out of them, that is surely
a very great absurdity! A rearrangement of particles should be able to produce
consciousness! No, what has life and consciousness has always had them and will
always have them. Why should not the whole of nature be of the same character?
The difference between the lower and the higher levels is then only this: what
exists on the higher levels in concentrated form is on the lower levels spread
out in a multiplicity of elements. (Lettre à Mlle Voland, 15 octobre 1759). It
is this thought that is developed more fully in ``Conversation between
d'Alembert and Diderot'' and in ``d'Alembert's Dream'', two dialogues that both
in form and in content belong among the classic works of philosophy.

d'Alembert makes an objection that is not answered. Even if one ascribes
original sensibility (in potential form) to the particles of matter, how can a
consciousness then arise through the joining together of such particles, a
consciousness that is not to have its seat in any of these particles but to
correspond to the connection among them all? ``Listen, philosopher,'' says
d'Alembert, ``I do see the aggregate, the tissue of small sensitive beings, but a
living being, a whole, a system, a self with consciousness of its unity! That I
do not see, no, that I do not see!'' --- It is thus held fast that here --- in
the
% --- p. 484 ---
% print: „Keden“ (p. 484) (misprint)
\opage{484}arising of consciousness --- there lies a problem that is not solved
by assuming sensibility as a general property of matter. Diderot thus
acknowledges that the monad cannot be explained by mechanical means: it is
impossible to derive the unity that characterizes consciousness by way of
