mechanical composition. --- Diderot does not hold fast to the clear insight that
thus comes to light in him by flashes. Memory and comparison follow for him (as
for Condillac) as a matter of course from the single sensations. Nevertheless
that objection shows how keenly Diderot has thought the question through. He
does not go by the beaten paths of materialism.

The difficulty of explaining the origin of conscious individuality recedes into
the background for Diderot all the more easily because all finite individuals,
by reason of the inner connection among them, make up one great whole: ``Do you
not grant that everything hangs together in nature, and that it is impossible
that there can be a gap in the chain? What do you mean, then, by your
individuals? There are no individuals, none at all. There is only one single
great individual: the whole!'' Thus he goes from the one limit of our knowledge
to the other, from individuality to totality. He stops for a moment in wonder at
what he sees at these limits; but his thought is too much in oscillation for the
problems to have time to settle.

A similar oscillation is felt in Diderot's ethical ideas. He takes a critical
stand toward Helvétius's attempt to explain all feelings as springing from the
striving after one's own advantage, and holds that there is in human nature a
foundation for the recognition of the right and the good, a foundation that can
never wholly disappear in any human being. With great enthusiasm he defends this
assertion in Holbach's salon, and in his earlier writings (especially in an
adaptation of one of Shaftesbury's books) he assumed a special moral sense. From
his letters it is clearly seen that he has come away from this last assumption.
What is called a moral instinct and shows itself in our involuntary actions or
judgments of actions is in reality the result of an infinite number of small
experiences that begin with the very beginning of life.
% --- p. 485 ---
\opage{485}A multitude of different motives make themselves felt here, but none
of them needs to come to our consciousness at the moment we judge or act.
Everything in us stems from experiences (tout est expérimental en nous); but we
need not become conscious of these experiences (Lettres à Mlle Voland,
2. Sept. 1762 and 4. Oct. 1767). Among these unconscious or forgotten
motives there are also some that concern ourselves, especially the need of
honor and of an immortal posthumous fame (on the significance of this last motive
Diderot carries on a lengthy correspondence with the sculptor Falconet). There
are in Diderot hints toward an investigation of the history of the development
of moral feeling, and the interesting thing is that his great enthusiasm for
``the motives of great and noble spirits'' is not weakened by seeing these
motives as fruits of development on the ground of experience. Yet he cannot
carry this conception through, especially not when he stands face to face with
the precepts of current social ethics. It is only in the individual that he
finds a natural development, not in society. Existing society offered rules and
institutions that seemed to him so unreasonable, especially when he compared
them with what was told of the life of savage peoples, that he could only
imagine them as having arisen through superstition and lust for power. Between
the man of nature and civilized man he could find no natural intermediate
links. How could a morality contrary to nature have arisen except through the
cunning and arbitrariness of the rulers? ``Examine all political, civil and
religious institutions closely: unless I am much mistaken, you will find that
the human race has for centuries been bowed under the yoke laid upon it by a
band of scoundrels. Beware of all who would introduce order! To order is always
to make oneself master of others by putting obstacles in their way''.
\textit{(Supplément au voyage de Bourgainville).} The age's lack of capacity to
find historical connection has hardly ever been expressed more clearly. Even
Diderot, with his great capacity for living and feeling his way into different
conditions, could find no other explanation than arbitrariness and lust for
power. The distance between the craving and longing of individuals and what
society offered, between the forces they felt in
% --- p. 486 ---
\opage{486}themselves and the narrow frame the existing order gave them for using
these forces, was too great for understanding to be possible. One could hope for
everything from the future, but one could find nothing in the past --- except
villainies. --- Religious faith in particular stood for Diderot merely as a
source of pernicious effects. It is more than jest when he says in a letter
that he would rather lay the blame on gods than on men. Belief in a God is ---
he maintains --- no harmless thing; it begets evil in two respects. In the first
place it inevitably brings with it a cult, and ceremonies and theological dogmas
soon take the place of natural morality and distort its precepts. In the second
place the great amount of suffering in the world conflicts with the idea of a
good God; one is then forced into every possible absurdity and
self-contradiction in order to gloss over this fact. Reason suffers as morality
suffers (Lettres à Mlle Voland, 20. Oct. 1760 and 6. Oct. 1765).

In Holbach's circle Diderot often discussed such questions. From his letters we
get a vivid picture of this circle. \textsc{Holbach} (1723 --- 1789) was a
German baron who had settled early in Paris, where he gathered about him some of
the most radical writers. He occupied himself with chemistry and (probably under
the influence of Diderot) also came to philosophical studies. There is hardly
any doubt that what Diderot said during his frequent visits to Holbach forms the
foundation of the most important of the latter's works, the work that has been
called the Bible of materialism: \textit{Système de la nature,} which appeared
pseudonymously in 1770. It is also stated in the preface that the author has had
help from several friends. Besides Diderot, the mathematician Lagrange, who was
tutor in Holbach's house, is thought to have collaborated. What Holbach himself
contributed is essentially the systematization. For in the book materialism is
set out as a system, a task that neither La Mettrie nor Diderot, who were spirits
partly more searching, partly more playful, had attempted. Of new thoughts it
really offers none. Its significance lies in the energy and indignation with
which every spiritualist and dualist
% --- p. 487 ---
\opage{487}assumption is pursued as harmful both in a practical and in a
theoretical respect.

Only then --- Holbach argues --- could it be necessary to assume spiritual
causes, a God over against the world, a soul over against the body, if material
nature were dead, passive, incapable of moving itself. But when there is now no
rest in nature, when motion is a fundamental property of matter, what need is
there then of spiritual causes? And besides, they explain nothing, but the
invoking of them is only an expression of our ignorance: one inserts the soul or
God where one cannot find the natural cause. It is in reality a remnant of the
savage's explanation of the phenomena of nature by the intervention of spirits.
Every time science has attempted a natural explanation, theology has fought for
the supernatural explanation. Of the mental we know nothing but that it is a
property attached to the brain. If it is asked how the brain has been able to
acquire this property, the answer runs: ``It is the result of an arrangement or
combination peculiar to the living being, by which a lifeless and senseless
matter ceases to be lifeless and acquires the capacity to sense by being taken
up into the living being. So it goes with milk, bread and wine when they are
taken up into the human organism''. (Système de la nature, I, p. 105). The
comparison we know from Diderot; but Holbach, so far as can be seen, does not
embrace with Diderot the assumption of sensibility as a fundamental property of
matter; he does mention it, but himself keeps to the conception that sensibility
arises through the combination of elements each of which by itself does not
possess that capacity. There is on this point a difference between Holbach and
Diderot that carries further-reaching consequences. For Holbach declares thinking
(consciousness) itself to be a motion, not indeed a motion of masses but a
molecular motion of the same kind as those that underlie fermentation, nutrition
and growth, motions that are not visible but which we infer from their effects.
(I, p. 15). There is much that is enigmatic about this motion, as about other
similar ones; but this enigma does not
% --- p. 488 ---
\opage{488}disappear by assuming a spiritual substance. ``Let us rest content
with the knowledge that the soul is moved and altered by the material causes
that act upon it. That gives us the right to conclude that all its activities
and faculties prove that it is material''. (I, p. 118). All science is then
physics. Ethics itself is only applied physics. In place of the imaginary
virtues and duties that were derived from man's relation to beings outside
nature there now comes a derivation of virtues and duties within man's own
nature. From the laws of nature it follows which paths we must take in order to
attain our purposes. In this way the concept of duty springs from the concept of
nature; for duty means precisely the path we must necessarily take in order to
reach our goal (II, p. 229). Each individual seeks his happiness; but reason,
``which is nothing but natural science applied to the conduct of man within
society'' (II. p. 186), teaches him that he cannot become happy if he will
separate his happiness from that of others, --- such, once and for all, is the
will of destiny (ordre du destin), --- and that on the other hand he who makes
men happy cannot himself be unhappy. In the last chapter of the work, which
contains ``an outline of the natural law'' (Abrégé du code de la nature), these
thoughts are developed in an enthusiastic language in which it has been thought
that Diderot's spirit can be recognized.

The assumption of a twofold kind of beings, spiritual and material, is according
to Holbach the source of the greatest evils for mankind. From the first, men
doubtless came involuntarily into the belief in spirits; they did not know the
causes of things and therefore quite naturally conceived them as personal
beings. But it was the priests' lust for power that first made the belief in
spirits into a system. And in particular these priests saw well what power the
mysterious has over men. Therefore they led them from belief in visible gods
(the sun and other objects of nature) to belief in invisible gods. Spiritualism
is theoretically so groundless that there can be no doubt ``that this system is
the fruit of a very profound and very interested policy on the part of the
theologians'' (I, 97): there was now, after all, an invisible part of man that
could be rewarded or punished in another world! The theologians are the true
manufacturers of gods (fabricateurs de la divinité).
% --- p. 489 ---
\opage{489}``When we will go back to the beginning, we shall always find that
ignorance and fear have created the gods; fancy, enthusiasm and deceit have
adorned or distorted them, weakness worships them, credulity keeps them alive,
custom respects them, and tyranny upholds them in order to profit by the
blindness of men''. In this utterance (II, p. 200) Holbach sums up his
philosophy of religion. He does not distinguish between natural and positive
religion. Once one engages with the representation of gods, a cult becomes
necessary; thereby the priests gain power, natural morality is distorted, and
persecution sets in. At the same time brooding over how evil can be reconciled
with the existence of God will lead to sophistical speculations. --- Holbach's
reasoning here quite recalls Diderot's, who probably had an influence on the
composition of this section. --- In religion as in society one had historical
facts for which one could find no natural basis and to which one at the same
time felt oneself in irreconcilable opposition. One then resorted to the theory
of arbitrariness, which seemed so simple. It is indeed in reality so simple that
it recalls the mythological theories of the childhood of the human race, which
the System of Nature meant precisely to root out. With his cunning priests
Holbach introduces a new kind of mythical beings.

He touches on a great problem: what value have religious representations when
they can no longer, as in the childhood of the human race, be used to fill the
gaps in our knowledge? But an answer to this question the philosophy of the
Enlightenment, because of its imperfect understanding of the forces of religious
life, could not give. If the world of the gods were really merely pasted on or
foisted upon humanity from without, if it had not sprung from the forces and
needs of the human spirit itself, then there exists no real religious problem.
A new generation and a new time were needed to take this question up. --- Only
Rousseau, whose solitude in his own age was brought about by his feeling its
sting before anyone else, tries his strength on it.

But before we go on to portray this remarkable man, it must still be remarked of
the Système de la nature that
% --- p. 490 ---
% scan: „Natureu“ (p. 490)
\opage{490}a certain doubleness makes itself felt in the concept of nature that
it takes as its foundation. On the one hand nature is defined as a being that
exists in itself, is its own cause, as an eternal substance, --- thus with
reminiscences of Spinoza. But on the other hand (and yet often in the same
breath, e.g. II, p. 189) it is granted that we know only the causes that act in
experience, not the first causes. Here the concept of nature is grounded on
experience, there on construction in thought. But what validity has it in either
of these forms? How far can experience lead us? What justification have
constructions in thought? None of these questions are raised. The philosophy of
the Enlightenment does not doubt its own enlightenment; it exists, after all, to
enlighten the others! --- And yet it was on a discussion of such questions
% scan: „Sporgsmaal“ (p. 490; the e-book's reading, set by sense: scan-artefact rule)
that the future of philosophy depended. But the spiritual atmosphere in France
was not calm enough to undertake it. In a distant German university town, on the
other hand, it was already in full swing when the Système de la nature appeared.

\section*{4.\quad Jean-Jacques Rousseau}

Rousseau's great achievement is to have brought to light the deep foundation
from which judgment could be passed between the philosophy of the Enlightenment
and the existing order. He sets up nature and immediate feeling as the
foundation of all valuation and demands of all culture and reflection that would
go beyond this foundation that they prove their justification by developing and
perfecting it; if they hinder and stunt it, they are of evil. For the first time
in modern times he raises \textit{the problem of culture.} From the time of the
Renaissance the work of culture had gone boldly forward in every domain: now a
voice was heard asserting that there was something wrong with the whole
movement. What gave occasion to Rousseau's first philosophical writing was a
prize question set by a French provincial academy, which called for an answer
to the question ``whether the renewal of the sciences and the arts had
contributed to the refinement of manners''. The question struck like lightning
into Rousseau's soul. It was to
% --- p. 491 ---
\opage{491}him, he says, as if he saw a wholly new world, and as if he himself
had become a new man! The new world was the world of personality, of living
feeling, of the inner life. He saw at once the disproportion between this world
on the one side and the existing order together with its critics on the other.
It is indifferent whether it was his thought from the start to answer the
question with No, or whether Diderot's daughter is right when she relates that it
was her father who advised him to answer in the negative. The negative answer is
only a formal paradox, which Rousseau more closely limits and explains in his
correspondence and in his later writings. But the violent collision between the
feeling that in the end is what values everything and the whole brilliant
intellectual and aesthetic development, that could come only in Rousseau; it was
prepared by his personality and by the course of his life.
\textsc{Jean} \textsc{Jacques Rousseau} was born in Geneva on 28 June 1712 of a
fairly well-to-do citizen family. His upbringing was of a kind that favored
fancy and indefinite feeling; there developed early in him what he himself calls
a romantic spirit (esprit romanesque), which led him to crave beyond the present
and to find his greatest enjoyments in the world of possibilities. After a
vagabond youth, which had the same romantic character that his fancy had already
assumed, but which also for a time brought him into circumstances that were
degrading and that had no favorable influence on his way of thinking, he went to
Paris, where he made his way as a teacher, as a private secretary, and later
chiefly as a copyist of music. His copying was for him what the grinding of
lenses was for Spinoza. He had a success with an opera and took the field for
Italian music as against French. Nothing suggested that he would win a
reputation in the world of thought and come to inaugurate wholly new tendencies
in the spiritual life. He had earlier had occasion to acquire a certain general
education, and had also occupied himself with philosophical reading. As a
contributor to the great Encyclopedia he came into the circle of the
``philosophers'' and was regarded as one of them. Through his answer to the
prize question mentioned he was led into the career of an author.
% --- p. 492 ---
\opage{492}His name became known, and as he went on treating the problem that
had so suddenly dawned on him, he came more and more into a polemical position
toward both the two great contending powers of the time, toward those who
attacked as well as toward those who defended the existing order. A new prize
question (``On the Origin of Inequality among Men'') gave him occasion for a
detailed eulogy of the state of nature at the expense of civilization. As he
had before denied that the renewal of the arts and sciences had been a good, so
he now denied that the exchange of the state of nature for social and civilized
life had been a good. The two prize essays mark the negative side of Rousseau's
appearance. A new period in his life began when he could withdraw into rural
solitude. His encyclopedist friends did not understand him. Something was
fermenting in him for which they, with all their criticism and wit, had no
sense. His feeling for nature and his enthusiasm for nature, which sustained him
in the last part of his life amid great bodily sufferings and amid real and
imagined persecutions, were closely bound up with his inclination to live in
immediate feeling. His inner life was so overflowing that he could find words
only with difficulty for what was stirring in him. At any rate he could seldom
find the words at the right moment; therefore he felt ill at ease in the salons.
Against the pointed, the refined, the articulated, in which the culture of the
mind had ended, he set the plain, the broad, the indefinite. He took an interest
in the chaotic beginning of life, in the elements that had not yet formed any
distinctly shaped world. In his moods of freedom in the woods at St. Germain or
Montmorency he thought he was living again the life of primitive man, before
culture had abolished the happy immediacy. The simple and elementary, the great
and simple relations of life, were for him venerable and full of sources of
joy. He understood what was stirring in the rearguard of the army of
civilization, among those whose enlightenment the Encyclopedists gave up as
hopeless and whom Voltaire called ``la canaille''. He found in immediate feeling
what can be common even though the life of representations is ever so
% --- p. 493 ---
\opage{493}differently developed. His own representations were the children of
his feeling. In his ``Confessions'' he says of himself that he felt before he
thought. And in his highest moments, moments such as he had them on his solitary
walks in nature, there was in his mind such a swelling and fullness, such a
resonance of countless indefinite representations, such a craving beyond all
bounds, that no representation, no image could express what he felt. The
independence of feeling he experienced not only through such states, in which it
was as good as sole ruler, but also through its influence on the
representations. His expectation of the future was dark, his memory of the past
bright; the content was determined by the nature of the mood. He has thus learned
from his own experience the psychological truth that feeling is just as original
and independent a side of mental life as knowledge, and that it by no means
merely behaves passively and receptively toward knowledge. The dark side of
Rousseau's character shows itself partly as sentimentality, partly as a
suspiciousness that rose to madness. A sinister example of how feeling can drive
representations forward and form an intricate system of them in order to find
expression and explanation is offered by one of Rousseau's last writings:
\textit{Rousseau juge de Jean Jacques,} in which he describes the systematic
persecution on the part of his former friends of which he believes himself the
object. The same systematic constructing that is here undertaken on the basis
of a morbid feeling is found also in his famous works: his philosophizing is in
reality, as he himself says of his religious faith, only an interpretation of
his feeling (exposition du sentiment).

In three works Rousseau has developed the conception of life that he sets in
opposition to the refinement and corruption of culture. In \textit{La nouvelle
Héloïse} (1761) he portrayed strong and deep love, the beauty and dignity of
marriage and family life, the nobility of resignation, the inwardness of
religious faith, the glory of nature --- subjects that had become foreign to the
time, and that drew from him tones that sounded new in the ears of the time and
marked a great turning point in poetic literature. In \textit{Émile} (1762) he
set forth a system of education that
% --- p. 494 ---
\opage{494}does not subdue nature but makes itself the servant of nature's
development, and he finds occasion besides to develop his religious views. In
\textit{Contrat social} (1762), finally, he sets forth his doctrine of the
social order that ought to take the place of the tyranny under which humanity
groaned.

With these works Rousseau regarded his task as ended. But he was not allowed to
cultivate his life in nature in peace. ``Émile'' was burned in Paris, and a
decree of arrest was issued against Rousseau. Now his unhappy years began. He
fled to Switzerland; but not even there did he find rest; in Geneva and Bern the
governments would not have him, and in Neufchâtel he suffered ill-treatment from
the population on account of his religious opinions. He then accepted Hume's
offer of an asylum in England, but in his morbid state soon conceived suspicion
of his friends there and fled back again to France, where he wandered about from
place to place until a sudden attack of illness ended his life (1778).

To find out Rousseau's real position on the problem of culture, one must not
stop at his paradoxical utterances in the two prize essays, but must connect
them with various utterances in letters and with the content of his later
writings. There then emerges, I believe, a surprisingly clear and significant
line of thought, which betrays a deep psychological understanding of the
conditions of man's spiritual life.

The state of nature, out of which man is torn by culture, he by no means
portrays in ideal colors. He does indeed reject Hobbes's portrayal of the state
of nature as a war of all against all; he holds that war presupposes partly
needs that man does not have in the state of nature, partly also a greater
intercourse among men than was possible; and he holds besides that Hobbes has
overlooked pity, which is an involuntary and original human feeling. But the
state of nature is for him a purely instinctive state, whose advantage over the
civilized state rests on there being a relation of equilibrium between needs and
the capacity to satisfy them. Man is guided by the impulse of self-preservation
(amour de soi) and easily finds means of fulfilling it. Emotion,
% --- p. 495 ---
\opage{495}fancy and reflection play no part. It is only life in common and
culture that awaken the capacity for comparison and reflection. Now the state of
equilibrium is abolished. The impulse of self-preservation is satisfied at the
expense of others and thereby becomes egoism (amour
propre)\textsuperscript{88}). Representations arise of goods that cannot be
attained, and the disproportion between needs and capacities thereby comes into
force. One now begins to reflect on the worth and meaning of life instead of
following instinct. Weariness of life and suicide, which were not known in the
state of nature, now become frequent. Anxiety about the future and about death
replaces secure tranquillity. Doubt, that unbearable state, takes the place of
the happy thoughtlessness of the state of nature.

Yet according to Rousseau's conception these dissolving and unhappy effects do
not set in at once. When he is to name which stage in the development of
humanity is the happiest, he does not point to the most primitive state but to a
state of incipient social life and civilization, which lies ``midway between the
carefreeness of the primitive state and the heated bustle of our self-love''.
This time was the world's real youth, which ought not to have been left behind.
Here reflection and refinement have not yet exerted their dissolving influence,
and on the other hand instinct has begun to give way to thoughts and
feelings\textsuperscript{89}). The most dangerous stage is the third; here the
dissolving forces spread. It is the stage of corrupt and over-refined culture.

When Rousseau was asked whether it was then his opinion that one should return
to that state which lies so near the primitive, his answer is that it is
impossible, as impossible as becoming a child again\textsuperscript{90}). One
cannot abolish error by going back to the state of ignorance. Once instinct has
been replaced by reflection, there is nothing else to do but to put a true and
natural knowledge in place of the false. ``When men are corrupt, it is better
that they be learned than ignorant'', says Rousseau in a letter (to Scheib, 15
July 1756), and with this he in reality gives the Enlightenment a recognition,
for it implies that intellectual culture does not increase corruption but rather
diminishes
% --- p. 496 ---
\opage{496}it. He wants a culture that does not divide and weaken feeling and
strength, a social life that does not make us turned outward and dependent. Only
in his own inner self, he says, does man find peace. Only he has lived much who
has felt life. But culture had brought doubt, slackness, outwardness and
restlessness. And it had also, through the division of labor, brought bondage:
social misfortune arose when the one saw that he could use the other's labor and
used the superfluous store he could gather to maintain him. All these evils had
to be remedied through a new ordering of life for the individual and for
society.

There were three domains in which Rousseau's ideas of ``the new world'' moved:
those of education, of religion and of the state. In ``Émile'' and in ``Contrat
social'' he has expressed these ideas. They roused resistance from the adherents
of the old and scorn from those of the new. His books were burned by the
authorities, Voltaire called him an arch-madman (archifou), Diderot ``the great
sophist''. Quite naturally: for neither of the parties had gone so deep to the
bottom of the problem as Rousseau, none had felt its innermost sting as he had.
The adherents of the existing order relied on a supernatural sanction, and the
Encyclopedists believed that they themselves had brought forth the true
enlightenment and made it accessible to those to whom it was worth the trouble to
give it. Why, then, these paradoxes and these plans for the future?

In his \textit{theory of education} Rousseau maintains that nature must be
allowed its free course, and that the educator's art must consist in removing
obstacles and procuring the most favorable conditions possible for capacities
and drives to unfold according to their own nature. One must not try to force
culture on from without, either by way of authority or by way of enlightenment.
Childhood has its purpose in itself, as every other period of life does, and is
not to be treated as mere preparation. One does not know the child, for one has
hitherto regarded it only from the standpoint of adults. It has a natural right
to free self-development. Therefore do not swaddle it, let it have its own
mother's milk, do not spoil it, let it follow its instinct of self-preservation
and make its own experiences, do not preach to it, do not teach it what it
% --- p. 497 ---
\opage{497}can learn for itself, do not awaken wishes and needs in it before it
can have them satisfied! --- The longer one can put off mental development, the
better. What matters is that the mind be full-grown, so that it shall not
languish by using its powers too early. If possible, bring the child to its
twelfth year without its being able to tell its right hand from its left: the
more quickly will the eyes of reason open in it when the time for that has come!
Let it grow up without prejudices, without habits and without knowledge!
Otherwise one does not come to know the child's own peculiar nature either. The
germ of character must have time to show itself, so that one can then take it
in the right way. And need and drive must have time to arise, so that one shall
not awaken aversion by forcing on it what cannot be appreciated. --- Education,
in other words, is to be negative, not positive. ``Positive I call'', says
Rousseau (in \textit{Lettre à M. de Beaumont,} the magnificent defense of
``Émile''), ``the education that aims at forming the mind before its time and at
giving the child knowledge of the duties of the man. Negative I call the
education that aims at perfecting the organs, the instruments of our knowledge,
before it gives us knowledge itself, and that prepares for reason by exercising
the senses. Negative education is not inactive; far from it; it does not give
virtues, but it forestalls vices; it does not teach truth, but it guards against
error; it prepares the child for everything that can lead it to the true when it
becomes able to understand the true, and to the good when it becomes able to
love the good''. This concept of negative education expresses very strikingly
Rousseau's real fundamental thought. Culture is to be the unfolding of nature,
not a shell, a heavy form forced on from without. Only that culture is genuine
which is nature itself at a higher stage of development. Therefore he urges
caution in ``introducing'' culture. Rousseau has a deeper eye for the peculiar
character of the life of the spirit than the adherents both of authority and of
``enlightenment''. Only what has developed naturally and what has been produced
by its own activity is genuine for him. Only through a development of culture of
a genuine kind can one leave the secure and
% --- p. 498 ---
\opage{498}carefree time of instinct and yet preserve the harmony between need
and capacity, between thought and feeling, between the outer and the inner. Like
so many mystics he has a fine sense for the conditions of spiritual growth. The
very framing of a concept such as that of negative education betrays this sense
and has a Socratic character. Rousseau nevertheless does not escape being the
child of his time. He does not have full confidence in the involuntary use of
the powers, for he sets in motion a shrewd educator and a whole system of
intrigues and arrangements so that Émile shall not come under any influences
other than those that supposedly suit his age. Systematic construction is
characteristic of Rousseau in every domain. His living feeling and enthusiasm
lead him to see what no one else could see; but it stops at the great grasp:
when the thought is to be carried through in detail, it becomes evident how far
he stands from the real world, and instead of letting himself be guided by real
experiences on the particular points, he gives free play to his constructive
understanding. Even at Émile's falling in love and wedding ``le gouverneur''
stands in the background and arranges everything --- and not always in a
negative and indirect way either. ---

It accords with the fundamental thought of Rousseau's pedagogy that the child's
\textit{religious conception} must not be imparted to it from without but is to
be drawn forth from it under the influence of the needs of the heart. In the
famous section ``The Profession of Faith of the Savoyard Vicar'', which is
inserted in ``Émile'', Rousseau gives us his religion. There is nothing new in
his religious ideas. It is the representations of ``natural religion'' or
``deism'' in which he finds the expression of his feeling. He will not bring any
proof of the validity of these representations, but sets them up as dogmas.
Matter cannot have its motion from itself, but the first cause of motion must be
a personal will. In opposition to Condillac's doctrine the essential difference
between sensation and thought is maintained, and in opposition to materialism
the difference between mind and matter as two substances. There are several
interesting remarks in Rousseau's development of this point, and it is of
particular historical interest that a countryman of Rousseau,
\textsc{Charles Bonnet},
% --- p. 499 ---
\opage{499}at about the same time in his psychological writings (of which the
most important is \textit{Essai analytique sur les facultés de l'âme.}
Copenhague 1760) criticized Condillac's attempt to trace everything in mental
life back to passive sensation, though it cannot be shown that Rousseau knew
these writings. In nature there is revealed a striving after purposes, a unity in
the whole plan, that bears witness to the working of a personal God. But
Rousseau differs here from the usual ``watchmaker philosophy'' of the time by
maintaining that this harmony and purposiveness in nature is not the reason why
he believes in God. The relation is precisely the reverse. His faith springs
from an immediate need of feeling. Doubt is to him an unbearable state; when his
reason wavers, his faith settles the matter on its own account. And only when
inner feeling has thus led him to faith can he find in nature indications that
point in the same direction as his dogmas. Although ``the Savoyard Vicar''
constantly seeks to show what is natural and reasonable in his assertions, he
nevertheless declares again and again that he will not philosophize or lecture
but only set forth what he feels, and he asks his hearer to find confirmation of
his assertions in his own feeling. The practical standpoint of feeling is
decisive. On the nature of God he will not brood, except in so far as he is
compelled to it ``by the feeling of the relations in which God stands to
him''\textsuperscript{91}). But it is above all in a famous letter to Voltaire
(18 August 1756), on the occasion of the latter's poem on the destruction of
Lisbon, that Rousseau decidedly maintains the inner, subjective source of faith:
he does not believe in God because everything in the world is good, but he finds
something good in everything because he believes in God. When in this letter he
defends optimism against Voltaire's criticism, he does indeed rely on the fact
that in the great, elementary relations of life there are sources of joy and
satisfaction that the refined man of the world does not know; he stresses in
particular ``the delightful feeling of existing'' (le doux sentiment de
l'existence indépendamment de toute autre sensation). He assumes besides that
the evils for the individual may be necessary for the great connection of the
world, and in the belief in immortality he has a last consolation. But the real
foundation of the optimism
% --- p. 500 ---
\opage{500}that he, in spite of his sickliness and his wretched circumstances,
maintains against Voltaire, living in honor, wealth and splendor, is his being
inwardly and personally gripped by religious feeling; it is this that enables
him to cry out to Voltaire: ``You enjoy, I hope!'' With respect to content the
religion of Rousseau and that of Voltaire were not different; ``natural
religion'' was common to them. But what a difference in inwardness and mood!
Rousseau has in an epoch-making way moved the religious problem from the domain
of the outward consideration and explanation of the world back to inner,
personal feeling and to the way in which this is attuned to life. What Pascal
was hindered by his Catholic dogmatism from carrying through, Rousseau came far
nearer to in spite of his deistic dogmatism. For a dogmatist he is, by the
quickness with which he lands in Cartesian spiritualism and in deistic theology.
Here, as so often in philosophy, it is not the result but the motivation that is
the new and the lastingly valuable thing. And the motivation is closely bound up
with the relation of dependence, so decisive for Rousseau's personality and cast
of mind, in which representation stands to feeling and need. The ``Savoyard
Vicar's'' last counsel is: ``Keep your soul always in such a state that you
constantly \textit{wish,
% scan: „onsker“ (p. 500; the e-book's reading, set by sense: scan-artefact rule)
} that there is a God; then you will never come to doubt it!''

That Rousseau's dogmas take the definite form they take is not, however, due
merely to the way in which he interprets his feeling. He has subjected the
representations to a criticism. In a letter (to M***, 15 January 1769) he says
that he has thought through the various systems and decided for the one that
seemed to him to have the fewest difficulties. Here, then, thinking is granted a
reacting influence on the postulates of feeling. When, e.g., the experience of
the evils in the world did not shake his faith in a good God, it was because, by
virtue of the doctrine of the two substances (mind and matter), he assumed that
matter set bounds to the carrying out of the divine purposes. He did not assume
a creation, but only an ordering of an already existing, perhaps eternal matter.
God is the good orderer and guide, but not almighty (see
% --- p. 501 ---
\opage{501}the letter just cited and his Lettre à M. de Beaumont). Here too,
then, Rousseau comes to the same result as Voltaire, although the two men stand
with so very different a mood before the problem of evil in the world.
Rousseau's religion is really joy and enthusiasm that a power can be traced in
the world which works for the good. He does not believe in the physical effects
of prayer. His prayer is an outburst of enthusiasm in which joy in nature at its
height\textsuperscript{92}) passes over into a hymn of praise to ``the great
Being'' that works everywhere but for which thought can find no concept; at its
height it becomes an ecstasy in which no word can express the deep and strong
mood, because the mind craves beyond all limits (Third Letter to Malesherbes).
The independence of feeling over against knowledge that Rousseau maintains shows
itself here in the fact that feeling at its height can find no adequate
expression in representations. From here there is only one step to the
knowledge that all religious representations, all dogmas, are symbols. This step
Rousseau's deistic dogmatism hindered him from taking.

His natural religion, which he believes to be independent of all tradition, he
sets in opposition to the positive religions. He is convinced that if one had
kept to the voice of the heart there would have been no other religions than
this one. But he was convinced that in his religion he had room for the real
kernel of Christianity. To the Archbishop of Paris he writes (Lettre à M. de
Beaumont): ``Monseigneur, I am a Christian, and a Christian at heart, according
to the teaching of the Gospel. I am a Christian, not as a disciple of the
priests, but as a disciple of Jesus Christ. My Master speculated very little
about dogmas but urged duties greatly: he did not prescribe so much articles of
faith as good works; he required faith only in what was necessary in order to be
good!'' The mysteries of Christianity he left alone; they did not concern the
decisive thing, which was the moral kernel. When weight was laid on what goes
beyond this kernel and on the definite dogmatic formulations, one ended in
unfairness, falsehood, hypocrisy
% --- p. 502 ---
\opage{502}and tyranny. All this dogmatic learning God is supposed to have
enjoined --- and on top of that to have set the punishments of hell for those
who could not become so learned! Only through books, written by men and
guaranteed by men, can one come to know these positive dogmas. The Gospel is the
most sublime of all books --- but it is still a book. Not on the leaves of a
book, but in the heart of man has God written his law (Letter to Vernes, 25
March 1758). ---

Rousseau had in his early youth let himself be led into going over to
Catholicism. Later he returned to Protestantism and took part in its worship,
reserving for himself the Protestant layman's right to free examination of all
dogmas by the measure of conscience and the heart. He was naturally branded as a
heretic by both churches; by the Encyclopedists he was regarded as a hypocrite
or as a muddled head who would probably end as a Capuchin. He himself called
himself the only man of the time who believed in God. ---

The third domain in which Rousseau believed he descried a new world was
\textit{the social and political.} Here too it becomes evident that he did not
give up the hope that the stunting and oppression of nature could be replaced
by a development that lets nature come into its own. In his ``Contrat social''
(I, 8) he even speaks very strongly of the progress made by man's giving up the
state of nature and entering social life by a (tacit) contract: ``While in the
social state he must do without several goods that he had from nature, he gains
in return others that are very great: his capacities are exercised and
developed; his representations are enlarged; his feelings are ennobled; his
whole soul rises to such a point that, if the abuses that attend the new
conditions did not often degrade him to such a degree that he sank below the
level from which he had set out, he would have to bless without ceasing the
happy moment that tore him forever from that level and made him a rational being
and a man instead of a dull and stupid animal.''

In his theory of the philosophy of law Rousseau forms the conclusion of a whole
series of attempts that begin in the struggles of the
% --- p. 503 ---
\opage{503}Reformation and aim at constructing the state on the basis of free
individual transfer. Rousseau did not invent the idea of the social contract,
but he uses it in order to be able to present society as having arisen in
accordance with nature: in the state of nature men lived (he thought) isolated;
the only transition to the life of the state that could make the state natural
was therefore free adherence and transfer. Through it the people comes into
being as a people, the individual transferring his absolute authority over
himself to the people as a whole. The sovereignty of the people is absolute and
inalienable. He transfers Hobbes's absolutist concept of sovereignty to the
people as a whole. He agrees with Hobbes that sovereignty can lie in one place
only, but instead of assuming with Hobbes that through the social contract a
submission to the governing power immediately takes place, he proclaims, like
Althusius, whom his expressions also recall\textsuperscript{93}), the principle
of the sovereignty of the people, and assumes that ``the general will'' takes up
into itself the will of all individuals. Like Althusius he distinguishes between
form of state and form of government and assumes only one form of state, but
various forms of government. The best form of government is an elective
aristocracy. But he rejects the division of powers and denies that sovereignty
can be exercised through representatives. The highest authority is and remains
with the people itself, which must assemble from time to time to give laws. As
soon as the people is assembled, all governmental authority ceases; all
magistracy is suspended. The legislative power --- as one with the people itself
--- is sovereign; the executive is its servant. The legislative power is the
heart, the executive is the brain: the brain can be paralyzed and the man can
still live, if the heart is intact.

The condition for the exercise of the sovereignty of the people is, according to
Rousseau, that the whole people can be assembled. Therefore the state must not
be too large; Rousseau's ideal was --- besides his own native state of Geneva
--- the small states of antiquity. The only form under which the sovereignty of
the people can be preserved in a large state is --- says Rousseau --- the
federal constitution. Rousseau had worked out a treatise on such a constitution
--- but this treatise was handed over by him to a friend, who
% --- p. 504 ---
\opage{504}destroyed it at the beginning of the Revolution so that it should not
do harm! It was, as Rousseau remarks, ``a wholly new subject, whose principles
had first to be set up''. Just before the French Revolution this subject was
treated by \textsc{Alexander Hamilton}, the founder of the North American
constitution of the Union, in ``The Federalist''. The French revolutionaries,
who otherwise took many slogans from ``Contrat social'', paid no heed either to
the hint mentioned of how the goods of a large and of a small state, of
centralization and of decentralization, can be united, or to the practical
attempt that was made in this direction across the
ocean\textsuperscript{94}). They kept only to that side of Rousseau's doctrine
by which the individual lets his will be wholly absorbed in the general will,
which proclaims itself through the decisions of the majority and has full
disposal over the life and property, education and religious practice of all
citizens. As Hobbes had the individual abdicate in favor of the sovereign
governing power, Rousseau had the individual abdicate in favor of sovereign
democracy.

There is a definite opposition between Rousseau's treatise on the origin of
inequality (of 1755) and his ``Contrat social'' (of 1762), --- but an
opposition of which he himself was surely aware. On closer consideration it is
clear that in the later account he meant to correct and supplement the earlier.
In his ``Discours'' he shows how economic inequality comes with the division of
labor, and how only later on the formation of the state by agreement sanctions
and fixes the difference between rich and poor. ``The laws'', he says
(Discours, p. 95), ``gave the weak new fetters and the rich new forces; they
definitively destroyed natural freedom, fixed forever the law of property and
inequality, made a cunning usurpation into an irrevocable right, and for the
future brought the whole human race under the yoke of labor, bondage and
misery''. Here, then, the original contract is conceived as a sanction of
inequality. In ``Contrat social'', on the other hand, it is said (I, 9) that
``far from destroying natural freedom, the original contract puts a moral and
lawful equality in place of the physical
% --- p. 505 ---
\opage{505}inequality that nature had been able to produce among men, and while
they may be unequal in strength and in mind, they now become equal by agreement
and by right''. In a note Rousseau adds that it is only under bad governments
that this equality is merely apparent; he grants that in fact the social state
is beneficial to men only when they all have something and when no one has too
much. There can hardly be any doubt that by these words Rousseau means to show
how the new account can be reconciled with the earlier. He is indeed right, too,
that law and right can be used in both ways: both to sanction existing relations
of inequality and to level them out. In the ``Discours'' he keeps to the first
side of the matter, which was indeed the one that most struck the eye in the old
society; in ``Contrat social'', which is to portray an ideal and therefore looks
away from actual conditions\textsuperscript{95}), he keeps to the other side and
urges what ought to happen: precisely because the course of things (already ---
as the ``Discours'' showed --- in the state of nature) always tends to abolish
equality, precisely for that reason --- it is said in ``Contrat social'' (II,
11) --- the power of legislation must always strive to maintain it, must see to
it that no one becomes rich enough to be able to buy another, and no one poor
enough to let himself be bought. That there is nothing fantastic in this
consideration the whole subsequent time has shown, it having been more and more
recognized as an essential task of the power of the state to even out social
oppositions. Rousseau was not a socialist, but had a clear eye for the influence
of social inequalities and for the drawbacks that go with the system of private
property. More than the earlier writers on natural law he has searched beyond
the formal, political principles and found the social question behind all
constitutional questions. Only to one thing was he, with his whole time, blind:
the significance of free associations. Once the state has come into being, it is
to regulate everything. Rousseau here comes into conflict with himself. For in
``Émile'' he lays weight precisely on individual development, on the unfolding of
the individual's natural peculiarity: but how can that become possible under the
tyranny of the ``general will''?
% --- p. 506 ---
\opage{506}Here lies a great problem, and it cannot surprise us that Rousseau has
not seen it: he moved, after all, in the midst of the arbitrariness of the old
regime, where neither the general nor the individual will could come forward; he
wanted to emancipate them both --- and he could, after all, quite calmly leave it
to the future to reconcile them. He had set his time problems enough. ---

In the history of philosophy Rousseau occupies a position that presents a
certain analogy with Leibniz's. They both bring forward the problem of
valuation, not being content with the mechanical explanation of nature and the
mechanical ordering of society, but asking about the significance of nature and
of society for human feeling, the source of all valuation. And in close
connection with this there stand in both of them the emphasis on the right of
individuality and the sense for the inner infinity of every individual. But the
carrying through of these thoughts was undertaken in very different ways by the
two so very different spirits. Leibniz sought to keep the scientific view of
nature by conceiving the laws it found as expressions of the harmony among the
self-unfolding of countless individual beings. The gradual transition from
obscurity to clarity was the fundamental law of all development in this
harmonious world-picture. Poor Jean Jacques did not find it so easy to find
harmony, either in himself or outside himself. In his ecstatic moments he
believed in it, he saw it with his mind's eye. But his monad had an obscure
depth in it that could not be cleared up but was precisely darkened more and
more, and neither in the world nor in society could he get everything to come
together into an intellectual harmony. His feeling was too strong to be
explained as confused thinking. Therefore he maintained the right of the
irrational. By the way of personal experience of life he had ended in a result
similar to the one Hume had come to by the way of epistemology: Hume had indeed
shown that all our knowledge rested on unprovable presuppositions. There were
then, seen both from the practical and from the theoretical side, problems
enough to take up for him who was to succeed in carrying philosophy further.

do not go further into the way in which Cusanus in later writings
\textit{(Possest} and \textit{De apice theoriæ)} modifies his ideas, especially
by stressing the activity of the highest principle and by conceiving this principle
as the unity of possibility and actuality, later especially as power (posse). Cf.
on this F. \emph{Fiorentino}: \textit{Il risorgimento
% print: „resorgimento“ (p. 508) (misprint)
filosofico nel Quattrocento.} Napoli 1885,
% --- p. 509 ---

Filosofi, med särskilt afseende på dens historiska betydelse.} Lund 1892, p.
22) disputes that the work ``Possest'' marks a different position from the one
taken in ``De docta ignorantia.'' But it seems to me that Fiorentino's
view is proved by the fact that Cusanus in ``Docta ignorantia'' (I, 26) expressly
declares that the infinite neither produces, is produced, nor proceeds
(Infinitas neqve generans, neqve genita, neqve procedens), whereas in
``Possest'' he lays very great weight on its activity. I grant that this
difference must not be stressed too strongly, since Cusanus in all his writings
operates with the relation complicatio --- explicatio, and so far cannot at any
stage disregard acting and proceeding.

\textsuperscript{14}) P.~83. \emph{Richard} \emph{Falckenberg}
\textit{(Grundzüge der Philosophie des Nicolaus Cusanus.} Breslau 1880, p. 54)
has pointed out that the relation complicatio --- explicatio comes to
mean something quite different when it is applied to the relation of the Deity to
the world (where it denotes a transition from something higher to something lower) and when it is
applied within the world (where it denotes a transition from lower stages of nature to
higher).

\textsuperscript{15}) P.~86. When \emph{Ludwig} \emph{Lange} (in his
interesting essay \textit{Die geschichtliche Entwickelung
% scan: „Entwickeluug“ (p. 509)
des Bewegungsbegriffes. ---} Philosophische Studien. Herausg. von W. Wundt III,
p. 350) remarks that for Cusanus, as the forerunner of Copernicus, the thought of the
relativity of place and of motion must have lain particularly near at hand, the relation is precisely the
reverse: it was the thought of the relativity of place and of motion that made him
the forerunner of Copernicus.

\textsuperscript{16}) P.~87. Concerning \emph{Paracelsus} (whose real name
was Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim) I must refer to Chr.
\emph{Sigwart's} excellent characterization (Kleine Schriften, I). Paracelsus was
born at Einsiedeln in Switzerland in 1493 and died, after a very restless life, at Salzburg in
1541. On his significance as a chemist and physician see \emph{Ernst} v. \emph{Meyer}:
\textit{Geschichte der Chemie.} Leipzig 1889, p. \textit{57}---61.
\emph{Julius} \emph{Petersen}: \textit{Hovedmomenter af den medicinske
Lægekunsts historiske Udvikling.} Copenhagen 1876, p. 21---24. ---
\emph{Cardanus} (b. at Pavia 1501, d. at Rome 1576) is more interesting for his
autobiography, which is a rarity for its frankness and is one of the
most peculiar documents of the Renaissance, than for his writings, of which
the most important \textit{(De subtilitate)} is a chaotic mixture of profundity,
fantasy and superstition. He ascribes to himself great powers of observation \textit{(De
vita propria.} ch. 23) both in science and in the practice of life; indeed, among his
scientific merits, which are recounted in a special chapter of the
autobiography (De vita propria. Kap. 44: Qvæ in diversis disciplinis digna
adinveni), he counts first and foremost, in the domain of natural science, that
he has ``brought the consideration of natural things back to a definite art and
method, which no one before him had attempted.'' History has not
been able to let him keep this honor.

coincide. Telesio's meaning is presumably that wisdom is a condition that cooperates in every single
virtue (since the task is always to find means of
self-preservation), but that magnanimity (which is called the summit of all the virtues, omnium
virtutum veluti apex) concludes the series of the virtues as the trait of character in
which they are all comprised as in their most perfect form. --- I do not go
further into Telesio's polemic, springing from misunderstanding, against
Aristotle's doctrine of virtue as habit. That a naturalistic thought should lie
at the root of this polemic (Fiorentino: Bernardino Telesio I, p. 316 f.)
I am unable to see.

Copernican system, and in his \textit{Dialogues on the Systems of the World} works
