\opage{511}\textsuperscript{25}) P.~105. The chief source for Bruno's biography is
the Inquisition's interrogations from his trial in Venice, which were first
published by \emph{Domenico} \emph{Berti} in his biography of Bruno (Turin
1868). Later Berti published fragments of the interrogations in Rome. Chr.
\emph{Sigwart} has collected testimonies on Bruno's appearance at German universities
(Tübingen Easter program 1880 and Kleine Schriften I). \emph{Dufour}
\textit{(Giordano Bruno à Genève.} Genève 1884) has published documents
on Bruno's stay in Geneva. --- An article in the Quarterly Review (October 1902),
\textit{Giordano Bruno in England}, contains some interesting remarks on the
very few traces of Bruno's stay in England that can be shown, apart from his
own statements. Thus one of the persons Bruno mentions in the \textit{Cena,}
\emph{Florio}, was a client of the Earl of Southampton (as was Shakespeare). This
Florio translated Montaigne's essays into English. --- In the poet Spenser the
author of the article thinks he finds traces of Bruno's \textit{Spaccio.}

\textsuperscript{26}) P.~110. \emph{Berti} \textit{(Giordano Bruno da Nola.}
Nuova edizione. Torino 1889, p. 196 ff.) concurs in the influence of Bruno on Shakespeare,
assumed by some German writers, through common acquaintances
or through books. Shakespeare came to London only a year after Bruno had
left it. As \emph{Robert} \emph{Beyersdorf} \textit{(Giordano Bruno und
Shakespeare.} Oldenburg 1889) has shown, an influence is nevertheless highly
improbable. In particular it seems to me decisive that no trace is found
in Shakespeare of the new astronomical ideas whose prophet Bruno was. Here, surely, there would
have been something for a Shakespearean imagination! --- Beyersdorf shows very finely
how differently Bruno and Shakespeare conceive the idea of the
constant change of natural phenomena and their passing over into one another. For the poet there is
here a testimony to the nothingness and wretchedness of human existence, whereas
for the thinker it is the unity and eternity of nature that reveals itself in its
glory in the midst of perishability. --- It must, however, be remarked here, as will
be shown more fully later, that Bruno also conceives the alternation of opposites
from its bitter and painful side. This comes out especially in the work \textit{De gl' heroici
furori,} and in this Bruno --- despite all his Neoplatonism --- is
different from Plato.

\textsuperscript{27}) P.~116. A friend of Berti's used the revolutionary period of 1849
to take copies of Bruno's trial in Rome, but did not finish. As for the
rest of the records of the trial, it was assumed until quite recently that it must be found in
the archive of the Inquisition in the Vatican. But to an inquiry from a German
Bruno scholar, Dr. \emph{Güttler}, there came from the Vatican the definite declaration
that neither the records nor the confiscated manuscripts were in the archive, and that
it was not known where they were. See on this Archiv für Gesch. d. Phil. VI, p. 344 f.

\textsuperscript{28}) P.~116. \emph{Schoppe}, a German scholar who had gone over
to Catholicism and was an eyewitness of Bruno's condemnation and death, names, in his
description glowing with hatred of heresy, among Bruno's ``horrible and utterly absurd
doctrines'' the assumption of innumerable worlds. --- When the Inquisition,
% --- p. 512 ---
% print: „d. 86“ (p. 512) (misprint)
\opage{512}on the Pope's order, put it to Bruno that the eight propositions extracted from
his writings had already been regarded as heretical by the most ancient Church,
it is quite possible that the assumption of several worlds may have been counted among
these old heresies. Later, of course, Galilei had to abjure the doctrine of the motion of the earth
as conflicting with Holy Scripture. --- Among the Protestants too
the assumption of several worlds was heretical. \emph{Melanchton} polemizes against
it as an ungodly doctrine, since Christ cannot have died and risen several
times. \textit{(Initia doctrinæ physicæ.} Corp. Ref. XIII, p. 220 ff.) ---
\emph{Campanella}, on the other hand, seeks in his \textit{Apologia pro Galilæo}
(Francofurti 1620, p. 9, 51) to establish that this doctrine is not heretical. ---
Cf. on the probable 8 counts of the indictment: F. \emph{Tocco}: \textit{Giordano
Bruno.} Firenze 1886, p. 86.

\textsuperscript{29}) P.~123. In the work \textit{De l'infinito universo e
mundi} (ed. Lagarde p. 343 f., 363) Bruno had already rejected the solid
spheres on physical and epistemological grounds. In \textit{De immenso,} I, 5
he finds this view confirmed by Tycho Brahe's investigations.
\emph{Tycho} himself drew the same consequences from his doctrine as Bruno. He says
thus in a letter to Kepler of April 1598 (Kepleri \textit{Opera} ed. Frisch.
1858, I, p. 44): ``I hold that all reality of the spheres, however one may
conceive them, must be excluded from the heavens, which I have learned from all the comets
that have appeared, ever since the new star of 1572, and which are in reality
celestial phenomena.'' (On the old view the comets were due to
exhalations from the earth and moved only in the sublunary world.) --- As F.
\emph{Tocco} \textit{(Opera latine di G. Bruno esposte e confrontate con le
italiane.} Firenze 1889, p. 318 f.) remarks, Bruno probably did not
know Tycho's works at first hand, since he does not use the excellent argument
against the solid spheres that the ``new stars'' afforded, and that Galilei later constantly
employed. (Cf. \emph{Tycho} \emph{Brahe's} work \textit{De nova stella}
(the edition of 1901) (fol. D. 2): ``That this star has changed both its
size and its color in a distinct manner is not a sufficient proof
that it belongs in the elemental region, below the sphere of the moon . . . .
For if it were possible that a new body \textit{came into being} in the ether itself,
which I have established above concerning this star on undeceiving grounds against
the opinions and dogmas of all investigators, --- then it will be regarded as far less
impossible and unreasonable that this new star undergoes a \textit{change} in
size and color.'') Nor does Bruno anywhere mention Tycho's peculiar
system of the world.

\textsuperscript{30}) P.~128. An interesting anticipation of Goethe's famous
words: ``\emph{Ihm} ziemt's die Welt im Innern zu bewegen,'' is found in \textit{De
immenso,}V\textit{,} 12: ``God or reason does not stand outside and make the world
revolve; for more worthy of him must be the inner principle of motion, which is the
own nature, the own soul, that everything has which lives in his bosom and in his
body.'' (\emph{Dignius} enim illi debet esse internum principium motus etc.).
--- For this inner principle, which underlies every being's
% --- p. 513 ---
\opage{513}impulse of self-preservation, Bruno, in the last work we have from his hand, the
\textit{Summa terminorum
metaphysicorum,} dictated during his stay in Zürich in 1591, uses the expression voluntas naturalis. --- Cf. \textit{Cena,}
Lagarde's ed., p. 163 f., 183 f. \textit{De l'infinito,} p. 370 ff. De la causa
242, 315, 320. ---

\textsuperscript{31}) P.~130. On the question of the relation between
the mental and the material, Bruno expresses himself somewhat differently in his
different writings. --- In the \textit{Cena,} p. 189, he will not inquire whether
mental substance is transformed into material substance and conversely, or not. In
\textit{De la causa,} p. 235 ff. (cf. \textit{Spaccio,} p. 409) it is maintained that
mental substance, just as well as material substance, persists through all
changes. At the same time \textit{De la causa,} p. 261 and 280 ff., maintains
the absolute unity of substance, the difference between mental and material
substance being due only to a differentiation (explication). Finally, he denies
in \textit{De gl' heroici furori,} p. 721, expressly the conversion of the material
into the mental and conversely. --- Not only the opposition between mind and matter,
but also the opposition between freedom and necessity is, according to Bruno, to fall away in
the highest principle, which he develops in a series of interesting propositions,
\textit{De immenso,} I, 11---12.

\textsuperscript{32}) P.~134. Bruno's atomism or doctrine of monads is found in
the didactic poem \textit{De triplici minimo,} which appeared at Frankfurt in 1591. It
occupies, as Lasswitz (\textit{Geschichte der Atomistik.} Hamburg und Leipzig
1889, I, p. 359--- 399) has shown, an interesting place in the history of the development of modern atomism.
Yet Lasswitz --- so it seems to me --- has not noticed
the contradiction in Bruno between his polemic against division to infinity and his
doctrine of the relativity of the concept of the atom. --- \emph{Felice} \emph{Tocco}, who at first (in
\textit{Opere latine di G. Bruno)} had assumed that Bruno also applied
atomism to the mental domain, has later (in his work \textit{Opere
inedite di G. Bruno.} Napoli 1891) corrected this assumption. He now finds an
inconsistency in Bruno, because the latter does not assume mental atoms just as well
as material ones. It is, however, a great question whether the concept of the atom is at all
suited to be applied to the mental side of existence, and it was
perhaps a right instinct that kept Bruno from making this
application, although, had he strictly held fast to the relativity of the concept of the atom,
it would not have involved all the consequences that at first glance
might seem to lie in it. --- When \emph{Tocco} (Opere latine di G. Bruno. p.
353), apropos of the expression monas monadum (of God), remarks that one cannot
see whether God is thereby distinguished from the other monads or thought of as their substance,
Bruno himself has clearly explained his meaning when he says: ``God is
the monad of monads, that is to say, the essential in all beings'' (\textit{Deus
est monadum monas, nempe entium entitas. De minimo.} ed. 1591, p. 17). ---
The universe is called a monad in \textit{De gl' heroici furori,} p. 724. --- This use
of the word monad is understood only by holding fast to the concept of relativity.

\textsuperscript{33}) P.~135. Of the transmigration of souls Bruno says (\textit{Spaccio,}
p. 410) that
% --- p. 514 ---
\opage{514}if one cannot accept it, it is nevertheless worth thinking about. In
the interrogation in Venice too (see \emph{Berti}: \textit{G. Bruno, 2,} ed. p. 402---408)
he expresses himself with a certain indefiniteness on this matter. Cf. on his treatment
of the doctrine of the transmigration of souls: F. \emph{Tocco}: \textit{Giordano Bruno,} p. 71---
75. --- He expresses himself most thoroughly on the relation between the world-spirit and the
individual souls in the \textit{Cabala,} p. 585---588.

\textsuperscript{34}) P.~147. In his \textit{Apologia pro Galilæo.} Francofurti
1622, p. 54, \emph{Campanella} says that he might perhaps, through the more recent investigations,
be compelled to assume several suns in the universe, so that it would not, as
he had hitherto assumed, have two centers, the sun and the earth, but many. Yet
he suspends his judgment. --- In his \textit{Realis philosophia} (1623) p. 10
he is likewise doubtful. --- Later, it is true, he inserted in his \textit{Universalis
philosophia seu Metaphysica} (Parisiis 1638), III, p. 71 some remarks
which developed how the matter would have to be conceived if Galilei were right (posito
qvod vera sint Galilei dogmata), but then added: ``Now judgment has been given in Rome
against Galilei, and with that what I had earlier [before those remarks]
written is established.'' --- A peculiar kind of verification!

\textsuperscript{35}) P.~168. The first account of the history of philosophy
in which Galilei has been given the place that is his due on account of his
clear consciousness of the method of thinking is J. F. \emph{Fries}: \textit{Die
Geschichte der Philosophie dargestellt nach den Fortschritten ihrer
wissenschaftlichen Entwickelung.} Zweiter Band. Halle 1840. Later
\emph{Prantl} \textit{(Galilei und Kepler als Logiker.} Münchener
Sitzungsberichte. 1875) has treated his doctrine of method and shown how it
eclipses Bacon's, and \emph{Tönnies} \textit{(Ueber die Philosophie des
Hobbes.} Vierteljahrsschr. für wiss. Philos. III) and \emph{Natorp}
\textit{(Descartes' Erkenntnisstheorie.} Marburg 1882, ch. 6) have established
Galilei's significant position at the entrance to modern philosophy, in
contrast to the traditional beginning with Bacon and Descartes.

\textsuperscript{36}) P.~173. \emph{Galilei}: \textit{Opere.} Firenze 1842 ff.,
XIII, p. 200 f. --- The German translation of the Discorsi (in ``Klassiker der
Naturwissenschaft'' No. 24, p. 57) has an inaccuracy here, through which the
simplification of the circumstances that Galilei has in mind drops out. Galilei's words
``dum externæ causæ tollantur'' (provided only that external causes are kept away) are
rendered, namely, by ``während äussere Ursachen hinzukommen.'' --- Galilei's thought experiment
appears most clearly in another place in the \textit{Discorsi} (Op. XIII, p. 221):
Mobile qvoddam super planum horizontale projectum mente concipio, omni secluso
impedimento. (\emph{I} conceive of a movable body thrown along a
horizontal plane, in such a way that every hindrance is excluded.) --- On the history of the
law of inertia cf. \emph{Wohlwill}: \textit{Die Entdeckung des
Beharrungsgesetzes.} (Zeitschrift für Völkerpsychologie. XIV---XV).

\textsuperscript{37}) P.~177. It is Natorp's merit (in his work on
Descartes's epistemology) to have been the first to draw attention to this
section of \textit{Il Saggiatore. (Opere de Galilei.} Firenze 1842 ff., IV, p.
332---338). ---
% --- p. 515 ---
\opage{515}The new doctrine was dangerous, since the denial of the reality of the sense qualities was thought to
conflict with the Catholic doctrine of the Eucharist, which held that the host kept its
sensible properties after its substantial transformation. Later Descartes and Leibniz
too had much trouble on account of this question.

\textsuperscript{38}) P.~178. As \emph{Prantl} has shown \textit{(Ueber Petrus
Ramus.} Münchener Sitzungsberichte 1878).

\textsuperscript{39}) P.~180. Cf. \emph{Freudenthal}: \textit{Beiträge zur
Geschichte der englischen Philosophie.} (Archiv für Gesch. der Philos. IV---V.)
--- Croom \emph{Robertson} in Academy. 1892, p. 110.

\textsuperscript{40}) P.~187. As a curiosity it may be mentioned that, just as there are those
who think that not Shakespeare but someone else, perhaps Bacon, wrote the
``Shakespearean'' tragedies, so a critical head in the most recent times has
found out that Bacon is not the author of the Novum Organum, and has stopped for a moment
at the possibility that Shakespeare might have written it, without, however,
daring to hold fast to this possibility. See on this Archiv für Gesch. d. Philos. I, p. 111.

\textsuperscript{41}) P.~194. On Bacon's relation to Plato see \textit{Nov.
org.} I, 105---124; II, 7---13. --- In \textit{De augmentis scientiarum,} III, 4
it is said: ``It is evident that Plato, that lofty mind, who surveyed everything as from a
mountain top, perceived in his doctrine of ideas that the forms are the proper
object of science.''

\textsuperscript{42}) P.~205. \textit{Discours de la méthode}
% print: „mèthode“ (p. 515) (misprint)
(1637), 2. partie. --- \textit{La vie de Monsieur Descartes.} [Par A. Baillet].
Paris 1691, I, p. 51---71. --- \emph{Millet}: \textit{Histoire de Descartes
avant} 1637. Paris 1867, p. 100 ff.

\textsuperscript{43}) P.~212. In the account given here I follow especially
Descartes's earliest sketch of a doctrine of method in \textit{Règles pour la direction
de l'esprit,} a work which, when carefully studied, removes many current
misunderstandings of Descartes. Cf. besides the third Meditation and the Reply
to the second set of objections, in which Descartes, at the request of others,
attempts a systematic exposition of his ideas. --- To the question of
how general propositions are formed from the single intuitions,
Descartes really gives only this answer: ``It is precisely the nature of our mind to form
general propositions from the knowledge of the single.'' \textit{(Resp. ed. sec. obj.).}

\textsuperscript{43\,b}) P.~213. Whereas Descartes in his doctrine of method
\textit{(Règles} etc.) begins by speaking of the clear and distinct intuition of
simple relations (intuition) and names the consciousness of ourselves as thinking
among the examples of such intuition, he later begins (especially at the beginning
of the 3rd Meditation) with the consciousness of ourselves as thinking beings and derives from
the simplicity and immediate clearness of this thought the significance of intuition. --- The
line of thought that underlies cogito ergo sum occurs already in
\emph{Augustinus} \textit{(De vera religione} cap. 49), indeed already in ancient
Indian philosophy.

\textsuperscript{44}) P.~214. At the end of the 3rd Meditation it is said: ``The
% --- p. 516 ---
\opage{516}possibility then alone remains that the representation of God is innate in me in the same
way as the representation of myself is innate in me.'' This is for Descartes
more than a comparison. For I cannot --- he thinks --- become conscious of myself
as a limited and imperfect being without an unconscious use of
the representation of a being raised above all limitation (3rd Medit.). --- To
Hobbes's objection: ``There is no innate representation; for what is
innate must always be present,'' --- Descartes answers \textit{(Resp.
tertiæ} X): ``When we say that a representation is innate, we do not mean that it
always appears before us; for in that sense there would be no innate
representation at all; but only that we have in ourselves the capacity to develop it.''
--- In \textit{Notæ in programma quoddam} Descartes says: ``Since I noticed that
there are thoughts in me which do not proceed from external objects or from the determination of my
will, but merely from my faculty of thinking, I called such
\emph{representations}, which are the \emph{forms} of those thoughts, innate, in order to
distinguish them from others, which come from outside or are produced by myself. In the same
sense we say that magnanimity, or that certain diseases such as gout or
stone, are innate in certain families, by which we do not mean that the children suffer from
these diseases in their mother's womb, but that they are born with a disposition or capacity to
contract these diseases.'' --- The part of Descartes's theological line of thought
that infers from the representation of God as the representation of an infinite being to
an infinite being as the cause of this representation is due perhaps to an
influence of \emph{Vives} (De \textit{anima.} 1538 p. 127 f.), by whom Descartes
was also influenced on several points in his psychology.

\textsuperscript{45}) P.~215. Cf. \emph{Natorp's} excellent account
\textit{(Descartes' Erkenntnisstheorie,} p. 55. ff., 76 f.). Natorp has
shown that the use of the concept of God in Descartes's epistemology is not of
so external a kind as it appears from the usual accounts. Yet
Natorp does not sufficiently emphasize what I believe one must lay the greatest
weight on: namely, that this whole epistemological use of the
concept of God was altogether unnecessary, since Descartes after all uses the causal principle
to establish the reality of the concept of God; when the causal principle is presupposed
valid, no theological guarantee is needed for the validity of knowledge.

\textsuperscript{46}) P.~218. The strict concept of substance is found in Descartes
\textit{Medit. III, Princ. phil.} I § 51. The lax concept of substance is found:
\textit{Resp. sec.} and \textit{Princ. phil.} I § 52. --- Descartes himself
\textit{(Princ. phil.} I, 51) draws attention to the double meaning of the word substance.

\textsuperscript{47}) P.~227. On Harvey's discovery and its prehistory see P.
Hedenius \textit{Om upptäcktan af blodomloppet.} (Upsala Universitets Årsskrift
1892). See especially on the relation between Descartes and Harvey p. 216 f., 277.
Descartes assumed that the heating of the blood in the heart caused it to be pressed out
into the body; he had thus not appropriated Harvey's thought of the heart as a
contracting muscle. --- Harvey too, to be sure, held fast to the old doctrine of
the heating of the blood in the heart, but did not apply it
% --- p. 517 ---
% scan: „Tone.“ (p. 517)
\opage{517}in this way. It was only \emph{Niels} \emph{Steensen} who definitely
showed that the heart is a muscle, and that there was no foundation for the
significance as the very source of life and the seat of the soul that had been ascribed to it from
ancient times. (Cf. \emph{Jul}. \emph{Petersen}: \textit{Bartholinerne.} Copenhagen
1898. p. 84 f.).

\textsuperscript{48}) P.~229. Descartes's localization of the soul in the pineal gland
was altogether arbitrary and was criticized by the anatomists of the time. \emph{Thomas}
Bartholin \textit{(Anatomia.} Lugd.
% scan: „Lngd.“ (p. 517)
Batav. 1651, p. 356 f.) objects partly that the nerves do not end in the pineal gland,
partly that it is so small that the representations would be mixed together [!] in it,
partly, finally, that it is placed where the ``excrements of the brain'' accumulate! In the
brilliant lecture that \emph{Niels} Steensen gave in Paris, and which is printed in
\emph{Winslöv's} \textit{Exposition anatomique} (4th part), he remarks that since
one does not know what fills the cavities of the brain, the doctrine of the animal spirits may be
just as good as that of the excrements of the brain. Against Descartes, whose general
method he credits with great merit, he objects that the pineal gland does not
stand in connection with any canal, and that it does not float freely, but hangs
together with the rest of the brain. --- What significance the pineal gland has is
not yet known. (\emph{Edinger}: \textit{Vorlesungen über den Bau der nervösen
Centralorgane.} 6. Aufl. p. 138). On Descartes's significance for the physiology of the nerves
cf. Huxley: \textit{Om den Hypothese, at Dyrene ere Automater.} (Tidsskrift
for populære Fremstillinger af Naturvidenskaben 1874). --- A remarkable utterance
of Descartes's is found in a letter to Mersenne (February 1649), namely that when
he denies the animal soul, he denies merely \textit{thinking} (cogitatio), not
\textit{life and sense perception}: vitam nulli animali denego, utpote qvam in solo
cordis calore consistere statuo; nec denego etiam \textit{sensum qvatenus ab
organo corporeo dependet.} This does not agree with other statements, especially not with
\textit{Resp. ad sextas obj.} § 9, where 3 degrees of sense perception are
distinguished: the first is merely a motion in the brain called forth by the impression
(cerebri motus), and this is common to animals and human beings; the second is the
immediate sensation of pain, pleasure, thirst, hunger, color, tone, taste, smell,
warmth etc., which arises in consciousness (in mente) as the effect of that
motion; the third is the judgments that, on the occasion of that motion, we pass
on external things. The sense perception he speaks of in the letter to Mersenne must be the
first of these degrees; but of it, it is not enough to say that it
\textit{depends} on the motions of the brain: it is nothing other than these and cannot
be called sensation. What he calls thinking in the letter must correspond to the
third degree. There is thus an unclarity with regard to the second degree; it is
precisely here that the transition takes place from motion (quantitative processes) to
consciousness (where different qualities of sense come to correspond to the
different quantities).

\textsuperscript{49}) P.~244. By his denial of necessary connection between
phenomena Malebranche is a forerunner of Hume. Perhaps Hume even got
motives for his theory of causation from Malebranche, whom he (as can be seen from his
\textit{Treatise,} I, 3, 14; 4, 5) studied eagerly. \emph{Mario}
\emph{Novaro} has
% --- p. 518 ---
% print: „p“ (p. 518) (misprint)
\opage{518}in his work \textit{Die Philosophie des Nicolaus Malebranche} (Berlin 1893, p.
44---50) drawn an instructive parallel between the theories of causation of Malebranche and of
Hume. --- Geulincx's philosophy too would present parallels to
Hume; but Hume hardly knew it.

\textsuperscript{50}) P.~256. \textit{Vita Thomæ Hobbes.} [Autore Rd. B. i.e.
Richard Blackbourne]. 1681, p. 14 f. Cf. Telesio's doctrine of sense perception
(above p 93). --- In his \textit{Vita carmine expressa,} p. 119 Hobbes
describes how, after long brooding over the nature of things, he
found out that there was only one single real thing [motion] in the world, although it
was ``falsified'' (sic) in many ways. --- F. Tönnies, whose energetic research in
most recent times has thrown so much light on Hobbes and his philosophy (see his
\textit{Anmerkungen über die Philosophie des Hobbes.} Vierteljahrsschrift für
wissenschaftliche Philosophie. III---V), has found a manuscript that
contains a treatise by Hobbes which, by its content, must have been composed
between the moment when the significance of the deductive method and then of motion
dawned on him and the moment when the subjectivity of the qualities of sense
dawned on him. This treatise, which is of interest with regard to the
historical development of the principle of the subjectivity of the qualities of sense,
Tönnies has printed in his edition of Hobbes's \textit{Elements of Law} (Oxford 1888).
--- Hobbes maintains that as early as 1630 [thus before he came to know Galilei]
he had held the conviction of the subjectivity of the qualities of sense. Cf.
\emph{Tönnies's} monograph on Hobbes \textit{(Hobbes' Leben und Lehre.}
Stuttgart 1896. p. 15).

\textsuperscript{51}) P.~261. Cf. Hobbes's treatise \textit{Of Liberty and
Necessity.} 3. ed. London 1685, p. 314, where it is said that as regards the definitions
of spontaneity, deliberation, will, inclination, drive, freedom, ``no other proof can
be given than every man's own experience when he
reflects on himself (by reflection on himself) and remembers what he himself
means when he says that an action is spontaneous'' etc.

\textsuperscript{52}) P.~262. In \textit{De Corpore,} IX, 9 Hobbes derives the
proposition that all change (qualitative change too) is motion from
the causal principle and the principle of inertia. --- His ``proof'' of the causal principle (Of
Lib. and Necess., p. 315) is as follows: ``If something had no cause, it could
just as well begin to come into being at the one moment as at the other; --- there
must then be a cause why it comes into being precisely at this moment!'' That here
precisely what was to be proved is presupposed, Hume has already shown. --- An
analogy to this is formed by his proof of the principle of inertia (De corpore, VIII, 10):
if a body at rest were surrounded by empty space, there would be no
reason why it should move more in the one direction than in the other, and
it would thus not move at all unless an external cause were added. Here
it is obviously presupposed that there are no ``inner'' causes. --- Possibly
this proof of the principle of inertia stems from Galilei. See his ``Dialoger over
Verdenssystemerne.'' 1st Day. (Strauss's German translation p. 21).

% --- p. 519 ---
\opage{519}\textsuperscript{53}) P.~264. Hobbes therefore really has no reason to
distinguish between definition and hypothesis. He says (De Corp., dedic.) that in
his logic, his Philosophia prima and his geometrical doctrine of motion he proceeds from
definitions, but in his physics from ``not unreasonable hypotheses.'' But those
definitions too are hypotheses. --- Hobbes requires, for the full understanding of a
phenomenon, the demonstration of a continuous progression from cause to effect. This
continua progressio (De corpore, IX, 6) recalls Bacon's latens processus
continuatus (Nov. org. II, 5---7). I do not consider it improbable that
Bacon's doctrine of the continuous process may have come before Hobbes's mind
when he had been led by another way to the idea that all change was motion. He
made the principle of his deduction what in Bacon was to be the last
result of numerous inductions. --- Likewise it is not improbable that
the name Philosophia prima for the second part of De corpore is due to Bacon, who
(De augm. III, 1) designates by this name the science of the general
fundamental propositions that hold for all domains.

\textsuperscript{54}) P.~284. A. D. \emph{Jørgensen} gives, in my view,
too lurid a picture of Hobbes's political theory, especially in his comparison between
Hobbes and Bishop Vandal. \textit{(Peter Schumacher Griffenfeldt,} I, København
1893, p. 218 f.). The moral limitation of the prince's physical right is found no
less in Hobbes than in the Lutheran theologian, and in Hobbes moreover with a
grounding that makes absolute sovereignty a means, not an end.
Cf. e.g. \textit{De cive} XIII, 3: ``The state is instituted for the sake of the
citizens'' (Civitas civium causa instituta est). --- In the older edition of
\textit{Leviathan} (ed. 1651, p. 193) the hope of influencing princes is expressed
somewhat more strongly than in the later one (ed. 1670, p. 172).

\textsuperscript{55}) P.~286. \emph{Freudenthal} has (Archiv für Gesch. de
Philos. VI, p. 191 ff., 380 ff.) brought forward Lord Brooke's work and shown the
interest that attaches to it.

\textsuperscript{56}) P.~286. On Culverwel see M. M. \emph{Curtis}: \textit{An
Outline of Locke's Ethical Philosophy.} Leipzig 1890, p. 9---18.

\textsuperscript{57}) P.~293. \emph{Colerus} \textit{(La vie de B. de Spinoza,}
tirée des écrits de ce fameux philosophe et du témoignage de plusieurs
personnes dignes de foi, qui l'ont connu particulièrement. A la Haye 1706, p.
14) regards Spinoza merely as Descartes's disciple in philosophy. \emph{Leibniz}
\textit{(Opera philos.} ed. Erdmann, p. 139) says of him that he has only
cultivated some seeds that Descartes had sown. This conception was long
dominant. \emph{Kuno} \emph{Fischer} and \emph{Falckenberg} hold fast to it in
their works on the history of modern philosophy. --- \emph{Joël} \textit{(Beiträge
zur Geschichte der Philosophie.} Breslau 1876), in opposition to this, emphasized
the great and lasting effect of Spinoza's studies of Jewish theology and
philosophy of religion. --- Chr. \emph{Sigwart} \textit{(Spinozas neuentdeckter
Tractat.} Gotha 1868) and \emph{Avenarius} \textit{(Ueber die beiden ersten
Phasen des Spinozischen Pantheismus.} Leipzig 1868) pointed --- on the basis
of the youthful treatise of Spinoza published by van \emph{Vloten} \textit{(Ad Benedicti de Spinoza opera
% --- p. 520 ---
% scan: „Frfaringen“ (p. 520)
% print: „Spinozichen“ (p. 520) (misprint)
\opage{520}quæ supersunt omnia supplementum,} Amstelodami 1862):
\textit{Kort Traktat om Gud, Mennesket og dets Lykke ---} to
the probability that Spinoza had been influenced by Giordano Bruno. ---
Finally \emph{Freudenthal} \textit{(Spinoza und die Scholastik.} In
the Festschrift for Zeller 1887) has shown to how high a degree Spinoza has used
scholastic concepts and proofs (especially in \textit{Cogitata metaphysica,} which
forms an appendix to Spinoza's exposition of the Cartesian philosophy; but
also in the Ethica). And the same scholar has later collected all the older biographies of
Spinoza and in general all documents that can throw light on his life and his
writings, in his book \textit{Die Lebensgeschichte Spinoza's in Quellenschriften,
Urkunden und nichtamtlichen Nachrichten.} Leipzig 1899. --- In my work
\textit{Spinozas Liv og Lære} (København 1877) I have given a popular
account of Spinoza and his philosophy. Later, repeated studies have led me
on single points to a different conception than in that work. I take
the opportunity to state that the picture used as title vignette in the
work mentioned, and which was taken from van Vloten's ``Supplementum,'' has since
been shown to represent --- not Spinoza, but one of his friends,
the philosopher and mathematician Tschirnhausen. A fine and, by all that can be
ascertained, genuine portrait of Spinoza is found in van Vloten and Land's new edition of
Spinoza's works.

\textsuperscript{58}) P.~298. I must also oppose A. D. \emph{Jørgensen's} reflections
(\textit{Nic}. \textit{Steensen,} p. 57) on Spinoza's relation to experience;
but on this point the section on Spinoza's
theory of knowledge will contain what is needed.

\textsuperscript{59}) P.~299. \textit{Studie zur Entwickelungsgeschichte des
Spinoza.} (Vierteljahrsschrift für wiss. Philos. VII) p. 161 ff., 334.

\textsuperscript{60}) P.~308. The first book of the ``Ethics'' develops the concept of substance and
the concept of God in a series of definitions, axioms and propositions. --- On
the connection between the concept of substance, the concept of God and the concept of nature cf.
Avenarius: ``Ueber die beiden ersten Phasen des Spinozischen Pantheismus,'' where
it is aptly shown that all three concepts, carried through consistently, meet in
one point in Spinoza. Yet Spinoza hardly kept the three currents of thought so
sharply apart from one another as they are kept in Avenarius's account. --- On
the relation between substance and modes one must note, besides the first book of the ``Ethics,'' Ep.
12 (in v. Vloten and Land's edition), where a distinction is drawn between the abstract and the
substantial conception, and Ep. 50, where it is declared that every determination is
a negation. --- The expressions natura naturans and natura naturata occur
already in Renaissance philosophers, mystics (Master Echardt) and scholastics.
According to \emph{Siebeck} (Archiv für Gesch. d. Philos. III, p. 370 ff.) they are said to
have their origin in the Greek \textit{φύσις} (as \textit{φύον} and as
\textit{φυόμενον}) and to have arisen through the translation into Latin of Greek
philosophical writings, probably in the thirteenth century. --- As regards
the exposition in the Ethics, the geometrical-deductive form is --- as already remarked --- only
a shell. In reality
% --- p. 521 ---
% print: „viss.“ (p. 521) (misprint)
\opage{521}it is a series of analyses that Spinoza undertakes, and by God or substance
he understands the comprehensive reality to which all phenomena belong, and
within which thought can therefore point them out. Cf. on this \emph{Harold}
\emph{Joachim}: \textit{A study of the Ethics of Spinoza.} Oxford 1901. p. 116
f. --- Cf. \emph{Descartes's} declaration (in Medit. VI) that by nature
in general (natura generaliter spectata) he understands either God himself or the connection of things
established by God (coordinatio rerum).

\textsuperscript{61}) P.~309. Cf., against this conception of Spinoza's concept of attribute maintained by
the elder \emph{Erdmann}: H. \emph{Bröchner}:
\textit{Benedict Spinoza.} København 1857, p. 47 ff. --- \emph{Mourly}
\emph{Vold} \textit{(Spinozas Erkendelsesteori.} Kristiania 1888, p. 242)
wrongly names Bröchner among those who interpret the attributes ``as predicates
necessary for our understanding, but accidental for God.'' Bröchner polemicizes
precisely against this conception.

\textsuperscript{62}) P.~311. Already in my work ``Spinozas Liv og Lære''
(1877) p. 100 I have pointed out this confusion in Spinoza. It has also been
brought forward by \emph{Windelband}: Geschichte der neueren Philosophie, I (1878),
p. 211 and by \emph{Tönnies}: Studie zur Entwickelungsgesch. des Spinoza.
(Vierteljahrssch. für wiss. Philos. 1883) p. 176 f.---\emph{Mourly} \emph{Vold}
(Spinozas Erkendelsesteori, p. 202) denies the confusion in Spinoza and
regards the doctrine of attributes as springing essentially from the endeavor to
ground a ``correspondence between idea and object.'' But when he concedes that
the doctrine of attributes in Spinoza also has a psychophysical significance, he must consistently
concede a confusion in Spinoza. For epistemology and psychophysics are two
different things, which is already seen from the fact that the ``objects'' are not merely
of a physical but also of a psychical kind; the problem of knowledge concerns, after all, both
the knowledge of the psychical and of the physical. --- The confusion in Spinoza is seen
clearly when one compares Eth.II, 7, Schol., where the relation between the concept of the circle
and the existing circle is used to illustrate the relation between
the attributes, with II, 17, Schol., where a distinction is drawn between the representation of
Peter (idea Petri) that corresponds to Peter's own body as its soul (mens
Petri), and the representation of Peter (idea Petri) that Paul has. The first
idea Petri has a psychophysical, the second an epistemological significance. Spinoza's
highly unfortunate usage of designating the soul (mens) as idea corporis has
favored the confusion. This usage stems from Aristotle by way of
Maimonides (see \emph{Hamelin}: \textit{Sur une des origines du Spinozisme.}
L'année philosophique. 1900. p. 24 f.), to whom Spinoza himself expressly
refers as regards the epistemological doctrine of identity, see
\textit{Eth.} II, 7 Schol. --- In German speculative philosophy (in Schelling
and Hegel) the confusion flourishes.

\textsuperscript{63}) P.~315. H. Morus: \textit{Demonstrationis duarum
propositionum, qvæ præcipuæ apud Spinozium} [sic] \textit{Atheismi sunt
columnæ, brevis solidaqve confutatio.} (Opera philosophica. Londini 1679, vol.
I, p. 619). --- On the different conceptions of Spinoza's concept of God there is an
instructive treatise by J. H. Löwe \textit{(Ueber Spinozas Gottesbegriff und
dessen Schicksale.} Appendix to
% --- p. 522 ---
% scan: „Tanke.“ (p. 522)
% print: „\emph{Erneste}“ (p. 522) (misprint)
% scan: „Pétit“ (p. 522)
\opage{522}Löwe's book: Die Philosophie Fichtes. Stuttgart 1862), which, however, does not mention More's
characteristic interpretation.

\textsuperscript{64}) P.~315. Cf. on this question \emph{Ed}.
\emph{Zeller's} remarks in Vierteljahrsschrift für wissenschaftliche
Philosophie, I, p. 285 f.

\textsuperscript{65}) P.~320. In Eth. II, 18 only the law now called
the law of contiguity is mentioned. But the law of similarity is presupposed in Eth. III, 27 and is named in Tract.
theol. polit. cap. 4 as an example of a mental law of nature.

\textsuperscript{66}) P.~327. A fuller account of Spinoza's ethics than
I can give here is found in my work ``Spinozas Liv og Lære,'' p. 120---146.

\textsuperscript{67}) P.~329. When it is said in Eth. V.38, Schol. and 40, Coroll.
that it is the \textit{intellectus,} not the \textit{imaginatio,} that is eternal, it seems
that only those individuals who rise above the stage of imagination (sensuous
representation) are organs of the divine activity of thought, which
can no more disappear than motion can. A statement
in the ``short treatise'' (2nd part, preface, no. 15) also points this way, to the effect that the soul can become eternal
when through knowledge and love it unites itself with the absolute
substance. --- The thought we meet here in Spinoza often comes forth in
the history of thought. I cannot go into it more closely here, but must
confine myself to some literary references. Plato's Republic, VII, p. 534 C
(Hejse's trans. of the Republic, 2nd part, p. 188). --- \emph{Chrysippos} (Diog. Laërt.
VII, 157). --- Maimonides (see Joël: Zur Genesis der Lehre des Spinoza, p. 66
ff. and Hamelin in L'année philos. 1900. p. 26 f.). --- \emph{Salomon} \emph{Maimon}:
Lebensgeschichte. Von ihm selbst geschrieben. Berlin 1792. II, p. 178 f. ---
\emph{Goethe}: Gespräche mit Eckermann. 4 Febr. and 1 Sept. 1829. ---
\emph{Wilhelm} von \emph{Humboldt} (see Haym: W. v. Humboldt, p. 637 f.). --- J. G.
\emph{Fichte}: Die Thatsachen des Bewusstseins, Stuttgart und Tübingen
% scan: „Tühingen“ (p. 522)
1817, p. 197 f. --- C. H. \emph{Weisse}: Die philosophische Geheimlehre von der
Unsterblichkeit des menschlichen Individuums. Dresden 1834. --- \emph{Louis}
Lambert (see Ravaisson: La philosophie en France au 19. siècle, p. 223). ---
\emph{Ernest} \emph{Renan}: Feuilles détachées. p. 392 f.

\textsuperscript{68}) P.~337. See on this Ludwig \emph{Stein}: \textit{Leibniz und
Spinoza.} Ein Beitrag zur Entwickelungsgeschichte der Leibnizischen
Philosophie. Berlin 1890. (Especially ch. 4).

\textsuperscript{69}) P.~341. The treatise of 1680 has no heading.
\emph{Erdmann}, who first brought it forward from the library in Hannover, gave it (in
his edition of Leibniz's \textit{Opera philosophica,} 1840) the title: De vera
methodo philosophiæ et theologiæ and assigned it to 1690---91. That it must be
of earlier origin is shown by both internal and external criteria, especially
the comparison with ``Petit discours de métaphysiqve,'' which was worked out in 1685 and
sent to Arnauld the following year. Cf. on this \emph{Selver}: \textit{Der
Entwickelungsgang der Leibniz'schen Monadenlehre bis 1695.} (Philosophische
Studien herausg. von W. Wundt, III), p. 433. \emph{Ludwig} \emph{Stein}:
\textit{Leibniz und Spinoza,} p. 117 ff. --- Stein, in his excellent
account of the history of Leibniz's development, lays too great weight on the influence
the study of Plato had on Leibniz. It
% --- p. 523 ---
\opage{523}is admittedly very characteristic that Leibniz, in the years so important for his philosophical
maturing, occupies himself so much with Plato and, among other things, quotes
the well-known passage in the Phaedo on final causes no less than twelve times.
But it is nevertheless symptom rather than cause. The conviction of the
legitimacy of final causes stood firm for Leibniz from the outset; it
sprang from his religious presuppositions, and all through his youth he had
sought means of bringing it into harmony with his scientific
theories. Plato could bring him nothing new here. --- In particular I find it
an unnatural explanation when Stein derives Leibniz's proposition of the identity of
substance and force from Plato's doctrine (expressed in a single passage) of the ``ideas'' as
active forces. Leibniz had, after all, been occupied with the concepts of force
and striving ever since 1670, and it is from his mathematical-physical studies that he
carries these concepts over into his philosophy and uses them to bring
the concept of substance to life. --- When several writers designate the advance Leibniz
made in the year 1680 as a \textit{substantialization of force,} I believe
that it would be more correct to reverse the relation and speak of a
\textit{conversion of substance into force.} It was in reality a dissolution
of Descartes's and Spinoza's concept of substance that was brought about by the treatise of 1680.

\textsuperscript{70}) P.~350. Leibniz's ``Tout comme ici'' has the same source as
Holberg's ``Ligesaa hos os,'' namely the comedy Harlequin empereur de la lune
(Gherardi's Théatre italien, vol. I). See Nouveaux essais, IV, 16, 12 (Erdmann,
p. 391 f.): On diroit quasi qve c'est dans l'Empire de la lune de Harléquin
tout comme ici. --- Besides this passage one must note with regard to the law of analogy:
letter to Arnauld, Nov. 1686 (Gerhardt's edition, II, p. 75 f.). De ipsa
natura (Erdmann, p. 157). Nouv. Ess. I, 1 (Erdmann p. 205) and III, 6, 14
(Erdmann, p. 312). Statements in letters (Gerhardt, II, p. 270; IV, p. 343).

\textsuperscript{71}) P.~352. \emph{Eduard} \emph{Dillmann} \textit{(Neue
Darstellung der Leibnizschen Monadenlehre.} Leipzig 1891) seems to me, in his
account of the doctrine of monads, which is in many respects instructive and interesting, altogether
to overlook the great significance that the law of analogy has for the
subjective completion of the doctrine of monads. Dillmann regards the faculty of representation as
given from the outset in the concept of the monad and takes the concept of phenomenon in Leibniz merely in a subjective
sense (phenomenon for). This conception is already refuted by the fact,
conceded by Dillmann himself, that Leibniz without further grounding
assumes that the monad represents the universe from the standpoint of its body, and that
he supports the assumption that the monad represents the whole universe by the fact that
every body, by virtue of the law of continuity, is affected by every change in
any part whatever of the world. (Cf. Dillmann, p. 301 ff., 342 ff.). ---
On Dillmann's hypothesis it would be impossible to understand why Leibniz takes
so dismissive a stand toward Berkeley's ideas as soon as he hears of them.

\textsuperscript{72}) P.~356. On the different ways in which the relation between
% --- p. 524 ---
\opage{524}Spinoza and Leibniz has been conceived in the course of time, see the first chapter of L.
\emph{Stein's} ``Leibniz und Spinoza.'' --- E. \emph{Dillmann} finds a
fundamental agreement between the two systems, but he thinks at the same time that
Leibniz's doctrine of the relation between God and the world is unassailable, \textit{and} he
lays no weight on the passages where Leibniz distances himself from Spinoza. (Neue
Darstellung, p. 472 ff.). Dillmann lets himself be led by his great and justified
admiration for Leibniz into playing the apologist for obvious
self-contradictions and evident accommodations. --- An instructive investigation of
the relation between the two systems has been undertaken by \emph{Robert} \emph{Latta} in his
treatise \textit{On the relation between the philosophy of Spinoza and that
of Leibniz} (Mind. 1899).

\textsuperscript{73}) P.~363. On the difference between perception and appétit see
Monadologie § 15. --- Passions as pensées confuses: \textit{Réplique aux
reflexions de Bayle} (Erdmann p. 188 a), as tendances ou
% scan: „on“ (p. 524)
des modifications de tendances: \textit{Nouv. Ess.} II, 20, 9 (Erdmann, p. 249 a).

\textsuperscript{74}) P.~365. Cf. a treatise (without heading) which is
printed in Gerhardt's edition, VII, p. 300 ff., where it is first said that all
factual data must have their ground, since the creative will that manifests itself
in them is not arbitrary, but acts according to grounds (ratio), and then:
``It is thus established that all truths, even the most contingent, have an
a priori justification (probatio) or a ground why they are rather than are
not. And this is precisely what the common saying maintains, that nothing happens without
a cause (causa), or (seu) that nothing exists without a ground (ratio).''

\textsuperscript{75}) P.~369. The law of the effect of contrast Leibniz already uses in
a letter from the beginning of the seventies (Gerhardt's edition, I, p. 61) to defend
optimism. Later he develops it especially (as \textit{lex lætitiæ)} in
\textit{De rerum originatione} (Erdmann, p. 149 f.). This
aesthetic-psychological argument is of ancient origin; it is found already in
\emph{Plotinos}, and is repeated (remarkably enough) by \emph{Augustinus}. Modern, on
the other hand, is the emphasis on the infinity of existence. Leibniz remarks that
Augustine does not yet know la grandeur de la cité de Dieu \textit{(Théodicée}
§ 19). Cf. \textit{Causa dei asserta §} 57---58.

\textsuperscript{76}) P.~374. In the preface to the first edition of
\textit{Vernünftige Gedanken etc.} Wolff says: ``I had indeed at the outset
resolved to leave the question of the connection between soul and body wholly
undecided; but since, by the reasons adduced in chapter 2, contrary to my expectation,
I was quite naturally led to Herr v. Leibniz's pre-established harmony, I have
retained it and placed this profound discovery in such a light as it
has not yet received.'' --- In the preface to the 2nd edition he expresses himself more precisely on
the relation of his doctrine to Leibniz's. Leibniz, he says, combined idealism [the
unbroken connection of the mental phenomena] with materialism [the unbroken connection of the material
phenomena], without examining each of them more closely by itself. That
Wolff now thinks he has done, and his result is that ``the dualists can unite
the theory of the idealists and of the materialists.'' --- This is in reality
% --- p. 525 ---
\opage{525}a correct determination of the difference between Leibniz and Wolff on this point:
Leibniz embraces the identity hypothesis (though with a spiritualist modification),
and Wolff embraces dualism (though with the assumption, taken from the identity hypothesis,
of the unbroken connection of the mental and of the material phenomena each
by itself). --- Very many of the objections that are usually advanced against
the identity hypothesis hold for the Wolffian theory, to which the name
``duplicism,'' which does not fit the real identity hypothesis at all,
fits very well.

\textsuperscript{77}) P.~390. Locke's friend Molyneux explained the apparent
contradiction between the two propositions (of which the one is found Essay, IV, 3, 10,
the other Essay, IV, 10, 5) by saying that the first passage states that God could by
supernatural means endow matter with the faculty of thought, whereas the second
passage speaks of matter without such supernatural influence (letter to Locke,
22 Dec. 1692). Locke declares this interpretation to be quite correct (letter of
20 January 1693). \textit{(The Works of John Locke,} 9. ed, London 1794, IX, p.
293---303.)

\textsuperscript{78}) P.~394. Locke does not really set up this triad
formally. Where he speaks of the need to leave the state of nature
\textit{(Civil Government,} II § 124---126) he names legislative power,
impartial judges and power to execute the laws as the three things that are needed.
Later (§ 136) he insists on the necessity that the same power that gives the
laws should not itself judge, since that would open the way to arbitrariness. But when
he (ch. 12---13) sets up three powers of the state and examines the relation
between them, this triad consists of the legislative, the executive and the
federative power. By this last Locke means an authority that represents
the state outwardly, towards other societies, in relation to which it finds itself in
the state of nature. Now since Locke states that the executive and the federative power
had best be united in the same hands (§ 147---148), the difference between them really
falls away, and since in another connection he has laid great weight on the distinction
between legislative and judicial power, the triad does to that extent come out clearly
in him. --- In the doctrine of the division of the power of the state Locke has, moreover, Buchanan, Hooker
and Sidney as predecessors. Cf. O. \emph{Gierke}: Joh. Althusius, p. 157, 163 f.

\textsuperscript{79}) P.~415. In the Scholium after the Definitions there is talk of ``the
true, absolute and mathematical space'' (and likewise of time). ``People in
general (vulgus),'' it is said, ``conceive quantities, on the other hand, only in relation
to sensible things'' (ex relatione ad sensibilia). --- But at the end of
Definitio 8 the ``true, physical'' mode of consideration is set in opposition to the
\textit{mathematical:} vere et physice --- as opposed to mathematice tantum! --- To
this belongs also the fact that Newton took the center of the world to be at rest (Principia,
III, 10, cf. 12 Coroll.), although he grounded the assumption of absolute
space precisely on the fact that no body could be shown to be absolutely at rest.

\textsuperscript{80}) P.~439. \emph{Ed}. \emph{Grimm} \textit{(Zur Geschichte
des Erkenntnissproblems,}
% --- p. 526 ---
% print: „phil.).“, no opening parenthesis (p. 526) (misprint)
% scan: „u'existait“ (p. 526)
% print: „puisque“, the quotation „puisque ... détruire.«“ has no opening » (p. 526) (misprint)
\opage{526}Leipzig 1890, p. 571---586) makes an interesting comparison between Hume's
two works. --- I cannot agree with Grimm that Hume's disowning of his
youthful work should derive from his really having come to another
standpoint. The motive was surely the same as the one that made his Dialogues on
natural religion a posthumous work: he wanted to be left in peace by the
orthodox. Cf. \textit{Letters of David Hume to Strahan,} Oxford 1888, p. 289
f., 303---330.

% print: „S. 141“, the anchor is on p. 441 (p. 526) (misprint)
\textsuperscript{81}) P.~141. Only in a single place (Treatise, II, 3, 9) does
Hume state that feelings or affects, besides arising through experience of goods and
evils, can spring from ``a natural impulse or an instinct'' (natural
impulse or instinct), but he then at once declares this instinct to be ``altogether
inexplicable.'' As examples of such feelings he names the desire for revenge,
the wish for happiness for our friends, hunger and other bodily drives.

\textsuperscript{82}) P.~441. Cf. an interesting statement in a letter to
Hutcheson: ``I wish from my heart that I could avoid drawing the conclusion
that, since morality, according to your view, is determined merely by feeling, it concerns
only human nature and human life. This has often been
urged against you, and the consequences of it are very significant.''
\emph{Burton}: \textit{Life and Correspondence
% print: „Correspondance“ (p. 526) (misprint)
of David Hume,} Edinburgh 1846, I, p. 119.

\textsuperscript{83}) P.~466. Il est absolument nécessaire pour les princes et
pour les peuples, que l'idée d'un étre supréme créateur, gouverneur,
rémunérateur et vengeur soit profondément gravée dans les esprits. Art.
Athéisme in \textit{Dict. phil.).} At the end of this article it is said that
there are fewer atheists now than before, because the true philosophers now acknowledge
final causes. ``The priest proclaims God to children, and Newton proves him
to the learned.'' --- In one of Voltaire's poems (to the author of the book Les trois
imposteurs) occurs the well-known line: Si Dieu n'existait pas, il faudrait
l'inventer.

\textsuperscript{84}) P.~468. In \textit{Lettres sur les Anglais,} XIII it is said
(on the occasion of Socrates's belief in his daimonion): Il y a des gens à la
vérité qui prétendent qu'un homme qui se vantait
% scan: „vantaít“ (p. 526)
d'avoir un génie familier, était indubitablement un fou ou un fripon, mais ces
gens-là sont trop difficiles. --- In \textit{Essai sur les moeurs et l'esprit
des nations} (Tome II, Chap. 9) it is said that Christianity must surely be
divine, puisque dix-cept siècles de friponneries et d'imbécilités n'ont pu
le détruire.'' Shortly before, the expression insolente imbécilité was used of a
teller of legends. --- Art. Fanatisme in Dict. phil.: Ce sont d'ordinaire les
fripons qui conduisent les fanatiques. --- It was not only religious and
ecclesiastical figures that Voltaire's mockery failed to do justice to. But one sees that even old
Socrates had to suffer for it. Elsewhere it falls upon Spinoza and upon the
naturalist \emph{Maillet}, whose anticipations of the
% --- p. 527 ---
% print: „l'inègalitè“ (p. 527) (misprint)
\opage{527}hypothesis of evolution Voltaire derided. All by virtue of the principle that what he did not understand
was stupidity or fraud.

\textsuperscript{85}) P.~468. Cf. D. \emph{Fr}. \emph{Strauss}:
\textit{Voltaire,} 3. Aufl., p. 330 ff.

\textsuperscript{86}) P.~470. \emph{Gneist} \textit{(Das Selfgovernment in
England,} 3. Aufl., p. 944) remarks: ``The spokesman of the new doctrines [namely
the new political doctrines in France] had before his eyes not the English constitution but
Blackstone's `Institutions,' in which the historical course of development of the whole
and the intermediate structure of self-government are lacking. Precisely this made
the description intelligible to French eyes.'' A mistake has crept in here, since
Blackstone's work did not appear until 1765, whereas ``Esprit des lois'' appeared in 1748.
The relation is precisely the reverse of what Gneist states: it is Montesquieu's
theory that influences Blackstone and thereby also gains considerable influence on
the political development in England. Cf. on this F. C. \emph{Montague's}
introduction to his edition of Bentham's ``Fragment on Government.'' (Oxford 1891,
p. 68). Montague also makes the apt remark that Montesquieu, at
the sight of the continental governments' system of oppression, was doubtless led to
stress the division of power more strongly than accorded with the English constitution and
the English theories. --- In \textit{The Federalist} No. 47---51 the founders of the
constitution of the North American Union, \emph{Madison} and
\emph{Hamilton}, examine Montesquieu's doctrine of the division of power in an interesting way
and discuss in particular how it is to be arranged when account is taken of the
fact that the legislative authority has a constant tendency to appropriate
the executive power.

\textsuperscript{87}) P.~482. F. \emph{Papillon}: \textit{Histoire de la
philosophie moderne dans ses rapports avec le développement des sciences de la
nature,} Paris 1876, II, p. 194 makes Diderot's philosophy proceed directly from
Leibniz. Against this see \emph{Knud} \emph{Ipsen}: \textit{Diderot.} p. 206 f. and
210 (where it is doubtless rightly urged that the collection of excerpts and
notes found in his works under the title ``Éléments de physiologie''
proves in how high a degree Diderot is influenced directly by his
studies in natural science).

\textsuperscript{88}) P.~495. Rousseau develops the difference between amour de soi and amour propre
in \textit{Discours} sur \textit{l'inégalité} (note no. 12),
and later in the writing \textit{Rousseau juge de Jean Jacques} (London 1780, p. 20
f.). Cf. further on this distinction my book \textit{Jean Jacques
Rousseau og hans Filosofi} (Copenhagen 1896) p. 99. This book gives a fuller
account of Rousseau's life and thought than there was room for here in the
general history of philosophy.

\textsuperscript{89}) P.~495. Discours sur l'inégalité, Amsterdam 1755, p. 80.
\textit{Lettre à M. de Beaumont} (Petits chefs d'oeuvre. Paris 1859, p. 304
f.). --- Whereas this happy condition is depicted here as following directly upon
the most primitive, animal condition, Rousseau elsewhere (e.g. in the
letter to the Maréchale de Luxembourg, 20 January 1763) depicts a more advanced
culture which still bears the stamp of simplicity, but which is corrupted by the
% --- p. 528 ---
\opage{528}introduction of the manners and wants of a great civilized country. Such, in
Rousseau's view, was the culture of Switzerland in his time, and he therefore fights eagerly
against introducing French customs (such as comedy). This question brought Rousseau into
sharp conflict with Voltaire and gave occasion to his \textit{Lettre à d'Alembert.}

\textsuperscript{90}) P.~495. Cf. letter to Mlle. D. M., 7 May 1764: On ne
quitte pas sa tête comme son bonnet, et l'on ne revient pas plus à la
simplicité qu'à l'enfance; l'esprit une fois en effervescence y reste toujours,
et quiconqve a pensé, pensera toute sa vie. C'est-là le plus grand malheur de
l'état de réflexion etc.

\textsuperscript{91}) P.~499. Souvenez-vous toujours que
% print: „pue“ (p. 528) (misprint)
je n'enseigne point mon sentiment, je l'expose. \textit{Émile,} IV (éd. Paris
1851, p. 326). Je ne voulais pas philosopher avec vous, mais vous aider à
consulter votre coeur (p. 344). Je ne raisonnerai jamais sur la nature de Dieu,
que je n'y sois forcé par le sentiment de ses rapports avec moi (p. 327).

\textsuperscript{92}) P.~501. Cf., besides the third letter to Malesherbes,
also \textit{Confessions,} XII (éd. Paris 1864, p. 608): ``I find no
worthier homage to the Deity than the mute admiration which the contemplation of
its works calls forth, and which is not expressed in definite acts . . . . In
my room I pray more seldom and more drily; but at the sight of a beautiful
landscape I feel myself moved, without being able to say why. I have read that a
certain bishop, visiting his diocese, found an old woman whose whole prayer
was only to say O! and said to her: Good mother, always pray thus; your prayer
is worth more than ours. My prayer is of this better kind.''

\textsuperscript{93}) P.~503. \emph{Gierke}: \textit{Althusius,} p. 201.
\emph{Rousseau}: \textit{Lettres écrites de la montagne} (6th letter).

\textsuperscript{94}) P.~504. \textit{Contrat social,} III, 15. --- Cf.
\emph{John} \emph{Morley}: \textit{Rousseau,} London 1891, II, p. 166---168, and
my essay
% scan: „Afhandliug“ (p. 528)
on Hamilton in ``Mindre Arbejder.''

\textsuperscript{95}) P.~505. Cf. \textit{Lettres écrites de la montagne.}
Lettre VI (éd. Amsterdam 1764, p. 219): Je ne sors pas de la thése générale . . .
Je ne suis pas le seul qui discutant par abstraction des questions de
politique ait pu les traiter avec quelque hardiesse.

\hhchapter{Sixth Book}\opage{1}

\begin{center}\textsc{The Philosophy of the German Enlightenment and Lessing.}\end{center}

\bigskip

\section*{1.\quad Characterization of the Thought of the Enlightenment}

In the middle of the eighteenth century the Wolffian philosophy was the dominant one in
Germany. It took the place of the renewal of Aristotelian and scholastic philosophy for
which Melanchton had laid the foundation, and acquired great significance for German
intellectual development, since by its clarity and sobriety it was well suited to
popularization. In this respect an important work had already begun before Wolff,
the philosopher of law \textsc{Christian Thomasius} laying
great weight on breaking through the barriers, hitherto so fixed, between the learned and
laymen. Among other things he began to lecture in German and to publish
philosophical works in that language, something that aroused much offense, so that
the board of censors even sent back one of his works with the message that ``one
could not censor any writing in which philosophical matters are taught in
the German language.'' Thomasius on the whole worked much, both orally and in writing,
to promote a free and enlightened treatment of moral and social conditions
in wider circles. In him there was, beside the critical and practical
tendency of his nature, a mystical-religious tendency, which explains how he
could for a time work together with the Pietists, not merely because the orthodox were
common enemies. The Pietist tendency, which developed in Germany from the end of the seventeenth
century, worked in the service of spiritual
% --- p. 2 ---
\opage{2}liberation by leading back to the inner experiences of mental life from
external, authority-bound literalism. The traditional dogmatics and the
external ecclesiastical order were pushed aside for the subjective inwardness of the
single individual. In the religious domain work was thus being done for the
emancipation of the individual, whereas the state-churchdom of the seventeenth century had compelled
individuals to merge in common religious forms. Now, with
personal inwardness, individual differences too could come forward; they
began to arouse more interest than the confessional differences, and soon
value and interest were ascribed to them, even if they did not agree with the scheme of
the penitential struggle that Pietism had set up from the first. The universal
priesthood was asserted; the right of laymen had of course to be acknowledged, since the great things
were accomplished just as well --- if not better --- in lay souls as in orthodox
priestly souls that had all the dogmatic rubrics in order. Pietism led
back to the natural, the practical, the useful, in leading away from
literalism and dogmatic scholasticism. In this it was akin to the other
tendencies of the time --- even to the Wolffian philosophy, although for a time it appeared
as its bitter enemy. Wolff and his disciples wanted to popularize philosophy,
as Pietism wanted to popularize religion. And the two tendencies were united in good
accord after Wolff had victoriously asserted his position. A whole series of
eminent philosophers of Wolff's school belonged to the Pietist tendency and
worked at one and the same time in the service of rational enlightenment and of religious
interiorization.

But quite other influences too than those that stemmed from Germany's own
philosophical and religious movements made themselves felt in the origin of the
so-called Enlightenment. The English philosophy of experience became the object of
eager study. Christian Thomasius is already, in his conception of the philosophy of law,
strongly influenced by Locke, and in the younger Wolffians Locke's
influence is refracted with Wolff's, so that their philosophy finally becomes a
combination of the thoroughgoing rationalism that had been learned from Wolff and the
philosophy of experience that Locke had founded. The secret was that Wolff's
rationalism could really only
% --- p. 3 ---
% scan: „Kontrastvirkning.“ (p. 3)
\opage{3}lead to the construction of a series of rubrics, and that, the more complete this
system of rubrics gradually became, the more there was bound to arise a hunger and thirst for
a content of experience that could fill it. There showed itself here a similar
effect of contrast to the one that had set Pietism up against orthodoxy in the
religious domain. In the philosophical domain this
effect of contrast appears in the great interest that empirical psychology attracts.
Not speculative metaphysics, but psychology grounded on experience came
more and more to be regarded as the fundamental science. The science of mental life,
as observation teaches us to know it, became the foundation on which
the aesthetic, moral and religious problems were worked out. This became an
important turning point in the history of psychology, since it gained greater
independence and drew nearer to natural science. Wolff had still
ascribed greater worth to speculative (``rational'') psychology than to empirical.
This now became otherwise. One sought to take experience as the foundation and only
later to examine how far one could get by starting from it. The most
eminent of the representatives of the philosophy of the Enlightenment, \textsc{Johann Nicolas
Tetens,} expresses this in a very clear way (in the preface to his
\textit{Philosophische Versuche über die menschliche Natur und ihre
Entwickelung.} Leipzig 1777. I. p. XIII): ``One ought not to begin the investigation
of the soul with metaphysical analyses, but only end with them. The
psychological analysis must come first. Once it has been brought about, the
metaphysical analysis, which consists only in the investigation of a few fundamental faculties and
modes of action, can very quickly be brought as far as it can go at all. If, on the
other hand, that empirical knowledge of the fundamental faculties is lacking, it is fruitless to
try to explain them from an organization that is to such a degree unknown to us.
To this is added, moreover, that however far one advances in metaphysical
psychology, the correctness of its propositions must nevertheless always be tested by means of
observations.'' \textsc{Kant} had already earlier expressed himself in a similar direction
\textit{(Nachricht von der Einrichtung seiner Vorlesungen in dem
Winterhalbjahre von 1765---66).} He asserts the necessity in philosophy of
proceeding analytically, not constructively, and
% --- p. 4 ---
\opage{4}what matters is then first and foremost a foundation of experience. He therefore begins his
philosophical course with empirical psychology, in which nothing can yet be
learned about the nature of the soul, indeed it cannot even be decided whether a soul exists!

It is this dominant interest in empirical psychology that, not least, gives
the German philosophy of the Enlightenment its peculiar stamp. Within this common
stamp manifold nuances appear, which, however, we cannot go into more closely
here. In the first volume of his \textit{Geschichte der neueren deutschen
Psychologie} (Berlin 1894) \textsc{Max Dessoir} has given a detailed
account of the way in which the psychological problems were treated by
the investigators of this time. Here we can dwell only on what has significance for
the general history of philosophy\textsuperscript{1}).

The psychology of the period of the Enlightenment is grounded first and foremost on Leibniz's thought
of the difference between obscurity and clarity as the fundamental difference in
mental life, and of representations as the elements of mental life. For the deeper-lying
motives and hints in Leibniz's psychology there was no eye.
It was the real period of splendor of rationalism. Enlightenment of the understanding was
the watchword, and everything in mental life that was not at once transparent was
conceived as a chaos of obscure representations. A practical consequence of this
intellectualist psychology was that people looked forward to the future with great confidence:
only light, and all will be well! A turning point came when it was recognized
that mental life has other elements than the intellectual. English psychology
from Shaftesbury and Hutcheson onward had clearly recognized this. Rousseau, whose
influence on the German development was extraordinarily great, had with
enthusiasm pleaded the cause of feeling and inveighed against the overvaluation of intelligence. And
finally Pietism had already worked in this direction. The period of rationalism
was succeeded by that of sentimentalism. The word ``sentimental'' dates from the
eighteenth century; it seems to have been formed by the English novelist Sterne
and was (at Lessing's suggestion) rendered in German by ``empfindsam.'' It was
in the endeavor to develop an aesthetic theory that the
peculiarity of feeling as an independent side of the life of consciousness was first asserted. J. G.
% --- p. 5 ---
\opage{5}SULZER (in essays in the publications of the Berlin Academy from the years 1751---52) and
MOSES MENDELSSOHN \textit{(Briefe über die Empfindungen} 1755) became aware, in their
investigations of aesthetic feeling, that here there was an
immediate and positive side of mental life which did not come into its own by
being depicted as a chaos of obscure representations that, on account of our
imperfection, were hindered from forming themselves into full clarity; according to Leibniz's and
Wolff's psychology feeling was only obscure, inhibited representation. The Wolffian
\textsc{A. G. Baumgarten} (\textit{Aesthetica} 1750) had been the first to use the word
aesthetics in the modern sense: the doctrine of the beautiful; but, true to his system,
he conceived aesthetics as the doctrine that set up rules for obscure
representing, thus for the lower part of the cognitive faculty, just as logic gives
rules for clear representing, thus for the higher part of the cognitive faculty.
The great interest in the inner events of mental life and in poetry and art
that was awakened in Germany in the middle of the century was bound to give birth to the need of a new
psychology, one that gave the life of feeling a positive and independent position in the
mental world. Mendelssohn shows very rightly (Brief IV. Philos. Schriften.
Verbesserte Auflage. Berlin 1771. I. p. 22) that if Baumgarten's conception were
right, the feeling for the beautiful would have to fall away with the advance of enlightenment,
and the higher beings, who are in possession of greater mental clarity, would then
be able with justice to complain of ``the wretched advantage that closes to them the
source of joy with which the lower beings are so richly provided.''
Characteristic, that precisely so pronounced a representative of the philosophy of the Enlightenment
should come to make this reflection! It is in the very interest of enlightenment that
he demands that the distinction between obscurity and clarity must not be the
only one to be made in mental life. The obscure --- he shows --- has in and
of itself nothing to do with pleasure and pain. He finds the condition of the feeling of pleasure
in an agreement between the manifold that makes itself felt in
the soul (or, in the case of sensual pleasure, in the nervous system); but
the feeling of pleasure itself is a positive force in our soul, not an inhibited state. In a
later work (\textit{Morgenstunden} 1786)
% --- p. 6 ---
\opage{6}Mendelssohn describes feeling as a faculty of valuation (Billigungsvermögen) and has thereby
pointed aptly to the important function that this side of the life of consciousness
performs\textsuperscript{2}). --- In his work \textit{Ueber die Deutlichkeit der
Grundsätze der natürlichen Theologie und Moral} (1762) Kant lays great weight
on the difference between cognition and feeling that Sulzer and Mendelssohn had
impressed upon us. ``Only in our day,'' he says (IV, 2), ``has one begun to see
that the faculty of perceiving the true is cognition, the faculty of feeling the good
is feeling, and that they must not be confused with one another.'' Kant is in this not only
influenced by his German predecessors, but by Hutcheson and Hume, and most of all by
Rousseau. --- But the decisive step was taken by TETENS with his
distinction between sensation (Empfindung) and feeling (Gefühl), which had hitherto
been used synonymously. ``Feelings,'' he says (Philos. Versuche. I. p. 168), ``mean,
in contrast to sensations, merely that a change or an impression in us and
upon us is felt, without our knowing, through this impression, the object that has brought
it about. Sensation, on the other hand, points to an object which, by means of the
sensible impression, we notice and, as it were, find present in us.'' Yet the two elements stand
so near one another that Tetens --- not to the advantage of clarity --- will use
the word feeling as a common designation for them both. He opposes Leibniz and
Wolff, who called all the elements of mental life representations, and wants this
word (in accordance with Hume's usage) restricted to denoting
reproductions. The faculty of forming and combining representations he calls
understanding, and his psychology then leads him to a tripartition: feeling, understanding and
will, such that the last two faculties denote the life of consciousness from the active side,
the first from the passive side. From Tetens this psychological tripartition
came to Kant, except that the latter carried out the distinction between
sensation and feeling more consistently. --- As to the significance that can reasonably be ascribed to
such psychological distinctions, people at that time were not clear. They were
inclined to construct a special mental faculty for each new psychological
distinction they found, and psychological research knew only by way of exception
higher tasks than mere description and classification. The important foundation
% --- p. 7 ---
\opage{7}for an explanatory psychology, which had been created by the doctrine of association of Spinoza and the English
investigators, was as good as not used. For all that, the psychology of the period of the Enlightenment
has had great significance in sharpening the sense for
self-observation, and it marks an important and lasting advance by its
recognition of feeling as an independent side of the life of consciousness.

Whereas the strong movement of feeling that was awakened in the middle of the century became in
France a womb of revolutionary thoughts, in Germany, where
both the sense for and the need of occupying oneself with public affairs were far
smaller, it found an outlet partly through psychological study, partly through artistic
production in the new tendency inaugurated by Herder and Goethe. It was the
intellectual and the aesthetic interests that stood in the front line.
It is therefore characteristic that the empirical psychology of the time lays so little
weight on the will, the active side of the life of consciousness. Everything turns on enlightenment and
on feeling. In deeper minds, however, a want is felt here too. \textsc{Friedrich
Heinrich Jacobi}, whose sentimentalism bears the stamp of the time, although --- as will
be described in a later connection --- as a philosopher he stands in sharp opposition
to the men of the Enlightenment, has in his first works spoken of the unhappiness
of a life of feeling that is cut off from the natural connection with action.
After an intimation that modern political conditions gave no possibility for
great feelings and characters to have effects outward, it is said in Jacobi's dialogue
\textit{Der Kunstgarten} (1779): ``Alas, the soul is little helped by feelings and
thoughts that have not proceeded from action and do not again aim at action . . .
Our most glorious knowledge serves us in the end only for idle contemplation, our
most exalted feelings only for solitary, barren enjoyment.'' It was the time of beautiful
souls and noble hearts; people believed themselves capable of the highest; there was
fermenting and roaring; there was ``Sturm und Drang''; the immediate need of the heart
was set against all reason, all rule and all convention, the original force and
simplicity of nature, which people thought they had found again, against the forms of culture and society;
chaos became the highest, and the capacity to produce new forms created from within
stirred really only in the poetic domain. This
% --- p. 8 ---
\opage{8}period of ferment, in which feeling determined representations, whereas the philosophy of the Enlightenment
had from the first asserted the reverse relation as the only possible one, was like
a confirmation by experience of the new psychology's doctrine of the independence of
feeling. It was the breakthrough of Romanticism in the midst of the camp of the Enlightenment. Through
many successive forms it dominated literature from now on and gave rebirth to human
imagination after the long intellectual labor. And, as will
appear, this whole artistic renaissance worked back upon the
philosophical development and gave it, at an important point of its history, a
fateful direction. ---

The psychological interest of the philosophy of the Enlightenment thus led it to its
limit. But in the classical time of the Enlightenment and in its typical representatives
this limitation was not felt. People thought themselves sufficiently equipped with
reason to be able in any case to be sure of going the right way,
even if they did not think they had gone the way to its end. An enlightened man grants
his descendants too that they will advance in enlightenment, and from the necessity of this
he does not draw the consequence that in himself there must still be found a good deal of
obscurity. In any case --- so it was reasoned --- what is needed for
blessedness our reason can perceive. But to this belonged, it was thought, first
and foremost faith in God and immortality; otherwise one could not feel
secure. In an infinity of expositions people took up and carried out \textit{the
``natural religion,''} which English and French writers had taught. But the
polemical relation in which natural religion was placed in France to
positive religion came out only in single cases in Germany. Protestant
theology was more elastic than Catholic. The Church and the
theological faculties were for a large part filled with Wolffians, who did not
acknowledge anything as revelation unless it satisfied the demands of reason,
but who at the same time thought, from the conviction of their hearts too, that they could establish
that the content of the biblical writings agreed with reason throughout. This
\textit{ecclesiastical rationalism} thus laid weight on a natural interpretation
of the miraculous content of the Bible, because it started from the assumption that Christianity must
agree with the
% --- p. 9 ---
\opage{9}religion of reason, indeed really was nothing but a historical proclamation of it.
Thus the reason that had been gathered from the experience and thinking of the preceding age
could be spread through the ecclesiastical organs over the whole
people. The Church became an organ of the Enlightenment with all its good and weak sides.
An important work of education was done in this way. Yet it was
