not everyone in whom natural and positive religion could be reconciled in so easy a
way. In this time of individualism, when so many different
motives were refracted in men's consciousness, the religious development of individuals had to
take the most different directions. A remarkable example of a course of development
from orthodoxy through Pietism to rationalism and from there to a position that
may recall the one Lessing, Herder and Schleiermacher later took has been
described by \textsc{Joh. Chr. Edelmann} (1698 --- 1767) in his autobiography
(edited by Klose, Berlin 1849). The literalism and externality of the orthodox drove
him over into Pietism, and he came into intercourse with sectarians and prophets. But
their hatred of reason and their lust for domination angered him, and in his anguish he then found out
that at the beginning of the Gospel of John one should not translate ``The \textit{Word}
was God,'' but ``\textit{Reason} (Logos) was God!'' If reason is God,
religion can contain nothing contrary to reason: with this the transition had been made from
Pietism to rationalism. But from the usual rationalism he parted
again when he read Spinoza's proposition that God is the \textit{immanent,
inner} cause of things, not their \textit{external} cause. His faith now became that God is the eternal
being in all things, inwardly one with every being. All that is true and
good in the world is God. The world is eternal. Christ was a man who led
men nearer to God by redeeming them from the false notions of
God and teaching them mutual love as the highest. The priests brought him down,
because they thought he wanted to overthrow their power, although he (like later
Edelmann and all his true followers) referred the rabble to the priests. The
Last Day breaks forth in every man who awakens from the slumber of
error. --- Edelmann thought that with the help of historical criticism and symbolic
interpretation the true religiousness could be found in the biblical writings. For
% --- p. 10 ---
\opage{10}\textsc{Hermann} \textsc{Samuel Reimarus} (1694---1768), one of the most zealous
champions of ``the truths of natural religion'' against materialists and other
ungodly men, the matter stood otherwise. Just as convinced as he
was that the purposiveness in nature (particularly the instincts of animals, on which
he wrote a special work) points to the origin of the world from a wise and
good God, and that in another life better and more lasting provision is made for human
blessedness than could be made in the present life, --- just as
convinced was he that the content of the biblical writings conflicted with the reason
and morality that natural religion enjoins. But this last conviction
he thought he must keep to himself. In all quietness he had sought to clarify
his thoughts on the biblical history and the biblical writings, and had worked out a
work which he called \textit{Apologie für die vernünftigen Verehrer Gottes,} and
in which he subjected the biblical literature to a sharp and dismembering
criticism from a historical, a scientific and a moral point of view alike.
Touching is the reason he gives for not publishing this work: he
fears that orthodox fanatics would rob him of the love of his wife and children
or else stir up a persecution that might fall upon them. ``The
reverend gentlemen,'' he says, ``must believe that an honest man causes his mind no
small torment when he must dissemble his whole life through.'' No one suspected what
the Hamburg professor, who had so finely conducted proofs both of God and of
immortality, had lying in his desk. \textsc{Lessing,} who through Reimarus's
family had obtained access to the manuscript after the author's death, published
fragments of it, declaring it to be a writing found in the library at
Wolfenbüttel. Later \textsc{David Strauss} (\textit{H.S}.
\textit{Reimarus und seine Schutzschrift.} Leipzig 1862) has given an abstract of
the whole work. What interests us here is especially Reimarus's general position.
Natural religion is enough for him; a revelation is therefore superfluous. But it
is moreover physically and morally impossible. God cannot by miracles break into his
own work, and he cannot, by revelations that are not imparted to all, and
that not all can even come to know, favor some above others.
Most of all, for Reimarus,
% --- p. 11 ---
\opage{11}the doctrine of the eternity of the punishments of hell conflicted with the true notions of God, and it
was this point that had first aroused his offense. Since, moreover, many
details in the biblical narratives aroused his misgivings, it is a
purely negative result that Reimarus gets out of his criticism. The only explanation
he could give of the origin of these narratives was that they were due to deceit on
the part of the Jewish priests and the apostles. The German professor's thorough research
thus led him to the same result to which a more light-footed reasoning had
led Voltaire. If it is not revelation, it is fraud: that is a
dilemma on which from this time many orthodox and freethinkers agreed from the bottom of their
hearts, and to which the religious debate is still often brought
back, as if since the time of Reimarus and Voltaire no new
points of view in the philosophy of religion had come forward.

More peaceably the relation between natural and positive religion took shape for
\textsc{Moses Mendelssohn} (1729 ---1786), who gave the most popular
expositions of the doctrine of natural religion. He was a Jew from Dessau who
had followed his Talmud teacher to Berlin and --- like Spinoza in his time ---
had worked his way into Western European literature, led by the need of an
intellectual culture going further than Hebrew literature could provide.
This was bound up with all the greater difficulty since at that time
Jews were forbidden to learn the German language. The young man's energy overcame all
obstacles; he learned Latin and German, and Locke and Wolff became his
favorite authors. His task was to state in elegant German (of which he became
master enough) what Wolff and his disciples had developed in many-volumed books
in a long-winded and pedantic exposition. He worked his way up to an admired
position in German literature, became the friend of Lessing and Kant, and stands as a type
of the popular philosophy of the day. He did not separate himself from his fellow believers, but
fought with zeal to procure them a better social position. In his interesting
work \textit{Jerusalem oder Ueber religiöse Macht und Judenthum} (1783) he sought
to show how the right fundamental propositions for ordering the relation
between state and church must lead to a freer position for his
% --- p. 12 ---
\opage{12}fellow believers in civil respects. It was his view that Judaism had no
dogmas beyond the content of the religion of reason, but that the Jewish religion
consisted in a law valid for the Jewish people. And since he now thought he could furnish
proof of the immortality of the soul (\textit{Phädon} 1767) and of the existence of a personal God
(\textit{Morgenstunden} 1786), there was for him the most beautiful
agreement between philosophy and religion. His proof of
immortality he grounded partly on the fact that the capacity to think cannot be explained
as a product of material composition, and that the soul, since it is thus
immaterial, must be imperishable, --- partly on the fact that a being destined for perfection
will not be able to be stopped on its way. The existence of God he proves
partly by the ontological proof taken from Descartes, partly from the
purposiveness of nature. The last-named work (Morgenstunden) came out only after
Kant's ``Kritik der reinen Vernunft'' had heralded a quite new period in
the history of philosophy. Mendelssohn declares in his preface that he knows well that
the school to which he belongs, the one ``that perhaps ruled too high-handedly in
the first half of the century,'' is no longer in repute. Newer tendencies have
come forward, which his ill health has kept him from becoming more closely acquainted
with; but he expresses the hope that ``the all-crushing Kant,'' whose
profundity he admires, will ``build up in the same spirit in which he has torn down.''
He had had greater confidence on his philosophy's behalf when, nineteen years
earlier, he published the most celebrated of his writings, the one in which he tried to
let Socrates speak as he would speak if he appeared in our days. ``After
so many barbarous centuries,'' it is said here (in the ``Anhang''), ``in which
human reason has had to slave for superstition and tyranny,
philosophy has at last lived to see better days. All parts of human
knowledge have made considerable advances through fortunate observation of
nature. Our very soul we have by this way learned to know better. By a closer
observation of its effects and states several data have been established
from which, by a tested method, more important consequences too can be drawn. The
most important truths of natural religion have, through this improvement of philosophy,
attained an evidence
% --- p. 13 ---
% print: „Behandlig“ (p. 13) (misprint)
\opage{13}that eclipses all the knowledge of the ancients.'' One understands from this pronouncement why
he called Kant, after his ``critique of all speculative theology'' had
appeared, ``the all-crushing!''

There remain to be mentioned some interesting attempts that were made, within the philosophy of the
Enlightenment, at treating \textit{the problem of knowledge.} The
Wolffian philosophy was indeed the dominant one; it was its fundamental thoughts that people sought
to work into the general consciousness. But greater weight was laid on
experience and the necessity of taking in material, and people sought in various
ways to combine Locke's philosophy with Wolff's. From this arose an
\textit{eclecticism} which does not quite coincide with the popular philosophy proper,
which kept nearer to Wolff. The chief seat of eclecticism was
the University of Göttingen, and its chief representatives were \textsc{Feder} and
\textsc{Meiners}, whereas the popular philosophy had its chief seat in Berlin,
from which Mendelssohn's writings went out, and where \textsc{Nicolai's}
\textit{Allgemeine deutsche Bibliothek} and \textsc{Biester's} \textit{Berliner
Monatsschrift} spread the thoughts of the Enlightenment among the educated public. Only a
few thinkers felt the problem that arose from having to grant that both Locke
and Wolff were right, having to admit the necessity both of taking in material and of
working up this material according to reason's own laws. These thinkers belong among
Kant's nearest predecessors in the domain of epistemology. The Leipzig professor
\textsc{C. A. Crusius} \textit{(Entwurf der nothwendigen Vernunftwahrheiten.}
Leipzig 1745) showed that the difference between sense perception and thinking does not coincide
with the difference between obscure and clear representing: sense perception can
surely be altogether clear and distinct! This demonstration forms an analogue to Sulzer's
and Mendelssohn's demonstration that the feeling of pleasure and pain is something other and more
than obscure representing. It naturally led Crusius to lay greater weight
on experience than Wolff consistently could. He distinguished sharply between the
reasons that lead us to perceive something and the causes by which things in
reality come into being (grounds of knowledge and real grounds), a distinction
Wolff and the whole dogmatic philosophy had blurred. He also refutes
Wolff's attempt to derive the principle of causality from the fundamental proposition of contradiction. And
as the problem of the relation between
% --- p. 14 ---
\opage{14}thought and reality was thus sharpened, Crusius also had to dispute the
validity of the ontological proof of God's existence, which of course amounted to this, that
if God could be thought, he must also exist. --- Still nearer to the decisive problem came
\textsc{Joh. Heinrich Lambert}, an investigator known also as a natural scientist and mathematician.
In his work \textit{Neues Organon}
(Leipzig 1764) he enjoins the necessity of beginning with experience and
applying the analytic method. We cannot begin with construction, since what matters
first and foremost is to determine rightly the single concepts with which we
are to operate. An anatomy of concepts must first be carried out in Locke's
manner. But it is not enough to find the simple concepts that are
contained in our experience; we must also find in how many different
ways they can be combined with one another. Thereby a transition is made from analysis
to construction; from the mere setting up of concepts one passes over to
discovering the fundamental propositions and postulates that lie in them. This transition
Lambert regards as quite easy. If one only begins with the simplest concepts and
advances without skipping any possible combination, one will be able to
carry out the construction with full certainty. Lambert is, however, clear that what
can be reached in this way can only be forms, not any real content; and he
raises in a letter (3 Febr. 1766) to Kant, whose thoughts at this time were moving
in the same direction as Lambert's, the question: ``whether and how far knowledge
of the form of our knowledge leads to knowledge of its content?'' To that extent he harbors
doubt about the justification of philosophical constructions, and comes to touch the
decisive turning point without, however, going further into the real problem. But
Kant honored his predecessor so highly that he would have dedicated the ``Kritik
der reinen Vernunft'' to Lambert, had the latter not died before the work's publication. Lambert
still belongs to the secure dogmatism of the philosophy of the Enlightenment, since he did not see what
had already dawned on Kant early, that the transition from analytic to
constructive method presupposes conditions that entail a limitation in principle
of our knowledge (cf. Kant's letter to Lambert 31 Dec. 1765). ---
% --- p. 15 ---
\opage{15}

Closest of all to Kant's fundamental thought came the South Schleswiger \textsc{Joh. Nic. Tetens} (who, after having
worked as professor of philosophy and mathematics at Bützow and Kiel, held a series of
high administrative posts in Copenhagen, where he died in 1807);
but he too had himself been set going by the work of Kant in
which the critical philosopher's fundamental thought first came forward (the Dissertation of
1770). Tetens's ``Versuche über die menschliche Natur'' is, in both psychological and
epistemological respects, the most important philosophical work in Germany in the
period immediately preceding Kant's chief work. In the psychological respect
we have already shown its significance. In his doctrine of knowledge
Tetens takes as his foundation a thought the holding fast of which would perhaps have brought greater
clarity into Kant's philosophy: namely, that all conscious apprehension is
apprehension of a relation. By every act of attention we lift what we
observe out from its surroundings: ``The word: see! expresses at least this
much, that the object I observe is a particular thing by itself.'' Observation is
a distinguishing, an ``Auskennen.'' (I. p. 273). The next step is conscious
comparison. Here too, by the very act of thought, a relation (of
likeness or difference) is fixed between things. A special class of relations we have in space
and time, which (as Kant had already taught in the ``Dissertation'') are forms
under which our knowledge orders the material taken up in sensations. ``As Herr
Kant has remarked, we do not form the concept of time by abstraction from the representation
of the objects we sense, but our own acts of sense, which have their succession
and duration even if no object is sensed, furnish the material for the abstraction of
the concept of time.'' (I. p. 398, cf. 277). The last kind of relation is found in
the relation of dependence (the causal relation), and here Tetens seeks in an unclear
way to mediate between Hume and Wolff. Without experience, he says (I. p.
320), I would certainly not suppose that the occurrence of one phenomenon would be
followed by a certain definite other phenomenon; but --- he adds --- this
supposition I state in a judgment which my understanding cannot but pass, and
which is therefore more than custom or association of ideas, is a true thought, although it
goes before experience. With this, of course,
% --- p. 16 ---
\opage{16}Hume's problem is not answered; Tetens has not shown the possibility that judgments our
understanding passes with logical necessity can have validity for real
events. When Kant read Tetens's ``Versuche,'' which he valued highly, and
which (according to what Hamann relates in a letter) was always to be found on his table,
he had already found the thought that could carry epistemology further
on this point.

\section*{2.\quad Gotthold Ephraim Lessing}

It has appeared in the foregoing that the so-called Enlightenment at several
points points beyond itself. It has, no doubt, a certain inclination to think itself
complete and to look down pharisaically on the darkness of the past; but it is at the same time an age
that is rich in possibilities, and for Germany it became a time of transition to a
magnificent period of poetic and philosophical flowering. In the most eminent
mind of this period the feeling of belonging to a period of transition expresses itself
with particular vividness. Although LESSING stood in a relation of personal friendship with
Mendelssohn and Nicolai, a friendship in which the latter were by no means
merely the receiving party, he nevertheless did not find himself as satisfied with the Enlightenment
as they. He felt a stranger in his time. Unsatisfied by the given forms of the life of the spirit,
he laid, like Socrates, the weight on the subjective, personal side
of the endeavor after truth. The hunt, he said, is better than the catch. By this
stress on the personal feeling of craving and striving he is the child of his time;
but it also made it possible for him to understand other times and positions
better than the men of the Enlightenment and of sentimentalism were otherwise able to. The difference
between times and positions comes out most, of course, when one keeps to the
final results, whereas in the inner striving, the subjective forces that
have given birth to the results, greater kinship may be found. Lessing's historical eye
is connected with his favorite idea of eternal striving. And that his eye was to so
high a degree directed toward the future, with hope of what it would bring, is connected
still more clearly with this idea.
% --- p. 17 ---
\opage{17}

This is not the place to go into Lessing's significance as a poet and as an
aesthetic writer, although it might well be of interest to trace the
fundamental character of the great seeker in all the different domains in which he worked.
Nor do we go more closely into his biography here, since it does not contain
data that are of significance for understanding him as a philosopher of religion. He was
born at Kamenz in Lusatia in 1729, studied at Leipzig, lived later in Breslau, in
Berlin and in Hamburg, occupied with poetic and aesthetic works, until in
1770 he became librarian at Wolfenbüttel. From his youth he had busied himself with
philosophical studies and made drafts of philosophical essays. But only in
his Wolfenbüttel period did this side of his interests come into the foreground,
especially during the polemic in which he became involved as the publisher of fragments of
Reimarus's ``Apology'' (the Wolfenbüttel Fragments). Here he waged a literary battle
against narrow-minded orthodoxy which is unique for the superiority in
the art of exposition, learning and wealth of ideas that he displayed. He died in 1781.

Lessing was fully aware that the most important capacity in him was the capacity for
criticism. He lacked creative capacity. But he possessed two things of value that
distinguished him above most of his contemporaries. He had a living thirst for
genuine, original spiritual content, in religious, philosophical and aesthetic
respects alike. And he had historical sense and great capacity to appreciate what
the past had brought forth of original spiritual content.

His historical sense is perhaps what sets him in sharpest opposition
to his contemporaries. If neither orthodoxy, Pietism nor rationalism
satisfied him or stood before him as forms in which religious life
could develop in the future, it was because he had a clear eye for the historical character of all
positive religion. Instead of finding the most important
form of appearance of Christianity in the biblical writings, over whose interpretation
men contended, he pointed back to the life and the whole religious development and
tradition from which these writings have proceeded, and which make their
origin explicable to us. It was not mere tactics when Lessing thus
% --- p. 18 ---
\opage{18}(during his defense of the publication of the Wolfenbüttel Fragments) maintained that
Christianity did not stand and fall with the Bible. He asserted that Christianity was
older than the Bible, and that it was not on book learning, not on reports of
``spirit and power,'' but on ever living, present ``spirit and power'' that
the future of Christianity depended. \textit{(Ueber den Beweis des Geistes und der
Kraft).} He comes out here against the overvaluation of book learning and against the
theological tutelage that had become general in the Protestant
Church as a consequence of Luther's zealous reference to the Bible as the rule of
doctrine. He pointed out that if Christianity was to be preserved, it must
have other supports than those to which orthodoxy had hitherto clung. He had
in his time greeted the appearance of the Herrnhuters with joy, since in this movement he saw
a turning away from orthodox externality, an interiorization that set life
above the letter. Christianity, he maintains against his orthodox opponent
Goeze, is essentially a matter of the heart, of feeling, and the criticism of the historical and
philosophical proofs does not touch those who believe in simplicity.

Yet Lessing, not only in his letters but also in his writings, has stated clearly enough
that he did not himself remain standing at the consideration of the
Christian religion as the historically revealed highest truth indicated here. In the
\textit{Duplik,} in the \textit{Antigoeze,} in \textit{Nathan der Weise,} in the
\textit{Erziehung des Menschengeschlechts}
% print: „Menchengeschlechts“ (p. 18) (misprint)
and in the \textit{Gespräche über die Freimaurer} he develops a whole
theory in the philosophy of religion, which is not only highly remarkable for its time, but
which is still to this day well suited to awaken reflection. --- Lessing's
peculiarity was that he furnished friends and opponents alike with new
arguments. By virtue of his great love of truth and his clear eye he was
often able to find a force on his opponents' side which they themselves did not suspect. He
has therefore sometimes been claimed by the Christian side (while at
other times he has been accused of dishonesty by the same side!). The world (even
the so-called Christian part of it) is simply not used to one's
helping one's opponents. But this care to bring out everything that could
clear up the problems has nevertheless
% --- p. 19 ---
\opage{19}not prevented Lessing from developing his own ideas in their full extent.

The starting point for the exposition of these ideas is best taken from a famous
pronouncement (in the ``Duplik''): ``Not the truth of which a man is in possession,
but the sincere effort he has spent to get at the truth, constitutes
the worth of man. For not by the possession of truth, but by the search
for it, do man's powers expand, and in this alone consists his ever
growing perfection. Possession makes one calm, lazy, proud . . . . If God held
all truth enclosed in his right hand, and in his left the one, ever
living striving after truth, though with the addition that I should always and eternally
err, and if he said to me: choose! --- then I would humbly
throw myself upon his left hand and say: Father, give me this! Pure
truth is indeed for thee alone!'' --- These words were directed both at the
orthodox and at the philosophers of the Enlightenment, and both needed to hear them. There
might, however, seem to be something Tantalean in the eternal seeking, especially since Lessing is
willing to accept the condition that he shall always err. But one
must notice that Lessing speaks hypothetically. He \textit{conceives} of a choice
between eternal seeking and error on the one side and mere possession of
the truth on the other. But he is evidently conceiving of a case that
does not occur. This is seen not only from the linguistic form, but also from
the grounding of the assertion that the worth of man does not depend on the possession of
truth, but on ``the sincere effort'' he spends to acquire it.
This worth is conditioned, namely, by man's powers being \textit{expanded} by
the search. Such an expansion would, after all, be impossible if absolutely
no result were reached, only constant disappointment. Then paralysis and contraction would
be the consequence, not expansion. In and of itself eternal striving without any
result whatever is a self-contradiction. It is another matter that every result attained is only
provisional and becomes the starting point for new striving. And this is, as the
following will show, precisely Lessing's meaning.

His definite relation to positive religion
% --- p. 20 ---
\opage{20}Lessing had already stated in his essay ``on the proof of the spirit and of power,'' and he comes
back to it more than once in his later writings. Even if the
historical foundation of Christianity were ever so certain, historical truths would nevertheless --- he declares ---
be unable to prove anything here. How can a knowledge of the eternal connection of things be grounded on
special, historical facts? How can it be demanded that, on account of certain events
1800 years ago, I should transform all my representations? History is one thing,
philosophy another. ``This is the ugly, broad ditch which I cannot get across, however
often and however earnestly I have attempted the leap!'' Lessing holds to this, that
however it may stand with the origin of Christianity, it has
left its effects in the development. In a fragment headed \textit{Die
Religion Christi} he states that while it is difficult to decide whether
Christ was more than a man, it is certain that he was a man. Let
us then keep to the religion of Christ, to the religion that Christ himself had
as a man; the question of the Christian religion, of the truth of the Church's
doctrine, must then be left in abeyance.

The religion Lessing professes is not grounded on single supernatural
events, but on the great inner connection in nature and history. The
various positive religions are for him links in this connection, since he
regards them as stages in the spiritual development of humanity. Instead of
mocking or being angered at the positive religions, he would rather (as he says in
the preface to ``Erziehung des Menschengeschlechts'') see in them ``the course in
which the human mind could alone develop in each single place
and shall develop further.'' What education is for the single man,
revelation is for the human race. By revelation the race is led forward from
lower to higher stages\textsuperscript{3}). The people of Israel learned, through
the relation of obedience to its God, who stood before it as the mightiest of all
gods, to accustom itself to the notion of the unity of the Deity, long before a
rational concept of this unity was possible. And through promises of reward and punishment it was
trained to do good and shun evil. Only later, through
acquaintance with
% --- p. 21 ---
\opage{21}other, more advanced peoples (Chaldeans, Persians and Greeks), could more ideal
religious notions develop in it. The strict discipline it had to
go through was necessary in order that teachers for the whole of humanity could come forth from
its midst. Christ was the first who enjoined purity of heart
with a view not to temporal reward and punishment but to another life. But both the New
and the Old Testament are only the elementary books of the human race, at which it
cannot remain standing, although it ought not to leave them before their content has
been sufficiently drilled in, and although it may be beneficial that the pupil
takes his elementary book for the highest science. The advanced pupil who
impatiently turns the last page of the book must beware of awakening premature
unrest in his weaker fellow pupils. But on the other hand it can also
be harmful to hold the pupil too long to the elementary book; one thereby easily makes
him hair-splitting and superstitious. The truths of revelation must be
transformed into truths of reason if the human race is really to appropriate
them, and Lessing tries, by a symbolic interpretation of the dogmas of the Trinity and of the
Atonement, to show what truths may lie hidden in the
dogmatic formulas. --- Education must reach its goal. The time must come when
man does not need the conviction of another life as a motive for his
action, but does the good for its own sake. Then the new, eternal
gospel, the third age, of which the enthusiasts of the Middle Ages already spoke,
will have come! The coming of this future we must patiently await. Through small
steps and by roundabout ways development goes forward. In ``Gespräche über die Freimaurer''
it is said: ``The Freemason waits calmly for the rising of the sun and lets the candles burn
as long as they will and can. He will not put out the candles too early, lest
he should later be obliged to light the stumps again.'' --- For Lessing
the significance of religion was in the end decidedly ethical. It is an education to will
the good for the good's own sake. The most important thing in Christianity was for him
(as he stated in the little dialogue \textit{Das Testament Johannis)} the
heartfelt exhortation to love. In the ``Freemason Dialogues''
% --- p. 22 ---
% print: „gansks“ (p. 22) (misprint)
\opage{22}(perhaps the most beautiful and clearest expression of Lessing's religious and also of
his ethical and social views) he conceives of the Freemasons, of whom he here
gives an idealized account, as a free brotherhood that wants to abolish the
barriers between men that religion, nationality and rank have hitherto set up.

Shortly after Lessing's death it aroused great attention when JACOBI, in letters to
Mendelssohn \textit{(Briefe über die Lehre des Spinoza.} 1785), asserted that
Lessing had declared himself an adherent of Spinoza. Since Spinoza still, even for
the spokesmen of the Enlightenment, stood as the epitome of all ungodliness, it was no
wonder that the assertion aroused not only attention but also grief and offense
in several of Lessing's friends, especially Mendelssohn.

Jacobi (a kind of modern Herbert of Cherbury) had traveled to Wolfenbüttel to
visit Lessing and get help from him in refuting Spinoza's doctrine. On this
occasion he showed Lessing Goethe's poem ``Prometheus,'' of which he had a
copy. He handed him the poem with the words: ``You have given so much offense,
so you shall for once be offended yourself!'' When Lessing had read it, he said:
``I have not been offended. All this I have long known at first hand .
. . . The point of view from which the poem is written is the same as my own.
. . . . The orthodox concepts of the Deity are no longer valid for me; I cannot
use them. `\textit{Ἓν καὶ Πᾶν!}
(i.e., One and All!) I can do no other. That is what this poem too amounts to, and I
must confess that it pleases me greatly.'' Jacobi: ``Then you are quite
in agreement with Spinoza?'' Lessing: ``If I am to name myself after anyone, I know of no
other.'' Jacobi admits in the course of the conversation that he cannot refute Spinoza and
prove his faith in a personal God distinct from the world, but that he helps
himself out of the fix by a leap, a salto mortale from knowledge over into faith. After
a rather wordy exposition by Jacobi, in which the latter seeks to shine with
his (not in all respects thorough) knowledge of Spinoza, Lessing says:
``Your salto mortale does not seem so bad to me, and I understand
% --- p. 23 ---
\opage{23}how a man with his head in the right place can in this way leap out head first
in order to get from the spot. Take me along, if it can be done.'' Jacobi: ``If
you will only step onto the elastic spot, it goes of itself.''
Lessing: ``Even that would require a leap which I dare not entrust to
my old legs and my heavy head.''

This is the main course of the famous conversation (6 July 1780). But there came out in
its course some utterances of Lessing on single points that are of particular
interest. --- Lessing declares that he cannot accept a personal God standing outside
the world. He is inclined, on the other hand, to think of God as the soul of the
world. In agreement with this is the fact that in several philosophical fragments dating
from his younger years he developed the thought that there cannot be anything outside
God, since God, by thus having something outside himself, would become limited and
finite. He asserts an inner, immanent relation between God and the world and will not
think of God in analogy with a human personality. With the idea of a
personal Deity in unchangeable enjoyment of its supreme perfection he could
not reconcile himself. He connected with it, as he said to Jacobi, ``such a
notion of infinite tedium that he became anxious and ill at ease
over it.'' It was natural that a thinker for whom constant striving was the
highest could not put up with a God finished once and for all. This is, moreover,
one of the points which show that Lessing's adherence to Spinoza must not be taken
all too strictly. For from Spinoza's concept of God becoming and development were excluded.
--- Lessing next speaks out against ``the human prejudice of regarding thought
as the first and foremost and deriving everything from it, whereas everything, thought
included, depends on higher principles. Extension, motion and thought are
evidently grounded in a higher force, which is far from exhausted by them.'' Here
Lessing polemizes against the theology rampant particularly in the Enlightenment, which
builds its proof of God on the purposiveness of nature. The pronouncement agrees entirely
with Spinoza, in whom thought as well as
% --- p. 24 ---
\opage{24}extension are attributes of substance, which besides them has infinitely many
other attributes. During the following conversations, however, Lessing referred also to
Hume's ``Dialogues,'' in which a related line of thought occurs. --- Finally
Lessing asks for a purely natural explanation of everything. A leap out into the
supernatural he will not engage in. On this point too he points
back to Spinoza, of whom he had earlier said in a letter to Mendelssohn:
``Spinoza is the first who was led by his system to the possibility that
all the changes of the body could spring solely from its own mechanical
forces.'' (It would, however, be more correct to say that it was the thought of this
possibility that led Spinoza to his system.)

Mendelssohn wanted to explain the whole conversation as a piece of mental gymnastics on Lessing's part.
This is, however, an impossible explanation, even if Lessing may have thought that his
sentimental friend could profit from such gymnastics, and even if it would
be wrong to ascribe to Lessing all of Spinoza's opinions. Lessing did not
attach himself to any definite system, but a circle of thoughts can be shown
which were the leading ones in him, in any case in his private chamber. It was not
merely indignation that Spinoza had so long been treated ``like a dead dog''
that led Lessing to plead his cause. On the whole a growing
interest in the decried thinker can be traced. Jacobi saw in him the most
consistent form of pure philosophy. Enthusiasts like Edelmann and pious orthodox like Jacobi's young
friend \textsc{Thomas Wizenmann} felt sympathy with Spinoza in so far as they could not
reconcile their religious feeling with the thought of a God distinct from the
world. \textsc{Goethe's} artistic-naturalistic faith and \textsc{Herder's}
religious-naturalistic faith also attached themselves with enthusiasm to the ``One and
All'' that Lessing had proclaimed\textsuperscript{4}). There expressed itself, from
various positions, a need of a deeper world-view than the
philosophy of the Enlightenment and the popular theology could give. But this need could only
be satisfied by the philosophical way when a thorough
investigation of the nature
% --- p. 25 ---
\opage{25}and range of human knowledge had first been undertaken. An investigation of this kind was needed not only
for the sake of the problem of knowledge itself, but also for the sake of the religious problem.
The year after that conversation between Lessing and Jacobi, which threw so sharp a
light on the religious position of the foremost men of the time, had taken place,
and the same year in which Lessing died, \textsc{Kant's} \textit{Kritik} \textit{der
reinen Vernunft} appeared.

\begin{center}---\end{center}


% --- p. 26 ---
\hhchapter{Seventh Book}\opage{26}

\begin{center}\textsc{Immanuel Kant and the Critical Philosophy.}\end{center}

\bigskip

\section*{1.\quad Characterization and Biography}

Every great work of the spirit has its fate. Since it offers a wealth of
motives, it may at different times be quite different sides and qualities that
make it an object of appropriation and admiration, and the thought or the chief
motive that guided the work's author need not be the one that determines its
lasting significance. In the time that has passed since ``Kritik der reinen
Vernunft'' appeared, a new edition has come out about every tenth year, and to
this very day the work is studied to an extent and with a thoroughness like no
other philosophical work. On its contemporaries the effect came above all from
the overthrow of the proofs of the religious assumptions, together with the
energetic assertion of the sublimity of the moral law and the demonstration of
its intimate connection with the spiritual nature of man. For a narrower circle
it was the treatment of the problem of knowledge that stood in the first line.
But here again weight could be laid on different sides. One could stress the
assertion of the capacity of reason for knowledge independently of experience,
or the limitation of the validity of this knowledge to the world of experience.
One could lay the weight on the idealist side of the system, according to which
reason determines what reality is; and one could lay the weight on the realist
side, according to which the activity of
% --- p. 27 ---
\opage{27}reason acquires real significance only when it receives its material
from a source to which it cannot itself penetrate. Finally, the chief interest
may turn either on the psychological analysis of the nature and working of
consciousness and of knowledge, or on the consequences drawn from it concerning
the conditions and limitation of knowledge. All these different motives have
determined the influence of the system on the time that followed, so that now
one, now another has predominated. It is the task of historical inquiry to show
the mutual relation of these different motives in Kant's philosophy and within
his course of development. Perhaps it will then be possible to lead them all
back to one fundamental motive, which unites in itself the practical and the
theoretical interest, the speculative and the empirical tendency, the
psychological and the epistemological task, and which Kant himself has
designated as \textit{the self-knowledge of reason in scientific form}
(Prolegomena § 35).

In Kant's view, thinking about existence begins \textit{dogmatically,} i.e.
with an involuntary, often naive confidence in its own power and in the
validity of its presuppositions. It therefore believes that it can solve every
task, penetrate to the innermost essence of existence. It is the time of the
great systems. Later there comes a time when it turns out that these edifices
of thought do not reach to heaven, and that the builders are not agreed among
themselves about the plan. It is the time of doubt, of \textit{skepticism.}
People mock the vain attempts and the mutual contradictions, and console
themselves, now with resignation, now with blasé indifference, over the
apparently wholly negative result. It is a natural reaction against blind
dogmatism. --- Kant turns against both tendencies. He holds that there is a
task which both the dogmatist and the skeptic neglect: to examine the nature of
our mind itself, of our knowledge, in order to discover what forms and powers
we have at our disposal for understanding existence, and how far these forms
and powers can carry us. The very fundamental form of all our knowledge Kant
then found in the unity which all knowledge seeks to bring about. At all its
steps knowledge is a gathering, a combining of what is scattered. The simplest
sense-image comes about through a working together of many different
impressions --- and
% --- p. 28 ---
\opage{28}the same stamp of unity is found in the greatest system that thought
can reach in its highest flight. --- To this extent the dogmatic systems spring
from a real, human need. One wants to embrace everything in one unified image.
They are attempts to realize what knowledge at all its steps tends toward. But
Kant then goes on to show that knowledge is bound to experience, and that this
search for unity, when it ventures beyond the limits of experience, entangles
itself in contradictions and in any case can furnish no proof of the validity of
its results. It goes with thought (to use one of Kant's many apt images) as it
would go with the dove if, because it is so easy to fly in the air, it were to
believe that it would be still easier to fly in empty space. It is precisely
the resistance that bears it up --- but it also, to be sure, sets limits to the
motion. --- The skeptics do the dogmatic systems an injustice by merely
considering them in their fully finished form. One ought to go back to their
origin, to examine what human power and need it is that has led to them, and
to what conditions the use of this power and the satisfaction of this need are
subject. --- Through such self-knowledge Kant will free the human mind from its
own earlier works, which easily become obstructing barriers for it. But at the
same time, with a clearer insight into conditions and limits, he will work on
with the same power from which the works of the past sprang, and he thereby
prepares the way for an understanding of these works to which mere negation and
criticism could not lead. \textit{Kant has thereby set the whole of the human
sciences their program.} He himself, it is true, worked only at the solution of
special philosophical problems. But the point of view he adopted here has a
general significance --- for the study of religion, art, literature and
language as well as for the study of institutions and forms of society. The
relations are analogous everywhere, and the task is essentially the same:
through the study of the powers that produced the work of the past, to set them
free to do, with clearer understanding, the deed of the future. What matters is
the demonstration and preservation of continuity, while the metamorphosis of
the powers goes on. In its deepest ground it was this striving that was astir in
Kant's
% --- p. 29 ---
\opage{29}great and profound labor of thought, and with it his central position
in the history of modern thought is given, even after one has once and for all
abandoned a great many of his own favorite doctrines. ---

Kant's life offers nothing sensational, nothing interesting or piquant. It was
a quiet, sensible life devoted to research. He lived as a plain burgher, with
no small touch of pedantry and philistinism. But out of the deep inner ground of
this unassuming and inconspicuous outward life great thoughts grew up that
illuminate human knowledge and human life. And the feeling for the great and
sublime --- which is the kind of aesthetic feeling that Kant understood and
described best --- perhaps thrives best in narrow circumstances, if only one
can catch sight of the sky. We unfortunately lack material for a portrayal of
Kant's inner, personal development. Those of his biographers who stood nearest
to him, and who immediately after his death gave portrayals of his life and
character (Borowski, Jachmann and Wasianski), give chiefly outward details and
open to us no insight into the inner mental motives that made themselves felt
during his development. His surviving letters date mostly from his later years.
We are therefore obliged to construct his spiritual development for ourselves
out of his writings. But before we attempt to solve this task, we must dwell a
little on the main points of his life.

\textsc{Immanuel Kant} was born in Königsberg on 22 April 1724. His father was
a saddler of Scottish descent; the name was properly Cant, but the philosopher
changed the C to K, so that it should not be pronounced as S. Both parents were
capable and sound natures, whose pietist piety let them bear the adversities
of life with gentleness. Kant's mother in particular had influence on him. Her
pietism did not make her blind to the beauty and glory of nature, to which she
sought to open her son's eyes. Kant often spoke later with enthusiasm of his
parents, and the tendency toward interiorization and toward the subjective side
of life which was the distinguishing mark of pietism set its stamp on his later
development. The pietism of Königsberg was of a particularly gentle and humane
kind. Yet Kant also felt the
% --- p. 30 ---
\opage{30}shadow sides of pietism in the formalism and the spiritual constraint
it brought with it, especially in the school, where fixed hours of prayer and
compulsory customs bred hypocrisy and unnaturalness. These experiences too came
to have influence on Kant's later attitude to religion. In the school the
ancient languages were chiefly cultivated, and all his life Kant was a sound
Latinist, on whom a Latin quotation fitting the occasion did not fail of its
effect. From his sixteenth to his twenty-second year he studied the philosophy
of Wolff and the physics of Newton at the University of Königsberg. His teacher
in these subjects was \textsc{Martin Knutzen,} one of the most independent of
the Wolffians. Kant was indeed enrolled as a theological student, but attended
only a few theological lectures. His circumstances were straitened. He made his
way by private teaching and later, from his twenty-second year on, took posts as
tutor with various noble families in East Prussia. Although he did not himself
think he had been a capable teacher, he nevertheless imbued several of his
pupils with his deep feeling for freedom and human dignity; for it is hardly an
accident that several of Kant's former pupils took the lead in the abolition of
serfdom. (At a later point in his life Kant is said to have declared: ``My
bowels turn over within me when I think of the serfdom in our country''.) The
position of tutor in the great houses brought Kant an experience of the world
that his retired life would otherwise not have been able to procure him, and
made him the polished man of society that, on the testimony of many, he could
be. But these years were also those in which he began to gather the wealth of
thought and knowledge that he displayed as soon as he first appeared as a
university teacher and author. At the age of 31 he returned (1755) to
Königsberg. In the same year he appeared both as lecturer and as author; he had
published only a single small treatise (on a question of physics) before. His
lectures were partly popular, for larger circles, on physical geography and
empirical psychology, partly strictly philosophical. An enthusiastic portrayal
of Kant as a teacher of philosophy in his younger days has been given by
\textsc{Herder,} who from 1762 was his hearer for some years (in the second
volume of \textit{Briefe zur Beförderung der Humanität).} He himself has spoken
of the principles of his
% --- p. 31 ---
\opage{31}teaching in a prospectus from this period \textit{(Nachricht von der
Einrichtung seiner Vorlesungen in dem Winterhalbenjahre von 1765---1766).} He
lays the weight, first, on a good foundation of experience, so that the young
students should not begin to speculate too early, and secondly, on teaching his
hearers not a finished philosophy but \textit{to philosophize.} And this for
the reason that a finished philosophy does not exist. Already in the first
period of his development, which may be reckoned from 1755 to 1769, he has
decidedly broken with dogmatism. He is in philosophical motion. Characteristic
of this period is the independent criticism he directs against his teachers
Newton and Wolff. In one of his most brilliant works, \textit{Allgemeine
Naturgeschichte und Theorie des Himmels} (1755), he criticizes Newton's denial
that the present arrangement of the solar system could be explained by
mechanical laws of nature, and puts forward the famous hypothesis that our
present system of heavenly bodies has developed out of a rotating primordial
nebula. In the very fixed connection between all the elements of the universe,
to which the laws of nature bear witness, he found a proof that the whole
universe has its ultimate ground in an absolute, all-embracing being. In this
way he here united his scientific and his religious conception, while he already
now rejected the current proofs of the existence of God. In his work
\textit{Einzig möglicher Beweisgrund einer Demonstration des Daseins Gottes}
(1763) he has developed this standpoint. His confidence in Wolff's dogmatic
constructions he had lost. It became his conviction that philosophy must
proceed by the way of analysis in order to arrive at certain and clear concepts.
In a series of works from the years 1762---63 he has discussed this question.
It is perhaps most probable to place at this point the influence that Kant, by
his own statements, received partly from Hume, partly from Rousseau. As I shall
try to show later, the sharp emphasis on analysis as the philosophical method
was bound quite naturally to bring him face to face with the problem of
causality as \textsc{Hume} had posed it. For this problem turned precisely on how we can
ground the assumption of a necessary relation between cause and effect when
these are
% --- p. 32 ---
\opage{32}two different things, so that the effect cannot be found by analysis
of the cause. \textsc{Rousseau's} strong emphasis on the right of feeling and
on the difference between knowledge and faith also produced a revolution in
Kant's line of thought. Hitherto, as a good philosopher of the Enlightenment, he
had placed man's essence and nobility in the understanding alone; now he learned
to find a deeper foundation, which could be common to the learned and the
unlearned, and in which the simplest laborer could stand on an equal footing
with the greatest thinker. And Rousseau's appeal to immediate feeling and faith
was bound to become all the more significant for Kant, as he was, after all,
precisely engaged in undermining the proofs on which the assumption of the
doctrines of natural religion had hitherto been grounded. On the whole Kant
was naturally bound to come, like Rousseau, to ascribe to intellectual
development a more \textit{indirect} significance for the life of the spirit
than he had at first done. His own critical labor of thought had here led him
in the same direction as Rousseau, and when the latter's \textit{Émile}
appeared, Kant was prepared to appreciate it. No wonder that on the day he had
got the book he gave up his customary walk at the fixed hour, to the great
astonishment of the people in the street. --- In his writings from this time he
lays great weight on psychology as the foundation of philosophy and
particularly of ethics, and appeals to Shaftesbury, Hutcheson and Hume as his
predecessors in this respect. Toward speculative constructions and systems he
is skeptical. In \textit{Träume eines Geistersehers erläutert durch Träume der
Metaphysik} (1766), one of Kant's wittiest writings, he shows how easy it is in
a certain sense to construct far-reaching spiritualist explanations, but at the
same time how unfinished and ungrounded the concepts are with which one
operates. His conclusion is: how much there is that we do not know --- but how
much there is, too, that we do not need to know! The Socratic ignorance, the
``philosophy of ignorance'' or the ``negative philosophy'', was at this time
(as is seen from his notes) a favorite thought of his. With his fondness for
Latin watchwords he would have used Cusanus's docta ignorantia, had he known
this expression.
% --- p. 33 ---
% print: „Syvaarskrigen“ (p. 33) (misprint)
\opage{33}

Until his 46th year Kant lived as a Privatdocent; the only public appointment
he held was a poorly paid post as under-librarian. The straitened times of the
Seven Years' War helped to prevent his obtaining a fixed position as a
university teacher. A professorship of ``poetry'' that was offered him he
declined. In 1770 he became professor of philosophy and in the same year
published a Latin treatise \textit{De mundi sensibilis atqve intelligibilis
forma et principiis} (on the form and principles of the world of sense and the
world of thought; in what follows we shall for brevity's sake refer to it as
``the Dissertation''), in which the fundamental thoughts of his definitive
philosophy come forward for the first time. In several statements found in his
letters and notes he has pointed to the year 1769 as the year in which his
fundamental view came into being. ``The year 1769'', he says thus in one place,
``gave me much light''. And in his last years he would properly acknowledge
only those writings which were later than 1769\textsuperscript{5}). The
thought that then dawned on him was that \textit{such forms and presuppositions
as are conditions for anything at all becoming an object of our knowledge must
have} \textit{validity for all experience.} This thought he applied in the
Dissertation to space and time as the forms of our sensuous intuition. The
second period in Kant's philosophical development (1769 ---1781) is marked by
the emergence of this thought and its application to all scientific knowledge.
But it testifies to the greatness of the problem and to the honesty of Kant's
labor of thought that he took 11 years to extend this application from sense
intuition to knowledge of the understanding. In the Dissertation it is only
sense intuition that is bound to subjective forms and presuppositions. The
world of sense is merely phenomenal; but with the help of the understanding we
can raise ourselves above it and know things in themselves. The world of
thought is real, the world of sense phenomenal. From letters and notes of the
seventies it is seen how much labor it cost before the conviction was grounded
that the understanding has its forms and presuppositions just as much as sense
intuition, and that therefore no scientific knowledge can carry us beyond the
phenomenal world of experience. When Kant discovered that knowledge of the
understanding, just as much as sense intuition, consists in a synthesis, a
synthesizing,
% --- p. 34 ---
\opage{34}combining activity of the mind, he was at his goal. But the result of
these many years of brooding Kant then, by his own statement, wrote down in
great haste, in the course of 4---5 months. He was therefore unable to lay much
weight on the form of exposition. Probably he also used earlier drafts,
composed at different times, without always examining carefully whether they
agreed entirely. As a result \textit{Kritik der reinen Vernunft} (1781) has
become a difficult book to read, not only on account of its content but on
account of its exposition. It is hardly credible, as one of Kant's biographers
relates, that Kant had his good friend the merchant Green test every sentence
in the book before it was written down. Had a practical man checked the
exposition, it would surely have become clearer. There is a great deal of
formality and no little scholasticism in it. Kant himself said of his book in a
note: ``When one leafs about in it, it seems to be the most pedantic thing of
all; and yet it is quite properly designed to abolish all pedantry''. Besides
contradictions and scholastic pedantries there are also needless repetitions,
which may confuse or weary. In spite of all this we nevertheless stand here
before an immortal masterpiece of philosophy, a work that marks a milestone on
the long wandering of human thought. By penetrating into the innermost nature of
knowledge Kant succeeds in finding the conditions on which it rests and the
limits beyond which it cannot lead. He shows us thought at once in its greatness
and in its limitation. His faith in reason is not slackened by this limitation:
for the barriers spring from the very nature of reason and are known according
to reason's own laws. Later research has subjected Kant's determinations of the
limits to a revision and has held, now that he drew the limits too narrowly,
now that he drew them too widely; it is in any case certain that they do not
lie precisely where Kant found them; but that does not diminish his greatness
as the one who has had the keenest eye for the form and working of knowledge and
for the significance of the problems of knowledge for the spiritual life as a
whole. --- Two years after the appearance of the chief work he gave
(in\textit{ Prolegomena)} a shorter and more accessible exposition of its line
of thought.
% --- p. 35 ---
\opage{35}

After the publication of Kritik der reinen Vernunft Kant set himself the task
of developing his ethical ideas. Already in the Dissertation he had abandoned
the psychological grounding of ethics that he had earlier embraced in
agreement with the Englishmen. In the moral law, as it immediately makes itself
known each time we feel ourselves obligated, he found reason at work in the
practical domain. In a fresh and clear exposition he has developed his
conception of the ethical in \textit{Grundlegung zur Metaphysik der Sitten}
(1785), but the chief work is \textit{Kritik der practischen Vernunft} (1788).
--- Kant needed one more chief work to complete his critical philosophy, which
was to embrace all sides of life. In \textit{Kritik der} \textit{Urtheilskraft}
(1790) he discussed the problems that arise from the beauty and purposiveness of
nature, and seeks to solve them by analogy with the way in which he had solved
the problem of knowledge and the ethical problem. In this work he gives profound
hints of a possible connection between the different domains which his critical
inquiries had earlier kept sharply apart from one another. ---

Kant lived his whole life in East Prussia. But he followed with great interest
everything that went on in the world, both in the physical world and in the
human world. Books of travel were his favorite reading, and physical geography
played, as already mentioned, a great part in his teaching. He kept up with the
development of the natural sciences, and not least he followed the political
events with eager attention. He was enthusiastic about the North American and
the French Revolution, and saw in the general interest with which people
throughout Europe followed these events a sign that humanity was advancing in
moral respects. News in natural science or news in politics was as a rule the
subject of his conversation with his table companions. After the publication of
his chief works Kant became a famous man. In the best men of the age he
awakened enthusiasm for his labor of thought and for his ideal view of life and
its tasks. People made pilgrimages from far away to remote Königsberg to get a
sight of him, and a number turned to him for advice in moral
% --- p. 36 ---
\opage{36}matters. He was in favor with Frederick the Great's powerful
minister Zedlitz, who followed his lectures through students' notebooks that
were sent to him from Königsberg; to him Kant dedicated Kritik der reinen
Vernunft. Frederick the Great himself cared nothing for German literature and
philosophy; in his younger years he had been an ardent Wolffian; later he held
to Bayle and Voltaire. But Kant was glad to live in the age of Frederick, under
a prince who at once conducted the government with a strong hand and allowed
thought to move freely. Kant did not consider his time an enlightened time, but
a time of enlightenment --- a time that is advancing in enlightenment. (See his
little treatise of 1784: \textit{Was ist Aufklärung?).}

But there came a time when in high places Kant came to be looked at with other
eyes. The great king's successor Friederich Wilhelm II, a dissolute man and a
weak character, who was given to spiritism and mysticism and was at the same
time frightened by the powerful movement in France, introduced a rule of the
clergy and a sharpened censorship. Zedlitz was dismissed: Wöllner, a bigoted
and narrow-minded man, was put at the head of the church and of education, and
a board of censors consisting of three theologians was set up. Attention was
directed in particular at Kant, the most important representative of free
inquiry, and attempts were even made to bring it about that Kant should be
forbidden to write! That, however, did not succeed. But the storm broke when in
1794 Kant published his work in the philosophy of religion, \textit{Religion
innerhalb der Grenzen der blossen Vernunft,} in which from his standpoint he
sought to show the significance of Christianity as a historical form for
ethical ideals, while he distanced himself decidedly from the orthodox
conception. Kant had been so cautious as to have the theological faculty in
Königsberg asked whether the content of the work fell under the theological
censorship, and when the answer was in the negative, he had obtained the
permission of the philosophical faculty of Jena for its
printing\textsuperscript{6}). But that did not prevent a royal letter,
procured by Wöllner, from being addressed to him, in which the most exalted
displeasure was expressed at his inquiries concerning religion, and further
unpleasantness was threatened if he continued in the same direction. It was an
unworthy treatment that the old thinker (
% --- p. 37 ---
\opage{37}he was now in his 70th year) here had to suffer. He had always spoken
with reverence of Christianity and its founder and had only used the right of
inquiry to test the relation of Christianity to human nature and reason. One
sees from Kant's papers that he conscientiously considered what he should now
do. He wrote on a slip of paper: ``Recantation would be base, but silence in a
case like this is the duty of a subject''. In his reply he then sought
frankly to show that he had not been guilty of any offense, but declared at the
same time that ``as His Majesty's faithful subject'' he would refrain from all
authorship in the direction of the philosophy of religion. There lay a
reservation in this: the promise, he held, applied only in this king's time ---
as long as he was \textit{this} king's subject. A few years later Friederich
Wilhelm II died, and his successor followed a more liberal policy. Kant now
took up his authorship in the philosophy of religion again and published (in
the preface to \textit{Streit der Facultäten} 1798) the history of the
conflict. This history is a revolting example of how narrow-minded fanaticism
often tries to stop the free life of the spirit. Fortunately it cannot be
stopped, and the ridiculous therefore unites with the revolting. Those who laid
hands on Kant's venerable figure have gained a place in history beside those
who laid hands on Galilei and forced him to say that the earth stands still.
The spirit stands still as little as the earth. ---

Kant's last years were a slow and sad dissolution of the power of thought that
had worked so tirelessly. Memory and the capacity for combination fell away;
obsessive representations, especially jingles and melodies from childhood,
forced themselves forward; uncanny dreams at night and restless agitation by
day tormented the old man. It has been conjectured that he suffered from a
disease of the brain. In the good intervals he sat at his desk to work on a
last, concluding work, of which some fragments are preserved. It bears the
stamp of decrepitude. Beside a few flashes of genius it is full of repetitions
from earlier writings. After a long wasting away Kant died on 12 February 1804.
% --- p. 38 ---
\opage{38}

\section*{2.\quad Course of Philosophical Development}

It is probably grounded not only in the history of philosophy but also in
experience from his own development when Kant says in one place that the first
step in philosophy is always dogmatic. And yet Kant does not appear in any of
the writings we have from his hand as a full-blooded dogmatist. From the first
he has a lively feeling of the scientific unfinishedness of the great systems
of speculative philosophy, and already in a treatise of 1758 he speaks with
irony of ``the gentlemen who are accustomed to throw away as chaff all thoughts
that have not passed through the treadmill of the Wolffian or some other famous
system''. Characteristic of \textit{the first period of his philosophical
authorship} (1755---1769) is that he is dissatisfied with the existing
doctrinal edifices of philosophy and seeks means to erect a new and more
thorough, if not so splendid, building. It is during this work that it dawns on
him that a speculative system must be preceded by an examination of the
concepts with which we operate, and that very great problems are contained in
these concepts. Metaphysics thereby becomes for him a doctrine of the limits of
knowledge, and he begins to speak of a critique of reason itself. When many
years later (in the preface to \textit{Prolegomena} 1783) he declared that it
was David Hume's criticism that \textit{woke him from his dogmatic slumber and
gave his inquiries in the domain of speculative philosophy a quite different
direction,} this awakening must probably be placed in the years 1762---63,
although it is a testimony to the independence and continuity of Kant's
philosophical thinking that it is impossible to point to any point in his
development where it would be absolutely necessary to assume a definite
influence from other authors in order to understand the later development. ---
Since, as regards the proof of the conception of Kant's course of development
set forth in what follows, reference is made to the treatise
\textit{Kontinuiteten i Kants filosofiske Udviklingsgang}
% scan: „Udviklingsgaug“ (p. 38)
(Det klg. danske Videnskabernes Selskabs Skrifter. 6. Række), we shall here
dwell only on some main points.
% --- p. 39 ---
\opage{39}

The positive and lasting value of those writings of Kant that precede 1769, the
year in which, by his own declaration, his definitive philosophy came into
being, rests chiefly on two trains of thought.

a) As already briefly touched on, Kant in his ``Allg. Naturgesch.'' attempts to
carry Newton's demand for a demonstrable cause (vera causa) for all phenomena
much further than the great natural scientist, to whom Kant himself looked up,
had believed possible. He thereby arrived at his famous hypothesis of the origin
of the solar system. A striving appears here in Kant that he never gave up.
Even in Kritik der reinen Vernunft (in the doctrine of method) he declares that
the wildest physical hypotheses are to be preferred to an appeal to the
supernatural. This zeal to build further on the natural causal series and to
avoid a break in it was connected with the fact that at the beginning of the
first period Kant's philosophy of nature and philosophy of religion stand in
intimate contact with each other. It was, he held, a false presupposition from
which one started when one assumed that nature, left to itself, would produce
only disorder and chaos. Not by chance, but according to its own laws, nature
produces order and purposiveness. The very mechanical order of nature that
embraces all phenomena, and according to whose laws the individual elements
work together, bears witness to a ground of unity for existence, to an infinite
power that stirs in the individual elements. The individual atoms are (as Kant
develops in an interesting treatise of 1756: \textit{Monadologia physica)}
points of force, not small extended parts, and the fact that they work together
in a law-governed way proves that there exists no original and absolute
separation between them. If each element in the world had its own separate
nature, it would be a matter of chance whether they fitted together in such a
way that a world-whole could come out of them. Their interaction would be
impossible if they were not all dependent on a common ground. In this ground of
unity the mechanical order of nature and the purposiveness of nature at once
find their explanation. Far from harboring fear of the demonstration of
physical causes by natural science,
% --- p. 40 ---
\opage{40}one should precisely rejoice that through it the great primordial
fact, interaction, the connection of nature, comes forward more clearly.

In the causal connection as a fundamental fact, then, Kant here finds the
foundation on which he theoretically builds his religious conception. There is
a remarkable kinship between his line of thought and Spinoza's, although he
quite certainly knew the latter only through expositions that did not let it
come into its own. --- The current proofs of the existence of God, on the other
hand, he already now rejects, especially the ``physico-theological'' one, which
would infer from the purposiveness of nature the necessity of assuming an
intervention by a power standing outside nature.

b) But at the same time as Kant found in the natural causal connection itself
the ``only possible ground of proof'' for a religious conception of the world, he
was making inquiries into the nature of our thinking. He found that it consists
in comparing and analyzing. Every judgment rests on a comparison between a
property and a thing: either the property fits the thing, or it does not fit.
We therefore constantly operate according to the principles of identity and of
contradiction; and can pass over from one concept to another only when the
latter can be shown in its identity with the first concept, that is, when I can
find the second concept by analysis of the first. Philosophy cannot, like
mathematics, begin by constructing and to that extent creating its concepts. It
must find them by analysis of experience --- but how then can it ground a
conviction that the analysis has been carried far enough, so that there are no
more marks to discover? The imperfection of earlier philosophy Kant derives
precisely from its operating with unfinished concepts, since it had hastily
passed over from analysis to construction, trusting that one must be able to
construct in philosophy just as well as in mathematics. Kant gives two
extraordinarily significant examples of such unfinished or ``surreptitious''
concepts. The one is the concept of mind, with which Descartes, Leibniz and
Wolff had operated in their spiritualist psychology. A complete concept of the
mental being that could justify ascribing to it an independent existence,
separated from matter,
% --- p. 41 ---
\opage{41}we do not have. We have an empirical concept of mental phenomena, but
empirical psychology cannot say whether a soul-substance exists or not. (The
work \textit{Träume eines Geistersehers} is a humorous demonstration of how easy
it is to build up a whole spiritualist system if one simply assumes the concept
of a soul-substance as given. Swedenborg's writings are used as the example.)
The other example is the concept of cause. If thinking is analysis, only such
relations are intelligible in which the second term can be derived from the
first. But can one, by analyzing one phenomenon, discover the necessity that
another phenomenon should occur? And that, after all, is what the concept of
cause designates! There is no contradiction in stopping at the first
phenomenon. But how then can the concept of cause be a valid concept? --- Kant
has here (first in the remarkable treatise \textit{Versuch den Begriff der
negativen Grössen in die Weltweisheit einzuführen} 1762) come by his own way,
but most probably guided by Hume's critical remarks, to the problem of
causality, and he lets it stand for the present as insoluble. But a very strong
collision must now take place in Kant's consciousness between the two trains of
thought, of which the one, in the interest both of natural science and of
religion, asserts the causal connection as the great primordial fact, and the
other asserts that this primordial fact itself is incomprehensible! Already in
``Allg. Naturgeschichte'' and ``Beweisgrund'' he had been at the problem of
causality, in that he had inferred a ground of unity for everything, since the
interaction between the elements would otherwise be incomprehensible. What has
happened in the treatise on negative magnitudes is a \textit{transposition of
the problem from the objective or metaphysical to the subjective or
epistemological form.} This transposition was naturally called forth by the
sharpened conviction that analysis must precede construction.

Since Kant, then, by analysis of a concept as important for real knowledge as
the concept of cause, had come up against a problem he could not solve, it is
no wonder that his whole mood at the close of the year 1762---63, so rich in
labor of thought (from which five significant treatises
% --- p. 42 ---
\opage{42}date), was decidedly skeptical. With irony he turns against ``the
thorough philosophers, whose number is constantly increasing'', and asks them to
solve for him the simple questions at which he has come to a stop. Out of this
mood sprang, a few years later, ``Träume eines Geistersehers''. There is no
period in Kant's life to which the expression ``awakening from dogmatic slumber''
fits so well as to this one. He himself later defined dogmatism as ``the
presumption of wanting to make one's way merely with pure knowledge from
concepts, according to principles which reason has long had in use,
\textit{without examining the manner in which, and the right by which, it has
arrived at them''} (Kritik der reinen Vernunft. 2. Aufl. p. XXXV). When Kant
defined dogmatism in this way, he cannot possibly have meant that when he wrote
the treatise on negative magnitudes and ``Träume'' he was still lying in
dogmatic slumber. In any case he then did himself an injustice. --- There are,
however, eminent Kant scholars who do not think that ``the awakening from the
dogmatic slumber'' can be placed so early. Against them the monograph mentioned
above attempts a detailed account, in that it takes the disagreement among Kant
scholars on this point in particular as evidence for ``the continuity in Kant's
philosophical course of development''. ---

\textit{The second period in Kant's course of development} (1769---1781), the
one that ends with his chief work, is taken up by the labor of finding the
possibility of a transition from analysis to construction. The year 1769, which
he himself has designated as a turning point, led him onto the thoughts that
are developed in the Dissertation the following year. A statement in one of
Kant's notes indicates clearly what the turning point consisted in: \textit{``I
found that many of the propositions which we regard as objective are in reality
subjective, i.e. contain the conditions under which alone we can perceive or
comprehend the objects''.} The discovery he made here he has himself compared to
Copernicus's. Just as it is owing to our standpoint on the earth that the
heavens are seen to move round us, so it is owing to the constitution of our
sense intuition that we apprehend things in space and time. What Newton called
absolute space and absolute time are only schemata or forms which we construct
when we
% --- p. 43 ---
\opage{43}notice the way in which we apprehend things. The laws of space and
time are
the laws of our sense intuition. But for that very reason everything that
experience can show us must also fall under these laws (for otherwise it could
not be intuited), and it is then understood how applied mathematics can
pronounce a priori laws for phenomena. But since in this way everything that is
intuited is apprehended by us according to the forms of our faculty of
intuition, it is not things in themselves (noumena) but only phenomena that we
apprehend by the help of sense perception.

The Copernican principle, that the knowledge of existence is determined by the
nature and modes of working of the knowing subject, Kant in the Dissertation
applies only to sense intuition. As regards the understanding, he does not yet
doubt, any more than before (in ``Beweisgrund''), that with the requisite
development it will be able to attain knowledge of things in themselves. But
the nature of the understanding is not examined more closely. Kant was
nevertheless right later in holding that his definitive philosophy had come into
being with the Dissertation; for the principle --- what for brevity's sake may
be called the Copernican principle --- had been set up, and it was now only a
matter of applying it throughout. It was in itself no wonder that Kant shrank
before admitting the impossibility of any scientific knowledge of things in
themselves. The old opposition, stemming from Plato, between noumena and
phaenomena, between existence as it is in itself and is known by thought, and
existence as it appears to sense perception, he had now apparently found a new
grounding for. And the sharp difference between intuition and understanding
also seemed to speak for their reach having to be different.

Yet it is seen from Kant's letters that shortly after the publication of the
Dissertation he felt a great difficulty in its results. How can concepts of the
understanding, which we form by the activity of our thought, have validity for
things that are altogether independent of us? Since these concepts (as e.g.
cause, substance, possibility, actuality and necessity) are formed by us, they
cannot after all be mere products of things; and in any case, if they were mere
products of experience, they
% --- p. 44 ---
% scan: „Forstanden.“ (p. 44)
\opage{44}could not be used to set up propositions that were to have validity
without being grounded on experience. Kant --- as is seen from letters and
notes --- proceeded in his treatment of this problem in such a way that he
examined the fundamental concepts (categories) with which we operate in our
attempts to know existence, and sought to reduce them to as small a number as
possible and at the same time to assure himself how many there are. The long
time between the Dissertation and ``Kritik der reinen Vernunft'' was spent on
such attempts. It can be seen that he tried different arrangements and
divisions. His attention was directed in particular to such concepts as express
a relation. He became clear that a relation can come about not only through
comparison but also through combination. Thus the concepts substance, cause and
interaction presuppose different combinations: combination of thing and
property, of cause and effect, of two causes. And when he thus found that we
operate with concepts that express our striving to combine the phenomena in
