different ways, in different forms, he had gained a point of view from which the
knowledge of the understanding, in spite of its difference from sense
intuition, nevertheless proved to be homogeneous with it. For when in the
Dissertation he had sought to show that space and time are our forms of
intuition, this was grounded on their being forms under which our faculty of
intuition \textit{orders and synthesizes} the given. They are grounded on a
``gathering and ordering power'' \textit{(vis animi,} omnes sensationes secundum
stabilem et naturæ insitam legem \textit{coordinans), and} they are themselves
\textit{schemata coordinandi} (Diss. § 15 D. E.). The understanding too now
proves to be a combining, synthesizing faculty; by it we seek to combine the
phenomena in certain mutual relations (e.g. as cause and effect). \textit{The
concept of synthesis,} which in the Dissertation was applied only to sense
intuition, thus now proved to fit the understanding as well. And now the
inference had to be drawn in a similar way as concerning time and space: only
when we can combine the phenomena in the way that our categories, which express
the forms of our understanding, indicate, only then can we understand! Synthetic
unity is the condition of all understanding as well as of all sense intuition.
% --- p. 45 ---
\opage{45}By the help of the categories we can therefore anticipate experience.
The Copernican principle is carried through --- but the impossibility of
knowing noumena, things in themselves, then becomes at the same time the
unavoidable consequence.

The combining principle that had been Hume's stumbling block now proved to Kant
to be the fundamental principle of all knowledge, from sense perception up to
the highest insight of the understanding. The applicability of this principle
draws the limit between what is intelligible and unintelligible for us. But it
was not enough for Kant to find, through analysis of the fundamental concepts,
the general form or type of the activity of the understanding. He wanted a
guarantee that \textit{all} the fundamental concepts had been found. He wanted
to set up a complete table of categories a priori. This he believed he could
achieve by taking the doctrine of judgments as his basis. Every judgment is a
combination of concepts and to that extent a synthesis (this is how he now
conceives the judgment, whereas in his treatises of 1762 he had held that the
predicate in the judgment must be able to be found by analysis of the subject).
As many kinds of judgments as there are, so many special kinds of synthesis, or
so many categories, must there be --- he concludes. The earlier logic's doctrine
of judgments, however, he must transform somewhat before he can use it. He then
finds four classes of judgments, each with three kinds, and so he gets twelve
categories. Far more significant than this attempt at systematization, both in
epistemological and in psychological respects, is Kant's general thought of
synthesis as the fundamental form of the activity of consciousness. He had here
found a concept that led both beyond the atomistic psychology that underlay
empiricism and beyond the spiritualist psychology on which most idealist systems
had hitherto built. Against empiricism, which would regard the unity of the mind
as a mere result of the manifold impressions, he asserts the activity of unity
as the fundamental character of mental life, which cannot be explained by
outward influence alone; against spiritualism, which does have an eye for this
fundamental character but would dogmatically lead it back to a mystical
substance behind consciousness, he asserts that our knowledge cannot carry us
further back than to the fundamental form and
% --- p. 46 ---
\opage{46}fundamental law of mental life as it appears in experience. At the
same time he has thereby gone beyond the psychology of the Enlightenment, which
kept to what is clearly conscious and seen through by the understanding.
Synthesis is the constant presupposition of consciousness, but need not itself
come forward as an object for consciousness. It can work blindly,
instinctively, as a hidden art in our innermost nature. --- Kant's theory of
knowledge was now complete, and he proceeded to work it out. We therefore pass
on to set it forth as it stands in his chief work.

\section*{3.\quad Epistemology (Kritik der reinen Vernunft)}

In setting forth the content of this work we do not follow the work's own
division, but an order that lets the great lines of the line of thought to which
the work owes its origin come forward more clearly. A natural system is thereby
put in place of the more artificial one that Kant himself followed.

\subsection*{a.\quad Subjective Deduction (Psychological Analysis)}

The critical philosophy differs from the dogmatic by examining the faculty of
knowledge itself and deciding, according to the result of this examination,
which tasks it can solve and which lie beyond its reach. But we know the
faculty of knowledge only from its activity in experience. The thing to do,
then, is to examine experience in order to see whether it might not be composed
partly of elements that could be owing to the faculty of knowledge itself, partly
of elements owing to the way in which it is roused to activity from without.
What is owing to the faculty itself Kant calls \textit{form;} what is owing to
influence from without he calls \textit{matter.} Nowhere has Kant methodically
carried out the analysis of experience by which he grounds the distinction
between form and matter that bears his whole epistemology. But on closer study
of the Dissertation and ``Kritik der reinen Vernunft'' one finds (as is shown in
% --- p. 47 ---
\opage{47}detail in the monograph on ``Kontinuiteten i Kants filosofiske
Udviklingsgang'' p. 26---28) that the forms are discovered when one notices what
is constant and universal in our knowledge, while the matter is what can change
and vary. Space and time are forms of our intuition: for whatever kind the
sensations may be, and however much they change, the forms of space and time in
which their content appears to us are the same; a space or a time does not
change, however it may be filled. If I abstract from all sense qualities,
something is still left: extension and succession. Further: whatever phenomena
we may have given, we understand them only when we can combine them as members
in definite relations, especially in the way
that the concept of magnitude and the concept of cause indicate. It is by a
judgment, a combining activity, that we call one phenomenon greater or smaller
than the other, or cause or effect in relation to the other. The same form of
combination (quantity or causality) can be applied even if the content is
quite different. --- Common to all the forms, according to what we already saw
above, is that they are the expression of a synthesis.

But Kant will not only prove that there are forms with which our knowledge
operates, but also decide how many and which these forms are. He holds that,
since we have to do here with what lies nearest of all to us, our own
knowledge, we must also be able to arrive at a complete and certain insight into
all its forms. This is evidently a dogmatic assumption. For the analytic method
that Kant employs can give no guarantee of completeness; full certainty can
never be attained that one has found all the forms. Nor can we be sure that we
have found the fundamental forms. The forms are the constant elements in
experience: from the constancy it is inferred that it is the faculty of
knowledge itself that is at work. But that is a hypothesis, and can never become
anything else. In the preface to the first edition of ``Kritik der reinen
Vernunft'' Kant remarks that ``the subjective deduction'' (i.e. the
demonstration of the forms of knowledge by means of analysis) might look like a
hypothesis, since it does after all aim at finding the cause of a given
% --- p. 48 ---
\opage{48}effect (namely of what is constant in experience); he holds,
however, that this is not so, and promises to prove it on another occasion. This
promise, however, he has not kept. His wish for a definitive result has here
made him a dogmatist. He could not resign himself to the only way out that is
given here: to operate with the foundation found by analysis as with a
hypothesis, leaving it to future inquiry to procure a still better foundation.
Kant was caught in the illusion that ``critique of reason'' was something that
could be done once and for all, and did not see that every attempt at critical
philosophy must start from presuppositions that are to a certain degree
dogmatic, and which it is the task of the critique of reason of the future to
treat. --- If we now look at the system of forms that Kant sets up, it
consists of three groups.

\textit{α}) \textit{Forms of intuition}. Space is the form of all intuition in
the domain of outer experience, time of all intuition in the domain of inner
experience. They are forms of \textit{intuition} (not forms of the
\textit{understanding}): for in space and time the parts are enclosed by the
whole, and make up the whole; one cannot represent to oneself the individual
part of space or of time except within the whole of space or the whole of time,
and there is only one space and one time. Space and time are \textit{forms,}
because every single experience presupposes them. They are the necessary
presuppositions that every experience must satisfy. --- As a gathering,
coordinating activity \textit{(synopsis,} a viewing-together, Kant calls it)
intuition in space and time has an active character in relation to mere
sensation (Empfindung), which gives us the individual qualities. But Kant
compares it above all with the higher degree of activity that lies in the
activity of the understanding, and designates it, in relation to that, as
receptivity. It does not yet give knowledge proper.

\textit{β) Forms of the understanding.} Intuition without concept is blind
(just as concept without intuition is empty). In intuition a multiplicity is
immediately combined into a whole. But knowledge arises only through this
combination being performed with consciousness, with an express turning of
attention, so that this act of attention \textit{(apperception} Kant calls it)
% --- p. 49 ---
\opage{49}becomes the common form or unity for the whole content. The unity of
consciousness and its identity with itself is the condition for the given
content being able to be synthesized. If, e.g., a line is to be known, it must
be drawn, i.e. its individual parts must be combined in a definite way, held
together by an activity of the mind that successively grasps the individual
parts, does not let go of the earlier ones when it passes on to the following,
and at last gathers them into a whole. The unity in this operation is the unity
of consciousness, and only by means of it does the line come into being as an
object for us. When I see the water freeze, I apprehend two states, fluidity
and solidity, in a relation of time, but at the same time in such a way that
the condition for the occurrence of the second lies in the first. Only by the
application of the concept of cause do I apprehend the transition from fluidity
to solidity as an objective event. --- The synthesis performed in examples such
as these Kant refers to the imagination, which forms a middle term between
intuition and understanding. When we become conscious of the forms according to
which the imagination works here, we have found the \textit{categories,} the
special kinds of synthesis in the domain of the understanding.

In setting up the system of categories Kant starts, as already touched on, from
his division of judgments into four classes. Corresponding to these he gets four
groups of categories, and corresponding to these in turn four groups of
fundamental propositions. To take a single example: to the hypothetical
judgments corresponds the concept of cause. For a causal relation between two
phenomena means that they are related to each other as the conditioning
judgment to the conditioned: \textit{when} the one phenomenon is given, the
other follows unavoidably. And the causal principle then states that such a
relation exists between every phenomenon and a certain definite other phenomenon.

The twelve categories, which it is superfluous to enumerate here, Kant himself
moreover leads back to two divisions: the mathematical and the dynamical
categories, \textit{the concept of magnitude} and \textit{the concept of cause}
can in reality be said to represent all the categories and to be the two chief
forms of the synthesis in which every knowledge consists. --- Such a reduction
is all the more necessary as the sharp difference between
% --- p. 50 ---
\opage{50}different classes of logical judgments that Kant assumed is
altogether untenable\textsuperscript{7}), so that one cannot by the doctrine of
judgments arrive at a system of different categories.

\textit{γ) Ideas of reason.} By reason in the wider sense Kant understands our
faculty of knowledge as a whole. By \textit{reason in the narrower sense} he
understands our faculty of knowledge in its tendency toward the
\textit{unconditioned} carrying through of synthesis. While intuition forms the
chaos of sensations into sense-images in space and time, and while the
understanding orders these sense-images in such connection as the concept of
magnitude and the concept of cause indicate, reason in the narrower sense
contains the demand for a completion of the series of members, for the
formation of absolute totalities --- thus an absolute beginning and limit of
space and time, absolute maxima and minima, absolute completion of the causal
series in a first cause\textsuperscript{8}). It is a continuation and completion
of the coordinating and synthesizing activity that intuition and understanding
already exercise. It is synthesis in its highest form. Concepts that designate
such an absolute completion Kant calls\textit{ ideas.} Whereas the word idea had
come in the literature of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries to mean the
same as representation, Kant goes back to Plato's usage, according to which
idea designates an object of thought that on account of its absolute character
cannot appear in experience. ``Plato'', he says, ``remarked very well that our
reason has a natural need to raise itself to cognitions that go much further
than that any object which experience can exhibit can ever be congruent with
them.''

Just as with the forms of intuition and the categories, Kant seeks with the
ideas too to prove that there is a certain definite number of them. There are
--- he holds --- three such ideas: the idea of the soul, the idea of the world,
the idea of God. For we seek a completed knowledge of inner experience, a
completed knowledge of outer experience and a completed knowledge of the origin
of everything that is. That these ideas are not invented but proceed from the
very nature of reason Kant will prove by their corresponding to the three forms
of syllogism that it was customary to distinguish in logic (the categorical,
the hypothetical
% --- p. 51 ---
% scan: „Virken:“ (p. 51)
\opage{51}and the disjunctive). This derivation is, however, very forced, far
more forced than the derivation of the categories from the kinds of
judgments\textsuperscript{9}). It falls away already through the fact that the
syllogism requires no other function of thought than the judgment, something
Kant himself had earlier shown (in a treatise of 1762 ``on the false subtlety of
the syllogistic figures''). Kant's unhappy love of systematization has made his
work more intricate than it needed to become. But in fact he is right that the
ideas of the soul, the world and God have sprung from the involuntary need of
consciousness for completion, to get the chain of thought hung up on a firm
hook, to form an absolute system as a counter-image of the synthesis that is the
fundamental form of thinking.

By analysis of our knowledge as it develops and works in experience, Kant
believes he has found all the forms of its working. But with the demonstration
of the forms, the demonstration of the justification of their use is not given.
Originally no doubt is harbored about this validity. There is a natural
tendency to ascribe absolute reality to forms of intuition, categories and
ideas alike. Reason acts before it tests. It wants to have its building finished
as soon as possible, and only afterwards does it examine whether the foundation
too was laid deep and firm enough. The first step of reason is dogmatic. When
it has learned wisdom by harm, it becomes skeptical. But the third step, which
presupposes mature and manly judgment, is the critical testing of the faculties
and reach of reason. For this the subjective deduction, which consists in
psychological analysis, is only the preparation. It shows what forms or laws our
knowledge follows according to its nature. The next question, which the
objective deduction is to answer, is this: to what conditions and limits is the
use of those forms subject? ---

As was already emphasized in the general characterization of Kant, it is one of
his chief merits that he has demonstrated what might be called \textit{the law
of the three stages,} a law that holds not only for the development of
knowledge but in analogous forms fits the development of the life of the spirit
as a whole. Kant has here indicated a point of view that plays a great part in
% --- p. 52 ---
\opage{52}later thinkers (Fichte, Hegel, St. Simon, Comte). It points to
development not proceeding in so straight a line as people in the period of the
Enlightenment were inclined to assume.

\subsection*{b.\quad Objective Deduction}

If space and time are forms in which we intuit everything, then no phenomena
can occur in experience that are not in space and time and do not obey the
laws of space and time. Applied mathematics thereby becomes valid; although it
rests on \textit{pure (independent of experience) reason,} it nevertheless has
\textit{validity for all possible experiences,} because it formulates only what
follows from the general laws of space and time. But on the other hand these
laws then also hold \textit{only} for things as they appear to us, for things
as \textit{phenomena} (Erscheinungen). For we have no right to make the
conditions of our apprehension into the conditions of the very essence and
subsistence of things, nor have we any right to regard our forms of intuition
as the only possible ones. Only from a human standpoint can we speak of space
and time. The mathematical laws are pure laws of reason, which hold for all the
experience human beings can have, --- and only with that experience and the
phenomena it can show us does our knowledge have to do.

The case is similar with the categories: since they are the forms of our
understanding, everything that we are to be able to understand must fall under
them, must satisfy the conditions they set. To experience belongs not merely
that something is intuited (in space or time or both), but also that the
various phenomena that are intuited are connected in a determinate way.
Experience in the strict sense requires not merely applied mathematics but also
applied logic. All phenomena must, if we are to understand them, fall under the
concept of magnitude and the concept of cause. The concept of magnitude
excludes gaps and leaps (non datur hiatus, non datur saltus): every increase or
decrease in extension or in degree must take place continuously. The concept of
cause excludes chance and absolute necessity (non datur casus, non datur
fatum): every phenomenon must, if the causal
% --- p. 53 ---
\opage{53}principle is to hold, stand in a relation of conditionedness to another
phenomenon, this again to a third, and so on. All the various fundamental
propositions that correspond to the categories can, as Kant in a single
place\textsuperscript{10}) suggests (unfortunately without developing this
thought further), be reduced to a single one: \textit{the fundamental
proposition of continuity.} The causal principle is only a particular form of
this general fundamental proposition, which demands a continuous connection.
That the fulfillment of this demand is a condition of experience, Kant shows in
the following way. If there is to be a difference between \textit{experience}
and imagination, experience must require a law-determined succession of the
phenomena, such that I cannot arbitrarily exchange the members (as I can in my
imaginings, dreams and fantasies), and such that no break in continuity occurs
(whereas in the world of dreams I can make leaps as great as you please). The
law of continuity (which, after all, comprises the law of the continuity of
extension and of degrees as well as the law that all phenomena stand in causal
relation) is valid for all phenomena, because it formulates the conditions
under which we can have real experience at all (as distinct from imagination).
It is the possibility of experience that we formulate in fundamental
propositions, which then hold a priori for all possible experiences. ---
Whereas Wolff vainly attempted to derive the causal principle from the
fundamental proposition of contradiction, that is, to give a purely logical
proof of it, Kant has here attempted to give an epistemological (or, as he
calls it with a barbarous scholastic expression, transcendental) proof of it, by
demonstrating its validity as a condition under which experiences can be made.
--- But here too (as with space and time) the limitation follows along with the
grounding. \textit{Only} as a condition of experience does the law of
continuity (the law of causality included under it) have validity. Just as
geometry would be a subjective figment of the brain if space were not a
condition of all outer experience, so the law of causality, and the law of
continuity in general, would be only a purely subjective maxim if it did not
state the condition of real experience. Our fundamental propositions anticipate
the form of experience --- but they do not hold beyond the domain of
experience, do not hold for anything that cannot come forth in
% --- p. 54 ---
\opage{54}experience. Experience is, as Kant expresses it, an empirical synthesis
which gives all other synthesis reality. We know only phenomena
(Erscheinungen), not things as they are in themselves, but only as they are
apprehended through the forms of our understanding, which (like the forms of
intuition) have significance only from a human standpoint.

As regards the ideas, an objective deduction (a ``transcendental'' proof) is
not possible. For since they denote something unconditioned, while everything
that can appear in experience is conditioned and limited, the foundation for a
proof that we had, in the case of the forms of intuition and the categories, in
the possibility of experience is lacking here. The ideas have their subjective
origin in reason's need of unity, but no object given in experience can be
congruent with them. An absolute totality, such as the ideas of reason under
various forms demand, experience cannot exhibit. We can go on advancing in
space, in time and in the series of degrees and conditions --- but whether
absolute completion is possible cannot be established. --- On the ideas,
therefore, no science can be built, as it can on the forms of intuition and the
categories.

It is a question whether there is the sharp difference between the three
classes of forms that Kant assumes. Continuity, causality, time and space too
have, in the shape in which Kant sets them up, an ideal perfection with which
no experience is congruent. Continuity is an idea to which only approximations
are found in experience. What Kant calls forms are in reality abstractions and
ideals that we, in accordance with the nature of our knowledge, set up and use
as standards and rules for our inquiry. The fundamental propositions therefore
become hypotheses, not proven truths. Experience in the strict meaning in which
Kant takes this word in his ``transcendental'' proof is itself an ideal, and
Hume, whose doubt about the causal principle Kant wanted to overcome, denied,
after all, precisely that there was experience in the meaning in which Kant
takes the word. Kant has thus not solved Hume's problem (which presumably
cannot be solved either); but his merit is to have brought forward a side of
the problem, or rather of our knowledge, which Hume had left
% --- p. 55 ---
\opage{55}aside, and he has thereby carried epistemology a mighty step forward. It
was his enthusiasm for the Copernican principle that led him to ascribe to his
line of thought a greater force of proof than it had. Instead of stopping at
the significance of the forms as types, exemplars and anticipations, he wanted
to give a compelling proof of their real applicability, and in this he did not
succeed. (Cf. more on this: ``Kontinuiteten i Kants filosofiske
Udviklingsgang'' p. 31---33).

\subsection*{c.\quad Phenomena and the Thing in Itself}

Kant's result from the investigation of pure reason was that our thinking does
indeed command forms and principles that do not spring from experience, but
that these nevertheless have no valid application beyond the domain of
experience. Their origin is not empirical, but only an empirical use can be
made of them. And since we have experience only by means of the application of
our forms of intuition and categories, everything we know is only phenomena,
not things in themselves. But then the questions naturally arise: what, then,
is this ``Ding an sich'', this ``Noumenon'', this ``Intelligible'', this
``transcendental object'' (under these various names the thing in itself occurs
in Kant)? --- and with what right is it assumed at all that there is any such
thing?

In putting these questions we must note that the problem of the thing in
itself, which came so strongly into the foreground during the first discussion
of Kant's philosophy, was not really Kant's main problem. His task was an
investigation of what faculty we possess for knowledge without building on mere
observations. And he found that it followed from the conditions of this
knowledge that it could concern only phenomena. His problem was the relation of
reason to experience, not the first origin of the content of knowledge.
Nevertheless it was natural that this problem, and the consequences that seemed
to follow from Kant's philosophy with regard to it, should attract special
attention.

To the question \textit{what} the thing in itself is,
% --- p. 56 ---
\opage{56}Kant answers that he does not know, and that he does not need to know
either, since it can never be met with in experience; everything that becomes
an object of experience is phenomenon. We do not even know whether the thing in
itself lies in ourselves or outside us. The concept noumenon or thing in itself
is merely a limiting concept, a purely negative concept, at which we arrive by
investigating the conditions of our knowledge, which are at the same time its
limits. But it nevertheless shines through Kant's manner of expression in
various places that he is inclined to think of the unknowable in idealist form,
perhaps most nearly as Leibniz's world of monads (in which connection it is
also of interest that Leibniz himself sometimes called the world of monads the
intelligible world as opposed to the world of sense). Kant did, to be sure,
firmly dispute the scientific justification of the use Leibniz had made of
analogy to construct his metaphysical idealism; but in the background of his
consciousness this view nevertheless seems to have maintained
itself\textsuperscript{11}). And, as will appear later, he ascribes practical
justification to analogy when he is to show the possibility of a faith where
knowledge is not possible. It is only so long as he speaks from a purely
theoretical point of view that he declares the Ding an sich a purely negative
concept.

Kant never doubted the existence of things in themselves. With the usual
conception he assumes an absolute reality, and his critique aims only at
grounding and limiting the knowledge we can have of them. But in the course of
his investigations he comes (though always in passing) to state
\textit{reasons for the assumption} that something other and more than
phenomena exists. Three such reasons appear in Kant. --- In the first place, it
would be an unreasonable and unjustified assumption that \textit{our} mode of
knowledge (in time and space and according to the categories of the
understanding) should be the only possible one. We would thereby, such is
roughly Kant's meaning, make ourselves guilty of the same error that was
committed before Copernicus by taking the earth's standpoint for the absolute
standpoint. The concept of the thing in itself thus marks that all our
knowledge is conditioned by our nature, --- that this nature of ours is a
contributing element in the way in which the objects of experience
% --- p. 57 ---
\opage{57}appear to us. --- In the second place: only as regards the form does
knowledge have its ground in our nature; the matter, the content, is given to
us (in the sensations); toward it we behave receptively. But it must surely
have a cause! In a reply to one of his critics Kant says: ``The objects, as
things in themselves, \textit{give} the matter for empirical intuitions; they
contain the ground by which sensibility is determined to act in its peculiar
way''\textsuperscript{12}). --- The third reason Kant finds, as we shall see
later, in the contradictions in which reason entangles itself by going beyond
the limits of experience, contradictions that in his opinion can be resolved
only by means of the distinction between phenomenon and thing in itself.

The difficulty that Kant's first critics found in his assumption of things in
themselves was connected with the second reason. Into the first and the third
they did not enter more closely. In his work \textit{David Hume über den
Glauben oder Idealismus und Realismus} (1787) \textsc{jacobi} sought to show
that Kant must consistently deny all existence outside our representations,
that is, profess a pure idealism [i.e. subjectivism]. The assumption of a
thing in itself as the cause of our sensations conflicts with Kant's doctrine
of the concept of cause as the expression of a form of the understanding whose
application is valid only \textit{within} the domain of experience. A similar
objection was made some years later by \textsc{g. E. Schulze} in his anonymous
book \textit{Ænesidemus} (1792). This objection cannot be refuted from Kant's
standpoint\textsuperscript{13}). It rests on Kant's own significant
fundamental thought, that the limitation of knowledge and its grounding are
closely connected.

Kant would have been consistent if he had merely maintained that the matter of
knowledge cannot be derived from its form, the varying and special elements not
from the constant and general frames. The possibility of experience ceases when
no sensations arise. But how sensations arise is a question with which the
critical philosophy (epistemology) has nothing to do. Hume had seen this
clearly when he (Treatise I, 3, 5) declared the first origin of sensation
inexplicable and added: ``And this question is of no significance either for
the task we have here set ourselves.'' Kant
% --- p. 58 ---
\opage{58}was, with regard to this question, placed in quite the same way as Hume.

On closer investigation it will appear (as shown in ``Kontinuiteten i Kants
filosofiske Udviklingsgang'', p. 33---35) that Kant sees in the Ding an sich
not merely the cause of the matter of knowledge but also of the determinate
forms in which we apprehend and order it. It is indeed also clear that the
question of origin must be raised with regard to the form just as much as with
regard to the matter. Especially as regards the apprehension of space, there
are in Kant manifold indications that the ground why we apprehend things in
precisely this determinate way (in three dimensions, etc.) must lie in the Ding
an sich\textsuperscript{14}). But he refers in general ``all extent and
\textit{connection''} in our observations to ``the transcendental object''
(Kritik der reinen Vernunft. 1. Aufl. p. 494; cf. also p. 653 f.; 660 f.)
--- Not merely in the matter of our knowledge, then, but also in its forms we
have an effect of the Ding an sich. And since the forms will be able to hold
only so long as the Ding an sich acts in a constant way, it is clear that the
knowledge we can build on the mere forms can only be hypothetical, --- while
on the other hand it becomes more than merely phenomenal, since it teaches us
how the Ding an sich acts. As soon as this point is brought forward and
unfolded in all its consequences, Kant's whole system is therefore altered.
Both the apriorism and the phenomenalism are limited, and the inconsistency
falls away. For all these three sides of Kant's philosophy are connected with
his absolute distinction between matter and form, a distinction that even on
purely psychological grounds raises serious misgivings.

Yet --- even when the Ding an sich is regarded as the cause of both form and
matter in our knowledge --- very little can be known about it: ``Gar nichts
bestimmtes'', says Kant (Prolegomena § 32 and 57). It stands as a great X,
which cannot be determined scientifically. And yet it is a determination of it
that has been attempted in all religions and in all speculative systems. Kant
here has the great merit of having determined \textit{the philosophical place
of religious and metaphysical speculations.} The conflict between positive and
natural religion, between spiritualism
% --- p. 59 ---
\opage{59}and materialism, between monism and pluralism, etc., concerns
precisely this X. Never before had the boundary between science and
speculation been staked out in so clear a way.

\subsection*{d.\quad Critique of Speculative Philosophy}

As regards the ideas, an objective deduction proved impossible. Nevertheless
the attempt has been made to lay the ideas of the soul, of the world and of God
at the foundation of sciences that rose high above experience. The result Kant
had reached through the general examination of the cognitive value of the ideas
he finds confirmed by a special critique of these supposed sciences, --- of
speculative psychology, speculative cosmology and speculative theology.

\textit{α. Critique of Speculative Psychology. ---} It rests on a fallacy when
it has been believed possible to set up a doctrine of the soul as a being
separate from the body. One infers from the unity that is the general form of
the activity of consciousness to the assumption of a simple substance behind
consciousness. From the synthesis one infers the substance. But this is
unjustified. The mere form of activity says nothing about the nature of the
being that lies at its foundation. Consciousness is not something simple, not a
single representation, but a form common to all representations. Psychology is
a purely empirical science, which cannot teach us anything about a being or
about properties (e.g. simplicity) that do not themselves come forth in
experience. Therefore it is also unjustified (as Kant develops especially in
the first edition of Kritik der reinen Vernunft) to make the difference
between material and mental phenomena into a difference between two kinds of
substances or beings; that would be to confuse a difference in our mode of
apprehension with a difference in the things themselves. What lies at the
foundation of the outer phenomena might, after all, be the same as what lies
at the foundation of the inner phenomena! The dualism would thereby fall away,
and with it all the difficulties that have been found in the interaction
between soul and body\textsuperscript{15}).

\textit{β. Critique of Speculative Cosmology. ---} The concept of
% --- p. 60 ---
\opage{60}the world or of nature as a whole presupposes that the concept of
magnitude and the concept of cause are extended beyond experience, which always
shows us only limited spaces and times and uncompleted causal series. A series
of contradictions (antinomies) thereby arises, since mutually conflicting
propositions can be proved: a sign that we have ventured beyond the limits of
our knowledge! --- Kant sets up four such antinomies (corresponding to the four
classes of categories and of logical judgments); but they can be reduced to
three, of which the first two concern the concept of magnitude, applied to
space, time and matter, the third the concept of cause.

1) \textit{Thesis:} The world must have a beginning in time and limits in
space; for an infinite series cannot be thought as given. \textit{Antithesis:}
The world can have no beginning and no limits, for otherwise an empty time
would have to precede its beginning and an empty space be outside it, and
neither the beginning nor the limit would then be comprehensible, since one
point of time or one place is not different from another in empty time and
empty space.

2) \textit{Thesis:} In dividing matter one must at last arrive at something
absolutely simple and indivisible (atoms or monads). \textit{Antithesis:}
Everything we can apprehend and represent is divisible, and the absolutely
simple and indivisible is an idea that can never be supported by experience.

3) \textit{Thesis:} In going back from effect to cause one must at last arrive
at a cause that is not in turn an effect; for otherwise one would never have
found the complete cause of anything! There must then be an absolute cause at
the beginning of the world's events, and perhaps also other absolute causes
within the course of the world (namely in beings with ``free'' will).
\textit{Antithesis:} An absolutely first cause is incomprehensible, since no
law connects it with its effect. There must surely be something that makes the
absolute cause begin to act at precisely this particular moment! ---

With regard to all three questions, then, we end according to Kant with
problematic judgments. There is a disproportion between our ideas and
experience: is it the former that are too large for
% --- p. 61 ---
\opage{61}the latter, or the latter that is too small for the former? We cannot
lay the blame on experience, since it is precisely the possibility of
experience that makes it possible to draw the boundary between category and
idea. The blame must therefore lie in the ideas or in the way in which we apply
them. --- According to Kant it is two different interests that manifest
themselves in the theses and in the antitheses. The theses express, he thinks,
the speculative standpoint of dogmatism, and they satisfy at the same time the
practical interest in the completion of the trains of thought, just as they are
popularly intelligible. The antitheses, on the other hand, appeal to
empiricism and to the purely scientific interest, whereas they contain
questionable practical consequences.

Toward the first two antinomies Kant takes a different position from that
toward the third. In the former --- he thinks --- both theses and antitheses
are false: the world is neither finite nor infinite, matter neither absolutely
divisible nor absolutely indivisible! The problems here fall away entirely when
we distinguish between our apprehension and the Ding an sich. Our apprehension
is a successive synthesis, which goes from member to member; here continuation
is always possible and completion impossible; every limit can be overstepped by
thought. But what thus holds for our apprehension --- that new tasks constantly
present themselves to it ---, that we have no right to transfer to things in
themselves. The idea of the world as a whole has for us only the significance
of constantly carrying our inquiry further and preventing us from premature
completion. --- It is easily seen that although Kant means to reject both
antitheses and theses, he in reality grants the antitheses to be right, as he
has indeed himself declared them to have sprung from the properly scientific
interest. For what the antitheses maintain is infinity in the sense of a
constant possibility of continuation, not given, completed infinity, which is a
contradiction\textsuperscript{16}). --- As regards the third antinomy, Kant
thinks that both thesis and antithesis can be correct, when the former is
understood of the Ding an sich, the latter of phenomena. In experience the
causal series is continued constantly, and no exceptions take place: if a
phenomenon were exempted from the law of causality, it could not, after all,
be distinguished from an illusion! But this constant conditionedness does not
hold for the thing in itself.
% --- p. 62 ---
\opage{62}Man as a being of experience, according to his phenomenal or
empirical character, is subject to the law of causality; but as Ding an sich,
as homo noumenon, according to his intelligible character, he can be regarded
as free. The intelligible character does not appear as phenomenon, but can be
regarded as the cause of the whole series of actions in which the empirical
character unfolds itself. --- Kant does not hereby mean to establish the
reality of free will, but merely to establish that if for practical reasons we
believe in the freedom of the will, such a belief will be compatible with the
lawfulness of the empirical character. He has not, however, succeeded. For how
can the intelligible character be the cause of the empirical one, when the
relation of time is not to find application to it? And when the empirical
character is seen as an effect of the intelligible one, an empirical
(phenomenal) explanation of the origin of character is thereby excluded.
Finally, the intelligible character itself is not ``freely'' chosen; Kant's
remarkable doctrine therefore becomes not a ``doctrine of freedom'' but a
fatalism of character: the intelligible character is unalterable --- and it
determines the whole series of a man's actions!

\textit{γ. Critique of Speculative Theology. ---} In the idea of God Kant
finds an expression of reason's need of complete completion. Such a completion
would be possible if thought could ground the assumption of a being necessary
in itself as the source of everything that has reality. It is thus an ideal of
knowledge that asserts itself here, and that it lies in the nature of human
reason to have such an ideal Kant finds confirmed by the fact that in science
one constantly works at leading all the forces in nature back to a single
fundamental force, and by the fact that in the popular religions a constant
tendency toward monotheism asserts itself. This ideal of knowledge has its
great significance. But it is another matter whether it is justified to make it
into an objective being (to hypostatize and realize it), indeed even to make it
into a personal being (to personify it).

1) The real proof of God's existence, the proof whose validity is presupposed
in all the other proofs that have been attempted, would be the
\textit{ontological} one, which derives God's existence from the very concept
we can form of him. It alone would lead to
% --- p. 63 ---
\opage{63}a complete completion of thinking, by leading to a concept whose
object would have to exist if one thinks it at all. We would then end in the
thought of something that has its ground in itself. --- But such a proof cannot
be given. From the concept of a thing the existence of the thing can never be
inferred. The concept can be entirely exact and complete, and yet it will be a
question by itself whether what is thus thought conceptually exists. For
existence is not a property like other properties: existence means merely that
the thing, as we think it in its concept (with all its properties), now also
really exists. The assumption of existence means the position of what is
thought in the concept and adds no new content. A hundred real thalers contain,
as far as the concept is concerned, no more than a hundred possible thalers.
There is no contradiction whatever in thinking something according to its whole
concept and yet thinking that it does not exist. --- Of existence we convince
ourselves by the fact that the thing belongs within the whole connection of our
experience, --- that there is a lawful connection between it and other things.
Outside the connection of experience we can give no proof of existence. Freedom
from self-contradiction is not enough for ascribing existence to the object of
a concept.

2) While the ontological proof starts from thought and seeks to get from it to
existence without using experience, the other proofs start from experience.
The \textit{cosmological} proof infers from the fact that something exists
(e.g. I myself) to an absolutely necessary cause of this. --- This proof
applies the causal principle beyond all possible experience, and it assumes at
the same time a completion of the causal series in an absolutely necessary
being, a being that has its ground in itself. The causal principle in itself
leads only from member to member in a constantly continued relation of
conditionedness, thus always only to finite causes, which must always again be
regarded as effects, and are thus only conditionally necessary; by assuming an
absolutely necessary being, the cosmological proof presupposes the validity of
the ontological proof, since it presupposes that there can be a being that has
its ground in itself, i.e. whose existence can be derived from its concept.
Such a completion is impossible for us: we cannot, even
% --- p. 64 ---
\opage{64}if we think of the Deity in the most exalted way, refrain from asking
whence it is. There lies here a true abyss for human reason --- an abyss that
can be thought filled only in an illusory way.

3) While the cosmological proof starts from the general experience that
something exists, the\textit{ physico-theological} proof starts from the order
and purposiveness that nature presents. --- But whence is it known that this
order and purposiveness is a matter of chance, --- that it does not follow from
the laws of nature according to which elements and forces act? (Cf. the
criticism of the physico-theological line of thought that Kant had already
given in his youthful writings). And even if one disregards this, the proof
leads only to the assumption of an orderer and master builder who has his
material given, not to the assumption of a creator. If one wants to arrive at
the assumption of an absolute being, one must use the cosmological and the
ontological line of thought, which have already been examined.

Neither by the way of pure thinking nor by that of experience, then, can a
proof of the existence of an absolute being be given, and the result obtained
earlier, that no scientific knowledge can be founded on the ideas, has thus
received its confirmation in the case of all three ideas. But the ideas do not
thereby lose their significance. Just as they have sprung from the very
structure of our mind, so they act as ideals and principles for our inquiry,
although they cannot be used for the knowledge of real existences. The idea of
an absolute totality leads us to demand and seek ever greater unity and
connection in our knowledge, keeps us from stopping too early. It becomes a
guiding thought for us that everything in the world stands in mutual, lawful
connection, \textit{as if} it had sprung from a ground of unity. The idea of
the soul has an analogous significance for research in the domain of inner
experience, and the idea of the world in the domain of outer experience. The
ideas have regulative, not constitutive significance. They guide and regulate
our advance within the domain of experience --- but by overstepping
(transcending) this domain they lose their significance, just as much as the
categories do. A ``transcendental'' knowledge there can be, according to Kant;
it consists in the knowledge of the presuppositions and principles on which our
% --- p. 65 ---
\opage{65}empirical knowledge rests; but a transcendent knowledge, a knowledge
that oversteps the domain of experience, there cannot be. (Kant, however,
sometimes uses the word ``transcendental'' in the same meaning as
``transcendent''). --- But should we --- Kant remarks --- arrive by another way
than that of scientific knowledge at the conviction of God's existence, then
the idea of an absolute being becomes of very great significance, since it
helps us to keep all sensuous and anthropomorphic representations away from
the thought of the Deity.

The result of the whole critique of speculative philosophy is that it wanted to
build a tower that could reach to heaven, but that there turns out to be
material only for building a house. About high towers and high-flying
metaphysicians there is --- says Kant --- usually much wind; that is nothing
for me; my place is the fruitful lowland of experience! --- Kant's speculative
successors, like HENRIK IBSEN's Master Builder Solness, thought that building
houses as dwellings for human beings was too slight a thing, and therefore,
like him, took to building castles in the air. For Kant it was no slight work
to labor in ``the fruitful lowland of experience'', if only one labored with a
wide horizon. And this he expresses in his doctrine of the ideas, which
enjoins that the highest thing is a never-resting striving that confidently
adds stone to stone, even though it knows that it always remains high up to
heaven. The thought expressed by Lessing of
eternal striving as man's true condition Kant has given a firm and deep
foundation in his doctrine of the fundamental form, mode of action and limits
of the human mind. But this thought has for Kant not merely theoretical
significance. It receives its full and proper significance in the practical
domain, as will appear in the consideration of Kant's ethics.

\subsection*{e.\quad Philosophy of Nature}

If we look back on Kant's epistemology, it is clear that, as it took shape in
``Kritik der reinen Vernunft'', it acquired a more constructive character, or,
as one can also express it, a more rationalist stamp, than it had
% --- p. 66 ---
\opage{66}in the years when the ``awakening'' probably took place, and when
analysis and empiricism gave it its stamp. The fundamental propositions that
condition experience Kant now thought, after all, that he could prove a priori.
As was suggested above, this proof did not succeed. But he thought himself so
certain on this point that he did not content himself with giving a deductive
proof of the causal principle, but also thought he could give such a proof of
the assumption of certain original forces of nature and laws of nature. In his
\textit{Metaphysische Anfangsgründe der Naturwissenschaft} (1786) he first
defines matter as the movable in space and then seeks to show that its essence
consists in an interplay of a repulsive and an attractive force. By the
repulsive force space is filled; it is therefore the first condition for matter
to be; but if it acted alone, \textit{matter would be dispersed in infinite
space;} there must then be an opposite force, which brings it about that the
repulsion does not go on to infinity, but that the parts of matter are held
together; --- if, conversely, attraction acted alone, \textit{all matter would
be gathered in one point.} Both forces therefore belong to the essence of
matter. --- Kant here takes the step that Newton did not dare to take: to
declare attraction a fundamental force. And in thinking that he can explain the
essence and subsistence of matter (the movable that we intuit in space) as the
result of the interaction of these two fundamental forces, he rejects atomism,
which he himself had professed thirty years earlier (in his ``Monadologia
physica''). By his attempt to derive matter from forces and by his application
of a constructive method in the philosophy of nature he paved the way for the
subsequent Romantic-speculative philosophy of nature. He moved further and
further away from the scientific mode of view that had intervened so mightily
in his philosophical development. Yet Kant himself --- in spite of his dynamic
constructions --- held fast to the strict scientific mode of explanation of all
material phenomena. From the concept of matter as the movable in space he
derives that all causes of material changes must be external, must be sought
in space outside the point that alters its state of motion. With this
fundamental proposition natural science stands and falls. All ``
% --- p. 67 ---
\opage{67}hylozoism'' (the assumption of inner forces or inner life in the
material points) would be the death of natural science. --- Of this derivation
of the law of inertia there holds what was already suggested in connection with
Kant's proof of the causal principle: that the demonstration of an idea as a
guiding thought for our inquiry is not the same as the proof of an objectively
valid law. But the zeal with which Kant enjoins the law of inertia shows that
he is not minded to abate the strict demands on the explanation of the
phenomena of nature.

The work on which Kant labored in his very last years was to show, by way of
construction, a transition from the general fundamental propositions that the
``Metaphysische Anfangsgründe'' had set up, to physics. This was an insoluble
task, and it was not merely the thinker's enfeeblement in old age that
prevented him from completing his work. But the attempt testifies to how strong
the constructive and rationalist tendency had gradually become in him.

\section*{4.\quad Ethics (Kritik der praktischen Vernunft)}

Kant's ethics is best known in its last form, in which it not only made a deep
impression on its age but has also in later times stood as the expression of a
typical ethical standpoint. What is at once characteristic and meritorious in
Kant's ethics must be sought, in the first place, in its finding the law of
man's right action in his own innermost being, seeing it as man's own law,
which acts practically in him if only he can truly become absorbed in himself
and become clear about himself. In the second place, in its having emancipated
the ethical from mere theory, from metaphysics and theology, and found an
independent foundation for it in man's practical nature. And in the third
place: although the moral law is found in man's own being, it nevertheless has
a strict and earnest character, points beyond man's individual limitation, lets
him see himself as a citizen in a great kingdom, and maintains the sublimity of
duty above every regard for self, every sensuous inclination, every immediate
impulse toward happiness. Kant sets his face against theology by maintaining
% --- p. 68 ---
\opage{68}the independence of ethics from religion, against the enlightenment of
the understanding by maintaining man's practical nature, the will, as what is
innermost in him, and against the idylls of the current doctrine of felicity by
letting the trumpet of unconditional tasks and demands sound. A feeling of
freedom and sublimity is the fundamental feeling in which this ethics lives.

Before we enter upon an account of it in detail, the account given earlier of
Kant's philosophical course of development must be supplemented by an
investigation of the process by which the Kantian ethics came into being.

Manifold elements have worked together here. As already suggested in the
biography, Kant's pietistic upbringing has left its effects in the strict
earnestness of his ethics. This remark was already made by his
contemporaries. \textsc{Schiller} writes to \textsc{Goethe} (22 Dec. 1798):
``There is still always something about Kant that makes one, as with Luther,
think of a monk who has indeed left his monastery but has not quite been able
to obliterate the traces of it''. Nevertheless, far too much weight has often
(e.g. by \textsc{Schopenhauer}) been laid on this point. When we see how
Kant's development actually proceeded, we find that the matter is not so
simple. Those after-effects from childhood have in many ways been modified by
the intervention of other elements, and on the other hand there were other
sides of Kant's nature that could lead him in the direction of ethical
rigorism. --- Before Kant's definitive ethics, two stages can be distinguished
in his course of development as an ethical thinker. (Cf. the fuller argument
in ``Kontinuiteten i Kants filosofiske Udviklingsgang''. ch. III).

\subsection*{a.\quad First Stage (1762--66)}

Very decisive was the influence of \textit{Rousseau.} It probably took place
at roughly the same time as the influence of Hume, that is, in the fertile
year 1762---63. In the ethical domain, as in the theoretical, dogmatism wanted
to regulate everything according to its ``eternal truths''. In opposition to
this, Rousseau demanded that one should learn to know human nature, and this
one could do only if one let it
% --- p. 69 ---
\opage{69}unfold freely, so that all theorizing and regulating received only an
indirect, negative significance. Imagined wants, mental as well as material,
were to be abolished. Not in the clarity of the understanding alone, but first
and foremost in feeling, in the inwardness and depth of the heart, lies man's
worth. Kant learned from Rousseau a new valuation of man. Earlier he had ---
as he himself has stated --- along with his age set enlightenment as the
highest thing and despised the rabble, who know nothing; Rousseau taught him
\textit{to honor men.} The idea of man's dignity as a personal being, --- an
idea that did not leave Kant at any stage of his later development and shows
us its continuity, --- Kant owes to the influence of Rousseau. --- Yet at this
time the study of the English moral philosophers (Shaftesbury, Hutcheson and
Hume) also worked upon Kant. To their writings he referred his hearers at this
time, and their thoughts he wanted to develop further. The distinction between
knowledge and feeling, which he carries through in psychological and ethical
respects, is due to this French and English influence; perhaps, however, also
to influence from Sulzer and Mendelssohn, his German predecessors on this
point.

Characteristic of this stage of Kant's ethics (according to his hints --- for
nothing more is extant from this period) is that all ethical judgments are led
back to a foundation of feeling. It is an immediate feeling that dictates them.
And the ethical feeling Kant describes particularly (in the small, interesting
work Beobachtungen über das Gefühl des Schönen und Erhabenen. 1764) as a feeling
of \textit{the beauty and dignity of human nature.} By this psychological
foundation this ethics differs decidedly from Kant's definitive ethics, in which
he disowns psychology, and he does not want merely to rely on
immediate psychological observation, but embarks on a comparative psychology,
investigating how the feelings of the beautiful and the sublime, to which the
ethical feeling belongs, vary among different races, among different
temperaments and between the two sexes. In a fragment from this time he says:
``In the first principles of ethical theory one must take account of the
different moral feeling of men, according to difference in sex,
% --- p. 70 ---
% print: „Værdighed“, the quotation „»Sand Dyd ...“ does not close (p. 70) (misprint)
\opage{70}age, upbringing and government, races and climates''. And in
``Nachricht von der Einrichtung seiner Vorlesungen 1765---66'' he announces
that in his lectures on ethics he will apply a method which is ``a fine
invention of our time'', and consists in first considering historically and
philosophically what happens, before showing what ought to happen. The point,
he continues, is to find man's lasting nature in order to be able to see what
perfection belongs to him in the state of crude simplicity, and what in that
of wise simplicity, and when he wants to raise himself above both.

Yet Kant does not assume, not even at this first stage of his ethics, that
immediate feeling is enough. ``True virtue can be built only on
\textit{fundamental propositions,} which are the nobler and more sublime the
more comprehensive they are. These fundamental propositions are not
speculative rules, but the consciousness of a feeling that lives in every human
breast, . . . the feeling of the beauty and dignity of human nature
\textit{(Beobachtungen über das Gefühl des Schönen und Erhabenen.} Königsberg
1764. p. 23). Here, then, there appears the trait characteristic of Kant's
ethics at all stages: the sublimity of the guiding ethical principle above
man's lower being. Kant remarks that there is a certain kinship between the
ethical feeling described and melancholy: for ``a soul whose strength is
limited feels a peculiar shudder when, filled with a great resolve, it sees the
dangers it has to pass through, and has before its eyes the hard but great
victory of self-conquest''. (Op. cit. p. 28). For the sanguine temperament,
therefore, this feeling does not lie within reach. The sanguine man's ethical
feeling has the stamp of beauty, not of sublimity, is without fundamental
propositions and dependent on momentary impressions (p. 34). --- Kant's
assertion of the necessity of general fundamental propositions stands in a
certain contradiction with his comparative method, which admits the possibility
of very considerable variations in the ethical feeling. Perhaps this
contradiction was one of the motives that led Kant beyond this first stage. The
last work in which this psychologizing ethics still prevails is ``Träume eines
Geistersehers'' (1766).
% --- p. 71 ---
% print: „afhængig“, for uafhængig (the author's slip) (p. 71) (misprint)
\opage{71}

\subsection*{b.\quad The Second Stage (1770--80)}

The turning point that came for Kant's philosophy at the end of the sixties
led, as shown earlier, to a sharp separation between sensibility and
reason, matter and form, and to an emphasis on reason and form as the
foundation of what is universally valid in our knowledge. It is possible that
Kant made the sharp distinction between reason and the sensuous in our being,
to which from this time on he also reckons feeling, earlier in the ethical
domain than in the theoretical. The transition probably took place in the
following way. When Kant already in the ``Beobachtungen'' laid such great
weight on fundamental propositions, it was because they denote the constant
and active elements in our nature as opposed to what is changing and passive.
But so long as the fundamental propositions were derived from feeling, were
only our consciousness of feeling, the foundation seemed to be uncertain and
empirical. With the prospect that opened up, after the discovery of the
Copernican principle, of a knowledge of reason independent of experience, an
endeavor to find for ethics too a foundation of reason independent of
experience naturally had to go hand in hand. In the ``Dissertation'' (1770) he
expressly distances himself from Shaftesbury's school --- reproaching it with
Epicureanism! Moral philosophy is now to be a pure science of reason. The moral
concepts are obtained not by experience but by pure reason itself. --- How
Kant's ethical conception took shape in the interval between the
``Dissertation'' and ``Kritik der reinen Vernunft'' we know only through some
fragments among Kant's posthumous papers. From a note of the seventies it is
seen that he laid weight on a ``practical idealism'', an ``idealism of reason,
of wisdom'', which consists in happiness being sought not outside us but in
ourselves. This thought occurs more fully worked out in a fragment published by
R. REICKE \textit{(Lose Blätter aus Kants Nachlass.} I. p. 9---16), which (as I
have sought to show in ``Kontinuiteten i Kants filosofiske Udviklingsgang''.
p. 43) very likely dates from the time immediately before the publication of
``Kritik der reinen Vernunft''. Just as the ultimate presupposition of all
knowledge of reason is the inner activity of
% --- p. 72 ---
\opage{72}thought (apperception), which makes coherent apprehension and
understanding possible, so too it is self-activity, the capacity to produce our
happiness ourselves, that is the firm ground of happiness. The matter of
happiness is sensuous, but its form is intellectual: for we preserve our
freedom and independence only when our willing is always in agreement with
itself. Morality is freedom under a universal law that expresses our agreement
with ourselves. It is thus the cause of happiness, and yet it does not have
happiness as its purpose. Neither morality nor happiness is dependent on
external results, on passive feelings or on the commands of authorities. ---
The standpoint expressed here thus finds the highest thing in the
self-activity by which the individual is the creator of his own happiness. By
its individualist and eudaemonist character it differs both from the earlier
standpoint and from the later one. But it marks an essential step in the
direction of laying the weight on the formal side of the ethical. Kant had here
reached a main point of his ethics: the inner relation between action and law,
which in his opinion could be present only when the law was purely formal; for
only then can the law be independent of experience. The distinction between
form and matter, between reason and experience, so important in Kant's
philosophy, he has here applied for the first time to the ethical.

\subsection*{c.\quad Third Stage (from 1785)}

In the transition to the definitive form that Kant's ethics assumed, three
different motives can be seen to have been at work: partly his psychological and
culture-historical conception, partly the conviction, gained through ``Kritik der reinen Vernunft'',
that the principles of pure reason are universal, valid for all
rational beings, and partly, finally, immediate observation and analysis of ethical
feeling as it expresses itself in practice.

\textit{α.} Kant had early been led to a \textit{developmental-historical
conception.} In his famous youthful work ``Allgemeine Naturgeschichte'' he had
put forward a hypothesis on the development of the solar system; in later treatises
he had discussed the prehistory of the earth and the origin of the human races. His constant
% --- p. 73 ---
\opage{73}interest in physical geography and in anthropology, subjects on which he gave
popular lectures, could not but keep his attention alive to the natural history
of man, even while his thought sought the ultimate grounds of our knowledge
and of our ethical judgments. Two of the most important thoughts of the doctrine of evolution are
already found in him: the principle of actuality, according to which the past must be explained
by causes we know from present experience, and the principle of the summation of small
effects into great and distant results. In the thought of development
he found the solution of \textit{Rousseau's problem} concerning the relation of culture
to individual happiness. As we have seen, he was strongly occupied with Rousseau
at once, when the latter's significant writings appeared (at the beginning of the sixties). At
the beginning of the eighties, after the publication of his main work, he again came
to concern himself with Rousseau's problem. It had become clearer and
clearer to him that individual happiness could not be the measure of the value of historical
development. On the whole there developed in him a dark view of human
nature, as experience and history teach us to know it. In
his notes and in his later published \textit{Anthropologie}, as well as
throughout his ethical writings and his writings in the philosophy of religion, we find this
empirical pessimism\textsuperscript{17}); the beauty of human nature, which he
had emphasized in ``Beobachtungen'', fades for him. We are a lazy, cowardly and
false race. Folly combined with a trait of wickedness (Thorheit mit einem
Liniamente von Bosheit) is the stamp of our race. Kant quotes in his ``Anthropologie''
with approval Frederick the Great's words to the optimistic Sulzer: ``My dear
Sulzer, you do not know what an accursed race we belong to''. One cannot without
strong repugnance watch the doings of men on the great stage of the world. Far greater
than the distress that nature inflicts on men is that which they inflict on
one another. The solution of the problem Kant finds in this, that development --- unconsciously
for the individuals --- leads toward a purpose of nature for the species, a
goal that is reached precisely through strife, wickedness and misfortune, and a goal that
individuals perhaps, if they became conscious of it, would not care about.
In a remarkable little work \textit{Idee zu einer allgemeinen}
% --- p. 74 ---
\opage{74}\textit{Geschichte in weltbürgerlicher Absicht} (1784) Kant develops this
thought, and takes it up again, with special regard to Rousseau, a few years later in
the treatise \textit{Muthmaasslicher Anfang des Menschengeschlechts} (1786).
The lots of the individual and of the species are different. As an animal being of instinct, the
single individual can reach full development; but man's peculiar capacities as a
rational being come to development only in the course of the species' history.
The development of reason requires long series of generations, for art is long, and
life short. What one generation has gained, the next can begin with, and
in this way a progress becomes possible in history, but a progress
which --- so long as the goal has not been reached --- brings greater suffering for the
individual than the instinctive life of the state of nature. Kant emphasizes in particular that
sexual maturity comes to man long before he is mature as a
being of culture, and that culture increases the inequality among men. If
individual happiness were the goal, man would have had to remain in the
instinctive life of Paradise; after he has broken with instinct --- a break that in the old
story is depicted as a fall --- and has entered upon the way of reason,
there is nothing else for it but to go the way to its end, so that self-won insight may
take the place of instinct in the regulation of life. In place of immediate
happiness there then comes worthiness of happiness through free self-activity as the goal
for the single individual. But the attainment of this goal presupposes the formation of
a free civil society, indeed, in the last instance, of a cosmopolitan
society\textsuperscript{18}). But a society in which the freedom of the individual, by
being bound by law, stands as compatible with the freedom of all others, develops only
because distress drives toward it. A constant strife is carried on among men in
their life together. They need one another, but their ambition and avarice
constantly bring them into strife --- individuals among themselves, and states among themselves.
This strife is necessary. For otherwise the species would perish from indolence,
and otherwise the faculties would not be developed. The trees in the forest seek to rob
one another of light and air, but thereby compel one another to seek light and
air in higher regions, and thereby attain in turn a beautiful, tall and
% --- p. 75 ---
\opage{75}straight growth. All culture and art, all social order is the fruit of antisocial
tendencies, whose mutual conflict compels to discipline and to develop the seeds of nature
to perfect proficiency. But on the way to perfect culture are found the
greatest sufferings. The time of transition is painful, and Rousseau was not altogether
wrong when he preferred the state of nature to half-civilization.

It is not Kant's meaning that a merely external harmony between the egoistic
interests should be the ideal and distant goal toward which history leads. The
highest culture includes morality; for only the good that springs from a
morally good disposition is more than illusion and glittering misery. Morality
thus stands here for Kant as the keystone of the education of humanity.

Now we find that Kant, the year after the publication of his ``Idee einer allgemeinen
Weltgeschichte'', for the first time declares (in \textit{Grundlegung zur Metaphysik der
Sitten.} 1785) that the moral law, as it expresses itself in the clearly
conscious conscience, aims precisely at this, that one should act so that the
rule one follows can become universal law, and that every human being
be treated as an end, not merely as a means. We see, then, that what Kant on his
definitive ethical standpoint presents as the content of the moral law or of duty
is \textit{an anticipation of the goal of historical development ---}
just as the a priori propositions in the theoretical domain, by means of the
concepts of magnitude and of cause, \textit{anticipated} the course of experience. The ideal,
drawn from human experience and human need, of a free society of
human personalities --- an ideal that again and again, under many
different forms, pushes forward in the history of ethics and of religion ---
denotes for Kant at once the \textit{final goal} of history, progressing through egoism,
antagonism, distress and sorrow, and the \textit{content} of the
moral law that makes itself known in the individual's inner self. Kant's ethics is the formulation
of a historical ideal, and is not so purely a priori as he himself supposed. As
in all formation of ideals, experience here too played its part\textsuperscript{19}) ---
The exalted, absolute, unconditional character that the moral law acquired for Kant
in opposition to the
% --- p. 76 ---
\opage{76}individual's sensuous nature and limited capacity is naturally explained by the fact that it is
the goal of the species that in the moral law makes itself known in the consciousness of the single individual. Therein
lies the marvelous in the moral law, as in all instincts of the species. The
great opposition that for Kant historically existed between the goals of the individual and of the species
led him to assume a no less sharp opposition between the
moral law and all empirically given elements in human nature.
Psychology seemed unable to fill this gap. Only by a leap
does Kant now pass from psychology over into ethics. While in ``Idee'' he had still
regarded morality as the highest step of cultural development, it later
(Kritik der Urtheilskraft. § 84) stood for him as an impossibility that any degree of
natural development could satisfy the unconditional
demand of the moral law. He kicks away behind him the historical ladder by which he had reached his
definitive ethics.

\textit{β}. The influence of Kant's epistemological investigations (in
``Kritik der reinen Vernunft'') makes itself felt very strongly in the development of
his ethics into its definitive form. Already the year after the publication of ``Kritik
der reinen Vernunft'' Kant was working on an exposition of the principles of ethics
(as is seen from a letter from Hamann to Hartknoch of 11 January 1782). Sharply
as he wishes to distinguish between theory and practice, they were nonetheless closely
connected for him. A main thought in ``Kritik der reinen Vernunft'' was, after all, that a
world of experience, a nature, comes into being for us only on the presupposition of
objective, universally valid laws. Kant has now expressly conceived the moral law by
analogy with the laws of nature: ``The validity of the will as universal law for possible
actions offers an analogy with the connection of existing things according to
universal laws, which is the formal side of nature'', --- and therefore the
moral law, the unconditional demand (the categorical imperative), can be expressed
thus: ``You shall act as if the fundamental proposition on which your action
rests were, through your will, to be made a universal law of nature''.
(Grundlegung zur Metaphysik der Sitten. 3. Aufl. p. 52. 81). Just as by
the law of causality we enter into the great real world, so the
% --- p. 77 ---
\opage{77}moral law thus opens to us access to an ideal world. There the question is
whether my representations are to have objective validity; here the question is
whether my actions are to have objective validity. The objective
rests everywhere on law. Already in the fragment that acquainted us with Kant's ethics at
its second stage, inner consistency, agreement
with ourselves in all our willing, was stressed as the decisive thing. This way of consideration is now
extended so that the purely individualistic falls away: the law of our action is to
be the law for a world of spiritual beings. I come into contradiction with
myself when I judge myself otherwise than I judge others!

But now experience can never ground a universal law; the possibility of experience
rests, conversely, on the validity of the law. This holds practically as well as
theoretically. Human nature as given in experience, which psychology and history
teach us to know, can therefore give us no foundation for the moral law.
Its origin is independent of all experience, cannot be explained at all
empirically or theoretically. Besides, it is the whole of human nature given in
experience that is to be subjected to the moral law and regulated by it: so
it cannot itself be the source of the law. Experience is always conditioned, but
the law is unconditioned. Reason must take its standpoint outside phenomena, if
it is to be able to subject everything to its unconditional law. This law does not thereby
cease to be the law of man's own innermost being: but it springs from that in
man which cannot appear in experience, from the intelligible in
man, not from man as phenomenon, from man as Ding an sich, as
noumenon, not from man as a sensuous being. Already in ``Kritik der reinen
Vernunft'' (1. Aufl. p. 553) it was declared that ``reason itself is no phenomenon
and is subject to no sensuous conditions'', and the whole doctrine of the
intelligible character shows that the peculiar and fateful turn that
Kant's ethics underwent already stood firm in principle for Kant when he wrote his
main work. In \textit{Kritik der praktischen Vernunft} (§ 5) it is said that
the mere form of the law has nothing whatever to do with phenomena, but
% --- p. 78 ---
\opage{78}makes man independent of everything in the world of phenomena. Man himself is thus
a citizen of two worlds: as a member of the intelligible world he gives the law to
himself as a member of the phenomenal world: he is at once lawgiver and
subject. He need not go beyond himself (only beyond his sensuous,
phenomenal being) to find the unconditioned. A ``You shall!'' exists for
man only because, besides belonging to the intelligible world, he also belongs
to the world of sense.

But thereby both the moral law itself and the possibility of its being
applied in the world of experience become altogether inexplicable. It becomes just as impossible
to explain ``how reason can become practical'' as to explain
how the intelligible world, things in themselves, are connected with the
phenomenal world. No mortal can see how the intelligible world
underlies the world of sense! ---

One sees the ascent in Kant's ethical idealism. In his zeal to assert the
loftiness of the moral law and the dignity of personality he raises them beyond
the world of experience, so that it becomes a riddle how they can have anything to
do with it. He places the foundation of the ethical beyond the limit of knowledge and
lets it share the fate of the disputed limiting concept in which his
theoretical thinking found its conclusion. Through his ever more sharply pointed
opposition to empiricism he approaches mysticism\textsuperscript{20}), and
he does indeed expressly declare that mysticism is less questionable in a
moral respect than empiricism (Kritik der praktischen Vernunft I, 1, 2 at the
end). Kant's rationalism was on the way to passing over into mysticism, just as in its
time mysticism (in the form of pietism) had contributed to the development of
