rationalism. --- There is here a decided inconsistency in his philosophy. Since the forms,
according to Kant, are gained by analysis of experience, they cannot be separated from
phenomena and placed in complete opposition to them. The forms are not
intelligible, they are gained by abstraction and analysis and cannot be regarded
as belonging to another world than the one in which they were found, even if
here they have the great significance of forming the foundation of all objective validity. This
must hold for the formal moral law,
% --- p. 79 ---
\opage{79}as well as for the forms of intuition and the categories. It is Kant's ethical interest
that leads him to assign the moral law a place in the intelligible
world (or rather to regard it as the entrance to this world), while he
does not think of assigning a similar dignity to the law of causality, which is analogous to
it. --- As so often, ethical idealism has by its overstraining
worked against itself. One does ethics no service by founding
it on something that lies beyond all experience. It is, after all, precisely in the world of experience
that the ethical is to live and work. --- What is significant in Kant's fundamental ethical
conception could very well have been preserved even if he had not turned his
back on psychology. The opposition between the ethical ideal and other elements in
our nature, which he has so energetically emphasized, is in reality taken from
psychological experience, and it is only a mythological expression that Kant gives this
experience by making it one with the opposition between the intelligible and the
phenomenal world.

\textit{γ.} In his ethical writings \textit{(Grundlegung} 1785 and \textit{Kritik
der praktischen Vernunft} 1788) Kant arrives at the statement of the principle of ethics
through \textit{analysis of the ordinary, practically given moral consciousness.}
He sets as the task of philosophical ethics to find and to think through the
principle that practical human reason involuntarily applies. He
presents first 1) the ethical phenomena or data, then finds out 2) the
law to which these bear witness, and finally 3) the force that works according to this law.

1) Already the ordinary moral consciousness is clear that the ethical value of an action
does not rest on what is attained or accomplished in the external world. Not the
external effects, but the inner will is what matters: nothing is good
but the good will! In the acting personality itself, not outside it, must
the good be found! Only that action is therefore good which springs from duty, or
from respect for the moral law. Neither custom and usage nor the experiences of the past
nor exemplars --- were they even the most exalted --- make an action good.
Every custom and every exemplar, every ideal given in experience must, after all,
itself first be tested and valued.
% --- p. 80 ---
\opage{80}Even the Holy One of whom the Gospel tells must be compared with our ideal
before we can acknowledge him. Neither a theological nor a psychological grounding of
ethics is therefore possible. Duty springs neither from authority nor from
experience. All feeling is empirical, sensuous, egoistic; even the so-called
moral sense and sympathy are at bottom only forms of the impulse toward happiness.
The decisive determination in the ethical is \textit{self-legislation}
(autonomy). From it follows the inwardness of the law; by being subject to the law of our own being
we are independent of experience and authority, and are at the same time
active, self-active.

Experience now shows that there are elements in man's nature which only reluctantly
bow to this inner law that is contained in practical reason. It is precisely
through this that we come to call it a law, and that its demands come to
stand as unconditional commands, categorical imperatives. There is talk of an
ought, which is nonetheless one with our innermost willing: but this innermost willing
meets resistance in ourselves. We have an inclination not to be
autonomous, not to follow the innermost law of our own will. Thereby the
ethical task assumes the character of \textit{duty,} moral necessitation, and the moral law
comes to stand as exalted above all empirically given elements in
our being.

All moral consciousness offers, according to Kant, these two features to analysis: the
inwardness of the law and its exaltedness, --- its unity with man's being and its
sharp opposition to man's phenomenon. Even in the worst scoundrel, Kant
asserts, these features can be traced. While in his youthful work
(Beobachtungen 1764) he admitted even very considerable variations in moral
feeling, he now, in a rather dogmatizing manner, makes human nature
more uniform than it is --- but this, too, becomes possible for him only by going
beyond experience.

Kant lays very great weight on the oppositions in human nature. Precisely
extreme cases, he thinks, show us best of all what different elements
and forces human nature encloses. The examples on which he bases
% --- p. 81 ---
\opage{81}his analysis are almost all taken from cases of conflict. The ethical
appears the more clearly in its peculiarity, the stronger the opposing
forces are, and the more other auxiliary motives than the purely ethical are kept out.
In ``the doctrine of method of pure practical reason'', which forms the concluding section of
``Kritik der praktischen Vernunft'', he therefore recommends cases of conflict, which
are for ethical analysis what the method of reagents is for chemical
analysis\textsuperscript{21}). But Kant does not hold merely to this, that the ethical
\textit{stands out most clearly} in cases of conflict between the ethical demand on
the one side, sensuous and egoistic interest on the other side. He declares
even that only in such states is the good will \textit{actually
present:} ``The state in which I, when certain of my purposes collide with the
moral law of duty, am conscious of preferring the latter, is not merely a
state that is better than others, but \textit{the only state good in
itself''.} \textsc{Schiller} caricatured this rigoristic tendency in Kant's ethics in a well-known epigram
by drawing the conclusion that one does one's duty only when one does
it with loathing. That was not Kant's meaning. As he himself bursts out in a dithyramb
to duty, the exalted power in man's inner self, so too it was his
meaning that duty should be practiced with cheerful boldness and enthusiasm. He was only somewhat
wary of the duties that came all too easily; he would see in them a sign
that one had not found one's proper duty. And he demanded that in the
relation of duty abstraction should be made from all self-interest and all immediate
allurement. The relation of duty is not to abolish the independence of the individual, but only
to limit it.

2) But what, then, is the \textit{content} of the law that, according to Kant, makes itself known
in every man's consciousness (whether he is able to formulate it or
not)? --- Since the law (on account of its inwardness and exaltedness) is to be
independent of all experience, the answer to this question seems to be
difficult. Kant answers consistently: the moral law is purely formal; it states
merely the form the will must have in order to be good. And the form is this, that the
principle I follow in my action must be capable of being laid down as the foundation of a
universal legislation, i.e.\ must be able to hold for all other rational beings in
% --- p. 82 ---
\opage{82}the same situation as I am in. The one who wills is to apply a universal measure
to himself, to regard his action as if by it he were about to create a
new nature. By means of this rule it will, Kant thinks, be easy in the individual cases
to find out one's duty, far easier than to attain happiness. That I may not
keep goods entrusted to me, that I may not lie, even if discovery is impossible, now follows
of itself: for if this right became universal, all trust between
men would fall away. The individual thus regards himself in his valuation as one
among many, and he limits his willing according to what the conditions of the
life together of the many require. Kant expressly distinguishes his moral principle from the old
rule that we must not do to others what we would not have them do to
us, a rule that can be interpreted purely egoistically. But there lies in his principle
more than the merely formal, mere logical consistency: there lies also the
presupposition that there are other interests than my own private ones, --- that there
are other personal centers in the world than myself. Should that be
something that can be known by the a priori way of pure reason? That I am a member of
a society whose welfare is my law, I know, after all, only through experience. And as we
have seen, Kant's ethics did in reality arise under the influence of
his culture-historical conception. He himself comes to admit that the
moral law is empirically and historically determined, not purely formal, when he says
\textit{(Tugendlehre} § 27): ``Legislating reason includes in its idea of
humanity in general the whole species''. That is, after all, an idea that has its
history, and a slow and laborious history! --- And Kant has also felt
the impossibility of getting anywhere with a purely formal principle, since all
action presupposes positive purposes and tasks. But if the categorical
imperative, the unconditional in the relation of duty, is not to be violated, the purposes
that are set up must be such as have an absolute value: otherwise it cannot
be made a duty to have them! The value of my personality --- such, roughly, is
Kant's line of thought --- rests on my capacity to follow the universal law in my
inner self; what purpose, then, can it be my unconditional duty to have? Only the
one, comes the answer: to respect
% --- p. 83 ---
\opage{83}the value of other personalities, which likewise is grounded on \textit{their} capacity
for self-legislation. While Kant's \textit{first ethical formula} was this: ``You
shall act so that the principle of your acting can serve as a universal
rule!'' --- his \textit{second} \textit{formula} becomes this: ``You shall act
so that you always treat humanity, in yourself as well as in every
other, as an end, never merely as a means!'' (Grundlegung. 3. Aufl. p. 66. ---
Kritik der prakt. Vernunft I, 1, 3. --- Tugendlehre. Einleitung § III---IV).
In his opinion the second formula can be derived from the first; but this is an
impossibility if the first is taken as purely formal. Both formulas
presuppose that we actually feel ourselves as members of a kingdom of personal beings. And
it is rather the first formula that springs from the second: as surely as the law
exists for the sake of personalities, not the reverse! Apart from what is artificial in
the derivation, it is a great and significant principle that Kant has stated. It is
the principle of personality in its noblest form, a thought that will live when Kant's
imperfect and unnatural grounding has long been forgotten, a thought of great ethical
value both as against the principle of authority, when this would be more than an
educative principle, and as against the external doctrine of utility and happiness, which holds
to the shells and forgets the kernel. ---

Kant himself, however, now maintained that his moral principle was purely formal,
an expression of pure reason. But then the question arises how this
intelligible law can determine our will as it works in experience? How can
the law become a \textit{motive? ---} In his zeal to assert the inwardness and
exaltedness of the law Kant had pushed psychology aside. He would not ground the
ethical on feeling, since feeling is a passive state, dependent on experiences.
But he cannot deny that action becomes impossible if feeling does not drive
the work. He then seeks to show that the very thought of the universal moral law
awakens in us a feeling of respect and reverence. Respect is, according to him, a
feeling that cannot be explained by experience; it is neither pleasure nor pain,
but pure interest, awakened by the loftiness of the law in our inner self, an effect that the thought
of this law produces on the mind. Here, then, is a motive that can set our
% --- p. 84 ---
\opage{84}empirical willing in motion. But it is, to be sure, a motive that is just as great a
riddle as the relation between the intelligible and the phenomenal world in general,
and, what is still more questionable: a motive whose possibility conflicts with Kant's
own conception of the causal principle as valid for all phenomena, inner and
outer; respect, after all, is not supposed to be explicable by phenomenal causes. Here again
Kant's ethical idealism has led him astray; but here again it is very
possible to separate the significant thought from the garb Kant gives it.

3) From the phenomenon, the moral consciousness of practical man, Kant went to
the law, and from the law he goes to the force. The law is the expression of a\textit{
consciousness of freedom.} Law and freedom are in a certain sense one; if one would distinguish
between them, we infer from the law back to freedom (Kritik der prakt.
Vern. § 6). The law proceeds from the will itself (Grundlegung. 3. Aufl. p. 104 ff.
--- Rechtslehre. Einleitung § IV). For the law is, after all, the fruit of self-legislation,
the expression of our autonomy as rational beings. By freedom Kant understands
\textit{first and foremost} originality, the capacity to act according to inner
principles and forces, independence of the given and of the external. --- But
Kant does not stop at this definition of freedom. Freedom involves for
him also \textit{the capacity to make an absolute beginning,} to initiate an
absolutely new causal series. This capacity is for him a necessary consequence of
originality and independence. But then ``freedom'' cannot be
found at all in the world of phenomena, which, as Kant has shown in ``Kritik der reinen
Vernunft'', offers no absolute beginnings. If freedom is to be the capacity for
absolute production of the motives\textsuperscript{22}) that determine the will working in
experience (something already contained in the doctrine of
respect), then it can be found only in the intelligible world (if one can act
and begin there --- since time, after all, does not hold!). Kant does not investigate whether
independence and the capacity for absolute beginning absolutely belong together. New centers
can, after all, form in the world, which, once they are formed, act independently of external
influence, according to an inner law. Kant makes each single will a god, instead
of letting it acquire its divinity through development and labor.
% --- p. 85 ---
\opage{85}

And besides the two definitions of ``freedom'' (as independence and as capacity for
absolute beginning) there comes, in a few places (Kritik der prakt. Vernunft.
Kehrbach's edition, p. 116 ff. --- Religion innerhalb der Grenzen der reinen
Vernunft, passim), a third: \textit{the capacity} \textit{to do just as well the
one as the other of two opposite things.} That Kant came to set up such a
monstrosity of a concept finds its explanation in the sharp opposition in which
he has set man's ideal (intelligible) being to man as he
appears in experience. As greatly as he thinks of the former, so meanly does he think
of the latter. There is a violent tension between the two poles, and it could not but
remain unexplained how man, whose innermost being is good (freedom
in the first sense is one with the good), could give room in himself to such motives as
experience attests. Kant explains it by assuming an equally
inexplicable capacity\textsuperscript{23}). --- Here again Kant is more in the right in the
facts he points to than in his theory of them. Human nature includes the
greatest oppositions within itself, seeds of good and seeds of evil. There is
a capacity to form ideals of exaltedness and purity, and there is perversity,
contrariness and filth. These oppositions must hang together in human nature; they
must have developed according to definite laws and under definite conditions. Kant,
who otherwise knew well enough the natural investigator's standpoint toward human affairs,
here made every solution impossible for himself by his unhappy dualism of ethics and
psychology. ---

\subsection*{d.\quad Special Ethics}

In two books that at many points bear the stamp of the weakness of old age,
\textit{Rechtslehre and Tugendlehre,} both published in 1797, Kant has set forth
his special ethics. The imperfection of these expositions is connected above all
with the systematizing that had gained the upper hand in the old thinker; but
at the same time, naturally, the one-sidedness of Kant's whole ethical conception expresses itself in
many particular questions. Above all signs of
% --- p. 86 ---
\opage{86}decrepitude and one-sidedness there nonetheless tower a series of noble and manly thoughts, Kant's
great legacy to the race.

The two books stand in a certain opposition to each other, in that the doctrine of right holds
to legality, the external agreement between my action and the law that
upholds the freedom of others as well as my own, while the doctrine of virtue also demands
morality: that the action is to spring from a disposition, an inner will to
acknowledge the law. The moral law (the categorical imperative) demands that my
will be limited by such conditions as the freedom of others requires. But
the observance of this limitation can come about from fear or from self-interest,
not merely from moral motives. The development toward the ideal state in
which no war takes place can proceed under the influence of many
different motives, which are not all properly moral. The opposition between
legality and morality is not absolute: for at the foundation of the establishment of
legality, at the foundation of the demand that there shall be laws, lies the
categorical imperative: \textit{``Es soll kein Krieg sein,} weder der, welcher
zwischen Mir und Dir im Naturzustande, noch zwischen uns als Staaten; denn das
ist nicht die Art, wie jedermann sein Recht suchen soll''. (Rechtslehre.
Beschluss). This confirms the assumption maintained above, that Kant's moral law
is an anticipation of the result of historical development. The legal order stands ---
although it requires only legality --- as a morally postulated means. ``Reason
obliges us'', says Kant (Rechtslehre § 49), ``by a categorical imperative to
strive after a state in which the constitution of society stands in as great
agreement with principles of right as possible''. Kant thus admits that the
realization of the highest moral purpose can also be prepared by the influence
of other than purely moral motives. And the very external securing of freedom that
the legal order makes possible is a condition for the inner moral disposition to be able to
develop (Lose Blätter aus Kants Nachlass. p. 528). In his foundational
ethical writings (``Grundlegung'' and ``Kritik der praktischen Vernunft'') Kant
states a sharper opposition between legality and morality than he can
maintain where the investigation goes into particulars.
% --- p. 87 ---
\opage{87}

Kant defines right as the sum of the conditions under which the will of the one
can be united with that of the other according to a universal law of freedom. There
is only a single innate right, which is attached to every human
personality, namely:\textit{ freedom, i.e.\ independence of the compelling arbitrariness
of every other, insofar as it can coexist with the freedom of every other
according to a universal law.} The right of property is thus grounded not merely in this, that
I have taken possession of a thing before anyone else takes possession of it (prior
occupatio), but first in this, that I acknowledge the equal right of others to what they first
have taken possession of. --- If anywhere, it is clear here that Kant's ethical
principles constantly presuppose the existence of a society as historically given. The
society itself Kant nonetheless conceives as having arisen by a contract that limits the
freedom of the individual by regard for the equal freedom of others. But he does not regard
this contract as a historical event. He uses the thought of it as a
guiding idea, a principle of reason for the valuation and development of
social relations. The historical origin of society he regards as a thing
indifferent in this connection. By this standpoint he marks a decided
advance over the mythologizing of the earlier teachers of natural law. Only he did not
raise the question how the principle of reason itself comes into being in
men's consciousness; here lies what is dogmatic in him.

Peculiar to Kant's doctrine of right is the strict carrying through of the individual's
rights of man, supported above all by a sharp distinction between person (a being with
self-legislation and accountability) and thing. A person must never be treated as
a mere means! From this proposition Kant derives not only personal freedom, but
also freedom of discussion and the right to a share in legislation.
Legislation must not decide anything about the people that the people could not will to
decide about itself, --- e.g.\ introduce an unalterable system of dogma that
abolishes the right to advance in enlightenment, or introduce hereditary nobility. --- With
enthusiasm Kant had hailed the North American War of Independence and the French
Revolution, and even in his doctrine of right he has not forgotten this enthusiasm. He
looked to the
% --- p. 88 ---
\opage{88}republic as the constitution of the future; but the republican spirit was nonetheless
more important to him than the external constitution, and a monarchy could in his opinion very
well be governed in a republican spirit. Paternal government he abhorred. The sovereign has
no right to make anyone happy against his will. Right has its origin in
freedom, not in happiness, and it is for freedom, not for happiness, that the sovereign
is to provide. Therefore punishment must not be meted out as a means to a good for society
or for the criminal himself, but solely and only for the reason that the criminal has
willed his action. Man would be treated as a means, as a thing, if
punishment were grounded in any other way than as retribution. Retribution is a
categorical imperative. Punishment must not be exercised in order to bring advantage, but is to be
exercised though it cause ever so much inconvenience. If a people were about to emigrate,
it ought first to execute the murderers! Fiat justitia, pereat mundus --- that means
in Kant's translation: ``Justice shall reign, even if all the rogues in the world
perish by it!'' ---

In his ``doctrine of virtue'' (individual ethics) Kant lays the weight above all on the
bearing of character that corresponds to his general conception of the ethical.
Virtue consists for him in strength of soul (fortitudo moralis), in the force and
dignity that follow from the consciousness of having the law for one's acting in one's
own inner self and of being bound through this law to a great whole.

The purposes that Kant's individual ethics sets are: 1) one's own perfection and 2)
the happiness of others. Not one's own happiness: for one strives after it involuntarily and
so eagerly that one regards it as the duty of others also to provide for it.
Nor the perfection of others: for only they themselves can provide for it;
perfection consists precisely in making oneself one's purpose according to one's
own concepts of duty. (As if happiness were so easy to win, and as if one did not
need help in one's own striving after the perfect!) --- 1) Under
the endeavor for one's own perfection belongs the development of all lower and higher
faculties, all culture. The point is to make the animal into man: ``What is
characteristic of man in opposition to
% --- p. 89 ---
\opage{89}the animal is the capacity to set himself purposes. Now if humanity in our own
person is the purpose, then there is bound up with this the duty to make oneself deserving of
humanity by culture'' --- first and foremost ``moral culture'', that is to say
the capacity to let one's actions be determined by the inner law. But everything that
makes man an active and useful member of society Kant derives from
human dignity: to be useless and superfluous is to degrade
humanity in one's person. A very characteristic section is: ``Von der
Kriecherei''. As a person man is of priceless value. Humble before the law in
his inner self, he is therefore to assert himself before all others, even were he to come
to stand before a seraph! Humility before others is not a duty, but can be
Pharisaism or even baseness, if one would win favor or advantage
by it. Therefore become not the slaves of men! Let not your right be trodden under
foot! Accept not benefits you can do without! Show steadfastness and
shun unworthy wailing under sufferings! Kneel to no one, for the ideal is within
you, and what can appear outside you can only be an idol! Deep bows and
many outward signs of courtesy are expressions of men's propensity to servility. And when
one makes oneself a worm, one cannot complain of being trodden under
foot! --- 2) With the second purpose that Kant sets up in individual ethics,
the happiness of others, there arises for him --- without his being clearly
conscious of it --- an extraordinarily difficult problem: is one in this to be guided
by the notions of happiness of others or by one's own? It is a problem
that leads into the innermost depths of personal life, especially when one, like Kant, has
so sharp a conception of personal dignity, determined by self-legislation.
Kant is very wavering here. Now he says that others have no
right to demand of me what I do not think will make them happy, and
speaks of the sour merit of promoting the true welfare of others although they do not
acknowledge it as such; now he says that I cannot do good to others
according to \textit{my} concepts of happiness, and that it cannot be called beneficence
when I deprive another of the freedom to become happy in \textit{his own}
way. --- The duties toward
% --- p. 90 ---
\opage{90}others Kant divides into duties of love and duties of respect, according as there is to reign
a relation of attraction and approach or a relation of distance.
The duty of respect follows directly from the first propositions of Kant's ethics.
He stands in a more difficult position toward love, partly on account of the sharply
cut independence he gives each single personality, partly on account of
the pessimistic conception he has of actual human nature.
Love must be limited by the other's right, for the other renounces his
human dignity when he does not himself have control over himself and his condition. Besides,
love is an immediate feeling and need that cannot be regulated by the commands of
reason. And as men actually are, it cannot be demanded that one
should feel delight in them. It is our duty to will them well and to do them good, and
this duty does not lapse with the sad experience that our race, when one
comes to know it more closely, is found exceedingly little lovable. The love of benevolence, not
of delight (amor benevolentiæ, non complacentiæ), is what can
be a duty. A harmony between approach and distance, between love and
respect, Kant finds in the relation of friendship: true friendship is indeed ``a rare bird,
to be likened to a black swan''; but black swans really exist. --- One
must, on the other hand, excuse Kant, as a bachelor, for having so imperfect an
understanding of marriage. He does not speak of it in the doctrine of virtue, but in the doctrine of right.
It is a contractual relation by which two persons of different sex bind
themselves to enter into sexual relations only with each other, not with others.
The sexual inclination Kant speaks of only as a purely isolated need in
human nature, sees it only from the purely sensuous side and has no eye for
its nuances and possible connection with some of the most ideal feelings.
% --- p. 91 ---
% print: „blossen Vernunft.“, the parenthesis of the heading does not close (p. 91) (misprint)
\opage{91}

\section*{5.\quad Philosophy of Religion (Kritik der praktischen Vernunft and Religion innerhalb der Grenzen der blossen Vernunft)}

\subsection*{a.\quad Morality and Religion}

Kant's ethics is autonomous --- is (or wishes to be) independent of all other
presuppositions than those that lie in man's innermost being, in the activity
that is his innermost nature, independent of physics and hyperphysics, of psychology and
theology. It must then be very difficult for Kant to demonstrate a natural
transition from morality to religion. For how can dependence be derived from
pure independence and self-activity? And yet it was early (from as far back as 1766, see
``Träume eines Geistersehers'') Kant's conviction that religion could only be
grounded on morality. The explanation lies in this, that the unconditional task that is
set man in his innermost self is to be solved by a finite, a limited
being. The moral law acquaints us with our inner freedom, and thereby with our independence
of the whole world of experience. But it is, after all, precisely to be carried through in
the world of experience, to permeate our personality completely. There then arises
a \textit{need of reason,} a moral want, which demands that the conditions be
fulfilled without which the complete realization of the ideal task is
impossible. The first condition is continued existence, for only by a progress going on
to infinity can the will come into perfect agreement with
the moral law. Personal immortality then becomes a postulate of faith. The second
condition is harmony between moral striving and the natural impulse toward happiness.
By experience it cannot be shown that virtue always leads to happiness or happiness
to virtue; where it happens, it is accidental. And yet the highest good must
include not merely virtue (the greatest good), but also happiness. There must in the last
resort be an agreement between the world of nature and that of freedom. There must then
be postulated a power that can bring harmony between the two worlds, so that
morality does not stand as a stranger in the world. Therefore the one who is
permeated by the moral demand is led to faith in the existence of a God.

Practical reason thus leads to convictions that
% --- p. 92 ---
\opage{92}concern something that lies beyond the limits that theoretical reason pointed out. The
X (Ding an sich) that theoretical reason had to leave undecided we gain
access to when we follow the need that practical reason calls forth in
us to postulate a perfect realization of the moral ideals. Kant
enumerates three postulates: the freedom of the will (which has already been discussed), the immortality of the
soul and the existence of God.

The need from which the postulates spring is not of a sensuous or
egoistic kind, but is a consequence of the presence and working of the moral law in
man's mind, thus of what is universal and universally valid in his being. It is
a pure need of reason (ein Bedürfniss der reinen Vernunft). But just as strongly
as Kant stresses the difference of this need from any wish whatever, just as
strongly does he stress its purely subjective character. The faith (or rather: the
hope) to which it leads is not itself a duty, although it is called forth by the law of duty.
There can --- says Kant --- be no duty to believe what cannot be
known. (Kritik der praktischen Vernunft. Kehrbach p. 151. 172 f.). Kant
thinks: when man feels the law in his inner self, he will also
\textit{unavoidably} feel the need to assume the conditions of its being
carried through. And in reliance on this unavoidability he also comes, in a
single connection, to declare it a duty toward oneself to have religion, since
otherwise one cannot keep one's moral conviction up. (Tugendlehre.
Beschluss. --- Lose Blätter p. 513). Indeed, the utterance even escapes him
that the ``right-minded'' may well waver in faith at times, but never give it up.
(Kritik d. pr. Vern. Kehrb. p. 175).

The question is whether the need of reason from which the postulates spring
is really universal, --- whether it is necessarily found in all individuals who
acknowledge an unconditional moral law and have an infinite ideal in their inner selves. Kant
has not seen that this question cannot be decided a priori, but must be answered
by means of psychological experience. On his own presuppositions he would
not be able to object anything against the one who, without wavering in his moral
conviction, but also without any ``postulates'' whatever, could look the eternal
disharmony between
% --- p. 93 ---
\opage{93}ideal and reality in the face. Indeed, he has even in a single place conceived
this possibility. The place is of special interest, since it states clearly what Kant
wished to attain by his postulates. ``We can'', says Kant (Kritik der
Urtheilskraft § 87), ``conceive a righteous man (such as Spinoza) who
holds himself convinced that there is no God and no future life
either: how will he judge of the purpose that is set him by the moral
law, which he honors in deed? From his obedience to this law he demands no
advantage for himself, neither in this nor in another world; unselfishly he will
solely and only bring about the good toward which that holy law directs all his
forces. But his striving is limited, and from the side of nature he may well now and
then expect an accidental concurrence, but not any lawful and regular
harmony with the \textit{purpose} he feels himself obliged and impelled to
realize. Deceit, violence, envy will always be rife around him,
although he himself is honest, peaceable and benevolent. The righteous whom he meets
are, by nature, which does not heed how worthy they are of happiness,
subjected to want and lack, sickness and untimely death, just as well as the other
animals on the earth. And they will go on being so until a vast grave swallows
them all together and hurls them, who could believe themselves the final end of creation,
back into the abyss of chaotic and purposeless matter from which they were
drawn forth''. Kant now thinks that one will not be able to hold fast to the
\textit{purpose} that the moral law leads us to set up without the religious
postulates. But his ethics would, after all, precisely abstract from all purposes and demand
a willing for the sake of the inner law itself --- whatever might come
of it! Only by an inconsistency can he set up the concept of \textit{the
highest good} (union of happiness and virtue) as an \textit{ethical} purpose; for the
first proposition of his ethics (Grundlegung p. 1) runs: ``Nothing can be conceived
in the world or outside the world that could without condition be called good, except
\textit{a good will.''} By his postulates (especially the second and third) he
in fact takes back the independence of ethics.

The postulates come forth when a need is felt to think
% --- p. 94 ---
% scan: „det.“ (p. 94)
\opage{94}the ethical together with the whole of the rest of our world-view. It is indeed a need
that does not stir in all, and ethically regarded need not stir either. But
Kant's great merit with respect to the philosophy of religion is nonetheless precisely this: in
a clearer and more deep-going way than had hitherto been done, to lead the religious problem
back to a personal need that is determined by the relation to ethical
ideals. The position of the religious problem at different times and in
different persons will rest on the presence of this need and on the
peculiar kind and manner in which it appears. Here there will, as experience shows,
be countless individual differences, which Kant's dogmatizing led him
to overlook. But with as sure a hand as that with which, in a theoretical
respect, he determined the philosophical place of the religious assumptions, he has here
found a corresponding determination of place as regards the practical and psychological side
of these assumptions.

\subsection*{b.\quad The Religious Postulates in Their Relation to Kant's Epistemology and to ``Natural Religion''}

By the postulates we come beyond the limits of knowledge. But how is that
possible, since the critique of reason has, after all, established that our forms of knowledge
simply have these limits? We have, after all, no further sets of forms of knowledge to
change to! Kant here lays weight on this, that the categories (it is here, as almost
always, the concept of cause that is chiefly in question) do not spring from experience,
but from the faculty of thought itself. He finds therein the possibility of using the categories
beyond the limit of experience or of phenomena to \textit{think} what the
postulates contain, even if we cannot \textit{know} it. For
knowledge a co-operation of intuition and thinking would be required. But intuition
is here excluded. The human cognitive faculty is characterized by
the difference between intuition and thinking, and by this, that all intuition is sensuous (in
time and space). A supersensuous intuition would be fanaticism, would lead to
lighting a ``magic lantern of figments of the brain''. --- Thus we conceive God as
cause of the world, our striving as continued and our ideal
% --- p. 95 ---
\opage{95}willing as a first beginning, although these concepts cannot be supplied with
intuitive data.

Even such a use of the forms of thought does not, however, agree with the critique of reason,
according to which concepts without intuition are empty (just as intuitions without
concepts are blind). And --- even if one grants such a use --- it is in
reality not the usual representations of God, freedom and immortality,
not what was understood by these words in ``natural religion'', that Kant can
express by his pure concepts. With intuition, after all,
\textit{the relation of time} \textit{must also fall away:} but how can there then be
talk of \textit{continued} existence (zukünftiges Leben), of beginning, of
creating? And if all data of experience are to be kept away, everything must be removed from
the representation of God that is owed to human psychology. We
know only an understanding that works its way forward to truth through successive and discursive apprehension and
discussion, and only a will that sets itself
purposes and thereupon seeks the means of reaching them. That does not fit the
unconditioned and infinite being, and it falls away with the relation of time. And if we ask
Kant what, then, is left of our psychological concepts when we
undertake so radical a change in them that they are to be applicable to
God, he answers clearly and candidly (although this answer is constantly overlooked in the
popular expositions of his doctrine): only \textit{the bare word} is
left! ``Name but one property'', he says, e.g.\ (Kritik d. pr. Vern. Kehrb.
p. 165), ``of which one could not show that, when everything anthropomorphic
is separated out, only the bare word is left, without our being able to connect the
least concept with it so as thereby to extend our theoretical knowledge.'' Similar
utterances are found in all Kant's main writings\textsuperscript{24}). More clearly
Spinoza could not have expressed himself. --- If it is asked how Kant can have attributed value to
the religious representations when they are theoretically altogether empty, the
answer is that according to Kant all religious representations are \textit{symbolic.} We
must help ourselves with analogies and symbols where the scientific use of our
concepts stops. The representations of a personal God and personal
immortality, too, then become only symbols for something that thought cannot express in adequate
form. It is
% --- p. 96 ---
\opage{96}no higher knowledge that is gained by passing over from knowledge to faith.
The ``need of reason'' here in reality takes poetry into its service. The postulates
are projections out into the unknowable of images that have formed in
the world of experience. --- There is, when one thinks through what lies herein, a
very great difference between Kant's religious standpoint and the religious standpoint
that ``natural religion'' formulated. Kant, like Lessing, had an
esoteric and an exoteric doctrine\textsuperscript{25}), even if he has not made
the difference between them altogether clear to himself, nor has seen all the consequences that
lie in the assumption of the symbolic character of the religious concepts, e.g.\ this one, that
symbols cannot be forced on anyone, but must be the object of free, individual
choice, so that my ``need of reason'' might perhaps find more appealing symbols than
those chosen by Kant. Kant has at the same time somewhat too hastily placed everything he felt a need
to believe in over into the Ding an sich, without investigating whether the different
postulates might not be mutually contradictory (e.g.\ God's omnipotence and
man's freedom --- cf.\ Religion innerhalb der Grenzen der blossen
Vernunft. 2. Aufl. p. 215 f. --- Lose Blätter p. 544). He has used
the limit of knowledge, as the woman in childbed in Holberg uses the screen, to
hide the various elements that he wants to be rid of in science, but wants to
keep for faith, without thinking that the strife will begin anew --- behind
the screen! For this demand we do make of our symbols, that they be
without self-contradiction.

The symbolic character of the religious representations is closely connected with the fact that
religious faith springs from a personal need. We seek forms in which we
can represent existence to ourselves as a kingdom in which what for us is of
the highest value comes fully into its own. On this point, too,
Kant's philosophy of religion --- with all its imperfections --- marks a great
advance over orthodoxy and the theology of the Enlightenment.

\subsection*{c.\quad Positive Religion}

As it is with the representations of natural religion, so it must also
be with the
% --- p. 97 ---
\opage{97}representations of positive religion. This consequence Kant drew in the remarkable work
\textit{Religion innerhalb der Grenzen der blossen Vernunft} (1793). Instead
of asking whether the representations of positive religion can stand before
the tribunal of natural science and of historical criticism, Kant asks about their
significance for human life in an ethical respect, asks what they
contain that can nourish and support life. And this is and remains, after all, always
the main question, for on its answer depends the value that can be attributed to
these representations (however the verdict of physics and of history may turn out).
That Kant keeps to Christianity as the positive religion lying nearest at hand
is natural. But it is remarkable to see that it is the dogmas of sin
and atonement that he especially discusses, precisely the dogmas for which the period of the Enlightenment had
least sense. He finds deep ethical truths contained in these dogmas,
in that what the Bible relates as external, historical events can be interpreted
as inner spiritual relations in man's mind, as the expression of contending
oppositions in the human will.

In the doctrine of sin and the fall Kant finds expressed a truth confirmed by experience:
that, in opposition to the inner willing whose law is the moral
law, there expresses itself a propensity to set the claims of sensuousness above those of reason. It is
law standing against law [as in Böhme God against God]; for it is not
sensuousness itself that is evil. Evil is the will that reverses the right
relation, according to which reason rules over sensuousness, and formulates
the opposite relation as its rule. The radical evil in man is this
perversion of the relation between the motives. Philosophical ethics takes it as a
fact, as something given in experience: the Bible presents the origin of radical evil
as a historical event, in that it lets man's good nature
precede his evil nature in time and the state of innocence be broken off by a
fall. By introducing a tempter it admits at the same time that an absolute explanation
cannot be given.

But beside radical evil there is always found in man a seed of
the good, which can be developed especially through admiration of exemplars. The capacity to respect
the good, even if one
% --- p. 98 ---
\opage{98}cannot practice it oneself, never altogether falls away. This capacity, from which the
moral consciousness develops, is the ideal in our nature, the inner heaven in
us in opposition to radical evil as the inner hell. There is given in our nature
an incomprehensible exemplar, an indwelling ideal, which in the Bible is presented
as the Son of God, who descends to earth and takes on human form.
The God-man is the idea of human nature in its perfection. Here again
what for the philosopher is an eternal relation is presented as a historical event:
the relation of the good, of the ideal, to human nature as a force
that stands in strong opposition to other tendencies in this nature. The struggle between
Satan and Christ is a struggle that is fought in the innermost depths of human nature.
In this struggle the God in us must suffer for what our evil will has done. The
new man who is to come into being suffers for the sins of the old. To this there corresponds in
our experience repentance, which presupposes a new direction of the will that takes over the
suffering bound up with working one's way out of the old will. This is
the ethical content of the dogma of atonement. The coming into being of the ideal man in us cannot indeed
become a completed process; only an approximation is possible; but from the
highest point of view the successive approximation is intuited and valued as a whole,
the relation of time being left out of consideration.

Kant is clearly conscious that this symbolic interpretation is altogether different from
historical interpretation. The latter he leaves to learned research.
He asserts that only through such symbolic-ethical interpretation do the religious books have
lasting ethical worth, and that this is in reality the way one goes and has always
gone when one has wished to make religion practically fruitful. And such
an interpretation is all the more justified, as man's moral capacities
have involuntarily exerted their influence already in the development of the religious
representations and given the revelations themselves their stamp. By a purely
external, historical way we can never come to know the ideal and the divine.
The highest exemplar always lies in our own spirit. Only through the God in us
do we know the God outside us; and that God in us is the only one before whom all
knees bow! (Lose Blätter p. 218). This God in us is the interpreter of
% --- p. 99 ---
\opage{99}everything that appears with the claim to be revelation. If Abraham
had held fast to it, he would not have wished to lay hands on his son; if
the judges of heretics had held fast to it, they would not have condemned anyone for the sake of his
dogmas. The moral law in us is more certain than any faith whatever. (Religion
innerhalb etc. p. 289 f.).

In Kant's opinion such wonderful things take place in man's inner self that
one has no need to assume external events to explain them --- especially
since every such explanation is illusory. The mysteriousness of the
events that the biblical narratives tell of he left undecided; but he
``honored the external garb for a doctrine that in the end is grounded on
testimonies that are indelibly preserved in the soul and need no miracles.''
(Religion innerhalb etc. p. 117).

Only this demand does he make, that the historical and dogmatic (``statutory'')
element in religion is more and more to be subordinated to the inner and ethical element.
Historical faith has only provisional and symbolic significance. The visible church
is to draw nearer and nearer to the true church, the invisible, in which each
individual stands in an inner and immediate relation to the highest truth. Then
the degrading difference between priest and layman will also cease; it is conditioned
by the necessity of historical learning in order to understand positive religion.
The kingdom of God is not a kingdom of priests. After the Reformation there has not been
any unconditional progress: whether one forbids laymen to read the Bible, or
one says: Search the Bible by all means, but you must not find anything else therein than what we
have found, --- it comes to the same thing! And then tell us rather at once what you have
found: then we shall spare ourselves our reading! (Lose Bl. p. 402). Still more burdensome for
the conscientious than the external observances that Catholicism demands is the
dogmatic confession of faith. If Christianity consists in that, then the word
does not hold: ``My burden is light!'' ---

Kant himself came to feel how strong an opposition there was between his interpretation of
Christianity and that of the church. Nevertheless he had the confident assurance that
religious development
% --- p. 100 ---
\opage{100}would go in the direction he had caught sight of. In this he may yet prove right,
although the religious oppositions have been sharpened in the time that has passed
since his work on the philosophy of religion appeared. For the philosophy of religion itself
this work was epoch-making, and it keeps its value for all times by its struggle
for the inner against the outer and by its assertion of the significance of the inner events of personal
life. In the psychology of religion and in the historical conception of
religion it leaves much to be desired. But it was the task of the new century
to supplement his thoughts in this respect.

% print: „Apellen“ (p. 100) (misprint)
\section*{6.\quad Speculative Ideas on an Aesthetic and Biological Basis (Kritik der Urtheilskraft)}

\subsection*{a.\quad The Two Worlds and Their Possible Unity}

In his \textit{Kritik der Urtheilskraft} (1790) Kant develops thoughts that point
beyond the limits within which his philosophy otherwise keeps itself. Instead
of the appeal to a moral faith, which in the earlier writings formed the
conclusion of his conception, his thinking here ventures on bolder prospects of
a great connection within which a unity of the oppositions he had hitherto held
apart from one another might be possible.

Kant had operated to a high degree with sharp distinctions. They had been
necessary to him for reaching his results. Only by distinguishing between
phenomena and things in themselves had he been able to carry through his proof
of the real validity of the knowledge of reason, and only by distinguishing
between the world of experience and the intelligible world had he thought he
could unite the originality and self-legislation of the will with the natural
determination of the empirical character. The two worlds, the phenomenal (that
of nature, of experience) on the one side, the intelligible (that of freedom,
of purposes) on the other, stand over against each other as though they were
wholly different and foreign to each other: this is the result of Kant's
epistemology and of his ethics, and
% --- p. 101 ---
\opage{101}his philosophy of religion has remedied it only in a rather external way,
through postulates. But in his great critical deliberateness he turns once more
against these results and asks whether it is really justified to regard those
oppositions as absolute and irreconcilable. --- Man himself is, after all, both
a natural being and an intelligible being, both phenomenon and thing in itself.
Here, then, is a point of unity for the two worlds! Man lives and acts in
nature, but is to follow, and can follow, the law of freedom, and through human
development in the world of experience the goal fixed by the ideal law is to be
striven for. So the two worlds cannot fall wholly outside each other: there must
be a ground of unity for nature and the moral world. --- And since Kant has
constantly operated with the distinction between our conception and the very
essence of things, was there not reason to ask whether the very assumption of
those oppositions might not be connected with the nature of our knowing mind?
It is not, after all, said that what stands as oppositions for us (with our
discursive thinking, which must distinguish and analyze in order to know) is
therefore so in the innermost ground of things! Just as Kant had already
intimated in ``Kritik der reinen Vernunft'' that what lies at the ground of the
material in our knowledge might be the same as what determines the forms in
which we order it, --- and that what lies at the ground of material phenomena
might be the same as what lies at the ground of mental phenomena, --- so now
too he finally discusses the possibility that the foundation of the world of
nature and of the world of freedom might be one and the same. He does as the
master builder does who takes down the scaffolding when the building is
finished: the distinctions Kant has used during his inquiry as means of
climbing upward he calls back when he is at the conclusion of the work. From
the very distinction between knowledge and existence he draws the conclusion
that this distinction --- which is, after all, made by our knowledge itself ---
cannot be absolute. But in this he relies on definite facts which lead him to
bring forward problems he had not hitherto treated, facts which show that
nature, according to its own laws, works in
% --- p. 102 ---
\opage{102}the direction of what our knowing and valuing mind desires and demands. Should
it then be foreign to the ideal?

\subsection*{b.\quad Aesthetic Consideration}

An aesthetic judgment is one by which we call a phenomenon beautiful or
sublime. The question then arises whether such judgments can have universal
validity, can be the expression of more than a purely individual satisfaction.

The beautiful is distinguished from the agreeable and the good by not resting
on the real existence of an object, but only on the image, the conception or
representation, that we have of it. Aesthetic satisfaction is disinterested and
free. It arises through a free play of the cognitive faculty, which is brought
about when an image makes our imagination and our understanding work together
in a harmonious way, the particulars of the image being easily and naturally
combined into a whole that is immediately understood. Neither the purely
material impression nor the pure concept plays a part here: mere material
gives no whole, and the pure concept gives an abstract rule, which appears as
constraint over against the material. In the English art of
gardening\textsuperscript{26}), in musical compositions, in the visual arts,
the single elements work together immediately into a conception of a whole that
satisfies an essential spiritual need in us. Kant lays very great weight on the
entirely immediate in the impression of beauty and underrates the more remote
representations that the image can awaken. Only ``free'' beauty (determined by
what Fechner has called the direct factor) is properly beauty; ``adherent''
beauty (determined by the associative factor) does not rightly bear the name of
beauty, since it presupposes definite representations. A flower, an arabesque, a
musical fantasia afford free beauty; the beauty of a human being is
``adherent,'' because it presupposes a representation of what it is to be a
human being.

Judgments about beauty (i.e. about free beauty) are subjective, insofar as they
spring from a feeling that the image awakens in us. But they may nonetheless be
universally valid, since the feeling is here determined by something that is
common to all
% --- p. 103 ---
\opage{103}men: the relation between the cognitive powers, the need of a harmonious
relation between the faculty of intuition and the faculty of comprehension.
Aesthetic judgments (judgments of taste) cannot be proved, but they can be
called forth by giving occasion for immediate intuition. The universal validity
is exemplary, i.e. it is reached by means of examples, not by rules. Therefore
aesthetic criticism is an art, not a science.

The sublime is likewise due to a disinterested satisfaction, but here the
relation is more complex. The great, the immeasurable, the infinite in extension
and in force overwhelms our faculty of apprehension and crushes our sense of
self. The mind is thereby brought to let go of everything finite and sensuous
and to feel in itself a power that is raised above every limitation: the power
to think the infinite ideas and to frame the unconditioned law. A higher kind
of self-assertion is thus awakened over against the mighty in nature, after a
preliminary inhibition. What is properly sublime, then, is not the outer
phenomena: they are only occasions for the great in ourselves to make itself
known. --- Here too universally valid judgments can be passed, since judgments
about the sublime are grounded in a feeling that must be capable of being
called forth in every sufficiently developed human being.

In the phenomena we call beautiful and sublime, nature now works \textit{according
to its own laws} to call forth in us a satisfaction independent of all egoistic
interest. This is a significant fact, especially since aesthetic feeling, by its
disinterestedness, is akin to ethical feeling!

Kant does not stop at investigating the valuation of the beautiful. He also
investigates the production of the beautiful in art. This production goes on
--- like the valuation --- without the guidance of abstract concepts,
predominantly involuntarily, and yet in such a way that what is produced
becomes an object of general recognition and comes to stand as an exemplar. Art
is the work of genius. Genius is ``exemplary'' originality: a disposition by
which nature gives art its rules. Genius does not work according to rules or
ideas, and yet rules can be derived and ideas found in its
works\textsuperscript{27}). The fact of genius thus shows --- like the fact of
the aesthetic
% --- p. 104 ---
\opage{104}judgment, --- that the world of nature and the world of freedom are not
absolutely separated, but must have a common foundation. These facts too we
must --- such is Kant's meaning --- take into account before we form our
concluding conception of existence.

\subsection*{c.\quad Biological Consideration}

Not only by producing beautiful and sublime phenomena and by working through
men of genius does nature show its agreement with the laws of our mind. In
organisms it presents beings of such a constitution that their single parts are
understood only as means or condition for the subsistence of the whole being.
There is here the same intimate connection between particulars and whole as in
the works of genius. In the organic world nature works as genius, in a way that
differs both from the mechanical production of a whole by the cooperation of
the parts and from the conscious joining of parts into a whole according to a
definite plan. Nature's organizing activity has no proper analogy with any of
the kinds of causality we know (Kr. d. Urth. § 65). We can make it intelligible
to ourselves only when we regard organisms \textit{as if} they were produced
under the guidance of the thought of a purpose (whether this is now thought of
as conscious or unconscious). But this is only a regulative principle; we may
not deny the possibility that the organic species and forms arose through a
natural process of development according to mechanical laws. The analogy that
exists among the organic forms might point to a common origin, so that nature
has reached, step by step, from the lowest forms to the highest. One could
imagine aquatic animals first becoming marsh animals and later land animals, so
that the forms suited to the circumstances replaced the less purposive ones.
(There are --- says Kant in Kr. d. Urth. § 80 --- probably few even among the
most acute naturalists through whose heads such a hypothesis, admittedly a
daring adventure of reason, has not passed!). ---

The whole opposition between mechanism and teleology, between arising through
the blind cooperation of the parts and arising through planned
% --- p. 105 ---
\opage{105}joining, is perhaps due only to the nature of our knowledge. Our understanding
proceeds discursively, goes from the parts to the whole and sees the whole as
their product; if it is to think of the constitution of the parts as determined
by the whole, it can do so only by thinking the representation of the whole as
the subjective cause of the formation and combination of the parts. For us,
therefore, mechanism and teleology form a great opposition. But in the ground
of nature, unknown to us, mechanical and teleological connection might well be
united in one principle --- only our reason is not able to frame this
principle!

With this thought, the most profound to be found in Kant, he takes up again a
line of thought that had occupied him much in his youth: namely, that the same
thing which makes causal relations between things possible also makes
purposiveness and harmony in nature possible. ``The continuity in Kant's
philosophical course of development'' shows itself most clearly of all at this
point. His speculative successors would begin precisely where he ended. For
Kant himself it was a last prospect, a concluding hypothesis, which was of
great value for inquiry, but could not be dogmatically set up as a starting
point. His marvelous ability to work at small things with great things in view
does not fail him here either. The account of his philosophy cannot end in a
more fitting way than with this characteristic trait of his personality as a
thinker.

\section*{7.\quad The Opponents of the Critical Philosophy}

A work like Kant's could not be understood at once. It discussed so many
problems, and discussed them in so interwoven a connection, --- it presented,
both by what it established and by what it denied, so peculiar a standpoint,
that it is no wonder its contemporaries could not pass a judgment that bore
witness to a full penetration into its peculiarity. Not all the judgments
passed on it have interest for the general history of philosophy. The
misunderstandings displayed on the part of the philosophy of the Enlightenment
and the Wolffian school
% --- p. 106 ---
\opage{106}bear witness only to the difficulty that one has, from an older, ingrown,
self-satisfied standpoint, in entering into a new line of thought. Not everyone
had such self-knowledge and modesty --- and at the same time so fine a faith in
truth --- as Mendelssohn displayed in the preface to his ``Morgenstunden.'' ---
Of considerable interest, on the other hand, is the opposition that Kant's
philosophy met with in a group of men who, in various forms, maintained the
significance of immediate certainty and of historical tradition, and in general
the significance of the mind's collected, concentrated activity, over against
Kant's analysis and criticism, which at so many points led him to sharp
separations between elements that in reality occur in indissoluble connection.
In great part these men do Kant an injustice, in that they overlook Kant's own
attempts to join again what he had separated only for the sake of inquiry and
clarity. And in part their objections are directed not merely against Kant's
philosophy, but against all philosophy, indeed against all inquiry whatever.
But they nonetheless form a salutary counterweight to Kant's analysis by
pointing to the living, concrete connection of things, and their opposition
relies, moreover, in principle on the thinker whom Kant had especially wished
to continue and to overcome, the same to whom he owed his awakening: Hume. On
experience, especially on feeling and historical experience, they relied in
their struggle against the philosophy of the Enlightenment, to which, in their
eyes, Kant was still to be reckoned. They carried Kant's opposition to the
Enlightenment so much further that they came into conflict with him as well.
Finally, they intimate points of view and ideas that worked in wide circles,
far beyond the philosophical domain, and that became of great significance for
the awakening of a new poetic and historical conception, a deeper understanding
of life as a whole.

a. Foremost in this group stands Kant's fellow townsman and friend \textsc{Johann Georg
Hamann}, the Magus of the North, as he has been called. It was through
religious experience that he learned to know the power of faith and the great
and conflicting forces of life. A religious breakthrough, which came to him
during a stay in London, where he had had occasion to experience the weak sides
of his character, became decisive for his whole life. There had been a mighty
% --- p. 107 ---
\opage{107}stirring in this deep, fermenting nature, which he himself (in a letter to Kant
of July 27, 1759) characterized by calling himself ``a man to whom the sickness
of his passions gives a strength to think and feel that a healthy man does not
possess.'' He felt himself to be like a man in a deep pit who at midday sees
stars that those who go about in the daylight cannot see. An intimate feeling
of the mystery of life and of the contradictions that existence presents to the
finite understanding, as soon as it does not stop at the surface, is Hamann's
distinguishing mark. He is fond of enigmatic hints and paradoxical propositions,
and his writings swarm with allusions to his chance reading, so that they are
often unintelligible without commentary. Baroque fancies alternate with
profound ideas and with mighty pathos, which makes intelligible the impression
he made on some of the greatest minds of the time. He stood not only for the
pious, who sighed over the Enlightenment and unbelief, as the prophet who
opened again the springs of the old faith, but he stood for the whole younger
generation as the one whose flight of spirit went higher than the reason of the
time could follow, and as the one in whom thought, imagination and feeling
worked together in a passionate concentration that came forward with tremendous
force against the prevailing rationalism and sentimentalism. But precisely
because his burning thirst could be satisfied only by a content of life that
streamed with collected power, he was a sworn enemy of all analysis. Already in
his first writing \textit{(Sokratische
Denkwürdigkeiten.} 1759) he declares it presumptuous to want to carry analysis
through to the last elements: that would, after all, be to want to grasp the
invisible essence of the Deity itself! Nature and history perhaps contain
riddles that only a power wholly other than our reason can solve! Therefore
Socratic ignorance is praised. Both our own existence and the existence of
things outside us we must \textit{believe} in; no other way to the assumption
of them is given. Faith is not a work of reason and therefore cannot be
overthrown by reason either. It does not build on grounds, any more than taste
and seeing do. Where ignorance stops, the divine genius helps us, which for
Socrates was of greater significance than all the wisdom of the world. --- The
ground of religion, he
% --- p. 108 ---
\opage{108}declares later (\textit{Zweifel und Einfälle.} 1770), lies in our whole existence
and is more comprehensive than the domain in which our knowledge moves.
Knowledge is the most abstract form of our existence. --- Only through passion
do abstractions get hands, feet or wings. Life is to be taken as a whole.
Philosophers separate what nature has joined together. To express this
concentrated content of life rightly, Hamann makes use of Bruno's principle of
the coincidence of opposites (coincidentia oppositorum), which he declares to
be worth more than the whole of Kant's critique. Reason (he writes to Kant as
early as 1759) --- as Hume has shown --- is given to you, not that you should
become wise by its help, but that you should know your folly and ignorance,
just as the law was given to the Jews to convince them of sin. Through
experience, tradition and language we get all that we can know.

With great interest Hamann followed the writings of Kant (``the little
Magister,'' later ``our Plato'') and was naturally occupied above all with
``Kritik der reinen Vernunft.'' Immediately after the work appeared he made a
draft of a criticism, which he nevertheless held back --- partly because he
noticed that ``his poor head, over against Kant's, was as clay against iron,''
--- partly so as not to offend Kant, to whom he stood in a debt of gratitude.
Only after Hamann's death (1788) was his \textit{Metakritik über den Purismum
der reinen Vernunft} printed. He saw in Kant's philosophy a failed attempt to
make reason independent of all tradition, faith and experience, and he
polemicizes especially against Kant's separation between matter and form and
between sensation and understanding. Why this violent, unwarranted, willful
separation of what nature has joined together? There is, after all, a constant
circulation! Intuitions rise without interruption into reason, and concepts
descend into sensation! --- In a letter written while he was reading
``Kritik der reinen Vernunft'' in proof sheets, he calls Kant the Prussian
Hume, but declares that he prefers the English one: ``Hume is still always my
man, because he has at least ennobled the principle of faith and taken it up
into his system. Our countryman keeps chewing the cud on his attack on
causality without thinking of the principle of faith. That does
% --- p. 109 ---
% print: „Königsberg“, no opening parenthesis before „f. 1730, d. 1788)“ (p. 109) (misprint)
\opage{109}not seem to me honest.'' (Letter to Herder of May 10, 1781.) And already in an
earlier writing \textit{(Des Ritters von Rosencreuz
% scan: „Rosencreux“ (p. 109)
letzte Willensmeynung über den göttlichen und menschlichen Ursprung der
Sprache.} 1772) he had said: ``Do you not know, then, philosophers, that there
is no physical bond between cause and effect, means and end, but a spiritual
and ideal one: namely, the bond of the collier's faith?'' And express reference
is made here to Hume. ---

It was not Hamann's way to write great works and give long developments of
thought. But his oracular sayings inspired \textsc{Herder} and \textsc{Jacobi}, who continued his
work, in that they, like him, appealing to Hume, set faith against reason. Yet
they were more children of the time than ``the Magus of the North,'' who has
been called ``the most believing among the believers'' (yet also ``the freest,
because he was the deepest''). Hamann was a believing Lutheran. Herder and
Jacobi stood far nearer to the Enlightenment, especially to its sentimental
form, although they fought the analyzing and grounding reason just as their
master did.

b. Hamann lived as a poor warehouse superintendent in Königsberg (b. 1730,
d. 1788). His view of life was established even before Kant was awakened from
his dogmatic slumber. \textsc{Johann Gotfried Herder} (b. 1744, d. 1803) was
as a young man Kant's hearer and was strongly influenced by the standpoint on
which Kant stood in the sixties. But in Königsberg he also met Hamann, and the
influence of the latter became the properly decisive one. With a great sense
for the original, the popular, what unfolds involuntarily, he worked to bring a
fresher and more vigorous spirit into literature. Goethe learned (as he relates
in ``Aus meinem Leben'') from Herder that the art of poetry was a gift to the
people, to the whole world, not a private inheritance for a few refined,
cultivated men. In the spirit of Rousseau, Herder maintained the right of the
natural and the human; but he had far more historical sense than Rousseau, and
in his view of nature he is influenced by Goethe, with whom, as
superintendent in Weimar, he stood in lively interaction until divergent views
on art and politics drew them apart from each other. In his chief work
\textit{(Ideen zur}
% --- p. 110 ---
\opage{110}\textit{Philosophie der Geschichte} \textit{der Menschheit.} 1784---91) he
collides with his former teacher Kant. Herder cannot accept that the goal is to
lie only in the species, not in the single individuals. Each single individual
is destined for such happiness and such development as is possible at the given
stage, but in order that this goal may be reached there must be interaction
among the individuals, and there must be a handing down of the acquired means
of culture from generation to generation.
It is this connection between individuals and generations that makes there be a
humanity --- and a philosophy of history. Already in unconscious nature ideal
forces are at work, which form and organize according to a definite type.
Leibniz's doctrine of monads is transformed in Herder into a doctrine of
organic forces, which work throughout nature in different degrees and at
different stages, in analogy with the force that works in our thought. ``The
force that thinks and works in me is by its nature as eternal a force as that
which holds suns and stars together . . . All existence is of the same kind,
one indivisible concept.'' (Ideen. I. p. 7---8). The thought that expressed
Kant's last presentiment is thus here laid at the foundation, and by means of
``the great analogy of nature'' a connection is found in everything, in the
universe as in history, a connection that also teaches us to find the bond
between science and religion. When Herder constantly uses the word nature in
his book, it is so as not to name God's name so often: ``Gott ist Alles in
seinen Werken!''

In this great connection of receiving and giving man too stands. His reason
can by no means go its own ways. The very word for reason, Fornuft, comes from
fornemme, to perceive, and points to our getting our thoughts through
tradition, language and outer influence. Reason is a product, not something
innate. Religion is the first form of spiritual culture. Before the first
abstract thoughts could be formed, there went a religious feeling of invisible
forces in nature. By this feeling man raises himself above the animal. The
disposition to humanity is older than reason. But it is developed only by
education, under the influence of exemplars. Man cannot develop everything out
of himself. And precisely because every single man becomes
% --- p. 111 ---
\opage{111}a man only by education, there is an education of humanity. Every single stage
of this development must be not merely a means to reach the next, but also an
end. All the means of the Deity are ends, and all its ends are means to higher
ends. Thus: ``What every man is and can be, that must be the end of the human
race. And what is that? Humanity and happiness in this place, in this degree,
as just this definite, peculiar link in the chain of culture that stretches
through the whole species.'' (Ideen. II. p. 118). --- By this line of thought
Herder corrects the violent opposition that existed for Kant's philosophy of
history between individual and species, and that had far-reaching consequences
for his ethics. But Herder contents himself with an enthusiastic declaration
and does not enter more closely into the great problems that the idea set up
contains when it is to be applied in particulars.

Herder's fundamental philosophical view, so far as it comes out clearly through
his lyrical and florid language, is borne by the thought that already played so
great a part in Kant's first writings: that the lawful connection of things
itself presupposes a ground of unity in existence. And this thought in turn led
Herder naturally to sympathy with Spinoza. He saw in Spinoza the most
consistent philosopher and found, through repeated study of his work,
nourishment for his need to get beyond all dualism between God and nature,
between mind and matter. A God existing outside the world conflicted for him
with the concept of God, with the concept of the world and with the concept of
space, and personality could not be a property of an infinite being. He
therefore decidedly distanced himself from Jacobi's horror of Spinoza. He had a
sense for the mystical side of Spinoza, while Jacobi saw in him only the
abstract rationalism (and neither of them saw the realistic side). He even
wrote to Jacobi: ``If you make the most inward, highest concept, which gathers
all in one, into a mere name, then it is you who are the atheist, not
Spinoza!'' It was Herder's hatred of all abstraction that led him beyond the
distinction between God and the world. He parted from Jacobi for the same
reason as he parted from Kant, and for the same reason as Hamann (who, for the
rest, could not
% --- p. 112 ---
\opage{112}understand his friends' negative and positive interest in Spinoza) took an
interest in Bruno's principle of coincidence. In his writing \textit{Gott}
(Gotha 1787) Herder took the side of Spinoza against Jacobi. His acquaintance
with Spinoza was not so thorough in particulars as Jacobi's; he reinterprets
Spinoza's view of nature in particular by putting into it his ``organic
forces,'' in general his modified Leibnizianism; but his writing did much to
awaken interest in what is deepest in Spinoza's philosophy. He himself was now
regarded as an apostate by the pious band that gathered about Hamann. His
religious standpoint had always been different from that on which the Magus of
the North, whom he so highly admired, stood. They were akin in the weight they
laid on the historical, the traditional, what has arisen involuntarily, in
opposition to the time's predilection for the clearly conscious and the
arbitrary. Herder was the one who first in earnest shook the current assumption
that religious representations were due to arbitrary fabrication and fraud on
the part of priests and princes. His sense for folk poetry also taught him to
see the original and nature-strong spirit of the old religious books. The need
for nourishment for all faculties at once asserted itself here; he wanted a
philosophy ``for the whole man,'' and this he found in the religious works that
stem from a time when the human mental faculties had not yet begun to work
separated from one another. It was a need that was more poetic than
philosophical --- and at the same time more poetic than religious. For Herder it
was always difficult to hold poetry, philosophy and religion apart from one
another; in this he is the most important forerunner of Romanticism. For the
understanding of religion he worked mightily by maintaining its immediate and
involuntary origin in the human spirit and by demanding that the religious
writings be read and understood in their own spirit. His own interpretation
was (without his always being clearly conscious of it) symbolic and ethical.
His standpoint is different both from that of orthodoxy and from that of
rationalism (in any case the current rationalism): in a certain sense a
continuation and further carrying out of Lessing's standpoint. Precisely
because he saw divine forces at work everywhere in nature, he felt no need to
set revelation in the narrower sense
% --- p. 113 ---
\opage{113}in sharp opposition to the general revelation that takes place through all the
life of nature and of man. In the 17th book of ``Ideen'' and in the writing
\textit{Von Religion, Lehrmeinungen und Gebräuchen} (Leipzig 1798) he has
developed his symbolic-ethical conception of Christianity. He found an
``enormous anti-Christianity'' in the prevailing church. Christ was for Herder
the spiritual savior of the species, who wished to form God-men who --- under
whatever laws they may live --- promote the welfare of others according to pure
fundamental propositions, and themselves, in patience, reign as kings in the
kingdom of truth and goodness. Christ's discourses are stamped with the purest
humanity. But out of his words speculative dogmas have been constructed, and
out of his symbolic actions magical processes have been made. (So wrote a
