bishop at the end of the last century!) Yet Herder did not doubt that the pure
religion of Christ would conquer.

In his criticism of Kant's doctrine Herder gave Hamann's ``Metakritik'' a
broader carrying through, without real originality. His significance is bound
up with the positive fullness that he partly brought, partly pointed to. And
when the diffuse writings \textit{(Metakritik,} 1799, and \textit{Kalligone,}
1800) in which he criticized Kant's philosophy appeared, the critical
philosophy had already been developed further by Kant's successors and led
into new paths, in part, to be sure, under the influence of the motives that
from the first had determined Hamann's and Herder's position toward it. ---

c. \textsc{Friedrich Heinrich Jacobi} (1743---1819), a spirited man of the world
and seeker after truth, one of the most characteristic representatives of the
``age of genius,'' contributed in his way a great deal to the peculiar direction
that German philosophy took after Kant. With great acuteness he had, as already
touched on, pointed out the great difficulties in Kant's doctrine of the Ding
an sich, and maintained that this doctrine must go if a consistent system was
to be reached. He was right in his criticism, but his intervention did not
concern the main problem Kant had posed
himself. The doctrine of the Ding an sich was only a consequence of Kant's
philosophy, not its main point. Instead of going back to Kant's
\textit{original} task and examining his method
% --- p. 114 ---
\opage{114}in order to find where the error lay, one sought --- in great part under the
influence of Jacobi's criticism --- to correct the error in the
\textit{finished} system. Jacobi himself felt unsatisfied with Kant's
philosophy for a reason similar to Hamann's and Herder's: because immediate
faith did not come into its right. And only faith can grasp the true. All
science aims at constructing, at producing its objects by an inner acting, at
dissolving everything into pure activity. We understand a thing only by
constructing it. Everything we comprehend we represent to ourselves as a link
in a series, in a complete connection, in which all differences are canceled.
The most consistent of all systems is subjectivism, which lets one's own ego be
the first link in the chain and derives the other links from it. Therefore
Jacobi saw in the turn Fichte gave to the critical philosophy the completion of
speculation. His open letter to Fichte (\textit{Jacobi an Fichte.} 1799) gives
perhaps the best insight into his philosophical conception. Earlier he had
maintained that Spinoza was the only consistent philosopher; now he set Fichte
higher, because the ego, consciousness itself, must after all necessarily be
the first link in the chain of knowledge. But common to all consistent
philosophy is that it must deny the original, the unconditioned, that which has
its ground and value in itself, the qualitative differences and peculiarities.
All philosophy aims at grounding and deriving, at reducing quality to quantity:
the immediate, the free and the original it therefore cannot comprehend. But
for that very reason --- Jacobi thinks --- it also shows itself the more
clearly, the more consistent philosophy becomes, that it cannot lead to the
truth, --- and it is for this reason that he urges and goads on to full
consistency, for only then does it become manifest that by this way the truth
is not reached. His letters on Spinoza impress this upon the philosophy of the
Enlightenment; his dialogues on idealism and realism show it against Kant; his
open letter to Fichte declares it most clearly and distinctly against this
``Messiah of speculation.'' And once more he had occasion to come forward with
his old thoughts against a new system, namely when Schelling thought he had
founded a new philosophy of religion by way of the philosophy of nature.
(Jacobi's writing: \textit{Von} \textit{den göttlichen Dingen.} 1811). Although
Jacobi was not himself a
% --- p. 115 ---
\opage{115}consistent thinker, he had a great sense for the consistency of systems and was
able with energy to bring the great lines of a train of thought to light.

That there is a reality different from consciousness, of this --- Jacobi
thinks --- no proof can convince us, since every proof moves within
consciousness. Immediate observation is a miracle, which we must assume if we
want to have truth: only through faith do things come to be for us. Only
through faith does God, the original source of everything, the fount of all
value in existence, come to be for us. God cannot be known, only believed. A
God who could be known would not be God. Indeed, it is even in the interest of
science that there be no God: for God's existence breaks off the series and
makes connection impossible! God reveals himself immediately in our inner being
(in the outer the true God cannot reveal himself), just as things reveal
themselves immediately to our senses. We perceive immediately that there is
something that is greater and better than we ourselves: we find God by finding
ourselves in God. And finally freedom, in the sense of the mind's ability to
intervene in the world of matter, can only be believed, not comprehended.
Freedom does not, indeed, consist in the unreasonable ability to determine
oneself without grounds; but since it is absolute self-activity, it is
inaccessible to science.

The opposition between science and faith that Jacobi maintained was connected
with the strong movement of feeling that dominated the time after Rousseau's
appearance. He himself gave expression to this tendency in poetic works. It is
the right of feeling that he maintains over against the objective grounds of
the understanding, indifferent to all individual emotion. In the moral domain
too he pleads the cause of individual feeling. ``The beautiful soul,'' which
unfolds itself out of inner germs without regulating itself by general
principles, resting securely and rocking itself in its moods, is to him the
highest, although he is not blind to the dangers to which it is exposed. He
pleads the cause of the exceptions over against the strict, universal law that
Kant had set forth in his categorical imperative, which seems to demand the
same conduct of all in all cases. Kant's moral law designates only
% --- p. 116 ---
\opage{116}the formal consistency in action, not the heart out of which one is to act. The
law exists for man's sake, not the other way round. The book of life must be
written before an index is made to it. A moral system is nothing but such an
index made afterwards! And then it wants to regulate life, to set up
universally valid rules without respect for individualities and exceptions!
Jacobi declares his opposition to this in the open letter to Fichte in the
often-quoted words: ``Yes, I am the godless atheist who will lie as Desdemona
lied in the hour of her death, will lie and deceive like Pylades, who gave
himself out to be Orestes, will murder like Timoleon'' etc.\textsuperscript{28}).

Jacobi, together with Hamann and Herder, has the merit of having held fast the
significance of that in life which cannot be converted into universally valid
knowledge. He fought for the right of immediacy, of reality and of
individuality, and thereby furnished important correctives to the direction on
which philosophy was about to enter, and on which he himself wished to goad it
on. But it was an illusion when he thought that the objects of his faith were
given by immediate revelation. In the first place, he takes the word faith in
two very different senses, partly of the involuntary trust in sense
observations, partly of the religious faith in what cannot be intuited. In the
second place, the content of his religious faith is a good old acquaintance:
the Cartesian spiritualism, which now, instead of the proofs the dogmatic school
had thought it could furnish, is proclaimed with Jacobi, as with Rousseau, as an
object of faith. But would the different individuals, the different ``beautiful
souls,'' really find the same content of faith in their inner being? From
feeling no definite content can be derived, only the general need to hold fast
the validity of what is of highest value. By fixing definite dogmas (even if
only the dogmas of ``natural'' religion) as the only form of satisfying this
need, Jacobi violates the inwardness and individualism of feeling for which he
otherwise makes himself the interpreter. And it is really only thereby that the
sharp opposition between his faith and his knowledge arises: his faith comes to
suffer under all the difficulties of the Cartesian spiritualism. It was in
% --- p. 117 ---
\opage{117}reality two kinds of philosophy that he had, in his faith and in his knowledge,
and it was then no wonder that he could complain that his head and his heart
conflicted with each other: he had taken it into his head that his heart could
beat only in an artificial way, and that this was the true nature.

\section*{8.\quad The Further Development of the Critical Philosophy}

The same need that led Kant's first opponents to raise a protest of feeling
against his work led his first independent disciples to try to bring the many
branching investigations and the numerous distinctions back to a few simple
principles --- preferably to a single principle. It was an endeavor that was
bound to arise naturally in thinkers whose enthusiasm for what was new and
great in Kant was united with a clear eye for his one-sidednesses. And to this
was added that, on closer discussion of Kant's doctrine, problems arose that
could not yet present themselves with full clarity to the founder himself, and
on whose treatment it depended what direction philosophy was to take after the
great turning point it had lived through. Three men in particular are to be
named here, Reinhold and Maimon as regards the theoretical problems, Schiller as
regards the aesthetic and ethical problems.

a. \textsc{Karl Leonhard Reinhold} was born in Vienna in 1758 and as quite a
young man became a novice in the Jesuit order; when this order was abolished,
to the great sorrow of himself and his comrades (which is described in a
letter printed in the biography published by his son), he entered a Barnabite
college. It was, however, zeal for study more than religious interest that
guided him in this step. He became teacher of philosophy at the college and was
strongly influenced by the rationalistic way of thinking that prevailed under
Joseph II. At last the opposition between his way of thinking and his position
as a monastic brother became so strong that at twenty-five years of age he fled
from the monastery. He now became a contributor to Wieland's journal ``Merkur''
and wrote there, among other things, his \textit{Briefe über die Kantische
Philosophie} (1786), a
% --- p. 118 ---
\opage{118}popular account through which Kant's doctrine first became properly known in
wider circles. When Reinhold had become professor at Jena in 1787, the
university there became a chief seat of the philosophical movement. Almost all
the philosophical tendencies that were developed in succession during the
attempts to continue Kant's inquiry arose in Jena. (Besides Reinhold himself:
Fichte, Schelling, Hegel, Fries, Herbart). Reinhold's chief work is his
\textit{Versuch einer neuen Theorie des menschlichen Vorstellungsvermögens}
(Prag und Jena 1789), which aimed at deriving the philosophy set up by Kant from
a single principle. Reinhold did not, however, remain at the standpoint he had
asserted in this work, and to which his significance in the history of
philosophy is bound. His great receptivity to the thoughts of others and his
disinterested love of truth made him change his standpoint repeatedly when he
thought he found significant progress in the solution of the problems in other
philosophical writers of the time (not always the most important). Already in
1793 he left Jena and went to Kiel, where he worked until his death in 1823.
For Danish literature he is of interest through his friendship with Baggesen
(of whom he has given a delightful characterization in his letters to Erhard).

Kant had not, according to Reinhold, gone back to the last presuppositions ---
or rather to the last presupposition. It was Reinhold's conviction that
philosophy could become true science only when it derived all its doctrines
from a single principle. Kant had, after all, not only distinguished sharply
between sensation and understanding and between theoretical knowledge and
practical faith, but he had also applied a double method: partly the analysis
of the forms of knowledge (the subjective deduction), which was essentially a
psychological investigation, partly the construction of the presuppositions of
experience (the objective deduction). These different methods and those
distinctions stood as an imperfection for Reinhold: he demanded a single
starting point, and from this starting point a single way. By this demand the
critical philosophy was led onto the way of speculation. The demand rests on a
confusion of the search for unity, which shows itself in all inquiry, with an
absolute principle: the unity
% --- p. 119 ---
\opage{119}that is sought always presupposes a given multiplicity that is to be ordered,
and is not in and for itself sufficient to express the ideal of knowledge. It
conflicts, moreover, with the nature of our thinking, since every inference
consists in the combination of several premises. But in their enthusiasm the
thinkers now set themselves an infinite ideal and believed themselves in
possession of powers to reach it. --- The principle that Reinhold lays at the
foundation he calls \textit{the principle of
consciousness.} All knowledge is representation (while not all representation
is knowledge), and the principle of consciousness now states that every
representation stands in relation partly to a subject, partly to an object, so
that it is partly to be distinguished from them, partly to be combined with
them. Consciousness itself consists in such a referring of the representation
to the subject and the object. Through a series of investigations Reinhold now
wishes to show in detail that all the forms and fundamental propositions set
up by Kant come forth through a closer carrying through of this first
principle, as more special ways in which representations are set in relation
(Beziehung) to subject and object. The element in the representation by which
it is referred to the subject is its form; the element by which it is referred
to the object is its matter. And since matter cannot be produced by form, the
object not by the subject, the assumption of a thing in itself becomes
necessary: there must be something in the representation that is not produced
by consciousness itself, but by a cause different from it. But since Reinhold
finds the essence of consciousness in a referring (beziehende) activity, the
representation of the thing in itself must necessarily become a
self-contradictory representation, since it is, after all, to concern something
that cannot be referred to the subject or apprehended by the subject's forming
activity. Reinhold accordingly declares: ``Of the reality of the thing in
itself only a contradictory representation, a mere illusion, is possible.'' And
he declares the connection between the mode of working peculiar to our activity
and the thing in itself to belong to ``the questions that no one will raise who
understands their meaning and knows the limits of what can be represented.''
(Versuch. p. 456. 460). But by this the problem of the thing in itself acquired
a far sharper and more provoking form than in Kant. Reinhold, after all,
stresses the unity
% --- p. 120 ---
\opage{120}and activity in consciousness far more strongly than Kant, and the enigma of
the eternal barrier, the self-contradiction in there having to be something
that at once \textit{had to} be thought and \textit{could not} be thought, came
forward all the more strongly thereby. --- It is especially against Reinhold's
doctrine that G. E. Schulze directed his ``Aenesidemus.'' It came forward more
and more clearly that either one must make greater concessions to Hume than
Kant had made, or one must boldly continue on the way Reinhold had entered
upon, and make the unity and activity in our knowledge absolute, whereby the
thing in itself would then have to fall away entirely. Reinhold's wavering in
his later period came from his being unable to decide for either of the two
possibilities.

b. With superior acuteness another of Kant's disciples, \textsc{Salomon Maimon},
took part in the discussion of the questions the master's doctrine led people
to raise. He was able at once to keep himself free from the dogmatizing into
which so many Kantians fell, and from the titanic speculation to which the
demand for the unity of the principle led over. The course of his life had
contributed to nourishing his critical independence. He was a Lithuanian Jew of
a poor family (born 1754), was trained as a rabbi and early distinguished
himself by acuteness and learning. But his thirst for knowledge led him beyond
the Talmud and Jewish theology. In his autobiography, which is a work of the
highest interest in psychological and cultural-historical respects, he
describes under what wretched conditions he had to work his way forward to
scientific knowledge. It was a Hebrew astronomy that he found by chance that
taught him that there was another science than the Talmudic. Laboriously he
taught himself the elements of the German language, and in order to be able to
share in the knowledge of the West he fled from his family (he had been married
already at eleven years of age!) and begged his way to Berlin, where he soon
awakened Mendelssohn's attention and interest. He now studied Wolff, Spinoza
and Locke. Since the imperfect aids that had stood at his disposal had compelled
him to supply what was lacking by his own acuteness, he had an ability to find
out what was
% --- p. 121 ---
\opage{121}essential in a line of thought and to draw the consequences from it, which let
him stand with independent criticism over against all the views he came into
contact with. Thus he stood also over against Kant's writings. From the remarks
he wrote down during his study of ``Kritik der reinen Vernunft'' there came
forth a work \textit{(Versuch über die Transscendentalphilosophie.} Berlin
1790), which gave Kant, who saw it in manuscript, occasion to declare that not
only had none of his opponents understood him as well as Maimon, but that in
general only few possessed in the same degree as he the acuteness necessary for
such investigations. In a series of writings, of which only \textit{Versuch
einer neuen Logik oder Theorie des Denkens} (Berlin 1794) shall be named here,
Maimon developed his epistemological views further. Theoretical thinking was
everything for him, --- both the highest perfection and the highest happiness.
In this he followed the older thinkers of his people (Maimonides, Spinoza).
After a long, wandering and insecure existence he lived his last years with a
Prussian landowner who took an interest in him. He died in the year 1800.

In Maimon we already find the criticism of Kant's philosophy that will probably
become the definitive one. --- Since, he says, we can discover the forms of
knowledge only by way of experience, we can prove neither their necessity nor
their completeness. We can obtain no guarantee that we have brought forward
\textit{all} the forms. And the very distinction between matter and form can
only be relative: there can be no pure matter, and just as little a pure form,
--- only approximations to them. The mere sensation is an idea in Kant's sense:
in spite of all possible degrees of approximation to a sensation in which form
plays no part, this extreme is nevertheless never reached. There are here two
limiting points or ideas: on the one side the single element in consciousness,
on the other side the perfect synthesis. Our knowledge moves in the interval.
It is a grasping, not an encompassing. Every time we try to form a total
representation, an all-encompassing thought, it turns out to be a
representation of something limited, something finite. --- Against Reinhold
% --- p. 122 ---
\opage{122}Maimon maintains the impossibility of setting up a single highest principle. The
``principle of consciousness'' set up by Reinhold expresses only what is common
to all fundamental propositions, and the special fundamental propositions cannot
be derived from it. Consciousness in general is an entirely indeterminate
concept. --- From Kant Maimon separates himself above all by denying the fact on
which Kant builds his ``objective deduction'': that we have \textit{experience}
(as something different from subjective representing). Even if Kant is right
that our thinking has at its disposal a system of categories, he is
nevertheless wrong in holding that we can \textit{in fact} apply these
categories to the given. For the given presents only relations of time, not
\textit{necessary} transitions. Only in the purely mathematical domain do we have
an objectively valid knowledge of reason, a ``real thinking.'' In empirical
judgments the consciousness of the subject, as a matter of mere fact, precedes
the consciousness of the predicate; the latter cannot be derived from the
former. It is otherwise in mathematics, and only there. Hume, then, is not
refuted by Kant, and he cannot be refuted at all. When Hume said that the
concept of cause was taken from experience, he understood by experience not, as
Kant did, a necessary order in the sequence of phenomena, but merely constant
observation, which produces custom and expectation in us. The causal principle
expresses a postulate, an idea that we seek to apply to phenomena, but whose
applicability can be shown only approximately. While Maimon thus takes an
intermediate position between Hume and Kant in his conception of the causal
principle, he takes up Kant's interesting intimations of the connection between
the concept of cause and the concept of continuity. There asserts itself, he
shows, a striving in our knowledge to reduce the opposition between phenomena
to the least possible. To seek out the cause of a phenomenon is the same as to
seek out its continuous coming into being, or to fill out the gaps between our
observations. What does one understand in natural science by the word cause but
a phenomenon's development and resolution, such that continuity is shown
between it and the preceding [and following]? Only by this continuity do
observations become experiences. The word experience therefore designates for
Maimon not a relation
% --- p. 123 ---
\opage{123}of necessity, but only a factual relation of continuity between the observed
phenomena. --- As regards the much-debated problem of the thing in itself, it
falls away entirely for Maimon in a certain sense. The thing in itself was,
after all, to be the cause of the ``matter'' in our knowledge; but there is no
pure matter according to Maimon; only in infinite approximation do we come to
matter, as to the determination of √2: hence the point in our line of thought
at which the question of a thing in itself can be posed lies infinitely far
away! That something is \textit{given} to us, or that our cognitive faculty
\textit{is affected,} means only that something arises in our consciousness
that cannot be derived a priori according to the general laws of consciousness
and of knowledge. The given is that in the representation of which we are
conscious of no activity. --- No faculty whatever contains the ground of its
special applications. But a thing, an object, can be given only in and for
consciousness. An object that is not an object for anyone is an impossible
thought, to be compared with an imaginary number (whereas the given, the point
where we are absolutely passive, was to be compared with an irrational number).
And even if one will ask about the cause of the given, this question cannot be
answered. For it cannot be decided whether the given springs from something
different from us or from our own cognitive faculty: we know only what appears
to our consciousness, and the cognitive faculty, apart from its functions, is
just as much a ``thing in itself'' as the unknown cause of the ``matter'' of
knowledge assumed by Kant and Reinhold. Both the concept of an absolute subject
and the concept of an absolute object are only ideas, limiting concepts, which
cannot be drawn into our knowledge\textsuperscript{29}). It is the task of our
understanding to \textit{grasp} phenomena, i.e. to understand them through
their mutual connection, through the \textit{law} of their relations. But the
imagination, which in turn is spurred on by our craving to reach the highest,
constantly seeks to extend our representations beyond all the limits of
experience and wants \textit{to encompass in one image} all the multiplicity
that is subject to law. Everything Kant calls ideas, concepts of an
unconditioned in various forms, Maimon derives not from reason but from the
imagination. The drive to totality in our knowledge has
% --- p. 124 ---
% print: „forsætte“ (p. 124) (misprint)
\opage{124}its ground in the drive toward the highest perfection; therefore it is
especially in the ethical and religious domain that the drive to form ideas
shows itself. But as soon as we represent such totalities \textit{as objects,}
we limit them and thus come to inhibit that drive. For every object must be
found within the continuous connection of knowledge. The striving for totality
is a perfection; but the representation of totality as an object is an
imperfection. It is not this representation, but that striving, that has
religious and ethical value. ---

Maimon calls himself a skeptic, not only over against the dogmatic philosophy,
but also over against the critical philosophy. It was the dogmatism of the
Kantians that provoked him to use this designation. In reality he has
intimated an epistemological view that was well fitted to lead beyond the
difficulties that had arisen during the discussion of Kant's works. Both as
regards the relation between thinking and experience (Kant's point of dispute
with Hume) and as regards the relation between knowledge and faith (Kant's
point of dispute with Jacobi) he had indicated points of view that lent
themselves to scientific carrying out. Maimon is the one among Kant's disciples
who has best continued his work (even if the old master liked his attempts to
continue his work as little as those of Reinhold and other ``hypercritical
friends'')\textsuperscript{30}). But the Romantic ferment of the time hindered a
continued development of the critical philosophy in the spirit by which Maimon
had been animated. The Romantic need of unity, the drive to revel in the
Absolute, to unite thinking with artistic vision, was too strong for Maimon's
critical and skeptical deliberateness to be able to hold interest. Its
speculative philosophy and its historians see Maimon's significance in his
being an intermediate link between Kant and the pure speculation initiated by
Fichte. But he has an independent and lasting significance and stands for
something far more than one of the ``superseded standpoints'' over which
triumphant speculation strode onward. ---

c. There is a certain analogy in course of life and in thinking between
Reinhold, Maimon and Schiller, in that all three in their youth had to free
themselves by flight from crushing circumstances in order to be able to
% --- p. 125 ---
\opage{125}reach the free development of the spirit they craved, and in that their task as
thinkers was the same under different forms: standing on the ground of the
critical philosophy, to bring about unity and harmony where Kant had put
distinctions and oppositions in the first line. \textsc{Friedrich Schiller}
(1759---1805), the great poet, whose biography it does not fall to the history
of philosophy to give, had throughout his whole life an intense philosophical
interest, even if by his own statement he felt his powers properly only in art,
and even if he finally used his philosophical theory to prove that the artist
alone is the true man, a proof that for him consistently marked the transition
from his philosophizing period to the magnificent poetic production of the last
decade of his life. It was not first the study of Kant that awakened his
philosophical interest. While he studied at the Karlsschule in Stuttgart, his
scientific interest was occupied by medicine and philosophy, and
speeches and treatises from this time bear witness that thoughts were already
taking root in him then which came to influence his later views. Of special
interest is \textit{Versuch über den Zusammenhang der thierischen Natur des
Menschen mit seiner geistigen} (1780), where it is developed that the pleasure
and pain bound up with the organic functions are not only of significance for
self-preservation, but also contribute to awakening and attuning or inhibiting
and depressing the mental powers, just as, conversely, mental pleasure and pain
react upon the organic condition. The ethical ideas Schiller declares at this
time betray the influence of Rousseau and of the English moral philosophers of
the eighteenth century. After his flight from Stuttgart (the Duke --- offended
by ``Die Räuber'' --- had forbidden him to publish anything but purely medical
writings) he immersed himself in the study of ancient poetic works, and from
this time on Greek humanity in art and life stood for him as the great ideal
that had shown itself in history in a happy period, but had been pushed aside
during the later development of culture. In a peculiar way this ideal combined
with the criticism of the state of culture to which Rousseau had led him. In
place of the vague notion of an unbound life of nature there now came the
view of the
% --- p. 126 ---
\opage{126}harmonious unfolding of life determined from within. In art he now saw a power
of life that without constraint, through involuntary harmonizing of drives and
powers, raises human life above the animal stage, just as in its symbols it
leads to grasping the truth long before the abstract thinker can reach it. And
not only the beginning of the higher life of the spirit, but also its summit,
is marked by art. Therefore Schiller says to the artists (in the poem
\textit{Die Künstler.} 1789):

Mit euch, des Frühlings erster Pflanze,

Begann die seelenbildende Natur;

Mit euch, dem freud'gen Erntekranze,

Schlisst die vollendende Natur. In art he saw man's proper distinguishing mark:

Die Kunst, o Mensch, hast du allein.

When Schiller wrote this poem, he already knew Kant's essays on the philosophy of
history, which had brought the problem of culture so strongly forward. He first
came to a more intimate immersion in Kant's writings in Jena, when he had become
Reinhold's colleague. The great thoughts found a well-prepared soil. Schiller,
who had had to struggle with outer obstacles as well as with conflicting drives
and doubting thoughts, knew how to value the master's struggle to find the
ground of truth and his maintaining of the ideal's elevation above the immediate
promptings of nature. But his artist's nature and his enthusiasm for the Greeks
did not allow him to give up the demand for the harmonious unfolding of human
nature as the highest. Thereby the problem was posed to him whose solution was
his contribution to the development of philosophy. It is characteristic that
from his artistic standpoint he makes the same demand that Hamann made from his
religious standpoint: that ``one must not separate what nature has joined.''
``Even in the purest utterances of the divine part of human nature,'' it says
in the treatise \textit{Ueber Anmuth und} \textit{Würde} (1793), ``the
sensuous part must not be pushed aside, and the triumph of the one must not be
grounded on the suppression of the other. Man's moral way of thinking
% --- p. 127 ---
\opage{127}is first secure when it springs forth from the whole human being as the united
effect of both principles, that is, when it has become nature to him.''
Therefore Schiller demands beauty and grace of moral action. Grace consists for
him in a harmony in the involuntary movements that accompany a freely willed
action, and that themselves point to a moral disposition in the mind. There
must be nothing forced, painful or crude in the action if it is to be perfect.
This demand, says Schiller, does not, to be sure, accord in its wording with
Kant's ethics. But --- he goes on --- the great thinker became the Draco of his
time, because it was not receptive to a Solon, and this led him to overlook
that the children of the house had not, after all, deserved that he should care
only for the slaves. Is the disinterested feeling in the noblest breast to be
made suspect because impure inclinations often usurp the name of virtue? And is
perfected humanity not found in the beautiful soul, which, led by immediate
feeling, performs the most painful duties and makes the most heroic sacrifices
with the ease of instinct? In the beautiful soul it is not the single actions,
but the whole character, that is moral. The beautiful soul has no other merit
than that it exists. Sensibility and reason, duty and inclination are in
harmony, and gracefulness is the outer expression of this. Yet Schiller
restricts the demand for grace to the actions that lie \textit{within} the
limits of human nature. Tasks may be set for man that lead him out to the very
limit of human capacity, where duty and inclination do not harmonize: here
strained struggle is the only possibility, and here the demand is to act with
dignity, to express the disharmony in such a way that the nobler power is
nevertheless seen in its superiority. --- A certain wavering asserts itself in
Schiller's line of thought. Harmony had to be the highest for him --- but he
doubts that it can be reached in all cases. Which stands highest, grace or
dignity: to this question he does not venture to give any definite answer. This
wavering is connected with his not having come (any more than Kant) to the
significance of differences of individuality in ethics. He speaks only of the
limits of human nature, not of the limits of the single
% --- p. 128 ---
\opage{128}individuality, and he confidently assumes that the limits lie in the same
place for all individualities. He says expressly: ``Our moral judgment brings
every individual under the measure of the species, and no other barriers than
the barriers of humanity itself are credited to man.''

In close connection with the problem of culture Schiller brings forward his
ideas in \textit{Briefe über die ästhetische Erziehung des Menschen} (1795). It
is the fundamental thought of ``Die Künstler'' that is developed here in detail.
The course of culture has led to the dissolution of the Greek harmony between
spirit and nature, reflection and imagination, universality and individuality.
It is the division of labor that causes the misfortunes under which we suffer.
The conflict of the powers leads to the progress of culture and is in so far a
gain for the species; but the single individuals become one-sided and crippled.
State and church, laws and manners, labor and enjoyment have become separated,
and each individual is only a fragment of a man. This can be remedied only by
the completion of culture. A pure command of reason cannot decide the matter,
for drives are overcome only by drives. It is, moreover, a sign of imperfect
culture when the moral character can be maintained only by sacrificing the
natural one, and when unity and connection can triumph only by violating
fullness and multiplicity. Only through aesthetic education is the solution of
the problem possible. Take hold of men in their idle hours, in their pleasures,
surround them with great spiritual forms, with symbols of the good, and let
seeming overcome reality without constraint, let art conquer nature. What
matters is to unite the involuntary fullness of natural life with the
independence and freedom of moral life, surrender to changing states with the
unity of personality, the material drive with the formal drive. In play this
task is solved. The powers there work according to their natural laws and yet
without being bound to material demands; they work from within, but without
self-constraint. Producing and receiving go together as one. Man is raised
above the influence of sensuous nature, and yet sensuous nature works according
to its own law. He determines himself with freedom; he is self-active; he is
guided by the formal drive; --- and yet sensibility and matter are not violated.
% --- p. 129 ---
\opage{129}The condition is that there be a certain superabundance of power that can be
applied to the free play of the functions. Where this has been reached lies the
proper beginning of human life. Man is only properly man when he plays. In the
free play of the powers human nature expresses itself many-sidedly and as a
totality, with the possibility of entering on special directions, a possibility
that is, however, not realized as long as the aesthetic state lasts. ``All
other exercises,'' says Schiller in the 22nd letter, ``give the mind a special
skill, but thereby also set a limit to it; only the aesthetic exercise leads to
the unlimited. Every other state into which we can come points us back to a
preceding one and needs a following one for its dissolution; only the aesthetic
state is a whole in itself, since it unites in itself all the conditions of its
arising and its continuance. Here alone do we feel ourselves as if torn out of
time, and our humanity expresses itself with a purity and wholeness
(Integrität), as though it had as yet suffered no impairment through the action
of outer powers.'' --- The \textit{aesthetic state} that Schiller describes is,
then, one in which all human powers work freely and harmoniously, without being
set in motion by outer needs, and without any single one being predominant. In
it he saw the completion of culture, not merely a means of subduing crudeness
and softening disharmony. ---

There has been dispute over whether Schiller in ``Briefe über ästhetische
Erziehung'' stands on the same standpoint as in ``Anmuth und Würde,'' or
whether he does not in the former set the aesthetic state as the highest, while
in the latter, as regards the limiting cases, he still reserved a place for
dignity beside grace. As we have seen, he really already proclaims grace as the
highest in ``Anmuth und Würde''; but still more decidedly it comes forward as
the fundamental thought in ``the aesthetic education'' that the highest is not
reached where there is not harmony and totality\textsuperscript{31}). There is
a ring of the Renaissance in Schiller's line of thought. Next after Kant's
pointing to the state of law built on the principle of freedom, no answer so
weighty has been given to the problem of culture posed by Rousseau as in
Schiller's setting up of the free and total play of the powers as the
% --- p. 130 ---
\opage{130}highest --- not merely as an end, but also as a means that can lead onward to
perfect culture. He is, however, clear that there is a long way to this goal,
and he thought, at any rate as regards himself, that he worked best for it
through art. ``Follow my advice,'' he wrote to a friend (letter to Erhard, May
26, 1794), ``and for the present let poor, unworthy and immature humanity look
after itself. Remain in the bright and quiet world of ideas and leave it to
time to carry the ideas into practical life!'' He himself, after concluding his
philosophical period (1789---95), worked at the presentation of ideas in
artistic form. The speculative philosophy that now began to develop he looked
upon with aversion, while even in the last year of his life he recalled with
enthusiasm the great circle of thought into which Kant had led him: ``The
speculative philosophy,'' he writes to Wilhelm von Humboldt (April 2, 1805),
``has driven me away with its hollow formulas, if it ever otherwise occupied
me. In this barren domain I have found no living spring and no nourishment for
myself. But the deep fundamental thoughts of the philosophy of the ideal are an
eternal treasure, and for their sake alone one must count oneself happy to have
lived in this time.'' --- A more beautiful epilogue could not be imagined for
the philosophy whose founding and first fortunes we have been occupied with
here.

\begin{center}---\end{center}


% --- p. 131 ---
\hhchapter{Eighth Book}\opage{131}

\begin{center}\textsc{The Philosophy of Romanticism.}\end{center}

\bigskip

\section*{A.\quad The Philosophy of Romanticism as an Idealist Doctrine of Development}

The spirit in which Kant's philosophy was carried further in Germany itself was
already determined by the objections of his first opponents and by his first
disciples' attempts at correction. People missed in him a comprehensive view, totality;
the living coherence of the spirit was violated by his analysis and distinguishing, and
they wanted ideas that could hold the whole content of the life of the spirit --- preferably all at
once! They appealed partly to religious faith, partly to artistic intuiting and
activity, as organs that let the fullness of life come into its own quite otherwise than
critical philosophizing did. And even on purely scientific grounds, it was held, the
critical philosophy was insufficient so long as all principles were not derived from a
single, absolute principle. What had kept Kant from such a formal completion of his
philosophy was the assumption that knowledge always presupposes something besides
itself, something that can never be drawn in but always withdraws: Ding an sich. But
this assumption led Kant's philosophy into a self-contradiction and was bound up,
besides, with his untenable distinction between the matter and the form of knowledge.
Let this assumption fall, then --- and nothing will prevent the consistent carrying through
of philosophy on the basis of Kant's own deepest thought of the nature of spirit as synthesis!
What in Kant had been the ultimate presupposition, the fundamental hypothesis, was now
drawn
% --- p. 132 ---
\opage{132}forth as the principle of beginning, from which a great systematic
construction was to be undertaken. It was a thought that filled young thinkers with
enthusiasm and made them overlook that it was in reality the philosophers' stone they
were seeking. All externality, isolation and dividedness in the spiritual life would
indeed vanish when unity was thus shown in everything, when all forms of life came to
stand as steps and phases through which one and the same infinite life expressed
itself! Not only the conscious life of the individual human being, but also the life of
the species in history and --- by way of analogy --- the life of nature would thereby be
seen in a wholly new light! And not merely a single side of the human life of the spirit
would find its explanation; if the guiding principle was grasped deeply enough, it must
lead beyond the distinction between science, religion and art and abolish all mental
disharmonies.

Such an ideal of knowledge may rightly be called romantic. It stands exalted and remote,
awakens longing and enthusiasm, and works more by this exaltedness than by the prospect of
clear and sober realization. That the ideal of knowledge could be formed in this way for
a whole generation is not explained by the preceding development of philosophy alone,
but is understood only through motives that lay in the whole spirit, need and tendency of
the age. A purely philosophical motive lay, to be sure, in the conviction awakened by Kant
of the originality and activity of the nature of spirit. It was then in itself a
justified thought experiment to try whether this originality and activity might not be
absolute, without limits and without conditions. But the audacity with which this
thought experiment was undertaken is understood only through other currents of the age.
The close of the eighteenth century was a time of strong agitation. --- The French
Revolution stirred up men's minds. It overturned what had hitherto stood firm, and
sought to raise a whole social edifice anew by way of construction. Even where its
practical ideals and consequences were not accepted, it nevertheless gave a sense for
absolute standpoints and for the ruthless carrying through of principles once laid down.
It is more than an analogy when the speculative
% --- p. 133 ---
\opage{133}movement in Germany has so often been compared with the contemporaneous
revolutionary movement in France\textsuperscript{32}). It is a movement of feeling that
finds vent in two different ways, according to the different inner and outer
conditions. --- At the same time Germany had its poetic golden age. In the poetry of
GOETHE and SCHILLER the artistic power had brought forth immortal images
as the expression of the craving and striving of life. Should the human spirit be more
powerless in the world of thought than in that of art? Should thinking not be able, in its
own domain, to reach a unity and harmony analogous to that which art yields in its own?
Indeed, should poetry and science not be one in their innermost nature, expressions of one
and the same creative power? The most characteristic representative of romantic poetry,
NOVALIS, sought in his unfinished work ``Heinrich von Ofterdingen'' to show poetry
as the innermost in everything. He regretted that poetry has a special name and that the
poets form a guild of their own. Poetry is, according to him, nothing other than the
peculiar mode of action of the human spirit: does not every human being, in every moment
of his life, compose and strive? The distinction between poetry and philosophy is,
according to Novalis, superficial and harmful; philosophy is only the theory of poetry,
and is to show us that poetry is one and all. The task was to find ``the secret word''
that solves all riddles in the inner and the outer world. (Novalis' Schriften. 4. Aufl.
I. p. 201. 286 ff. --- II. p. 240 ff.). The difference between the romantic philosopher
and the romantic poet is here this: while the poet regards philosophy as the interpreter
of the poetry of life that is found in everything, the philosopher will rather conceive
poetry as an intuitive, figurative form of the thought that stirs in everything.
--- As the third in the alliance, religion came forward. There was stirring in the age
--- as the appearance of Hamann, Herder and Jacobi already bore witness --- a need of a
deeper religiousness than the flat and dry rationalism. Nor could the sentimental
religion of feeling satisfy. If it is now the business of thinking to show us the unity
in everything, can the philosophical striving then be essentially different from the
religious need, which also, after all, seeks out beyond the oppositions of life and
their unrest? And must not a reconciliation of religion and science be reached, if only
one conceives the
% --- p. 134 ---
\opage{134}nature of reason thoroughly and consistently enough? Not by taking reason
captive, but by going back to the innermost nature of the spirit, which lies at the ground
of religion as well as of science, will the philosophy of Romanticism solve the religious
problem. Thus in his work \textit{Ueber die Religion, Reden an die Gebildeten unter
ihren Verächtern} (1799) SCHLEIERMACHER sought to demonstrate the necessity of
religion for the depth and harmony of the life of the spirit. --- In the development of
natural science at the close of the century, discoveries and ideas came forward that
could lead to laying greater weight on the unity in nature than the immediately
preceding period had done. The discovery of galvanism, the founding of the new chemistry
(after Lavoisier) and of comparative anatomy must in many ways give a new view of nature.
And Goethe, whose poetic works exercised so great an influence on those spiritually stirred
in the age, was led precisely by his studies in natural science to a presentiment of an
inward unity in everything, a presentiment that his studies of Spinoza had nourished in
him and that had already exercised influence on Herder. The Goethe-Herderian view of
nature furnished the foundation and the direction for the speculation of Romanticism. In
particular, Goethe's theory of colors with its polemic against the mechanical explanation
of nature, and his ``Metamorphose der Pflanzen'' with its fundamental thought of an inner
unfolding through the various organic forms, gained a significant and fateful influence
on the speculative philosophy of nature. And in his ``Faust'' Goethe had given passionate
vent to the boundless craving for a knowledge that penetrates into the innermost of
existence. Schelling was the first who rightly valued Goethe's great poem, which then
existed only as a fragment: ``To the contradiction that springs from unsatisfied desire
for knowledge of things the poet has attached his images in the poem that is the Germans'
own poem, and he has opened an ever fresh source of enthusiasm, which by itself alone was
able to rejuvenate the science of this age and to spread over it the breath of a new life.
Whoever would penetrate into the sanctuary of nature, let him nourish himself on these
tones from a higher world and drink in already in his youth the power that goes out in
dense rays of light from this work and moves the
% --- p. 135 ---
\opage{135}world's innermost!'' (SCHELLING: \textit{Ueber das akademische Studium.}
Vorlesung XI). --- Finally, Spinoza's system, which had recently been drawn forth from the
darkness of neglect and was acknowledged by friends and foes alike as the ideal of
philosophy, exercised an overwhelming power both by its thoughts and by its strict form
of unity. --- There was thus no lack of motives that could lead men to try to raise bold
systematic edifices.

The method became predominantly deductive and constructive. Confirmation by experience was
held to be unnecessary --- in the confidence that ``the inner type of all things'' revealed
itself in thought just as well as in the whole of existence. (Cf. Schelling, loc. cit.).
The material used in the systematizing had been procured by the labor of the preceding
age. What the philosophy of Romanticism really wants is to create a systematic form for
everything that had come forth in Kant's epistemology and ethics, in Lessing's and
Schiller's aesthetic ideas, in Goethe's poetry, in Herder's historical thoughts and in
Hamann's fermenting religious spirit. Systems as such are not productive, but presuppose
the productive powers. If we now look at the romantic systems in philosophy, we must say
that just as little as romantic poetry succeeded in obscuring the great figures of Goethe
and Schiller, which on the contrary shine forth again after the romantic period with
undiminished splendor, just so little did romantic philosophy succeed in giving the
spiritual content that that series of great spiritual heroes had brought forth such a new
form that these heroes should now have significance only as forerunners. Whoever seeks
real nourishment will often prefer to go back behind the systematizers to the original
sources. The speculative period in Germany at the beginning of our century can, moreover,
by no means measure itself with the period of the great systems in the seventeenth century
in originality and productive power, in rigor and in significance for the treatment of
problems. This does not exclude that the eminent men who stand as representatives of the
philosophy of Romanticism, in their eager striving to form the content of the life of the
spirit into a coherent whole, have thrown light on several problems and uttered
significant ideas whose time will not be over with that of the systems. In literary
% --- p. 136 ---
\opage{136}respects most of these thinkers have harmed their continued influence by the use
of a scholastic terminology, a kind of jargon, that makes their writings hard of access to
those who have not themselves learned to think in this language.

\subsection*{1.\quad Johann Gottlieb Fichte}

\subsubsection*{a.\quad Biography and Characterization}

It is a chief peculiarity of German thought, right from the mysticism of the Middle Ages
on, that it asserts the independence, inwardness and validity of the spiritual life and
lays this assertion at the foundation of its world-view. What is inner and original in us
stands as a light in which we --- consciously or unconsciously --- see everything in heaven
and on earth. The greatest deed of the German people, the Reformation, was a struggle for
free, inward conviction against ecclesiastical authority. The critical philosophy founded
by Kant was a continuation of the Reformation, being a return, leading still further, to
the innermost sources of all knowledge and valuation. Kant's first disciple, Joh. Gottl.
Fichte, possessed not only the capacity for self-absorption, the mystical vein that leads
down into the depths of the inner life, but also the unbending strength of will and the
strong self-feeling without which the conviction of the eternal right and supremacy of the
inner over the outer cannot be held fast and carried through. He was the son of a Saxon
peasant, born at Rammenau in Upper Lusatia on 19 May 1762. His vigorous character, whose
shadow sides were obstinacy and pride, he inherited from his mother, as indeed the
temperament of eminent men so often comes from the mother's side. As a child he helped at
the loom or tended the flock of geese. He distinguished himself by the attention with which
he followed the sermons and by the sure memory with which he could reproduce them. Here
his sense for spiritual things found its first nourishment, and thereby at the same time
the occasion for his further education was given. A landowner from the neighborhood came
too late to church one Sunday
% --- p. 137 ---
\opage{137}and was then referred to the goose-boy to learn what the pastor had said.
Astonished at the boy's abilities, he resolved to take charge of him and help him to study.
Fichte's last years at school were a time of strong agitation: Lessing was just then
waging his theological struggle, and his polemical writings made an unforgettable
impression on the young student. From 1780 on he studied theology, philology and
philosophy at Jena and Leipzig. His circumstances were straitened. His benefactor had
died, and from home he could get little or no help. He had a hard struggle to endure
against his mother, who wanted at any price that he should be a pastor, while his own
plans aimed at a free, many-sided development of his abilities. He was on the point of
despairing from want when in the year 1788 he got a place as private tutor in Zürich.
During his stay here his plans ripened, insofar as the need to influence his age through
thought and word became vividly conscious to him. But the direction of this activity and
the means by which he was to act still stood dark to him. It is characteristic of his
personality that the will thus goes before the thought. All his life long he is driven
as by an inner power to work in the domain of ideas, but he is always able only imperfectly
to convert this inner need into the form of thought, although all his life long he works
restlessly at new and more perfect expositions of his system. And his philosophy itself
rests precisely on the fundamental thought, which he more than any other thinker has
brought forward and impressed, that our innermost being is a willing, an acting, and that
all representing and thinking is conditioned by this practical capacity, the inmost root
of our ego. In a letter from his youth he declares: ``I will not merely think, I will
act . . . I have only one passion, only one need, only one complete feeling of myself,
this: to act outward. The more I act, the happier I feel.'' --- A great good for him, both
for the clarifying of his purposes and for the polishing of the unbridled harshness of his
character, was that here in Zürich he came to know the excellent woman who later became his
wife, Johanna Rahn, Klopstock's niece. Their correspondence shows how well she understood
all sides
% --- p. 138 ---
\opage{138}of his nature. She stood faithfully at his side in good and evil days. ---
The tutoring in Zürich did not last long, especially because Fichte found that the parents
needed education no less than the children, and therefore set up a weekly censure for the
parents which drew their attention to the pedagogical faults they had committed in the
course of the week! --- He set out wandering again, to educate himself further and to find
a sphere of activity. During a stay in Leipzig (1790) he studied Kant's works for the first
time, and with that his life got its decisive turning point. ``I live,'' he writes in a
letter, ``in a new world since I have read Kant's `Kritik der praktischen Vernunft'.'' He
now found definite problems set for his thinking and definite principles for the practical
influence on the age that he longed to exert. Kant himself he came to know the year after
in Königsberg. To introduce himself to the old master, he worked out a writing
\textit{(Versuch einer Kritik aller Offenbarung),} which he laid before him, an application
of Kant's doctrine to the philosophy of religion, which Kant himself had not yet treated.
The writing won not only Kant's recognition, but since it appeared (through a
misunderstanding) anonymously, it was taken by many to be a work by Kant himself. With this
Fichte had broken through; the way to literary and scientific activity now lay open to him.
He now accepted his betrothed's offer to set up house with the help of her fortune. In the
following years he published writings on the French Revolution and on the freedom of the
press, in which he asserted the justification of the efforts for freedom against the
reaction that the terrorism of the revolutionary period had begun to produce. Fichte
treats practical problems before he immerses himself in the purely speculative
problems\textsuperscript{32\,b}). To these last he was led over naturally when in 1794 he
was called as professor to Jena (after Reinhold). Here he unfolded an energetic and
brilliant activity as a teacher and developed his peculiar system, which was first set forth
in \textit{Grundlage der gesammten Wissenschaftslehre} (1794), but was later reworked again
and again, partly so that the system might become more perfect, partly so that it might
become more accessible. In neither of these two respects did Fichte ever satisfy
% --- p. 139 ---
\opage{139}himself. The best access to a knowledge of his philosophical view is given by a
later treatise, \textit{Erste Einleitung in die Wissenschaftslehre} (1797), with whose help
a preliminary characterization of Fichte's standpoint will be attempted here.

There can, according to Fichte, be two philosophical systems, each consistent in itself.
The one he calls idealism, the other dogmatism. What philosophy is to explain is
experience. Our experience contains thoughts of things. Now one can either (with dogmatism)
derive the thought from the thing, or (with idealism) the thing from the thought. Which of
the two possibilities one chooses depends on what sort of man one is. A philosophical
system is not a dead piece of furniture that one can have or part with at pleasure; it
springs from the innermost soul of man. The choice will depend on whether the feeling of
independence and activity or the feeling of dependence and passivity has the upper hand in
us. Yet --- Fichte stresses --- on closer investigation it will appear that idealism is
already better placed than dogmatism on purely theoretical grounds. For from the mere thing,
from bare being, one will never be able to derive a thought, a consciousness of the thing
and of being. It is the inconsistency of dogmatism that it is a doctrine, a system of
thought, and yet cannot establish the possibility of there being thoughts at all. Dogmatism
(to which belong materialism, spiritualism, Spinozism) is therefore an impossible
philosophy. Idealism, on the other hand, starts from thinking itself as what is original,
and from it will be able to derive --- not, to be sure, the things themselves, which indeed
are never given either, but experience, our definite representations of things. The task
of the Wissenschaftslehre is now precisely to show how our representations of things spring
from the activity of thought, in that this activity by its nature comes to set itself
definite limits. The Wissenschaftslehre starts from the presupposition that there can be
nothing in the ego that is not the fruit of the ego's own activity. While Kant went back
from the given multiplicity in the content of consciousness to the unity that embraces it,
Fichte, conversely, will start from the original activity of the ego and derive its special
forms from it. If his work succeeds, he will at last have constructed actual empirical
consciousness. He holds that
% --- p. 140 ---
\opage{140}philosophy to be false which does not agree with experience. --- Of the method
Fichte used in this investigation we shall speak in the special exposition of the
Wissenschaftslehre. Here only the spirit and direction of Fichte's teaching were to be
indicated.

His ethics and doctrine of right Fichte set forth in \textit{Naturrecht} (1796) and
\textit{Sittenlehre} (1798), the latter of which is probably the most significant work he
produced.

It lay in Fichte's energetic and vehement character as well as in the given circumstances
that his activity at Jena did not unfold without frictions and serious struggles, which
at last led to a catastrophe. Besides disputes with philosophical colleagues who could not
follow him in his reform of the Kantian philosophy, he also came into conflict with the
theologians, who took offense that on Sundays he gave lectures to the students on practical
ethics, and with the students, because he sought to reform the rough life of the Burschen
that had flourished from of old. This last conflict even led to Fichte's being
% print: „bler“ (p. 140) (misprint)
assaulted in his house and leaving Jena for a time. But the most serious and most
significant struggle was the \textit{Atheism Controversy} (1799). For this to be
understood, Fichte's standpoint in the philosophy of religion must be characterized. It
proves to be closely connected with his opposition between idealism and dogmatism. It
might indeed seem as if in Fichte's philosophy there could be no room at all for any
principle beyond human thought, beyond the human ego; for Fichte wanted, after all, to
derive everything from thought, from the ego. But already in the first exposition of the
Wissenschaftslehre this frequent misunderstanding was rejected. Fichte does indeed lay down
the proposition that everything that is in consciousness must be a product of the ego; but
he shows at the same time that there is a very great deal in our consciousness that we are
not conscious of having produced. The ego we know in experience is always limited, is
placed in a system of limits, has objects (non-egos) over against it that it has not itself
produced. There must then be at work in consciousness a more comprehensive principle than
the finite (empirical) ego; only in this principle, which Fichte calls the pure or the
infinite ego, can the ground be sought of the world of objects or limits in which our
finite ego
% --- p. 141 ---
\opage{141}is placed. The ultimate ground of the limitation by which the finite egos and
their limits come to be cannot now be found by the theoretical way; for what can limit an
infinite activity? If, on the other hand, our conscience is right that the highest thing is
labor and striving, then we understand why there is a finite world: for without resistance
no labor, without means no purposes. The actual world is a material for our duty. And the
assurance that the resistance can progressively be overcome, that we can always do our duty
and work our way forward toward full spiritual freedom as our highest goal, is grounded on
the idea of an order of things that makes conscientious action possible and gives it its
full effect, an order of things that does not indeed come forth in sensuous experience, but
of which I myself feel myself a member every time I act from purely ideal motives. The
essential thing in religion is now that man builds on such a moral world-order, on this
divine that is exalted above everything perishable, and regards each of his duties as
sprung from this order and as contributing to its development. For it is not an ordering
that is finished once for all; it is constantly in development. And just as little is it an
accidental ordering, which would in turn presuppose an ordering being outside it. That man
personifies his experiences of this world-order into a particular being is harmless, if only
it serves to make the thought of it living for his consciousness. But when he thinks of God
as a potentate on whose favor future feelings of pleasure depend, then it is an idol he
worships, and then he is rightly to be called an atheist. Indeed, every attempt to comprise
the infinite principle (the pure ego, the moral world-order) in the form of the concept
founders; to comprehend is to limit. As soon as something is comprehended, it ceases to be
God, and every so-called concept of God is necessarily the concept of an idol! ---

These views Fichte developed in his treatise \textit{Ueber den Grund unseres Glaubens an
eine göttliche Weltregierung} (1798) and, after charges had been raised against him, partly
in sharpened form in the masterly polemical writings \textit{Appellation an das}
% --- p. 142 ---
\opage{142}\textit{Publikum} and\textit{ Gerichtliche Verantwortungsschrift} (1799). ---
The course of the controversy was this. After an anonymous pamphlet had raised an outcry
on the occasion of Fichte's treatise, the Electoral Saxon government had it confiscated and
complained to the government at Weimar that atheistic doctrine was being taught at the
University of Jena, which was also attended by Electoral Saxon subjects. Fichte answered
this with the polemical writings just named. At Weimar they would have preferred to hush the
matter up. They did not want to offend the Electoral Saxon government, nor did they want to
stop Fichte's activity. They wished only that Fichte would keep quiet. But that was against
his nature, and he addressed a defiant letter to a member of the government at Weimar. All
the privy councilors, Goethe among them, were now embittered, and Fichte was dismissed in a
sharp form. It was a flagrant encroachment on the freedom of teaching that was thereby
committed, since the government in its letter arrogated to itself a judgment on Fichte's
doctrine. Despite repeated steps on the students' part, the government held to its
decision, and Fichte had to leave Jena.

For a number of years he now lived as a private man in Berlin, occupied with new
expositions of his system and with popular lectures. It has been thought that a difference
of principle in standpoint can be found between the writings he published from this time
and the Jena writings. A difference there certainly is; but it can be called one of
principle only if one conceives the ``Wissenschaftslehre'' in its first form as an attempt
to derive everything from the individual, finite, empirical ego. As we have seen, such a
conception is incorrect. Already in Fichte's first writings he does not really teach a pure
idealism by his own definition, for he does assume something that acts in us without our
becoming conscious of it. When he calls it an ego, it is the analogy with conscious activity
that he uses. Only by the extension of the ego from the empirical to the infinite ego, which
becomes possible through this analogy, can Fichte hold fast to his idealism and conceive
everything actual as phenomenon or symbol of thought. There is a certain mystical vein in
Fichte already in his earlier writings; he felt himself different from the older mystics
only in this, that they were inclined to represent the highest to themselves
% --- p. 143 ---
\opage{143}as something given, as something that could be attained once for all, while for
Fichte it was an infinite that constantly demanded new labor. \textit{(Sittenlehre}
§ 12). --- In his later writings he now teaches that the thought (the infinite ego) of which
everything is phenomenon is itself only phenomenon of an absolute reality, an infinite
power, a life, a light that comes to our knowledge only in broken rays. He thus stresses
more than before the mystical (or dogmatic) element lying beyond all conscious thought,
which he had already had an eye for in his first exposition of the Wissenschaftslehre. With
this there follows a change in feeling, --- insofar as it should not, conversely, be the
change of feeling that has called forth the altered conception. While Fichte in his first
writings stresses rather the restless striving and acting, the constant activity, so that
his religion too, which consists in faith in a moral world-order, is essentially ``die
Religion des freudigen Rechtthuns,'' --- he later lays more weight on devotion to the life
that stirs in us and wells up in us without our willing and reason being able to produce
it. Characteristic in this respect is the writing \textit{Anweisung zum seeligen Leben}
(1806), while Fichte's general philosophical and psychological views, as they took shape
in his later years, are most accessible in the posthumous writing \textit{Die Thatsachen des
Bevusstseins.} --- With the changes named there also follows naturally a change of front in
Fichte's polemic. Hitherto he had attacked orthodoxy and dogmatism. Now he attacked the
idea-forsaken ``Enlightenment,'' the empty and negative tendency of the understanding that
was content with its meager concepts but lacked all deeper spiritual sense. And this polemic
gains a peculiar interest from its giving him occasion to set forth his conception of the
historical development of the spiritual life. This is in the remarkable writing
\textit{Die} \textit{Grundzüge des gegenwärtigen Zeitalters} (1806). He distinguishes here
five periods in the development. First the \textit{instinct of reason} rules, in that a
group of individuals arises (the normal people) among whom life is ordered in noble and
perfect forms without either science or art being necessary. When the normal people, in
consequence of natural events, are scattered among the animal peoples of nature, the
struggle begins between
% --- p. 144 ---
% scan: „Berlin,“ (p. 144)
\opage{144}culture and rawness. And the second period arises when what the instinct of
reason leads to is set up by eminent individuals as law and norm for the others. This is the
period of \textit{authority}. Against authority rises the impulse toward freedom and the need
to comprehend. It overthrows authority --- but with it also the reason that had
involuntarily given authority its content and value. Only individual willfulness and
sensuality remain in the period of \textit{empty freedom}. With contempt one turns from the
darkness of the past, secure in the concepts won, which one makes the measure of everything
without having any notion of what it takes to comprehend anything. The character of this
time is ``Auf- und Ausklärung.'' It is plainly enough his own contemporaries that Fichte
means to characterize hereby. As the mark of the fourth period he gives \textit{the science
of reason,} true and many-sided understanding, with full consciousness of the greatness of
the task. But mere knowledge is not enough; the goal is reached only when there forms an
\textit{art of reason,} an art that aims at ordering all human relations according to the
science of reason. --- As Fichte himself points out, the third period stands in decided
opposition to all the others. It has a negative stamp, while positive powers (instinct and
authority, or science and art) rule in all the others. It is a period of transition --- and
Fichte thus really assumes three stages (like Kant and Schiller), a positive, a negative and
a new positive one, so that the new positive powers work their way forward through the
dissolution. Dissatisfied with modern times, especially with the critical and rationalist
tendency of the eighteenth century, he awaits a new age with a deeper need and better
sources for the understanding of life.

The great events of the time soon gave Fichte occasion to speak still more urgent words to
his age and his people. After the battle of Jena Berlin was occupied by the French, and
Fichte went to Königsberg, where for a time he taught at the university. When this city too
was occupied by the enemy, he stayed for a time in Copenhagen, where he came to stand close
to the brothers Ørsted. After the conclusion of the peace he returned to Berlin, which for
several years still had a French garrison. It was
% --- p. 145 ---
\opage{145}Prussia's time of rebirth, and Fichte belonged to the circle of excellent men who
by thought, word and deed worked for national restoration. In the winter of 1807---8 he
delivered in Berlin his famous \textit{Reden an die deutsche Nation.} The struggle with arms
is over for the present; now what matters is a struggle in the domain of characters and
ideas. Of its outer life the nation is no longer master. But the education of the new
generation is still in its power. This it must use to bring forth a generation that has the
capacity to set itself great purposes and to sacrifice itself for them. What matters is to
awaken the whole people, not merely a single class, and what matters first and foremost is
to make an independent development of character possible. The starting point must be sought
in an original need and drive that is found in every human being; for education cannot bring
anything into a human being for which no germ whatever is found in him. Every human being
needs esteem, to be esteemed by others at least, if he does not yet feel the need to esteem
himself. At its height this need gives birth to the capacity for the free and independent
formation of exemplars for one's action. Only such freely and independently formed
exemplars can set a living feeling in motion; what is taken in from outside does not act so.
The German people in particular will be receptive to such an education by virtue of its
sense and zeal for spiritual freedom and inner independence in faith and thought. It is,
after all, the people from which Luther's Reformation, Kant's philosophy and Pestalozzi's
pedagogy have come forth. --- It was Pestalozzi's fundamental thoughts that Fichte here
carried through on a larger scale. During his stay in Switzerland he had come to know the
great educator\textsuperscript{33}).

When the University of Berlin was founded (1810), Fichte became professor there. At the
outbreak of the War of Liberation he had plans (as already in 1806) of going along as an
orator. It did not happen. But he nevertheless became a victim of the war, being infected by
a hospital fever that his wife had contracted in nursing the wounded, and he died on
27 January 1814.
% --- p. 146 ---
\opage{146}

\subsubsection*{b.\quad The Wissenschaftslehre}

It is the ``Wissenschaftslehre'' in its original form that constitutes Fichte's most
important contribution to the philosophical discussion, and to it we shall here keep. ---

The task is to find the first fundamental proposition of all knowledge. If we turn our
attention to our ordinary consciousness, we find that we can think both of ourselves (the
ego) and of something that is not ourselves (the non-ego). But even when we think of the
non-ego, this happens only by virtue of a mental activity, an activity of the ego. The
non-ego exists for us only through an activity of the ego, through a ``positing.'' We feel
ourselves perhaps bound or compelled to represent to ourselves definite things to which we
ascribe reality: but this binding or compelling presupposes something that is bound or
compelled. Limitation presupposes something that is limited. The presupposition of all
knowledge is the free, infinite activity of mind which in each single representation
appears determinate or bound, but which is not bound absolutely to any single one. In our
immediate consciousness this original activity does not appear; there we find only its
single products. Of our willing and acting we never become immediately conscious. Limits and
results we notice, not that which is limited and which brings forth the results. The first
fundamental proposition therefore does not really concern a fact, but an act (not a
``Thatsache,'' but a ``Thathandlung''), as Descartes indicated by his Cogito, ergo sum and
Kant by his synthesis. To discover this original activity (the pure ego) reflection and
abstraction are needed, the capacity to hold fast the thought of an undivided and unlimited
activity for which the opposition between subject and object, action and result, does not
hold. A kind of higher intuition is required, an intellectual intuition, to grasp what does
not appear to immediate apprehension and yet cannot be formed into a concept either, since
every concept presupposes opposition. Mental energy and independence are needed to discover
this innermost active kernel of our being. Most people would sooner be able to regard
themselves as a piece of lava in the moon than
% --- p. 147 ---
% scan: „ud ledes“ (p. 147): one word; a gap in the word is no division
\opage{147}as pure mental activity. The assumption of a peculiar soul distinct from the
body, as a ``being'' or a ``substance'' by itself, such as spiritualist metaphysics sets it
up, is therefore wholly rejected by the ``Wissenschaftslehre.'' (In a later writing Fichte
declares this in a very plain way: ``The existence of a soul is absolutely denied. This
whole concept is rejected as a bad fiction. And this is not something inessential, but it
is a very essential criterion of our system. With the presupposition of such a soul one can
neither get into this system nor remain in it.'' \textit{Die Thatsachen des Bewusstseins.
% scan: „Bcwusstseins“ (p. 147; the e-book's reading, set by sense: scan-artefact rule)
} Stuttgart und Tübingen 1817. p. 105 f.).\textsuperscript{34})

But that first fundamental proposition of a mental activity as the source of everything in
consciousness does not explain that something other than the ego itself is posited in
consciousness. A second fundamental proposition must therefore be laid down, which cannot
be derived from the first. If the first is formulated thus: \textit{The ego posits itself,}
the second comes to run: \textit{The ego posits a non-ego.} This second fundamental
proposition is found, like the first, by reflecting on what is given in consciousness. Now
there arises a necessity of connecting the two propositions with each other, of bringing
about a synthesis by the connection of thesis and antithesis, and this becomes possible by
laying down as the third fundamental proposition: \textit{The ego posits a limited ego in
opposition to a limited non-ego.} By this synthesis we get back to immediate consciousness,
which can be explained neither by assuming that the ego is posited absolutely, nor by
assuming that the non-ego is posited absolutely, but only by the assumption of a mutual
limitation, a reciprocal action of ego and non-ego. --- The presupposition of this
limitation and reciprocal action is always the unity of consciousness. When the ego and the
non-ego are placed in opposition to each other, this very opposing presupposes that it is
the same consciousness that posits both members of the opposition.
