The method Fichte employs may be called the antithetical. First a proposition is laid down
that brings out an essential moment of the matter; then a proposition that brings out an
opposite moment (which is also contained in the matter, but cannot be derived from the
first); and both are then sought to be united. The
% --- p. 148 ---
\opage{148}necessity of seeking a union of the opposed propositions lies in the first
fundamental proposition itself, that everything in consciousness is due to an indivisible
mental activity; for from this it follows that the relation of opposition cannot be
fundamental. However limited our consciousness (the finite, empirical ego) may be, the pure
ego nevertheless acts in it as the ultimate source not only of all its acting, but also of
all its suffering.

We do not follow Fichte in his continued use of this method, by which every synthesis
always appears again as thesis, in order by combination with a new antithesis to lead to a
new synthesis. The method has its great value, but in the particulars became arbitrary and
unfruitful in Fichte's hands, because its application demands a more detailed analysis of
experience, here, that is, a fuller psychology, than was at his disposal. What he wants to
achieve is a derivation of the forms and fundamental propositions that in Kant were still
laid down purely schematically. The principle of identity he finds contained in the first
fundamental proposition: the proposition A = A holds originally of the ego in its pure,
self-identical, constant activity. The form of time comes forth when various acts of the ego
(positing of ego, positing of non-ego) are to be possible in such a way that they are
dependent on one another in a definite order. The form of space comes forth when various
determinations in the non-ego are to be posited each by itself and yet without interruption
and without being dependent on one another in a definite order of time. The causal principle
is contained in the third fundamental proposition, which demands mutual limitation, i.e.
reciprocal action of ego and non-ego. When the various determinations of the non-ego are
also conceived as mutually dependent on one another (as in natural science), the concept of
action has been involuntarily transferred from the ego, whose nature it expresses, to the
non-ego. --- Only the general forms of empirical consciousness, not the special, individual
content of experience, can and will Fichte deduce\textsuperscript{35}).

In the whole world-picture that forms itself for ordinary consciousness, we have then,
according to Fichte, the product of an involuntary activity unconscious to ourselves. As we
project the sense qualities, so we project time, space, logical identity, causality.
% --- p. 149 ---
\opage{149}From this it does not follow that our world-picture is an illusion. The concept of
illusion can be applied only as the opposite of reality, but this opposition falls away
here, or rather: the true reality is in the activity which, without our noticing it, brings
forth the world-picture in our consciousness, and this activity is a \textit{necessary,
lawful} activity. Only philosophical reflection, which must be well distinguished from
ordinary, practical consciousness, discovers that deep-lying power at work in all finite
egos, and thereby understands at the same time how the same world-picture forms itself for
all egos. This is Fichte's solution of the problem of knowledge. ---

Both in order to understand Fichte's method and his result, one must hold firmly that the
second fundamental proposition cannot be derived from the first. In this his antithetical
method differs from Hegel's so-called dialectical method. And from this there follows too a
limitation of purely theoretical philosophy, on which Fichte himself lays the very greatest
weight, and which is in the highest degree characteristic of his system. For the question
then arises: why does the ego (the pure ego) produce or posit a non-ego within itself? why
is the pure, identical activity broken? why does the straight line of the original activity
become a curve? Fichte answers that to this question no answer can be given theoretically.
To explain that breaking (Anstoss) or bending one would have to assume a force besides the
absolute force, and that is a self-contradiction. Only from our moral consciousness, which
sets striving and labor, struggle to attain great purposes, as the highest, do we win an
understanding. For labor presupposes limits, struggle presupposes resistance. That a world
of non-egos, of objects, is set before us has, then, the ethical significance that labor and
struggle become possible. Nature is the material for our duty. Object means a standing-against,
and a standing-against means resistance. Without a system of limits no ethics. Our highest goal
is the freedom and independence that is won by combating all hindrances to our ego. --- The
practical philosophy thus contains the key to the theoretical.

Both the practical and the theoretical philosophy presuppose
% --- p. 150 ---
\opage{150}the first fundamental proposition. The weight that Fichte, in his setting up of
this fundamental proposition, lays on the original activity as the first element in our
being becomes of special significance for ethics. There is an original need of action for
action's own sake, apart from outer occasions and tasks. Both in conscience and in natural
impulse this need makes itself known. Kant's categorical imperative, which he himself could
not explain, becomes intelligible through this original need of activity at any price, and
no less is the unruliness of the sensuous drives understood by it. The single things or
objects in nature stand for us from the first only as means or limits for the satisfaction
of our lower or higher drives. Our conception of the world is from the first practical.
``The whole system of our representations,'' says Fichte in the ``Wissenschaftslehre''
(2. Aufl. p. 288), ``depends on our need and our will.''

\subsubsection*{c.\quad Ethics}

When the original craving and activity is attached to definite objects, according to the
peculiar character of each single individual, it appears as natural impulse and aims at
enjoyment. Through enjoyment I become dependent on the objects. But by virtue of the infinite
in that craving and activity, which is the expression of my independence over against
everything given, all objects, there can develop in me a consciousness, a reflection, that
shows me other possibilities besides what is immediately given. On this my freedom rests. It
is one and the same primal impulse that expresses itself both in natural impulse and in the
reflection and impulse toward freedom that can release me from every sensuous relation of
dependence. Natural impulse and the impulse toward freedom need not stand in conflict with
each other either: for the satisfaction of the single natural want can take place in such a
way that it becomes precisely a means to greater freedom and independence. Thereby the
ethical law is given: \textit{each single action shall lie in a series that leads me to
complete spiritual freedom.} Thereby the infinite ego is realized in the world of
experience. The limits posited are overcome. It is an infinite goal, but a constant
approximation is possible,
% --- p. 151 ---
\opage{151}in that every purpose attained is made a new starting point. --- When there is
harmony between the two forms in which the primal impulse expresses itself (natural impulse
and the impulse toward freedom), we have a feeling of self-esteem, a feeling of pleasure that
is very different from sensuous enjoyment and would preferably not be called pleasure at all.
In the opposite case we have a feeling of self-contempt. The capacity for having such
feelings is called conscience. Only the action that springs from conscience is moral. To act
on authority is unconscionable. The first commandment is: \textit{You shall act according to
the conviction of your duty!} And this conviction is won by comparing the action
contemplated not merely with the conception I have of it at the moment, but with every
conception I could think of getting of it, thus by trying whether I could own the action in
all eternity. --- Moral evil springs from inertia, dependence, --- inertia toward reflection,
toward raising oneself above what is momentarily given, reluctance to go beyond the present
state, a tendency to stay in the given track. Inertia then leads in turn to cowardice and
falsehood, slavery being preferred to toil, and seeming being used as a cover for what one
will not defend in open struggle. --- But how is it possible that the impulse toward freedom
can be awakened where it does not stir? Man cannot, after all, release his own power! The
answer to this lies in the doctrine of an instinct of reason that Fichte later developed in
``Grundzüge des gegenwärtigen Zeitalters,'' but which is already found in the
``Sittenlehre.'' In some individuals the original spiritual need can be so strong that in a
way inexplicable to themselves and others it raises them above what is sensuously given.
They have a kind of ``Genie zur Tugend.'' They then act as awakening exemplars for the
others. At this point lies, for Fichte, the explanation of the rise of positive religions.
Quite naturally, such individuals endowed with deeper spiritual power, and likewise those
who are influenced by their personality, come to regard what has developed in them and goes
out from them as a miracle. Out of their empirical ego it certainly cannot be explained. The
assumption of such a miracle has its significance when it serves as a means of awakening the
% --- p. 152 ---
\opage{152}slumbering attention and energy. It is thus of great and decisive significance
that man lives together with other human beings. Only among human beings is he a human
being. And in reality the many individuals have only a single goal: the realization of the
idea of the ego. My personality is not, for me, the highest, ethically regarded. But it is
the only means by which \textit{I} can work for the highest. My goal is reached also when
others act ethically. When each follows his conviction, all will work to develop the highest
and most inward independence and to realize reason in a society of free beings. What in
religious language is called the communion of saints means the presentation of the pure ego
in the whole of rational beings. Over against this infinite goal the individual is a mere
means and instrument and of vanishing significance. What matters for the individual is to
annihilate his individuality --- not in mystical absorption, but in active doing for the
eternal goal. --- In his later writings Fichte expresses himself still more severely about
this vanishing significance of the individual personality, in strange contradiction with the
weight he otherwise lays on individuality\textsuperscript{36}). At last, then, individuality
becomes for him what ought not to be, a limitation that is to be abolished, a negation that
is taken back. The pure ego crushes the empirical one. It is a nemesis that here overtakes
Fichte. He has sought an absolute foundation for his ethics by putting it in inner connection
with his speculation, but precisely thereby comes at last to abolish his ethics. Yet on his
way, before he plunges into this speculative abyss, he has found ethical thoughts of lasting
value. ---

Of Fichte's special ethics his conception of church and state is to be mentioned. ---
The church he conceives as an association of individuals for the awakening and
strengthening of ethical conviction. The common foundation for this is symbols, figurative
forms in which the highest thoughts can influence all, the uneducated as well as the
educated. Only through such symbols does general and mutual spiritual influence become
possible. For as regards the highest thoughts themselves in their pure, scientific form, it
will be impossible to bring about general understanding and agreement.
% --- p. 153 ---
\opage{153}The symbol is generally accessible through its figurative form and at the same time
indeterminate in its interpretation. On this its value rests. Even if the ethical teacher of
the people does not ascribe literal truth to the symbol, he will nevertheless be able to use
it when he does so with enthusiasm and with a living wish to act upon the spiritual life of
others\textsuperscript{37}). But the spirit of Protestantism demands that all symbols be
developed into clearer and more perfect forms. Every symbol (the representations of a
personal God and of a personal immortality too, not merely the representations of the
positive religions) is only a makeshift symbol. What furnishes the measure for the symbols is
the degree to which they are able to make the thought of a higher, ethical world-order plain
and living. --- Just as every ecclesiastical symbol is a makeshift symbol, so every given
state is only a makeshift state. The state has to do only with the outer being of man, and
according to Fichte a sharp distinction is to be made between the doctrine of right and
ethics. The doctrine of right rests on the principle that whoever (no matter for what reason)
will live together with others must restrict his freedom out of regard for the freedom of
others. The relation of right rests on the mutual recognition of this. The state's only
task is to maintain the relation of right, and where necessary it compels the individual to
recognize the freedom of others (as regards body, property and self-preservation). But Fichte
does not find the state imperfect merely so long as this outer security is not brought
about. He maintains (and in this he plainly goes beyond the concept of a mere state of law or
police state) that the state can demand that property be recognized by all only when it
strives to bring it about that all come to possess property. Everyone ought to be able to
live by his labor. There ought to be neither needy nor idlers in the state. Charity is only a
wretched and ambiguous expedient. Already in his ``Naturrecht'' and his ``Sittenlehre'' he
hints at thoughts in the direction of what has since been called socialism. In
\textit{Geschlossener Handelsstaat} (1800) he wants world trade handed over to the state, so
that the inner economic development within each single nation can proceed more independently
and naturally. He does not fear that the intercourse between the nations will suffer by this;
it is science, not
% --- p. 154 ---
\opage{154}trade, that carries this intercourse, insofar as it has real value. Fichte is, as
has rightly been said (see GUSTAV SCHMOLLER's study of Fichte in ``Jahrbücher for
Nationalökonomie und Statistik.'' 1865), the first German social writer. His political
theory, despite his sharp distinction between right and morality, nevertheless proves in the
end to be borne by ethical points of view. In his expositions of the doctrine of right and
of the state from his later years he lays weight on this, that the state, which is to educate
from compulsion and through compulsion to freedom, cannot reach this goal without working to
procure for all individuals property, leisure and the means of higher culture. ---

\subsection*{2.\quad Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling}

\subsubsection*{a.\quad The Period of the Philosophy of Nature}

Schelling is the classic philosopher of Romanticism. Fichte still stands close to the critical
philosophy and distinguishes carefully between consciousness and its content; he can be called
a Romantic on account of the craving for the boundless that in him replaces Kant's thought of
continual progress. But in Schelling there is the genuinely Romantic need to revel in a content
that is taken in more by intuiting and symbolism than by testing thought. Thus he revels first in
nature and art, later in religion. With this need to revel it was no wonder that, although he
began as Fichte's disciple and collaborator, he soon found Fichte's ego too meager. His
intellectual tendency went toward great, symbolic intuitions in which the oppositions of things
could at once bring each other out and be seen in their connection. Beholding was for him the
highest, and when in his speculation he laid weight on oppositions, it was in order to give his
thought-images fullness and relief. Fichte, on the other hand, brought out the oppositions because
they were the condition of work, struggle and development. Fichte's philosophy was really ethics
through and through; Schelling did not concern himself with ethics at all.

Schelling was born at Leonberg in Würtemberg on January 27,
% --- p. 155 ---
\opage{155}1775. Already at the age of fifteen he came as a student to Tübingen, and here, like the rest
of the student youth, he was strongly taken up with the French Revolution; he was supposed to be
the author of a German translation of the Marseillaise, which led Duke Karl, known also from the
story of Schiller's youth, to proceed harshly against the young student. His first studies were
theological; he was interested in mythology and the historical interpretation of the Bible. Soon,
however, he threw himself into philosophical studies, immersing himself in Kant, Fichte and
Spinoza. In various treatises from the years 1794 and 95 he developed Fichte's
``Wissenschaftslehre'' further. A stay in Leipzig as tutor to two young noblemen gave him the
opportunity for studies in natural science, and here he wrote his first work in the philosophy of
nature: \textit{Ideen zur einer Philosophien der Natur} (1797). From the first he conceived his
philosophy of nature as a supplement to the ``Wissenschaftslehre''; later it led him to set
himself in opposition to it, and a very sharp polemical relation thereby arose between the two
former friends. From 1798 he worked as professor at Jena, whither the influence of Goethe,
Schiller and Fichte had called him. Here in Jena the Romantic school was really constituted. The
brothers Schlegel with their gifted wives, Novalis, Tieck, Steffens and others met here with
Schelling, and in this ``republic of despots'' there was an overflowing of poetic, religious,
philosophical and scientific ideas, now in conflict, now in accord. Friedrich Schlegel writes to
Schleiermacher: ``Hier gehts ziemlich bunt und störend durcheinander --- Religion und Holberg,
Galvanismus und Poesie''. And Dorothea Schlegel gives a similar description: ``Es geht so recht
kunterbunt her mit Witz und Philosophie und Kunstgesprächen und Herunterreissen''\textsuperscript{38}).
For the time being it was at this period the enthusiasm for nature and art that was strongest in
Schelling; the religious enthusiasm of Novalis and Tieck even awakened in him, by way of
opposition, an antireligious enthusiasm, which found expression in an ``Epicurean confession of
faith'' in poetic form, which was to have been printed in the Schlegels' ``Athenäum'' but was held
back on Goethe's advice. Schelling later had part of it printed in his journal for
% --- p. 156 ---
\opage{156}speculative physics; it is now available in full in ``Aus Schellings Leben''. Leipsig
1869. I. p. 282 ff. The following lines characterize Schelling's philosophy of nature --- also in
the sense that it looks better in verse than in prose.

Darum, ist eine Religion die rechte,

Müsst sie in Stein und Moosgeflechte,

In Blumen, Metallen und allen Dingen

So zu Luft und Licht sich dringen,

In allen Höhen und Tiefen

Sich offenbaren in Hieroglyfen . . . .

Hinauf zu des Gedankens Jugendkraft,

Wodurch Natur verjüngt sich wiederschafft,

Ist \textit{eine} Kraft, ein Pulsschlag nur, \textit{ein} Leben

Ein Wechselspiel von Hemmen und von Streben.

Besides ``Ideen'', there must be named as expositions of the ``philosophy of nature''
\textit{Erster Entwurf eines Systems der Naturphilosophie} (1799) and \textit{Einleitung zu
seinem Entwurf eines Systems der Naturphilosophie, oder: Ueber den Begriff der spekulativen
Physik} (1799). In \textit{System des transscendentalen Idealismus} (1800) he presents ``the
philosophy of nature in its connection with the Wissenschaftslehre'' and proclaims artistic
intuition as the only organ that makes possible the apprehension of spirit and nature, subject and
object, in their inner unity, the only standpoint where the oppositions of life, particularly the
opposition between theory and practice, fall away. In the year 1801 he began an abstract
systematic exposition of his doctrine \textit{(Darstellung meines Systems} in vol. 2 of
``Zeitschrift für spekulative Physik''), but did not complete it. In \textit{Methode des
akademischen Studiums} (1803), on the other hand, we have in a freer form an encyclopedic
exposition of Schelling's philosophical ideas as they took shape at the close of his first period.
A new turn, and soon after a remarkable halt in his production, set in with his departure from
Jena (1803). But before we follow him into the second great period of his thought, that of the
philosophy of religion, we must give an exposition and characterization of the ``philosophy of
nature''. ---

It was from the first in the name of idealism itself that Schelling
% --- p. 157 ---
\opage{157}demanded a more positive recognition of nature than Fichte's system, for which nature was only
a limit or a means, could afford. The very secrets of the spiritual world can be solved only when
we learn to understand nature, so that it is no longer an alien power to us. In Fichte nature is
only object; but the object can be understood only if in its essence it is of like kind with the
subject. Nature is comprehensible only if it bears the stamp of spirit. And if the forces that
work in spirit can already be found in nature, then it can be understood how spirit develops out
of nature. Nature then stands as the Odyssey of spirit, as its striving to get back to itself and
its inwardness from the form of externality in which it is placed in nature. The way from nature to
spirit must be just as possible as the way from spirit to nature (in ``Kritik der reinen Vernunft''
and in ``Wissenschaftslehre'').

Modern natural science had sought to make everything in nature into motion, to explain everything
by the interaction of material parts. If this explanation exhausts the essence of nature, then
either everything ideal must be denied, or else one must assume that it comes into nature from
outside. But to explain what is purposive in nature by the influence of a divine understanding,
that is, says Schelling (Ideen. 2. Ausg. p. 63), not to philosophize but to indulge in pious
considerations. And besides, the chief philosophical problem remains: namely \textit{how we know}
the whole system of causes and effects that makes up nature, --- how this system \textit{comes to
be for us.} The natural scientist lives in nature as an immediately given reality; but the
philosopher of nature asks how it can be given to us. (Cf. Ideen. 2. Ausg. p. 4; 27 f.). The same
problem appears as the question of the origin of the faculty of sense (sensibility) in nature.
How can the organism become its own object? (Erster Entwurf. p. 174)\textsuperscript{39}).

No one will be able to deny that a real problem lies here, and that it is clearly posed, both from
the standpoint of idealist philosophy and from that of real science. There must --- if the
spiritual side of existence is to be comprehensible --- be other forces at work and other
properties to be found in nature than
% --- p. 158 ---
\opage{158}those that mechanical natural science knows and has expressed in its laws. Schelling's
solution, now, is that the same duality of a force going out into the infinite and a limiting
force, which Fichte has demonstrated in consciousness, must be found in the whole of nature. Since
the life of consciousness rests on opposition (duplicity), the whole of nature, out of which the
life of consciousness develops, must also present opposed forces, only in lower potencies, or, to
recall Leibniz (see: System des transscendentalen Idealismus. p. 190), all forces in nature are
representing forces of different degree. Matter is slumbering spirit, spirit in equilibrium, and
spirit is matter in development. But Schelling does not stop at such a general principle or
postulate. He believes he can demonstrate in detail the steps by which nature rises to spirit. He
starts from the spiritual forces and thinks of them as at work in nature in lower ``potencies''.
In a treatise \textit{Ueber den wahren Begriff der Naturphilosophie} (Sämmtl. Werke. I, 4. p. 84
f.) he has clearly stated his method: ``To see the objective in its first coming-to-be is possible
only by \textit{depotentiating} the object of all philosophizing, which in the higher potency is =
ego, and then constructing from the beginning with this object reduced to the first potency.'' One
is thus to infer from the higher degrees to the lower. Schelling does not investigate whether this
is possible (since one and the same object can of course have other forms of state in its lower
degrees than in its higher). His ``construction'' is therefore in reality also a
poetic-symbolic interpretation, by which the forces and forms of nature are conceived as stepwise
approximations to the life of consciousness. Like all metaphysical idealism he builds on analogy,
but he has such great confidence in it that on its basis he believes he can build up a
``speculative physics'', which is not merely to show us the results of natural science in a new
light, but even in the end to take the place of natural science. Nature is understood only ``from
within'', by being seen as visible spirit. By adopting a purely external and empirical point of
view Boyle and Newton have corrupted physics, just as Bacon corrupted philosophy! Mathematical
astronomy does not, after all, teach us to know the real essence of the planetary motions! The
innermost essence of natural phenomena is understood,
% --- p. 159 ---
\opage{159}namely, according to Schelling, not by explaining the one with the help of the other, but by
their all springing from a common ground of which they are, each in its own way, symbolic
expressions; it is in this that the unity of nature consists. Thus the three dimensions of space
express the inner relations within the Absolute, namely unity, opposition and the combination of
both; the circular motion of the heavenly bodies is a symbol of the All, which spreads out in all
directions but always returns to itself; in the causal relation there appears, in an externally
different way, what in the Absolute is in infinite unity, etc. (Schelling's dialogue
\textit{Bruno} 1802). The empirical natural scientist does not see the symbolic significance of
natural phenomena; he explains the external symbol and thinks he has thereby explained everything.
\textit{(Methode des akad. Studiums.} Vorlesung XI: Ueber die Naturwissenschaft im Allgemeinen).

The Romantic element in Schelling's philosophy of nature lies not in the problem as he originally
poses it to himself, but in the boldness with which he puts his symbolic interpretation of nature in
place of science's laborious attempt to explain nature by the mutual connection of the individual
phenomena. He overlooks that the unity of nature can be established scientifically only through
this connection, which he scorns. On this point lies the decisive difference between Schelling's
philosophy of nature and such attempts of thought as those of Spinoza and Leibniz, which precisely
took the real connection as their foundation. Not even as confirmation by experience does Schelling
think he needs the empirical: since speculative construction presents ``the inner type of all
things, which by virtue of the common origin must be one'', it is sufficient to itself and can
penetrate into regions from which experience is excluded by insurmountable limits!

Let us look a little in detail at Schelling's attempt to demonstrate spirit in nature. --- The
various phenomena and forces are to be shown to be ascending potencies. And at the same time on
every step, within every potency, there is to be shown a relation of opposition (or of duplicity,
or of polarity), as a lower degree of the relation of opposition that appears in consciousness
between subject and object (ego and non-ego). The concepts \textit{potency}
% --- p. 160 ---
\opage{160}and \textit{polarity} are the fundamental concepts of Schelling's philosophy of nature. With
their help he constructs the scheme in which the various natural phenomena get their place. He
arranges them so that there is (in every case symbolically) an ascent to higher steps (potencies)
and on each step a new opposition (polarity) in analogy with the oppositions on the lower steps.
The qualitative differences here give way to differences in degree and in form. It is interesting
to see that Schelling's Romantic attempt to give a speculative natural philosophy, just as much as
exact natural science, resolves all qualitative differences into quantitative ones. Schelling has
himself drawn attention to this likeness between the ``philosophy of nature'' and atomism, and on
account of it wants to call his doctrine dynamic atomism. The difference is that while mechanical
atomism explains everything by a relation between material parts, the ``philosophy of nature''
explains everything by a relation between forces. But in the clarity and rigor with which the
general thought is applied, Schelling stands far behind atomism. The general scheme he has
constructed for himself with the help of the concepts of potency and polarity is filled in in a
highly arbitrary manner, often by a mere play with words, so that the name ``philosophy of
nature'' has rightly acquired an ill sound in scientific ears. Yet it is of historical interest to
get a survey of Schelling's symbolism of nature.

In the absolute principle \textit{(Urgrunden),} which lies at the ground of everything, there is
absolute unity between subject and object. At no point in existence is this unity abolished; but
now the one, now the other pole can have the preponderance: on this quantitatively different
relation between the poles rests the difference between the various potencies. In \textit{nature}
the objective, in \textit{spirit} the subjective pole has the preponderance. If the Absolute can be
represented by A = B (where A means subject, B object), nature can be represented by A = B+, spirit
by A+ = B (where the plus sign above denotes the predominant pole). Within nature three potencies
are distinguished. The first appears in the elementary, attracting and repelling forces that hold
the structure of the world together; \textit{gravity} is the characteristic
% --- p. 161 ---
\opage{161}expression of this first potency. In \textit{light,} as well as in magnetism, electricity and
chemical process --- the second potency ---, there shows itself a combination of what has been
isolated by the separating forces, which is already like an intimation of what the process of
knowledge is in the spiritual domain. In \textit{organic life ---} the third potency --- there
appears a world in miniature, a system of processes that are both ends and means for one another
mutually, and in whose capacity for sensation (sensibility) spirit in nature at last breaks through
its limits. The potencies of \textit{spirit} appear in the three activities: \textit{cognition,
action} and \textit{art.} In artistic intuition Schelling found the highest form of the life of
the spirit when he wrote his ``System des transscendentalen Idealismus''. ``Art is at once
philosophy's only true and eternal organ and its document, which ever anew attests what
philosophy is unable to present in the external, namely the unconscious in acting and producing
and its original identity with the conscious. Art is the highest for the philosopher, because it
as it were opens to him the holy of holies, where what is separated in nature and history, and
what in life and action as well as in thinking is eternally split apart, burns as in one flame,
in eternal, original union. The intuition which the philosopher forms of nature in an artificial
way is for art the original and natural one.'' (System. p. 475). --- It is consistent that a
philosopher who builds his system with the help of poetic symbolism ends by proclaiming art the
highest. For him, as for Novalis, everything is really poetry; the process of nature is an
unconscious poetry that breaks forth with consciousness in and for man.

It was not Schelling's meaning that nature was literally the prehistory of spirit. His philosophy
of nature differs from the modern doctrine of evolution not only in disdaining the mechanical
connection but also --- which for that matter is bound up with it --- in denying a
\textit{factual} transition from one ``potency'' to the other. The one step does not arise
\textit{out of} the other, but the producing activity itself of nature or of the Absolute, which
appears in experience not itself but only in its products, comes to full unfolding only through
a series of
% --- p. 162 ---
\opage{162}forms. Each one of these forms springs from the infinite producing itself, not from other
forms. There is in the Absolute an eternal unity of subject and object, which does not need to
develop through the potencies of nature and spirit, which are only its different reflections in
the medium of experience. This Schellingian standpoint, which was in essentials also Goethe's, was
dominant among many eminent natural scientists, who saw the kinship of the forms of nature but
could not reconcile themselves to the thought of a real descent. For them the kinship consisted in
the interior of nature, in the creative imagination of the Deity, or however they expressed it,
not between the actual, existing groups of natural beings themselves. --- In essentials such a
conception was also held by Schelling's friend and disciple, \textit{Henrik Steffens;} although he
lays more stress on the individual and the historical, he did not assume a \textit{real}
development in nature by which the later forms should have come into being from the earlier. He
expressly declares himself against ``a gradual transition from one form to the other'', although
he assumes ``one formative force, which goes connecting through all shapes''. \textit{(Indledning
til filosofiske Forelæsninger.} Copenhagen 1803. p. 81 f.). --- On the other hand \textit{Oken,}
and the Danish investigators \textit{Olufsen} and\textit{ F. C. Sibbern} assumed a \textit{real}
development, a development of the forms in time.

\subsubsection*{b.\quad The Problem of the Philosophy of Religion}

There came about, as already mentioned, a break and soon after a halt at a certain point of
Schelling's development. He had come forward as a producer very early; his first philosophical
work is from his nineteenth year. The period of Romanticism offers not a few examples of such
early-ripe and early-arrested productive power. In Schelling the break and the halt were connected
partly with the fact that the path he had struck out on could not lead him further than he had
come once he had given utterance to his bold ideas, partly with the fact that a new problem
appeared before him, and partly, finally, also with purely personal circumstances.
% --- p. 163 ---
\opage{163}

The new problem that appeared before him was the religious one. As we have seen, Novalis's
religious enthusiasm called forth an opposite mood in Schelling. In the Jena period he was too
taken up with nature and art for the more practical problems to arise in him. In a letter from the
beginning of the year 1806 he says: ``During my retirement in Jena I was less reminded of life,
but constantly and powerfully of nature, to which almost all my inquiry was confined. Since then I
have learned to see that religion, public faith, the life of the state is the point around which
everything moves.'' (Aus Schellings Leben. II. p. 78). It was one of his disciples,
\textit{Eschenmayer,} who brought him to occupy himself with the religious problem. Eschenmayer
maintained in an interesting little work \textit{(Die Philosophie in ihrem Uebergang zur
Nichtphilosophie,} Erlangen 1803) that religion was a sphere that lay higher than philosophy. For
even if philosophy knows how to overcome all oppositions and to demonstrate the Absolute as the
highest unity, there remains the question how then the individual oppositions, the various
potencies, arise, and that is answered only in faith in a creating God. Philosophy is unable to
ground the existence of a finite world split into oppositions, a world of differences and
potencies, different from the absolute unity in which speculation sees the highest. Schelling
acknowledged that differentiation contained a great problem, but he held fast that this problem
must be capable of solution within philosophy. Philosophy must be extended; but there was no reason
to conceive religion and philosophy as two wholly different things. He contends that it is indeed
impossible to derive difference from identity, plurality from unity: but precisely for that reason
he has, after all, maintained in his philosophy that opposition (difference, plurality) is a
principle just as original as unity. A \textit{living} unity is one that has the oppositions not
outside itself but within itself, however strong a tension there may be between them. In the work
\textit{Philosophie und Religion} (1804), which he wrote after having moved from Jena to Würzburg,
he acknowledges that in nature and history forces are stirring that point to a tension so strong
that it cannot be derived from the very idea of the
% --- p. 164 ---
\opage{164}absolute unity, a tension that is to be brought into harmony through the various steps of nature
and history. Earlier he had called nature the Odyssey of spirit; now he uses this expression of
history as well. The untamed and irrational in nature and history bears witness to a falling away
from the eternal idea, to a disharmony that has come in and is to be reconciled. But he maintains
against Eschenmayer, as a few years later in a polemic against Fichte, that such opposition and
strife is necessary in order that life and harmony may come to be. Without opposition no life.
These thoughts were nourished in Schelling, especially after he had settled in Munich, by the
study of the old mystics, first and foremost Jacob Böhme, who at this time in general enjoyed a
renaissance; St. Martin in France and Franz Baader in Germany renewed his line of thought. In the
most significant and brilliant work of Schelling's period of the philosophy of religion:
\textit{Philosophische Untersuchungen über das Wesen der menschlichen Freiheit und die damit
zusammenhängenden Gegenstände} (1809), Schelling seeks to show that only if one assumes, as he has
done in his philosophy, an original opposition in the Absolute, in the essence of the Deity, a
dark, irrational ground that is clarified and harmonized by the very development of the life of
the divine being, only then is one justified in conceiving God as a personal being. His philosophy
of nature, with its potencies ascending step by step, he here gives a religious significance.
Personality does not develop except through opposition to and on the basis of a natural
foundation, through strife with resisting forces. Finite beings have this opposition, this basis,
\textit{outside themselves.} If the infinite being is to be personality, it must have the relation
of opposition \textit{within itself:} there must be in God something that in itself is not God
but can become so. Theism, says Schelling in a polemic against Jacobi, can be built up on the
ground of naturalism; but from a pure theism, from rationalism's ``enlightened God'' or from the
natureless God of ordinary theology, it is impossible to ground the existence of nature.
\textit{Given} oppositions can be overcome --- and in this life consists; but from a pure unity
given oppositions cannot be explained. In the original difference Schelling sees --- still in
Böhme's footsteps --- the germ of
% --- p. 165 ---
% print: „Karakter, Det“ (p. 165) (misprint)
\opage{165}evil. By following the deep need for egoism, for detached self-assertion, man follows a will
that goes back to the first ground of things. All evil consists in a striving back to the chaos out
of which the order of nature has proceeded. And by this it is understood that nature always shows
us a residue that is impenetrable to the understanding and cannot be brought under definite laws;
it is
the old chaos, which has not wholly vanished. But without chaos, without strife and dissolution, no
real unity; without discord love does not become manifest. Had God been to avert evil, he would
have had to abolish his own personality: in order that evil should not be, God himself would have
to not be! ---

Schelling's remarkable work, a mixture of profundity and fantasizing, has philosophical interest
in that it concedes something irrational, that is, something impenetrable to the thinking that
Schelling knew and knew how to practice, and to that extent establishes that speculative
philosophy cannot reach its goal but must concede to the critical philosophy that knowledge has
limits. To that extent it heralds a reaction against speculation and has a certain realistic
character. It is of interest besides in that it opens a new discussion of the concept of God and
investigates the conditions under which an absolute and infinite being can be conceived as
personality. In accordance with Böhme's proposition: without opposition no consciousness, an
opposition \textit{within} God's essence is then postulated as the condition for his being
conceivable as personality. On this thought is built \textit{philosophical theism,} as it was
later developed, on the basis of Schelling's resumption of Böhme's ideas, by eminent thinkers such
as C. H. WEISSE (1801---1866) (in his work \textit{Das philosophische Problem der Gegenwart.} 1842,
and later in his \textit{Philosophische Dogmatik.} 1855---62) and HERMANN LOTZE. --- The difficulty
for philosophical theism consists in this, that when the opposition whose overcoming is to be the
condition of God's personality is an inner one, lies in God's own essence, it cannot be quite in
earnest. The struggle then becomes only a game, a divine jest. The personal life that we know, and
of which alone we can form a concept, must struggle with \textit{external}
% --- p. 166 ---
% print: „Henseenee“ (p. 166) (misprint)
\opage{166}limits; a personal life whose inner forces are not constantly partly nourished, partly checked
by external circumstances is unthinkable for us. As regards Schelling in particular, it was not
even his meaning that a \textit{successive} process should take place in the Deity; the strife is
not to precede the peace; there is to be in God nothing first and nothing last, but an eternal
circulation. By this the whole only becomes really incomprehensible; every attempt to think such an
eternal circulation ends in dizziness. Already Arnauld, in his criticism of Descartes's doctrine of
God as cause of himself (see the first volume of the present work p. 237), demonstrated the
self-contradiction therein. Weisse, accordingly, also saw clearly that there could be meaning in
the whole thought only if one assumed a real, historical development of God's essence in time. But
that conflicts with the concept of God as the absolute being, and the difficulty for philosophical
theism is thus not made any
less\textsuperscript{40}). ---

We have seen the break in Schelling's philosophical producing. Soon after comes the halt. At the
end of the treatise of 1809 he promises an exposition of the philosophy of spirit on the foundation
he had now gained. But despite various starts and announcements, even rather noisy announcements,
the fulfillment of this promise failed to come. His productivity was checked. Perhaps it was
connected with the loss of his brilliant wife that a hypochondriac mood took hold of him. But in
any case Hegel's appearance and victorious advance in the philosophical domain also contributed
much to holding Schelling back. In quiet he worked out his philosophy of religion in lectures at
Erlangen and Munich, and what came from him publicly was almost nothing but bitter sallies against
the victorious rival in Berlin. When, after Hegel's death, the so-called left wing of his school,
with Strauss and Feuerbach at its head, drew radical consequences from his doctrine in religious
respects, Schelling let himself be called to Berlin (1841) by the Romantic King Friedrich Wilhelm
IV as a kind of philosophical rescuer. Now the publication of the thoughts that had occupied him so
long was expected. But his appearance in Berlin was a fiasco. His later doctrine came out in print
only after his death, which occurred in 1854.
% --- p. 167 ---
\opage{167}It consists of a \textit{Philosophie der Mythologie} and a \textit{Philosophie der Offenbarung}
and aims to show how that Odyssey of spirit, that progressive reconciliation and harmonizing of the
restless and conflicting forces, takes place through the development of religious consciousness.
One and the same process extends through the mythologies into Christianity and through the
development of Christianity to free religion. In detail this exposition is of no
interest\textsuperscript{41}); Schelling deals quite as arbitrarily with the facts of the science
of religion as in his youth with the facts of natural science, and his ideas now in his later days
lack the titanic boldness and Romantic mood that distinguished so many of the thoughts of his
youth.

\subsection*{3.\quad Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel}

\subsubsection*{a.\quad Characterization and Biography}

Goethe, in a conversation with Eckermann (Feb. 17, 1831), characterized the relation between the
first and the second part of Faust thus: ``The first part is almost entirely subjective;
everything proceeds from a more entangled, more passionate individual. In the second part there
is almost nothing subjective; there appears here a higher, broader, brighter, more passionless
world''. German philosophy in its development from Kant on through the various systems offers a
parallel to the difference Goethe found between the two parts of his great work. It begins in
Kant and Fichte, and is continued in part in Schelling, with subjective inquiry and craving, with a
sharp distinction between ideal and reality. And it closes in Hegel's system with a reconciliation
with reality through immersion in its various regions, what was there divined and sought as a
distant ideal being now supposed to have been found as the very kernel of things. What Goethe
wanted to express in the second part of Faust, the reconciliation with reality won through
historical experience and faithful work, was the same as what Hegel wanted to express in his
system in opposition to the critical philosophy and to Romanticism. And the parallel fits also in
% --- p. 168 ---
\opage{168}another respect, in that transitions and details are often no less difficult to understand in
Hegel's system than in the second part of Faust.

What first strikes the reader of Hegel's writings is the abstract character of his developments
and the many technical expressions with which he operates. It is this that especially deters
present-day readers. But for one who is able to penetrate this shell there is another trait of
character that comes most to stand in the foreground, and that must stand in the foreground when
Hegel's physiognomy as a thinker is to be rendered with historical justice. It is the great
interest in the content of the life of the spirit in all forms and at all stages. Hegel was,
despite his speculative method and his abstract form of exposition, nevertheless a realistic
nature. He had a lively need to immerse himself in the objective powers of life. His thinking
sought to be a re-thinking, a translation of the fullness of life into the form of thought. In
order that the rich content might become the property of thought, it had to be formed into a
circle of thoughts in which the individual links hung together just as intimately as the
individual moments of existence do, so that no single one of these can be touched without the
whole circle trembling. With the help of his dialectical method Hegel believed he could present
such a circle of thought. It has gone so tragically for him here that precisely this method, which
for him was the way to reach the highest in the domain of thought, has prevented his thoughts from
gaining a form and a grounding that could give them the lasting significance they deserve.

Hegel was born in Stuttgart on August 27, 1770. He studied theology in Tübingen together with
Schelling, five years his junior. Besides theology he cultivated natural science and philosophy;
he was especially taken up with Rousseau and Kant. --- 1793---96 he lived in Bern as a private
tutor. For the understanding of Hegel's religious development and of his position on one of the
deepest problems of his later philosophy, the position of the individual toward the whole, the
notes from the Tübingen and Swiss periods, first brought to light by ROSENKRANTZ \textit{(Hegels
Leben.} Berlin 1844) and HAYM \textit{(Hegel und seine Zeit.} Berlin 1857), are of the greatest
value. Hegel's consideration of the
% --- p. 169 ---
\opage{169}person of Christ is decidedly rationalist, in the spirit of the eighteenth century; what is new
and peculiar lies in his consideration of Christianity and its position in world history. Hegel's
historical consideration led him beyond the age of the Enlightenment and places him close to
Lessing; but the result is nevertheless very different from
Lessing's. Hegel's ideal in this period was classical antiquity, the sunlit utopia that has found
its most beautiful expression in Schiller's poem ``Die Götter Griechenlands''. In enthusiasm for
this ideal he met with his friend the poet Hölderlin, and he himself sought (in the poem
``Eleusis'') to give his feeling poetic expression. But the foundation of his conception was a
consideration of scientific value. His study of history had taught him to call those times happy
in which men gathered in unity around great common tasks, and in which the individual really was
a part of the whole, did not come forward with subjective criticism toward it, but was animated
by it and absorbed in it. Such a time was classical antiquity, and over against it Christianity
really stood for Hegel as a phenomenon of dissolution. Like S. Kierkegaard later, Hegel lays
weight on Christianity's being the concern of the individual, and precisely from this point of
view he passes judgment on it. When the universal and common vanished because of the corruption
of the times and the destruction of civil freedom, the individual was asserted at the expense of
the whole, and through this Christianity won its power. Values vanished from life in order to be
transferred to the life after death. In his consideration of religion Hegel stands here at the
same stage as Feuerbach later, but his special criticism of historical Christianity as the
religion of individuals, and that means here in Hegel of the weak and corrupted, has really found
its counterpart only in Nietzsche\textsuperscript{41\,b}). The thought that the universal and
common is what is right, the tendency to assert the whole at the expense of the parts, which later
became to so high a degree the sustaining element in Hegel's ethics and in his consideration of
life and history, found its first peculiar expression in his enthusiasm for antiquity. Vanished
antiquity was the ideal; it lay bright and great; at the subjective, critical, rationalist
tendency of the present Hegel feels the same disgust as Fichte in his ``Grundzüge des
gegenwärtigen
% --- p. 170 ---
\opage{170}Zeitalters''; where Fichte looked with hope toward the future, Hegel looked with longing back
toward the past, but the dark view of the present is common to all the great Romantics. In his
criticism of the Christianity of the present Hegel stood close to Schelling in this period; he
followed the latter's production with admiration, and declared himself almost a pupil. His
maturing into an independent thinker took place during his stay in Frankfurt, where in 1796---1800
he had a position as private tutor. Here his philosophy came into being. In a letter to Schelling
(Nov. 2, 1800) he writes: ``The ideal of my youth had at the same time to transform itself in me
into a system'', --- an utterance that is characteristic of his philosophy. To be sure, the ideal
lay in the past, in classical antiquity. But when he now proclaims that the ideal must be
translated into a system, it means that he wants to break with the Romantic longing and with
Romanticism's capricious relation to the reality of the present. The danger and difficulty of such
a transition lies in this, that while the ideal means distance, lack of closure and an open
horizon, the system is to give a coherent and conclusive understanding. In the translation it then
easily happens either that the ideal accommodates itself too much to reality, or that reality is
reinterpreted according to the ideal. And Hegel's system came to suffer from both defects. The
reality that he shows to be the revelation of an ideal content he has himself all too often given
an idealistic reinterpretation. His whole system therefore stands on the ground of Romanticism.
But Hegel nevertheless had a deep sense of the real, especially of historical reality, and his
enthusiasm for the classical times did not weaken his interest in the present. He made penetrating
studies of contemporary conditions; thus during his stay in Switzerland he studied the financial
constitution of the canton of Bern down to the smallest details.

From 1801 on Hegel worked as Docent in Jena. The University of Jena was, of course, the hearth of
the philosophical movement from the time when Reinhold came forward here as champion of Kant's
philosophy; here Schiller, Fichte and Schelling worked; here in these same years Herbart and Fries
also studied. For a time Hegel and Schelling worked together. They published a journal in which
Hegel polemicized against the ``philosophy of reflection'', which
% --- p. 171 ---
\opage{171}was unable to rise to the idea of the absolute unity of subject and object and to see
everything in its light. This criticism applied especially to Kant, Fichte and Jacobi. But the ways
parted on account of the two men's different intellectual tendencies. Schelling's strength was
intuition, the quick grasp, the great intimation; but patient execution in detail did not suit him.
And with the rapid acquisition of a new standpoint there followed --- all through his youth --- a
rapid abandonment of it as well. Hegel developed slowly, but from the moment when his system stood
before him in its main outlines (1800), it did not change, and his whole remaining life was
absorbed in the further execution of the method he considered the right one. As he had broken with
the ``philosophy of reflection'' on account of its dualistic doctrine of subject and reality, so
he broke with Schelling on account of his formlessness in thinking, his lack of a fixed method. The
break was proclaimed in the preface to \textit{Phänomenologie des Geistes} (1807). In Schelling's
philosophy, it is said here, the Absolute appears as the night in which all cats are gray, since
it is depicted as the unity or identity of all differences. Schelling does indeed acknowledge the
oppositions, since he of course operates with the scheme of polarity; but that is precisely a mere
scheme, which does not let real development come into its own. Schelling is like a painter who has
only two colors on his palette and thinks he can render everything with them. What matters is to
show how the various elements of existence pass over into one another with inner necessity. Only
through this intimate connection between everything in the world is it made clear that the
Absolute is not dead being, resting unity, but process, life, spirit. It is the dialectical method
that Hegel here demands; it really contains within it, as will be shown later, his whole system.
In ``Phänomenologie des Geistes'' he wants to give an introduction to the system by showing how
ordinary consciousness develops into speculative consciousness, rises through various stages or
forms to the knowledge that truth is neither dead being (substance) nor mere subjectivity, but a
living unity of both, --- a knowledge that the individual consciousness will now be able to reach
all the more easily since ``the
% --- p. 172 ---
\opage{172}world-spirit has had the patience to go through all these forms in the long extension of time
and to take upon itself the enormous work of world history, in which at every stage it worked out
all the content that was possible there''. (Phänomenologie. Vorrede). The course of development
that this work, unique of its kind, depicts is then at once that of the individual and that of the
species; it is at once a psychology and a history of culture that is given, --- and in the
exposition the two are so entangled in each other that one often does not know which of them one
has before one. The historical examples that one glimpses through the abstract exposition Hegel
uses only as types, which will repeat themselves again and again when human consciousness works
under the same conditions. Consciousness is always driven forward by its own inner law, since it
must take on a new form or rise to a new stage whenever its theoretical and practical results do
not correspond to its presuppositions. The fault always proves in the end to lie in consciousness
itself, and therefore it is compelled to change its presuppositions or its standard, until ---
when the very standpoint of pure science is reached --- the opposition between presupposition and
result, concept and object, is abolished. ---

The battle of Jena and its consequences brought about Hegel's emigration to South Germany. He lived
to such a degree in speculative thoughts that this catastrophe did not set his patriotic feeling in
motion. On the day before the battle he had even, with interest and speculative curiosity, seen
``the Emperor, this world-soul'' ride out to reconnoiter, and the night before the battle he had
finished working out his ``Phänomenologie'' (see his letter to Schelling of May 1, 1807). (The
preface, however, was written only some time later). He felt himself a spectator at a
world-historical play and was now merely concerned to find a quiet place. For a time he worked as
an editor in Bamberg. After that he became rector of the gymnasium in Nuremberg (1808---16). Here
he published his chief work \textit{Wissenschaft der Logik} (1812---16), an exposition of all
the fundamental scientific concepts, developed according to the dialectical method. Naturally the
wish had to arise in him to work at a university again. 1816---18 he was professor in Heidelberg,
where he published his
% --- p. 173 ---
\opage{173}\textit{Encyclopädie der philosophischen Wissenschaften im Grundrisse} (1817), and for the rest
of his life he worked at the University of Berlin, where he published his \textit{Grundlinien der
Philosophie des Rechts} (1821). In the Berlin period he stood at the height of his influence,
partly through his magnificent systematics, which seemed to provide a wide and living frame for the
whole spiritual content of the age,
and which therefore soon gathered a large school around him, partly through his conservatism in the
philosophy of right and of religion, which was convenient to those in power. It was the time of
broken political promises and of ecclesiastical reaction in Germany, and yet Hegel taught the ideal
truth of the existing order of the state and of the ruling religion! However unattractive the forms
this tendency in Hegel took, --- especially in his sallies against oppositionally minded thinkers
who came to suffer under the displeasure of those in power, --- there is nevertheless no doubt that
his conservatism sprang from his idealistic conception. It was his conviction that the idea was
not so powerless as to be unable to penetrate reality, and not only nature but also the state: ``Of
nature it is granted that philosophy is to know it as it is, that the philosophers' stone lies
hidden \textit{in nature itself,} that it is in itself rational, and that knowledge is to grasp
this \textit{actual} reason present in nature . . . But the ethical world, the state, is not to be
so fortunate that reason has gained power and might in it, asserts itself in it and dwells in it.
The spiritual universe is, on the contrary, to be abandoned to chance and arbitrariness, is to be
\textit{God-forsaken!''} (Phil. des Rechts. Vorrede). By this conviction of his one understands his
indignation toward those who believed they had more reason than that which had historically
developed in the state. On this point Hegel stands close to the so-called historical school, which
regards the legal order as a historical work raised above all individual reflection and willing.
He even declared that philosophy always comes too late to teach how the world ought to be. Thought
is the last product of the world-process. When reflection awakens, it is a sign that a historical
form of life is concluded. ``The owl of Minerva begins its flight only when dusk has fallen!'' ---
Hegel's conservatism ought
% --- p. 174 ---
\opage{174}really to have led him to lay far greater weight on the method of experience than he does. For
when thought always comes afterward and cannot anticipate the new, how is it then possible to find
truth by the way of pure thinking, of the dialectical method?

Hegel died of cholera on November 14, 1831. A few years later his disciples published his collected
works, partly from lecture manuscripts (philosophy of religion, aesthetics, history of philosophy
etc.).

\subsubsection*{b.\quad The Dialectical Method}

What Hegel calls the dialectical is for him 1) a property of all our thoughts which makes the
individual thought necessarily lead over to others, but also 2) a property of things which makes
the individual thing necessarily belong together with others. Thereby, for him, the way by which
thought reaches truth can at the same time immediately express the innermost life of existence
itself. In our thinking existence, existence thinks itself in us.

1) Since every concept is limited, it leads, when consistently thought through, over to its
opposite, its negation. Every concept (and especially the fundamental concepts, the categories)
comes forward with the claim to express the whole of reality, the whole content of experience; but
precisely this claim leads to the demonstration of its limit, thus to the negative. (It goes, then,
with the individual concepts as it goes, according to the ``Phenomenology of Spirit'', with the
various stages of human consciousness, which by their own consistency lead beyond themselves. There
is a dialectic of concepts, just as there is a dialectic of standpoints). But through the negation
a new position emerges: for what is negated is only a determinate, limited content, not all content
whatever. The negation thus means that a new concept comes into force. And since this new concept
is determined by its relation to and its memory of the earlier concept, it becomes richer than the
latter. The new concept that is formed includes the old one within it, taken up into a larger
connection.
% --- p. 175 ---
\opage{175}The negation is then a \textit{sublation} also in the sense that the negated concept is lifted
up into a higher unity. A unity of opposites comes into being, which comprises both the original
concept and its opposite. ``In this way now'', says Hegel in the introduction to his Logic, ``the
system of concepts is to form itself and be completed by unceasing, pure progress, taking up nothing
from outside''. --- The Hegelian system therefore unfolds through triads, each concept that is set
up being negated, and thereupon the unity of opposites, the higher unity that holds both the
position and the negation, being set up, --- so that this in turn may be subjected to the same
process. If we thus begin with the most abstract thought of all, the concept of being, this thought
turns over into the thought of nothing, because pure, differenceless being without content and
determinacy is the same as non-being. If both thoughts are combined, the concept of becoming is
obtained; for to become is both to be and not to be, since it is the transition from one state to
another. But the concept of becoming then leads in turn to the concept of properties that come to
be or are dissolved, etc.

2) But this forward-driving dialectic is now the expression of the self-development of
\textit{existence}. In our thinking the pulse of existence itself beats, and with the same rhythm as
everywhere. Every finite phenomenon points, by virtue of its limitation, beyond itself, is only a
moment in the whole great connection. In asserting this objective dialectic Hegel has, as is seen
from his application of it in detail, two experiences especially in view. First, the passing of
opposites into one another precisely by virtue of the relation of opposition, as in the
psychological effect of contrast, in the alternation of life and death, light and darkness
(excessive light abolishes sight, as does pure darkness), in the social domain the passing of
strict right into crying wrong (summum jus, summa injuria) etc. At the high point of development
dissolution begins: that was the law by which Hegel wanted to construct nature and history for
himself. But second --- and this is the most essential point of view --- he is thinking of how the
results of the earlier stages determine the development at the later ones. The child's innocence
is sublated by the unrest of doubt, of reflection and of passion; but through this
% --- p. 176 ---
% print: „desvære“ (p. 176) (misprint)
\opage{176}purgatory a firm, harmonious character develops, in which the immediacy of childhood returns in a
higher form. The seed-corn must be dissolved for the plant to come into being; but in the plant what
is essential in the seed-corn is preserved. What Hegel wanted to express by his doctrine of the
dialectic as world-process is, then, a conviction of the conservation of force and the subsistence
of values in existence. In his mystical language: the memory of the world-spirit preserves
everything; perishing means merely a sublation of external existence, not the annihilation of what
is essential. Never, surely, has so magnificent an attempt been made to carry through the
conservation of force and the subsistence of values in the spiritual domain. When Hegel stood at
the turning point at which the ideal was translated for him into a system, it meant that he no
longer doubted the subsistence of values in existence. As long as ideal and reality are still
sharply distinguished, so long does it remain undecided whether values might not vanish in
existence (so that the time of the ``happy times'' would be over once and for all), even if the
elementary forces were not lost but maintained themselves under new forms. ---

Important ideas thus lie concealed behind the dialectical method. But first and foremost it must
be noted that speculative philosophy here for the first time set up an independent and peculiar
method by which pure reason could develop according to its own inner law. Hegel's Logic is the
first resolute answer to Kant's ``Kritik der reinen Vernunft''. Had Hegel been right, then the
task that Kant regarded as insoluble would have been solved: to ground knowledge of existence by
thought's own way. Since negation is a purely logical operation, which is always in our power, we
would, if Hegel were right, always be able to spin the thread of thought further on our own, since
from any concept whatever new positive concepts could be conjured forth. But unfortunately that is
not how matters stand. It is indeed always in our power to negate, and again to negate the
negation, --- but the negation of the negation always leads us back to the original position, just
as $-(-2)$ is 2 and not a new number. Only if by negating non A I could get (not A again, but) B,
only then could the thread of thought a priori be
% --- p. 177 ---
\opage{177}spun on into the infinite. It is therefore also only apparently that Hegel brings forth the
system of our fundamental scientific concepts by a purely dialectical way. In reality the triad
(position --- negation --- higher unity) is only a scheme into which he more or less arbitrarily
brings the content of experience
into it. It is also a correct remark, which one of Hegel's English disciples has made, that ``he was
far more anxious to show how the higher category is \textit{intimated} (is suggested) by the
lower, than to prove that the lower is \textit{self-contradictory} without the higher; and when
this is not proved, the dialectic loses its compelling necessity.''\textsuperscript{41\,c}).

Hegel's dialectical method is a continuation of Fichte's antithetical method. But Fichte saw
clearly that the antithesis (as a positive proposition) could not be derived from the thesis. The
various propositions that were set up against one another were for him only different attempts to
express the given; each proposition means a new incision of thought, and the synthesis then
combines what they have each accomplished separately. The new position is thus always won from
experience. But according to Hegel the antithesis should always be derivable from the thesis. ---
Like Fichte's antithetical method, Schelling's method of potentiation or depotentiation was also a
forerunner of the dialectical method. Hegel here marks the conclusion of Romanticism's endeavor
toward a purely idealistic construction of the world-view. And it went with him historically as it
should according to his own dialectical law, in that thought, once it had properly reflected on
what this thoroughgoing speculative idealism was really driving at, sought its way over to wholly
different starting points and methods, and Hegel himself became at most a moment in a ``higher
unity''.

\subsubsection*{c.\quad The System}

Hegel's system falls, in accordance with the fundamental law of the dialectic, into three parts.
The beginning is made with \textit{logic,} which for Hegel is not merely a doctrine of the forms of
our thinking, but an exposition of the eternal thoughts that lie at the ground of existence. He
himself recalls the idea of the Logos as the world-creating and
% --- p. 178 ---
\opage{178}world-ordering principle. Both in the world of nature and in that of spirit there reign
universal thoughts and laws, which logic presents in their pure, abstract form, by showing how the
one concept develops out of the other. --- The second part of the system is the \textit{philosophy
of nature,} which presents the thought-content of existence not in logical abstraction but in the
form of ``externality'', in space and time. The transition from logic to the philosophy of nature
is to take place with dialectical necessity. It is one of the most difficult points for Hegel's
method. In reality the transition naturally takes place through the abstraction on which logic
builds being sublated by the thinker's returning to the experiences from which he has extracted the
abstract concepts he operated with in the logic. --- The philosophy of nature has rightly been
called the partie honteuse of the Hegelian system. Hegel operates with the concepts of natural
science with still greater arbitrariness than Schelling. Already Schelling had put Kepler (in his
``Mysterium cosmographicum'') and Goethe (in his theory of colors) above Newton; Hegel goes further
along the same path. It was a Romantic attempt to displace the mechanical view of nature (an
attempt in which no account was taken of the decisive change that had taken place in Kepler's
views, see the first part of this work). Hegel aims, like Schelling, to arrange the concepts of
natural forces and natural forms so that nature can be seen step by step to work its way up from
mere externality to the inwardness of spirit. The most important steps are: mechanics, physics,
organics. But just as little as in Schelling do these steps mean a real development. Hegel declares
expressly (Encyclopädie § 249): ``Nature is to be regarded as a system of steps, of which the one
necessarily proceeds from the other . . . but not so that the one should be produced \textit{in a
natural way} (natürlich) out of the other, but in the inner idea that constitutes the ground of
nature. \textit{Metamorphosis} belongs only to the concept as such; only its change is development
. . . Such nebulous and at bottom sensuous representations as the so-called \textit{origin} of
plants and animals from water, and then the \textit{origin} of the more developed animal
organizations from the lower etc., thinking consideration must decline.'' This
% --- p. 179 ---
\opage{179}utterance is characteristic of the \textit{idealist} doctrine of development, for which the
strict mechanical derivation of one natural form from others is externality and sensuousness, a
sin against the pure self-movement of the ``idea''. --- The third part of the system is the
\textit{philosophy of spirit.} The transition takes place by the form of externality in which the
idea appears in nature being sublated again. Inwardness, independence of time and space, take the
place of nature's material divisibility and extension. Although here too the demonstration of the
dialectical necessity is hard going, the emergence of mental life nevertheless contains no
difficulty of principle for Hegel, since he of course conceives the idea, the spiritual principle,
as what is innermost, what really subsists in nature. Hegel's philosophy is really philosophy of
spirit from first to last, an attempt to make the science of spirit the absolute science, just as
materialism is an attempt to make the science of matter the absolute science. When one of Hegel's
disciples (the elder ERDMANN) has characterized his system as panlogism, on account of the
pervasive endeavor to form all the content of existence into abstract categories and to conceive
the movement of thought as a world-law, that is to lay too great weight on the form of Hegel's
system. It is surely more correct when another of his disciples (ROSENKRANZ) has characterized the
system as philosophy of spirit. The dialectical method really aims to show that everything hangs
together as intimately as the thoughts in the mind, forms one great totality, as they do, and that
the right expression for the essence of existence is therefore: everything is spirit, and spirit
is everything. Kant's ``synthesis'' has here become a world-principle. --- The philosophy of
spirit naturally falls, like the philosophy of nature, into three parts. First \textit{subjective
spirit} is treated (in the series of steps: soul, consciousness, reason), the spiritual life in
individual subjects, --- thus the content of what one would now call psychology. Then comes
\textit{objective spirit,} the spiritual life as it expresses itself in historically appearing
forms of society and institutions. Here belong right, morality (Moralität) and ethical life in
family, civil society and state (Sittlichkeit as distinct from Moralität). The higher unity of
subjective
% --- p. 180 ---
\opage{180}and objective spirit is \textit{absolute spirit,} the totality of spiritual life in existence,
``spirit in its congregation'', where every difference between the individual and what fills and
sustains the individual has fallen away. As forms of absolute spirit are named: art, religion and
(speculative) philosophy.

This highest step itself, the culmination of the dialectical movement, must nevertheless be a step
on which \textit{human} spiritual life, the only one we know, stands. But Hegel keeps this in a
certain ambiguity. Although art, religion and philosophy are human endeavors, he nevertheless
conceives them essentially as forms of life of the \textit{world-spirit}. A naive admission that
these forms of life are nevertheless realized, and, so far as we know, only realized, at a definite
place in the universe, Hegel does make in his philosophy of nature, when he (Encyclopädie § 290
cf. 280) seeks to show that the planets are more perfect globes than the suns, and that the earth
in turn is the most perfect planet! Most perfect must here, after all, mean: best suited to the
development of the life of the spirit. But what then is the rest of the universe for? Old Böhme's
heavy doubts (see the first part) might then arise here again! Despite all his dialectic Hegel has
not been able to rise above the geocentric and anthropocentric (earthbound and man-bound)
standpoint that we are, once and for all, compelled to take. No dialectic can teach us to jump over
our own shadow. ---

Of particular interest (both for the history of culture and philosophically) are two sections of
Hegel's philosophy of spirit: his doctrine of right and the state and his doctrine of religion.

\subsubsection*{d.\quad Philosophy of Right}

Hegel's youthful ideal had been the ancient state, which stood as a divine
power, enveloping and absorbing all individuals, in contrast to the modern
individualistic conception, for which the state existed by a contract between
individual egoisms. In his \textit{Philosophie des Rechts} (a more detailed
development of what in the system is called the objective spirit) he
accordingly later also sets ethical life proper
% --- p. 181 ---
\opage{181}(Sittlichkeit), as it appears in the life of the family, civil
society and the state, in opposition partly to right (das abstrakte Recht) as
the expression of the individual will, partly to ``morality'' as the
expression of the subjective conscience, which in its isolation from the
objective powers of society turns into sheer arbitrariness, into evil! Only
within society can right and morality thrive; they are branches of a whole,
not wholes by themselves. In the ethical communities the good has its
subsistence as in a world animated by it. What is decisive here is not
individual consciousness and arbitrariness. There is in the ethical world
something that goes beyond the consciousness of the single individual. In this
sense Antigone in Sophocles proclaims that no one knows whence the laws come,
that they are eternal. The lives of the single individuals are regulated by
ethical powers which do indeed find their points of attachment in them, but
are not dependent on them. Indeed, Hegel even declares (§ 145): ``Whether the
individual is, is indifferent to objective ethical life, which alone is the
abiding, the power by which the life of individuals is governed''. Yet the
individual first finds its proper sphere in it, is free only by living in it,
and the relation between the single individual and society is then so intimate
that faith and trust are not the right words, since they still presuppose a
certain relation of difference. It is a new and higher nature that has taken
the place of the natural will in ``Sitte''. Where the ethical substance (the
spirit of the family, of society, of the state) thus prevails, the individual's
particular duties spring from it with necessity and are not difficult to find.

Of the ethical communities the state, again, is the most important. It unites
in itself the essence of the family and of civil society as the higher unity of
both. It is the full actuality of the ethical idea. Here spirit has realized
