itself in a far more perfect way than in nature, where it is still asleep. It
is ``God's march in the world'' that the state exists; it is to be honored as
an earthly deity. --- Just as the single individual's duties follow immediately
from his station in society, without his needing to work them out by
speculation, so the constitution of the state, too, proceeds from its essence.
The constitution does indeed develop in time, historically, but it cannot be
made; it is not ``ein Gemachtes''. As
% --- p. 182 ---
% scan: „nnder“ (p. 182)
\opage{182}empirical proof that constitutions cannot be made, Hegel points to
the constitution that had been worked out by speculation and that people tried
in vain to introduce during the French Revolution, and to the constitution,
rational in and for itself, that Napoleon tried to force upon Spain. It is the
great merit of Hegel's philosophy of right that it so decidedly stresses the
connection of constitutional life with the whole historical character of the
state, a character pointing beyond every single individual's wishes and
thoughts. He thereby stands close to the historical school and to positivism.
\textsc{Auguste Comte}'s first independent work (Systéme de la politique
positive. 1822) accordingly also met (as is seen from a letter from Comte to a
friend in Berlin, 10 Dec. 1824) with a very good reception from Hegel, just as
Comte felt an interest in what he heard of Hegel's lectures on the philosophy
of history, although Hegel struck him as ``encore trop métaphysique'' and
seemed to him to let ``spirit'' figure rather too much: Je n'aime point du tout
son \textit{esprit,} auquel il fait jouer un rôle si singulier. (See
\textit{Littré:} Auguste Comte et la philosophie positive. 2. éd. p. 157).

Hegel did not, however, wish simply to renew the ancient political theory,
whose one-sidedness he admitted. The modern state is to be the organization of
freedom. Civil society, the family and the single individuals are to have their
particularities and interests satisfied in the state. What the state demands as
duty is to be the individual's proper right. The great end of the state should
not and cannot be attained without the adherence of the narrower communities
and of the individuals \textit{(nicht ohne} das eigene Wissen und Wollen der
Besonderheit, die ihr Recht behalten muss. § 260). But in his more detailed
working out Hegel nevertheless makes the objective element wholly dominant.
Even that modest ``nicht ohne'' is not respected \textit{---} as we have indeed
already heard that ethical life as objective substance is indifferent to the
being or non-being of the single individuals! For a thinker who sees in the
state, mark well not the idea or ideal of the state but the historically given
state, the earthly deity, substantial reason, the ideals, criticisms and
reasonings of single individuals must stand as subjective opinions and wishes,
a self-importance, a ``Besserwissen'', that fails to recognize the deep truth in
what historically exists.
% --- p. 183 ---
\opage{183}In accordance with the principle: ``Es sollen die Wissenden
regieren, \textit{οἱ ἄριστοι,} nicht die Ignoranz und die Eitelkeit des
Besserwissens'', Hegel finds the proper representation of the state in the
bureaucracy: ``Die Regierung ruht in der Beamtenwelt''. In Germany,
particularly in Prussia, he saw this principle realized. It was the most
satisfying sight that met him when, in his lectures on the philosophy of
history (in the twenties), he concluded with a survey of the state of Europe.
Thus far had ``God's march in the world'' come. The speculative reactionary did
not see that the foot of the Deity was already lifted for new, mighty strides,
which for the time being burst every \textit{system ---} without, however, being
able to obstruct the prospect of the world of \textit{ideals}.

In the preface to his philosophy of right Hegel makes a spiteful attack on the
Kantian FRIES in Jena, who in 1817 had taken part in the German students'
festival at the Wartburg, so scandalous to the reactionaries, and had declared
there that ``among a people in which a genuine public spirit prevails, the
conduct of every public affair will receive its life from below, out of the
midst of the people, as living communities, held together by the bond of
brotherhood, dedicate themselves to every work aimed at the education and
welfare of the people''. So, exclaims Hegel, the ethical world is to be handed
over to the subjective contingency of opinions and arbitrary wills, and the
more than thousand-year labor of reason is to be pushed aside for personal
feeling! In his zeal to ``convert the ideal into a system'' Hegel becomes
unjust to those who could not find the existing system ideal. History has
proved Hegel wrong; it has shown that only through the free adherence of the
people does the state gain strength. To consolidate the German Empire founded
by war, Bismarck at once introduced universal suffrage.

\subsubsection*{e.\quad The Philosophy of Religion}

With respect to religion, too, Hegel's demand is this: immersion in what has
developed historically, not subjective reasoning or individual feeling, --- but
then also the promise that thought will find its own essence again in the work
of history, which is indeed the world-spirit's own work! He sets his face both
against
% --- p. 184 ---
\opage{184}rationalism and against orthodox theology. Orthodoxy clings to the
literal expressions of the dogmas and does not see that with increasing
culture, reflection and enlightenment the time of immediate, unprejudiced
religion is past. Rationalism, on the other hand, makes the concept of God
empty and finite, places God outside the world, the infinite outside the
finite, and perhaps despairs altogether of a knowledge of God. And when one
(like Schleiermacher) tries to remedy this by an appeal to feeling, one does
not thereby get beyond one's own subjectivity. Mere feeling cannot establish
its own justification; its value depends on its content and object. Feeling
cannot be the decisive thing: man has it in common with the animal --- and if
it depended on feeling alone, the dog would be the best Christian!

The task of the philosophy of religion is now to lead beyond this opposition
between literalism on the one side and rationalism and subjective feeling on
the other. Philosophy certainly cannot produce religion. But it can know the
religion that is, and examine the relation between religion and the rest of
man's view of life. And on closer consideration it turns out that the more
philosophy attains its full development, the more need, interest and content it
has in common with religion.

Speculative philosophy seeks, after all, to know the unity of existence through
all oppositions, to understand it as an infinite spirit that contains and
comprehends everything. But this same thing is what is expressed in the
religious dogmas: they too seek, after all, --- in the highest forms of
religion --- to express that everything in the end springs from an infinite
spirit! The difference between religion and philosophy is only that in
religion the content is apprehended in the form of \textit{imagination}, so
that what for the philosopher are eternal fundamental relations, the
expression of an eternal truth valid for all times, is intuited as a historical
event and in the form of the image. What is to be apprehended philosophically
as moments in one and the same concept appears to the religious imagination as
independent opposites, set over against each other in an external way, so that
it is only in the religious \textit{cultus} that a concrete unity of the divine
and the human is realized, as the single individual becomes one with
% --- p. 185 ---
\opage{185}the highest spiritual. (``Der Cultus ist, sich diesen høchsten,
absoluten Genuss zu geben --- da ist Gefühl darin; da bin ich mit meiner
besondern Persönlichkeit dabei''. \textit{Philos. der Religion.} 2. Aufl. I.
p. 215 f.). --- The external, figurative, historical form falls away when
philosophy converts the content of religion into the form of thought. The
difference between religion and philosophy consists only in this difference
of form.

Hegel seeks to show how the various religions can be arranged in a series of
stages that leads dialectically from the most elementary forms to the highest
religion, the one in which the concept of religion has come to its full
development, since in it the Deity is in earnest apprehended as spirit. This
religion is Christianity. Humanity, says Hegel, has not needed to wait for
philosophy in order to receive the consciousness of the truth. In religion the
truth is there --- in the form of imagination. Philosophy does not seek to
overturn religion, only to convert the truth it contains into the form of
thought. What religion sums up in a concrete image, philosophy develops
analytically in abstract thoughts; the relation is as that between the
clenched and the outstretched hand. --- How Hegel conceives this is seen from
some examples. --- In the notion of creation God and the world are set in
opposition to each other; the latter is seen as the product of the former.
For thinking this opposition cannot hold: for if the infinite had the finite
outside itself, it would of course be limited by it --- and so not be
infinite. The truth in the dogma of creation is that the finite does not exist
in isolation, independently, but always points beyond itself; the essence of
the finite is to have a limit, but precisely through the limitation, the
negation, it hangs together with the whole content of existence, is taken up
into and determined by the infinite. --- In the dogma of the atonement this
relation between the infinite and the finite is expressed in a still more
striking way. God himself is dead, as it says in an old hymn: thus with his
infinity undiminished God enters into the finite world, negates himself (in
the incarnation) and cancels this negation again (through the suffering, the
death and the resurrection). In the great images of dogmatic language it is
thus established that
% --- p. 186 ---
\opage{186}finitude and suffering themselves are a divine moment, so far from
excluding the connection with the highest. Thereby existence has received its
explanation for us. What makes up the pain and the anguish in finite existence
is precisely what shows it as a member in an infinite connection.

In his speculative zeal Hegel overlooked that for the believer in revelation
precisely the decisive thing is that the dogma is more than an image. Every
positive religion must assume that at certain points the difference between
symbol and reality falls away --- that is the condition for the very concept
of revelation having validity. In the closing words of his \textit{Vorlesungen
über die Philosophie der Religion} he accordingly also states that the
disharmony between faith and reflection does indeed fall away for the
philosopher when he immerses himself in the essence of the religions and finds
in it again the highest ideas of thinking; but the philosophers are, after
all, only a small part of humanity --- and he then finds himself forced to
close with the words: ``How the age is to find its way out of its disharmony
must be left to the age itself, and it is not immediately the business of
philosophy''. --- Moreover, Hegel overlooks that a change of form may very well
mean an opposition in principle. Hegel interprets the dogma of creation and
the dogma of the atonement as symbolic expressions of the connection between
the elements of existence, of the infinite life-process that pervades
everything and from which we are not loosed even when we feel most bitterly
the limitation and pain of finitude. His own vigorous and manly way of taking
life shows itself here. But even if this interpretation were the right one,
--- even if it really were such an experience of life that had found symbolic
expression in those dogmas, it is nevertheless a quite different view of life
from Hegel's that emerges when creation means a supernatural act, and when the
atonement means a historical event by which the supernatural God suffered and
died as a man. With the change of form, which Hegel presents as wholly
innocent, there in reality follows a transition from a dualistic world-view to
a naturalistic or monistic one. This soon came to light in the debate on the
philosophy of religion within Hegel's school. He himself appears here as the
Romantic who seeks
% --- p. 187 ---
% scan: „Myudighed“ (p. 187)
\opage{187}back to the old forms of the life of the spirit and yet transforms
them according to his need. And it is precisely the abiding truth in Hegel's
philosophy of religion that the religious representations of the past can have
continued value for us only when we can in one way or another find in them an
expression of our own experiences and our own thoughts. That naturally does
not lead to any historical interpretation; for the nourishing value of the
representations may depend on many displacements; but if such a finding again
is not possible at all, then the representations of the past are only learned
curiosities. --- It was a great ideal that stood before Hegel: to show that in
history no value had been lost, --- even if it was an ideal that his own system
was unable to carry out. And in particular his psychology, which made thought
the only element of consciousness, was not suited to serve as a foundation for
this inquiry. In this respect his rival, whom we shall now describe, decidedly
has the advantage over him.

\subsection*{4.\quad Friedrich Ernst Daniel Schleiermacher}

\subsubsection*{a.\quad Characterization and Biography}

The demand that Reinhold had set up in his time, that philosophy should be
derived from one single principle, found its most resolute execution in Hegel,
and the Jena school --- so one could call the whole series Reinhold --- Fichte
--- Schelling --- Hegel, because it was at the University of Jena that their
thoughts were first developed --- could seem to form a dialectical process that
in its advance gave birth to one system after another with inner (perhaps even
``world-historical'') necessity. To demonstrate this process of development
over and over again was the Hegelians' favorite undertaking: in this way, after
all, their master's ideas were derived historically --- by his own method. As
we have seen, quite other moving forces than the inner dialectic also played a
part. And in any case the Hegelians were embarrassed by a man who, in their
master's period of glory, stood at his side with great spiritual authority, and
who already
% --- p. 188 ---
\opage{188}long before had influenced the thinking and striving people of the
time by the weight of his distinctive personality, without its being possible
to fit him into that series of stages, toward which he stood precisely in a
position of opposition. Schleiermacher's position in the history of philosophy
is characterized by his keeping the spirit of the critical philosophy alive
within the sphere of the Romantic philosophy, a combination made possible by
his Socratic personality, which possessed in a rare degree the capacity to
combine full and intimate devotion with clear reflection. He had in his
personality what Hegel thought he had in his system, the union of opposites in
living unity.

\textsc{Friedrich Schleiermacher} was born on 21 November 1768, of a family of
clergymen. His grandfather had been strongly moved by the radical kind of
pietism in which subjective feeling led to opposition to the established
church, and he had staked his own and his family's existence on it. The father
was a practical nature; his rationalist tendencies were pushed back by the need
to act practically on people. Enthusiastic about the religious life of the
Herrnhuters, he placed his son, when the latter was 15 years old, in their
educational institution at Niesky, from which he later passed on to the
seminary at Barby. Schleiermacher himself, all his life through, ascribed a
decisive significance for his spiritual life to his youth among the
Herrnhuters. His nature had indeed already expressed itself before; in a
vindication of his views (1801) he says: ``My way of thinking has no other
ground than my distinctive character, my innate mysticism, my culture
proceeding from within.'' It was a chief trait in him that he set his personal
stamp on everything he took in from without. But the Herrnhut religiosity, with
its intimate life of feeling, its retirement, its endeavor that the religious
content should be lived through in the innermost depths of the single soul,
while at the same time life together with like-minded souls was zealously
cultivated, gave him a stamp he never lost. Later too he felt himself a
``Herrnhuter of a higher order''. Higher --- for Herrnhutism soon became too
narrow for him. He needed a fuller life with people than the cloistered
seclusion allowed, and above all there
% --- p. 189 ---
\opage{189}stirred in him an intellectual need and a doubt that led him beyond
the anxious theology taught by his Herrnhut teachers. After a hard clash with
his father he had his wish fulfilled of going to study at
Halle. Here he came to know the theology and philosophy of the Enlightenment,
and soon also Kant's writings. It is of great importance for understanding
Schleiermacher's development to hold fast (what DILTHEY, in his excellent but
unfortunately unfinished \textit{Leben Schleiermachers} (1870), has shown on the
basis of Schleiermacher's youthful notes) that he had found his decisive
standpoint before he came under the influence of the Romantics and before he
came to make a study of Spinoza. At the University of Halle, and later during
his stay with a noble family in the country and as a clergyman in a provincial
town, he had been led through solitary study and reflection to his distinctive
religious standpoint, which brought about for him a harmony between his
critical intelligence and his living feeling. This standpoint was the result of
the conflict between Herrnhut religiosity and critical philosophy. He never
gave up the conviction that in feeling man's innermost life is lived, and that
feeling --- and feeling alone --- brings it into immediate relation to the
highest. But he learned from the critical philosophy the definite conditions
and limits to which human knowledge is subject. Still more sharply than Kant
himself he maintains that all representations that go beyond experience have
only symbolic value. It was not only the representations of Christian theology
% scan: „Teoløgis“ (p. 189; the e-book's reading, set by sense: scan-artefact rule)
but also the favorite dogmas of the theology of the Enlightenment, of a
personal God and personal immortality, that thus now took on another meaning
for him. What was distinctive of Schleiermacher --- and what makes him one of
the most significant figures in the history of the philosophy of religion ---
was now that what criticism dissolved and denied validity as objective truth
did not need for him to lose its religious value, if it could stand as the
symbolic expression of an experience that man has in his innermost life of
feeling. And these experiences of feeling, the inner moods that can never be
fully expressed in words, were for him the properly religious. In the
purgatory of the critical philosophy he let the finite and
% --- p. 190 ---
\opage{190}external in his faith be consumed and kept a kernel that now became
so much the more valuable for having stood its test. But he did not take over
Kant's philosophy as it stood. On the contrary, he took a very critical stand
toward it, so critical that he has even been accused of injustice toward the
great master whose disciple he really remained. His criticism concerned in
particular the external way in which Kant combined morality and religion.
Schleiermacher showed (as is seen from the \textit{Denkmale der inneren
Entwickelung Schleiermachers),} published for the first time by Dilthey in the
appendix to the biography) that from purely ethical motives no inference can be
made to anything that lies beyond knowledge. He thus completes Kant's endeavor
to free ethics from dogmatic assumptions by overturning Kant's own moral
theology. Only after his views had thus taken shape through his own criticism
came the study of Jacobi and Spinoza and the connection with the Romantic
school. Here he now saw a fully formed world-view and an endeavor to gather the
whole fullness of life into a form of unity that rose above every external
barrier. But in face of these new movements he kept his wonderful capacity to
combine devotion with criticism, a capacity that quite naturally hangs together
with the spiritual impulse of self-preservation, whose satisfaction requires
both, both the taking in of what has nourishing value and the rejection of the
opposite. For this need Schleiermacher had an open eye. The assertion of the
significance of the single individuality already comes forward in his youthful
notes and becomes a chief thought of his all his life through. This emphasis on
individuality made him critical of Spinoza's and Schelling's systems, however
deeply he sympathized with their striving for a unified conception. Moreover,
he found the limits of knowledge overstepped in these systems, and he did not
find the significance of immediate feeling recognized. But the great movement
of thought and imagination of Romanticism gave him fullness and breadth of
view and opened to him spheres for which he had hitherto had no eye. The
friendship with \textsc{Friedrich Schlegel} became a turning point for him
here. Romanticism's remarkable mixture of individualism and
% --- p. 191 ---
\opage{191}mysticism met him here in a pronounced form\textsuperscript{42}).
However different the two friends were, their life together was nevertheless
fruitful owing to Schleiermacher's great capacity to understand another
individuality and to convert what could be learned from it into the forms of
his own life. Schlegel too, restlessly oscillating as he was, felt polemically
disposed toward the attempts to close philosophy in a system; only with him it
was rather his arbitrariness, with Schleiermacher besides individualism above
all the critical sense, that was decisive here. Schleiermacher found his own
tendencies in Schlegel in a chaotic and restless form. And through Schlegel he
came into touch with the rest of the Romantics' circle, which gave him rich
occasion to use his talent for separating kernel from shell in such a way that
what connects kernel and shell is nevertheless not overlooked. --- One fruit of
the two friends' collaboration was the ``Fragments'' in the brothers Schlegel's
``Athenäum''. ---

The first work in which Schleiermacher expressed himself at length was
\textit{Ueber die Religion. Reden an die Gebildeten unter ihren Verächtern}
(1799). Here he sharply separates religion --- in a way that will be considered
more closely later --- from knowledge and morality, and determines immediate
intuition and feeling as its organ, but on the other hand seeks to show that
intellectual, moral and aesthetic culture only becomes complete by leading back
to the immediate living in the feeling of the infinite (the universe or the
world-spirit) as that which encompasses and bears all individualities and all
finite existence. Spinoza is praised as the one who was pervaded by the lofty
world-spirit, so that the infinite was his beginning and end and the universe
his only and eternal love. In a later edition there is added to this an
enthusiastic eulogy of Novalis as the one who, in the domain of art, strove in
a direction similar to that of Spinoza in the domain of thinking. While these
speeches describe religious feeling as that which lets man feel himself, with
his whole individuality, one with the eternal and infinite, the next work,
\textit{Monologen} (1800), takes the matter up from the standpoint of
individuality itself, maintaining the
% --- p. 192 ---
\opage{192}significance of personal independence and distinctiveness. As we have
seen, the conviction of the positive significance of individuality had arisen
early in Schleiermacher. It marks his opposition not only to Spinoza and
Schelling, but also to Kant and Fichte, who assumed a universal moral law valid
for all. It stood firm for him that ``every human being is to express humanity
in \textit{his} own way, with a distinctive mixture of its elements, so that it
may reveal itself under all possible forms, and so that in the fullness of
space and time all the differences it holds in its bosom may be developed''.
Humanity is not to be a uniform mass. (See especially the 2nd Monologue). ---
In these two works Schleiermacher expressed, in a more indefinite and rhetorical
form, the fundamental thoughts that it became the task of his life to carry out
and maintain in theory and practice. He was a decidedly practical nature. When
he laid weight on individual development, it was not in order to favor
isolation and the retired cultivation of one's own self. In his view, energetic
assertion of one's own personality, ``self-presentation'', was the only way in
which one can influence others. For one cannot intervene quite directly in the
personal life of others. From this side, then, individualism became for him a
means. No more than Socrates was he prevented by the need for self-knowledge
from influencing others. His work as a clergyman had sprung from the need to
unite the two. It consisted for him in an endeavor to lead individuals to
reflection on themselves and on the deepest foundation of their life, to
immediate living in the eternal and infinite, to liberation from everything
finite and sensuous. The dogmas were for him only symbols that could be used as
auxiliary representations in this process of interiorization and liberation.
Such a conception of the clergyman's work was possible only in an age that,
partly in the form of rationalism, partly in the form of Romanticism, took a
free attitude toward the dogmas of the church, and even then it gave strong
offense, just as it also aroused scandal that Schleiermacher moved in circles
that were anything but churchly. In clerical circles he seems not to have felt
at ease, and in another age he would perhaps hardly have taken up the clerical
calling. In a letter from the year 1802 we read: ``Preaching is now the only
means of
% --- p. 193 ---
\opage{193}exercising personal influence on the common way of thinking of the
mass of men''. Later, during Prussia's unhappy period and during the reaction
after the War of Liberation, he showed his strength and his courage by pleading
the cause of national independence and personal freedom through sermons and
editorial work and in the church struggles.

It was during his stay in Berlin as chaplain at the Charité hospital
(1796---1802) that Schleiermacher came to know life in larger and variously
marked circles, entered the atmosphere of the Romantic school and published his
first writings. After he had then been a clergyman in a provincial town for
some years, he came to Halle as professor of theology (1804), where he worked
not only through theological but also through philosophical lectures. Studies
of Greek
philosophy, especially of Plato (whose dialogues he translated), had widened
his horizon and confirmed him in his standpoint. Schelling's philosophy he had
greeted with joy. He thought that when idealism recognized the distinctive
character of the life of nature, it would also come to recognize the religious
life as something different from the mere life of thought and will, so that a
``higher realism'' could emerge. In Schelling's system he saw only formalism,
since the unity of subject and object, of thinking and being, was for him only
an abstraction; only living feeling could reach beyond these oppositions.
Moreover, he did not find individual existence sufficiently brought out. In
Halle he now worked together with HENRIK STEFFENS, and in the modification this
man gave to the Schellingian doctrine he found his own views expressed. In
Steffens's writings on the philosophy of nature, which rested far more than
Schelling's on independent studies in natural science, it appears as a
fundamental thought that in nature, from the lowest stages to the highest and
through the progressive development of the globe and of organic life, a
pervasive \textit{individualizing tendency} shows itself, and in such a way that
the more individualized a natural form is, the more it bears the stamp of
infinity, i.e. the fuller the content and the greater the oppositions it
holds. A proposition such as this: ``The stage that most encloses the infinity
of nature within itself is the most individual'' (
% --- p. 194 ---
\opage{194}Steffens: \textit{Beiträge zur innern Naturgeschichte der Erde.}
Freiberg 1801, p. 273), could not but appeal to the author of the
``Monologues'' and of ``Speeches on Religion''\textsuperscript{43}). A later
work, in which Steffens developed this thought in connection with his general
ideas about knowledge \textit{(Grundzüge der philosophischen
Naturvissenschaft.} Berlin 1806), was the philosophical exposition with which
Schleiermacher is said to have agreed most, and on which he himself perhaps
(according to a remark of Steffens's, p. XXII) had some
influence\textsuperscript{44}). --- The battle of Jena put an end to
Schleiermacher's work in Halle. He now went to Berlin, where by sermons and in
other ways he sought to strengthen courage and national feeling. He occupies an
eminent place in the series of men to whom Germany owes its national rebirth.
When the University of Berlin was founded, he became professor of theology
there, but also lectured on philosophy and its history. At the same time he
worked as a preacher on large circles. As a political liberal he was in bad
odor in the period of reaction. It went so far that for a time he could not
write by post at all, since his letters were opened. The government was also
against his conduct in church affairs. Schleiermacher, who himself belonged to
the Reformed Church but by his whole standpoint could not attach great weight
to confessional differences, was in favor of the king's plan for a union of the
two Protestant confessions; but he strongly disapproved of the intention to
introduce the union by compulsion.

It could not be otherwise than that the positive content of religion, the more
Schleiermacher entered into theological and ecclesiastical work, should come to
play a greater part in his expositions. In the later editions of the
``Speeches'' and in his chief work \textit{Der christliche Glaube} (1821---22)
this comes out clearly. But one will not be able to show any difference in
principle between the standpoint in the first edition of the ``Speeches'' and
in the work that is probably the greatest Protestant theology has produced since
the time of the Reformation. He himself had the feeling of being the same. When
he had conceived the plan of his doctrine of faith, he wrote to a friend of his
youth (1818): ``A
% --- p. 195 ---
\opage{195}dogmatics, which I have at last overcome myself to write, will show
you that I am still quite the same as in the `Speeches on Religion'.'' And a
few years later (1822), on the occasion of the third edition of the
``Speeches'', he repeats this remark. He felt himself in very sharp opposition
to the pietism and literalism that had grown up around him. It was not in such
a way that he had imagined his youthful thought of a renewal of religious life
would be fulfilled. At first he had wanted to gain recognition for religion as
an essential and sustaining side of the life of the spirit. Later his thought
had been a renewal of Protestantism. He looked forward to the founding of the
University of Berlin because he hoped to be able to found there ``a
theological school that could develop Protestantism, as it now is, further and
bring it new life'' (letter to Brinckmann, 17 Dec. 1809). But the fundamental
thoughts on which this school was to be built were in reality those he had
expressed in ``Reden über die Religion''. That he himself did not think he had
changed his views is certainly no proof; but a closer inquiry will show that
the relation between the youthful writings and the concluding theological work
is this: what was first indicated in broad outline and in rhetorical form later
received its more definite development, after Schleiermacher's theory of
knowledge and ethics had developed (in the way that is seen in the works
\textit{Dialektik} and\textit{ Philosophische Sittenlehre)}, which appeared
after his death), and after he had, through further theological studies, gained
a more thorough acquaintance with the historical forms in which religious
feeling had found expression within Christianity. The view that all dogmas had
arisen through reflection on immediate experiences of feeling he never gave up.
On the other hand, even when he set about working out his doctrine of faith, he
was not quite sure where the boundary lay between the properly religious (what
he calls in a letter the immanent dogma, by which are probably meant the
representations inseparable from religious feeling at its height) and the
mythological (what he calls the transcendent or mythical dogma). (Letter to
Blanc, 23 March 1818).
% --- p. 196 ---
\opage{196}What gives Schleiermacher's philosophy of religion its great and
abiding interest is the clear way in which he conceives the relation between
feeling and representation in the religious domain. The consequence of his
conception would certainly have led him much farther away from the
ecclesiastical conception than he himself thought he had come. He did indeed
see clearly that he felt himself more at one with others than they with him; in
a letter from one of his last years (to Reichel, 3 April 1832), after touching
on the opposition and misunderstanding of which he is the object ``from the
exalted on both sides'', he utters the beautiful words: ``I am learning at least
for myself, in quiet, to be at one with many who think themselves very far
removed from me, and in that lies a peculiar, life-refreshing power''. What is
Romantic in Schleiermacher lies precisely in his overlooking the great
difference it makes whether one regards the dogmas as symbols of human feelings
or as authentic proclamations of the eternal truth. He took a great step toward
a deeper understanding of religious phenomena; but at the same time he gave the
religious a quite different place and significance from the one ecclesiastical
tradition ascribes to it. His whole Socratic personality was needed for him to
be able, with the conception he had, to work in the service of the church.
Early on he had to defend himself against the charge of dishonesty and improper
accommodation. He then pointed with pride to the fact that his abilities could
well make another occupation possible for him, were it not precisely his desire
and his calling to use them in the work of a clergyman, and with regard to the
relation between his religion and his philosophy he declared: ``I am convinced
that I really have the religion I am to proclaim, even if I should have a quite
different philosophy from most of my hearers. Nor is there in me any unworthy
cleverness or reservatio mentalis, but I give the words precisely the meaning
that a human being gives them \textit{while he is absorbed in religious
contemplation} (indem er in der religiösen Betrachtung begriffen ist), only not
another meaning besides''. (Aus Schleiermachers Leben. III. p. 284). This
% --- p. 197 ---
\opage{197}statement is characteristic in that it relegates the difference
between religious representations to the philosophical, i.e. the theoretical
domain, and in that he maintains that the religious representations, when
feeling is at its height, in fact take on another meaning than in calmer
moments\textsuperscript{45}). It is at the height of feeling that it creates its
forms for itself or seizes those that are handed down; then it shows itself as
the dogma-creating power, and it is in this, the real hour of the birth of
religion, that Schleiermacher wished to regard it; there the lines converge, and
there he also found the point of contact between his line and many others that
in their further course even went in the opposite direction. ---

Schleiermacher's life in Berlin, vexed by opposition from without and from
above, was beautified by the happiest home life. After a short illness, during
which he kept his full clarity and spiritual freedom to the last, he died on 12
February 1834.

\subsubsection*{b.\quad Dialectic and Ethics}

We shall be able to form a notion of the harmony that existed for
Schleiermacher between religious feeling and scientific thinking if we first
examine how far, by the way of thinking, he arrives at results that allow
religious feeling to move freely, and then how far, by starting from religious
feeling, he arrives at results that allow thinking to move freely.

In his theory of knowledge he seeks to mediate between Kant and Schelling. It
was clear to him that Schelling overstepped the limits of knowledge, and in his
\textit{Dialektik} he accordingly sought to give a new determination of those
limits. By dialectic he understood the doctrine of the principles of the art of
philosophizing. It forms the preparation for philosophy as a systematic
science. It is the task of philosophy to find the inner connection of all
knowledge, and dialectic now discusses the very conditions of a knowledge.
These fall into two parts: for it belongs to knowledge that each single thought
hangs together with other thoughts, and that to the single thought there
corresponds a
% --- p. 198 ---
\opage{198}real being. These two parts cannot be separated. If knowledge is to
be valid, there must correspond to the relation between our lower and higher
concepts lower and higher kinds of existence, so that, just as the higher
concepts contain the ground of the lower, the higher existence contains the
ground or force that reveals itself in the lower existence in a multiplicity of
phenomena. And in a similar way there must correspond to the connection between
concepts expressed in judgments a real connection between the things that are,
a causal relation. By this assertion of an agreement between knowledge and
being Schleiermacher separates himself from Kant, whose critical scruples he
passes lightly over, borne by the Romantic need to immerse himself in
existence. On the other hand he recalls Kant by his determination of limits.
For the identity of thinking and being is indeed for him a presupposition of
all knowledge; but it is a presupposition that cannot itself become a
knowledge --- although for the other Romantics it was the very highest
knowledge. Schelling's attempt to set up a doctrine of absolute identity led,
for Schleiermacher, merely to the setting up of more or less felicitous
schemata. He here takes up Kant's doctrine of the ideas, defining idea as a
problematic concept, a concept that designates a limit for thought which
thought never reaches, let alone gets beyond. In all our knowledge there are two
elements, one due to the organic function, sense perception and experience,
another due to the intellectual function, which appears as construction and
speculation. Neither of the two elements can be wholly lacking. Empiricism is
right that the being of the single things is not wholly absorbed in the
concept; but it is not right if it asserts that the being of the single things
is the whole of being. Speculation is right that all particulars must have
their ultimate ground in the source of all being and knowledge; but it hovers
between knowledge and poetry when it believes it can derive things from this
ultimate source by the way of construction. The idea of God as the unity of
thinking and being is the presupposition that, consciously or unconsciously,
lies at the basis of all knowledge; but it can only be constructed as a formal
schema. With it is combined the idea of the world as the totality of the
multiplicity
% --- p. 199 ---
\opage{199}of all that is. As the idea of God is the formal point of departure
(terminus a qvo), so the idea of the world is the real conclusion (terminus ad
qvem) toward which our knowledge moves without ever reaching it. For no more
than the point of departure can the end point be converted into real knowledge.
As every knowledge we have contains construction and empirical material in
varying proportions to each other, so every knowledge we have also lies at a
certain point between the point of departure and the end point. All our
knowledge is in this respect provisional. It is the task of scientific
criticism to compare our actual knowledge with the ideal of knowledge; it is in
the theoretical domain what conscience is in the practical domain. An absolute
systematic completion is impossible, and in particular it lies in the stated
relation between speculation and empirical material that philosophical systems
set themselves an impossible task when they seek to derive the finite from the
infinite and to give the inner physics of the infinite being. Only in religious
feeling is the unity of opposites lived; science is unable to grasp it, either
in its meaning as principle or in its meaning as totality. The images in which
that feeling finds expression nevertheless fall under scientific criticism.
Only such images are admissible as express both the difference between the
idea of God and the idea of the world and the inseparability of both ideas. The
two ideas are correlata: no God without the world, and no world without God.
All images that do not conflict with this rule the philosophical art can admit.
But just as it emphasizes against speculative philosophy that the latter gets
no further than giving schemata, so it maintains against the religious
representation that this gets no further than giving images. The expression
person, e.g., can, used of God, only be an image; likewise the expression
force, and whatever others one might wish to use. Atheism is for the most part
only the rejection of the validity of images and anthropomorphisms.

Just as the unity of thinking and being is the presupposition of all knowledge,
so the unity of willing and being is the presupposition of all action. For as
knowledge would be impossible if there were no point of unity for thinking and
being, so
% --- p. 200 ---
\opage{200}action would become impossible if the will were absolutely alien and
isolated in the world. The external world must be receptive to our
intervention and able to take into itself the ideal stamp of our will. At the
basis of all conscience lies the idea of a unity of willing and being, an idea
that cannot be different from the idea of a unity of thinking and being, but,
no more than that idea, can be formed into a scientific concept.

By this consideration dialectic leads over into \textit{ethics.} Its place in
the whole system of science Schleiermacher indicates in the following way. The
presupposition and final end of all knowledge (or action) was, after all, the
unity of thinking (or willing) and being. At every stage of existence we know,
one of these two elements predominates. The science of the part of existence
where being predominates over thinking and willing, nature over reason, is
called physics, which is again divided into natural history (empirical physics)
and natural science (rational physics). The science of the part of existence
where thinking and willing predominate, or work toward predominating, over
being, reason over nature, is called ethics, which is again divided into two
parts, history (empirical ethics) and moral doctrine (rational ethics). But all
these oppositions are relative. No nature without reason and willing! Nature is
``a diminished ethics''; it shows us the will at a series of stages --- in
inorganic form, in plant life and animal life and --- at the summit --- in man.
Without this unity of nature and reason, ethics proper would not become
possible. It is a further and higher development of something that already
makes itself known in nature. (Cf. Dialektik § 213---214). --- It was on this
point that Schleiermacher found in Steffens's philosophy of nature a necessary
supplement to his doctrine. He could not, like Kant and Fichte, set ethics in
sharp opposition to nature. He demanded (already in his \textit{Kritik der
bisherigen Sittenlehre,} 1803) that ethics be brought into connection with
science as a whole, and in this respect he set up Spinoza and Plato as
exemplars. He therefore emphasizes with great force that no absolute beginning
of ethical development can be assumed. (Philos. Sittenlehre § 103. 124. 325).
It is always a given foundation, a relative harmony, that can
% --- p. 201 ---
\opage{201}serve as point of departure and of attachment. And in this way
ethics enters into relation not only with nature but also with history, since
every ethical development begins at a certain point of the development of the
species. The single human being has in his innate organs results of the
exercise of the preceding generations (Philos. Sittenlehre § 147---148). ---
Although Schleiermacher's doctrine of development is reached predominantly by
the way of construction and has an idealist stamp, he nevertheless here
indicates a point of view that has been much discussed in modern biology. Only
he thinks that such organization of the nature of the species can be spoken of
first in the case of man. The animal species remain standing at the same point.
Development, then, takes place in nature, but not in the sense of a real
transition from form to form.

The relation in which ethical development stands to nature is a relation of
reciprocal action. The ethical process consists partly in an organizing,
shaping and forming activity, partly in a symbolizing, expressing and
designating activity. To the first kind of activity belongs man's striving to
make himself master of nature. The single individual takes possession of and
works a part of nature and thereby makes it his property, and men together form
a legal community that secures intercourse. To the symbolizing activity belong
all the ways in which man gains expression and form for his spiritual life and
so puts something into the world that has value only as a sign of inner life.
In individual form such a striving expresses itself in religion's need to
create poetic forms for feeling, since feeling is in itself incommunicable
(unübertragbar). Art conditions the possibility of bringing individual
distinctiveness to intuition and thereby bringing about spiritual intercourse
with others. Art is for religion what language is for
science\textsuperscript{46}). Therefore every individual must in a certain sense
be an artist. The universal form of symbolizing is science, which expresses
what is common, identical and therefore communicable in the life of
consciousness. --- Thus the whole development of culture falls under ethical
development, and ethics is in a radical way freed from the subjective and
formal mode of consideration,
% --- p. 202 ---
\opage{202}which prevailed to so high a degree in Kant and Fichte. In his
``Monologues'' Schleiermacher was still impatient that material culture (what
he later called organizing activity) played so great a part in life, and he was
inclined to see the ethical only in the endeavor to express one's distinctive
personality (in symbolizing). But in his maturer conception he seeks to unite
the two. A symbolizing striving that does not recognize the significance of
natural points of departure he now calls (Philos. Sittenlehre § 209) the cynical
one-sidedness; an organizing activity without a sense for symbolizing he calls
the economic one-sidedness.

One misses in Schleiermacher's ethics a deeper entering into the subjective
oppositions and conflicts. He describes the ethical process without stopping at
the crises. And yet it is a chief merit of his ethics that it so clearly sets
forth the significance of individuality. He does indeed grant Kant and Fichte
that reason is one and the same in all; --- but he adds that the nature of the
single individual is not exhausted by this common element. When the species in
fact splits into a multiplicity of individuals, each one can gain ethical value
only when he expresses the common human nature in a quite definite and
distinctive way. In an ethical respect there will therefore be something in the
single individual's action that cannot be transferred to or hold for that of
others. If he has not been present in his action with his whole and full
distinctiveness, then his action is imperfect, then he has not been wholly
active. Because of this individualizing of the manner of action there are
points where each one must be his own judge. But because he is his own judge,
he is not his own teacher\textsuperscript{47}). In the concept of personality
it lies not only that the single individual sets himself apart from others, but
also that he has others beside him. Already in the ``Monologues''
Schleiermacher had set up the proposition: ``Keine Bildung ohne Liebe''. The
clearer the sense the single individual has for his own distinctiveness, the
greater the sense he must also gain for that of others. It is imagination that
is the organ here. Conversely, one also becomes conscious of one's own
distinctiveness only within the species. Later
% --- p. 203 ---
\opage{203}Schleiermacher also emphasizes the division of labor, which assigns
the single individual a definite calling according to his nature. In this lies
a warning against regarding one's individuality as fully finished so long as it
has developed only in isolation or in narrow circles. --- In his personal
experience Schleiermacher had learned to know the value of individuality. He was
a virtuoso at discovering and associating with different personalities. He
found, as he says in a letter (to Henriette Herz, 17 Dec. 1803), no human being
insignificant ``who has something distinctive and who presents human nature
from one side or another''. And it was a precept of duty in his ethics that
everyone \textit{should} be distinctive and act in his own distinctive way. In
this way, after all, the individualizing tendency in nature is also carried
further. ---

In a series of academic treatises (which, besides the ``Kritik der bisherigen
Sittenlehre'', were all that Schleiermacher himself published on ethics) he
treated the fundamental ethical concepts of duty, virtue and the good, and
showed that they do not designate different parts of the content of ethics, but
different sides from which one and the same content can be regarded. The
concept of the good, which for him is one with the concept of the full
realization of spirit or reason in nature (through organizing and symbolizing),
ought to be laid at the foundation, since duty and virtue receive their real
grounding only through it. ---

\subsubsection*{c.\quad Faith and Knowledge}

Dialectic and ethics were to show how far thought and will can reach when they
develop according to their own laws. As the third chief form of the human life
of the spirit Schleiermacher sets religion, whose source and seat is in
feeling, and his endeavor is now to show that it can develop according to its
own laws, independently of the other forms and without interfering in their
independent development, --- and yet in such a way that only in religious
feeling are full harmony and reconciliation won.

In his ``Speeches on Religion to the Cultured among Those
% --- p. 204 ---
% print: „Troeslæren“ (p. 204) (misprint)
\opage{204}Who Despise It'', Schleiermacher opposes in particular two religious
standpoints: the one from which religion is conceived as a doctrine (revealed
or grounded on mere reason), and the one from which religion is conceived as a
means for morality. It consists, he maintains, in the \textit{immediate}
consciousness that everything finite is in and through the infinite, everything
temporal in and through the eternal. While knowledge goes from thought to
thought, from phenomenon to phenomenon, and while the will is directed toward
definite tasks, feeling rests immediately in itself, raised above all
opposition. (Feeling is for Schleiermacher one with ``immediate
self-consciousness'', from which he distinguishes ``objective
self-consciousness'', which is a kind of self-recognition. Der christliche
Glaube § 3). Knowledge and action depend on special talents; in them man acts
in a one-sided way and in face of objects that are different from himself. But
in feeling there is the fine, infinite movement in which the single
individual's full individuality can unfold, and in which individuality is
nevertheless precisely irradiated by the infinite. In a description of religious
% scan: „religiose“ (p. 204; the e-book's reading, set by sense: scan-artefact rule)
feeling it is a matter of seizing the moment in which the inner life stirs
whole and undivided, before it appears in thought and image or in will and
action. It is the point where the universal and the individual meet, before the
difference between subject and object has yet come into force. In this
immediate feeling the individual stands as dependent, not dependent on anything
finite whatever, toward which a reaction might be possible, but absolutely
dependent. And this absolute feeling of dependence becomes a consciousness of
God as soon as reflection awakens and seeks an expression for that on which we
are dependent with our whole passive and active being: for ``by the expression
God is meant precisely the whence \textit{(das Woher)} of our receptive and
self-active existence''. (Der christliche Glaube § 4,4).

It has been thought that a difference in principle between the ``Speeches'' and
the ``Doctrine of Faith'' is to be found in this: that in the former religion is
depicted more as an immediate feeling of unity than as a feeling of dependence,
the latter expression first occurring in the ``Doctrine of Faith'', --- and in
this: that religion, especially in the first edition of the ``Speeches'',
% --- p. 205 ---
\opage{205}is described as conditioned by the intuition of the universe or the
world-all, whereas the ``Doctrine of Faith'' makes a definite distinction between
God and the world. The standpoint of the first work has even been called
monistic, that of the second dualistic\textsuperscript{48}). But already in the
``Speeches'' the religious relation is described as a relation of dependence,
insofar as one goes back to the point where consciousness in the single moments
first comes into being, the point where as yet no difference asserts itself.
Here, at the root of consciousness, the universal and the individual meet: but
the individual, which is only coming into being, must evidently be dependent.
And when in the ``Speeches'' (especially the 1st edition) expressions such as
universe or world-all are mostly used, Schleiermacher himself has repeatedly
emphasized that what makes the world a whole is precisely God (Philos.
Sittenlehre § 287 and note 2 to the second speech in the 3rd edition). When in
the ``Dialectic'' and the ``Doctrine of Faith'' he distinguishes between God and
the world, he means by the world the totality, by God the unity, and he
affirms, as we have seen, a close connection between these two concepts. --- His
ideas underwent an unfolding, but his feeling of having remained the same did
not deceive him.

Both in the ``Speeches'' and in the ``Doctrine of Faith'' it is definitely
maintained that no concepts and propositions belong to the proper essence of
religion, but that they are all derived, due to reflection on the immediate
states of feeling. As we have already seen, the word God designates the origin
(das Woher) of the peculiar feeling of dependence. It is by virtue of a need
for expression and communication that words and images are sought for the
feeling that is in itself unutterable. If these images are taken as literal
truth, mythology results. It is the task of the doctrine of faith to convert
the figurative expressions of feeling into proper expressions, or at any rate
to give the figurative expressions a definite limitation. No proposition in the
doctrine of faith may
be derived from another proposition, but every proposition is to be drawn
immediately from religious experience and only afterwards compared with other
propositions. (Chr. Gl. § 17). The only proof there can be any question of for
such propositions is, then, that others come to have the same experiences as
the expositor. All dogmas that cannot in this
% --- p. 206 ---
\opage{206}way be traced back to immediate experiences of feeling
Schleiermacher therefore rejects, or at any rate he declares them to be symbols
that are not necessary expressions of religiosity. So the representations of
the personality of God, of personal immortality, of creation, of the first
human beings, of the origin of sin, etc. He denies that religious experience
can lead to assuming that the connection of nature is broken. There would in
that case be a relation of opposition between the consciousness of God and the
consciousness of the connection of nature; but there can --- Schleiermacher
asserts --- never arise from religious interest a need to conceive a fact in
such a way that its conditionedness by the connection of nature would be
canceled by its dependence on God, since these two relations coincide.
\textit{Miracle} therefore becomes only the religious name for an event, for
what has aroused religious attention and to which a special value therefore
attaches. Revelation does not mean a doctrine but a fact of religious
significance that cannot be explained from the historical connection.
Christians assume such a revelation in Christ, because only by assuming him as a
sinless archetype who appeared historically can they explain to themselves
their consciousness of redemption, i.e. the experience that what hindered their
consciousness of God and by this hindering caused them suffering has now been
cleared away. Religious feeling is in itself a feeling of blessedness; but since
it constantly occurs in consciousness together with other feelings, which are
determined by man's nature as a finite and sensuous being, and since these
feelings can partly accord with, partly hinder religious feeling, there arises
an opposition between religious pleasure and religious pain. And the
canceling of religious pain is something the Christian can make intelligible
to himself only if there has appeared in Christ an exemplar whose pure
consciousness of God propagates its redeeming and reconciling power through the
congregation to the single individuals who are set before the image of his
personality. There is the same relation between the consciousness of redemption
and faith in Christ as the pure exemplar as between the feeling of dependence
and the representation of God. In both places the inference is from effect to
cause.
% --- p. 207 ---
% scan: „mod“ (p. 207)
\opage{207}

The great question becomes whether the justification of such an inference can
be shown. From a pure state of feeling no inference can be made, without the
help of other experiences, to the cause that has aroused it, --- and such other
experiences Schleiermacher must consistently keep away. That feeling, because
of its need for diffusion and intensification (so excellently described in his
time by Hume), leads to the formation of representations of ideal beings is a
psychological fact; but this process leads, as Schleiermacher himself
acknowledges elsewhere, only to symbols. Feeling's need for symbolism is
confused by Schleiermacher with its significance as a fact pointing to the
presence of a quite definite cause. As a philosopher he keeps to symbolizing;
but he could become an ecclesiastical theologian only because he confused
symbolizing with a causal explanation. And this confusion then brought him into
open conflict with his own philosophy. His theory of knowledge declared the
concept of an absolute being impossible to carry through; but his theology
forced him to set up such a concept. His philosophy of nature declared that no
absolute beginning could be conceived; but his Christology forced him to assume
an absolute point of beginning in the appearance of Christ, since through him
something was supposed to have entered history that could not be explained by
the preceding historical development.

Schleiermacher's philosophy of religion is --- like Hegel's --- an attempt at
restoration. Characteristic of it is that it defends religion by showing its
significance for the life of the spirit as an interiorizing, infinitizing and
harmonizing power, and does not, conversely, judge the life of the spirit by
its relation to religion as the highest norm. A standard is thus presupposed
that lies beyond that of religion itself. Schleiermacher closes his exposition
of the Christian doctrine of faith with a statement that recalls the closing
words of Spinoza's Ethics: not a single one of the propositions he has set up in
his work loses its meaning, he asserts, even if there is no continued
subsistence of personality after death (§ 158). It is thus the life we know and
live in the world of experience that is to be deepened and
% --- p. 208 ---
\opage{208}developed, and from its needs the highest standard is drawn. And
whereas the positive religions sought not only to create peace and harmony in
the mind, but also represented knowledge and morality, religion according to
Schleiermacher has nothing at all directly to do with these domains.

That it was an essential change he made in the concept of religion, he was
clearly aware. Neither Protestantism nor Christianity at all had for him
reached its final form. A constant development had to take place in the
religious domain too, and it was the task of free theology to guide this
development. Neither the doctrine of faith nor Christian ethics was for him
given once and for all; the writings of the New Testament contain only the
conception of the first generation. This holds especially in the case of
ethics, that it must constantly be altered and developed --- as regards both
motives and results: ``There is no exposition of ethics that could continue to
hold for all the ages of the Christian church, but every exposition has full
value only for a certain period.'' \textit{(Christliche Sitte.} p. 69. cf.
p. 94 f.). --- This grand conception the church has not adopted. Had
Schleiermacher lived in our day, it would have been far more difficult for him
``to feel
% scan: „fole“ (p. 208; the e-book's reading, set by sense: scan-artefact rule)
himself at one with many who think themselves far removed from him.''

Schleiermacher's philosophy of religion is distinguished from Hegel's by its
more correct psychology. It is a main point that religion is referred to
feeling, not to mere thinking. Even if the dogmas are dissolved into symbolism,
something nevertheless remains: the experiences of feeling that led to the
production and acceptance of the dogmas. The problem is whether they fall away
or subsist or are converted into other forms when the objective truth of the
dogma is rejected. Schleiermacher himself assumed a subsistence, neither a
falling away nor a conversion. In that he was wrong. But his standpoint was
whole and harmonious. He knew an undulation between feeling and knowledge, but
he did not understand Jacobi's complaints at being a Christian with his heart
and a heathen with his understanding. And by his fine understanding of the
nature and conditions of personal life he stands as one of the most eminent
spirits within the circle of Romanticism.
% --- p. 209 ---
\opage{209}

\section*{B.\quad The Philosophy of Romanticism as a Pessimistic View of Life}

\subsection*{Arthur Schopenhauer}

\subsubsection*{a.\quad Biography and Characterization}

Schopenhauer's philosophy arose on the same spiritual soil as the idealist doctrine of
development, and yet in sharp opposition to it. The spiritual kinship shows itself in the
bold attempt to solve the problem of existence by a purely subjective path; the
opposition appears partly in Schopenhauer's critical conception of knowledge, partly in
his sharp emphasis on what is disharmonious and irrational in existence. Schopenhauer,
like Schleiermacher, is a critical philosopher; he puts the problem of knowledge before
the problem of existence, and he lays far greater weight on experience and immediate
intuition than Fichte, Schelling and Hegel. Like Schleiermacher, he came to his
philosophy while working to appropriate Kant's thoughts and carry them further. He
regarded himself as Kant's true heir and denied that anything of significance had
happened in philosophy between Kant and himself, although his debt to Fichte and
Schelling was no doubt greater than he would admit. But while Schleiermacher embraces an
idealist optimism and believes, just as Hegel does, in the development of reason through
nature and history, Schopenhauer takes an altogether unique place in the whole of
European thought by breaking with the fundamental presupposition of the harmony of
existence on which Western theology and philosophy had hitherto always rested, more or
less decidedly, and by --- appealing to the experience of the misery of life --- setting
up the proposition that the innermost kernel of existence is a blind, unbridled, never
resting and never satisfied need. Thus not only the problem of knowledge but also the
problem of valuation is posed here in an entirely different way, and answered in an
entirely different direction, than in the preceding group of thinkers, whom he therefore
also regarded as his antipodes. But in his solution of
% --- p. 210 ---
\opage{210}the problem of valuation, no less than in his solution of the problem of
existence, Schopenhauer stands decidedly on the ground of Romanticism. He continues its
opposition to rationalism and ``enlightenment''; his philosophy is a thoroughgoing
doctrine of the limitation and impotence of reason. He sympathizes with Romanticism's
turning back to the Oriental spirit, which is pessimistic in contrast to Western
optimism. Not only with Romanticism but also with orthodoxy did he sympathize, since he
found the greatest significance of Christianity in its pessimism. The optimistic
elements in Christianity he ascribed to the after-effect of Judaism. In a remarkable
fragment (\textit{Neue Paralipomena} § 446) (written 1852 at the earliest) he expresses
his sympathy with Romanticism and orthodoxy in opposition to humanism and materialism.
Since his philosophy is thus closely bound up with his experience of life and his view
of life, his expositions too --- apart from the epistemological investigations ---
acquire a personal and living character, a strength and a brilliance, which give them a
literary value that the works of his speculative antipodes almost entirely lack. The
ability to discuss philosophical questions in clear and vivid form, which distinguished
the French and the English school, Schopenhauer --- whose culture was also in large part
English and French --- has at his command in a high degree, and in him it is joined with
one of the most peculiarly marked personalities known to modern literature.

\textsc{Arthur Schopenhauer} was born in the then still free city of Danzig on 22
February 1788. His father was a rich merchant, an ardent champion of his city's freedom,
who, when Danzig became Prussian, moved with his family and his business to Hamburg in
spite of all brilliant offers. The son was to be brought up as a man of the world: ``My
son'' --- said the father --- ``shall read in the great book of the world''. Arthur was
therefore educated in France and England and spent part of his early youth traveling
with his parents round Europe. Then he was placed in a merchant's office in Hamburg,
since his father would not yield to his wish to go to the university. Here in Hamburg,
by his own account, his pessimistic
% --- p. 211 ---
% print: „Hilden“ (p. 211) (misprint)
\opage{211}view of life was founded. ``In my seventeenth year, without any learned
schooling, I was seized by the misery of life, just as Buddha was in his youth, when he
saw sickness, old age, pain and death. The truth which spoke loudly and clearly out of
the world overcame the Jewish dogmas which had also been impressed upon me''. (Neue
Paralipomena § 656). It was certainly not merely what the young man saw around him that
determined his result here (as presumably also with Buddha or with the originator of the
Buddha legend). His temperament, his whole personality expressed itself in it.
Schopenhauer must be called ``burdened'' from birth. There was insanity both in his
father's and in his mother's family. His father was an energetic but harsh and irritable
nature, who suffered from unmotivated attacks of anxiety. He is said to have taken his
own life in a fit of derangement. Arthur Schopenhauer inherited his father's
temperament. Melancholy, anxiety and suspicion tormented him. Already as a boy he
brooded over the wretchedness of men. For when he was not harboring suspicion toward
others, or when his vehemence and unbridled self-esteem did not overwhelm him, his
susceptibility to suffering led him to feel pity for others. On a journey in the south
of France he could not share his mother's delight in the beautiful landscape, because he
could not help thinking of the wretched life led in the dilapidated huts they passed.
Already here he was exercised in the thought he later expressed in his chief work in
answer to the optimists' appeal to the beauty of nature: ``Zu \textit{sehen} sind diese
Dinge freilich schön; aber sie zu \textit{sein} ist ganz etwas Anderes''. But there were
also other elements in him that kept him from seeing life in a bright light. Strong
sensual drives stirred in him, which left him no peace and which he could not master,
but which again and again ``drew him from the heights of heaven to the dust of the
earth''. In youthful poems from the Hamburg period he has depicted the inner struggle
between his striving to lead a life of thought with his gaze on the great and lofty, and
the constant pull and snare of voluptuousness. When in his philosophy of life he found
the solution of the riddle of the world in the belief that an unbridled, never satisfied
need stirs in everything, he built here too
% --- p. 212 ---
\opage{212}on inner experience. His choleric mood, which bred bitterness and vehemence,
his strong self-esteem and ambition, which chafed at the lack of recognition, and his
sensuality all gave him material at first hand. And what was Tantalean in the need he
felt lay not only in its unbridledness but especially in the opposition in which it
stood to the other need that stirred in him, the need to lead a life of intuiting and
thinking. He was a contemplative nature, and in this respect had inherited the
temperament and gifts of his mother, Johanna Schopenhauer, the novelist well known in
her day. All three of the parts of which, according to Plato, the human soul consists
--- thought, the sense of honor and self-esteem, the sensual drive --- were thus marked
here in extreme form and were bound to come into conflict with one another. When in his
solution of the problem of existence he would conceive the world by analogy with his own
microcosm, it was clear that no harmonious picture could come of it. In a fragment from
the year 1814 he speaks against the assumption of a unity in man's nature: ``Inner
discord is his nature, as long as he lives''. And such an inner disharmony he then found
in the whole of existence.

After the father's death the mother moved to Weimar, where she was soon received into
the circles of Goethe and Wieland. After much resistance the son got his way and was
allowed to study. With zeal and brilliant results he threw himself into classical
literature, natural science and philosophy. His resolve was now fixed that he would
devote his life to thinking. As he said to Wieland: ``Life is a precarious business; I
have resolved to spend mine in thinking about it''. His stay with his mother in Weimar
came to have great significance for him through his acquaintance with Goethe. The young
pessimist and the great optimist met in an interest in the theory of colors. They worked
together for a time, but to Goethe's great dissatisfaction Schopenhauer --- who
otherwise, like the other Romantic philosophers, took Goethe's side against Newton ---
parted from him by giving a physiological explanation of the color qualities, whereas
Goethe believed he had given a physical one. Goethe nevertheless followed Schopenhauer's
% --- p. 213 ---
\opage{213}activity as an author with interest, and felt especially attracted by the
weight he laid on immediate intuiting in contrast to speculation and reflection. From
the old master the young man, full of self-esteem, who was already complaining bitterly
of the world and of men, received this advice in his album:

Willst du dich deines Werthes freuen,

So musst der Welt du Werth verleih'n.

Schopenhauer pursued his academic studies in Göttingen and Berlin. There G. E. Schulze
(the author of ``Ænesidemus''), here Fichte was his teacher in philosophy. But it was
Plato and Kant who became his real masters. His critical sense gave him an interest in
Kant's epistemological investigations, whose significance he found misjudged by Kant's
successors. But what gave Plato and Kant a special significance for him was that in
Plato's opposition between the clear world of ideas and the obscure world of sense, and
in Kant's opposition between the law-governed world of phenomena and the ``thing in
itself'' lying beyond all concepts and laws, he found expression for the dualism between
thought and will, contemplation and ardor, which his personal experience had impressed
upon him. --- Besides Plato and Kant, the study of the sacred writings of the Hindus (in
Anquetil du Perron's Latin translation) also played its part in the development of his
views. Already the Hindus had stopped at the problem that was for Schopenhauer the chief
philosophical problem: the problem of physical and moral evil. He set Buddhism and
primitive Christianity so high because these religions were faith in a redeemer more
than in a creator. The wonder which according to Plato is the beginning of philosophy
has --- says Schopenhauer --- the character of dismay and sorrow. And the problem
becomes so sharp because evil, although it is that which ought not to be, must
nevertheless have its germ in the very kernel of the world, since it cannot, after all,
arise out of nothing. Here lies ``the punctum pruriens of metaphysics, which puts
humanity in an unrest that can be quieted neither by skepticism nor by criticism.''

It was, however, the epistemological grounding of his
% --- p. 214 ---
\opage{214}system that he worked out first. True to his fundamental proposition of
standing toward life as a thinking spectator, he withdrew in the year 1813 --- while the
youth of Germany were streaming to the colors to free the fatherland, and everything was
filled with war fever and the clash of arms --- to secluded Rudolstadt, and in this
idyllic retreat wrote his doctoral dissertation \textit{Ueber die vierfache Wurzel des
Satzes vom zureichenden Grunde} (1813). He means to show here that all our
representations stand in a law-governed connection, which appears in four forms: 1) as
the relation between ground and consequent, 2) as the relation between cause and effect,
3) as relations of space and time, 4) as the relation between motive and action. After
once more insisting on the important difference between ground and cause, the work aims
to show that the principle of causality works involuntarily and immediately in every
sense perception, since by a construction of which we are not conscious we intuit the
cause of our sense-sensations as external objects in space. Schopenhauer means thereby
to correct Kant's sharp distinction between intuition and understanding. More than he
would admit, he is here influenced by Fichte's Wissenschaftslehre.

As regards the limits of knowledge, Schopenhauer comes to the same result as Kant. Since
by the nature of our mind we bring all our representations into such a connection as the
principle of sufficient reason demands, and since we know nothing that is withdrawn from
this great law of connection and relativity, we do not know the absolute essence of
things, the thing in itself. But he now parts from Kant by asserting that there is
nevertheless a way to penetrate to the kernel of existence, even if it cannot be done by
the way of the knowledge of the understanding. We can penetrate into the fortress by an
underground passage. For Kant has overlooked (or at any rate only hinted at it in his
doctrine of practical reason and of the intelligible character) that the kernel of
existence must be in us, in our own inner being. We carry the ``Ding an sich'' within
us. The craving and striving that express themselves in our pleasure and pain, our fear
and our hope, in all feelings and in all willing, are a revelation of the kernel of
existence and give us a key to the understanding of the whole of nature. When we
% --- p. 215 ---
\opage{215}keep to the standpoint of the knowledge of the understanding, the world is
only phenomenon, only representation. But by using the analogy with our own need and
willing we discover that the essence of the world is will --- in many forms and degrees.
--- These are the fundamental thoughts of Schopenhauer's chief work \textit{Die Welt als
Wille und Vorstellung} (1819).

It was during a four-year stay in Dresden that this work took shape in him. In character
it has a certain kinship with Spinoza's ``Ethics'', in so far as it comprises a whole
series of different problems, in mutual connection, within one frame. It gives, in
progressive development, theory of knowledge, world-view, aesthetics and ethics. And the
different ideas, according to a remark from 1813 (Neue Paralipomena § 630), had grown
together imperceptibly, so that he would not be able to say which of the different parts
of his system had formed itself first. It grew up in him like the child in the mother's
womb. Philosophy as total intuition or world-view was in his conception an art rather
than a science. By virtue of the principle of sufficient reason science goes from
proposition to proposition, from phenomenon to phenomenon, from point to point in space
and in time. But the philosophical art forms a total intuition which no longer contains
the answer to a Why, any more than it makes a new Why possible, but answers the last,
decisive question: \textit{What} is the world? This total intuition forms itself in the
philosopher in the moments when it becomes possible for him to hold himself in a purely
objective, intuiting attitude and to grasp the great, typical features of life. The task
then is to translate this total intuition into concepts, and by this endeavor philosophy
is distinguished from the fine arts, which remain at intuition and therefore give only
fragments and examples, no rule and no whole. This conception of
philosophy\textsuperscript{49}) is developed in notes of Schopenhauer's which date from
the years 1811---1818 and are put together as §§ 1---29 of the ``Neue Paralipomena''
edited by \textsc{Griesebach}. (Cf. also ``Welt als Wille und Vorstellung''. Part 2. Ch.
7, 34 and 36). We shall no doubt hit Schopenhauer's thought if we compare philosophy as
an art with historiography,
% --- p. 216 ---
\opage{216}which likewise lies on the border between science and art. And this comparison can
