then be carried further, since philosophy as an art, according to Schopenhauer,
presupposes the critical philosophy, just as historiography presupposes historical
criticism. When Schopenhauer thinks that no philosopher before him had held this
conception, he is mistaken. Metaphysical idealism in all its forms --- especially in
Leibniz, Herder and Schelling --- is built on a total intuition which illuminates the
innermost of the world by means of the analogy with what stirs in man's own inner being.
On such an inference from analogy rests Schopenhauer's artistic beholding of existence
too. Schopenhauer's answer to the question \textit{What:} ``The innermost essence of the
world is will!'' --- is not new either; Kant, Fichte and Schelling had already solved the
riddle of the world in this direction, even if Schopenhauer has expressed the thought
with greater energy.

Schopenhauer's work can be compared with a drama in four acts (just as Spinoza's
``Ethics'' was a drama in five acts). The \textit{first book} treats of the world as
phenomenon, subject to the principle of sufficient reason. It contains Schopenhauer's
epistemology, which had already been laid down in the ``Vierfache Wurzel''. From the
world as mere representation we go back to the will as the innermost essence of the
world; therein lies the solution of the riddle of existence. In the \textit{second book}
the different grades and forms of the will in nature are described more closely, and
the will to life is depicted as the blind need for existence that stirs in everything,
working its way up from grade to grade, taking knowledge into its service, and at last
awakening to consciousness of its whole wretchedness. The question arises whether a
deliverance from this unblessed, restless craving is not then possible. The
\textit{third book} then points to art: in the aesthetic contemplation of nature and of
life it is as if the wheel of time stood still, the will brought to rest. But along this
path deliverance succeeds only in single moments. If the goal is to be reached
completely, it can --- as the \textit{fourth book} shows --- only be done by wholly
abolishing one's will to live, in pity or in asceticism. Existence is a tragedy. In
Schopenhauer the drama does not get the bright, reconciling close it has in Spinoza. ---
% --- p. 217 ---
\opage{217}

After completing his work Schopenhauer made a journey to Italy and stayed for a longer
time particularly in Venice. From brooding over the riddles of existence he here once
more plunged into the life of the world. On a walk with his beloved he met Byron, who was
also staying in Venice at this time. Both the philosophical and the poetic pessimist knew
how to accept the goods the wicked world offered. From all that had been able to hold
him in Italy he nevertheless tore himself loose and returned home to Germany to work as
a lecturer in philosophy. He qualified as a lecturer in Berlin, on which occasion he had
a clash with Hegel. His activity as a lecturer did not succeed. This way of working for
philosophy did not suit him. Besides, out of defiance he set his lectures at the same
hours as those in which Hegel gave his most frequented course. After making a further
journey he chose (1831) Frankfurt as his place of residence. With great business ability
he had saved his fortune, which was threatened by a bankruptcy, and from now on he led a
solitary, quiet life, occupied with study and writing. His pessimism was strengthened by
the slight attention that fell to the lot of his work. In his indignation he could
imagine no other cause for it than a conspiracy of the envious professors of philosophy.
It was the disciples of Schelling and Hegel who now occupied most of the chairs in
Germany, and Schopenhauer, for whom Fichte, Schelling and Hegel were only ``the three
great windbags'', could not but feel still greater contempt for the epigones. With
justice he was indignant at the mixing of theology and philosophy that flourished. On
the other hand he had only few words of recognition for the critical work in the domain
of the philosophy of religion and the history of religion that proceeded from the school
of Schleiermacher and of Hegel. In the natural sciences he believed he found new
confirmations from experience of his doctrine of the will to life; he collected them in
his work \textit{Der Wille in der Natur} (1836), in which he himself believes he has
given the most thorough and clearest exposition of his cosmological doctrine. It deals
with the subject treated in the second book of the chief work. His ethical views he
developed in \textit{Die beiden Grundprobleme der Ethik} (1841). --- From the forties
on, but especially from
% --- p. 218 ---
\opage{218}the beginning of the fifties, his writings began to arouse more attention.
Several men of letters attached themselves to him and worked to spread the knowledge of
his books. There appeared (1844) a new edition of the chief work with the addition of a
second part, which, in sections corresponding to those of the first part, gives further
developments of its content. Later he also published \textit{Parerga und Paralipomena}
(1851), two volumes of shorter, popular essays which illuminate various of his ideas.
--- It was the pessimistic mood, after the hopes of 1848 had been shattered and reaction
had set in in every domain, that bred receptiveness to Schopenhauer's view of life. To
this was added the dissolution of the Hegelian school, which in turn awakened a sense of
and a need for the critical philosophy, which was after all so essential a part of
Schopenhauer's system, just as he now also found greater support in his admiration for
Kant, who for many had stood as a standpoint long since overcome. His brilliant
exposition won him, once he began to become known, a large circle of readers. Greedily
he received the incense now offered to him, and with strictness he held his disciples to
procuring him every laudatory review that appeared. Not a drop of his late fame would he
lose. His old age became a happy time for him, and in spite of his pessimism he wished
for a long life. He himself had always followed the direction toward redemption from the
ardor of the will given in the third book of his chief work more than that given in the
fourth book. An ascetic he was not, although he admired the ascetics and stood with great
emotion before the pictures of St. Francis and Rancé, these men who had wholly overcome
the world within themselves. From the ardor of the sensual drives old age had now freed
him, to his great relief. His friend and biographer GWINNER relates: ``On this theme the
old man overflowed with exalted thoughts and deeply moving feelings''.
\textit{(Schopenhauers Leben.} Leipzig 1878. p. 526 f.). A stroke of the lungs suddenly
put an end to his life on 21 September
% --- p. 219 ---
\opage{219}1860.

\subsubsection*{b.\quad The World as Phenomenon for Science}

In the exposition of Schopenhauer's philosophy we follow the four books of the chief
work, and the first point is then the world as representation or as phenomenon. Only
sensation is immediately given, and it corresponds only to the changes of our body. A
conception of the world as external comes about only through the understanding, which
cannot be separated from sense perception, at once referring the sensation to an
external cause, which is conceived as acting in time and as removed from our body in
space. This act of the understanding does not come to our consciousness but takes place
involuntarily and unconsciously. At one stroke space, time and causality are released,
these forms that lie preformed in our cognitive faculty. Only through causality in
immediate connection with time and space does external observation become possible. This
theory Schopenhauer sets in opposition to Kant's, according to which the concept of
cause first comes into play when the sense images have been formed by means of the forms
of space and time. But he agrees with Kant that the causal principle cannot be grounded
on experience, since sense observation itself, after all, first becomes possible through
its involuntary application. And from the causal principle there follow, according to
Schopenhauer,
in turn the law of inertia and the law of the conservation of matter as necessary
consequences. --- The theory of the principle of causality as at work in sense intuition
itself Schopenhauer hardly developed except under the influence of Fichte, whose lectures
``on the facts of consciousness'' he heard in Berlin. A comparison between Fichte's and
Schopenhauer's doctrine on this point establishes such an agreement that Schopenhauer,
had his ideas been used in this way by another author, would surely have complained of
brazen plagiarism and found in it a new testimony to human baseness. The theory
mentioned has played a part in modern physiology of the senses, since HELMHOLTZ takes it
as the basis of his work on the sensations of tone\textsuperscript{50}). It is not
conclusive, however; for it must be asked whether that capacity to project and to
localize has not come about by development, and whether experience and the association
of representations have not had an influence on this development. Schopenhauer denies
% --- p. 220 ---
\opage{220}this. ``Physiologically,'' he says (Vierfache Wurzel, § 21), ``the intellect
[i.e. the cognitive faculty, whose forms are time, space and causality] is a function of
the brain, which the brain learns from experience just as little as the stomach learns to
digest or the liver to secrete bile.''

But when thus the whole way in which the world exists for us is due to forms of our
cognitive faculty, the whole world is and remains for us only representation, or rather
a series of representations held together by the principle of sufficient reason. This
does not mean that it is a lie or a seeming; its empirical reality is not shaken
thereby: our experience, after all, comes about precisely through the use of those
forms. The consequence, on the other hand, seems to be materialism, since every
phenomenon is to find its explanation through another according to the law of inertia
and the law of the conservation of matter, which, after all, according to Schopenhauer
are supposed to follow immediately from the law of causality. And it is precisely
Schopenhauer's opinion that the goal and ideal of natural science must be a complete
materialism. He even declares knowledge itself to be a product of the brain, and repeats
(in his lecture manuscripts) a well-known forceful saying of the French author CABANIS in
the following statement: ``Just as the stomach digests, the liver secretes bile, the
kidneys urine, etc., so the brain secretes representations.'' Yet according to
Schopenhauer materialism is right only so long as we are speaking of the world as
phenomenon or representation. Materialism founders not only on the fact that the series
of material causes goes on to infinity, and that it cannot explain the different forces
of nature, but first and foremost on the fact that the whole materialistic world-picture
is only our representation, not a thing in itself. The center of gravity of existence
thereby falls back into the subject, whose states are what is immediately given. All
matter exists only for a knowing being and in its representation.

We seem, then, to be moving here in a circle: matter produces a representation, and
matter is itself only an object of representation! This difficulty falls away when it is
held fast that time, space and causality --- the principle of reason in its different
forms --- do not hold for the thing in itself. The world
% --- p. 221 ---
\opage{221}as representation (to which matter itself also belongs) is only the outer side
of existence. As soon as we ask \textit{what} it is that comes forth before us in the
infinite series of phenomena, ordered according to the principle of reason, the
principle of reason itself can of course not help us. Were we merely representing,
knowing beings, the question could not be answered. Only when inner experience is brought
into connection with outer experience can the answer be reached. The will which is the
innermost in man must also be the innermost in the world. Only from man can the world be
understood. Our inner being must have its root in what is not phenomenon but thing in
itself. The will is Mephistopheles, who comes forth as ``des Pudels Kern''. If one does
not accept this, nature in all its causal series becomes unintelligible; but the veil
falls when we take what stirs in us as will to be one with what stirs at the different
grades of natural causality. (The clearest statement of this is in ``Der Wille in der
Natur'', at the end of the section on physical astronomy). --- With this explanation
Schopenhauer does not think he oversteps the limits of knowledge. There does arise, to be
sure, the difficulty that our life of will unfolds before us in the form of time, and
that the single acts of will are subject to the law of motivation (the fourth of the
forms in which the principle of sufficient reason appears). How, then, can the will,
which is itself phenomenon and is known only through representation, be made one with
the thing in itself? This difficulty seems (as KUNO FISCHER \textit{Arthur
Schopenhauer.} Heidelberg 1893. p. 239 remarks) to have dawned on Schopenhauer only in
working out the second volume of the chief work, which appeared 25 years after the first.
He has to admit that the will too can only be phenomenon; but, he says, it is the
phenomenon that is one with our own subject, that which stands in the most intimate and
closest relation to us, where we therefore have the thing in itself most immediately
before us and in the very lightest veiling. It is the primal phenomenon (an expression
Schopenhauer borrows from Goethe's theory of colors) by means of which we make all other
phenomena intelligible to ourselves. If anyone should ask what, in turn, the will is in
itself, no answer can be given to that. (Welt als Wille und Vorstellung. II. Ch. 18, 26
% --- p. 222 ---
% print: „Villen“ (p. 222) (misprint)
\opage{222}and 41). --- It is clear that by this limitation of his solution of the riddle
Schopenhauer in reality admits that he has not solved the riddle. For a primal phenomenon
is and remains, after all, a phenomenon, even if it is the one that lies nearest to us.
The fundamental presupposition that precisely what lies nearest to us should be the
kernel of existence Schopenhauer has not examined. On examination it would turn out that
the whole problem of knowledge was really posed anew\textsuperscript{51}). This point is
of no slight significance for Schopenhauer's philosophy; for only if the will is
absolutely one with the thing in itself has he the right to regard it as groundless, as
raised above the law of grounding; if it is phenomenon, albeit primal phenomenon, it must
in this respect share the fate of all other phenomena.

Even if the will is regarded as phenomenon, there is a question Schopenhauer has passed
by, namely the one which Hume and Fichte, each from his side, raised: how far we can
immediately observe ourselves as willing. Schopenhauer proclaims an immediate observation
of the will, just as he proclaims that what this observation shows us is the innermost
nerve of existence. His psychology is romantic, like his cosmology. And the psychological
difficulty becomes all the greater since knowledge and will, in his conception, are
supposed to be absolutely (toto genere) different. The will in itself is groundless,
whereas knowledge everywhere works according to the law of grounding; the will is
eternal and unchangeable, whereas everything we know, and knowledge itself, comes into
being, develops and changes. Moreover, the will is the master of knowledge. It is the
will that guides the course of our representations without our noticing it. And
knowledge is from the first only a means for the will. In order that the individual may
be able to satisfy the will to life, it must know its relations to other things; all our
knowledge is, after all, only a sum of such relations. No wonder that knowledge cannot
open to us the access to the Absolute! With full right the mysticism of all ages,
especially Christian mysticism, has maintained the limitation of the natural light! ---
By regarding knowledge as an instrument of the will Schopenhauer becomes a forerunner of
the modern doctrine of evolution, of which his very expression \textit{will to life}
reminds us.
% --- p. 223 ---
\opage{223}But Schopenhauer's psychological concept of will is very elementary. By will he
understands need, striving and craving (the Greek \textit{θέλημα}), not the capacity for
deliberation and decision (the Greek \textit{βούλησις}); he expressly wants (Neue
Paralipomena § 149) the concept restricted to what is common to the animal and man. As
he limits the concept on this side, he extends it on another side, in that he describes
all feelings and emotions as manifestations of will and in consequence rejects the
setting up of feeling as a distinct side of conscious life. Thus not only all striving
and wishing, but also pleasure and pain, hope and fear, love and hate are manifestations
of will. It is the constant, blind impulse of self-preservation, the will to life, that
stirs in all these forms, that spurs on or checks the development of knowledge, and that
gives consciousness unity and connection; on its identity, not on the identity of
consciousness, the identity of the personality rests. --- Schopenhauer's personal
experiences have here led him to insist on differences which Romantic philosophy ---
especially the Hegelian system --- was inclined to blur. From his own inner being he knew
the sharp opposition between thought and need; his intellectual and aesthetic gifts led
him in one direction, his sensuality, anxiety and irritability so often in quite other
directions, and in these elementary forces he then saw outbursts of the obscure power
that drives us and everything onward. It was a significant plea against intellectualism
that was thereby entered, although it set up an unnatural cleavage as the normal state.
This cleavage between knowledge and will is necessary to Schopenhauer's pessimism: for
it is the blind, irrational will that explains to him that the world is --- as it is.

\subsubsection*{c.\quad The World as Will}

What thus appears to our self-consciousness, our inner experience, as willing, appears,
according to Schopenhauer, to our outer experience as our material body. To him this is
immediately evident. There is no causal relation between the will and the body; they are
one and the same thing, which is
% --- p. 224 ---
\opage{224}given to knowledge as body and to our self-consciousness as will. The
difference arises from the different modes of apprehension, the outer and the inner.
Muscular activity is thus not the effect of the will but its sensible phenomenon. For the
will is identical not only with the brain but with the whole body, and not only with the
force that moves the muscle but also with that which forms the muscle out of the blood.
The different organs and functions correspond to the different drives. --- Schopenhauer
thereby gives the concept of will a new extension, beyond the domain of conscious life.
It becomes for him one with everything that is called force of nature. The different
forces of nature are only particular forms of a willing at work in the whole of nature.
Matter is the visible form of the will. The difference between blind force of nature and
deliberate action is only a difference of degree and concerns only the phenomena, not
the essence that reveals itself in them. When Schopenhauer thus leads the concept of
force back to the concept of will, instead of --- as is usual --- going the opposite way,
this is in accordance with his fundamental proposition that what is mediately known is
to be led back to what is immediately known. All force of nature is conceived by analogy
with what we know in ourselves as willing. What really goes on in impact, in attraction,
in the turning of the magnetic needle, in the chemical process, in organic growth,
becomes clear to us only when we conceive it as different degrees and forms of willing.
In ``Der Wille in der Natur'' Schopenhauer seeks to show this in detail.

Schopenhauer's adherence to the identity hypothesis appears, like so many of his views,
without closer grounding. It is not impossible that here --- as in his whole doctrine of
the will --- he got his motives from Fichte, who in his lectures on ``the facts of
consciousness'', at which he had Schopenhauer as a hearer, explained that the body is
the outer, material form under which the ego must appear in order to be able to struggle
with the material barriers, since matter can be displaced from its space only by another
matter. In Fichte, then, a grounding is attempted; in Schopenhauer there is merely a
proclamation. And besides, Schopenhauer commits a
% --- p. 225 ---
\opage{225}very great inconsistency in letting the brain, without more ado, produce the
representations. On this point, then, he speaks altogether materialistically and without
feeling any sting, whereas otherwise he has scornful words enough for the materialists.
His standpoint is this: the representation of the world is a product of matter (in the
brain); but matter itself (the brain included) is only a phenomenon of the will, existing
for sensible representation, while the will is the absolute reality. The unpsychological
cleavage between representation and will shows itself here in its most glaring form. The
Romantic artist's view of existence, which by Schopenhauer's own account led him to his
system, has let him pass lightly over glaring contradictions. ---

Schopenhauer's philosophy of nature recalls Schelling's. Just as Schelling seeks to show
an ascending series of ``potencies'' in nature, through which matter rises to spirit, so
Schopenhauer distinguishes a series of grades through which the will rises from the
purely elementary forms to the clearly conscious ones. Lowest stands purely mechanical
interaction, where cause and effect are not of different nature and where the relation
between them can be made immediately intuitive. With the more special forces of nature
(heat, electricity, etc.) the relation becomes less transparent because of the
dissimilarity between cause and effect. And the causal relation becomes still more
mysterious in the organic domain, where the cause appears as a rousing impulse (Reiz),
since there is far more in the effect than in the cause. Finally, in conscious beings,
the cause becomes motive --- but here, as it happens, self-observation reveals to us the
inner nature of the causal relation, so that we discover that it is a willing. The will
strives for the highest possible objectivation, that is, phenomenal, objective
appearance. This striving is one with the very need to exist. Hence the infinite wealth
of forms and grades in nature! Every grade attained is a barrier beyond which there is
craving. The unity and kinship in nature are understood from its being one and the same
will that stirs in everything; the diversity and multiplicity, from the infinite impulse
to exist being unable to come to a stop at any
% --- p. 226 ---
% print: „sa“ (p. 226) (misprint)
\opage{226}grade or to be contained in any form. And the one form stands in the way of
the other; hence the struggle in nature, especially in the domain of plant and animal
life. The restlessness of the will shows itself also in the motions of the globes
through cosmic space without rest and without goal. But in the world of living beings
the inner discord in the world-will appears most clearly (die dem Willen wesentliche
Entzweiung. Welt als Wille und Vorstellung, I, § 27). Everything presses forward to
existence, if possible to organic existence, and then in turn to as high a form of life
as possible, and in this throng struggle and mutual destruction arise. Men and animals
devour one another and devour the plants, which in turn devour air, water and other
substances. Everywhere ``Gedränge und Gewirre'', and therefore chase, anxiety and
suffering! --- Through pictures of the life of nature, which he takes from his rich
reading, Schopenhauer illustrates this more closely.

In this struggle for self-preservation consciousness, among other things, then arises.
It is from the first only a means of self-preservation, since it brings the advantage
that motion can be released before the impression (der Reiz) comes, the motive
anticipating it. At one stroke the world then comes into being as representation. But
through the representations, its products, the will to life continues to work. When we
represent life to ourselves as a good and therefore strive to preserve it and develop
it, this is due to an influence, unconscious to us, of
the world-will on our representations. It deludes us with goods and constantly awakens
new expectations, so as to be able to cling to existence by new paths. We are ourselves
one with this will to life; therefore we must live, and because we must live we think
that life is good. We are driven forward from behind, while we believe we steer by our
freely chosen purposes. This holds not only for the self-preservation of the individual
but also for the preservation of the species through propagation. The individual feels
here the strongest need, and in its satisfaction the highest pleasure --- and yet he is
thereby only a means for the will's striving after continued subsistence through the
species. Even in the individual choice in the relation of the sexes he is led, without
knowing it, toward the individual who together with him can
% --- p. 227 ---
\opage{227}bring the best offspring into the world. At the bottom, everywhere, lies the
blind, universal need for existence.

While the optimist is blindly taken in by this obscure deceiver, the pessimistic
thinker sees through the illusion and discovers that life is a business that does not
pay. For the proof of this Schopenhauer refers to experience, which sufficiently
establishes the suffering and nothingness of life. But a proof from experience would not
be exhaustive. Therefore (see Welt als Wille und Vorstellung, I, § 58---59 and II, Ch. 28
and 46) the a priori consideration, which rests on the very nature of feeling or of will,
becomes what is really decisive. Only the feelings of pain are positive: in them stirs
the constant need and ardor that keeps life up and drives it forward. Whenever a passing
damping of this inner fire is attained, the need being satisfied, the feeling of
pleasure arises; its nature is negative, only the sign of a want filled. By an illusion
it nevertheless stands before us as a positive state\textsuperscript{52}). On the whole,
then, the feelings of pain are also the strongest. We notice pain, but not
painlessness, sorrow, but not freedom from sorrow, fear, but not security. Well-being is
an entirely negative state. Health, youth, freedom --- the greatest goods --- we do not
notice until they are gone. And while habit dulls enjoyment, it creates the possibility
of new suffering if what we are used to ceases. --- The wretchedness that thus lies at
the bottom the great multitude does not notice; the geniuses discover it more easily,
because the mental powers stir most strongly in them and their wishes are more lively;
resistance and disappointment are then felt all the more strongly. --- This whole result
agrees very well with the assumption set up earlier, that the law of grounding does not
hold for the world-will. The world-will is, both practically and theoretically, a
problem, an irrational principle, something which cannot and is not to be comprehended.
---

As one sees, Schopenhauer gets something quite different out of his philosophy of
nature than Schelling does. Through the different grades of nature the tension grows
stronger and stronger, until at last it breaks out into the light of consciousness and
thereby gets its sharpest form. There is a more realistic character about his view of
nature than
% --- p. 228 ---
\opage{228}about Schelling's\textsuperscript{53}). This shows itself also in the
distinction he draws between the etiology of nature, the demonstration of the efficient
forces and causes, and the philosophy of nature, the interpretation of the absolute
essence that manifests itself in these forces. Had he only held fast to this
distinction! But it does not keep him from sallies against the mechanical view of
nature, which, to be consistent, he ought to have let unfold independently, so that he
could then afterward attempt his metaphysical interpretation. And closely connected with
this is the fact that he, as little as the other Romantic philosophers, assumes a real
development in nature, proceeding step by step in time. He does hint at the influence of
need and use on the development of the organs, but he regards it as a mistake on the
part of LAMARCK when the latter assumes a historical course of development from lower to
higher species. Schopenhauer regards the different forms and grades of nature as
expressions of the world-will, radiating from it, but not in real connection with one
another. And yet with his ``will to life'' and by his great emphasis on the significance
of throng and struggle in nature he stands as a forerunner of the doctrine of evolution
in the form Darwin later gave it. He has an eye for the efficient cause Darwin appeals
to, although he does not grant that this cause can produce the differences of species in
nature. These stand for him as Plato's ideas, as eternal forms for the outbursts of the
unbridled will; an origin they have not.

Even more than by his realistic tendency he comes into opposition to Schelling by his
pessimistic interpretation. His personal conception of life here decidedly comes to
color his cosmology, and his keen power of observation and deep indignation give his
expositions, in so far as they move in the domain of human life, a highly marked
character. It is through his philosophy of life that he has above all influenced wider
circles.

\subsubsection*{d.\quad Redemption through Artistic Contemplation}

The knot is now tied; the question is whether it can be untied. It is characteristic
of Schopenhauer's directions toward a solution that
% --- p. 229 ---
\opage{229}they address themselves exclusively to the individual. History is for him a
play of accidents, like the frost flowers on the windowpane or the figures in a
kaleidoscope, and he assumes no progressive development through the race by which evil
could be eliminated. The will is the same at all grades --- however different knowledge
is! It is a great psychological riddle how this can be possible. Knowledge arises as a
means in the service of the will; but however good this means may be, it gains no
reacting influence on the will itself. On the other hand, in some cases it is supposed to
be possible for knowledge to tear itself wholly loose from the service of the will,
whereby man's individuality is then abolished and he is wholly absorbed in disinterested
contemplation. Thus when one ``loses oneself'' in the beholding of a work of art. This
upheaval and liberation, where the will vanishes and pure beholding reigns, can be
explained only by a sudden breakthrough of the faculty of intuition. One now stands in a
purely contemplative relation to the world --- and one can do so only when one forgets
that one belongs to it. With the will, suffering too falls away. Only through art does
this become possible. Science goes on constantly further in the series of grounds, and
the will always strives restlessly further. But art is everywhere at the goal; it
presents things in their eternal rest, ``under the aspect of eternity''. Schopenhauer
especially praises Netherlandish art for the still, will-less state of mind that
expresses itself in it, and that was necessary for so objective a beholding to become
possible. But the highest art for him is music, which immediately presents the will, the
world-will in its rising and falling, in its elementary and in its complicated forms,
and gives us its secret history, its checks, struggles and torments. It is in reality we
ourselves who are the taut, struck and quivering string! --- But a strong exertion is
required to hold fast the artistic relation to existence, and only few have energy
enough for it. The will, with its never resting need and misery, always presses on. The
geniuses are in a particularly high degree endowed with the capacity to enjoy in the
image what one flees in naked reality.
% --- p. 230 ---
\opage{230}

The opposition between art and life demonstrated by Kant and Schiller is driven by
Schopenhauer to the uttermost extreme. He overlooks the sympathetic absorption in the
object, which in turn presupposes that we ascribe a value to it. The value of art will in
the end fall away if there is no value of life at all. With a variation on Goethe's
album verse one could say: ``If you would ascribe worth to art, you must ascribe worth to
life!'' --- It is clear, further, that Schopenhauer necessarily needs a will for the very
artistic liberation from ``the will''; for --- as he rightly says --- exertion is
required to hold fast the artistic contemplation. For the energy with which ideal
purposes are upheld Schopenhauer has no expression, since he denies the possibility that
the elementary ``will to life'' can undergo a metamorphosis. In return he must then
posit one of the abrupt transitions in which his system is so rich.

\subsubsection*{e.\quad Practical Redemption}

Even in the geniuses the artistic redemption from life is only momentary and never
complete. A perfect calming, a decisive quietive, art does not afford, only a passing
consolation. The world-will, which stirs so mightily in us all, as if each of us were
the whole, drives us at the same time to commit encroachments on one another. The
deterrent authority of the state does indeed damp wrongdoing, but the true overcoming of
egoism first comes forth when we bethink ourselves that it is one and the same being that
stirs in us all, so that the tormentor in his innermost ground is one with the tormented,
although in his illusion he thought himself an entirely different being from his victim.
True remorse of conscience and true virtue arise from a presentiment of the illusion of
individuation. Love of mankind in particular presupposes the knowledge of the unity of
all. Since every joy, according to Schopenhauer's psychology, presupposes the removal of
a pain, love can aim only at relief and therefore appears as pity. In pity Schopenhauer
sees ``the ethical primal phenomenon'', and he declares it inexplicable unless one
presupposes the unity of all in the last ground.
% --- p. 231 ---
\opage{231}From it the highest virtues, justice and love, develop.

But the absolute quietive is attained only by those who wholly deny the will to life in
themselves through complete resignation. Only the great ascetics and saints reach so
high that the will to live no longer works in them. Asceticism, then, is not
mortification in order to attain blessedness in another world, but is the involuntary
consequence of the impulse of self-preservation, the need to continue one's own existence
and that of the species, having fallen away. In Buddhism and primitive Christianity
examples of this are found. For him who has seen through the torment of existence and the
illusion of individuation there are no more motives, only quietives. Thereby one glides
over into Nirvana, a state that stands as a nothing for those whose highest reality is the
world of sense. Schopenhauer expresses himself on this in the following way (Welt als
Wille und Vorstellung. II. Ch. 48): ``At its highest point my doctrine takes on a
negative character, and so ends with a negation. For here it can speak only of what is
negated or given up; what is gained and grasped instead it is compelled to describe as
nothing, and it can only add the consolation that it is only a relative, not an absolute
nothing. For when something is nothing of all that we know, then it is certainly nothing
at all for us. But from this it does not follow that it is absolutely nothing, namely
that from every possible standpoint and in every possible sense it should be nothing. It
follows only that we are limited to a purely negative knowledge of it, and this may very
well be due to the limitation of our standpoint.'' (Cf. with this Schopenhauers Briefe,
herausg. von Griesebach. p. 210 f; 359). --- The philosopher sees in the involuntary dying
away the highest form of redemption. But just as little as the saint needs to be a
philosopher, just as little does the philosopher need to be holy. The philosopher has
only to set forth his conception of the world in clear concepts, and he then finds the
ascetic's ecstasy to be the highest ideal, an ideal before which he bows in reverence,
even if for his own person he goes other ways. ---

Here again --- as with artistic redemption --- Schopenhauer fails to give us an
explanation of where the energy, the \textit{will}, comes from that can tear us loose
from ``the will to
% --- p. 232 ---
\opage{232}life''. Even if it is a negative, an inhibiting will, it is nevertheless a
will that is required, and in the ascetic far more clearly than in the genius. Besides,
this break with the will cannot, after all, take place without a break with the will's
forms of manifestation, which were supposed, after all, to be subject to the law of
grounding! Already by his declaration that pity is a psychologically inexplicable
phenomenon he sins against his own theory of knowledge. At several points (besides those
mentioned, also in his explanation of spiritualistic phenomena, which occupied him much
in his later years) he lets, in complete conflict with the spirit of the critical
philosophy, ``the thing in itself'' break through the series of phenomena. Quite apart
from this, there appears for Schopenhauer the great difficulty that presents itself in
every attempt to derive everything from one principle, namely how opposition and discord
within the one world-will (die dem Willen wesentliche Entzweiung) is possible, and
further, how it is possible to explain the diversities of phenomenal existence from the
one principle that stirs in everything. It was this problem that Böhme wrestled with in
his religious speculations; it was this that Tschirnhausen put to Spinoza and Eschenmayer
to Schelling. One of Schopenhauer's disciples, \textsc{Frauenstädt}, made a similar
objection to his master. Schopenhauer's answer (in letters from the autumn of 1853)
really maintains only that the diversities \textit{must} have their ground in the thing
in itself, but does not say how\textsuperscript{54}).

Schopenhauer's radical pessimism is a phenomenon of great interest for the history of
culture. On the way in which he seeks to ground it, not much weight is to be laid.
Neither his proofs from experience nor his attempt at psychological deduction hold good
when they are to ground absolute pessimism. Yet it would not be justified to conceive the
whole as a mere outburst of his peculiar temperament. Every significant individuality is
a point of vantage for the human race, from which it catches sight of possibilities and
of sides of existence that would otherwise not be brought out. And the energy and freedom
of spirit with which Schopenhauer lays bare the disharmonies and the dark sides in nature
and culture have brought it about that the problem of valuation has
% --- p. 233 ---
\opage{233}entered an entirely new phase. Veiling of facts and blunting of problems will
now on this point be more difficult than before. That has its great theoretical and
practical significance. And this gain is not shaken by Schopenhauer's truly Romantic
attempt to make his feeling of life the feeling of the whole of existence. While his
antipodes within the Romantic doctrine of development always strive, after all, to hold
back their personalities, so that the content of thought might develop according to its
own laws, Schopenhauer's philosophy has a more individualistic character, also in that he
makes arbitrary leaps of thought where a transition is to be formed between ideas each of
which stands firm for him in his individual philosophy of life, although he cannot show
any objective, really grounded connection between them. Fortunately, by his own
epistemology, which takes up Kant's investigations again, he has himself put forward
correctives. He stands, like Schleiermacher, as an interesting example of how critical
philosophy and a markedly individual conception of life are united. By their very
personalities these men illuminate the great problem of the relation between thought and
life, even if their own solution should not be the definitive one.

\section*{C.\quad An Undercurrent of Critical Philosophy in the Period of Romanticism}

Schleiermacher and Schopenhauer stand as eminent testimonies that Kant's
thoughts had not come into their full right through the constructions of
Fichte, Schelling and Hegel. Kant was no superseded standpoint; in the midst of
the apparent sole dominion of Romantic speculation he always had a circle of
faithful and understanding followers. There was always an undercurrent which,
though it was not able to break through the speculative overcurrent before it
got help from natural science and historical criticism, is nevertheless of
great importance, partly for philosophical inquiry itself through its results,
partly for the history of
% --- p. 234 ---
\opage{234}philosophy as a testimony that the continuity in the history of
thought was not broken off by the speculative philosophers' adventures of
thought. First and foremost we must mention here a whole series of men who did
not come forward with the claim to be philosophers by profession, but whose
view of life had been determined by Kant's philosophy, and who faithfully
preserved this view of life during their activity in larger or smaller circles.
In several regions of Germany associations were formed of men of the most
various age and station for the common study of Kant, and there were many
individuals, in part among the most distinguished men of the time, who were
able to preserve the kernel of the master's thought while disregarding the
inessential in the forms in which he had clothed it. It is of particular
interest to see that in the circle of the men to whom Germany owes its
spiritual and political rebirth after the defeats at the beginning of the
nineteenth century there are not a few of Kant's disciples. Besides
Schleiermacher and Fichte we must mention here \textsc{Wilhelm Von
Humboldt}, who organized the educational system in Prussia, and \textsc{Theodor
Von Schön}, who carried through the abolition of serfdom. ``In contrast with
the raw reality we see the statesmen of that time approach the problems of
agrarian legislation, of freedom of trade and of the constitution of the towns
with the idealism of the Königsberg school'' (Gneist.) As regards Denmark, we
may mention here the great jurist \textsc{A. S. Ørsted}, who in his youth was an
ardent Kantian, and who in his old age declared \textit{(Af mit Livs og min Tids
Historie.} Copenhagen 1851. I. p. 35) that the influence Kant's ethics had had
on his mind had never at any time been lost. Ørsted says in this connection:
``When one of the statesmen who had had a part in leading Prussia's rebirth,
and who had always remained true to the spirit from which it went forth
(Minister of State von Schön), received on the occasion of his official jubilee
a beautiful and warm tribute from his fellow citizens, he testified that if he
had accomplished anything useful for his fatherland, he owed it to the way of
thinking which his great teacher Kant had implanted in him, and that he must
therefore lead the thanks that had been brought to him back to the source of
which he was only a little brook. Without otherwise being able to make any
comparison, I am seized
% --- p. 235 ---
% scan: „ban“ (p. 235)
\opage{235}by a similar feeling when I think about what Kant has been to me and
to many others in my fatherland.'' Yet it was not only Kant's influence as an
ethicist that held its ground despite the Romantic overcurrent. The strict
demand he had made of grounding, and the critical understanding he had gained
of the limits of knowledge, made a great many of his disciples regard the
speculative turn that philosophy took with his most prominent successors with
indignation and contempt. In an exceptionally clear and interesting way this
is seen in the ardent Kantian, the physician \textsc{Joh. Benj. Erhard}, whose
autobiography and correspondence \textsc{Varnhagen Von Ense} has published. In a
letter of May 19, 1794, he says (with reference to Fichte): ``The philosophy
that \textit{proceeds from} one fundamental proposition and dares to derive
everything from it is and remains always a sophistical trick; but the
philosophy that \textit{ascends to} the highest fundamental proposition and
presents everything else in perfect harmony with it, without deriving it from
it, is the true one . . . Kant's philosophy does not reign at all among his
disciples; for they want to make reason \textit{constitutive . . .} I have
already once written to Reinhold about it and proved to him that a theory of
representations is impossible; only an analysis of them is possible.'' All our
judgments, Erhard next shows, are formed by analysis. This holds in the
empirical sciences, and it holds also in philosophy, where ``we attain all our
knowledge by \textit{analysis of the concepts formed by us without reflection;}
if one does not attend to this, one constructs for oneself a system of the
original concepts, instead of knowing the actual system.'' The misgivings
Erhard expresses here were shared by several of his friends, thus also, as
already suggested, by Schiller. The famous jurist \textsc{Anselm Feuerbach}
likewise says in a letter that ``he who has drawn nourishment from Kant's
spirit and knows that play with empty concepts is not philosophy'' cannot share
the enthusiasm with which the new philosophy was received by most.
\textit{(Biographischer Nachlass.} 2. Ausg. I. p. 51). And Wilhelm von Humboldt
felt, precisely at the time when Hegel stood at the height of his fame, the
need to give a character portrait of Kant permeated by deep admiration, in
which Kant is praised for having, by his critical
% --- p. 236 ---
\opage{236}work, given philosophical analysis its proper foundation, for having
united ``a perhaps unsurpassed dialectic'' with ``a sense for the truth that
cannot be reached by this way'', and for having taught philosophizing rather
than philosophy, for having awakened to seeking rather than communicated
results. \textit{(Ueber Schiller und den Gang seiner Geistesentwickelung. ---}
Introduction to \textit{Briefwechsel zwischen Schiller und Wilhelm v. Humboldt.}
Stuttgart und Tübingen. 1830. p. 45---49).

At the same time as Erhard expressed his misgivings about the constructive turn
in philosophy, two of Fichte's hearers in Jena worked out critiques of the
``Wissenschaftslehre'' which became for them introductions to long labor of
thought. \textsc{Fries} and \textsc{Herbart} both set themselves the task of
working further in Kant's spirit, since they could not acknowledge as the right
one the way by which Fichte wanted to carry Kant's philosophy further. Each in
his own way they seek to give a further elaboration to the psychological
foundation on which Kant's philosophy in reality --- though he was loath to
admit it --- rested. Thereby they gain great importance for the history of
psychology. They maintain the right and importance of empirical psychology over
against the speculative constructions. Their sober intellectual tendency and
their able insight into natural science place them in several respects as
representatives of a line of thought that one does not usually date back to the
period of Romanticism. In line with them there later came \textsc{Beneke},
whose merits also lie mainly in the domain of psychology. If these three
investigators were able only to maintain and continue an undercurrent, not to
break through the overcurrent, it came from the subdued, reserved quality of
their nature. Their domain was the empirical and criticism, not the world of
striking ideas and brilliant views. But their quiet work has borne its fruit.

\subsection*{a.\quad Jacob Friedrich Fries}

Like Schleiermacher, Fries came out of the Moravian Brethren and bore marks of
it in his spiritual life, partly in the weight he lays on feeling as the
foundation of faith and presentiment, partly --- by a natural effect of
contrast --- in the criticism he
% --- p. 237 ---
\opage{237}directs at the influence feeling can have in making knowledge
dogmatic and in paralyzing the will. And like Schleiermacher he worked his way
by independent thinking out of the confessional limitation that reigned at the
Herrnhut school in Niesky, where he came in the year 1792, 19 years old.
According to what he himself has stated (in notes used by \textsc{Henke}:
\textit{Jacob Friedrich Fries.} Aus seinem handschriftlichen Nachlasse
dargestellt. Leipzig 1867), it was personal experience and psychological study
that brought him away from positive faith. In vain he had exerted himself and
struggled to force in himself the devout moods that were demanded in the
Herrnhuters' many quiet hours; he now saw that it was his own natural feeling
and imagination that he had wanted to drive up to an artificial height. He also
came to have ethical misgivings about the doctrine of atonement. But religious
life did not thereby lose its importance for him. Like Schleiermacher, he found
a symbolic value in the religious representations, and despite all dogmatic
negation he felt spiritually akin to the Moravian Brethren, with several of
whose members he kept up a warm friendship all his life. His philosophical
development was determined by his being introduced to Kant's philosophy already
at the Herrnhut college, where it was presented to the pupils especially in the
form Reinhold had given it. Only in secret could Fries read Kant's own works,
and here it particularly interested him to see the way by which Kant had come
to his results. The psychological analysis on which Kant laid so much weight in
his early writings, and which in his ``Kritik der reinen Vernunft'' is called
the subjective deduction, but which he pushed more and more aside, became in
Fries's eyes the most important thing. But Fries already now missed in Kant a
thorough treatment of the psychological foundation of epistemology, and he set
himself as his life's task to bring it about.
After leaving the Herrnhut college he studied in Leipzig, where the
psychologist \textsc{Plattner} gained a great and lasting influence on his views, and
then in Jena, where Fichte was just then at the height of his power and his
fame. Fichte's Wissenschaftslehre did not satisfy him
% --- p. 238 ---
% print: „(1812.“, no closing parenthesis (p. 238) (misprint)
\opage{238}at all. He found his first demands on scientific method unfulfilled
by this attempt to set up one single highest principle and to proceed from it.
First psychological description, then analysis and abstraction --- and only
then, if possible, a construction, which can nevertheless never become anything
but hypothetical --- these were the fundamental propositions Fries had already
gained, partly by his own thinking, partly by his ardent study of mathematics
and natural science, which he had begun in Niesky and continued in Jena. Even
before he came to Jena, he had worked out a series of essays in which he showed
the importance of empirical psychology for the philosophical problems. The
objections he had to make against speculative philosophy, and which Fichte's
lectures aroused in him, he wrote down, and on the basis of them he later
worked out his polemic: \textit{Reinhold, Fichte und Schelling} (1803,
published again 1824 under the title \textit{Polemische Schriften.} I), a book
which first made his name known, and which still has great interest through
its characterization of philosophical method. For some years he lived as a
private tutor in Switzerland and continued his philosophical and scientific
studies. Then he worked as a lecturer in Jena, in opposition to the speculative
philosophy that reigned in this hearth of Romanticism. As professor in
Heidelberg he published \textit{Wissen, Glaube und Ahndung} (1805), a popular
presentation of his epistemological and religious-philosophical views, and
then his chief work \textit{Neue Kritik der Vernunft} (1806---7), in which he
took up Kant's line of thought and sought to correct it and carry it further.
Besides Kant he was also influenced by Jacobi, whose emphasis on immediate
consciousness and on feeling agreed with his conviction of the fundamental
importance of psychological experience. But while Kant wanted to prove too much
and thereby led astray into a new dogmatism, Jacobi wanted to prove too little
and thereby really remained standing outside philosophy. In a polemic (against
Schelling), \textit{Von deutscher Philosophie Art und Kunst} (1812), Fries has
developed more closely his relation to Kant, Jacobi and the philosophy of
Romanticism. Throughout the last part of his life (1816---43) Fries worked as
professor in Jena. Because of his
% --- p. 239 ---
\opage{239}liberal political views, which he had developed in novels and
pamphlets, it was a special joy to him to come back to Karl August's duchy,
since this little country was the only one where the promises given by the
princes after the Wars of Liberation, of the introduction of constitutions of
estates, had been fulfilled. As Kant's disciple Fries laid great weight in his
ethics on the feeling of personal dignity and insisted that a vigorous personal
life could unfold only in a public life permeated by the ideas of honor and
justice; ``it is'', he says in his Ethics published in 1818 (p. 377), ``the
disgrace of peoples to slave for the private purposes of single men or single
estates, and the true demand for civil freedom amounts to this, that only the
public purposes are valid in the state''. In this spirit he sought to influence
the academic youth, who now after the war had returned to their studies; he
wished thereby also to work against the coarseness by which the earlier
student life had been marked. Energetically he warned against secret
societies, whereas he sympathized with the formation of a general German
students' union, by which the bond knit by the common struggle against the
conqueror of the world could be preserved. His participation in the Wartburg
festival of 1817, where speeches were held in this spirit, and where, in
imitation of Luther's burning of the papal bull, a number of (really or
supposedly) reactionary books were burned, raised a storm against him which
Karl August, who was favorably disposed toward him, sought in vain to avert.
From the Prussian and Austrian side his dismissal was demanded, and when Sand,
one of Fries's hearers, had murdered the writer Kotzebue (who stood as a symbol
of reaction and foreign influence), it became necessary to give way, yet in
such a way that Fries gave up only the professorship of philosophy and instead
took over a professorship of physics. Already in Heidelberg he had combined
teaching in physics and in philosophy, a proof of the thoroughness of his
scientific training. He has published a mathematical philosophy of nature, a
physics and a popular astronomy, works that won him the recognition of Gauss
and Alexander von Humboldt. This side of Fries's activity is significant in
that he maintains the strict mechanical view of nature, which the Romantic
% --- p. 240 ---
\opage{240}philosophy of nature had believed it could push aside as an
accident. It was Fries's conviction, which he has expressed among other places
in his \textit{Geschichte der Philosophie, dargestellt nach den Fortschritten
ihrer wissenschaftlichen Entwickelung} (1837 ---40), a work outstanding for its
time, that it is the strict scientific conception of the phenomena of outer
and inner experience that first really gives the philosophical problems of
modern times their sting. From this side he sympathizes with Spinoza, whose
identity hypothesis he embraces, while he opposes Spinoza as a constructive
philosopher. In his \textit{Psychische Anthropologie} (1820---21) he builds on
self-observation and physiology and gives interesting contributions both to the
doctrine of sense perception, to the doctrine of the association of
representations (the psychical mechanism) and to the doctrine of the unity and
activity of mental life at all stages. With all its defects this work is a
forerunner of the psychology of the most recent times. ---

Fries always regarded himself as a Kantian. Two years before his death he
still writes to his friend and disciple the theologian \textsc{De Wette}: ``As regards
the belief in Kant's victory in the future, I think thus: when clear and firm
science is once again demanded in the philosophical domain, then we shall be
proved right. But when that will happen, I do not know''. (Henke p. 268). But
it was not his intention to approve Kant's philosophy as it stood. He missed a
psychological foundation for the self-knowledge in which, according to Kant,
the critical philosophy was to consist. Self-observation is to show us in what
forms our knowledge (reason in the widest sense, working both in sense
perception and in thinking) involuntarily works. From psychological experience
the fundamental concepts that express these forms are then extracted by
abstraction (not induction). But the result we can reach in this way can only
be probable; there is no absolute guarantee that we have really found the right
fundamental concepts. Only that knowledge can be apodictic which builds on the
forms of the self-activity of the knowing mind; but this self-activity is never
unconditioned, since it must always be awakened by impressions it does not
itself produce; and even where we (as in logic and mathematics)
% --- p. 241 ---
\opage{241}have found pure forms of thought by abstraction, the knowledge that
can be built on them is only purely formal. Nevertheless Fries assumes that a
complete system of fundamental concepts (categories and ideas) can be set up,
by whose help we can survey the whole domain of the knowledge of nature. He
thinks that Kant succeeded in the complete enumeration of the fundamental
concepts, and in his own exposition he therefore also follows Kant's system.
There is a problem here that Fries has not seen sharply. He admits that all
psychological experience is \textit{fragmentary:} it is only by reflection, by
``re-consciousness'', an attention directed toward our own involuntary mental
activity, that we discover the forms we use immediately and involuntarily, and
this reflection takes place successively and occasionally and is never
completed. But nevertheless we are thereby to discover the \textit{constant}
and \textit{unchangeable} way in which our reason works. (See especially ``Neue
Kritik'', I. p. 198---200). Rightly Fries says that ``the whole secret of
philosophy lies hidden here.'' This secret he has not unveiled to the degree he
himself thinks. Both Kant's systematics and Jakobi's faith have here exercised
too great an influence on him and prevented him from carrying the analysis
sufficiently far. --- Add to this, moreover, that Fries speaks mostly of the
psychological analysis that shows the subjective condition of knowledge, not so
much of the logical analysis by which we go back from what is objectively given
to the conditions of its being understood (Kant's objective deduction). ---

Another chief objection to Kant on Fries's part is that Kant nourished the
illusion of being able to give a proof of the objective validity of knowledge.
Fries agrees with Maimon that Kant has only shown that we in fact have and use
certain categories (qvæstio facti), but not that we have the right to use them
(qvæstio juris). The objective validity of our knowledge cannot be proved. We
cannot compare knowledge and existence, but only mediate, reflected knowledge
with immediate knowledge. Truth does not mean the agreement of knowledge with
its object, but the agreement of mediate knowledge with immediate knowledge;
every grounding therefore becomes in the end subjective. (Neue Kritik. I. p. 288 ---
% --- p. 242 ---
\opage{242}295. Polem. Schr. p. 124, 351---354). Kant pointed to this but did
not hold fast to it, which in turn has led his speculative successors to
confuse the relation between the subject of knowledge and its object (a
relation that does not fall outside knowledge itself) with a causal relation,
and to revel in mystical ideas of the unity of thinking and being.

Against speculative philosophy Fries maintains not only that we can set up no
conclusive \textit{constitutive} principles, but only regulative ones. He
states besides that the real philosophical work in any case lies in the
regressive, analytical method, which on the basis of what is given leads to the
discovery of the fundamental concepts that condition understanding. Speculation
leads easily to intellectual laziness; only criticism necessarily makes one
diligent. Idealism and dogmatism are not --- as Fichte thought --- the greatest
opposites. Idealism can be just as dogmatic as materialism, when it does not
examine its own presuppositions. Only in their results, not in method, do they
stand opposed to each other; but of the greatest importance is the opposition
that concerns method, the real art of philosophizing, and here it is criticism
that forms the opposite of all dogmatism, whether this appears in idealist or
in materialist form (Polem. Schr. p. 257). The system is not so important as
the method. The system has importance by bringing order and clarity into our
knowledge; but whoever hopes to attain more by its help, whoever wants to
extend his knowledge by the system, deceives himself (Neue Kritik § 70).

The limit of our knowledge is marked for Fries by the fact that in science we
can form no completed series, can reach no concluded whole. Everything in
material nature is subject to the laws of physics, everything in mental nature
to those of psychology, and by way of analogy we can imagine that the same
relation between a material outer and a mental inner is found everywhere. But
even by this way we do not get beyond the finite --- and there is on the whole
no scientific way from the finite to the infinite and eternal. Only by faith
can the eternal be grasped. Faith arises when the limits to which our knowing
is always subject are thought of as removed --- hence by a negation.
% --- p. 243 ---
\opage{243}Every phenomenon, every object of knowing is limited, and the faith
that an eternal being lies at the ground of the world of phenomena can
therefore arise only by way of negation. Positive concepts of the eternal we
cannot form. Every positive representation of it (as in the usual notions of
God and immortality) is figurative, and if one wants to shape it into
knowledge, one gets mythology. Likewise it is impossible to derive the finite
(the phenomena) from the eternal; the speculative attempts at this lead only to
philosophical novels, which everyone tells in his own way. There is only one
truth; therefore it is one and the same reality which we regard in science as
the finite world of phenomena and in faith as upheld by an eternal principle,
--- just as it is the same phenomenal world which we regard in physics from the
outer, in psychology from the inner side. Like Kant, Fries distinguishes the
ideas, as representations of absolute totality, from the concepts, whose object
is always limited and relative. But he parts from Kant and the Romantics by
maintaining that the ideas arise by a negative way. For faith, however, more is
required than merely the negation of the limits; faith is a conviction grounded
on interest, on the feeling of value. And even if the content of faith cannot
be represented except in a symbolic way, certain phenomena can nevertheless be
interpreted as revelations of the eternal that is inaccessible to thought. In
the beautiful and the sublime in nature the presentiment of the eternal as the
true essence of things has its foundation, and the highest beauty and
sublimity is that which a human being's personality can offer. For Fries there
is a close kinship between aesthetic and religious feeling, far more than in
Schleiermacher, of whom his philosophy of religion, however independently it is
developed, reminds us in a high degree. \textit{(Handbuch der
Religionsphilosophie und philosophischen Aesthetik.} Heidelberg 1832). Since
Fries's theoretical philosophy was far more definitely and fully developed than
Schleiermacher's, he also keeps himself freer than the latter from any real or
apparent adaptation to church doctrine. His symbolism is far freer and less
dogmatic. In Christianity he criticized especially its favoring of passive and
humble feelings and its
% --- p. 244 ---
\opage{244}doctrine of atonement, which conflicts with ethics. In Kant's idea
of man's personal dignity he found the clear and complete development of a
thought which the Greek and the Christian teaching had not yet been able to
carry through, a thought which can reach its realization only through the
public life in the state; for only there is man's personal cultivation
completed. Through his calling the individual is bound in his inner development
to society, and in this Fries finds the justification for regarding ethics,
with Aristotle, as a part of political theory, although the fundamental thought
of ethics stands higher than all political theory. ---

Scorned by Hegel, and still scorned by those who nourish a Romantic admiration
for the philosophy of Romanticism\textsuperscript{55}), the sober-minded
investigator has nevertheless developed, in his theory of knowledge, in his
psychology and in his ethics alike, thoughts that constantly prove their
validity and value.

\subsection*{b.\quad Johann Friedrich Herbart}

This thinker --- the most eminent of the men of the critical undercurrent ---
called himself a Kantian of 1828\textsuperscript{56}). This implies that he at
once places himself on the foundation for philosophizing given by Kant and
thinks he has carried thinking a step further. His admiration for Kant did not
exclude a sharp criticism, which went still further than Fries's. With Fries he
has in common what the latter called the regressive or analytical method.
Already as Fichte's hearer in Jena he became clear that one cannot derive
everything from one principle. A principle that included everything in itself
could only be the conclusion of thinking, not its beginning. How will one get
the derivation going from one single principle? How can one thought pass over
into another thought? Already here one notices the tenacious adherence to the
principle of identity, to the proposition that every thing is what it is, which
is the characteristic mark of Herbart's thinking. All becoming and change
contain a contradiction, since identity is thereby constantly canceled. The
Romantic systems with their evolutions from an absolute principle were
therefore for Herbart an uninterrupted series of contradictions, constant
% --- p. 245 ---
\opage{245}sins against the fundamental law of thought. These misgivings
Herbart laid before his teacher Fichte, who could not but acknowledge the
acuteness of his young hearer, although it went against his own favorite
concept of the ego, which Herbart found altogether self-contradictory, because
the ego was to be at once unity and plurality, and because it was to become and
unfold itself.

It was against great resistance from those nearest to him that Herbart, who was
born in Oldenburg on May 4, 1776, followed his interest in philosophical
thinking, with which the interest in theoretical and practical pedagogy went
hand in hand. After his student years in Jena he lived --- like several other
German philosophers --- some years as a private tutor with a patrician family
in Switzerland, and here the real foundation of his philosophy came into being.
He agreed with Kant that experience shows us only phenomena. But while Kant
carefully wants to hold fast to the opposition between phenomenon and thing in
itself, Herbart argues (in a sketch of a ``Wissenslehre'' worked out in Bern)
that representation must nevertheless in the end always point to something
that is represented, and that is not itself in turn a representation of
something else, but is different from all representing. What is different from
all representing (which Herbart later calls the reals) we must think in such a
way that the contradictions contained in the concepts of experience (first and
foremost in the concept of the ego, from which Herbart took his point of
departure) fall away. With this the program was given with which Herbart in
the year 1802 began his activity as a lecturer in Göttingen. --- His course of
development, which offers no small philosophical interest, is described in an
essay by \textsc{Robert Zimmermann}: \textit{Perioden in Herbarts philosophischem
Geistesgang} (Sitzungsberichte der philos. hist. Klasse der kaiserl. Akademie
der Wissenschaften. 83. Bd. Wien 1876). Herbart's later life offers no striking
features. The quiet, conservative man was absorbed in his studies and lectures
and in his pedagogical endeavors. After some years of activity in Göttingen he
occupied Kant's chair in Königsberg for a long series of years, but his last
years he spent again in Göttingen, where he died in 1841. --- Already in two
significant writings of
% --- p. 246 ---
% print: „(1813“, no closing parenthesis (p. 246) (misprint)
\opage{246}1808 \textit{(Hauptpunkte der Metaphysik and Allgemeine praktische
Philosophie)} Herbart had stated his views. His investigations concern partly
metaphysics (which for him means both epistemology and the treatment of the
problem of existence), partly psychology, partly ethics. In his
\textit{Einleitung in die Philosophie} (1813) he gave an excellent propaedeutic,
which has lasting value for all who want to learn to philosophize without at
once swearing by a system. Although the fundamental thoughts of Herbart's own
philosophy naturally come forward at several points, this book is carried
throughout by the spirit of the critical philosophy, the very spirit of seeking
and testing thought. \textit{Lehrbuch zur Psychologie} (1816) carries further
what ``Hauptpunkte der Metaphysik'' (§ 13) had already suggested as ``elements
of a future psychology''. Even before Herbart published this textbook, his
great psychological work \textit{(Psychologie als Wissenschaft, neu begründet
auf Erfarung, Metaphysik und Mathematik)} had been worked out, although it
appeared only in 1824---25.
Finally he presented in \textit{Allgemeine Metaphysik nebst den Anfängen der
philosophischen Naturlehre} (1828---29) his treatment of the problem of
knowledge and the problem of existence.

\textit{α.} From experience one proceeds, and one must proceed. But, says
Herbart, experience does not immediately give us any knowledge. It is not
knowledge, but is first to become so by being thought through. The compulsion
experience exercises over us is an insurmountable point of departure, beyond
which no line of thought is possible. But if we cannot go back, we can go
forward. And we must go further, since the sensations we receive do not lie in
us as a loose aggregate, but order themselves in forms and series that present
tasks for thinking. Until these tasks are solved, thinking gets no rest. It is
perhaps a labor of patience that is required here, when the demands of strict
logic are to be reconciled with what experience offers. But here one is
nevertheless always on firm ground, since one builds on experiences and does
not construct castles in the air. The age has been incredibly spoiled by those
who simply laid down one single principle and one single method, and this has
led to the corruption of the sciences and has awakened in many an aversion
% --- p. 247 ---
\opage{247}to philosophy. Only by regular investigation can this aversion
disappear.

In every sensation something certain and definite is given, which must be taken
as it is. An \textit{absolute position} is given. This is not to be understood
as if sensation were a copy or immediately gave us a knowledge of things.
Things in themselves we do not know --- that is a proposition dogmatism will
never be able to overthrow. But we know that they are; by sensation itself they
are posited. And even if we want to call what our sensations contain seeming,
this very seeming becomes unthinkable if one does not assume a being. The
proposition must therefore be set up: \textit{So viel Schein, so viel
Hindeutung auf Sein.} (Hauptpunkte. p. 20). Every single sensation points to a
single thing that is, a single position. It is, says Herbart, a chief
proposition in all metaphysics, first set up by the old Eleatics, that
\textit{what is is absolutely simple.} As soon as it is thought with inner
oppositions, a task arises for thinking, since identity is canceled. But this
does not exclude that there can be several things that are, since each single
thing that is is the object of absolute position. The relation between the
different things that are concerns only thinking, which compares and combines,
not the things that are themselves, each by itself.

Now when experience shows us becoming and change, we have here a seeming at
which we cannot stop. The task is to find the being that lies at the ground.
The problem had first dawned on Herbart through Fichte's ego, which was to be
in constant self-activity. Later he saw that the same problem lay in all
change, and he therefore also later put Fichte side by side with the old
Heraclitus; the former's assertion: ``The ego posits itself,'' and
Heraclitus's: ``All flows'', are both grounded on experience, but at neither of
them can one stop. Herbart adds yet another problem to these, the so-called
problem of inherence, which arises because one and the same thing is to have
several properties. Under this problem too the concept of the ego falls,
insofar as the ego is to include an inner multiplicity in itself.
% --- p. 248 ---
% print: „Forskel p,“ (p. 248) (misprint)
% print: „(det i sig selv ligesaa uforanderlige,“, no closing parenthesis (p. 248) (misprint)
\opage{248}

The necessity of assuming a \textit{multiplicity} of things that are (reals)
springs from the attempt to explain the experiences of changes and of things
with several properties; --- to explain means for Herbart to remove the
contradictions. Every thing is what it is. When it now appears in experience
with another property than before, this cannot be understood by the thing
itself alone, but requires the assumption of one or more other reals, to which
our conception relates it. The difference with which the real A now appears to
me in comparison with its earlier appearance can be explained by the fact that
I now think it together with B. A has not changed, but I have put it together
with B (in itself equally unchangeable). Thus A keeps its unchangeability,
although experience shows it to us changed. The causal principle expresses,
according to Herbart, precisely this, that a thing is not changed by acting;
the causal relation is thus a timeless relation! Activity (which is indeed a
change) appears in experience only because we set the thing in relation to
another thing. And when a thing appears with several properties, this likewise
is only because we compare it with other things. Put together with B, A looks
different from when it is put together with C or D or E etc. (One and the same
thing is different in the dark and in the light, for the eye and for the ear
etc.). --- The method Herbart uses to remove the contradictions of the concepts
of experience he himself calls the method of relations \textit{(Methode der
Beziehungen).} Not in the single real itself, but in the relation in which we
set it to other reals, lies the ground of what experience shows us. But this
relation is inessential, accidental for the real itself. It is a matter of
complete indifference to A whether we compare it with B or not. Our setting in
relation and comparing is an accidental point of view \textit{(zufällige
Ansicht).}

Although Herbart, against Kant, maintains the necessity of inferring from the
phenomena to the things in themselves (from ``Schein'' to ``Sein''), he
nevertheless really comes himself to the result that there is a very great
opposition between the phenomena and the reals. In ``Psychologie als
Wissenschaft'' (§ 149, Anm. 2)
% --- p. 249 ---
\opage{249}Herbart states consistently that to appear as phenomenon (das
Scheinen) is no essential property of what is, but that every true explanation
of the sensible world must lead to presenting being a phenomenon (das Scheinen)
as purely accidental to being. Being and phenomenon then have wholly different
natures. The true reality does not become, is not altered, is not increased or
diminished; it is subject to the strict law of identity. It is what it is and
needs no development. There is a multiplicity of reals, and from this it is
understood that we, who cannot help putting together and comparing, experience
changes and compound properties. But each single real is in itself (as
absolute position) independent of all others. --- The peculiar character of the
yield of Herbart's attempt to correct the concepts of experience appears in two
propositions: 1) Im Reiche des Seins giebt es gar keine Ereignisse (Allg.
Metaphysik § 235); 2) Jedes Kontinuum ist von der Realität ausgeschlossen
(Allg. Metaphysik § 209).

Now Herbart obviously removes the supposed contradictions from the reals only
by laying them over into our representing and thinking. If nothing is to
happen in the world of the reals, things must go on all the more lively in the
world of representations and thoughts, where indeed, among other things, those
contradictions arise, are treated and are resolved. The inner unrest that is
felt before the problems are solved Herbart has himself felt and described. So
these great inner events should then be only seeming! Since Herbart grounds his
psychology not only on experience but also on metaphysics, this consequence
cannot be kept away. It would nevertheless be a misunderstanding to regard
Herbart as an extreme realist. Of the real nature of the reals we can,
according to him, know nothing, hence not whether they are material or mental
either. Undeniably the materialist notion of absolute, unchangeable atoms agrees
better with Herbart's reals than the notion of mental beings would do; and
Herbart has himself stated (against metaphysical idealism) that the experiences
from inner nature have no prerogative over the experiences from outer nature in
determining the notions of the nature of the reals. Nevertheless he cannot help
using analogies
% --- p. 250 ---
\opage{250}from our mental phenomena. So when he calls the real's preservation
of its identity with itself despite the relation to other reals
\textit{self-preservation.} The concept of self-preservation is justified only
when there is a real resistance to overcome in order that identity may be
preserved, and when a work is performed, when, therefore, something
\textit{happens}. Self-preservation is acting (and so far change), not merely
