being. It is the self-preservation of the reals that comes forward especially
in the beings to which we ascribe force and life, and which in our inner
experience comes to our consciousness as sensation. And Herbart admits that the
only example of self-preservation accessible to us is our own sensations (Allg.
Metaphys. § 329). It then becomes clear, and is also admitted by his most acute
disciple and interpreter (\textsc{Drobisch}: \textit{Ueber die Fortbildung der
Philosophie durch Herbart.} 1876. p. 20), that Herbart in his way --- like
metaphysical idealism --- thinks the reals by analogy with our own inner
states\textsuperscript{56\,b}). But two contradictions remain standing in his
system: between the two propositions that from seeming one must infer being and
that seeming is accidental to what is --- and between the two propositions that
what is is unchangeable and that what is strives after self-preservation.

\textit{β}. The conflict that has shown itself here between Herbart's
metaphysics and psychology he pushes aside by virtue of the presupposition that
metaphysics, which is to test all concepts of experience, must also form the
foundation of psychology. Psychology is to build not only on experience but
also on metaphysics, and, as we have already seen, the problem of the ego is
merely a particular form of the problems of inherence and of change and is
solved when these are solved. The soul is a real like other reals; its
sensations and representations are its expressions of self-preservation. A
sensation arises in the soul when it has to preserve its nature over against
another real. And since the real that lies at the ground of the mental
phenomena is now assumed to be another than the one that lies at the ground of
the material phenomena, Herbart lands in a spiritualism that differs from the
usual (Cartesian) one in that the beings
% --- p. 251 ---
\opage{251}between which the interaction takes place are not of different
kinds\textsuperscript{57}).

The necessity of assuming a soul-real lies in the fact that our representations
always stand in mutual connection and interaction. Partly they fuse together
(by assimilation), namely when they are closely akin, partly they combine into
groups (complexions), namely when they are mutually different in kind (like
color and tone), partly they inhibit one another, namely when they are of the
same kind without being able to fuse. The fact that they cannot remain
unaffected by one another, or ununited and unconnected, shows that they are
expressions of self-preservation of one and the same representing being. They
always have a tendency to make up one single activity, insofar as they do not
inhibit one another. By assimilation and complexion a total force arises, which
expresses what we call our ego (which is thus a result and not a principle),
and which comes to have a decisive influence on what can be taken up in us in
the future. Only what can fuse with (be apperceived by, Herbart calls it) the
dominant groups of representations can win mental subsistence. The
apperceiving groups of representations make up the character of the
personality.

Herbart's psychology has its great importance by proceeding from the single
elements (sensations and representations) as the foundation of all mental
phenomena. He thereby strikes into the way first trodden by Hume and Hartley,
which a few years after the appearance of Herbart's great psychology was
followed again in England by James Mill. Herbart is one of the most eminent
representatives of the psychological tendency that regards the multiplicity of
elements as the foundation in mental life, and the unity of consciousness as
merely the product of their interaction. What the English call association
Herbart calls assimilation (association by similarity) and complexion
(association by contiguity). It is a lasting merit he has earned by putting the
simple elements in place of the faculties of the soul still embraced by Kant,
and by demanding that the mental phenomena be explained by the interaction of
these elements according to definite laws. Through the works that have
proceeded from him and from the many able psychologists of his school
% --- p. 252 ---
% print: „grundet der“ (p. 252) (misprint)
\opage{252}\textsc{(Drobisch, Waitz, Zimmermann, Volkmann, Nahlowsky, Steinthal,
Lazarus),} psychology has made great progress. --- Yet the spiritualist
assumption of a soul-substance stands in strange contradiction with this
emphasis on the multiplicity in mental life as the fundamental thing. If
Herbart, instead of grounding psychology on metaphysics, had grounded it
exclusively on experience, he would have found in the fact that there is no
incoherent multiplicity in consciousness an essential contribution to the very
characterization of the life of consciousness, and he would have set himself
the task of showing how this characteristic trait (consciousness as
synthesizing activity) manifests itself in detail in the psychological laws. As
it is, he ends in a psychological atomism and comes into conflict with
experience by ascribing to each single representation a tendency to eternal
subsistence\textsuperscript{58}). --- And the elements from whose cooperation
he wants to explain everything in consciousness are only elements of
cognition. Feeling and willing are to be merely products of relations between
representations: feeling arises when a representation is pressed by
counteracting tendencies, so that it cannot move freely, and drive when a
representation works its way up against obstacles and thereby more and more
affects other representations, partly by awakening them, partly by pushing them
back. Psychological observation does not confirm this doctrine of Herbart's,
that feeling and willing are always derivative in relation to cognition.

It was surely Herbart's endeavor to make psychology an exact science that
guided him, both when he proceeded from the multiplicity of elements as
foundation and the unity of consciousness as mere product, and when he
conceived feeling and willing as mere resultants of opposing representations.
As the title of his chief psychological work shows, he wants to ground
psychology not only on experience and metaphysics, but also on mathematics. A
possibility of this he finds in the fact that representations increase and
decrease in clearness, or, as he expresses it, rise and sink, and that this
rising and sinking is conditioned by the mutual relations of the
representations. Here it is their mutual inhibition that is decisive.
% --- p. 253 ---
\opage{253}Herbart's mathematical psychology aims at finding definite laws for
the mutual inhibition of representations. Now a difficulty lies here for him in
the fact that the forces with which the single representations seek to
maintain themselves in consciousness cannot, like physical forces, be measured
by a motion in space; it is indeed only a figurative expression when one speaks
of the rising and sinking of representations. We lack a measure in mental
mechanics. For lack of such a measure Herbart proceeds from the fundamental
proposition that the sum of inhibition in consciousness at each moment is as
small as possible, since all representations strive to maintain themselves. It
then remains to determine mathematically how the inhibition (obscuring) must be
distributed among the various representations that are given simultaneously or
are striving upward, if it is to be the least possible. --- Despite what is
interesting in this line of thought, Herbart has not succeeded in showing an
agreement between the results he could thus derive by mathematical means and
mental observations, any more than the fundamental proposition he built on can
be said to be valid. Its validity rests on the assumption of representations as
independent forces. But if the nature of the life of consciousness is to be
synthesizing activity, the single element has no absolutely independent energy:
whether it can subsist in consciousness despite its opposition to other
elements will depend not on itself alone, but on the total energy that
consciousness can command for its synthesizing activity. The more energetic
the synthesis is, the more mutually opposed representations can be embraced
without inhibiting one another. And there is the further point that
representations are not the only elements. In a state of feeling a
representation that is favored by a dominant feeling can go on being far more
uninhibited than it should be according to its relation to other
representations. --- Herbart's school has, in fact, also let his mathematical
psychology drop; at any rate it has not carried it further. But even if Herbart
erred in his attempt, the attempt itself is a testimony to his energetic
searching and to his firm conviction that lawfulness in
% --- p. 254 ---
\opage{254}the domain of mental nature is no less than in the domain of
material nature\textsuperscript{59}).

\textit{γ.} According to Herbart there is no scientific principle that can
combine in itself the explanation of reality and the demonstration of value.
The science of valuation (which Herbart calls aesthetics in the widest sense)
must therefore be kept separate from the science of the reality of things. In
this distinction between theory and practice, too, Herbart is a Kantian. Here
too he opposes the philosophy of Romanticism, whose principle of unity was to
contain at once the explanation of reality and the standard for valuation. For
himself the difference between these two things becomes all the more
necessary, since theoretical science, in his conception, ends with the
assumption of relationless reals, while valuing judgments concern precisely
not realities but relations between realities. When we call something
beautiful or ugly, praiseworthy or disgraceful, it is the relation between the
properties of things, or between the different tendencies in a single man, or
between the wills of different men toward one another, that we have in view.
--- The specifically ethical judgments differ from aesthetic judgments in
general in that they concern something which can not merely be possessed as a
thing of value, but which conditions the unconditioned value of the person
himself.

Just as important as it is to subject the concepts of experience to a testing
criticism, just so important is it to test the concepts of valuation,
especially the ethical ones. We often pass valuing judgments without noticing
it, and therefore false accessory notions can easily creep in; motives other
than the purely ethical can be stirring and be mixed up with these. The task
then is to bring out the simple fundamental relations that valuation concerns,
in order to discover by which practical ideas we are guided. A practical idea
is an exemplar that involuntarily hovers before us in our judgment when we
clearly judge the harmonious or disharmonious relation between a man's
conviction and his action, or between the striving of several men in relation
to one another. There can be disharmony between what a man considers right and
the actual direction of his will; such a relation we
% --- p. 255 ---
\opage{255}disapprove of as conflicting with \textit{the idea of inner
freedom.} Or the energy with which he strives to satisfy his conviction may be
too slight and the conviction itself too feeble; such a relation we disapprove
of by virtue of \textit{the idea of perfection.} In a similar way \textit{the
ideas of right, of equity and of benevolence} manifest themselves in our
judgments concerning the relation between different personal wills toward one
another. But these judgments are only certain and universally valid when the
relations come forward pure and clear, and when extraneous interests are kept
away. Both an individual and a social development must take place before man
comes to the standpoint where the practical ideas determine valuation. It is a
matter of fixing sufficiently strong groups of representations around them, so
that they can become a power in the soul. That Kant could pronounce his
categorical imperative was a testimony to what development has taken place.
Yet he is wrong in holding that the practical ideas must always announce
themselves through a violent constraint. He who is able to form the practical
ideas and keep them awake in himself will also experience how mild their
dominion can be.

In his ethics Herbart is influenced by the English ethicists of the eighteenth
century, perhaps especially by Adam Smith, whose ``impartial spectator'' makes
precisely such valuations as Herbart desires. But Herbart wants to keep away
any closer psychological explanation of the ethical judgments, just as he also
wants to disregard every practical purpose and foundation for valuation. He
wants human relations of will to be valued as one values pieces of music. His
ethics has an aesthetic stamp, and too little is noticeable in him of the fact
that ethical judgments, where they are genuine and primitive, spring from a
will and are grounded on the thought of a practical purpose that is striven
for. Nevertheless Herbart's ethics has interest through its clear description
and analysis of the most important relations of will, as well as through its
endeavor to maintain the independence of ethics from theology. This last has
all the more interest since Herbart, in religious respects no less than in
political, was a conservative man. In his faith he held to the Protestant
Church, but he insists,
% --- p. 256 ---
\opage{256}despite his theologizing philosophy of religion, that the concept of
God is always thought by means of psychological and ethical determinations that
are taken from man. It then depends on the ethical ideas being developed in
their purity and independence, in order that the concept of God may become the
right one. Herbart's theoretical philosophy offers no points of attachment for
theology\textsuperscript{60}), and his philosophy of religion therefore stands
in a rather loose connection with his other views. Only one notices a
consequence of his psychology when he insists on the importance of the form and
content of the religious ideas making them able to fill men's minds, to form
great and strong (apperceiving) groups of representations in them.

\subsection*{c.\quad Friedrich Eduard Beneke}

In a letter to Herbart (May 22, 1824) Beneke writes: ``Independently of each
other we have arrived at the conviction that psychology needs a thoroughgoing
reform, if it is to solve the task that is set it.'' About the task that is set
psychology the two investigators were not entirely agreed. They both set it the
task of showing that what Kant --- and after him Fries --- called the forms
were results of mental processes, not originally ready-made modes of action.
Even more energetically than Herbart, Beneke conceives them as mental products,
whose genesis through law-determined processes of development it is the
business of psychology to show. But while Herbart wants to ground psychology
not only on experience but also on ``metaphysics'', which here means on an
investigation of the nature of existence that precedes psychological
investigation, Beneke maintains that psychology is the fundamental
philosophical science, since the concepts of all the other philosophical
sciences are mental products, and psychology itself he wants to treat merely as
an empirical science. It is indeed the task of philosophy to lead to a
world-view; but its nearest object is nevertheless the life of consciousness
itself --- partly because this has most interest for us, partly because we know
this side of existence immediately, while the material side is only
% --- p. 257 ---
\opage{257}known through consciousness, partly, finally, because --- before we
proceed to the highest problems --- we must test the powers of the human mind.
In thus making empirical psychology the foundation of all philosophy, Beneke
reminds us of the English school, and he also acknowledges himself to be
Locke's disciple. Only in Germany, he says, do they not know that psychology,
and with it the whole of philosophy, builds on experience; that is why they are
there so far behind in philosophy in relation to other peoples, who have let
themselves be taught by Bacon, Locke and Hume. Even Kant does not hold fast to
the method of experience, but denies it as soon as he passes from critique to
positive development. His speculative successors have, despite all their
brilliance, only harmed philosophy. They gained a great following because they
profited from the enthusiasm Kant had awakened. But this whole speculative
period is to be regarded only as a phenomenon of cultural history; not
refutation, but historical explanation is what is needed over against these
bold systems.

When Beneke expressed himself in this way about philosophy and about the
philosophy of the time (in the work \textit{Die Philosophie in ihrem
Verhältnisse zur Erfahrung, zur Spekulation und zum Leben.} 1833), he had
fought his first battles and published his most important works. In his
student days he had been influenced especially by Fries (through the latter's
friend and disciple De Wette) and by Schleiermacher. Jacobi too had great
influence on him through his insistence on the importance of immediate
observation; but Jacobi's dread of analysis and proof repelled him. At 22 years
of age he conceived the plan of working toward a reform of philosophy, which
was suffering under the wild speculations, and in the same year (1820) he
habilitated at the University of Berlin. In a couple of smaller works he
developed his conception of the task and method of psychology, and he gave
well-attended lectures as Privatdozent. But after the publication of his
\textit{Physik der Sitten} (1822), a counterpart to Kant's ``Metaphysik der
Sitten'', his name --- although he published an able defense --- was struck
from the list of lecturers, without his succeeding, despite repeated attempts,
in obtaining information about the reasons for this step. Only the minister,
who was a patron of Hegel, declared
% --- p. 258 ---
\opage{258}to him that a philosophy which did not derive everything from the
Absolute did not deserve its name! Perhaps it had been inferred from the title
that Beneke taught materialism, although by ``physics'' he meant here only an
attempt at a natural, empirical grounding. The book itself is of no small
interest for the history of ethics, since it speaks for a psychological
grounding of the ethical standpoint and seeks to show how the ethical judgments
develop through reflection on the way in which feeling is set in motion over
against human actions, one's own and others'. Beneke treats the ethical
judgments in quite a similar way to that in which Schleiermacher treats the
propositions of faith, and there is hardly any doubt that Beneke is here
influenced by Schleiermacher's lectures. Moreover he maintains --- in agreement
with Jacobi and in opposition to Kant's absolute and universal morality --- the
importance of the individual presuppositions in determining what is right and
duty in the single case.

Beneke's ethics, however, shows an interesting development. In ``Physik der
Sitten'' he rejects every real content in ethics, every objective valuation,
since such a valuation --- he thinks --- conflicts with the principle that every
ethical valuation is to be traced back to the motives. The ethical criterion is
determined only subjectively, as the self-agreement of the individual: he who
follows his conscience (``Werthgebung'') acts morally. Beneke stands here in a
similar position to the one Kant held at the second stage of his ethics; only
he deviates by maintaining that the individual's peculiar ``Werthgebung'' can
in turn be subjected to a valuation. About 1830 Beneke teaches, under the
influence of Bentham, whom we shall come to discuss only later, that the
subjective consideration not only does not exclude, but precisely presupposes,
an objective principle, a real content. As in Bentham, this becomes the
principle of welfare, to which he gives an interesting underpinning in his
chief ethical work \textit{Grundlinien der Sittenlehre. Versuch eines
natürlichen System derselbers} (1837---40). Five points of view for the
objective valuation he sets up here: the character of the human faculties that
are furthered or inhibited; the degree in which the single faculty is
developed; the multiplicity of mental results; the duration of these;
% --- p. 259 ---
\opage{259}the unmixed progress that is won through them (Sittenlehre I.
p. 132). It is Beneke's great merit to have first transplanted the objective
principle of English ethics onto German soil.
While his predecessors from Kant on had wanted to raise
ethical valuation above every regard for the effects of actions, whereby ethics
acquired a predominantly subjective character, Beneke holds fast to the way in
which actions intervene in the weal and woe of living beings as determining for
ethical valuation, even if this valuation differs from the juridical one by
aiming directly at the disposition from which the actions
proceed\textsuperscript{61}). ---

When his teaching in Berlin had been stopped, he worked for some years in
Göttingen, and from here he published his most significant work with the
unpretentious title \textit{Psykologische Skizzen} (1825 ---27). A place was
nevertheless opened to him again at the University of Berlin, and in straitened
circumstances, without the reigning Hegelianism allowing him to advance to
professor ordinarius, he unfolded a rich activity as lecturer and author in
psychological, pedagogical and ethical directions. His pedagogical writings in
particular found entry into large circles. --- On the first of March 1854 he
drowned; probably, broken down by long illness and by despondency, he took his
own life in a fit of derangement. ---

While Herbart seeks to understand the life of consciousness in its various
forms and at its various stages as the mechanical product of a multiplicity of
single elements (through their fusions, complexions and inhibitions), Beneke's
psychological theory has a more biological character. He conceives the
development of the life of consciousness as a growth from given germs or
dispositions, which he calls the \textit{primary faculties} (Urvermögen); by
these are meant the faculties of sense perception and of motion; --- according
to Herbart, on the other hand, the soul is a tabula rasa before other reals,
by entering into relation to it, awaken its self-preservation. The primary
faculties are bound up with need and striving. The impressions from without
that can bring them to full unfolding they seek involuntarily. And under the
influence of outer experiences new faculties are constantly formed, since the
earlier influences do not entirely disappear but leave traces or dispositions
that act
% --- p. 260 ---
\opage{260}as co-determinants in the later influences. Therefore a constant
interaction takes place between the conscious and the unconscious. By the
concept of faculty Beneke wants to express precisely only the unconscious inner
conditions that, from the first and later at every stage, work together with
the outer experiences. We are indeed not able to separate distinctly what stems
from the outer experiences from what is due to the inner conditions; but there
is no doubt about the constant cooperation of the inner and the outer. Beneke
subjects the whole relation between the conscious and the unconscious to an
interesting investigation. Of other psychological phenomena that are discussed
in his rich chief work (whose most important content he later presented in
shorter form in his \textit{Lehrbuch der Psychologie als Naturwissenschaft.}
1833), we may mention the importance of the relation of contrast for the
feelings, and the tendency of mental elements to spread their stamp over the
whole mental state (Beneke calls this process equalization; it is perhaps
better called expansion). When so many elements and laws determine the
development of the life of consciousness, it is no wonder that the higher
stages can be so different from the lower that they do not seem explicable
from them. But just as little as one can see in the germ of a cherry tree any
hint of the cherries, which first appear as fruits on the developed tree, just
as little can one find the higher forms preformed in the lower forms of mental
life. The forms of higher mental life are neither innate, nor have they come
into the soul from without, but they arise during the development of the soul
according to its peculiar laws. --- Beneke's psychology would deserve a
monographic treatment that investigated its relation both to the older
psychology (especially Hume and Tetens) and to that of the most recent times.

Beneke himself, however, is not entirely clear about the biological character
of his psychology, and he does not always hold fast to it. In his great zeal to
plead the cause of psychological inquiry over against speculative philosophy,
he praises inner experience, not only at the expense of abstract thinking but
also at the expense of outer experience, maintaining that it is far clearer and
more exact than the latter, which is to show itself especially in the fact that
here we can follow the single elements in their cooperation. But
% --- p. 261 ---
\opage{261}this seems to presuppose that the mental products can be wholly
seen through in their arising from the elements, which conflicts with the
difference in quality between elements and products that Beneke otherwise so
rightly emphasizes. ``Let us not forget'', he says (Skizzen II, p. 329 f.),
``that the joining together itself is also something, and that, even if the
result contains in itself no more than the sum of its elements, it is
nevertheless --- precisely as sum and as an organically joined whole --- not
only different from each single one of its elements, but also from a mere
heaping up of them''. In every such organic joining (e.g. in the arising of a
new faculty) there must always be something that is not transparent to
self-observation, just as everywhere in nature the arising of new qualities
poses the greatest problems. And in the domain of outer nature one is able far
more clearly than in the domain of inner nature to show the conditions under
which new qualities arise.

When Beneke has thus come to overestimate the perfection of psychology as a
science (or at least its prospect of becoming perfect), it is surely also
because he ascribes to it great importance as the fundamental philosophical
science. It is from the psychological consideration that we orient ourselves in
existence. The principles of the philosophy of nature are taken from
psychology: since in our inner experience we have access to knowing a part of
existence \textit{as it is in itself,} we naturally conceive the part of
existence that we know only as outer, objective being (material nature)
\textit{by analogy with} ourselves. The forms and laws of the mental world we
therefore transfer by way of analogy to material nature. The philosophy of
nature which Beneke thus adopts differs from Schelling's by being conscious of
its hypothetical character and by assuming only an analogy between the mental
and the bodily, not, as Schelling would, an identity of them. And while
Schelling believed he could put this idealist interpretation, which builds on
analogy, in place of the mechanical explanation of nature, which he regarded as
an error, Beneke holds fast to the justification and necessity of a
thoroughgoing material explanation of all material phenomena of nature. Thus he
acknowledges the attempts
% --- p. 262 ---
\opage{262}to give a purely physiological-anatomical explanation of the
phenomena of insanity, however much he insists on the importance of the
psychical symptoms. In this respect he joins Spinoza's conception (see
especially his book \textit{Das Verhältniss von Seele und Leib.} 1826. p. 219
f.; 243 f.), although other statements point rather to a conception akin to
Herbart's, in that they amount to saying that the difficulties of the
interaction between the two dissimilar elements fall away when one thinks of
it as taking place between the soul and the being analogous to the soul that
lies at the ground of the material elements. Beneke did not attain to clarity
about the choice that is to be made here\textsuperscript{62}). --- Just as the
inference by analogy in the philosophy of nature leads us to conceive all
material beings as members of a series descending from our own station in
existence, so it leads us in the philosophy of religion to form
representations of higher beings in likeness to ourselves. All religion and all
science of religion, however refined and spiritualized this may be, is nothing
but anthropomorphism. And since the distance between God and man is probably
far greater than it is between man and worm, --- since moreover in the
philosophy of religion we lack the support that the philosophy of nature has in
mechanical natural science, --- the religious representations are objects of
faith, and the essential task of the philosophy of religion becomes partly to
investigate the psychological development of the representations religion
uses, partly to fathom the spiritual need itself that seeks its satisfaction in
religion. In the following statement Beneke's conception of the philosophy of
religion as applied psychology appears clearly and interestingly: ``No longer
will the philosophy of religion subdue and cut down the historically conceived
religious dogmas according to a preconceived, narrow norm; but in seeking to
reconstruct all the forms in which the supersensible reveals itself and has
revealed itself to the human mind, and to derive and interpret them on the
basis of the most deep-going self-knowledge, it brings them --- at once
acknowledging them all and subjecting them to a sharp test --- into the organic
connection in which they have gradually developed from the
% --- p. 263 ---
% print: „Religionsfilosof“, the quotation „»Psykolog ...“ does not close (p. 263) (misprint)
\opage{263}first beginning of human culture right up to our days. Here again,
then, it is psychology that has the task of unraveling and illuminating the
multiplicity, at first sight confusing and wrapped in darkness''. (Die
Philosophie etc. p. 27).

Both as ``psychologist, philosopher of nature (cosmologist), ethicist and
philosopher of religion''\textsuperscript{63}) the investigator, misjudged in
his time, stands as a forerunner of thoughts that in the following generation
found a more fruitful soil than he had had before him in Germany's
Romantic-speculative age.

\section*{D.\quad Transition from Romantic Speculation to Positivism or to Positive Faith}

\subsection*{a.\quad Criticism of Hegel and Dissolution of the Hegelian School}

The philosophical situation in Germany when Hegel died (1831) was this: a
speculative school, founded by eminent thinkers, had won a decided
supremacy, while the opposition from the side of the critical philosophy and of
specialized research stirred only in smaller circles. It therefore became an event of
great significance that within speculative philosophy itself there arose an
opposition to the conclusion which the thought of Romanticism had found in Hegel's
system. There were thinkers who would not give up speculation, but who did not see
its consummation in Hegel; they set themselves the task of keeping Hegel's fundamental thoughts,
but of letting him, with his whole system, be absorbed in a higher unity, that is, of treating him
as he had treated the preceding philosophers. And the supplement which the
Hegelian system was supposed to need was fetched partly from the sphere of experience, partly from
that of positive faith. Thus Schelling, who had held himself
back as long as Hegel lived, now announced a new philosophy which was to bring
speculation into a harmonious relation both to empirical knowledge and to religion. He was called by Friedrich
Wilhelm IV to Berlin
% --- p. 264 ---
\opage{264}to counteract Hegelianism, and in his lectures here he set forth
that by a purely rational way only a knowledge of the general
possibilities and laws could be reached, while the knowledge of the real, which is always single and
individual, demands an act of will springing from the personal need which
cannot rest content with possibilities and general laws. The transition from that
rational philosophy to this knowledge grounded on faith and will
Schelling called a transition from negative to positive philosophy. Only positive
philosophy can maintain the personality of God, which was the chief problem with which
Schelling had been occupied ever since 1809, and which now became the problem about which
interest gathered in the first decades after Hegel's death. In Hegel's
philosophy of religion, after all, a reconciliation between
thought and faith was, in his opinion, to have been reached. But soon after his death it became a point of dispute whether
Hegel's philosophy could be said to lead to the assumption of a personal God and a
personal immortality\textsuperscript{64}). Schelling and the thinkers who stood
near him, especially C. H. WEISSE (1801--- 1866) and \textsc{The Younger Fichte}
(1797---1879), maintained that Hegel's system was pantheism, but undertook by
way of thought to build up a theism which was not to deny pantheism, but to
take it up into itself as into a higher power. They sought to show that all
fundamental thoughts gather at last in the idea of personality, and that this idea must stand
as the expression of the highest reality, just as they (by a further working-out of
what Schelling had stated in his treatise on freedom in the year 1809) sought to
establish the possibility of ascribing the character of personality to an infinite being.
Yet at bottom they all come to admit that theism cannot be grounded
scientifically. Schelling's transition from negative to positive philosophy was in
reality a transition from thought to faith. The younger Fichte, in whom
the tendentious aim is stronger than the thinker's interest, returns to the popular
theology's God, finished once for all. Weisse, at once the most acute
and the most profound of these thinkers, goes back to Schleiermacher, whose
philosophy of religion he carries further in an interesting way by maintaining the
close connection of religious feeling with ethical purposes and
% --- p. 265 ---
\opage{265}tasks. In his bold religious thinking he resolutely draws the consequence that
a God who is to be a personality must also be subject to development in time,
and he insists on the real causal connection as the bearer and frame of all ideal
content in existence. He professes (in agreement with Lamarck) a theistic
evolutionism. An existence relatively independent over against God becomes possible only
through the elements of the Deity themselves being in an infinite process of elevation. From
the eternally becoming nature in God springs the material process of nature, after
the divine will has received its outward expression in the fundamental laws of mechanics
(especially in the law of inertia), which make possible a richer individualization of the
divine content of nature. Through the material development of nature there goes a
constant struggle between the organic and the purely mechanical, a struggle which is the
condition for the rise of mental life. --- But the program of speculative theism,
which calls for a scientific grounding of the assumption of a personal God,
is in fact pushed aside in Weisse too for an appeal to personal faith
as the only power that can here lead to the goal.

In a direction similar to that of speculative theism went the views in the philosophy of religion
developed by \textsc{Karl Christian Friedrich Krause}
(1781---1832), which --- together with his views in the philosophy of law --- were set out in fairly
accessible form in his work \textit{Urbild der Menschheit}
(1811). Krause, however, does not care for the expression personality and will not use it of
God. He designates his conception as \textit{panentheism,} because it maintains that
God has the world in himself, is not absorbed in the world. Krause's philosophy, developed in a long series of writings,
which possesses the obscurity of mysticism but also its noble
qualities, gained particular significance for the philosophy of law, since he stresses the idea of
humanity as an organic whole and as the image of the divine
archetype, and since he regards law as the form of this organic whole's
development of life. This standpoint made possible a conception at once idealistic and
reformatory, which formed a characteristic contrast to Hegel's
conservative doctrine of right and has been of no slight significance for the development of
free and humane ideas. Through the works of his disciples,
% --- p. 266 ---
% print: „Venste“ (p. 266) (misprint)
\opage{266}especially \textsc{Heinrich Ahrens's}, Krause's views gained influence on
wider circles, also outside Germany (especially in Belgium and in Spain). In
the philosophy of religion, on the other hand, the ideas of Schelling and Hegel and their
consequences became of the greatest significance. ---

Within Hegel's own school the sharpening of the problem of the philosophy of religion gave
occasion to a split. Some Hegelians held that the master's philosophy, rightly
understood, agreed with the current faith and with the doctrine of the Church. Other Hegelians
declared that, consistently followed, it must come into irreconcilable conflict with these.
Strauss, who himself belonged to the latter, compared this opposition with
that between Right and Left in parliamentary assemblies, and it soon became
customary to speak of the Hegelian Right and the Hegelian Left. The adherents
of the latter were also called the Young Hegelians. The most eminent
Right Hegelians were \textsc{Göschel, Rosenkranz} and \textsc{J. E. Erdmann}.
The Hegelian Left, which unquestionably gained the greatest significance for the development of
thought, is represented by \textsc{David Friedrich Strauss} and \textsc{Ludwig
Feuerbach} in the domain of the philosophy of religion, by \textsc{Arnold Ruge} and
later by \textsc{Karl} \textsc{Marx} and \textsc{Ferdinand Lassalle} in the
domain of the philosophy of law and of society.

Among all these thinkers Feuerbach stands in the front rank. The transition from
Romanticism to positivism, from speculative thought to a view of life and world-view built on scientific
experience, takes place in an extraordinarily characteristic way in the course of development of this energetic man.
In this course of development a whole criticism of the philosophy of Romanticism is contained, and it stands
at the same time as typical of many a personal development of life from the faith of childhood to the
conviction of manhood grounded on thought and experience. It was Strauss
whose \textit{Leben Jesu} (1835) posed the religious problem anew in all
its sharpness; but Feuerbach gave one of the most important contributions to its elucidation in
the following decades.

It was not exclusively the religious problem, however, with which the philosophical
work of the thirties and forties was occupied. An epistemological
discussion of great value for its time,
% --- p. 267 ---
\opage{267}not least through its criticism of the speculative method, was undertaken by
\textsc{Adolph Trendelenburg} in his \textit{Logische Untersuchungen} (1840).
Trendelenburg lays great weight on the philosophical problems arising on
the ground of experience. It is reflection on what empirical knowledge yields that
leads to philosophy. The problem of knowledge Trendelenburg seeks to solve by
pointing out motion as a determination common to thinking and being:
the motion of thought in intuition and construction has its parallel in the motion
to which all material phenomena can be traced back. And when
the motion of will is determined by the thought of a purpose, Trendelenburg finds
an analogy to this too in material nature, since he holds it impossible
to understand organic phenomena without granting the concept of purpose validity
in the knowledge of nature; of the insufficiency of a purely mechanical view of nature
he is vividly convinced, however far he stands from speculative
philosophy of nature. He emphasizes the finitude and limitation of our knowledge and holds,
with Kant, that it is impossible to give our fundamental concepts such an extension that they
could be applied to the Absolute. The power of our thought is to behold the subdued rays,
broken in a play of colors; but it does not therefore deny the pure light from which
they come. As men on whom Trendelenburg's philosophy has exerted significant
influence may be named Søren Kierkegaard and Albrecht Ritschl. --- Besides
this epistemological work Trendelenburg has published a work in the philosophy of law
of great value \textit{(Naturrecht auf dem Grunde der Ethik.}
1860)\textsuperscript{65}). And finally he has worked as an eminent investigator
in the domain of the history of philosophy. Here his endeavors met those of
Hegel's disciples, to whom a series of great, in part monumental works on
various periods of the history of philosophy are owed. \textsc{Eduard Zeller} and
J. E. \textsc{Erdmann}, later \textsc{Kuno Fischer} are especially to be named here.
During the struggle of the systems a natural need was felt for historical and comparative
orientation, and the history of philosophy as a special discipline really first came
into being in this period.
% --- p. 268 ---
\opage{268}

\subsection*{b.\quad David Friedrich Strauss and the Religious Problem}

Already as a young student Strauss (who was born in 1808 in Ludwigsburg and
studied theology and philosophy in Tübingen) had raised the question whether the historical
components of the Bible, especially of the Gospels, belonged to what for Hegel
was the eternal thought-content of religion, or whether they were merely to be reckoned to the
form of representation in which this content appears to the popular
consciousness. In his \textit{Leben Jesu} (1835) he later sought to establish that
in the evangelical history there is present neither history nor conscious
invention (the dilemma with which the orthodox theologians are wont to operate), but myth,
that is to say unconscious poetry, whose motives were partly the religious ideas that
animated the time and the people (especially the messianic idea), partly the mighty impression
which the founder of Christianity had made on his disciples. What the Gospels give
us is therefore --- as Strauss later expressed it --- not ``the Jesus of
history'', but ``the Christ of faith''. As a purely historical person Jesus is really
quite unknown to us; only ``the Christ of faith'' is a being with definite features. In a
concluding treatise to ``Leben Jesu'' it is set forth that the idea of the God-man
cannot find application to a single individual, but that only the whole human race,
appearing in an infinity of individuals, can through its constant suffering,
striving and working realize the divine. What the doctrine of the Church states
about Christ can keep its validity when it is transferred to humanity. In
a later work \textit{(Die christliche Glaubenslehre in ihrer geschichtlichen
Entwickelung und im Kampfe mit der modernen Wissenschaft dargestellt,}
1840---41, translated into Danish by H. Brøchner) Strauss showed that the reconciliation
between Christianity and philosophy which Hegel thought he had reached became possible only
by Christianity's being conceived as monism (doctrine of unity), while it is nevertheless
in reality a decided dualism. In Christianity, after all, the unity of the divine and the human
is realized in only one individual --- all other
individuals fall outside! And in that one individual the unity of God and
man becomes possible only in the form of suffering and through the intervention of supernatural powers!
% --- p. 269 ---
\opage{269}From several sides, then, it is precisely in Christianity that the opposition between the two
worlds, the divine and the human, appears. Indeed, primitive Christianity even gives up
letting the divine world permeate the human and lives in the
expectation that the former will in the near future burst the latter in a supernatural way!
--- The consequence for Strauss becomes a sharp opposition between believers
and non-believers and an energetic protest against all attempts at reconciliation.

Strauss's merit with regard to the religious problem is that of having asserted the concept of
myth or unconscious poetry against the current dilemma: history
or conscious invention. This concept expresses unequivocally what was
designated by Kant, Herder and their successors by the expression symbol. It has
the advantage that it sets the definite task of showing why precisely these
images were formed; it has a more historical tone than the expression symbol. Strauss
did not go more closely into the question which mental powers and drives
lead to the great images and symbols which through the popular religions have
become the property of the species --- what it is that sets the whole ideal-forming
process going. He later acknowledged that Feuerbach had given a weighty
answer to this question.

It had been Strauss's thought to found a free, critical theology. But his
heretical views made it impossible for him to obtain any theological teaching post. He
lived therefore as a private man, for a long time occupied with literary and
biographical studies. Thus he wrote interesting books on
Ulrich v. Hutten, Voltaire and others. Toward the end of his life he returned
to thinking in the philosophy of religion, in that in the work \textit{Der alte und der
neue Glaube} (1872) he wished to show how the religious problem stood
--- not only, as in his earlier works, when the consequences were drawn from
speculative philosophy, --- but also when the consequences were drawn from modern
natural science. He had here set himself a task for which he was not equal. He
was more scholar than thinker, and more artist than scholar. The book was written with
brilliant clarity of style, but lacked depth and inwardness in its conception
% --- p. 270 ---
\opage{270}of the religious and consistency in the standpoint which it sought to maintain against
materialism. In the aesthetic view of life, especially in music, he found a
surrogate for the religious cult, a testimony to how little he had
thought through all sides of the religious problem. After a hard and painful
illness, which he bore with the greatest gentleness and strength of character, he died in the year 1874.

\subsection*{c.\quad Ludwig Feuerbach's Psychology of Religion and Ethics}

This energetic and richly endowed thinker is a fine example of how the
personal kernel can go on being essentially the same although it
appears in the most different forms. It was one and the same interest that moved him at all his changing
standpoints. From his earliest
youth he felt a need for full and positive human life, for ``soulful
satisfaction'', for occupying himself with the questions whose answering
decides the value that life has for man, and whose answering is therefore also for
man a matter of conscience. It was --- according to what he himself stated in his later
years in a self-characterization --- this need that first led him to
theology and then to philosophy, and within philosophy again from
speculative philosophy to a standpoint which roughly coincides with what the
French philosopher Auguste Comte calls positivism. Thought was for him always
the servant of life. He regarded himself as a positive thinker whose criticism and
polemic (which in the eyes of his contemporaries were what was most prominent in him) were only
means to separate the husks from the kernel in religion. He wished to penetrate
to the living human need that lies behind the religious
representations, and therefore he directed so sharp a criticism against these. So far
was the essence of man from being absorbed for him in thought, that he says of himself
(when he was urged to write his autobiography): ``It is impossible for me
to express what moves me most deeply; how much more impossible must it
then be for me to write it and to give up my inner self to the indiscreet
public.'' And in another place
% --- p. 271 ---
\opage{271}he says: ``How far behind our very being do our thoughts, by which we seek to bring
our being to consciousness, nevertheless remain.'' This
incommensurability between thought and personality must be firmly kept in mind if
one would understand this ever fermenting and seeking, ``dissatisfied''
spirit\textsuperscript{66}).

Ludwig Feuerbach was born in Landshut in 1804 of a highly gifted family. His father
was the famous jurist Anselm v. Feuerbach, and several of his brothers have
distinguished themselves in art and science. He studied theology in Heidelberg, but soon
went over to philosophy, which he studied under Hegel in Berlin. The discord in
his inner self which he could not get resolved in theology was ended by Hegel's philosophy,
and he regarded Hegel, who had made him a philosopher, as his second
father. For some years he worked as a lecturer in Erlangen, but then withdrew.
Partly he seems to have lacked gifts for oral presentation, partly he was
opposed from the theological side, since it did not remain hidden that he was
the author of the radical work \textit{Gedanken über Tod und
Unsterblichkeit} (1830). He then withdrew to the country and took up his abode
at Brucksberg, a factory in which he had a share as his wife's dowry,
and from here he unfolded a rich activity as an author. In a series of
excellent works he treated subjects from the history of modern philosophy. Of these
especially to be noted is his \textit{Pierre Bayle,} in which the opposition between
theology and philosophy is strongly stressed, and the independence of ethics from theology
is maintained. Already here his definitive standpoint in the philosophy of religion is
clearly seen, though it first comes forward clearly and definitely in his chief work
\textit{Wesen des Christenthums} (1841). While Strauss, like Hegel,
kept essentially to the content of the dogmas, Feuerbach goes back to the
source of the dogmas in human feelings and drives, in fear and hope, in
longing and desire. His task is not the impossible one of formulating the content of the dogmas
in scientific concepts, but of understanding their origin psychologically.
From the official documents of religion he goes back to the spiritual and
inward life which has found expression in them. And as critical as he is toward
the dogmas, so sympathetic is he toward the source from which they come. On this rests
% --- p. 272 ---
% print: „Feyerbachs“ (p. 272) (misprint)
% scan: „nnd“ (p. 272)
\opage{272}the great difference there is between his relation to religion and Voltaire's.
Feuerbach goes much further in criticism and negation than the French freethinker ---
but nevertheless stands with far more understanding and appreciation before what is inwardly
moving in religion than Voltaire with his dilemma: madness or
knavery! The studies and experiences of the intervening time had not been
wasted. There is a great and characteristic difference between the freethinkers of the eighteenth and of the nineteenth
century (when one keeps to the freethinkers who think). It
was Feuerbach's endeavor in the philosophy of religion (as it was at about the same time
\textsc{Lyell's} in geology) to understand the formations of the past by the help of the
forces that are still at work at the present day. It is the so-called
principle of actuality that underlies his well-known proposition that all
theology is psychology. --- In grandeur of plan, in depth and energy none of
Feuerbach's other works can be compared with ``Wesen des Christenthums'', although both he
himself and his friends have placed his \textit{Theogonie}, published in 1857, above it.

The break with speculative philosophy which had been accomplished for Feuerbach
as far as the conception of religion is concerned had consequences for his whole
philosophical conception. In \textit{Grundsätze der Philosophie der Zukunft}
(1843) he gives a program for a new philosophy, in which --- in remarkable
agreement with utterances in Schelling's ``positive philosophy'' --- it is maintained that
only the individual is real, and that this real is unutterable,
impenetrable to thought, and therefore to be grasped only with passion.
Reality is not a theoretical concern, but ``eine Frage auf Tod und
Leben''. The object of modern philosophy is not what lies beyond
experience, but man himself, with nature as his foundation. --- Later on
he developed in the work \textit{Gottheit, Freiheit und Unsterblichkeit} (1866)
his views on the spiritual and the material; this work stands in his
production roughly as Strauss's ``old and new faith'' stands within his. In his last
years, which were unhappy through want of livelihood and illness, he was occupied with an ethics;
interesting fragments of this work were published after his death (1872) by
Grün.
% --- p. 273 ---
% print: „Erkerealist“ (p. 273) (misprint)
\opage{273}

Already in his ``Pierre Bayle'' Feuerbach had demanded an ``analytic-genetic''
philosophy, and a somewhat more detailed program he had given in his ``Grundsätze''.
But beyond a general demand in this direction he got neither here nor in
his later works. He never entered upon epistemological
investigations, and even where he appears as an epistemological realist he retains something
dogmatic and mystical in his line of thought. And he had no inkling that the demand he
made was already being fulfilled by the works of Comte and Mill. When he arrived
at positivism, it had long since been founded in the French and English
schools. The case is similar with his ethics. There is here something
tragic in Feuerbach's position within the philosophical development of our
century. He lived in a period of transition, and he came to suffer from it. He
had used so much strength in working his way out of speculation that he
later lacked energy, drive and time for a positive and scientific working-out of
his new standpoint. But on the other hand he stands as one of the most
pronounced characters, one of the most truth-loving men of the nineteenth
century. And he is one of the most important champions of a humane
view of life. Humanism was the name he himself held most fitting
for his tendency. --- We shall now dwell more in detail first on his
philosophy of religion, next on his general philosophical standpoint,
finally on his ethics.

\textit{α.} Schleiermacher had determined religious feeling as the
feeling of dependence, but had left open whence this feeling got
its objects. Feuerbach now sought to show that feeling itself
\textit{produces} its objects, so that these do not merely express it, but
spring from it. In place of the mere feeling of dependence he puts
the trust of the heart and the living wish, and finds the peculiarity of faith in this, that
man's wishes are in it freed from the fetters of reason and of nature. What
is the object of man's innermost craving and longing stands in faith as
something objectively real, as the Absolute. The opposition between wish and
reality is annulled. While therefore Schleiermacher sought to show that every
conflict between faith and knowledge rested on misunderstanding or on this, that
% --- p. 274 ---
\opage{274}neither faith nor knowledge had reached its consummation, according to Feuerbach
the most peculiar religious phenomena arise precisely through the inward craving
for the fulfillment of the heart's wishes bursting the barriers set by reason, and
at their culmination the religious phenomena therefore acquire an antirational character.

With energy and profundity Feuerbach has gone back to the
psychological foundation of religion, men's wishes, need and hope. The wish is, he says
(in ``Theogonie''), the religious primal phenomenon, the theogonic principle. This
assertion is grounded in ``Wesen des Christenthums'' by a consideration which has
general philosophical interest.

Man cannot reach beyond his own being; all conceptions and thoughts bear
his own stamp. The objects to which he relates himself therefore teach us his being,
since they are only occasions for him to unfold his being. Only by
virtue of man's own nature does an object gain power over him. And from the first
man has no ground to set barriers to his being. He gives
himself over confidently to all representations and ascribes unlimited validity to them.
In particular it lies in the nature of feeling that it tends to make its
object infinite, to regard it as real. Doubt can first arise when man
comes to know his barriers, and when the understanding begins to distinguish between the
subjective and the objective, a distinction that is not known at the standpoint of
faith. For faith is precisely faith in the absolute
reality of subjectivity\textsuperscript{67}). --- Now it is not everything subjective that becomes
the object of religious faith. Religion arises by virtue of a discrimination, a
valuation: what man regards as divine is not the indifferent,
but that to which he ascribes the highest value. Every man who has a highest
purpose has a God. What man praises and extols is God for him; what he
blames and rejects is the ungodly. God is the book in which man has
inscribed his highest feelings and thoughts. Man's heaven is a
collection of flowers formed by choice within the flora of this world. This
holds of the heaven of civilized man as well as of that of natural man,
% --- p. 275 ---
\opage{275}only that the former, on account of his culture, does not expose himself in such a way as
the latter. From man's God and heaven one can therefore come to know his own longing and
craving. In the divine attributes we have the attributes which man at the
given stage values most highly. That God is personality means: personal
life is the highest. That God is love means: there is nothing that stands
above the loving mind. In the Christian religion God suffers: that is
to say: suffering for others is divine. And in a similar way, in order to
understand religion, we must everywhere make subject what in it is predicate, and
conversely. In Christianity the principle of religion comes forward in its whole depth and
fullness. The mind, the life of feeling, here acquires an inwardness and a strength, but also
an infinity, which paganism did not know; suffering was felt more strongly, and
love was therefore also felt all the more inwardly. The levity of the Olympian gods
was wrecked on the distress of the heart, but the God of the Christians is a tear of love
shed in the deepest concealment over human misery. ---
The world of wishes and ideals man regards in religion as an
independent world beyond, the real world, in sharp opposition to the
present world, the world of finitude, of suffering and of struggle.

But, one might say, how can religion be derived from the infinity of the mind, from
the omnipotence of feeling, since in religion man feels himself precisely finite,
imperfect and sinful! --- Feuerbach explains this feeling as a kind of
contrast effect: man, who has involuntarily put everything over into his God,
now feels himself, in contrast to this, poor and wretched. He sees his own
being in God and must then indeed feel empty and poor when he sees himself in
opposition to God. But in God his being is also well preserved. Man can in
God enjoy his being in far richer fullness than by keeping to his limited
actual nature. --- Another objection runs thus: ``In theology, after all, a distinction has long since
been made between God's being and the attributes we ascribe to him, and
Schleiermacher in particular developed this distinction!'' To this Feuerbach answers
that if one annuls the divine attributes, one annuls the
% --- p. 276 ---
\opage{276}divine being. That distinction is a fruit of skepticism and unbelief. Genuine
faith does not make it. And what does one keep back when one takes all attributes
away? The history of religion shows that as long as one cares to know something
about God, one also knows something. In its classical time religion does not know that
distinction. What Feuerbach is concerned with on the whole is to hold the religious
phenomena up before consciousness in their peculiar, primitive, involuntary
character. Only with religion in its original form will he have to do, not
with the religiosity modified by criticism and more or less scientific culture.
Within Christianity he thus insists on the difference between
original and modern Christianity. Christianity too has had its
classical times, and only these interest Feuerbach, not ``the modern world's
dissolute, characterless, comfortable, belletristic, coquettish, epicurean
Christianity.'' But not even the theologians --- he holds --- now know what
Christianity is. The point has been broken off the original Christian opposition
between this world and the world beyond. Protestantism signifies in
reality an entirely new view of life, different from that of primitive Christianity. Its
morality is purely human; only its faith leads back to original
Christianity. The miracles it relegates to the past, and the Last Day to an
indeterminable future --- and yet faith in the imminent end of the world
belongs to what is innermost in the Christian faith and cannot be separated from
the rest of the content of faith; for this world must pass away if the world of infinite wishes
is to come. The secret of modern Christianity is therefore, according to
Feuerbach, that the theogonic wish, the primal phenomenon, is no longer present. ---

This is Feuerbach's theory in the philosophy of religion. If we now ask what value he
ascribes to religion, it is, as already touched on, very far from the case that he
takes up a polemical attitude toward it where it is original and genuine. Religion is
--- in its classical period --- the only way in which man can
become conscious of his nature and of the tasks it sets, --- the only way to
self-understanding and self-absorption.
% --- p. 277 ---
\opage{277}And it gives man a great horizon, enlarges his sensuous consciousness by
letting his own being stand before him as something beyond, exalted and infinite.
But on the other hand religion brings with it questionable effects. When the
believer has everything in his God, and when the supernatural powers are for him the
true reality, he cannot feel any need of family life, science, art
and the life of the state. The drive toward culture cannot come into being in him. Religion and
culture have the same purpose, and the more man hopes to reach by the one of
these ways, the less will he seek by the other; there will be an inverse
relation between them. It is moreover no altogether harmless projection that takes
place when man sees his ideals as attributes of an absolute being
which stands as different from himself. The more the difference between God and
man is insisted on, the more it will come to this, that the attributes (goodness,
justice etc.) are taken in an entirely different meaning when they are used of God
and when they are used of man. Man must then take his own conscience and
his own reason captive in order to obey the divine will, even if this
commands something that conflicts with what is humanly called goodness and
justice. Here lies the source of fanaticism, the source of all the dismal
phenomena that the history of religion presents. The two sides that religion presents
to valuation Feuerbach finds clearly expressed in Christianity's doctrine of
faith and love. Love annuls all barriers, makes all one in spite of everything
that may separate them; but faith sets barriers between them again, awakens
hatred of heretics and lovelessness. Love is only a predicate of God, and the
divine subject has other demands to make than those of love; one cannot
infer from what love demands to what God demands. Herein lies
for Feuerbach the necessity of going away from the standpoint of religion. He
protests, however, against his own standpoint being purely negative. He
acknowledges the value of the divine attributes, but precisely therefore he will not
have them attached to a divine being as a subject different from them.
The true atheist is he for whom these attributes
% --- p. 278 ---
\opage{278}are nothing, not he for whom their subject is nothing. The attributes first come
into their own by being separated from the presupposed subject. This holds especially
of love, the disposition in which the unity of the human race expresses itself. It
existed before Christianity. Christ was the image under which the unity of the species
dawned on the popular consciousness. And even where faith in Christ has
vanished, the true being of Christ continues to subsist wherever love
reigns. --- According to Feuerbach, therefore, no real values are lost by
giving up religious faith. What is given up is only the projection. We no longer go
over the river to fetch water, because we have discovered that the water we
fetched in reality came from the river. ---

Without being able to enter into any more detailed criticism of Feuerbach's
philosophy of religion, I must yet point out that in his doctrine of feeling or
the wish as productive (the theogonic wish) he does not sufficiently attend to
the reciprocal relation between feeling and the other sides of the life of consciousness. In and of itself
feeling can produce nothing --- and yet ``the wish out of itself and only out
of itself'' (Theogonie p. 57) is to bring forth the representation of God. Feeling can only
act selectively, intensifyingly and idealizingly on representations which are already
present and which man has either from tradition or from his own
experience. The wish itself is determined by the experiences man believes he has
had concerning the relation between his ideals and the actual course of things.
The ideals he projects as divine attributes, and when faith is strong
it sees in the bearer of these attributes a victor over all the resistance of reality.
The special forms which the religious representations take are determined
by representations which have arisen beforehand, by the most different ways. ---
As regards Feuerbach's valuation of religion, he is perhaps somewhat too
optimistic in his assumption that nothing is lost by giving up religion.
Even if religion does not contain, and cannot contain, anything but man's
being, it might well be that this content worked far more strongly in the form
religion gives it than it otherwise can. In any case there might be
% --- p. 279 ---
% scan: „Udtatelse“ (p. 279)
\opage{279}natures that were accessible to stronger influence only when it comes in
this definite form. This great problem still remains unsolved. ---
Finally, Feuerbach has overlooked that there can be no question of a strict proof of his proposition that all
theology is psychology. The philosophy of religion can only
show the possibility of explaining all religious representations as
psychological products; but that they are in reality nothing other and nothing more cannot
be proved. From the content of faith agreeing with human wishes nothing
can in and of itself be inferred for or against. There might perhaps be one who could
accept Feuerbach's method and yet reject his result, holding fast, in
passionate assurance, to the reality of that toward which the boundless craving of the mind
is directed. That was at least one form under which the religious
dispute could be continued after Feuerbach's contribution; perhaps more will appear.

\textit{β}. If all theology is psychology, all philosophy must of course be so
too, and Feuerbach had thus come by way of the philosophy of religion to the
standpoint on which Fries and Beneke had long since placed themselves. In
his ``Grundsätze der Philosophie der Zukunft'' he proclaims man ---
nature, man's basis, included --- as the only object of philosophy,
anthropology therefore --- physiology included --- as the
universal science. The little witty work is full of striking propositions,
but has something oracular in its form that robs it of the value it would have been able to gain
through a full working-through of its thoughts. It proclaims the right of the
individual fact and of sense perception, but does not go more closely into the
problems that thereby arise about the relation between experience and science,
between sense perception and thinking, between psychology and epistemology. Feuerbach
here stood at his limit.

There is a similar obscurity in his relation to materialism in his later
writings. Feuerbach studied physiology with zeal and wrote an enthusiastic
review of \textsc{Moleschott's} ``Lehre der Nahrungsmittel'' (1850), in which
he comes out with the following utterance: ``The doctrine of foodstuffs is of great
ethical and political significance. Foodstuffs become blood,
% --- p. 280 ---
\opage{280}blood becomes brain and heart, thoughts and feelings. Human fare is
the foundation of human culture and feeling. If you would improve the people, then
give them better food instead of declamations against sin. Man is
what he eats. (Der Mensch ist, was er isst).'' And he adds that when the common people
get better food (peas instead of potatoes), a coming revolution will have
better prospects of succeeding. This utterance (which is found reprinted in
\textit{Nachlass.} II. p. 90) has often been used from the theological side to
show how deep Feuerbach had sunk. It shows his ability to impress forcefully and
paradoxically what he wants to bring out --- but at the same time certainly also
obscurity on decisive points, namely concerning the relation between ``man''
and his ``basis''. However much Feuerbach in this and in later utterances seems to
approach materialism, he nevertheless did not himself find the expression materialism
descriptive of his view. (See Nachlass. II. p. 307). In his opinion
man cannot be regarded as a mere product of matter. One must start from man,
not merely see him as a result, as materialism does. For ``life,
sensation, thinking is something absolutely original, of genius, uncopiable,
irreplaceable, inalienable.'' The task then is to find an Archimedean point between
materialism and spiritualism, so that man is regarded both as a material
and as a spiritual being. \textit{(Werke,} X, p. 162 f.). --- What holds
Feuerbach back from drawing the consequence to which his materialistic-sounding
utterances might lead is the same principle with which he works in his
philosophy of religion, the principle of subjectivity one might call it, the principle that
the ultimate ground of knowledge can be found only in man, not outside him.
This principle he applies first against theology and speculation, later against
materialism; but there with far greater clarity than here.

\textit{γ.} Feuerbach's ethical conception underwent several changes. Early
he maintained the independence of ethics from religion and theology, and it was then the ethics of Kant and
Fichte that he first referred to (thus in ``Pierre Bayle''). In ``Wesen des
Christenthums'' he referred, as already mentioned, to the love of humanity as
the feeling in which the unity of the species made itself known
% --- p. 281 ---
\opage{281}in and for the single individual. Later he stressed the impulse toward happiness as the
foundation of ethics in a way that led me in my book \textit{Filosofien i
Tyskland efter Hegel} (1872) p. 84 f. to designate his ethics as ``the morality of
egoism''. This, however, has proved, through the moral-philosophical fragments of Feuerbach published by Karl Grün in the year 1874 (in ``Nachlass'' I.),
to rest on a
misunderstanding. For Feuerbach the happiness of the individual is not the purpose of morality, but
its presupposition. For only he who knows from his own experience what it is to suffer
want and wrong can feel pity for others. Pity and love of humanity
presuppose that the agent himself has an impulse toward happiness --- something Feuerbach
asserts especially against Schopenhauer, who makes pity the
foundation of morality although he rejects the impulse toward happiness. Pity consists in making
others' impulse toward happiness one's own. Ethics acknowledges no isolated impulse toward happiness,
no happiness of one's own without the happiness of others. As two human beings belong to the physical origin of man,
so two human beings belong also to the origin of morality. Through the relation between the two sexes
nature has solved the problem of the transition from the egoistic impulse toward happiness to
the acknowledgment of duties toward others. The relation of the sexes forms the foundation of morality
by putting a two-sided or many-sided impulse toward happiness in place of the isolated one. As
the existence of the single individual is bound to that of others, there arise feelings of
belonging together and of community; one's own impulse toward happiness is limited, and there is now only
a question of duties toward ourselves in the sense of indirect duties toward others. ---
Conscience is not a special faculty, implanted once for all, from which
a whole ethics could be derived a priori. Conscience is only another
word for disposition, heart, pity, humanity. It arises first as bad
conscience, after the act. Bad conscience is pity joined
with the sting of being conscious that one is the cause of the sufferer's misfortune. It
presupposes that I can feel the other's impulse toward happiness, so that in my own inner self I
feel the violation of this impulse and have the accusing image of the sufferer in my soul.

Although Feuerbach expressed his ethical views only in sketches and fragments,
they are of no slight interest, partly for
% --- p. 282 ---
\opage{282}showing in what direction the thoughts of this sharp critic and untiringly working
spirit went concerning such important questions, partly for the agreement
between them and views that had already been developed beforehand by the
real founder of modern positivism, Auguste Comte. --- Within the history of German
thought Feuerbach stands as the one who most energetically
accomplished the transition from Romantic speculation to critical self-understanding, and
led back anew to the discussion of the first presuppositions of all our
knowledge and all our valuation.

\subsection*{d.\quad Karl Marx's Speculative Socialism}

The greatest theorist of modern socialism is a disciple of Hegel and of
Feuerbach. Through Feuerbach KARL MARX (1818---83) was led to a radicalism
that acquired a definite direction when in France he became acquainted with St. Simon's
ideas. Feuerbach now became too individualistic for him, but Hegel's dialectical
method gave him a frame for the picture of the mighty course of social development
through history. From the philosophy of Romanticism he kept the presupposition that
strict science consists in deriving everything from one principle, and in his endeavors
to carry socialism over from the world of utopias onto the firm ground of science
he built on the thought that all social order and all spiritual culture (or,
as he calls it, all ideology) is determined through and through by economic
production and its conditions. This is what has been called the materialist
conception of history. In his chief work \textit{Das Kapital,} whose first volume
appeared in 1867, Marx wishes to show that economic production of necessity
runs through a series of stages (``Entwickelungsphasen''), none of which can be
skipped, although the duration of the development can be shortened when the necessary insight
is present. Modern capitalism, which by many (especially by
``bourgeois'' political economy) is held to be the only possible order of production,
has arisen under definite historical conditions whose time will one day be
past. It reaches its culmination when all wealth is gathered in a few hands,
while at the same time the want of the propertyless workers has risen to the
utmost. Then comes the reversal with dialectical
% --- p. 283 ---
% print: „memlig“ (p. 283) (misprint)
\opage{283}necessity: the expropriators are expropriated! They had ``negated'' the small owners; now
they are themselves ``negated'' by the organized proletarians, who through universal
suffrage have got the power of the state into their hands. By this great revolution, which
the Marxists await as the earliest Christians awaited the Day of Judgment, the
social problem is definitively solved. All means of production now become the common
property of society.

Thus the constructive method of Romanticism was used to shape a social
gospel in the midst of the age of realism. And while contemporary natural science
more and more put the doctrine of slow and quiet development in place of an older
time's theory of catastrophes, the assumption of a development through the collision of
opposites became, through Marxism, dominant in wide circles. Moreover the
``materialist conception of history'' challenged the criticism of cultural history by its theory
that all ideal culture was only a reflex of economic conditions. And although
Marx thought he had given a purely objective theory of the future social
development, independent of all subjective, ethical principles, his line of thought, on closer
consideration, rests in the end on an ethical postulate, namely on the fundamental proposition,
reminiscent of Kant's ethics, that the worker is not to be a mere means for
production, but that the relation is to be precisely the reverse. (Cf. Das
Kapital. I. 2. Aufl. p. 645). --- On all these points such great
difficulties have arisen that the socialist movement will be compelled to seek
a new theoretical foundation if it would avoid building on untenable dogmas.
But Marx's giant work keeps its value in the history of thought through the
mastery with which an immense material of social experiences is ordered in a
grandly planned systematic form.

\subsection*{e.\quad Philosophy in the North}

Only at quite few points in the general history of philosophy is there occasion
to dwell on thinkers from the Scandinavian North. The philosophical
movement has here consisted predominantly in an independent appropriation of
philosophical ideas that were developed in the larger countries, an appropriation which has indeed
been
% --- p. 284 ---
\opage{284}of significance for the course of the life of the spirit in the North, but has not led to results
that intervened decisively in the general development of thought. The critical and
especially the Romantic philosophy thus won disciples in the North too. If
something peculiar is to be named in the way in which the philosophy of Romanticism was
taken up here, it must be that the practical, personal interest,
the interest in the ethical significance of ideas, makes itself strongly felt. And here
there appears again a characteristic difference between the development in Sweden and in
Denmark.

In Sweden there already comes forward in \textsc{Thorild}, at the beginning of the nineteenth
century, the thought which for Swedish philosophy at its culmination came
to express the absolute reality: the idea of existence as a living,
harmonious whole. Under the influence of Kant, Fichte and Schelling a
series of thinkers, among whom especially the energetic \textsc{Benjamin
Höijer} must be named, developed this idea further, until \textsc{Christopher Jacob} \textsc{Boström}
(born in Piteå 1797, died in Upsala 1866) systematically completed the ``rational
idealism''. The world which sense perception and experience show us cannot, according to Boström,
