be the true one, because it presents external oppositions in space, and because
it develops in time. When German speculation sought to show the
essence of the Absolute as engaged in constant development, this was, according to Boström, a sign
that it had not raised itself sufficiently above experience. Even Hegel is
an empiricist when he lets the idea unfold itself through the positing and annulling of
opposites! Only in the thought of an eternal personality whose ideas are in turn
(finite) personalities in mutual harmony does thought, for Boström and the Swedish national school
founded by him, find its conclusion. Not only against the
idealist doctrine of development of German philosophy, but also against the Christian theology's
doctrine of creation and atonement does Boström polemicize in his zeal to
hold fast the true reality in its pure, absolute perfection. It was his
fundamental proposition that the higher explains the lower, the perfect the imperfect.
Rational idealism is an ethical idealism: since the highest for us is a
harmonious society of independent personalities, the idea of such a
society is used to give the answer to
% --- p. 285 ---
\opage{285}what the ``thing in itself'' is that underlies the sensuous world of phenomena.
Boström's philosophy is a Platonism with the modification that it
conceives the ideas as concrete personalities, not as abstractions.
Idealism has here become a speculative
philosophy of personality\textsuperscript{68}).

While Swedish thought asserted the principle of personality in the ideal world,
Danish thought aimed rather at asserting it in the world of experience. Both
\textsc{Treschow} and \textsc{F. C. Sibbern} met German speculation with a
sound realism in their conception of the world, and with a sense for psychological
experience which kept wild speculations away. When Hegel's philosophy too had
made its entry into Denmark, where aestheticians and theologians especially attached themselves to
it, Sibbern wrote an able and pertinent criticism of it (1838). ``All my
philosophy'', Sibbern once said, ``aims at studying life and reality''.
Abstract and speculative construction could be nothing for him. Philosophy
must start from a given foundation, which it is a matter of analyzing. It is not
only the general ideas and laws that make existence intelligible to us: we must
also know the factually given starting points from which the processes of development in
existence take place. It is a chief thought in Sibbern's world-view (especially
developed in his \textit{Spekulativ Kosmologi} 1846) that all development takes place
sporadically, from different, often apparently mutually conflicting
starting points. Therefore his conception of development could not become as
idealistic as Hegel's. While Boström found Hegel too empirical because he
assumed a development, Sibbern's objection to Hegel is that he does not assume
a \textit{real, historical} development. And to this doctrine of development as
sporadic he gave an extraordinarily interesting application both in his
theory of knowledge and in his philosophy of religion. Since the knower himself is always only
one of many sporadic elements in existence, he will not be able to survey
it in its totality; on the other hand no one other than he will be able to
experience how the universal life stirs at this particular point. Thereby
Sibbern came to maintain the limits of knowledge against speculation \textit{(Om
Filosofiens Begreb.} 1843. § 21) and to maintain
% --- p. 286 ---
\opage{286}the significance of the single subjectivity against ecclesiastical dogmatism
(university programs of 1846 and 1847). --- In his psychological works
he has given contributions of lasting significance especially in the doctrine of the feelings. His book
\textit{Om Forholdet mellem Sjæl og Legeme} (1849), a work significant for its time,
shows how he sought to bring his psychological theories into
agreement with physiological experiences. He declares himself against the
dualistic conception; it is one and the same life that appears as
the life of consciousness and as material life\textsuperscript{69}).

In a more radical way \textsc{Søren Kierkegaard} came forward against Romantic
speculation and against its claim to have reconciled the oppositions of life and of
existence. His chief thought was that the different possible views of life stand
so sharply against one another that a choice must be made --- hence the watchword
\textit{Either---Or, ---} and a choice by which the single
personality must decide out of itself --- hence the watchword \textit{the
single individual.} He himself designated his thinking as qualitative dialectic, by which
he meant to designate the opposite of the Romantic speculation's doctrine of
continuous development through inner, necessary transitions. This doctrine was in
Kierkegaard's eyes fantastication, but a fantastication to which he had felt himself
drawn. Brilliantly gifted as thinker and poet, he had especially a
wonderful ability to let reflections unfold, and he endows the
possibilities of thought with a power of vividness and a wealth of mood that is
unique in our literature. He was supported in this by an art of language that made
it possible for him to shape words so that all the small waves on the great sea of mood
became visible and all nuances of thought came into their own. Often he plays with
language; it is as the warrior who plays with his weapons. But passionately as
he loved the life in thought and mood and the cultivation of the art of language, there was
nevertheless a still stronger need that led him beyond the world of possibilities to
a life in reality and earnestness. A bottomless melancholy made him feel the
insufficiency of the intellectual and aesthetic life, while on the other hand
this melancholy led him --- through the need for diversion ---
% --- p. 287 ---
\opage{287}to the great aesthetic-philosophical production that fills his first great
period as an author (1843---46). He was a Romantic in gifts and mood, and
precisely this meant that he learned from his own experience how hard the way can be from
the world of reflection and fantasy through the narrow pass of decision (of the Either ---Or)
to the striving of the single individual in the world of reality.

Qualitative dialectic appears in Kierkegaard's epistemology in the
sharp opposition between thought and existence. Even where thought can find
a connection, it is not said that this can be held fast in the practice of life. As
long as one lives, so long are we in becoming and thus face the uncertain, since
there is no guarantee that the future will be like the past. We know
backward, but live forward. A purely objective decision is impossible here. Therefore
a system of thought that was to comprise existence is impossible. Only an abstract,
purely logical system is possible. Such a system can perhaps, as an abbreviation,
contain the experience made hitherto in its broad outlines; but life constantly leads to
new possibilities and new choices. Besides, there are also at the same time such great
differences and oppositions present that the thought is not to be found that could
comprise them all in a ``higher unity''. And in any case the
single, individual existence will not be able to come into its full right in such a
system. When for Kierkegaard religious truth could appear only in
the form of the paradox, this is a natural consequence of his theory of knowledge; for
the paradox expresses the relation between an existing spirit and the eternal truth.
He insists expressly that when he says that the object of faith is
the paradox, it is no concession; the highest, the eternal can be had only
through a subjective choice without objective grounding, indeed in conflict with what
objective grounding leads one to assume. Outside subjective faith itself
there is no criterion of truth: subjectivity is the truth.

In Kierkegaard's ethics qualitative dialectic appears partly in his conception
of choice, the decision of the will, partly in his doctrine of the stages. He denies
decidedly that there is any analogy
% --- p. 288 ---
% print: „Spændighed“ (p. 288) (misprint)
\opage{288}between spiritual development and organic development. In the
spiritual domain no successive unfolding takes place that could make
the transition from deliberation to resolution, or from one view of life (one
``stage'') to another, intelligible. Continuity is broken at every such
transition. --- As regards choice, psychology is supposed to be able to show only possibilities
and approximations, motives and preparations. The choice itself comes with a jerk, a
leap, whereby something entirely new (a new quality) is posited. Only in the world of
possibilities is there continuity; in the world of reality decision always takes place
through a break in continuity. But --- one might ask --- can this jerk
or this leap then not be made an object of psychological observation?
Kierkegaard's answer is not clear. He declares that the leap lies between two
moments, between two states, of which the one is the last state in
the world of possibilities, the other the first state in the world of reality.
From this it would seem to follow that it cannot be observed. But from this it would
in turn follow that it must take place unconsciously, --- and the possibility that there could
be an unconscious continuity behind the oppositions appearing in consciousness
could not be rejected. It is therefore by a fiat that Kierkegaard maintains the concept of the leap.
--- In his doctrine of the different views of life (or, as he calls them with a
less happy expression, ``stages'') he is able to hold fast
the necessity of the leap only by conceiving the views of life (the three
chief forms: aesthetic, ethical and religious view of life) in their clearly and firmly
marked, fully finished, indeed even extreme form. The depiction of the
aesthetic stage in particular presents figures of whom it must be said that they have
run themselves aground. It is therefore no wonder that the possibilities that can be shown
psychologically fall short. Experience shows, after all, that where a development takes place
it happens while the forms still have a certain indeterminacy; from one entirely
finished form to another, development is mostly impossible. Even if one should
appeal to the law of contrast effect, this can find application only where
some tension still remains, where life has not congealed. ---
Already by this strong stress
% --- p. 289 ---
\opage{289}on the leap in every decision Kierkegaard prevents himself from obtaining a
real content, definite real tasks, for his ethics. The decision, after all, is to
rest not at all on the value of the content for man and the power which the content, through
this value, can gain over man. And Kierkegaard's ethics becomes still more formal
as the concept ``the single individual'' unfolds its consequences for
him. The more the single individual is isolated from the species, the less can it obtain
definite, real purposes and tasks. In the end, then, Kierkegaard pushes the ethical
stage out entirely, and only the two possibilities remain: to live aesthetically or
to live religiously. What did not fall under one of these two possibilities was
philistinism for him. The choice became: either enjoyment or suffering, either the giving up of
personal life or out into the tension and pain which the relation to the
eternal truth necessarily brings for a temporal being! The ability to span
strong oppositions and to bear the suffering that follows from it became
more and more for Kierkegaard the criterion of the height and value of a view of life. It
is a standard directly opposed to the natural need and direction of life, and there
expresses itself here in Kierkegaard an outright life-hostile tendency. In his later
years, accordingly, he read Schopenhauer's writings with great interest.

It was under the influence of this line of thought that he caught sight of the great
problem (already stressed by Schopenhauer and Feuerbach) of the relation between
primitive Christianity and modern Christianity, not in a dogmatic but in an ethical respect.
His violent polemic against the established Church in his last days came as a
natural consequence of his whole course of development. In ``the Christianity of the New
Testament'' he found his criterion of the highest view of life (the highest
``stage'') fulfilled. That the established Church now considered itself in continuity with
the Christianity of the apostles was in Kierkegaard's eyes an insolent presumption, and in
his \textit{Øjeblikke} he carried through with great pathos and cutting mockery the
thesis: the Christianity of the New Testament does not exist! --- Thus the
harmony which the thought of Romanticism had thought to find between knowledge and faith, between
culture and religion, was burst. It was a work for which
% --- p. 290 ---
\opage{290}Kierkegaard by his whole nature was suited. He was not one of those who were able
to open ways to a solution by posing the problems in new forms or widening
the horizon by way of experience. But he has passionately asserted anew the qualitative
differences and decisions which speculation was inclined to efface,
and he has thereby worked for the power and fullness of life and enriched
far more than those who stand near him in view of life and
standpoint\textsuperscript{70}).

\begin{center}---\end{center}


% --- p. 291 ---
\hhchapter{Ninth Book}\opage{291}

\begin{center}\textsc{Positivism.}\end{center}

\bigskip

\noindent For the spiritual life of the nineteenth century two intellectual tendencies are characteristic:
Romanticism and positivism. The first proceeds from the needs of the heart and from the
ideals of thought, the second seeks its support in what is factually given; for by the word
\textit{positive} is meant first and foremost the same as \textit{real.} The two
tendencies thus seem to be as opposed as can well be. They proceed from opposite
starting points. And yet there is an inner kinship between them. They are borne by the same
interest and rest on the same presupposition. Both are animated by a need of
full spiritual content and of absorption in great realities. Romanticism wishes to grasp
reality just as much as positivism does; only the former believes it can grasp it by
the subjective way, while the latter will build on objective facts. The
common presupposition is that an ideal which stands wholly outside
reality is a false one. Therefore men turn away from the eighteenth century's criticism by the understanding
and immerse themselves with enthusiasm in the great course of development of nature and of history.
The concept of development reigns both in Romanticism and in positivism. Men seek especially
to find the continuous connection within history which the age of Enlightenment and
Revolution had broken apart. A more thorough understanding of the past and of
the conditions for the development of the spiritual life forms an essential part of the significance of both
tendencies in the history of thought. Even though it must be said that the
spiritual oppositions --- the oppositions in the domain of faith and of
% --- p. 292 ---
\opage{292}views of life --- have steadily grown sharper in the course of the nineteenth century,
it is nevertheless the great debt we owe to these two intellectual tendencies that they have
taught us to enter into standpoints which are essentially different from our
own. By means of the historical sense, which is a form of human
sympathy in general, a bridge has been thrown over oppositions which could not be
overcome by logical discussion. This marks a turning point in the history of the
human life of the spirit. A new organ has been acquired. What
Immanuel Kant set up as the program of the human sciences: to find the
moving forces which have produced the works of the past, to investigate their laws and
their range, and thereby to set them free to do the work of the future, --- this
Romanticism and positivism have each in its own way sought to fulfill.

It would therefore be wrong to regard positivism merely as a reaction against
the philosophy of Romanticism. It would be wrong even chronologically; for
the origin of positivism lies in the time before the full development of Romanticism.
It was not surfeit with the one tendency that led to the
other, even though positivism found more favorable conditions for spreading in wider
circles once the dominion of Romanticism had been broken.

Yet there is one very essential point in which the two tendencies from the very outset
diverge from each other. In its enthusiasm for the unity of thought Romanticism overlooked
the multiplicity of reality, and in its assurance of the truth of the ideal it overlooked
the strict mechanical conformity to law to which everything must submit that is to
attain subsistence in the world of reality. Since positivism takes its
starting point in what is factually given, it opens itself to the differences
and oppositions of reality and strives to find the laws according to which phenomena arise and
develop in the real world. Its difficulties and problems therefore come
to lie at other points than those of Romanticism. Positivism seeks to go up from what is
factually given toward the unity of thought and the validity of the ideal, while
Romanticism went the opposite way. The great thinkers of positivism assume just as
confidently that it must be possible to climb from below upward
% --- p. 293 ---
\opage{293}as the Romantics assumed that one must be able to climb from above downward.
Comparative consideration must decide which way is the better.

While the philosophy of Romanticism had its home in Germany, positivism has
its home in France and England. National differences show themselves here
in a characteristic manner. The English school, which in Hume had reached a certain
conclusion, now revives and appears in new forms, which still preserve the
realistic stamp that distinguished English thought right from the Middle Ages
onward. Only when the word positivism is taken in a wider sense does it also include
the main tendency in the English philosophy of the nineteenth century. Its most important
spokesmen have protested against being called positivists --- but they
were then thinking of the narrower sense of the word, in which it designates Auguste
Comte's philosophy. It does not diminish the significance of modern English philosophy
that it is here presented as that which has completed and extended the
way of looking at things which Auguste Comte --- the second great figure of French philosophy
beside Descartes --- had shaped in its broad outlines. And
all the less so, as Comte himself stood in considerable debt to the older English school.

Both France and England have in our century made valuable contributions to
the development of philosophical thought which cannot be brought under
positivism, even where this word is taken in the wider sense. But in the general
history of philosophy we must lay the chief weight on the most significant
tendency, and therefore also let it furnish the title for the Book that treats
French and English philosophy in the nineteenth century.
% --- p. 294 ---
\opage{294}

\section*{A.\quad Comte and French Philosophy}

\subsection*{1.\quad Philosophy in France in the First Decades of the Century}

\subsubsection*{a.\quad The Renewal of the Principle of Authority}

The French Revolution had wished to throw off the bridge to the past. The age of the Church and of the
old faith was to be over. But even before the Revolution's opponents
had triumphed outwardly, it became evident that as a spiritual power the Church was not
defeated. Eminent writers praised religion for its significance in the
service of humanity and for the poetry it shed over life, and amid the
mighty upheavals there were those who sought an absolutely fixed point in the
general swell of the waves. With the outward shipwreck of the Revolution, moreover, the
ideas of the eighteenth century, as the French philosophers and their
English predecessors had maintained them, also seemed to have played out their part. They had
--- so history now seemed to testify --- been unable to lead to any fixed
social order, while the Church had maintained and renewed itself ``in spite of the syllogism,
the scaffold and the epigram'', to use an utterance of the principle of authority's
most important representative, \textsc{Joseph De Maistre} \textit{(Le pape.} 14. éd.
p. 477). In defiance of everything the eighteenth century had thought and fought for,
a theological school now sought to lead all ordering of human life and all
understanding of existence back to supernatural principles. This school has
more interest for the history of literature than for that of philosophy, and I therefore confine myself
here to some characteristic features from de Maistre's chief works, while,
as regards the tendency as a whole, I refer to the account in
\textsc{Georg Brandes:} \textit{Reaktionen i Frankrig} (2nd ed. 1892).

When modern philosophy, as the preceding sections of this work have shown,
supports itself on natural science, partly as a further application of its
results, partly as a discussion of its presuppositions, de Maistre seeks to
deprive it of this support. He disputes that there can be purely physical
% --- p. 295 ---
\opage{295}causal explanations. What is material cannot --- he asserts --- be a
cause. A physical cause is a self-contradiction\textsuperscript{71}). All material
motion is derived from original impulses, which can only stem from
spiritual beings. In the consciousness of the influence of our own will we have a
proof that motion begins with an act of willing. Scientific
explanations, such as, e.g., the origin of water by the combination of oxygen and hydrogen,
the origin of ebb and flood by the influence of sun and moon, the influence of chemical processes
on the formation of the strata of the earth, de Maistre therefore declares to be
``dogmas'' which may rightly be doubted. Yet he is quite willing to let the learned
amuse themselves in the domain of natural science, provided only they do not apply consequences
from it to social and religious affairs. It is not science but faith
that is to govern men. The truths that sustain life God proclaims not
through the academies but through the authorities in Church and State. It is prelates,
noblemen and high officers of state who are to teach the nations what is
true and false in the moral and the spiritual domain. History has now
furnished proof of the impotence of human reason to guide
men. How few are able to think correctly! And no one is able
to think correctly about all things. Then it is best to begin with
authority. The ground of all misfortunes is that speech has been set free. It
began with the Reformation --- one of the greatest crimes men have
committed against God! And it was continued in the philosophy of the eighteenth century --- one of the
most shameful episodes in the history of the human mind! The philosophers of the eighteenth century
preached error as religion. They were not in good faith, but had formed
a conspiracy (la cabale) against what is holy. Voltaire --- this
blasphemous buffoon (bouffon sacrilège) --- gave himself the appearance of
pleading the cause of innocence, although the innocence of Calas is not proven. By setting Locke
on a pedestal he has only shown his fanaticism and at the same time his lack of
patriotism. --- An end to the misfortunes will come only when the absolute
infallibility of the Pope is acknowledged. Without it the universal character of the Church cannot be
maintained, social peace cannot be preserved, and
% --- p. 296 ---
% print: „kunnne“ (p. 296) (misprint)
% print: „der,“ (p. 296) (misprint)
\opage{296}the sovereignty of princely power cannot be upheld. It is a mysterious
principle that is here appealed to: but everything is mystery in the social and in the
physical world. Reason condemns war --- and yet war reigns throughout all
nature as a mysterious means to the subsistence of life. The executioner is
the horror of society --- and yet at the same time a force that holds society up: take
away this incomprehensible social factor, and chaos will take the place of order!
Only tradition and authority, not human reason, can guide us in this
world, which everywhere presents terrible mysteries. Nothing therefore is more
ridiculous than the assumption that man should gradually have raised himself from
barbarism to science and civilization. ---

These ideas, which de Maistre develops especially in his
\textit{Soirées de St. Petersbourg,} a series of dialogues which
are assigned to 1809 but appeared only after his death, in the year 1821, turn upside
down everything that thought had sought to build up ever since the days of the Renaissance.
As so often, there is here a kinship between the opposites. Just as unhistorically
and uncomprehendingly as the philosophers of the eighteenth century had stood toward the Church
and the Middle Ages, just as unhistorically and uncomprehendingly did de Maistre and the men
of his tendency stand toward the philosophy of the eighteenth century, --- only with the difference
that the wicked philosophers now took the place of the wicked priests as the source of
all evil. The philosophy of the eighteenth century was regarded as a deliberate
conspiracy against authority, as a purely arbitrary process. And this was in
good agreement with the fact that authority itself was conceived as what is purely
arbitrary, commanding from without or from above. Hereby there arose again a new likeness with
the philosophy of the eighteenth century: for when all knowledge is to be built on authority,
its self-activity must be subdued, its free unfolding of its inner possibilities
denied. De Maistre therefore consistently comes --- just as Condillac did
--- to assume the complete passivity of man. It is then no wonder that the
possibility that man should have arrived at civilization by the way of natural development
appears to him as utterly absurd.
% --- p. 297 ---
\opage{297}

\subsubsection*{b.\quad The Psychological School}

The significance of the authoritarian school lay in its passionate bringing forward of the value of the
historical powers, in opposition to the psychology of the Enlightenment and the Revolution,
which saw in the heart and understanding of the single individual an independent
force. But as the principle of authority was conceived here, it was an external, brutal
principle; its inner connection with mental life was not investigated --- and could
not be investigated from this standpoint, since every independent value that was
ascribed to the individual's own inner life would entail a limitation of the absolute
authority. Philosophically, therefore, as already remarked, the authoritarian school stood
(when certain mystical stirrings, of which it itself becomes afraid, are discounted)
on Condillac's standpoint. All the greater is the interest of seeing how, out of
Condillac's own school, through the use of psychological observation and reflection,
a deeper psychology develops, which places itself in definite opposition both
to the French philosophy of the Enlightenment and to the new authoritarian school.

When the Revolution broke out, Condillac had triumphed. His philosophy became the
official one, and his adherents occupied the philosophical section in the
National Institute established by the Convention. Before this philosophical academy
the physician PIERRE JEAN GEORGES CABANIS in the winter of 1797---98 read a series of memoirs on
the relation between soul and body, which were printed in the Academy's transactions and later in
expanded form appeared as a book (1802) under the title: \textit{Rapports du physique et
du moral de l'homme.} Cabanis speaks of Condillac with great appreciation, but
modifies his doctrine on essential points. Condillac lays the weight exclusively
on the external senses; according to him man receives from the surrounding world in a
passive manner the whole content of his consciousness and all its forms. Cabanis
reproaches him for not having taken account of that in consciousness which corresponds
to the organism's own inner states. Impressions constantly come to the brain
from the various inner organs, and besides, the state of the brain and nerves themselves
always plays a part as well. There is an obscure feeling or sense perception which is
% --- p. 298 ---
\opage{298}immediately bound up with the subsistence of life, independently of external sense impressions, and which
has therefore already been present before the individual is at birth brought into
relation to the great surrounding world, from whose influences Condillac derives everything in
consciousness. Cabanis introduced the feeling of life into modern psychology. With this
the passivity toward the surrounding world was already limited; for in the feeling of life the
individual has an original fund which gains influence on everything it later
takes into itself, and gives it color and stamp. And Cabanis brings instinct into close
connection with the feeling of life. In instinctive actions too he finds facts
that are incompatible with Condillac's theory. Instinct presupposes a fund of
original force, which is released by impressions from the inner functions of life, as
is shown especially in the reproductive and parental instincts. Cabanis
lays so great weight on the concept of instinct that he even hints at the thought that
a universal instinct might be at work in all processes of nature, a thought in
which the germ of Schopenhauer's philosophy of nature has rightly been found. It
was not, however, Cabanis's intention to put forward a philosophical system. He wishes to
proceed in a purely psychological and physiological way and not to answer the ultimate
questions. Although in a single place he expresses himself in a strongly materialistic way (in that
he lets thought be secreted in the brain, as bile is in the liver), it would nevertheless
be wrong to assign his work to the materialistic literature proper.
His standpoint is characterized by the following statement (Rapports,
XI, 8. éd. Peisse p. 597): ``It took a long time before men came to
acknowledge only a single force in nature; perhaps an even longer time will be needed
to acknowledge rightly that, since we cannot compare this force with anything
else, we cannot form any true notion of its properties.'' In a
later work \textit{(Lettre sur les causes premières)} he gave a
fuller development of his thoughts, which departs still further from materialism
than the famous chief work had done.

Napoleon did not regard Condillac's school with favorable eyes. It did not, after all,
content itself with investigating our sensations and representations; beside
its \textit{ideology}
% --- p. 299 ---
\opage{299}(so DESTUTT DE TRACY, an ardent Condillacien, called the doctrine of the
origin of representations, cf. his work \textit{Eléments d'Idéologie}
1801) it also busied itself with theories of morality and law in the spirit of the eighteenth
century. Napoleon derived all the misfortunes of France from the ``ideologists'', and in any
case he would rather think for France, just as he acted for it. He
suppressed the Académie des sciences morales et
politiques established by the Convention, and writings of a freer philosophical content could no longer appear in
France. Destutt de Tracy had to have his commentary on Montesquieu printed
anonymously in America in English translation. The ideologists withdrew into
narrower circles. In particular there gathered around Cabanis and Destutt de Tracy in
Auteuil a band of younger men who were interested in philosophical studies.
From this circle came forth France's first psychologist of this century, MAINE DE
BIRAN (b. 1766, d. 1824).

Biran held administrative posts under the Revolution, the Empire and the Restoration
and was a member of legislative assemblies. It was not, however,
the great outward events of the time that filled his mind. He was a good
patriot, but lacked the inclination and the capacity for outward action. The great historical
drama worked upon him by strengthening the emotions in his own mind,
emotions which he early observed both with the interest of the theorist and with
an inward longing for peace and harmony within. His constitution must have been
of such a nature that the relation between the passive and the active, the involuntary
and the voluntary, or, as he himself aptly designates it, between
temperament and character, became for him a theoretical and practical problem all his life
long. Of this his \textit{Journal intime} bears witness, the most remarkable of the
works he left behind (published by E. Naville in his book: \textit{Maine
de Biran. Sa vie et ses pensées.} 1857), which contains entries from the
beginning, the middle and the end of his life as a thinker. How early and how
definitely his peculiar problem presented itself to him can be seen from a statement
from the period when he still adhered to Condillac's doctrine (27 May 1794). ``What is
properly the so-called mental activity? I
% --- p. 300 ---
\opage{300}always feel the state of the soul determined by this or that bodily state . . .
If I could some day undertake a connected piece of work, I might have
a wish to investigate in what degree the soul is active, in what degree it can
alter the external impressions, increase or diminish their strength by the
attention it directs upon them, and try how far it is master of
this attention . . . It would be highly to be wished that a man practiced in observation
would analyze the will, as Condillac has analyzed
the understanding.'' At the same time he complains of the constant shifting and streaming in his
inner states (cette révolution perpétuelle, cette roue toujours mobile de
l'existence), which hinders fixed moods and gives rise to doubt and unrest even toward
what he seeks with honest will to hold fast.

In his first works Biran kept to the doctrine of Condillac and Cabanis. But
gradually he laid ever more weight on the activity which in his
view comes immediately to our consciousness in the effort of will. ``The self
makes itself known to itself through the inner sense in the effort or
the movement of will, which the soul perceives (aperçoit) within itself as a product
of its activity, as an effect that has its cause in its will.''
\textit{(Rapports du physique et du moral de l'homme,} Oeuvres philos. 1841.
IV, p. 75). Here there is for Biran an original fact which puts an end to
Condillac's doctrine of passivity. But he does not forget --- constantly
repeated inner experiences saw to that --- the involuntarily arising sensations and
moods. He reproached the moralists who write on the problem of happiness for
giving themselves up to general reflections and postulates and believing that one can
immediately command one's feelings and inclinations. Wholly independently
of our conscious willing a multitude of changing phenomena stir within us,
which the self finds before it when it becomes conscious of itself, and which must stem from
another inner cause than the self. There is also, outside the self or consciousness
and independently of the relation to the surrounding world, a series of inner phenomena which
self-observation discovers, but which can subsist without it. (Journal intime. 24
Oct. 1814). This theory of
% --- p. 301 ---
% print: „\textit{M}\textit{è}\textit{moire“ (p. 301) (misprint)
\opage{301}sensations that were to subsist outside the self aroused great attention and much opposition
in the small philosophical society which Biran gathered about him in Paris, and in whose meetings
men such as the physicist Ampère, the historian Guizot and the philosopher Royer Collard
took part. Only Ampère joined Biran definitely. They were both agreed in
setting the immediate consciousness (apperception immédiate)
% scan: „immódiate“ (p. 301)
of the energy of will as the central psychological fact. But outward from it
mental life fades off into the unconscious, and when the act of self-consciousness sets in, the
self finds a whole series of elements given --- in any case it hears their
echo. So also on awakening from torpor or on reflection upon
habitual states. In a hitherto unprinted \textit{Mémoire sur
les perceptions obscures} (of 1807), which has been brought to light by \textsc{Alexis
Bertrand} (La psychologie de l'effort et les doctrines contemporaines. Chap.
2), Biran had sought to explain this opposition between the passive and the
active in mental life physiologically by assuming different cooperating
nerve centers. He also uses the phenomena of somnambulism to illuminate
the duality within us. In his zeal for exact self-observation and for supplementing
self-observation by other sources of psychological knowledge Biran is a
forerunner of modern psychology. From his psychological
standpoint he declares himself definitely against the authoritarian school, which attributed no significance to man's free
self-activity. Only through absorption in the nature and laws of mental life
can one, Biran maintains, find the point where the origin of the moral and religious
relation lies. The men of the authoritarian school, who wholly disregarded
the individual nature of the soul and ``ex abrupto'' set up authority as the
foundation of all science, lacked in his eyes love of truth and
were led merely by the need to act, to work upon men. And they
fell, he continues, into skepticism and materialism, in that they made
the soul purely passive and let its whole direction be determined from without, by authority!
(Journal intime. 28 July 1823).

In the immediate consciousness of self-activity Biran sees the primitive and
fundamental principle of all our knowledge. In it not only does our own
self proclaim itself to us; but since
% --- p. 302 ---
\opage{302}self-activity meets resistance, we obtain consciousness of the existence of the material world.
The self-activity we are aware of is in fact the soul's acting upon the
organism, where there is always a certain resistance to overcome.
% scan: „overvindé“ (p. 302)
Thus Biran gives a spiritualistic interpretation of the consciousness of our acting
and of the checking of our acting that may take place; and thereby there is gained at the same time
an explanation of the opposition between our willing proper and what is involuntary in
our inner states. Yet he does not adhere to the Cartesian doctrine of the soul as
a substance: we know the self only as active force; there could be no immediate
consciousness of the substance. --- The force or acting which we thus perceive
in ourselves serves us as a type to which we refer all external phenomena.
We come to know in our self-consciousness the concepts of force, cause, unity and identity,
and only because we can draw these concepts from the primitive inner fact,
concepts which are very different from concepts of kinds, can we apply them to the
phenomena of experience. --- Neither external sense perception nor authority, but the
immediate consciousness of our self-activity is the foundation of all our
knowledge. Concerning the reality of this foundation Biran harbors no doubt; modern
psychology will hardly be able to grant, however, that he has overcome Hume's doubt
about the possibility of an immediate apprehension of causality\textsuperscript{72}). ---

Biran's most important writings were published only long after his death. He
worked for a time on a larger work which was to comprise all his
psychological studies \textit{(Essai sur les fondements de la psychologie);} but
political circumstances prevented him from finishing it for publication, and
later he laid his draft aside in order to work out a new exposition
\textit{(Nouveaux essais d'anthropologie).} Both works were published in 1859 by
Naville (Oeuvres inédites de M. de Biran). The reason why in his last
years he rejected his older exposition was that he had caught sight of a
deeper layer in the soul than those he had hitherto taken into account in his
reflections. Hitherto he had described the currents which spread from the feeling of life
over the whole inner life, and, in opposition to them, the feeling of
energy in which our self seeks to work
% --- p. 303 ---
% print: „\textit{la vie de l'esqrit}“ (p. 303) (misprint)
% scan: „humaine.“ (p. 303)
\opage{303}its way out of the passive and involuntary. In the feeling of energy he had in stoic
fashion found his refuge amid the outer and inner emotions. But this refuge was
not enough for him in the long run. It did not suffice against the unrest in the outer and in the
inner world. The need awakens in him for an absolutely fixed point of support, for a
devotion of another and higher kind than that to the moods of the feeling of life, a
devotion to something that is independent of the soul's own imperfect activity,
and which yet comes not from without but from within. He uses Kant's distinction
between noumena and phenomena and seeks his firm standing ground in the inner relation to
something that lies beyond all phenomena. It is the fundamental thoughts of religious mysticism
in which he now lands by the way of his own independent experience, at the same time
as the study of the Gospel of John, De imitatione and Fénelon replaces the study
of Descartes and Leibniz, which in its time had in turn replaced the study of Condillac
and Cabanis. Biran's religiosity takes on no confessional character. He
holds fast that religious feeling cannot be produced from without; it must arise
involuntarily, and just as involuntarily under its influence the
images take shape in which the soul finds the notion of the eternal and infinite
expressed. Religion is feeling rather than faith; faith is subordinate to feeling.
What our spiritual activity can do here is to bring about receptivity
for the higher life, the spiritual life proper, \textit{la vie de l'esprit} in
opposition to the active life in will and reason, \textit{la vie humaine,} which
again is opposed to the currents of the feeling of life, \textit{la vie animale.} This higher
life Biran also designates as ``the mystical life of enthusiasm'', ``the highest stage
the human soul can reach, in that, so far as it lies with it, it makes itself one
with its highest object and thus returns to the source from which
it has sprung''. (Oeuvres inédites. III. p. 541. 521).

But Biran's diary shows that his passion for psychological observation and
reflection did not fall away with his passing over to mysticism. Again and again
he discusses the question how far the psychological causal explanation can
reach with respect to the most inward and highest states. Now it is said that those who
seek to explain everything by natural causes cannot
% --- p. 304 ---
% print: „(Jornal“ (p. 304) (misprint)
\opage{304}be prevented from asking whether even the highest state of blessed rest and
contemplation, where the soul is in ecstasy and feels itself under divine
influence, --- whether even that might not be explained by the working of organic
moods, so that heavenly bliss would be replaced by unrest and
tossing as soon as the organic state changed. Now it is declared as
settled that the idea or feeling which the soul has of the perfect, the great, the beautiful
and the eternal cannot spring from the soul itself; moral and religious truths
have another source than psychological truths. (Journal intime. 26 August
1818 and 19 September 1818). Right up to the last leaves of the diary there is discussed
in particular the question how our own mental activity in thinking and in
concentration of the mind can prepare the way for that higher devotion by virtue of the
constant reciprocal action between the active and the passive in us: and how, it is
then asked, can one distinguish between what as a consequence of such concentration
wells up from the soul's own ground and what is due to the influence of divine
forces? Beyond a ``whether --- or'' (soit---soit) Biran does not get,
however great his need to hold fast that when we seek to penetrate into
truth, truth also seeks to penetrate into us. (Journal intime. October 1823).

Only few had knowledge of Maine de Biran's thought before his writings --- for
the most part long after his death --- were made public. To these few
belonged first and foremost the famous physicist \textsc{André-Marie Ampére} (b.
1775, d. 1836), who stood in lively oral and written communication with him and
together with him found the starting point of philosophy in the immediate consciousness
of the energy of the self. Ampère acknowledged his friend's priority on this point, but
while Biran all his life continued to circle about this one point, Ampère sought to
give a detailed psychological and epistemological theory. Philosophical studies
occupied him to a high degree; beside his scientific and mathematical
lectures he also lectured on philosophy. Ørsted's discovery of
electromagnetism led him into the brilliant series of investigations which
have especially made his name famous; but he did not forsake his old
% --- p. 305 ---
\opage{305}love, and in his later years he was occupied with studies on the
encyclopedia and classification of the sciences, which led to the publication of his
\textit{Essai sur la philosophie des sciences} (first volume 1834, second volume
with introductions by Ste. Beuve and Littré 1843), in which several of his
interesting psychological and philosophical ideas were expressed. Later his
correspondence with Biran and some fragments of a treatise were published with
an introduction by his son, under the title: \textit{Philosophie des deux Ampère,}
publiée par \textsc{Barthélemy St. Hilaire} (Paris 1866). (Of the son's philosophy,
however, there is not much in the book).

Ampère stands as a philosopher to Biran roughly as he stands as a physicist
to Ørsted. In Ørsted's discovery he divined a single example of
a general law, which he succeeded in developing mathematically and demonstrating
experimentally. Electromagnetism was extended by him into the electrodynamic theory.
The influence of the electric current on the magnetic needle led him to discover the
influence of electric currents on one another and the influence of the earth
on electric currents. Biran's observation of the relation between the active and
the passive in mental life led Ampère to two series of investigations, partly to
an investigation of how our sensations and representations involuntarily
combine prior to and independently of conscious activity, partly to an
investigation of how the scientific knowledge of existence becomes
possible on the basis of the mind's conscious use of its faculties. By the first
investigation he has given interesting contributions to the psychological
doctrine of association, by the second to epistemology.

In psychological respects Ampère applies the same method as the English
association psychologists. He does not --- like Biran and most other
French psychologists --- stop at description, but seeks to explain
the origin of compound phenomena of consciousness by the fusion and combination
of simpler elements. A fusion (concrétion) takes place, e.g.,
between the sensation of color and the sensation of resistance, which enter into so close a
combination that one is inclined to take such compound
combinations for simple and
% --- p. 306 ---
% print: „fuldet“ (p. 306) (misprint)
\opage{306}primitive ones. It is only analysis that discovers that a
fusion has taken place, and that our own involuntary activity and the limits it
meets have thereby played an essential part. Another example of concrétion
is had in recognition, where the present sensation of an object and the
reproduction of an earlier sensation fuse together. By the same process
Ampère further explains that when during the performance of an opera one has the text
before one, one can immediately \textit{hear} the words, while without the help of the
text one would not be able to hear them. The words one reads and the sounds one hears
fuse immediately together\textsuperscript{73}). It was this kind of explanation
which, according to Ste. Beuve, made Ampère's psychological lectures so attractive.

In the very fundamental fact on which he was agreed with Biran, the immediate
consciousness of self-activity, Ampère makes a distinction which Biran did not
grant. He distinguishes between self-consciousness (autopsie [i.e. heautopsie],
later: émesthèse) and the muscular sensation, showing that this latter
sensation we have also when another person moves our arm or our leg. In
one's own movement self-consciousness is the phenomenon that contains the cause,
the muscular sensation the phenomenon in which the effect appears. Precisely through the fact
that the muscular sensation can also be produced by another, I discover that I
myself am in some cases the cause of it. In this experience, then, the
causal relation dawns upon me. Immediately I have it given only in my own
activity, and all other acting I therefore apprehend by analogy with this. Together
with the immediate consciousness, at which Biran stopped, there works according to
Ampère the faculty of apprehending relations, the cognitive faculty proper. It is by
it that we apprehend the relation between cause and effect, between places in space and time,
etc. And it is by it alone that we can know more than mere phenomena.
However true it is, according to Ampère, that everything that appears to us is only
phenomenon, he is nevertheless convinced that the relations (rapports, relations) which
obtain between the phenomena among themselves without depending on the phenomena's
qualitative character have absolute (noumenal)
% --- p. 307 ---
\opage{307}validity. The mere concepts of kinds, which are obtained by comparison and abstraction,
have no higher validity than the sense qualities which make up their content.
But the concepts which express pure relations and modes of coordination, such as
causality, number, time and space, hold absolutely and form the bridge by which our
knowledge reaches from the world of phenomena to that of noumena. On this point
Ampère declares himself definitely against Kant, whom he otherwise highly admires. No
less definitely does he declare himself against Reid, who assumes an immediate observation
of external reality, whereby according to Ampére he confuses a ``concrétion'' with an
elementary observation. Noumenal reality (matter in itself as the cause
of sense impressions, the soul in itself as the cause of our own acting, God as the
cause of everything) we discover only by way of inference and in the form of hypothesis. What we
immediately apprehend is only phenomena, but the relations, independent of the qualities,
which we intuit between the phenomena hold for the noumena too. By
relations Ampère means the same as what Boyle and Locke called the primary qualities.

On this question Biran at first inclined to Reid's view. When his
philosophical friend had eagerly urged him to study Kant, he became more of a
Kantian than Ampère cared for. Against the latter's theory of relations he maintains (in
a conversation which is mentioned in Journal intime 30 Oct. 1816) that a very
great difficulty is bound up with making the transition from the consciousness of our own
activity (the fundamental fact common to Ampère and Biran) to the assumption of external
causes. Here, according to Biran, is an abyss over which analysis and induction cannot
carry us. From the fact that I am not the cause of a passive state in me it cannot
be inferred that there is necessarily a cause which produces everything that I
do not produce. We are ourselves causes, and therefore it is natural for us to
apprehend other things as causes: but that is no proof! --- When Ampère held
that the absolute validity of relations was proved by the fact that all inferences we draw
from our theories of relations are confirmed by experience, Biran answers (in a
hitherto unprinted letter, used by A. Bertrand: La psychol. de l'effort p. 188):
``What
% --- p. 308 ---
% scan: „Udg;“ (p. 308)
\opage{308}experience can teach us whether the forms of the coordination of phenomena are absolutely in
things or only in the mind that apprehends? Can this doubt of reflection
ever be cleared up by an external experience? Do not both possibilities agree equally
well with the phenomena?'' --- To this Ampère has hardly been able to give any
satisfactory answer from his theory of relations\textsuperscript{74}).

In his world-view Ampère is a Cartesian. He divides the sciences into
cosmological and noological sciences, of which the first concern the
material, the latter the mental phenomena. The noological sciences are to be
studied after the cosmological, partly because these show us the use of the
human faculties for the knowledge of the world and thereby throw light on these faculties'
nature, partly because the knowledge of the world, especially of man's physical nature,
which they give, is of importance for understanding man's intellectual and
moral faculties. As regards Ampère's classification of the sciences in
detail, it is very intricate and cannot in simplicity and clarity measure up to
the one Auguste Comte set up at about the same time. But there are in his ``Essai
sur la philosophie des sciences'' many interesting remarks, and if he
had been able to carry out his wish to give not only a classification but also
an exposition of the most important truths, methods, problems and hypotheses in
the various domains, there is no doubt that so excellent a thinker and
investigator would have produced an excellent work and an interesting corrective to
Comte's system. --- At about the same time as Ampère and Comte the
woman mathematician \textsc{Sophie Germain} (b. 1776, d. 1831) was also busied with ideas on
the course of development of the sciences in its connection with the standard of truth
which lies in the very nature of human knowledge. Under the evident
influence of Kant she shows that by reason of the nature of our consciousness we have a
need of unity, order and connection, a need which guides us not only in
scientific inquiry but also in the moral and aesthetic domain. Her
philosophical work \textit{Considérations générales sur l'état des sciences et
des lettres aux différentes époques de leur culture} (published 1833, new ed.
1879 in ``Oeuvres philosophiques de Sophie
% --- p. 309 ---
\opage{309}Germain'' by H. Stupuy) aims to show that the same type guides us in
science, morality and art. ``There is only one single type of the true. In
morality, in science, in literature, in art we always seek the
unity, order and proportion of existence among the parts of one and the same whole.''
The causal principle is only a special form of this general principle. We find
application for the causal principle when we do not see the object we are investigating in
its whole. It shows itself to us as a fragment, and we then ask what
unity encloses it. We see it as a part and seek the whole to which
it belongs. This need of unity and wholeness has led to bold systems, to
arbitrary use of analogies and to the assumption of mystical causes. But it has
also led to many happy ideas, and the progress of science depends on its
being alive. The coherence in the history of science depends on it. But men
gradually learn to put methods in the place of systems and to ask
\textit{how and how much} in the place of \textit{why.} Instead of
creating the world according to the whims of his imagination man learns to trace out
the real connection of the world, and when it thus gradually succeeds in finding
a great unity in everything, the imagination will regain in surer form what it
has lost by its bold images having been displaced by critical inquiry. ---

While in the philosophical closets of Biran and Ampère a thinking was developing which
led beyond the reigning Condillacism, this was defeated in philosophical
teaching by the appearance of Royer Collard and Victor Cousin. ROYER COLLARD'S
lectures at the Sorbonne (1811---14) introduced Reid as a philosophical classic in
France. He laid great weight on psychological inquiry in the direction of the Scottish school
and emphasized the significance of instinctive apprehension and of immediate moral
conviction as against the limited point of view and abstract
analyses of ideology. This was at the expense of the sharpness of the problems; an appeal to sound
common sense all too often took the place of an argument. But a new
tendency had been inaugurated, and the eye was opened to sides of the spiritual life which the
hitherto reigning school had left in shadow. Royer Collard's considerable
% --- p. 310 ---
\opage{310}personality gave his appearance as a philosopher a peculiar weight. His successor
\textsc{Victor Cousin} (b. 1792, d. 1867) was an enthusiastic speaker with great
talent for awakening the interest of the young. Young himself, he shared the young's
expectation that with the free constitution and the fall of military despotism there would
come a brilliant time for French spiritual life. His teaching had a
decidedly historical stamp. He brought the history of philosophy into academic
teaching in France. His own philosophical points of view he got partly from
the Scots and Royer Collard, partly from Biran and Ampère, in whose philosophical
gatherings he took part. Biran saw well enough that Cousin ``was hunting on his
preserves''; but he expected to get a share of the game, since Cousin's teaching would
produce receptivity for his own great psychological work when it came
(which unfortunately it did only some thirty-odd years after Biran's death).
Cousin combined Reid's theory of the immediate apprehension of absolute
reality with Biran's doctrine of the consciousness of our own self-activity and with
Ampère's doctrine of absolute relations. And with this he later also united
Schelling's and Hegel's doctrine of absolute reason. On journeys in Germany
he had come to know German speculative philosophy, after \textsc{Md. de
Staël's} book \textit{De l'Allemagne} (which was written in 1810, but could appear only
after Napoleon's fall) had given a general impression of German
philosophy from Kant's time. Cousin's philosophy became an eclecticism which from the
various systems drew out what supposedly had lasting value:
the systems were each by itself incomplete, but none of them wholly false!
The standard for the choice was at first psychological observation after the pattern of Reid
and Biran, later the universal reason of Schelling and Hegel, and in the
last part of Cousin's career --- when after the Revolution of 1830 he had become
official director of all philosophical teaching in France --- the chief doctrines of natural
religion and of Cartesian spiritualism. The boldness and the
inspiring quality of his first appearance\textsuperscript{75}) as a philosophical teacher
were damped by his historical studies and his official position. Aptly has
Renan, who moreover long after Cousin's death expressed in warm words what he
owed him, cited
% --- p. 311 ---
\opage{311}him as an example of the fact that it is not good for philosophy to win an all too
complete victory. It must be added that the victory was only outward. Napoleon
had looked with pleasure on Royer Collard's appearance, and it was the July Monarchy that
supported Cousin.

Cousin's most important work is, Du \textit{vrai, du beau, du bien,} his
lectures of 1818, which were published by Garnier twenty years later in their
original form, but in later editions were mutilated by Cousin himself, whom
the heresies of his youth now embarrassed. It was this work that made so great an
impression on Renan. Besides this, one must seek his ideas in the prefaces to five volumes of
\textit{Fragments philosophiques,} in which he treats subjects from the history of
philosophy. In the preface to the first of these volumes (1826) he presents his
characteristic doctrine of ``impersonal reason'', in which he has combined
Reid, Ampère and Schelling. It is by means of the psychological method, by
deepening self-observation, that he believes he has reached a point to which
not even Kant had penetrated, a point where the apparent subjectivity and relativity of the necessary
principles vanishes, in that there is revealed
an involuntary grasping of truth as the foundation of all logical reflection and
of all setting up of necessary concepts. Only by becoming an object of
reflection does reason become subjective; in itself it is a light which, independently
of all personal differences, shines within every human being as a
universal revelation.

While Cousin did indeed believe that he was supporting himself on psychological observation, but very
soon rose above it on the wings of rhetoric and fancy,
\textsc{Théodore Jouffroy} (1796 ---1842) had a greater and more faithful interest in
psychological inquiry. He did, to be sure, keep one-sidedly to self-observation and
disdain other sources of psychological knowledge, in that in a strictly
spiritualistic fashion he distinguished between psychology and physiology as two subjects which
had nothing to do with each other. But he was in earnest --- a whole
series of investigations shows it --- about getting clear on the relation between
self-observation on the one side and natural science and philosophical
speculation on the other. He does not have Cousin's romantic virtuosity in
throwing bridges over abysses. His philosophy sprang
% --- p. 312 ---
% print: „franke“ (p. 312) (misprint)
\opage{312}from his purely personal need of clarity in knowledge, after he had through a
hard struggle seen the theological notions lose their value for him. But
although there is a strong personal interest in his thinking, it does not lead him
to compromise or to content himself with solutions that do not
fully satisfy his thought. Rather, he then stops at the recognition
that the solution of the problem is unattainable. ``There are'', he says in one of his
lectures \textit{(Mélanges philosophiques.} 3 éd. p. 350 f.), ``two ways
in which the man who thinks can obtain peace in his soul and rest for his
mind; the first is to possess, or believe one possesses, the truth concerning the
questions that interest humanity; the second is to see clearly that
this truth is inaccessible, and to know why it is so. . . Since the
facts we can observe are limited, the inferences we can
draw from these facts are so likewise. Science therefore has its
horizon, beyond which it cannot see; it is its task gradually to
determine this horizon. At this outermost limit of its domain it must part
from poetry, which alone can go further. This separation is its duty
toward humanity, toward which it has the task of discovering the truth, and
which has only all too often suffered from having hoped for and sought the truth where
it was, and for ever will be, inaccessible to it.'' --- It is far more
by the manly way in which Jouffroy faced the problems than
by his treatment of them in detail that he stands as a fine and attractive
figure in the history of French philosophy. In so far as he points to
definite results, these go in the direction of the eclecticism founded by Cousin.

\subsubsection*{c.\quad The Social School}

When Cousin's disciple \textsc{Damiron} in the year 1828 published a work on French
philosophy in the nineteenth century, he set up eclecticism as the higher unity
or the right mean as against the Condillacian school on the one side and the
theological school on the other. The peculiar
% --- p. 313 ---
\opage{313}intellectual work of Biran and Ampère, which went deeper than eclecticism, had not come before
the public. But in the second edition (which came out the same year) he found himself
induced to speak of the ideas of Saint-Simon and Auguste Comte, although he
admitted that he could not clearly see their significance. At that time only
Comte's first writings were available. Saint-Simon's career, on the other hand, was concluded. The germ had been
laid from which modern socialism and positivism were to develop.

\textsc{Saint-Simon} (whose full name was Claude Henri de Rouvroy, comte de
Saint-Simon) was more a journalist and social reformer than a philosopher. But he gains
significance for the history of philosophy through his living conviction that a new
social order becomes possible only if a new world-view makes its way.
And this new world-view can, of this he is no less convinced, only be
built up on the foundation of the positive sciences. Saint-Simon himself had not
received any scientific education. As a young man (he was born in 1760) he took part
with bravery in the North American War of Independence. Thereafter he threw himself
into industrial enterprises, renounced his noble rank during the Revolution,
took to speculating in national lands and appeared as a ``grand
seigneur sansculotte''. He was in prison during the Reign of Terror, but was freed at
Robespierre's fall. His wealth he used (as long as he had it) not only
to live in high style, but also to prepare the scientific and social
reform of which he had early conceived the thought. He surrounded himself with men of science from
the Polytechnic and the Medical School in order to train himself to write an
encyclopedia of the sciences. His great plans he did not give up because he became
poor; on the contrary, he worked with ever greater zeal. He had a rare
capacity for drawing eminent men to himself and getting them to work with him and
for him. Augustin Thierry and Auguste Comte were for a time his secretaries and
collaborators and called themselves with pride his pupils, until their ways parted.
While Saint-Simon in his earlier period had put the production of
a new encyclopedia in the first line, because only on the foundation of such a one could
a new catechism be worked out, after
% --- p. 314 ---
\opage{314}the upheavals of 1814---15 he believed he could proceed directly to the new organization of society,
whose main feature was that industrial and economic life should stand in the first
line and the government system proper take a subordinate place. In place
of noblemen and jurists, great industrialists and men of science were now to
stand as the heads of society. The final purpose was to be that
the working class, the class that suffers most, should be helped forward in intellectual
and economic respects. While in France after the Restoration men were absorbed in
constitutional and parliamentary struggles, Saint-Simon declared that it is the
social renewal that matters, that the external form of government is indifferent, and
that a government is on the whole only a necessary evil. As the leading motive to carry
the new order he at first thought of insight into the harmony of interests, much
as Helvetius and later Bentham conceived it. But in his last years
he appealed to the love of man (philanthropy) and wished to found a new
Christianity, which consisted essentially in the commandment of love, while at the same time it
differed from the old Christianity by letting earthly life come into
its full right and not making it a means to a supernatural existence. The
individual right of property can in his view be founded only on the
universal utility which this institution offers, not on the single
person's claim in and for itself. What matters now is association in order to
exploit the earth. It is things, not men, that are to be governed. As his
disciples later expressed it: in place of the mutual exploitation of men by
one another the exploitation of the globe is to come. The state is to gather the
human forces for great works, such as the building of canals and roads, drainage,
cultivation. Labor and brotherhood was Saint-Simon's watchword. Surrounded by a small
circle of adherents he died in 1825.

As Saint-Simon by his political program stood in opposition to both of the
contending parties of his day, the Liberals as well as the Legitimists, so in the
domain of ideas he stood in opposition both to the theological school and to the philosophy of the eighteenth
century. Significant here is the way in which he
conceives and evaluates the Middle Ages already in writings
% --- p. 315 ---
% print: „Saints-Simons“ (p. 315) (misprint)
\opage{315}from 1807 and 1813. The Middle Ages are for him a great period of organization. The
civilized world was held together by brotherhood and common faith. The priests were
not, as Voltaire thought, charlatans, but the most advanced part of the
nation. Since the medieval system has fallen before criticism and
revolution, we live in a spiritual and social chaos. Negation and egoism
flourish. What matters is to reach a new organic period, and the spiritual power that
is to lead to it can be none other than positive science, which
it is a matter of putting into a system. Saint-Simon's friend the physician BURDIN put forward, in a
conversation with him, ideas on the development of the sciences which Saint Simon took up, and
which contain interesting intimations of positivism. All sciences
began on the foundation of a small number of experiences and therefore had in their
first period the character of guesses, often fantastic guesses. Astronomy
began as astrology, chemistry as alchemy. As experience advances,
the sciences pass from a conjectural to a positive form. Mathematics,
astronomy, physics and chemistry have already reached the positive form;
physiology and psychology are on the point of doing so. Finally philosophy too will
become a positive science; it is due to the imperfect state of the particular sciences
that there is still so great a distance between general science and
the special sciences. On this conception of the history of the sciences
Saint-Simon built his hope of a new world-view on a purely scientific
foundation. The expression \textit{positive philosophy} he was the first to use. Further than
the general thought he did not get. He was not the man to
carry through a great, connected work. And yet he marks a decisive
turning point. By his recognition of the Middle Ages as a distinct period of culture
he betrays a historical sense which was rare at the time when he appeared. And
he thereby succeeds in being able to conceive history as a continuous
process of development. While in the period of Enlightenment the Middle Ages had come to stand as
an arbitrary interruption of development, they now stood as a period of spiritual
and social organization after a preceding period of dissolution. In return the
period
% --- p. 316 ---
\opage{316}after the Middle Ages came to stand as an age of dissolution. Criticism and liberalism
are for him only means of getting the obsolete system out of the way, and are not
themselves a new system. Such a system had first to be developed, and in Saint-Simon's
conviction it could not be reached except on the foundation of empirical science. The
time must come when humanity would build its faith and its morality on experience and
science. Only by this way can there arise a new total conception of
existence about which all can gather, so that life can again be carried on with
united forces.

This doctrine of Saint-Simon's his school generalized, in that throughout history it
distinguishes between critical and organic periods. In Kant and Fichte, indeed already
in Rousseau, a similar opposition occurs. Such a conception was bound
naturally to come forward in an age that had seen criticism overthrow an old
order of things in the domain of faith and of society without being able to produce a new
order and without being able to root out the need of one. However much there was of
charlatanry in Saint-Simon, he nevertheless had on a decisive point a
correct historical eye and felt the spiritual and social needs of the time. It thereby becomes
understandable that he had a great historian and a great philosopher
among his disciples.

In Saint-Simon there is found only the germ of socialism. The germ was developed in his
school\textsuperscript{76}), which reshaped his doctrine in such a way that he would not
have acknowledged it. They wished to restrict the right of inheritance and to entrust to
the state the distribution of the product of labor according to each person's capacity and work. The school took on
more and more a fantastic and utopian character. A new hierarchy was set up
with ``Father'' ENFANTIN at its head; but the school was dissolved when Enfantin came out with
ordinances concerning the sexual relations of the faithful, which brought conviction and
imprisonment for the leaders. Before these last extravagances the sober and
critical elements had withdrawn. The enthusiasm that had bound
the Saint-Simonians together --- the enthusiasm for the goal of completing man's dominion over nature
by the cooperation of human forces --- was nevertheless not
without fruit.
% --- p. 317 ---
\opage{317}A great part of France's railways, canals, factories and banks owe
their coming into being to former Saint-Simonians. The cutting through of the isthmuses of Suez and
Panama was a Saint-Simonian thought. It was pupils from the
Polytechnic School who in particular had joined the new
doctrine with enthusiasm. This school, which had been established by the Convention, was the home of the
sciences which according to Burdin and Saint-Simon had already become positive, and
which had the calling to form the foundation of the faith of the future. Positive
philosophy is the philosophy of the Polytechnic School, while eclecticism reigned at the
École normale (where teachers were trained for the higher
educational institutions). The real founder of positivism, Auguste Comte,
himself a pupil of the Polytechnic School, speaks in a letter (Lettres à Valat. p.
229) of the hidden and involuntary strife between \textit{Normaliens} and
\textit{Polytechniciens,} which in his eyes was a special form of the strife
between the metaphysical and the positive school. It was the philosophy of the Polytechnicians
that was to become France's most significant contribution to the history of philosophy in
the nineteenth century.

\subsection*{2.\quad Auguste Comte}

\subsubsection*{a.\quad Biography and Characterization}

At the root of the rise of modern positivism lies the development of the
empirical sciences in the last centuries, and in particular the magnificent
advance in the domains of chemistry and physiology which the French
naturalists began at the end of the eighteenth and the beginning of the
nineteenth century. One by one all the domains of nature had been drawn under
the scientific principles and methods which Kepler, Galilei and Newton had
established. LAVOISIER and BICHAT had continued in chemistry
and physiology what the founders of modern natural science had accomplished in
the domains of astronomy and physics. The question now is: what significance
has this whole development for our view of life and our world-view?
Positivism's answer is:
% --- p. 318 ---
\opage{318}Should it be the case that the progress of science is a joy only to
the specialists and to the industrialists? Should it not be a change in the
whole spiritual life of man, in human faith and conduct of life, that results
from all the domains of nature being subject to the method of the empirical
sciences? There is, after all, in the human mind an involuntary need to apply
the same method and the same theory everywhere. Now when we understand nature
by explaining its phenomena according to the laws that experience points out,
are we then, in our faith and in our way of conducting and ordering life, to
be able to build on an entirely different foundation? In fact we find that
empirical science constantly exerts a determining influence on men's religious
and speculative representations, however much these are asserted to have
sprung from entirely different sources. A certain degree of positivism is
found in every world-view. But now all the domains of nature have been drawn
under \textit{positive science,} i.e.\ under the knowledge that builds on facts
and on the laws which experience establishes for these facts. The moment then
seems to have come when that influence is no longer to be hidden and limited,
but when men can consciously and resolutely use in their view of life and
world-view only such representations as positive science can recognize and
confirm. There is still lacking, to be sure, a positive science of the
spiritual life of man; it must then be the task of positivism to found one.
If that succeeds, what then stands in the way of carrying out the program of
positivism? --- The task Auguste Comte set himself was a double one: to make
the human sciences into a positive science, and then to give a systematic
exposition of the chief facts, chief laws and chief methods of all the
positive sciences. The foundation for the world-view of the future would
thereby be given. The time of theology and speculation was over; the positive
philosophy now stood as the only possible tendency. The questions that man
cannot get answered with the help of positive science would then gradually
fall away.

There nevertheless always remains a difference between positive science and
positive philosophy. For it is not the single isolated facts, nor the special
laws, that can condition
% --- p. 319 ---
\opage{319}a world-view. The human mind seeks, as Comte expressly emphasizes,
unity in method and in doctrine. The positive philosophy first comes into
being when the single positivities are worked together into a whole. The
point, then, is to unite positivity and generality or totality. Positivism
therefore cannot use the given as it immediately lies before us, but must
submit it to a working-up, unite it into a whole. Here the difficulty of
positivism comes to lie; for in this working-together there is necessarily
need of hypotheses and presuppositions, and the question then is on what their
validity rests.

Auguste Comte finds his philosophical predecessors in the eighteenth century.
He refers especially to Diderot and Hume, to Kant and the Scottish school. But
he admires de Maistre and regards the Middle Ages as the last
\textit{organic} period we have had. It was his conviction that only by
carrying out positivism in faith and conduct of life would we regain the unity
and harmony in our spiritual and social life which was lost through modern
criticism and through the Revolution. Side by side with the enthusiasm for
positive thinking there goes in Comte the fervent, at last mystical love of
humanity, a need of feeling that demanded its satisfaction with such energy
that it several times threatened to burst his consciousness. The founder of
positivism felt himself spiritually akin to the mystics of the Middle Ages.
And at last he even wanted to found a new religion, which was to be positive
in a sense other than the one in which people are accustomed to speak of
positive religion. ---

\textsc{Auguste Comte}'s life shows us how the various motives that led to his
work developed in him. He was born on 19 January 1798 in Montpellier. His
family was strictly Catholic. By his own account (Cours de
philosophie positive. Tome VI. Préface personelle) he was scarcely fourteen
years old when he ``ran through all the essential degrees of the revolutionary
intellectual tendency and felt the need of a general political and religious
regeneration.'' Perhaps it was precisely the rapid development that led him
away from the representations of his childhood which brought it about that
the need of settled dogmas and definite symbols became so vivid in
% --- p. 320 ---
\opage{320}his later years, after his best strength had been spent on his main
philosophical work. The period in which he was seeking was only short, and he
