did not reap sufficient experience of what value such a period can have for
the freedom, inwardness and fullness of personal life. He came to share the
age's aversion to the \textit{critical} periods. Already as a boy he was
refractory toward all compulsion and all regulation; but full of reverence
before intellectual and moral superiority. (Cf.\ the characterization he gives
of himself as a young man in a letter printed in \textsc{Littré}: \textit{Auguste Comte et la
philosophie positive,} 2. éd. p. 493). In the year 1814 he entered the
Polytechnic School in Paris. This school for the exact sciences, founded by
the Convention, he later regarded (cf.\ a letter to Stuart Mill of 22 July
1842) as the first germ of a true scientific corporation. It comprised the
sciences that had decidedly reached the \textit{positive} stage, and it was for
him the foundation on which all higher education should build. There was,
moreover, among the school's pupils a republican temper and a brotherhood
which united them in a common enthusiasm over the significance their subjects
could have for the development of culture. It was this that won Saint-Simon's
ideas so great a following among the school's pupils. The thought of
positivity and the thought of humanity sprouted forth together. The
reactionary government used, in the year 1816, a demonstration against a
teacher as the occasion for closing the school and sending the pupils home.
But Auguste Comte could not bear to live away from the center of the movement.
In spite of his parents' prohibition he came back to Paris the same year to
continue his education. He studied biology and history to supplement his
polytechnical training, and acquired an excellent encyclopedic foundation. He
earned his living by teaching mathematics. Of great significance for his
development was his coming into close relation with Saint-Simon. He writes of
this in a letter from that time (1818): ``Through collaboration and friendship
with one of the men who see farthest in the domain of philosophical politics I
have learned a host of things which I would have sought in vain in books, and
my mind has, in
% --- p. 321 ---
% scan: „kar“ (p. 321)
\opage{321}the half year I have been in contact with him, made greater progress
than it would have made in three years had I been alone. This work has
developed my conception of the political sciences and has besides indirectly
raised my representations of the other sciences, so that I have noticed that I
have got more philosophy in my head and a more correct, more elevated view of
things.'' \textit{(Lettres à Valat.} p. 37). What Comte owed to Saint-Simon was
partly the notion of the necessity of a new spiritual authority in place of
the hierarchy of the Middle Ages, which in the opinion of both had been an
admirable institution for its time, partly the interest in the social
question, with which the sharp emphasis on the opposition between militarism
and industrialism is connected. In a treatise of 1820 \textit{(Sommaire
appréciation de l'ensemble du passé moderne)} Comte dates the dissolution of
the old social system back to the twelfth century, finding the first germs of
this dissolution in the emancipation of the communes and in the introduction
of the positive sciences into Europe by the Arabs.
Thereby the ground was laid for the industrial system founded on labor
gradually taking the place of the territorial system founded on conquest, and
for positive science replacing theology. Even if Comte had already, by his own
path, arrived at similar ideas, his relation to Saint-Simon nevertheless
hastened his development, and it was with great injustice that Comte later
regarded it as a great misfortune for himself that he had come to know
Saint-Simon\textsuperscript{77}). The two men were, however, too different in
their nature and line of thought to be able to go on working together. The
break came when Comte felt his independence. In principle they came to
disagree about the place science was to take in relation to labor and to the
new ``priesthood'' Saint-Simon had in mind in his later years. As we have
seen, the latter, in the last part of his career, pushed the theoretical
reformation aside in order to think directly of the practical one. In this
Comte disagreed with him. The last work in which Comte still calls himself a
pupil of Saint-Simon occasioned the break; Saint-Simon dissociated himself
from it, and Comte later published it in his
% --- p. 322 ---
\opage{322}own name. This work, whose title was: \textit{Plan des travaux
scientifiques nécessaires pour réorganiser la société} (1822,
published again in 1824 under the title: Politique positive), marks Comte's
breakthrough as an independent thinker. The most important obstacle to the
development of civilization he sees in the constant preponderance of the
revolutionary tendency, especially in freedom of conscience and the
sovereignty of the people, which are critical, not organic, principles. There
is lacking the capacity to enter into a coherent circle of representations and
to recognize a rationally grounded authority. A new social system cannot be
constructed all at once, but must develop successively. That is sufficiently
proved by the many failed constitutions in the most recent history of France.
The fundamental condition for working together toward a common goal is a
common way of thinking and temper. The old society had such a common
foundation in theology. In order that the new society may get a corresponding
foundation, there must first be brought about a comprehensive edifice of
thought that can come forward with the same authority as that with which the
results of the single sciences come forward in the special domains. Most
important of all is that politics be made a positive science. While in the
mathematical, physical and biological domains one recognizes definite laws for
all phenomena, one still believes that in the social domain one can intervene
at one's own discretion, e.g.\ introduce a thought-out social system without
further ado. This belief will fall away when the conformity to law of human
relations is recognized. And such a conformity to law Comte seeks to point out
in the close connection that exists at every point in history between the
social organization and the whole of civilization, that is to say, between the
order of society and spiritual development as this appears in science, art and
industry. Civilization in its turn springs from man's instinctive need of
perfection\textsuperscript{78}). The various stages that civilization runs
through Comte, relying on the history of the sciences, reduces to three: the
theological, the metaphysical and the positive, and he seeks to show how
definite stages in social development correspond to them. Since \textit{the
law of the three stages} is a
% --- p. 323 ---
\opage{323}chief point in Comte's philosophy, the detailed account of it must
be deferred to the exposition of that philosophy. --- This writing of Comte's aroused great attention among politicians, historians
and scientists alike. Guizot, the mathematician Poinsot, Alexander von
Humboldt, the Duke of Broglie and others expressed their approval. It went so
deep that it led beyond the contending parties, while at the same time it did
justice to what was of value in their tendencies. But Comte's real plan had
still not been carried out. Only now did he proceed to the chief work of his
life: to give an encyclopedia of the content and methods of the positive
sciences. He writes to his friend Valat (1824): ``I will work all my life and
with all my powers at the founding of the positive philosophy.'' And at about
the same time he writes to another friend (Gustave d'Eichthal) that his real
task is ``an encyclopedic recasting of all our positive knowledge, which in
reality ought to be conceived as a single mass.'' A few years later he set out
his ``positive philosophy'' for the first time before a small but select
audience (to which there belonged, among others, A. von Humboldt, Poinsot, the
mathematician Fourier, the political economist Dunoyer, the physicians
Broussais and Esquirol, the engineer Hippolyte Carnot).

Comte supported himself by literary work and by teaching mathematics. He had
married a young, gifted Parisian woman. Very early the relationship seems to
have become less happy, partly because Comte's parents were against the union
(which in their eyes was already abominable through having been contracted in
civil form), partly also, as is seen from a characteristic letter to Valat
(16 Nov.\ 1825), because Comte had not found in his wife the qualities he
valued most in a woman: ``devotion of heart and gentleness of character,
together with the kind of subordination which the feeling of her husband's
intellectual superiority can inspire in her,'' qualities which ``it is
certainly very difficult nowadays to find united in a woman of outstanding
intellectual gifts.'' Comte wishes these qualities to his friend's bride in
such a way that it shines through clearly that he
% --- p. 324 ---
\opage{324}misses them in his own wife. She had been too independent for him.
She showed, however, great faithfulness and energy during an attack of mental
illness which --- no doubt chiefly as a result of overwork --- struck Comte. He
was placed in an asylum, and his parents sought to use the opportunity to
bring him under their influence and wanted to place him in a monastery.
Madame Comte, whose civil marriage the parents had wished to pass over in
silence, asserted her right and demanded that her husband be placed in his own
home, and her nursing then succeeded in bringing back his mental health, so
that he could resume his interrupted lectures. (Comte's parents nevertheless
had him --- while he was still insane --- married in church, and thereby
relieved their hearts of the mortal sin of having given their consent to the
civil marriage).

Now there followed for Comte a series of vigorous and happy years, in which he
worked out and published his main work, \textit{Cours de philosophie positive}
(in 6 volumes, 1830---42). The content of each single volume he first thought
through at length on solitary walks. As far as the material was concerned, he
could rely on his great memory. When the meditations were concluded, he wrote
them down in the course of a comparatively short time. Little weight was
thereby laid on the form of the exposition. His style is heavy, unaesthetic,
and suffers from repetitions and a heavy use of technical expressions; but it
is distinguished by clarity, thoroughness and weight, and bears the stamp of
energy and earnestness. Often (especially in the last three volumes of the
work, which deal with the social sciences) the stream of thought becomes so
mighty that it carries the reader along. Comte sought to work for the positive
philosophy in a popular way through public lectures. From the twenties on,
former pupils of the Polytechnic School had held popular lectures on natural
science round about the country. In the year 1830 Comte and some of his
comrades founded the Association polytechnique, which was to work in this
direction. For a long series of years (until the coup d'état of 1851 put an
end to it) Comte gave free public popular lectures, first on astronomy, later
(after 1848) on positive philosophy as a whole. In a little writing,
\textit{Discours sur l'esprit positif} (1844),
% --- p. 325 ---
% print: „Hitorikeren“ (p. 325) (misprint)
\opage{325}he has set out the general considerations with which he introduced
his astronomical course; it gives the best introduction to Comte's
philosophy. ---

A fixed official position Comte never obtained. After 1830 he had hoped for a
professorship in the history of the positive sciences, for which he was in the
highest degree qualified; but an approach to Guizot, now so powerful, was
without result. In his Mémoires Guizot even, by an incomprehensible lapse of
memory, presents it as though it were the first time he saw this man, with
whom he had nevertheless, in the years of opposition in the twenties, had so
many conversations and felt a community of thought. Nor did he obtain a
professorship of mathematics at the Polytechnic School, although he had for a
year temporarily filled this post in a manner that won general recognition. He
had to be content with the more modest position of répétiteur and of examiner
at the entrance examination, in which last capacity he made annual tours of
the provinces.
This last post too, to which one had to be elected annually by the teaching
council of the Polytechnic School, he lost when in the preface to the last
volume of the ``Cours'' he had made a sharp attack on mathematical
specialism and its arrogance. It was now, he held, biologists and sociologists
who were to stand in the front rank in intellectual respects: the supremacy of
the mathematicians was over, since the more concrete domains had been drawn
under positive scientific treatment. The provocative manner in which he
expressed this caused him not to be re-elected examiner, and he was now again
reduced to living by private teaching. English and French admirers and friends
(among the English are to be mentioned Stuart Mill and the historian Grote,
among the French the learned Littré) nevertheless made his economic
circumstances easier for him by giving him support.
--- In his domestic circumstances too it came to a crisis, his life together
with his wife coming to an end after a long period of growing discord. Yet his
wife continued in the finest manner to show her interest both in his ideas and
in his personal circumstances.

Amid all these conflicts and the emotions they
% --- p. 326 ---
% print: „Instutionerne.“ (p. 326) (misprint)
\opage{326}caused, and after the great exertion of strength he had spent in the
twelve years he worked on his main work, it came to a new nervous crisis, not
indeed so severe as the earlier one, but yet of such a kind that, in his own
expression in a letter to Stuart Mill, there was ``danger
cérébral''\textsuperscript{79}). Other circumstances worked together in this
crisis and gave it its peculiar character. He had come to know a woman who
became for him what Beatrice was for Dante: the one toward whom his need of
feeling, which he had carried all his life without getting satisfaction for it
in any intimate relationship, could find a complete outlet. For the first time
he came to know the whole inwardness of mood and of devotion, and this young
woman, whose name was Clotilde de Vaux, continued, when she died after the
lapse of a year, to stand for him as the representative of humanity (just as
Beatrice for Dante was that of theology), to whom he addressed his daily
thoughts and the ``solemn outpourings of noble feeling'' (solennelle effusion
des sentiments généreux), as he called his prayers. She became the genius who
inspired him to his second main work, which was to systematize the feelings,
just as the first had systematized the ideas. This work appeared under the
title \textit{Politique positive ou traité de sociologie, instituant la
religion de l'humanité} (4 volumes, 1851 --- 54). In a letter to Stuart Mill
(of 14 July 1845) Comte states that the new work, the plan for which he had
already formed earlier, had received its decisive character during that crisis
and the ``méditation exceptionelle'' it brought with it. For it dawned on him
that the second part of his philosophical activity ought to differ from the
first in this, that feeling should get as great a place in it as the
understanding had in the former. Now that the purely theoretical work has been
done, the point is its social application, and this consists essentially in a
systematization of the human feelings, a consequence of the systematization of
ideas and an indispensable basis for the systematization of institutions.
--- Had the new work aimed only at this, it would not have marked any decisive
opposition to the earlier one, but a continuation and extension or deepening
of it. In reality it went, as the title already shows, far
% --- p. 327 ---
\opage{327}further. It was to found a new religion. And whereas the earlier
work started from the world or nature and on the basis of the knowledge of
nature sought to arrive at an understanding of man, this objective method was
now to be replaced by the subjective one, which started from man, regarded the
whole of nature from the human point of view, and humanity itself as the
highest being (le grand être). In subjective absorption in the thought of
humanity, in fervent devotion to it, consisted the new religion, whose high
priest Comte soon felt himself to be. He would not give up the positive
philosophy; its content was to be the dogmas of the new religion, the religion
of humanity; but he added cult and practice. In his \textit{Catechisme
positiviste ou sommaire exposition de la religion universelle} (1852) he has
given a shorter exposition of what the ``Politique positive'' develops at
great length.

This last turn in his line of thought had been prepared by what he called his
``hygiene of the brain'' (hygiène cérébrale), which consisted in his
abstaining on principle from all study and absorbing himself solely in the
working out of his works. Thereby he would keep disturbance away and see to it
that the unity of the plan was held fast. Earlier he had pursued far-reaching
studies, and his solid memory enabled him now to use what he had gathered at
that time. Together with this isolation from everything new in science and
literature, an isolation which brought with it the cessation of all real
discussion and of critical testing of his own ideas, there went absorption in
music, Italian and Spanish poetry, and the reading of De imitatione Christi.
He demanded of every positivist that he read every day in a poetic masterpiece
at least as much as corresponds to a canto of Dante. The writing De imitatione
he regarded as a great poem on human nature; in his reading he everywhere put
humanity in place of God, and so found in the old mystical book an aid to a
fervent entering into the life of humanity. According to an eyewitness's
description of Comte in his last years, his whole being was pervaded by
gentleness and goodness. He had, however, had the disappointment that his most
famous disciple Littré, and several with him,
% --- p. 328 ---
\opage{328}withdrew from him when he passed from appearing as a philosopher to
feeling himself the high priest of the religion of humanity, just as he
himself had withdrawn from Saint-Simon when the latter voiced a similar
pretension. After the long and severe labor of thought, the mythological need
of childhood had now, favored by the cerebral hygiene, broken through again,
and on this last part of his way he was followed by only a
few\textsuperscript{80}). Yet the new religion of humanity has its
congregations and its places of worship round about in France, England, Sweden
and America. This religion without theology is a characteristic sign of the
times. For Comte himself it was a resting place where his thought gathered the
memory of the greatest and best it had found in humanity's knowledge and
action, and from which it looked with hope toward the future that could be
expected for the constantly progressing species. Love as principle, order as
foundation and progress as goal! that was the motto of the religion of
humanity. --- On 5 September 1857 Auguste Comte died.

\subsubsection*{b.\quad The Law of the Three Stages}

Our knowledge runs through, according to Comte, \textit{three stages of
development,} which can be pointed out in the case of each single science. The
more intricate and composite the subject matter of a science, the longer it
will be before it has run through this scale. The abstract sciences come first
to the definitive stage, the concrete ones later. In Comte's opinion the point
of time has now come when the most concrete of all the sciences, the science of
society (sociology), is about to enter the third stage. With that the circle
is closed, and a retrospect becomes possible.

The first stage is \textit{the theological.} Here a very limited number of
observations lies at the basis, and imagination therefore plays the greatest
part. The explanation of natural phenomena, the connecting bond between the
given facts which the human mind by its constitution cannot do without, is
found at this stage in the intervention
% --- p. 329 ---
\opage{329}of personal beings. It is only with the help of the representations
of gods and spirits that man can from the beginning make the world
comprehensible to himself. Herein lies the great benefit these representations
have rendered to the development of human knowledge. Had these representations
not been available, and had the wish to find again the working of those beings
in what happened round about in nature not asserted itself, the activity of
knowing would not have got under way; the original torpor would have
persisted. The understanding man believes he gains at this stage is,
moreover, absolute; for beyond those divine beings he thinks of nothing, and if
he can explain a natural phenomenon by their intervention, he has nothing more
to search for. Therefore man at first has no doubt at all about the
possibility of reaching an absolute knowledge. --- In practical respects the
theological representations have exerted an influence no less important. They
have furnished a firm and common ground for moral and social life. This stage
of development is the time of authority. Men live in a common trust in
unshakable powers.
In politics the age of kingship corresponds to this.

The theological stage comprises a series of steps. In fetishism a mental life
like the human one is ascribed directly to the objects of nature. In
polytheism, the step most characteristic of the theological stage, material
objects are deprived of their immediate life, and the source of their motions
and changes is sought in various beings, mostly invisible, who form a higher
world. The transition from fetishism to polytheism is the most important step
taken within the theological stage. The god is removed from the natural
phenomenon to which he corresponds, and thereby the notion of matter as living
can be replaced by the notion of matter as subject to the law of inertia. It
is owing to the beginning capacity for observation and induction that this
transition is made. In monotheism the distance and the opposition between the
principle from which the explanation is taken and the phenomena that are to be
explained are still greater. It is therefore vague and brings with it less
spiritual community than polytheism.
% --- p. 330 ---
\opage{330}It forms the transition to the second great stage: \textit{the
metaphysical.} Here the explanation is found not in personal beings but in
abstract ideas, principles and forces. There prevails here a striving to
reduce various phenomena to one principle, a striving which already within the
theological stage leads over from fetishism to polytheism and from polytheism
to monotheism. The metaphysical stage continues this striving by assuming as
many forces as there are peculiar groups of phenomena, thus a chemical force, a
vital force, etc. At last the striving is then to reduce all these various
forces to one fundamental force, one fundamental being, Nature, an equivalent
of the concluding unity that monotheism made possible at the theological
stage. Common to these first two stages is the tendency to seek absolute
solutions. Metaphysics, just as much as theology, seeks to explain the inmost
nature of things, the origin and destiny of all things, and the manner in which
the phenomena are produced. The difference is only that the abstract is put in
place of the concrete, argumentation in place of fantasy. As great a
preponderance as fantasy had over observation at the first stage, so great a
preponderance has argumentation here.

Comte conceives the metaphysical stage essentially as a stage of transition and
as a process of dissolution. Argumentation bores its way into the theological
circle of representations, points out the contradictions there, puts constant
ideas or forces in place of the incalculable wills, but thereby weakens the
living impression and the authoritative influence of the powers that are
assumed to rule in nature and in human life. Something new it cannot build up;
real equivalents it cannot give. In practical respects the dissolution shows
itself in the rule of doubt and egoism. The individual is torn out of the
living connection with society, and the understanding is cultivated at the
expense of feeling; Comte even speaks in his later years of the long revolt of
the understanding against the heart. In politics it is the age of the peoples,
as the first stage was that of the kings; the jurists are the leading men;
society is conceived as having arisen by contract, and the state is built on
the principle of the sovereignty of the people.
% --- p. 331 ---
% scan: „Forhold.“ (p. 331)
\opage{331}

At the \textit{positive} stage both fantasy and argumentation are subordinated
to observation. Every proposition that is put forward concerns a fact, either a
special or a universal fact. Agreement with facts is the only criterion. Not,
however, to be understood as though it were the single, isolated facts that
are stopped at. Positivism is as far from empiricism as from mysticism: just as
little as it departs from the facts in order to lose itself in supernatural
beings or in abstract principles, just as little does it scatter itself in
incoherent observations. But instead of seeking absolute \textit{causes and}
tracing the production of things out of them, it seeks the \textit{laws} of
phenomena, that is to say, the constant relations that subsist between the
observed phenomena. Whether it is thoughts and feelings or impact and gravity
that are to be understood, the relations under which they appear are the only
thing our knowledge can ascertain. Science builds on the invariability of the
laws of nature, which first dawned on thought with the founding of
mathematical astronomy among the Greeks, but in modern times has been found
again in one domain after another. Bacon, Galilei and Descartes stated this
principle and thereby stand as the founders of the positive philosophy. Even
if the laws that hold in the particular have not yet been found everywhere, an
irresistible analogy now leads us to apply that great philosophical principle
of the invariability of the laws of nature to all phenomena and events.

Whereas the first two stages showed us a striving to reduce everything in
existence to an absolute principle, whether this was thought of in theological
or in metaphysical form --- as God or as Nature ---, it follows from the
nature of the positive philosophy that such an absolute and objective
conclusion is not possible. The strict demand for confirmation by experience
makes it impossible to reduce everything to one principle; experience always
shows us only a limited connection, and there will always be many phenomena
and events which it will not be possible to bring into connection with the
others. There are groups of phenomena (at least as many as there are
% --- p. 332 ---
\opage{332}different sciences that cannot be reduced). The many laws cannot be
reduced to a single one. Only a subjective, not an objective unity can our
knowledge reach. The subjective unity consists in the same method being
applied everywhere, which brings with it uniformity and convergence of the
various theories. (Quant à \textit{la source intérieure} des théories humaines
. . . nos connaissances tendent vers une entière systématisation. Discours
p. 24). Subjectively regarded, then, we get only a single science. And it can
become common to all human subjects. The positive method brings about unity
not only within the consciousness of the single subject, but also between the
various subjects. Thereby the positive philosophy becomes the intellectual
foundation of society among men. Even now it is only on subjects that have
been drawn into the domain of positive science that agreement prevails among
men, while otherwise opinions go in the most various directions. Catholicism,
as long as it ruled without intellectual competition from the side of
scientific thought, offered a spiritual community which stands as a model of
what the positive philosophy will one day bring. The positive philosophy finds
in the subjective unity that lies in the concept of humanity the only possible
equivalent of what the concept of God was for the theological philosophy and
the concept of nature for the metaphysical philosophy.

The connection of theory and practice is far closer at this stage than at the
first two. For knowledge of the laws of phenomena makes it possible for us to
intervene in the future development of phenomena, and the wish to be able to
do this is a contributing motive in the transition from the first two stages
to the third. See in order to be able to foresee (voir pour prévoir!) is the
motto of positive science. To this third stage therefore corresponds industry,
in the sense of man's working-up of nature. Yet the consideration must not here
be restricted to external nature. If there are also laws for man's states and
actions, individual and social development, no less than the purely physical,
can come to be determined by knowledge.
% --- p. 333 ---
% scan: „Utvirlsomme“ (p. 333)
\opage{333}

Comte points out (see especially ``Discours sur l'esprit positif'' p. 41---44)
that all the various meanings in which the word \textit{``positive''} can be
used fit the philosophy he calls the positive. Positive can mean the same as
\textit{real,} and the positive philosophy will, after all, first and foremost
build on facts. It also means \textit{useful} as opposed to idle, and the
positive philosophy, after all, aims at the improvement of our individual and
social existence, seeks to be more than the mere satisfaction of curiosity. By
the positive we also often mean \textit{the certain and indubitable, and} it
is, after all, the task of the positive philosophy to lead us beyond the
constant doubt and debate of the earlier philosophies. The positive can
further mean \textit{the precisely determined, and} the positive philosophy
will, after all, put the laws, the constant and determined relations, in place
of the
indeterminate and shifting representations of earlier stages. Finally,
``positive'' is also used as the \textit{opposite of negative, and} that fits
the third stage, whose task it is to organize, whereas the second stage
essentially signified a process of dissolution. The positive philosophy cannot,
indeed, use the explanations with which the theological philosophy rests
content; but it wages no direct battle with them. It even concedes that it is
as impossible to bring a proof for the rejection of the beings in which one
believes in the theological philosophy as to bring a proof for their
acceptance. No one has ever brought a proof that Apollo or Minerva did not
exist; the belief in them fell away when it no longer fitted together with the
whole spiritual condition. Not only does the positive philosophy not polemize
against the theological; it also seeks to do it full justice, by investigating
historically the conditions of its rise and evaluating its influence on human
development. Such an understanding was not possible at the earlier stages,
where one absolute theory stood over against another, and where each single
system had to regard it as its task to annihilate the others.

Only one peculiarity of the positive stage does not lie in the word
``positive'' itself. It is that it everywhere puts \textit{the relative} in
place of the absolute. But this
% --- p. 334 ---
\opage{334}relative character follows for Comte necessarily from the other
marks of the positive philosophy. When it puts the law in place of the cause,
it stops at a mere relationship, at a relation. It asks: how? not: why? The
inner production and the first grounds it does not seek. The single laws,
moreover, cannot be reduced to a single law, and in any case there remains the
relativity that arises from our always regarding the world from man's point of
view. All knowledge presupposes an opposition between the individual and the
surrounding world. Kant therefore rightly distinguished between the subjective
and the objective, and deserves an eternal admiration because by this
distinction he put an end to the absolute philosophy, although he was not
sufficiently positive in his thinking to be able to prevent his successors from
returning to it\textsuperscript{81}). Although the world presupposes man if it
is to be known, it can nevertheless exist without him. And although man
depends on the world, he is nevertheless not a result of it. (L'homme dépend
du monde, mais il n'en résulte pas. Catéchisme positiviste. \textit{2.} éd.
p. 146). In vain has materialism sought to abolish the independence and
self-activity (spontanéité) of organic life by exaggerating the significance of
the influence of the inorganic surrounding world. The duality remains. ---

The law of the three stages Comte derives from the history of the sciences,
thus by the way of experience. But after he has set it up, he seeks to show
that it can be derived from what we know of the nature of the human mind; the
induction is confirmed by a deduction. For the human mind cannot do without
modes of view and concepts that can bring connection among the single facts.
Before the bond between the phenomena can be found by investigating the
phenomena themselves, as at the positive stage, it must be found in the
mythological representations that arise involuntarily, or in the metaphysical
ideas that are formed by giving these representations a more abstract and
constant form. At the same time the human mind has an inclination to conceive
everything after its own likeness, to carry its own inner feeling over into
things. That is
% --- p. 335 ---
\opage{335}an easy way of gaining an explanation. But if men did not trust that
the explanation could easily be found, they would not engage in any
investigation. ---

It would be interesting to make a comparison between Comte's law of the three
stages and similar thoughts in Kant, Fichte, Hegel and Saint-Simon, indeed
already in Rousseau and Lessing. Beside characteristic divergences there would
turn out to be agreement at least on the one point, that the spiritual life of
man, after the period when authority ruled in theory and in practice, has had a
period when criticism, reflection and doubt performed a dissolving work, after
which the point now is to reach a standpoint with a positive and common
foundation for faith and conduct of life. It is a great historical experience
that has been formulated by the thinkers named in the law of the three stages.
As far as Comte is concerned, it is really only the first and the third stage
that stand out with a definite characterization. One often gets the impression
that Comte really assigns to the metaphysical stage all such endeavors in
thought and life as he harbors an antipathy toward. He sympathizes with the old
Catholic system, in which he sees one of the most marvelous productions of the
human spirit, and he sympathizes with that system of the future which, on the
ground of empirical science, was to lead to a new spiritual community. The
intervening critical and revolutionary period he looked on with aversion,
although he had to concede that it had performed an indispensable work. The
various marks he adduces of the metaphysical stage do not necessarily hang
together. In particular it will not be possible to find a connection between
the tendency to explain the phenomena by assuming specific forces or faculties
and the overvaluation of the intelligence or the predominance of egoism. That
tendency appears at a certain point within the history of each single science
and cannot be used to characterize the common human development; in any case
it can very well be united with the recognition of the central significance of
the life of feeling and of the reality of the sympathetic feelings. An
overvaluation of the intelligence is found perhaps quite as much among
cultivators of the special sciences
% --- p. 336 ---
% scan: „saare,“ (p. 336)
% print: „Posivitet“ (p. 336) (misprint)
\opage{336}as among speculative philosophers. At the conclusion of his main
work Comte did, after all, feel vividly the opposition in which he stood to
scientific specialism, and he expressed it so strongly that it had drastic
personal consequences for him. But for this opposition between the positive
philosophy and positive special research he finds no place in his doctrine of
the three stages. And yet it is a very essential characteristic of modern times
that the division of labor in the scientific domain has advanced so far that an
intellectual unity, a common world-view, becomes harder and harder to reach.
Here there surely lies a greater problem of the history of culture than in any
of the defects Comte finds in the metaphysical stage. It was Comte's enthusiasm
and sanguineness that kept him from seeing this clearly. The problem of the
relation between positivity and generality --- of the possibility of reaching
a general world-view on ``positive'' ground --- did not stand sharply enough
before him. That is connected, as will appear later, with his shortcomings in
respect of epistemology. The positive stage itself is therefore unclearly
drawn in several respects. Thus it remains unclear how narrowly the positive
philosophy binds us to the facts before us. How far may we depart from these
by the way of hypothesis? What justification has a hypothesis that is a
logical consequence of given experiences but cannot be verified? What
justification has a faith that cannot indeed be derived from experience, but
yet does not conflict with experience? Such questions, extraordinarily
important for the relation between science and view of life, Comte passes by.

Absolute boundaries between the various stages Comte does not really assume,
although he has not sufficiently emphasized the unity of human thought through
all the stages. It was not his opinion that the theological stage was wholly
without positivity. The influence of experience has always asserted itself,
e.g.\ in the transition from fetishism to polytheism and from polytheism to
monotheism; but as long as the circle of experience was small, its influence
could not become one of principle. It is nevertheless the forward-driving power
of experience that expresses
% --- p. 337 ---
\opage{337}itself in the metaphysical principles. These represent in reality
groups of experience which are demanded to be withdrawn from mythological
arbitrariness. Metaphysics systematized, as Comte says in one place (Discours
sur l'esprit positif, p. 36), the opposition of nascent science to the old
theology. As long as the positive spirit was still only little developed, it
could not formulate its own tendencies, and it then used metaphysics as its
organ. Thus knowledge moves forward through continuous transitions. A complete
breakthrough and a general dominion of \textit{esprit positif} Comte by no
means expected at the beginning of his career.
He writes to Valat on 30 March 1825: ``Although I hope for some use from my
endeavors, I do not hide from myself that in my lifetime they will not be able
to produce any remarkable result, even if they should be able to give an
impulse to all minds that are capable of taking part with effect in the great
work, something which only the future will be able to show.'' Later, when
under the influence of his cerebral hygiene and of the mystical absorption in
his ideas he had lost all understanding of what was going on around him in the
scientific and the political world, he cherished a greater and ever increasing
sanguineness in this respect.

Whether Comte laid most weight on the negative character of the second stage or
on its significance as a necessary intermediate link, it was his conviction
that the decisive battle in the spiritual world would come to be fought between
Catholicism and positivism. Repeatedly in his letters to Stuart Mill he
expresses the wish that a direct debate between these two tendencies --- with
the exclusion of Protestantism, deism and other inconsistent intermediate forms
--- might come about. It was to him a significant sign of the times that the
Catholics now demanded freedom of teaching, while the ``metaphysical'' school
(Cousin, Guizot, Thiers, Villemain) demanded that the state monopoly be
maintained. Both schools had thereby denied their principles, the former the
principle of authority, the latter the principle of freedom. But if discussion
and teaching became free, he hoped that the metaphysical school's fear would be
% --- p. 338 ---
\opage{338}fulfilled, while Catholicism would then stand over against a new
adversary it had not known before. He only regretted that the representatives
of Catholicism had become inferior since de Maistre's time. That the
oppositions sharpened, and that Catholic orthodoxy became ever stricter and
more systematic, was for him fully understandable, after the revolutionary
movement had betrayed the tendency to build spiritual and social development on
an entirely different foundation from that of authority. In the face of these
radical prospects de Maistre had inculcated ultramontanism as the only
consistent religious system, and it had succeeded in shattering Gallicanism,
whose fate other intermediate standpoints too would come to share. Comte
therefore rejoices that his friend Valat, in a breakthrough of religious faith,
took the step fully back to pure Catholicism, without stopping at any
intermediate standpoint, although in the beautiful letter he wrote to Valat on
that occasion (25 August 1843) he made no secret of his doubt that Catholicism
could now bestow the peace and harmony which in its classical time it could
give to those who had the highest intellectual and moral development of that
day. In particular he refers in this respect to the misgivings about the dogma
of the eternal damnation of those who practice the highest morality even if
they reject every article of faith, a dogma which is nevertheless
indispensable to the whole Catholic organism.

\subsubsection*{c.\quad The Classification of the Sciences}

By philosophy Comte understands the whole system of human concepts. This
systematizing can, as we have seen, take place in three different ways.
Hitherto the theological and the metaphysical method have ruled; Comte himself
believes he is the first to carry out the systematization by the positive
method, that is to say, by the same method as that by which the concepts or
laws are won within the single sciences. It is the task of the positive
philosophy to gather and order the laws that have been extracted from the
facts. By thus connecting what occurs scattered in the various
% --- p. 339 ---
\opage{339}sciences, it seeks to remedy the drawbacks the division of labor
brings with it in the domain of knowledge. Comte regards it as hopeless to
attempt to reduce all special laws to a single one, as the theological and the
metaphysical philosophy had each in its own way attempted. The positive
philosophy would certainly become more perfect if that were possible; but
experience speaks against it, since it presents diversities that cannot be
reduced. While the unity of the positive philosophy does not consist in all
laws being reduced to a single one, it comes out clearly, on the other hand, in
the common method, which everywhere proves applicable, and which, in spite of
the irreducible diversities, points to a uniformity in the various classes of
phenomena. To each of these classes there corresponds a peculiar science, and
the classification of the sciences therefore becomes the most important task of
the positive philosophy.

Comte's classification of the sciences orders them in \textit{the sequence in
which each of them historically entered the positive stage.} Here comes first
mathematics, then astronomy, physics, chemistry, biology and sociology. But
this sequence shows us at the same time a progressive transition from
\textit{simplicity} in the phenomena considered to
\textit{compositeness} (complication). The simpler a science's content is, the
more quickly will it be able to run through the various stages; the more
complex the phenomena that are to be investigated, the longer it will be
before the childhood diseases are overcome. Biology and sociology therefore
come last in the series. The simpler the relations a science concerns, the more
\textit{universal validity} will it at the same time have; for the simpler
relations recur in the more composite ones. Mathematics holds for all
phenomena, and the most concrete sciences, biology and sociology, have the
\textit{narrowest extension.} (This relation between généralité décroissante
and complication croissante Comte could have found demonstrated in logic's
doctrine of the inverse relation between the content and the extension of
concepts). Finally, the methods of the various sciences also present a
corresponding sequence. The simpler and more universal a science's foundation
is, the greater the preponderance the \textit{deductive} method gains over the
\textit{inductive.} Thus
% --- p. 340 ---
\opage{340}mathematics is the most deductive science, sociology the least
deductive. In sociology the demonstration of the historical course of
development plays the greatest part; after this has been established by the
inductive way, the task then becomes to deduce it from human nature, as Comte
himself has attempted by his setting up of the law of the three stages. The
inductive foundation of mathematics is so simple that one often overlooks it
and regards mathematics as a pure science of reason. But a pure science of
reason there is not at all. Even mathematics is a natural science; its
concepts, just as much as those of all other sciences, stem from experience.
But the facts mathematics concerns are so simple that one can consider them as
easily in fantasy as in reality, and that one can abstract from the physical
and chemical properties of bodies. Number, extension and motion are properties
we can represent to ourselves just as well in an indeterminate medium thought
of as including all the bodies of the universe as in the real bodies
themselves. This explains the apparent independence of mathematics from
experience. On the foundation of fantasies of space and number the
mathematical deductions can unfold unconcerned about experience. If
mathematics had no foundation in experience at all, it would be altogether
impossible to understand how the mathematical deductions could be applied to
the study of real nature. --- Between the as good as purely deductive method of
mathematics and the as good as purely inductive method of sociology lie the
other chief methods, each corresponding to its chief science. Through
astronomy's use of deductively set up hypotheses that are confirmed by
observation, we come to the experimental method of physics, to the rational
method of division of chemistry, and to the comparative method of biology; this
last forms the transition to the historical method of sociology.

The six groups of concepts or laws that Comte thus sets up in the ``Cours de
philosophie positive'' he regards as irreducible. In the transition from one
sphere to the other a leap takes place; a new principle comes into force which
cannot be derived from the preceding one. It is in Comte's eyes materialism to
seek to derive the higher (i.e.\ more complex,
% --- p. 341 ---
\opage{341}more limited and more inductive) science from the lower. Just as
little can any of the single groups be made the all-embracing one. And the
same discontinuity that thus for Comte prevails between the six groups of
fundamental concepts prevails also within each single one of them. The various
branches of physics will thus --- he asserts --- always remain separate from
one another. It is with the organic species as with the physical forces. The
concept of species would, says Comte, entirely lose its scientific
significance if one were to admit transformations of one species into another
under the influence of the external conditions of life. Between the plant and
the animal world in particular he maintains ``a real and deep discontinuity,
which cannot be effaced by any transition whatsoever.''

This point in Comte is an instructive example of how tendencies of thought can
turn over into their opposites. The difference of the positive philosophy from
the metaphysical was to consist, after all, in laws being put in place of ideas
or forces, and relative explanations being put in place of absolute ones. But
Comte in reality himself sets up a Platonic world of ideas through his
irreducible groups of concepts. He takes the discontinuity too dogmatically,
instead of taking it as a mere fact, a fact which is perhaps due only to the
imperfection of science. By his emphasis on the discontinuity in existence he
sets his positivism in the sharpest opposition to German Romanticism, which
sought to dissolve all differences in ideal continuity. It is, as Comte also
concedes, the constant task of science to reduce the diversities, the breaks
in the continuity of the phenomena, to the least possible. Every discontinuity
can therefore signify only a provisional limit. And the later development of
science, precisely in the period that begins with the conclusion of Comte's
main work (c.\ 1840), has indeed led to demonstrating or conjecturing
continuity where Comte had considered it impossible. Thus the law of the
conservation of energy, in particular the doctrine of heat as a form of motion,
and the demonstration of the identity of light and electricity have given an
insight into the unity of nature for which Comte had no room in his system. In
the organic domain the
% --- p. 342 ---
\opage{342}hypothesis of evolution has led to the well-founded assumption that
species signify only stages in, or offshoots of, connected processes; in
particular it has become harder and harder to maintain sharp boundaries
between the animal and the plant world. Comte already pronounced against the
hypothesis of evolution as it existed in his time (in Lamarck's form); and his
disciples (Charles Robin, Littré) have since been eager opponents of it. This
much can be said without anticipating anything: that the relation between
continuity and discontinuity has proved to be more intricate than Comte had
supposed in his philosophy.

The connection between the various domains rests, according to Comte, on this,
that the preceding domain, as the simpler and more universal, lies at the
basis of the following, more complex and special one (even if the latter
cannot be derived from the former). Mathematics is the most abstract and
universal science, and within mathematics, again, the theory of number is
simpler and more universal than geometry and the theory of motion; it
therefore becomes the rational basis of the whole system of our positive
knowledge. Comte has here overlooked that there are fundamental concepts of our
knowledge that are still more simple and universal than the concept of number,
namely the concepts of identity and difference, as these are conceived in
logic: not only as identity and difference between magnitudes, but also
between qualities. In his series of branches of knowledge Comte has thus not
got the first member in. Moreover, a difficulty comes up for him when he
teaches that geometry and the theory of motion --- which in abstraction and
universality come right after the theory of number --- hold for all phenomena,
the former in so far as these are conceived in equilibrium (from the static
point of view), the latter in so far as they are conceived in motion (from the
dynamic point of view). Extension and motion are forms only of material
phenomena, not of mental phenomena, and since Comte himself rejects
materialism because it introduces the points of view of the lower science into
the higher and seeks to \textit{derive} man from the world, not merely to
point out his dependence on the world, the science of mental phenomena does not
fit into Comte's sequence of the sciences, in which each preceding one is to
hold for the following ones,
% --- p. 343 ---
\opage{343}although these are more special. Logic and the theory of number hold
directly for the science of mental phenomena as well as for the science of
material phenomena; but this cannot be said of geometry and the theory of
motion, as long as one does not, with consistent materialism, regard the
phenomena of consciousness without further ado as extended in space. The
classification of the sciences is not so simple a matter as Comte presupposed.
His system presents here a difficulty similar to the one we have already
pointed out in Hobbes (in the first part of this work, p. 264 f.). Comte
himself would not concede this. He does not regard psychology as a special
science and therefore gives it no independent place in the series either. He
denies the possibility of self-observation. One observes --- he
says\textsuperscript{82}) --- all phenomena with one's mind (esprit); but with
what, then, is one to observe one's mind? One cannot, after all, divide one's
mind into two parts, of which the one acts while the other investigates how it
goes about it! Yet Comte concedes that the feelings can be observed more easily
than thinking, because, as he believes, they have a different organ from it.
Our intellectual activities must be studied in their products and results or
in the organs to which they are tied. Instead of setting up psychology as an
independent science, Comte distributes the psychological investigations
between biology and sociology. Biology alone would not let the fact that the
individual's mental life is determined by the influence of history and of
society come into its own. It is thus by a purely objective way that Comte
wants the life of consciousness studied. It was meritorious that the objective
method was emphasized so strongly in opposition to the purely subjective and
spiritualist psychology of Cousin and Jouffroy. But Comte has not seen that the
subjective method in reality always lies at the basis of the objective one,
and he has on the whole not let the peculiarity of the phenomena of
consciousness come into its own. Whereas elsewhere he emphasizes discontinuity
more strongly than is defensible, here he emphasizes it too little. There
would, as already indicated, also have arisen a difficulty for his
classificatory system if the qualitative
% --- p. 344 ---
\opage{344}peculiarity of the phenomena of consciousness were to be stressed;
they would break the sequence, since, even if they are in and for themselves
simple and elementary, they are in fact tied to the most complicated material
phenomena. Should they then be placed first or last? --- Comte sets himself in
definite opposition not only to spiritualism but also to the psychology of
Condillac, which he reproaches for conceiving the single individual as purely
isolated, and also for taking account only of the external influences, not of
the inner conditions. The single individual is a scholastic abstraction; only
the species is a reality. (Cours\textsuperscript{2} VI, p. 590). In biological
respects Comte found the most important work done in Gall's physiology of the
brain, if one disregarded his unfortunate doctrine of localization. Gall's
list of mental faculties would indeed, Comte concedes, have to be considerably
reduced; but no fewer than ten could be assumed; between ten and fifteen
faculties was what he was most inclined to assume (Lettres à Stuart Mill.
p. 51---55). Gall, Comte believes, first brought the study of the intellectual
and moral functions into the positive stage and maintained the significance of
the inner dispositions. This admiration of Comte's for Gall conflicts with his
own conception of the relation between the metaphysical and the positive stage;
for Gall's doctrine of faculties presents all the marks of ``metaphysics.'' ---
If one asks how Comte unites the assumption of 10---15 peculiar faculties with
the unity of the life of consciousness, the answer is that this unity is,
according to Comte, not original but a result, resting on the harmony between
man's various tendencies and forces (Cours\textsuperscript{2} III, p. 545).
--- The problem of the relation between discontinuity and continuity extends
into the life of consciousness and appears here in a way that demands its own
peculiar investigation, an investigation, however, that Comte does not come to
take up, because he carves psychology up into a biological and a sociological
part, without the central psychological questions getting room to come
forward. On this point Comte is supplemented by the new English school, which
% scan: „sem“ (p. 344)
lays a peculiar weight precisely on psychology.
% --- p. 345 ---
\opage{345}

\subsubsection*{d.\quad Sociology and Ethics}

More than half of Comte's chief work --- the last three and largest volumes ---
treats of the science of society (sociology --- as he calls it with a word
of his own coining, which in spite of all philological misgivings has now made its way
through). It comprises an essential part of psychology, the whole of
political economy and ethics, together with the philosophy of history. Just as Comte
protests against treating the psychology of the single individual apart from the
spiritual development of the whole species, so he also protests against
political economy and ethics being isolated from the general theory of society, and the later
development of these sciences has proved him right in this
protest\textsuperscript{83}). Neither psychology, political economy nor ethics
can be treated without regard to human development through history.
In all the different scientific domains Comte points out the relation between
statics and dynamics. The world is regarded statically in geometry, dynamically in
the doctrine of motion. Within physics and chemistry forces are regarded partly in equilibrium,
partly in activity. In the organic domain statics is represented by
anatomy, which investigates organization, dynamics by physiology, which
investigates functions. To sociology there belong partly a social statics, which
studies the constant conditions of existence of society, partly a social dynamics, which
studies the laws of the steady development of society: the fundamental idea of the former is order,
of the latter progress. Statics and dynamics belong closely together, for order and progress
mutually condition each other --- something which neither the reactionary nor the
revolutionary school has seen.

\textit{a) Social statics.} Society forms a whole, within which all
elements stand in the most intimate interaction, so that one of them cannot be
altered without more or fewer of the others undergoing a corresponding alteration.
Thus, e.g., the political and social constitution is closely connected with the whole of
civilization. There is a close connection between ideas, manners and
institutions, and no external authority --- whether of revolutionary or
reactionary kind --- is able to accomplish anything by
% --- p. 346 ---
\opage{346}forcing upon society institutions which do not correspond to the prevailing ideas and
manners. Naturally the institutions in turn react upon ideas and manners; but
this reaction presupposes a longer undisturbed subsistence and is most strongly
prominent in the childhood of the human race. The ideas and the manners, too, stand
in mutual interaction. It is the task of political institutions to regulate
the common life which has developed involuntarily during the progress of humanity in
intellectual, moral and physical respects. The elements which play the greatest
part in this development will in the end become the ruling ones in society.
Authority rests on free co-operation, not the reverse.

Within social statics \textit{ethics} finds, on an essential side, its
place. The ethical laws express the solidarity in all human life. This
solidarity is discovered involuntarily, as men follow their need of
fellowship. It is self-contradictory to explain the origin of social life out of
calculation of the utility man can have from living together with others. Utility
can only show itself after a sufficiently long common life has taken place, and
can therefore not be the original motive for the common life's taking place. Comte
here sets himself in opposition to the explanation frequent in the eighteenth century,
which stopped at the shrewd calculation of isolated individuals. In his
view an instinctive impulse to social life, independent of personal calculation,
asserted itself originally; feeling here, as on the whole,
precedes knowledge. In this view of his Comte is, by his own account,
a disciple partly of Hume and Adam Smith\textsuperscript{84}), who led him beyond
the current theory of egoism, partly of Gall, who assumed definite organs of the brain for the
social instincts. Comte finds the first germ of sociability at the stage
in the animal world where the sexes are separate and where care for
offspring appears. Yet even in man the egoistic inclinations at first
have the upper hand over the social inclinations, which latter Comte, in order to
designate them in their marked opposition to egoism, designates as altruism
(from alter, one's neighbor). Nor is personal interest to be rooted out.
Altruism would become a vague and unfruitful love if it did not
% --- p. 347 ---
\opage{347}acknowledge the need of personal satisfaction both in others and in the
individual himself. What matters is that the egoistic instinct be subordinated,
and this happens through the successive development of intelligence and sympathy. Through
sympathy intelligence is freed from working in the service of egoism alone, and
through intelligence the eye for social solidarity is sharpened. The social
state favors the sympathetic feelings. As the individual extends his feeling
to embrace the whole species, he obtains through this social expansion
satisfaction for his need to make himself eternal, seeing the continued
life of the species as a continuation of his own life.

As isolated and single the individual is only an abstraction. The social unit is
the family, where the first germs appear of the dispositions which
characterize the social organism. Here the individual learns to go beyond
himself, to live in others, at the same time as it obeys its most energetic
instincts. It is the most intimate society. It is a unity, not a
combination (union, not association). Co-operation no doubt also plays a part in
the family, but not the chief part, as in the larger societies, which rest on common
labor and on the supplementing made necessary by the division of labor. By performing a
definite labor each individual and each family exercises a social function. The
authority which is to direct this function must proceed from society itself and
found its power on the confidence it inspires and the free adherence it
finds. Every society will inevitably come to have a government. While in the
individual life it is the personal instincts, and in the family sympathy, that
rule, in the larger society it will essentially be the intellectual faculties
that act to order it. A certain intellectual community is necessary for a
society; the co-operation of interests and immediate sympathy are not
sufficient. Positive science has a very great significance for ethics,
for it will be a matter of determining as exactly as possible the real, direct
or indirect influence which every action, inclination or feeling
has on human existence, both on the single individuals and on
society as a whole.

It was, according to Comte, the great merit of Catholicism that it
% --- p. 348 ---
\opage{348}emancipated morality from politics, to which in the polytheistic period it had been
wholly subordinated. This emancipation found its expression in the doctrine of the two powers
and of the independence of the spiritual power from the temporal. But Catholicism showed
itself unable to satisfy the growing intellectual
needs of men, and metaphysical criticism began its dissolving work. Moreover
Catholicism furthered egoism by letting the individual be occupied with his own
salvation, whereby it no doubt gained a mighty motive, but hindered the free and pure
unfolding of the sympathetic and high-minded feelings. Only the positive
intellectual tendency directly favors the unfolding of these feelings by impressing upon us
that our whole development takes place \textit{within} society, so that it is
the individual and not society that is an abstraction. In social life the
egoistic inclinations must in many ways be checked; only the social drives
can unfold freely, and the heightened activity which the unlimited horizon thus opened
brings with it contains a source of happiness, of inner
satisfaction, which is independent of external rewards. The concept of duty
springs from the view of the whole (esprit d'ensemble) which positive philosophy
asserts, and which shows the single individual as a member of the whole species, so
that the rules for its action must follow from a universal order of things, not
merely from purely individual interests. The highest idea in the ethical domain
is the idea of humanity as that whose development is uninterruptedly determined by the
co-operation of all individual and social organs. Comte polemicizes against the sharp
separation between private and public functions. This distinction is purely
empirical and comes forward only in times of transition, when a new civilization is
developing, and when the new elements have difficulty in finding their
place. It did not exist among the Greeks and Romans, nor in the theocracy of the Middle
Ages; it first came forward at the end of the Middle Ages, especially after the
industrial upswing which followed the abolition of serfdom.
The masses of the proletariat have since that time not truly been incorporated into
the social system. And only with such an incorporation comes the right
personal self-respect, which consists
% --- p. 349 ---
\opage{349}in feeling oneself a fellow worker within a great whole. One day such a
feeling will ennoble even the humblest occupation, namely when through
\textit{positive} education the consciousness has become alive of the significance of every single
endeavor for society as a whole.

It was Comte's conviction that what was needed for the time being was political
quiet, the avoidance of great political upheavals, so that ideas, feelings and manners
could undergo the involuntary change which the positive stage will bring with it.
The most important social difficulties were in his eyes not political, but chiefly
moral, and could be overcome only through the influence of ideas and manners.
In him the concept of duty decidedly preponderates over the concept of right.
His philosophy contains no elements for a philosophy of law and political theory proper.
For he holds the belief that institutions will easily develop once ideas and manners are
changed. Here, already in his first and proper chief work, there asserts itself a
utopian tendency, arisen as a reaction against the preceding period's
strong emphasis on individual rights as well as against the many
constitutional struggles with which the age was occupied. He thought that a comparatively
short-lived ``progressive dictatorship'' would suffice to bring about the
quiet ripening of ideas and feelings which was a necessary condition
for the Occident to arrive at its lasting social institutions, and for
the great Revolution to obtain its positive counterpart.

\textit{β) Social dynamics.} One important law which belongs to social dynamics
we already know: the law of the three stages. In the intellectual domain, as
Comte emphasizes, progress can most easily be demonstrated. But to the different stages
of intellectual development there correspond, as we indicated in the exposition of
the three stages, stages of development of a social and political kind. To the
theological stage corresponds the \textit{military.} Its significance consists in this, that
regularity and discipline, necessary conditions of political organization,
are implanted and developed. Forces are gathered about pressing common purposes. Just as
the first spiritual authority necessarily had to be theological, so
the first governments necessarily had to
% --- p. 350 ---
\opage{350}be military. Only external force could gather and hold together. And only
through war does society grow at the earliest stages of development. War in turn brings
slavery: in order that the warriors might have free disposal of their force,
the economic labor had to be done by slaves. To the transitional period which in
intellectual respects is designated as the metaphysical there corresponds in the social and
political domain a period in which the \textit{jurists} (``the legists'') rule. A
defensive military organization takes the place of the earlier offensive one. The
warlike spirit gradually gives way to the productive spirit. The middle classes
push forward and demand political rights. It is the task of the ruling jurists
to weigh the different claims against one another. It is a vague and restless
transitional stage, the social phase in which we still find ourselves. To the
positive stage corresponds the \textit{industrial} phase, in which the producing
forces determine the arrangement of institutions and the distribution of power. Social
questions now take the place of political ones. The proletarians gradually
discover that political revolutions cannot solve the great social
problems whose sting they feel most of all. They will naturally sympathize with
the endeavor of positive philosophy to set duties above rights,
so that the attention of all may be directed to solving the task which is the
properly social one: to procure for all access to spiritual development and access to
work. There will therefore be a natural understanding between proletarians and
positive philosophers.

This demonstration of humanity's solidary course of development becomes of great
significance for ethics, which thus belongs not only to social statics
but also to social dynamics. Not only is the social feeling strengthened
by the demonstration of the solidary development, but an essential part of the content of ethics
can be determined only on a dynamic basis. For the task of ethics is to
contribute to the development of the specifically human qualities --- in contrast
to the animal and vegetative ones. And here ethics has its presupposition not only in
what social dynamics teaches about the different stages, but already in the
results of comparative biology,
% --- p. 351 ---
\opage{351}which show how the animal functions, the higher one comes up in the series of
animals, play an ever greater part in relation to the vegetative ones. In man
the specifically human qualities, intelligence and sociability, in turn develop in
relation to the animal ones, which Comte --- following Gall's
interpretation of the brain --- finds expressed in the stronger development of the frontal region of the
brain in relation to the part of the brain which lies nearest the spinal cord.
Within the human species Comte assumes an ever further-reaching development of
intelligence and sympathy (altruism), the condition for the single individual's being able to
make himself one with the species. Although Comte is an opponent of Lamarck's
doctrine of evolution, he nevertheless acknowledges the great influence which uniform and steady
exercise has on faculties and qualities. The nobler tendencies in our nature will through
social life be ever further developed; the baser instincts will gradually be
weakened, partly by self-control, partly by lack of exercise, or they will
gradually be compelled to serve the social order itself. --- A more definite form
Comte is unable to give his ideas on this point, partly because he lacks
the doctrine of the displacement of motives founded by Spinoza and Hartley, which
English psychology later carried further, partly also because he could not
make use of the close connection which evolutionism assumes between the development of the individual and of
the whole species.

In concluding his exposition of human ethics, Comte declares that when
one wishes to compare the morality of positive philosophy with religious morality,
one must not forget that while the former is scarcely thought out and cannot work through
regular institutions, the latter is fully developed through centuries of
spiritual labor and has for long ages found support in a great social
apparatus. In his later years --- after the remarkable nervous crisis in the middle of the
forties --- he became more sanguine and no longer held fast to the
conviction that we stand only at the beginning of the development.
% --- p. 352 ---
\opage{352}

\subsubsection*{e.\quad Theory of Knowledge}

Although Comte has not made the theory of knowledge the object of special
investigation and exposition, the whole of positive philosophy nevertheless rests clearly
enough on definite epistemological presuppositions, and in some places (especially
in the last volume of ``Cours'' and then in ``Discours sur l'esprit positif'') he
expresses himself on it at greater length. It will be of great interest to attempt a
determination of Comte's epistemological standpoint.

Positive philosophy is, according to Comte's express and repeated declarations, not
empiricism. Already in 1825 he shows in an essay \textit{(Considérations
philosophiques sur les sciences et les savants),} that an absolute empiricism is
impossible. Science does not consist in a mere accumulation of facts. Its essential
task is the connection of facts; it consists of laws, not of mere
facts. No isolated fact is incorporated in science; it becomes so
only when the isolation is removed by its being connected --- at least by means of a
hypothesis --- with another fact. Comte even makes the interesting
remark (Cours\textsuperscript{2} IV, p. 300) that no isolated and purely
empirical observation can be certain. It was indeed also, as we have seen, through
the necessity of a bond between phenomena that Comte made it
intelligible that our knowledge must pass through the theological and the
metaphysical stage before it can reach the positive. At the positive stage
the laws of phenomena are sought, that is to say a factual connection between them.
The connection can be brought about in two ways. Either it is a question of
simultaneously given phenomena, and then the explanation is gained by demonstrating
similarity in the relations and laws which hold for different groups of phenomena.
Or else it is a question of successively appearing phenomena, and then the task is
to demonstrate a continuous connection between them. In the first case we have
a static, in the second case a dynamic explanation. Whether we explain
\textit{par similitude} or \textit{par filiation,} we connect phenomena
in such a way that we can foresee their occurrence. And in both cases
we satisfy our mind's need of unity and find again
% --- p. 353 ---
\opage{353}the constant in the midst of the variations. (Discours sur l'esprit positif, p. 20---21).

Comte's theory of knowledge does not go beyond these developments, interesting in themselves,
on this point. He does not pursue the connecting activity of the mind
more closely, although he regards it as fundamental: \textit{tout se réduit
toujours à lier!} A closer investigation would here have led him further into
subjective psychology than he wished and considered possible. Nor does
he enter into the question what validity can be ascribed to those laws of similarity
and of succession. He expresses himself somewhat waveringly on this point. Now he says
that science has nothing to do with the first fundamental propositions; they
spring up involuntarily in the human mind and cannot be discussed.
(Discours sur l'esprit positif. p. 46). Here he approaches Reid's theory of knowledge built on common
sense. Now, on the other hand, he says that the principle of
the invariability of natural laws, on which positive science rests, cannot
be grounded a priori, but will always in the end prove to rest on simple
observation and induction (Discours. p. 17). This last consideration would
evidently, if carried through consistently, drive him over into pure empiricism and into the
difficulties in which it finds itself with regard to the causal principle,
difficulties which first came clearly to light through Stuart Mill's
significant resumption of Hume's problem. --- When Comte expects that
the principle of the invariability of natural laws will gradually make its way in
all domains, it is, as already remarked, because he thinks that an
irresistible analogy will compel us to carry it through. It will, as he declares
in one of his older essays, in the long run be impossible for the human
mind to think positively in some domains, metaphysically or theologically in
others. It will strive after unity in method and theory. Here, then, the power of habit
is at work, to which Hume already pointed. But habit can explain only the principle's
psychological power over the mind, not its real validity. The sting of the problem of knowledge proper
Comte has not felt. He sought to systematize positive
% --- p. 354 ---
\opage{354}knowledge; but he did not set himself the task of discussing the ultimate
foundation of this knowledge.

From another side, however, Comte approaches the problem of knowledge, namely in his
emphasis on the relativity of knowledge. He finds it, as we have seen, to be
an essential characteristic of positive philosophy that it everywhere puts
the relative in place of the absolute which was sought in the earlier forms of
philosophy. The relativity of knowledge he grounds in two ways. In the first place,
positive science can teach us only relations of similarity and of succession between
things, not the absolute causes of things, nor the very inmost
nature of the things between which those relations obtain. The relations themselves, too, stand
as mere facts which cannot be fathomed further. In the second place,
all our knowledge is determined by the relation between our organism and its environment
--- Comte even speaks of ``the great elementary dualism between the understanding and
the milieu'' --- and in such a way that the environment does affect and determine
the understanding and gives it its material, but the working up takes place, as in
the process of nutrition, according to the laws of our own organization and in its forms. There is
therefore a relation partly to the subject, partly to the object, which asserts itself in
all knowledge. In this biological epistemology\textsuperscript{85}) Comte
feels himself a successor of Aristotle, Leibniz and Kant
(Cours\textsuperscript{2} VI, p. 620 ff. Catéchisme positiviste, p. 150 f.).
It leads him to see that our knowledge can reach only an approximation to
reality; but on account of his practical standpoint he does not come to
discuss the question how far our knowledge can rightly be said to
be a reflection of reality. It is enough for him that the knowledge we
have can be used practically for orientation. On the other hand he lays great weight on this, that
the very subject to which knowledge stands in relation undergoes change and
development. All knowledge is determined by the stage of development which the individual and
