the species have reached. All our knowledge therefore has a historical character.
Sociology leads, as already the doctrine of the three stages has shown, no less
than biology to an emphasis on the relativity of knowledge. As long as biology and
sociology
% --- p. 355 ---
\opage{355}were not yet developed in positive form, the relativity could be overlooked, as
happened in the whole period when mathematics stood as the chief science. Now
the scepter has passed to sociology. It is sociology to which it belongs to state the
concluding scientific points of view.

That Comte thus came to stress the biological and sociological point of view
for our knowledge, or in other words came to see knowledge as determined
by man's nature, needs and degree of development, brought with it an important change in
his philosophical standpoint. From the first he had laid the chief weight on ``the
necessary and rational subordination of the concept man to the concept
world'' (Cours\textsuperscript{2} III, p. 188); now he lays more and more weight
on the subjective side of knowledge. Knowledge comes to stand for him
essentially as the satisfaction of a subjective need, and he regards
every means of reaching such satisfaction as justified. The need of
knowledge becomes for him an artistic need. He asserts the justification of
following the simplest hypotheses and disregards the necessity of a
confirmation by experience. In what relation the satisfaction of the need of unity
and simplicity in the conception of the world stands to positive reality he does
not discuss, occupied as he more and more became with the mystical world to
which he had gained access after the nervous crisis and the ``méditation
exceptionelle'' it brought with it. His plan now became to set a subjective system
in place of the objective system which had been set forth in ``Cours''. Hitherto
he had explained man by the world; now he would explain the world from man.

\subsubsection*{f.\quad Comte as Mystic}

Comte's great work as a thinker was done with his exposition of positive
philosophy. But later this stood for him only as an introduction to the highest
mysteries. Of the psychological causes of this change in his views
we have already spoken. We shall now merely mention briefly what the ideas were
which occupied him in his last years. If they have no
% --- p. 356 ---
\opage{356}significance as scientific thoughts, they nevertheless have significance as symptoms.

In his positive philosophy Comte had gone from the world to man; he had
advanced from the abstract and universal relations to the more complicated
--- and man is the being that lives under the most complicated relations. Now
he will go from man to the world, will with full consciousness take up the
subjective standpoint which men in the childhood of the species took as their basis without
being conscious of it. The world is now regarded as the supporting foundation of
human life. From the most complicated --- and therefore the highest ---
standpoint in existence the lower stages are now to be looked back upon. Within
human nature it was in the exposition of positive philosophy necessarily
intelligence that had come to stand in the first line. It is through intelligence that we
know the laws of existence, and it is its influence on feeling that leads
to new manners and institutions. Now feeling is set in the first line, and it
becomes the task to enlighten intelligence by means of the heart. In place of
analysis and the specialties synthesis, the unified conception, is now set. But only a
subjective unity in our knowledge is possible. The forces of existence cannot, as
positive philosophy has established, be reduced to absolute unity. But a
unity in conception can be gained by regarding the whole of existence (so far as we
know it) in relation to humanity. But Comte now feels the necessity of
making a change in his earlier classification of the sciences, namely
that of separating ethics from sociology and setting it up as the seventh
fundamental science. For when humanity is to be the point of unity about which
all thoughts gather and from which they go out, then the task is to immerse oneself in
human nature in its whole fullness. But in sociology it is properly
only thought and action that become of significance; the feelings play a
part there only as motives, and since the different motives can on the whole
balance one another, there will from a purely sociological point of view be no reason
to lay great weight on the feelings. Ethics now becomes precisely the most
complicated science of all by bringing forward an element which
% --- p. 357 ---
\opage{357}in sociology still stood as subordinate. The addition of ethics as an
independent member in the system of the sciences thus takes place in accordance with
the law of advance from the more abstract to the more
concrete\textsuperscript{86}). All sciences are now to be regarded as parts of
ethics and to be cultivated with it in view, so that each single one is treated as
preparation for the following, more complex one, until we land in ethics, the
concluding science. Care must be taken that analysis does not again gain the upper hand,
and all studies should be dropped which do not further our knowledge of
the order of nature and our ability to adapt ourselves to it, or which cannot
serve as guidance for our activity. New chief works should be composed which
can reduce the fundamental sciences to their necessary extent. ---
Characteristically Comte now (in \textit{Politique positive} and in
\textit{Catéchisme positif)} calls the chief doctrines of positive philosophy ``the
positive dogma''. His thought seeks rest, and he becomes impatient with every
investigation that leads away from immediate absorption in the religion of
humanity. Feeling stands for him high above knowledge and action, which have
value only through their results, which moreover are dependent on external circumstances,
while feeling causes direct and inner satisfaction. And from this follows in turn
the precedence of art over science. The source of art is in feeling. It gently leads
the abstract considerations of the theorists back to reality, while it
instills in the practical men a noble interest in great ideas. Its physiological origin
lies in the involuntary movements which are bound up with the feelings and
express our inner states, while they also react upon these. It
forms ideal types which by steady contemplation perfect our thoughts and
instincts. In the priests of the religion of humanity philosophy and poetry are to melt together.

The religion of humanity, of which Comte regarded himself as the founder, is a worship
of humanity as \textit{le grand être,} in which we all have a share,
the sum of all deceased, now living and future beings who in a free way
have worked for human progress and happiness in small or great circles. It is
an ideal concept; for only those will live in the continued
% --- p. 358 ---
\opage{358}memory of the species who have devoted themselves to it and worked for it. In drawing up a
positivist calendar, in which every month and every day is named after men
who have had significance for the development of humanity, Comte himself has given
directions for a public cult, which consists in periodically recurring,
enthusiastic and grateful remembrance of the benefactors of the species. In the private cult
persons who have stood nearer to the individual will represent for him the
ideal of the species. Those who have put themselves in the way of progress --- as, e.g.,
the Emperor Julian and Napoleon, ``ces deux principaux rétrogradeurs que nous offre
l'ensemble de l'histoire'' --- will be remembered in the positivist cult only
in order to receive ``the deserved periodical flogging''. The single individual's
dignity rests on its absorption in ``the great being'' through the smaller and
larger circles (family, fatherland, etc.) within it. Toward the
preservation and perfecting of this being all thoughts and actions are to be directed.
Altruism (vivre pour autrui) contains at once the highest duty and the
highest happiness.

The direction of the cult as well as of education is, according to Comte, to be entrusted to a
priesthood consisting of encyclopedically trained philosophers, who are also to
be poets and physicians. Through their authority, resting on free acknowledgment, they will
gain influence on public opinion. Comte seeks on the whole to carry over
into the religion of positivism analogies to ``everything great and heartfelt which
the Catholic system of the Middle Ages has realized or at least sketched''.
Sociocracy, the social order he has in mind, is far more akin to
theocracy than to the intervening individualist period with its
``endless agitation''. Indeed, Comte even seeks further back. Precisely because
positivism has completely worked itself free of the old prejudices, it will
be able without misgiving to resume the fetishistic view of nature and
ascribe life and soul to everything in nature. That will give language force and favor
the artistic imagination, and it will quicken the feeling for everything that can
serve the subsistence and development of ``the great being''. Every animal species is regarded as a
human being that has been arrested in its growth (un grand être plus ou moins
avorté). It is the time of images
% --- p. 359 ---
\opage{359}that now comes again after the long critical period. The new religion
then regards cosmic space as ``the great medium'' in which the earth, ``the great
fetish'', has formed itself. The great fetish has in turn let its mighty
elementary forces rest and has sacrificed itself out of longing that ``the great
being'', in which the highest perfection appears within a narrow frame,
should develop. (The highest beings are, as Comte already taught in
``Cours'', also the most dependent). The great medium, the great fetish and the
great being make up the positivist trinity. ---

Comte also gives hints concerning the constitution of the future sociocracy.
The idea of right is to disappear completely. No one possesses any other right than that of
doing his duty. Individuals are regarded not as separate beings but as
so many organs of the great being. The directing power in external affairs
belongs to the industrial chiefs (bankers, manufacturers and landowners). These
\textit{patricians} are by their wealth freed from covetousness and will be able to
ennoble labor by taking it on by free choice, motivated by the highest
personal feelings. Their task is to direct industrial labor in such a way
that all can come to share in family life, which is the foundation of human
happiness. It is in the interest of the proletarians that capital be concentrated
in the hands of a few patricians; thereby a common and intelligent direction becomes
possible. The time of the middle class is past. The patricians correspond to the nutritive organs in
the organism. Over against them stand the cerebral organs, the organs of reason
\textit{(the philosophers),} of heartfelt feeling \textit{(the women)} and of
energy \textit{(the proletarians).} While the patricians chiefly represent
order, the proletarians represent progress. It is the business of the philosophers (or
priests) to find out what the welfare of ``the great being'' demands; the business of the women
is to awaken the right feeling to drive the work. Philosophers and women will
sympathize with the proletariat and find support in it against possible encroachments
on the part of the patricians, and the proletarians have in public opinion and in
refusal of co-operation a means of preventing abuse on the part of the spiritual or
temporal authorities. ---
% --- p. 360 ---
\opage{360}

Comte's utopia has the interest which such descriptions can have when they come
from eminent minds with an eye for the tendencies of the age. One traces his
historical presuppositions, just as in Plato's Republic a multitude of
features from Greek conditions have been found again. His sketch of a religion of the future has significance partly
as the testimony of an earnest and heartfelt man that all is not done with
criticism and negation of the views of life of the past, partly in that it is
the idea of humanity and of love that he makes the center. What he would not
admit was that, provided only this idea can come to dominion, the
religious representations would be able to develop with individual freedom and in great
multiplicity among those who feel a need of them. Hardly many will share the taste
Comte displays in his arrangement of a cult of the future, apart from
some brilliant thoughts, e.g. about a new calendar with the names of historical personalities
in place of the unknown names of saints. Many will think that the real
religious problem only begins where Comte's religion ends, namely with
the question how the development of the world is related to the development of
the human species and its ideals. Comte's new trinity gives no answer
to this. --- Just as little as Comte will give individuality freer play in
religious respects, just as little will he do so in political respects, so that he
even wholly excludes the concept of a legal order and of a representative
constitution. Public opinion and the strike will hardly be sufficient
correctives when there are no fixed forms of public and private life to
which those in power are bound. --- Most characteristic is the suppression of
free inquiry in the face of the closed ``positive dogma''. It can be excused only
as an effect of the cerebral hygiene which the tired thinker, after his energetic
labor, had had to impose on himself. But it would conflict with the spirit of his
own most excellent work if his proposals were followed.
% --- p. 361 ---
\opage{361}

\section*{B.\quad John Stuart Mill and the Renewal of English Philosophy in the Nineteenth Century}

In England the clash between the thought of the eighteenth and of the nineteenth century was not
so violent as in France and in Germany. The English people's wonderful ability
to carry out radical upheavals without breaking the continuity of its
development displays itself also in the philosophical domain. There does
indeed appear (as already remarked in the first part), after the time of Hume and Adam Smith, an ebb
in English philosophy. In the domain of epistemology Hume had drawn such
radical consequences from the preceding English philosophy of experience that there
was hardly anything to be done for the time being from that standpoint. The practical,
political and religious interests, moreover, came into the first line. The men who
held fast to the philosophical interest at the transition to the new century,
Jeremy Bentham and James Mill, are accordingly guided essentially by practical interest.
The ethics and psychology of the older English school were taken into the service of the ideas of reform. And
here it is remarkable to see in how different a way essentially the
same circle of thoughts is made fruitful in England and in France. There is not
the heaven-storming quality in Bentham and James Mill that there is in the French
philosophers of the Enlightenment; but there is a concentration of thought on definite
purposes and a sense for practical application
% scan: „Anvendélse“ (p. 361)
of general principles, which forms a salutary contrast to the
pointed phrases and declamations of the revolutionary Frenchmen. The English do not like
to fire off their artillery into the air; they care about hitting their target,
even if the thunder of the cannon sounds less resounding. Through their practical sense and
their steadfast upholding of the principles of the older English school those
two men mark significant extensions of the best in the eighteenth century into
the new time. They brought up a young generation which could receive the thoughts of the new time
without forfeiting the yield of the preceding time's intellectual labor. Stuart Mill's
personality as a thinker obtains a central position in the
% --- p. 362 ---
\opage{362}history of English philosophy by the fullness and understanding with which he
is able to take up into himself the thoughts of the old and of the new time and to work them over
in such a way that with him a whole renewal of English philosophy sets in.
He resumes Hume's problems on a broader basis, at once with greater
consistency and with greater many-sidedness. With conscientious energy he holds fast to
the points of view of the older school as long as it is possible for him, without concealing
the difficulties and without lacking an eye for the significance of the new experiences. He
has, as regards both theoretical and practical problems, carried out a
work of survey and of reckoning of the greatest significance for the spiritual and social development of the nineteenth
century, and in the forties and fifties he was
undoubtedly the greatest philosophical thinker of the age. Then came the doctrine of evolution with
its new points of view.

Critical philosophy and Romantic speculation, however, also made their way
into the English life of the spirit and gave it mighty impulses. A deepening and an
enlargement became possible for which the older English school, left to itself, could hardly
have prepared the way. Against empiricism the tendency which Schiller
had called ``the philosophy of the ideal'' asserted that there were spiritual values which
the philosophy of experience had not been able to explain. In England this
tendency was represented by Coleridge and especially by Carlyle. In the latter Goethe's
humanism and Fichte's doctrine of personality are transformed into a peculiar historical
view of life, which has intervened powerfully in the development of many individuals and
given forceful guidance for preserving, in the struggle with the problems of the age and amid
the century's sharp oppositions, the inmost kernel of the personal life.
There was one question, however, which Carlyle always pushed aside, in so far as he
did not answer it by cutting the knot. It was this: how this
assertion of the value of the personal life is related to the attempts to find
a thoroughgoing conformity to law both in the spiritual domain and in the rest of
existence. Here lies the epistemological problem which in the spirit of critical
philosophy is taken up by inquirers such as Whewell
% --- p. 363 ---
% scan: „Jfremy“ (p. 363)
\opage{363}and Hamilton, and which Stuart Mill then treats in the direction of absolute empiricism.

\subsection*{1.\quad Philosophy in England before 1840}

\subsubsection*{a.\quad The Philosophy of Reform}

\textsc{Jeremy Bentham} (born in London on February 15, 1748, died June 8,
1832) belongs rather to the history of jurisprudence and of philanthropy than to that of philosophy.
But he intervened powerfully in the development of philosophical ethics by the energy
with which he declared and applied the principle that every action and every
institution is to be judged by the tendency it has to further happiness and
keep unhappiness away. He would found all ethics and all jurisprudence on the one
fundamental proposition that well-being is to be preferred to ill-being. Only prejudices,
especially religious prejudices, and the lust for domination could, he thought, hinder the open
acknowledgment of this principle, and we therefore also see men follow it
everywhere where they use their reason without external and internal hindrances. The principle
of the greatest possible happiness for the greatest possible number, or, as it is also
called, the principle of utility (by utility is understood the tendency to produce happiness),
is according to Bentham a self-evident principle: it grounds all practical valuation,
but itself needs no grounding. So he sets it up
already in his first writing, which appeared in the year of Hume's death.\textit{ (A Fragment on
Government.} 1776. Chap. 1. § 48. Here \textit{The principle of utility} is said
to be ``the principle which contains the only reason [reason] that does not in turn
depend on any higher reason, but is itself the one, fully sufficient reason
[the sole and all-sufficient reason] for every kind of action''.)

This principle, however, Bentham did not discover himself. It had been set up in a similar formulation
by Hutcheson and by several after him. Bentham himself declares (in
\textit{Deontology),} that he has it from Priestley. But it was, he says, in
an interesting statement about his course of development (Fragm. on Gov. Chap. 1. § 36
% --- p. 364 ---
\opage{364}Note), the reading of the third part of Hume's ``Treatise,'' that made the scales fall from
his eyes. He had been brought up in an orthodox Tory family, in strictly
conservative views. He had regarded Charles I as a martyr and rebellion as an
impiety. His legal studies had later led him to the natural-law doctrine
of the original contract, from which it was deduced that when the prince broke his
obligations, the subjects were no longer obliged to obey him.
This doctrine he now broke with, influenced by Hume, partly because no
conclusion of any such contract could be demonstrated in history, partly because, even if one
assumed an original contract, there still remained the question to be answered
\textit{why} one should keep contracts or promises at all. The
only possible answer to this question is: the keeping of contracts is to
the advantage of society, and therefore each single individual ought to keep his promises;
if he does not keep them, he ought to be punished, for the suffering the punishment brings
him is amply outweighed by the good that the keeping of promises brings
society (Fragm. Chap. 1. § 42). Thereby the theory of natural law is replaced by
the theory of utility, the original contract by the principle of utility. And this transition
has, as Bentham himself emphasizes, the great significance that we now pass from the world of
fictions over into the world of facts. For whether an action or an
institution is useful or not must be demonstrable in experience.
Discussion will therefore now consist essentially in the ascertaining of facts. The right
of free criticism of actions and institutions is therefore of extraordinary significance.
There could --- Bentham thinks --- be no danger in such freedom of expression.
For every institution that is really useful will have those as its defenders
who draw utility from it, and so there will be no lack of answers to charges. --- In
his later writings Bentham preferred to speak of \textit{the principle of
happiness} rather than of the principle of utility.

Through his principle of utility Bentham came to make front on two sides. He came forward
as a severe critic of the traditional institutions and especially of
the chaotic English legislation. His proper field is the censure of the
existing legal and social order (censorial jurisprudence, see Fragm. on Gov.
% --- p. 365 ---
\opage{365}Preface). He brought forward and chastised existing abuses with such effect that
it has been said of him that he worked against his own fame: the
evils he attacked disappeared to such a degree that later one could not
sufficiently appreciate the significance of the labor that made them
disappear! --- In the Italian philosopher of law \textsc{Beccaria} he saw in this
domain his most important predecessor. Beccaria had already set up the principle of
the greatest happiness for the greatest number as the purpose of laws and applied it in his
criticism of criminal law. Bentham gave it a far more comprehensive application.
While he thereby came into sharp conflict with the conservatives, he opposed
on the other hand the French revolutionaries' appeal to natural law and
their setting up of general rights of man. Rights the individual has, in
Bentham's view, only in so far as the welfare of the whole society brings this
with it. And he thought that the proclamation of the rights of man led to
favoring egoism, which was strong enough already, while what mattered was precisely
to get the individual to submit to the sacrifices the good of the majority demanded. When
nevertheless in revolutionary declamations people spoke of natural and inalienable
rights, that was for Bentham only ``nonsense upon stilts''.

In his chief philosophical work \textit{Principles of Morals and Legislation,} which
appeared in 1789, Bentham goes more into detail with regard to the application of the principle of utility.
He investigates which feelings of happiness are to be preferred to
others, and in this demands regard for the certainty of the feeling of pleasure, for
its intensity, duration, propinquity, purity and capacity to propagate itself. He
investigates further by what rewards and punishments men can be led
to perform actions that bring happiness, and in close connection with this, what
different motives determine men's actions in general, and what
moral value they have. Everywhere he shows himself strong in distinction, definition and
classification. In his domain he is something of a scholastic. Of particular
interest is his investigation of motives. For it is by no means the case that he
overlooks their significance. On the contrary, the principle of utility itself gives
% --- p. 366 ---
% scan: „af.“ (p. 366)
\opage{366}him a standard for the valuation of the inner sources of actions. Those motives are to be
called good which prove to work in the direction of harmony between the individual's own
interests and those of others, bad those which lead to separating the interests. The
motive that will most surely of all lead in the direction of what the principle of utility demands is
benevolence (good-will, benevolence): ``the demands of utility are neither more nor less
than what the most comprehensive and enlightened benevolence requires''. Then comes
the need of others' esteem, the wish to win their love, religion, and
finally the individual impulse of self-preservation and the wish for enjoyment, advantage and
power. (Princ. of Mor. and Legisl. Chap. X. § 29---42).

Bentham's chief interest was the reform of legislation in a humane direction:
codification of the laws (the very word ``codification'' he coined), so that
everyone can know and understand them, and so as to keep abuses and costs away,
improvement of the prison system, and the development of the constitution into a democracy
through the introduction of universal suffrage. In his struggle for the reforms he uses
the principle of utility as his starting point. And since he constantly proceeds from it, he takes
it as a dogmatic principle, as settled, and feels no need to
investigate on what its acknowledgment is grounded. He does not see that a similar question can be put
to him to the one he himself put to the adherents of natural law.
As he asked them why one ought to keep one's promise, so
one can ask him why one is to work for the happiness of the many. Logically
self-evident it is not. If one investigates what possibilities of an answer to
this question are to be found in Bentham, one gets no clear result
out of it. As we have seen, he declares the demands of the principle of utility to be the same as the demands of
comprehensive and enlightened benevolence. So far one might believe that
the acknowledgment of the principle of utility as a standard springs, according to Bentham too, from
sympathetic feelings. In Bentham personally it probably was so.
He was a man easily moved to pity and sympathy, just as he
was also, for his own part, very susceptible to pain. But he
lacked the ability to enter into the moods and states of others, and moreover
the many prejudices and hindrances springing from egoism
% --- p. 367 ---
\opage{367}which he met on his way did not give him any great
notion of the power of disinterested sympathy in the world. While his own
sympathy led him not only to work his whole life long, theoretically and
practically, to further human happiness, a labor which brought him
himself neither advantage nor external honor, and while it moreover inspired in him a great hope that
the demands of the principle of utility would make their way, he nevertheless built, both in his
activity and in his hopes, rather on there proving to be among men's
egoistic interests a harmony which made it possible
for the general happiness to be reached, provided only each individual energetically and shrewdly
worked for his own happiness. It is the harmony of well-understood interests on which he
properly builds. In a writing which was composed on the basis of his notes
by one of his disciples and appeared after his death
\textit{(Deontology)} this side of his view comes out especially strongly.
He here takes a standpoint which recalls that of Helvetius; he also always
rated this French author very highly. Although disciples of Bentham have
protested against the views developed in the said writing being without further ado
ascribed to Bentham himself, it is nevertheless not improbable that it contains a part
of Bentham's views of whose relation to other parts he himself had not made
himself clear. All virtue is here traced back to individual prudence, which sees that one
must serve others in order to receive services from them in return, and the hope for the future
is built on public opinion gaining greater and greater significance, and on
its becoming more and more insight into the harmony of well-understood interests
that determines the judgments of public opinion. The notion of this great
harmony inspired Bentham, just as Adam Smith was inspired by the harmony of
economic interests. Bentham has properly extended what in
Smith is political economy to make up the whole of ethics. He builds on a
conception of the species as consisting of isolated individuals, each striving
eagerly to procure for himself as many goods as possible at as little cost
as possible. Even so great an admirer of Bentham as Stuart Mill has nevertheless
declared that he knew only ``the business side of human life'' (the business
% --- p. 368 ---
\opage{368}part of human affairs)\textsuperscript{87}). Only it must be held fast that
Bentham himself did not stand in any ``businesslike'' relation to his views
and endeavors\textsuperscript{88}).

Early on Bentham's ideas gained influence on men who were active in public
life, and when he learned what resistance his ideas of reform met with on the part of state
and church, he himself became more politically interested and more anticlerical
than he had previously been. But no school proper or closed party
formed itself around him. He lived very retired and worked
properly only through his writings. Toward the end of his life his
tendency got its own organ (Westminster Review), which entered into sharp opposition to
the journals of the old parties (Quarterly Review and Edinburgh Review). Bentham's
friend James Mill and the latter's son Stuart Mill were the most active contributors.
The adherents of Bentham's principle of utility were commonly called Utilitarians, a word which
Stuart Mill (Levned. Danish trans. p. 81) believes he brought into currency, although
Bentham himself had already used it. Like the word positivism, the
word utilitarianism, too, designates rather different views; for an ethical view
is not completely characterized by the standard it applies in
valuation. The ethical problem contains more questions than this. A
utilitarian (in a wider sense) need not, in particular, conceive the
psychological foundation of ethics in the same way as Bentham. ---

Among Bentham's collaborators \textsc{James Mill} stands in the first rank. His
philosophical significance consists especially in this, that he seeks to supply the
psychological foundation which Bentham's ethics lacked. In this respect his
education at the University of Edinburg, where he heard lectures by
Dugald Stewart, a disciple of Reid, had given him a preparation. Later
he is influenced by Thomas Brown, whose philosophical standpoint forms a transition
between the older Scottish school's appeal to induction, instinct or common
sense and pure association psychology. But on James Mill's definitive
standpoint the study of Hartley had the greatest positive influence. He was born in
the south of Scotland on April 6, 1773, and grew up in humble
% --- p. 369 ---
\opage{369}circumstances. His father was a village shoemaker. His mother was of a more well-to-do family, and
it was owing to her self-respect and ambition that the son's good intellectual
abilities received sufficient development. Later James Mill received support from a
landowner, Sir John Stuart, in whose family he became tutor. In Edinburgh
he studied theology, but it seems that he early gave up the thought of
becoming a clergyman, even if his theological views only much later (and still
later than his son relates in his Autobiography) developed in a radical direction. In
his thirtieth year he went to London, where he made his living by literary
work. These became straitened years for him, when he married and had a numerous
family which he had to support with his pen. In this hard struggle for
existence he nevertheless did not give up the struggle for humane purposes, any more than he
abated his gradually developed radical views. The chief work from
this period of his life is \textit{History of British India,} in which he gives
a sharp criticism, but one built on thorough knowledge, of the East India Company's
government in India. It is characteristic of English conditions that Mill
was nonetheless appointed in the Company's service when he applied for a vacant post; one
held to the knowledge and was not afraid of the criticism. Soon he rose to a
very high position and gained great influence on the Indian administration. Of great
significance for him was his acquaintance with Bentham, which became a firm friendship
that lasted in spite of passing ill feelings and clashes between the two sharply
marked and self-assured men. Mill worked for the application of the principle of utility
in a whole series of philanthropic and political domains. His endeavors in these
directions are still interesting and instructive to follow; \textsc{Alexander
Bain} gives in his \textit{work James Mill. A Biography} (London 1882) a
detailed survey of his labors from year to year. Mill worked not only
through his writings, but quite as much through his conversations with a circle of younger
men who gathered around him, members of the radical political party and
contributors to the Westminster Review. He is the spiritual father of the first
parliamentary reform. With a zeal and a sharpness which at times became too strong even for
Bentham, who otherwise did not
% --- p. 370 ---
\opage{370}mince matters, he attacked the aristocracy and the hierarchy. From his
study he directed the great class struggle which brought English politics
onto new paths. He showed himself a more practical politician than Bentham by
not proclaiming universal suffrage without further ado, but restricting
the program to the emancipation of the middle class. It was his conviction that
the suffrage could be extended to larger circles only as
enlightenment and instruction spread. From a politics which rested on
general popular enlightenment and suffrage and was guided by the principle of utility, he expected
an unlimited progress for the human race. For him, as
for Bentham, the decisive thing was that men should be enlightened about their interests and
be allowed to follow their reason. He proceeded, like Bentham, predominantly
deductively. The principle of utility was for him too an eternal truth from which
it was only a matter of drawing the consequences. Neither he nor Bentham had a sense
for the manifoldly nuanced concrete circumstances under which the general
ethical and legal-philosophical principles were to be applied. To give laws was for
Bentham far from so difficult a matter as Montesquieu had thought. Bentham did indeed
write a special essay ``on the influence of time and place on
legislation''; but he nevertheless thought that --- especially under the influence of
prejudices and of zeal to defend traditional abuses --- the
significance of historical circumstances was exaggerated. What in James Mill marks an
advance in relation to Bentham is the endeavor to give a more definite
foundation for the general principle of valuation from which the ethical and
political propositions were to be deduced. To this he was led by the psychological
studies which he steadily continued during his official activity and during his
philanthropic and political endeavors, and which found their conclusion in his
famous work\textit{ Analysis of the Human Mind} (1829).

This work is of great significance in the history of psychology as the most
thoroughly carried-through attempt to trace all mental phenomena back to association
between representations. It resumes the attempt which Hartley had in his time
made in the same direction. There is far greater clarity and fullness in James
% --- p. 371 ---
\opage{371}Mill's exposition than in Hartley's. He not only explains all phenomena in
consciousness as arisen through association, but all association he in turn traces
--- in a somewhat artificial way --- back to association between
representations which have frequently occurred together (what has later been called
association by contiguity). It is the principle of simplicity that is at work here. James Mill
sets up as a rule that as few original facts as possible are to be acknowledged.
Just as Bentham would build the whole of ethics on the one proposition that pleasure is
to be preferred to pain, so James Mill would build the whole of psychology on
the one proposition that what has once been experienced can be recalled again when
experiences which occurred together with it in time or space are repeated. --- If
this proposition could bear the whole of psychology, psychological theory would
undeniably gain a quite extraordinary simplicity and perspicuity. And at the same time
the prospect would be opened of so consistent a carrying through of
the philosophy of experience as the older English school had not yet known. Not
only all single representations each by itself, but also all
combinations of representations would then be wholly determined by what had appeared
to consciousness from without. An unlimited prospect of influencing the
human life of the spirit and determining its direction opened here; for through
legislation, education and in general the ordering of external circumstances one determines
the combinations of representations which come to rule in men.
Association psychology thus gives access not only to understanding
men's representations as they have once and for all combined and formed
themselves, but also to deciding which representations and
combinations of representations are to rule in the future. It could be
the foundation both for criticism and for new formation, a mighty weapon against prejudices by
demonstrating their origin, and a means of progress by putting new,
justified combinations of representations in the place of the prejudices. --- Beside
Hartley's influence that of Helvetius shows itself here. The book ``De l'esprit'' was in Mill's
circle a favorite work, just like ``Observations on Man''.

When now association psychology, in the form in which it here appears, is to serve
as the foundation for the acknowledgment of the principle of utility,
% --- p. 372 ---
% scan: „Fremstilling.“ (p. 372)
\opage{372}James Mill --- following Hartley --- lays strong weight on this, that
association can lead not only to one representation calling up another
representation or awakening a feeling of pleasure or pain, but also to
several representations and feelings entering into so close a combination that they cannot
be separated, and that the new whole they together make up has qualities which
the parts each by itself do not have. The new whole formed by association
can, as James Mill expresses himself in the clearest exposition he has given
of this (Appendix B to the polemical writing \textit{Fragment on Mackintosh,} an
essay of classic significance in psychology), itself become a supporting principle
in human nature (a substantive principle of human nature). One can
therefore not infer from the nature and value of a feeling to its origin. It
has given occasion to many disputes and misunderstandings that these two things,
value and origin, have been confused. It has been believed that a mental
faculty must either be absolutely original, or else that the factors
to which it owes its coming into being must be homogeneous with it. Mental
processes have been compared with mechanical combinations, and it has been overlooked that they must often be
conceived by analogy with chemical processes. This mistake has led to
either (as in ``the selfish system'') tracing, for the sake of clarity and simplicity,
all feelings back to egoism, or assuming several different original
kinds of feelings (some selfish, others disinterested). By means of
association psychology, on the other hand, the view can be grounded that the
disinterested feelings have developed out of elementary feelings just as much
as the egoistic ones. As Butler already demonstrated, egoism proper cannot be
original, since it presupposes conscious calculation; but just as little is
disinterested benevolence original: it develops through pleasure and pain
being very early transferred from the nearest and more elementary causes to
more remote ones, which stand in connection with them as conditions and means of their
working. Secondary feelings form themselves, which are attached to something that
was at first a means but gradually comes to stand as a purpose. Thus
motives which at first have value only as conditions of action can
acquire independent value;
% --- p. 373 ---
\opage{373}and the unconditional value we ascribe to the moral feeling or conscience
thereby obtains its explanation. The welfare of others, which at first was only a means to
the individual's welfare, can secondarily become a purpose for him. James Mill expected,
by virtue of this possibility, great things of the political education a people
undergoes by living under a good constitution. He says of this in an essay
(``Education'', written 1818): ``When the political machine is such that the
great objects of desire are seen to be the natural rewards of great and
noble conduct, of considerable services to humanity and of the high-minded
and benevolent cast of mind from which great endeavors in the service of humanity
proceed, then one will also naturally find zeal to acquire the
qualities which lead to admirable actions spread abroad in
humanity: such qualities as great intelligence, perfect
self-control and all-conquering goodness!'' --- And secondary feelings and
qualities can be just as firm and immediate as the primary ones. Nor
will --- Mill asserts --- the analytic investigation of the origin of such secondary
feelings and qualities through association weaken the value they can
have for us: ``Gratitude remains gratitude, resentment remains
resentment and generosity generosity in the consciousness of those who feel them, --- after
the analysis as before it. He who can trace such feelings back to their
elements does not cease to have them, any more than he who never thought
of investigating them . . . . They are constituent parts of human
nature. How we are affected by having them is a matter of experience which everyone
knows from himself. Their working is what it is, whether they are simple
or compound. Does a compound motive cease to be a motive as soon as it is
discovered that it is compound?'' (Fragm. on Mackintosh. p. 51 f.). ``The
disinterested nature of a feeling is not impaired by the consideration that it has come into being through
one of the great psychical processes by which we with great probability
explain the coming into being of the other habitual states of human consciousness
(habitual states)'' (ib. p. 421). Mill here answers an objection which both
then and later was often made against the psychological
% --- p. 374 ---
\opage{374}explanation of the origin of the moral feeling --- not only against the explanation
the older association psychology gave, but also against the one the doctrine of evolution has given.

But in the very statement of Mill's just quoted it is implied that the deductive application
of association psychology has its definite difficulties and limits. First
the concrete states must be studied in their \textit{historical} coming into being before
their elements can be discovered. By the reference to immediate experience it is
admitted that the matter is not so simple as it might seem according to the
principles of association psychology. The new qualities of the product
cannot, after all, be deduced from the factors! And the historical element which thus
asserts itself in the individual's life of consciousness as a --- at least
provisional --- hindrance to analysis appears in far higher degree in the
social and political domain as a barrier to the deductive application of
the principle of utility. The Utilitarians of the older school satisfied only in a very
imperfect way the principle of experience which it was their task and their
pride to assert.

It was now precisely the irreducible, that which resists analysis, on which
the philosophy of Romanticism laid weight. With great passion the most important
representative of the Romantic school in England in particular asserts that in life which does not seem
intelligible by mechanical explanation, the original and unique which all
personal and historical development presents.

\subsubsection*{b.\quad The Romantic Philosophy of Personality}

Bentham and James Mill are two mighty rocks that jut into the new
century, and against which the waves of Romanticism break. It was of
extraordinarily great importance for the life of the spirit in England that the
new currents met such superior representatives of the old time, so firm of
character. The interaction between the old and the new thereby became as
fruitful as it seldom is. The clash between the two tendencies was sharp and cut
deep into many a personal development, but it gave birth to forms and endeavors
in the view of life and in thought that
% --- p. 375 ---
\opage{375}have epoch-making importance for the life of the spirit in Europe as a whole.

Through \textsc{Samuel Taylor Coleridge} (1772---1834) the new German
literature and philosophy of the age of Romanticism gained influence in England.
In his youth he had (as he relates in his \textit{Biographia litteraria}) been
an adherent of Hume and Hartley. But he was repelled by the eighteenth
century's attempt to lead all mental phenomena back by analysis to elementary
functions, and by the endeavor to demonstrate mechanical laws for the life of
the mind: the unity and activity of the mind were lost! The study of German
philosophy led him decidedly away from the English school. As a good Romantic he
reveled in absolute ideas, in which the differences and oppositions of the
finite world faded and vanished. He set the whole, intuited by presentiment,
against the piecemeal work of empiricism, synthesis against analysis. In his own
opinion he anticipated some of Schelling's ideas; so thoroughly had he lived
himself into the speculative line of thought that he could continue it on his
own in the same direction as its original founders. Occasionally, in editing his
writings, he confused pieces he had translated from Schelling with his own
compositions, which gave occasion to charges of plagiarism. This poetic,
enthusiastic spirit, who was quite as much poet and preacher as thinker, could
not properly distinguish between what he had himself conceived and what he had
found in others. What he took from German philosophy was above all Kant's
distinction between reason (in the narrower sense), as the faculty of ideas of
the unconditioned, and understanding, as the faculty of categories that make
limited knowledge possible. This distinction he used above all to find a
reconciliation between thought and religion. All the objections the preceding
age had held to be decisive were now --- not exactly rejected, but --- set down
to the account of the ``understanding'' and pushed aside by an appeal to the
deeper conception of ``reason.'' Behind this appeal there lay hidden the
awakening sense for what in history and in life escaped, or had hitherto
escaped, scientific explanation. It was a protest against the
% --- p. 376 ---
% scan: „Thesis.“ (p. 376)
\opage{376}sufficiency of the science developed hitherto, a protest that was
given and taken as a new solution, a new foundation. Coleridge did not get
beyond presentiment and annunciation. He worked mostly through conversations
(or rather through his monologues before listeners). His great work on the
agreement between philosophy and Christianity, to which he referred his
listeners at the difficult points, he never got written. He placed himself in
opposition both to the philosophy of the eighteenth century (Hume and Voltaire)
and to the ecclesiastical theology that had stiffened into outward forms and
formulas. Like the German systematizers of Romanticism, he wished to bring about
a higher unity of reflection and dogmatic faith. In his fundamental thoughts he
recalls the so-called right wing of Hegel's school. He found an explanation of
the Trinity, e.g., by applying the schema thesis, antithesis and synthesis, which
from Fichte's time on played so great a role in German speculation. (Under the
evident influence of Schelling's later doctrine, however, he is in danger of
deducing a quaternity, since he posits God as ``the absolute will or identity''
= prothesis, as the foundation for the interplay of thesis and antithesis that
is harmonized in synthesis! See \textit{Table Talk}, 8 July 1827.) But coherent
thinking was not Coleridge's affair. It is surely apt when he has been called a
religious epicurean. He reveled in religious thoughts and feelings and in ideas
that could furnish symbols for them. But he was a weak character. He could
master neither his conduct of life nor his line of thought. He fled, as
\textsc{Carlyle} (who in \textit{Life of Sterling}, chap. VIII, gives an
interesting characterization of him) has said, from life into the world of
theosophic dreams; what he gave was ``transcendental moonshine,'' which showed
many a young doubting and seeking nature the old things in a new light, but did
not contain any really new life. A man who was himself for a time strongly
influenced by Coleridge, the friend of Carlyle and of Stuart Mill, John
Sterling, has said of him: ``His misfortune was that he appeared at a time when
there was a man's work to be done --- and he did not do it. He had not
sufficient strength of character; doctrines he had ceased to believe in he
professed, in order to avoid the unrest of strife.'' What this
% --- p. 377 ---
% scan: „Signs.“ (p. 377)
\opage{377}charge, which Sterling repeats in a letter to Carlyle, is aimed at is
not clear. But when it is speculation and fantasy that become the chief organs
of religious thought, it easily happens that more doctrines are acknowledged
than one can really turn into personal property.

Meanwhile, Coleridge had awakened a new sense and new ways of seeing in many of
the younger generation. No less a man than Stuart Mill, who was otherwise not
favorably disposed toward German speculative philosophy, has placed him beside
Bentham and regarded these two men as the two great fertilizing minds (seminal
minds) of their time. Mill's own great and honest attempt to learn from both of
them we shall later have occasion to bring forward. Most of those whom
Coleridge influenced for the time being would not learn from Bentham as well,
but were led through the ``moonshine'' to orthodoxy, and soon to a more
pronounced orthodoxy than the old. Perhaps Carlyle is right when he says that
had there been no Coleridge, there would have been no Anglo-Catholic movement
(Puseyism). Several of the men of this movement at any rate began with poetic
and speculative ideas before the positively ecclesiastical line of thought
gathered speed\textsuperscript{89}). That the oppositions in the domain of the
view of life sharpen in the course of the nineteenth century --- at any rate as
regards the outward formulas --- is something to which the life of the spirit
of every country bears witness.

\textsc{Thomas Carlyle} (1795---1881) found nourishment for his spirit in a
wholly different side of German philosophy. Not a higher speculative knowledge,
but a more vigorous assertion of the value of personality, a new faith, was what
he gained through the study of German poetry and thought. Through the German
poets he was led to the German thinkers; through Schiller and Goethe he was led
to Kant and Fichte. He saw clearly that the Scottish school had not overcome
Hume's doubt by its appeal to instinct \textit{(Signs of the Times} 1829),
whereas Kant and his successors went to work more thoroughly
% scan: „grnndigere“ (p. 377)
and attacked Hume, and the mechanical philosophy in general, at the center, not
in the outworks. Like Coleridge, Carlyle lays particular weight on the
distinction between understanding and reason; it was for him from the first the
% --- p. 378 ---
% print: „cèleste“ (p. 378) (misprint)
\opage{378}most characteristic thing in Kant's philosophy \textit{(State of German
literature.} 1827). But Goethe was and remained the great prophet of his youth.
However different his heavy Scottish nature, in which the mists did not wholly
vanish even on clear days, was from Goethe's bright humanism, Goethe was
nevertheless his model, and his confession of faith was the same as Faust's.
From Kant he took into his definitive philosophy above all the distinction
between the thing in itself and phenomena. All that nature shows us is only
phenomena. The ``philosophy of clothes,'' which he sets forth in his profound and
humorous work \textit{Sartor Resartus} (1833), rests on the thought that just as
little as the clothes make the man, so little has one fathomed existence because
one knows the phenomena. Existence is and remains an unfathomable wonder, which
must fill us with reverence. The world is the garment of the Deity. Natural science
merely demonstrates the outward mechanism, but the kernel of existence is not
thereby reached. Nature is a great symbol, a revelation of ideas that cannot be
grasped by means of any scientific method. The world is no dead machine, as
science would make it. Even the purely outward connection --- the clothes --- is
inexhaustible and beyond survey from our little corner of existence. And however
far our experience and our thought might be able to reach, beyond the forms of
space and time we do not get, and they are after all only forms of knowledge;
they too belong to the garments of the Deity, which are forever woven anew. The
wonder of existence hides itself from us because from dull habit we take the
forms for realities, and because our first fundamental propositions are often
only assumptions we are accustomed to and therefore do not call into doubt. But
what is philosophy other than a constant struggle against habit? It is
``transcendental'' precisely because it oversteps (transcends) the sphere of blind
habit. It is then the task of philosophy to awaken anew the feeling for the
wonder of existence when the mind is dulled by mechanical representations. ``The
man who cannot wonder, and who does not constantly wonder and worship --- were
he President of innumerable scientific societies and did he carry in his single
head the whole Mécanique céleste and Hegel's philosophy and the sum of the work
of all observatories and laboratories --- is but a pair of spectacles behind
% --- p. 379 ---
\opage{379}which there is no eye. Let those who have eyes look through him, then
he may be of some use.'' (Sartor Resartus. I, 10).

It is easy to see that Carlyle applies the distinction between the thing in
itself and phenomena not in the spirit of Kant but in the spirit of Romanticism.
For Kant it was the task of science to find the lawful connection of phenomena,
and the concept of the thing in itself marked the limit of this endeavor. But
Romanticism despises and cancels the scientific endeavor to link phenomenon to
phenomenon according to definite laws. One never comes to an end that way, after
all, and one does not reach the kernel of things! Carlyle himself, like his hero
in Sartor Resartus (Book II. Chap. 3 and 7), had a time in his youth when the
world was to him a dead machine. (\textsc{Froude}: \textit{Thomas Carlyle.} I.
p. 101)\textsuperscript{90}). The study of Hume, Gibbon and d'Alembert had
robbed him of the religious conception of his childhood. For a time he was
wholly absorbed in mathematical studies, and his first literary work was a
translation of Legendre's Geometry. It was then that he was led through Mme. de
Staël to German literature, and Goethe's great world opened itself to him.
``Four years ago,'' he writes to Goethe in 1824, ``I read Faust on the
mountains of my Scottish homeland, and then it was my dream that I might reveal
to you, as to a father, all the pains and wild wanderings that my heart, whose
innermost secrets you seem to know so completely, has gone through.'' Like
Faust he grew impatient with science. What is the use of being able to dig a few
feet deeper than one has reached hitherto, when there is still an infinitely
long way left? Or, as he later said in a conversation with Charles Darwin, how
ridiculous is it not to care whether a glacier moves a little faster or a little
slower, or moves at all! As a good Romantic he believed in Goethe's optics and
would not grant the physicists the right to criticize it. His hints of a view
of nature recall Schelling's, especially the eleventh lecture on ``Methode des
akademischen Studiums,'' where it is stated, among other things, that ``the ideas
\textit{symbolize themselves} in things,'' and that ``empiricism apprehends
reality quite
% --- p. 380 ---
\opage{380}independently of its meaning, since it is the nature of the symbol to
have a life of its own in itself'': natural science thus takes as absolute
reality what is only symbol.

But it is not outward nature that interests Carlyle. Man is for him the real
revelation, the true Shekinah, the highest symbol. No analysis can exhaust his
essence. Locke and his successors sought to analyze and mechanize the mind
through and through. And in particular men sought to make the whole conduct of
life mechanical, to lead it back to the mechanics of the feelings of pleasure and
pain, to make the principle of utility the rule, and to exclude every original,
spontaneous, independent action. Bentham and utilitarianism are objects of
Carlyle's sharp criticism and bitter scorn. He ascribes to the principle of
utility only a negative, dissolving significance. It may be serviceable for
criticizing the old order of things, but not for producing a new one. It puts a
dead mechanism of interests in place of the living, personal morality that
springs from the heart's yearning to fulfill its inner ideals. As eagerly as
Carlyle polemicizes against what he calls the ``philosophy of cause and effect,''
just as eagerly does he polemicize against an ethics that builds on ``profit and
loss'' (virtue by profit and loss), and he sees in Bentham's theory a solution of
the problem: ``Given a world full of knaves, to show how virtue becomes the
result of their united endeavors.'' \textit{(On Heroes and Heroworship.} Lect.
VI). What Carlyle holds against the analytical psychology and the doctrine of
utility is not least that they lay too great weight on conscious reflection.
Everything great comes into being and ripens in silence. Only a man who can keep
silent becomes a great man; and a great deed that is done with full
consciousness of its greatness is in reality a small deed. Rightly do the poets
sing hymns to the night. Full, clear consciousness makes everything small and
mechanical. The highest truth can exist for man only in the form of the symbol:
the symbol speaks and is silent, reveals and conceals at once.

Toward theological dogma Carlyle is no more favorably disposed than toward
natural science and empirical philosophy. Only in the form of the symbol can man
have the truth. But symbols
% --- p. 381 ---
% print: „Heroworschip.}“ (p. 381) (misprint)
% print: „enson.“ (p. 381) (misprint)
\opage{381}grow old and wear out like clothes, and new ones must be formed in
place of the old. Philosophy, which is a struggle with habit, has in particular
to struggle with the habitual and mechanized religious representations. Carlyle
describes his standpoint as \textit{natural} supernaturalism. It is divine forces
that work in us and outside us. But they work in an inward, natural way. As the
living garment of the Deity is constantly woven anew in outward nature, so the
inner sense constantly fashions new forms for the life of the spirit. Each
individual has to find his symbol and his religion, just as he has his deed to
cast into the ever-flowing stream of time. ``By \textit{religion},'' says
Carlyle \textit{(On Heroes and Hero-Worship.} Lect. I), ``I do not understand
the church-creed a man professes, the articles of faith he will sign . . ., but
that which a man practically believes (often \textit{without} declaring it to
himself, and still less to others) --- that which a man practically lays to heart
and holds for certain concerning his inner relation to this mysterious
universe.'' To speculate further on the essence of the Deity is useless. We have
each of us enough to do in performing the deed that lies in our power. Carlyle's
religious conception is nevertheless clearly enough the same as Goethe's, and as
Fichte's in his later writings (``Grundzüge des gegenwärtigen Zeitalters'' and
``Wesen des Gelehrten''), to which he even refers explicitly. Fichte was the one
among the German philosophers with whom Carlyle most sympathized. The thought of
the Deity pervades everything, the spiritual and the physical world; every
spiritual being is a spark from it. Whether his concept of God is theistic or
pantheistic, he will not decide. John Sterling, in a letter that contains a
criticism of Sartor Resartus, had objected among other things that the God spoken
of in the book is no personal God; Carlyle declares it an abstract question that
he cannot or will not discuss. (Life of Sterling. Part II, Chap. 2). --- In his
later years he declared that it was best for the time being to keep silent about
religion. Its time will come again; but the dishonesty must first be done away
with (Froude: Thomas Carlyle. II. 2. p. 394).

Carlyle's protest both against empirical and critical science and against
theology was bound to make him lonely. He felt himself also
% --- p. 382 ---
\opage{382}a stranger in his time. It was a time dissolved by skepticism and
analysis, a decrepit (decadent) time, the age of mechanism. Spirit was lacking
and faith was lacking. Faith is the expression of the truth of life, mysterious
and indescribable like all the activities of life. But next after the end of the
Roman world there has been no time so skeptical, untrue and decadent as the
eighteenth century, whose after-effects reach into the nineteenth century. It is
a time in which no ideal can grow or flower. (On Heroes. Lect. V. --- History of
the French Revol. Vol. I, Chap. 2). The law of the three stages appears plainly
here in Carlyle, who very likely has it from Fichte and the Saint-Simonians. But
more strongly than any of the other writers in whom this law appears, he speaks
out about the wretchedness of the time. Both in speech and in writing he
complains of having come into being in so miserable a time. His mighty fantasy,
his intense and easily stirred mood, and his deep melancholy, which was
constantly reinforced by bodily infirmity (dyspepsia), made him dwell in
particular on the dark sides of the time, which he exaggerated in comparison with
those of earlier times. He found it hard to imagine that this time could be a
time of transition to a better, positive time, as according to the law of the
three stages it should be. He himself really assumes no gaps in development: it
is a misunderstanding, he says, to believe that the phoenix burns itself up
completely and then lies as a heap of ashes until a new bird comes into being in
a miraculous way; no, destruction and creation go hand in hand, and the new
garment is woven in the very midst of the process of the old one's dissolution
(Sartor Resartus Chap. 7). But Carlyle was not himself able to find the new
threads. He is convinced that none of the spiritual works of the past is lost:
``Whatever mechanical science and spiritual torpor may say, man and his universe
are eternally divine, and what the past has possessed of nobleness and of divine
revelation can and shall not be lost.'' (Life of Sterling. Part I. Chap. 8).
This conviction of the subsistence of values he will not, like Coleridge and
Hegel, ground by a symbolic interpretation of dogmas and customs. But he wants
the same reverence, the same wonder, the same energy in renunciation and in
work, to which the faith of the
% --- p. 383 ---
\opage{383}past partly bore witness and which it partly conditioned, preserved
for the conduct of life of the future. By this endeavor his standpoint is
understood, his opposition at once to scientific criticism and to ecclesiastical
faith. He seeks the foundation for the preservation of values much farther
within personality than analysis and tradition can reach. The living garment of
the divine force that never dies must be woven from within. But will these inner
forces now also be capable of being awakened after the time of dissolution in
which we are placed? Carlyle is thrown back and forth between faith in the
subsistence of values, or of the inner forces, and the dark picture the age
presented. The picture became, as it seems, even darker and darker to him. In
his youth he was indignant at Bentham's philanthropy, in his old age at
Gladstone's zeal for England's political and material development. In a
conversation in March 1867 (see Caroline Fox's diaries) he declares that the
whole thing is going downhill and means nothing to him. Like ``a mourning
Jeremiah'' he strikes up the old lament he had begun to chant forty years
earlier, and still can find no bright spots. The more vigorous faith of his
younger days weakened in his later years.

The cause of Carlyle's dark view of the time cannot be sought merely in his own
melancholy and easily wounded heart. It lies also in the very unrest and doubt of
the time, in the ever sharper opposition between the contending powers in the
domain of the spiritual life, the ever advancing settlement between the old and
the new, a settlement in which debit and credit are so extraordinarily difficult
to apportion. We have seen a whole series of thinkers, right from Rousseau,
Lessing and Kant, stand before this problem. Few could by their whole nature feel
the sting as sharply as the Scottish peasant's son who, starting from the strict
Presbyterian faith, had lived through the spiritual powers of the time and
tested them in his personal life. The problem will follow the race on its way
until ``the third kingdom'' comes --- if it comes. That Carlyle saw nothing but
darkness around him came from the strict demands he made on the solution of the
problem. It was his indwelling ideality, his own inner light, that made the
darkness around him so deep. He says somewhere that to every young and
% --- p. 384 ---
\opage{384}fiery mind that enters this world with a great goal before its eyes
and with a clear view of life, the world will appear as bad: for what else should
its strength and heroism be used for? Were the world good, he would be of no use!
It is thus human strength and ideality that make the world appear as evil: evil
is the shadow of ourselves, a shadow that does not stay outside us but stretches
into our own mind. Man's misfortune comes from his greatness, from the infinite
that stirs in him and to which he cannot give vent in the forms of finitude.
(Sartor Resartus. II, 9. --- Life of Sterling. I, 5).

But the cause lay also in Carlyle's being an incorrigible Romantic. He had all
Romanticism's lack of ability to discover the ideality in the constant, faithful
work that adds link to link and through the small is led to the great. He has
only scorn for science and for all coherent endeavors in the practical domain.
And yet precisely he, who has spoken such beautiful, and often such loud, words
on the significance of silence and of quiet preparation, should naturally have
been able to come to understand that proud buildings can rise from stones each
of which by itself is insignificant. That is the faith that lies behind the
detailed investigations of science. But inquiring natures Carlyle did not
understand. For men like Stuart Mill, Faraday, Charles Darwin and George Grote
he has only superficial mockery to spare. Froude (II, 2. p. 259) says of him:
``He fought against Darwin's doctrine of the transformation of species; but I
could see that he feared it might be true!'' His idealism was shy, because he
lacked understanding of the significance of intellectual and practical work. His
faith in the personal life was not so firmly established that he could trust
that it would surely subsist, however much analysis and criticism were applied to
it. The kernel of life can surely bear a purgatory. Carlyle is right that we
cannot live on criticism, but he did not see the ideal forces that could lie
behind the critical work. On this point the Romantic became a philistine.

When Carlyle speaks out on what is to bear the spiritual and social life in the
future, he points to what in
% --- p. 385 ---
\opage{385}his conviction has also borne it in the past: reverence for heroes,
for the great men. The infinite force that works and symbolizes itself in
everything appears above all in man, and most especially in the great man. As in
Fichte, faith in the rise and significance of the chosen spirits stands in close
connection with faith in the working of the Deity in all finite beings. By
heroes or great men Carlyle understands the leaders and models of men, the
founders of everything that the multitude of men strive to accomplish and
attain. All the works we see realized around us in the human world have had
their first germ in the mind of the great man. There the invisible forces work
that, after the time of quiet conception and pregnancy, at last set the new into
the visible world. The history of great men is therefore the soul of world
history. The hero can appear as prophet, poet, statesman, but in all his shapes
he represents the great, collected force of life, as opposed to all externality,
partiality and limitation. Before them the deep need of reverence, the divine
spark in all, breaks forth. (On this point too we are reminded in Carlyle of
Fichte, especially of the latter's ``Reden an die deutsche Nation''). It is the
hero who finds the hidden thoughts of existence and of the times and proclaims
them to others in word and deed, and thereby leads the race forward. More than
ever, such heroes are needed in our time, an enlightened aristocracy to lead
men. The great social gulf that the whole of history proclaims grows broader and
broader in our day. Already in ``Sartor Resartus,'' before his social writings
proper, Carlyle points to it (in the chapter ``Helotage,'' III, 4), lamenting
the bodily and spiritual hunger of the many. Popular education and emigration on
a great scale are the means he points to for relieving the distress. He misses
new prophets and new Hengists and Horsas to set these means to work. But to go
more closely into the social question was not Carlyle's bent; for that he
despised philanthropists, political economists and politicians far too much. In
its place he turned to history, in order to bring forward great figures and
models, in case they might have an awakening
% --- p. 386 ---
\opage{386}and concentrating effect on the slack and divided race. It is
through his historical writings above all that Carlyle has worked on wider
circles. It is through these writings that his thoughts work on more and more
people in our day. For many he has himself been one of the heroes he wrote
about, one of those who have the ability to feel, see and express the needs of
the time and the thoughts of the time. Of his significance as a historian we
shall not speak here; it belongs before another forum. Only we find Romanticism
again in him in the excessive weight he lays on what is original, spontaneous,
inexplicable in the great figures. He makes no real attempt to show the
dependence of the great on the race --- although greatness does after all show
itself also in the great capacity to run into debt, because the spiritual sense
and consumption of the great are greater than those of others. Only a mystical
explanation of ``the hero'' does Carlyle give, by regarding him as an incarnation
of the infinite force that works in everything. Here too the Romantic shyness of
analysis and of the ``philosophy of cause and effect'' shows itself.

Carlyle does not, however, go as far as a later conception that finds ``the goal
of history'' in the great men. He regards them as the great causes, and thus as
the great servants. He proclaims the worship of heroes --- but he sees clearly
that to ``be worshipped by'' or to rule over a stupid mass is no heroic deed.
``Hero-worship,'' he says \textit{(Past and Present.} I, 6), ``yes, my friends,
but consisting first and foremost in our having a heroic mind ourselves. A whole
world of heroes --- not a world of bunglers, where no hero-king can rule --- that
is what we strive for.''

\subsubsection*{c.\quad Critical Philosophy}

In the same year in which James Mill's ``Analysis,'' which marked a vigorous
resumption of the work of English philosophy of experience, appeared (1829), the
``Edinburgh Review'' brought out an essay by \textsc{William Hamilton},
\textit{Philosophy of the Unconditioned,} by which the critical philosophy was
transplanted onto English ground. Hamilton was born in Glasgow in 1788 and had
studied there and at Oxford. When his epoch-making essay appeared, he was
% --- p. 387 ---
\opage{387}professor of history at the University of Edinburgh, after having lived
for a number of years as an advocate. His starting point as a philosopher lies
in the Scottish school founded by Reid, which marked a reaction against Hume's
skeptical and negative results. Reid and his successors sought to correct these
results by more exact psychological observation, but were led in their zeal to
set up a whole series of original faculties and instincts. All too often they
dismissed the results of analysis and criticism with an appeal to ``common
sense'' --- an appeal that called forth Kant's apt remark that one proves one's
common sense by using it, not by invoking it, and that Hume's common sense might
be just as sound as Reid's. Kant appears here (in the introduction to the
``Prolegomena'') as advocate for Hume, to whom he owed so much. But he sought in
his own way to refute Hume, and thereby came to have the same opponent as Reid
and his disciples. William Hamilton now seeks to combine the doctrines of Reid
and Kant. In the essay mentioned and in a series of essays following upon it,
which were likewise published in the ``Edinburgh Review,'' and among which
\textit{Philosophy of Perception} (1830) is especially to be noted, he developed
his peculiar views, which were of no small interest in epistemological and
religious-philosophical respects. These essays he later published collected
under the title \textit{Discussions on Philosophy.} In 1836 he became professor
of philosophy at Edinburgh, and there, until his death (1856), he gave
well-attended lectures on psychology and logic, which became of great
importance for philosophical development in Scotland. The lectures were later
published under the titles \textit{Lectures on Metaphysics} (2 vols.) and
\textit{Lectures on Logic} (2 vols.). Hamilton was an acute thinker, an eager
seeker after truth, akin to Lessing in spite of his Scottish gravity; he was
also in possession of comprehensive learning in the history of philosophy.

In his essay on the philosophy of the unconditioned, which is a criticism of
Schelling and Cousin, and in part also of Kant, Hamilton seeks to show that only
the conditioned and limited can be an object of knowledge, and that the attempts
to set up a philosophy
% --- p. 388 ---
% scan: „Uendel ighed“ (p. 388): a gap in the word
\opage{388}of the unconditioned cannot be carried through. But he gives not only
criticism; he gives the outline of a whole epistemology, which on particular
points he worked out further in his later writings. His main proposition is:
\textit{to think is to set conditions} (to think is to condition). By this he
means that everything we are to be able to apprehend and comprehend we determine
by its relation to something else that conditions and limits it. An absolute
whole we cannot apprehend; every whole is for us always part of a greater whole.
An absolute part we can just as little apprehend; every part can in turn be
thought of as divided and is thus a whole. An infinite whole we cannot apprehend
either; for an infinite time would be required to go through all its parts.
Thus neither the absolutely limited nor the absolutely unlimited can be an object
of knowledge. Our knowledge concerns the conditionally limited. The philosophy
of the unconditioned, which credits itself with the ability to construct a
scientific concept of the unconditioned as that which is to be at once absolute
totality and infinity, sins against the nature of our knowledge. In a later
appendix to the essay (Discussions p. 577 ff: \textit{Conditions of the
Thinkable}) it is developed how all knowledge consists in a judgment that
connects two terms: therewith the relativity of all thought is given. All
knowledge rests, moreover, on a relation between subject and object; beyond this
opposition we cannot get, unless with Schelling we are willing to sink into the
absolute unity in a mystical way, whereby all knowledge is excluded. Another
relation that plays an essential role in our knowledge is the relation between
thing and property: the thing and the property are known only in relation to
each other. In the closer determination of things we determine them in time
(protensively) or in space (extensively) or with respect to the degree of their
properties (intensively); but all these determinations are relative: the one
determination of time, space or degree presupposes the other. The concept of
cause too Hamilton brings under what one might call the epistemological law of
relation \textit{(law of relativity).} He takes it as a limitation of our
knowledge that we understand things only by finding their causes. We are not
able to think
% --- p. 389 ---
\opage{389}an unconditioned beginning. When a phenomenon begins, this can for us
be only apparent. Just as little can we think an unconditioned cessation. The
disappearance of a phenomenon too can be only apparent for us. When we seek the
conditions of the phenomenon, this means that we connect it with other
phenomena, regard it as a term in a relation --- because of our impotence to
think an unconditioned! Every existence is for our knowledge relative, is bound
to a preceding existence. As soon as something new is added to what exists that
is more than a transformation of the earlier into a new form, and as soon as
something is taken from what exists that does not come again under a new form,
we stand before the incomprehensible. Cause and effect cover each other and can
