be found again in each other. The concept of cause is thus not, as Reid and Kant
each in his own way assumed, an independent, isolated concept. It is a
particular form of our consciousness's general way of working, a particular
example of the fundamental law that our knowledge by its nature can grasp only
the conditionally limited.

By this epistemological law of relation Hamilton has cast light on an essential
side of our knowledge. In place of Reid's appeal to the instincts of common
sense and in place of Kant's scholastic table of categories he has put an
analysis of the fundamental forms of the knowing consciousness and has
demonstrated a common characteristic mark for them. Psychology is for him the
fundamental philosophical science. Consciousness is for the philosopher what the
Bible is for the theologian, and the original testimonies of consciousness must
be taken as true, since they lie at the foundation of all our knowledge. On this
point Hamilton sometimes speaks just like Reid. ``The root of our nature cannot
be a lie'' --- therefore the assumption of an opposition between consciousness
and its object, which immediate consciousness according to Hamilton entertains,
must be true. This is Hamilton's simple solution of the problem of the existence
of a world independent of consciousness. The problem is thereby hardly allowed
to come forward. ``Natural realism'' has, for Hamilton, right on its side.

On the particular psychological and logical questions that Hamilton has treated
with great acuteness and learning we cannot
% --- p. 390 ---
\opage{390}enter here\textsuperscript{91}). We must, on the other hand, dwell
on the consequences Hamilton draws from the limitation of knowledge. The value
of philosophy cannot for him, naturally, depend on its bringing us absolute
truth. Its value depends altogether not on the finished results, but on the
constant release of mental energy into activity and striving. By speculation our
mental forces are exercised. Lessing is right when he places the eternal search
above the possession of truth. A waking error is better than a sleeping truth.
Philosophy does not lose its value because it ends with an acknowledgment of our
ignorance grounded on insight into the conditions of our knowledge (docta
ignorantia, as Hamilton calls it with Cusanus). Before it reaches this its
conclusion, it has developed and exercised the noblest mental forces.

This ignorance concerning the absolute essence of existence rests on the fact
that our thought ends in a dilemma whose horns are equally inconceivable. Were
we to know the unconditioned, it would have to stand before us either as an
unconditionally limited, an absolute totality, or else as an unconditionally
unlimited, an infinite in time, space and degree; but neither of the two can be
grasped by us, because both conflict with the law of relativity. Hamilton does
not think, however, that we must or can remain stuck in this dilemma. For by
virtue of the logical principle of the excluded middle between two mutually
contradictory possibilities, one of the two assumptions \textit{must} be true.
(The logical principles thus have for Hamilton not --- like the law of relation
--- validity only for our knowledge, but are laws of things, not merely laws of
thought. See on this Discussions p. 577 f.). There is then here not merely room
for a faith, but necessity for a faith. We have learned that our knowledge is no
measure of existence, and we have learned that a choice must be made. The idea of
an unconditioned is not, as Kant thought, a positive idea that has its natural
root in the nature of our knowledge; it signifies on the contrary the negation
of all knowledge. While Coleridge held to Kant's doctrine of ideas, Hamilton
parts from Kant precisely on this point. He finds the possibility and the
necessity of a faith given in this, that, as regards the idea of the
unconditioned, we stand before two
% --- p. 391 ---
\opage{391}possibilities that are both inconceivable, and between which we must
nevertheless choose with logical necessity.

The choice is determined, according to Hamilton, by practical, moral motives. We
need an unconditioned being that can uphold and secure the subsistence of our
mind. And in the representation of this being we lean on the analogy with our
own being. Hamilton does not agree with Kant in his criticism of spiritualistic
psychology. Consciousness, he says (Lectures on Metaphysics. I. p. 158), is
indeed the condition of all inner phenomena; but it is itself only a
phenomenon; there must lie something behind it whose property it is, and this
must be something different from what lies behind material phenomena. The same
relation as there is between our mind and our body we assume --- by an analogy
--- between the unconditioned spiritual being we believe in and the world of
relativities that knowledge presents to us. Through this analogy Hamilton makes
the transition from philosophy to theology. The end of philosophy is the
beginning of theology. But he says at the same time that no difficulty arises in
theology that does not already appear in philosophy. And his own doctrine
confirms it: for that unconditioned being which is to be the object of faith is
set up by an inference from analogy and is thus to \textit{stand in relation to}
the world as the soul to the body; but then it becomes, after all, conditioned,
relative! Hamilton has not shown the possibility of escaping, by passing over to
faith, the epistemological difficulties he himself has so energetically
demonstrated. He agrees with Fichte that a God who could be comprehended would be
a conditioned being; but a God who is placed in relation to a world would, even
if he could not be comprehended, be a conditioned being, and if he is to be
maintained as an unconditioned being, his concept would contain a
self-contradiction. --- As regards the content of faith, there is confirmed here
in Hamilton what we have been able to establish in a whole series of thinkers
from Leibniz's time on: that every attempt at a speculative or religious
world-view must, consciously or unconsciously, lean on an inference from analogy.
--- Hamilton's whole standpoint, which is characterized by his psychological
starting point, his critical analysis of the
% --- p. 392 ---
\opage{392}conditions and limits of knowledge, at once with an adoption and a
correction of Kant's line of thought, and finally his philosophy of religion
grounded on analogy, recalls such German inquirers as Fries and Beneke.

Two years after Hamilton's death his disciple \textsc{Henry Mansel} gave a
series of lectures at Oxford, which are published under the title \textit{Limits
of Religious Thought} (Danish translation by N. Teisen: ``Grænserne for den
religiøse Tænkning.'' Odense 1888). Here he draws from Hamilton's doctrine the
consequence that a scientifically grounded theology is impossible, because our
knowledge cannot reach the unconditioned. But at the same time he maintains that
no objections can be raised from scientific thought against revelation; only if
we had an absolute knowledge, a philosophy of the infinite, could revelation be
refuted. And in agreement with Joseph Butler's ``Analogy'' --- a work that has
altogether played a great role in religious discussion in England in our century
--- he maintains that the difficulties and contradictions that can be
demonstrated in the theological assumptions occur within every attempt at a
conclusive world-view, even if it moves on the foundation of nature and reason.
From this he concludes that the difficulties arise --- not from revelation, but
from the limitation of reason. We must then believe what we cannot comprehend.
It is our duty to assume the personality of God, although it is for us
self-contradictory that an unconditioned being should be a personality, since
personality presupposes opposition and limitation. We must believe in the dogma
of the atonement and in the dogma of eternal punishment, even if these dogmas
conflict with our notions of love and justice. What is love and justice in our
eyes is perhaps not so in God's! We see only the part, not the whole. If our
horizon were widened, we would apprehend everything differently! Just as
Hamilton had already taught that it is owing to an imperfection of our nature
that we apprehend things as causes and effects, so Mansel teaches that human
ethics hangs together with limited human nature, for which reason no inference
can be drawn from the ethics of man to the ethics of the Deity. For
% --- p. 393 ---
\opage{393}man it is, e.g., a duty to forgive, because he needs a bridle on his
selfishness; but this grounding of the necessity of forgiveness cannot hold for
God!! --- Both human thought and human conscience are thus here cut off from all
influence on the valuation of religious representations. Without rudder and
without compass, according to Mansel, man is to sail the ocean of religion.
Whether the theological voyage will go better in this way is perhaps a question
--- until such time as the superhuman thought and the superhuman conscience that
are to escape the logical and ethical difficulties have been demonstrated.
Mansel's philosophy of religion was at first received with great approval as a
good weapon against rationalism and speculation. But people seem to have come
back somewhat from the first enthusiasm\textsuperscript{92}), having discovered
that it was a weapon that easily wounded the one who used it. It is also clear,
after all, that however much one may wish to inculcate the necessity and the
possibility of leaping from thought and conscience into faith, man cannot, even
by the boldest salto mortale, once and for all leap over his own shadow. ---

Besides Hamilton and his disciples there must still be named an inquirer who in
a fruitful way brought Kant's epistemology to bear in England. \textsc{William
Whewell} (1795---1866), who worked at the University of Cambridge first as a
natural scientist (mineralogist), later as a philosopher, published in 1837 his
work \textit{History of the Inductive Sciences,} which some years later was
followed by \textit{Philosophy of the Inductive Sciences, founded upon their
History} (1840). In these works he sought by the historical road to establish
the correctness of Kant's fundamental thoughts, which, to be sure, he did not
always apprehend with sharpness and clarity. He stands on the ground of the
English school in maintaining that all knowledge develops on the foundation of
experience. Both the human sciences and natural science are inductive sciences.
But induction does not mean merely the collecting and juxtaposing of facts; it
means the grouping of the facts under a guiding thought, their reduction under a
general law. And the history of the inductive sciences now proves that this
grouping and reduction become possible only when there are already at work in
the inquirer
% --- p. 394 ---
\opage{394}ideas and points of view that can make possible the discovery of the
law of the facts' connection. The facts must be connected by a mental act whose
possibility must lie in the nature of the mind. Every inquirer therefore starts
from presuppositions that cannot be derived from the particular facts each taken
by itself. By a closer investigation of the way in which inquirers such as
Kepler and Newton came to their discoveries, this conception of the method of
induction is further illuminated. Kepler had the concept of an ellipse
beforehand, just as Newton had the concept of attraction, and only because these
concepts were present in advance did their discoveries become possible. It is
not Whewell's opinion that such concepts lie fully finished in the mind, but
that no discovery can be made without the cooperation of a mental activity that
follows its own laws. Even if the special ideas (as, e.g., of ellipse and of
attraction) have themselves developed under the influence of experience, we
nevertheless come back at last to fundamental concepts that are the expression
of nothing other than the laws of the cognitive faculty itself, which assert
themselves in all experience, from the simplest sense perception to the most
comprehensive induction. By attending to the way in which our knowledge works,
we find a series of forms or fundamental concepts --- the concepts of time and
space as the foundation of mathematics, the concept of cause as the foundation
of the mechanical sciences, the concept of purpose as the foundation of the
organic sciences, and the concept of duty as the foundation of ethics ---
concepts that according to Whewell cannot be reduced to simpler forms or derived
from observation. He contents himself with setting them up in a series without
subjecting them to a closer examination, and his conception thereby acquires a
likeness to Reid's, whereas Hamilton, as we have seen, made an interesting
attempt to demonstrate the various fundamental concepts as various expressions of
the epistemological law of relation. Nor does he apprehend the relation between
philosophy and theology with the critical sharpness that distinguishes Hamilton.
His significance lies in the preparatory work he has contributed toward a theory
of induction. Here he has in a significant way illuminated the method of
induction as a \textit{method of discovery,}
% --- p. 395 ---
% scan: „Bevismotodc“ (p. 395)
% print: „Forgrundeen.“ (p. 395) (misprint)
\opage{395}whereas --- as his great opponent Stuart Mill showed --- the method of
induction as a \textit{method of proof} did not come into its own with him. For
one who occupied himself particularly with the history of the inductive sciences,
the point of view so energetically stressed by Whewell was bound, quite naturally,
to come especially into the foreground.

\subsection*{2.\quad John Stuart Mill}

\subsubsection*{a.\quad Biography and Characterization}

\textsc{John Stuart Mill}, James Mill's son, was born on 20 May 1806 in
London. He is an example of early intellectual development, but he also
developed under a high pressure of intellectual influence that a less vigorous
and original nature could hardly have endured, and that left lasting
consequences in him too, both in his intellectual tendency and for his bodily
health. His father taught him himself. At three years old he began Greek and
soon after arithmetic; at the same time he naturally learned English reading and
grammar. Latin he began when he was eight. History he learned on his own from
detailed works, and then gave his father an account, on walks, of what he had
read. After a great part of Greek and Roman literature had been gone through, he
began logic when he was twelve years old, and here too what he had read on his
own was gone through and discussed thoroughly on walks. Then followed reading in
political economy and a careful study of Demosthenes and Plato, with particular
regard to argument and method. Very early the boy had to teach younger brothers
and sisters, and thereby got practice in mastering and applying what he had
learned. There was no cramming. The father endeavored that understanding should
keep pace step by step with instruction, indeed preferably go ahead of it:
``What could be found out by thinking,'' says Stuart Mill in his autobiography
\textit{(Levned.} Danish trans. by Vilh. Arntzen, p. 34), ``my father never told
me until I had exhausted my
% --- p. 396 ---
% scan: „A.“ (p. 396)
\opage{396}strength in finding it out myself.'' --- Mill recommends the way in
which he himself was taught for imitation. He thinks that what he achieved here
any boy or girl of fairly good abilities and a healthy nature could achieve. Even
if what was demanded often lay beyond the child's ability, Mill nevertheless
holds it pedagogically right to make such demands: ``A pupil from whom nothing
is ever demanded that he cannot do never does what he can do!'' He would never
admit that this upbringing, which, as he says, had given him a quarter of a
century's start over his contemporaries\textsuperscript{93}), had exercised any
questionable influence on his development and on his health. And yet there is
hardly any doubt that a mental crisis he later went through, as well as a
nervous debility from which he suffered all his life from his thirtieth year on,
were in great part consequences of the one-sided and forced development of his
childhood years. That at least was the view of his friends (see A. BAIN:
\textit{John Stuart Mill.} A Criticism. London 1882). Mill would never admit
that work could be harmful. Although an eager philosopher of experience, he was
nevertheless so spiritualistic that he denied all essential influence of
physiological dispositions and states. Therefore he not only believed that
mental development could be hastened without harm to health, but he also did not
acknowledge any original difference between individuals. It was always a
foundation of the hope he had for the future of humanity that all qualities of
character were effects of upbringing and of outward, social conditions, so that
by pedagogical and social reforms one would be able to alter human characters to
indeterminable degrees and in the same direction. In this respect he constantly
paid homage to the doctrine of Helvetius, of which his father and Bentham were
such eager adherents. --- Apart from the physical consequences of the forced
upbringing, it suffered also from the defect that it was only the understanding,
not feeling and fantasy, that was developed. The whole spontaneous unfolding of
moods and images was checked under this strictly rationalistic upbringing.
Whereas in his old age, in his autobiography, he recommended the way in which he
had been brought up,
% --- p. 397 ---
\opage{397}he had at an earlier stage himself felt its drawbacks. In a
conversation of 1840, which the Quaker Caroline Fox records in her diaries, he
says expressly that he will not recommend the early intensive strain in the
upbringing of all children, since it easily comes at the expense of the
liveliness of childhood and favors reflection at the cost of activity. ``I have
never been a boy,'' he said, ``have never played cricket; it is better after all
to let nature go its own ways.''

Another point on which Mill's autobiography must also be corrected by what has
come to light by other roads about his development is what he relates about his
religious notions in childhood. He relates in the autobiography that he received
no religious upbringing at all, since his father had long since given up all
religious faith. Supported by definite recollections on the part of members of
the family, Bain (in his biography of James Mill) has shown that Stuart Mill
remembered wrongly as regards the definitive change in his father's religious
standpoint. In Stuart Mill's childhood his father still went to church, and the
son with him, and the rest of the family continued to do so later too. Definite
utterances of Stuart Mill as a boy are preserved that show that he read the
Bible with enthusiasm. But the father began very early to discuss religious
questions with the boy. He taught him not to break off a line of thought or let
go of a problem out of a feeling of religious devotion before he had found out
whether it could be solved or not. He impressed upon him what was for him the
decisive difficulty not only in the faith of the church but also in faith in a
good and almighty Creator: the impossibility of reconciling the experience of the
physical and moral evil in the world with such a faith. It was Butler's
``Analogy'' that had led James Mill to the purely negative standpoint he took in
religious respects in his later years. Not for the first and only time has a
work of defense here had the opposite effect from that intended --- here,
however, by its depth and consistency. The line of thought into which Stuart Mill
was thus early led determined his later position on the religious problem, even
when, after a mental crisis, he took a more positive standpoint, and even in his
posthumous essays in the philosophy of religion
% --- p. 398 ---
\opage{398}the after-effects of the father's conversations with the little boy
are to be felt.

A year of his early youth (1820---21) Stuart Mill spent in the south of France
with a brother of Bentham's, who had an estate there. He ascribes to this stay a
great influence on his development. Above all there was awakened in him a love
of France and an interest in French literature and politics to which he remained
faithful all his life. The French historical writers later, at an important
point in his development, gained great influence on him, and he found in the
French a capacity for enthusiasm and for self-renewal that he often missed in
his own countrymen. After his return home he pursued legal studies and studied
Bentham's writings. In Bentham he found an idea that could bring coherence into
all notions and endeavors. He felt himself a new man when he had made a
penetrating acquaintance with Bentham's ``principle of utility.'' He says of this
in the autobiography (Levned. p. 68 f.): ``This principle gave unity to my
notions of things. I now had a conviction, a faith, a doctrine, a philosophy,
indeed a religion in the best sense of the word, the spreading and inculcating
of which was to be the chief task of my life. I pictured to myself a great
number of changes in the condition of men that were to be carried through by
this doctrine . . . . . The prospect of progress that Bentham opened for me was
sufficiently wide and brilliant to make my life bright and to give my endeavors a
definite form.''

With zeal Mill joined the band of young men who strove to work for the
philosophical and political ideas of Bentham and James Mill. Hartley's
psychology, Malthus's political economy and Bentham's moral philosophy were the
foundation on which they worked. The ``Westminster Review'' was their organ, in
which Stuart Mill's first larger essays were printed, and what they fought for
first and foremost was freedom of expression and the extension of the suffrage.
They hoped that if only full access were given to enlightenment and knowledge,
all social problems would be solved. By prudent self-control the workers would be
able to prevent the strong increase of population, which is a chief factor in
pressing
% --- p. 399 ---
\opage{399}wages down. Class rule would be broken through the extension of the
suffrage. Human notions would be altered, and through them in turn human
character, by virtue of Hartley's doctrine of inseparable associations. Despite
all the zeal with which these ideals and prospects for the future were held
fast, Mill nevertheless states that the expression ``thinking-machine,'' which
has often wrongly been applied to Bentham's adherents, really fitted him in this
period. As he expected the regeneration of the human race not through
disinterested love of justice but from ``the enlightening influence of the
cultivated understanding upon the selfish feelings,'' so in himself it was
essentially the understanding that had the floor. ``My zeal,'' he says in his
autobiography, ``was in this period of my life not much else than zeal for
speculative opinions. It did not have its root in any genuine benevolence or
sympathy with the human race, though these qualities had their due place in my
ethical conception. Nor did it stand in connection with any ideal elevation. And
yet my fantasy was very receptive to this feeling; but there was at that time a
stoppage in its natural nourishment, poetic culture, while there was a
superabundance of what stood in conflict with it, logic and analysis. Add to this
that my father's teaching had a tendency to undervalue feeling.'' (Levned p.
112). It was the rationalism of the eighteenth century that here, through Stuart
Mill's upbringing, continued its effect far into the new century, nourished and
goaded by the constant struggle against prejudices and sentimental declamations.

There came upon Mill, when he was twenty, a mental crisis that on essential
points gave him another view of life. The foundation of his whole mental life
suddenly collapsed for him. He fell into a state of dejection in which he asked
himself whether he would now really feel happy if everything he expected of
intellectual and political progress were realized --- and he had to answer No.
Life now became heavy and desolate to him. He performed his work purely
mechanically, but it seemed to him as if the source of mental life in him had
dried up. Constant analysis had made everything cold for
% --- p. 400 ---
\opage{400}him. The psychology by which he had been brought up had indeed seen
that the feelings are influenced and altered by the development of
representations, but had not seen that deep and strong feelings can be produced
and preserved in this way only when they get sufficient nourishment through
spontaneous experiences and through constantly fresh and immediate influence. Now
he felt like one who is stranded at the beginning of his voyage, with a
well-equipped ship and a rudder --- but without a sail! --- It was a reaction
against the violent strain of childhood and early youth and against the
one-sided development of the understanding. And it was at the same time a
reaction against the line of thought of the eighteenth century, a reaction that
was bound quite naturally to come forth in a young man who had been brought up in
the thoughts of the old time and stood in the midst of those of the new, even if
he had not yet let them come in over his threshold. --- The mental crisis was
resolved for Mill through new experiences, new ideas and a new human
relationship. --- He was deeply moved by a touching passage in a biography and
so learned that the source of feeling was not exhausted in him: ``I was no
longer hopeless; I felt that I was neither a stick nor a stone.'' Thereby he
gained new courage. He immersed himself in the poets, of whom Wordsworth above
all came to have great significance for him. He learned what indispensable
spiritual nourishment poetry can give; hitherto he had been inclined, with
Bentham, to fear that it would impart false notions to men. He learned to give
the unconscious and the spontaneous their due in life, and found out how
important it is not to stare at one's own happiness as the final purpose, but to
set oneself a higher purpose: then happiness will be found in the endeavor to
realize it. ``Only those are happy who have their gaze directed on something other
than their own happiness . . . . Ask yourself whether you are happy --- and you
will cease to be so!'' --- To this were added new studies, especially of the
French historians (Guizot, Michelet, Tocqueville), who taught him that
institutions and laws develop according to natural laws; they correspond to the
stage of development of society and of views, and their perfection must be
regarded in relation to this stage, and only to a certain degree can the order
that
% --- p. 401 ---
\opage{401}progress follows be altered by arbitrary intervention. In particular
the writings of Comte and the Saint-Simonians made a strong impression on him. He
came to know the difference between critical and organic periods, and Carlyle's
works acted on him as a mighty poetry of personality. He saw that one could not,
as he had hitherto believed with his father and Bentham, treat human affairs
purely deductively, or ascribe to outward conditions a wholly determining
influence. He came --- which was after all also the most consistent course for an
adherent of the philosophy of experience --- to give experience its full due. In
his religious views too this crisis and its resolution intervened, although he
does not speak of this point more closely in the autobiography, where he says
only that he now saw the significance of the development of the inner man. The
foundation of the religious views he developed in his posthumous essays was laid
in these years, as will later be shown more closely. By Bentham's friends he was
regarded as an apostate, while in other circles he was received as one who had
broken with sectarian prejudices in order to grasp the truth. In a remark
recorded by Caroline Fox, Mill's friend John Sterling says of him that he has
sacrificed the position of undisputed leader of a mighty party for the higher
honor of being a private in the army of truth, and Sterling hopes that Mill's
books will work to give the feeling of reverence the place in life that so many
have denied it. --- But what a stirring of feeling and self-forgetfulness had
begun, and what a widened historical view and religious sense had developed,
gained its proper fullness in his life only through his acquaintance with the
woman who later became his wife, and to whom he himself ascribes a wholly
overwhelming influence on his mental development, and whom he regards as a
supremely superior mind. By his overflowing eulogies of her he set his friends,
and --- especially by his autobiography --- his readers, a riddle, since he seems
to ascribe to her everything he has accomplished. The secret is no doubt that
Eros, here as so often, has been the great teacher, who has given an eye for
ideals and a sense for intimate, personal qualities, and has set feeling in a
motion that does not
% --- p. 402 ---
\opage{402}stop at the object that has awakened it. This explains why those
nearest to Mill and his friends could see nothing extraordinary in the woman who
for him was a genius of the highest rank. One of his brothers, who knew her well,
used to say that she was an able and remarkable woman, ``but nothing like what
John took her for.'' Where Mill gives a closer account of what he owes her, he
exempts his purely scientific works (his Logic and the theoretical parts of the
Political Economy) from her influence, whereas he characterizes her as the one
who had the freest and boldest eye for the ideal and for what the future might
bring, while at the same time she possessed a great sense for concrete, factual
conditions and a lively ability to make them vivid, just as she also had a sure
apprehension of the relative significance of different points of
view\textsuperscript{94}). One understands that Mill here found something he
had missed all his life, and to which his upbringing had made him less
receptive, until it came to meet him in personal reality. He found his Beatrice,
as Comte found his.

Stuart Mill entered practical activity early, being employed already at
seventeen in the service of the East India Company, where he gradually rose to
fill the high post his father had held at the last. For a time he directed the
education department, later the Indian government's correspondence with the
Indian princes and with foreign states, and at last, as Chief Examiner of the
Indian Correspondance, had the superintendence of the whole administration. His
activity in these positions has won great recognition from competent quarters,
and on the dissolution of the India Company he was offered a seat in the new
``Indian Council,'' which, however, he declined for reasons of health. In his
leisure he continued his studies. In his younger days he was an eager member of
a debating club in which Bentham's disciples discussed philosophical, literary
and political questions with young men from other circles, partly Tory lawyers,
partly Coleridgians. As an author he worked for a long time only in reviews and
newspapers. His most important essays he collected in a series of volumes under
the
% --- p. 403 ---
\opage{403}name \textit{Dissertations and Discussions.} His definitive views on
philosophical questions were founded around 1830. Of influences from a later
time must especially be named those he received from Comte, with whom he stood
for a long time in lively correspondence, and from Carlyle, whom he admired as a
prophet but could not follow as a philosopher. --- In those essays one finds the
astonishing balance and many-sidedness that distinguish Mill's line of thought.
After the strict school of clear thinking he had gone through in his childhood
had been supplemented by richer experiences, he was able to show appreciation
and to cast light in many directions.

The reaction against the line of thought of the eighteenth century, and in
particular against the ways of seeing that derived from Bentham and James Mill,
acted more strongly on Mill's social, literary and religious conception than on
his general philosophical (epistemological and moral-philosophical) standpoint.
In Caroline Fox's diaries we meet him in the circle of eminent men who
frequented the house of the gifted Quaker family in
Falmouth\textsuperscript{95}). Mill had gone out to Cornwall to nurse a brother
who was ill with consumption. The utterances and conversations of his that are
reported bear an intimate, personal stamp, and bear witness to a deep
seriousness about life and its tasks. He speaks much in a Carlylean spirit, and
in that circle one hardly had the feeling of being in the company of one of the
most radical men of the century. Later, when the book ``On Liberty'' appeared,
the eager listener felt deeply indignant (as, for that matter, she had also felt
at Carlyle's ``Life of Sterling''). For Mill there was no contradiction between
the philosophy of personality into which he had been led and the strictly
rational consideration of knowledge and life that he applied in his inquiry. His
significance rests in an essential respect precisely on his having freed the
philosophy of personality from the Romantic character, shy of knowledge, that it
had in Carlyle. For him personal inwardness and enthusiasm were not incompatible
with an untiring search for grounds and causal explanation. He learned ---
after his crisis --- that one can have a great view of life without therefore
fearing or despising thought. That Carlyle could never get into his head.
``Poor fellow,'' he said of Mill, ``
% --- p. 404 ---
\opage{404}he has had to work his way out of Benthamism, and the emotions and
sufferings he has gone through have helped him to thoughts that never came into
Bentham's head. But he is all the same far too eager to prove everything. If
John Mill got to heaven, he would hardly be content until he had found out how
everything was arranged. For my part I should not care much about the machinery
of the place, but should quite give up the question whether there was to be an
artisan class or a working class among the angels.'' \textit{(Memories of old
Friends from the Journals of Caroline Fox.} 6 June 1842). In humorous form
Carlyle has here aptly indicated the difference between himself and Stuart Mill.
Yet it should perhaps be added that if heaven is not reserved especially for
Romantics, insight into and work with the mechanism of life would be necessary
to prepare the way to heaven. And besides, heaven must be assumed to furnish
satisfaction for the intellectual need as well as for every other personal need.
What Carlyle reproaches Mill with, he could just as well reproach Socrates with,
who imagined, after all, that in the other world he would spend the time as here
in testing and inquiring. --- A comparison between the way in which Stuart Mill
speaks of Carlyle in his autobiography and the way in which Carlyle in
conversation and letters (see e.g. Froude II, 1. p. 74; II, 2. p. 419) spoke of
Mill, even just after the latter's death, establishes which of the two men had
the better ability and the more honest will to understand and to appreciate.
Carlyle, who himself always had the valve open and loudly preached the gospel of
silence, could not reconcile himself to the subdued quality in Mill's
personality. And when he had had to give up the hope of getting an unconditional
adherent in Mill, he had almost nothing but scorn and mockery to spare for him.
---

Stuart Mill attached an extraordinarily great practical significance to the
purely theoretical debate carried on in modern philosophy between empiricism and
speculation. All false assumptions and tendencies in the moral, religious and
social domain would --- he thinks --- be invincible if one did not refute the
claim that truths can be won by immediate intuition, by the road of pure
thought, independently of experience
% --- p. 405 ---
\opage{405}and observation. This claim in reality makes an assumption its own
proof! Never has a better means been devised for securing the preservation of
all ingrown prejudices! In opposition to this Mill sets the derivation of all
knowledge from experience and the explanation of all intellectual and moral
qualities by means of the laws of the association of representations. Here there
are tasks enough to solve, whereas the intuitive philosophy, which marks the
reaction of the nineteenth century against the eighteenth, favors human
indolence while at the same time being a bulwark for every kind of conservative
prejudice. It was this line of thought (see Levned. p. 226 f. 277 f) that lay at
the foundation of the working out of his two chief philosophical works
\textit{System of Logic} (1843) and \textit{Examination of Sir William
Hamilton's Philosophy} (1865). --- In his Logic he has for the first time given a
theory of induction, systematized the methods of experience, just as Aristotle
systematized the methods in which deductive reasoning moves. Aristotle had as his
predecessors the Greek philosophers and sophists, and as foundation the eager
discussions that were held in Athens, especially in the Socratic schools. Stuart
Mill built on the history of modern natural science through three centuries and
on an analysis of the forms in which its work has moved. His work marks the most
thoroughgoing presentation of empiricism in epistemology that has been given,
just as his father in his ``Analysis'' had carried empiricism through in the
psychological domain. There appears in the foundation of Mill's Logic a clear and
fateful influence of his father's psychological theory, a theory that he later
(partly in the notes to a new edition of the ``Analysis,'' partly in the work on
Hamilton's philosophy) gives up, without becoming aware of what effect this
giving up really has on epistemology. His great love of truth, which shows itself
in his untiring readiness to go into objections and let them have their full
effect, has also opened his eyes to truths for which at the beginning of his
career he did not yet have an eye. He began writing his Logic in 1830, and still
in the last edition of the work on Hamilton's philosophy, at the end of his life,
he makes modifications in his conception that
% --- p. 406 ---
\opage{406}arose from his uninterrupted work with the problems. Whereas he
starts from James Mill's conception of consciousness as a series or heap of
independent elements, which are brought into connection with one another in a
purely external and really inexplicable way according to the laws of
association, he ends by acknowledging the unity and connection in consciousness
as a fundamental psychological fact. ``The uniting principle,'' which Hume
wished to push aside, Mill has now acknowledged as a cornerstone. This marks a
break with the older English school whose range Mill was not aware of.

Besides the purely philosophical writings named (to which must still be added an
interesting book on Auguste Comte), there is a whole series of significant
writings of ethical, social and political content. To these belong his
\textit{Principles of Political Economy} (1848), in which work he conceives
political economy as a part of the whole theory of society and carries through a
distinction between the laws of production and the laws of distribution, a
distinction that makes it possible for him to acknowledge what is justified in
the socialist systems. (It was, however, only in the second edition of the book,
1849, that this acknowledgment properly came forward.) Whereas he had hitherto,
in the footsteps of his father and Bentham, fought against class rule and for
personal freedom, it was now clear to him that behind political emancipation
there stood a far more serious question, the social one. The Saint-Simonians had
already opened his eyes to it. That he did not lose sight of the significance of
personal freedom is shown by the book \textit{Om Friheden} (1859). In the essay
\textit{Utilitarianismen} (translated by G. Brandes under the title: Moral,
grundet paa Nytte- eller Lykkeprincipet) he defends the ethical doctrine of
utility against its opponents, and in the work \textit{Om repræsentativ
Regering} (1860) he gives his political theory.

Mill had a seat in Parliament 1865---1868 and won recognition for his clarity and
expert knowledge, although he spoke above all on the most unpopular questions.
Gladstone has in a letter (of 19 Dec. 1888, cited in GOMPERZ: \textit{John
Stuart Mill.} Ein Nachruf. Wien 1889. p. 46) expressed himself on Mill's
parliamentary activity in the following way: ``Mr. Mill's
% --- p. 407 ---
\opage{407}eminent gifts of mind were well known to us all before he entered
Parliament. What his conduct there revealed to us, to me at least, was the
uncommon nobility of his character. I used at that time in conversation to call
him the saint of rationalism . . . . On the other hand he was indeed a
philosopher, but not a man of fixed ideas. He united the sound sense and
practical tact of the statesman with the lofty independence of a solitary
thinker. I need not say that I greeted his appearance with joy and deeply
regretted his disappearance, and that in the interest of the whole House of
Commons. He was a boon to us all. In every party, within every political
tendency, such men are, I must confess with pain, rare.'' --- The reason Mill was
not re-elected was partly that his religious views were used against him, partly
that his radical political ideas went too far for the class of voters who had
elected him the first time.

During a stay in Avignon Stuart Mill died on 5 May 1873. In him passed away one
of the greatest, most honest and noblest minds of the nineteenth century. The
course of his life, as he himself has depicted it, is a source of instruction for
everyone who strives, just as his writings cast light on some of the most
important subjects of human thought\textsuperscript{96}).

\subsubsection*{b.\quad Inductive Logic}

Mill's chief strength as a thinker lies in his untiring discussion, his
unwearied turning and twisting of problems in order to reach their ultimate
presuppositions. In the later editions of the \textit{System of Logic,} in which
account is taken of the objections raised against his theories, his
exposition takes on a dialogical character. Just as the author of a dialogue, when
it truly deserves its name, endeavors to let the different
standpoints come forward in as clear and characteristic a form as possible,
so it is also Mill's endeavor to do full justice to the views and objections of his opponents;
he does not really regard them as
opponents, but as fellow workers. That his understanding of
% --- p. 408 ---
\opage{408}other standpoints had its limit goes without saying; it was the same
limit that his personality and his historical starting point as a thinker
set to his inquiry altogether. This limit stands out to a critical examination
all the more clearly as the psychological foundation of his whole
epistemology shifts under him, without his seeming to have become
aware of it. Whoever would assess Mill must first and foremost see him as
the great seeker. His merit in philosophy does not stand or fall with
the answer to the question whether he succeeded in carrying through empiricism in
so absolute a form as even Hume had not yet conceived it.

It is the logic of experience that Mill sets over against the logic of pure thinking, partly in
opposition to it, partly as an extension of it. Pure thinking cannot
extend our knowledge, but only lead us to preserve agreement among our
representations. New truths, however, are obtained only by observation and experience, and the
question then arises by what paths, on the basis of observation, we can
prove the new truths. It is on the proof, not on discovery itself, that Mill
lays the chief weight. His guiding interest is to let all assumptions
pass through a purgatory before they enter the heaven of truth. How
assumptions arise in the first place interests him less; it is the justification
that matters. The significance and practical worth of philosophy rest for Mill,
as for Carlyle, on its being a struggle with habit. The assumptions which have
formed in the individual by involuntary association of representations, or which
he has received by tradition, must be sifted and tested, so that one can
exclude prejudices that hinder progress. For his great hope of the advance of
the human race the consistent tracing back of all assumptions to
experience stood as an essential support.

Apart from such cases in which a general proposition is laid down by an
authority, as with theological and juridical propositions, every
general proposition, Mill maintains, is only a summing up of a series of particular
observations. Deductive logic, which begins with general propositions,
% --- p. 409 ---
% scan: „sig.“ (p. 409)
\opage{409}therefore presupposes an inductive logic, which shows how we arrive at these
general propositions from the particular observations. Pure thinking
always presupposes experience. If, e.g., I reason thus: ``All men are
mortal --- the Duke of Wellington [who was still living when Mill wrote his Logic]
is a man --- therefore the Duke of Wellington is mortal'', --- then it is
clear that, in order to have the right to set up the first proposition, about the mortality of
\textit{all} men, I must really be certain that the Duke
of Wellington too will die. In reality, says Mill, I do not infer from the death of
\textit{all} men to Wellington's death, but I infer from a great
series of experiences of the death of particular men to the death of this particular man,
Wellington. If I really knew that \textit{all} men were
mortal, I should not need to infer at all, since Wellington's mortality would be
included in the general mortality. My inference is then really this:
John is mortal, Thomas is mortal, etc., etc. --- so Wellington is presumably
mortal too. At the bottom of every syllogism whose major premise is not established
by authority there lies, then, in reality an \textit{inference from particular
to particular.} This is the form of inference from which both induction and
deduction spring, --- first induction, and then deduction. The beginning
of the whole process of knowledge consists in two phenomena (man and death, e.g.)
occurring together for me. The next time the first of them occurs,
the expectation of the second will then occur. If this expectation is confirmed, I sum up
all these experiences in a \textit{general} proposition, that is to say, in a
proposition which gives me \textit{all my experiences} in brief compendium. More it
cannot give me, if I am not to make an unjustified generalization. All
inference is therefore from particular (or particulars) to particular (from
particulars to particulars). This inference occurs already in children. When
the child sees the flame on which it has burned itself before, it draws its hand
back, not because it has set up any general proposition, but because the sight
of the fire immediately calls up the representation of pain. Animals too can
infer in this way, for not only the
% --- p. 410 ---
\opage{410}burned child, but the burned dog too shuns the fire. (Logic. Book II. Chap. 3 § 3).

Mill of course sees clearly that this immediate transition from an observation
to a representation or an expectation is merely an association, whose
justification has first to be tested. It is an association of the kind to which
James Mill sought to reduce all association, association ``by contiguity'': we
have often seen A and B together, and now expect B because A occurs again. But can
\textit{proof} now be given of the validity of such an expectation? For what is at issue
in logic is not what we acknowledge as valid, but what we
\textit{ought} to acknowledge as valid (Evidence is not that which the mind does or
must yield to, but that which it ought to yield to. Logic. Book III. Chap. 21.
§ 1). By what right, then, do we infer from the occurrence of one phenomenon (A) to the occurrence of another,
different from it (B)?

On the basis of the history of the empirical sciences, a basis in whose
use Mill acknowledges having had predecessors in Comte, Whewell and John Herschel
(On the Study of Natural Science. London 1830), he now sets up four
chief methods by whose help one can distinguish between valid and invalid
connections of representations. The very detailed exposition of these methods
(whose indefinite main features Herschel had given) is one of the most important parts of
Mill's work. Here we can keep only to one main point, the weight Mill lays
on the negative cases, the experiences in which a phenomenon does not occur, although
the circumstances otherwise, save for a few particular ones, are the same as in the experiences
in which it does occur. In such cases the \textit{method of difference,}
the chief inductive method, finds application. (It is suggested by Bacon as one of the
most important ``instantiæ solitariæ''). In the particular circumstances by which an
experience that presents the phenomenon differs from an experience that does not
present the phenomenon, we must then see something that stands in causal connection with
it (either as its cause or its effect or in such a way that both
are effects of the same cause). Only then, therefore, can we rightly expect B after
A, when it has been shown that with the absence of
% --- p. 411 ---
\opage{411}A follows the absence of B. And we then need only two cases, one positive and one
negative, to establish a law concerning the relation between A and B.

Only in very simple cases, however, is the inference so simple. In complicated
conditions, where many different elements act together, we must first resolve the
phenomenon into its particular elements, then by simple inductions investigate
how each of these acts, then again by deduction find out what the
result of their combined action will be, and finally by observation
show that what we have inferred or calculated also really agrees with
experience. The whole process of knowledge thus consists of three members, induction,
deduction and verification. --- So far is Mill from failing to recognize the significance of the
deductive method that he even sees a proof of a science's
perfection in the role deduction plays within it. What he
insists on is only that all deduction rests in the end on inductions and must
be confirmed by the agreement of its results with experience. He rejects
pure thinking only when it would begin without a foundation in experience and end without
confirmation by experience.

The method of difference itself, which is to bear the whole edifice of knowledge, is, as Mill
clearly sees, demonstrative only if we proceed from the assumption that there is such a connection in
nature that what has once happened will happen again when exactly the same
conditions occur. The uniformity of nature, or the law of causality, is thus the
presupposition of the validity of all our inferences concerning real
phenomena. In discussing how the causal principle is proved, Mill takes
up the great problem which Hume and Kant had discussed. He answers it in Hume's
spirit, but in such a way that he would illuminate it from the logical side, whereas Hume
declared it logically insoluble and went straight over to giving a psychological
explanation of how the assumption of a causal connection could have arisen.

Mill denies that the causal principle is founded on immediate belief, intuition
or instinct. In the first place, belief or instinct are not proofs. A strong and
firm association of representations can produce a conviction that cannot be
shaken by
% --- p. 412 ---
\opage{412}any counter-proof; but its strength is not itself a proof. On the other hand,
Mill holds, every assumption of cause can be suspended and ``instinct'' pushed aside.
Anyone who is accustomed to abstraction and analysis, and whose imagination can
move freely, will not find it impossible to conceive an absolute chaos in which
phenomena follow one another in ever-changing ways, without any definite
law. (Logic III, 21, 1. 4). And often we are compelled to stop at mere
``collocations'', a sum of factually given conditions which cannot in turn be
shown to be caused. Nor, indeed, have men at all times believed
in the law of causality; they have assumed ``chance'' and ascribed reality to
``free will''. Nor, in order to understand the validity of empirical science, need we
assume that the law of causality holds for all phenomena, if only we assume it
valid for the domains in which our investigation moves; the motion of the planets may,
e.g., be subject to definite laws, even if wind and weather are not. And we
lack all right to extend the validity of the law of causality further than to the part of the universe
known to us. Experiences can be grounded only by experiences; the very
foundation of empirical science must be established by way of experience. Experience
must tell us how far we can rely on experience; we have no higher
authority to appeal to. We must make experience its own measure.
\textit{(We make experience its own test.} Logic. III, 4, 2).

The causal principle itself, then, is to be grounded on experience and proved by
induction. Our conviction that a phenomenon does not occur unless a certain
definite other phenomenon goes before it is grounded on our having experienced
such a connection between phenomena countless times. The situation with the conviction of
the validity of the law of causality for the particular phenomenon is thus the same as with
the conviction that the Duke of Wellington will die. Here too it is an
inference from particular to particular. But Mill holds that the law of causality rests
on so many experiences that it may rightly be said to be the most
comprehensive generalization we possess. By giving our more limited
pieces of knowledge a support in it, we raise their certainty to a higher level.
% --- p. 413 ---
% print: „Erkendessesteori.“ (p. 413) (misprint)
\opage{413}

Yet it was precisely the justification of connecting two representations (e.g.
A and B) in the future, because they had previously occurred together, that inductive
logic was to establish; the ``inference'' from particular to particular is, after all, only an
association. But we have in reality come no nearer to seeing that
justification by being told that it is grounded on the causal principle,
when this principle itself in turn proves to be grounded on inference from
particular to particular --- that is, on association, however countless the
repetitions that strengthen this association. (In the causal principle A is ``the occurrence
of a phenomenon'', B ``the occurrence of a certain definite other phenomenon''). Mill moves in
a circle\textsuperscript{97}), or rather: he does not really get off
the spot. What he has really attained by his reference to the causal principle as the ultimate basis of
the particular inductions is only to establish that the most
indissoluble associations will be able to hold up the looser, more unstable ones; a
new habit can be strengthened by an old habit of kindred nature. But that is
no proof.

Mill has surely let himself be carried too far by his zeal to root out all
a priori principles. He has --- like so many of his opponents ---
confused the assumption that a principle springs from the very nature of consciousness with
the proof of its real validity. He is right that, however much a principle
has its ground in the nature of our consciousness, its real validity is not
thereby proved. But it might be that there were hypotheses which we were driven by the nature of our
consciousness to set up, and which it was the task of empirical science
to test in detail. The task of scientific knowledge will then
be partly the making precise, partly the verifying of involuntarily posited
presuppositions. Mill harbored suspicion every time it was maintained that involuntary
assumptions could become of significance for knowledge; he feared that one would at once
smuggle in a dogma. A march on the spot was the nemesis his
suspiciousness brought down on his own epistemology.

An inference from particular to particular does not in reality exist, if
by inference one understands a process that leads \textit{with necessity}
from the one assumption to the
% --- p. 414 ---
\opage{414}other, and if one will not abolish the difference between inference and mere
association of representations. If the transition from the one particular to the other is to be
justified, this can only be done by the likeness between the first particular and an
earlier one: I infer that, since B\textsubscript{1} corresponded to A\textsubscript{1}, B\textsubscript{2} will correspond to A\textsubscript{2}. It
is an analogy that here guides the transition, and on a test of the analogy's
validity the decision as to the justification of the transition depends. Mill too comes
to admit the significance of the relation of likeness for all inferring (Logic. II, 3, 3 and III,
3, 1); but he does not see that this abolishes the possibility of an inferring from
particular to particular such as he has described it, and that the
principle of identity becomes the ultimate presupposition of all inference, whether
it appears in inductive or deductive form. A blind coupling together of
representations gives no logical connection: only where the relation of identity can be
shown is the blindness removed\textsuperscript{98}).

But the logical fundamental propositions themselves Mill regards, in consequence of his pure
empiricism, as grounded on experience. I experience early that light and darkness,
motion and rest, past and future are different and incompatible
predicates. I experience that I cannot at the same time believe something and not believe
it. Belief and non-belief are incompatible mental states. From this I then
derive by generalization the proposition that what is self-contradictory cannot be
true. But to this proposition there can belong no necessity that goes
beyond what experience teaches. Even if we stop at certain assumptions which we cannot
reject without feeling self-contradiction, we may not therefore infer
that they are in themselves, in reality, impossible. There may be
associations of representations that are so firm that we cannot dissolve them. But
the history of science shows us examples enough that what at one time was
regarded as unthinkable was nevertheless true. When we see that inconceivable things in
the course of time become conceivable, the inconceivability of the opposite of an
assumption cannot be any proof of the correctness of this assumption. What is
possible and real we learn only by way of experience, not through subjective
criteria. --- Of the two questions, whether there are self-contradictions
% --- p. 415 ---
\opage{415}that are more than factually indissoluble associations of representations, and whether we
have the right to assume that the self-contradictory cannot exist, it is
evidently the latter that has the greater interest for Mill. He even expresses himself
in his later writings (Examination of Sir William Hamilton's Philosophy. 2.
ed. p. 67) doubtfully as to whether the incompatibility of two mutually contradictory
assumptions is grounded on the original nature of our consciousness or springs
from experience. To change the logical principles, he remarks
(ib. chap. 21), experiences would be required which the conditions of our life do not make possible. But in
any case he holds fast that a subjective necessity cannot prove an
objective reality. What Mill overlooks here is the stimulating,
forward-driving force of self-contradiction. It is the self-contradiction in some of the inferences we draw
from experience that sets us problems and spurs us to work to procure
the self-contradiction away --- by extending experience. If we did not constantly use
self-contradiction as a criterion, our thinking would soon fall asleep.

The mathematical fundamental propositions are for Mill, like the logical fundamental propositions and
the causal principle, mere generalizations from experience. Mathematics
is indeed a science of reason which by way of thinking leads to necessary
results. But it rests on fundamental propositions that can only have been taken from
experience. That two magnitudes which are equal to one and the same third are
equal to each other is a proposition of experience and nothing more. Likewise it is a
proposition of experience that two straight lines that have intersected will always
diverge. The geometrical definitions contain elements from experience,
although these elements of experience are represented as more perfect and more exact than
experience presents them. The definition of the circle thus implies that all
the radii are equal, which they cannot be shown to be in any real circle.
All real circles nevertheless contain greater or lesser approximations
to the ideal circle about which geometry proves its propositions, and the
greater the approximation, the greater the validity the application of these
propositions acquires in reality. We make a leap from the approximately equal
to the absolutely
% --- p. 416 ---
\opage{416}equal, because we can thereby derive consequences; and in applying these
consequences we then take the degree of approximation into account. Geometry thus rests
on hypotheses, or, if one will, on fictions. If geometry is to have real
validity, the presupposition is that the nature of space corresponds to the
observations we have used to form our ideal hypotheses or
fictions. But whether space is so constituted everywhere in the world we cannot
know a priori. --- Had Mill gone more closely into the idealization which
leads to the setting up of the hypotheses of geometry, his whole epistemology would
perhaps have taken on another character, since he would have seen that one may very well
acknowledge an a priori element in our knowledge without therefore assuming that
assumptions about the nature of existence can be founded on it without further ado.

Mill's attempt to carry through empiricism and to make earnest of the doctrine of the
blank tablet cannot, then, be said to have succeeded. But by venturing the
attempt he has, through his acute and ramified investigations, thrown
light on the nature of our knowledge. The attempt itself may be regarded as a counterpart
to Hegel's dialectical method: whereas Hegel would develop truth by the
self-unfolding of pure thought, Mill would develop truth by
piecing together independent representations taken up from without. ---

A peculiarity of Mill's epistemology is the dependence in which it stands
on his psychological presuppositions. He builds his logic on his father's
psychology. Association by contiguity as the fundamental form of all connection of representations,
and indissoluble association as the explanation of what stands as inconceivable: these
are the means he operates with. \textit{Psychology} is for him
the fundamental science which bears all other sciences. The laws of association are the
fundamental laws of all our knowledge.

Mill has not himself given any exposition of psychology, but has in his Logic
treated its method and in other writings (``Examination'', 1865, and in the notes
to James Mill's ``Analysis'', 1869) treated particular psychological questions in an
% --- p. 417 ---
\opage{417}interesting way. The exposition of psychology with which in his later years he
most nearly sympathized was the one his friend and disciple \textsc{Alexander
Bain} gave in his two chief works \textit{The Senses and the Intellect} (1856) and
\textit{The Emotions and the Will} (1859). But in these works the strict
association psychology, as James Mill taught it, is abandoned, and
the relation of likeness is --- under the influence of William Hamilton --- acknowledged as the
condition of all association of representations, association by contiguity included.
Mill associates himself with this in his notes to the ``Analysis''. The relation of likeness should
thus, to be consistent, now have gained a greater influence in epistemology than Mill
had granted it in his Logic, where, as we have seen, he grounded all
inference on association by contiguity. He did indeed already in the Logic (I, 3,
11; 5, 6) acknowledge the relations of likeness and of difference as distinct, irreducible relations;
but he did not investigate more closely the role these relations play in all
connection of representations and all thinking.

Even in his later writings Mill would hold fast to Hume's and James Mill's conception
of consciousness as a series of states, only he adds: --- real
or \textit{possible} states. But he finds a difficulty at which his
predecessors had not stopped. In memory and expectation the
presupposition is contained that \textit{I myself and no other} have had at another time,
or will have, such a state of consciousness as I now have the representation of.
There must then be more in consciousness than the particular members that make up the series.
How can a series know that it is a series, --- that it has past members
and will have new members? The presence of \textit{a bond} is here made evident
between the particular members of consciousness, the particular sensations and
representations, a bond that is just as real as the particular members themselves and
is not a mere product of thought. If we are to have a name for this original
connecting element in our consciousness, we must call it our ego or our self.
(Examination. Chap. 12. The most characteristic and decisive statements were
first added in the later editions). In the notes to the ``Analysis'' (II. p. 175)
Mill expresses himself thus: ``There is a certain bond between all the members of the series which
makes me say that these were sensations
% --- p. 418 ---
\opage{418}of a person who was the same person throughout . . . . and this
bond constitutes for me my self''. Further than this --- Mill adds --- we can
at least not get by way of psychological analysis. With this,
association psychology is definitively abandoned. Mill has, as has been aptly
said, opened a trapdoor in the middle of his own philosophy. For Hume ``the
uniting principle'' consistently stood as a riddle, because he proceeded from the particular sensations
and representations as the only reality. When Mill now acknowledges the
uniting bond as just as real as the particular elements, he corrects the whole
concept of consciousness from which Hume, and after him James Mill, proceeded.
The laws of association can now only be special forms of ``the uniting
principle'', and the English school has thus by its untiring analysis
corrected its own principle\textsuperscript{99}). It brings contradictions into
Mill that he shows the relation of likeness and the bond to be realities, although he
builds his logic on purely external and accidental association. But it bears witness to
the honesty and acuteness of his search that he thus arrives at results which
lead beyond his own original presuppositions. ---

A peculiar application that Mill makes of the laws of association must still be mentioned. He
seeks to show how belief in an external world can be explained from them.
--- What I know of the world, I know through my sensations. But does there
then exist in reality a world in the sense of something different from my
sensations? --- What is really given are the sensations I have at
this moment. But besides, in memory and expectation I have representations of
possible sensations, representations which by repetition and association can
come to form fixed, coherent groups. And these groups continue to
stand before us in the same way in our representation, whether they are given as
sensations or not. We thereby get the representation of something that stands fast,
whether we perceive it or not. What is the so-called ``external'' object
other than the regular possibility that certain sensations recur in the
same way as I have had them before? --- In the assumption that there exists
% --- p. 419 ---
\opage{419}something independent of my consciousness I am confirmed when I experience that other
sentient beings have a similar regular series of sensations to my
own. --- What I mean by ``matter'' is then nothing but a permanent
possibility of sensations. It is the fixed and common associations of representations
that lead us to set up the concept of matter. And since we find that the
concept of cause holds within the series of our sensations and representations,
we involuntarily apply it also to the whole series, the whole sum of our
sensations and representations, and regard matter as their cause. --- The
practical belief, the strong inclination to assume an external world, is for Mill
no proof. By virtue of the principle of fixed association he holds that such an
assumption is not necessary. One need not assume anything existing other than
consciousness --- only that besides the consciousness really given one must also
assume the \textit{possibility} of new states of consciousness. It is clear that in
this ``possibility'' Kant's ``thing in itself'' lies hidden. When Mill says
(Examination. 2. ed. p. 189): ``The not-self might be merely a form in which
consciousness represents to itself the possible modifications of the self'', then it must
be asked whether the self can itself turn these possibilities into realities, so that
its changes of state could be understood out of itself. If the answer is yes,
the self will stand as creating its inner world out of nothing; if the answer is no, one must
either deny the causal principle or assume a reality besides the self. Mill does
not go more closely into this side of the matter and in general brings out too little the
connection in which the problem of the reality of an external world stands with the problem of causality.

\subsubsection*{c.\quad The Principles of Ethics}

Nowhere does Stuart Mill's peculiar position within the history of thought
show itself more clearly than in his ethics. Brought up in the spirit of the eighteenth century,
he seeks with honest will to make the points of view of the new age his own; but since
the presuppositions are taken from the old school, while the goal he would reach and
the points of view he acknowledges are due to the influence of new
% --- p. 420 ---
\opage{420}motives, there appears at decisive points in his line of thought a
duality which he himself does not always notice. In the ethical domain this
duality consists in his holding fast to the principle of utility, which he had learned to acknowledge in Bentham's school,
but wishing to supplement it by bringing it into
agreement with the philosophy of personality, whose ethics is of a more subjective
kind. He saw clearly that this task is the most important one for the future of ethics,
although he did not succeed in giving a theoretical solution of it. The
spiritual crisis he went through at a certain point of his development was conditioned
precisely by this problem. That in practice, in the art of life, in his great and
significant activity, he united in a rare degree regard for the inner development of the
personal life with regard for the outer effects of particular actions,
his biography bears witness. But the theory of this art he was not
able to give.

The reason why he did not succeed in this must doubtless be sought chiefly in his great
piety toward Bentham and his father. He had at one time, in the subjectively
strongly agitated period after that crisis, spoken out strongly against Benthamite
utilitarianism, which he reproached for taking a purely external
business standpoint. Now he believed he had got beyond the reaction against the
view into which he had been initiated in his early youth, and he now came forward
as its defender --- without being clear how far he himself had
altered the theory whose defender he would be. He did not distance himself sufficiently
from the older utilitarianism, and at particular points his
theory is also determined more by it than, to be consistent, it should be. That is why his
treatise ``Utilitarianism'' has become one of his least clear writings.

A clear and natural measure in ethical valuation we obtain --- of this Mill is
constantly convinced --- only by keeping to the effects of actions. If we ask
\textit{why} an action is good, the decision will in the end always
depend on whether it produces feeling of pleasure at some point or other and in some
extent or other. Human nature is once and for all so constituted that it
desires nothing which is not either the whole of happiness, a
% --- p. 421 ---
\opage{421}part of happiness or a means to happiness. Every action is judged and must be
judged according to the degree in which it leads toward what is thus always
the ultimate object of human desire. In this consists the application of the principle of utility.

To the question \textit{whose} happiness it is that is to furnish the measure
of valuation, Stuart Mill answers: ``Not the agent's own greatest happiness, but the
greatest total sum of happiness''. And this assertion he grounds not, as
Bentham in the ``Deontology'', by pointing to the harmony of well-understood egoistic
interests, but by giving a psychological explanation of the origin of the moral
feeling. It is the moral feeling that makes it possible for us to strive
to produce happiness, even if it is not our own happiness that we produce.

Stuart Mill does not take the moral feeling to be innate, but to be a highly
composite product. Its most important elements are sympathy, fear, religious
feeling of various kinds, experiences of the effects of actions, self-esteem,
desire for the esteem of others. In its extraordinarily composite character must be
sought the cause of the mystical character with which the notion of moral
obligation appears. There is a great quantity of feelings that must be rooted out
before one can do anything that conflicts with what one regards as right.
The association between those various elements is besides so strong that
the feeling appears with an indissoluble unity. And since the laws of association are
laws of nature, the moral feeling is a natural feeling, notwithstanding that it has a
history of its genesis. It is, after all, natural for men to speak, to draw
inferences of reason, to till the soil and to build cities, and yet these
skills are not innate, but acquired. If any single element in the
moral feeling were innate, it would have to be sympathy. But the greatest weight must
be laid on the fact that social life accustoms all individuals to having a common
interest, to working with united forces, to constantly taking account of
one another. There forms a kind of instinct that leads individuals to
solidarity in feeling and in action. And the more social life develops by
the barriers between the different
% --- p. 422 ---
\opage{422}classes being broken down, the more solidarity grows. The feeling of unity can become
a religion when it is constantly favored by education and by
the ordering of institutions and is enjoined by public opinion. There
takes place through social life an education of egoism, so that even if
regard for others was at first only a means, it later becomes itself an
end. Whereas Bentham --- at any rate in practice --- proceeded from
self-interest as the universal motive, Stuart Mill was convinced of the
reality of disinterested feelings. Thus he remarks, in his interesting
essay on Plato, apropos of the doctrine of the dialogue Gorgias that it is better
to suffer than to do wrong: ``The advance which `Gorgias' marks is one of the
greatest that has ever been made in moral culture, namely the development of
a disinterested choice of duty for its own sake, such that this choice
signifies a higher state than that in which selfish inclinations are sacrificed
to a more remote selfish interest''. (Diss. and Disc. III, p. 340).

Stuart Mill thus embraces an individual doctrine of development, like Spinoza,
Hartley and James Mill. The principle of indissoluble association serves him ---
like his predecessors --- to ground and explain the inner foundation of
ethics, while the principle of utility serves to ground the judgment of particular
actions. In clarity and simplicity, however, his exposition cannot measure itself with
Spinoza's and James Mill's. There is a certain wavering in him as to what is
original and what is acquired, and he also entangles himself in a
difficulty his predecessors did not know, by assuming
differences of quality between feelings. One feeling of pleasure is to be able not only to
be stronger, more lasting, more unmixed with pain, more fruitful in
happiness-bringing effects, more common to many than another feeling of pleasure; it
is also to be able to be of a qualitatively higher kind, which shows itself in that
whoever has experienced it seeks it, even if it can be obtained only by
going through great suffering, and prefers it to the greatest possible quantity of
another feeling of pleasure. The question is whether the ``difference of quality'' Mill here
posits does not find its explanation precisely in certain feelings of pleasure being
sanctioned and favored
% --- p. 423 ---
\opage{423}by the moral feeling whose origin Stuart Mill himself has sought to
explain. In any case the question whether there are qualitative
differences between feelings is far too complicated a question to be
solved by the simple proof Mill adduces. ---

While Stuart Mill, by laying so great a weight on the subjective foundation and
by assuming a difference of quality between feelings, moves far away from
Bentham's standpoint, he is still far too much a Benthamite in distinguishing between
the value of the action and the value of the acting personality and in holding that ethics
has to do only with the former. Precisely from a utilitarian standpoint this
distinction must be untenable. For since every motive contains possibilities of far
more actions than the particular one being judged at the moment, valuation must
extend to it as well. Even if the particular action does not give rise to
effects that conflict with the principle of welfare, actions may nevertheless spring from the same
motive which must be condemned, and the motive itself becomes in
such cases ethically questionable. It is consistent that valuation goes
back to the source. In the book ``Om Friheden'' the distinction mentioned plays, as
will appear, a large role too.

\subsubsection*{d.\quad Social Ethics}

Of the whole series of ethical and economic questions which Mill has
treated in his various writings and essays, only a few will be brought forward here
to illustrate his ethical standpoint.

α. \textit{Individual and Society.} (Om Friheden. 1859). --- Mill fought for
emancipation and self-development. But he experienced that political freedom does not
bring with it real, spiritual freedom and independence. In place of the physical
compulsion that is gradually displaced, public opinion, the
moral police, easily steps in. And this tyranny is more dangerous than the political one, since it leaves
fewer ways of escape open, penetrates into daily life and makes the soul itself a
slave. One follows the current, even when it concerns only which pleasures one
is to enjoy, instead of following
% --- p. 424 ---
\opage{424}one's own drive and one's own judgment. In England especially, says Mill, the yoke of public
opinion is heavy, while the yoke of the law is lighter than in other countries. A great danger
