threatens here: the rule of the masses, the rule of collective mediocrity. The mass
must certainly always be led by individuals --- but it prefers to take its opinions
from people who do not stand too high above it. And yet the impulse to everything
that is noble and wise always comes from individual outstanding people. The few
original people are the salt of the earth! --- Mill will, however, have no cult
of great men. All they can demand is full freedom to
utter the new ideas. Power to compel others would first and foremost corrupt
the great themselves. The means of avoiding that danger, which lies in the tyranny of public
opinion and in the lowering of the level by the rule of the masses, is \textit{freedom,}
the only constant, never-failing source of progress, because it creates
as many independent centers of improvement as there are personalities.

As a general fundamental proposition for the interference of others in the affairs of the individual,
Mill lays down that an individual's freedom of action may be restricted only
when an interference is necessary to prevent his conduct from bringing suffering
on others. Care for the individual's own good is not sufficient ground for
such interference. The only part of his conduct for which the individual owes
society an account is the part of it that concerns others. --- By interference
Mill understands partly physical compulsion, partly the spiritual
compulsion that lies in the judgments of others. In the latter respect he distinguishes between ``moral disapproval or
condemnation'' and ``expression of displeasure or withdrawal of esteem''. (Om Friheden.
Danish trans. p. 142). This, however, is a very fine distinction, since to withdraw
my esteem from an individual is to inflict a pain on him --- if, that is, he
sets store by my esteem; and if he does not, my ``disapproval'' will surely not pain
him either. The distinction is just as difficult as that between
actions which have effects only for ourselves and actions which have
effects for others as well. Whoever does not develop his personality, or who shows
a lack of prudence and personal dignity, can thereby
% --- p. 425 ---
\opage{425}deprive others of a power to which they rightly had a claim. Precisely when one maintains, as
Mill does, that what matters is to get as many independent starting points as
possible, it is impossible to mark off any domain that could not acquire
significance beyond the limits of individuality. This distinction between what
concerns the individual himself and what concerns others is as little tenable as
the previously mentioned distinction between the value of the agent and the value of the
action. And in both places Mill would precisely by virtue of the principle of utility have been able to
arrive at a more correct conception. ---

The importance of as great a freedom as possible Mill insists on as regards both opinions
and actions. --- If an opinion is true, what harm is there then
in its being freely discussed? Should it contain only a part of the truth, then
only free discussion can decide how great a part of the truth it makes up. And only by
being kept alive through discussion does it gain influence on characters and
actions. Even if, finally, an opinion could be useful without being
true, its utility must nevertheless be discussed just as well as its truth; in our days
--- Mill holds --- the utility of opinions plays quite as large a role as their truth.
--- As for actions, they cannot of course have as great a freedom as
opinions. But Mill maintains that the value of the different ways of living
must be tested in experience, and that this can only be done by giving
differences of character as much scope as is possible without causing
others suffering. It is a condition of the individual's own happiness as well as of
individual and social progress that its own character, and not custom and usage,
determine its manner of acting. Strong drives and desires are a good; they are the
stuff of which heroes are made, and men do not act badly because their
desires are strong, but because their conscience is weak. ---

Even if the boundary between individual and society is not so easy to draw as Mill
thinks, he has nevertheless by his investigation (which, moreover, takes up Kant's
fundamental thought in his ``Rechtslehre'') shown that the burden of proof always lies on
whoever would
% --- p. 426 ---
\opage{426}have freedom restricted, just as he has impressed the responsibility that is
attached to every moral judgment.

\textit{β. The Woman Question.} (Kvindernes Underkuelse. 1869). ---
The question of woman's right is for Mill only a single side of the great
question of emancipation. Here too what essentially matters is the struggle against the abuse of
power, the removal of the hindrances to the free unfolding of personality,
the abolition of the right of the stronger and of all external authority where this is not
necessary as protecting and educating. Besides, in his investigation of
this question he finds application for his favorite theory of indissoluble
association, to explain the opinions that hinder development. The
notions people have of the female nature rest, he maintains, only on habit
and tradition, not on real experience. What we call the ``female
nature'' is only an artificial product. Only by opening the barriers that have hitherto
been set to the development and use of female capacities can one come to know the
real female nature. It is the same line of thought as in the book on
liberty: compulsion must go, so that experience can be gained. It is a practical
application of the method of difference. But Mill believes he knows the result beforehand;
he maintains that the mental capacities of women and men are equal --- an
assumption which is of course not necessary to ground equality of rights.

\textit{γ. The Question of Representation.} (Om den repræsentative Regering.
1861). --- In discussing this question too Mill pursues his
main thought: how freedom can be secured not only against the despotism of individuals and
estates, but against the despotism of the majority. He discusses the dangers and advantages of
democracy. The constitutions between which the struggle now stands are in
reality only two: democracy and bureaucracy. The only possible solution
is that democracy take bureaucracy into its service and merely reserve to itself
superintendence and control. Parliament should represent only the decision of will in
the state; for drafting laws it is not suited; for that commissions of experts
should be appointed. To secure the right of the minority in decisions
Mill recommends, among other things, proportional representation.
% --- p. 427 ---
\opage{427}Clear as his eye is, as the book on liberty also shows, for the defects
of democracy, he nevertheless sees clearly how shortsighted are those who sigh for
a despotism in order to get their plans of reform carried through. They forget that the
development of the people itself is the most important condition of continued progress, and they do
not see that a good despotism in a fairly civilized country is even more
harmful than a bad one, because it is far more enervating to the spirit and strength of the people.

\textit{δ}. \textit{The Social Question.} (Principles of Political Economy.
1848). --- In the course of Mill's development it became more and more clear to him that the
social question takes precedence over the political. His democratic
conviction he never gave up; but partly, as we have already seen, he came to have
an open eye for the defects of democracy, partly there formed for him an
ideal of the future which lay far beyond the democratic program. Without great
social changes individual and political freedom would in any case
not really be able to benefit all.

Already in a letter from the year 1842 (to Robert Barcley Fox, printed in Caroline
Fox's Diaries. II. p. 272) Mill speaks of the significance of the social question:
``I believe that ever since the changes that took place in the constitution
through Catholic Emancipation and the Reform Act, a great part of the ruling
class, especially younger men, have gradually had their eyes opened, and the progress of Chartism
is producing, I believe, the feeling that those who govern must strive, both from duty and from
prudence, to a far higher degree than they have long been accustomed to, to
look after the temporal and spiritual interests of the poor''. But he must add:
``As to the means, on the other hand, of curing or even merely alleviating great social
evils, people are just as far from harbor as they were before''. To a
definite solution Mill did not come later either. He acknowledges openly that here there are
two fundamental thoughts, both of which he must hold fast, although in their consequences ---
at any rate apparently --- they conflict with each other. They are
the ideas of individualism and of socialism, of which Mill (Levned. p. 259)
declares that they are diametrically opposed to each other. How it is then possible to
unite them,
% --- p. 428 ---
% print: „imponener“ (p. 428) (misprint)
% print: „Undersøgelselse“ (p. 428) (misprint)
\opage{428}he declares he does not know; that he leaves to the future. It was his
conviction that we do not yet know either of the two systems in its best
possible form. We know neither yet what free self-activity in its highest degree
and form can accomplish, nor what possibilities there are for a thoroughgoing social
ordering of the external conditions of life. Nowhere perhaps do Mill's great qualities show
themselves so clearly as here. Together with a great hope for the future, indeed perhaps precisely
supporting himself on it, he takes up a critically discussing position toward the different
possibilities that experience presents. What is merely handed down and customary does not impress
him; he calmly investigates the conditions of its subsistence and looks to see
whether these conditions might not be replaced by others.

In his investigation of the socialist systems he took up a far more
unprejudiced standpoint than the economists of his time were wont to. That followed from
the spirit of his philosophy. He could not, like the usual opponents of
socialism, see in the right of inheritance and the right of private property dogmas that did not
need to be grounded. The way in which the yield of production is distributed
depends, in his conception, to so high a degree on the actual social order and
on the habit and will of men that it was a great piece of sleight of hand when
the economists were wont to regard the mode of distribution now prevailing as
grounded on eternal natural necessity. As regards private property in particular, it
was not introduced for any of the reasons for which it is now upheld.
Originally society, for the sake of peace, maintained the individual in the possession of
what he had once and for all seized. Whether this arrangement is to be
retained for the future or replaced by an arrangement such as socialist
systems conceived, that is now an open question, and a question which is the
object of discussion through all classes in the civilized countries. Mill
finds precisely what is peculiar to our time in this, that all principles are discussed, and that
even those who suffer most under the existing institutions take part in
the discussion of the value and justification of these principles. It is the first time in
history that this has been the case. What will the result be? Mill answers
(Principles of
% --- p. 429 ---
\opage{429}Polit. Economy. II, 1, 3): ``If I may venture a conjecture, the decision will
probably depend chiefly on one consideration, namely which of the two systems
is consistent with the greatest degree of human freedom and self-activity.
Once the means of sustaining life are secured, the need of freedom is the
strongest of all the personal wants of men, and it grows in strength,
instead of diminishing, the more the intellectual and moral faculties are developed . .
. An education which taught men, or social institutions which
commanded them, to give up control over their own actions in order to obtain
comfort and abundance, be it in ever so high a degree, or to
renounce freedom for the sake of equality, would rob them of one of the
most exalted characteristics of human nature''. Now Mill does think that
this objection to socialism is often exaggerated, and he maintains that the
compulsion this system would entail would deserve to be called freedom in comparison with
the compulsion under which the great working class now lives. But he sees no
reason to give up the system of private property, if only the laws will do
as much to prevent its drawbacks as they now do to aggravate
them. The present order favors the development of selfishness to a
degree which is not in itself necessary, even if the system of private property
is retained. The socialists wrongly blame competition for all social
evils. They forget that where there is no competition, there is monopoly and with it
taxation of the industrious in favor of the idle. Competition among
the workers themselves certainly presses wages down; but all other competition
is to the good of the workers by making the necessaries of life cheaper. Not
competition, but the subjection of labor to capital is the cause of the
drawbacks. (IV, 7, 7).

What according to Mill essentially matters is, by vigorous intervention on
the part of the state, to raise the whole level of the working class, its demands on life and
on itself. What matters is to reach by peaceful means such an advance as the
French working class gained by the French Revolution. By improved
education, by the parceling out of land and by an emigration carried through on a large
% --- p. 430 ---
\opage{430}scale the working class will be able to attain such a social position
and to have acquired such ideal and material needs that, in order not to
lower the level and diminish wages, it will show the necessary self-control
and avoid improvident increase of population, even if this effect only
occurs in a later generation that has grown up under the more favorable conditions.
(II, 11, 2). But Mill also expected much of the free associations
(trade unions and especially productive associations) and followed their development in
France and England with great interest. Their chief significance he saw in their
favoring the virtues of independence: justice and self-control. In such
smaller circles experiments in a socialist direction could moreover be made
which might become of significance for the continued discussion of the social question.

\subsubsection*{e.\quad The Religious Problem}

In the writings Stuart Mill himself published he touches only in passing
on religious questions. Most fully in the work on Hamilton's philosophy. He
here disputes two conceptions. The one (which Hamilton too, from his standpoint,
had disputed) was the one Schelling and Hegel had asserted, that by
way of pure thinking a scientific concept of God could be set up, a concept
of an absolute and infinite being, the author and end of all things. Mill maintains that
in the religious question too we must proceed from experience, and that it must
be the contemplation of nature that leads us to the assumption of a God. He seems
also to hold that it is possible to ground such an assumption, and in
accordance with this he maintains (in his work on Comte and positivism) that
even if one assumes with Comte the law of the three stages, there will still remain on the
positive stage \textit{open questions,} and that one may very well
hold fast to theological assumptions, provided only these are framed so that they do not
come into conflict with what experience teaches. The other conception Mill disputes
is the one Hamilton and especially Mansel embraced, that even if the scientific
investigation of the concept of God as the absolute and
% --- p. 431 ---
\opage{431}infinite, almighty and all-good being should lead to self-contradictions and to
consequences that conflict with what the human conscience must maintain,
we must nevertheless believe in such a being, since neither our logic nor our ethics can
find application to the Deity. Against this doctrine Mill expresses himself with great
indignation. ``If'', he says (Examination. 2. ed. p. 103), ``instead of
the glad tidings that there exists a being in whom all the excellences which the
highest human thought can conceive are found in a degree inconceivable to us,
I am told that the world is governed by a being whose attributes are infinite,
without our knowing what they are, any more than we can understand what
principles it follows in its government, except that `the highest human
morality which we are able to conceive' does not sanction them, ---
convince me of it, and I will bear my fate as well as I can. But when I am
told that I am to believe this and at the same time call this being by
names which express the highest human morality, then I say in plain
words that I will not. Whatever power such a being may have over me, there is one
thing it shall not be able to do: it shall not compel me to worship
it. I will call no being good who is not what I mean
by it when I apply this word to my fellow creatures; and if such a
being can sentence me to hell, well then, to hell I will go''.

From this forceful statement, which aroused great attention and offense and was
used against Mill by political opponents, one will see what for Mill was
the kernel of the religious problem, namely the moral impossibility of acknowledging
a higher measure of moral valuation than the human one. Already
Bentham had (in Deontology. Part. I. Chap. 8) spoken out sharply against calling
an attribute in God love which in man would be the opposite of
love; that is to call a dagger thrust a kiss! And according to what Stuart Mill
relates in his Levned (p. 42), it was the impossibility of reconciling the evil in
the world with belief in an almighty and all-good creator that determined James Mill's
rejection of all religious assumptions and made him feel a certain sympathy with the
% --- p. 432 ---
\opage{432}Manichaean assumption of a good and an evil principle that struggle with each other for
dominion in the world. For his own part Stuart Mill did not express himself
definitely in any of the writings that appeared in his lifetime. It was certainly
not from fear of men that he refrained from uttering his views. What he
did utter was enough to brand him as a man who departed to a high degree
from the usual religious notions. His utterances were indeed used
as a means of agitation against him, and a church organ declared, when he was dead:
``His death is no loss to anyone, for he was a gross unbeliever, however nicely he
behaved, and a very dangerous person. The sooner the `lights of thought' who hold
the same opinions as he go to the same place where he has gone, the better it will
be both for church and state''. What opinions Mill held, even the
church organ, which was hardly in doubt about Mill's fate after death, would have had
trouble saying. The explanation must be sought in his not himself finding his ideas
on the religious problem fully developed; the question was for him in
reality open, and he would not speak publicly about it before he
had satisfied his own demands for clarity and thoroughness. Even his
friends knew no more of his religious standpoint than has been
set out above, until his \textit{Essays on Religion} appeared some time after his
death. Of the three essays this work contains, two (on the utility of religion
and on theism) were not finished; only the third (on nature) did he himself consider
worthy of publication. --- A contributing reason for his reticence
may perhaps also have been that he would not mix several problems
together, but have them discussed each by itself. He felt no need to fire off
his artillery in all directions at once. The secret of the great
influence which, in spite of his radical standpoint, he gained in his time has partly
lain in his taking one point at a time. As he himself said to a
friend: ``I spare no prejudice, but I attack one at a time''.

The fundamental thought of the essay \textit{on nature} is that one cannot set up
nature, as it is without human
% --- p. 433 ---
\opage{433}intervention, as a model for man, any more than one can
infer from it an all-wise, all-good and almighty author. Nature can impress us by
its might and power; but its conduct bears the stamp of terrorism and injustice;
it gives to those who have, and is merciless to those who have not. The
only possibility of uniting belief in a God with experience of the
real world consists in the assumption that the Deity is indeed good, but not
almighty. Omnipotence must be sacrificed to goodness. In the essay \textit{on theism}
this is developed more closely. The author of the world order has been obliged to conform
to conditions that were independent of his will. The matter and the force in the
world are not created; their properties and laws are independent of the
will of the orderer of the world. It is then no wonder that there are so many
imperfections! Everything that checks the tendency, traceable in nature, to
produce something purposive and good must be put down to the account of the material
hindrances with which the Deity has to struggle. The mood that will
be peculiar to the religion of the future must be the inspiring feeling of
being the Deity's fellow worker, a feeling that cannot without self-contradiction be
united with belief in an almighty God. What the Deity's will is can only
be discovered by attending to everything in nature that tends toward general
welfare and a higher development of life. In this struggle between the good and the evil
forces in the world even the slightest contribution can be of significance. To do something,
however little it may be, to further the victory of the good is the most living
and strengthening thought that can animate a man. This thought will be a
leading thought in the religion of the future! --- Already in a letter of 1841 (to Robert
Barclay Fox, see Caroline Fox's Diaries. II, p. 260) Mill mentions this thought,
referring to the Saint-Simonians' doctrine of continuing the work of creation.

One point in Mill's polemic against Hamilton first becomes properly intelligible when one
knows that he conceived the Deity as a limited being. For he cannot
understand all the difficulties Hamilton finds theoretically in the concept of God,
% --- p. 434 ---
\opage{434}namely not how the law of relativity can be a hindrance to holding fast
this concept in thought. God is thought in relation to the world --- what contradiction
is there in that? asks Mill. He surely presupposes here his own concept of a
limited God; for the self-contradiction is of course present only so long as
the Deity is to be thought as an absolute and infinite being --- and yet in relation to
something that is not itself, so that it is thus conditioned and limited, i.e. becomes
relative! --- It was not logical but ethical reasons that led Mill to his
standpoint in the philosophy of religion, which recalls the one Voltaire and Rousseau took.

When Mill, from the tendency to purposiveness and heightened life which can be traced in the world
alongside wholly opposite tendencies, infers the assumption of a
Deity, this inference is shaken if a purely scientific explanation
of purposiveness and the development of life were possible. Mill rejects
the dogma of creation because every phenomenon must be explained by another phenomenon; but
must not for the same reason the inference too which he believes he can draw from
purposiveness and the development of life be rejected, since here too
definite natural causes must be sought in each particular case? It is these causes that
the hypothesis of evolution seeks to show, and Mill does indeed declare that if
the hypothesis of evolution is adopted, it will not indeed make impossible the assumption of a
creative intervention, but will nevertheless greatly weaken the proof of such an
assumption. ``Let us leave this remarkable hypothesis to the fate which
the progress of science reserves for it''.

Even if religion could not be proved, it will --- in Mill's
conception --- not fall away so long as it is of benefit to man. Mill
investigates in a separate essay \textit{the utility of religion.} Religion has
this in common with poetry, that it springs from a need of grander and
more beautiful images than those prosaic life brings with it. Human life
will, in spite of all progress, continue to be so wretched and narrow that man
will always need greater breadth and height for his destiny. Imagination
must be freed from the limitation that positive experience brings with it. Even if
% --- p. 435 ---
\opage{435}religion differs from poetry by the weight it lays on the real
significance of ideals, the essential thing in all religion is nevertheless that feeling and longing
are directed in a forceful and earnest way toward an ideal object. This condition
is fulfilled by Comte's religion of humanity better than by any of the religions that embrace
belief in God as the author of the world. The feeling of unity with humanity, of deep
sympathy with its welfare and progress, is a disinterested feeling which does not
contain anything that can become questionable in a logical or ethical respect. Only
one form of supernatural belief is there that is neither illogical nor immoral,
namely the one described above, which regards nature as the product of a struggle
between a good and wise being on the one side and on the other either
matter (as Plato assumed) or an evil principle (as the Manichaeans assumed). Whoever
embraces this belief can be sure that the evil in the world is not a work
of the being he worships. Even if this belief could not be proved, even
if it is rather a hope than a belief, true wisdom of life nevertheless demands that it be
held fast with all one's might. It brings with it a bright and cheerful way of taking life,
and it does not exclude reason and criticism. By one-sidedly and needlessly turning
one's gaze toward what is dark, narrow and unhappy in life one only hampers one's
capacity for action. The hope that beyond the limit set to our experience
there are good forces and an immortal life has its essential significance in
giving the scale of the feelings a greater extent. Mill ascribed significance to belief in immortality
especially for the sympathetic feelings; he even at times placed the whole
significance of religion at this point, as when he said to a friend who had
lost one of those nearest to him: ``In my view the only
lasting value of religion consists in alleviating the feeling of complete separation which is so
dreadful in a great sorrow''. But in his work on the philosophy of religion he dwells
also especially on the significance Christianity has had and has in
setting up an exalted model for the race; it is far more by its
image of Christ than by its idea of God that Christianity has worked. And the
% --- p. 436 ---
\opage{436}influence of this model will --- Mill maintains --- not fall away because one conceives it in a
purely historical, human manner. ---

Mill's religion has this in common with Kant's, that it is rather a hope than a belief.
He is quite clear that the decisive question is this: ``Is it
irrational to let oneself be determined by the imagination to a hope for whose
realization one may perhaps never be able to give any probable ground? Must
one combat this hope as a departure from the principle of reason which bids us
regulate our feelings as well as our opinions according to strict proofs?'' Mill
holds that on this point there will long be dispute among thinkers, and that each
of them will decide it according to his temperament. But he holds as well that the
question itself has not received the serious discussion its great significance demands.

Mill's own solution leaves one side of the problem standing. If the good
principle struggles with material chaos, there must nevertheless be a world order
that embraces them both and makes the struggle possible. Struggle is interaction, and
interaction presupposes an order of things that makes it possible for the
different acting forces to meet. Thus the old problem rises
again behind Mill's solution. Mill's critics in the philosophy of religion in
England\textsuperscript{100}), who for the most part operate with Hegelian weapons,
have especially brought forward this point, while they have not felt the ethical
sting of the problem as strongly as Mill. --- Psychologically regarded, Mill has passed over a factor
that plays a large role in religion, namely the need of absolute absorption and
rest in a being that is not itself placed in the struggle of life. This need is in
the religions curiously at odds with the need of having in the Deity a
living and struggling model. The religious problem is sharpened when both
spiritual needs demand satisfaction at once.

But Mill's greatness does not lie in his results. His pure empiricism he
succeeded in grounding and carrying through as little as Plato succeeded in
carrying through his pure idealism. This comparison lies all the closer
as Mill was all his life a great admirer of Plato. One can apply
to him what he himself says of
% --- p. 437 ---
\opage{437}Plato (Levned p. 24): ``I have always felt that the name Platonist belongs with far
greater right to those who have been trained in and have endeavored to
apply Plato's mode of investigation than to those who have only adopted certain of his
dogmatic propositions''. Mill's significance in the history of philosophy consists precisely in
his mode of investigation, in the way in which he has set experience and
critical thinking to work in a whole series of theoretical and practical
domains. He has awakened a philosophical spirit which is of greater significance than any
single one of his results. --- And with this we leave the thinker at once all of a piece
and ever striving, logically clear and
% scan: „øg“ (p. 437)
strongly moved by feeling, who in his development at once reflects
the problems of his time and gives weighty help in their treatment.

\section*{C.\quad The Philosophy of Evolution}

The general fundamental thought on which the positivist philosophy rests is
that our views are to be built on observations. In explaining the
phenomena that experience presents, we are then to rely on causes that can
themselves be demonstrated in experience. Positivism is really only a carrying-through of
the demand for ``true causes'' that Kepler and Newton made. As Auguste
Comte has shown, the difference between the various main forms of philosophy depends
on which causes one assumes. But even if one adheres to this principle, there may
still be room for significant oppositions. Comte and Stuart Mill stopped at
the conception of the causal relation as a relation between two different phenomena
which for us simply were, as a matter of fact, connected. They laid no weight on that side
of the causal relation by which, the more it is deepened and seen through, it shows us a
continuous connection between the phenomena. Therefore they did not come to see the
close connection there is between the concept of cause and the concept of evolution. In the
social domain this latter concept does, to be sure, play
% --- p. 438 ---
\opage{438}an essential role with them; but it does not become determinative for their whole
view of nature. They laid too great weight on the differences that experience
presents, and did not see that all knowledge aims at reducing them as much
as possible. They stopped at the problem of how new forms arise. Within
the individual they assumed a development, and in the species likewise, through the influence of traditions
and institutions. But that the concept of evolution could become a leading
thought for the whole conception of the world they did not see, and the limits of their thinking
were in great part determined by this.

The change in the view of nature that \textsc{Charles Darwin's} discoveries and
hypotheses brought about may with good reason be compared with the changes
caused by Copernicus and Bruno, Galilei and Newton. Copernicanism enlarged
the world and made it infinite; the earth and human life no longer stood
as that about which everything turned. Newton showed that a fixed lawfulness
holds in the whole great world, since the distant globes follow the same laws that
hold here on earth. Darwin's view of nature signifies a similar widening of
the gaze as regards organic life. In the domain of living beings
no great connection, no general law of origin and development, had yet been
demonstrated. It had been shown by \textsc{Caspar Friedrich Wolff} and \textsc{Karl Ernst Von Baer}
that the single organism develops through a series of
stages from a germ that bears no likeness to the fully developed
individual. It has been shown by \textsc{Spinoza, Hartley} and \textsc{James
Mill} that a psychological development can take place in the single individual, through
which, by virtue of the laws of association, mental forms take shape that
resemble the original foundation as little as the forms of the grown organism
resemble those of the germ. And the historical school, founded by \textsc{Montesquieu}
and flourishing after the Revolution especially in France and Germany, had asserted
the concept of development with regard to the origin of social and political forms.
\textsc{In the philosophy of Romanticism} the concept of evolution likewise played a great
role. The inward connection of the individual thing with the whole was held fast, and
existence was conceived as a series
% --- p. 439 ---
% scan: „uansélige“ (p. 439)
\opage{439}of steps on which the content of the world appeared in ever higher forms. But
the use that was made there of the concept of evolution was a purely ideal one. Development was not
conceived as a process by which one phenomenal form
arose out of another; the continuity was thought to lie in the ideal kernel of existence, not
between the single phenomena. And no one asked after the efficient causes
that could lead over from one step to the next. A great example of
how new forms and states can take shape by virtue of laws that constantly
hold was, on the other hand, given in \textsc{Kant's} and \textsc{Laplace's} hypothesis of
the development of the solar system out of a primeval nebula through the influence of definite physical and chemical
relations, and in \textsc{Lyell's} theory of the origin of
the present state of the earth's surface through the constant action of the same
physical and chemical causes that are at work to this day. Darwin's doctrine
holds that the organic species arise because constant
variations of the organic forms take place, but that only those variations can survive which
under the given conditions of life (physical conditions and relations to other living
beings) offer certain purposive properties. It is this that he
figuratively designates by the expression ``the struggle for existence.'' When the conditions of life
then continue to be the same through long periods, the purposive
properties will be fixed and heightened. Darwin has widened the view of nature and let us
discover an immeasurable course of development out of which the species now living have
come forth. And on the other hand he has sharpened the eye for small things,
in that he has taught us to see, in the often inconspicuous causes that are at work around
us, the forces by whose quiet but uninterrupted working the living
species have arrived at the forms under which they now appear to us.

What was new in Darwin's doctrine was not the general thought that organic species and
forms have arisen through natural causes. This thought had come forward in many shapes
before him. His significance lies in his having supported it by
demonstrating definite causes that work in the direction of such a new formation. The
concept of evolution itself is, as already indicated, so closely bound up with
the concept of cause and the concept of continuity
% --- p. 440 ---
\opage{440}that it could come forward as a leading idea before Darwin gave it the
mighty confirmation of experience through his investigations. Thus HERBERT
SPENCER had, several years before Darwin's epoch-making work appeared, already adopted
the hypothesis of evolution, and in particular he had (in the first edition of his Psychology)
shown what significance this hypothesis had through the possibility that the
properties and faculties that cannot find their explanation in the single
individual's experience could be explained by the experience of the whole species. It was an
extension of the philosophy of experience, by which it became possible for it to let
points of view that hitherto only the speculative and critical philosophy had asserted
come into their own more fully than had happened before. Later Spencer has,
in a detailed, systematic exposition, sought to show the concept of evolution to be
a principal concept to which our experience and our thinking lead us back from all sides.

\subsection*{1.\quad Charles Darwin}

\subsubsection*{a.\quad Biography and Course of Development}

The justification for drawing this great naturalist into the history of philosophy
lies --- in a similar way as with Copernicus, Kepler, Galilei and Newton ---
first and foremost in this, that his method and his results have significance far
beyond his special field and mark a turning point for scientific
research and for the view of nature
% scan: „Natnropfattelsen“ (p. 440)
as a whole. Quite shortly after the idea of his hypothesis had arisen
in him (1837), twenty years before his famous work appeared, he wrote in his notebook:
``My theory will lead to a whole philosophy.'' But it was not only through its
consequences, not only by raising the question of how the new theory
bore on the whole world-view, that Darwin acquired significance for philosophy. He
has also himself treated psychological and ethical questions and expressed himself on
the limits of knowledge. And as we know him through his autobiography and
his letters, he stands before us as a peculiar Socratic
% --- p. 441 ---
\opage{441}figure in the research of our time, venerable by his energy, his love of truth and his
feeling of humanity.

\textsc{Charles Darwin} was born at Shrewsbury on 12 Feb. 1809. After having
tried medical studies in Edinburgh and then theological
studies in Cambridge, without having got anything out of it, his early awakened
interest in natural history led him to go along on a voyage round the world that the ship
``Beagle'' made from 1831---1836. The observations he made on this voyage
form the first foundation of his theory. He had compared the present fauna of South America
with the extinct species and wondered at the likeness in structure
alongside the differences, especially in size. He had compared
the animal species in the northern part of South America with those in the southern part, and
here too found likeness and difference combined in a peculiar way. But above all
he had wondered to find on the Galopagos Islands, some 150 miles from
South America, an animal and plant world that quite recalled
South America's, although it consisted of species that were found nowhere else in the world:
the species occurred only on these islands, but they belonged to genera that were found on
the nearest mainland. It was as if one and the same fundamental form had been transformed partly
to live on the mainland, partly on the islands. And besides, each one of
the islands had its peculiar species, which were not found on the other islands. How is
this kinship on the one side, this difference on the other, to be
explained? With this problem Darwin returned home from his great voyage, and he
spent his whole life answering it. He lived in the country near
London under the happiest circumstances, uninterruptedly occupied with collecting
facts that could throw light on his problem. The question to be
solved was why precisely such forms and properties are preserved and developed as
are of benefit to animals and plants under the conditions in which they live. What had
struck Darwin was precisely the variation in forms and properties in accordance
with the conditions of life. He started from the assumption that there must be a natural cause
of this --- but which? The reading (in the year 1838) of \textsc{Malthus's} work on
the population question set
% --- p. 442 ---
\opage{442}his thoughts going. Malthus showed that living beings have a
tendency to multiply to a higher degree than the quantity of the means of nourishment can
increase. But then, Darwin concluded, living beings must surely be one another's
opponents, must fight or compete with one another for access to what they need in order
to live. Life is and must be a ``struggle for existence,'' and the individual or
the group of individuals that for some reason or other has acquired a faculty or an
organ that the others lack, and that suits the circumstances, will more easily hold its own in
the struggle than the others. The multiplication of the species will take place chiefly through them, and
forms that lack this faculty or this organ will gradually die out. And
when a group of living beings has to live in a limited space, this will be
all the more easily done, the more different forms there are
within the group, since their wants will thereby more easily be able to be
satisfied. When all have to live on one and the same thing, not
so many can live as when there is difference in food. It is therefore an advantage in
the struggle for existence that a capacity for variation is present in a species.

Already at the beginning of the forties Darwin worked out a treatise in which
he set forth his theory, but he laid it aside in order to undertake further
investigations. In the middle of the fifties he began the final redaction of
his work, and this appeared in 1859 under the name of \textit{Origin of Species.} (Danish
translation by J. P. Jakobsen. 1872). To it was joined a long series of
other writings, of which the most important in philosophical and psychological respects
are \textit{Variation of Animals and Plants under Domestication} (1868),
\textit{Descent of Man} (1871, Danish translation by J. P. Jacobsen 1874) and
\textit{Expression of the Emotions in Men and in Animals} (1872). --- Darwin's
long, faithful work in the service of science ended only with his death on
19 April 1882\textsuperscript{101}). Three years before, he had written in
his autobiography: ``I believe that I have acted rightly in devoting my life to
science. I feel no remorse for having committed any sin, but I have
again and again regretted that I have not done more direct good to my
fellow men.'' ---
% --- p. 443 ---
\opage{443}

\subsubsection*{b.\quad Theory and Method}

The result of Darwin's research was a victory for the principle of natural
causes and for the assertion that nature makes no leaps. It had indeed earlier
been assumed that the varieties are due to definite natural causes; but the
species themselves were regarded as supernaturally produced or at any rate as inexplicable. Continuity
was now demonstrated in a domain where hitherto one had either assumed
supernatural intervention and interruption or had stopped at original,
inexplicable differences, or at the most had appealed to an inner
impulse of development that was to lead from one step to the next. By the
explanation Darwin gave of the origin of species, through the struggle for existence,
he moreover threw a light on the conditions of life, not only physical but also
mental life, which is quite as important as the solution of the special
task he had set himself. It was an old English thought that he, without
knowing it, took up again. For his ``struggle for existence'' recalls Hobbes's ``war of
all against all.'' The English have always had an eye for the conditions of life and for
the necessity of putting force into the effort to master them. By this is
conditioned the peculiar mixture of empiricism and idealism that is often
regarded as a contradiction. Their sense for practical circumstances as they
simply are does not, however, dull their conviction of the value of the inner forces, even
if they do not express it in the mystical or speculative way into which the thinkers of the Continent
often lapse.

The explanation Darwin gives of the origin of species is entirely in the spirit
of positivism, and it was therefore inconsistent when Comte's disciples took up a
dismissive attitude toward the new hypothesis. The cause to which Darwin appeals is
given, \textit{positive.} He declares in a letter that to say that the species
were created thus or thus is no scientific explanation,
but only a pious way of saying that it is as it is. And according to other
statements, when at the close of the ``Origin of Species'' he spoke of
the first forms of life as having been created, he meant only that we know nothing of how
life arises;
% --- p. 444 ---
\opage{444}later he expressly regretted that out of regard for common opinion he
had used the word ``created.''

The expression \textit{the struggle for existence} is figurative. It is meant to designate the
dependence of one being on another and on the conditions of life, and in such a way that
not only the single individual is thought of, but also its offspring. A
plant that grows on the edge of a desert must struggle for life, that is to say, its
subsistence depends on how little moisture it can make do with. An even
greater role than the relation to physical conditions is played in the organic
world by the relation to other living beings. Mistletoes on the same branch ``struggle''
with one another for room and nourishment; but they also struggle with other fruit-bearing
plants, since their multiplication depends on whether the birds swallow their seeds rather than
those of the others, so that sowing can take place to a higher degree. While the expression the struggle for
existence designates the organism's adaptation to the living or lifeless
environment, Darwin designates by the expression \textit{natural selection} the
other side of the relation, namely the way in which the conditions of life
favor certain properties --- ``the principle according to which every variation, however
slight, that is useful to the individual is preserved.'' There is struggle everywhere in
nature. It is always a matter of: to be or not. Every being subsists by virtue
of a victory it has won at some time or other of its life. And
the struggle for existence is in turn a consequence of the strong multiplication of organic
beings. The whole economy of nature becomes unintelligible to us if we for a single
moment forget that each single species seeks to increase extraordinarily strongly, and
that there is always some obstacle or other that checks or stops its spread,
even if we cannot always catch sight of it. It is because of this
collision between spread and obstacle that a selection becomes
necessary. The individuals that offer purposive variations survive, the
others die out; thus the rise of differences is favored, and there take shape
at last the species that are now in the eyes of so many essentially different. We have here a key
to understanding how forms of different kinds can be related to
one another, since with increasing divergence of character they develop out of
% --- p. 445 ---
\opage{445}a common fundamental form. What C. F. Wolff had shown for the different organs
of the same individual, that in spite of their unlikeness they develop out of certain simple rudiments,
Darwin showed for the different species within the organic world as a whole.

Darwin's method is an interesting model for inductive research. His
course of development as a researcher presents with unusual clarity the three
main stages that a truth built on experience runs through. The first foundation
of his theory was, as we saw, the observations made on the voyage. They
called forth the idea, the provisional hypothesis, and --- after the reading of Malthus ---
the explanation by deduction from the strong impulse of multiplication in its relation to
the conditions of life. The third link in the series of labors was the verification,
the confirmation by experience. It consisted essentially in four groups of facts.
The English animal breeders had for many years produced new races by ``artificial selection.''
They noticed small variations, suited to their purposes, in
the different individuals, and then, by seeing to it that only individuals which
offered such variations propagated the species, succeeded in breeding new forms. What
happens here consciously and methodically happens through ``natural selection'' unconsciously
and in a more irregular way. The second fact that confirms the theory is the
kinship of extinct species with species now living. They can as a rule be ranged as
links in groups now existing and be conceived as lower forms of development of these.
The third fact lies in the geographical distribution of the species, which is best understood
by assuming that different forms and properties in related beings have
arisen through the spread of the stock over tracts of different character.
That the lowest beings are the most widely distributed is explained by their
seeds and eggs being small and well fitted to be carried far and wide by water and current.
Finally the agreement there can be in the embryonic state between
animal forms that, when fully grown, differ greatly from one another, testifies to a distant
kinship, and rudimentary organs (which are found especially in the embryonic state) likewise become
intelligible only on the assumption of such a kinship.

There was a remarkable kinship between Darwin's character
% --- p. 446 ---
\opage{446}and the direction and method of his research. What distinguished him as a researcher was
his open and childlike mind, for which nothing was mean and insignificant.
Everywhere he divined a connection. Nature was to him not a dead collection of
objects to which the naturalists were to give name and number, but a living
reality, where the subsistence and growth of the one depends on that of the other. The insect and
the flower, the bird and the plant, the mold and the worm, the life of animals, their structure,
their ornaments, their love and their fights, all this stood for him in mutual
connection and could only in an unnatural way be separated. The word natural history
he has made a truth. With the childlike openness toward nature there was joined
in him the manly understanding that fixed, definite laws hold
everywhere, and that even the highest in nature is not withdrawn from such laws, but
precisely shows its highness by developing by virtue of these laws. He used to
say that one could not be a good observer if one could not speculate.
It was not possible for him to see anything new in nature without at once forming a
hypothesis about how it could have come to be. But on the other hand he had
a peculiar capacity for seizing an objection and holding it fast. He followed
what he called the golden rule, of noting down every fact and every
thought he came across that conflicted with the results he had reached. Very
few objections were therefore made against his views that he had not himself
noticed and sought to answer. He was in this respect more critical than
several of his adherents; these sometimes thought that he laid too much
weight on the objections that could be made against his doctrine. He was fully
aware that his hypothesis really cannot be proved directly. Of one of his
critics he writes in a letter: ``He is one of the very few who see that the change of species
cannot be directly proved, and that my doctrine will sink or
swim according as it is able to group and explain the phenomena. It is
remarkable how few judge it in this way, which is the one right
way.'' The proof of his doctrine he found in the ``thread of thought'' (the intelligible
thread) with which
% --- p. 447 ---
\opage{447}it connects a whole series of facts. His doctrine was for him not a dogma but a
means of work, a light over nature that could produce more light.
The significance of scientific hypotheses is, after all, not least that of giving occasion for
continued research: we try whether it is possible to connect \textit{all} our
experiences in the way we have succeeded in connecting \textit{some} of them;
we learn what we are to ask nature about. In this respect Darwin's
doctrine of the origin of species by natural selection has been extraordinarily
fruitful. It teaches us everywhere in natural science to trace the significance
that a property, a faculty or a form has in the struggle for existence. It starts
from the assumption that nothing can subsist or develop
% print: „udvilke“ (p. 447) (misprint)
that does not have a definite significance in the whole connection of life.

\subsubsection*{c.\quad The Limits of the Theory}

Darwin acknowledges a limit to his research in the question of the first
origin of the individual differences between which both
artificial and natural selection take place. A selection presupposes something
that can be selected, differences and variations. Darwin takes it as a fact
that such variations arise, and the more frequently, the more favorable
the conditions of life are, and the more developed a species already is. He admits that
``we are very ignorant on all points concerning the causes of variability,'' and
the enigma of the origin of the original variations became for him for a time
all the greater, as he was inclined to ascribe to external circumstances a
very slight direct influence. In a letter to Huxley shortly after the ``Origin of
Species'' had appeared, he writes (25 Nov. 1859): ``You have very
acutely found a point that has greatly perplexed me: if --- as
I believe --- external conditions produce little \textit{direct} effect, what
the devil determines each particular variation?'' (See already the letter to Hooker of
23 Nov. 1856). Later he came to ascribe to the conditions of life a greater
direct influence on the variations (see his letters to Carus 4 May 1869, to
Wagner 13 Oct. 1876, to Neumayr 9 March 1877). In ``
% --- p. 448 ---
\opage{448}Variation of Animals and Plants under Domestication'' (Chap. 22---26)
Darwin discusses the question more closely and emphasizes not only the direct action of the conditions of life
but also the effect of the use or non-use of organs and faculties. (See
also the ``Descent of Man'' ch. 4). --- There is all the more reason
in studying Darwin to be attentive to this point, as his critics
have often confused the original origin of the variations with the natural
selection of properties that have come to be through such varying. ``Natural
selection,'' says Darwin against this (Variation of Animals and Plants.
London 1868. II p. 272), ``depends on the best endowed individuals remaining
alive under different and complex circumstances, but has nothing whatever to do with
the original cause of any change whatsoever in structure.'' Darwin's hypothesis
concerns chiefly the effects of selection among the variations, not
the origin of the variations. Naturally he assumed that there were causes of this
too; but it was not the main thing for him to find them. Every hypothesis must
build on a certain foundation that it cannot draw into the proof along with it. There
is then no contradiction in Darwin's taking the variations essentially merely as
factually given, and it is a strange objection that has sometimes been
directed against him that he builds on ``chance.'' Darwin does indeed use
a few times the expression ``chance-variations,'' thus in the letter to Hooker mentioned above,
but by it he means variations whose cause is not known, and he
himself declares the expression inexact. Variability depends more on the
nature of the organism than on the character of the surroundings (More Letters from Ch. Darwin
I. p. 377); this explains its mysterious character. Darwin declares (in
a letter of 1881: More Letters I. p. 391) that the discovery of the causes of variability
will be one of the most important tasks of the research of the future. ---
Just as Darwin regarded the first origin of the variations as enigmatic in
several respects, so he also declared the origin of life as a whole to be
an unsolved enigma.

On the other hand Darwin found no reason to assume that in the origin of the human
species from lower forms quite
% --- p. 449 ---
\opage{449}peculiar forces were at work. As soon as the conviction had dawned on him
that the species had arisen by natural development, it became clear to him that
the human species could form no exception to this. But in the ``Origin of
Species'' he contented himself with hinting that the new doctrine would also
be able to throw light on man and his history; there was no room here for
special investigation of a single species of living beings. When Darwin later
took up this question in detail (in the work ``On the Descent of Man''), it
was, as he declares in a letter, partly because he was accused of
not daring to come forward with his views on this point. He stood here even
more alone than on the general question of the origin of species. Even men
like Lyell and Wallace, who otherwise adhered to him, became doubtful here.
Darwin himself felt no conflict between feeling and the impulse of research. Man's
real worth and highness was for him not diminished by his having developed
from lower forms. Against the theological and romantic conception that
regards man as a fallen angel he set the realistic
conception of man as an animal that has developed into a mental
being. Neither in mental nor in bodily respects did he assume more than
differences of degree between man and animal. There is, he asserts, a far greater
leap between the mental faculties of one of the lowest vertebrates (the lamprey or
the lancelet) and those of one of the highest apes than there is between the apes' and
men's mental faculties. And he shows how difficult it is to draw
the boundary between mere instinct and reason proper. The very fact that
animals can learn by harm shows that one dare not deny them reason. And
the case is similar with memory, the sense of beauty and sympathetic
instincts.

It has sometimes been concluded from Darwin's doctrine that there must really
take place an uninterrupted progress in perfection in all living beings, and
one has then found a great objection to the doctrine in the fact that the lowest organic
forms continually go on existing. Here too Darwin himself has already answered
the objection. Natural
% --- p. 450 ---
% print: „man“ (p. 450) (misprint)
% scan: „angaar.“ (p. 450)
\opage{450}selection does not necessarily bring progress with it. What use would an
intestinal worm or an earthworm have of more perfect organs than it has? An
organ that does not help in the struggle for existence takes up room and force to
no use. Where circumstances for some reason or other exclude strong
rivalry, it is perfectly intelligible that a form of life remains as it
is through immeasurably long periods of time. (Origin of Species ch. IV. p. 154---155.
Cf. ch. X. p. 422 f). Natural selection can only make every organic
being as perfect as it needs to be in order to rival or ``struggle
for existence'' with other organic beings, and the remarkable thing, according to
Darwin, is that experience shows us so few cases where such perfection
is not present. But perfection must always be measured by the relation to
the conditions of life. (The natural selection of each species implies improvement
in that species \textit{in relation to its conditions of life.} Letter to Lyell.
25 Oct. 1859). In this it is then also implied that natural selection can sometimes
bring about a regression to simpler and more elementary forms of life, namely when
the conditions of life for some reason or other are simplified, so that various
organs become superfluous, if they do not become harmful. There is no
inherent or necessary tendency in organic beings to rise upward on
the ladder of organization. (Variation etc. I. p. 8).

\subsubsection*{d.\quad Ethical-Religious Consequences}

Apart from the objections that point to supposed self-contradiction or
disagreement with experience, objections of an ethical-religious kind have also been raised against Darwin's
theory, and that not only from the theological side; even
so radical a thinker as Eugen Dühring has here taken offense on ethical grounds
and expressed himself in the most violent way against the theory. The very idea of the struggle for
existence seems to many incompatible with an ethical conception of life: how
are love of mankind and conscience to be reconciled with this idea?

As regards the ethical objection, it is so far from being the case
% --- p. 451 ---
\opage{451}that Darwin has overlooked it, that he has with full consciousness discussed the ethical
problem in connection with his theory. As a moral philosopher he stands at a standpoint similar
to the one that Shaftesbury and Hutcheson founded, and that in the nineteenth
century Comte and Spencer carried further, only that Darwin's natural-historical
point of view and his doctrine of natural selection give a broader basis for
the whole standpoint.

Darwin finds in the fact that man is the only being that can with
certainty be designated a moral being the greatest difference between him
and the animal. But from this it does not follow that the moral feeling should not have
developed in a natural way, and there is nothing in it either that conflicts
with the struggle for existence or with natural selection. One must only hold
fast that the properties and faculties that natural selection fosters are not
only such as are for the good of the single individual, but also
such as are for the good of the whole group or species. In all such
animals for which it is most fortunate to live in close association, those
individuals that found the greatest pleasure in the company of others would most easily escape dangers. And
since the continued subsistence of the species depends on the preservation of the very often
helpless offspring, it will be easy to understand how the love of parents
for their offspring can have been developed by natural selection. Experience shows that
animals sometimes expose themselves to danger to save other animals. A tribe or
group of animals or men in which mutual compassion and the
need to help one another prevail will be especially fortunately placed in the struggle for
existence, more fortunately than other groups where each cares only for himself,
and where the forces are not united toward a common end. Thus in the
single individual, by virtue of the law of natural selection, properties can be preserved and developed
that are beneficial to the subsistence of society, not especially to that of the single
individual. Not only the selfish but also the unselfish feelings
have their natural history. However great the distance may be between what
stirs in animals when they show love and self-sacrifice for one another, and the
highest human morality, there are between the two countless
% --- p. 452 ---
\opage{452}degrees, and one has at no point the right to assume that natural development is
interrupted. Within the human world itself there are, after all, very great
distances in moral respects. There are states and forms of human
life that stand even far below what animal life can show us. Darwin declares that
he would rather be descended from the ape that risked its life to save its
keeper than from the savage who delights in torturing his enemies, kills his
children without remorse, treats his wives as slaves and is himself a slave of
the most dreadful superstition\textsuperscript{102}).

The moral feeling presupposes, according to Darwin, besides the desire to live together
with others (sociability) and the capacity for compassion with others (sympathy), also the capacity
to remember and compare. When these presuppositions are present,
past actions will be able to be drawn forth and judged by what the strongest (in
the moment of remembrance, if not at all moments the strongest) feeling demands.
When the faculty of speech is developed, mutual praise and blame will act on the single
individuals. A public opinion will take shape. Further, constant habit and
practice in working for common interests will root and strengthen the social
motives and instincts. Perhaps an inheritance of dispositions in this direction will also
take place. --- A confirmation by experience of his moral-philosophical theory
Darwin finds in the investigation of the properties that at different times and among
different peoples have been acknowledged as virtues, and of the different extent
of the circles of individuals whose weal and woe the moral feeling has at
different times taken into account.

The very theory of natural selection thus shows us that not every
adaptation, every selection, every form of the struggle for existence is approved. From
lower forms of this struggle we are led over to higher forms, first and foremost
to a stage where a valuation of the forms of the struggle can take
place\textsuperscript{103}). ---

It was found not only that Darwinism was an immoral doctrine, but also that it was
a materialistic and godless doctrine.

Darwin has nowhere expressed himself on the relation between the mental and the
material. He keeps to the fact that mental life
% --- p. 453 ---
% print: „Instinskter,“ (p. 453) (misprint)
\opage{453}in men and animals is, as a matter of fact, bound up with the activity of material organs and
so far can be studied as natural history like other organic phenomena. He
therefore investigates the development of mental life through the struggle for life from lower to
higher steps, and the definite laws of this development. In this there is nothing
materialistic. Just as he declares the origin of life an unsolved problem,
so he would surely also have declared the origin of mental life
unexplained; perhaps the two problems coincided for him. Darwin has made
interesting special psychological investigations, namely, besides those on the
moral feeling, on the sexual feelings and instincts, on instincts
in general, on the expression of the emotions, on the development of the child in its first year.
One finds all through his writings, often where one does not expect it (e.g. in the
little book on the influence of earthworms on the formation of mold), interesting
psychological traits. But to discuss the principles of psychology itself was not his business.

If by materialism one merely means the reduction of phenomena to
definite natural laws that exclude supernatural intervention, then Darwin is
certainly a materialist. The organic forms have, according to him, not stood as
fully finished ideals before the Creator's imagination, to be thereupon set into
material reality, but they are results of long processes of development
from the most inconspicuous beginnings, under the constant action of
the conditions of life. Darwin has widened the domain of natural connection; he has
brought it about that the habit of thinking positively and doing without theological causes has
increased among naturalists and thereafter also in wider circles. In principle
nothing new has in a certain sense been added by this; for the principle of natural causes
had long since been laid down --- but it is not frequent in
the history of science that this principle finds so brilliant an application as
here. When in recent times several English theologians have accepted Darwin's doctrine,
they help themselves by placing the creative act at the beginning of life,
when the primeval form or forms arose, and natural selection then becomes for
them the way, fixed by the Deity, in which the single species arise. To
this
% --- p. 454 ---
\opage{454}expedient Darwin himself, however, could not resort. In no less a degree than Stuart Mill
he found it impossible to reconcile the suffering and the disharmonies in the world with
the providential government of an almighty being. He was no pessimist; he had the
conviction, which to be sure he found very difficult to prove, that
happiness in the world decidedly outweighed unhappiness. But natural
selection, which brings suffering and unhappiness with it and breeds hatred and cruelty no
less than love and gentleness, could not in his eyes be regarded as a means
in the hand of a providence. Should the ichneumon wasp have been created on purpose to devour
living caterpillars, the cat to play with the mouse? Already in his writings (especially
``Variation.'' II. p. 432) he expressed himself in this direction, still more strongly in
his letters and in his autobiography. It was the fact of evil that he again
and again came back to when he was invited to express himself in religious
respects. When he came home from his great voyage he still
believed in revelation, and when he published the ``Origin of Species'' he was still
a theist. But little by little, without any painful break, his
views changed, and he at last declared himself (in a piece of the
autobiography written in the year 1876) an \textit{agnostic,} that is to say, one who is conscious
that our knowledge cannot solve the problem. The expression had first (1859) been
used by Darwin's friend and disciple Huxley (who on this point was influenced by
William Hamilton). As little as he could reconcile himself to the thought that
the world as it is was due to conscious intention (design), so little could he
reconcile himself to the thought that it should be a result of chance (chance
or brute force). ``The safest conclusion,'' he wrote to a young man who
wanted to know his opinion, ``seems to me to be that the whole question lies beyond
the reach of the human understanding. But man can do his duty.''

Agnosticism really means that what stands for us as a dilemma need not
be one in itself, since there could be more possibilities besides those
that are for us the only ones: design---chance. Darwin ends with the same result as
Kant in the ``Kritik der Urtheilskraft,'' who declared that the
% --- p. 455 ---
\opage{455}distinction between mechanism and teleology perhaps belonged to the oppositions that we must set up by
virtue of our knowledge, but that we had no right to
take as valid for existence itself.

\subsection*{2.\quad Herbert Spencer}

\subsubsection*{a.\quad Biography and Characterization}

The year before Darwin's famous work appeared, Herbert Spencer drew up an outline of
a systematic exposition that was to show the significance of the concept of evolution
in the various domains. His earlier works had led him to
conceive this concept as a principal concept in our knowledge, and he now wished to
devote his life to carrying out this conception in detail. As he was
without means, it was his wish to be enabled with the government's help to
carry out his plan. He was warmly recommended by men who knew his earlier
works, men such as the philosophers Stuart Mill and Fraser (Hamilton's successor in
Edinburgh), the historian Grote, the physiologist Huxley, the botanist Hooker and
the physicist Tyndall. The work was reckoned first at seven, later at ten volumes; in the
actual execution it came to comprise nine volumes. Although Spencer obtained no
government support, he has nevertheless with great perseverance, and in spite of his
often failing strength, carried his plan through: the first part of the work
\textit{(First Principles)} began to appear in the autumn of 1860, and the
last part (the conclusion of the \textit{Principles of Ethics)} appeared in the spring of 1893.
The intervening parts treat biology, psychology and sociology. It will be of
interest to see how the thought of this comprehensive work arose and
matured\textsuperscript{104}).

\textsc{Herbert Spencer} was born at Derby on 27 April 1820. His father was an
excellent schoolmaster, who laid great weight on the view that sound mental development
comes only through self-education, and therefore sought to get his pupils to think
and observe on their own. Spencer showed an early interest in natural science
and history. It was his delight to follow the development of
% --- p. 456 ---
% scan: „kan“ (p. 456)
\opage{456}insects; in his father's library he made himself acquainted with books of
various content, and together with his brothers he eagerly discussed
scientific, political and religious questions. His parents were
Methodists; but the father gradually became dissatisfied with the clerical
organization of this communion and joined the Quakers, without, however, adopting their
special doctrines; what appealed to him was their ``unpriestly system.''
The son Herbert then went on Sundays with his father to the morning service of
the Quakers and with his mother to the evening service of the Methodists. The result was
that in the end he could not bear to hear Bible texts. Later Spencer came to live
in the house of an uncle who was a clergyman (of the Broad Church tendency), an
excellent man who took an eager part in the agitation for the repeal of the Corn Laws
and had merits in the regulation of poor relief. Spencer's critical position
toward all far-reaching attempts to order social relations by the intervention of the power of the state,
and his great faith in free development, were founded and
nourished by the religious and political views he met with in his
early youth. It was intended that he should be a schoolmaster, like his father;
but for a number of years he worked as a civil engineer. Mathematical studies and
mechanical inventions together with political agitation filled a great part of
his time. The first works mentioned from his hand are articles on
the proper sphere of governmental authority and a treatise on the nature of sympathy, in
which he set forth a theory similar to the one Adam Smith had in his time
given. Already earlier he had, through his natural-historical studies, become an
adherent of the theory of the natural development of species. He has himself declared that
the study of Lyell's geology, which in the older editions combated Lamarck's theory,
was precisely what led him (in the year 1839) to see the correctness of the theory of
natural development. This also had an influence on his religious
notions, which changed without his being able to trace the decisive change
back to any definite point of time. In his first considerable work,
\textit{Social Statics} (1850), he conceived social development by analogy
with organic development, a conception that also plays
% --- p. 457 ---
\opage{457}a great role in his later writings. The perfect unfolding of life is here for him a divine idea
that is to be realized, and of which nature offers intimations and approximations.
Spencer has himself declared that in this work he was influenced by Coleridge
and through him by Schelling. This theological mode of consideration he later
abandoned for a purely factual demonstration of development under its various
forms. The greatest influence on his theory of development he himself
ascribes, already for this period, to ``the truth that Harvey's
embryological investigations first dimly indicated, that was later grasped with greater
clarity by [the anatomist] Wolff, and that received its definite form from von
Baer, the truth that all organic development is a change from a state of
homogeneity to a state of heterogeneity.'' This truth, which had been
found valid for the development of the single organism, stood for Spencer as valid
for development in all domains, and it dawned on him at the same time that in
all domains development takes place. In a little essay on
the development hypothesis from the year 1852 he makes a comparison between
the theory of development and the theory of creation, and assumes --- relying on the variations of domestic animals and cultivated
plants, on the difficulty of distinguishing between species and variety,
and on the likeness of different forms in the embryonic state --- that the species have acquired
their present forms by development under the influence of external circumstances.
Decisive for his whole point of view was the working-out of his \textit{Principles
of Psychology} (first edition 1855). What is significant about this work is that
--- although it takes its stand on the ground of the philosophy of experience --- it insists on
the impossibility of explaining the individual consciousness out of the single
individual's experiences alone. All earlier empiricism had trusted that it was only
a matter of finding the experiences the single individual has, in order to understand its
conscious life. It was a conviction that had not only theoretical but
also practical significance. For if man's conscious life is determined merely by
the individual's own experience, there opens up a prospect of giving it, through purposive
arrangement of education and social relations, the stamp one wishes.
Stuart Mill and Comte built to a great extent their
% --- p. 458 ---
\opage{458}hopes for the future development of the species on this conviction, although both these
thinkers' deep understanding of historical development stood in a remarkable
conflict with it. Spencer now arrived at the conviction that development in the
mental as well as in the material domain proceeds very slowly,
through countless intermediate links and stages, of which none can be skipped. It is
the constant influence of the conditions of life that carries life forward to new forms,
among others also to the forms with which it now appears. We cannot therefore
understand the conscious life of the single individual from the experiences to which it has itself
been subject, but must go back to the experiences of the species. And it is not here
only the traditions that are at work; in the innermost structure of our mind, in the way
in which representations are combined, and in the direction in which feelings and
drives unfold, hereditary tendencies are at work that become intelligible only by
assuming an after-effect of the experiences of preceding generations. Heredity
had hitherto stood as a curiosity to which no significance was ascribed outside
single striking examples; now it came to stand as a constantly co-operating
factor even in the very highest forms of life. It was this widening of
the horizon in the psychological domain that led Spencer to search out
the general laws of development, and at the same time to investigate whether these laws might not
be derivable from the fundamental laws of our knowledge itself. With this the idea of
his philosophy of evolution was given. The first outline of it appeared in an
essay \textit{Progress, its Law and Cause} (1857). (Danish translation in
``Mindre Afhandlinger af Herbert Spencer.'' Copenhagen 1877). Here he carried through the
thought that all development is a transition from homogeneity to heterogeneity, and
sought to derive it from the law of the conservation of energy. In the first edition of
``First Principles'' he still sets up only this one form of the law of evolution;
later he supplemented it with two others: evolution as a transition from dispersion
to coherence and as a transition from an indefinite to a definite state. And thereafter
the publication of the great work went forward.

There were several preliminary works besides those mentioned. In a series of essays
that were published in various
% --- p. 459 ---
\opage{459}journals, Spencer had already, before the working-out of his great work, treated
various subjects of a philosophical, natural-scientific, sociological, aesthetic and
ethical kind. His systematic works are only further, broad (often far too broad)
