elaborations of what is laid down in these short, clear and often also in form
masterly essays, which are published collected in three volumes of \textit{Essays}, and
which are perhaps the part of Spencer's production that will last longest.

During the working-out of the first edition of his Psychology, Spencer through
overexertion brought on himself a nervous debility that he has never since got over. He came
to suffer from chronic sleeplessness. At last it threatened that he would have to give up
all work. But in later years (from 1890) he has in his advanced age not only
been able to complete his work, but also with life and vigor to take part in the newest discussions (called forth by
Weissmann's hypothesis) in the domain of the biological doctrine of evolution.
The last thing he has published is \textit{Facts and Comments} (1902), a
collection of short essays. He declares that it will be his last book.

The most decisive question in evaluating Spencer's theory becomes whether,
by the extension he gives to empiricism and positivism with
the help of the concept of evolution, he has succeeded in reaching the reconciliation of hitherto mutually conflicting
views at which he aims. But even if he should not have succeeded in this,
--- even if old problems, after having passed through the purgatory of
the philosophy of evolution, rose up in a new form --- his
widening of the psychological horizon and his demonstration of the concept of evolution
as the principal concept of special research do not lose their significance. It must, in
evaluating his work, be held fast that it was in this widening and this
demonstration that his real new thought consisted, not in the setting-up of any definite
epistemological or psychological theory. Moreover it cannot be otherwise
than that during the working-out of a work that extends through some thirty-odd
years unevennesses and inconsistencies in the treatment must arise, especially
when his views on single points change before the completion of the work.
% --- p. 460 ---
\opage{460}

Spencer's works do not give us much access to knowledge of his inner life. The
impression one gets is that he is not so subjective a nature as Mill and Comte,
in spite of all their positivism, were. Yet one finds between his long inductions
and deductions, between his formulas of evolution and his statements of fact, utterances
of warm feeling and quiet enthusiasm. He does not have, like Mill, the need
to influence men directly. The doctrine of evolution has opened his eyes to
the hard struggle in which everything living is placed, and to the difficulties with which
especially man's spiritual and social life has to contend. It has taught him that
ideals that to the preceding generation still seemed able to find their
realization in the nearest future presuppose a long series of intermediate links
that must all be gone through, and therefore come to lie as an immeasurably
distant goal for the wandering of the species. Therefore resignation comes to play a
great role in the view of life that arises on the basis of his doctrine. Not as
if it were his opinion that the present should altogether fade or be sacrificed for
the distant goal. But in such a way that the present is not understood merely by being seen in its
connection with the past out of which it has developed, but only when one at the same time
holds fast that it is a transition to a more developed state. Spencer surely
belongs himself among those of whom he speaks in the words with which his great work
closes (Princ. of Eth. II, p. 433): ``The highest ambition of the good man
will be to have a share --- even if it is an extremely small and hidden share --- in the
development of what is human (`the making of Man'). Experience shows us examples of
interest arising from the pursuit of altogether unselfish ends; and in
the course of time there will be more and more of those whose unselfish end is
the further development of humanity. When from the heights of thought they behold the distant
form of the life of the species, which they themselves will never come to enjoy, but which
will first fall to the lot of a distant posterity, they will feel a quiet joy in
helping toward its coming.''

The year after Spencer had conceived the idea of his philosophy of evolution,
Darwin's book on the origin of species appeared, through which the doctrine of evolution acquired a wholly new and
firmer basis. Darwin
% --- p. 461 ---
\opage{461}names Spencer in the preface among his predecessors and later calls him (in a letter
to Ray Lankester 15 March 1870) ``the greatest living philosopher in England.''
Darwin's whole theory fitted excellently into Spencer's system, only that Spencer
--- with all acknowledgment of the significance of natural selection --- laid more
weight on direct development through the use of the faculties under the influence of circumstances
than Darwin did in his earlier years. --- Of no small
interest is it that Stuart Mill, who at first was doubtful about
Spencer's evolutionist psychology, later declared himself convinced that
not only in the individual but in the race, through inherited dispositions, a
mental development takes place. This changed conviction he expressed the year before
his death in a letter to the physiologist Carpenter (printed in the latter's Mental Physiology.
p. 486).

\subsubsection*{b.\quad Religion and Science}

Spencer begins his systematic exposition \textit{(System of Synthetic
Philosophy)} with a section on the Unknowable\textsuperscript{105}). It
contains a doctrine of the limits of knowledge and at the same time examines the
relation between religion and science. It is to show what validity can be
ascribed to the scientific world-view that the remaining parts of the system
seek to build up. There is here something inexpedient in the manner of
exposition of which Spencer has not been aware. Neither epistemology nor the
philosophy of religion can attain full clarity and grounding when they are not
connected with psychology --- but psychology comes only far along in the system!

The line of thought in the first section is as follows. In recent times
religion and science stand as opposites. This comes from religion's wanting to
solve problems that only science can solve, and from science's wanting to
intrude upon domains where only religion belongs. Every religion has hitherto
sought to give a theoretical explanation of existence, presenting itself as an
unveiling of the riddle of the world. Different as the religions are, they
nevertheless agree in this, that they would be
% --- p. 462 ---
\opage{462}revelations of something that would otherwise be unknown. The difference
between the lower and the higher religions consists in this, that the lower ---
fetishism, and polytheism as well --- think that it is very easy to form a
notion of what is at work in existence. It is above all the belief in the
spirits of ancestors that forms the foundation of primitive theology. One has,
no doubt, a presentiment that the world is at bottom a riddle; but this
presentiment is very weak, and the riddle is held to be easily solved. In the
higher religions ever more weight is laid on the mystery, and it comes at last
to this, that every image, every thought becomes inadequate to express the
innermost of all things, and it is declared a blasphemy to think the Deity in
the way in which alone we \textit{can} think it. The religious development will
be complete when it is recognized that the mystery is greater than the
religions have hitherto assumed. The religions assumed a relative mystery, a
mystery that could be unveiled. But the mystery is absolute when no image, no
thought any longer suffices. The contradictions to which the religious notions
constantly lead arise from the wish to assume an absolute cause. Whether one
will assume that the world has produced itself, or that an external cause has
produced it, one ends in the contradiction that something should be able to be
the cause of itself; in the first case the world would have to be the cause of
itself, in the second case the being that has produced the world. The more
special contradictions in the religious notions --- between omnipotence on the
one side, goodness and justice on the other, between justice and grace etc.
--- are, as Mansel has already shown, only special consequences of that
fundamental contradiction.

But it now fares, Spencer continues, with the underlying scientific concepts
just as it fares with the religious attempts to express the innermost nature of
existence. Concepts such as time and space, motion and force, consciousness and
personality are clear and serviceable so long as we keep within the limited and
relative world of experience, but lead to contradiction when we would use them
as expressions of the nature of an absolute being. Our scientific knowledge
moves --- as regards both the outer and the inner world --- in the midst
% --- p. 463 ---
\opage{463}of a multiplicity of constant changes, without our being able to see
either beginning or end, either the first cause or the final end. It follows,
moreover, as Hamilton and Mansel had already shown, from the very nature of our
knowledge that we comprehend only the finite and limited. All knowledge
presupposes a distinguishing; but the Absolute cannot be distinguished from
anything else, since there can be nothing besides it. Spencer adds that all
knowledge also presupposes an apprehension of likeness, a referring of what is
to be known to something kindred; but the Absolute cannot be kindred with
anything else, since there can be nothing besides it.

Yet Spencer does not grant Hamilton and Mansel that the Absolute is a purely
negative concept. Knowledge must assume that there is other and more than it can
comprehend. Its activity consists in distinguishing, apprehension of likeness,
determining and limiting; but there must be something that is determined and
limited, something that is formed, and that has subsistence independently of
the determinate form it receives for our consciousness. What thus forms the
constant foundation, for us indeterminate, of the whole content of our
knowledge, we represent by analogy with what we sense as our own \textit{force}
in muscular exertion. There is a force to which it is owing that anything at
all can become an object of our consciousness. It is this force which not only
produces the individual changes that we distinguish and apprehend, but which
also underlies that in us which persists through all changes. A concept of this
force we cannot form; we can only approach it by successively thinking away the
limits under which the unknowable force appears in each individual case in our
experience. It is, then, the primitive sensation of force that in the end gives
our knowledge its content, both in the shifting changes and in what remains
constant while these take place (something constant under all modes).

Religion and science will in the end be able to meet in the conviction that the
innermost essence of existence is unknown and incomprehensible to us, whereas we
can have a scientific knowledge of the way in which it manifests itself
% --- p. 464 ---
\opage{464}in the world of experience. Our consciousness of existence is, seen from the
one side, religion, seen from the other side, science. The strife will cease
when the limit of knowledge is fixed in the right way; then religion will not
draw anything that can be comprehended under \textit{its} authority, and
science will not draw anything that cannot be comprehended under \textit{its}
authority. There can be no strife between our intellectual and our moral
faculties: it therefore cannot be our duty to believe something that contains a
self-contradiction. It cannot, as Mansel assumed, be our duty to think God as
personal and yet infinite, when personality and infinity exclude each other.
Our duty can only be to submit to the limits of our knowledge and to acknowledge
the mystery that really is there. When the concept of personality cannot serve
as an expression of the Absolute, it is not because it is too high a concept,
but precisely because it is too narrow a concept. A divine psychology we cannot
give, and the strife between religion and science continues so long as the
adherents of religion claim for themselves an intimate acquaintance with what is
an eternal mystery, and therefore set up concepts that can be attacked by
criticism.

Spencer is fully aware that his attempt to mediate between religion and science
will meet with resistance. Men need living and concrete notions, need to
represent what underlies all things as a being akin to themselves, and only
when this need can find expression in their faith can their faith gain
influence on their actions. So long as there has not developed an
\textit{organic morality,} which lets man act ethically from inner need, so long
is it of importance that the influence of religious opinions should not be
lost. Every faith stands in a definite relation to the stage of development on
which man stands, and a hasty rejection of religious faith will therefore easily
let the imperfections of our nature come forward more than they did while the
old faith ruled. In any case so profound a spiritual revolution cannot take
place without pain. He who is impatient because he finds that the process of
transition lasts too long must remember that in every religion, even the
lowest, there is ``a soul of truth'', --- that even the lowest
% --- p. 465 ---
\opage{465}religions give their adherents something they could not get in any other
way, --- and that all forms of faith are links in a great process of
development that is still far from its end. If he considers this, he will more
readily put up with the sophistical reasons by which traditional opinions are
defended, with the unworthy flattery with which men worship their deity, with
the arrogance of ignorance, which far surpasses the arrogance of science, and
with the condemnation of actions that proceed from unselfish compassion and pure
love of the good. ---

One misgiving about this doctrine of the relation between religion and science,
which Spencer does not touch upon, is that the Absolute and the Relative are
distinguished in an all too external way\textsuperscript{106}). Through this
relation of opposition the Absolute itself becomes relative. That the opposition
between the Absolute and the Relative cannot consistently be so external on
Spencer's own conception is seen from his statement that a completed concept of
the Absolute could be reached only by the removal of \textit{all} limits and
relations: such a removal is, after all, an infinite process, and we cannot,
therefore, in reality set the Absolute and the Relative over against each other
as two \textit{finished} concepts. When, moreover, Spencer states in some places
that the Absolute, which for him is one with the Unknowable, works through all
phenomena, the inner as well as the outer (thus First Principles § 34, 46 and
93), then its essence must manifest itself in the forms and laws under which the
phenomena appear; it cannot in reality be wholly unknowable, and Spencer is
wrong to declare the chief concept of experience, the concept of evolution,
wholly invalid as regards ``the Absolute''. It would be a self-contradiction if
the general laws and forms that experience presents should have no significance
whatever for what lies behind or beyond experience. No proof can be given that
evolution should concern only the shell of existence and not its kernel at all.
A dualism has here remained in Spencer.
% --- p. 466 ---
% print: „des“ (p. 466) (misprint)
\opage{466}

\subsubsection*{c.\quad Philosophy as Unified Knowledge}

The problem of the relation between religion and science arises not only every
time a special science draws a new phenomenon within its domain, but also when
an attempt is made to unite the various truths that the special sciences have
found into universal truths. It is, according to Spencer, the task of philosophy
to carry further the work of demonstrating unity in the multiplicity of
phenomena, which the special sciences each carry on in its own domain, by
seeking laws that are common to all our various domains of experience. The
point is to find a highest truth from which the fundamental propositions of
mechanics, physical and psychological principles and social laws can be
derived. We should then have founded a philosophy as completely unified
knowledge (completely unified knowledge).

Philosophy begins with a provisional assumption of the validity of the
fundamental propositions on which all thinking rests. This provisional
assumption is justified later by the consequences drawn from it agreeing with
experience. The validity of an assumption can only be established by its
agreement with all other assumptions. Truth can for us consist only in complete
agreement between our representations (representations of things) and our
observations (presentations of things). When our expectations and our
observations do not agree, the assumption from which we started has been
invalid. The complete establishment of an assumption's validity by its agreement
with all other assumptions leads us again to that working together of all
knowledge into unity in which philosophy consists. But this also implies that
every demonstration of the validity of individual assumptions presupposes the
validity of the activity of thought by which we find things like or different.
This activity of thought underlies all knowledge, both observation and
inference, whatever it concerns. Every proof presupposes this
\textit{primordial act,} and its validity therefore cannot be disproved; a
disproof is, after all, also a proof.

We think always in relations. Next after the relation of likeness and
% --- p. 467 ---
\opage{467}difference, the relation of succession and that of coexistence are of
importance. The relation of coexistence is derived from the relation of
succession: we represent as simultaneous such different phenomena as can be
represented just as well in the one order as in the other. The fundamental
experience that underlies every apprehension of likeness or difference,
succession or coexistence, we already know; it is the sensation of force: of
something that offers resistance or produces change, and that we represent to
ourselves by analogy with our own sensation of effort. Matter and motion are
only manifestations of force, and time and space are forms of manifestations of
force. Both in the domain of inner and in that of outer experience the concept
of force is the ultimate concept to which we come back. We rightly distinguish
between the self and the not-self; but both are only different ways in which
the concept of force manifests itself. The matter and content of our thinking
are all the different forms of force.

The concept of force is thus of a symbolic kind. It is the ultimate symbol (the
ultimate symbol). It points back to our subjective experience, by analogy with
which we apprehend everything else. Spencer here recalls the metaphysical
idealism that uses this analogy to solve the problem of existence. He concedes
that if we had the choice between reducing the mental elements to the material
or the material to the mental, we should have to choose the latter. It is
absurd to reduce the known to the unknown; an intelligible hypothesis we get
only when we reduce the unknown to the known, and thus regard the objective,
material elements as being in their essence of the same nature as the
subjective elements of our consciousness. In his ``Principles of Psychology''
§ 63 Spencer says: ``Let me say here, once for all, that if we were obliged to
choose between the two possibilities, of reducing mental phenomena to physical
phenomena and of reducing physical phenomena to mental phenomena, this latter
possibility would stand as the more reasonable (the most acceptable) of the
two.'' But such a reduction Spencer considers impossible, since we cannot avoid
making the mental elements clear to ourselves by means of forms and relations
that are taken from external
% --- p. 468 ---
\opage{468}nature. A clear intuition of the nature of consciousness we get only by
using images from the material world. Moreover, we cannot derive and explain
the physical phenomena from the mental phenomena. We must therefore stop at the
difference between psychical and material phenomena and content ourselves with
showing that the same laws of experience hold for both kinds of manifestation
of force.

Now it is, according to Spencer, a fundamental presupposition of all science
that force neither arises nor passes away in existence. All thinking consists in
setting something in relation to something else. If, now, force were to perish,
or if force arose out of nothing --- which in outer experience would show itself
in matter's being annihilated or arising, or in motion's being interrupted or
beginning, --- then we should have a relation between something and nothing or
between nothing and something; but a relation one of whose terms has vanished
from consciousness or has not arisen in it is a self-contradiction. The force
that must thus always be assumed to persist is not any relative, phenomenal form
of force, but the absolute force that stirs in all things, and so we here come
back again to the thought that an Absolute must underlie all the phenomena of
experience, the fundamental thought common to religion and science. It is the
business of empirical science to demonstrate the special transitions that take
place between the various forms of force. But the principle of the conservation
of force itself cannot be proved by way of experiment, since every experiment,
on closer reflection, turns out to presuppose its validity. All weighing and
measuring presupposes, after all, that the unit we take as a basis does not
change while the weighing or measuring goes on. If the force with which the
weight tends toward the earth varies while the chemical experiment that is to
determine the atomic weight is being performed, then the conclusion drawn from
the experiment is invalid. The conservation of force is therefore a principle or
a postulate on which all investigation of the real world rests.

For Spencer, as for Hamilton and for Kant, the principle of the conservation of
force coincides with the causal principle. We shall also find that several of
the natural scientists who set up
% --- p. 469 ---
\opage{469}the principle of the conservation of force on experimental grounds assumed
that it was really a proposition of reason, so that what mattered was to show
how it manifests itself in experience. So Robert Mayer, Joule and Colding.
There is, however, surely a distinction to be made here. For there could, after
all, be lawfulness in nature even if force arose and force passed away,
provided only that this arising and passing away were bound to definite
conditions. One could imagine that when the condition A was present, B always
arose, although B in quantitative respect might be put = A + x, and that when
the condition C was present, D always arose, although D was = C---y. In that
case the causal principle would hold without the principle of the conservation
of force holding. This shows that this latter principle is a more special
principle than the causal principle, when the latter merely expresses a rule for
the occurrence of phenomena. All regularity in nature would not be gone because
the law of the conservation of force did not hold. It is another matter that we
wish, as far as possible, to establish that just as in the logical inference
there is no more than was already in the premises, so in the real effect, too,
there is no more than was already in the cause; for thereby the principle of
causality and the principle of grounding will be brought into the greatest
possible agreement with each other. Even without this complete analogy with
logical grounding, however, the causal relation could have validity. Therefore
Spencer's deduction does not suffice, even if he is right that every attempt to
prove the conservation of force experimentally in a certain sense presupposes
it.

From the principle of the conservation of force Spencer derives that motion
goes in the direction of greatest attraction or least resistance, --- that all
motion is rhythmical, --- and that all phenomena are subject to evolution and
dissolution. By this road he passes from the consideration of philosophy as
unified knowledge to his consideration of philosophy as the doctrine of
evolution. But before we follow him to this consideration, we must first ask
what consequences Spencer draws from the law of the conservation of force with
regard to the relation between the mental and the
% --- p. 470 ---
\opage{470}material phenomena. It has not been Spencer's intention to discuss this
problem in particular, and one finds in his writings, as they now stand, a
certain wavering on this point, which is explained by Spencer's having changed
his conception in the interval between the various editions of his books,
without this change having been carefully carried through at every point in the
new editions. Hence arise the contradictory utterances that are found in
him\textsuperscript{107}). At first (in the first edition of ``Principles of
Psychology'' and ``First Principles'') he conceived the relation between the
mental and the material after the likeness of the relation between the various
forces of nature, and assumed a transition from the material to the mental just
as from motion to heat. The arising of sensations is thus explained by the law
of the conservation of force. Insofar as one should wish to find (as some
critics did find) materialism in this conception, Spencer reminded them that
matter and motion are for him in the end only symbolic expressions for the
unknowable force that stirs in all things. But later he became aware that the
arising of the phenomena of consciousness could not be derived from the
principle of the conservation of physical energy. In particular, the arising of
sensation out of motion, as an equivalent for the latter, is incompatible with
the doctrine of the continuity of motion. In later editions, therefore, Spencer
conceived the relation between the mental and the material according to the
identity hypothesis, in such a way that they stand as two phenomenal forms of
the unknowable force, mutually irreducible. With regard to the doctrine of
evolution, which is the main thing for Spencer, it comes to the same which
hypothesis one holds to. For whether one assumes a relation of interaction or a
relation of identity between the mental and the bodily, evolution in both
domains can present the same fundamental features, and that is what is decisive
for the philosophy of evolution. According to the identity hypothesis, to be
sure, mental evolution cannot be explained by deduction from the conservation of
physical force; but the material process corresponding (obverse) to mental life
can nevertheless be explained in this
way\textsuperscript{108}). When Spencer in his doctrine of evolution explains
all evolution by the laws of matter and motion, and yet uses examples from
psychology and
% --- p. 471 ---
\opage{471}sociology no less than from astronomy and physiology to illustrate the forms
of evolution, this is justified by the fact that the mental phenomena, whichever
hypothesis one starts from, are assumed to be bound in a lawful way to material
phenomena.

\subsubsection*{d.\quad Philosophy as the Doctrine of Evolution}

The unified knowledge that philosophy seeks is won, according to Spencer, not
only by a demonstration that there is a common presupposition on which all
inquiry rests, but also by the demonstration of a law that is common to all
phenomena that experience presents. Spencer systematizes positivism partly by
reducing all positive knowledge (knowledge of facts) to a common presupposition,
partly by setting up a common law or form for everything positive, all phenomena.
Every phenomenon has its history: it comes into being for us, and it vanishes
again for us. Each single science describes the history of \textit{its}
phenomena; the point now is to examine whether these various historical
processes do not present common features, so that \textit{a general law of
evolution} can be set up. It then turns out that all evolution more or less
clearly presents three different characteristic features, which together give us
the complete concept of evolution. --- As already remarked, Spencer had at first
set up only one characteristic feature of evolution, namely the transition from
homogeneity to heterogeneity. Later he saw that there were quite simple forms of
evolution in which this feature was wholly subordinate, and that, moreover, in
order to be able to distinguish sharply between processes of evolution and of
dissolution, it was necessary to set up yet a third characteristic feature.

1) \textit{Evolution as concentration} (or integration). When a phenomenon
comes into being, there takes place a gathering, combination and concentration
of elements that previously occurred in a dispersed state. When a cloud forms in
the sky or a heap of sand on the beach, an evolution of the simplest kind has
taken place, the process consisting almost exclusively in a gathering and
heaping up. Such a process of concentration took place, according to the
hypothesis of Kant and Laplace, at the
% --- p. 472 ---
% print: „Arbejsdeling“ (p. 472) (misprint)
\opage{472}first coming into being of our solar system out of the primeval nebula,
whose parts were previously in a more dispersed state. All organic growth takes
place through the taking up into the organic tissue of elements that were
hitherto found dispersed in the surrounding world. A psychological example is
had in every generalization, every formation of general concepts and laws: we
thereby concentrate in a single thought a whole multitude of different
observations and representations. Social evolution consists first and foremost
in a joining together of individuals or groups of individuals who formerly
lived in a more dispersed state.

2) \textit{Evolution as differentiation.} Only in the very simplest cases can
evolution be described as a mere process of concentration. There will not only
take place a separation of the whole mass from its surroundings; but within the
mass thus set apart special concentrations will in turn take place, so that the
evolution becomes compound. And in the course of evolution these special
concentrations will come forward more and more, so that on comparing the
earlier and later stages we find a transition from homogeneity to heterogeneity.
In the evolution of the solar system there occurs a separation between
different globes, each with its peculiarity. Organic evolution advances from the
homogeneous germ to the organism furnished with different kinds of tissue and
with differently built and differently acting organs. The whole of organic life
has, according to the hypothesis of Lamarck and Darwin, been more homogeneous at
earlier stages, the differences of species now existing being due to evolution
from common ancestral forms. The senses develop, when we compare earlier and
later stages, from a less distinct and less exact faculty of apprehension to
ever greater distinctness and exactness, so that more differences can be
apprehended. Mental life is measured not only by its concentration but also by
its richness. In the evolution of society different estates and classes are
formed through the division of labor.

3) \textit{Evolution as determination.} In a process of dissolution, too,
differences arise in a hitherto homogeneous mass. To distinguish evolution from
dissolution it must then be added that in evolution there occurs a transition
from a more indeterminate
% --- p. 473 ---
\opage{473}and disordered state to a more determinate and ordered state. Evolution
advances from a chaos whose parts are dispersed and homogeneous to a gathered
whole whose parts are heterogeneous and at the same time stand in a determinate
connection with one another. Thus the solar system, the organism, consciousness
and society are more or less ordered wholes. This third point of view really
arises from the combination of the first two: an ordered whole is one in which
differentiation of the parts and concentration of the whole go hand in hand
with each other.

Everywhere in existence --- in the great and in the small, in the mental and in
the material world --- processes of evolution of the kind now described take
place. The philosophy of evolution formulates, on the basis of a comparative
consideration of these processes, the fundamental features of the general
history of every phenomenon. But what has thus been found inductively must now
be grounded deductively by being derived from the law of the conservation of
force.

In the first place, a concentration of homogeneous parts will arise when they
are acted upon in a homogeneous way by the same force. This happens when heaps
of withered leaves or heaps of sand or clouds form under the influence of the
wind. Natural selection works in this way by requiring quite definite variations
of the living beings that are to be able to subsist under definite conditions:
thereby these are set apart as new species from those not fit to live. In the
second place, when a homogeneous whole has formed, differences will arise when
the homogeneous parts are acted upon by heterogeneous forces. And when
difference in the state of the parts has thus been produced, homogeneous forces
will act differently upon them. An organic species will vary under different
physical conditions, and even if the varieties are subjected to a homogeneous
influence, this will nevertheless not have the same effect on them all. ---
This follows from the conservation of force, which would be abolished if the
same causes produced heterogeneous effects on homogeneous objects, or
heterogeneous causes produced homogeneous effects on homogeneous objects, or the
same causes homogeneous effects on heterogeneous objects.
% --- p. 474 ---
\opage{474}

In order to understand Spencer rightly one must remember that his doctrine of
evolution does not apply to the world as a whole, of which, owing to the
relativity of knowledge, we can form no notion, but that it applies to the
individual wholes that arise within the circle of our experience. It has
sometimes been objected against him that his ``evolution'' becomes
incomprehensible if it is to begin as an absolute homogeneity; whence --- it is
asked --- are the differences then to come? Spencer himself declares expressly
(First Principles. § 116, 149, 165) that he speaks only of limited phenomena,
and that he assumes only a relative homogeneity and heterogeneity, just as the
concepts of concentration and differentiation, simplicity and complexity, must
also be taken in a relative sense. ``Since we know,'' says Spencer, ``no
absolute dispersion or absolute concentration, change can never be anything but
a transition from a more dispersed state to a less dispersed state, from looser
coherence to firmer coherence. Likewise, since no concrete phenomena present
absolute simplicity, --- since nothing is absolutely uniform, --- since we
nowhere find complete homogeneity, the transformation in reality always takes
place in the direction of greater compositeness, or increased multiplicity, or
a higher degree of heterogeneity. This qualification the reader must constantly
keep hold of''\textsuperscript{108\,b}). \textit{If} one could imagine the
whole universe in a state of complete equilibrium, where wholly homogeneous
centers of force were distributed with absolute homogeneity over the whole of
space, then everything would remain in equilibrium for all eternity. But such a
thought is excluded already by the fact that no limit can be set to space. Of
all homogeneous masses that we know it holds that they will necessarily become
differentiated in a lower or higher degree. ---

Evolution must (naturally, when it is not interrupted from without) necessarily
lead to a state of equilibrium in which both concentration and differentiation
have reached their culmination. As regards human evolution this state means the
highest perfection and bliss, consisting in the greatest possible harmony between
men and nature, and among men themselves. But since the external
% --- p. 475 ---
% scan: „Fremskriden.“ (p. 475)
% print: „betwen“ (p. 475) (misprint)
\opage{475}influences constantly continue to exert their effect, this state of
equilibrium will not be able to maintain itself in the course of time. Evolution
will be followed by dissolution when energy is lacking to preserve, under the
continued influences, the harmony between concentration and differentiation. And
through the various stages of dissolution one ends up in a new chaos. --- Just
as processes of evolution go on uninterruptedly within the circle of our
experience, so processes of dissolution of greater and smaller wholes also go on
uninterruptedly.
% scan: „nafbrudt“ (p. 475)
Even if our solar system too --- and all solar systems ---, as some natural
scientists think, should have the germ of dissolution within it, there will
always be a possibility of new formations of systems, since there will always
be external forces to set the processes of evolution going. All motion is
rhythmical, and evolution and dissolution will therefore alternate endlessly.

While Hegel in his idealist doctrine of development guaranteed an eternal
progress, the ``higher unities'' (which correspond to Spencer's harmony between
concentration and differentiation) always becoming the foundation for new
evolutions, Spencer, as a good positivist and by virtue of the doctrine of the
relativity of knowledge, cannot say anything about whether evolution or
dissolution is the stronger process in existence. By virtue of his dualistic
conception of the relation between the Absolute and the Relative he will not
even ascribe any absolute significance to evolution (nor, therefore, to the
whole rhythm of evolution and dissolution). Here, as already shown, a
contradiction comes out in him, since he acknowledges a connection between the
phenomena and the unknowable order of things that underlies them (the
connection between the phenomenal order and the ontological order). Only this he
holds firmly, that just as little as we can set limits to time and space, just
as little can we set limits to the force that works in the world of phenomena.
But his proper task he has accomplished by his characterization of the history
that every phenomenon runs through.
% --- p. 476 ---
% scan: „antage.“ (p. 476)
\opage{476}

\subsubsection*{e.\quad The Concept of Evolution in the Domain of Biology and Psychology}

It is in the biological and the sociological domain that Spencer moves with the
greatest expert knowledge. A biological idea gave, as we have seen, the impulse
to his whole system, and this biological idea (of evolution as differentiation)
he in turn connected directly with a sociological idea (of the division of
labor). Social life is for him a form of life that obeys the general laws of
life, and the same holds for mental life and the ethical life. Biology is thus
the dominant concrete science in his system. It is the evolution of life at all
stages and under all forms that his inquiry will follow.

Life consists in a constant adaptation of inner relations to outer. In a living
body an impression from without produces not only a direct effect but also an
indirect effect, a state being called forth whereby the living being becomes
able to meet a following change in the surrounding world. An inner activity is
set going which comes, or can come, to be of use on a later occasion. The organic
tissue has two apparently opposite properties which in combination make
adaptation possible. It has a plasticity that lets the impressions from without
send a tremor through the whole organic mass, or at least through large parts of
it; and it has a polarity, a definite manner of arrangement of the ultimate
organic particles, which Spencer calls the physiological units and regards as far
simpler than the cells but more compound than the chemical molecules, a polarity
which brings it about that the effect of the impressions on the organic mass is
determined predominantly by the mass's own constitution. The formation of the
organic mass in the first place is an obscure question. Spencer rejects the
assumption of the arising of organic \textit{forms} out of inorganic matter. He
is, on the other hand, inclined to assume that organic mass of a wholly
\textit{structureless} kind was formed at a certain definite point in the
cooling process of the earth's surface. Since this original organic mass was
without definite structure, this assumption is thus not one with the assumption
of a first organism. There has been organic life without organization. (See
especially
% --- p. 477 ---
\opage{477}the Appendix to the first volume of ``Principles of Biology''.) The organic
forms have arisen successively under the action of outer conditions on inner.
By virtue of the general laws of evolution, constant external influences produce
differences in the mass, first and foremost a difference between the surface and
the interior; and through the different ways in which the different parts react
to the impressions, they gradually take on a different nature. Spencer even sets
up the proposition that function precedes structure, and that it is the constant
functioning in a definite way that produces the definite structure that the
individual organs possess. This direct influence of the surroundings on the
organic tissue is really presupposed by the doctrine of natural selection; this
selection takes place precisely among the incipient structures called forth by
the direct influence, among the various variations that the organic mass
undergoes under the external influence. Even where the variations arise from
other, unknown causes, it is nevertheless only when favorable modes of action are
bound up with these so-called ``spontaneous variations'' that natural selection
can preserve them. (Princ. of Biol. § 61). The change that can take place in the
structure through a certain constant functioning will be able to be inherited
when it comes to produce an alteration in the organic polarity, that is, in the
manner peculiar to this particular organism in which the physiological units are
arranged.

Darwin's doctrine of natural selection (which Spencer prefers to call the
doctrine of the subsistence of the most purposive forms of life: the survival of
the fittest) Spencer acknowledges in the fullest measure and with great
admiration. But just as little as Darwin himself does he think that selection
can explain everything. Without the assumption of the inheritance of acquired
characters the origin of species is for him incomprehensible, and he has
therefore in recent years carried on a polemic against ``the natural scientists
who would be more Darwinian than Darwin himself'', especially against the
Weissmannian hypothesis, which denies all influence of practiced functions on the
cells that contain the germ of the offspring, and must therefore derive all
evolution from natural selection. Especially in the case of the higher organic
beings, which have a
% --- p. 478 ---
% print: „Indflydele,“ (p. 478) (misprint)
\opage{478}developed nervous and muscular system, he thinks that the influence that the
use of the powers has on the organization plays a considerable part. He ascribes
to the question not only biological but also ethical and social significance.
``If'', he says in his essay \textit{Factors of Organic Evolution} (1886), ``a
nation is altered as a whole by the inheritance of the effects that the nature
of its members undergoes through the forms of daily activity that its
institutions and conditions of life determine, then these institutions and
these conditions of life must mold the citizens far more quickly and completely
than they could if the only cause of adaptation is the more frequent survival
of individuals that have varied in a favorable direction''. The ethical and
social responsibility thus becomes greater when one assumes the inheritance of
acquired characters than when everything rests on selection. It is this that
gives the problem so great an interest in Spencer's eyes. ---

Consciousness too is an activity that arises in the adaptation of living beings
to their surroundings. When the impressions grow in number, the adaptation to
them can only become exact if they are ordered in a series, as happens in
consciousness. Psychology is to that extent a part of biology. But Spencer here
distinguishes between objective and subjective psychology. It is really only
objective psychology, the one that studies the life of consciousness through the
material functions to which it is bound, that belongs in the series of the
concrete sciences. Subjective psychology, which builds on immediate
self-observation and wins its results by analysis of it, stands in the same
relation to all other sciences as the subject in general stands to the object;
it is the science of subjective existence, while all other sciences together
concern objective existence. Therefore subjective psychology is a science wholly
unique of its kind. (Princ. of Psychol. § 56. --- Classif. of the Sciences. 3.
ed. p. 26 b).

Like Stuart Mill, then, Spencer maintains the independence of psychology in
opposition to Comte's overlooking of it. And he differs at the same time from the
older English school in maintaining that one cannot regard consciousness as a
mere
% --- p. 479 ---
\opage{479}sum of sensations and representations, since there is always something that
connects these and maintains the unity of the circle of representations against
attempts to divide it. There must --- Spencer teaches --- be something
substantial in consciousness as opposed to all shifting forms, but this
substantial something we cannot know, since it does not come forth in any single
state, although every state is a particular form of it.

For all the peculiarity with which the life of consciousness appears in
subjective experience, it nevertheless presents the same fundamental features as
life and as evolution in general. Its evolution consists in progressive
concentration, differentiation and determination. All the transitions take
place gradually, and it is therefore wrongly that faculties differing in essence
have been distinguished in the soul. From reflex movement through instinct and
memory to reason, from the simplest distinguishing and recognizing to the
highest scientific act of thought, there is a continuous series of stages. The
qualitative and quantitative richness of consciousness corresponds to the
richness of the living being's relations to the surrounding world. There is
always a correspondence between the life of consciousness and the external
relations the individual has to do with. There is a continuous series of stages
from the intestinal worm in an organic tissue to a Newton or Shakespeare whose
thought embraces the world.

With regard to the question of the origin of knowledge Spencer makes a stand
against Leibniz and Kant on the one side, Locke and Mill on the other side. He
combats empiricism, which does not see that the matter of experience is always
taken up and worked over in a manner determined by the original nature of the
individual, and which moreover comes to lack a criterion of truth. An original
organization is needed to explain the influence that impressions have on the
different individuals; and there is needed, every time one would ground an
assertion, a criterion consisting in this, that the opposite would contain a
self-contradiction. In the innate nature of the individual and in the logical
principle on which we rely in every inference we thus have something a priori,
something that cannot be derived from experience. To that extent Spencer grants
Leibniz and Kant that they are right as against Locke and Mill.
% --- p. 480 ---
\opage{480}But only so long as it is a question of the experience of the single
individual. For the single individual there exists an a priori, but not for the
species. For the conditions and forms of knowledge and feeling that are found
originally in the single individual, and therefore cannot be derived from its
experience, are due to inheritance from earlier generations. The forms of
thought are one with the accumulated and inherited changes of structure that are
latently present in every newborn individual and are gradually unfolded by its
experiences. And their first origin, then, is empirical after all: the fixed and
universal relations between things must in the course of evolution form fixed
and universal connections within the organism; by the incessant repetition of
absolute external uniformities there are bred in the species necessary forms of
knowledge, indissoluble connections of thought, which express the net yield of
the experience of perhaps millions of generations right down to the present
time. The single individual cannot take apart what has thus become an ingrown
connection in the organization of the species, and therefore it brings with it
in its innate nature the foundation on which the necessary truths are built.
(See Princ. of Psychol. § 208, 216 cf. First Princ. § 53: Absolute uniformities
of experience generate absolute uniformities of thought). Although the inductive
school has, in Spencer's opinion, gone too far when it would derive everything by
way of induction, whereby induction itself comes to hang in the air, he would
nevertheless, if he must choose, rather count himself of Locke's school than of
Kant's. For \textit{in the end}, according to him too, all knowledge and all
forms of thought nevertheless stem from experience. Max Müller has held that
when Spencer conceded that there is something in consciousness that is not a
product of one's own experience, he is a pure Kantian (a thorough Kantian). But
Spencer has answered this: ``The evolutionist point of view is wholly empirical.
It distinguishes itself from the older view of the empiricists by the extension
it gives this view . . . . But Kant's view is evidently absolutely
unempirical''. (Essays. III. p. 274. 277).

Spencer is, however, struck here by his own criticism of empiricism when he
assumes that the species at any stage whatever of its
% --- p. 481 ---
\opage{481}evolution has been able to receive influences from without without there
being, for receiving these influences and determining their results, any
previously given organization. There is here an unclearness in his psychology
that goes back to his biology. For his proposition that function determines
structure seems unable to be understood otherwise than as saying that the
organic tissue at the lowest stage behaves absolutely passively toward the
influences that produce activity in it. Such a relation of absolute passivity is,
however, excluded by his own definition of life as adaptation --- and does not
in reality take place even where it is inorganic beings that are acted upon,
since surely the stone is affected otherwise by heat than the wax. ---
Moreover, Spencer has overlooked that the \textit{validity} of our knowledge is
not absolutely guaranteed by the first presuppositions' being derived from the
experiences of countless generations. This establishes at most that these
presuppositions have hitherto proved practically serviceable in the struggle
for existence. A proof of their absolute truth cannot be built on
it\textsuperscript{109}). ---

Even more than knowledge, feeling, according to Spencer, presupposes a
foundation that is original for every individual and received from the species.
The constant interaction with the surrounding world, the constant struggle with
the conditions of life, engenders a tendency to moods for which one does not
always succeed in finding clear expression in representations. So it is with the
sympathetic feelings, e.g. the little child's pleasure at a smiling face, its
pain at a sorrowful or threatening face. The feeling of justice, the immediate
indignation at encroachment, can arise without there being any distinct concept
of the limits of the individuals' freedom of action. Spencer objects to the
earlier utilitarians that they let the conscious insight into the effects of
utility precede the appearance of the actions and motives that are valued. In
order to experience that sympathy is beneficial, one must first act
sympathetically without deliberation. It is thus feeling that makes it possible
to discover utility, not the discovery of utility that calls forth the feeling in
the first place. It is from the constant education to which man is subjected
through the interaction of the conditions of life that Spencer expects continued
changes and progress in
% --- p. 482 ---
\opage{482}human emotional life, not from the mere communication of finished
knowledge. He opposes the proposition from which Comte, especially in his
earlier writings, started, that ideas rule the world. It is feeling and
character that drive the work, and which ideas become dominant will depend on the
character of the people, which in turn rests on a foundation inherited from
earlier generations.

\subsubsection*{f.\quad The Concept of Evolution in Sociology and Ethics}

For Spencer's sociology the relation between individual and species that his
biology and psychology have found becomes of decisive significance. When every
individual has an original foundation for its character that goes back to the
earlier history of the species, the evolution of social life will not be able to
be changed suddenly by the influences that one may be able to exert on the
single individuals through reforms in education and constitution. Spencer has
not so immediate a hope for the future as that which animated Bentham, Mill and
Comte. Evolution advances slowly, because it is the very natural foundation in
the individuals, not merely their thoughts and knowledge, that must be changed.
During his stay in America Spencer, in a conversation, strongly censured the
abuses in the public life of the United States, which he derived from the fact
that the country had got its constitution, good in itself, by a happy accident,
but also had only \textit{got} it; it had not grown forth spontaneously, and
therefore it was no wonder that its consequences turned out other than had been
imagined. When an American friend asked whether instruction and the spread of
political knowledge would not remedy this, Spencer answered: ``No. It is
essentially a question of character, and only in a subordinate sense a question
of knowledge. It is a common illusion that instruction can be a universal remedy
for political evils''. Changes of character take place, according to Spencer,
only through a race's standing for generations in direct interaction with the
real conditions of life. Only through practical adaptation, through the
development and exercise of the powers that are used in the struggle of life, do
firm characters and healthy feelings arise. In his work on education Spencer
% --- p. 483 ---
\opage{483}therefore impresses the necessity of the child's gaining experiences on its own
account, coming itself to know natural relations and to feel the effects of its
own actions. Screens are to be used as little as possible, since they involve
double work: first adaptation to the screen, and then to what lies behind the
screen, the real relations. The child had best burn itself; otherwise it does
not rightly learn to shun the fire. And what holds of the character of the
individual holds of that of the race, and of the whole species. In his largely
and broadly planned work \textit{Principles of Sociology} Spencer seeks to
illustrate this by means of an extensive material, drawn especially from the
races standing lowest. Together with a circle of collaborators he has published,
under the title \textit{Descriptive Sociology}, a series of tabular surveys
(supported by references to sources) of the conditions of cultural history among
various peoples. In a lively written book, \textit{The Study of Sociology}, he
has discussed the difficulties with which a purely scientific sociology has to
contend.

It is a favorite proposition of Spencer's that societies and constitutions
grow, but are not made. He demonstrates in detail the analogies between a
society and an organism. The single individuals correspond to the cells, or
rather perhaps to the physiological units. Both within society and within the
organism the common life is to a certain degree independent of the fate of the
single units each taken by itself. But there is a great and significant
difference between society and the organism: while in the latter consciousness
(where it is present) is bound to the central organs, in relation to which the
other organs and units have only subordinate significance, in society it is
precisely the single units that have consciousness, while the central
organization as such has no consciousness of its own. In the organism the parts
exist for the sake of the whole; in society the whole exists for the sake of the
parts. On this difference between society and organism, according to Spencer,
no less weight must be laid than on the analogies between them. (Cf. Princ. of
Sociol. § 222. cf. Princ. of Ethics. II. § 102, 137). For on it rests the
fundamental proposition, whose correctness the history of social life
establishes, that centralization always has significance only as a necessary
% --- p. 484 ---
\opage{484}means, while the decisive thing always remains what goes on in the single
individuals, where human life proper is led. In social life as in individual
education the point is to reduce screens and tutelage to the least possible,
since they always complicate and retard evolution by necessitating a double
adaptation, first to the artificial, then to the natural relations. Experience
shows that wherever demands that have their root in nature are enjoined by
external authorities, obedience to the authorities comes to take the first place
at the expense of the practical relation to natural reality. And experience
shows as well that artificially set up and appointed authorities do not work as
ably and purposively as the free, individual forces themselves. The social
machinery uses too much force to reach its end --- and easily reaches other ends
than those intended. The single individuals experience far more urgently than
the authorities of the state a direct connection between labor and yield.
Although Spencer theoretically holds fast (what he had already taught in
``Social Statics'') that the land is the property of the whole people, he
declares himself, from aversion to ``officialism'', against the state's taking
over the cultivation of the land, as the ``Nationalists'' propose. Quite apart
from the financial difficulties of the state's taking over the land,
difficulties that in Spencer's view would in and of themselves make the
proposal impossible to carry out, the notorious imperfection of state
administration in comparison with private administration is in his eyes
sufficient to reject it. (See Appendix B to Princ. of Ethics. Part. IV).

Experience shows us societies at the most different stages of evolution; the
degree of evolution is measured here as everywhere by concentration,
differentiation and determination. But there is an opposition that in
sociological --- and no less in ethical --- respect stands in the first line. It
is that between militarism and industrialism. Two types of society appear here,
of which the first prevails especially at lower stages and gradually, but very
slowly and with many fluctuations, gives way to the second. The military
society arises from the necessity of defending the social group against external
enemies,
% --- p. 485 ---
\opage{485}often also from the drive to acquire livelihood and power at the expense of
other groups. Characteristic of this type is the absolute subordination of the
individuals to the whole. They are means, not ends. Obedience becomes the highest
duty. Peaceful labor at procuring the means of subsistence is left to women and
slaves. In industrial society, on the other hand, labor stands in the first
line. The main thing here is the free, personal intercourse between the
individuals, their working together in the service of common interests. Instead
of the mixture of savagery and submission that the military type fosters, the
industrial type sets the individuals freely over against one another and lets
them learn in daily intercourse to attain their ends in such a way that they
acknowledge the equal right of others to attain theirs. It is a discipline that
gains influence on characters, manners and constitutional conditions. While the
regulating apparatus under the military type was all in all, it now becomes more
and more restricted to the office of maintaining peace and right among the
members of society. For carrying out the functions that the state formerly
attended to as a kind of providence, voluntary associations are formed, insofar
as the spontaneous working together of individuals is not sufficient. While
formerly it was society that stamped its impress on the single individuals, it
is now more the single individuals who order society according to their needs.
--- The struggle between militarism and industrialism is still undecided. After
long years of peace militarism got a new upswing on the Continent, in which for
the second time the Bonaparte family, the greatest of all modern curses (that
greatest of all modern curses, the Bonaparte family), intervened in the course
of things, and now it flourishes in all countries more or less and introduces
its spirit and type again in other domains too than the purely military.
Compulsory regulation now takes the place of free self-development in a series
of domains. In the ideal of social democracy, of an army of workers, each with
his appointed occupation and his appointed wage, the same type expresses itself,
and it is then no wonder that socialism, like militarism, thrives best in one
and the same country, Germany. (Princ. of Ethics. II § 26, 72). And the
prospects of improvement are for the present not bright: ``
% --- p. 486 ---
\opage{486}So long as the European nations divide among themselves the parts of the earth
that are inhabited by lower peoples, with cynical indifference to the rights of
these peoples, it is foolish to expect that within each single one of those
nations a tender regard for the right of individuals should be shown on the part
of the government''. (ib. § 119). --- Yet Spencer descries the possibility of a
third type, which stands as high above industrialism as the latter stands above
militarism. The industrial type is easily carried into the one-sidedness of
everything's being directed to labor for the sake of gain. The third and higher
type of human life will be one in which free devotion to activities that are
immediately satisfying, and do not merely serve as a means of existence, comes
to occupy a far greater place than now. Within our present social order it is
especially efforts and institutions for the furtherance of intellectual and
aesthetic ends that contain indications in the direction of the third
type\textsuperscript{110}).

The closer working out of what this highest type of human life contains within
it belongs to ethics, not to sociology. For this type of the future is,
according to Spencer, the goal toward which all ethical striving moves. So long
as this goal has not been reached, no strict ethics is possible: the realization
of absolute ethics presupposes a perfect human life in a perfect society.
According to Spencer, scientific ethics is a system of deductions from the
highest laws of biology and of the general doctrine of evolution. But he
concedes that such deductions cannot hold without further ado. At the imperfect
stages the conditions are so intricate that only approximations to the
absolutely right and compromises between the absolutely right and what the
subsistence of life under the actual conditions requires become possible. But
relative ethics must constantly be checked and regulated by keeping the ideal
principles of absolute ethics in view. Ethics must construct a picture of the
conditions on which the perfect life rests, without at once directing itself by
whether these conditions are already actually present now. If we compare
ethical development at various stages, we find that it bears the general
characteristic marks of all evolution. Ethical action presents greater
concentration and
% --- p. 487 ---
\opage{487}coherence than unethical action: compare e.g. self-control with
dissoluteness, truthfulness with mendacity! It likewise presents greater
richness in differences, greater differentiation: for he who merely looks after
his own egoistic interest gets a narrower range of vision and range of action
than he who works for others as well; all of a man's faculties and possibilities
do not come to
development when he will work only for selfish ends, and the highest degree of
development can therefore be present only where the individual's activity
furthers the welfare of others. Finally, the more perfect ethical conduct also
bears the stamp of greater determinateness than the less perfect: it takes
definite considerations into account and sets definite limits to the
individual's own impulses and to those of others, which in themselves might
spread into the indeterminate; conscientiousness, justice and moderation are
examples of this.

In the perfect type of life the development of the individual will be limited
only by the equal right of others to development; the individual will,
moreover, spontaneously, from his own inner need, refrain from encroachment on
the healthy development of others, and for his part help it forward as much as
lies in his power; finally, it will not be necessary, for the attainment of more
remote ends, to undertake labor that does not bring immediate satisfaction.

The construction of these conditions for the perfect form of life rests on the
principle of welfare. Spencer does indeed criticize the utilitarianism of
Bentham and Mill; but only because it is too empirical, too inclined to keep to
the nearest effects of actions without catching sight of the more remote ones,
which can be established only by way of deduction. Here, as in his theory of
knowledge, he seeks to show that the empirical and the a priori conception can
be united by means of the philosophy of evolution. The significance of a priori
(``intuitive'') ethics he finds partly in its maintaining the significance of
deduction and setting up ideal principles that are not directly built on
experience, partly in its finding a deeper psychological foundation for ethical
feeling than the individual's own experience can afford. In his construction of
the doctrine of right he comes to the same result as Kant: that the fundamental
right is freedom for the individual, insofar as
% --- p. 488 ---
% print: „Eth.«“ (p. 488) (misprint)
\opage{488}he does not come to commit encroachment on the equal freedom of others; this
is, after all, as stated, the first characteristic mark of the perfect type of
life. This agreement of Spencer's with Kant, which surprises him himself (see
Appendix A to Princ. of Eth. Part. IV), cannot surprise us, since we have seen
Kant's ethics and doctrine of right proceed from an evolutionist line of
thought. The great significance of a priori ethics consists in not letting
itself be entangled in regard for the nearest effects of actions; but it is
mistaken in thinking that the ethical principles are not in the end determined
by regard for whether the actions cause happiness or unhappiness. And even if
there is an a priori foundation for ethical feeling, independent of individual
experience of happiness, this very foundation is in turn to be explained as the
result of the doing and suffering of earlier generations. In his closer
conception of ethical feeling Spencer parts from Kant by assuming that the
feeling of duty belongs only to a certain stage of evolution. The feeling of duty
consists in an inner control that one feeling exerts over another; but with
advanced evolution such control will be unnecessary; there will have been formed
an ``organic morality'' which makes the performance of the actions required by
the ethical principles as spontaneous and as immediately satisfying as the
mother's care for the child and the artist's absorption in his work already are
now. Man will then be completely adapted to the social state --- and the latter
to him.

Until perfect evolution is reached, we must make do with compromises. As a
strict science ethics is not possible before the highest stage of life. Spencer
thus really assumes that no ethics can be given before it is --- superfluous!
Paradoxical as this may seem, there might nevertheless lie in it a correct
recognition of the difficulties of principle with which every attempt at a
scientific ethics has to contend under the intricate conditions under which we
have to lead our life. Perhaps one must even go still further than Spencer, in
his great confidence in the victorious course of evolution, has thought
necessary; in particular, he takes too little account of individual differences
and their influence on ethical determinations\textsuperscript{111}). --- We
shall bring
% --- p. 489 ---
\opage{489}forward some examples to illustrate what Spencer means by the opposition
between absolute and relative ethics.

Sociology has shown us that the present stage of development of the human race
is characterized by a conflict between militarism and industrialism. In this
period of conflict the freedom of the individual will in many ways be more
limited than absolute ethics permits. Slavery is an institution that belongs to
militarism. With the development of industrialism personal freedom comes into
force in ever wider circles. But through the worker's dependence on the employer
something constantly maintains itself of the relation of obedience in which the
slave stood to the master, although the relation now rests on contract, and so
on consent and obligation on the part of both parties. Whether this can ever be
wholly changed we cannot know; the task of relative ethics, on the other hand,
is to impress the necessity of as great an approximation to the ideal relation
of equality as the conditions in any way permit. --- While slavery existed, the
poor enjoyed the protection of the masters, which was often paternal. With the
abolition of unfreedom has followed the abolition of protection, and with it in
turn the sufferings that the struggle for existence brings. By state compulsion,
then, men have sought to remedy this through the arrangement of poor relief,
since it was clear that the principle of the subsistence of the best adapted
could not be allowed to prevail in all its severity. But the intervention of the
state has here caused greater evils than were to be remedied: it has protected
the weak and incapable, made it possible for them to bring offspring into the
world, and maintained them at the expense of the able and industrious! Men have
wanted to soothe their feeling of the suffering that is in the human world by
applying a system that on closer consideration makes evil worse. The present
system of state aid is a kind of social opium-eating. The sufferings that
evolution once and for all brings with it cannot be escaped. And they are not
escaped by letting feelings that have their proper domain in more personal
relations and within the family gain influence on the arrangement of political
and social relations. Family ethics and state ethics must not be confused; the
former concerns the rearing of helpless offspring, the latter the ordering
% --- p. 490 ---
\opage{490}of the mutual relations of adults. When adult age is reached, no state aid is
to hinder the conditions of life from taking effect. It is another matter with
free charity, which uses its own means, while the state \textit{extorts} its
means. But it too will only be able to hinder superfluous suffering and soften
the necessary; if it goes further, it weakens the vital power of the race. ---
Spencer must himself concede, however, that just as there are many transitional
forms between the child and the adult, so there is room for many compromises
between family ethics and state ethics. These systems do not form so thoroughgoing
an opposition in principle to each other as one would think from many of
Spencer's utterances. Spencer's correct fundamental thought is that compassion
with suffering must not exclude the discipline through interaction with the real
conditions of life that is necessary for the healthy development of the
individual and of the whole race.

In its crudest form the struggle for existence favors egoism. But altruism,
which has its root in sympathy, slowly works its way forward, first in the form
of care for the helpless, later also in other and higher forms. There is no
absolute opposition between them: evolution will lead to such a change of human
nature that the individual finds his highest happiness in devotion, without,
however, hampering by his intervention the independent development of the other,
and that, on the other side, no one is so egoistic as to wish to be the object of
an absolute self-sacrifice by another individual. What now characterizes the
exceptionally highly placed may be expected one day to characterize all: for
what the best human nature is capable of lies within the compass of human nature
as a whole, and evolution is not ended so long as there is still a possibility
of a fuller and richer life through the unfolding of faculties that at once bring
the individual himself immediate satisfaction and do others good. Free activity
and unfolding of life which is more than a means to a future end is, as we have
seen, what is characteristic of the higher type of life to which Spencer looks
forward. Already now there are, as we have also seen, actions and efforts that
bear this stamp, so that ``the third kingdom'', to which Spencer
% --- p. 491 ---
\opage{491}with so many other thinkers in the nineteenth century looks forward, does not
lie only in the future.

\section*{Appendix}

In English literature there remain to be mentioned some works of a more special
nature that are of interest for philosophical thought in general. These are the
logical works of Boole and Jevons and the ethical work of Sidgwick.

After Stuart Mill had treated inductive logic in such a way that the limits of
the probative force of the purely inductive method came clearly to light,
\textsc{George Boole} in his work \textit{An Investigation of the Laws of
Thought} (London 1854) gave a new exposition of deductive logic, in which he
assigned to deduction the significance of deriving all the combinations of
certain concepts that are logically possible when a definite connection between
these concepts is given. The task of deduction is thus to give exhaustive
information about the logical value of a given judgment. Boole's method is
acute, but very artificial in its form. His fundamental thought was carried out
in a far simpler form by \textsc{Stanley Jevons} in a series of works that began
with \textit{Pure Logic or The Logic of Quality apart from Quantity} (1864) and
ended with \textit{Principles of Science} (1874). Jevons takes the content of
concepts, not their extension, as his basis, and thereby brings out more sharply
the difference of pure logic from pure mathematics. He also carries through
(what Hamilton and several before him had already begun by quantifying the
predicate) the principle of identity far more sharply, already in the
formulation of judgments, than had hitherto been done in logic --- if some long
unprinted treatises of Leibniz are excepted. His logical work goes far more into
particulars in its exposition of the methods of research than Mill's logic.
Jevons's logic has a considerable epistemological interest through the clear way
in which it establishes that a deductive inference underlies every induction,
the proof of the correctness of an induction always consisting in this, that
deduction from the proposition tentatively set up leads back to the given
% --- p. 492 ---
\opage{492}experiences, neither to more nor to less than them. Since deduction in turn
presupposes the validity of the logical principles, the incorrectness of pure
empiricism is thereby established. In the last years of his life (1877---79)
Jevons published in ``Contemporary Review'' a very sharp criticism of Stuart
Mill's philosophy, in which he sets pure empiricism in the sharpest opposition
to evolutionism and attaches himself decidedly to Spencer's philosophy.

\textsc{Henry Sidgwick} by his work \textit{Methods of Ethics} (1877) gave
ethical discussion new life and new clarity. In particular he drew attention to
the fact that behind the name utilitarianism there were hidden two different
ethical systems, of which the one took egoism, the other altruism as its basis,
while they both saw the ethical standard in the principle of welfare. He
undertakes a careful investigation of how far the two systems can each reach by
itself. He also seeks to show that the current moral propositions (the morality
of Common Sense) all lead back to utilitarianism, and that the gaps or
contradictions found in them can be made to vanish when one carries through
this unconscious utilitarianism\textsuperscript{112}).

\hhchapter{Tenth Book}
\label{ch:tiende-bog}

\begin{center}\textsc{Philosophy in Germany 1850--1880.}\end{center}

\bigskip

\noindent \opage{493}Of the two great tendencies in nineteenth-century philosophy it was
positivism that had best maintained its connection both with the thought of the
eighteenth century and with empirical science. The philosophy of Romanticism, by
contrast, was a definite and conscious attempt at reaction against both these
tendencies; it wanted even to do over again what had been founded with the rise
of natural science in the seventeenth century. In Germany, the hearth of
Romanticism and of its philosophy, that tendency was the dominant one at the
middle of the century. The adherents of the critical undercurrent were the only
ones who held fast to continuity with the other sciences --- leaving aside
Schopenhauer and Feuerbach, who at that time still stood as solitary thinkers
for whom the hour of recognition had not come.

As little as positivism was to be explained as a reaction against Romanticism,
so little is the philosophical movement which takes place in Germany after the
middle of the century to be explained as a continuation of Franco-English
positivism. It has its presuppositions in Germany itself. It receives its
problems above all from the renewed rise of natural science toward the middle
of the century. Not only do natural-scientific studies and results now become
the object of more general interest than in the earlier part of the century,
when poetry, religion and speculative philosophy had laid claim to men's minds;
\opage{494}natural science itself now returned, with clearer consciousness, to the great
principles its founders had in their day set up. The demand for an
understanding of outer nature as a series of demonstrable causes and effects ---
in other words, for a mechanical explanation of nature --- was now asserted
again, as in the seventeenth century. And at the same time a new and
comprehensive law of nature was discovered and demonstrated: the law that in
