Schelling had put forward \opage{559}in mythologizing and speculative form. He would soften
the paradox by pointing out that every time a new phenomenon [a new quality]
arises within our experience, we really have an absolute beginning. (Cursus p.~79.
Logik p.~191.) But the difference is that what is new and beginning in our
experience awakens wonder and gives thought a problem that can occupy it, whereas
that sharp opposition between absolute identity and change makes thought's work
hopeless once for all. Not merely a difference but a conflict between thinking
and reality is what Dühring here comes to lay down. --- When one has the choice
between assuming such a conflict and assuming that existence is as incapable of
being concluded as thinking is, this latter possibility seems preferable. There
is a constant interplay between thought and reality: as inquiry advances there
shows itself new continuity behind the apparent discontinuity, and so far reality
confirms thought's ideal; but new discontinuity is also discovered where there
seemed to be continuity in what is given, and the problem of how far reality can
be understood is then posed anew. In Dühring the dogmatist has got the upper hand
of the critical philosopher, on account of his great zeal to let reality come
into its own.

On the other hand Dühring lays very great weight upon the inner connection
between thinking and reality. Existence itself continues on into our thinking,
where this unfolds according to its true essence. To the relation between
premisses and conclusion (ground and consequent) there corresponds, in the real
processes, the relation between cause and effect. To logic's principle of
identity there corresponds the single thing's identity with itself,
notwithstanding that it occurs in different connections. To our thinking's
combinations and deductions there corresponds nature's unity and the interplay of
forces in the arising of phenomena. We do not thereby conceive nature on the
analogy of human consciousness, but as operating in such a way that human
knowledge gets a material to investigate that corresponds to its own
constitution. And even if our analysis will never be able to exhaust the great
connection in nature, \opage{560}the necessity does not cease of maintaining the kinship
between what operates in things and what operates in the understanding.

What appears in our scientific principles is according to Dühring the fruit of
forces that have long worked in a determinate direction before coming to clear
consciousness. Consciousness and thought rest upon something that is as little
consciousness and thought as the moving mechanical force is itself a phenomenon
of movement. But it is a warranted hypothesis to represent to ourselves the
ground of our thinking activity --- a ground not appearing in consciousness ---
as agreeing with the ground of nature's connection showing itself to us to be
ordered in accordance with the understanding. (Nat.\ Dial.\ p.~155, 225. Logik
p.~173. Leben, Sache etc.\ p.~303.) What makes us think is thus the same as what
makes nature operate.

This last train of thought now gradually gains such preponderance over Dühring
that in his later writings he conducts a violent polemic against the critical
philosophy, which maintains that we do not know things in themselves, because our
knowledge is determined not merely by the nature of things but also by our own
nature. He sees in that conception a bogging-down of science, a hypocritical
accommodation of thought's results to what the need to assume a world beyond
demands. Here again it is the law of the determinate number that underlies the
matter: number is an example of our commanding concepts which express what is, in
such a way that between reality and the concept no insertion conditioned by the
constitution of the I takes place at all. (Logik p.~165.)

As sharply as Dühring elsewhere emphasizes the opposition between thinking and
being, so definitely does he here emphasize the possibility of their completely
covering one another. There he has formal knowledge chiefly in view, here real
knowledge. But they cannot be kept wholly apart, as is shown by the fact that the
law of the determinate numbers precisely sets inquiry new tasks --- namely, to
find out why changes occur just when those determinate numbers are reached.

It is Dühring's merit with respect to recent epistemology that he sets the
problem of the relation between quality and \opage{561}continuity, between the determinate
turning points and the connected processes, in so clear and distinct a light. His
whole standpoint is determined by a contention between criticism and positivism,
and contains an invitation to a closer investigation of the relation between
those two tendencies.

\subsubsection*{β.\quad Conception of the World}

Dühring lays great weight upon the development of a \emph{world-schematism},
which is to give a fully formed picture of actual existence's general features.
In this the task of the philosophy of reality consists. It is to lead to a system
of experience, whereas the earlier metaphysics was a kind of alchemy which sought
by mystical ways to fathom existence's essence. --- At this point he recalls
Comte and Spencer. He is in his ``schematism'' more abstract than Spencer and
less original than Comte.

My system, he says, knows not two realities but only a single one --- nature and
its parts. He approaches materialism in emphasizing that everything in the world
has a material side, and that by following the material phenomena in their
intuitable connection one must be able to find everything that has reality. But
he will not stop at the mere phenomena. Thereby he distances himself from ``the
usual, rather coarse materialism''. He often uses the word \emph{matter} in the
sense of \emph{being, world-medium, the bearer of all that is actual}. But he
expressly emphasizes that the concept of matter must be widened and deepened so
that it becomes clear that the dispositions to the phenomena of consciousness are
found in nature just as much as the possibilities of all other phenomena.
\emph{The philosophical concept of matter} contains more than the physicists' and
the chemists', since it is to be the concept of what underlies all bodily and
spiritual states and comprehends the whole and full reality. (Cursus p.~62, 75.
Leben, Sache etc.\ p.~302\,f.) Materialism is for Dühring only a ``pedestal'', a
real foundation, an outer, mechanical frame for the conception of the world and
the view of life --- not the exhaustive, ample explanation of existence itself.

\opage{562}A doctrine one does not expect to find in Dühring is the assumption of
\emph{purposes} in nature. To understand him rightly on this point one must
notice that he distinguishes between purpose (\textit{Zweck}) and intention
(\textit{Absicht}). (Logik p.~203.) When he ascribes validity to the concept of
purpose for our conception of nature, it is because the forces and dispositions
operating in nature always exhibit certain tendencies, work in certain
directions, and above all because they \emph{operate together} and thereby make
nature appear as a systematic unity. Those tendencies do not always lead --- as
little in outer nature as in conscious human life --- to completed results. But
whether the goal is reached or not, \emph{the combined operation of manifold
elements} appears as a characteristic principal feature of all processes. In
apprehending nature one must attend not merely to the general laws but also to
the directions and tendencies of the processes that go on, and to the types and
forms in which nature's activity appears. Nature forms a scale of stages, the
lower forms of existence being the foundation of the higher. The measure by which
we distinguish between lower and higher forms can be sought only in the results
of the different tendencies, in the degree to which they lead to their natural
goal. And the last goal must be the arising of beings which not only exist and
operate but also become conscious of their existence and their operating: only as
the foundation of the history of conscious beings has the history of the
mechanical whole of nature a meaning; a thoroughly unconscious world would ---
says Dühring (Cursus p.~104) --- be a foolish half-measure, a theater without
actors and without spectators. And that the phenomena of consciousness are, on
the other hand, essentially to be regarded as purposes is seen from the fact that
unconscious and conscious operation can accomplish one and the same thing; it
would be mere luxury for men and animals to become conscious of their impulses
and motives, if it were only a question of attaining outer results, and if we
were not here facing something that was in itself purpose. Our feelings in
particular --- the feeling of love, the social feeling --- do not have their
value merely by being means or motives leading to actions necessary for life's
\opage{563}subsistence; they have immediate value as expressions of a higher stage of life
than the purely elementary one. (Cursus p.~158\,f. Der Werth des Lebens,
2.~Aufl., p.~241.)

If one were to object to this last thought that conscious life is nevertheless
not always bound up with pleasure, but that pain occupies so great a place that
conscious life does not seem to be a real ``purpose'', Dühring would point to
what he calls \emph{the law of difference} --- a law which under different forms
and names plays a great part in recent psychology. (The most suitable name would
be: the law of ratio.) For Dühring it is not merely a psychological law but a
world-law. The antagonism of forces is a principal feature in the
world-schematism. All expression of force, all movement and all development is
conditioned by distance, difference, opposition. All consciousness too
presupposes difference. Without difference, no sensation. Within consciousness
the same holds. Life's play would lose its attraction if there were no resistance
and hindrance to overcome, and if need and satisfaction did not succeed one
another. It is existence's rhythms and differences that make it valuable for us:
our feeling of life is set in motion by the transitions between mutually
different states. Without what is harsh, bitter and painful, the deep
satisfaction in life would not be felt. --- The same emphasis upon feeling's
being determined by oppositions which made Schopenhauer a pessimist makes Dühring
an optimist. Schopenhauer is, as regards the ``law of difference'', more
consistent than Dühring, in so far as he assumes that unrest and movement lie as
an original tendency in the world-ground's nature; whereas for Dühring's
philosophy it becomes a great riddle how successive differences and rhythmically
changing states could have succeeded the resting being which that philosophy
assumes in virtue of the law of the determinate number.

The \emph{combination} of the different forces is what makes development
possible. Whether this combination leads to a state of equilibrium or to a new
movement, the tendencies of the several forces are preserved in the development's
result. A constant strife between the forces would be an absurdity --- but it is
\opage{564}not found in nature. The avoidance of the absurd is a natural-logical principle.
Only in exceptional cases does this principle lead to untenable forms being
annihilated and dissolved. As a rule nature takes the positive way. Therefore, on
Dühring's view, the idea of the struggle for existence is false: it one-sidedly
emphasizes the negative point of view and lays the weight upon antagonism instead
of upon combination. Dühring gives Lamarck's theory the preference over Darwin's.

\subsubsection*{γ.\quad Ethics}

The ethical has according to Dühring its foundation in the human impulses. Only
its foundation --- for nature can err, and therefore a closer development and
correction is necessary. The higher a being stands, the greater the possibility
that it goes wrong. Besides, what matters ethically is to combine elements which
from nature's hand are not yet connected, but are perhaps even in mutual strife.

% [p. 565]
The germs of the good Dühring finds, like Comte, in the sympathetic instincts.
Nature has itself seen to it that another's suffering determines our own feeling
in a painful way, and there is perhaps no feeling that has undergone so
conspicuous a development in the course of culture as this one. It does not lead
to subduing and abolishing our own individuality. On the contrary, ethical
development consists both in an individualization and in a socialization; the two
necessarily belong together, since the full development of the single
individuality first becomes possible in a more highly developed society. Under
more imperfect social conditions the free, distinctive development of individuals
is hindered. But since our present states are essentially built upon compulsion,
they constantly hamper that development. A free society --- the germs of which
are given in the organizations formed by free association --- will first let both
individuality and community come into their own. In such a society all relations
of production and of consumption would be brought under social direction, so that
the individual's whole interest can be attached to the work and not to the work's
yield. Only thereby does \opage{565}a thoroughgoing ennoblement of life become possible.
From socialism Dühring's conception differs partly in that he thinks of free
labor communes and not of an absolute centralization of
production,\footnote{On Dühring's position on the social question, and on the
different standpoints he has taken here, I refer to B. \emph{Friedländer}: \textit{Die
vier Hauptrichtungen der modernen socialen Bewegung.} Berlin 1901.} partly in
that he does not regard it as necessary that development should be interrupted by
a historical miracle: the building of the future will on his view arise, not ---
as Karl Marx holds --- through evil increasing, but through the good growing
quietly. On this point too Dühring is decidedly an optimist, however much
baseness he may think he can establish in the world. He is a definite opponent of
pessimism. Only the pessimism of indignation (\textit{Entrüstungspessimismus}),
as represented by Byron and called forth by determinate social conditions, has
his approval; whereas he despises the Romantic ``pessimism of the beyond'' and
the ``pessimism of rottenness'' frequent in the higher classes.

Beyond the feeling for the good forces that work their way forward within the
human world, there arises a \emph{universal affect} when the gaze is raised to
the great unity of which the human world is only a single ramification --- when
the thinker feels himself as belonging to that unity and as moved by its forces
--- and when the thought of his own fate is taken up into the thought of the
great order of things, within which so many good germs have been able to unfold.
---

Not only by the problems it poses, but also by the noble, antique style in which
it is carried through, and by the connection it establishes between thinking and
personality, Dühring's philosophy stands as one of the most characteristic
attempts of thought in the generation that followed Romanticism's fall and
natural science's new rise at the middle of the nineteenth century. The year 1880
forms here a characteristic turning point, in that a circle of the more
considerable investigators conclude their activity about that time --- namely,
besides Dühring, Lotze, Fechner, Darwin and Spencer; shortly before, Lange had
succumbed. In a separate work some principal forms of the history of philosophy
in the following quarter-century are to be presented.

\opage{566}
\textsuperscript{1}) P.~4. Only a single point shall be touched on here, which could not well find a place in the
text. Wolff had transformed the Spinoza-Leibnizian identity hypothesis into an external parallel theory, which could
rightly bear
% scan: „hære“ (p. 566; the e-book's reading, set by sense: scan-artefact rule)
the name duplicism. (Cf. note 76 to the first volume). It was this theory that had especially aroused offense among
his theological opponents; but for other reasons too it could not but be found difficult, and it became the object
of much criticism and was soon abandoned by several Wolffians. An acute and independent thinker, Kant's teacher,
\emph{Martin} \emph{Knutzen} in Königsberg, who could as little put up with the usual doctrine of interaction as with
Wolff's external parallelism, sought a solution of the difficulty by taking up again Leibniz's thought of the
ultimate elements of matter as ``representing'' (psychical) beings. With this the heterogeneity of the elements
which, on the assumption of an interaction between soul and body, were to act on one another, fell away. The
soul-monads were taken to differ from the body-monads only in degree, not in essence. The Cartesian dualism, which
Wolff had renewed in his own way, thereby fell away, and the problem of the relation between soul and body was
widened into a problem of the interaction of things in general. Knutzen thereby set up a theory that was later
developed by Herbart and especially, in a characteristic way, by Lotze. --- Cf. \emph{Benno} \emph{Erdmann}:
\textit{Martin Knutzen und seine Zeit.} Leipzig 1876. p. 64---97. --- A similar theory was, moreover, set up by the
eclectic Berlin academician \emph{Prémontval}. See \emph{Dessoir}: \textit{Geschichte der neueren deutschen
Psychologie} I. p. 45.

\textsuperscript{2}) P.~6. ``It is usual to divide the faculties of the soul into the cognitive faculty and the
faculty of desire, and to count the feeling of pleasure and pain as belonging to the faculty of desire. But it seems
to me that the soul's approval, approbation and satisfaction, which are nevertheless properly very different from
desire, lie between cognition and desire. We regard the beauty of nature and of art with pleasure and satisfaction,
without the least stirring of desire . . . . It seems to me
% --- p. 567 ---
\opage{567}most expedient to give the soul's satisfaction or dissatisfaction, which is indeed a germ of desire but not
desire itself, a name of its own . . . I will call it the faculty of valuation (Billigungsvermögen), in order thereby
to distinguish it both from the knowledge of truth and from striving after the good,'' \emph{Mendelssohn}:
\textit{Morgenstunden.} Berlin 1786. p. 118---119.

\textsuperscript{3}) P.~20. That Lessing uses the concepts of education and revelation in a figurative sense there
can be no doubt, given his own declaration in the preface that the positive religions represent the course of
development of the human spirit. To speak popularly he had to speak anthropomorphically. His standpoint appears
clearly in some philosophical fragments from his younger years (e.g. \textit{Das Christenthum der Vernunft}) and in
the conversation with Jacobi. --- The account of Lessing's standpoint that is given in the text has, with a few
changes, been printed as part of my essay \textit{Apologi for Lessing} in Nordisk tidsskrift, published by the
Letterstedt Society. 1889.

\textsuperscript{4}) P.~24. As regards Jacobi's rendering of the famous conversation, both the thoughts and the often
highly characteristic expressions testify that we have Lessing himself speaking before us. Herder declared:
``Lessing ist so dargestellt, dass ich ihn reden sehe und höre'', Cf. \emph{Erich} \emph{Schmidt}:
\textit{Lessing.} II. p. 667. --- As remarked in the text, one must naturally not take Lessing's ``Spinozism'' quite
literally and externally. See on this the interesting investigation in C. \emph{Hebler}:
\textit{Lessing-Studien.} Bern 1862. Ch. 5. --- Jacobi sent Herder a copy of the account of the conversation with
Lessing. In his reply Herder (who was at that time Superintendent in Weimar) declared that, by unexpectedly finding
a fellow believer in Lessing, he had been strengthened in his adherence to the divine Spinoza, whose philosophy,
however, he does not embrace on every point. He moreover points out to his ``dear extramundane personalist'' that
his salto mortale is impossible, ``denn wir sind in der Schöpfung auf ebnem Boden''. (R. Haym: \textit{Herder nach
seinem Leben und seinen Werken.} II. Berlin 1885. p. 275 f.). --- \emph{Goethe} joined Herder, although his
artistic standpoint led him to lay greater weight on the incomprehensibility of that which cannot take on a
definite, individual form. In Weimar Spinoza was eagerly studied in the winter of 1784---85. An interesting document
from this study is a recently found little essay, written in Frau v. Stein's hand, probably from Goethe's
dictation. It shows clearly how Goethe sought to arrange Spinoza's ideas for himself in his own way. Cf. on this
\emph{Dilthey's} essay: \textit{Aus der Zeit der Spinoza-Studien Goethe's} (Archiv für Geschichte der Philosophie.
VII). --- Jacobi was dismayed at Herder's adherence to Lessing and showed Herder's letter to \emph{Wizenmann} (whose
relation to Jacobi is described by the words: ``I love his spirit and marvel at his unbelief''), but must here again
have been dismayed when the young man, a positive believer, answered Jacobi's question as to what he thought of
Herder's confession of faith: ``
% --- p. 568 ---
\opage{568}I have the same faith''. What appealed to Wizenmann in Spinoza was the inward relation in which God in
his doctrine stands to nature. (Goltz: \textit{Thomas Wizenmann.} Gotha 1859. I. p. 342 f.). On the other hand
Wizenmann agreed with Jacobi in finding Goethe's poem ``Prometheus'' blasphemous (ib. p. 311). In the anonymous work
\textit{Die Resultate der Jacobischen und Mendelsohnschen Philosophie,} kritisch untersucht von einem Freiwilligen
(Leipzig 1786) Wizenmann afterwards took Jacobi's side in the dispute against Mendelssohn, since he too contested the
possibility of a religion of reason. In a note to ``Kritik der practischen Vernunft'' (I, 2, 2) Kant speaks of
Wizenmann as ``a fine and clear head, whose early death is to be lamented''.

\textsuperscript{5}) P.~33. As regards the more detailed grounding of my conception of Kant's development, I must
refer to my monograph: \textit{Kontinuiteten i Kants filosofiske
% scan: „filosofiskc“ (p. 568; the e-book's reading, set by sense: scan-artefact rule)
Udviklingsgang} (Det kgl. danske Videnskabernes Selskabs Skrifter. 6. Række. 1893), where the references to the
sources are found. --- When Kant (see my monograph mentioned above, p. 6) says in several places in his letters that
Kritik der reinen Vernunft is the fruit of twelve years' work, \emph{Emil} \emph{Arnoldt} \textit{(Kritische Excurse
auf dem Gebiete der Kant-Forschung.} Königsberg 1894. p. 182) would count these twelve years back from the time when
Kant wrote the book down, which in his opinion happened in the year 1778. This might in itself be quite reasonable;
but when one also takes into account other passages (cited on the same page of the monograph) which point directly to
the year 1769 as the decisive turning point, it becomes more natural to count the twelve years from the publication
of the work. In favor of the year 1766 it could be said that Kant, in his announcement \textit{(Nachricht} etc.) of
lectures for 1765---66, for the first time uses the expression ``Kritik der Vernunft'' of the epistemological task he
has set himself. But then a distinction must be made between the beginning of reflection and its first result. This
latter, and with it the decisive, turning point must in any case be put at 1769. --- I take the opportunity to remark
that, when I worked out the fourth chapter of the monograph and showed in it that Kant's theory of the intuition of
space arose through a subjectivizing of Newton's world-space, a transposition from sensorium dei to sensorium
hominis, --- I did not know the second part of \emph{Vaihinger's} \textit{Kommentar zu Kants Kritik der reinen
Vernunft,} in which a similar explanation is given. My essay was worked out in the summer of 1892, the same year in
which Vaihinger's work appeared.

\textsuperscript{6}) P.~36. The book has a prehistory which is not without interest and which has only recently been
fully illuminated by \emph{Dilthey} \textit{(Der Streit Kants mit der Censur über das Recht freier
Religionsforschung.} Archiv für Gesch. d. Philos. III. p. 418 ff.) and \emph{Emil} \emph{Fromm} \textit{(Immanuel Kant und
die preussische Censur.} Hamburg und Leipzig 1894). The book consisted of several essays, which began to appear
separately in the Berliner Monatsschrift. But when the second essay was to be printed, the board of censors imposed a
ban. The editor of the journal complained to the King, and the matter came before the council of ministers. But just
at that same time the ministers received a very ungracious
% --- p. 569 ---
% scan: „det.“ (p. 569)
\opage{569}royal letter, because they had not shown themselves willing to go along with further steps against the
press. They were told that they ``were pleading the cause of the so-called men of enlightenment'', and the King
expressed the expectation that, by watching over literature, they would protect positive religion and thereby in
turn the order of the state. (A characteristic causal series!) Under these circumstances the council of ministers
resolved that the decision of the board of censors must stand. It was then that Kant published the essays, collected
as a book. --- The expressions I have used of Wöllner in the text are too mild, if Frederick the Great was right
when, in his day, on a proposal to raise him to the nobility, he answered with the following marginal note: ``Der
Wölner ist ein betriegerischer und intriguanter Pfaff, weiter Nichts'' (E. \emph{Fromm} p. 19). Cf. also
\emph{Emil} \emph{Arnoldt}: \textit{Beiträge zu dem Material der Geschichte von Kant's Leben und
Schriftstellerthätigkeit in Bezug auf seine ``Religionslehre'' und seinen Conflict mit der preussischen
Regierung.} Königsberg 1898. (It is shown here, among other things, that Kant --- for what reason is uncertain ---
got the philosophical faculty in Jena, not in Königsberg, to give the imprimatur).

\textsuperscript{7}) P.~50. Already S. \emph{Maimon} and \emph{Herbart} criticized Kant's division of judgments and
the use he made of it in his theory of knowledge. --- Cf. the investigation of the relation between primary and
secondary judgments in my \textit{Formel Logik. ---} On Kant's division in relation to the divisions current before
him see \emph{Adickes}: \textit{Kants Systematik als systembildender Factor.} Berlin 1887. p. 30---41.

\textsuperscript{8}) P.~50. Kant, who on the whole is very loose in the use of his terminology, often lets the wider
and the narrower meaning of the word reason pass into one another. This holds also with regard to the meaning in
which he takes it in the title of his main work, since by the pure reason he means to investigate he thinks
sometimes of the capacity for knowledge independent of \emph{experience}, sometimes particularly of the capacity for
\emph{knowledge} of \emph{something} that cannot become an \emph{object} of experience. Cf. on this H.
\emph{Vaihinger}: \textit{Commentar zu Kants Kritik der reinen Vernunft.} I. Stuttgart 1881. p. 453 f.

\textsuperscript{9}) P.~51. Cf. on this \emph{Schopenhauer} in his \textit{Kritik der Kantischen Philosophie,} which
forms an appendix to \textit{Die Welt als Wille und Vorstellung,} first part. (6. Aufl. Leipzig 1887. I. p.
572---577). --- A. \emph{Riehl} \textit{Der philosophische Kriticismus.} I. Leipzig 1876. p. 441. 446.

\textsuperscript{10}) P.~53. Kritik der reinen Vernunft. I. Aufl. p. 229. --- Cf. my essay on Kontinuiteten i Kants
filosofiske Udviklingsgang. p. 16 f.

\textsuperscript{11}) P.~56. Kant's criticism of Leibniz's doctrine of monads is found in Kritik der reinen Vernunft.
I. Aufl. p. 265 f. --- From Kant's notes it seems to follow that in his lectures he did not, theoretically either,
hold fast to the unknowability of the Ding an sich as sharply and definitely as the consequence of his
epistemological investigation properly demanded. Cf.
% --- p. 570 ---
% scan: „ban“ (p. 570)
% print: „Poulsen“ (p. 570) (misprint)
% print: „S 57.“, no point after S (p. 570) (misprint)
\opage{570}\textit{Reflexionen Kants zur kritischen Philosophie.} Aus Kants handschriftlichen Aufzeichnungen
herausgegeben von \emph{Benno} \emph{Erdmann}. II. Leipzig 1884. Nr. 1151; 1156---58. \textit{Lose Blätter aus
Kants Nachlass.} Mitgetheilt von R. \emph{Reicke}. I. Königsberg 1889. --- Cf. on Kant's pedagogical and didactic
accommodations as a lecturer the interesting remarks in \emph{Emil} \emph{Arnoldt}: \textit{Kritische Excurse auf
dem Gebiete der Kant-Forschung.} p. 387---399; 402---403; 454. --- \emph{Max} \emph{Heinze} \textit{(Vorlesungen
Kants über Metaphysik aus drei Semestern.} Abhandlungen der phil. hist. Classe der kgl. sächs. Gesellsch. der
Wissensch. 1894. p. 658) grants Arnoldt that Kant --- according to what is available --- must have expressed
himself more cautiously in his lectures than in his writings, but adds: ``Manches klingt da allerdings recht
dogmatisch, da er die kritische Einschränkung nicht stets beifügt; aber dann neigt \textit{er innerlich auch
diesen dogmatischen Sätzen zu.''} This statement aptly expresses a result that can be drawn from the manuscripts of
Kant's lectures (partly by himself, partly by his hearers) which have been brought to light in recent years by B.
Erdmann, Reicke, Arnoldt and Heinze. --- One more remark shall be taken from Heinze's essay (ib. p. 518). Whereas
Kant, as is seen from his ``Nachricht'' of 1766, earlier began his philosophical course with empirical psychology,
he later, as notes taken at his lectures show, went back to the order followed by the Wolffians, in which psychology
came after ontology and cosmology. --- \emph{Benno} \emph{Erdmann} \textit{(Einleitung zu Kants Prolegomena.}
Leipzig 1878. p. LXV) and O. Riedel \textit{(Die monadologischen Bestimmungen in Kants Lehre vom Ding an sich.}
Hamburg und Leipzig 1884) have shown how the doctrine of monads persisted in the background of Kant's
consciousness. In his excellent book on Kant \textit{(Immanuel Kant. Sein Leben und seine Lehre.} Stuttgart 1898)
\emph{Friedrich} \emph{Paulsen} very strongly emphasizes that Kant, in spite of his critique of reason, always held
fast to a certain vague metaphysical idealism as his final conviction. It was not Kant's intention to root out
metaphysics; he only wanted to give it other grounds than those on which it had hitherto relied. Yet Paulsen aptly
remarks of the lecture notebooks through which alone we know Kant's metaphysics: ``Freilich, sollten wir Kant
allein aus diesen Heften kennen lernen, dann würden wir wohl niemals zu einer deutlichen Vorstellung von seiner
Denkart kommen, wahrscheinlich es auch nicht der Mühe wert halten'' (p. 237).

\textsuperscript{12}) P.~57. The first reason: Kritik der reinen Vernunft. I. Aufl. p. 26 f. 34 f. 286.
Prolegomena. Riga 1783. p. 163 f. --- The second reason: Kritik der reinen Vernunft, I. Aufl. p. 19. 288. 494. 637.
Prolegomena p. 104 f. Grundlegung zur Metaphysik der Sitten. 3. Aufl. p. 106. Ueber eine Entdeckung, nach der alle
neue Critik der reinen Vernunft durch eine ältere entbehrlich gemacht werden soll. Königsberg 1790. p. 56. It is this
last passage that is translated in the text. Since the translation is free, the German text is given here: Die
Gegenstände, als
% --- p. 571 ---
% scan: „Analyse.“ (p. 571)
\opage{571}Dinge an sich, geben den Stoff zu empirischen Anschauungen (sie enthalten den Grund, das
Vorstellungsvermögen seiner Sinnlichkeit gemäss zu bestimmen).

\textsuperscript{13}) P.~57. It is of no use, with A. \emph{Riehl} (Der philosophische Kriticismus. I. p. 434), to
distinguish between ground and cause. For the matter is given only through the faculty of representation being
affected; the relation of time cannot be kept out. The real contradiction in Kant surely lies rather precisely in
this, that he will apply the concept of cause to the Ding an sich without daring also to apply the relation of time.
For Kant himself sought to disarm the objection by distinguishing between thinking and knowledge (Kritik der
practischen Vernunft. I. Aufl. p. 94 f. and the preface to Kritik der reinen Vernunft. 2. Aufl.): in mere thinking
we operate with the pure category; to real knowledge belongs sense intuition. But the merely ``thinking''
application of the concept of cause itself nevertheless becomes meaningless when the relation of time may not also
be applied. --- This whole problem presents itself differently, partly when Kant's concept of time is subjected to a
revision, partly when Kant's proof of the validity of the causal principle is restricted to the extent within which
alone it really has significance. --- The whole doctrine of the ``Ding an sich'' appears with a more realist stamp in
the 2nd edition of ``Kritik der reinen Vernunft'' than in the 1st edition, something to which \emph{Jacobi} and
\emph{Schopenhauer} already drew attention. But in the main point and in the main difficulty both editions agree,
and the most important difference between them is to be found on another point (namely, as remarked in
``Kontinuiteten i Kants filosofiske Udviklingsgang'' p. 28. 55 f.: in that the psychological analysis, the subjective
deduction, recedes more in the later edition, as well as in the ``Prolegomena'', and the whole weight is laid on the
objective or transcendental deduction). --- Cf. on the significance of the ``Ding an sich'' in the critical
philosophy, once Kant's errors have been corrected, my essay \textit{Filosofiske Problemer} (Universitetsprogram
1902), p. 50 f. I am unable to see that any epistemology which will not derive the ``matter'' of knowledge from its
``form'' can avoid positing a ``Ding an sich'' at some point or other. It seems to me that this side of the problem
has not come into its own in the otherwise interesting and acute essay by my young friend Mag. art. \emph{Anton}
\emph{Thomsen}: \textit{Bemerkungen zur Kritik des Kantischen Begriffes des Dinges an sich.} (Kantstudien. 1903).

\textsuperscript{14}) P.~58. To the quotations cited in the monograph must be added the letter to Reinhold of 12 May
1789: ``Das Realwesen von Raum und Zeit und der erste Grund, warum jenem drei, dieser nur eine Abmessung zukommt, ist
uns unerforschlich''. Further, Reflexionen II. Nr. 1187---88, where Kant distinguishes between the succession and
the ground of the succession. ---

\textsuperscript{15}) P.~59. Kant's statements are not entirely clear, but nevertheless seem to tend rather in the
direction of the identity hypothesis. \emph{Benno} \emph{Erdmann} (Einleitung in die Prolegomena. p. LXV) and O.
\emph{Riedel} (Die monadol.
% --- p. 572 ---
\opage{572}Bestimmungen. p. 7; 27 f.) interpret Kant's statements in the direction of a theory like the
``monistic-spiritualistic'' hypothesis set up by Martin Knutzen (see note 1) and later by Herbart and Lotze. Against
this speaks: 1) Kant expressly rejects the assumption of a soul-substance, which Knutzen, Herbart and Lotze alike
embrace. 2) The possibility on which he dwells is: ``Eben dasselbe, was in einer Beziehung körperlich heisst, würde
in einer andern zugleich ein denkend Wesen sein''. (Kritik. 1. Aufl. p. 359). 3) Kant rejects three hypotheses,
namely dualism, materialism and pneumatism (Kr. 1. Aufl. p. 379), the last of which is surely a ``monistic
spiritualism''. 4) In any case Kant differs from the monistic spiritualists in definitely denying the possibility of
an interaction between matter (as phenomenon) and the soul (as phenomenon): ``Das commercium der Seele mit der
Materie als Phänomen kann gar nicht gedacht werden; denn das müsste im Raum sein. Die Seele ist aber kein Gegenstand
äusserer Anschauung''. Reflexionen II. Nr. 1197 (cf. Nr. 1131). Cf. also Lose Blätter I. p. 160. Tugendlehre. 2.
Aufl. p. 66. In a notebook of Kant's lectures of 1793---94, recently brought to light (by \emph{Emil}
\emph{Arnoldt}: Kritische Excurse p. 502), it is likewise said: ``Die Körper als Körper können auf die Seele nicht
wirken und umgekehrt, weil Körper gar nicht Relationen auf ein denkendes Wesen haben können. Die äussere Relation,
in der ein Körper mit einer Substanz steht, ist nur im Raum, also muss diese Substanz auch im Raum, mithin ein Körper
sein.''

\textsuperscript{16}) P.~61. In Kritik der reinen Vernunft 1. Aufl. p. 549 note Kant does indeed seek to foist a
dogmatic line of thought on the antitheses; but he does not succeed. It is indeed also clear that the contradictory
opposite of absolute completion is not absolute (given) infinity, but non-completion (continual progress). Kant's
doctrine of the antinomies appears very early in him, and he seems originally to have wanted to use it as the
foundation for the critique of the whole of dogmatic metaphysics. It is an artificial schematism, devised later,
that leads him to distinguish between three ideas, to which three different critical investigations must then also
correspond, and the doctrine of the antinomies was then restricted to the investigation of the concept of the world.
Cf. on this question Fr. \emph{Paulsen}: \textit{Immanuel Kant.} p. 209---213.

\textsuperscript{17}) P.~73. In his essay \textit{Kant als Vater des modernen Pessimismus} \emph{Eduard} von
\emph{Hartmann} (Zur Geschichte und Begründung des Pessimismus. 2. Aufl. Leipzig 1891) has in a tendentious way
exaggerated the pessimistic side of Kant's conception. In particular he makes Kant depict the disproportion between
culture and individual happiness in far stronger terms than he actually uses. When Kant
\textit{(Anthropologie.} 2. Aufl. p. 314) speaks of ``Perfectionirung des Menschen durch fortschreitende Cultur,
wenn gleich mit mancher \emph{Aufopferung} der \emph{Lebensfreuden} desselben'', Hartmann (p. 104) renders the
last words without further ado by: ``
% --- p. 573 ---
% print: „Ksnts“ (p. 573) (misprint)
\opage{573}auf \emph{Kosten} ihrer \emph{Lebensfreuden}'', which sounds far stronger and can be understood
absolutely. When Kant \textit{(Kritik der Urtheilskraft.} 2. Aufl. p. 392) speaks of culture's increasing inequality
and torments, Hartmann (p. 104) uses this statement as if it were Kant's last word on this matter, which, as the
context shows, it is not.

\textsuperscript{18}) P.~74. In the work \textit{Zum ewigen Frieden} (1795) Kant develops the line of thought of
``Idee'' and ``Muthmasslicher Anfang'' with particular regard to the possibility of the cessation of wars through the
formation of a world-embracing union. As in the two earlier essays, Kant here abstracts entirely from moral motives
and sympathetic feelings and merely investigates which egoistic interests can be assumed to work in the direction of
the ideal end: a state of right that embraces all men. Yet he declares that it is a \emph{duty} to use the mechanism
of the interests in this direction. --- Kant has taken up, on a more deep-going psychological foundation, Lessing's
idea of the education of the human race. He expressly defends this idea against \emph{Mendelssohn}, who (in his
\textit{Jerusalem)} held that there could be talk of education and progress only for the single individual, not
for the species. (See Kant's essay: \textit{Ueber den Gemeinspruch: Das mag in der Theorie richtig sein, taugt aber
nicht für die Praxis.} 1793). --- On the significance that \emph{Rousseau} probably had for Kant in the transition to
the definitive form of his ethics I have expressed myself in \textit{Jean Jacques Rousseau og hans Filosofi} (1896).
p. 106--- 108 and in the essay \textit{Rousseaus Indflydelse paa den definitive Form for Kants Etik} (Oversigt over
det kgl. danske Videnskabernes Selskabs Forhandlinger. 1896).

\textsuperscript{19}) P.~75. Cf. what I remarked in this respect about Kant's ethics in my work \emph{Om}
\emph{Grundlaget} for den humane \emph{Etik}. (1876). p. 52.

\textsuperscript{20}) P.~78. It was Kant's formalism that brought him close to mysticism. \emph{Hamann} rightly spoke of ``a
mystical love of form'' and ``a gnostic hatred of matter'' as traits that could characterize Kant's philosophy
\textit{(Metakritik.} Schriften ed. Roth. VII. p. 7, cf. his oral statements to Kant VI. p. 227, see also p. 212.
213). --- One of Kant's disciples, C. A. \emph{Willmans}, wrote a dissertation \textit{De similitudine inter
Mysticismum purum et Kantianam religionis doctrinam} (Halis Sax. 1797), of which Kant --- with some reservation ---
reprinted a piece as an appendix to \textit{Streit der Facultäten.} Later Kant found himself prompted to make a still
more definite reservation, so that his doctrine should not be confused with a doctrine of the possibility of
supersensible experiences, a possibility he definitely rejected as self-contradictory. See the statement of Kant
reprinted in R. \emph{Reicke}: \textit{Kantiana.} Königsberg 1860. p. 81 f., and \emph{Jachmann}: \textit{Immanuel
Kant geschildert in Briefen an einen Freund,} Königsberg 1804. p. 116 ff.

\textsuperscript{21}) P.~81. Cases of conflict as examples (the method of reagents): \textit{Kritik}
% --- p. 574 ---
% scan: „fl.“ (p. 574)
\opage{574}\textit{der practischen
% print: „prachtischen“ (p. 574) (misprint)
Vernunft} (Kehrbach's edition). p. 36. 112. 186 ff. \textit{Anthropologie.} 2. Aufl. p. 243. \textit{Tugendlehre.}
Einleitung § IX. (In the last-named place it is developed that virtue is strength, and that strength is known only
by resistance!). --- See also the first chapter of the essay: \textit{Ueber den Gemeinspruch: Das mag in der Theorie
richtig sein, taugt aber nicht für die Praxis} (1793). The passage cited in the text immediately following is found
in this essay.

\textsuperscript{22}) P.~84. Cf. Reflexionen Kants. II. Nr. 1534: ``Das Vermögen die Motive des Willens schlechthin
selbst hervorzubringen ist die Freiheit. Dieser Actus beruht nicht selbst auf dem Willen, sondern ist die
Spontaneität der Causalität des Wollens''. --- Freedom in this sense is not a capacity to choose: ``Die Freiheit ist
ein positives Vermögen, nicht etwa zu wählen, denn hier ist keine Wahl, sondern das Subject zu bestimmen''. (Lose
Blätter. I. p. 570).

\textsuperscript{23}) P.~85. \emph{Herbart} has already \textit{(Gespräche über das Böse.} Königsberg 1817. p.
145---147) pointed out two meanings of the word ``freedom'' in Kant. I agree with \emph{Jodl} \textit{(Geschichte der
Ethik in der neueren Philosophie.} II. Stuttgart 1889. p. 30---37) that three different meanings of this word must be
distinguished in Kant. --- As I have shown in my \textit{Etik} (ch. 5), the meanings of the vague word are by no
means exhausted with this.

\textsuperscript{24}) P.~95. Kritik der reinen Vernunft. 1. Aufl. p. 695 ff. Prolegomena. 1. Aufl. p. 174. 179.
Kritik der Urtheilskraft. §§ 59. 88. 91 Anm.

\textsuperscript{25}) P.~96. This appears clearly from the information that \emph{Emil} \emph{Arnoldt} has recently
given about Kant's lectures in his \textit{Kritische Excurse auf dem Gebiete der Kant-Forschung}. See, besides what
is cited in note 11, also Arnoldt's work cited, p. 465 f., where Kant's lectures on the philosophy of religion are
especially discussed, in which he used the current religious usage without drawing attention to the modifications
in the meaning of the concepts which criticism and symbolism bring with them.

\textsuperscript{26}) P.~102. It is quite characteristic of the history of the development of taste that, whereas
Kant in his \textit{Beobachtungen über das Gefühl des Schönen und Erhabenen} (1763) mentions ``in Figuren
geschnittene Bäume'' (p. 4) as an example of beautiful phenomena, it is said in \textit{Kritik der Urtheilskraft}
(1790) that ``the English taste in gardening'', precisely by its approach to the grotesque and by its avoidance of
all constraint, gives ``taste in the designs of the imagination'' occasion to show its greatest perfection. (§ 22
Anm.).

\textsuperscript{27}) P.~103. In the period immediately preceding (the Sturm und Drang period) the word genius had
been in fashion. It expressed a craving into the boundless, a wish to free oneself from all rules and laws. Every
unclarity and unruliness found it easy to adorn itself with this word. ``The word genius'', says \emph{Goethe} (Aus
\textit{meinem Leben.} Book 19), ``was so misused that it was even considered necessary to
% --- p. 575 ---
% print: „Papire“ (p. 575) (misprint)
\opage{575}banish it from the German language. And so the Germans might perhaps have deprived themselves of this
word, seemingly foreign but belonging to all peoples in equal degree, had not the sense for the highest and best,
founded anew by a deeper philosophy, happily gained power.'' That Goethe here alludes to Kant's definition of genius
in Kr. d. Urth. is seen from what precedes, where it is said of the genius period's misuse of the word genius: ``It
was still long until the time when it could be declared that genius is the power in man that gives law and rule
through doing and acting''. --- There is a certain connection between Kant's concept of genius and his conception of
the consciousness of synthesis. In every consciousness a hidden art is exercised in the synthesizing activity which
is the essence of all consciousness, but which need not itself be an object of consciousness. And the laws and rules
for thinking and acting that can be set up consciously are in the end derived from that hidden art. The quality of
genius then denotes only the culmination of a form of activity that is present in all mental life.

\textsuperscript{28}) P.~116. In \textit{Eduard Allwills Papiere} (Vermischte Schriften. 1780) Jacobi depicted a
``beautiful soul'' who insists on the right of the exception and uses it for excesses. But although Allwill's conduct
is evidently disapproved of by Jacobi, he nevertheless later, in his own name (Jacobi an Fichte. p. 32), uses the
example of Desdemona, which is already used by the hero in ``Allwills Papire'' (p. 236) to defend the right of
individual feeling to make exceptions. --- The expression ``beautiful soul'' was perhaps taken up by Schiller and
Goethe from ``Allwills Papiere'' (p. 229). Yet the expression goes back to Rousseau. --- When I have somewhere called
Jacobi a modern Herbert of Cherbury, it may be added that the similarity also shows itself in that Jacobi, like
Herbert, wished for a sign in confirmation --- only it did not come. \emph{Wizenmann} relates in a letter from
Jacobi's estate Pempelfort near Düsseldorf that Jacobi, as they sat in the garden one evening, said: ``Here I often
sit and look at the setting sun and then imagine the joy that would flame up in me if a miracle of God's grace
assured me of his existence. Then I stand up, inspired by the thought: God! and would like to go out, call together
the whole world and proclaim him to it.'' His enthusiasm thus did not fall away because the sign did not come. When
he heard the evening wind rustle in the trees of the garden, and nature stirred for him in its depth and sublimity,
it was his conviction: ``Das ist doch nicht die Macht eines Chaos, die mich so harmonisch durchregt!''
(\emph{Goltz}: Thomas Wizenmann. I. p. 310 f).

\textsuperscript{29}) P.~123. In Maimon there is a certain wavering with regard to the concept of the thing in
itself. The comparison with an imaginary number(√-a) is found in \textit{Kritische Untersuchungen} (Leipzig 1797) p.
158. 191. But according to other passages the thing in itself (like matter and form) is an idea that can be
represented approximately, like the irrational number √2. Thus Maimon expresses himself when he leaves it open where
the thing in itself is to be sought: in an absolute object or an absolute subject (e.g. \textit{Versuch
% --- p. 576 ---
% scan: „Værdifulde.“ (p. 576)
% scan: „Rige.“ (p. 576)
\opage{576}einer neuen Logik.} Berlin 1794. p. 142). The solution may perhaps be sought in this, that Maimon, where
he altogether rejects the Ding an sich, is thinking of Kant's conception of it, whereas he himself has another concept
of it, according to which the contradictions fall away. In \textit{Philosophisches Wörterbuch} (Berlin 1791) --- with
regard to form and clarity Maimon's best work --- it is said: ``I differ from Herr Kant merely in the following way:
according to him things in themselves are the foundation, existing outside us, of their phenomena in us . . .
According to me, on the other hand, the knowledge of things in themselves is nothing other than \textit{the complete
knowledge of phenomena . . . .} We continually approach the knowledge of them, the more complete our knowledge of
phenomena becomes'' (p. 276 f.). And with this agrees a note in his autobiography \textit{(Salomon Maimons
Lebensgeschichte. Von ihm selbst geschrieben.} Berlin 1792. II. p. 43), where it is said: ``The nature of irrational
numbers shows us that, without having any concept of \textit{a thing as object in itself}, one can nevertheless
determine its relation to other things''.

\textsuperscript{30}) P.~124. Some years after Maimon's first writings there appeared \emph{Jakob} \emph{Sigismund}
\emph{Beck's} abstract of Kant's writings, in which he came to a result similar to Maimon's, namely that
epistemologically there could be no question at all of a thing in itself, and in which an attempt was made to show
how forms of intuition and categories denote different stages of development of the activity of the understanding
through which alone there are things for us. It is of interest to see how different thinkers strike out on the same
path, but it is not necessary to go further into Beck's expositions. Interesting information about his personal
relation to Kant is obtained from the letters from Beck to Kant published by R.\emph{Reicke} (Reicke: \textit{Aus
Kants Briefwechsel.} Königsberg
% scan: „Königsherg“ (p. 576; the e-book's reading, set by sense: scan-artefact rule)
1885) and from the letters from Kant to Beck published by \emph{Dilthey} (Archiv für die Geschichte der Philosophie.
II). (These letters have since been included in the new edition of Kant's writings undertaken by the Berlin
Academy, in the 11th and 12th volumes).

\textsuperscript{31}) P.~129. With regard to the relation between the two essays cf. F. \emph{Ueberweg}:
\textit{Schiller als Historiker und Philosoph.} Leipzig 1884. p. 242---248 and F. \emph{Jodl}: \textit{Geschichte der
Ethik in der neueren Philosophie.} II. Stuttgart 1889. p. 56 f. cf. p. 507 f. I cannot, however, agree with the
result of these two authors, that Schiller constantly holds fast to a relation of opposition between grace and
dignity. Not only does he already indicate in the older essay that grace, harmony, is what is highest in value, but
he does so still more definitely in ``Briefe üb aesth. Erz.''. Thus it is said in the 27th letter: ``In the midst of
the fearful realm of forces and in the midst of the holy realm of laws the aesthetic formative drive builds at a
third realm, the realm of joy, of play and of seeming, in which it takes from man the fetters of all relations and
frees him from everything that is called constraint, in the physical as in the moral domain.'' And Schiller finds
this third realm realized where ``man with bold simplicity and calm innocence goes through the most intricate
relations and has neither
% --- p. 577 ---
% scan: „auf.“ (p. 577)
% print: „Str.“ (p. 577) (misprint)
% scan: „auf.“ (p. 577)
\opage{577}need to injure another's freedom in order to assert his own, nor to throw away his dignity in order to
show grace''. Thus a union of grace and dignity (which were earlier set up as opposites) in the aesthetic state, in
which the opposition between the physical and the moral has also fallen away.

\textsuperscript{32}) P.~133. This comparison comes out in an interesting way in one of \emph{Friedrich}
\emph{Schlegel's} fragments in \textit{Athenäum:} ``Die Französische Revolution, Fichtes Wissenschaftslehre und
Goethes Meister sind die grössten Tendenzen des Zeitalters. Wer an dieser Zusammenstellung Anstoss nimt, wem keine
Revolution wichtig scheinen kann, die nicht laut und materiell ist, der hat sich noch nicht auf den hohen weiten
Standpunkt der Geschichte der Menschheit erhoben.'' (Athen. 1, 2. p. 56) --- Yet \emph{Baggesen} had often hinted at
a similar comparison, first admiringly, later indignantly. Cf. in the latter respect his statement in a letter to
Erhard of 17 May 1797 about ``die neuesten Ichtischen und Fichtischen Sanskulotterien a priori, die jetzt in
Deutschland auf die politischen Sanskulotterien a posteriori in Frankreich gefolgt sind.''

\textsuperscript{32\,b}) P.~138. A more special demonstration of the way in which Fichte's independent philosophy
developed has been given --- on the basis of hitherto unprinted manuscripts of Fichte --- by \emph{Willy}
\emph{Kabitz} in his work \textit{Studien zur Entwickelungsgeschichte der Fichteschen Wissenschaftslehre aus der
Kantischen Philosophie.} (Berlin 1902). Of particular interest is --- besides the decisive influence of Kant's
writings --- the preceding influence of Rousseau and Pestalozzi (work cited p. 8) and the later influence of
``Ænesidemus'' (work cited p. 56).

\textsuperscript{33}) P.~145. On the influence that Fichte's later writings have had on the spiritual development
in Denmark, through \emph{Grundtvig}'s being so strongly influenced by them in his youth, I have made some remarks in
my account of philosophy in Denmark in the nineteenth century in P. Hansen's danske Literaturhistorie.

\textsuperscript{34}) P.~147. Fichte thinks of the relation between the ego and the body thus: the body is the
outer material form under which the ego must appear in order to be able to struggle with the material limits. Since
the non-ego appears in the form of space, the ego must do so too: ``Matter can be displaced from its space only by
other matter; therefore the mind, as a force that is to act in a material world, must itself be matter, thus an
immediately given body, determinate and limited in space . . . The resistance lies in matter; therefore the force
must also be taken up into the medium of matter.'' \textit{Die Thatsachen des Bewusstseins.} 1817. p. 81. 83. Cf.
already \textit{Naturrecht} § 5, and \textit{Sittenlehre} § 9 (Nr. V). --- Compare this view of Fichte's with Kant's
view mentioned in note 15.

\textsuperscript{35}) P.~148. Fichte often declared that the special content of experience and of life cannot
be deduced from general principles. Most clearly and finely perhaps in his lectures \textit{Ueber das Wesen des
Gelehrten} (
% --- p. 578 ---
% scan: „idelhele“ (p. 578)
\opage{578}Berlin 1806) p. 33 f. ``Life in time can be comprehended only in general, according to its essence, as
the presentation of the one, original and divine life; but in the particular, according to its real content, it must
be immediately lived and experienced; and only in and through this experience can it be reproduced in representation
and in consciousness . . . . In each single part of human life something remains over which does not go wholly into
the concept and therefore cannot be anticipated or replaced by any concept either, but which must be immediately
lived if it is to come into consciousness at all. This is called the domain of bare and pure empiricism or
experience.'' If one overlooks this, one will ``forfeit life itself, in striving to explain it out completely''. ---
Among what must thus be taken as given, Fichte counts first and foremost each single ego's definite, individual
peculiarity, ``the point at which we find ourselves when we begin to use our freedom'', and which conditions the path
we afterwards describe. (\textit{Wissenschaftslehre.} 2. ed. p. 267). For even if an ethical explanation can be given
of the limitation of the pure ego to finite egos, no explanation is thereby given of the definite individual
peculiarity in the single ego. In his later expositions Fichte calls this splitting into peculiar individualities a
``projectio irrationalis''.

\textsuperscript{36}) P.~152. Cf. on this my \textit{Etik} VIII, 4. --- J. H. \emph{Löwe}: \textit{Die Philosophie
Fichtes.} Stuttgart 1862 p. 155---158 has clearly illuminated the opposition in which Fichte's doctrine of
individuality stands to other elements in his system.

\textsuperscript{37}) P.~153. In his youthful work \textit{Kritik aller Offenbarung} (Königsberg 1793. p. 225) Fichte
even declares that the living wish to exercise spiritual influence and the sure conviction that this can happen only
by means of the representation of a revelation can produce an at any rate momentary faith through the influence of
enthusiasm on the imagination. A wish that the revelation may be true can be justified, he thinks, when this wish is
itself ethically motivated (ibid. p. 216).

\textsuperscript{38}) P.~155. Fr. Schlegel's and his wife's letters to Schleiermacher are found in \textit{Aus
Schleiermachers Leben.} In Briefen. 3. Bd. Berlin 1861. p. 129. 132---134. --- On the peculiar way in which Fr.
Schlegel transposed Fichte's Wissenschaftslehre into romantic ``irony'' reference must be made here to S.
\emph{Kierkegaard}: \textit{Om Begrebet Ironi.} Copenhagen 1841. p. 287---320. Yet it must be well noted with regard to
Kierkegaard's account of Schlegel that he takes account only of the novel ``Lucinde'', which marks an extreme point of
oscillation in Schlegel's movement of thought. In the fragments in the journal \textit{Athenäum} and elsewhere
Schlegel developed the concept from a far more significant side, as an expression of the capacity to immerse oneself
in single domains or individuals as though they were everything, and thereby to see them in their peculiarity, a
capacity that presupposes an inner infinity in the one who possesses it; one must oneself be a world in order to be
able to understand others as peculiar parts of the world. (Cf.
% --- p. 579 ---
\opage{579}Athenäum I. 2. p. 31 f.). It is a concept that expresses the historical method from an essential side,
but which can indeed be turned so that it swings out into pure arbitrariness and sensuality. The Romantic school was
in constant oscillation. Romanticism swings between unbridled self-feeling (the pure ego being made one with the
empirical ego) and mystical self-surrender (the empirical ego vanishing in the pure, infinite ego), the interval
between the two poles is filled by a living need to revel in all the forms of the life of the spirit (poetry,
philosophy, religion) --- preferably all at once. No poetry and no science could in the end satisfy this need. No
wonder that in the end it led so many over to the old Catholic Church, which in doctrine and cult is still untouched
by the modern distinction between the different domains of the spirit. Thus Dorothea Schlegel wrote to Schleiermacher
later on (1806 or 7): ``Trost, Mittheilung, Liebe, Musik, Malerei und wohlthätige Thränen finde ich in der Kirche''.
(Aus Schleiermachers Leben. III. p. 416). In Schelling there corresponds to this transition the transition to the
period of philosophy of religion in his speculation.

\textsuperscript{39}) P.~157. When Schelling says: ``Sensibilität als Phänomen steht an der Grenze aller
empirischen Erscheinungen, und an ihre Ursache als das höchste ist in der Natur alles geknüpft'' (Erster Entwurf p.
174), this statement recalls Hobbes's proposition that of all phenomena in nature the most remarkable is this, that
anything at all can become a phenomenon, so that, while the phenomena are the condition for knowing everything else,
sense perception is in turn the condition for the knowledge of this condition. De corpore XXV, I. (Cf. the account
of Hobbes's philosophy in the first volume of this work. p. 266).

\textsuperscript{40}) P.~166. A detailed account of Weisse's system of philosophy of religion I gave in my day in my
book \textit{Filosofien i Tyskland efter Hegel} (Copenhagen 1872) p. 181---219. On philosophical theism in general I
have had occasion to make some remarks at the end of my essay \textit{Lotze og den svenske Filosofi} (Nordisk
Tidsskrift, published by the Letterstedt Society. 1890).

\textsuperscript{41}) P.~167. In ``Filosofien i Tyskland efter Hegel'' p. 121---149 I have given a survey of
Schelling's later doctrine.

\textsuperscript{41\,b}) P.~169. The characterization of Hegel's conception of Christianity in the notes from his
youth I owe to Mr. Mag. art. \emph{Anton} \emph{Thomsen}.

\textsuperscript{41\,c}) P.~177. \emph{Ellis} Mc. \emph{Taggart}: \textit{Hegel's Treatment
% print: „Treatement“ (p. 579) (misprint)
of the subjective notion.} (Mind. 1897). p. 164. Cf. the same author's essay \textit{The Changes of method in Hegel's
Dialectic} (Mind. 1892). --- Cf. also F. C. \emph{Sibbern's} acute remarks on the different kinds of triadic
relation (``trilogies'') that appear in Hegel: \textit{Hegels Philosophie betragtet i Forhold til vor Tid.}
Copenhagen 1838. p. 125---132. Sibbern aptly remarks that the Hegelian logic in its spiral
% --- p. 580 ---
% scan: „ktr.“ (p. 580)
\opage{580}course has no consistent room for real synthetic unities, i.e. such unities as are formed when two
elements that stand on the same line \textit{meet} one another (as when two feelings, each of which has arisen by
ways of its own, meet, or when thought and feeling meet after each has developed with a certain independence). In
Hegel, consistently, the second member should always be derived from the first.

\textsuperscript{42}) P.~191. Cf. note 38 above. --- On Schleiermacher's conception of Fr. Schlegel's personality,
which he had to defend not only against opponents but also against those closest to him, see \textit{Aus
Schleiermachers Leben.} In Briefen. I. p. 320. 349 ff. The last statement in particular testifies both to
Schleiermacher's sense for other personalities (particularly for that in them which connects their shell with their
kernel) and to his faithful and chivalrous disposition. It will stand as one of the most important documents when a
comparative ethics of friendship comes some day to be written.

\textsuperscript{43}) P.~194. The lectures that Steffens gave in Copenhagen in 1802, and which became of such great
significance for the life of the spirit in Denmark through the awakening influence they had on Grundtvig and
Oehlenschläger, are in large part an account of the fundamental thoughts of the ``Beiträge'', only with the addition
of aesthetic and historical considerations, whereby the line of thought is extended from the domain of the
philosophy of nature to that of the philosophy of spirit. Cf. \textit{Indledning til filosofiske Forelæsninger.}
Copenhagen 1803. p. 91. 107 f., where the at once individualizing and universalizing tendency in nature is
emphasized. See moreover on these lectures my essays on Steffens in ``Tilskueren'' (1902) and in ``Nordisk
Universitetstidsskrift'' (1903).

\textsuperscript{44}) P.~195. \emph{Dilthey} (\textit{Leben Schleiermachers.} p. 351) remarks that especially the
first draft of Schleiermacher's ethics, which dates from 1804, recalls in its content the writings of Steffens
mentioned here. --- When the University of Berlin was to be opened, Schleiermacher declared that it was desirable to
appoint Steffens in order to avoid one-sidedness both in philosophy and in natural science, and that for his own
part he particularly wished for this appointment, since his lectures on ethics would thereby find a foundation in
general philosophy; to achieve this he was willing in the first years to forgo a considerable part of his salary.
(Aus Schleiermachers Leben. IV. p. 175). It did not succeed, however. Steffens went instead to Breslau, and only
several years after Schleiermacher's death to Berlin.

\textsuperscript{45}) P.~197. Compare with this Fichte's view mentioned in note 37.

\textsuperscript{46}) P.~201. When it has been said that for Schleiermacher religion was a variety of the sense for
art (see \emph{Albrecht} \emph{Ritschl}: \textit{Schleiermachers Reden über die Religion und ihre Nachwirkungen auf
die evangelische
% print: „ewangelische“ (p. 582) (misprint)
Kirche Deutschlands.} Bonn 1874. p. 53 cf. 91 f.), it is rather the reverse that is correct: it is the sense for art
that for Schleiermacher is
% --- p. 581 ---
% scan: „»umiddelbar«.“ (p. 581)
\opage{581}a kind or variety of the religious need to express the relation of feeling to the unity of life. Cf. W.
\emph{Bender}: \textit{Schleiermachers Theologie mit ihrem philosophischen Grundlegen.} Nördlingen 1876---78. I. p.
163. The correctness of Bender's conception is seen especially from ``Philosophische Sittenlehre'' § 290.

\textsuperscript{47}) P.~202. \textit{Philos. Sittenlehre} § 343: ``Where the individual is what is properly
ethically productive in actions, there only the agent himself can be his judge''. --- Cf. \textit{Die christliche
Sitte} p. 65: ``Insofar as an action has its ground in the individuality of the man, no one other than he himself can
judge it. But in this respect each is only his own judge, not his own teacher''. --- Perhaps it is characteristic
that this last remark occurs only in Schleiermacher's ``Christian'' ethics, not in the ``philosophical'' one; but
from a philosophical point of view too it is correct, and it finds its grounding in his whole doctrine.

\textsuperscript{48}) P.~205. J. E. \emph{Erdmann}: \textit{Grundriss der Geschichte der Philosophie.} Berlin 1866.
II. p. 465. 477. Cf. also \emph{Weissenborn}: \textit{Darstellung und Kritik der Schleiermacherschen Dogmatik.}
Leipzig 1849. p. 40---65, and \emph{Alb}. \emph{Ritschl}: \textit{Schleiermachers Reden über die Religion} etc. p.
59. --- A more correct conception is put forward by W. \emph{Bender}: \textit{Schleiermachers Theologie.} I. p.
173---175. --- \emph{Delbrück} found the ``Doctrine of Faith'' pantheistic and incompatible with the 2nd edition of
the Speeches (Aus Schleiermachers Leben. II. p. 366 f.), --- thus took the reverse view of it from that which
Erdmann and Ritschl took. --- When Schleiermacher in the ``Doctrine of Faith'', instead of the expression
``feeling'', also uses the expression ``immediate self-consciousness'', he himself explains this in ``Philos.
Sittenlehre'' thus: ``The expression `immediate self-consciousness' has its advantages, since many assign feeling
only to a lower region; but the word self-consciousness cannot be used without the addition `immediate', since
otherwise one thinks of reflected self-consciousness. Therefore the expression `feeling' is the best.''
\textit{Philos. Sittenlehre} § 253. --- A difference between the conception of religion in the ``Speeches'' and in
the later writings, on which great weight has often been laid, is this, that religion is there depicted as a purely
passive feeling, whereas later (and, as \emph{Dilthey} has shown, already in sermons contemporary with the
``Speeches'') the practical character of religion was more emphasized. I believe, however, that here too the
standpoint of the ``Speeches'' is often characterized somewhat one-sidedly; this holds e.g. of \emph{Jodl's}
otherwise excellent account of Schleiermacher's standpoint in his ``Geschichte der Ethik''. For it is an express
doctrine in the ``Speeches'' that ``in order to take up into himself the life of the world-spirit and to have
religion, man must first have found humanity, and he finds it only in and through love''; --- and the development of
humanity is not concluded; it goes on uninterruptedly anew from manifold individual starting points (2. Rede). Since
religion is conceived as that which provides the highest point of view for, or rather the fundamental mood in,
participation in human life and its
% --- p. 582 ---
% print: „arbejdede“ (p. 582) (misprint)
\opage{582}development, the religious feeling is by no means merely passive. When Schleiermacher calls it the music
of life, it is a music that serves not merely for mental entertainment but also to deepen the interest in work, even
if it does not itself directly set definite tasks, any more than it sets up definite theoretical
% print: „teoretiske, Antagelser“ (p. 582) (misprint)
assumptions. Here too there is only a difference of degree between the ``Speeches'' (I. ed.) and the later writings.
In the ``Doctrine of Faith'' (§ 9) Schleiermacher distinguishes definitely between aesthetic religiousness, where the
highest is the beauty of the soul, and teleological religiousness, where the highest state is not one of rest, but
at the same time works for the advance of the ``Kingdom of God''. This distinction is unknown (any more than the
``Dialectic's'' distinction between God and the world) in the ``Speeches'', where the whole relation is left more
indefinite. --- In the ``Dialectic'' too a closer determination of the relation between feeling and the other sides
of mental life is given than in the ``Speeches''. See especially Appendix C § LI: ``Es [das Gefühl] scheint bisweilen
allein hervorzutreten und darin Gedanke und That unterzugehen; aber dies scheint nur, es sind immer Spuren des
Wollens und Keime des Denkens oder umgekehrt beides, wenn auch wieder scheinbar verschwindend, darin mitgesetzt.''

\textsuperscript{49}) P.~215. The consideration that leads Schopenhauer to call philosophy an art does not, as will
easily be seen, coincide with the one I have put forward in my essay \textit{Filosofi som Kunst} in ``Mindre
Arbejder''.

\textsuperscript{50}) P.~202. Cf. also \emph{Helmholtz's} \textit{Handbuch der physiologischen Optik. 2.} Aufl. p.
248 f., where Fichte's work ``Die Thatsachen des Bewusstseins'' is mentioned with recognition, and where it is then
added that what is correct in Schopenhauer's corresponding expositions must for the most part be traced back to this
source. --- Possibly, however, Schopenhauer was also influenced on this point, in his theory of the principle of
causality, by hints in his teacher G. E. \emph{Schulze}. Cf. \emph{Ernst} \emph{Fischer}: \textit{Von G. E. Schulze zu
A. Schopenhauer.} Ein Beitrag zur Geschichte der Kantischen Erkenntnisstheorie. Aarau 1901. p. 68 and 102. Yet
Fischer is decidedly wrong when he declares that Schopenhauer could learn nothing from the lectures he heard from
Fichte in Berlin (among others on ``Die Thatsachen der Bewusstseins''). It should moreover be noted that Fichte was
strongly influenced by Schulze's ``Ænesidemus'', so that both influences may have combined here.

\textsuperscript{51}) P.~222. The difficulty mentioned was already emphasized by \emph{Herbart} in his criticism of
Schopenhauer's main work immediately on its appearance (reprinted in Herbart's \textit{Sämttl. Werke.} XII). It is
not impossible that Herbart's objection led Schopenhauer --- despite his great contempt for this and other critics
--- to the closer explanations in the second volume; it is striking that he here repeatedly returns to it. That these
explanations do not remove the difficulty is at bottom granted also by P. \emph{Deussen} (Archiv für Gesch. d. Phil.
III. p.
% --- p. 583 ---
% scan: „Gaug“ (p. 583)
% scan: „bar“ (p. 583)
\opage{583}164), who seeks to defend them, but in fact goes back from Schopenhauer to Kant --- In a conversation with
Karl Bähr in the year 1856 Schopenhauer declared that he had read Herbart's review only once in his life, namely
when it appeared in 1820. \textit{(Gespräche und Briefwechsel mit Arthur Schopenhauer.} Aus dem Nachlasse von Karl
Bähr. Leipzig 1894. p. 19). It may nevertheless well have had its effect for all that.

\textsuperscript{52}) P.~227. See on this psychological theory my \textit{Psykologi.} VI E, 6.

\textsuperscript{53}) P.~228. Schopenhauer in his philosophy of nature, as regards the conception of organic life, is
strongly influenced by the French investigators Cabanis, \emph{Bichat} and \emph{Lamarck}. Cf. an interesting essay by
\emph{Paul} \emph{Janet}: \textit{Schopenhauer et la physiologie française.} (Revue des deux mondes. 1880).

\textsuperscript{54}) P.~232. Cf. \emph{Lindner} und \emph{Frauenstädt}: \textit{Arthur Schopenhauer. Von ihm.
Ueber ihn.} Berlin 1863. p. 592 ff. --- Frauenstädt is surely right when he (work cited p. 434 f.) argues that
Schopenhauer in the first edition of his main work has a more subjectivist conception than later, in that he was at
first inclined to regard the individual differences as merely phenomenal, but later (especially in ``Parerga und
Paralipomena'') assumes that they have their ground in the thing in itself. --- Cf. \textit{Schopenhauers Briefe,}
herausg. von Griesebach p. 211.

\textsuperscript{55}) P.~244. See thus W. \emph{Windelband}: \textit{Geschichte der Philosophie.} Freiburg 1892. p.
492. --- The disparaging way in which Th. \emph{Graae} in his book on Uwe Jens Lornsen occasionally speaks of Fries is,
on the other hand, due rather to a lack of acquaintance.

\textsuperscript{56}) P.~244. Against this utterance (which is found in the preface to his Allgemeine Metaphysik)
protest was made from the side of strict Kantianism. In a letter (of 26 March 1833) Herbart then declares that he has
called himself a Kantian because the changes he has made in the interior of the science, especially by his criticism
of the metaphysical starting points and his transformation of psychology, are of subordinate significance in relation
to the great fundamental features of philosophizing set up by Kant. Moreover he has the same enemies as Kant:
speculative theology and the remnants of the old scholasticism. (See \textit{Ungedruckte Briefe von und an Herbart.}
Herausg. von R. Zimmermann. Wien 1877. p. 101---103).

\textsuperscript{56\,b}) P.~250. Cf. already G. \emph{Hartenstein}: \textit{Die Probleme und Grundlehren der
allgemeinen Metaphysik.} Leipzig 1836. p. 532. ``Was aus dem Gegensatze der Vorstellungen folgt (die, als
Selbsterhaltungen der Seele, das \textit{einzige} Beispiel darbieten, wo das wirkliche Geschehen uns erkenntbar wird),
muss überall, wo entgegensetzte Selbsterhaltungen in Einem Realen eintreten, ein Analogon finden.'' --- Cf. with this
my essay \textit{Filosofiske Problemer} (Universitetsprogram 1902), p. 64, and note 52.

\textsuperscript{57}) P.~251. Herbart's theory of the relation between soul and body
% --- p. 584 ---
\opage{584}thus stands closest to the one set up by Martin Knutzen and Prémontval (see note 1). Within Herbart's
school this theory has been developed by, among others, \emph{Ludwig} \emph{Strümpell}: \textit{Grundriss der
Psychologie.} Lepzig 1884. Ch. 15---16.

\textsuperscript{58}) P.~252. Cf. on this my \textit{Psykologi.} V B, 6. --- Moreover Herbart's psychology and
metaphysics here again come into conflict with one another: for if he really succeeds in explaining the unity of
consciousness by the interaction of the elements, he does not need the metaphysical explanation of the unity and
connection in consciousness by a soul-substance; and if he starts from the soul-substance from the outset, he cannot
take the unity for a mere product. --- The ``apperceiving masses of representations'' correspond roughly to what in my
Psykologi (V B, 5) I call the real self.

\textsuperscript{59}) P.~254. Among Herbart's merits in the domain of theoretical philosophy his treatment of logic
should not be forgotten (in \textit{Hauptpunkte der Logik} 1808 and in \textit{Einleitung in die Philosophie).} Of
interest is especially his reduction of the doctrine of judgments, in that he rejects all divisions except that into
affirmative and negative, and his hint at the doctrine of the quantification of the predicate concept. See especially
``Einleitung'' § 53. In the attempt to reduce the artificial classification of logical judgments, which played so
great and fateful a role in Kant, Herbart moreover has Maimon as a predecessor.

\textsuperscript{60}) P.~256. \emph{Lotze} remarks in his excellent account of Herbart's philosophy
\textit{(Geschichte der deutschen Philosophie seit Kant.} Leipzig 1882) that Herbart consistently had to conceive God
as a real which, without relation to other reals, could unfold no activity. (§ 72). This criticism also hits Leibniz
and --- Lotze himself. --- With regard to immortality Herbart's philosophy is, as Lotze also remarks, really all too
favorably placed, since by virtue of the doctrine of the eternal reals it leads not only to an individual immortality
but also to ``the inconvenient assumption of the eternal pre-existence of the soul!''

\textsuperscript{61}) P.~259. In an interesting way \emph{Fr}. \emph{Jodl} \textit{(Geschichte der Ethik in der
neueren Philosophie.} II. p. 251---266) has characterized Beneke's place in the history of ethical thought by
emphasizing his opposition to Kant and to speculation, his being influenced by the English school (particularly
Bentham, one of whose works he translated) and his position as Feuerbach's predecessor. --- Mag. art. \emph{Anton}
\emph{Thomsen} has in his essay \textit{Ueber die Entwickelung der ethischen Theorie Benekes} (Archiv für die
Geschichte der Philosophie. XVI, 2. 1903) shown the interesting difference between Beneke's earlier, predominantly
subjective standpoint (in ``Phys. d. Sitten'') and the later, more objective standpoint influenced by Bentham (in
``Sittenlehre''). The text of my account has been changed in the 2nd edition in accordance with Thomsen's result. ---
Interesting biographical information on Beneke is given by O. \emph{Gramzow}: \textit{Fr. E. Benekes Leben und
Philosophie} (Bern 1899). (Cf. my review of this work
% --- p. 585 ---
% scan: „paavist.“ (p. 585)
\opage{585}in Göttinger gelehrte Anzeigen 1901. Nr. 2). --- \emph{Kuno} \emph{Fischer} has (see his work
\textit{Hegels Leben, Werke und Lehre.} Heidelberg 1901. I. p. 157 f.) examined the documents concerning Beneke's
dismissal and found no trace of Hegel's participation. He derives the dismissal from ``the privy councillors' fear of
demagogues''.

\textsuperscript{62}) P.~262. Cf. the interesting remarks on Beneke's position on the problem of soul and body in
\emph{Ueberweg's} \textit{Grundriss der Geschichte der Philosophie der neunzehnten Jahrhundert.} 9. Aufl. von
\emph{Max} \emph{Heinze}. 1902. p. 133 note.

\textsuperscript{63}) P.~263. Beneke is of interest also as a logician, in that he (already in his \textit{Lehrbuch
der Logik.} 1832) showed that it is the content of concepts, not in the first instance their extension, that matters
in logical thinking (§ 21. 57), and in that he led the doctrine of inference back to the principle of substitution,
whereby inference becomes a simple ``taking up of one judgment into another'', the concepts being ``divided'' (or, as
it has later been called, quantified) (§ 170). --- Beneke and his disciples hold that William Hamilton, in his
doctrine of the quantification of the predicate, made himself guilty of plagiarism of Beneke. See \emph{Dressler}:
\textit{Characteristik der Werke Benekes.} (Appendix to the 3rd printing of Beneke's ``Lehrbuch der Psychologie''. p.
299). --- Beneke's logic aroused attention in England. \emph{Stuart} \emph{Mill} writes in a letter to Bain (1844):
``I am reading a book on logic by a German professor named Beneke, which he sent me after reading mine, and which had
previously been recommended to me by Austin and Herschel as agreeing with the spirit of my theories. This agreement is
present to a certain degree, although his book is more psychological than my plan entailed. Although I consider much
of his psychology unsound, because he has not properly grasped the principle of association (he now and then comes
