very near to it), there is much in it of a thought-provoking kind.'' (A. \emph{Bain}: \textit{John Stuart Mill.} A
Criticism. London 1882. p. 79).

\textsuperscript{64}) P.~264. On the dispute concerning the belief in immortality see \emph{Poul} Møller: \textit{Om
Muligheden af Beviser for Menneskets Udødelighed.} (Efterladte Skrifter. V) and my book \textit{Filosofien i Tyskland
efter Hegel,} p. 17---29. --- The last-named work also gives a detailed account of Schelling's later doctrine and of
the philosophy of Weisse and of the younger Fichte.

\textsuperscript{65}) P.~267. A detailed account of Trendelenburg's philosophical views is given in my book on
Filosofien i Tyskland efter Hegel (p. 222---246).

\textsuperscript{66}) P.~271. The self-characterization that Feuerbach gave in the statements cited only quite
recently became known through \emph{Wilhelm} \emph{Bolin's} book: \textit{Ludwig Feuerbach, sein Wirken und seine
Zeitgenossen.} Mit Benutzung ungedruckten Materials. Stuttgart 1891. --- A new, critical edition of Feuerbach's
writings has been begun by W. Bolin and Fr. Jodl.

\textsuperscript{67}) P.~274. This line of thought of Feuerbach's will receive illumination and
% --- p. 586 ---
\opage{586}confirmation from what is developed in my \textit{Psykologi} V B. 4 and VI F. --- Feuerbach has in part a
predecessor for his psychological theory in Hume. Cf. the first part of this work.

\textsuperscript{68}) P.~285. With regard to the course of development of Swedish philosophy reference must be made to
\emph{Axel} \emph{Nyblæus's} great work \textit{Den filosofiska forskningen i Sverige från slutet af adertonde
% scan: „ådertonde“ (p. 586)
århundradet,} framstäld i sitt sammenhang med filosofiens allmänna utveckling. Lund 1873 ff. Cf. also the same
author's essay \textit{Om den Boströmska Filosofien} (Lund 1883) (offprint from Ny svensk tidsskrift). --- In my essay
\textit{Filosofien i Sverig} (Nordisk Tidsskrift, published by the Letterstedt Society 1879) I have given a more
detailed characterization and criticism of Swedish philosophy.

\textsuperscript{69}) P.~286. A more detailed characterization of Sibbern and his philosophy I have given in
``Tilskueren'' 1885. (Reprinted in ``Mindre Arbejder''. 1899). --- On Danish philosophy in the nineteenth century cf.
my article in P. Hansen's Literaturhistorie vol. 2. In a somewhat more detailed form this survey is reproduced in
\textit{Archiv für die Geschichte der Philosophie.} 2. Bd.

\textsuperscript{70}) P.~290. In a philosophical respect the most important of Kierkegaard's writings are:
\textit{Begrebet Angest} (1844). \textit{Stadier paa Livets Vej} (1845). \textit{Uvidenskabelig Efterskrift} (1846).
--- With regard to the more detailed grounding of the characterization of Kierkegaard given in the text I must refer
to my book \textit{Søren Kierkegaard som Filosof} (Copenhagen 1892). --- On Kierkegaard's dogmatic standpoint
interesting demonstrations are found in Chr. \emph{Schrempf}'s essay: \textit{Kierkegaards Stellung zu Bibel und
Dogma.} (Zeitschrift für Theologie und Kirche. Freiburg in Br. I. p. 179---229).

\textsuperscript{71}) P.~295. While de \emph{Maistre} by his principle of authority and by his emphasis on war
recalls Hobbes, by his doctrine of causation he recalls Malebranche, whom he also mentions with great admiration,
just as he also follows him in his mystical-pantheistic intellectual tendency, as when he speaks of the divine ocean
that shall one day take up all things and all men. He feels himself that he stands here at the border of heresy,
for he adds at once: Je me garde cependant de vouloir toucher à la personnalité, sans laquelle l'immortalité n'est
rien. (\emph{Les} Soirées de St. Petersbourgh. 7. éd. II. p. 203).

\textsuperscript{72}) P.~302. Cf. on this question my \textit{Psykologiske Undersøgelser.} (Det kgl. danske
Videnskabernes Selskabs Skrifter. 6. Række) p. 68---81. --- When Biran speaks of sensations that fall outside the
self, he means by the self more or less what in my \textit{Psykologi} (V B, 5) is called the real self, the central
and more active part of the content of consciousness. Outside the formal self, which expresses the connection and the
unity in consciousness, no sensations can fall. --- In his criticism of Condillac Biran had a predecessor in Charles
\emph{Bonnet} \textit{(Essai analytique sur les facultés de l'âme.} Copenhague 1760).

\textsuperscript{73}) P.~306. See, on the phenomena of concretion, \textit{Philosophie des deux Ampère.} p. 316 f.
\textit{Essai sur la philosophie des sciences} (1834) p. LVIII ff. ---
% --- p. 587 ---
\opage{587}A. \emph{Bertrand} \textit{(La psychol. de l'effort} p. 62) uses the expression \textit{concrétion}
wrongly, in that he uses it of free association between two different representations; for that kind of combination
Ampére uses the expression \textit{commémoration.} When I recognize the tree, it is concrétion; when I see the tree
again and then come to think of the dog that lay at the root of the tree last time, it is commémoration. --- I
regret that I did not know Ampère's account when I wrote the chapter on immediate recognition in my ``Psykologiske
Undersøgelser''. But it is a great joy to me to see how close an agreement there is between his conception and the
one I have developed.

\textsuperscript{74}) P.~308. Ampère, moreover, makes the difference between his theory and Kant's greater than it
is, by ascribing to Kant the conception that the relations, the forms of coordination, stand in no connection
whatever with things in themselves.

\textsuperscript{75}) P.~310. Of Cousin's first appearance as a philosophical teacher \emph{Jouffroy} gives an
interesting characterization in his \textit{Nouveaux Mélanges philosophiques} (2. éd. p. 85---95). --- \emph{Renan}
\textit{(Feuilles detachées,} 4. éd. 1892. p. 298 f.) has expressed himself about Cousin, and about what he owes
him, in the following way: A travers une foule de défauts, quel haut sentiment de l'infini! quelle vue juste du
spontané et de l'inconscient! quel accent religieux, inoui depuis Malebranche, quand il parle de la raison! Que l'on
comprend bien les traces que gardèrent de ce premier enseignement des hommes tel que Jouffroy! Je connus le cours de
1818 sous les ombrages d'Issy vers 1842. L'impression fut sur moi on ne peut pas plus profonde. J'ai la conscience
que plusieurs des cadres de mon esprit viennent de là . . . M. Cousin a été non un de mes pères, mais un des
excitateurs de ma pensée.

\textsuperscript{76}) P.~316. On the relation between Saint-Simon and his school see \emph{Paul} \emph{Janet}:
\textit{Saint-Simon et le Saint-Simonisme.} Paris 1878. --- In the characterization of Saint-Simon I rely
especially on \emph{George} \emph{Weill}: \textit{Saint-Simon et son oeuvre.} Paris 1894 and on Chr. \emph{Adam}:
\textit{La philosophie en France} (Première moitié du 19e siècle). Paris 1894. --- On the relation of the
Polytechnic School to Saint-Simonism cf. G. \emph{Pinet}: \textit{L'Ecole polytechnique et les Saint-Simonisme.}
(La Revue de Paris. 15 May 1894). --- While Saint-Simon's writings are incoherent and make only constant fresh
starts, his school produced a coherent development of doctrine, namely the one edited by \emph{Hippolyte}
\emph{Carnot}, the \textit{Doctrine de Saint-Simon} (1829), which gives the content of \emph{Bazard's} lectures, and
which in time lies before the fantastically extravagant period that ended with the dissolution of the school. The
further development that the doctrine of critical and organic periods received in ``Doctrine de Saint-Simon'' surely
took place, however, under the influence of \emph{Auguste} \emph{Comte's} first important work (Plan des travaux
scientifiques nécessaires pour réorganiser la société. 1822); although he still called himself Saint-Simon's
disciple, he was nonetheless fully emancipated. ---
% --- p. 588 ---
% print: „Sain-Simonisternes“ (p. 588) (misprint)
\opage{588}In his Autobiography (Danish trans. p. 164---169) \emph{Stuart} \emph{Mill} speaks in an interesting way
of the significance that the Saint-Simonians' doctrine of critical and organic periods had for him. --- The whole
doctrine had, as was shown earlier, first been developed by Kant and Fichte, the first thinkers who saw both that
criticism and the Revolution had triumphed and that they could nevertheless not be the last word of history. In
Rousseau and Lessing the same thought is dawning. --- Moreover, Lessing's ``Erziehung des Menschengeschlechts'' was
one of the Saint-Simonians' favorite books.

\textsuperscript{77}) P.~321. Comte's disciples go a step further than the master, in that they maintain that it is
rather Saint-Simon who learned from Comte than the latter from the former. \emph{Littré}: \textit{Auguste Comte et
la philosophie positive.} 2 éd. p. 90 f. \emph{Robinet}: \textit{Notice sur l'oeuvre et sur la vie d'Auguste
Comte.} 2. éd. p. 139. Even if Saint-Simon --- as is natural --- did not remain uninfluenced by the gifted younger
men who worked together with him, it nevertheless stands firm that he had developed his main thoughts before he came
into contact with Comte. The priority with respect to the idea of a positive philosophy as the new spiritual
authority that was necessary after the age of criticism and revolution cannot be denied to Saint-Simon. But --- as
\emph{Georges} \emph{Weill} (Saint-Simon et son oeuvre. p. 208---210), who has clearly demonstrated this, rightly
remarks --- Comte's great significance is not in reality diminished by it.

\textsuperscript{78}) P.~322. Instead of perfecting, \emph{Comte} later (Cours de philosophie positive. 2. éd. IV.
p. 262. 264) prefers to use the expression development (developpement), because a moral valuation might lie in the
word perfecting.

\textsuperscript{79}) P.~326. In a letter to Stuart Mill of 27 June 1845 he says: Le trouble a consisté en
insomnies opiniâtres, avec mélancolie douce, mais intense, et oppression profonde, longtemps mêlée d'une extrême
faiblesse. He connects the attack with the fact that a few days before he had begun to work out his new work, and
adds: \textit{L'ensemble de ma composition aura beaucoup gagné à cette période exceptionelle,} où ma méditation
était loin d'éprouver l'atonie de ma motilité. --- The year after, when Chlotilde de Vaux had died, he confessed
that the feeling that had arisen in him toward her had contributed to that nervous crisis. (Lettres d'Auguste Comte à
Stuart Mill, p. 413 f.). --- Madame Chlotilde de Vaux's husband had been sentenced to penal servitude for life for a
degrading crime, but she regarded her marriage as indissoluble, and the relation between her and Comte therefore did
not go beyond an intimate friendship.

\textsuperscript{80}) P.~328. Of the two most important writings on Comte, Littré's maintains that Comte's real
significance ends with the publication of ``Cours de philosophie positive'', while \emph{Robinet's} regards
``Politique positive'' as the real conclusion and polemicizes against Littré as an ungrateful and uncomprehending
apostate. --- It follows of itself that Stuart Mill's
% --- p. 589 ---
\opage{589}recognition of Comte applies only to the first period. The correspondence between them ceased when Comte
stood at the entrance to the second. In his work \textit{Auguste Comte and Positivism} (1865) Mill has given an
interesting valuation of Comte's doctrine in both of its stages. --- The schism that Littré caused has, moreover,
later repeated itself within the circle of the ``orthodox'' positivists. Some of these (with \emph{Lafitte} at their
head) hold that the positivist priesthood is to work upon the heart through the intelligence, while others (with the
Englishman \emph{Congreve} at their head) hold that positivism must triumph, as Christianity did in its time, through
direct appeal to proletarians and women, so that the heart must be worked upon without its happening through the
intelligence. See on this \emph{Caird}: \textit{The social philosophy and religion of Comte.} Glasgow 1885. p. 171
ff.

\textsuperscript{81}) P.~334. \textit{Cours de philosophie positive.} 2\textit{.} éd. VI. p. 612: Kant a
réellement mérité une éternelle admiration en tendant, le premier, d'échapper directement à l'absolu philosophique
par sa célèbre conception de la double réalité, à la fois objective et subjective, qui indique un si juste sentiment
de la saine philosophie. Cf. \textit{Discours sur l'esprit positif.} p. 24. \textit{Catéchisme positiviste.} 2. éd.
p. 8 and 150. --- According to what Comte himself states in one place, he did not read Kant's chief work. Yet he
early came to know his ideas at second hand. In a letter to Valat of 3 Nov. 1824 he states that in Kantianism there
are ``very good things alongside a mass of extravagances'', and he protests against Cousin's account of Kant being
regarded as valid: Cousin est bien loin de comprendre la portée des Idées-mères du philosophe de Koenigsberg. Yet he
here counts Kant as belonging to the metaphysical stage, and draws a parallel between his own relation to Kant and
Galilei's relation to the Peripatetic physics. --- The only writing of Kant's that he knew is the little treatise
``Idee zu einer allgemeinen Weltgeschichte'', which his friend Gustave d'Eichthal translated for him (1824), and
which he admired greatly. Had he known it six or seven years earlier, he could, he says, have spared himself the
trouble of working out his treatises [of 1820 and 22]. Letter to Eichthal of 10 Dec. 1824. --- On Comte's relation
to ``metaphysics'' cf. the interesting discussion in \textit{Bulletin de la société française de philosophie.}
January 1903. (Report of the meeting of 27 Nov. 1902).

\textsuperscript{82}) P.~343. The first time Comte touches on the question of the possibility of self-observation
is in \textit{Lettres à Valat} p. 89 (letter of 24 Sept. 1819). In his treatise \textit{Examen du traité de
Broussais sur l'irritation} (1828) (reprinted in the interesting collection \textit{Opuscules de philosophie
sociale,} Paris 1883, which contains the most important of Comte's works before the publication of Cours de
philosophie positive) he praises Broussais for his polemic against self-observation and remarks: One can observe
one's feelings when they are not too strong, because they depend on an organ other than that of observation; but
one's own intellectual activity one cannot observe, for then observer and object would be identical, and who would
then
% --- p. 590 ---
% scan: „done“ (p. 590)
% print: „siécle.“ (p. 590) (misprint)
\opage{590}make the observation? What has won subjective psychology a large following in the last ten years [before
1828] is, he thinks, the justified criticism of the ideology of Condillac and Helvetius, which regarded our knowledge
as the mere product of external influences, without taking into account the necessity of inner dispositions; but
this criticism had been better given by Bonnet and Cabanis, and above all by Gall and Spurzheim. (Opuscules p.
293---296). In \textit{Cours de philosophie positive} (I p. 32 f.; III p. 564; VI p. 605. 2. éd.) he repeats his
polemic against self-observation, remarking as well that an elementary analysis cannot be applied to the most
complicated phenomena of all. --- Since he assumed that self-observation was nevertheless possible as regards the
feelings, he has given a practical proof of it in one of his letters to Valat, in which he analyzes the motives
that underlie his activity as an author (28 Sept. 1819). --- On the whole question I refer to my Psykologi I, 8.

\textsuperscript{83}) P.~345. Cf., as regards political economy, the interesting treatise by \emph{Ingram}:
\textit{Nationaløkonomiens nuværende Stilling og Udsigter.} (Translated from the English). p. 16 ff. --- To Mill,
who had told him of his plan to write a political economy, Comte stated that although political economy properly
belongs to sociology as a whole, it can nevertheless do provisional service by being treated in isolation, especially
when the working out is undertaken by so good a head as Mill. \textit{Lettres à Stuart Mill.} p. 231 f. 254 f. Cf.,
on the other hand, \textit{Cours de la philosophie positive.} (2. éd.) IV. p. 255: Toute étude isolée des divers
éléments sociaux est donc, par la nature de la science, essentiellement stérile, à l'exemple de notre économie
politique, fût-elle même mieux cultivée.

\textsuperscript{84}) P.~346. Cf. \textit{Cours de philosophie positive.} 2. éd. IV p. 392. Also \textit{Lettres
à Stuart Mill.} p. 121: --- cette noble école, qui . . . fut certainement la plus avancée de toutes celles du
dernier siècle. --- p. 275: C'est à l'école écossaise et non, comme beaucoup d'autres, à l'école germanique, que
j'ai dû la première rectification des graves aberrations, à la fois
% print: „foîs“ (p. 590) (misprint)
morales et intellectuelles, propres à ce qu'on appelle l'école française: je n'oublierai jamais combien ma propre
évolution a été d'abord redevable surtout à quelques lumineuses inspirations de Hume et d'Adam Smith. --- (By the
Scottish school Comte evidently means the whole tendency that began with Shaftesbury and Hutscheson, not what is
called the Scottish school in a narrower sense: Reid and his successors). --- I may perhaps add the remark here that
the fundamental conception on which I build in my various ethical writings developed in me especially in the study of
Comte, as my treatise \textit{Om Grundlaget for den humane Etik} (Copenhagen 1876) will also bear witness.

\textsuperscript{85}) P.~354. It is therefore not correct to say with \emph{Fiorentino}: \textit{Manuale di storia
della filosofia,} 2. ed. Napoli 1887. p. 581, that Comte takes account only of the relations between objects among
themselves, not of the
% --- p. 591 ---
\opage{591}relations between object and subject. To be sure, he has not drawn the consequences of this latter
relation.

\textsuperscript{86}) P.~357. See on this \textit{Politique positive.} IV p. 187; 233 f. \textit{Catéchisme
positiviste.} p. 165 f. 222. --- In his later period Comte also makes another characteristic change in his
classification. He sums up in a series (15) of propositions the most general principles of the positive philosophy,
and gives this ``systematization of the positive dogma'' the name of \textit{philosophie première.} The name he takes
from Bacon. Then comes \textit{philosophie seconde:} the series of the seven fundamental sciences, which are,
however, again divided into two groups: \textit{philosophie naturelle} (the first five sciences) and
\textit{philosophie morale} (the last two sciences). Politique positive IV p. 226. --- In the Catéch. pos. (p. 167
f.) he speaks a little differently, mathematics, astronomy, physics and chemistry making up \textit{cosmology,} and
biology, sociology (in the narrower sense) and ethics \textit{sociology.}

\textsuperscript{87}) P.~368. In his essay on Bentham (Dissertations and Discussions. I) --- where the utterance
quoted is found --- \emph{Stuart} \emph{Mill} says: ``Bentham conceives the world as a collection of persons, each
pursuing his separate interest or pleasure, and who can be kept from colliding more than is necessary by hope and
fear under the influence of the law, of religion and of public opinion''. (p. 362). --- \emph{Leslie}
\emph{Stephen} (\textit{\emph{The} Utilitarians.} I. London 1900. p. 314 and 325) remarks that the manuscript of the
``Deontology'', which is now at University College in London, seems to show that Bentham was essentially the author
of this work, and that the editor, who was probably not very intelligent, is responsible only for some rhetorical
exaggerations, especially in the second part.

\textsuperscript{88}) P.~368. By my distinction between the motive of valuation and the motive of action I have
sought to avoid the difficulty that arises for Bentham when the question of the justification of the principle of
utility comes up. Cf. my \textit{Etik} ch. III, 1---2; 18 and the first treatise in my \textit{Etiske
Undersøgelser.}

\textsuperscript{89}) P.~377. Cf. J. H. \emph{Newmann}: \textit{Apologia pro vita sua.} London 1879. p. 10. 189 f.
--- See also L. E. \emph{Fløystrup}: \textit{Den anglokatholske Bevægelse i det nittende Aarhundrede.} Copenhagen 1891.
p. 28. 30 and \emph{George} \emph{Worley}: \textit{The Catholic Revival of the 19th Century.} London 1894. p.
45---51. --- Coleridge's philosophical ideas are perhaps best got to know in brief from his work \textit{Church and
State,} where Appendix B sets out his doctrine of reason and understanding, and where Appendix E develops his
relation to earlier philosophers. In \textit{Biographia literaria} I chap. 12 he develops his ideas in Schelling's
terminology and with a \textit{very} extensive use of Schelling's own sentences. --- Sterling's utterances about
Coleridge are found in \textit{Journals of Caroline Fox} (28. january 1842) and in a letter to Carlyle (in the
latter's \textit{Life of Sterling} p. 273).

\textsuperscript{90}) P.~379. See, besides \emph{Froude}: \textit{Thomas Carlyle} (London 1882---
% --- p. 592 ---
\opage{592}84), also \emph{Dilthey's} characterization of Carlyle in Archiv für Geschichte der Philosophie IV, and
\emph{Leslie} \emph{Stephen's} in \textit{The Utilitarians} III. p. 462---477.

\textsuperscript{91}) P.~390. In my \textit{Psykologiske Undersøgelser} p. 58 I have touched on Hamilton's merit
in regard to the doctrine of association in setting up the law of the whole (law of redintegration). Of older
writers there should have been named here, besides Kant and Fries, also \emph{Beneke}: \textit{Psychol. Skizzen.} I.
p. 382 ff., and already Chr. \emph{Wolff}: \textit{Vernünftige Gedanken von Gott, der Welt und der Seele des
Menschen.} § 238. Hamilton may have known both these writings. --- In my \textit{Formel Logik} § 18 I have touched on
Hamilton's standpoint in logic. --- In my work \textit{Den engelske Filosofi i vor Tid} (Copenhagen 1874) there is a
fuller discussion of Hamilton. --- Among Hamilton's disciples and critics it has been much discussed how he conceives
the knowledge of the so-called primary qualities of things (extension and form): whether it too is determined by the
subject, or whether we are here to know things as they are in themselves. \emph{Stuart} Mill found (in his
\textit{Examination of Sir William Hamiltons} Philosophy\textit{)} here a contradiction of Hamilton's doctrine that
all knowledge is relative, conditioned by the relation between object and subject. \emph{Mansel}
\textit{(Philosophy of the Conditioned.} London and New-York 1866. p. 84) and \emph{Veitch} (\textit{Hamilton.}
Edinburgh and London 1882. p. 179) interpret their teacher as assuming a relative knowledge of the primary qualities
(which are thus primary only in relation to the secondary ones, the qualities of sense usually so called).
\emph{George} \emph{Grote} (\textit{Minor Works.} p. 293) thinks that Hamilton changed his standpoint with respect to
this question, so that in the dissertations found in his edition of Reid's works he assumes a knowledge of the
primary qualities in themselves, whereas earlier he assumed only a relative knowledge of them. \emph{Leslie}
\emph{Stephen} expresses himself in a similar direction on this point in Hamilton (\textit{The Utilitarians.} III.
p. 385---401).

\textsuperscript{92}) P.~393. Cf. \emph{Masson}: \textit{Recent British Philosophy}. 3. ed. London 1877. p. 252 f.
--- \textit{Edinburgh Review.} July 1884. p. 218.

\textsuperscript{93}) P.~396. Yet there was one among these whose early development and early learning is quite as
remarkable as Mill's, namely \emph{William} \emph{Rowan} Hamilton (b. 1805, d. 1865), famous for his optical and
mathematical discoveries (not to be confused with the philosopher William Hamilton). At three years old he could read
and do sums; at four he was proficient in geography; at five he could translate from Latin, Greek and Hebrew and was
familiar with Homer, Milton and Dryden; at eight he read Italian and French and improvised Latin poems; before he
was ten he studied Arabic and Sanskrit, and when he was twelve he wrote a Syriac grammar. And all this with full
preservation of bodily and mental health. He appropriated everything without effort and with understanding. He had a
strong feeling for poetry, was a friend of Wordsworth, and was himself the author of fine poems. From his ninth year
on he was already a good swimmer, so that his bodily development
% --- p. 593 ---
% scan: „Syesmaader,“ (p. 593)
% scan: „Philosophy«.“ (p. 593)
\opage{593}was not neglected. \textit{Nature.} 3. May 1883. --- If one compares his development with Mill's, and both
with that of other children, one gets an impression of how very different the original foundation is on which the
work of education builds.

\textsuperscript{94}) P.~402. Cf. \emph{Stuart} \emph{Mill}: \textit{Levned.} Danish trans. p. 190 f. 243. 245. 256.
--- \emph{Bain} (\textit{John Stuart Mill.} A Criticism. London 1882. p. 163---174) gives an interesting
characterization, grounded on various testimonies and on psychological investigation, of the relation between Mill
and his wife. --- \emph{Theodor} \emph{Gomperz} (\textit{John Stuart Mill.} Ein Nachruf. Wien 1889. p. 18) describes
a visit to Stuart Mill's house. Mill's wife takes part in the conversation, especially by interjecting ``brilliant and
telling words'', and even when the discussion passes over into the purely philosophical domain, ``her husband,
listening almost with devotion, asked her opinion, which she put forward in clear and well-ordered form''.

\textsuperscript{95}) P.~403. See \textit{Memories of old Friends from the Journals of Caroline Fox.} Edited by
Horace S. Pym. (Tauchniz Edition. Leipzig 1881). I. p. 150 ff. II. p. 218 f. (cf. 77. 143). --- These diaries give a
most interesting glimpse into the spiritual life of a whole series of distinguished English thinkers, poets and men of
science. For a long series of years Caroline Fox wrote down every evening what she remembered of the utterances of
the eminent guests in her parents' house.

\textsuperscript{96}) P.~407. In my book \textit{Den engelske Filosofi i vor Tid.} Copenhagen 1874. p. 47 I was led by
my criticism of some of Mill's views, --- a criticism I still maintain, --- to use disparaging expressions about Mill
which I would not use now, which I already had struck out in the German translation (Einleitung in die englische
Philosophie unserer Zeit. Uebers. von Dr. H. Kurella. Leipzig 1889), and which Mill's posthumous treatises on the
philosophy of religion, which were not available at the time, moreover refute. Repeated occupation with Mill and his
writings has increased my admiration for him. --- An excellent characterization of Stuart Mill's personality and
significance has recently been given by \emph{Leslie} \emph{Stephen} in the third volume of his work \textit{The
Utilitarians.} (London 1900).

\textsuperscript{97}) P.~413. This circular reasoning has been demonstrated with great force and sharpness by
\emph{Stanley} \emph{Jevons} in the fragments of the ``Examination of J. S. Mills Philosophy'', which his early death
prevented him from completing. See \textit{Pure Logic and other Minor Works.} London 1890. p. 254 ff. From his correct
criticism of Mill on this point, however, Jevons draws all too far-reaching consequences with regard to Mill's
significance as a thinker as a whole. --- See also \emph{Arne} \emph{Löchen}: \textit{Om Stuart Mills Logik.}
Kristiania and Copenhagen 1885. p. 165 ff. Jevons's criticism had already been published in ``Contemporary Review''
1877---79, so that Löchen was able to profit by it. But Löchen's work is rich in interesting and instructive remarks
and investigations, and gives a good characterization of Mill as logician and epistemologist.

% --- p. 594 ---
% print: „establist“ (p. 594) (misprint)
% scan: „partienlar“ (p. 594)
% print: „imposibility“ (p. 594) (misprint)
\opage{594}\textsuperscript{98}) P.~414. On this I already built my criticism of Mill's epistemology in my earlier
account. See \textit{Den engelske Filosofi i vor Tid} p. 37 f. (On p. 37, instead of: ``comparison is the condition
of synthesis'' there should stand: ``synthesis is the condition of comparison''). --- In his essay \textit{Criteria
of truth and error} (Mind 1900. p. 15) \emph{Henry} \emph{Sidgwick} remarks: I think it impossible to establish the
general truths of the accepted science by processes of cogent inference on the basis of merely particular
premisses; and I think the chief service that J. S. Mill rendered to philosophy, by his elaborate attempt to perform
this task, was to make this impossibility as clear as day.

\textsuperscript{99}) P.~418. In my \textit{Psykologi i Omrids paa Grundlag af Erfaring} (Copenhagen 1882. 4. ed.
1898) I have tried to make ``the unifying principle'' the guiding point of view and to show how both the laws of
association and the laws of sensations lead back to this principle, which Kant (under the name of synthesis) had
already made the basis of the conception of consciousness. It has therefore surprised me more than once to be
counted without further ado among the adherents of the English school. \emph{Paul} \emph{Carus} (\textit{Primer of
Philosophy.} Chicago 1893. p. 175) thus names me among ``the psychologists who hold that the doctrine of association
gives a key to all the problems of the soul''. \emph{Wundt} (\textit{Physiologische Psychologie.} 4. Aufl. Leipzig
1893. II. p. 482) has named me among ``the representatives of association psychology'', who hold that ``all mental
processes can be derived from the associations''. Already in my book on English philosophy (1874) I criticized
association psychology, the conception that makes the sensations and representations in their independence the real
in consciousness and regards association as an external connection between them, inessential to themselves. And
through the whole of my Psykologi there runs a criticism of this conception, combined, to be sure, with attempts to
preserve the truths it has led to discovering. I also believe that association psychology can be corrected only by
seeking out its own hidden presuppositions, not by assuming a special faculty of thought or ``apperception'' which
should cancel or limit the associations. Cf. my \textit{Psykologiske Undersøgelser} p. 5 --- 6 and 59 --- 67.

\textsuperscript{100}) P.~436. A survey of the attempts in the philosophy of religion in England before and after
Mill's time is given by O. \emph{Pfleiderer}: \textit{Die Entwickelung der protestantischen Theologie in Deutschland
seit Kant und in Grossbritannien seit 1825.} Freiburg 1891. (The account of Mill's views in this work is, however,
not accurate. Pfleiderer commits a bad historical error on p. 407 by having Hamilton, who had died 9 years before
Mill's ``Examination'' appeared, reply to Mill's criticism!!). --- Cf. also N. H. \emph{Marshall}: \textit{Die
gegenwärtigen Richtungen der Religionsphilosophie in England und ihre erkenntnisstheoretische Grundlage.} Berlin
1902. --- The somewhat naive and often not very profound character of Mill's treatises on the philosophy of religion
speaks for the correctness of \emph{Leslie} \emph{Stephen's} conjecture (\textit{The Utilitarians.} III.
% --- p. 595 ---
% print: „Americane“ (p. 595) (misprint)
% scan: „Fxempler“ (p. 595)
\opage{595}p. 86) that Mill did not know Hume's writings on the philosophy of religion, any more than he seems to have
known the ``Treatise''.

\textsuperscript{101}) P.~442. A somewhat fuller biography and characterization of Darwin I have given in my popular
sketch: \textit{Charles Darwin.} Copenhagen 1889. (Studentersamfundets Smaaskrifter Nr. 91---92). Some passages of
this little book will be found again in the account. --- The chief source is \textit{The Life and Letters of Charles
Darwin, including an autobiographical chapter.} Edited by Francis Darwin. London 1887. (Translated in ``Bibliotek for
de tusen hjem''). To this must be added the later published \textit{More Letters of Charles Darwin.} A record of his
work in a series of hitherto unpublished letters. Edited by Francis Darwin and A. C. Seward. London 1903.

\textsuperscript{102}) P.~452. It is not impossible that this utterance is owed to the recollection of the well-known
scene at the meeting of naturalists in Oxford in 1860 between Huxley and the Bishop of Oxford (see Life and Letters.
II. p. 320 ---22), --- except that Huxley preferred the ape as ancestor not to a savage but to --- the Bishop of
Oxford.

\textsuperscript{103}) P.~452. Cf. my remarks on the relation between Darwinism and ethics in \textit{Grundlaget for
den humane Etik} (1876). p. 30---39, and in \textit{Etiske Undersøgelser} (1891). p. 22 f.; 32---38.

\textsuperscript{104}) P.~455. For Spencer's biography and course of development I use, besides utterances in his
writings (especially the interesting remarks in the essay \textit{The Classification of the Sciences, with Reasons for
Dissenting from the Philosophy of M. Comte.} 3. ed. p. 31, 34, 46), above all a short biography by Prof.
\emph{Youmans}, based on information from Spencer, in the American periodical \textit{The Popular Science Monthly}
(March 1876), which I translated at the time in my translation of ``Mindre Afhandlinger af Herbert Spencer''
(Copenhagen 1877), and a draft of a speech by Youmans, found in the report of a celebration for Spencer in New York in
the autumn of 1882. (\textit{Herbert Spencer on the Americans, and the Americans on Herbert Spencer.} New York 1882.
p. 68---76).

\textsuperscript{105}) P.~461. This first part of ``First Principles'' has been translated into Danish under the title
\textit{Religion og Filosofi} by S. \emph{Hansen} (Copenhagen 1887).

\textsuperscript{106}) P.~463. Already in my book \textit{Den engelske Filosofi i vor Tid} (1874) p. 123 f., 132, 145
f. I put forward this objection.

\textsuperscript{107}) P.~470. In the year 1876 I drew Spencer's attention to these contradictions in a private
letter, and in his answer he explained them in the way stated, remarking that he had not until then noticed them.

\textsuperscript{108}) P.~470. Cf. \textit{First Principles.} 3. ed. p. 318 f. ``Although the evolution of the
various products of human activity cannot be said directly to furnish examples of the accumulation of matter and the
dissipation of motion [which Spencer assumes in every evolution, the parts of the whole that is forming losing their
independent motion],
% --- p. 596 ---
\opage{596}they are nevertheless \textit{indirect} examples of it.'' p. 391: ``The phenomena that are subjectively
apprehended as changes in consciousness are objectively apprehended as nervous processes, which science now interprets
as processes of motion.'' --- \textit{Principles of Psychology.} 2. ed. I. p. 508: ``Although the evolution of mind
itself cannot be explained by a series of deductions from the conservation of force, it is nevertheless possible that
its correlate (its obverse). The evolution of physical changes in a physical organ, can be so explained.''

\textsuperscript{108\,b}) P.~474. Strangely enough, even the most acute of Spencer's English critics, \emph{James}
\emph{Ward}, has overlooked this in his work \textit{Naturalism and Agnosticism} (London 1899), interesting in
epistemological respects. He puts, e.g., ``the universe'' without further ado in place of ``a universe''. Cf. the
work named, I. p. 192 with 187.

\textsuperscript{109}) P.~481. Already in \textit{Den engelske Filosofi i vor Tid} (1874). p. 171---173 I put
forward this criticism of Spencer's theory of knowledge. In my \textit{Psykologi} VII C, 4 I have discussed this
subject again.

\textsuperscript{110}) P.~486. An interesting criticism of Spencer's sociology is found in \emph{Émile}
\emph{Durckheim}: \textit{De la division du travail social.} Paris 1893. p. 218---247.

\textsuperscript{111}) P.~488. Cf., concerning the difficulties for a scientific ethics, my work \textit{Etiske
Undersøgelser.} Copenhagen 1891. --- An instructive criticism of Spencer's attempt to ground ethics immediately on
biology (on the organic force and breadth of life instead of on its value as experienced in pleasure and pain) ---
and thereby of Spencer's inclination to apply a deductive method in ethics, is given in \emph{Henry}
\emph{Sidgwick's} \textit{Lectures on the Ethics of Green, Spencer and Martineau.} (London 1902). (Thus Sidgwick
states: So long as life is partially painful, it may still be true in any particular case that conduct conducive to
maximum quantity of life is not conducive to maximum of pleasure. p. 148. --- Sidgwick also emphasizes the
possibility of a conflict between what the development of the individual organism and what the development of the
social organism requires. p. 143 f).

\textsuperscript{112}) P.~492. In the concluding section of the German translation of my book on modern English
philosophy I have already named the works of Boole, Jevons and Sidgwick, besides several others that I must pass
over here. (\textit{Einleitung in die englische Philosophie unserer Zeit.} Leipzig 1889. p. 243---249).

\end{small}
